chunks.title: Diffie-Hellman
chunks.content:
Term: Diffie-Hellman (DH)
Definition: The original public-key key exchange protocol, allowing two parties to establish a shared secret over an insecure channel. Quantum-vulnerable.
Technical Note: Broken by quantum computers via Shor's algorithm. Being replaced by Key Encapsulation Mechanisms (KEMs) such as ML-KEM.
Category: algorithm | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: RSA
chunks.content:
Term: RSA
Definition: A widely used classical public-key algorithm based on the difficulty of factoring large numbers. Vulnerable to quantum attacks via Shor's algorithm.
Technical Note: Common key sizes: 2048, 3072, 4096 bits. Being replaced by ML-DSA for signatures and ML-KEM for key exchange.
Category: algorithm | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: DSA
chunks.content:
Term: DSA (DSA)
Definition: Digital Signature Algorithm, a classical FIPS 186 signature scheme based on discrete logarithms. Deprecated by NIST IR 8547 alongside RSA and ECDSA due to quantum vulnerability.
Technical Note: Broken by Shor's algorithm. Common key sizes: 1024–3072 bits. No longer approved for new systems after 2030 per NIST IR 8547.
Category: algorithm | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: Elliptic Curve Cryptography
chunks.content:
Term: Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC)
Definition: A classical public-key algorithm using the mathematics of elliptic curves. More efficient than RSA but equally vulnerable to quantum attacks.
Technical Note: Common curves: P-256, P-384, P-521, secp256k1 (Bitcoin), Curve25519.
Category: algorithm | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: ML-KEM
chunks.content:
Term: ML-KEM
Definition: Module-Lattice-Based Key Encapsulation Mechanism, the NIST-standardized PQC algorithm for key exchange (formerly Kyber). Defined in FIPS 203.
Technical Note: Variants: ML-KEM-512 (128-bit security), ML-KEM-768 (192-bit), ML-KEM-1024 (256-bit).
Category: algorithm | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: ML-DSA
chunks.content:
Term: ML-DSA
Definition: Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Algorithm, the NIST-standardized PQC algorithm for digital signatures (formerly Dilithium). Defined in FIPS 204.
Technical Note: Variants: ML-DSA-44, ML-DSA-65, ML-DSA-87 corresponding to security levels 2, 3, 5.
Category: algorithm | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: SLH-DSA
chunks.content:
Term: SLH-DSA
Definition: Stateless Hash-Based Digital Signature Algorithm, a conservative NIST-standardized hash-based PQC signature scheme (formerly SPHINCS+). Defined in FIPS 205.
Technical Note: 12 variants: combinations of SHA-256/SHAKE, 128/192/256-bit security, and fast/small trade-offs.
Category: algorithm | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: FN-DSA
chunks.content:
Term: FN-DSA
Definition: FFT over NTRU-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Algorithm, based on Falcon, and planned for FIPS 206. FIPS 206 remains in development; no Initial Public Draft or final standard has been published.
Technical Note: Variants: FN-DSA-512 (Level 1) and FN-DSA-1024 (Level 5). Known for very small signatures but requires careful floating-point implementation.
Category: algorithm | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: FrodoKEM
chunks.content:
Term: FrodoKEM
Definition: A conservative lattice-based KEM algorithm based on the "plain" Learning With Errors problem, offering strong security guarantees at the cost of larger key sizes.
Category: algorithm | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: HQC
chunks.content:
Term: HQC
Definition: Hamming Quasi-Cyclic, a code-based KEM selected by NIST as an additional standard. Uses error-correcting codes for security.
Category: algorithm | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: Classic McEliece
chunks.content:
Term: Classic McEliece
Definition: A code-based KEM with very large public keys but extremely conservative security assumptions. One of the oldest post-quantum proposals.
Category: algorithm | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: XMSS
chunks.content:
Term: XMSS (XMSS)
Definition: eXtended Merkle Signature Scheme, a stateful hash-based digital signature algorithm standardized in RFC 8391 and NIST SP 800-208.
Technical Note: Like LMS, XMSS is stateful and each key can only sign a limited number of messages. Required by CNSA 2.0 for firmware and software signing.
Category: algorithm | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: LMS/HSS
chunks.content:
Term: LMS/HSS (LMS)
Definition: Leighton-Micali Signature / Hierarchical Signature System. A stateful hash-based signature scheme for firmware and software signing.
Technical Note: Standardized in RFC 8554. "Stateful" means each key can only sign a limited number of messages.
Category: algorithm | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: AES
chunks.content:
Term: AES (AES)
Definition: Advanced Encryption Standard, a symmetric encryption algorithm. Relatively safe from quantum attacks (just double the key size: AES-256).
Technical Note: Quantum attacks via Grover's algorithm halve the effective security level, so AES-128 becomes ~64-bit. AES-256 remains secure.
Category: algorithm | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: Shor's Algorithm
chunks.content:
Term: Shor's Algorithm
Definition: A quantum algorithm that can efficiently factor large numbers and compute discrete logarithms, breaking RSA and ECC.
Category: algorithm | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: Grover's Algorithm
chunks.content:
Term: Grover's Algorithm
Definition: A quantum algorithm that speeds up brute-force searches, effectively halving the security level of symmetric ciphers and hash functions.
Category: algorithm | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: ECDSA
chunks.content:
Term: ECDSA (ECDSA)
Definition: Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm, a classical signature scheme used in TLS, Bitcoin, and many other systems. Quantum-vulnerable.
Category: algorithm | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: ECDH
chunks.content:
Term: ECDH (ECDH)
Definition: Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman, a classical key agreement protocol. Quantum-vulnerable and being replaced by ML-KEM.
Category: algorithm | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: X25519
chunks.content:
Term: X25519
Definition: An elliptic curve Diffie-Hellman key exchange function using Curve25519. Widely used in TLS 1.3 and the basis for hybrid PQC key exchange.
Technical Note: Combined with ML-KEM-768 to form the X25519MLKEM768 hybrid key exchange, now deployed by major browsers and cloud providers.
Category: algorithm | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: X448
chunks.content:
Term: X448
Definition: An elliptic curve Diffie-Hellman key exchange function using Curve448, providing higher security than X25519. Quantum-vulnerable.
Category: algorithm | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: Ed25519
chunks.content:
Term: Ed25519
Definition: A high-performance digital signature algorithm using the Edwards curve Curve25519. Used in SSH, TLS, and Solana.
Category: algorithm | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: Ed448
chunks.content:
Term: Ed448
Definition: An EdDSA signature algorithm using the Edwards curve Curve448, providing 224-bit security. Quantum-vulnerable.
Category: algorithm | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: SHA-256
chunks.content:
Term: SHA-256
Definition: Secure Hash Algorithm producing a 256-bit digest. Used extensively in Bitcoin and TLS. Quantum-safe at current key sizes.
Category: algorithm | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: HKDF
chunks.content:
Term: HKDF (HKDF)
Definition: HMAC-based Key Derivation Function, used to derive cryptographic keys from a shared secret. Essential in TLS 1.3.
Category: algorithm | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: Keccak-256
chunks.content:
Term: Keccak-256
Definition: The hash function used by Ethereum, based on the SHA-3 algorithm family. Produces 256-bit digests.
Category: algorithm | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: secp256k1
chunks.content:
Term: secp256k1
Definition: The elliptic curve used by Bitcoin for digital signatures. Quantum-vulnerable and a key concern for cryptocurrency PQC migration.
Category: algorithm | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: Kyber
chunks.content:
Term: Kyber
Definition: The original name (CRYSTALS-Kyber) for the lattice-based KEM standardized by NIST as ML-KEM in FIPS 203. Often still referenced in older documents and libraries.
Technical Note: Kyber was selected from the NIST PQC competition Round 3. It was renamed to ML-KEM for the final standard.
Category: algorithm | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: Dilithium
chunks.content:
Term: Dilithium
Definition: The original name (CRYSTALS-Dilithium) for the lattice-based signature scheme standardized by NIST as ML-DSA in FIPS 204.
Technical Note: Dilithium was selected from the NIST PQC competition Round 3. It was renamed to ML-DSA for the final standard.
Category: algorithm | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: Falcon
chunks.content:
Term: Falcon
Definition: The NTRU-lattice-based signature scheme selected by NIST as the basis for the planned FN-DSA standard. FIPS 206 remains in development with no published Initial Public Draft or final standard.
Technical Note: Falcon uses fast Fourier transforms over NTRU lattices. NIST plans to use the FN-DSA name when FIPS 206 is published.
Category: algorithm | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: SPHINCS+
chunks.content:
Term: SPHINCS+
Definition: The original name for the stateless hash-based signature scheme standardized by NIST as SLH-DSA in FIPS 205. Very conservative security assumptions.
Technical Note: SPHINCS+ relies only on the security of its underlying hash function, making it a strong fallback if lattice assumptions are broken.
Category: algorithm | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: BIKE
chunks.content:
Term: BIKE (BIKE)
Definition: Bit Flipping Key Encapsulation, a code-based KEM that was a NIST PQC Round 4 candidate. Uses quasi-cyclic moderate-density parity-check codes.
Category: algorithm | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: SHA-3
chunks.content:
Term: SHA-3
Definition: The third generation Secure Hash Algorithm standard (FIPS 202), based on the Keccak sponge construction. Includes SHA3-256, SHA3-512, and SHAKE variants.
Technical Note: SHA-3 provides an independent alternative to SHA-2 with different mathematical foundations. Used in SLH-DSA parameter sets.
Category: algorithm | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: SHAKE
chunks.content:
Term: SHAKE
Definition: Extendable-Output Functions from the SHA-3 family (SHAKE128, SHAKE256). Unlike fixed-length hashes, SHAKE can produce output of any desired length.
Technical Note: Used in SLH-DSA-SHAKE parameter sets and as a key derivation mechanism in several PQC algorithms.
Category: algorithm | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: EdDSA
chunks.content:
Term: EdDSA
Definition: Edwards-curve Digital Signature Algorithm, the family of signature schemes including Ed25519 and Ed448. Offers high performance and resistance to side-channel attacks.
Technical Note: EdDSA is deterministic (no random nonce), reducing implementation risks. Quantum-vulnerable via Shor's algorithm.
Category: algorithm | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: ChaCha20-Poly1305
chunks.content:
Term: ChaCha20-Poly1305
Definition: A modern authenticated encryption with associated data (AEAD) cipher combining the ChaCha20 stream cipher with the Poly1305 authenticator. Quantum-safe at current key sizes.
Technical Note: Widely used in TLS 1.3, WireGuard, and SSH as an alternative to AES-GCM. Efficient in software without hardware AES acceleration.
Category: algorithm | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: Triple-DES
chunks.content:
Term: Triple-DES (3DES)
Definition: A legacy symmetric cipher that applies DES three times to each block. Being phased out in favor of AES due to its small 64-bit block size.
Technical Note: Still found in legacy payment systems (DUKPT) and some government systems. NIST deprecated 3DES after December 31, 2023.
Category: algorithm | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: P-256
chunks.content:
Term: P-256
Definition: A NIST standard elliptic curve (also called secp256r1 or prime256v1) widely used in TLS, FIDO2, and government systems. Quantum-vulnerable.
Technical Note: Part of the Suite B / CNSA 1.0 algorithms. Combined with ML-KEM-768 in the SecP256r1MLKEM768 hybrid key exchange.
Category: algorithm | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: P-384
chunks.content:
Term: P-384
Definition: A NIST standard elliptic curve (secp384r1) offering 192-bit security. Used in high-security TLS configurations and government systems. Quantum-vulnerable.
Technical Note: Combined with ML-KEM-1024 in the SecP384r1MLKEM1024 hybrid key exchange for NIST Level 5 security.
Category: algorithm | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: Ascon
chunks.content:
Term: Ascon
Definition: A lightweight authenticated encryption cipher selected by NIST as the standard for constrained environments (IoT, embedded devices). Very low resource requirements.
Category: algorithm | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: RIPEMD-160
chunks.content:
Term: RIPEMD-160
Definition: A 160-bit cryptographic hash function used in Bitcoin address generation (combined with SHA-256). Quantum-safe at current output sizes.
Category: algorithm | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: SM2
chunks.content:
Term: SM2
Definition: China's national standard elliptic curve public-key algorithm for digital signatures and key exchange, managed by OSCCA. Quantum-vulnerable.
Technical Note: Combined with ML-KEM-768 in the curveSM2MLKEM768 hybrid key exchange for Chinese PQC migration.
Category: algorithm | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: PBKDF2
chunks.content:
Term: PBKDF2
Definition: Password-Based Key Derivation Function 2, used to derive cryptographic keys from passwords. Applies a pseudorandom function (typically HMAC-SHA) iteratively.
Technical Note: Used in BIP39 to derive seed bytes from mnemonic phrases (2048 iterations of HMAC-SHA512).
Category: algorithm | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: X25519MLKEM768
chunks.content:
Term: X25519MLKEM768
Definition: A hybrid key exchange algorithm combining X25519 (classical ECDH) with ML-KEM-768 (post-quantum KEM). Both shared secrets are combined via HKDF so the result is secure if either algorithm holds.
Technical Note: Deployed in Chrome, Firefox, and Cloudflare TLS 1.3. Uses concatenated shared secrets fed through HKDF-SHA256 for the final key.
Category: algorithm | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: sntrup761
chunks.content:
Term: sntrup761
Definition: A lattice-based key encapsulation mechanism used in OpenSSH hybrid key exchange. Combined with X25519 to provide post-quantum protection for SSH connections.
Technical Note: Available in OpenSSH since version 9.0 as sntrup761x25519-sha512. Being superseded by mlkem768x25519-sha256 in newer OpenSSH versions.
Category: algorithm | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: Winternitz One-Time Signature
chunks.content:
Term: Winternitz One-Time Signature (WOTS+)
Definition: A hash-based one-time signature scheme used as the building block for LMS and XMSS. Each key pair can only sign one message safely.
Technical Note: The Winternitz parameter (w) controls the trade-off between signature size and computation time. Larger w = smaller signatures but more hash operations.
Category: algorithm | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: ECIES
chunks.content:
Term: ECIES (ECIES)
Definition: Elliptic Curve Integrated Encryption Scheme, used in 5G networks to conceal subscriber identity (SUCI). Combines ECDH key agreement with symmetric encryption.
Technical Note: 5G defines three SUCI protection profiles: Profile A (ECIES with Curve25519), Profile B (ECIES with P-256), and Profile C (ML-KEM for post-quantum protection).
Category: algorithm | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: DRBG
chunks.content:
Term: DRBG (DRBG)
Definition: Deterministic Random Bit Generator. An algorithm that produces a sequence of pseudorandom bits from a secret seed value. NIST SP 800-90A defines three approved mechanisms: CTR_DRBG, Hash_DRBG, and HMAC_DRBG.
Technical Note: CTR_DRBG (AES-based) is the most widely deployed, used by OpenSSL and the Linux kernel. All three mechanisms use symmetric primitives and are quantum-safe.
Category: algorithm | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: ECC
chunks.content:
Term: ECC (ECC)
Definition: Elliptic Curve Cryptography — a public-key cryptosystem based on the algebraic structure of elliptic curves over finite fields. Offers smaller key sizes than RSA for equivalent classical security, but like RSA it is fully broken by Shor's algorithm on a CRQC.
Technical Note: Common curves: P-256, P-384, P-521 (NIST), Curve25519 (X25519/Ed25519). ECC is used extensively in TLS, SSH, code signing, and PKI. NIST SP 800-186 and CNSA 2.0 mandate migration away from ECC to ML-KEM and ML-DSA before 2030.
Category: algorithm | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: LMS
chunks.content:
Term: LMS (LMS)
Definition: Leighton-Micali Signature — a stateful hash-based signature scheme standardised in NIST SP 800-208 and RFC 8554. Based on one-time Lamport signatures aggregated via a Merkle tree. Approved by CNSA 2.0 for firmware and software signing.
Technical Note: LMS is stateful: each leaf in the Merkle tree can only be used once. An HSM must persist the current leaf index in NVRAM and never reuse it — failure leads to catastrophic key compromise. LMS key sizes: ~1,616 bytes (pub) to 64 bytes (priv). PKCS#11 v3.2 mechanism: CKM_LMS.
Category: algorithm | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: HAWK
chunks.content:
Term: HAWK
Definition: A lattice-based PQC signature candidate in the NIST signature on-ramp, designed as an integer-only alternative to FN-DSA (Falcon). Eliminates floating-point side-channel hazards that complicate Falcon implementations.
Category: algorithm | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: MAYO
chunks.content:
Term: MAYO
Definition: A multivariate signature candidate in the NIST signature on-ramp. Produces very small signatures (~420 bytes at NIST Cat 1) with relatively small public keys, derived from the Oil-and-Vinegar trapdoor.
Technical Note: MAYO-2 lost ~30 bits of security in the 2025 Ran wedge attack. Reparameterisation to odd-characteristic fields restores the original target.
Category: algorithm | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: UOV
chunks.content:
Term: UOV (Unbalanced Oil and Vinegar)
Definition: A multivariate signature scheme using more vinegar variables than oil variables. A NIST signature on-ramp candidate with tiny signatures but large public keys.
Technical Note: The 2025 Ran wedge attack pushed 3 of 4 UOV parameter sets below their declared security level. Odd-characteristic-field reparameterisation is the proposed fix.
Category: algorithm | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: SQIsign
chunks.content:
Term: SQIsign
Definition: An isogeny-based PQC signature candidate in the NIST on-ramp. Smallest combined public key + signature of any PQC candidate (~148 bytes at NIST Cat 1) — fits in a single network packet.
Technical Note: Cousin scheme SIKE was broken in 2022 by the Castryck–Decru attack. SQIsign avoids the structural exploit but constant-time signing is still an open implementation challenge.
Category: algorithm | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: FAEST
chunks.content:
Term: FAEST
Definition: An MPC-in-the-Head signature candidate in the NIST signature on-ramp. Builds a signature out of a simulated multi-party computation over the AES block cipher.
Technical Note: Security reduces to the one-wayness of AES, which is among the best-studied symmetric primitives. Signatures are kilobytes — large versus multivariate or isogeny candidates.
Category: algorithm | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: MQOM
chunks.content:
Term: MQOM (Multivariate Quadratic on MPC-in-the-Head)
Definition: An MPC-in-the-Head signature candidate in the NIST on-ramp whose security reduces to the hardness of solving systems of multivariate quadratic equations.
Category: algorithm | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: SDitH
chunks.content:
Term: SDitH (Syndrome Decoding in the Head)
Definition: An MPC-in-the-Head signature candidate in the NIST on-ramp whose security reduces to the hardness of syndrome decoding (the same combinatorial problem underlying code-based KEMs).
Category: algorithm | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: SNOVA
chunks.content:
Term: SNOVA
Definition: A multivariate signature candidate in the NIST PQC signature on-ramp. Combines UOV-style trapdoors with a noncommutative algebra structure.
Technical Note: Most SNOVA parameter sets were broken by the 2025 Ran wedge attack and require reparameterisation to remain candidates.
Category: algorithm | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: WOTS+
chunks.content:
Term: WOTS+ (Winternitz One-Time Signature Plus)
Definition: A hash-based one-time signature primitive that signs a message digest by walking chains of n-byte hash values. Used as the leaf-signing component inside SLH-DSA (FIPS 205) and the hypertree layers of LMS / XMSS.
Technical Note: FIPS 205 fixes the Winternitz parameter lg_w=4. Chain lengths trade signature size against hash-round cost. A WOTS+ key signs exactly one message — reuse leaks the private key.
Category: algorithm | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: FORS
chunks.content:
Term: FORS (Forest of Random Subsets)
Definition: The few-time signature layer inside SLH-DSA (FIPS 205) that actually signs the message digest. Sits between the WOTS+ leaves and the hypertree, signing a k-subset of values using a-level hash trees.
Technical Note: FORS parameters (k, a) directly control signature size and resistance to multi-target attacks. FORS is few-time rather than one-time: pseudorandom message-derived indices give a negligible reuse probability across SLH-DSA's lifetime.
Category: algorithm | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: HMAC
chunks.content:
Term: HMAC (HMAC)
Definition: Hash-based Message Authentication Code, a keyed construction that combines a secret key with a hash function (e.g. SHA-256) to provide message integrity and authenticity.
Technical Note: Used as the basis for HMAC_DRBG and HKDF, both already in this glossary. HMAC's security depends on the underlying hash function, not on hardness assumptions broken by Shor's algorithm — it remains safe at existing key/output sizes against quantum attack, unlike RSA/ECC.
Category: algorithm | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: AES-GCM
chunks.content:
Term: AES-GCM (GCM)
Definition: Galois/Counter Mode, an authenticated-encryption (AEAD) mode for AES that combines counter-mode encryption with a GHASH-based authentication tag in one pass.
Technical Note: The default AEAD mode in TLS 1.3 and most modern protocols. Nonce reuse under the same key is catastrophic — it can leak the authentication key. AES-CCM is the alternative AEAD mode used where GCM's parallelism isn't needed.
Category: algorithm | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: AES-CCM
chunks.content:
Term: AES-CCM (CCM)
Definition: Counter with CBC-MAC, an authenticated-encryption (AEAD) mode for AES that combines counter-mode encryption with a CBC-MAC authentication tag.
Technical Note: Common in constrained environments (Bluetooth LE, Zigbee/802.15.4, some IoT/OT protocols) where GCM's parallel-friendly design matters less than CCM's simpler hardware footprint.
Category: algorithm | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: Rainbow
chunks.content:
Term: Rainbow
Definition: A multivariate-quadratic digital signature scheme and NIST PQC Round 3 finalist, eliminated in 2022 after a rank-based cryptanalysis attack recovered a Rainbow private key on a single laptop in about a weekend.
Category: algorithm | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: Saber
chunks.content:
Term: Saber
Definition: A module-lattice-based key encapsulation mechanism and NIST PQC Round 3 finalist alongside Kyber and NTRU; not selected because NIST judged Kyber (now ML-KEM) the stronger overall combination of security and performance among the lattice KEMs.
Category: algorithm | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: Picnic
chunks.content:
Term: Picnic
Definition: A signature scheme built from symmetric primitives and zero-knowledge proofs rather than a hard math problem; a NIST PQC Round 3 alternate candidate not standardized, mainly due to large signature sizes and slow performance relative to SLH-DSA and ML-DSA.
Category: algorithm | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: GeMSS
chunks.content:
Term: GeMSS (Great Multivariate Short Signature)
Definition: A multivariate-quadratic signature scheme and NIST PQC Round 3 alternate candidate, notable for very large public keys; not selected for standardization.
Category: algorithm | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: NTRU
chunks.content:
Term: NTRU
Definition: A lattice-based key encapsulation mechanism built on the NTRU problem, one of the oldest practical lattice cryptosystems (1996) and a NIST PQC Round 3 finalist; not selected as ML-KEM (Kyber) became the primary standardized lattice KEM.
Technical Note: NTRU Prime, a variant designed to avoid the extra algebraic structure of cyclotomic-ring NTRU, produced the sntrup761 parameter set already in this glossary — used in some early hybrid TLS/SSH PQC deployments.
Category: algorithm | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: XMSS-MT
chunks.content:
Term: XMSS-MT (XMSS^MT)
Definition: A multi-tree variant of XMSS that chains multiple XMSS trees hierarchically, extending the total number of signatures a single key pair can produce.
Technical Note: Standardized in RFC 8391 alongside single-tree XMSS, and by NIST SP 800-208.
Category: algorithm | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: LM-OTS
chunks.content:
Term: LM-OTS (Leighton-Micali One-Time Signature)
Definition: The one-time signature primitive underlying LMS: each LM-OTS key pair is valid for exactly one signature, and many are combined via a Merkle tree to build a reusable LMS key.
Category: algorithm | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: TLS
chunks.content:
Term: TLS (TLS)
Definition: Transport Layer Security, the protocol that secures HTTPS web traffic. TLS 1.3 is the current version.
Technical Note: PQC integration uses hybrid key exchange (e.g., X25519 + ML-KEM-768) to maintain backward compatibility.
Category: protocol | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: X.509
chunks.content:
Term: X.509
Definition: The standard format for public key certificates used in TLS, email signing, and code signing.
Category: protocol | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: Public Key Infrastructure
chunks.content:
Term: Public Key Infrastructure (PKI)
Definition: The system of Certificate Authorities, digital certificates, and registration authorities that manages public keys and enables secure communication.
Category: protocol | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: Certificate Signing Request
chunks.content:
Term: Certificate Signing Request (CSR)
Definition: A message sent to a Certificate Authority to request a digital certificate. Contains the public key and identity information.
Category: protocol | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: Certificate Authority
chunks.content:
Term: Certificate Authority (CA)
Definition: A trusted organization that issues digital certificates, verifying the identity of certificate holders.
Category: protocol | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: Key Encapsulation Mechanism
chunks.content:
Term: Key Encapsulation Mechanism (KEM)
Definition: A method to securely establish a shared secret key between two parties. The PQC replacement for traditional key exchange.
Technical Note: Unlike Diffie-Hellman, KEMs work via encapsulation (encrypt a random secret with a public key) and decapsulation (decrypt with the private key).
Category: protocol | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: 5G-AKA
chunks.content:
Term: 5G-AKA
Definition: 5G Authentication and Key Agreement protocol, the primary authentication mechanism in 5G networks.
Category: protocol | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: SUCI
chunks.content:
Term: SUCI (SUCI)
Definition: Subscription Concealed Identifier, a privacy-protecting identifier used in 5G that encrypts the subscriber's permanent identity.
Category: protocol | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: OpenID4VCI
chunks.content:
Term: OpenID4VCI
Definition: OpenID for Verifiable Credential Issuance, a protocol for issuing digital credentials to wallets.
Category: protocol | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: OpenID4VP
chunks.content:
Term: OpenID4VP
Definition: OpenID for Verifiable Presentations, a protocol for presenting digital credentials from a wallet to a verifier.
Category: protocol | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: SSH
chunks.content:
Term: SSH (SSH)
Definition: Secure Shell, a protocol for encrypted remote login and command execution. PQC integration adds ML-KEM hybrid key exchange.
Category: protocol | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: IPsec
chunks.content:
Term: IPsec (IPsec)
Definition: Internet Protocol Security, a protocol suite for encrypting and authenticating IP traffic. Used in VPNs and site-to-site connections.
Technical Note: PQC integration via IKEv2 multiple key exchange (RFC 9370) adds ML-KEM alongside classical DH.
Category: protocol | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: IKEv2
chunks.content:
Term: IKEv2 (IKEv2)
Definition: Internet Key Exchange version 2, the protocol used to establish security associations in IPsec VPNs. PQC migration adds ML-KEM key exchange.
Category: protocol | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: EMV
chunks.content:
Term: EMV (EMV)
Definition: Europay/Mastercard/Visa, the global standard for chip-based payment card authentication. Uses RSA and ECC signatures that are quantum-vulnerable.
Technical Note: Over 14 billion EMV cards are in circulation globally. Offline authentication relies on RSA/ECC signatures vulnerable to quantum forgery.
Category: protocol | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: S/MIME
chunks.content:
Term: S/MIME (S/MIME)
Definition: Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions, a standard for email encryption and digital signing. PQC integration via ML-KEM and ML-DSA.
Category: protocol | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: CMS
chunks.content:
Term: CMS (CMS)
Definition: Cryptographic Message Syntax, a standard for digitally signed, encrypted, or authenticated data. Foundation for S/MIME and code signing.
Technical Note: Multiple IETF RFCs define PQC integration: RFC 9629 (KEM in CMS), RFC 9882 (ML-DSA in CMS), RFC 9814 (SLH-DSA in CMS).
Category: protocol | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: OpenPGP
chunks.content:
Term: OpenPGP
Definition: An open standard for email encryption and signing based on PGP. PQC integration adds composite ML-KEM+ECC encryption and ML-DSA+ECC signatures.
Category: protocol | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: Signal Protocol
chunks.content:
Term: Signal Protocol
Definition: The encryption protocol used by Signal, WhatsApp, and other messengers. Updated with PQXDH to add ML-KEM-1024 for post-quantum security.
Category: protocol | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: PQXDH
chunks.content:
Term: PQXDH (PQXDH)
Definition: Post-Quantum Extended Diffie-Hellman, the post-quantum key agreement protocol used by Signal (and optionally WhatsApp). Combines X25519 with ML-KEM-1024 to establish session keys.
Technical Note: Deployed by Signal in September 2023. The shared secret is derived from both the classical X25519 exchange and an ML-KEM-1024 encapsulation, ensuring security if either algorithm is broken.
Category: protocol | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: FIDO2 / WebAuthn
chunks.content:
Term: FIDO2 / WebAuthn
Definition: Web authentication standards enabling passwordless login using public-key cryptography. Currently relies on quantum-vulnerable ECDSA/EdDSA.
Category: protocol | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: Credential Activation
chunks.content:
Term: Credential Activation
Definition: A TPM 2.0 protocol (TPM2_MakeCredential / TPM2_ActivateCredential) for securely delivering a credential to a specific TPM, proven by the TPM demonstrating possession of the corresponding EK private key. PQC migration uses ML-KEM-768 encapsulation against the EK per TCG V1.85.
Technical Note: The Privacy CA encapsulates a secret against the EK public key; only a TPM holding the matching EK private key can decapsulate and release the credential.
Category: protocol | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: BB84
chunks.content:
Term: BB84
Definition: The first quantum key distribution protocol, proposed by Bennett and Brassard in 1984. Uses four quantum states in two conjugate bases to establish a shared secret key.
Technical Note: Alice encodes random bits in rectilinear (+) or diagonal (x) bases. Bob measures in a randomly chosen basis. After basis reconciliation over a classical channel, only matching-basis bits form the sifted key.
Category: protocol | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: QUIC
chunks.content:
Term: QUIC
Definition: A modern transport protocol built on UDP, providing encrypted connections with lower latency than TCP+TLS. The foundation of HTTP/3.
Technical Note: QUIC integrates TLS 1.3 directly, so PQC migration via hybrid key exchange (X25519MLKEM768) applies to QUIC connections as well.
Category: protocol | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: WireGuard
chunks.content:
Term: WireGuard
Definition: A modern, high-performance VPN protocol using state-of-the-art cryptography (ChaCha20, Curve25519). PQC integration is being developed.
Technical Note: PQC migration involves adding ML-KEM hybrid key exchange to the Noise protocol framework used by WireGuard.
Category: protocol | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: DTLS
chunks.content:
Term: DTLS (DTLS)
Definition: Datagram Transport Layer Security, the UDP equivalent of TLS. Used in IoT (CoAP), WebRTC, and VPN protocols. DTLS 1.3 adds PQC support.
Category: protocol | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: mTLS
chunks.content:
Term: mTLS
Definition: Mutual TLS, a TLS mode where both client and server present certificates for authentication. Common in microservices, zero-trust architectures, and API security.
Technical Note: PQC migration for mTLS requires updating both client and server certificates to PQC or hybrid algorithms.
Category: protocol | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: OCSP
chunks.content:
Term: OCSP (OCSP)
Definition: Online Certificate Status Protocol, used to check whether an X.509 certificate has been revoked. An alternative to Certificate Revocation Lists (CRLs).
Category: protocol | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: DNSSEC
chunks.content:
Term: DNSSEC (DNSSEC)
Definition: DNS Security Extensions, a suite of protocols that add cryptographic authentication to DNS responses. Uses digital signatures to prevent DNS spoofing.
Technical Note: PQC migration is challenging due to DNS packet size limits. Larger PQC signatures may require protocol changes or new transport mechanisms.
Category: protocol | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: ACME
chunks.content:
Term: ACME (ACME)
Definition: Automatic Certificate Management Environment, the protocol used by Let's Encrypt and other CAs to automate certificate issuance and renewal.
Technical Note: ACME will need updates to support PQC certificate types as the Web PKI transitions to quantum-safe algorithms.
Category: protocol | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: ACVP
chunks.content:
Term: ACVP (Automated Cryptographic Validation Protocol)
Definition: A protocol, not a program: JSON messages over HTTPS through which a client registers an algorithm implementation's capabilities with a NIST test server, downloads the generated test vector sets, and uploads its responses for checking. NIST's servers that speak it are the ACVTS (Automated Cryptographic Validation Test System), operated for CAVP; CAVP, not ACVP, issues algorithm validation certificates, and CMVP validates whole modules to FIPS 140-3.
Technical Note: Source: ACVP JSON Specification, draft-ietf-acvp-spec-01 (Library: NIST-ACVP) §1 Abstract, §6 (JSON over HTTP[S]), §8 Encoding; NIST CAVP project page (csrc.nist.gov/projects/cryptographic-algorithm-validation-program) for ACVTS and certificates. A passed vector-set disposition is not itself a validation; running public ACVP-Server sample vectors is not one either. The .req/.rsp request and response files belong to ACVP's predecessor, the CAVS tool (e.g. SHAVS §6.2.1), which the CAVP page lists as deprecated by ACVTS.
Category: protocol | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: PQ3
chunks.content:
Term: PQ3
Definition: Apple's post-quantum secure messaging protocol for iMessage, providing Level 3 security with ML-KEM key exchange and periodic re-keying.
Technical Note: PQ3 uses a ratcheting design that regularly re-establishes quantum-safe shared secrets, protecting past and future messages.
Category: protocol | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: MACsec
chunks.content:
Term: MACsec (MACsec)
Definition: IEEE 802.1AE Media Access Control Security, providing Layer 2 encryption for Ethernet frames. Used to secure LAN traffic between switches and endpoints.
Technical Note: MACsec relies on AES-GCM (quantum-safe) for encryption but uses ECDH/ECDSA for key agreement, requiring PQC migration for the key exchange.
Category: protocol | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: KMIP
chunks.content:
Term: KMIP (KMIP)
Definition: Key Management Interoperability Protocol, an OASIS standard for communication between key management systems and cryptographic clients.
Technical Note: KMIP 2.1+ includes support for post-quantum key types and algorithms.
Category: protocol | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: CMP
chunks.content:
Term: CMP (CMP)
Definition: Certificate Management Protocol (RFC 4210), used for managing X.509 certificates including enrollment, updates, and revocation. PQC support via RFC 9810.
Category: protocol | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: JWT
chunks.content:
Term: JWT (JWT)
Definition: JSON Web Token, a compact token format for securely transmitting claims between parties. Widely used in API authentication and OAuth 2.0.
Technical Note: JWTs typically use RSA or ECDSA signatures which are quantum-vulnerable. PQC JWT support (ML-DSA) is being standardized via JOSE working group.
Category: protocol | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: JSON Web Signature
chunks.content:
Term: JSON Web Signature (JWS)
Definition: A standard (RFC 7515) for digitally signing JSON payloads. JWS is the mechanism that makes JWTs tamper-proof — the signature covers the JOSE header and payload.
Technical Note: PQC migration requires new JWS algorithm identifiers (e.g., ML-DSA-44, ML-DSA-65) registered via the IETF JOSE PQC draft. Signature sizes grow from 64 bytes (ES256) to ~2,420 bytes (ML-DSA-44).
Category: protocol | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: JSON Web Encryption
chunks.content:
Term: JSON Web Encryption (JWE)
Definition: A standard (RFC 7516) for encrypting JSON payloads. JWE provides confidentiality for JWT claims using a two-layer encryption model: a Key Encryption Key (KEK) wraps a Content Encryption Key (CEK).
Technical Note: PQC migration replaces ECDH-ES key agreement with ML-KEM encapsulation. The KEM ciphertext replaces the encrypted key in JWE compact serialization.
Category: protocol | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: JOSE
chunks.content:
Term: JOSE
Definition: JSON Object Signing and Encryption, the IETF framework encompassing JWS, JWE, JWK, and JWA specifications. JOSE defines how to sign, encrypt, and represent cryptographic keys in JSON format.
Technical Note: The IETF JOSE working group is standardizing PQC algorithm identifiers (ML-DSA, ML-KEM, SLH-DSA) for use in JOSE headers. The framework was designed for algorithm agility — only the "alg" header value changes.
Category: protocol | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: OpenID Connect
chunks.content:
Term: OpenID Connect (OIDC)
Definition: An identity layer built on OAuth 2.0 that provides authentication via ID tokens (JWTs). Widely used for single sign-on across web and mobile applications.
Technical Note: OIDC ID tokens are signed JWTs. PQC migration requires authorization servers to sign ID tokens with ML-DSA and clients to verify PQC signatures. JWKS endpoints must serve PQC public keys.
Category: protocol | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: Demonstrating Proof-of-Possession
chunks.content:
Term: Demonstrating Proof-of-Possession (DPoP)
Definition: An OAuth 2.0 extension (RFC 9449) that binds access tokens to a specific client by requiring a proof-of-possession JWT with each API request, preventing token theft and replay attacks.
Technical Note: Each DPoP proof is a JWS signed with the client's key. With PQC, every API request includes a ~4 KB ML-DSA signature in addition to the access token, potentially exceeding HTTP header size limits.
Category: protocol | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: JSON Web Key Set
chunks.content:
Term: JSON Web Key Set (JWKS)
Definition: A JSON document (RFC 7517) containing a set of public keys used to verify JWTs. Authorization servers publish JWKS endpoints so resource servers can fetch signing keys.
Technical Note: ML-DSA public keys are ~2 KB each (vs 32 bytes for EC). JWKS payloads grow significantly during PQC migration, especially with key rotation maintaining multiple active keys.
Category: protocol | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: Rosenpass
chunks.content:
Term: Rosenpass
Definition: A post-quantum key exchange protocol designed as a companion to WireGuard VPN. Performs a separate key exchange using Classic McEliece and the pre-standard round-3 Kyber-512 (not FIPS 203 ML-KEM) and feeds the resulting key into WireGuard.
Technical Note: Rosenpass runs alongside WireGuard rather than modifying it, adding PQC protection without changing the WireGuard protocol itself.
Category: protocol | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: SignedData
chunks.content:
Term: SignedData
Definition: A CMS (Cryptographic Message Syntax) structure defined in RFC 5652 that carries digitally signed content. The foundation of S/MIME email signatures.
Technical Note: Contains the original content, signer certificates, and one or more SignerInfo structures with the actual signatures. PQC migration requires updating the signature algorithms.
Category: protocol | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: EnvelopedData
chunks.content:
Term: EnvelopedData
Definition: A CMS structure for encrypted content using key transport (RSA) or key agreement (ECDH). Being superseded by AuthEnvelopedData with KEM-based encryption for PQC.
Technical Note: Traditional EnvelopedData uses RSA key transport, which is vulnerable to quantum attacks. RFC 9629 defines KEMRecipientInfo as the PQC replacement.
Category: protocol | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: KEMRecipientInfo
chunks.content:
Term: KEMRecipientInfo
Definition: A CMS recipient info type defined in RFC 9629 that uses Key Encapsulation Mechanisms (KEMs) instead of RSA key transport for encrypting content-encryption keys.
Technical Note: Enables ML-KEM-based encryption in S/MIME and CMS. The sender encapsulates a shared secret to the recipient's KEM public key, then derives the content-encryption key.
Category: protocol | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: Certificate Revocation List
chunks.content:
Term: Certificate Revocation List (CRL)
Definition: A signed list published by a Certificate Authority containing the serial numbers of certificates that have been revoked before their expiration date.
Technical Note: CRLs are periodically published and can become large. OCSP provides real-time revocation checking as an alternative. PQC migration requires CRLs to be signed with quantum-safe algorithms.
Category: protocol | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: Certificate Transparency
chunks.content:
Term: Certificate Transparency (CT)
Definition: An open framework (RFC 9162) that requires all publicly-trusted TLS certificates to be logged in publicly auditable logs, enabling detection of misissued certificates.
Technical Note: CT logs are Merkle trees of certificate records. The Merkle Tree Certificate (MTC) design builds directly on CT infrastructure, replacing individual certificate signatures with batch Merkle inclusion proofs.
Category: protocol | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: Hybrid Public Key Encryption
chunks.content:
Term: Hybrid Public Key Encryption (HPKE)
Definition: A standardized framework (RFC 9180) for hybrid public-key encryption that combines a KEM, a key derivation function, and an AEAD cipher into a composable primitive.
Technical Note: HPKE is used in TLS ECH (Encrypted Client Hello), MLS messaging, and several IETF PQC drafts. It can be instantiated with ML-KEM for post-quantum security by substituting the KEM component.
Category: protocol | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: MQTT
chunks.content:
Term: MQTT (MQTT)
Definition: Message Queuing Telemetry Transport, a lightweight publish/subscribe messaging protocol for IoT. MQTT 5.0 supports TLS 1.3 transport security.
Category: protocol | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: LoRaWAN
chunks.content:
Term: LoRaWAN
Definition: Long Range Wide Area Network, a low-power WAN protocol for IoT. Uses AES-128 pre-shared keys. Maximum payload of 222 bytes makes PQC KEM infeasible inline.
Category: protocol | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: Matter
chunks.content:
Term: Matter
Definition: Smart home interoperability standard (formerly Project CHIP). Uses the CASE protocol with ECDSA P-256 for device attestation. PQC migration requires protocol specification update.
Category: protocol | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: CoAP
chunks.content:
Term: CoAP (CoAP)
Definition: Constrained Application Protocol, a lightweight RESTful protocol designed for IoT devices. Runs over UDP with DTLS for security. Maximum payload of ~1,024 bytes makes PQC key exchange challenging.
Category: protocol | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: NB-IoT
chunks.content:
Term: NB-IoT (NB-IoT)
Definition: Narrowband IoT, a cellular connectivity standard for low-power wide-area (LPWA) devices. Offers 62.5 kbps uplink bandwidth, making PQC handshake overhead a significant concern.
Category: protocol | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: Connection Coalescing
chunks.content:
Term: Connection Coalescing
Definition: An HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 optimization where a single TLS connection is reused for requests to multiple hostnames sharing the same IP address and TLS certificate, amortizing PQC handshake overhead across domains.
Technical Note: With PQC hybrid handshakes adding 10-20KB overhead, connection coalescing becomes a critical mitigation — reducing the number of handshakes proportionally reduces total bandwidth impact.
Category: protocol | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: GOOSE
chunks.content:
Term: GOOSE (GOOSE)
Definition: Generic Object Oriented Substation Event. A high-speed multicast protocol in IEC 61850 for protection relay tripping with 4ms delivery requirements.
Technical Note: GOOSE uses HMAC-SHA256 for per-message authentication (quantum-safe). The quantum vulnerability lies in the RSA-based key distribution channel that seeds the HMAC keys.
Category: protocol | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: DNP3-SA
chunks.content:
Term: DNP3-SA (DNP3-SA)
Definition: DNP3 Secure Authentication (IEEE 1815.1). Challenge-response authentication for SCADA using HMAC-SHA256 with pre-shared Update Keys.
Technical Note: Session authentication uses HMAC (quantum-safe). PQC impacts the RSA-based Update Key distribution. ML-KEM-768 ciphertext (1088 bytes) fits within DNP3 2048-byte fragment limit — a clean single-fragment migration.
Category: protocol | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: DLMS/COSEM
chunks.content:
Term: DLMS/COSEM (DLMS/COSEM)
Definition: Device Language Message Specification / Companion Specification for Energy Metering. Used globally for smart meter communication with security suites based on AES and ECDSA/ECDH.
Technical Note: Security Suite 1 uses AES-GCM-128 + ECDSA P-256 + ECDH P-256. PQC key exchange (ML-KEM-768 at 1088 bytes vs ECDH at 33 bytes) creates a 33x bandwidth increase that is significant at scale for millions of meters.
Category: protocol | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: ICCP/TASE.2
chunks.content:
Term: ICCP/TASE.2 (ICCP)
Definition: Inter-Control Center Communications Protocol. Used for real-time data exchange between utility control centers, secured via TLS.
Technical Note: ICCP links are internet-facing and carry real-time grid state data — the highest-priority PQC migration target under NERC CIP-012.
Category: protocol | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: DICOM
chunks.content:
Term: DICOM (DICOM)
Definition: Digital Imaging and Communications in Medicine. The standard protocol for transmitting, storing, and sharing medical images (X-ray, CT, MRI). DICOM supports TLS for transport security; PQC migration requires updating both the transport layer and any encrypted archives of imaging data.
Category: protocol | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: SDA
chunks.content:
Term: SDA (SDA)
Definition: Static Data Authentication. The simplest EMV card authentication method where the issuer pre-signs static card data with RSA. Vulnerable to card cloning since the signature never changes.
Technical Note: SDA uses a single RSA signature over static data. A terminal verifies this signature against the issuer CA certificate chain. Being deprecated in favor of DDA/CDA.
Category: protocol | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: DDA
chunks.content:
Term: DDA (DDA)
Definition: Dynamic Data Authentication. An EMV card authentication method where the card generates a unique RSA signature per transaction, preventing cloning attacks.
Technical Note: DDA requires the card chip to perform RSA signing using its private key. The terminal verifies via the EMVCo CA certificate chain (Root → Network CA → Issuer CA → ICC).
Category: protocol | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: CDA
chunks.content:
Term: CDA (CDA)
Definition: Combined Data Authentication. The strongest EMV offline authentication method, combining dynamic RSA signature with the application cryptogram in a single operation.
Technical Note: CDA binds the authentication and transaction authorization into one cryptographic operation, preventing man-in-the-middle attacks between card and terminal. Most modern EMV cards use CDA.
Category: protocol | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: ARQC
chunks.content:
Term: ARQC (ARQC)
Definition: Authorization Request Cryptogram. A symmetric MAC generated by the EMV card chip using a shared secret with the issuer, proving the card is genuine during online authorization.
Technical Note: ARQC uses 3DES or AES-based MAC computation with issuer-derived session keys. Being a symmetric operation, ARQC generation is inherently quantum-safe.
Category: protocol | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: ARPC
chunks.content:
Term: ARPC (ARPC)
Definition: Authorization Response Cryptogram. A symmetric MAC generated by the issuer in response to an ARQC, proving the issuer authorized the transaction.
Technical Note: ARPC is the issuer-to-card counterpart of ARQC. Together they form a mutual authentication mechanism. Both use symmetric crypto and are quantum-safe.
Category: protocol | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: 3-D Secure
chunks.content:
Term: 3-D Secure (3DS)
Definition: A payment authentication protocol for card-not-present (e-commerce) transactions. Version 2.0 uses ECDSA challenge signing and risk-based authentication.
Technical Note: 3DS 2.0 challenge signatures use ECDSA P-256, which is quantum-vulnerable. The frictionless flow relies on device fingerprinting and behavioral analysis (quantum-safe). PQC migration targets the challenge signing component.
Category: protocol | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: ACARS
chunks.content:
Term: ACARS (ACARS)
Definition: Aircraft Communications Addressing and Reporting System. A digital data link for transmitting short messages between aircraft and ground stations via VHF radio or SATCOM.
Technical Note: ACARS messages are limited to 220-byte blocks. ML-DSA-65 signatures (3,309 bytes) require 15+ blocks, making in-band PQC authentication infeasible without protocol redesign or gateway-mediated signing.
Category: protocol | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: CPDLC
chunks.content:
Term: CPDLC (CPDLC)
Definition: Controller-Pilot Data Link Communications. A text-based ATC communication system replacing voice with structured data messages between pilots and air traffic controllers.
Technical Note: CPDLC operates over SATCOM with 600ms RTT and supports up to 1,024-byte messages. PQC signature authentication is feasible (ML-DSA-44 fits in 3 blocks) but adds latency to safety-critical ATC clearances.
Category: protocol | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: ADS-B
chunks.content:
Term: ADS-B (ADS-B)
Definition: Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast. A surveillance system where aircraft broadcast their GPS-derived position, altitude, and velocity on 1090 MHz, receivable by ground stations and other aircraft.
Technical Note: ADS-B transmits unauthenticated 112-bit messages (14 bytes payload) with no encryption or signing. The message size is far too small for any PQC signature. Authentication requires out-of-band verification or protocol redesign.
Category: protocol | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: Agent-to-Agent Authentication
chunks.content:
Term: Agent-to-Agent Authentication (A2A)
Definition: Mutual authentication between autonomous AI agents using cryptographic credentials, enabling secure communication, task delegation, and transaction execution without human intermediation.
Technical Note: A2A authentication typically uses mTLS with PQC certificates (ML-DSA for signing, ML-KEM for key exchange). Per-message signing adds bandwidth overhead — at 10K messages/second, ML-DSA-65 signatures add significant bandwidth compared to ECDSA, requiring careful protocol design.
Category: protocol | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: Secure Multi-Party Computation
chunks.content:
Term: Secure Multi-Party Computation (MPC)
Definition: A cryptographic technique allowing multiple parties to jointly compute a function over their combined inputs while keeping each party's input private from the others.
Technical Note: MPC enables collaborative AI model training across organizations without revealing proprietary data. Quantum impact varies by protocol: garbled circuits rely on symmetric crypto (Grover-resistant with larger keys), while secret-sharing schemes may need PQC for the communication channels.
Category: protocol | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: CCC Digital Key
chunks.content:
Term: CCC Digital Key
Definition: A specification by the Car Connectivity Consortium (CCC) enabling smartphones to function as vehicle keys via NFC, BLE, or UWB. CCC Digital Key 3.0 uses ECDH P-256 key agreement and ECDSA P-256 certificates, both quantum-vulnerable.
Technical Note: NFC transport limits APDUs to 256 bytes, making ML-KEM-768 ciphertext (1,088 bytes) require 5 APDUs per key exchange. BLE (512-byte L2CAP frames) and UWB (symmetric ranging, quantum-safe) handle PQC migration more gracefully. Owner-to-friend key sharing adds another quantum-vulnerable certificate chain.
Category: protocol | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: CAN Bus
chunks.content:
Term: CAN Bus (CAN)
Definition: Controller Area Network, the dominant in-vehicle serial bus protocol with an 8-byte (CAN 2.0) or 64-byte (CAN FD) payload per frame. CAN buses connect ECUs for powertrain, chassis, and body functions.
Technical Note: CAN 2.0 payload (8 bytes) cannot carry any PQC signature in a single frame — even the smallest ML-DSA-44 signature (2,420 bytes) requires 303 CAN frames. CAN FD (64 bytes) is slightly better but still impractical for per-message PQC signing. Automotive Ethernet (1,500-byte MTU) is the PQC-feasible bus for ADAS and infotainment zones.
Category: protocol | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: RFC 9794
chunks.content:
Term: RFC 9794
Definition: IETF Informational RFC (June 2025) that defines terminology for post-quantum/traditional (PQ/T) hybrid schemes, so that protocols, standards and organisations use the word "hybrid" consistently. It is a reference terminology guide and does not set protocol rules.
Technical Note: Defines terms such as PQ/T hybrid scheme, PQ/T hybrid KEM, PQ/T hybrid digital signature, PQ/T hybrid composite scheme, PQ/T hybrid combiner, PQ/T parallel PKI and multi-certificate authentication. Its Security Considerations section says the document itself does not have a security impact on Internet protocols and that the security considerations for each hybrid protocol belong in that protocol's own specification (for TLS 1.3 key exchange, RFC 9954). A test rule such as "both components must complete, no silent downgrade" is test practice, not an RFC 9794 requirement.
Category: protocol | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: IKE_SA_INIT
chunks.content:
Term: IKE_SA_INIT
Definition: The initial phase of the IKEv2 protocol. It negotiates cryptographic algorithms, exchanges nonces, and performs a Diffie-Hellman exchange.
Category: protocol | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: IKE_INTERMEDIATE
chunks.content:
Term: IKE_INTERMEDIATE
Definition: An optional phase introduced in IKEv2 to transmit large amounts of data, such as post-quantum key shares, before authentication completes.
Category: protocol | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: IKE_AUTH
chunks.content:
Term: IKE_AUTH
Definition: The completion phase of the IKEv2 handshake. It authenticates the previous messages and establishes the first IPsec Security Association (CHILD_SA).
Category: protocol | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: Header
chunks.content:
Term: Header (HDR)
Definition: The encrypted exchange header found at the start of an IKEv2 packet. Contains the SPIs, version, exchange type, and flags.
Category: protocol | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: Encrypted Payload
chunks.content:
Term: Encrypted Payload (SK)
Definition: The secure container wrapping IKEv2 payloads like Identifiers (IDi/IDr), Certificates (CERT), and Authentication (AUTH) data.
Category: protocol | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: Messaging Layer Security
chunks.content:
Term: Messaging Layer Security (MLS)
Definition: IETF group-messaging protocol (RFC 9420, July 2023) that scales end-to-end encryption to large groups using TreeKEM. Deployed by WhatsApp, Cisco Webex, AWS Wickr, and Google Messages.
Technical Note: Post-quantum ciphersuites are defined in draft-ietf-mls-pq-ciphersuites (ML-KEM + ML-DSA). Hybrid combiners are specified in draft-ietf-mls-combiner.
Category: protocol | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: TreeKEM
chunks.content:
Term: TreeKEM
Definition: The asynchronous ratcheting tree at the heart of MLS. Members are leaves of a binary tree; each branch holds a shared secret derived from its children, so Add / Remove / Update operations only touch the O(log N) nodes on the affected path.
Technical Note: TreeKEM uses HPKE (RFC 9180) to encrypt path updates between members and provides both forward secrecy and post-compromise security.
Category: protocol | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: EST
chunks.content:
Term: EST (Enrollment over Secure Transport)
Definition: IETF certificate enrollment protocol (RFC 7030) used by devices to request, renew, and re-key X.509 certificates over TLS. Common in IoT, enterprise PKI, and 802.1X NAC enrolment.
Technical Note: Often deployed alongside ACME (web-facing) and CMP (enterprise / 3GPP) as part of an automated CLM stack. PQC migration of EST mostly inherits from the underlying TLS and CSR algorithm choices.
Category: protocol | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: PSK
chunks.content:
Term: PSK (Pre-Shared Key)
Definition: In TLS 1.3, a symmetric key issued by the server after a full handshake and presented by the client on reconnection to enable session resumption — feeding into the Early Secret stage of a faster resumed handshake, optionally with 0-RTT early data.
Technical Note: PSK-based resumption is itself symmetric-key and therefore not directly threatened by a quantum computer, but the PSK is only as trustworthy as the full handshake that established it — if that handshake's key exchange was classical (not hybrid ML-KEM), a harvested session ticket carries the same exposure forward.
Category: protocol | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: SNI
chunks.content:
Term: SNI (Server Name Indication)
Definition: A TLS extension carried in the ClientHello that tells the server which hostname the client is connecting to, so a single IP address can serve TLS certificates for multiple domains. Sent in plaintext in standard TLS.
Technical Note: Because the ClientHello (and SNI within it) is unencrypted, it reveals which site a user is visiting even though the connection content is protected — a metadata leak Encrypted Client Hello (ECH) closes by encrypting the ClientHello using a key published in DNS. SNI/ECH is a transport-metadata concern orthogonal to PQC key exchange, not solved by it.
Category: protocol | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: Registration Authority
chunks.content:
Term: Registration Authority (RA)
Definition: The entity in a PKI that verifies a certificate applicant's identity and authorizes issuance, then forwards the approved request to the Certificate Authority (already in this glossary) for signing.
Technical Note: Separating the RA and CA roles lets an organization outsource identity vetting while keeping signing authority centralized.
Category: protocol | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: OAuth
chunks.content:
Term: OAuth (OAuth 2.0)
Definition: An authorization framework (RFC 6749) that lets an application obtain limited access to a resource on a user's behalf via short-lived tokens, without handling the user's credentials directly.
Technical Note: OpenID Connect, already in this glossary, is an identity layer built on top of OAuth 2.0.
Category: protocol | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: COSE
chunks.content:
Term: COSE (CBOR Object Signing and Encryption)
Definition: The binary, CBOR-based counterpart to JOSE, used where compact encoding matters — IoT, constrained devices, WebAuthn/FIDO2 attestation.
Technical Note: The IETF COSE and JOSE working groups are standardizing the same ML-DSA/ML-KEM/SLH-DSA algorithm identifiers across both formats.
Category: protocol | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: LAMPS
chunks.content:
Term: LAMPS (Limited Additional Mechanisms for PKIX and SMIME)
Definition: The IETF working group producing PQC and composite-signature specifications for X.509 certificates, CMS, and S/MIME — including the composite ML-DSA drafts this hub's own email-signing workshop implements.
Category: protocol | Complexity: advanced

metadata.acronym: Limited Additional Mechanisms for PKIX and SMIME

chunks.title: VPN
chunks.content:
Term: VPN (Virtual Private Network)
Definition: A broad term for tunneling protocols — IPsec, WireGuard, TLS-based VPNs — that extend a private network across a public one.
Technical Note: PQC migration for VPNs generally means adding a hybrid post-quantum key exchange to the underlying IKEv2, WireGuard, or TLS handshake.
Category: protocol | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: RFC 8446
chunks.content:
Term: RFC 8446
Definition: The original IETF standard defining TLS version 1.3, published August 2018. TLS 1.3 removed legacy cipher suites, mandated forward secrecy, and reduced the handshake to 1 round-trip. Obsoleted by RFC 9846 (July 2026), which re-specifies TLS 1.3 under the same version number.
Technical Note: TLS 1.3 is the foundation for PQC key exchange integration. RFC 8446 (now RFC 9846) defines the "key_share" extension that hybrid PQC groups (e.g., X25519MLKEM768) plug into without protocol changes.
Category: standard | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: FIPS 203
chunks.content:
Term: FIPS 203
Definition: The NIST standard defining ML-KEM (Module-Lattice-Based Key Encapsulation Mechanism), published August 2024.
Category: standard | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: FIPS 204
chunks.content:
Term: FIPS 204
Definition: The NIST standard defining ML-DSA (Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Algorithm), published August 2024.
Category: standard | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: FIPS 205
chunks.content:
Term: FIPS 205
Definition: The NIST standard defining SLH-DSA (Stateless Hash-Based Digital Signature Algorithm), published August 2024.
Category: standard | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: FIPS 140-3
chunks.content:
Term: FIPS 140-3
Definition: The U.S. government standard for validating cryptographic modules. Hardware and software must pass FIPS 140-3 testing to be used in federal systems.
Category: standard | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: CNSA 2.0
chunks.content:
Term: CNSA 2.0
Definition: NSA's Commercial National Security Algorithm Suite 2.0, mandating PQC adoption timelines for national security systems.
Category: standard | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: Common Criteria
chunks.content:
Term: Common Criteria (CC)
Definition: An international standard (ISO/IEC 15408) for evaluating the security properties of IT products, used globally for government procurement.
Technical Note: The Common Criteria Recognition Arrangement (CCRA) is a 31-nation mutual recognition agreement: national Certification Bodies (e.g., BSI for Germany, ANSSI for France, NIAP for the US) issue CC certificates that are accepted across all member states. The EUCC is the EU-specific adaptation managed by ENISA.
Category: standard | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: EUCC
chunks.content:
Term: EUCC (EUCC)
Definition: EU Cybersecurity Certification Scheme — the European Union's harmonized product security certification scheme based on Common Criteria, managed by ENISA under the EU Cybersecurity Act (2019).
Technical Note: EUCC certificates are valid across all 27 EU member states, eliminating the need for per-country certification. ENISA maintains the Agreed Cryptographic Mechanisms (ACM) list specifying which PQC algorithms are approved for EUCC-certified products. National Certification Authorities (e.g., BSI, ANSSI) issue EUCC certificates.
Category: standard | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: eIDAS 2.0
chunks.content:
Term: eIDAS 2.0
Definition: The EU regulation establishing a framework for electronic identification and trust services, including the European Digital Identity Wallet.
Category: standard | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: NIS2 Directive
chunks.content:
Term: NIS2 Directive
Definition: The EU Network and Information Security Directive 2 (Directive 2022/2555), requiring operators of essential services and digital service providers to implement strong cryptographic controls. Transposed into national law across EU member states by October 2024.
Technical Note: NIS2 mandates risk-based security measures including encryption and cryptographic key management. ENISA guidance links NIS2 obligations directly to PQC migration timelines, making it a key compliance driver for EU organisations.
Category: standard | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: PKCS#12
chunks.content:
Term: PKCS#12
Definition: A file format for storing a private key together with its X.509 certificate, commonly used for importing/exporting credentials.
Category: standard | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: FIPS 206
chunks.content:
Term: FIPS 206
Definition: The planned NIST standard for FN-DSA (FFT over NTRU-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Algorithm, based on Falcon). FIPS 206 is still in development; NIST has not published an Initial Public Draft or final standard.
Category: standard | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: FIPS 186-5
chunks.content:
Term: FIPS 186-5
Definition: The NIST Digital Signature Standard defining RSA, ECDSA, and EdDSA. Being deprecated in favor of PQC signature algorithms per NIST IR 8547.
Category: standard | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: NIST IR 8547
chunks.content:
Term: NIST IR 8547
Definition: NIST Internal Report setting the PQC transition timeline: quantum-vulnerable public-key algorithms are deprecated after 2030 and disallowed under NIST standards after 2035. Final since 27 October 2026; it replaced the initial public draft of 12 November 2024.
Technical Note: Covers RSA, ECDSA, EdDSA, finite-field and elliptic-curve DH and MQV at every key size of 112 bits of security or more. It recommends ML-KEM-768 as the default ML-KEM parameter set and allows a hybrid key-establishment scheme to be FIPS 140-validated when one input is approved.
Category: standard | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: NIST SP 800-131A
chunks.content:
Term: NIST SP 800-131A
Definition: NIST Special Publication providing guidance on transitioning the use of cryptographic algorithms and key lengths. Defines which algorithms are approved, deprecated, or disallowed for federal use.
Technical Note: Revision 3 (2019) deprecated SHA-1 and 2TDEA. A future revision is expected to align with NIST IR 8547 timelines, formally disallowing RSA, ECDSA, and DH after 2035.
Category: standard | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: NIST SP 800-208
chunks.content:
Term: NIST SP 800-208
Definition: NIST recommendation for stateful hash-based signature schemes LMS and XMSS, used for firmware signing and secure boot.
Category: standard | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: RFC 9629
chunks.content:
Term: RFC 9629
Definition: IETF standard defining how to use Key Encapsulation Mechanisms (KEMs) in the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) for encrypted messaging.
Category: standard | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: PCI DSS
chunks.content:
Term: PCI DSS (PCI DSS)
Definition: Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard, requiring strong cryptography for cardholder data protection. Quantum threatens its RSA/ECC foundations.
Category: standard | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: HIPAA
chunks.content:
Term: HIPAA (HIPAA)
Definition: Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act, the U.S. law requiring encryption of protected health information. Patient data faces HNDL risk.
Category: standard | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: IEC 62443
chunks.content:
Term: IEC 62443
Definition: International standard series for industrial automation and control systems (IACS) cybersecurity. Critical for IoT and energy sector PQC migration.
Category: standard | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: SLSA
chunks.content:
Term: SLSA (SLSA)
Definition: Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts — a security framework (originally from Google) that defines increasing levels of supply chain integrity guarantees, from basic build provenance to fully hermetic, reproducible builds.
Technical Note: SLSA levels depend on cryptographic attestations signed during the build process. If those signatures use quantum-vulnerable algorithms (ECDSA, RSA), the entire SLSA guarantee collapses once quantum computers can forge attestations.
Category: standard | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: in-toto
chunks.content:
Term: in-toto
Definition: An open-source framework for securing the integrity of software supply chains by defining and cryptographically verifying each step of the build and release process. Each step produces a signed attestation (a "link") forming a verifiable chain.
Technical Note: in-toto link metadata is signed with the functionary's private key. PQC migration requires upgrading all functionary keys to ML-DSA to prevent quantum forgery of supply chain attestations.
Category: standard | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: NIST SP 800-227
chunks.content:
Term: NIST SP 800-227
Definition: NIST Special Publication providing recommendations for Key Encapsulation Mechanism (KEM) implementation, including guidance on parameter selection and secure use of ML-KEM.
Category: standard | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: NIST IR 8545
chunks.content:
Term: NIST IR 8545
Definition: NIST Internal Report documenting the selection of HQC as an additional KEM standard, providing a code-based alternative to lattice-based ML-KEM.
Category: standard | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: RFC 9370
chunks.content:
Term: RFC 9370
Definition: IETF standard defining multiple key exchanges in IKEv2, enabling hybrid classical + PQC key exchange for IPsec VPNs.
Technical Note: Allows adding ML-KEM alongside classical Diffie-Hellman in a single IKEv2 handshake without breaking backward compatibility.
Category: standard | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: RFC 9881
chunks.content:
Term: RFC 9881
Definition: IETF standard defining how to use ML-DSA digital signatures in X.509 certificates and Certificate Revocation Lists (CRLs).
Category: standard | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: RFC 9882
chunks.content:
Term: RFC 9882
Definition: IETF standard defining the use of ML-DSA signatures in the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS), enabling PQC-signed messages and documents.
Category: standard | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: ISO/IEC 18013-5
chunks.content:
Term: ISO/IEC 18013-5
Definition: International standard for mobile driving licences (mDL), defining the data model, security mechanisms, and device engagement protocols for digital identity documents.
Category: standard | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: BSI TR-02102
chunks.content:
Term: BSI TR-02102
Definition: German Federal Office for Information Security (BSI) Technical Guideline series on cryptographic recommendations, covering TLS, IPsec, SSH, and general algorithms.
Technical Note: TR-02102-1 covers general recommendations; TR-02102-2 through TR-02102-4 provide protocol-specific PQC migration guidance.
Category: standard | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: NIST SP 800-57
chunks.content:
Term: NIST SP 800-57
Definition: NIST Special Publication 800-57: Recommendation for Key Management. Defines the seven-stage key lifecycle (pre-operational, operational, post-operational, etc.) and cryptoperiod guidance.
Category: standard | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: PKCS#11
chunks.content:
Term: PKCS#11
Definition: A standard API (also called Cryptoki) for accessing cryptographic hardware like Hardware Security Modules (HSMs), smart cards, and tokens.
Technical Note: Defines C-language function calls for key generation, signing, encryption, and object management. PKCS#11 v3.2 adds CKM_ML_KEM_* and CKM_ML_DSA_* mechanisms for PQC.
Category: standard | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: BIP44
chunks.content:
Term: BIP44
Definition: Bitcoin Improvement Proposal 44, defining a multi-account hierarchy for deterministic wallets using derivation paths like m/44'/0'/0'/0/0 (purpose/coin/account/change/index).
Technical Note: Builds on BIP32 (HD wallets) and BIP43 (purpose field). Enables standard derivation paths across different cryptocurrencies and wallet implementations.
Category: standard | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: SP 800-90A
chunks.content:
Term: SP 800-90A
Definition: NIST Special Publication defining three Deterministic Random Bit Generator (DRBG) mechanisms: CTR_DRBG (AES-based), Hash_DRBG (SHA-based), and HMAC_DRBG. Published June 2015 (Rev. 1).
Technical Note: All three DRBGs are built on symmetric primitives (hash functions, HMAC, block ciphers), which Shor's algorithm does not break; whether a given DRBG is adequate against quantum attack depends on the primitive and security strength chosen (Rev. 1 CTR_DRBG also allows three-key TDEA). That is engineering judgment, not a NIST statement. CTR_DRBG is the default in OpenSSL. Rev. 2 is not yet a draft: NIST published a pre-draft call for comments on 2025-09-04 (closed 2025-11-04) announcing plans for a new DRBG construction based on SHAKE extendable-output functions; no draft text has been published.
Category: standard | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: SP 800-90B
chunks.content:
Term: SP 800-90B
Definition: NIST Special Publication providing methods for validating entropy sources used as input to DRBGs. Defines health tests (repetition count, adaptive proportion) and min-entropy estimation procedures. Published January 2018.
Technical Note: The NIST Entropy Source Validation (ESV) program under CMVP uses SP 800-90B to certify hardware entropy sources. The NIST EntropyAssessment tool on GitHub implements the min-entropy assessment methods.
Category: standard | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: SP 800-90C
chunks.content:
Term: SP 800-90C
Definition: NIST Special Publication describing constructions for Random Bit Generators (RBGs) that combine entropy sources with DRBGs. Defines RBG1, RBG2, RBG3, and RBGC construction classes. Published September 2025.
Technical Note: Completes the SP 800-90 series. Specifies how to combine multiple independent entropy sources for defense-in-depth, using XOR and conditioning functions to ensure combined output retains entropy even if one source is compromised.
Category: standard | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: BIP-360
chunks.content:
Term: BIP-360
Definition: Pay-to-Merkle-Root (P2MR), a draft Bitcoin soft fork that adds a new native SegWit output type (version 2, bc1z… addresses) working like Taproot with the elliptic-curve key-spend path removed. It contains no post-quantum signature of its own: its authors (Hunter Beast, Ethan Heilman and Isabel Foxen Duke) intend to offer a separate proposal for that upon further research. Earlier drafts were titled P2QRH.
Technical Note: P2MR addresses use bech32m encoding (bc1z…). Every spend reveals a leaf script and a control block. The BIP says P2MR outputs are resistant to long-exposure attacks (keys exposed for longer than needed to confirm a spending transaction), and that protection against short-exposure attacks, where a key is exposed in the mempool while a transaction waits to be confirmed, may require post-quantum signatures. In the BIP's depth-1 example the P2MR witness is 135 bytes, against 66 bytes for a Taproot key-path spend.
Category: standard | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: Solana Improvement Document
chunks.content:
Term: Solana Improvement Document (SIMD)
Definition: The formal proposal process for Solana protocol changes, analogous to Bitcoin BIPs and Ethereum EIPs. SIMD-0461, a proposed Falcon (FN-DSA) signature-verification syscall, was closed by its author on 2026-06-17; a commenter in the thread says Falcon-512 and Hawk-512 verifiers already work as on-chain programmes without protocol changes.
Category: standard | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: SUIT
chunks.content:
Term: SUIT (SUIT)
Definition: Software Updates for Internet of Things (RFC 9019). A CBOR-based manifest format for secure firmware updates, providing metadata, conditions, and signature verification for OTA delivery.
Category: standard | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: RFC 7228
chunks.content:
Term: RFC 7228
Definition: Terminology for Constrained-Node Networks. Defines device Class 0/1/2 based on RAM and Flash memory constraints, used to categorize IoT device capabilities for protocol selection.
Category: standard | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: NIST RMF
chunks.content:
Term: NIST RMF (RMF)
Definition: NIST Risk Management Framework (SP 800-37) — a six-step lifecycle process (Categorise, Select, Implement, Assess, Authorise, Monitor) for managing information security and privacy risk in federal and commercial systems.
Technical Note: Step 1 (Categorise) uses FIPS 199 impact levels (Low/Moderate/High) to classify systems. For PQC, categorisation directly informs which controls from SP 800-53 apply, including post-quantum cryptographic requirements.
Category: standard | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: ISO 27005
chunks.content:
Term: ISO 27005
Definition: ISO/IEC 27005 — the international standard for information security risk management. Provides a structured methodology for identifying assets, assessing threats and vulnerabilities, evaluating risk, and selecting risk treatment options.
