Technical Note: ISO 27005 uses a likelihood × consequence matrix to produce a risk level. For PQC, the threat is a CRQC; the vulnerability is use of RSA/ECC; the consequence is full plaintext exposure of harvested data. Risk treatment options: mitigate (migrate to PQC), accept, transfer, or avoid.
Category: standard | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: FIPS 199
chunks.content:
Term: FIPS 199
Definition: Federal Information Processing Standard 199 — NIST's standard for categorising federal information and information systems. Defines three impact levels (Low, Moderate, High) for confidentiality, integrity, and availability that drive control selection in the NIST RMF.
Technical Note: High confidentiality impact (per FIPS 199) triggers the most stringent cryptographic requirements. Under CNSA 2.0, High-impact systems face the earliest PQC migration deadlines.
Category: standard | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: GDPR
chunks.content:
Term: GDPR (GDPR)
Definition: General Data Protection Regulation — EU Regulation 2016/679 requiring appropriate technical and organisational measures to protect personal data. The "appropriate technical measures" clause is interpreted to require state-of-the-art encryption, creating an implicit obligation to migrate to PQC as quantum threats mature.
Technical Note: GDPR Art. 32 ("Security of processing") obliges controllers and processors to implement encryption commensurate with the risk. As CRQC timelines become clearer, regulators are expected to interpret Art. 32 as mandating PQC readiness for long-retained personal data.
Category: standard | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: PIPL
chunks.content:
Term: PIPL (PIPL)
Definition: Personal Information Protection Law — China's primary data privacy law (effective November 2021), requiring data processors to adopt security measures protecting personal information. Mandates localisation of certain data and restricts cross-border transfers, making PQC migration relevant for multinational organisations with Chinese data subjects.
Category: standard | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: CCPA
chunks.content:
Term: CCPA (CCPA)
Definition: California Consumer Privacy Act — U.S. state law (effective 2020, amended by CPRA in 2023) granting California residents rights over their personal data. Data breaches of unencrypted personal information trigger mandatory notification, incentivising strong cryptography including PQC for long-retained data.
Category: standard | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: LGPD
chunks.content:
Term: LGPD (LGPD)
Definition: Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados — Brazil's data protection law (Law 13.709/2018), modelled on GDPR. Requires appropriate technical security measures for personal data. Brazilian DPA (ANPD) guidance on cryptographic adequacy is expected to align with global PQC migration timelines.
Category: standard | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: PDPA
chunks.content:
Term: PDPA (PDPA)
Definition: Personal Data Protection Act — Singapore's primary data protection law administered by the PDPC. Requires reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data. Singapore's CSA has published PQC guidance referencing PDPA obligations for organisations managing long-retained personal data.
Category: standard | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: DORA
chunks.content:
Term: DORA (DORA)
Definition: Digital Operational Resilience Act — EU Regulation 2022/2554, applying to financial entities and their ICT service providers from January 2025. Requires ICT risk management, resilience testing, and third-party risk oversight. PQC migration readiness is expected to be assessed under DORA's ICT risk management chapter.
Technical Note: DORA Art. 6 mandates a comprehensive ICT risk management framework including cryptographic controls. EBA and ESMA technical standards under DORA are expected to reference ENISA PQC guidance as it matures.
Category: standard | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: CycloneDX
chunks.content:
Term: CycloneDX
Definition: An OWASP standard for Software and Cryptography Bills of Materials (SBOM/CBOM). CycloneDX v1.6 introduced the Cryptography Asset type, enabling machine-readable inventory of all cryptographic algorithms, keys, certificates, and protocols in a system.
Technical Note: CycloneDX CBOM components include: algorithms (name, parameterSets, primitive), certificates (subject, validity, signatureAlgorithm), keys (algorithm, size), and protocols (type, version, cipher suites). Tooling: IBM Quantum Safe Explorer, Keyfactor.
Category: standard | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: CAVP
chunks.content:
Term: CAVP (CAVP)
Definition: Cryptographic Algorithm Validation Program — the NIST/CCCS program that validates implementations of Approved algorithms and their components. Testing runs black-box through NIST's ACVTS, which speaks the ACVP protocol; implementations that complete it get an algorithm validation certificate on the CAVP validation list. Algorithm validation is a prerequisite of FIPS 140-3 module validation under CMVP.
Technical Note: Source: NIST CAVP project page (csrc.nist.gov/projects/cryptographic-algorithm-validation-program): an algorithm is listed on a module certificate as an Approved security function only after it completes the algorithm validation process. ACVP sub-specifications and ACVTS testing exist for ML-KEM (FIPS 203), ML-DSA (FIPS 204) and SLH-DSA (FIPS 205). Only the ACVTS production environment, used by accredited labs, creates CAVP certificates; passing public sample vectors does not.
Category: standard | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: NERC CIP
chunks.content:
Term: NERC CIP (NERC CIP)
Definition: North American Electric Reliability Corporation Critical Infrastructure Protection standards. Mandatory cybersecurity requirements for bulk electric system operators.
Technical Note: CIP-012 mandates encrypted inter-control-center communications (ICCP/TASE.2) — the highest-priority PQC migration target in the energy sector. CIP-013 requires supply chain risk management including vendor PQC readiness.
Category: standard | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: IEC 61850
chunks.content:
Term: IEC 61850
Definition: International standard for communication networks and systems in substations. Defines GOOSE, MMS, and Sampled Values protocols for protection and control.
Technical Note: GOOSE messages have a 4ms delivery requirement for protection relay tripping. HMAC authentication is quantum-safe, but asymmetric key distribution for HMAC seeds requires PQC migration.
Category: standard | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: IEC 62351
chunks.content:
Term: IEC 62351
Definition: Power systems management and associated information exchange — security standard. Covers TLS profiles, GOOSE authentication, and key management for power systems.
Technical Note: Part 3 covers TCP/IP security (TLS for MMS/ICCP), Part 6 covers GOOSE peer-to-peer authentication using HMAC, and Part 9 defines key management architecture for power systems.
Category: standard | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: IEEE 2030.5
chunks.content:
Term: IEEE 2030.5
Definition: Smart Energy Profile 2.0 standard for distributed energy resource communication using certificate-based device authentication.
Technical Note: Each DER (solar inverter, battery, EV charger) has a unique IEEE 2030.5 device certificate signed by the utility CA. Fleet-wide PQC certificate reissuance is required for migration.
Category: standard | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: GINA
chunks.content:
Term: GINA (GINA)
Definition: Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act (2008). US federal law prohibiting discrimination based on genetic information in health insurance and employment. Genetic data decrypted via HNDL attacks could enable discrimination that GINA was designed to prevent.
Category: standard | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: 42 CFR Part 2
chunks.content:
Term: 42 CFR Part 2
Definition: US federal regulation providing additional privacy protections for substance use disorder patient records beyond HIPAA. Records protected under Part 2 carry heightened stigma risk if quantum-decrypted, as disclosure can lead to criminal prosecution, employment loss, and social ostracism.
Category: standard | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: 21 CFR Part 11
chunks.content:
Term: 21 CFR Part 11
Definition: FDA regulation establishing criteria for electronic records and electronic signatures in the pharmaceutical industry. Requires validated cryptographic controls for data integrity. Any PQC migration in pharma must maintain Part 11 compliance throughout the transition.
Category: standard | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: ARINC 653
chunks.content:
Term: ARINC 653
Definition: Avionics Application Standard Software Interface (ARINC 653). An RTOS partitioning standard that isolates safety-critical software functions in separate memory/time partitions on shared hardware.
Technical Note: Each ARINC 653 partition has a fixed memory budget and CPU time window. PQC libraries must fit within these constraints alongside existing avionics functions, limiting algorithm choice.
Category: standard | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: DO-178C
chunks.content:
Term: DO-178C
Definition: Software Considerations in Airborne Systems and Equipment Certification. The primary standard for certifying safety-critical avionics software, defining five Design Assurance Levels (DAL A through E).
Technical Note: Adding a PQC cryptographic library to a DAL-A system (e.g., Flight Management System) requires MC/DC test coverage, traceability, and independent verification. Recertification costs $2-10M and takes 12-24 months.
Category: standard | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: DO-326A
chunks.content:
Term: DO-326A
Definition: Airworthiness Security Process Specification. The FAA/EASA standard for addressing cybersecurity threats to airborne systems, requiring threat assessment and security controls for type certification.
Technical Note: DO-326A mandates that cryptographic protections be evaluated against evolving threats including quantum computing. Aircraft manufacturers must demonstrate PQC readiness as part of the airworthiness security risk assessment.
Category: standard | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: International Traffic in Arms Regulations
chunks.content:
Term: International Traffic in Arms Regulations (ITAR)
Definition: US export control regulations (22 CFR 120-130) governing the export and transfer of defense articles and services, including military cryptographic systems listed on the US Munitions List.
Technical Note: ITAR Category XI covers military cryptographic equipment. PQC implementations for military aircraft or defense satellites require State Department export licenses. No license exceptions exist for embargoed destinations.
Category: standard | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: Content Credentials
chunks.content:
Term: Content Credentials (C2PA)
Definition: A technical standard by the Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity that embeds cryptographically signed metadata into digital content to verify its origin, creation method, and edit history.
Technical Note: C2PA signs the claim in each manifest with a COSE_Sign1 signature and X.509 certificate chains to create tamper-evident provenance chains. C2PA 2.4 allows ECDSA, RSASSA-PSS and Ed25519 signatures, all quantum-vulnerable, and its allowed list holds no post-quantum algorithm, so moving to ML-DSA signatures would take a revision of the specification. Provenance signed today stays forgeable beyond Q-Day.
Category: standard | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: ASIL
chunks.content:
Term: ASIL (ASIL)
Definition: Automotive Safety Integrity Level, a risk classification defined by ISO 26262 ranging from QM (quality management, no safety requirement) to ASIL-D (most stringent). Higher ASIL levels demand tighter crypto verification latency budgets and redundancy requirements.
Technical Note: ASIL-D systems (braking, steering) require fail-operational crypto with dual-path verification (PQC primary + classical backup) and hardware watchdog timers. Verification must complete within 10-15ms. ASIL-A/B systems can tolerate fail-safe degradation with relaxed timing.
Category: standard | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: TISAX
chunks.content:
Term: TISAX (TISAX)
Definition: Trusted Information Security Assessment Exchange, a standard for information security assessments in the automotive supply chain governed by VDA (German Association of the Automotive Industry) and ENX.
Technical Note: TISAX v7 (expected 2027) is anticipated to add PQC readiness criteria. OEMs requiring TISAX compliance from Tier-1 and Tier-2 suppliers will cascade PQC requirements through the supply chain. Assessment scope will likely cover key management, firmware signing, and cryptographic inventory.
Category: standard | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: AUTOSAR
chunks.content:
Term: AUTOSAR
Definition: AUTomotive Open System ARchitecture, a standardized software architecture for automotive ECUs. AUTOSAR Classic Platform provides the SHE-based Crypto Service Manager (limited to AES/CMAC). AUTOSAR Adaptive Platform offers a flexible Crypto Service Manager that can integrate PQC algorithms.
Technical Note: AUTOSAR Adaptive Platform is the key enabler for automotive crypto-agility. Its Crypto Service Manager abstracts algorithm selection behind a provider interface, allowing OEMs to swap ECDSA for ML-DSA without modifying application software. Classic Platform ECUs (80%+ of deployed fleet) cannot be upgraded to PQC without hardware replacement.
Category: standard | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: ISO 15118
chunks.content:
Term: ISO 15118
Definition: An international standard for vehicle-to-grid communication enabling Plug & Charge: automatic mutual authentication between electric vehicles and charging stations using X.509 certificates over TLS.
Technical Note: ISO 15118 uses a PKI hierarchy (OEM Root CA → Vehicle Sub-CA → Vehicle Leaf Cert) with ECDSA P-256. PQC migration requires updating the entire Plug & Charge PKI to hybrid certificates, affecting vehicle OEMs, Charge Point Operators (CPOs), and eMobility Service Providers (eMSPs).
Category: standard | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: IEEE 1609.2
chunks.content:
Term: IEEE 1609.2
Definition: The security standard for Wireless Access in Vehicular Environments (WAVE), defining V2X message signing, certificate formats, and the Security Credential Management System (SCMS) for pseudonym certificate issuance.
Technical Note: IEEE 1609.2 currently mandates ECDSA P-256 for V2X message signing and ECIES for encryption. A PQC amendment (expected 2025-2026) will add ML-DSA and ML-KEM support. The SCMS uses butterfly key expansion to generate millions of unlinkable pseudonym certificates — this mechanism must be adapted for PQC key sizes.
Category: standard | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: FedRAMP
chunks.content:
Term: FedRAMP (FedRAMP)
Definition: Federal Risk and Authorization Management Program — a U.S. government-wide program that provides a standardized approach to security assessment, authorization, and continuous monitoring for cloud products and services used by federal agencies.
Technical Note: FedRAMP authorization requires FIPS 140-2/140-3 validated cryptographic modules. As NIST finalizes PQC standards, FedRAMP-authorized cloud service providers will need to migrate to quantum-resistant algorithms to maintain their Authority to Operate (ATO). Timeline aligns with CNSA 2.0 milestones.
Category: standard | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: EAL
chunks.content:
Term: EAL (Evaluation Assurance Level)
Definition: Common Criteria scoring scale from EAL1 (lowest) to EAL7 (highest) that grades the depth and rigor of a product's security evaluation. Higher EAL means more design analysis, more testing, and stronger evidence requirements — not necessarily a more secure product.
Category: standard | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: CSWP 39
chunks.content:
Term: CSWP 39 (NIST Cybersecurity White Paper 39)
Definition: NIST CSWP 39 — Considerations for Achieving Crypto Agility — Strategies and Practices (final, December 2025). Defines a 5-pillar crypto-agility model (inventory, governance, lifecycle, observability, assurance) across a 4-tier maturity ladder (Partial → Risk-Informed → Repeatable → Adaptive).
Category: standard | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: NIS2
chunks.content:
Term: NIS2 (Network and Information Security Directive 2)
Definition: EU directive (2022/2555) requiring enhanced cybersecurity controls across critical-infrastructure sectors. Transposition deadline October 2024; enforcement ongoing across member states. Mandates appropriate cryptographic measures without naming PQC explicitly.
Category: standard | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: eIDAS
chunks.content:
Term: eIDAS (electronic IDentification, Authentication and trust Services)
Definition: EU regulation governing electronic identity and trust services across member states. eIDAS 2.0 introduces the EU Digital Identity Wallet with phased PQC-relevant milestones for high-risk and full PQC adoption.
Category: standard | Complexity: intermediate

metadata.acronym: electronic IDentification, Authentication and trust Services

chunks.title: CRA
chunks.content:
Term: CRA (Cyber Resilience Act)
Definition: EU regulation (2024/2847) imposing cybersecurity requirements on products with digital elements. Entered force December 2024; full obligations apply 11 December 2027 (reporting obligations from September 2026).
Category: standard | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: SOC 2
chunks.content:
Term: SOC 2 (Service Organization Control 2)
Definition: AICPA audit framework evaluating a service provider's controls against the Trust Services Criteria (security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality, privacy). Cryptographic-control adequacy is evaluated within the security criterion.
Category: standard | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: ISO/IEC 27001
chunks.content:
Term: ISO/IEC 27001 (Information Security Management Systems)
Definition: International standard specifying requirements for an Information Security Management System (ISMS). Annex A.10 covers cryptography. Does not mandate PQC directly but the control framework drives PQC adoption.
Category: standard | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: STIG
chunks.content:
Term: STIG (Security Technical Implementation Guide)
Definition: DISA-maintained configuration standards that lock down DoD information systems and components. STIGs prescribe specific cryptographic-suite choices, with ongoing updates to reflect CNSA 2.0 / FIPS 140-3 alignment.
Category: standard | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: CSPN
chunks.content:
Term: CSPN (Certification de Sécurité de Premier Niveau)
Definition: ANSSI's first-level security certification scheme for IT products. Faster and lighter than full Common Criteria; PQC products began entering CSPN catalogue in 2025.
Category: standard | Complexity: intermediate

metadata.acronym: Certification de Sécurité de Premier Niveau

chunks.title: NIST IR 8528
chunks.content:
Term: NIST IR 8528
Definition: NIST Internal Report (October 2024) that down-selected the PQC signature on-ramp to 14 second-round candidates across four mathematical families: MPC-in-the-Head, multivariate, isogeny, and lattice. Superseded by NIST IR 8610 (May 2026), which closed the second round and advanced nine candidates to the third round.
Category: standard | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: CA/B Forum SC-081v3
chunks.content:
Term: CA/B Forum SC-081v3
Definition: CA/Browser Forum ballot (April 2025) that phases TLS certificate maximum validity from 398 days down to 200d (2026), 100d (2027), and 47d by March 2029. Forces every public-trust TLS deployment onto automated CLM.
Category: standard | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: OMB M-23-02
chunks.content:
Term: OMB M-23-02
Definition: US Office of Management and Budget memorandum (November 2022) requiring federal agencies to maintain an annual cryptographic inventory and a prioritised PQC migration plan through 2035.
Technical Note: OMB M-23-02 is the policy backstop behind much of the federal PQC inventory cadence; it sits alongside CNSA 2.0 (NSS deadlines 2030/2033) as the recurring forcing function for cryptographic posture programs in federal scope.
Category: standard | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: NSM-10
chunks.content:
Term: NSM-10
Definition: National Security Memorandum on Promoting United States Leadership in Quantum Computing While Mitigating Risks to Vulnerable Cryptographic Systems, signed May 4, 2022. Directs NSA, CISA, and NIST to inventory cryptographic systems and sets migration timelines for National Security Systems.
Technical Note: Implemented via OMB Memorandum M-23-02, which required agencies to submit cryptographic inventories.
Category: standard | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: FIPS 140-2
chunks.content:
Term: FIPS 140-2
Definition: The predecessor to FIPS 140-3 for validating cryptographic modules. NIST's CMVP stopped accepting new FIPS 140-2 submissions in 2021; many previously validated modules remain listed during a multi-year transition to FIPS 140-3.
Category: standard | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: CNSA 1.0
chunks.content:
Term: CNSA 1.0
Definition: NSA's original Commercial National Security Algorithm Suite (2015), specifying classical algorithms — RSA-3072, ECDH/ECDSA P-384, SHA-384, AES-256 — for protecting National Security Systems.
Technical Note: Superseded by CNSA 2.0 (2022, already in this glossary), which adds PQC algorithms and sets adoption timelines.
Category: standard | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: NIST SP 800-56A
chunks.content:
Term: NIST SP 800-56A
Definition: Recommendation for Pair-Wise Key-Establishment Using Discrete Logarithm Cryptography — the NIST standard specifying Diffie-Hellman and elliptic-curve (ECDH) key-agreement schemes.
Category: standard | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: NIST SP 800-56B
chunks.content:
Term: NIST SP 800-56B
Definition: Recommendation for Pair-Wise Key-Establishment Using Integer Factorization Cryptography — the NIST standard specifying RSA-based key-transport and key-agreement schemes.
Category: standard | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: NIST SP 800-56C
chunks.content:
Term: NIST SP 800-56C
Definition: Recommendation for Key-Derivation Methods in Key-Establishment Schemes — the NIST standard specifying the two-step (extract-then-expand) key-derivation approach used to turn a shared secret from SP 800-56A/B, or a PQC KEM, into usable keying material.
Category: standard | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: NIST SP 800-186
chunks.content:
Term: NIST SP 800-186
Definition: Recommendation for Discrete Logarithm-based Cryptography: Elliptic Curve Domain Parameters — the NIST standard specifying the NIST curves (P-256, P-384, P-521) used throughout TLS, X.509, and other classical or hybrid cryptography.
Category: standard | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: RFC 8391
chunks.content:
Term: RFC 8391
Definition: The IETF specification for XMSS (eXtended Merkle Signature Scheme) and XMSS^MT, the stateful hash-based signature schemes also standardized by NIST SP 800-208.
Category: standard | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: RFC 8554
chunks.content:
Term: RFC 8554
Definition: The IETF specification for LMS (Leighton-Micali Signatures) and its multi-tree variant HSS, the stateful hash-based signature schemes also standardized by NIST SP 800-208.
Category: standard | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: NIST IR 8105
chunks.content:
Term: NIST IR 8105
Definition: Report on Post-Quantum Cryptography (April 2016) — NIST's original report announcing the PQC standardization project and surveying the state of quantum-resistant cryptography at the time.
Category: standard | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: NIST IR 8309
chunks.content:
Term: NIST IR 8309
Definition: Status Report on the Second Round of the NIST PQC Standardization Process (July 2020), narrowing the KEM and signature candidates to the finalists and alternates that became ML-KEM, ML-DSA, FN-DSA, and SLH-DSA.
Category: standard | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: NIST IR 8413
chunks.content:
Term: NIST IR 8413
Definition: Status Report on the Third Round of the NIST PQC Standardization Process (July 2022), announcing the selection of ML-KEM, ML-DSA, and FN-DSA for standardization and continued fourth-round evaluation of alternate KEMs (BIKE, Classic McEliece, HQC, SIKE).
Technical Note: SIKE was withdrawn after a 2022 cryptanalytic break; HQC was later selected via NIST IR 8545, already in this glossary.
Category: standard | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: PKCS#1
chunks.content:
Term: PKCS#1
Definition: The RSA Cryptography Standard, specifying RSA encryption and signature padding schemes (PKCS#1 v1.5, OAEP, PSS) used across TLS, S/MIME, and code signing.
Category: standard | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: PKCS#7
chunks.content:
Term: PKCS#7
Definition: The Cryptographic Message Syntax standard for signing and encrypting arbitrary data, superseded by and largely synonymous with IETF CMS — the basis for S/MIME and code-signing signature formats.
Category: standard | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: PKCS#8
chunks.content:
Term: PKCS#8
Definition: The standard syntax for encoding a private key, optionally password-encrypted, independent of its algorithm — the format OpenSSL's genpkey produces for RSA, ECDSA, and PQC key types alike.
Category: standard | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: Post-Quantum Cryptography
chunks.content:
Term: Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC)
Definition: Cryptographic algorithms designed to be secure against attacks by both classical and quantum computers.
Technical Note: PQC algorithms are based on mathematical problems believed to be hard for quantum computers, such as lattice problems, hash functions, and error-correcting codes.
Category: concept | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: Quantum Computing
chunks.content:
Term: Quantum Computing
Definition: A type of computing that uses quantum-mechanical phenomena like superposition and entanglement to perform calculations exponentially faster than classical computers for certain problems.
Category: concept | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: Q-Day
chunks.content:
Term: Q-Day
Definition: The hypothetical future date when a quantum computer becomes powerful enough to break current public-key cryptography (RSA, ECC).
Category: concept | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: Harvest Now, Decrypt Later
chunks.content:
Term: Harvest Now, Decrypt Later (HNDL)
Definition: An attack strategy where adversaries collect encrypted data today with the intention of decrypting it once quantum computers become available.
Category: concept | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: Encryption
chunks.content:
Term: Encryption
Definition: The process of converting readable data (plaintext) into an unreadable format (ciphertext) using an algorithm and a key, so only authorized parties can read it.
Category: concept | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: Digital Signature
chunks.content:
Term: Digital Signature
Definition: A mathematical scheme that proves the authenticity and integrity of a digital message or document, analogous to a handwritten signature.
Category: concept | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: Public Key
chunks.content:
Term: Public Key
Definition: A cryptographic key that can be shared openly. Used to encrypt data or verify digital signatures.
Category: concept | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: Private Key
chunks.content:
Term: Private Key
Definition: A cryptographic key kept secret by its owner. Used to decrypt data or create digital signatures.
Category: concept | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: Key Pair
chunks.content:
Term: Key Pair
Definition: A mathematically linked public key and private key used together for encryption/decryption or signing/verification.
Category: concept | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: Hybrid Cryptography
chunks.content:
Term: Hybrid Cryptography
Definition: Using both classical and post-quantum algorithms together during the transition period, providing security even if one algorithm is broken.
Category: concept | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: Crypto Agility
chunks.content:
Term: Crypto Agility
Definition: The ability of a system to quickly switch between cryptographic algorithms without major redesign, critical for adapting to PQC.
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: Qubit
chunks.content:
Term: Qubit
Definition: The basic unit of quantum information, analogous to a classical bit but capable of existing in superposition of 0 and 1 simultaneously.
Category: concept | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: Superposition
chunks.content:
Term: Superposition
Definition: A quantum property where a qubit can represent both 0 and 1 at the same time, enabling quantum computers to explore many solutions simultaneously.
Category: concept | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: Lattice-Based Cryptography
chunks.content:
Term: Lattice-Based Cryptography
Definition: A family of PQC algorithms based on the hardness of problems involving mathematical lattices. The basis for ML-KEM and ML-DSA.
Technical Note: Key problems: Learning With Errors (LWE), Module-LWE, Ring-LWE. Offer good performance and key sizes.
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: Hash-Based Signatures
chunks.content:
Term: Hash-Based Signatures
Definition: Digital signature schemes whose security relies only on the properties of hash functions. Very conservative security but can be stateful.
Technical Note: Stateful: LMS/XMSS (must track which keys are used). Stateless: SLH-DSA/SPHINCS+ (larger signatures).
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: Code-Based Cryptography
chunks.content:
Term: Code-Based Cryptography
Definition: PQC algorithms based on the hardness of decoding random linear error-correcting codes. Used by Classic McEliece and HQC.
Category: concept | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: Security Level
chunks.content:
Term: Security Level
Definition: NIST defines 5 security levels for PQC algorithms. Level 1 ≈ AES-128, Level 3 ≈ AES-192, Level 5 ≈ AES-256.
Technical Note: Level 1: comparable to breaking AES-128. Level 5: comparable to breaking AES-256. Most deployments use Level 3.
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: Key Exchange
chunks.content:
Term: Key Exchange
Definition: The process by which two parties establish a shared secret key over an insecure channel. In PQC, replaced by Key Encapsulation Mechanisms.
Category: concept | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: Quantum Advantage
chunks.content:
Term: Quantum Advantage
Definition: The point at which a quantum computer can solve a specific problem faster than any classical computer. Also called "quantum supremacy."
Category: concept | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: WebAssembly
chunks.content:
Term: WebAssembly (WASM)
Definition: A binary instruction format that enables near-native performance in web browsers. Used by PQC Today to run OpenSSL and liboqs in-browser.
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: HSM
chunks.content:
Term: HSM (HSM)
Definition: Hardware Security Module, a dedicated physical device for managing and protecting cryptographic keys. Must be updated for PQC support.
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: Entanglement
chunks.content:
Term: Entanglement
Definition: A quantum phenomenon where two qubits become correlated so measuring one instantly determines the state of the other, regardless of distance.
Category: concept | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: HD Wallet
chunks.content:
Term: HD Wallet (HD)
Definition: Hierarchical Deterministic Wallet, a cryptocurrency wallet that generates all key pairs from a single seed phrase using BIP32/39/44 standards.
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: BIP39
chunks.content:
Term: BIP39
Definition: Bitcoin Improvement Proposal 39 defines mnemonic seed phrases (12 or 24 words) used to back up and restore cryptocurrency wallets.
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: EUDI Wallet
chunks.content:
Term: EUDI Wallet
Definition: European Union Digital Identity Wallet, a mobile wallet for storing and presenting digital credentials under the eIDAS 2.0 framework.
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: Qualified Electronic Signature
chunks.content:
Term: Qualified Electronic Signature (QES)
Definition: A digital signature with the legal equivalence of a handwritten signature under EU law, requiring a qualified certificate and a secure creation device.
Category: concept | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: MILENAGE
chunks.content:
Term: MILENAGE
Definition: The set of cryptographic functions (f1–f5) used in 5G authentication. Based on AES and generates authentication vectors.
Category: concept | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: Encapsulation / Decapsulation
chunks.content:
Term: Encapsulation / Decapsulation
Definition: The two operations of a Key Encapsulation Mechanism. Encapsulation creates a shared secret using a public key; decapsulation recovers it using the private key.
Technical Note: Unlike Diffie-Hellman key exchange, KEMs are asymmetric: the sender encapsulates, the receiver decapsulates. This is the core operation of ML-KEM.
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: Learning With Errors
chunks.content:
Term: Learning With Errors (LWE)
Definition: A mathematical problem believed to be hard for quantum computers, forming the security foundation of ML-KEM, ML-DSA, and FrodoKEM.
Technical Note: Variants include Ring-LWE (structured, faster) and Module-LWE (used in ML-KEM/ML-DSA, balancing security and performance).
Category: concept | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: NTRU Lattice
chunks.content:
Term: NTRU Lattice (NTRU)
Definition: A lattice-based cryptographic family using polynomial rings, providing the mathematical basis for FN-DSA (Falcon). One of the earliest PQC proposals (1996).
Category: concept | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: Hybrid Key Exchange
chunks.content:
Term: Hybrid Key Exchange
Definition: Combining a classical key exchange (e.g., X25519) with a PQC KEM (e.g., ML-KEM-768) in a single handshake, ensuring security even if one algorithm is broken.
Technical Note: Deployed today as X25519MLKEM768 in Chrome, Firefox, and major cloud providers. IETF draft-ietf-tls-ecdhe-mlkem defines the TLS 1.3 integration.
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: Composite Certificate
chunks.content:
Term: Composite Certificate
Definition: An X.509 certificate encoding both a classical and a PQC key/signature under a single composite OID. Both signatures must verify. Requires all relying parties to support the composite OID — legacy-incompatible.
Technical Note: Defined in IETF drafts: composite ML-KEM (draft-ietf-lamps-pq-composite-kem) and composite ML-DSA (draft-ietf-lamps-pq-composite-sigs). Both the public key and the signature are RAW CONCATENATIONS with the ML-DSA component FIRST — no ASN.1 wrapper — so a verifier splits at ML-DSA's fixed length. Each profile also fixes a traditional hash that tracks the CURVE (P-256 → SHA-256, P-384 → SHA-384); the SHAxxx in a profile name is the pre-hash applied to the message, not the traditional algorithm's hash. Neither OpenSSL 3.6.3 nor 4.x registers any composite algorithm, so stock OpenSSL cannot parse these certificates at all.
Category: concept | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: Related Certificate
chunks.content:
Term: Related Certificate (RFC 9763)
Definition: A binding mechanism (RFC 9763) that links two independent X.509 certificates — one classical, one PQC — to the same end entity via a SHA-256 hash in a RelatedCertificate extension. Legacy systems only process the classical cert; PQC-aware verifiers check both and verify the binding hash. Distinct from Alt-Sig, which embeds a PQC signature inside a single certificate's extensions.
Technical Note: The RelatedCertificate extension (OID 1.3.6.1.5.5.7.1.36) carries a hash of the related cert and a pointer. Each certificate is individually valid, enabling backward compatibility — unlike composite certificates which require composite OID support.
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: Alt-Sig Certificate
chunks.content:
Term: Alt-Sig Certificate
Definition: A single classical X.509 certificate with PQC key and signature embedded in X.509 extensions: SubjectAltPublicKeyInfo (2.5.29.72), AltSignatureAlgorithm (2.5.29.73), and AltSignatureValue (2.5.29.74). Informally called the "Catalyst" approach (NSA). Legacy validators ignore the unknown extensions; PQC-aware verifiers check both signatures.
Technical Note: Defined by ITU-T X.509 (2019) §9.8 — NOT by an IETF draft. (This entry previously credited draft-ietf-lamps-cert-binding-for-multi-auth, which is a different mechanism and is itself expired.) Distinct from Related Certificates (RFC 9763), which uses two separate certificates bound by a hash; Alt-Sig keeps everything in one certificate. Verified against OpenSSL 3.6.3: it validates the classical signature and ignores the alt-signature extensions entirely, which is what gives backward compatibility — and also means a legacy validator provides NO quantum protection even though it reports success.
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: Chameleon Certificate
chunks.content:
Term: Chameleon Certificate
Definition: A single X.509 certificate that encodes a classical "delta" variant inside a DeltaCertificateDescriptor extension (OID 2.16.840.1.114027.80.6.1). PQC-aware verifiers reconstruct the classical certificate from the delta; legacy systems see a standard classical cert.
Technical Note: Defined in draft-bonnell-lamps-chameleon-certs (DigiCert, Entrust). More bandwidth-efficient than related certs (RFC 9763) because only one certificate is transmitted. STATUS: the draft is an INDIVIDUAL submission that EXPIRED on 2026-04-21 and was never adopted as a LAMPS working-group document — there is no draft-ietf-lamps-chameleon-certs, and the work was not renamed or absorbed elsewhere. Treat it as a dormant design worth understanding, not an active standards track.
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: TBSCertificate
chunks.content:
Term: TBSCertificate
Definition: "To Be Signed" certificate — the core unsigned structure inside an X.509 certificate containing version, serial number, issuer/subject DNs, validity period, SubjectPublicKeyInfo, and extensions. The CA signs this structure to produce the final certificate.
Technical Note: In DER encoding, TBSCertificate is a SEQUENCE. The outer Certificate SEQUENCE wraps TBSCertificate + signatureAlgorithm + signatureValue. PQC algorithms like ML-DSA and SLH-DSA are specified in the outer signatureAlgorithm AlgorithmIdentifier.
Category: concept | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: AlgorithmIdentifier
chunks.content:
Term: AlgorithmIdentifier
Definition: An ASN.1 SEQUENCE containing an OID that identifies a cryptographic algorithm, plus optional parameters. Appears in X.509 certificates to specify signature algorithms (signatureAlgorithm field) and public key algorithms (SubjectPublicKeyInfo.algorithm).
Technical Note: PQC algorithms defined in FIPS 203/204/205 use absent parameters (no NULL) per their respective X.509 profile RFCs (RFC 9881, RFC 9909). The OID for ML-DSA-65 is 2.16.840.1.101.3.4.3.18; SLH-DSA-SHA2-128s is 2.16.840.1.101.3.4.3.20.
Category: concept | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: Hybrid Certificate
chunks.content:
Term: Hybrid Certificate
Definition: An X.509 certificate using both classical and PQC algorithms during the transition period, maintaining interoperability with legacy systems.
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: SCADA
chunks.content:
Term: SCADA (SCADA)
Definition: Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition, industrial control systems used in power grids, water treatment, and manufacturing. Quantum-vulnerable via legacy crypto.
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: V2X Communication
chunks.content:
Term: V2X Communication (V2X)
Definition: Vehicle-to-Everything communication, enabling cars to exchange safety data with infrastructure and other vehicles. Uses ECDSA P-256 certificates that are quantum-vulnerable.
Category: concept | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: CBDC
chunks.content:
Term: CBDC (CBDC)
Definition: Central Bank Digital Currency, a digital form of fiat money issued by central banks. Requires quantum-safe cryptography for long-term trust.
Category: concept | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: DRM
chunks.content:
Term: DRM (DRM)
Definition: Digital Rights Management, technology protecting copyrighted content through encryption. Systems like Widevine, PlayReady, and FairPlay face quantum threats to their key hierarchies.
Category: concept | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: KMS
chunks.content:
Term: KMS (KMS)
Definition: Key Management System, software for generating, storing, rotating, and auditing cryptographic keys. Must be upgraded to support PQC key sizes and algorithms.
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: TPM
chunks.content:
Term: TPM (TPM)
Definition: Trusted Platform Module, a hardware chip providing secure key storage, platform integrity measurement, and cryptographic operations. PQC support being added via TCG specifications.
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: Endorsement Key
chunks.content:
Term: Endorsement Key (EK)
Definition: A TPM 2.0 primary key in the Endorsement Hierarchy (TPM_RH_ENDORSEMENT = 0x4000000B), provisioned by the manufacturer and used to establish trust in the TPM. Per TCG V1.85, EK migrates from RSA-2048/ECC-P256 to ML-KEM-768 (TPM_ALG_MLKEM = 0x00A0) and is used for KEM-based Credential Activation.
Technical Note: Non-migratable, non-duplicable, factory-provisioned. ML-KEM-768 public key = 1184 B; ciphertext = 1088 B (FIPS 203).
Category: concept | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: Attestation Identity Key
chunks.content:
Term: Attestation Identity Key (AIK)
Definition: A restricted TPM 2.0 signing key used for TPM2_Quote — signing PCR values to prove system state to a remote verifier. Per TCG V1.85, AIK migrates from RSA-2048/ECC-P256 to ML-DSA-65 (TPM_ALG_MLDSA = 0x00A1, FIPS 204 Cat III).
Technical Note: ML-DSA-65 public key = 1952 B; signature = 3309 B. AIK certificates are issued by a Privacy CA or by TPM vendor direct attestation.
Category: concept | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: Storage Root Key
chunks.content:
Term: Storage Root Key (SRK)
Definition: The primary key of the TPM 2.0 Storage Hierarchy (TPM_RH_OWNER = 0x40000001). All user-created keys are wrapped under the SRK. Per TCG V1.85, the SRK migrates to ML-KEM-768 for child-key wrapping, which drove the TPM_BUFFER_MAX increase from 4096 B to 8192 B.
Technical Note: Not exportable. ML-KEM wraps child TPM2B_PRIVATE blobs via KEM-derive.
Category: concept | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: Device Identity Key
chunks.content:
Term: Device Identity Key (IDevID)
Definition: IEEE 802.1AR Initial Device Identity — a long-lived, factory-provisioned key used to prove device identity in network onboarding. PQC migration is tracked in an IEEE 802.1AR PQC amendment and requires hardware refresh (ML-DSA-65 per TCG V1.85 Part 2 Table 206).
Technical Note: Used in 802.1X network access, FIDO Device Onboard, and supply-chain provenance attestation.
Category: concept | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: Platform Configuration Register
chunks.content:
Term: Platform Configuration Register (PCR)
Definition: A TPM register that accumulates integrity measurements (hash chains) of platform state: firmware, boot loader, kernel, and optionally application code. TPM2_Quote signs PCR values with the AIK to produce a verifiable attestation report.
Technical Note: Extend-only: PCR_new = hash(PCR_old || measurement). 24 PCRs on TPM 2.0; SHA-256 is the standard bank.
Category: concept | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: Code Signing
chunks.content:
Term: Code Signing
Definition: Digitally signing software executables and scripts to verify their authenticity and integrity. PQC migration replaces RSA/ECDSA signatures with ML-DSA or SLH-DSA.
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: Secure Boot
chunks.content:
Term: Secure Boot
Definition: A hardware-enforced chain of trust that verifies each component in the boot process is signed by a trusted authority. Requires PQC-capable signature verification.
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: QKD
chunks.content:
Term: QKD (QKD)
Definition: Quantum Key Distribution, a method of distributing encryption keys using quantum physics rather than mathematical hardness. Distinct from PQC and requires specialized hardware.
Technical Note: QKD (e.g., BB84 protocol) uses photons to detect eavesdropping. Unlike PQC, it requires dedicated fiber or satellite links and cannot run on standard networks.
Category: concept | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: QBER
chunks.content:
Term: QBER (QBER)
Definition: Quantum Bit Error Rate, the fraction of sifted key bits where Alice and Bob disagree despite using the same measurement basis. A QBER above ~11% indicates eavesdropping.
Technical Note: In BB84, an eavesdropper measuring in the wrong basis introduces a 25% error rate on intercepted qubits. The theoretical QBER threshold for secure key generation is approximately 11%.
Category: concept | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: Sifted Key
chunks.content:
Term: Sifted Key
Definition: The subset of raw key bits where both parties used the same measurement basis during QKD. Typically about half the transmitted bits survive sifting.
Category: concept | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: Privacy Amplification
chunks.content:
Term: Privacy Amplification
Definition: A post-processing step in QKD that uses universal hash functions to distill a shorter, provably secret key from a partially compromised key by removing any information an eavesdropper may have obtained.
Technical Note: The output key length depends on the estimated information leakage. Uses hash functions (e.g., SHA-256) to compress the corrected key, reducing Eve's knowledge to negligible levels.
Category: concept | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: No-Cloning Theorem
chunks.content:
Term: No-Cloning Theorem
Definition: A fundamental quantum mechanics result proving it is impossible to create an identical copy of an unknown quantum state, providing the theoretical basis for QKD security.
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: Trusted Node
chunks.content:
Term: Trusted Node
Definition: A physically secured relay point in a QKD network where keys are decrypted and re-encrypted to extend range beyond single-link limits (typically ~100 km for fiber).
Technical Note: Trusted nodes are a practical necessity but a security concern: compromising any node reveals all keys routed through it. This is a major architectural limitation of current QKD networks.
Category: concept | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: Cryptographic Inventory
chunks.content:
Term: Cryptographic Inventory
Definition: A comprehensive catalog of all cryptographic algorithms, protocols, keys, and certificates in an organization, essential for planning PQC migration.
Category: concept | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: OTA Updates
chunks.content:
Term: OTA Updates (OTA)
Definition: Over-the-Air updates, the process of remotely delivering firmware or software to devices. Signature verification must be quantum-safe to prevent forgery.
Category: concept | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: EHR
chunks.content:
Term: EHR (EHR)
Definition: Electronic Health Records, digital patient medical records that require long-term confidentiality. Prime targets for Harvest Now, Decrypt Later attacks.
Category: concept | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: SBOM
chunks.content:
Term: SBOM (SBOM)
Definition: Software Bill of Materials, a formal record of the components in a software product and their supply-chain relationships. Increasingly required alongside CBOM for security compliance.
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: TEE
chunks.content:
Term: TEE (TEE)
Definition: Trusted Execution Environment, an isolated processing environment on a processor that protects code and data. Must be updated for PQC algorithm support.
Category: concept | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: DUKPT
chunks.content:
Term: DUKPT (DUKPT)
Definition: Derived Unique Key Per Transaction, a key management scheme for payment terminals that derives a unique symmetric encryption key for each transaction from a Base Derivation Key.
Technical Note: The symmetric DUKPT derivation chain is quantum-safe. The quantum vulnerability is at the Key Injection Facility where RSA-2048 key transport wraps the BDK. Compromising the BDK exposes all past and future transaction keys.
Category: concept | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: Root CA
chunks.content:
Term: Root CA
Definition: The top-level Certificate Authority in a PKI trust hierarchy. A Root CA issues a self-signed certificate that serves as the trust anchor — all certificates in the chain ultimately derive their trust from it.
Technical Note: Root CAs are installed in OS and browser trust stores. PQC migration for Root CAs is highest priority since a compromised root breaks the entire chain. CNSA 2.0 requires Root CAs to use ML-DSA-87 by 2030.
Category: concept | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: Fulcio
chunks.content:
Term: Fulcio
Definition: The Certificate Authority component of Sigstore. Fulcio issues short-lived (~20 minute) X.509 certificates that bind an OIDC identity to an ephemeral signing key.
Technical Note: Fulcio is the primary PQC upgrade point in the Sigstore ecosystem. Migrating Fulcio to ML-DSA certificates automatically protects all downstream consumers without developer intervention.
Category: concept | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: Rekor
chunks.content:
Term: Rekor
Definition: The transparency log component of Sigstore. Rekor is an immutable, append-only log that records every signing event — signature, certificate, and artifact hash — for public auditability.
Technical Note: PQC migration increases Rekor entry sizes significantly (~200 bytes for ECDSA vs ~3,600 bytes for ML-DSA-65). Storage overhead is the primary cost of PQC migration in Sigstore.
Category: concept | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: Keyless Signing
chunks.content:
Term: Keyless Signing
Definition: A code signing approach where no long-term private keys are managed by the developer. Identity-based trust (via OIDC) replaces key-based trust, with ephemeral keys generated per-signing event.
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: Time Stamping Authority
chunks.content:
Term: Time Stamping Authority (TSA)
Definition: A trusted service (RFC 3161) that proves a digital signature was created at a specific time. Essential for code signing, where signatures must remain valid after certificate expiration.
Technical Note: PQC migration requires TSAs to issue timestamps signed with quantum-safe algorithms. A quantum-vulnerable timestamp means an attacker could backdate forged signatures.
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: Extended Key Usage
chunks.content:
Term: Extended Key Usage (EKU)
Definition: An X.509 certificate extension that restricts the purposes for which a certificate can be used — for example, Code Signing (OID 1.3.6.1.5.5.7.3.3), Server Authentication, or Client Authentication.
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: Software Supply Chain
chunks.content:
Term: Software Supply Chain
Definition: The entire pipeline from source code to deployed software, including dependencies, build systems, artifact registries, signing infrastructure, and distribution channels. Every link in this chain is a potential attack surface.
Category: concept | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: Build Provenance
chunks.content:
Term: Build Provenance
Definition: A cryptographically signed attestation documenting how a software artifact was built — including the source repository, build system, entry point, and build parameters. Answers the question "who built this and how?"
Technical Note: Build provenance is a core requirement of SLSA Level 1+. Without quantum-safe signatures on provenance attestations, an adversary with a quantum computer could forge provenance for malicious artifacts.
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: CRQC
chunks.content:
Term: CRQC (CRQC)
Definition: Cryptographically Relevant Quantum Computer, a hypothetical future quantum computer powerful enough to break RSA, ECC, and other classical public-key cryptography.
Technical Note: Estimates vary, but a CRQC would need thousands of stable logical qubits. Most timelines estimate 2030-2040 for CRQC capability.
Category: concept | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: Forward Secrecy
chunks.content:
Term: Forward Secrecy
Definition: A property of key exchange protocols where compromise of long-term keys does not compromise past session keys. Each session uses ephemeral keys that are discarded.
Technical Note: Also called Perfect Forward Secrecy (PFS). Critical for TLS 1.3 and a reason hybrid PQC key exchange is preferred over static key transport.
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: Side-Channel Attack
chunks.content:
Term: Side-Channel Attack
Definition: An attack that exploits physical characteristics of a cryptographic implementation (timing, power consumption, electromagnetic emissions) rather than mathematical weaknesses.
Technical Note: PQC algorithms like FN-DSA require careful floating-point implementation to resist side-channel attacks. Constant-time implementations are essential.
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: Certificate Chain
chunks.content:
Term: Certificate Chain
Definition: A linked sequence of X.509 certificates from a leaf (end-entity) certificate up through intermediates to a trusted root CA, establishing a chain of trust.
Category: concept | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: Root of Trust
chunks.content:
Term: Root of Trust
Definition: A foundational component (hardware or software) that is inherently trusted and used as the starting point for a chain of trust in a system.
Technical Note: PQC migration requires updating roots of trust (TPM, secure boot firmware, root CA certificates) to quantum-safe algorithms.
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: Key Rotation
chunks.content:
Term: Key Rotation
Definition: The practice of periodically replacing cryptographic keys with new ones, limiting the exposure window if a key is compromised.
Technical Note: PQC migration involves key rotation from classical to hybrid or pure PQC keys across all cryptographic infrastructure.
Category: concept | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: Non-Repudiation
chunks.content:
Term: Non-Repudiation
Definition: A property of digital signatures that prevents a signer from denying they signed a message. Essential for legal documents, contracts, and financial transactions.
Category: concept | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: SD-JWT
chunks.content:
Term: SD-JWT (SD-JWT)
Definition: Selective Disclosure JSON Web Token, a credential format that allows holders to reveal only specific claims from a signed token without exposing all data.
Technical Note: Used in the EUDI Wallet ecosystem alongside mdoc format. Each claim is individually salted and hashed for privacy.
Category: concept | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: mDL
chunks.content:
Term: mDL (mDL)
Definition: Mobile Driver's License, a digital credential stored on a smartphone conforming to ISO/IEC 18013-5. Uses mdoc format with cryptographic device binding.
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: mdoc
chunks.content:
Term: mdoc
Definition: Mobile Document, a CBOR-based verifiable credential format defined in ISO/IEC 18013-5. Uses Mobile Security Objects (MSO) for issuer-signed data integrity.
Category: concept | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: CBOR
chunks.content:
Term: CBOR (CBOR)
Definition: Concise Binary Object Representation, a compact binary data serialization format (RFC 8949). Used in mdoc credentials, IoT protocols, and WebAuthn attestations.
Category: concept | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: Verifiable Credential
chunks.content:
Term: Verifiable Credential (VC)
Definition: A tamper-proof digital credential that can be cryptographically verified. Issued by a trusted authority and held in a digital wallet for presentation to verifiers.
Technical Note: W3C Verifiable Credentials and ISO mdoc are the two major formats. PQC migration requires updating the signature algorithms used by issuers.
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: Selective Disclosure
chunks.content:
Term: Selective Disclosure
Definition: The ability to reveal only specific attributes from a digital credential without exposing all contained data. A key privacy feature of SD-JWT and mdoc formats.
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: BIP32
chunks.content:
Term: BIP32
Definition: Bitcoin Improvement Proposal 32, defining Hierarchical Deterministic (HD) wallets. Enables deriving an entire tree of key pairs from a single master seed.
Technical Note: Uses HMAC-SHA512 for key derivation. Supports hardened and normal derivation paths (e.g., m/44'/0'/0'/0/0).
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: UTXO
chunks.content:
Term: UTXO (UTXO)
Definition: Unspent Transaction Output, Bitcoin's model for tracking coin ownership. Each transaction consumes existing UTXOs and creates new ones.
Technical Note: PQC migration for Bitcoin must handle UTXOs locked by quantum-vulnerable ECDSA scripts, potentially requiring a network-wide migration.
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: SUPI
chunks.content:
Term: SUPI (SUPI)
Definition: Subscription Permanent Identifier, a 5G subscriber's permanent identity (usually based on IMSI). Protected by encrypting it as SUCI before transmission.
Technical Note: SUCI conceals the SUPI using ECIES (Profile A/B) or ML-KEM (Profile C) to prevent IMSI-catching attacks.
Category: concept | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: Fully Homomorphic Encryption
chunks.content:
Term: Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE)
Definition: An encryption scheme that allows computations to be performed on ciphertext, producing encrypted results that match operations on the plaintext.
Technical Note: FHE is lattice-based and believed to be quantum-safe. Used for privacy-preserving cloud computing, but remains computationally expensive.
Category: concept | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: Zero-Knowledge Proof
chunks.content:
Term: Zero-Knowledge Proof (ZKP)
Definition: A cryptographic method where one party proves knowledge of a value without revealing the value itself. Used in privacy-preserving authentication and blockchain.
Technical Note: PQC-compatible ZKP constructions (e.g., lattice-based, hash-based) are active areas of research for quantum-safe privacy systems.
Category: concept | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: DER
chunks.content:
Term: DER (DER)
Definition: Distinguished Encoding Rules, a binary encoding format for ASN.1 data structures. The standard encoding for X.509 certificates, keys, and ECDSA signatures.
Category: concept | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: DER (Distributed Energy Resource)
chunks.content:
Term: DER (Distributed Energy Resource) (DER)
Definition: Distributed Energy Resource. Solar inverters, battery storage systems, and EV chargers connected to the distribution grid. Not to be confused with DER the ASN.1 encoding (Distinguished Encoding Rules).
Technical Note: DERs authenticate via IEEE 2030.5 certificates (ECDSA P-256). PQC migration requires fleet-wide certificate reissuance to ML-DSA-65.
Category: concept | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: PEM
chunks.content:
Term: PEM (PEM)
Definition: Privacy Enhanced Mail, a Base64-encoded format for storing cryptographic objects (certificates, keys, CSRs). Recognized by "-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----" headers.
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: Derivation Path
chunks.content:
Term: Derivation Path
Definition: A hierarchical path notation (e.g., m/44'/0'/0'/0/0) used in HD wallets to deterministically derive child keys from a master key following BIP32/BIP44 standards.
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: Quantum Error Correction
chunks.content:
Term: Quantum Error Correction
Definition: Techniques to protect quantum information from decoherence and errors during computation. Essential for building practical, large-scale quantum computers.
Technical Note: Current quantum computers lack sufficient error correction for cryptanalysis. Advances in error correction directly affect CRQC timelines.
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: Interoperability
chunks.content:
Term: Interoperability
Definition: The ability of different cryptographic implementations, libraries, and systems to work together correctly. Critical during PQC migration when classical and quantum-safe systems must coexist.
Category: concept | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: Hybrid Mode
chunks.content:
Term: Hybrid Mode
Definition: An operational mode where both classical and post-quantum cryptographic algorithms run in parallel, ensuring security even if one algorithm is broken.
Technical Note: Recommended by NIST, BSI, and ANSSI as the preferred transition strategy. Applied to key exchange, signatures, and certificates.
Category: concept | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: QTSP
chunks.content:
Term: QTSP (QTSP)
Definition: Qualified Trust Service Provider, an organization authorized under eIDAS 2.0 to issue qualified electronic signatures, seals, timestamps, and certificates.
Category: concept | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: Attestation
chunks.content:
Term: Attestation
Definition: A cryptographically signed statement vouching for the authenticity or properties of a device, key, or credential. Used in FIDO2, TPM, and digital identity systems.
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: Key Binding
chunks.content:
Term: Key Binding
Definition: Cryptographic proof that a credential is bound to a specific holder's key, preventing unauthorized transfer or replay of digital credentials.
Category: concept | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: Crypto Discovery
chunks.content:
Term: Crypto Discovery
Definition: The automated process of scanning an organization's systems to identify all cryptographic algorithms, keys, certificates, and protocols in use. The first step in PQC migration.
Technical Note: Tools like SandboxAQ AQtive Guard and IBM Guardium automate crypto discovery to build a Cryptographic Bill of Materials (CBOM).
Category: concept | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: RLP
chunks.content:
Term: RLP (RLP)
Definition: Recursive Length Prefix, Ethereum's serialization encoding for transactions, blocks, and account state. Used to encode transaction data before signing with ECDSA.
Category: concept | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: Base58Check
chunks.content:
Term: Base58Check
Definition: A Bitcoin-specific encoding format that converts binary data to a human-readable alphanumeric string with a built-in checksum for error detection.
Technical Note: Omits confusable characters (0, O, I, l). Used for Bitcoin addresses, WIF private keys, and extended public/private keys.
Category: concept | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: Harvest Now, Forge Later
chunks.content:
Term: Harvest Now, Forge Later (HNFL)
Definition: An attack strategy where adversaries record digitally signed data today, planning to forge signatures once quantum computers can break the signing algorithm. Also called Trust Now, Forge Later (TNFL); the two terms are interchangeable and used equally across the platform.
Technical Note: While HNDL targets confidentiality (encrypted data), HNFL / TNFL targets authenticity and integrity — firmware updates, certificates, and legal documents signed with RSA/ECDSA become forgeable. HNFL (Harvest Now, Forge Later) and TNFL (Trust Now, Forge Later) name the same risk: the Applied Quantum framework and the simulation use TNFL; the learning content uses HNFL.
Category: concept | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: Trust Now, Forge Later
chunks.content:
Term: Trust Now, Forge Later (TNFL)
Definition: The same risk as Harvest Now, Forge Later (HNFL): data signed and trusted today can be forged once a quantum computer can break the signing algorithm. TNFL and HNFL are interchangeable — the Applied Quantum framework and the simulation use TNFL; the learning content uses HNFL.
Technical Note: Targets authenticity and integrity (signatures, certificates, firmware, legal documents) rather than confidentiality. See also Harvest Now, Forge Later (HNFL).
Category: concept | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: Cipher Suite
chunks.content:
Term: Cipher Suite
Definition: A named combination of cryptographic algorithms used together in a TLS connection — specifying the key exchange, authentication, bulk encryption, and hash algorithms.
Technical Note: TLS 1.3 cipher suites (e.g., TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384) are simpler than TLS 1.2, separating key exchange from the cipher suite. PQC adds new key exchange groups like X25519MLKEM768.
Category: concept | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: TLS Handshake
chunks.content:
Term: TLS Handshake
Definition: The initial negotiation between client and server that establishes a secure TLS connection — agreeing on cipher suites, exchanging keys, and authenticating the server.
Technical Note: TLS 1.3 completes in 1 round-trip (1-RTT). PQC key exchange increases ClientHello size significantly (ML-KEM public keys are ~1,184 bytes vs 32 bytes for X25519).
Category: concept | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: Key Lifecycle
chunks.content:
Term: Key Lifecycle
Definition: The complete management process for cryptographic keys from creation to destruction, typically comprising 7 stages: generation, storage, activation, rotation, deactivation, compromise response, and destruction.
Technical Note: Defined by NIST SP 800-57. PQC migration adds complexity — organizations must plan parallel classical and PQC key lifecycles during the transition period.
Category: concept | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: Merkle Tree
chunks.content:
Term: Merkle Tree
Definition: A binary tree of hash values where each leaf contains a hash of a data block and each internal node contains a hash of its children. The foundation of stateful hash-based signature schemes.
Technical Note: In LMS/XMSS, each leaf holds a one-time signature key pair. The tree height determines the maximum number of signatures (2^h). The root hash serves as the public key.
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: One-Time Signature
chunks.content:
Term: One-Time Signature (OTS)
Definition: A signature scheme where each private key must be used to sign exactly one message. Reusing a key leaks information that allows signature forgery.
Technical Note: LMS and XMSS use Merkle trees of OTS keys to enable multiple signatures from a single public key. Strict state management is required to prevent key reuse.
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: P2PKH
chunks.content:
Term: P2PKH
Definition: Pay-to-Public-Key-Hash, a Bitcoin address format (starting with "1") that hides the public key behind a hash until the first spending transaction.
Technical Note: Provides some quantum protection for unspent outputs since the public key is not exposed. Once spent, the public key is revealed on the immutable blockchain and becomes harvestable.
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: AUSF
chunks.content:
Term: AUSF (AUSF)
Definition: Authentication Server Function, a 5G core network function that handles subscriber authentication using the 5G-AKA protocol and interfaces with the UDM for credential verification.
Category: concept | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: SIDF
chunks.content:
Term: SIDF (SIDF)
Definition: Subscription Identifier De-concealing Function, the 5G core component that decrypts the SUCI (concealed subscriber ID) back to the SUPI (permanent ID) using the home network private key.
Technical Note: SIDF uses ECIES (Profile A/B) or ML-KEM (Profile C) decapsulation to recover the subscriber identity. A key target for PQC migration in 5G networks.
Category: concept | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: UDM
chunks.content:
Term: UDM (UDM)
Definition: Unified Data Management, a 5G core network function that stores subscriber profiles, authentication credentials, and subscription data. Works with the AUSF for 5G-AKA authentication.
Category: concept | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: Person Identification Data
chunks.content:
Term: Person Identification Data (PID)
Definition: The digital identity credential in the EUDI Wallet ecosystem, containing core attributes like name, date of birth, and nationality issued by a national authority.
Technical Note: PID is the identity credential issued by a PID Provider; a Wallet Unit without a PID stays Operational and can still receive other attestations, but cannot present a PID. Must be cryptographically bound to the wallet holder's key to prevent transfer.
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: Relying Party
chunks.content:
Term: Relying Party
Definition: An entity (organization, service, or application) that relies on a digital credential presented by a holder to make trust decisions — such as granting access or completing a transaction.
Technical Note: In the EUDI ecosystem, relying parties use OpenID4VP to request and verify credentials. They can only request attributes they are authorized to see (selective disclosure).
Category: concept | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: Wallet Instance Attestation
chunks.content:
Term: Wallet Instance Attestation (WIA)
Definition: A cryptographic proof that a digital identity wallet app is a genuine, certified instance running on a secure device. Required by issuers before they will provision credentials.
Technical Note: Attests to the wallet's integrity, certification status, and device security. Prevents credential issuance to compromised or counterfeit wallet applications.
Category: concept | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: Entropy
chunks.content:
Term: Entropy
Definition: A measure of unpredictability or randomness in data. In cryptography, high entropy means data is difficult to predict, which is essential for secure key generation and nonce creation.
Technical Note: Min-entropy is the most conservative measure: -log2(max probability of any single outcome). NIST SP 800-90B defines methods for estimating entropy of physical noise sources.
Category: concept | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: CSPRNG
chunks.content:
Term: CSPRNG (CSPRNG)
Definition: Cryptographically Secure Pseudo-Random Number Generator. A PRNG whose output is computationally indistinguishable from true randomness, suitable for cryptographic key generation.
Technical Note: Typically implemented as DRBGs (SP 800-90A) seeded from hardware entropy sources. Examples: /dev/urandom (Linux), CryptGenRandom (Windows), crypto.getRandomValues (Web Crypto API).
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: TRNG
chunks.content:
Term: TRNG (TRNG)
Definition: True Random Number Generator. A hardware device that generates random numbers from physical phenomena such as thermal noise, shot noise, or clock jitter.
Technical Note: Processor random-number instructions are not raw TRNG output. Intel's DRNG guide says RDRAND returns values from an SP 800-90A-compliant DRBG (AES CTR_DRBG) and RDSEED returns seed values from an SP 800-90B/C-compliant enhanced non-deterministic RNG; Arm documents RNDR as returning a number from an approved RBG whose DRBG is reseeded from an approved entropy source. In NIST terms, the physical noise source is one part of an entropy source (SP 800-90B), which in turn seeds a DRBG (SP 800-90A).
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: QRNG
chunks.content:
Term: QRNG (QRNG)
Definition: Quantum Random Number Generator. A device that generates random numbers from quantum mechanical phenomena such as photon detection, vacuum fluctuations, or quantum beam splitting.
Technical Note: A quantum process is the noise source; like any noise source it still needs a stochastic model, health tests and an SP 800-90B entropy assessment, and a product's claims rest on its own certificate. For example, CMVP Entropy Validation Certificate #E63 covers ID Quantique's Quantis IID QRNG chips (physical noise source; checked 2026-09-24). A simulated QRNG is not evidence about a QRNG.
Category: concept | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: Min-Entropy
chunks.content:
Term: Min-Entropy
Definition: The most conservative measure of entropy, defined as the negative base-2 logarithm of the probability of the most likely outcome. Used by NIST SP 800-90B for entropy source validation.
Technical Note: For a uniform byte distribution, min-entropy = 8 bits per byte. There is no typical figure for real sources: min-entropy is estimated per noise source from its raw samples, and for non-IID data SP 800-90B takes the minimum of all its estimators' results (§6.2). The NIST SP 800-90B EntropyAssessment tool computes these estimates.
Category: concept | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: SCT
chunks.content:
Term: SCT (SCT)
Definition: Signed Certificate Timestamp — a cryptographic proof from a Certificate Transparency log server that a certificate has been submitted and will be publicly logged. Required by Chrome for all TLS certificates since 2018.
Technical Note: SCTs are embedded in certificates (via a TLS extension or OCSP stapling) and signed by the CT log's private key. In the Merkle Tree Certificate (MTC) design, SCTs are replaced by Merkle inclusion proofs, which also prove CT log membership without a separate signature.
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: Merkle Tree Certificate
chunks.content:
Term: Merkle Tree Certificate (MTC)
Definition: A certificate format that replaces individual per-certificate digital signatures with a compact inclusion proof in a Merkle tree. A single CA signature on the tree root covers the entire batch, dramatically reducing TLS handshake sizes for post-quantum algorithms.
Technical Note: For a landmark subtree of ~5.4 million certificates, the inclusion proof is 736 bytes (23 sibling hashes × 32 bytes); a standalone certificate over ~3,000 certificates needs 384 bytes. The handshake still carries the server's public key and CertificateVerify signature. For ML-DSA-44 that is about 4,668 bytes with a landmark certificate and 6,736 bytes with a standalone one (one CA cosignature), against 10,522 bytes for a leaf-plus-intermediate chain: roughly 56% and 36% smaller.
Category: concept | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: Merkle Tree Certificate Authority
chunks.content:
Term: Merkle Tree Certificate Authority (MTCA)
Definition: A Certificate Authority that collects certificate assertions into a Merkle tree, signs the root hash, and distributes inclusion proofs to subscribers. The MTCA replaces individual certificate signatures with batch-level tree signing.
Technical Note: The MTCA role is defined in draft-ietf-plants-merkle-tree-certs. Unlike traditional CAs that sign each certificate individually, an MTCA signs once per batch. A transparency service publishes signed roots for client synchronization.
Category: concept | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: Inclusion Proof
chunks.content:
Term: Inclusion Proof
Definition: A compact chain of sibling hashes from a leaf to the root of a Merkle tree, proving that a specific item (such as a certificate) is part of the committed batch. Verification requires only hash recomputation, not signature verification.
Technical Note: The proof size is O(log₂ N) where N is the number of leaves. For 2²³ (~8.4 million) leaves, the proof contains 23 sibling hashes (736 bytes at 32 bytes per SHA-256 hash). Domain-separated hashing (0x00 for leaves, 0x01 for internal nodes per RFC 9162) prevents second-preimage attacks.
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: Certificate Bloat
chunks.content:
Term: Certificate Bloat
Definition: The significant increase in TLS certificate chain sizes caused by post-quantum signature algorithms. An ML-DSA-44 signature is 2,420 bytes compared to 64 bytes for ECDSA P-256, so a leaf-plus-intermediate ML-DSA-44 chain with its CertificateVerify signature carries about 9.9 KB of keys and signatures (more with ML-DSA-65/87 or longer chains), which can break constrained clients and slow connection setup.
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: Batch Signing
chunks.content:
Term: Batch Signing
Definition: A cryptographic technique where a single digital signature covers multiple items simultaneously by signing a hash that commits to the entire set. In Merkle Tree Certificates, the CA signs the tree root once to authenticate potentially millions of certificates.
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: Domain-Separated Hashing
chunks.content:
Term: Domain-Separated Hashing
Definition: A technique that prepends a unique prefix byte to hash inputs depending on their type, preventing one type of hash from being confused with another. In Merkle trees, leaf hashes use prefix 0x00 and internal node hashes use prefix 0x01, as specified in RFC 9162.
Technical Note: Without domain separation, an attacker could construct a leaf whose hash matches an internal node, enabling second-preimage attacks. The 0x00/0x01 prefix convention is defined in RFC 9162 (Certificate Transparency v2).
Category: concept | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: Cosigner Quorum
chunks.content:
Term: Cosigner Quorum
Definition: A trust mechanism in Merkle Tree Certificate deployments where relying parties accept a signed subtree only after a configured set of external witnesses (cosigners) have co-signed it, preventing a compromised CA from silently issuing fraudulent certificates.
Category: concept | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: Account Abstraction
chunks.content:
Term: Account Abstraction (AA)
Definition: An Ethereum protocol feature (EIP-4337) that enables smart contract wallets with arbitrary signature verification logic. This allows users to switch from ECDSA to PQC signatures (ML-DSA or FN-DSA) today without a protocol hard fork.
Technical Note: EIP-4337 smart accounts verify PQC signatures on-chain at higher gas cost (~300k–500k gas per PQC signature vs ~21k for ECDSA). Combined with EIP-7702 (code delegation for EOAs), this provides a two-phase PQC migration path for Ethereum.
Category: concept | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: Information-Theoretic Security
chunks.content:
Term: Information-Theoretic Security
Definition: A security guarantee that holds regardless of the adversary's computational power, including quantum computers. QKD achieves this for key distribution because its security is derived from the laws of quantum physics rather than mathematical hardness assumptions.
Technical Note: Distinguished from computational security (used by PQC), which assumes the adversary has bounded computational resources. Information-theoretic security means that even with unlimited computing power, an attacker cannot break the scheme.
