Technical Note: PQC via oqsprovider: install liboqs + oqs-openssl-provider, configure in /etc/ssl/openssl.cnf: [provider_sect] oqsprovider = oqsprovider_sect. OpenSSL 3.5+ includes ML-KEM and ML-DSA in the default provider without needing oqsprovider. TLS PQC: openssl s_server -groups x25519:mlkem768 starts a hybrid TLS 1.3 server. Applications using OpenSSL 3.x via libssl inherit PQC support automatically.
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: Compliance Gap Analysis
chunks.content:
Term: Compliance Gap Analysis
Definition: A systematic comparison of an organization's current cryptographic posture against regulatory requirements, identifying where PQC migration is needed to meet compliance deadlines. Evaluates frameworks like CNSA 2.0, DORA, NIS2, and sector-specific mandates across multiple jurisdictions.
Technical Note: A PQC compliance gap analysis typically covers: (1) algorithm inventory vs. approved algorithms, (2) certificate lifecycle vs. regulatory deadlines, (3) vendor PQC readiness vs. contractual obligations, (4) data retention periods vs. HNDL exposure windows. Multi-jurisdiction organizations must reconcile overlapping requirements.
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: Quantum Risk Exposure
chunks.content:
Term: Quantum Risk Exposure
Definition: A measure of an organization's vulnerability to quantum computing threats, combining data sensitivity, cryptographic algorithm usage, data retention periods, and the estimated timeline to a cryptographically relevant quantum computer (CRQC).
Technical Note: Quantum risk exposure is typically assessed across four dimensions: Quantum Exposure (HNDL/HNFL window overlap), Migration Complexity (infrastructure depth and algorithm diversity), Regulatory Pressure (compliance deadline proximity), and Organizational Readiness (crypto-agility maturity and team capability).
Category: concept | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: Board Fiduciary Duty
chunks.content:
Term: Board Fiduciary Duty
Definition: The legal obligation of corporate board members and executives to exercise due care in protecting organizational assets, including digital assets threatened by quantum computing. Failure to plan for known cryptographic risks may constitute a breach of fiduciary responsibility.
Category: concept | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: PQC Migration Budget
chunks.content:
Term: PQC Migration Budget
Definition: The estimated total cost of transitioning an organization's cryptographic infrastructure to post-quantum algorithms, including hardware upgrades, software updates, staff training, compliance certification, and operational overhead during the hybrid transition period.
Technical Note: Key cost drivers: HSM firmware upgrades ($50K–$500K per cluster), certificate re-issuance across PKI hierarchy, application code changes for larger key/signature sizes, re-certification costs (FIPS 140-3, Common Criteria), and potential performance infrastructure upgrades to handle increased computational and bandwidth requirements.
Category: concept | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: Key Size Impact
chunks.content:
Term: Key Size Impact
Definition: The significant increase in cryptographic key and signature sizes when migrating from classical to post-quantum algorithms. ML-KEM public keys are 800–1568 bytes (vs. 32–91 for ECC), and ML-DSA signatures are 2420–4627 bytes (vs. 64–72 for ECDSA), affecting APIs, protocols, and storage.
Technical Note: Practical impacts: JWT tokens may exceed HTTP header limits, TLS handshakes require additional round trips, certificate chains grow 10–50x, PKCS#11 buffer sizes need adjustment, and database column widths for stored keys must be expanded. Performance budgets for latency-sensitive applications (payments, IoT) require careful re-evaluation.
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: Middlebox Compatibility
chunks.content:
Term: Middlebox Compatibility
Definition: The ability of network intermediary devices (firewalls, load balancers, DPI appliances, TLS inspection proxies) to correctly process PQC-sized TLS handshakes and certificates without dropping, truncating, or rejecting connections due to unexpected packet sizes.
Technical Note: ML-KEM-768 adds ~1100 bytes to TLS ClientHello; some middleboxes with hardcoded buffer limits will drop oversized handshakes. Testing strategy: deploy hybrid TLS (X25519+ML-KEM-768) in monitoring mode before enforcement, use QUIC where possible to avoid TCP middlebox issues, and coordinate with network security vendors on firmware updates.
Category: concept | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: Cryptographic Debt
chunks.content:
Term: Cryptographic Debt
Definition: The accumulated technical risk from hardcoded algorithm choices, missing abstraction layers, and tight coupling between application logic and specific cryptographic implementations, making PQC migration more difficult and costly.
Technical Note: Common sources: hardcoded "RSA-2048" strings in config files, direct OpenSSL API calls without provider abstraction, fixed-size key buffers, algorithm-specific serialization formats, and certificate templates that assume specific key types. Crypto-agile architecture eliminates this debt by design.
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: Performance Budget
chunks.content:
Term: Performance Budget
Definition: The allocation of computational resources (CPU cycles, memory, bandwidth, latency) for cryptographic operations within an application or system. PQC algorithms have different performance profiles than classical algorithms, requiring budget redesign during migration.
Technical Note: ML-KEM-768 encapsulation is ~5x faster than ECDH P-256 but produces larger ciphertexts. ML-DSA-65 signing is comparable to Ed25519 but verification is slower and signatures are ~36x larger. SLH-DSA is orders of magnitude slower for signing but provides hash-based security without lattice assumptions. Architecture decisions must balance security level, performance, and bandwidth constraints per use case.
Category: concept | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: Fleet Migration
chunks.content:
Term: Fleet Migration
Definition: The coordinated process of upgrading cryptographic configurations across an entire fleet of servers, endpoints, IoT devices, and network appliances to support post-quantum algorithms, typically executed in phased rollouts with rollback capability.
Technical Note: Fleet migration phases: (1) inventory and dependency mapping, (2) canary deployment to 1–5% of fleet, (3) staged rollout with health checks, (4) enforcement with monitoring, (5) legacy algorithm sunset. Configuration management tools (Ansible, Terraform, Chef) must be updated to manage PQC-specific parameters like hybrid key exchange groups and larger certificate chains.
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: Certificate Rotation at Scale
chunks.content:
Term: Certificate Rotation at Scale
Definition: The operational challenge of replacing certificates across large infrastructure deployments when migrating to PQC algorithms, complicated by larger certificate sizes, new CA hierarchies, and the need to maintain backward compatibility during the transition period.
Technical Note: Key considerations: ACME/cert-manager automation must support PQC certificate types, multi-CA coordination when different CAs adopt PQC at different rates, certificate transparency (CT) log compatibility with larger PQC certificates, and monitoring for mixed classical/PQC certificate environments. Expect 10–50x increase in certificate chain sizes affecting TLS handshake latency.
Category: concept | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: Quantum-Safe Research Data
chunks.content:
Term: Quantum-Safe Research Data
Definition: Research datasets, publications, and intellectual property that require long-term confidentiality (20–50+ years) and integrity protection, making them particularly vulnerable to Harvest Now, Decrypt Later attacks and requiring early PQC adoption.
Technical Note: High-risk research domains: genomics and bioinformatics (patient privacy regulations extend decades), classified defense research (50+ year confidentiality), pharmaceutical R&D (patent-sensitive data during 20-year exclusivity periods), and financial modeling (proprietary algorithms with long competitive value). Research institutions should prioritize encrypting data at rest with hybrid PQC schemes.
Category: concept | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: Formal Verification
chunks.content:
Term: Formal Verification
Definition: Mathematical proof techniques used to verify that cryptographic algorithm implementations correctly conform to their specifications, providing stronger assurance than testing alone. Critical for PQC algorithms where implementation subtleties can introduce vulnerabilities.
Technical Note: Active PQC formal verification efforts: NIST PQC standards are being verified using tools like EasyCrypt, Jasmin, and CryptoVerif. Lattice-based schemes require careful verification of polynomial arithmetic and sampling. Side-channel resistance claims also benefit from formal verification of constant-time implementation properties.
Category: concept | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: Passive Discovery
chunks.content:
Term: Passive Discovery
Definition: A network analysis technique that inspects encrypted traffic in-flight without injecting any packets. Used to detect and classify cryptographic algorithms across TLS, SSH, IKEv2, and OT protocols by analyzing observable handshake metadata on a SPAN port or network tap.
Technical Note: Tools like CryptoNext COMPASS and pqc-flow operate in passive mode — zero packets are injected, making them safe for production environments including OT/ICS. Observable data includes ClientHello cipher suites, server certificate algorithms, key exchange group identifiers, and SSH algorithm negotiation. Cannot validate whether a remote endpoint actively supports PQC — only detects what is being used in current flows.
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: Active Scanning
chunks.content:
Term: Active Scanning
Definition: A network assessment technique that initiates real connections to target endpoints to probe which cryptographic algorithms they support. Unlike passive discovery, active scanning actively negotiates TLS/SSH/IKEv2 handshakes to discover PQC readiness.
Technical Note: Tools like pqcscan (Anvil Secure, Rust-based) and SSLyze probe endpoints by attempting handshakes with specific algorithm sets. Key metrics collected: supported PQC algorithms, hybrid key exchange groups, TLS versions, certificate details, and risk scores. Active scanning requires network access and generates detectable connection attempts — should be coordinated with security operations before running at scale.
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: TVLA
chunks.content:
Term: TVLA (Test Vector Leakage Assessment)
Definition: A statistical methodology for detecting side-channel information leakage in cryptographic hardware implementations. Uses Welch's t-test to determine whether power consumption during cryptographic operations is statistically correlated with secret key data.
Technical Note: TVLA has a non-specific fixed-vs-random test and specific tests on chosen intermediate values. The non-specific test flags any input-dependent difference, including leakage of public data such as ciphertexts, so for lattice-based PQC (ML-KEM/ML-DSA) a failing result does not by itself show that a secret leaks. Labs therefore add specific tests on the stages that handle secrets: NTT/INTT transform, polynomial multiplication, and modular reduction. |t| > 4.5 (the common threshold from Goodwill et al., 2011) indicates statistically significant leakage.
Category: concept | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: Interoperability Matrix
chunks.content:
Term: Interoperability Matrix
Definition: A compatibility mapping showing which combinations of client and server PQC algorithm configurations successfully negotiate a shared secret. Used during the lab testing phase of PQC migration to identify which vendor combinations are compatible, require fallback, or are incompatible.
Technical Note: Key findings from production interop testing: Chrome 130+ (hybrid X25519+ML-KEM-768) is compatible with Cloudflare, AWS, and OQS test servers. Pure PQC clients (no classical component) are rejected by Cloudflare's server policy. Legacy TLS 1.2 servers reject all PQC ClientHello extensions — connection succeeds via fallback but PQC is not used. Use test.openquantumsafe.org for reference server testing.
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: Crypto Inventory
chunks.content:
Term: Crypto Inventory
Definition: A comprehensive catalog of all cryptographic assets across an organization — including algorithms in use, key sizes, certificate types, library versions, protocol configurations, and their locations across code, infrastructure, and third-party systems.
Technical Note: Crypto inventory differs from CBOM in scope: CBOM is code-level (source and binaries), while a crypto inventory spans network traffic (passive discovery), endpoint configuration (active scanning), and code analysis. A complete inventory combines all three: passive network probes (CryptoNext COMPASS, pqc-flow) + endpoint scans (pqcscan) + CBOM generation (CBOMkit). Typical enterprise inventory phase: 2–4 weeks for network + 1 week for endpoint scans.
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: Performance Baseline
chunks.content:
Term: Performance Baseline
Definition: A set of established metrics for classical cryptographic algorithm performance (ECDH, RSA, ECDSA) used as a reference point to measure the overhead introduced by PQC algorithms. Enables data-driven decisions about hardware capacity, latency budgets, and migration sequencing.
Technical Note: Critical baselines for PQC migration: TLS handshake latency (classical: 8ms LAN, 68ms WAN), IKEv2 SA setup (classical: 38ms LAN, 240ms WAN), certificate size (RSA-2048: 1.2KB). PQC overhead vs baseline: hybrid TLS ~1.2x handshake latency, pure-PQC IKEv2 up to 53x SA setup time on WAN. Tools for baseline measurement: PQC-LEO (open source), VIAVI TeraVM (commercial), Keysight CyPerf (freemium).
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: Security Association
chunks.content:
Term: Security Association (SA)
Definition: A set of negotiated cryptographic algorithms (encryption, integrity, PRF) agreed upon between two network peers.
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: Nonce
chunks.content:
Term: Nonce (Ni)
Definition: A random cryptographic value (typically 32 bytes) sent by the Initiator (Ni) or Responder (Nr) to prevent replay attacks and contribute to key derivation.
Category: concept | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: HSS
chunks.content:
Term: HSS (Hierarchical Signature System)
Definition: RFC 8554 stateful hash-based signature scheme that composes multiple LMS trees into a single signing capability with extended lifetime. PQC-relevant for firmware / software signing where the key state can be tracked.
Category: concept | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: KEM
chunks.content:
Term: KEM (Key Encapsulation Mechanism)
Definition: Cryptographic primitive that produces a ciphertext encapsulating a fresh shared secret under the recipient's public key. ML-KEM (FIPS 203) is the NIST-standardised PQC KEM; classical examples include RSA-KEM and DHKEM.
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: KDF
chunks.content:
Term: KDF (Key Derivation Function)
Definition: Cryptographic function that derives one or more secret keys from a shared secret, password, or master key. PQC handshakes use HKDF (RFC 5869) to expand the KEM-output shared secret into traffic keys and resumption keys.
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: PKI
chunks.content:
Term: PKI (Public Key Infrastructure)
Definition: Framework of policies, processes, and components that issues, distributes, validates, and revokes digital certificates. PQC migration of PKI requires new certificate, CRL/OCSP, and timestamp signature algorithms (e.g. ML-DSA).
Category: concept | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: MPC-in-the-Head
chunks.content:
Term: MPC-in-the-Head (MPCitH)
Definition: A signature design that proves knowledge of a secret by simulating what a multi-party computation would output, then revealing just enough of the simulation to be verifiable. Used by FAEST (AES-based), MQOM (multivariate quadratic), and SDitH (syndrome decoding).
Technical Note: MPCitH signatures are typically kilobytes — larger than lattice or multivariate — but security reduces to well-studied symmetric or combinatorial assumptions rather than newer algebraic structures.
Category: concept | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: Isogeny-Based Cryptography
chunks.content:
Term: Isogeny-Based Cryptography
Definition: PQC algorithms built on the hardness of finding isogenies (structure-preserving maps) between supersingular elliptic curves. Offers the smallest combined public key + signature sizes of any PQC family. SQIsign is the leading on-ramp candidate.
Technical Note: The earlier isogeny KEM SIKE was broken in 2022 by the Castryck–Decru attack. SQIsign uses a different mathematical structure that avoids the same exploit, but the field is young and conservative deployments treat it with caution.
Category: concept | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: Multivariate Cryptography
chunks.content:
Term: Multivariate Cryptography
Definition: PQC algorithms based on the hardness of solving systems of multivariate polynomial equations (usually quadratic) over a finite field. Produces tiny signatures and large public keys. Candidates include UOV, MAYO, QR-UOV, SNOVA.
Technical Note: The 2025 Ran wedge attack hit several UOV / MAYO / SNOVA parameter sets. Reparameterisation to odd-characteristic fields restores security; QR-UOV was unscathed.
Category: concept | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: PQC On-Ramp
chunks.content:
Term: PQC On-Ramp
Definition: NIST's ongoing standardization process for additional post-quantum signature algorithms beyond the August 2024 winners (ML-DSA, SLH-DSA, FN-DSA). Documented in NIST IR 8528 (Oct 2024); aims to provide algorithmic diversity beyond the lattice family.
Technical Note: Nine third-round candidates remain across four families: MPC-in-the-Head (FAEST, MQOM, SDitH), multivariate (UOV, MAYO, QR-UOV, SNOVA), isogeny (SQIsign), and lattice (HAWK). Earliest projected standardization window is 2027.
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: Cryptographic Posture Management
chunks.content:
Term: Cryptographic Posture Management (CPM)
Definition: The continuous, iterative management discipline of knowing what cryptography you have, keeping it healthy, and proving it across certificates, libraries, application software, and key material. Distinct from crypto-agility (capability) and from a CryptoCOE (operating model).
Technical Note: CPM is organised around five pillars (Inventory, Governance, Lifecycle, Observability, Assurance) and a six-stage operational loop (Discover → Classify → Score → Remediate → Attest → Reassess) wrapped in a strategic annual PDCA cycle.
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: Certificate Lifecycle Management
chunks.content:
Term: Certificate Lifecycle Management (CLM)
Definition: The provisioning, rotation, revocation, and retirement workflow for X.509 certificates across an enterprise. Becomes mathematically impossible to run manually under CA/B Forum SC-081v3's 47-day TLS cert validity (March 2029).
Technical Note: Modern CLM is driven by ACME (RFC 8555), EST (RFC 7030), and CMP (RFC 4210). Shadow-cert discovery via Certificate Transparency logs is a standard input. Forrester TEI 2025 modelled 312% ROI on CLM automation for one vendor — treat as upper bound.
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: CryptoCOE
chunks.content:
Term: CryptoCOE (Cryptographic Center of Excellence)
Definition: An organisational operating model that centralises ownership of cryptography across an enterprise — answering 'who owns it?' for crypto-agility (capability) and CPM (program).
Technical Note: This module's ROI model assumes about 50% lower PQC transition cost for organisations with a CryptoCOE in place before 2028; it is an illustrative assumption, not a sourced figure. The CryptoCOE typically owns standards, exception handling, KMS / HSM platform decisions, and library / vendor approvals.
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: Classical Security Bits
chunks.content:
Term: Classical Security Bits
Definition: The cost of the best known classical attack on an algorithm, measured in equivalent brute-force operations — not the key length. RSA-2048 reaches only ~112 bits because the General Number Field Sieve (GNFS) factors large numbers sub-exponentially. ECC P-256 reaches ~128 bits because Pollard's rho is fully exponential, costing exactly k/2 bits where k is the key size. Under Shor's algorithm on a quantum computer, both reach 0 — all classical asymmetric algorithms are fully broken regardless of key size.
Technical Note: Source: NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 Rev 5 Table 2 (RSA-2048 = 112 bits). Quantum resource estimates: Gidney & Ekerå 2021 (RSA) and Roetteler et al. 2017 (ECC).
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: Hypertree
chunks.content:
Term: Hypertree
Definition: The multi-layer Merkle structure at the core of SLH-DSA. d layers of trees each of height h/d: the bottom layer authenticates a FORS public key; higher layers each authenticate a WOTS+ public key; the root of the topmost tree is the SLH-DSA public key.
Technical Note: Increasing d makes signing faster (-f variants) but enlarges the signature. Decreasing d (-s variants) yields smaller signatures at the cost of more hash work per layer. Same security level at any choice of d within a parameter set.
Category: concept | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: CKA_EXTRACTABLE
chunks.content:
Term: CKA_EXTRACTABLE
Definition: PKCS#11 key attribute controlling whether a key's raw value may leave the token. When CK_FALSE, the private/secret key can be used for operations but never exported in the clear — the basis of HSM key custody.
Technical Note: Paired with CKA_SENSITIVE. A non-extractable, sensitive key can still be wrapped for backup only if CKA_WRAP_WITH_TRUSTED / policy allows; otherwise it is bound to the token for life.
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: CKA_SENSITIVE
chunks.content:
Term: CKA_SENSITIVE
Definition: PKCS#11 key attribute that, when CK_TRUE, prevents a key's value from being revealed by C_GetAttributeValue — the token refuses to disclose the raw secret.
Technical Note: Combined with CKA_EXTRACTABLE=CK_FALSE to give a key that can be used but never read out.
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: CKA_TOKEN
chunks.content:
Term: CKA_TOKEN
Definition: PKCS#11 attribute marking an object as persistent on the token (CK_TRUE) versus a temporary session object (CK_FALSE) that disappears when the session closes.
Category: concept | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: C_GenerateKeyPair
chunks.content:
Term: C_GenerateKeyPair
Definition: PKCS#11 function that generates an asymmetric key pair (public + private) directly inside the token, so the private key can be created non-extractable and never exists outside the HSM.
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: C_WrapKey
chunks.content:
Term: C_WrapKey
Definition: PKCS#11 function that encrypts (wraps) one key with another so it can be exported or backed up as ciphertext — e.g. AES key-wrap of a data key under a key-encryption key.
Technical Note: The wrapped key's CKA_EXTRACTABLE must be CK_TRUE for C_WrapKey to succeed.
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: C_EncapsulateKey
chunks.content:
Term: C_EncapsulateKey
Definition: PKCS#11 v3.2 function for KEM encapsulation: given a recipient's public key it produces a ciphertext plus a freshly derived shared-secret key object — used for ML-KEM (FIPS 203).
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: CKM_AES_KW
chunks.content:
Term: CKM_AES_KW
Definition: PKCS#11 mechanism for AES Key Wrap (RFC 3394) — deterministic, authenticated wrapping of key material under an AES key-encryption key, with an integrity check value.
Technical Note: CKM_AES_KWP (RFC 5649) is the padded variant for wrapping keys whose length is not a multiple of 8 bytes.
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: CPC Code
chunks.content:
Term: CPC Code (CPC)
Definition: A Cooperative Patent Classification symbol (e.g. H04L9/0852) that categorizes a patent by subject matter. Jointly developed and maintained by the USPTO and the European Patent Office, CPC codes are hierarchical — sections (letters) subdivide into classes, subclasses, groups, and subgroups, with longer codes indicating more specific technology.
Technical Note: The USPTO replaced its own classification system (USPC) with CPC on January 1, 2013. A single patent typically carries several CPC codes.
Category: concept | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: Priority Date
chunks.content:
Term: Priority Date
Definition: The earliest date an inventor can claim to have disclosed an invention, typically from an earlier-filed provisional or foreign application. It is the date patent examiners use to judge whether the claimed invention is novel against prior art.
Technical Note: The priority date often equals the filing date, but not always — a later non-provisional filing can claim priority back to an earlier provisional.
Category: concept | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: Filing Date
chunks.content:
Term: Filing Date
Definition: The date a complete patent application was formally submitted to the patent office. It anchors the start of prosecution and (for the earliest non-provisional filing in a family) the patent term calculation.
Category: concept | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: Issue Date
chunks.content:
Term: Issue Date
Definition: The date a patent is formally granted and becomes enforceable — sometimes called the grant date. It marks the end of examination, when the patentee gains the legal right to exclude others from the claimed invention.
Category: concept | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: Independent Claim
chunks.content:
Term: Independent Claim
Definition: A patent claim that stands alone and defines the invention completely without referring to any other claim. Every patent has at least one. Independent claims set the broadest scope of protection; dependent claims narrow an independent claim by adding further limitations and must be read together with it.
Category: concept | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: Wallet Unit Attestation
chunks.content:
Term: Wallet Unit Attestation (WUA)
Definition: A credential issued by the Wallet Provider that attests to the authenticity and security properties of a wallet instance. Without a valid WUA, no PID Provider will issue credentials.
Category: concept | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: Qualified Electronic Attestation of Attributes
chunks.content:
Term: Qualified Electronic Attestation of Attributes (QEAA)
Definition: An attestation of attributes issued by a Qualified Trust Service Provider, carrying legal weight across all EU member states.
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: Public Body Electronic Attestation of Attributes
chunks.content:
Term: Public Body Electronic Attestation of Attributes (PuB-EAA)
Definition: An attestation issued by a public body on the basis of an authentic source.
Category: concept | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: Device Binding
chunks.content:
Term: Device Binding
Definition: Cryptographic proof that the entity presenting a credential controls the private key the credential was bound to at issuance.
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: Wallet Secure Cryptographic Device
chunks.content:
Term: Wallet Secure Cryptographic Device (WSCD)
Definition: The secure hardware storing an EUDI wallet's private keys. Can be local (device secure element, eSE, TEE) or remote (cloud HSM).
Category: concept | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: Wallet Secure Cryptographic Application
chunks.content:
Term: Wallet Secure Cryptographic Application (WSCA)
Definition: The firmware or software managing cryptographic operations inside the WSCD.
Category: concept | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: Cloud Signature Consortium API
chunks.content:
Term: Cloud Signature Consortium API (CSC API)
Definition: Standard API for remote signature creation services, used by QTSPs for remote qualified electronic signatures. Version V2.2 was published in November 2025.
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: Unlinkability
chunks.content:
Term: Unlinkability
Definition: Privacy property ensuring that multiple presentations by the same credential holder cannot be correlated across different Relying Parties.
Category: concept | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: Data Minimization
chunks.content:
Term: Data Minimization
Definition: The GDPR principle (Article 5(1)(c)) requiring collection of only the personal data necessary for a specific purpose. Selective disclosure enforces it cryptographically rather than by policy.
Category: concept | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: Trusted List
chunks.content:
Term: Trusted List
Definition: A machine-readable registry of Qualified Trust Service Providers published by each EU member state, enabling cross-border trust verification.
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: eIDAS Trust Framework
chunks.content:
Term: eIDAS Trust Framework
Definition: The cross-border mechanism ensuring mutual recognition of digital identities, wallets and qualified attestations across all 27 EU member states.
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: Remote HSM
chunks.content:
Term: Remote HSM
Definition: A Hardware Security Module operated by a provider rather than held on the user's device. The EUDI ARF supports both local WSCD and remote WSCD (HSM) models.
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: mso_mdoc
chunks.content:
Term: mso_mdoc
Definition: The CBOR-encoded mobile document credential format defined by ISO/IEC 18013-5, carrying a Mobile Security Object signed as a COSE_Sign1 structure. Optimised for proximity presentation over NFC or BLE.
Category: concept | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: SD-JWT VC
chunks.content:
Term: SD-JWT VC
Definition: The Selective Disclosure JWT Verifiable Credential profile (draft-ietf-oauth-sd-jwt-vc), built on base SD-JWT (RFC 9901). Uses the dc+sd-jwt media type, which replaced vc+sd-jwt in November 2024.
Category: concept | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: COSE_Sign1
chunks.content:
Term: COSE_Sign1
Definition: A CBOR Object Signing and Encryption single-signer signature structure (RFC 9052), used by ISO 18013-5 mdocs to sign the Mobile Security Object.
Category: concept | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: LDAP
chunks.content:
Term: LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol)
Definition: The protocol used to query and update directory services such as Microsoft Active Directory — the store of user accounts, groups, and credentials that authentication systems rely on.
Technical Note: LDAP channels are typically secured with StartTLS or LDAPS (LDAP over TLS), so LDAP's own PQC exposure is really the TLS layer beneath it: the handshake needs hybrid ML-KEM key exchange, and any client-certificate authentication needs an ML-DSA-capable CA chain. LDAP simple binds that send credentials in the clear (no TLS) remain a separate, non-quantum risk.
Category: concept | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: OpenSSL
chunks.content:
Term: OpenSSL
Definition: The most widely deployed open-source cryptography and TLS toolkit, providing both a command-line tool and the libssl/libcrypto libraries that a large share of Linux, network appliance, and application-layer software links against for TLS and general cryptographic operations.
Technical Note: OpenSSL 3.5 (April 2025) added ML-KEM and ML-DSA to its default provider, so any application linked against system OpenSSL 3.5+ gains hybrid PQC TLS support without code changes — the same mechanism the oqsprovider add-on supplied for older 3.x releases. Distinct from OpenSSL Provider, which is the plugin architecture that makes this pluggable.
Category: concept | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: Governance, Risk, and Compliance
chunks.content:
Term: Governance, Risk, and Compliance (GRC)
Definition: The organisational function that measures, reports on, and governs risk — as distinct from a SOC, which detects and responds to it. GRC produces the instruments a board uses for oversight, a CISO uses to manage a program, and internal audit uses to verify it.
Technical Note: For a PQC migration, GRC is what turns a cryptographic inventory (a CBOM) into board-level risk reporting, tracks migration milestones against regulatory deadlines, and provides the audit trail that a program actually happened rather than merely being claimed.
Category: concept | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: WAF
chunks.content:
Term: WAF (Web Application Firewall)
Definition: A filtering layer, typically deployed alongside a reverse proxy or CDN edge node, that inspects HTTP(S) requests for application-layer attacks (SQL injection, XSS, and similar) before they reach an origin server.
Technical Note: Because a WAF sits inline with TLS traffic — often terminating it itself — its PQC readiness follows the same path as any other TLS termination point: the underlying TLS stack needs hybrid ML-KEM key exchange, and certificate validation needs to tolerate the larger ML-DSA certificate chains.
Category: concept | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: Executive Order
chunks.content:
Term: Executive Order (EO)
Definition: A directive issued by the U.S. President to federal agencies, carrying the force of law without requiring Congressional approval. Executive Order 14412, "Securing the Nation Against Advanced Cryptographic Attacks" (June 22, 2026), is the order currently driving federal PQC migration deadlines.
Technical Note: EO 14144 (January 2025) first added PQC provisions to federal cybersecurity policy; EO 14306 (June 2025) narrowed them. EO 14412 superseded both, setting concrete deadlines (FIPS 203/ML-KEM key establishment by Dec 31 2030, FIPS 204/ML-DSA signatures by Dec 31 2031 for High Value Assets) and is implemented via OMB Memorandum M-26-15.
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: CVE
chunks.content:
Term: CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures)
Definition: A standardized identifier system for publicly known cybersecurity vulnerabilities, maintained by MITRE with CISA sponsorship, so a single CVE ID can be cross-referenced across advisories, scanners, and databases like the NVD.
Category: concept | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: VEX
chunks.content:
Term: VEX (Vulnerability Exploitability eXchange)
Definition: A machine-readable statement, typically paired with an SBOM, declaring whether a product is actually affected by a specific known vulnerability (CVE) — cutting down alert fatigue from CVEs that exist in a dependency but aren't reachable or exploitable in that product.
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: Composite Signature
chunks.content:
Term: Composite Signature
Definition: A signature format that concatenates a post-quantum signature (e.g. ML-DSA) with a traditional signature (e.g. ECDSA or Ed25519) into one value that verifies as a unit, remaining secure as long as either underlying algorithm holds.
Technical Note: Distinct from a Composite Certificate, which is the X.509 container that can carry a composite signature. Standardized by the IETF LAMPS working group's composite ML-DSA drafts.
Category: concept | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: Logical Qubit
chunks.content:
Term: Logical Qubit
Definition: A fault-tolerant unit of quantum information built from many physical qubits combined via quantum error correction. Estimates of when a quantum computer could break RSA or ECC are expressed in logical qubits, not physical ones.
Category: concept | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: Physical Qubit
chunks.content:
Term: Physical Qubit
Definition: A single physical two-level quantum system (e.g. a trapped ion, superconducting circuit, or photon) used as a qubit before error correction. Many physical qubits — current estimates range from hundreds to well over a thousand, depending on the error-correction code — are needed to form one reliable logical qubit.
Category: concept | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: Fault Injection
chunks.content:
Term: Fault Injection
Definition: An active implementation attack that deliberately induces a physical fault — voltage or clock glitching, laser pulses, electromagnetic pulses — during a cryptographic operation to force an incorrect computation and leak secret material.
Technical Note: Distinct from a Side-Channel Attack, which passively observes normal operation rather than disturbing it.
Category: concept | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: Quantum Supremacy
chunks.content:
Term: Quantum Supremacy
Definition: A milestone at which a quantum computer performs a specific computation infeasible for any classical computer in a practical time, regardless of whether that computation is useful.
Technical Note: Largely superseded in current usage by the more application-relevant term Quantum Advantage, also in this glossary.
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: Entropy Source Validation
chunks.content:
Term: Entropy Source Validation (ESV)
Definition: The CMVP process for validating an entropy source — the combination of a noise source, health tests and an optional conditioning component that produces random bitstrings for a random bit generator — against NIST SP 800-90B. An accredited laboratory tests the entropy source and submits it through NIST's Entropy Source Validation Test System (ESVTS), and a validated entropy source may be referenced by certificate number in multiple modules without being recertified.
Technical Note: Source: NIST SP 800-90B (January 2018), Section 3 'Entropy Source Validation' (p. 9) and Glossary (p. 62); NIST CMVP Entropy Validation Announcements page, 'ESV Program Rollout' of April 13, 2022 and 'Entropy Source Validation Test Server' of March 24, 2022 (page footer 'Updated August 21, 2026'); NIST ESV-Server README (usnistgov/ESV-Server). SP 800-90B states that validation provides additional assurance that adequate entropy is provided by the source. ESVTS runs the SP 800-90B Entropy Assessment Library to analyze entropy sources, and its Prod environment is available to NVLAP-accredited labs with the 17ESV accreditation scope.
Category: concept | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: Known-Answer Test
chunks.content:
Term: Known-Answer Test (KAT)
Definition: A kind of cryptographic algorithm self-test in which a module operates an algorithm on a set of known input vectors and compares the result to the known expected output; if the calculated output does not equal the known answer, the self-test fails. The FIPS 140-3 Implementation Guidance calls it the most common way to meet an algorithm self-test requirement, alongside comparison tests and fault-detection tests.
Technical Note: Source: CMVP Implementation Guidance for FIPS 140-3 and the Cryptographic Module Validation Program (last update August 19, 2026), IG 10.3.A (pp. 102-103, quoting ISO/IEC 19790:2012 Section 7.10.3.2) and General Notes 6-7 (p. 115). General Note 7 permits a KAT to verify equality by comparing a hash of the calculated output to a hash of the known expected output; that hash function must itself be self-tested first. For ML-KEM, ML-DSA and SLH-DSA the guidance describes KATs that use fixed, predetermined values (pp. 110-112).
Category: concept | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: Cryptographic Algorithm Self-Test
chunks.content:
Term: Cryptographic Algorithm Self-Test (CAST)
Definition: A conditional self-test that a FIPS 140-3 cryptographic module performs on the cryptographic functions of each approved algorithm it implements, before the algorithm's first operational use. A CAST may take the form of a known-answer test, a comparison test or a fault-detection test.
Technical Note: Source: CMVP Implementation Guidance for FIPS 140-3 and the Cryptographic Module Validation Program (last update August 19, 2026), IG 10.3.A 'Cryptographic Algorithm Self-Test Requirements' (pp. 102-103, quoting ISO/IEC 19790:2012 Sections 7.10.3.1 and 7.10.3.2) and General Notes 5 and 8 (p. 115). Unless otherwise stated, CASTs are performed on the algorithms and parameters (for example key sizes, curves, modes) that an approved service uses. The requirement also applies to allowed algorithms with a claim of security and to legacy algorithms, but a CAST is not required before first execution in the non-approved mode.
Category: concept | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: Pairwise Consistency Test
chunks.content:
Term: Pairwise Consistency Test (PCT)
Definition: A conditional self-test that a cryptographic module must perform on every public and private key pair it generates; the Implementation Guidance treats it as separate from a cryptographic algorithm self-test. For ML-KEM key pairs it consists of encapsulating a shared secret with the encapsulation key and decapsulating the result with the decapsulation key, and it passes if the two shared secrets are equal. It is not required when a key or key pair is imported from outside the module's cryptographic boundary.
Technical Note: Source: CMVP Implementation Guidance for FIPS 140-3 and the Cryptographic Module Validation Program (last update August 19, 2026), IG 10.3.A (p. 103, quoting ISO/IEC 19790:2012 Section 7.10.3.3) and its Additional Comment 1 (pp. 115-116). For key pairs generated for SP 800-208 (LMS, XMSS) or FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA), the PCT may be limited to confirming that the resulting public and private key share the same key identifier.
Category: concept | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: Sensitive Security Parameter
chunks.content:
Term: Sensitive Security Parameter (SSP)
Definition: In FIPS 140-3, the term that covers both critical security parameters (CSPs) and public security parameters (PSPs). For example, an AES-GCM initialization vector is considered an SSP (a PSP or a CSP) within the module validation, and SSP establishment is the process by which CSPs or PSPs are securely shared within a module or between two or more entities.
Technical Note: Source: CMVP Implementation Guidance for FIPS 140-3 and the Cryptographic Module Validation Program (last update August 19, 2026), IG D.A 'Acceptable SSP Establishment Protocols' (p. 176), IG D.B 'Strength of SSP Establishment Methods' (p. 178) and IG C.H Additional Comment 10 (p. 155). FIPS 140-3 and NIST SP 800-140B Rev. 1 use the term (SP 800-140B expands the abbreviation) but do not define it.
Category: concept | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: Security Policy
chunks.content:
Term: Security Policy
Definition: The vendor-provided, non-proprietary document that the CMVP requires for a cryptographic module; its required content comes from ISO/IEC 19790 Annex B and ISO/IEC 24759 Section 6.14 as modified by NIST SP 800-140B. Its sections follow the Annex B order, from 'General' to 'Mitigation of other attacks', and any section that does not apply is marked as such. Among other things it records the module's cryptographic boundary, the approved modes of operation and how each is configured, and a table of the module's sensitive security parameters.
Technical Note: Source: NIST SP 800-140B Rev. 1, CMVP Security Policy Requirements (November 2023), Abstract (p. i), 'Security Requirements' (pp. 3-5) and section 2.4 (p. 9); FIPS 140-3 (March 22, 2019), section 3.3. For example, the vendor-provided non-proprietary security policy must list all vendor-affirmed security methods (p. 5).
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: Cryptographic Boundary
chunks.content:
Term: Cryptographic Boundary
Definition: The explicitly defined perimeter that establishes the boundary of all components — the set of hardware, software or firmware components — of a cryptographic module. FIPS 140-3 test requirements have the tester verify that the module's block diagram indicates this boundary, and the module's security policy must define it precisely and list any hardware, software or firmware excluded from it.
Technical Note: Source: CMVP Implementation Guidance for FIPS 140-3 and the Cryptographic Module Validation Program (last update August 19, 2026), IG 9.5.A (p. 85) and IG 2.3.B (p. 27), both quoting the ISO/IEC 19790:2012 definition; NIST SP 800-140 (March 2020), assertions AS02.15, AS02.17 and AS02.18 (pp. 3-5); NIST SP 800-140B Rev. 1 (November 2023), pp. 7 and 9. The test requirements set the boundary rule separately for hardware, firmware and hybrid modules; a hybrid module's boundary is the composite of its hardware component boundary and the disjoint software or firmware component boundary.
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: Protection Profile
chunks.content:
Term: Protection Profile (PP)
Definition: In Common Criteria, an implementation-independent statement of security needs for a type of target of evaluation (TOE). It describes the TOE type and the security functional and assurance requirements expected of it, and is typically written where a user community, a regulator or a group of developers wants to define a common set of security needs. A Security Target for a specific product may conform to one or more Protection Profiles.
Technical Note: Source: Common Criteria for Information Technology Security Evaluation, Part 1: Introduction and general model (CC:2022 Revision 1, November 2022), clause 3.68 (p. 22), 5.2.2.3 (p. 30), 6.3.3.2 (p. 39) and Annex B.2.1 (p. 125). Clause 10.1 (p. 66) says a PP is intended to describe a general TOE type, so it may be used as a Security Target template for any TOE of that type.
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: Security Target
chunks.content:
Term: Security Target (ST)
Definition: In Common Criteria, an implementation-dependent statement of security requirements for a specific target of evaluation (TOE), based on a security problem definition. It is a document that describes the TOE, the conformance claims, the security problem, the security objectives and the security requirements, and it is typically produced by the developer. It may conform to one or more Protection Profiles.
Technical Note: Source: Common Criteria for Information Technology Security Evaluation, Part 1: Introduction and general model (CC:2022 Revision 1, November 2022), clause 3.82 (p. 24), 5.2.2.3 (p. 30), 12.1 (p. 89) and Annex D.2.1 (p. 149). Before and during the evaluation the ST specifies what is to be evaluated; after the evaluation it specifies what was evaluated.
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: Target of Evaluation
chunks.content:
Term: Target of Evaluation (TOE)
Definition: In Common Criteria, the set of software, firmware and/or hardware, possibly accompanied by guidance, that is the subject of an evaluation. A TOE may be an IT product, a part of an IT product, a set of IT products, a unique technology that can never be made into a product, or a combination of these, and the Security Target must outline its physical and logical scope.
Technical Note: Source: Common Criteria for Information Technology Security Evaluation, Part 1: Introduction and general model (CC:2022 Revision 1, November 2022), clause 3.90 (p. 25) and clauses 5.3.1-5.3.2 (p. 33). The CC says the relation between the TOE and any IT product matters in one respect: the evaluation of a TOE containing only part of an IT product should not be misrepresented as the evaluation of the entire IT product.
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: Modules In Process List
chunks.content:
Term: Modules In Process List (MIP)
Definition: The CMVP list of cryptographic modules on which the CMVP is actively working. For each submission it shows the module name, vendor name, standard and status together with the date the module went into that status. Because validation is a joint effort of the CMVP, the laboratory and the vendor, the list gives some indication of which of them has the action. Participation is voluntary, the list does not necessarily include all modules being tested or reviewed, and posting on it does not imply or guarantee FIPS 140 validation.
Technical Note: Source: NIST CMVP Modules In Process List page (csrc.nist.gov), 'Last Updated: 10/3/2026'; FIPS 140-3 CMVP Management Manual, Version 2.7 (April 9, 2026), section 4.2 (p. 31) for the voluntary-participation and no-guarantee statements. Per the page, a module moves from Pending Review to Review only after the lab pays the NIST Cost Recovery fee. Status values shown include Pending Review, Review, Comment Resolution - Lab, Comment Resolution - CMVP, Pending Resubmission, Cost Recovery and Finalization; the page does not describe each state and points to the CMVP Modules In Process page for details.
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: Cryptographic and Security Testing Laboratory
chunks.content:
Term: Cryptographic and Security Testing Laboratory (CSTL)
Definition: An independent, NVLAP-accredited laboratory (also written 'CST lab') that tests cryptographic modules for the CMVP. It tests a module to the FIPS 140-3 requirements for the security level and embodiment, and produces a written test report for the CMVP Validation Authorities, who review it. Vendors submit a module and its documentation to the accredited CSTL of their choice.
Technical Note: Source: FIPS 140-3 CMVP Management Manual, Version 2.7 (April 9, 2026), sections 1.1 (p. 1), 2.6.1-2.6.2 (p. 13) and 2.6.3 (p. 15). A CSTL can conduct algorithmic testing and verify compliance with the algorithm standards (there may be additional requirements beyond what is CAVP-tested), review the module's documentation and source code, and perform the required testing in accordance with the test requirements, SP 800-140x and the Implementation Guidance.
Category: concept | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: CCRA
chunks.content:
Term: CCRA (CCRA)
Definition: Common Criteria Recognition Arrangement — a 31-nation mutual recognition agreement under which national Certification Bodies issue and accept IT product security certificates based on ISO/IEC 15408 (Common Criteria).
Technical Note: CCRA member nations include the US (NIAP), UK (NCSC), Germany (BSI), France (ANSSI), Japan, South Korea, Australia, and Canada. A CC certificate issued by any national CA is valid across all member states. The EU operates the EUCC as a stricter harmonized adaptation managed by ENISA.
Category: organization | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: NIST
chunks.content:
Term: NIST (NIST)
Definition: National Institute of Standards and Technology, the U.S. agency leading PQC standardization through its Post-Quantum Cryptography project.
Category: organization | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: ETSI
chunks.content:
Term: ETSI (ETSI)
Definition: European Telecommunications Standards Institute, producing PQC migration guides and standards for European industry.
Category: organization | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: IETF
chunks.content:
Term: IETF (IETF)
Definition: Internet Engineering Task Force, developing PQC integration into internet protocols like TLS, SSH, and IKEv2.
Category: organization | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: ANSSI
chunks.content:
Term: ANSSI (ANSSI)
Definition: French National Cybersecurity Agency, publishing PQC recommendations and cryptographic certifications for France and Europe.
Category: organization | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: BSI
chunks.content:
Term: BSI (BSI)
Definition: German Federal Office for Information Security, providing PQC migration guidelines and recommendations for German government systems.
Category: organization | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: 3GPP
chunks.content:
Term: 3GPP (3GPP)
Definition: The partnership project that develops specifications for mobile telecommunications including 5G security architecture.
Category: organization | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: NSA
chunks.content:
Term: NSA (NSA)
Definition: National Security Agency, the U.S. intelligence agency that publishes CNSA 2.0 and mandates PQC adoption timelines for national security systems.
Category: organization | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: CISA
chunks.content:
Term: CISA (CISA)
Definition: Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, the U.S. agency coordinating PQC migration for critical infrastructure and publishing product category lists.
Category: organization | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: ENISA
chunks.content:
Term: ENISA (ENISA)
Definition: European Union Agency for Cybersecurity, publishing PQC guidelines and coordinating quantum-safe transitions across EU member states.
Category: organization | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: GSMA
chunks.content:
Term: GSMA (GSMA)
Definition: Global System for Mobile Communications Association, leading the Post-Quantum Telco Network Taskforce for PQC integration in mobile networks.
Category: organization | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: CA/Browser Forum
chunks.content:
Term: CA/Browser Forum
Definition: An industry body of Certificate Authorities and browser vendors that governs Web PKI certificate standards, including PQC certificate adoption rules.
Category: organization | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: NCSC
chunks.content:
Term: NCSC (NCSC)
Definition: UK National Cyber Security Centre, publishing PQC migration guidance and a 2035 deadline for full transition to quantum-safe cryptography.
Category: organization | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: OSCCA
chunks.content:
Term: OSCCA (OSCCA)
Definition: China's Office of State Commercial Cryptography Administration, managing China's independent cryptographic standards including SM2 and PQC competitions.
Category: organization | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: ISO/IEC JTC 1
chunks.content:
Term: ISO/IEC JTC 1
Definition: Joint Technical Committee 1 of ISO and IEC, the international standards body for information technology including cryptographic standards (SC 27).
Category: organization | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: EuroQCI
chunks.content:
Term: EuroQCI (EuroQCI)
Definition: The European Quantum Communication Infrastructure initiative, a pan-EU program to deploy a quantum communication network across all 27 member states combining terrestrial fiber and satellite links.
Category: organization | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: Sigstore
chunks.content:
Term: Sigstore
Definition: An open-source project (Linux Foundation) for keyless code signing. Developers authenticate with their existing identity (GitHub, Google) and receive short-lived certificates, eliminating long-term key management.
Technical Note: Sigstore centralizes crypto in two services: Fulcio (CA) and Rekor (transparency log). Upgrading these to ML-DSA automatically provides PQC protection to all downstream ecosystems (npm, PyPI, Kubernetes).
Category: organization | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: PQCA
chunks.content:
Term: PQCA (PQCA)
Definition: Post-Quantum Cryptographic Alliance, a Linux Foundation project bringing together industry and academia to advance PQC adoption through open-source software.
Category: organization | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: OQS
chunks.content:
Term: OQS (OQS)
Definition: Open Quantum Safe, an open-source project providing C library (liboqs) implementations of post-quantum algorithms and integrations with OpenSSL, BoringSSL, and other libraries.
Category: organization | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: ASD
chunks.content:
Term: ASD (ASD)
Definition: Australian Signals Directorate, Australia's national cybersecurity agency. Published aggressive PQC migration timelines with a 2030 deadline for full transition — five years ahead of the US.
Category: organization | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: CCCS
chunks.content:
Term: CCCS (CCCS)
Definition: Canadian Centre for Cyber Security, Canada's technical authority on cybersecurity. Published the ITSM.40.001 PQC migration roadmap for the Government of Canada.
Category: organization | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: CRYPTREC
chunks.content:
Term: CRYPTREC (CRYPTREC)
Definition: Cryptography Research and Evaluation Committees, Japan's organization for evaluating and recommending cryptographic algorithms for government use.
Category: organization | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: KpqC
chunks.content:
Term: KpqC (KpqC)
Definition: Korean Post-Quantum Cryptography project, South Korea's national initiative to develop and standardize its own PQC algorithms including HAETAE, AIMer, SMAUG-T, and NTRU+.
Category: organization | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: ITU-T
chunks.content:
Term: ITU-T (ITU-T)
Definition: International Telecommunication Union — Telecommunication Standardization Sector. Study Group 17 (SG17) is developing PQC standards for telecommunications infrastructure.
Category: organization | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: NCCoE
chunks.content:
Term: NCCoE (NCCoE)
Definition: NIST National Cybersecurity Center of Excellence, collaborating with industry to develop practical PQC migration guidance and reference architectures.
Category: organization | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: BIS
chunks.content:
Term: BIS (BIS)
Definition: Bank for International Settlements, the international financial institution that published the quantum-readiness roadmap (Paper 158) for the global financial system.
Category: organization | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: CACR
chunks.content:
Term: CACR (CACR)
Definition: Chinese Association for Cryptologic Research, the organization that ran China's independent PQC competition and is shaping the NGCC (Next-Generation Commercial Cryptographic) standards program.
Category: organization | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: IETF PLANTS Working Group
chunks.content:
Term: IETF PLANTS Working Group (PLANTS)
Definition: The IETF working group responsible for standardizing Merkle Tree Certificates and related post-quantum PKI infrastructure. Adopted draft-ietf-plants-merkle-tree-certs in January 2026.
Category: organization | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: CMVP
chunks.content:
Term: CMVP (CMVP)
Definition: Cryptographic Module Validation Program — a joint NIST and CCCS program that tests cryptographic modules against FIPS 140-3 requirements. Validated modules appear on the NIST CMVP validated-modules list with a certificate number, recording that an accredited laboratory tested that module version against FIPS 140-3 at the stated security level; the Approved algorithms inside it must first complete CAVP algorithm validation.
Technical Note: PQC FIPS 140-3 validation for ML-KEM (FIPS 203) and ML-DSA (FIPS 204) modules began in 2024. Validation cycles take 12–18 months; procurement requiring FIPS 140-3 validated PQC must account for this lag. Check: csrc.nist.gov/projects/cmvp.
Category: organization | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: CC
chunks.content:
Term: CC (Common Criteria)
Definition: International standard (ISO/IEC 15408) for security-product evaluation. Country-specific schemes (BSI Germany, ANSSI France, NIAP US, CCS Canada, etc.) run evaluations; results mutually recognised through the CCRA. EUCC succeeds the SOG-IS MRA in the EU.
Category: organization | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: CSA
chunks.content:
Term: CSA (Cyber Security Agency of Singapore)
Definition: Singapore's national cybersecurity authority. Publishes the Cybersecurity Code of Practice and PQC readiness guidance for critical-information-infrastructure operators. Note: also used for Cloud Security Alliance (separate org).
Category: organization | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: ITSM (CCCS)
chunks.content:
Term: ITSM (CCCS) (Information Technology Security Management series)
Definition: CCCS Canada's technical-guidance document series (ITSM.40.xxx, ITSAP.xx.xxx). The PQC-relevant entry today is ITSAP.00.017 — Preparing your organization for the quantum threat to cryptography.
Category: organization | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: MAS
chunks.content:
Term: MAS (Monetary Authority of Singapore)
Definition: Singapore's central bank and integrated financial regulator. Publishes Technology Risk Management Guidelines and circulars that cover cryptographic-control expectations for financial institutions.
Category: organization | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: KISA
chunks.content:
Term: KISA (Korea Internet & Security Agency)
Definition: South Korea's national agency for cybersecurity and internet governance. Operates the K-CMVP cryptographic-module validation programme and co-administers the KpqC competition with academic partners.
Category: organization | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: MSIT (Korea)
chunks.content:
Term: MSIT (Korea) (Ministry of Science and ICT)
Definition: South Korea's policy ministry for science, ICT, and broadcasting. Co-sponsors the KpqC standardization competition with KISA and the National Intelligence Service.
Category: organization | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: DISA
chunks.content:
Term: DISA (Defense Information Systems Agency)
Definition: US Department of Defense combat-support agency that runs IT infrastructure for the joint warfighter. Maintains the STIG library that locks down DoD system configurations, including cryptographic-suite controls.
Category: organization | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: TCG
chunks.content:
Term: TCG (Trusted Computing Group)
Definition: Industry consortium that publishes the TPM (Trusted Platform Module) and DICE (Device Identifier Composition Engine) specifications. PQC-relevant work covers TPM 2.0 PQC algorithm additions and attestation-quote signing.
Category: organization | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: ISO
chunks.content:
Term: ISO (ISO)
Definition: International Organization for Standardization, a Geneva-based body that develops and publishes international standards.
Technical Note: Develops cryptographic standards jointly with IEC through ISO/IEC JTC 1 (already in this glossary).
Category: organization | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: IEC
chunks.content:
Term: IEC (IEC)
Definition: International Electrotechnical Commission, the international standards body for electrical and electronic technologies.
Technical Note: Jointly operates ISO/IEC JTC 1 with ISO, the committee responsible for IT security standards including cryptographic techniques.
Category: organization | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: IEEE
chunks.content:
Term: IEEE (IEEE)
Definition: Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers, a professional association that publishes technical standards — including IEEE 1609.2 (vehicular communications) and IEEE 2030.5 (smart grid), both already in this glossary — now being updated for PQC.
Category: organization | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: OMB
chunks.content:
Term: OMB (OMB)
Definition: Office of Management and Budget, the U.S. executive-branch office that issues implementation guidance directing federal agencies on PQC migration planning and budgeting.
Technical Note: Issued M-23-02 (2022, cryptographic inventories) and M-26-15 (2026, the operative PQC migration schedule under EO 14412), both already in this glossary.
Category: organization | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: DoD
chunks.content:
Term: DoD (DoD)
Definition: Department of Defense, the U.S. military department that mandates CNSA 2.0 compliance for National Security Systems and drives PQC migration timelines across defense contractors and suppliers.
Category: organization | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: OASIS
chunks.content:
Term: OASIS (OASIS)
Definition: Organization for the Advancement of Structured Information Standards, a nonprofit consortium that develops open standards — including KMIP, already in this glossary, which now extends to PQC key types.
Category: organization | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: NIAP
chunks.content:
Term: NIAP (NIAP)
Definition: National Information Assurance Partnership, the U.S. Common Criteria certification body operated jointly by NSA and NIST; issues CC certificates recognized under the CCRA (both already in this glossary).
Category: organization | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: W3C
chunks.content:
Term: W3C (W3C)
Definition: World Wide Web Consortium, the standards body for web technologies including WebAuthn and Verifiable Credentials, which are incorporating PQC algorithm support for web authentication and digital credentials.
Category: organization | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: OWASP
chunks.content:
Term: OWASP (OWASP)
Definition: Open Worldwide Application Security Project, a nonprofit foundation producing widely used application-security guidance (e.g. the OWASP Top 10) that is beginning to address crypto-agility and PQC migration risk for software developers.
Category: organization | Complexity: beginner

chunks.title: PCI SSC
chunks.content:
Term: PCI SSC (PCI SSC)
Definition: PCI Security Standards Council, the payment-card-industry body (founded by the major card brands) that maintains PCI DSS and is issuing PQC migration guidance for payments.
Category: organization | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: MITRE
chunks.content:
Term: MITRE (MITRE)
Definition: A U.S. nonprofit operating federally funded R&D centers, best known in security circles for maintaining the CVE program and the ATT&CK adversary-tactics framework.
Category: organization | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: GlobalPlatform
chunks.content:
Term: GlobalPlatform
Definition: An industry association that standardizes secure-element and trusted-execution-environment specifications used in SIM cards, secure elements, and IoT hardware roots of trust, now extending its specifications to PQC-capable secure elements.
Category: organization | Complexity: advanced

chunks.title: Cloud Security Alliance
chunks.content:
Term: Cloud Security Alliance (CSA)
Definition: A nonprofit industry association publishing cloud-security best practices, distinct from Singapore's Cyber Security Agency (also abbreviated CSA — see that entry). Runs an active Quantum-Safe Security working group producing PQC migration guidance for cloud providers and customers.
Category: organization | Complexity: intermediate

chunks.title: Australia — ISM December 2024 Update
chunks.content:
Country: Australia
Organization: Australian Signals Directorate
Type: Milestone | Phase: Guidance
Period: 2024–2024
Title: ISM December 2024 Update
Description: ASD updates ISM with specific PQC requirements (ISM-1917) including ML-DSA-87, ML-KEM-1024, SHA-384/512, AES-256 by 2030.

Main Topic: Information Security Manual Last updated: December 2024 Guidelines for Cryptography Cryptographic fundamentals Purpose of cryptography The purpose of cryptography is to provide confidentiality, integrity, authentication and non-repudiation of data.
Key Takeaways: Organizations must transition from DH to ECDH or PQC algorithms by 2030; ML-DSA and ML-KEM are the approved asymmetric PQC algorithms for digital signatures and key encapsulation; SHA-3 is approved exclusively for use within ML-DSA and ML-KEM; Full disk encryption is required for data at rest protection; Cryptographic equipment must be ASD-approved or meet Common Criteria evaluations based on data classification.
Migration Timeline: Years mentioned: 2024, 2030; Keywords: prohibited, deprecat
Regions / Bodies: Regions: United States, United Kingdom, Canada, Australia, International, Bodies: NIST, NSA, ACSC/ASD
Compliance Frameworks: FIPS 140-3, Common Criteria, SP 800-57 (Key Mgmt)
Standardization Bodies: NIST, ISO/IEC, ISO, IEC, CMVP (NIST)
Phase Rationale: The document represents a Guidance phase event as it provides "Guidelines for Cryptography" and specifies controls that organizations "should" comply with, such as using ECDH in preference to DH.
Mandate Level: Mandatory
Sector Applicability: Government; Critical Infrastructure
Migration Urgency: Critical Deadline
Historical Significance: This update marks the Australian Signals Directorate's explicit inclusion of NIST-standardized PQC algorithms (ML-DSA, ML-KEM) into national security guidelines with a defined 2030 sunset date for legacy Diffie-Hellman.
Key Dates: 2030: DH will not be approved for use beyond this year; December 2024: Document last updated
Dependencies: Requires implementation of ML-DSA and ML-KEM in cryptographic modules; Contingent upon ASD approval of High Assurance Cryptographic Equipment (HACE) for classified data.

chunks.title: Australia — ISM June 2025 Cryptography Guidelines Update
chunks.content:
Country: Australia
Organization: Australian Signals Directorate
Type: Milestone | Phase: Guidance
Period: 2025–2025
Title: ISM June 2025 Cryptography Guidelines Update
Description: ASD releases the June 2025 revision of the ISM Guidelines for Cryptography, updating controls including ISM-1917 (development and procurement of new cryptographic equipment and applications ensures support for ML-DSA-87, ML-KEM-1024, SHA-384, SHA-512 and AES-256 by no later than 2030) and restating that DH, ECDH, ECDSA and RSA will not be approved beyond 2030.

chunks.title: Australia — ACSC Annual Cyber Threat Report 2024–25 — Prepare for PQC as one of 4 'Big Moves'
chunks.content:
Country: Australia
Organization: Australian Signals Directorate
Type: Milestone | Phase: Guidance
Period: 2025–2025
Title: ACSC Annual Cyber Threat Report 2024–25 — Prepare for PQC as one of 4 'Big Moves'
Description: ASD's ACSC Annual Cyber Threat Report 2024–25 recommends businesses and network owners focus on 4 'big moves', one of which is to prepare for post-quantum cryptography, warning that a cryptographically relevant quantum computer is on the horizon and that effective transition plans will be critical to operating in 2030 and beyond, so planning must start now.

Main Topic: The ACSC Annual Cyber Threat Report 2024–25 outlines the current cyber threat landscape in Australia, emphasizing state-sponsored actors, cybercrime, and the strategic priority of preparing for post-quantum cryptography.
Key Takeaways: Businesses must prepare for post-quantum cryptography as a national priority; Effective transition plans are critical for operating in 2030 and beyond; Organizations should implement best-practice logging, replace legacy IT, and manage third-party risk; State-sponsored actors continue to target critical infrastructure and telecommunications providers
Migration Timeline: Effective transition plans will be critical to operating in 2030 and beyond
Regions / Bodies: Regions: Australia; Bodies: ASD, ACSC
Compliance Frameworks: Essential Eight Maturity Model
Phase Rationale: The document is a national threat report that identifies PQC as a strategic priority and mandates planning for the post-quantum era, representing a policy and awareness phase rather than a technical implementation phase.
Mandate Level: Recommended
Sector Applicability: Government; Critical Infrastructure; Telecommunications; Technology
Migration Urgency: Long-Term
Historical Significance: Highlights Australia's explicit designation of PQC as a national priority and sets a 2030 horizon for operational readiness in a post-quantum world.
Key Dates: 2030: operating in a post-quantum computing world
Dependencies: Requires effective transition plans to start now; Enables secure operations in 2030 and beyond

chunks.title: Australia — Commonwealth Cyber Security Posture in 2025
chunks.content:
Country: Australia
Organization: Australian Signals Directorate
Type: Milestone | Phase: Guidance
Period: 2025–2025
Title: Commonwealth Cyber Security Posture in 2025
Description: ASD report to Parliament on cyber security measures implemented across Australian government entities for the 2024–25 financial year, drawn primarily from the annual ASD Cyber Security Survey for Commonwealth Entities. It recommends entities start preparing for post-quantum cryptography by locating and assessing algorithms that will need to transition, and encourages all organisations to be prepared by 2030 by moving to more secure forms of encryption.

Main Topic: The document reports on the cyber security posture of Australian government entities for the 2024–25 financial year, focusing on Essential Eight implementation and general security metrics.
Key Takeaways: Entities should start preparing for Post Quantum Cryptography by locating and assessing algorithms that will need to transition; Organizations should continue to implement Essential Eight mitigation strategies to at least Maturity Level 2; Entities should prioritize effective logging to identify malicious activity; Supply chain risk assessments should be a core output for new IT procurements
Regions / Bodies: Regions: Australia; Bodies: Australian Signals Directorate (ASD), Department of Home Affairs, Joint Committee of Public Accounts and Audit (JCPAA)
Compliance Frameworks: Essential Eight; Protective Security Policy Framework (PSPF); Public Governance, Performance and Accountability Act 2013
Phase Rationale: The document is a government report on cyber security posture that includes a recommendation to start preparing for PQC, representing an early awareness/planning phase rather than a specific technical standard or mandate.
Mandate Level: Recommended
Sector Applicability: Government
Migration Urgency: Exploratory
Historical Significance: Represents a national government report explicitly recommending the start of PQC preparation (algorithm inventory) for federal entities, signaling the beginning of the assessment phase in the Australian public sector.
Dependencies: Requires locating and assessing algorithms that will need to transition to more secure forms of encryption

chunks.title: International — Paper 158 Quantum Roadmap
chunks.content:
Country: International
Organization: Bank for International Settlements
Type: Milestone | Phase: Guidance
Period: 2025–2025
Title: Paper 158 Quantum Roadmap
Description: BIS publishes Paper No 158, "Quantum-readiness for the financial system: a roadmap" (July 2025), a framework to support the financial system in the transition to quantum-safe cryptographic infrastructures, emphasising the need to start the transition today with broad awareness and cryptographic inventory as critical foundations.

Main Topic: A framework and roadmap for the financial system's transition to quantum-safe cryptographic infrastructures, emphasizing early action, inventory, and hybrid migration strategies.
Key Takeaways: Start the transition today with broad awareness and cryptographic inventory; Post-quantum cryptography is a viable near-term solution but requires coordinated planning for performance and integration; Avoid viewing the change as simple algorithm replacement; Ensure security through cryptographic agility, defence in depth, hybrid models, and phased migration; Quantum key distribution has long-term potential but faces immediate infrastructure challenges.
Migration Timeline: Years mentioned: 2025
Regions / Bodies: Bodies: BIS, national security agencies
Phase Rationale: The document is a published BIS Paper (No 158) providing a strategic framework and roadmap for quantum-readiness, representing a high-level planning and guidance phase rather than a technical specification or mandate.
Mandate Level: Recommended
Sector Applicability: Finance; Banking
Migration Urgency: Near-Term
Historical Significance: Provides a central bank perspective on quantum readiness, emphasizing that the transition is not a simple algorithm replacement but requires systemic changes like agility and hybrid models.
Key Dates: early 2030s: critical systems quantum-safe
Dependencies: Requires broad awareness and cryptographic inventory as critical foundations; Enables coordinated planning for hybrid models and phased migration.

chunks.title: Canada — PQC Best Practices Published
chunks.content:
Country: Canada
Organization: Canadian Forum for Digital Infrastructure Resilience (CFDIR) Quantum-Readiness Working Group (QRWG)
Type: Milestone | Phase: Guidance
Period: 2023–2023
Title: PQC Best Practices Published
Description: The Quantum-Readiness Working Group (QRWG) of the Canadian Forum for Digital Infrastructure Resilience (CFDIR) publishes version 03 of the Canadian National Quantum-Readiness Best Practices and Guidelines, advising Canadian businesses, organizations, and Critical Infrastructure owners and operators to begin planning a transition to quantum-safe cryptography through preparation, discovery and quantum risk assessment phases.

Main Topic: Canadian Forum for Digital Infrastructure Resilience (CFDIR) best practices and guidelines for quantum-readiness covering algorithm selection, hybrid approaches, and migration planning.
Key Takeaways: Organizations must plan an orderly transition to quantum-safe cryptography over the next few years; Hybrid cryptography standards and technology are recommended for migration; Third-party vendors should be assessed using specific PQC roadmap questions; Cryptographic agility is essential for future-proofing systems; Critical Infrastructure owners need to inventory current cryptographic uses immediately.
Migration Timeline: NIST on-track to publish first set of PQC standards in 2024; transition expected over many years; planning should occur now as changes are still years away.
Regions / Bodies: Regions: Canada; Bodies: Canadian Forum for Digital Infrastructure Resilience (CFDIR), Quantum-Readiness Working Group (QRWG), Bank of Canada, Government of Canada (GC).
Compliance Frameworks: CCCS ITSM.40.001
Standardization Bodies: U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST).
Phase Rationale: The document provides a structured framework of best practices and guidelines for assessing quantum risks and prioritizing migration, rather than enforcing a specific regulatory mandate or defining technical standards.
Mandate Level: Recommended
Sector Applicability: Government; Finance; Banking; Critical Infrastructure; Technology; All Sectors
Migration Urgency: Near-Term (1-3yr)
Historical Significance: Represents a comprehensive national guidance framework from Canada, published in June 2023, that bridges the gap between high-level policy and technical implementation for federal departments and industry stakeholders.
Key Dates: 2024: NIST expected to finalize PQC standards; 2025: Post-standardization period begins; 2030: Post-quantum period begins
Dependencies: NIST finalization of PQC standards; vendor development of quantum-safe products; organizational inventory of cryptographic use cases

metadata.sectorApplicability: Government; Finance; Banking; Critical Infrastructure; Technology; All Sectors

chunks.title: Canada — CCCS PQC Migration Roadmap Published
chunks.content:
Country: Canada
Organization: Canadian Centre for Cyber Security
Type: Milestone | Phase: Guidance
Period: 2025–2025
Title: CCCS PQC Migration Roadmap Published
Description: CCCS publishes ITSM.40.001 Roadmap for migration to PQC for Government of Canada. Effective June 23 2025.
