Key Takeaways: India has established a Task Force under the National Quantum Mission to oversee the phased transition to PQC; The roadmap recommends launching PQC/hybrid solution pilots in high-priority systems; A National PQC Testing & Certification Program is recommended to ensure product security; The document emphasizes the need for crypto agility and quantum resiliency in national digital infrastructure; Indigenously developed quantum-safe products should be progressively adopted where feasible.

chunks.title: Germany — BSI Signals Future Hybrid PQC Key Exchange for TLS
chunks.content:
Country: Germany
Organization: Bundesamt für Sicherheit in der Informationstechnik
Type: Milestone | Phase: Guidance
Period: 2026–2031
Title: BSI Signals Future Hybrid PQC Key Exchange for TLS
Description: BSI TR-02102-2 (version 2026-01) states BSI intends to recommend quantum-safe mechanisms in TLS (in hybrid use with recommended classical mechanisms) as soon as suitable standards have been adopted -- not yet a formal recommendation, and not a mandate. The sole use of classic (EC)DHE key agreement is only recommended until the end of 2031, and BSI intends to recommend the hybrid mechanisms SecP256r1MLKEM768 and SecP384r1MLKEM1024 from the Internet-Draft draft-ietf-tls-ecdhe-mlkem as soon as the corresponding RFC has been adopted.

Main Topic: BSI Technical Guideline TR-02102-2 provides recommendations for TLS versions, cipher suites, and key lengths, including a timeline for discontinuing classical mechanisms and adopting hybrid quantum-safe key agreement.
Key Takeaways: BSI recommends hybrid quantum-safe key agreement mechanisms for TLS once suitable standards are adopted; Sole use of classical key agreement is only recommended until the end of 2031; TLS 1.2 is recommended only until the end of 2031 due to lack of standardized quantum-safe key agreement mechanisms for that version; DSA and DHE cipher suites are discontinued from the end of 2029; RSA signatures with PKCS #1 v1.5 padding are discontinued
Migration Timeline: 2029: Discontinuation of DSA and DHE cipher suite recommendations; 2031: Sole use of classic key agreement mechanisms ends; TLS 1.2 recommendations discontinued; 2032+: TLS 1.3 recommended
Regions / Bodies: Regions: Germany; Bodies: Federal Office for Information Security
Compliance Frameworks: TR-02102-1; TR-02102-2
Standardization Bodies: Federal Office for Information Security
Phase Rationale: The document represents a planning and recommendation phase, outlining future discontinuation dates for classical algorithms and signaling the intent to recommend hybrid PQC mechanisms once standards are available.
Mandate Level: Recommended
Sector Applicability: All Sectors
Migration Urgency: Long-Term (3-5yr, planning horizon)
Historical Significance: This is a key national guideline from Germany's BSI that sets concrete deadlines for the deprecation of classical TLS mechanisms and establishes the framework for future PQC adoption in TLS.
Key Dates: 2029: Discontinuation of DSA and DHE cipher suite recommendations; 2031: End of recommendation for sole use of classic key agreement mechanisms; 2031: Discontinuation of TLS 1.2 recommendations; 2032+: TLS 1.3 recommended
Dependencies: Requires adoption of suitable standards for quantum-safe mechanisms in TLS; Enables recommendation of quantum-safe mechanisms in hybrid use

chunks.content:

Type: Milestone | Phase: Deadline
Period: 2030–2030
Title: Quantum-Vulnerable Public-Key Algorithms Deprecated
Description: Under NIST IR 8547 (final, October 2026), quantum-vulnerable public-key algorithms (RSA, ECDSA and finite-field or elliptic-curve DH and MQV at 112 bits of security or more; EdDSA at 128 bits or more) are deprecated after 2030: they may still be used, but with a security risk the user accepts, and they are disallowed after 2035. chunks.title: United States — GSA PQC Buyer Guide v1.0
chunks.content:
Country: United States
Organization: General Services Administration
Type: Milestone | Phase: Guidance
Period: 2025–2025
Title: GSA PQC Buyer Guide v1.0
Description: GSA Federal Acquisition Service Post-Quantum Cryptography Buyer’s Guide; acquisition guidance for agencies procuring PQC via Best-in-Class contracts.

Main Topic: A GSA Federal Acquisition Service guide providing federal agencies with practical guidance on acquiring and implementing Post-Quantum Cryptography products, services, and solutions to protect against quantum computer attacks.
Key Takeaways: Agencies must inventory all CRQC-vulnerable systems and submit to ONCD and CISA; Transition to PQC standards may take 10 to 20 years due to integration complexity; Organizations should develop cryptographic agility to adjust encryption mechanisms quickly; Sensitive data remains relevant for years making the harvest now, decrypt later threat urgent
Migration Timeline: NIST anticipates 10 to 20 years from algorithm standardization to full integration; initial CRQC-vulnerable system inventories due May 4, 2023; annual inventory and funding assessments required following initial submission
Regions / Bodies: United States; U.S. General Services Administration (GSA); National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST); Office of the National Cybersecurity Director (ONCD); Department of Homeland Security (DHS); Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA); Office of Management and Budget (OMB)
Compliance Frameworks: Federal Information Processing Standards (FIPS) 203; FIPS 204; FIPS 205; FISMA; National Quantum Initiative Act of 2018 (Public Law 115-368); Quantum Computing Cybersecurity Preparedness Act (Public Law 117-260); National Security Memorandum (NSM)-10
Standardization Bodies: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)
Phase Rationale: This document provides acquisition guidance and implementation steps for federal agencies to procure PQC products, aligning with the "Guidance" phase of defining how to execute the transition rather than just setting policy or technical standards.
Mandate Level: Recommended
Sector Applicability: Government; Critical Infrastructure
Migration Urgency: Near-Term (1-3yr)
Historical Significance: Represents one of the first specific buyer’s guides issued by a major federal procurement body (GSA) to operationalize the transition to NIST-standardized PQC algorithms for government contracts.
Key Dates: May 4, 2023: initial CRQC-vulnerable system inventories due; August 13, 2024: NIST PQC standards released; November 2024: NIST IR 8547 initial public draft issued; January 10, 2025: NIST IR 8547 initial public draft closed; July 2024: White House Report on Post-Quantum Cryptography published
Dependencies: Procurement of PQC products via GSA contracts; Implementation of PQC in federal IT systems; Annual submission of system inventories and funding assessments to CISA/ONCD

chunks.title: International — RFC 9881 ML-DSA in X.509
chunks.content:
Country: International
Organization: Internet Engineering Task Force
Type: Milestone | Phase: Standardization
Period: 2025–2025
Title: RFC 9881 ML-DSA in X.509
Description: RFC 9881 — Algorithm identifiers and conventions for using ML-DSA (FIPS 204) in Internet X.509 certificates and CRLs.

Main Topic: Specification of algorithm identifiers and encoding conventions for using the Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Algorithm (ML-DSA) in Internet X.509 certificates and Certificate Revocation Lists.
Key Takeaways: Conforming CA implementations MUST use specific OIDs for ML-DSA signatures in certificates and CRLs; The parameters component for ML-DSA algorithm identifiers MUST be absent; ML-DSA public keys cannot be used for key establishment or encryption, restricting keyUsage bits; Only the pure variant of ML-DSA is specified, excluding the pre-hash variant; Private key seed format is RECOMMENDED for efficient storage of both private and public keys.
Compliance Frameworks: FIPS 204
Standardization Bodies: IETF; NIST
Phase Rationale: This document is a published RFC (Released) that standardizes the use of ML-DSA in X.509, representing the formalization phase of PQC adoption rather than a timeline or mandate.
Mandate Level: Informational
Sector Applicability: All Sectors
Migration Urgency: Exploratory
Historical Significance: First RFC to define algorithm identifiers for NIST-standardized ML-DSA in X.509 certificates, enabling pure post-quantum digital signatures in the Internet PKI.
Dependencies: Requires FIPS 204 finalization; Enables ML-DSA adoption in X.509 certificate chains.

chunks.title: International — RFC 9941 SSH PQ-Hybrid Key Exchange
chunks.content:

Type: Milestone | Phase: Standardization
Period: 2026–2026
Title: RFC 9941 SSH PQ-Hybrid Key Exchange
Description: RFC 9941 — sntrup761x25519-sha512 PQ-hybrid key exchange for the SSH protocol.

Main Topic: Specification of a hybrid SSH key exchange method combining Streamlined NTRU Prime sntrup761 and X25519 with SHA-512.
Key Takeaways: Implementations should announce and accept sntrup761x25519-sha512@openssh.com as an alias for interoperability; The shared secret MUST be encoded as a string rather than mpint to prevent side-channel attacks; Clients and servers MUST abort if received public keys do not match expected lengths of 1190 or 1071 bytes; The hybrid construction aims to remain secure if either the classical or post-quantum algorithm is secure.
Standardization Bodies: IETF
Phase Rationale: This document is a published RFC (Released) that standardizes a specific hybrid key exchange method for SSH, representing a formalization of a widely deployed implementation rather than a policy mandate or research phase.
Mandate Level: Informational
Sector Applicability: All Sectors
Migration Urgency: Near-Term

Description: RFC 9370 — Multiple key exchanges in IKEv2; allows integration of PQC (including hybrid post-quantum key exchanges alongside (EC)DH) in IKEv2, for the IPsec protocol suite.

Main Topic: Extends IKEv2 to support multiple successive key exchanges, enabling hybrid post-quantum and classical key agreement mechanisms.
Key Takeaways: Hybrid key exchanges combine classical and PQC secrets to ensure security if any component is secure; IKE_INTERMEDIATE exchanges allow fragmentation for large PQC payloads; The protocol maintains backward compatibility with standard IKEv2 if additional exchanges are not supported; Multiple PQC algorithms can be used to hedge against risks in individual new algorithms
Standardization Bodies: IETF
Phase Rationale: This document is a published RFC (Released) that defines a protocol extension mechanism rather than a specific migration phase or regulatory mandate. It provides the technical framework for hybrid PQC integration in IKEv2.
Mandate Level: Informational
Sector Applicability: All Sectors
Migration Urgency: Long-Term

Dependencies: Requires assignment of new Transform Type 4 identifiers for PQC algorithms; Depends on RFC 9242 (IKE_INTERMEDIATE) and RFC 7383 (IKE Fragmentation)

Country: International
Organization: Internet Engineering Task Force
Type: Phase | Phase: Standardization
Period: 2026–2026
Title: RFC 10024 — PQ/T Hybrid Key Agreement for TLS 1.3
Description: RFC 10024, 'Post-Quantum Traditional (PQ/T) Hybrid Key Agreement Mechanisms for TLS 1.3' (Proposed Standard), defines three hybrid ML-KEM + ECDHE key agreement groups for TLS 1.3 — X25519MLKEM768, SecP256r1MLKEM768 and SecP384r1MLKEM1024 — and their TLS Supported Groups code points. Published August 2026, superseding the draft-ietf-tls-ecdhe-mlkem Internet-Draft this row previously tracked.

Main Topic: This draft defines three hybrid key agreement mechanisms for TLS 1.3 that combine the post-quantum ML-KEM with ECDHE.
Key Takeaways: Three new hybrid groups (X25519MLKEM768, SecP256r1MLKEM768, SecP384r1MLKEM1024) are defined for TLS 1.3; The X25519MLKEM768 group is recommended for general use due to wide deployment of X25519; SecP256r1MLKEM768 and SecP384r1MLKEM1024 are intended for FIPS-compliant environments requiring certified classical implementations; The draft obsoletes experimental Kyber768 code points in the TLS registry.
Regions / Bodies: Regions: None detected; Bodies: IETF, NIST
Compliance Frameworks: FIPS 140-3 (implied by "FIPS-approved"), NIST SP 800-56C, NIST SP 800-135, NIST SP 800-227
Standardization Bodies: IETF, NIST
Phase Rationale: The document is an active Internet-Draft in the IETF process, specifically defining standardization parameters for hybrid key exchange, which represents the standardization phase of PQC adoption.
Mandate Level: Recommended
Sector Applicability: All Sectors
Migration Urgency: Near-Term
Historical Significance: This draft establishes the specific hybrid group identifiers (X25519MLKEM768, etc.) that will become the standard for post-quantum secure TLS 1.3 key exchange, obsoleting earlier experimental Kyber code points.
Dependencies: Requires NIST FIPS 203 finalization; Enables hybrid PQC adoption in TLS 1.3 stacks.

Main Topic: Defines X.509 OIDs and structures for ML-KEM public keys in certificates.
Key Takeaways: ML-KEM is specified for use in X.509 PKI certificates at three security levels; ML-KEM and Kyber are not compatible; NIST defines security levels based on reference schemes like AES and SHA-2; Object identifiers for ML-KEM are assigned by NIST; Private key formats for ML-KEM are specified in this document
Regions / Bodies: Bodies: Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF), US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)
Standardization Bodies: Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF), US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)

Description: ASD Information Security Manual (Guidelines for cryptography, June 2025): taking into account projected advances in quantum computing, DH, ECDH, ECDSA and RSA will not be approved beyond 2030 and will need to be phased out in favour of ASD-approved post-quantum algorithms; the development and procurement of new cryptographic equipment and applications is to ensure support for ML-DSA-87, ML-KEM-1024, SHA-384, SHA-512 and AES-256 by no later than 2030.

Main Topic: Joint statement by 18 EU member states urging the transition to post-quantum cryptography to mitigate the "store now, decrypt later" threat.

Mandate Level: Recommended

Migration Urgency: Critical Deadline

Description: NÚKIB declared its support for the Position Paper on Quantum Key Distribution published on January 26, 2024 by ANSSI, BSI, NLNCSA and the Swedish National Communications Security Authority, sharing its concerns about QKD and its main statement that the clear priorities should be the migration to post-quantum cryptography and/or the adoption of symmetric keying.

Main Topic: Czech Republic's NÚKIB supports a position paper prioritizing post-quantum cryptography over Quantum Key Distribution for long-term security.
Key Takeaways: Transition to post-quantum cryptography or symmetric encryption is the priority over relying on quantum-vulnerable public-key cryptography; Long-term research on quantum key distribution is desirable but not feasible as a sole reliance; Organizations should prepare for quantum threats by adopting quantum-resistant cryptography; NÚKIB has already implemented post-quantum cryptography for its web portal security
Regions / Bodies: Regions: Czech Republic; Bodies: NÚKIB, ANSSI, BSI, NLNCSA, Swedish Armed Forces

Mandate Level: Informational
Sector Applicability: Government
Migration Urgency: Long-Term
Historical Significance: Represents a national cybersecurity agency explicitly aligning with the European consensus that PQC is the priority over QKD for protecting against quantum threats.
Key Dates: 19 September 2024: Letter of Support published; beginning of 2024: Position paper on Quantum Key Distribution published

chunks.title: Denmark — Transition to Quantum-Safe Cryptography
chunks.content:
Country: Denmark
Organization: SAMSIK
Type: Milestone | Phase: Guidance
Period: 2023–2023
Title: Transition to Quantum-Safe Cryptography
Description: Informational guidance for citizens, authorities and businesses on the quantum threat to current encryption; cites NIST/BSI/NCSC as reference sources. No binding organizational deadline stated — early 2030s used only as a working threat-timing assumption, not a compliance date.

Main Topic: Overview of the threat from quantum computers to current cryptography and guidance on preparing for the transition to quantum-safe cryptography.
Key Takeaways: Organizations should prepare for the transition to quantum-safe cryptography as current systems are vulnerable; Hybrid algorithms can be used for systems with highly sensitive data before final standardization; Crypto agility is recommended to minimize work for future updates; Candidate algorithms should not be used until final standardization is complete
Migration Timeline: NIST PQC standard expected to be ready in 2024; vulnerable algorithms to be replaced over a number of years
Regions / Bodies: Denmark; Bodies: SAMSIK (implied by title/source context, though text mentions Global Risk Institute, NCSC, BSI, NIST, DHS, ETSI, ANSSI as references)
Standardization Bodies: NIST; ETSI

Mandate Level: Informational
Sector Applicability: Government; All Sectors
Migration Urgency: Long-Term
Historical Significance: Represents early national guidance (2023) from Denmark on PQC transition, aligning with global expert expectations and NIST standardization efforts.

chunks.title: Finland — Quantum-Safe Encryption Transition Guidance Published
chunks.content:
Country: Finland
Organization: Finnish Transport and Communications Agency — Cybersecurity Centre

Period: 2026–2026

Description: Traficom's National Cyber Security Centre publishes a guidance website on the quantum threat to current encryption, with advice for organisations on moving to quantum-safe encryption; it urges starting a cryptographic inventory immediately because of the 'collect now, exploit later' threat. No compliance deadline is stated.

Main Topic: Publication of guidance by Finland's Traficom Cyber Security Centre on transitioning to quantum-safe encryption methods.
Key Takeaways: Organizations should conduct a cryptographic inventory immediately; Prepare for quantum threats early due to potential secret development; Protect long-term confidential data such as health and personal records; Utilize the "harvest now, decrypt later" risk model to justify immediate action
Regions / Bodies: Regions: Finland; Bodies: Traficom, Cyber Security Centre
Phase Rationale: The document represents a guidance publication phase, providing advisory information on transitioning to quantum-safe encryption rather than a technical standard or mandate.
Mandate Level: Recommended
Sector Applicability: Government; Healthcare; All Sectors

Historical Significance: Represents official guidance from Finland's national communications authority (Traficom) on PQC transition, highlighting the "harvest now, decrypt later" threat.
Key Dates: 6.3.2026: Guidance published; 11.5.2026: Information event for experts
Dependencies: Requires cryptographic inventory; Enables participation in expert information event

chunks.title: Sweden — National Recommendations for the Transition to Quantum-Safe Cryptography
chunks.content:
Country: Sweden
Organization: Nationellt Cybersäkerhetscenter (part of FRA)
Type: Milestone | Phase: Deadline
Period: 2026–2035
Title: National Recommendations for the Transition to Quantum-Safe Cryptography
Description: Two-tier recommended timeline under the Swedish Cybersecurity Act's all-hazards requirement: high-risk data (business secrets, sensitive personal/health data) quantum-safe by end of 2030; full transition for all use cases by end of 2035. References EU DORA (Reg. 2022/2554) for the financial sector and the EU NIS Cooperation Group's coordinated PQC roadmap (June 2025).

Main Topic: National recommendations from Sweden's NCSC for the transition to quantum-safe cryptography, including timelines and algorithm guidance.
Key Takeaways: Organizations subject to the Cybersecurity Act must inventory current cryptographic solutions; Transition to PQC should be elevated to management level; Recommended PQC algorithms include ML-KEM, ML-DSA, SLH-DSA, LMS, and XMSS; Migration targets are set for 2030 and 2035.
Migration Timeline: Milestones: 2030: Ready; 2035: Ready
Regions / Bodies: Regions: Sweden; Bodies: NCSC Sweden (Nationellt cybersäkerhetscenter vid FRA)
Compliance Frameworks: Cybersäkerhetslag (2025:1506); FIPS 203; FIPS 204; FIPS 205; FIPS 186-5; NIST SP 800-56A; NIST SP 800-56B; NIST SP 800-208
Standardization Bodies: NIST; IETF; ETSI; 3GPP; ISO; CEN/CENELEC; SIS
Phase Rationale: The document provides national recommendations and a timeline for transition, indicating a planning and preparation phase rather than immediate mandatory enforcement or final completion.
Mandate Level: Recommended
Sector Applicability: All Sectors

Historical Significance: Represents Sweden's national guidance for PQC transition, aligning with EU and global standards.

chunks.title: Switzerland — Quantum Computers and Post-Quantum Cryptography — Technology Brief
chunks.content:
Country: Switzerland
Organization: National Cyber Security Centre (Switzerland)

Period: 2025–2025
Title: Quantum Computers and Post-Quantum Cryptography — Technology Brief
Description: Technology brief outlining what a quantum computer is, why it challenges certain cryptographic methods and what post-quantum cryptography is; it recommends a carefully planned migration and creating an SBOM or CBOM as a sensible first step. No compliance deadline is stated.

Main Topic: A technology brief by NCSC Switzerland explaining quantum computers, post-quantum cryptography standards, and migration recommendations for organizations.
Key Takeaways: Implement hybrid methods combining conventional and PQC methods to mitigate risk; Create a Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) or Cryptographic Bill of Materials (CBOM) to understand cryptographic reliance; Approach migration carefully to avoid weakening overall security with hasty solutions; Design systems for cryptographic agility to support various protocols and algorithms
Migration Timeline: IBM plans to build a quantum computer with 100,000 qubits by 2033

Compliance Frameworks: FIPS 203; FIPS 204; FIPS 205
Standardization Bodies: NIST; IETF

Mandate Level: Informational
Sector Applicability: All Sectors
Migration Urgency: Long-Term
Historical Significance: Represents a national cyber security centre's formal guidance on PQC migration, emphasizing hybrid approaches and cryptographic agility for general organizational readiness.
Key Dates: 2033: IBM plans to build a quantum computer with 100,000 qubits

chunks.title: Jordan — Quantum-Resistant Encryption Roadmap for the Financial Sector
chunks.content:
Country: Jordan
Organization: Central Bank of Jordan (CBJ)
Type: Milestone | Phase: Policy
Period: 2026–2026
Title: Quantum-Resistant Encryption Roadmap for the Financial Sector
Description: The Central Bank of Jordan announced a sectoral roadmap for transitioning the financial and banking sectors to quantum-resistant encryption: integrating quantum-related risks into institutional risk registers, strengthening governance, inventorying cryptographic assets, prioritizing migration based on risk assessments, and piloting quantum-resistant encryption in virtual and non-operational environments, leading to full adoption within a defined timeframe. No deadline date is given.

Main Topic: The Central Bank of Jordan has released a sectoral roadmap for transitioning the financial and banking sectors to quantum-resistant encryption.
Key Takeaways: Financial institutions must inventory cryptographic assets and prioritize migration based on risk assessments; Pilot tests of quantum-resistant solutions should be conducted in virtual and non-operational environments; Stakeholders including suppliers and technical partners must coordinate to ensure business continuity during the transition; Quantum-related risks must be integrated into institutional risk registers and governance frameworks.
Migration Timeline: full adoption of quantum-resistant systems within a defined timeframe
Regions / Bodies: Regions: Jordan; Bodies: Central Bank of Jordan
Phase Rationale: The document describes the launch of a roadmap for transitioning to quantum-resistant encryption, representing a strategic planning and preparation phase rather than a specific technical implementation or standardization milestone.
Mandate Level: Recommended
Sector Applicability: Finance; Banking
Migration Urgency: Long-Term
Historical Significance: Represents a proactive commitment by a national central bank to enhance the readiness of its financial sector against future quantum computing threats, aligning with international best practices.
Dependencies: Requires coordination among financial institutions, suppliers, and technical partners; Enables full adoption of quantum-resistant systems within a defined timeframe.

chunks.title: France — Post-Quantum Cryptography Transition Roadmap Declaration
chunks.content:
Country: France
Organization: Banque de France
Type: Milestone | Phase: Policy
Period: 2026–2026
Title: Post-Quantum Cryptography Transition Roadmap Declaration
Description: Banque de France press release on the G7 Cyber Expert Group (CEG) declaration on the progress of a coordinated roadmap for the financial sector's transition to post-quantum cryptography. The declaration calls for integrating this preparation into governance and risk management and planning migration according to systems' exposure and systemic importance: critical systems are to be migrated by 2030-2032 and all other systems by 2035, with targets that may be re-evaluated as technology evolves. It is consistent with work undertaken at European level by the European Commission and, in France, by the Banque de France and the ACPR since 2022.

Main Topic: G7 Cyber Expert Group roadmap for the financial sector's transition to post-quantum cryptography, endorsed by Banque de France and ACPR.
Key Takeaways: Integrate PQC preparation into governance and risk management; plan migration based on system exposure and systemic importance; migrate critical systems by 2030-2032 and all other systems by 2035; foster cooperation between public, private, and academic actors
Migration Timeline: Critical systems migrated by 2030-2032; all other systems by 2035
Regions / Bodies: Regions: France; Bodies: G7 Cyber Expert Group (CEG), Banque de France, ACPR, European Commission
Phase Rationale: The document represents a policy/guidance phase event, establishing a coordinated roadmap and framework for the financial sector's transition rather than a technical specification or standard.
Mandate Level: Recommended
Sector Applicability: Finance; Banking; Critical Infrastructure
Migration Urgency: Critical Deadline
Historical Significance: Represents a coordinated G7-level roadmap for the financial sector, aligning national efforts (France, EU) with international cooperation for PQC transition.
Key Dates: 2030-2032: critical systems migration; 2035: all other systems migration
Dependencies: Requires cooperation between public, private, and academic actors; depends on technology evolution and threat monitoring

chunks.title: United Kingdom — Quantum Computing (Tech Horizons Report)
chunks.content:
Country: United Kingdom
Organization: ICO
Type: Milestone | Phase: Guidance
Period: 2024–2024
Title: Quantum Computing (Tech Horizons Report)
Description: ICO notes that quantum computing could undermine specific types of encryption protecting most of today's digital communications, recalls UK GDPR/DPA 2018 obligations to take appropriate technical and organisational measures considering the state of the art, says organisations should be crypto-agile, and supports the NCSC's recommendation that large organisations start planning their PQC transition now. No compliance deadline stated.

Main Topic: Overview of quantum computing technology, its potential impacts on encryption and data privacy, and guidance for organizations on preparing for the transition to post-quantum cryptography.
Key Takeaways: Organizations should start planning their transition to post-quantum cryptography now by identifying at-risk datasets; Do not rush to transition before final standards-compliant products are available; Maintain crypto-agility by keeping encryption use under regular review; Be aware of "harvest now, decrypt later" risks where actors collect data to decrypt later with quantum computers
Migration Timeline: Estimates for quantum computer materialization range from five to 30 years
Regions / Bodies: Regions: United Kingdom; Bodies: Information Commissioner's Office (ICO), National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), National Quantum Computing Centre (NQCC), Regulatory Horizons Council, Data Protection and Digital Information Commission (DRCF) counterparts
Compliance Frameworks: Data Protection Act 2018 (DPA 2018); UK GDPR
Standardization Bodies: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)
Phase Rationale: The document is a Tech Horizons Report from the ICO, providing high-level guidance and risk assessment rather than a specific implementation phase or mandate.
Mandate Level: Recommended
Sector Applicability: All Sectors
Migration Urgency: Long-Term
Historical Significance: Represents regulatory guidance from the UK ICO on data protection implications of quantum computing, aligning with NCSC technical advice.
Dependencies: Requires final standards-compliant products to be available before transitioning

chunks.title: Norway — Quantum Migration (Kvantemigrasjon) Guidance
chunks.content:
Country: Norway
Organization: NSM
Type: Milestone | Phase: Guidance
Period: 2023–2026
Title: Quantum Migration (Kvantemigrasjon) Guidance
Description: NSM guidance recommends that organisations begin with a detailed assessment of their operations and cryptographic use, plan a phased transition to new standards with suppliers, and await standardised solutions rather than make rushed quantum-safe-cryptography procurements.

Main Topic: NSM guidance for Norwegian organizations on risk assessment and migration to quantum-safe IT systems and cryptographic solutions.
Key Takeaways: Organizations should conduct risk assessments of their IT systems for quantum vulnerabilities now; Migration to quantum-safe systems is time-consuming and costly, requiring early planning; Many organizations lack full visibility into their current cryptographic usage, complicating replacement efforts; NSM provides advice and assistance for the quantum migration process.
Regions / Bodies: Regions: Norway; Bodies: NSM (Nasjonal sikkerhetsmyndighet)
Phase Rationale: The document is a guidance publication from NSM advising organizations to begin risk assessments and planning for quantum migration, representing the initial awareness and assessment phase of national PQC adoption.
Mandate Level: Recommended
Sector Applicability: All Sectors
Migration Urgency: Near-Term
Historical Significance: Represents official guidance from the Norwegian National Security Authority (NSM) urging immediate risk assessment for quantum vulnerabilities in national IT infrastructure.
Dependencies: Requires international new quantum-safe standards to be finalized; Enables secure data protection for the future.

chunks.title: India — Q-SAFE Expert Committee on Quantum Technology Risk
chunks.content:
Country: India
Organization: Reserve Bank of India
Type: Milestone | Phase: Discovery
Period: 2026–2026
Title: Q-SAFE Expert Committee on Quantum Technology Risk
Description: RBI constitutes an eight-member expert committee for a Quantum Secure and Adaptive Financial Ecosystem (Q-SAFE), convened by Dr. Anil Prabhakar (IIT Madras), to evaluate the financial sector's cryptographic inventory through a Cryptography Bill of Materials (CBOM), assess crypto agility, evaluate industry preparedness for quantum-safe cryptography including vendor tools, and recommend a roadmap and framework to quantum-secure the Indian financial system; its report is due within six months of its first meeting (per RBI's May 25 press release).

Main Topic: The Reserve Bank of India has constituted the Q-SAFE expert committee to examine quantum technology risks and opportunities in the financial sector.
Key Takeaways: Financial institutions must evaluate cryptographic inventory using a Cryptography Bill of Materials (CBOM); Quantum computing poses risks to existing encryption systems via harvest now decrypt later attacks; The RBI Q-SAFE committee will recommend a roadmap to quantum-secure the Indian financial system; Industry preparedness for quantum-safe cryptography adoption needs assessment regarding vendor tool maturity
Migration Timeline: Committee to submit report within six months from the date of its first meeting
Regions / Bodies: Regions: India; Bodies: Reserve Bank of India (RBI), Department of Science & Technology (DST), Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY)
Phase Rationale: The document describes the formation of an expert committee to examine risks and recommend a roadmap, representing an initial exploratory and planning phase rather than a specific implementation or standardization milestone.
Mandate Level: Informational
Sector Applicability: Finance; Banking
Migration Urgency: Exploratory
Historical Significance: Represents a significant step in India's regulatory response to quantum threats, establishing a dedicated body to assess cryptographic inventory and prepare the financial system for quantum-safe transitions.
Key Dates: May 25: Press release issued; Six months from first meeting: Committee report submission deadline
Dependencies: Requires the submission of the Q-SAFE committee report; Enables the development of a roadmap and framework for quantum-securing the Indian financial system

chunks.title: Indonesia — National PQC Migration Roadmap Task Force — Inaugural Meeting
chunks.content:
Country: Indonesia
Organization: Badan Siber dan Sandi Negara (National Cyber and Crypto Agency)
Type: Milestone | Phase: Discovery
Period: 2026–2026
Title: National PQC Migration Roadmap Task Force — Inaugural Meeting
Description: BSSN-led National Task Force for Quantum-Resistant Cryptography Preparation held its inaugural meeting 2026-06-25 at BSSN headquarters (Bojongsari, West Java); one planned output is a draft Presidential Regulation on a quantum-resistant cryptography migration roadmap. Task force formation, not yet an issued regulation — no compliance deadline exists. Source is a first-party account by a named task force member (Dr. Rudi Rusdiah), not a BSSN press release; treat accordingly.

Main Topic: Inaugural meeting of Indonesia's National PQC Migration Roadmap Task Force, led by BSSN, to develop a presidential regulation for post-quantum cryptography migration.
Key Takeaways: Indonesia has established a national task force to create a PQC migration roadmap and presidential regulation; The banking sector is critically vulnerable to Harvest Now, Decrypt Later attacks due to reliance on RSA and ECC; China is pursuing an independent PQC standardization path (NGCC) distinct from NIST standards; Global PQC migration is accelerating with specific deadlines in the US, UK, and China; Interoperability testing and cryptographic asset inventory are immediate priorities for the Indonesian task force
Migration Timeline: US Federal migration before 2035; UK Roadmap 2028–2035; China NGCC launch February 2025; China standardization completion in 3 years; China mass migration in 5 years; China consolidation in 10 years; US high-risk migration deadline 2030; US full quantum-resistant security 2035; Q-Day estimated early 2030s
Regions / Bodies: Indonesia; BSSN; ABDI; United States; NIST; United Kingdom; NCSC UK; Canada; Australia; ASD; Singapore; CSA Singapore; China; ICCS

Standardization Bodies: NIST; ICCS (China Cryptography Standardization Technical Committee)

Mandate Level: Mandatory
Sector Applicability: Government; Finance; Banking; Telecommunications; Technology
Migration Urgency: Near-Term

Dependencies: Requires completion of cryptographic asset inventory; Depends on finalization of NIST and Chinese standards; Enables development of Presidential Regulation on PQC Migration Roadmap

chunks.title: Germany — BSI: VS-IT Umstellungsfristen fuer Post-Quanten-Kryptografie vereinbart
chunks.content:

Type: Milestone | Phase: Deadline
Period: 2025–2025
Title: BSI: VS-IT Umstellungsfristen fuer Post-Quanten-Kryptografie vereinbart
Description: BSI, together with manufacturers of IT security products for protecting classified information (VS-NfD), set binding deadlines for the transition to quantum-safe cryptography; at a workshop convened by BSI in September it was agreed that IT security products able to counter the threat of future quantum computers should be available from 2030 at the latest.

Main Topic: The German Federal Office for Information Security (BSI) has established binding deadlines with IT security product manufacturers for the transition to post-quantum cryptography for classified information protection.
Key Takeaways: IT security products for classified information (VS-NfD) must support post-quantum cryptography by 2030; The BSI estimates a cryptographically relevant quantum computer is likely realizable within 16 years; The agreement ensures long-term availability of secure IT for state secret protection; The collaboration establishes a foundation for future-proof technology competence in Germany
Migration Timeline: Milestones: 2030: IT security products for VS-NfD must be available to effectively counter threats from future high-performance quantum computers
Regions / Bodies: Regions: Germany; Bodies: BSI (Bundesamt für Sicherheit in der Informationstechnik)

Mandate Level: Mandatory
Sector Applicability: Government; Defense
Migration Urgency: Critical Deadline
Historical Significance: Represents a concrete national mandate from the German BSI setting a 2030 deadline for PQC-enabled IT security products for classified data, signaling advanced government adoption.

chunks.title: United States — FAA Request for Information: Post Quantum Cryptography Support (RFI 697DCK-26-RFI-PQC)
chunks.content:

Organization: Federal Aviation Administration

Period: 2026–2026
Title: FAA Request for Information: Post Quantum Cryptography Support (RFI 697DCK-26-RFI-PQC)
Description: The FAA issues Request for Information 697DCK-26-RFI-PQC seeking industry input on capabilities and readiness to support the transition of the National Airspace System (NAS) and its Air Traffic Control infrastructure, and of FAA business systems, to Post-Quantum Cryptography; responses due April 10, 2026.

Main Topic: Request for Information regarding Post-Quantum Cryptography migration strategies for FAA enterprise IT and National Air Space safety-critical systems.
Key Takeaways: FAA seeks industry input on PQC migration for both enterprise IT and safety-critical NAS systems; Transition requires balancing federal mandates with high costs and complex recertification processes; Vendors must address cryptographic agility and hybrid key wrapping capabilities; Migration strategy evaluation includes "One-Stop Shop" vs "Best-of-Breed" approaches; Long-lived data protection (HNDL) is a critical concern for enterprise IT.
Migration Timeline: Response deadline April 10, 2026; CRQC projections less than 10 years
Regions / Bodies: Regions: United States; Bodies: FAA, NIST, CISA, OMB, ICAO, Eurocontrol, RTCA

Standardization Bodies: NIST; ICAO; Eurocontrol; RTCA
Phase Rationale: This document is a Request for Information (RFI) seeking industry input on PQC migration strategies, representing an exploratory/planning phase before final acquisition strategy.
Mandate Level: Mandatory

chunks.title: France — AMF Sets 2026 Priorities, Names Quantum Computing in Cyber Inspections
chunks.content:

Description: AMF's 2026 priorities announcement states that, in the area of cybersecurity, it will support implementation of the European DORA Regulation, conduct inspections of the robustness of regulated market participants' cybersecurity systems, and begin to include anticipation of the impact of quantum computing in these inspections.

Main Topic: The AMF outlines its 2026 strategic priorities, including the integration of quantum computing impact anticipation into cybersecurity inspections for financial market participants.
Key Takeaways: The AMF will include anticipation of quantum computing impact in cybersecurity inspections for 2026; The AMF will support the implementation of the European DORA Regulation on digital operational resilience; The AMF will finalize its roadmap on artificial intelligence for the financial sector; The AMF will accompany the transition to the MiCA regime with the transitional period ending on 30 June 2026

Migration Urgency: Near-Term

chunks.title: Uruguay — National Cybersecurity Strategy 2024-2030 Commits to Quantum-Resistant PKI

chunks.title: United States — HAWK Withdrawn from the Additional Signatures Process
chunks.content:
Country: United States

chunks.content:

Type: Milestone | Phase: Deadline
Period: 2029–2029
Title: CII Full PQC Adoption Deadline
Description: Milestone 3 (Full PQC Adoption) for Critical Information Infrastructure sectors — government, strategic, defence, power, telecom, transport and BFSI — by 31 December 2029: complete enterprise-wide PQC/hybrid (classical + PQC) adoption, operate PQC-only trust chains and ensure all digital signatures are quantum-safe, making PQC the default across all systems and business processes. Other enterprises have until 31 December 2033.

Main Topic: A strategic roadmap and testing framework for India's transition to Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) and Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) under the National Quantum Mission.
Key Takeaways: India has established a phased PQC migration roadmap with specific deadlines for Critical Information Infrastructure (CII) and regular enterprises; The National Quantum Mission Task Force has defined a testing and certification framework for PQC products aligned with global standards; Hybrid PQC mechanisms are recommended as the primary mitigation strategy alongside QKD; Vendor readiness and supply chain PQC capability are identified as critical risks to migration timelines; Cryptographic inventory and risk assessment are mandatory preparatory steps before migration.
Migration Timeline: Milestones: 31 Dec 2027: CII Resiliency Organisation Preparatory stage; 31 Dec 2028: CII Migration of High Priority Systems; 31 Dec 2029: CII Full PQC Adoption; 31 Dec 2033: Regular Enterprises Full PQC Adoption

chunks.content:
Country: United States
Organization: National Institute of Standards and Technology
Type: Milestone | Phase: Standardization
Period: 2026–2026
Title: NIST IR 8547 Final Published
Description: NIST publishes the final NIST IR 8547, Transition to Post-Quantum Cryptography Standards, replacing the November 2024 initial public draft. It deprecates quantum-vulnerable public-key algorithms (RSA, ECDSA and finite-field or elliptic-curve DH and MQV at 112 bits of security or more; EdDSA at 128 bits or more) after 2030 and disallows them under NIST standards and guidelines after 2035, recommends ML-KEM-768 as the default ML-KEM parameter set, and supports the federal deadlines set by Executive Order 14412 and OMB M-26-15.

Main Topic: NIST’s approach to transitioning from quantum-vulnerable cryptographic algorithms to post-quantum digital signature algorithms and key-establishment schemes.
Key Takeaways: NIST has published a final report detailing the transition from quantum-vulnerable to post-quantum cryptographic standards; The report identifies existing quantum-vulnerable standards and the quantum-resistant standards to which IT products and services must transition; The report supports the implementation of Executive Order 14412 and OMB Memorandum M-26-15; Federal agencies are directed to prioritize the migration of their most sensitive systems to post-quantum cryptography

Compliance Frameworks: Executive Order 14412; OMB Memorandum M-26-15
Standardization Bodies: NIST

Mandate Level: Mandatory
Sector Applicability: Government
Migration Urgency: Near-Term
Historical Significance: This is the final publication of NIST IR 8547, providing the definitive technical roadmap for the US federal government's transition to post-quantum cryptography in response to Executive Order 14412.
Dependencies: Requires implementation of Executive Order 14412 and OMB Memorandum M-26-15; Enables migration of federal agency sensitive systems to post-quantum cryptography.

Title: TCG TPM 2.0 Library Specification V185 — Part 2: Structures
Description: Definitions of the constants, flags, structures and unions used to communicate with the TPM in Version 185 (published March 12, 2026). chunks.title: Transition to Post-Quantum Cryptography Standards
chunks.content:
Reference: NIST IR 8547
Title: Transition to Post-Quantum Cryptography Standards
Description: NIST's final transition plan (October 2026) for moving from quantum-vulnerable public-key algorithms to post-quantum standards. Every quantum-vulnerable signature and key-establishment parameter set in NIST standards (RSA, ECDSA and finite-field or elliptic-curve DH and MQV at 112 bits of classical security or more; EdDSA at 128 bits or more) is deprecated after 2030 and disallowed under NIST standards and guidelines after 2035. ML-KEM-768 is the recommended default ML-KEM parameter set, HQC becomes approved once its FIPS is published, and a hybrid key-establishment scheme can be FIPS 140-validated when at least one input comes from an approved scheme. It supports Executive Order 14412 and OMB M-26-15, which set earlier federal deadlines for the most sensitive systems: post-quantum key establishment by 31 December 2030 and signatures by 31 December 2031.

chunks.title: PKCS #11 Specification Version 3.2 (OASIS Standard)
chunks.content:
Reference: PKCS11-V32-OS-OASIS
Title: PKCS #11 Specification Version 3.2 (OASIS Standard)
Description: PKCS#11 v3.2 finalized as an OASIS Standard (3 June 2026), technically identical in content to the prior Committee Specification Draft 01 / Committee Specification 01 — no substantive changes after Working Draft 13 (16 April 2025) per the spec's own Appendix C Revision History. Adds post-quantum mechanisms: ML-KEM (CKM_ML_KEM 0x00000017, CKM_ML_KEM_KEY_PAIR_GEN 0x0000000f), ML-DSA (CKM_ML_DSA 0x0000001d, CKM_ML_DSA_KEY_PAIR_GEN 0x0000001c, CKM_HASH_ML_DSA_*), and SLH-DSA (CKM_SLH_DSA, CKM_SLH_DSA_KEY_PAIR_GEN). Introduces C_EncapsulateKey() and C_DecapsulateKey() for KEM operations, and C_WrapKeyAuthenticated()/C_UnwrapKeyAuthenticated(). New key types: CKK_ML_KEM (0x49), CKK_ML_DSA (0x4a), CKK_SLH_DSA (0x4b). New attributes: CKA_PARAMETER_SET, CKA_ENCAPSULATE, CKA_DECAPSULATE, CKA_SEED.

chunks.content:
Reference: OpenID4VP-Spec
Title: OpenID for Verifiable Presentations 1.0
Description: OpenID4VP 1.0 defines an OAuth 2.0-based mechanism for requesting and delivering credential presentations. It supports multiple credential formats, DCQL queries, cryptographic and non-cryptographic holder-binding models, and use with the Digital Credentials API. The specification does not mention EUDI or by itself mandate use in EUDI Wallet flows; deployment profiles determine applicability and allowed cryptographic algorithms.

chunks.content:
Reference: IETF-Token-Status-List
Title: OAuth Status List (draft-ietf-oauth-status-list-20)
Description: IETF specification for a compact bit-array status list to check validity states of credentials (valid revoked suspended). Provides privacy-preserving revocation: the verifier cannot determine which specific credential is being checked from the status list position alone. Used in EUDI Wallet ecosystem for credential revocation checking without revealing holder identity to the issuer.

chunks.title: Rosenpass: Formally Verified Post-Quantum Protocol for WireGuard
chunks.content:
Reference: Rosenpass-Protocol
Title: Rosenpass: Formally Verified Post-Quantum Protocol for WireGuard
Description: Defines the Rosenpass protocol for adding post-quantum key exchange to WireGuard. Runs a separate handshake that combines Classic McEliece 460896 (static keys) with Kyber-512 (ephemeral keys), both NIST round-3 submissions rather than the FIPS 203 ML-KEM standard, and passes the resulting key to WireGuard as a pre-shared key (PSK). Handshake packages are 1092, 1132 and 176 bytes, plus a 64-byte EmptyData acknowledgement. Security is analysed symbolically with ProVerif; a CryptoVerif proof is in progress.

Authors: Rosenpass e.V.

chunks.title: JSON Web Key (JWK)
chunks.content:
Reference: RFC 7517
Title: JSON Web Key (JWK)
Description: Defines the JWK format for representing cryptographic keys as JSON. JWKS endpoints publish public keys for JWT signature verification. PQC migration significantly increases JWKS response sizes: ML-DSA-65 public keys are 1952 bytes vs 65 bytes for P-256, challenging HTTP header limits and caching strategies.

chunks.title: The OAuth 2.0 Authorization Framework
chunks.content:
Reference: RFC 6749
Title: The OAuth 2.0 Authorization Framework
Description: Defines the OAuth 2.0 authorization framework enabling secure delegated access using access tokens. Access tokens and ID tokens issued by authorization servers are typically JWTs signed with RSA or ECDSA. PQC migration requires updating JWT signing across all OAuth authorization servers and resource server token validation.

chunks.content:

Description: Defines DPoP for binding OAuth 2.0 tokens to a client public key using signed proof-of-possession JWTs. DPoP proof JWTs use ECDSA signatures that are quantum-vulnerable. chunks.content:
Reference: Europol-FS-ISAC-PQC-Financial-2026
Title: Prioritising Post-Quantum Cryptography Migration Activities in Financial Services
Description: Europol, FS-ISAC, and QSFF joint guidance for financial institutions on prioritising PQC migration. Introduces a Quantum Risk Score framework covering shelf life of data, exposure, and severity. Provides migration complexity assessment and cryptographic antipattern identification for financial sector risk management.
Type: Industry Report | Status: Published
Authors: Europol; FS-ISAC; Quantum Safe Financial Forum
Algorithm Family: Lattice-based; Hash-based
Security Levels: 
Migration Urgency: High
Industries: Finance & Banking; Government & Defense
Region: PQC-REGION-EU

Protocols: TLS
Infrastructure Layers: Points of Sale (PoS) terminals; Hardware-intensive use cases; Public key cryptography inventory.
Standardization Bodies: EMVCo; FS-ISAC.
Migration Timeline: Solution availability scales ranging from available now or less than 1 year to uncertain or greater than 3 years; Migration Time Score factors include execution cost and external dependencies with 1 to 3-year roadmaps.

Reference: RFC-9964
Title: RFC 9964 — ML-DSA for JOSE and COSE
Description: This document specifies JSON Object Signing and Encryption (JOSE) and CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE) serializations for Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Standard (ML-DSA) defined in NIST FIPS 204. chunks.title: The Learning with Errors Problem
chunks.content:
Reference: Regev-LWE-Survey
Title: The Learning with Errors Problem

chunks.content:
Reference: VIAVI-PQC-Migration-WP-2026
Title: Testing, Measuring and Managing PQC Migration: The Hidden Cost of Quantum-Safe Security and How to Plan PQC Migration
Description: Real-world scale performance benchmarking of PQC migration using VIAVI TeraVM Security Test on Dell R6625 hardware. Tests ML-KEM-768 hybrid (X25519Kyber768) against classical X25519 on HAProxy TLS and Strongswan IKEv2 VPN. Finds 32% throughput drop, 3500%+ latency increase (web pages 48x slower), and 75% reduction in VPN tunnel setup rate. Covers NGFWs enterprise impact and mitigation via hardware acceleration and TLS session resumption.

chunks.content:
Reference: arXiv-2603-01091-HNDL-Rekeying
Title: Quantifying Harvest-Now-Decrypt-Later Threats: An Empirical Analysis of Rekeying Defences
Description: Empirical analysis of HNDL attack economics across TLS 1.2, TLS 1.3, QUIC, and SSH. Quantifies adversarial storage cost feasibility; proposes aggressive rekeying and hybrid PQC as defences. References production deployments by Cloudflare, Apple PQ3, AWS, and Google Chrome. chunks.content:
Reference: NIST-SP-800-38D
Title: Recommendation for Block Cipher Modes of Operation: Galois/Counter Mode (GCM) and GMAC
Description: NIST SP 800-38D specifies GCM and GMAC for AES. GCM provides authenticated encryption using a 96-bit (12-byte) nonce and a 16-byte authentication tag appended to ciphertext. Nonce uniqueness per key is mandatory — reuse lets an attacker recover the keystream and forge authentication tags (SP 800-38D §8). Used as CKM_AES_GCM in PKCS#11 v3.2.

chunks.content:
Reference: IETF RFC 5649
Title: Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) Key Wrap with Padding Algorithm
Description: RFC 5649 extends RFC 3394 AES Key Wrap with a padding scheme for arbitrary-length plaintexts. The 8-byte Alternative Initial Value (AIV) includes a fixed 4-byte constant (0xA65959A6) and a 4-byte plaintext length. Wrapping a 32-byte DEK produces 48 bytes. Used as CKM_AES_KEY_WRAP_KWP in PKCS#11 v3.2.

chunks.title: HMAC-based Extract-and-Expand Key Derivation Function (HKDF)
chunks.content:
Reference: RFC 5869
Title: HMAC-based Extract-and-Expand Key Derivation Function (HKDF)
Description: RFC 5869 defines HKDF: HKDF-Extract(salt, IKM) → PRK binds input keying material to a salt; HKDF-Expand(PRK, info, L) derives L bytes bound to a context string preventing cross-protocol key reuse (§3.2). Used in TLS 1.3, IKEv2, and PQC envelope encryption to derive AES wrapping keys from ML-KEM shared secrets per SP 800-56C Rev 2 §4.

Public comment period closes June 16, 2026.

Authors: NIST; Quynh Dang; Dustin Moody; Andrew Regenscheid; Hamilton Silberg

Title: How to factor 2048 bit RSA integers with less than a million noisy qubits
Description: This arXiv preprint estimates that RSA-2048 could be factored in less than a week with fewer than one million noisy qubits under stated assumptions, including a 0.1% gate error rate, one-microsecond surface-code cycles and ten-microsecond control reaction time. chunks.content:
Reference: ref-kim-ecdlp
Title: New Quantum Circuits for ECDLP: Breaking Prime Elliptic Curve Cryptography
Description: This Cryptology ePrint preprint proposes lower-depth Shor circuits for prime-field ECDLP and reports model-based fault-tolerant estimates. One example estimates P-224 at 1.4 minutes with about 107 million physical qubits or 14.3 hours with about 670000 physical qubits. These are conditional resource estimates from a non-peer-reviewed preprint, not evidence that the required hardware exists or a universal break time for elliptic-curve cryptography.

chunks.content:
Reference: ref-pont-downtime
Title: Downtime Required for Bitcoin Quantum-Safety
Description: This arXiv preprint models one Bitcoin transition scenario and calculates a non-tight lower bound of 1827.96 cumulative downtime hours under its assumptions. The result is an analytical lower bound, not an operational plan, observed outage or mandatory migration schedule. Its statement about quantum devices arriving within a decade is an author premise, not an established deadline.

chunks.content:
Reference: arXiv-2603-28627
Title: Shor's Algorithm is Possible with as Few as 10,000 Reconfigurable Atomic Qubits
Description: Demonstrates that Shor's algorithm for breaking RSA and ECC can be executed with as few as ~10,000 reconfigurable neutral atom qubits — an order of magnitude fewer than prior estimates. Reference: RFC-6750
Title: RFC 6750
Description: This specification describes how to use bearer tokens in HTTP requests to access OAuth 2.0 protected resources.  Any party in possession of a bearer token (a "bearer") can use it to get access to the associated resources (without demonstrating possession of a cryptographic key).  To prevent misuse, bearer tokens need to be protected from disclosure in storage and in transport. [STANDARDS-TRACK]

Title: Transport Layer Security (TLS) Cached Information Extension
Description: Defines the TLS cached_info extension, also applicable to DTLS, so peers can identify previously cached certificate or certificate-request data by fingerprint and omit unchanged handshake payloads. It reduces repeat-handshake bandwidth but does not change the certificate's signature algorithm or make a classical certificate post-quantum secure. PQCtoday migration note: caching can reduce repeated transmission of large certificate chains, but it is not a substitute for PQ-capable authentication and certificate formats.

sourcePassages: The current version of the Internet Key Exchange Version 2 (IKEv2) protocol, specified in RFC 7296, supports traditional digital signatures.
This document specifies a generic mechanism for integrating post- quantum cryptographic (PQC) digital signature algorithms into the IKEv2 protocol.
it outlines how Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signatures (ML-DSA) and Stateless Hash-Based Digital Signatures (SLH- DSA), can be employed as authentication methods within the IKEv2 protocol
This document specifies the use of pure mode for signature-based authentication in IKEv2, where the message is signed directly along with domain separation information.
PQC signature algorithms are generally modeled to achieve strong unforgeability under adaptive chosen-message attacks

Reference: TCG-PC-Client-Platform-TPM-Profile-v1.07
Title: TCG PC Client Specific Platform TPM Profile for TPM 2.0, Version 1.07 (Published)
Description: TCG PC Client Platform TPM Profile for TPM 2.0, Version 1.07 (23 March 2026), written against TPM Library version 185. Makes ML-KEM and ML-DSA mandatory for PC platform TPMs (the TPM must support ML-KEM-768 or ML-KEM-1024 and ML-DSA-65 or ML-DSA-87), requires a TPM that ships with EK certificates to carry one for RSA 3072 or ECC P-384 together with one for ML-KEM-768 or ML-KEM-1024, and adds chunked transfer to the CRB interface for the larger post-quantum commands and responses.

chunks.content:
Reference: draft-ietf-tls-cert-abridge
Title: Abridging Certificate Chains in TLS
Description: Proposed TLS Certificate Compression scheme using a shared dictionary of root and intermediate WebPKI certificates. chunks.content:

Title: FAEST: Fast AES-based Tight Signature (Round 2 Specification)
Description: AES-based MPC-in-the-Head signature using the VOLE-in-the-Head paradigm. Security reduces directly to AES — the most-studied symmetric cipher in existence — making FAEST the most conservative foundation among the MPCitH candidates. chunks.content:
Reference: SDitH-Round2-Spec
Title: SDitH: Syndrome Decoding in the Head (Round 2 Specification)
Description: MPC-in-the-Head signature built on the syndrome decoding problem for random linear codes over finite fields — one of the most-studied hard problems in code-based cryptography, dating to McEliece (1978). chunks.content:
Reference: UOV-Round2-Spec
Title: UOV: Unbalanced Oil and Vinegar (Round 2 Specification)
Description: Original UOV construction by Kipnis-Patarin-Goubin (1999). Public key is a system of multivariate quadratic polynomials with the secret oil/vinegar partition hidden inside. Tiny 96 B signatures at NIST L1; large public key (~66 KB raw, ~1.2 KB compressed) and private key (~237 KB). 2025 Ran wedge attack pushed three of four parameter sets (uov-Ip, uov-III, uov-V) below their security targets; reparameterisation in odd-characteristic fields restores security.

chunks.content:
Reference: SQIsign-Round2-Spec
Title: SQIsign: Compact Signatures from Quaternions and Isogenies (Round 2 v2.0 Specification)
Description: Isogeny-based signature scheme — the only post-quantum candidate built on supersingular elliptic-curve isogenies. Smallest combined public-key+signature of any PQC candidate by a wide margin: SQIsign-I (NIST L1) is pk=64 B, sig=177 B (up from 148 B in Round 1, traded for a 20× signing speedup). Round 2 redesign switched to higher-dimensional isogenies, simplifying the security analysis and dramatically improving performance. chunks.title: HAWK: Module Lattice Isomorphism Signature (Round 2 Specification)
chunks.content:
Reference: HAWK-Round2-Spec
Title: HAWK: Module Lattice Isomorphism Signature (Round 2 Specification)
Description: Lattice signature that eliminates FN-DSA's floating-point Gaussian-sampling pain — pure integer arithmetic on a rank-2 module lattice with a Gram matrix as the public key. Compact 555 B signatures at NIST L1 — smaller than both ML-DSA and FN-DSA — and dramatically easier to implement in constant time on constrained hardware. Security rests on newer assumptions: the Search Module Lattice Isomorphism Problem (smLIP) and the One-More-Shortest-Vector Problem (omSVP). NIST flagged these for further community analysis; Round 2 included a refined omSVP definition addressing a discrepancy found during evaluation.

chunks.title: PQC Continuity: Downgrade Protection for TLS
chunks.content:
Reference: draft-sheffer-tls-pqc-continuity
Title: PQC Continuity: Downgrade Protection for TLS
Description: Proposes a TLS-layer mechanism for servers to make a cached commitment that they support PQC key exchange. Clients that have cached the commitment refuse future connections that omit PQC, providing protection against active MITM downgrade attacks that suppress ML-KEM negotiation during the quantum transition. Introduces the concept of a downgrade limit (cached duration) analogous to HSTS for HTTP.

chunks.title: Circle's Post-Quantum Security Roadmap: Securing blockchains smart contracts and digital assets for the quantum era
chunks.content:
Reference: Circle-PQC-Roadmap-2026
Title: Circle's Post-Quantum Security Roadmap: Securing blockchains smart contracts and digital assets for the quantum era
Description: Three-phase PQC migration roadmap for Circle (USDC issuer) and the Arc blockchain. Catalogs seven quantum attack vectors on the full blockchain stack (at-rest forgery via EVM ecrecover; retroactive privacy loss; consensus disruption; history rewrite; P2P session compromise via libp2p/Noise; RPC interception; on-spend). Readiness phase: SLH-DSA-SHA2-128s on-chain precompile for smart-account signature verification; X-Wing hybrid KEM (ML-KEM-768 + X25519) for TLS 1.3 and encrypted memos; TEE-based private execution environment (AWS Nitro/SGX/TDX). Transition phase: dual-mode USDC smart contracts; post-quantum ecrecover override; multi-sig cold storage; encrypted mempool. Switch phase: full PQ validator signatures; account recovery (dual-key BIP-39 derivation; TEE-attested ZK proof; off-chain). Policy section covers quantum flag day regulatory implications for stranded USDC assets. Co-authored with Dan Boneh (Stanford).

Description: Three-author governance and systems-architecture analysis of organizational identity in the PQC transition. chunks.title: Exploiting ML-DSA bugs
chunks.content:
Reference: Bernstein-MLDSA-Bugs-2026
Title: Exploiting ML-DSA bugs
Description: Cryptanalysis paper by Daniel J. Bernstein demonstrating exploitability of ML-DSA software vulnerabilities. Reproduces two distinct bug patterns (Dilithium 1.0 implementation flaw + PlayStation 3 ECDSA-style randomness reuse) as ML-DSA software variants, each forging signatures in ~1 second on a laptop core. Provides open-source attack demos that recover equivalent secret keys from public keys + a small number of signatures. Estimates breakable-key rates over time for ML-DSA solo vs. Ed25519+ML-DSA hybrid, arguing quantitatively for hybrid signature deployment.

chunks.title: Delegated Credentials for TLS and DTLS
chunks.content:
Reference: RFC-9345
Title: Delegated Credentials for TLS and DTLS
Description: Defines a TLS 1.3-or-later mechanism allowing a certificate holder to issue a short-lived delegated credential for TLS or DTLS authentication while retaining compatibility with peers that do not support it. The credential is bound to the end-entity certificate, is normally limited to seven days absent another application profile, and has no independent early-revocation mechanism. It can decouple an endpoint signature algorithm from CA issuance support, but the RFC does not itself define a PQ algorithm or PQ migration requirement.

chunks.title: ENISA — SBOM Adoption State of Play 2026: Survey Results and Analysis
chunks.content:
Reference: ENISA-SBOM-Adoption-2026
Title: ENISA — SBOM Adoption State of Play 2026: Survey Results and Analysis
Description: ENISA survey-based analysis of Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) adoption across the EU (June 2026). Reports survey results on adoption readiness, formats (SPDX/CycloneDX), tooling and SDLC lifecycle integration, barriers and supplier requirements; finds the EU Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) is the primary accelerator, with 79% of organisations expecting to reach SBOM maturity before the CRA becomes fully applicable. Foundational to crypto-asset inventory and CBOM for PQC migration.

Authors: ENISA; European Union Agency for Cybersecurity

Title: Executive Order 14412 (June 22, 2026): Securing the Nation Against Advanced Cryptographic Attacks
Description: U.S. Executive Order signed June 22 2026 mandating federal post-quantum migration: agencies name a PQC migration lead within 30 days; OMB issues guidance to inventory High Value Assets and submit migration plans within 90 days; a NIST migration pilot completes by 2027; HVAs and high-impact systems transition to PQC for key establishment (FIPS 203) by Dec 31 2030 and digital signatures (FIPS 204) by Dec 31 2031; covered contractors comply by 2030; CISA and NIST publish CBOM minimum elements and accelerate FIPS 140-3 validation.

Published: 2026-06-22 | Updated: 2026-06-22

Standardization Bodies: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)

chunks.content:
Reference: draft-ietf-jose-hpke-encrypt
Title: Use of Hybrid Public Key Encryption (HPKE) with JOSE
Description: Defines how JWE uses HPKE in two modes: Integrated Encryption (HPKE encrypts the payload; the header carries only "alg", the JWE Encrypted Key is the encapsulated secret, IV and tag are empty) and Key Encryption (HPKE wraps the CEK; the encapsulated secret goes in "ek"). chunks.content:
Reference: KLEPTO-2022-Kyber-Backdoor
Title: Backdooring Post-Quantum Cryptography: Kleptographic Attacks on Lattice-based KEMs
Description: Practical kleptographic (SETUP) backdoor demonstrated in Kyber/ML-KEM key generation — the generated public key covertly leaks the secret key to whoever holds the backdoor key. Validated end-to-end on TLS 1.3. A deliberately-subverted implementation, not a math or quantum-computer break: proof that a correctly-specified PQC algorithm can still be broken today via a compromised implementation or supply chain.

chunks.content:

Title: SALSA: Attacking Lattice Cryptography with Transformers
Description: First published use of transformer models (the same architecture family behind modern LLMs) to attack LWE-based lattice cryptography — recovers sparse binary secrets for small-to-mid LWE dimensions (up to n=128). Does not threaten standardized ML-KEM/ML-DSA parameter sets, but establishes AI-assisted cryptanalysis as an active, real research direction against lattice-based PQC, not a hypothetical one.

chunks.title: On the Practical Exploitability of Dual EC in TLS Implementations
chunks.content:
Reference: KLEPTO-2014-DualEC-Backdoor
Title: On the Practical Exploitability of Dual EC in TLS Implementations
Description: The definitive practical demonstration of the NSA-inserted Dual_EC_DRBG kleptographic backdoor (Young-Yung SETUP construction, applied to an elliptic-curve PRNG) working end-to-end against real TLS implementations, including RSA BSAFE and OpenSSL-FIPS. sourcePassages: Brotee and Subasish Das Abstract: Post-quantum cryptography (PQC) is moving from evaluation to deployment as NIST finalizes standards for ML-KEM, ML-DSA, and SLH-DSA. This survey maps the space
upward, we examine protocol integration (TLS, DNSSEC), PKI and certificate hygiene, and deployment in constrained and high-assurance environments (IoT, cloud, finance, blockchain). We also

chunks.content:
Reference: Sigstore-Algorithm-Registry
Title: Sigstore Algorithm Registry (architecture-docs)
Description: Sigstore's source of truth for algorithms recommended across its ecosystem. Clients are not required to implement every listed algorithm and may implement others; compatibility with the Public Good Instance requires at least one registry algorithm. ML-DSA-44/65/87 pure variants are listed for sign/verify but explicitly marked experimental, not fully functional and not operational within Sigstore. The registry therefore documents integration work, not a production-wide replacement of ECDSA or proof that every Sigstore client supports ML-DSA.

chunks.content:
Reference: PKCS-11-Cryptographic-Token-Interface-Profiles-Version-3-2-O
Title: PKCS #11 Cryptographic Token Interface Profiles Version 3.2 (OASIS Standard)
Description: Defines the conformance profiles that PKCS#11 v3.2 conformance is measured against. Section 7 of the base specification states that an implementation is a conforming Provider only if it meets one or more provider profiles specified here, so the base spec mandates no mechanism on its own. Specifies Baseline Provider, Complete Provider, Extended Provider, Authentication Token, Public Certificates Token and HKDF TLS Token, plus Baseline and Extended Consumer. Baseline Provider requires a CKO_PROFILE object with CKP_BASELINE_PROVIDER and explicitly requires no mechanisms. Edited by Tim Hudson (Cryptsoft); supersedes Profiles v3.1.

Reference: PKCS-11-Cryptographic-Token-Interface-Usage-Guide-Version-3
Title: PKCS #11 Cryptographic Token Interface Usage Guide Version 3.2
Description: Companion guidance to PKCS#11 v3.2 and a normative reference of it. v3.2 moved the session-state model, the user/login model and the object-access matrix out of the base specification and into this document — the spec says only that CK_STATE holds the session state 'as described in [PKCS11-UG]'. Auditing session, login or private-object access behaviour against the base specification alone will therefore find no governing text. Note the process asymmetry: this is a non-standards-track Committee Note that the Standard nevertheless cites normatively. Edited by Dieter Bong (Utimaco); supersedes the v2.40 Usage Guide.
Type: Standard | Status: OASIS Committee Note 01
Authors: OASIS PKCS11 Technical Committee
Algorithm Family: 
Security Levels: 
Migration Urgency: Medium
Industries: HSM Vendors; Government; Finance; PKI; Defense
Region: PQC-REGION-GLOBAL
Published: 2025-04-15 | Updated: 2025-04-15

Main Topic: Guidance on using PKCS #11 Version 3.2, including session-state, user/login models, and object-access matrices.

Standardization Bodies: OASIS
Leaders: Valerie Fenwick (Chair); Robert Relyea (Chair); Dieter Bong (Editor); Dina Kurktchi-Nimeh (Substantial contributions)

Description: IACR ePrint / EUROCRYPT 2018 paper introducing Ouroboros Praos, the proof-of-stake consensus protocol Cardano runs. Reference: Wormhole-Docs-VAAs-Guardian-signature-scheme
Title: Wormhole Docs — VAAs (Guardian Signature Scheme)
Description: Official Wormhole documentation for VAAs (Verifiable Action Approvals) — the cross-chain message-attestation format signed by Wormhole's 19-member Guardian network. Each Guardian independently ECDSA-signs a keccak256 double-hash of the message body; once 13 of 19 (two-thirds supermajority) signatures are collected, they are combined with the message into a VAA. A plain M-of-N multisig, not an aggregated threshold signature.

chunks.content:
Reference: Arbitrum-Docs-Inside-AnyTrust-DAC-BLS-signing
Title: Arbitrum Docs — Inside AnyTrust
Description: Official Arbitrum documentation for the AnyTrust protocol. AnyTrust chains use a Data Availability Committee (DAC, N members, 2-of-N honesty assumption): each member signs (data hash, expiry) with a BLS key; once enough signatures are collected the sequencer aggregates them into 'a BLS aggregated signature (over the BLS12-381 curve)' forming a DACert, posted to the L1 inbox contract. No mention of ECDSA for this specific mechanism — it is BLS end to end.

Title: Internet2 report on a PQC backbone demonstration
Description: Internet2 reports a March 2026 demonstration with Ciena and Purism over a 1,390-mile Albuquerque-Las Vegas path, measuring 10 Gbit/s line rate, less than 1 ms latency and jitter, and zero packet loss. chunks.content:

Title: Securosys announcement of the Primus HSM CyberVault series
Description: Securosys announces optional PQC support in its CyberVault series and says the series implements HSS/LMS and XMSS. Description: Cuts the logical-qubit cost of Shor's factoring algorithm by computing approximate modular exponentiations with a Residue Number System, removing the assumption that n-bit arithmetic needs an n-qubit register. Title: Reducing the Number of Qubits in Quantum Discrete Logarithms on Elliptic Curves
Description: Applies the same Residue Number System compression to the elliptic-curve discrete logarithm problem, reaching 3.12n + o(n) qubits — the most space-efficient polynomial-time ECDLP algorithm published. Estimates 1,193 logical qubits for a 256-bit curve at 2^38.98 Toffoli gates across 22 runs, against 2,043 for RSA-3072 at comparable classical security.

Title: Agile, post-quantum secure cryptography in avionics
Description: The authors construct hybrid authenticated key-encapsulation variants for HPKE using X25519 with ML-KEM, and optionally ML-DSA, then integrate them into an ARINC 653 software partition. Title: Evaluation of Time-Critical Communications for IEC 61850 Substation Network Architecture
Description: A 2015 experimental paper measuring GOOSE end-to-end latency on a 100 Mbit/s laboratory substation network. It reports averages of 26 microseconds at 30% load, 310 microseconds at 50% load, and 1.1 milliseconds when sampled-value traffic is added. The paper states that Type 1-A messages require less than four milliseconds, but cites secondary literature for that statement rather than reproducing or validating the normative IEC text. It tests no cryptography or PQC overhead, so use it as historical lab evidence, not a current IEC conformance source or PQC performance budget.

algorithms like RSA and ECC are at risk of becoming obsolete. Recognizing this, the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) led a global effort to standardize PQC

sourcePassages: This document has been prepared by the 3GPP Task Force, and contains an example set of algorithms which may be used as the authentication and key generation functions f1, f1*, f2, f3, f4, f5 and f5*.
(It is not mandatory that the particular algorithms specified in this document are used — all seven functions are operator-specifiable rather than being fully standardised).
Annex 2 gives a specification of the block cipher algorithm which is used as a cryptographic kernel in the definition of the example algorithms.
The example algorithm set makes use of the following components: - A block cipher encryption function, which takes a 128-bit input and a 128-bit key and returns a 128-bit output.
The algorithm set is designed to be secure whether or not OP is publicly known; however, operators may see some advantage in keeping their value of OP secret.

Title: RFC 9925 — Unsigned X.509 Certificates
Description: RFC 9925 defines id-alg-unsigned for X.509 containers used where the consumer is not expected to verify a certificate signature, such as some out-of-band trust-anchor uses. Receivers may accept it only when signatures are not being verified; validators must reject it in a certification path. It updates RFC 5280 and can avoid pointless large self-signatures, but it is not a general way to bypass certificate authentication.

chunks.content:
Reference: TSA-SD-PIPELINE-2021-02G
Title: TSA Security Directive Pipeline-2021-02G
Description: Renews without substantive revision cybersecurity measures for covered critical pipeline and LNG owner/operators. Requirements apply to Critical Cyber Systems and include a TSA-approved Cybersecurity Implementation Plan, incident-response and assessment plans, network segmentation, and access controls using MFA or commensurate compensating controls. The directive specifically requires encryption when OT services are allowed to traverse the IT system; it does not state a general rule that all data in transit must be encrypted. It is not PQC-specific. PQCtoday migration note: any future cryptographic change must be reflected in the operator's approved, scoped implementation plan.

chunks.title: The Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP)
chunks.content:
Reference: RFC-7252
Title: The Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP)
Description: Defines CoAP, a lightweight RESTful request/response protocol for constrained nodes and lossy networks. Its DTLS binding includes NoSec, PreSharedKey, RawPublicKey, and Certificate modes; RawPublicKey is mandatory to implement, and the public-key modes require support for TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_128_CCM_8 with secp256r1. It is not PQC-specific. PQCtoday migration note: deployments using those public-key modes rely on classical elliptic-curve cryptography and need a separately specified transition path.

Title: JSON Web Token (JWT) Profile for OAuth 2.0 Access Tokens
Description: Defines an interoperable JWT profile for OAuth 2.0 access tokens, including required claims, the 'at+jwt' type, and resource-server validation rules. Title: PROFINET Security Whitepaper (PI, V1.05, Feb 2019)
Description: PROFIBUS & PROFINET International white paper (V1.05, Feb 2019) setting out the security concept for PROFINET protocol extensions, aligned with IEC 62443. Defines three PROFINET Security Classes - 1 Robustness (e.g. changeable SNMP default strings, read-only DCP, signed GSD files), 2 Integrity + Authenticity (cryptographically protected cyclic and acyclic communication, confidential configuration data), 3 Confidentiality (adds encryption) - using device certificates for start-up key negotiation and a MAC over cyclic frames (HMAC-SHA256 best performer, not finally selected).

chunks.title: A practical implementation of virtualized protection system with IEC61850 under Docker
chunks.content:
Reference: Torres-ICREPQ-2024-341
Title: A practical implementation of virtualized protection system with IEC61850 under Docker
Description: UPV/EHU conference paper (ICREPQ'24) simulating a Docker-virtualised IEC 61850 substation protection system and showing that adding virtual IEDs raises the tripping communication delay (37 ms baseline, about +3 ms with 1 extra IED and +44 ms with 7). Documents the IEC 61850-5 transfer-time classes TT0-TT6 (TT0 >1000 ms, TT1 1000 ms, TT2 500 ms, TT3 100 ms, TT4 20 ms, TT5 10 ms, TT6 3 ms for trips and blockings).
Type: Research Paper | Status: Published
Authors: E. Torres, N. Escobar, P. Eguia, O. Abarrategi, D.M. Larruskain, V. Valverde, G. Buigues (University of the Basque Country UPV/EHU)

Region: PQC-REGION-GLOBAL

Main Topic: The document presents a practical simulation of a virtualized Substation Automation System (SAS) using Docker to evaluate how the number of virtual IEDs affects communication latency and tripping performance under the IEC 61850 standard.
