The Government & Defense module teaches the federal post-quantum policy layer — the instruments that turn post-quantum cryptography from an engineering preference into a procurement requirement. It covers the CNSA 2.0 suite and precisely what it replaces from CNSA 1.0, the dated CNSSP 15 milestones that bind National Security Systems, the National Security System versus federal civilian distinction that decides which deadline applies to a given system, the Federal PKI certificate profile pair (one published and classical, one draft and post-quantum), and how the requirement propagates outward through procurement to contractors who never touch an NSS. It carries genuine dated deadlines rather than advisory guidance: the CNSSP 15 dates for National Security Systems and, for federal civilian high value assets and high impact systems, the Executive Order 14412 dates.

## Key Concepts

- **CNSA 2.0 replaces every public-key line of CNSA 1.0 and almost nothing else.** Key establishment moves from ECDH P-384 / RSA-3072 to ML-KEM-1024 (FIPS 203); general-purpose signatures move from ECDSA P-384 / RSA-3072 to ML-DSA-87 (FIPS 204); software and firmware signing moves to LMS or XMSS (NIST SP 800-208), with ML-DSA-87 also approved for it. AES-256 is unchanged and SHA-384 becomes SHA-384 or SHA-512. That asymmetry is the central budgeting lesson: "replace all cryptography" is the wrong model, because the symmetric half of the estate survives the transition intact
- **Level-5 parameters only.** CNSA 2.0 approves ML-KEM-1024 and ML-DSA-87 exclusively. ML-KEM-512, ML-KEM-768, ML-DSA-44 and ML-DSA-65 are FIPS-approved but not CNSA 2.0-approved — an NSS-specific narrowing of the NIST standards, not a restatement of them
- **Firmware signing moved first, and NSA said why.** Three stated reasons: NIST had already standardised the algorithms, the use case is more urgent than others, and stateful hash-based signatures have the longest cryptanalytic history — so their performance costs matter least here. LMS and XMSS are the approved SP 800-208 schemes (all parameter sets; NSA recommends LMS with SHA-256/192) and the multi-tree variants HSS and XMSS^MT are not allowed. Validated ML-DSA-87 is also approved for software and firmware signing, but NSA wants LMS and XMSS adopted now where possible because validated implementations have been available longer; ML-DSA can make sense when a signing strategy needs more signatures than a single LMS or XMSS key can reasonably provide, or in distributed signing environments
- **The dated CNSSP 15 milestones** (as stated in the CNSA 2.0 FAQ Ver 2.2, October 2026):
  - **1 January 2027** — CNSA 2.0 algorithms will be required in all new acquisitions for NSS
  - **31 December 2030** — all NSS equipment and services that cannot support CNSA 2.0 must be phased out unless otherwise granted an exception; NSA also expects encryption to be broadly quantum resistant by default by this date
  - **31 December 2031** — CNSA 2.0 algorithms are mandated for use, unless otherwise noted, to achieve full quantum resistance for NSS
  - **2035** — the goal set in NSM-10 for achieving quantum resistance; NSA intends that all NSS will be quantum-resistant well ahead of 2035
- **The advisory and the FAQ state different dates.** The September 2022 advisory carried a per-equipment-type timetable running from 2025 to 2033; the CNSA 2.0 FAQ (Ver 2.2, October 2026) says that the update to CNSSP 15 set several dates and states them as listed above. The FAQ does not restate the advisory's 2033 date
- **NSA does not require hybrids for NSS, and that is not a prohibition.** The FAQ states NSA "has confidence in CNSA 2.0 algorithms and will not require NSS developers to use hybrid certified products for security purposes," while explicitly allowing that "product availability and interoperability requirements may lead to adopting hybrid solutions." This is routinely misreported as a ban. NSA also acknowledges some protocols may need hybrid-like constructions simply to carry the larger ML-KEM-1024 and ML-DSA-87 objects
- **NSA's four stated objections to hybrids**: added protocol and library complexity (extra negotiation, error handling, modified APIs, more testing); interoperability becomes harder because every party must share both component algorithms _and_ the hybridisation method; it buys a second transition later when classical components are eventually dropped; and more security products fail from implementation flaws than from cryptanalysis, so added complexity is itself a risk. These are the strongest published arguments against the hybrid-by-default posture most of the commercial world has adopted — and the opposite of what ETSI specifies for European trust services
- **Naming drift is an inventory problem.** The September 2022 advisory names the algorithms CRYSTALS-Kyber and CRYSTALS-Dilithium because FIPS 203/204 did not exist yet; the October 2026 FAQ (Ver 2.2) calls the same algorithms ML-KEM-1024 and ML-DSA-87. The two documents name the same algorithms differently. Estate inventory tooling must search both vocabularies, because a search for "Kyber" will not find documents written after standardisation
- **NSS and federal civilian are governed by different instruments.** CNSSP 15 carries the CNSA 2.0 dates and binds National Security Systems. Federal civilian agencies follow the Quantum Computing Cybersecurity Preparedness Act, OMB M-23-02 / M-26-15 and Executive Order 14412 (22 June 2026): inventory, reporting and migration plans, plus **dated PQC deadlines for high value assets and high impact systems** — key establishment by 31 December 2030 and digital signatures by 31 December 2031 — which exclude National Security Systems, whose CNSSP 15 requirements and timelines NSA describes as comparable. Which stack applies to a system is the first question to answer, because it determines which dates apply
- **The federal mandate stack**:
  - **Quantum Computing Cybersecurity Preparedness Act (2022)** — Law. Federal civilian executive-branch agencies. Requires inventory of CRQC-vulnerable cryptographic systems and migration, with OMB reporting. The statute is what makes the rest of the stack enforceable rather than advisory
  - **OMB M-23-02** — To comply with NSM-10, directs agencies to submit a prioritised inventory of CRQC-vulnerable cryptographic systems (excluding National Security Systems) by 4 May 2023 and annually thereafter until 2035, or as directed by superseding guidance
  - **OMB M-26-15** — Implements the accelerated migration set by Executive Order 14412 (22 June 2026), and fulfils OMB's responsibility under the QCCPA to issue guidance directing each agency to prioritise critical IT for migration to PQC and to plan that migration. Each agency submits a PQC migration plan within 120 days, phased from discovery (2026–2027) through pilots (2027–2028), prioritised key-establishment migration (2028–2030) and signature migration (2031) to full migration (2035). It does not apply to National Security Systems
  - **Executive Order 14306** — Sustains and amends prior federal cybersecurity direction, including the PQC provisions driving the CISA product-category work
  - **Executive Order 14412 (22 June 2026)** — Section 4(b) directs OMB to require agencies to move all high value assets and high impact systems (not National Security Systems) to PQC for key establishment by 31 December 2030 and for digital signatures by 31 December 2031. Section 6(c) directs the FAR Council to publish, within 180 days, a proposed rule requiring covered contractors to comply by 31 December 2030 with NIST FIPS, including all applicable FIPS incorporating PQC-compliant algorithms; the order directs a proposed rule, it is not itself that rule
  - **CNSS Policy 15** — The instrument that actually carries the CNSA 2.0 dates, for National Security Systems
  - **NIST SP 800-171 Rev. 3** — Reaches nonfederal systems processing Controlled Unclassified Information: contractors, universities and suppliers who never touch an NSS. NIST states that it supersedes Rev. 2 (February 2020), but DoD's CMMC briefing (cleared for open publication 21 January 2025) says CMMC assessments remain against Rev. 2 until DoD formally adopts Rev. 3 through rulemaking
- **Federal PKI has two certificate profiles, and only one is binding.** The Common Policy X.509 Certificate and CRL Profile is published, in force, and classical (RSA, SHA). A separate PQC profile dated **21 April 2026** is a **DRAFT**, adding ML-DSA and ML-KEM for CITE testing starting from v2.2 of the Common Policy profiles. A draft is not contractually bindable — teaching the pair side by side is crypto agility as an actual document lifecycle rather than a slogan. Separately, the Federal PKI page announced that the Federal Bridge Certification Authority (FBCA) G4 would be replaced by the FBCA G5 starting 27 August 2026 to meet federal cryptographic-strength requirements (applications may need new intermediate CA certificates in their trust stores), and under the Common Policy CA private keys must be held in cryptographic modules validated to at least FIPS 140 Level 3
- **The 1 January 2027 date is a requirement with exceptions, not an automatic ban.** CNSA 2.0 algorithms will be required in all new NSS acquisitions; the FAQ (version 2.2, October 2026) says that where no CNSA 2.0 compliant product meeting the need is available on 1 January 2027, a deployment may, if needed, be accepted on a vendor's contractual commitment to provide a CNSA 2.0 update, combined with a realistic deployment plan that prioritises partial quantum resistance and meets the 2030 deadline for full quantum resistance, and NIAP Policy Letter #33 (effective 1 January 2027) says government contracts must include language requiring products used in NSS to implement PQC or be updateable to implement PQC
- **The CSfC PQC Guidance Addendum is a draft.** Version 1.0 draft .5 (4 April 2025) sets out a planned timeline, subject to change, that aims for all CSfC solutions to implement post-quantum cryptography by 2030. NSA's CNSA 2.0 FAQ (version 2.2, October 2026) says NIAP will begin archiving the certificates of partially quantum-resistant and quantum-vulnerable products generally within a year of fully quantum-resistant products coming on the market, that it expects this archiving to start in late 2027, and that products with archived certificates will not comply with CNSSP 11 and will not be appropriate for NSS
- **Algorithm support is not the only procurement gate.** CNSSP 11 requires commercial IA and IA-enabled IT products bought to protect information on NSS to comply with the NIAP program (agencies select evaluated products from the NIAP Product Compliant List) and, where applicable, the FIPS cryptographic validation programs; the CNSA 2.0 FAQ says NIAP and FIPS validation are required in most circumstances
- **The CISA PQC product category list is broader than CNSA 2.0.** It names ML-KEM (FIPS 203), ML-DSA (FIPS 204), SLH-DSA (FIPS 205) and the stateful hash-based signatures of SP 800-208, and says organizations should acquire only PQC-capable products in the categories it lists as widely available; NSA does not approve SLH-DSA, HSS or XMSS^MT for National Security Systems

## Workshop / Interactive Activities

The workshop has 3 hands-on tools:

1. **CNSA 1.0 → 2.0 Suite Comparator** — which suite lines are replaced and which survive, with NSA's own stated rationale per line. Makes the "symmetric primitives survive" point concrete rather than asserted
2. **Federal Mandate Explorer** — pick a system type and see which instruments bind it, and critically, whether it has a dated deadline at all
3. **Federal PKI Profile Pair** — the classical certificate profile beside the draft PQC profile, and why a draft cannot be cited as binding

## Related Standards

CNSSP 15 carries the dates for National Security Systems. The QCCPA and OMB M-23-02 / M-26-15 carry inventory, reporting and migration-plan obligations for federal civilian systems, and Executive Order 14412 sets dated PQC deadlines for their high value assets and high impact systems (key establishment by 31 December 2030, digital signatures by 31 December 2031). NIST SP 800-171 Rev. 3 reaches nonfederal systems handling Controlled Unclassified Information (DoD's CMMC briefing, cleared for open publication 21 January 2025, says CMMC assessments remain against Rev. 2 until DoD formally adopts Rev. 3 through rulemaking), and Executive Order 14412 directs a proposed FAR rule requiring covered contractors to comply with NIST FIPS, including all applicable FIPS incorporating PQC-compliant algorithms, by 31 December 2030. CNSSP 11 requires commercial IA and IA-enabled IT products bought for National Security Systems to comply with the NIAP program and, where applicable, the FIPS cryptographic validation programs, and NIAP Policy Letter #33 sets the timeline for post-quantum requirements in NIAP evaluations. The Federal PKI Common Policy certificate profile is in force and classical; a draft profile dated 21 April 2026 adds ML-DSA and ML-KEM for CITE testing. Underlying algorithm standards are FIPS 203 (ML-KEM), FIPS 204 (ML-DSA), FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA, named by the CISA list but not approved for NSS) and NIST SP 800-208 (LMS/XMSS). RFC 8603 profiles the earlier CNSA suite for X.509. Related guidance includes the NSA CSfC PQC Guidance Addendum (draft), the CISA PQC product category list (2026) and the CMMC 2.0 model.

Cross-reference: the **Hybrid Cryptography** module reaches a different default — hybrid recommended or mandated — and the **Trust Services** module covers ETSI TS 119 312 V2.1.1, which incorporates PQC transition requirements, including hybrid cryptographic schemes. Same algorithms, different authorities, different defaults. Which applies is a jurisdiction question, not a cryptography question.

chunks.title: Healthcare PQC — Module Summary
chunks.content:
# Healthcare PQC — Module Summary

## Overview

Intermediate-level module (60 min, 5 workshop steps) covering post-quantum cryptography migration for the healthcare industry — a sector with the highest density of irreplaceable biometric data, long data retention requirements (PHI, genomic records), life-critical medical device security, and complex regulatory obligations under HIPAA, GDPR Article 9, and FDA cybersecurity guidance.

## Key Topics

- **Biometric data profiles and irreplaceability**: Healthcare holds uniquely irreplaceable biometric data — unlike passwords, biometrics cannot be rotated when compromised. PQC protection priority is driven by replaceability and lifetime sensitivity:
  - Fingerprint (512-byte template, irreplaceable — unique ridge patterns, recommend ML-KEM-768 + ML-DSA-65)
  - Iris (256-byte template, irreplaceable — stable for life, unique per person, ML-KEM-768 + ML-DSA-65)
  - Facial Geometry (2,048-byte template, partially replaceable with difficulty — angle/aging variants, ML-KEM-768 + ML-DSA-65)
  - Voiceprint (4,096-byte template, irreplaceable — voice patterns change gradually with age but remain matchable for 20+ years; compromised voiceprints enable long-term spoofing of voice-authenticated medical commands, ML-KEM-768 + ML-DSA-44)
  - DNA-SNP profile (5 MB genomic data, truly irreplaceable — single lifetime record, highest risk, ML-KEM-1024 + ML-DSA-87)
  - Retinal scan (384-byte template, irreplaceable — vessel patterns are stable and unique, ML-KEM-768 + ML-DSA-65)
- **Pharmaceutical IP and HNDL risk windows**: Drug compound structures (20-year patent protection — active development data encrypted today is HNDL-exposed during critical patent window), clinical trial data (FDA 21 CFR Part 11 governs electronic records and signatures and requires audit trails to be kept at least as long as the records they cover; the retention period itself comes from the applicable predicate rule — for IND investigators, 21 CFR 312.62(c): 2 years after the marketing application is approved, or 2 years after the investigation is discontinued and FDA is notified — plus sponsor, jurisdiction and contract terms, such as the EU Clinical Trials Regulation 536/2014 Art. 58 minimum of 25 years for the trial master file; determine the period before sizing HNDL exposure), genomic research datasets (participant-linked data stays sensitive for the participant's lifetime and affects relatives, among the longest HNDL exposures in healthcare; the module models it as a 75-year site estimate)
- **Patient privacy regulatory landscape**: HIPAA Security Rule (45 CFR § 164.312 — encryption and decryption of electronic PHI under the access-control standard, and encryption of electronic PHI in transmission, are each an "addressable" implementation specification: implement it if reasonable and appropriate, or document why not and implement an equivalent alternative measure if reasonable and appropriate), HIPAA's 18 direct identifiers that constitute PHI, GDPR Article 9 special category data (biometric and genetic data may be processed only under an Article 9(2) condition such as explicit consent, health-care provision or research, with appropriate safeguards), GDPR Right to Erasure (Article 17) conflicts with blockchain-based health record immutability, a 6-year retention requirement for HIPAA compliance documentation such as policies, procedures and risk assessments (45 CFR § 164.316(b)(2)); how long the medical records themselves are kept is set by state law and is often longer
- **Medical device security**: FDA premarket cybersecurity guidance (current edition 3 February 2026, first issued September 2023 — nonbinding recommendations, including cryptography that is expected to stay cryptographically strong throughout the service life of the device; the guidance does not name quantum computers or PQC algorithms). Section 524B of the FD&C Act separately requires sponsors of "cyber devices" — devices that include software, can connect to the internet and could be vulnerable to cybersecurity threats — to submit a plan to monitor, identify and address postmarket vulnerabilities (including coordinated vulnerability disclosure), to design, develop and maintain processes and procedures that give reasonable assurance that the device and related systems are cybersecure, and to provide a software bill of materials (SBOM), in 510(k), PMA, PDP, De Novo and HDE submissions. IEC 62443-4-2 (component-level security for medical OT), implantable devices (pacemakers, insulin pumps) with 10–15 year in-body lifetimes requiring ultra-low-power crypto — BLE/NFC pairing security models must migrate. Post-market: under section 524B(b)(2)(A) of the FD&C Act, manufacturers of cyber devices must make updates and patches available for known unacceptable vulnerabilities on a reasonably justified regular cycle.
- **Hospital information systems**: EHR/EMR systems (HL7 FHIR R4/R5 API security — OAuth 2.0 + SMART on FHIR, token signing must migrate to ML-DSA), DICOM medical imaging (no DICOM supplement adding PQC digital signature support exists yet — DICOM Supplement 217 is titled "Neurophysiology Waveforms" and is unrelated; radiology report signatures are defined in DICOM PS3.15's Digital Signatures profile, which supports pluggable algorithm registration via OID, so ML-DSA would need a new signature algorithm identifier registered under that existing framework once proposed and ratified), telehealth TLS sessions (encryption in transit is an addressable HIPAA specification — TLS 1.3, specified in RFC 9846, with an ML-KEM hybrid key agreement as defined in RFC 10024, for video conferencing APIs), pharmacy dispensing systems (barcode/NFC verification, label authentication with ML-DSA-44). In the US, the ONC health IT certification criteria for certified EHR software that cover end-user device encryption, integrity and trusted connection (§ 170.315(d)(7)–(d)(9)) refer to NIST-approved encryption and SHA-2 or stronger hashing and name no post-quantum algorithm
- **HIPAA compliance and PQC timeline**: The HIPAA Security Rule in force (45 CFR Part 164 Subpart C, eCFR text current to 23 September 2026) names no encryption algorithms and sets no post-quantum date; HHS lists OCR's proposed rewrite of it separately from the rule in effect (HHS page last reviewed 7 August 2026), so plan migration phases against your own risk and treat any specific HIPAA year you see quoted as a guess. Covered entities and business associates face OCR audits, so a documented migration plan helps show that quantum risk was assessed.
- **Data retention vs. HNDL intersection**: PHI retention 7+ years, genomic data 75+ years — any asymmetrically encrypted data retained beyond the CRQC horizon is vulnerable to retrospective decryption. Forward secrecy alone does not protect archived records encrypted to long-lived RSA/ECDH public keys; re-encryption of archived data at rest with ML-KEM-derived keys is required.

## Workshop Steps

1. **BiometricVaultAssessor** — Inventory biometric data types by replaceability tier, template size, and storage system; map each to recommended ML-KEM/ML-DSA variant; calculate vault re-keying scope and estimated data re-encryption time for a hospital network with 500K patient records
2. **PharmaIPCalculator** — Model HNDL exposure for drug development data by pipeline stage (discovery, preclinical, Phase I–III, FDA review, post-market), each with a site-estimated number of years until the data stops being sensitive (from 20 years at discovery to 2 years post-market); calculate risk score by stage and current encryption algorithm; output migration priority ranking
3. **PatientPrivacyMapper** — Map HIPAA 18-identifier PHI categories to encryption requirements; model GDPR Article 9 data flows for cross-border patient data (EU → US); identify Right to Erasure conflicts with immutable record stores; design crypto-shredding approach using ML-KEM key deletion
4. **DeviceSafetySimulator** — Assess implantable and connected medical device crypto: pacemaker BLE pairing (ML-KEM constrained variant), insulin pump NFC session, MRI scanner DICOM TLS; model post-market surveillance timelines for firmware crypto updates under FDA's premarket cybersecurity guidance; its PQC readiness checklist is module-authored, derived from FDA's service-life cryptography recommendation
5. **HospitalMigrationPlanner** — Build a phased migration plan for a 5,000-bed health system: EHR TLS/FHIR API signing, DICOM signing, telehealth TLS, pharmacy dispensing, biometric vault, PHI archive re-encryption; map against HIPAA compliance checkpoints and OCR audit readiness milestones

## Key Data Points

- DNA-SNP genomic data: 5 MB per patient, truly irreplaceable — requires ML-KEM-1024 (strongest PQC KEM) + ML-DSA-87 for any genomic database that may be retained 50+ years
- Retinal scan template: 384 bytes; irreplaceability = highest protection tier despite small size
- HIPAA PHI breach cost: average $9.77M per healthcare breach (IBM Cost of a Data Breach Report 2024) — quantum-enabled mass decryption of archived RSA-encrypted PHI would be catastrophic
- DICOM image study size: 50 MB–500 MB per study; ML-DSA-65 signature (3,309 bytes) adds negligible overhead (<0.01%) to study payload
- HL7 FHIR API token: JWT signed with RS256 (RSA-2048) — replace with ES384 (ECDSA P-384) now, migrate to ML-DSA-44 (ML-DSA-44, ML-DSA-65 and ML-DSA-87 are registered for JOSE and COSE in RFC 9964, May 2026)
- Implantable device power budget (a planning assumption, not a measurement): a pacemaker-class device has a very small power budget, and this module treats ML-KEM-512 and AES-128-CCM as feasible there
- PHI re-encryption scope (assuming about 7 years of retained records; state medical-record rules vary): 7 years × average hospital 10M records × 256-byte AES key blob = ~17 GB of key material to be re-wrapped with ML-KEM-768; operational planning required for batch re-encryption
- GDPR Article 83 fine for special category data breach: up to 4% of global annual turnover or €20M — EU enforcement of quantum-vulnerable genomic data protection expected post-2030
- Genomic HNDL window: 75-year retention starting 2026 = data exposed through 2101 — far beyond any CRQC projection; absolute priority for immediate ML-KEM migration

## Standards Referenced

- HIPAA Security Rule (45 CFR Part 164) — PHI encryption standards and administrative safeguards
- GDPR Articles 9, 17, 32 — Special category data, Right to Erasure, technical security measures
- FDA Cybersecurity in Medical Devices guidance (current edition 3 February 2026, first issued September 2023) — nonbinding recommendations for premarket submissions, including cybersecurity management plans for vulnerabilities found after release; FD&C Act section 524B for cyber-device submissions
- IEC 62443-4-2 — Security for Industrial Automation and Control Systems: Component Requirements
- HL7 FHIR R4/R5 — Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (API security)
- RFC 9846 — The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.3 (July 2026)
- RFC 10024 — Post-Quantum Traditional (PQ/T) Hybrid Key Agreement Mechanisms for TLS 1.3 (August 2026)
- ONC health IT certification criteria § 170.315(d)(7) end-user device encryption, (d)(8) integrity, (d)(9) trusted connection
- DICOM PS3.15 — Digital Signatures profile (pluggable algorithm registration; no PQC signature supplement exists yet)
- NIST SP 800-111 — Guide to Storage Encryption Technologies for End User Devices
- FIPS 203 (ML-KEM) — key encapsulation for PHI archive re-encryption and FHIR API session keys
- FIPS 204 (ML-DSA) — digital signatures for DICOM radiology reports and FHIR audit logs
- FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA) — stateless signing for long-lived genomic data provenance records
- 21 CFR Part 11 — Electronic Records and Electronic Signatures (FDA audit trail integrity)
- NIST SP 800-66 Rev. 2 — Implementing the HIPAA Security Rule

## Cross-References

- `data-asset-sensitivity` — PHI and genomic data sensitivity classification (GDPR/HIPAA mapping)
- `kms-pqc` — hospital KMS for PHI archive re-encryption key management
- `hsm-pqc` — HSM-protected signing keys for DICOM report signing and FHIR token issuance
- `iot-ot-pqc` — connected medical device and implantable device PQC constraints
- `digital-id` — patient identity verification, mDL integration for clinical authentication
- `tls-basics` — telehealth TLS 1.3 migration and FHIR API transport security
- `compliance-strategy` — HIPAA/GDPR compliance framework integration for PQC migration documentation
- Quiz: 15 questions (hpq-001 through hpq-015)

chunks.title: Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) & HSM Key Custody
chunks.content:
# Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) & HSM Key Custody

## Overview

This advanced Hardware Infrastructure module (LM-076) was split out of LM-019 _Confidential Computing & TEEs_. It covers fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) as the way to protect data in use by trusting mathematics instead of hardware, and how an HSM can hold the FHE secret key, and what its decryption policy can and cannot protect. TEEs, remote attestation and the TEE-HSM channel stay in LM-019.

One ~45-minute route: nine learn sections in learning order (what FHE is and promises; schemes, data types and noisy results; where FHE is used; the cost and how it is being reduced; keys, operations and AES data; the quantum threat; standards and compliance; the HSM as key custodian; open-source implementations), eight exercises and two workshop steps (eight flow scenarios and six hands-on concept views).

## Key Concepts

- **FHE trusts mathematics, a TEE trusts hardware** (not sourced in the Library) — the server computes directly on ciphertexts and never sees input or output, and there is no enclave to attest. The cost is speed (orders of magnitude slower than computing in the clear). FHE does not prove the result is correct: ciphertexts are malleable.
- **What "fully homomorphic" promises** — Gentry (STOC 2009): a scheme "that allows one to evaluate circuits over encrypted data without being able to decrypt". It does not promise exact results (CKKS is approximate), speed (the ICO: "several thousand times slower than processing plaintext"), integrity (NCSC: FHE provides "only confidentiality"), or that decrypted results can be shared freely.
- **Four schemes in ISO/IEC 28033 (drafts)** — BGV and BFV (exact integers, ISO/IEC 28033-2), CKKS (approximate real and complex numbers, 28033-3) and TFHE/CGGI with FHEW (bits and small integers, 28033-4; the part is titled look-up-table evaluation). The Library records ISO/IEC 28033 as under development; the current stage of each part is not sourced in the Library. Every ciphertext carries noise that grows with each operation; bootstrapping refreshes it. CKKS is fixed-point approximate arithmetic: read results by rounding to a trusted precision.
- **Which scheme for which data** — BFV/BGV for exact values (counting, matching, private lookups), CKKS for real numbers and machine-learning inference, TFHE for comparisons and lookup-table logic (Microsoft SEAL README).
- **Where FHE is used** — in production for private lookups (Apple, BFV) and Microsoft Edge's password breach check (SEAL); peer-reviewed for private set intersection, genome-wide association studies, biometric search and AI inference; small, slow AI training; pilots for official statistics; a regulator sandbox for cross-border financial-crime intelligence. The sources show it used where a small query or simple computation can wait seconds to hours and the data could not otherwise be shared.
- **Cost and acceleration** — reported overheads range from thousands of times (ICO) to about a million times (DARPA estimate, 2021). GPUs, FPGAs, simulated and fabricated accelerator chips and better algorithms report large speedups, each against its own baseline; no source shows DARPA DPRIVE's within-ten-times goal met. TEEs, MPC, differential privacy and federated learning trade cost against different trust assumptions.
- **Standards and compliance** — FHE is not among FIPS 140-3 approved security functions, has no generally approved CNSA 2.0 solution and no Common Criteria certification; only the conventional cryptography around it can be validated. The HomomorphicEncryption.org Security Standard v1.1 (2018) is a community standard. Under the GDPR, encryption is not anonymisation (EDPB draft Guidelines 02/2026).
- **One small secret key, many large public keys** — the secret key can be regenerated from a 32-byte seed; the public encryption, relinearization, rotation and bootstrapping keys are large and need integrity protection. There is no standard encoding yet: no PKCS#11 or KMIP object type and no X.509 OID.
- **FHE does not work directly with AES** — an AES ciphertext has no structure a server can compute on. Transciphering runs the symmetric cipher's decryption inside FHE; TFHE-rs ships it for Kreyvium and AES-128-CTR.
- **Quantum threat** — lattice-based FHE has no known quantum break (it rests on the (Ring-)Learning With Errors family behind ML-KEM). The parts around the scheme, such as classical key exchange and signatures on the key set, are usually still classical and need a post-quantum fix.
- **The HSM as FHE key custodian** — generate a non-extractable 32-byte seed in the HSM, derive the secret key inside it, sign the parameter set and evaluation-key hashes with ML-DSA, decrypt under policy with an audit log, and back the seed up only HSM to HSM. The HSM can run key generation and decryption but not homomorphic evaluation. A bootstrappable CKKS evaluation-key set (3.94 GB as exported) streams out of the token in 1,001 bounded calls: measured 473 s on one MX95 Cortex-A55 core with a 16.7 MiB token peak, and 213.8 s on one core or 84.0 s on six MX95 Pro cores once the token caches work between calls (64.5–123.6 MiB peak; about 16 MiB at about twice the time with the cache off). On the board the CPU, not the 1 Gb/s link, is the limit (54 MB/s at best). This is a deployment pattern; no FHE library or paper defines an HSM role. No standard PKCS#11 mechanism exists.
- **The decryption-oracle limitation** — an unrestricted or insufficiently checked HSM decryption interface can become a key-recovery oracle, and decrypted CKKS results seen by others can leak key information even from honest computations. Single-HSM decryption therefore trusts the authorized release path and relies on a decryption policy (approved result shapes, rounding, noise flooding for CKKS, budgets, audit) plus compensating controls; BFV, BGV and TFHE need negligible decryption-failure probability. Measured: the flood width follows the published analysis (Li, Micciancio, Schultz and Sorrell 2022, Corollary 2: log2 sigma = s/2 + 1/2 log2(24 q n) + log2 B, q = (replicas + 1) x maximum decryptions; the first version was 10.3 bits narrower and counted one copy of the key). At CKKS default parameters, flooding for 30 bits of statistical security over 10,000 releases and four replicas needs sigma = 2^43.1 and leaves -12.8 bits in the noise-study emulation, and the token refuses the release. A second parameter set (META-BTS bootstrapping twice per refresh, scale 2^90, sigma = 2^69.1) keeps 11.10, 11.25 and 11.34 bits at program depth 0, 1 and 3 end to end on a Mac, and with the token on the boards 11.37, 11.20 and 11.26 bits (MX95 Pro) and 11.19, 11.14 and 11.32 bits (MX95), within 0.3 bits of the Mac, against a bar of 10 bits: a thin margin of about 1.1-1.4 bits, set by the paper's exact sizing, at about twice the bootstrap time, 3 multiplications between refreshes instead of 9 and a 12 % larger key set. Each board generated the 4.41 GB key set in 96.9 s (MX95 Pro) and 99.2 s (MX95), with every limb equal to the reference. The earlier board runs at the narrower width (22.78 bits on the MX95 Pro, 22.59 on the MX95) are kept as records of that run. The noise is drawn with floating-point Box-Muller and rounded: the time of one draw depends on the value drawn (about 21 ns of 230-390 ns, measured on both MX95 boards), the time of a whole release showed no measurable dependence, the noise is a rounded continuous Gaussian rather than the discrete Gaussian of the published analysis, and a constant-time sampler is a tracked next-development item. Threshold decryption removes the single point of trust at the cost of more parties and ceremony.
- **Threshold FHE** — split the key across several parties so no single decryptor exists. OpenFHE (BFV, N-of-N) and Lattigo (BGV, t-of-N) implement it. For CKKS, a 2-of-2 Lattigo prototype at the real parameters works (joint keys bootstrap at 24.3–24.5 bits; 4.10 GB of shares per party), but flooding for third parties at the default parameters fails as with one token (the corrected width is wider, so it fails by more), and a crafted request sent to one party returns that party's whole share, so each token needs its own independent approval. One share alone decrypts nothing (-27.8 bits); the joint secret has about 384 non-zero coefficients against 192; a decryption share at level 0 is 0.5 MB (1.05 MB switched to the owner's public key). Key-recovery attacks have been reported on t-of-N threshold decryption (IACR ePrint 2026/031, preprint); t-of-N such as 2-of-3 is not recommended, and whether the attacks apply to a fixed 2-of-2 split is not established.
- **Key rotation without decrypting stored data** — the token streams one key-switching key from the old secret to a new token-generated one (31.5 MB, byte-identical to Lattigo), and the FHE server switches stored ciphertexts to the new key (precision 28.7 → 27.1–27.3 bits). Security officer only; the old seed is retired after the rotation manifest is signed, and the token commits a signed retirement record before it destroys it; the server deletes the rotation key. The token refuses a user or public session, the same seed, a different parameter set, a copy of a token-made key as the new secret, going back from new to old, a second target for the same old secret, and a looser decryption policy. One switch took 36.5 ms at the top level and 10.1 ms at level 0 on a Mac. Not established: whether a holder of the old secret can read switched ciphertexts without the original.
- **Cross-checks with other libraries** — OpenFHE v1.6.0 CKKS at N = 2^16 (128-bit-checked settings): 80 keys, 13.26 GB, one bootstrap at 13.3 bits; That run counted one test rotation; the keys bootstrapping needs are 79, 13.09 GB. Lattigo-layout keys ran in OpenFHE with equal precision through a format bridge. The HSM's own key export now runs in OpenFHE as it is: a third parameter set (registry ID 4) takes OpenFHE v1.6.0's primes, digits and key list at its 128-bit-checked settings; the token streamed all 79 keys (6.56 GB) in 17.8 s on an M5 Max with an 83.5 MB peak, 0 mismatches over 12,483 evaluation-key limbs, and OpenFHE bootstrapped once, its default refresh, with only the token's keys at 13.28 bits against 13.20 with its own; owner release only. OpenFHE's iterative bootstrapping (two rounds: EvalBootstrap with numIterations 2 and a precision argument) works with the same 79 keys, nothing changed on the token, and raises the precision: one round 13.2 bits; two rounds 21.1 bits at the setting OpenFHE's example recommends (precision 8, the measured bits minus 5) and 31.7 to 31.8 bits at the best settings found (precision 19 to 20; a freshly encrypted ciphertext is 32.1 bits in the earlier run); through the token's owner release 30.5 bits when the ciphertext's true scale is applied and 27.0 bits when the release is read at face value, because OpenFHE's scale after a bootstrap differs from 2^52 by 6 to 7 parts in a billion and the token's input carries the scale only as a power of two. Below precision 19 the result is about 13.2 plus the precision; above 20 it falls (28.0 at 22, 24.2 at 24; not investigated); the best setting came from a sweep, not from a documented rule. The token's keys and OpenFHE's own agree within 0.4 bit. The cost is about twice the time (about 6 s against 3.2 s on a shared Mac) and one level (7 left instead of 8; keeping 8 needs a chain depth that OpenFHE refuses at N = 2^16; it asks for N = 2^17); peak memory is unchanged at 16.6 GiB. One Mac, no board, one seeded input, four runs per setting up to precision 15 and two above, the variant that raises the modulus first only. The token's export of this set was also generated on both MX95 boards in 145 s (MX95) and 142 s (MX95 Pro), about 2.4 minutes each, and streamed to a Mac in about 3 minutes (181 s and 178 s), with all 1,565 pieces matching the reference and the token-signed manifest; OpenFHE itself ran only in a container on a Mac, not on a board. Lattigo reproduces Microsoft SEAL v4.1.2 CKKS decryptions exactly. TFHE-rs 1.8.1 published test vectors: 28 of 36 byte-identical on a Mac and both MX95 boards; the 8 FFT outputs differ from upstream bytes but are identical across our platforms and decrypt correctly.
- **An encrypted risk-scoring service** — a reference service scores 32,768 customers per request on CKKS ciphertexts made under the token's keys (logistic regression on the UCI credit-default dataset, CC BY 4.0; a cubic in place of the sigmoid, 3 multiplications, no refresh). On 6,000 held-out rows: AUC 0.717298 encrypted against 0.717299 in plaintext and the same decision on all 32,768 slots; about 200 ms of server time per batch on an M5 Max, while encrypting a batch takes the data owner 3.6 s. The same service, built as a static binary for each processor, also ran on an x86-64 virtual machine (12 virtual CPUs of an AMD Ryzen AI 9 HX 370, token in a container on the Mac: 277 ms per batch, median of three repetitions, 273-305 ms over all 8 jobs; server peak 1,311 MiB; key set admitted with 40 ms to verify and 100 ms to assemble; about 13,000 requests an hour by server time alone; whole run 47 s) and on an MX95 Pro board (6 Cortex-A55 cores, 15.4 GiB) with the token on the base MX95 board, which exported its 4.41 GB key set in 124 s (35.7 MB/s, 83 MiB peak): 4.29 s per batch (median of three, 4.16-4.66 s over all 8 jobs), about 21 times the Mac; server peak 1,870 MiB; key set admitted with 170 ms to verify and 497 ms to assemble; 600 requests an hour one at a time with the 184 MiB upload and 840 by server time alone; whole run 202 s. The scores were identical on all three machines (21.00 bits against the plaintext cubic, the same decision on every slot at 0.5 and 0.25, AUC 0.717298 against 0.717299). The service admits keys only with the token's ML-DSA-65-signed manifest, needs only the relinearization key, speaks TLS 1.3 with X25519MLKEM768 and a client certificate, and refuses about 40 tested bad inputs; only the owner can decrypt a score (owner release). Limits: classical test certificates, one tenant, memory only, 3 multiplications and one batch size, one run per machine; the first virtual machine run and the board run use the published test seed (a third run, on the virtual machine with the token on the MX95 Pro reached over KMIP, used a random seed generated in the token and gave the same accuracy) (the secret key is public, so they measure time, memory and correctness, not secrecy), the x86 run is a virtual machine whose cores were not pinned, and the board's service listens on loopback behind an ssh tunnel with TLS inside it.

## Workshop / Interactive Activities

_FHE + HSM Flows_: step through eight scenarios (CKKS and TFHE single-HSM custody, OpenFHE and Lattigo threshold FHE, what fits in the HSM, Kreyvium transciphering, CKKS key rotation, and CKKS shared 2-of-2 decryption). Each step shows who holds which key and which data state, and a quantum overlay marks the links a quantum computer breaks.

_FHE concepts, hands-on_: six interactive views (noise budget and bootstrapping, encoding and rounding, programs as FHE circuits, key streaming and chunk size, key rotation without decrypting, shared 2-of-2 decryption). In the key-rotation view the user picks who starts a rotation and what the new secret is and sees what the token refuses; in the shared-decryption view the user toggles independent approvals and flooding and sees the measured outcome.

## Related Standards

- `ISO-IEC-28033`
- `tfhe-rs-v1.8.1`
- `openfhe-v1.6.0`
- `lattigo-v6.2.0`
- `fhe-rs-v0.1.1`
- `IACR-ePrint-2025-075`
- FIPS 203 (ML-KEM-768) and FIPS 204 (ML-DSA-65) for post-quantum signing and sealing of the key set and the seed backup

chunks.title: HSM & PQC Operations
chunks.content:
---
module_id: hsm-pqc
title: HSM & PQC Operations
track: Infrastructure
difficulty: advanced
duration: 90 min
workshop_steps: 4
---

# HSM & PQC Operations

## Topics Covered

- HSM architecture for PQC (FIPS 140-3 levels, on-prem vs cloud side-by-side)
- PKCS#11 v3.2 PQC mechanisms (CKM*ML_KEM*_, CKM*ML_DSA*_, CKK\_\* key types)
- On-prem HSM deep dive (Thales Luna 7.9.0 or newer, Entrust nShield v13.8+ (ML-KEM: v13.8.3+), Utimaco Quantum Protect)
- Cloud HSM deep dive (AWS CloudHSM, Azure Dedicated HSM, Google Cloud HSM)
- Side-channel attack surfaces (NTT power analysis, EM emanation, fault injection, ML-DSA hedged signing)
- HSM firmware migration (upgrade paths, dual-partition strategy, FIPS re-validation)
- What the lab tests for an HSM (CAVP algorithm certificates, the CMVP module certificate and Security Policy, IG 10.3.A self-tests and pairwise tests, CMVP submission scenarios)
- Stateful signature state management (LMS/HSS NVRAM persistence, CNSA 2.0)
- FIPS 140-3 (CMVP) and CAVP PQC validation tracking

## Workshop

1. PKCS#11 PQC Simulator — 8 operations with classical comparison and on-prem vs cloud notes
2. Vendor Comparison — Interactive matrix with PQC Maturity Score (0-100)
3. HSM Migration Planner — 4-phase firmware migration wizard
4. FIPS Validation Tracker — CMVP/CAVP PQC validation status per vendor

## Vendor statements on the Learn tab (checked 23 October 2026 unless stated)

- Entrust nShield (CMVP #5329 and #4745, nShield 5s, FIPS 140-3 Level 3): the approved-algorithm lists of both certificates contain no PQC algorithm. The PKCS#11 interface gained the PQC algorithms one release at a time; ML-KEM and SLH-DSA were available through nCore before PKCS#11. Security World v13.9.0 release notes (revision 1.4, 14 September 2026): section 3.9 adds ML-DSA to the nShield PKCS#11 API (CKM_ML_DSA_KEY_PAIR_GEN, CKM_ML_DSA, CKM_HASH_ML_DSA and the _SHA256, _SHA512, _SHAKE128 and _SHAKE256 variants; firmware v13.8 or later and the PostQuantum feature enabled). Section 3.4 (ML-KEM) and section 3.5 (SLH-DSA) each say "This functionality is currently only available via nCore." Later releases changed that: v13.9.3 (12 December 2025) section 3.4 adds ML-KEM to PKCS#11 (CKM_ML_KEM_KEY_PAIR_GEN and CKM_ML_KEM; firmware v13.8.3 or later) and v13.9.5 (24 April 2026) section 3.8 adds SLH-DSA to PKCS#11 (12 parameter sets). v13.9.6 (29 July 2026) adds FPGA acceleration of ML-KEM on mid- and high-speed models. CAVP certificate A7990 (PQSDK 1.4.1) lists LMS KeyGen, SigGen and SigVer; the Entrust pages read do not describe HSS or XMSS. An nShield 5s module is on the CMVP Modules in Process list, which is a queue position, not an outcome.
- Thales Luna and Utimaco (SLH-DSA): Thales's Luna Network HSM 7 "Post Quantum Algorithms" page says "ML-DSA and ML-KEM algorithms are available using Luna HSM Firmware 7.9.0 or newer" and that LMS-HSS is available in Luna HSM Firmware 7.8.9 and newer; that page and Thales's Luna HSM Firmware v7.9 release post do not list SLH-DSA. Utimaco's Quantum Protect page offers ML-KEM, ML-DSA, LMS and XMSS (with HSS and XMSS-MT) and says "More algorithms such as SLH-DSA are on the roadmap."; its algorithm list shows "SLH-DSA (FIPS 205) in progress". Entrust's v13.9.0 release notes describe SLH-DSA as available via nCore.
- AWS CloudHSM (hsm2m.medium, CMVP #4703, Marvell LS2 HSM Family, FIPS 140-3 Level 3): ML-DSA-44/65/87 keys are generated and used in the HSM through vendor-defined PKCS#11 mechanisms (CKM_CLOUDHSM_ML_DSA_KEY_PAIR_GEN, CKM_CLOUDHSM_ML_DSA, CKM_CLOUDHSM_EXT_MU_ML_DSA); AWS's PKCS#11 library is documented as compliant with PKCS#11 version 2.40. No ML-KEM mechanism is documented (the CloudHSM CLI key generate-asymmetric-pair category lists only ec, ml-dsa and rsa). Two statements are unreconciled and the page prefers neither. AWS documentation: "Starting September 1, 2026, ML-DSA is available in FIPS mode for hsm2m.medium clusters." and, on cluster modes, "In FIPS mode, only Federal Information Processing Standard (FIPS) validated keys and algorithms can be used." The NIST Security Policy for CMVP #4703 (dated January 29, 2026) lists "ML-DSA (non-compliant)" (use "Key generation, sign, verify") and "ML-KEM (non-compliant)" (use "Key generation, Asymmetric key encapsulation and un-encapsulation") in Table 6, "Non-Approved Algorithms Not Allowed in the Approved Mode of Operation", lists the services CN_PQC_GENERATE_KEY_PAIR, CN_PQC_CRYPTO_SIG_GEN and CN_PQC_CRYPTO_SIG_VERIFY in Table 11, "Non-Approved Services", and the note under the table says "The indicator is success for all non-approved services only when the partition is operated in the non-approved mode. The non-approved services will fail FIPS POLICY MISMATCH when partition is operated in the approved mode." The certificate lists no PQC algorithm among its approved ones and its latest update on NIST's page is 26 February 2026. "Available in FIPS mode" (an AWS cluster setting) and "listed on the certificate" are different claims; ask AWS which statement applies to a given cluster. AWS-LC 3 (CMVP #5298 and #5314) is a separate Level 1 software module that approves ML-KEM but not ML-DSA and does not change the HSM certificate.
- Google Cloud: the Cloud KMS algorithms page lists its PQC signing algorithms (ML-DSA-44/65/87 including external-mu, SLH-DSA-SHA2-128S) and key encapsulation algorithms (ML-KEM-768, ML-KEM-1024, X-Wing) for the software protection level; its tables for the HSM and single-tenant HSM protection levels list none. Google's Cloud HSM architecture page says Cloud HSM uses Marvell LiquidSecurity HSMs (certificate #4399) in FIPS 140-2 Level 3 certified hardware.
- Certificates read: Thales Luna T7 #5450 lists ML-KEM, ML-DSA and LMS; Kryptus (ASI-HSM) #5282 lists ML-KEM and ML-DSA; Crypto4A #5497 lists ML-KEM, ML-DSA, SLH-DSA and LMS; Sansec #5503 lists ML-KEM, ML-DSA and SLH-DSA; Luna M7 #5300 lists only LMS; Luna K7 #4684 (firmware 7.8.x), nShield 5s #5329 and #4745 and Marvell LS2 #4703 list no PQC algorithm.

## Side channels and hedged signing

- The vector cards describe attack classes and the countermeasure techniques discussed for them. Whether a given HSM implements a technique is stated, if at all, in the vendor's documentation and the module's Security Policy. NIST SP 800-140F section 6.2 (March 2020) reads in full "No additional requirements at this time", so CMVP has no approved non-invasive test metrics. FIPS 140-3 IG 12.A: "If a cryptographic module has been purposely designed, built and publicly documented to mitigate one or more specific attacks, this section is applicable and AS12.01 through AS12.04 (as applicable) shall be addressed regardless if the vendor of the module wishes to address the claim or not."
- ML-DSA hedged signing, FIPS 204 section 3.4: hedged is the default variant; "The use of fresh randomness during signing helps mitigate side-channel attacks"; the deterministic variant "should not be used on platforms where side-channel attacks are a concern and where they cannot be otherwise mitigated". PKCS#11 v3.2 lets the caller choose CKH_HEDGE_PREFERRED, CKH_HEDGE_REQUIRED or CKH_DETERMINISTIC_REQUIRED, so which variant a given HSM uses by default is a property of that product (module documentation and Security Policy).

## Stateful signatures in an HSM

- NIST SP 800-208 section 8.1 (p. 28): "In order to prevent the possible reuse of an OTS key, when the cryptographic module accepts a request to sign a message, the cryptographic module shall increment the leaf index of the private key (q in LMS, idx in XMSS, idx_sig in XMSSMT) and shall store the incremented leaf index value in nonvolatile storage before exporting a signature value or accepting another request to sign a message." IG C.N Resolution 12 has the tester confirm it. How a product recovers after a power failure is product behaviour (Security Policy and administrator guide).

## What the lab tests (Learn > HSM Firmware Migration)

A PQC-capable HSM is checked in four places. CAVP is NIST's algorithm validation program (tests specified in ACVP documents). CMVP is the cryptographic module validation program whose Validation Authority is a joint effort of NIST and the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security: a module's certificate lists its approved algorithms and the Security Policy published with it lists its services. A CAST is a cryptographic algorithm self-test run by a validated module; a PCT is a pairwise consistency test on a generated key pair; a CSTL is an accredited testing laboratory.

- Algorithm certificates (CAVP): NIST's ACVP specification drafts (2 October 2026) cover ML-KEM (keyGen, encapDecap), ML-DSA, SLH-DSA and LMS (keyGen, sigGen, sigVer). CAVP overview page: "Cryptographic algorithm validation is a prerequisite of cryptographic module validation." and "Due to this structure, ACVTS testing is entirely black-box. The implementation is never provided to NIST or the CAVP in order to receive a validation certificate." ML-KEM draft section 6.1: "For the encapsulation key check, the server will generate a potentially valid or invalid encapsulation key ek. The IUT SHALL determine if the provided ek is valid based on [FIPS203] Section 7.2." Not covered (ML-DSA draft section 6.2.2): "An ACVP server will not test the zeroization of intermediate values, security strength of the deterministic random bit generators (DRBGs), or incorrect length signatures or public keys." LMS draft section 6.2.2: "ACVP does not test the inability of an implementation to export a private key. ACVP does not provide any guarantees on the inability to reuse private OTS pairs of an implementation." IG C.N Background (last modified September 2024): "CAVP tests are undergoing development with testing available for LMS but not yet for XMSS, HSS, or XMSSMT." No ACVP specification is published for XMSS, XMSS^MT or HSS (October 2026).
- Module certificate (CMVP) and Security Policy: CAVP overview page: "For an algorithm implementation to be listed on a cryptographic module validation certificate as an Approved security function, the algorithm implementation must meet all the requirements of FIPS 140 and must successfully complete the cryptographic algorithm validation process. However, a product or implementation does not meet the FIPS 140 module validation requirements by simply implementing an Approved security function and acquiring validations for each of the implemented algorithms." A Security Policy keeps approved and non-approved items apart (the policy of CMVP #4703 has "Table 10 Approved Services" and "Table 11 Non-Approved Services" and lists non-approved algorithms in its Tables 4, 5 and 6). IG 2.4.A: "the algorithm shall be included in the Security Policy's list of non-approved algorithms allowed in the approved mode of operation with no security claimed (see SP 800-140B). However, the module's certificate shall not include these algorithms as they do not claim any security and are not used to meet any requirement of FIPS 140-3." The question to put to a certificate is whether ML-DSA (or ML-KEM, SLH-DSA, LMS) is among its approved algorithms and which approved services use it.
- Self-tests (FIPS 140-3 IG 10.3.A, last modified 19 August 2026): "The requirements of this IG apply prior to the first operational use of the cryptographic algorithm." GeneralNote8: "For all algorithms that require a CAST (e.g., approved algorithms, allowed algorithms with a claim of security as permitted by an IG, and legacy algorithms per IG C.M), a CAST shall be performed prior to first time algorithm execution in the approved mode; but CASTs are NOT required (but are certainly permissible) prior to first time algorithm execution in the non-approved mode." ML-KEM: "if the module implements ML-KEM encapsulation, the module shall have a CAST for the ML-KEM encapsulation mechanism." and Note21: "The ML-KEM decapsulation CASTs shall cover both the implicit rejection and (unnamed) non-rejection paths." ML-DSA: "if the module implements digital signature generation, the module shall have an ML-DSA digital signature generation CAST for either the 'hedged' or 'deterministic' algorithm (per FIPS 204 Section 5.2)." LMS: "If the module implements LMS signature generation then it shall also implement key generation and shall have CASTs for both LMS signature generation and key generation." Pairwise consistency test (Additional Comments 1): "Though not a CAST, a pairwise consistency test (PCT) shall be conducted for every generated public and private key pair for the applicable approved algorithm (per ISO/IEC 19790:2012 Section 7.10.3.3)." For ML-KEM the PCT encapsulates a shared secret K with ek and decapsulates with dk, and passes if the two K values are equal. For key pairs generated from stored seeds (FIPS 203, FIPS 204) a PCT is only required prior to the first exportation of the seed or key pair or prior to the first operational use of the key pair after the seed has been generated within the module. IG D.S Scenario 1 (last modified 9 April 2026): "ML-KEM shall be CAVP tested via 'ML-KEM EncapDecap' for all implemented parameter sets (ML-KEM-1024, ML-KEM-512, ML-KEM-768) and functions (Decapsulation, Encapsulation). The module shall implement the encapsulation and decapsulation key checks specified in FIPS 203 Sections 7.2 and 7.3".
- Which submission for a firmware update (CMVP Management Manual version 2.7, 9 April 2026, section 7.1; twelve submission scenarios): "An updated version of a previously validated cryptographic module can be considered for a revalidation rather than a full validation depending on the extent of the modifications from the previously validated version of the module." Full Submission (FS): "If modifications are made to hardware, software, or firmware components that do not meet any of the below revalidation criteria, then the cryptographic module shall be considered a new module and shall undergo a full validation testing by a CSTL and submitted as a FS." Algorithm Update (ALG): "Code or configuration changes are not permitted under this revalidation scenario." CVE: "Changes shall not introduce new features or cryptography". Update (UPDT): "An updated cryptographic module can be considered in this scenario if less than a 30% of security changes were made to the module. Security changes include impacts to: approved / allowed security functions/algorithms, SSPs, approved security services, self-tests, and security states within the FSM. None of these, assessed individually, can exceed 30% of changes." and "The CMVP upon review, may determine that the changes are >30% and shall be submitted as an FS." The summary table (section 7.1.14) gives UPDT a new certificate and a new sunset date and requires the latest guidance, CAVP testing and, where IG 9.3.A applies, ESV testing. Adding ML-KEM, ML-DSA or SLH-DSA changes the approved algorithms, approved services and self-tests, which are categories counted toward the 30% limit; whether a given release is an UPDT or an FS is decided by the CMVP on the lab's submission.

## Key Standards

- FIPS 140-3 (Cryptographic Module Validation) and its Implementation Guidance (IG 10.3.A, IG D.S, IG C.N, IG 12.A)
- CMVP FIPS 140-3 Management Manual (version 2.7, 9 April 2026)
- PKCS#11 v3.2 (OASIS Standard, 3 June 2026)
- FIPS 203/204/205 (ML-KEM, ML-DSA, SLH-DSA)
- NIST SP 800-208 (Stateful Hash-Based Signatures)
- CNSA 2.0 (NSA)

Vendor algorithm availability and validation evidence are shown from shared, product-specific capability records with source links, checked dates and the recorded review state. Availability, approved mode and inclusion on a named CMVP certificate are separate facts; missing records remain unknown. Version-specific documentation examples and integration scenarios do not establish support for another firmware, parameter set or environment.

chunks.title: Hybrid and Composite Cryptography
chunks.content:
# Hybrid and Composite Cryptography

## Overview

The Hybrid Cryptography module teaches how to combine classical and post-quantum algorithms during the quantum transition, and what that choice costs. It runs in this order: why hybrid; the risks of hybrid compared with pure PQC, for key establishment and for signatures; which national agencies, standards bodies and companies recommend hybrid or accept pure PQC; hybrid KEM construction (X25519MLKEM768, combiners); hybrid KEMs in TLS 1.3; implementation and validation (SP 800-227, FIPS 140-3 IG D.S); HPKE; hybrid signatures (non-separability, Silithium); and finally hybrid certificates (seven X.509 formats plus chameleon certificates as a historical design).

## Key Concepts

- **Hybrid cryptography** combines classical and PQC algorithms so that security holds even if one component is broken
- **Pure PQC risks (what hybrid guards against)**: young schemes can fall to classical cryptanalysis (SIKE and Rainbow, per the Czech NÚKIB annex); in 2026 the BSI advised against Classic McEliece in new developments after new structural cryptanalysis and noted that a hybrid with Classic McEliece still keeps at least classical security; new implementations can carry exploitable bugs (Bernstein 2026: a small change in ML-DSA software is exploitable in 1 second on 1 laptop core, and far fewer Ed25519+ML-DSA keys than ML-DSA-only keys are estimated to be breakable for years after the first quantum attack)
- **Risks of hybrid KEMs**: an unsound combiner (ETSI TR 103 966: a "concatenation only" hybrid key is not secure against active adversaries; SP 800-227 approves specific combiners); fallback to classical-only when a client retries after a failed hybrid attempt (backwards-compatible hybrids can be open to downgrade, ETSI TR 103 966); larger messages (X25519MLKEM768 key share 1,216 bytes vs 32) and, in IKEv2, extra pre-authentication key exchanges raising denial-of-service risk; HPKE Auth modes cannot use ML-KEM or hybrids containing it; FIPS 140-3 approval only under the five IG D.S conditions (X-Wing cannot yet meet them)
- **Risks of hybrid signatures**: stripping one signature when verifiers accept either component (ETSI TR 103 966: such a backwards-compatible hybrid can be less secure than the PQC algorithm alone; fix: require both, or a non-separable construction per RFC 9955); certificate rollback where a server keeps classical certificates (individual draft draft-sheffer-tls-pqc-continuity proposes clients remember PQC support); more complex and less researched than hybrid confidentiality (UK NCSC); a PKI that issues both signature types or two parallel PKIs (NCSC prefers a single migration to a fully post-quantum PKI; the NSA tells national security systems to use a parallel PKI, not several algorithms in one certificate); no universally accepted hybrid certificate format (GSMA PQ.03 finds recommending hybrid certificates premature); composite ML-DSA-65 + ECDSA P-256 signatures of about 3.4 KB; no FIPS 140-3 IG section on composite signatures
- **Risks common to both**: added complexity and attack surface (NSA: more products fail through implementation or configuration errors than through algorithms; Dutch PQC Migration Handbook: hybridisation may increase attack surface); every party must support all components and the same combination method; removing the classical part later is a second transition; for some formal properties hybrids may be no stronger, or even weaker, than their components (NSA: a matter of significant debate); something marketed as hybrid is not necessarily quantum resistant; overhead of two algorithms, judged low when hybrid only sets up a session key (Dutch handbook)
- **Who recommends hybrid**: ANSSI (France) insists on hybrid wherever PQC is deployed in the short and medium term, mandatory in the French regulated perimeter, except hash-based signatures (SLH-DSA, XMSS, LMS); its recommendations are not a regulatory obligation elsewhere. BSI (Germany) TR-02102-1 currently recommends quantum-safe methods only in hybrid use; classical-only key agreement is recommended until the end of 2031. The Dutch AIVD/CWI/TNO handbook recommends hybrid especially when deploying before mature implementations exist. The EU ECCG Agreed Cryptographic Mechanisms v2.0 recommends hybrid mode for long-term confidentiality (the v3 draft adds that lattice mechanisms should not be used standalone); ENISA's 2026 hybridization report is explicitly not a recommendation
- **Who accepts pure PQC**: the NSA will not require hybrid for national security systems and counts only NSA-identified hybrids (such as its IKEv2 profile) as CNSA 2.0 compliant; the UK NCSC uses hybrid only where needed (interoperability, implementation security, protocol constraints); the Czech NÚKIB accepts hybrid or standalone ML-KEM and ML-DSA at security level 5; NIST approves ML-KEM and ML-DSA on their own and says combining can be advantageous during migration (SP 800-227); Canada's Cyber Centre (ITSP.40.111 version 5) recommends ML-KEM and ML-DSA and phases out classical schemes used without a post-quantum scheme by the end of 2035, without discussing hybrid
- **Standards bodies and industry**: ETSI specifies hybrid key exchange (TS 103 744) and describes trade-offs (TR 103 966) without mandating it; the IETF standardizes both hybrid TLS groups (RFC 10024) and pure ML-KEM groups (draft) and does not choose for deployers; Google Chrome, Cloudflare and AWS deploy X25519MLKEM768; Cloudflare targets 2029 for full post-quantum security including authentication
- **NIST SP 800-227** describes how to combine key-establishment mechanisms securely (§4.6): a suitably designed classical/PQC combination can retain security if one component remains secure. Compatibility with existing systems depends on the protocol and the mechanisms each participant supports — the combination itself does not provide it. §3.3 recommends appropriate side-channel protections such as constant-time implementations; migration to pure PQC is driven by algorithm maturation rather than calendar deadlines alone
- **SP 800-227 approved KEM parameter sets**: ML-KEM-512 → NIST Category 1 (AES-128 equivalent, constrained/IoT, short-lived sessions); ML-KEM-768 → Category 3 (AES-192 equivalent, default for TLS 1.3 and most internet traffic); ML-KEM-1024 → Category 5 (AES-256 equivalent, CNSA 2.0 and high-assurance/federal systems). This module's advice: HNDL risk and data-retention window should drive the choice, and ciphertext that must stay secret past ~2035 should use Category 3 or 5 rather than Category 1
- **Hybrid KEM in a FIPS 140-3 validated module (CMVP IG D.S, last modified 9 April 2026)**: IG D.S "Scenario 2" is a hybrid of an approved ML-KEM plus one or more non-ML-KEM schemes combined through an approved key combiner (SP 800-227 §4.6.2); the non-ML-KEM may be approved or non-approved (examples: X25519, X448). To claim Scenario 2, a module must implement at a minimum all five of: (1) an approved ML-KEM; (2) one or more non-ML-KEM (approved or non-approved); (3) an approved key combiner (a concatenation of the shared secrets fed into an SP 800-56C one-step or two-step KDF, HKDF included, or an SP 800-133 §6.3 method: concatenation, XOR, or key extraction using HMAC; the IG describes the §6.3 route only for combining ML-KEM shared secrets with those of approved key-agreement schemes, IG D.F Scenario 1 or 2); (4) the module does not offer arbitrary hybrid combinations but enforces a pre-defined set of hybrid schemes (e.g., SecP256r1MLKEM768, X25519MLKEM768, SecP384r1MLKEM1024); (5) for each set, the module controls at minimum the shared-secret sequencing logic (e.g., concatenation order). If any is missing (e.g., a library with an approved ML-KEM and X25519 but no approved key combiner, or one with the first three items that does not enforce a set of combinations or control sequencing), Scenario 2 cannot be claimed and any non-approved non-ML-KEM scheme offered must be restricted to the non-approved mode only. A non-approved component such as X25519 is classified as a "non-approved but allowed algorithm with no security claimed" (IG 2.4.A; listed in the Security Policy, not on the certificate); it may be used only inside the approved hybrid, enforced by the module itself (not used for other purposes in approved mode, not offered as an independent approved service such as a separate API call in a software library; operator guidance in the Security Policy cannot enforce it). The claimed security strength of the hybrid comes from the ML-KEM, and the hybrid service is then an approved security service. The Security Policy records the claim in the Security Function Implementation table as "KEM-Hybrid" or "KEM-Hybrid-Full" (entry names such as "KEM-Hybrid X25519MLKEM768"); the non-approved half is listed with the caveat "no security claimed" citing IG D.S Scenario 2 and IG 2.4.A (CMVP KEM Hybrid guidance, last updated 8 April 2026). "KEM-Hybrid" applies when a module meets items 1 to 5 but not the extra conditions for "KEM-Hybrid-Full", and it can still be an approved service, even for a software library offering it to a calling application. IG D.S Additional Comment 8: the TLS 1.3 hybrid key exchange (draft-ietf-tls-ecdhe-mlkem-01, now RFC 10024) may meet Scenario 2 using the SP 800-56C HKDF as the approved combiner with one of SecP256r1MLKEM768, X25519MLKEM768 or SecP384r1MLKEM1024 (the specifications may still be in draft form); the X-Wing hybrid KEM "cannot yet meet the requirements of Scenario 2" even though it uses an SP 800-56C one-step KDF, because at a minimum SP 800-133 needs an update to approve the X-Wing seed generation method (seed expansion using SHAKE is not currently in SP 800-133). Separately, the CAVP prerequisites page (updated 22 September 2026) lists X-Wing keyGen and encapDecap tests; CAVP states that acquiring validations for each implemented algorithm does not by itself meet the FIPS 140 module requirements. Self-tests: every approved scheme in the hybrid must be self-tested individually under IG 10.3.A; for the ML-KEM part, under IG 10.3.A (known-answer self-tests for each ML-KEM function implemented: encapsulation, decapsulation, key generation; decapsulation tests cover both the implicit-rejection and non-rejection paths; on at least one of ML-KEM-512, -768 or -1024 as implemented in approved mode); IG D.S says there is currently no separate self-test for the approved key combiner or for the non-approved half, beyond self-testing any approved algorithms used within (e.g., KDFs). CAVP testing: the IG lets the approved pieces be tested separately (the ML-KEM and, with a non-approved other half, the approved algorithms beneath it such as KDFs), or end-to-end tests of the full hybrid scheme "if available within CAVP", with the IG to be updated after they become available; no hybrid-KEM specification appears in the ACVP specification index (pages.nist.gov/ACVP) as of 23 October 2026. Do not confuse with IG 1.B "Hybrid Modules" (new 19 August 2026), which concerns a module whose boundary combines a software or firmware component with a disjoint hardware component and has nothing to do with hybrid key exchange
- **Hybrid combiner construction (SP 800-227 + SP 800-56C-Rev2)**: concatenation order is fixed per protocol (TLS 1.3 per RFC 10024 §4.3: X25519MLKEM768 uses `ML-KEM_ss || X25519_ss`, while SecP256r1MLKEM768 and SecP384r1MLKEM1024 use `ECDHE_ss || ML-KEM_ss`; per its §5, SP 800-56C-Rev2 approves this when the first secret comes from a FIPS-approved scheme, so ML-KEM goes first where X25519 is used, and ECDHE goes first for the NIST curves, whose certified implementations are more widely available; SP 800-227 §4.6.2, September 2025, approves its key combiner when at least one shared secret in any position comes from an approved scheme); SP 800-56C permits either HKDF (HMAC-based extractor with SHA-256/384/512) or KMAC128/256 as the combiner; dual-PRF assumption means the combined secret is safe as long as _either_ input looks uniform to the attacker, so a future break of ML-KEM or of X25519 alone does not break the session key; SP 800-227 §4.6.3 says the domain-separation input should be used to uniquely identify the composite scheme in use (for example the two component schemes, order of composition, choice of parameter set, key combiner, KDF)
- **Combiners compared**: TLS 1.3 hybrid groups (RFC 10024) feed the concatenated secrets into the TLS 1.3 HKDF key schedule and rely on the handshake transcript to bind the key shares; X-Wing (draft-connolly-cfrg-xwing-kem-11) computes SHA3-256(ss_M || ss_X || ct_X || pk_X || XWingLabel), hashing the X25519 ciphertext and public key but not the ML-KEM ones; composite ML-KEM (draft-ietf-lamps-pq-composite-kem-23) uses the same shape, SHA3-256(mlkemSS || tradSS || tradCT || tradPK || Label), for twelve pairings, and its MLKEM768-X25519 entry uses the X-Wing label (hex 5c2e2f2f5e5c); the CFRG concrete hybrid KEMs (draft-irtf-cfrg-concrete-hybrid-kems-04) use SHAKE256 as PRG and SHA3-256 as KDF and state that MLKEM768-X25519 is identical to X-Wing; ETSI CatKDF (TS 103 744) forms psk || k1 || k2 and runs one KDF (HMAC, KMAC or HKDF) with a context holding all public keys and ciphertexts of both components, which the composite draft calls the more conservative choice, while CasKDF chains one KDF stage per component
- **What makes X-Wing different**: it leaves out the ML-KEM ciphertext and public key, relying on the specifics of ML-KEM-768's Fujisaki-Okamoto transform; the draft warns the combiner "cannot be assumed to be secure, when used with different KEMs"; if SHA3-256, SHA3-512 and SHAKE-256 are modelled as random oracles its IND-CCA security is bounded by ML-KEM-768's and the gap-CDH security of Curve25519; it claims MAL-BIND-K-PK and MAL-BIND-K-CT, which ML-KEM alone does not achieve; its private key is a 32-byte seed expanded with SHAKE256 into both component keys (public key 1,216 bytes, ciphertext 1,120 bytes, shared secret 32 bytes), the reason FIPS 140-3 IG D.S says it cannot yet meet Scenario 2; the composite ML-KEM draft calls X-Wing and its MLKEM768-X25519 entry "largely interchangeable", the one difference being X-Wing's joint seed keygen, so an X-Wing implementation is a compliant composite implementation but not the reverse
- **ML-KEM decapsulation and implicit rejection (FIPS 203 §§6.3 and 7.3)**: input checks can fail; for example, ML-KEM-768 requires a 1,088-byte ciphertext. After the required checks pass, an internal re-encryption mismatch selects a fallback shared secret derived from the secret rejection value `z` and the received ciphertext, without exposing the mismatch through an error or timing. Normal library argument and operational errors still apply. If tampering triggers this path, the receiver obtains a different secret; in a protocol deriving an AES-GCM key from it, authentication fails and unauthenticated plaintext must not be released. Implicit rejection conceals the internal ciphertext-validity result; a later authentication failure can also occur after valid decapsulation and does not directly disclose that result. Protocol error handling and timing must preserve this distinction. Successful decapsulation alone does not confirm a shared key: use protocol authentication or key confirmation.
- **Implementation considerations**: correct results alone do not show that an implementation protects its secrets; constant-time techniques help prevent execution time or memory access from revealing secret values, but do not mean every call takes the same number of milliseconds (SP 800-227 §3.3 recommends appropriate protections; effectiveness depends on the implementation and device). ML-KEM encapsulation requires fresh, unpredictable random input: an attacker who knows the 32-byte `m` can reproduce the encapsulation with the recipient's public key and recover the shared secret (FIPS 203 §3.3). In an X25519 + ML-KEM hybrid, a leak of only the X25519 secret can still be covered by a suitable combiner through the uncompromised ML-KEM secret; a leak of both secrets or the final session key loses that protection. For HSM/TPM devices, check the manufacturer's documentation for which protections exist and which settings affect them — do not assume a PQC-protection switch exists
- **CNSA 2.0** (NSA): its FAQ (v2.2, October 2026) quotes CNSSP 15 as requiring CNSA 2.0 algorithms in all new NSS acquisitions by 1 January 2027, says that by 31 December 2030 NSS equipment and services that cannot support CNSA 2.0 must be phased out unless otherwise granted an exception, and that by 31 December 2031 CNSA 2.0 algorithms are mandated for use, unless otherwise noted; it also says specific deadlines depend on equipment type; NSA will not require NSS developers to use hybrid certified products for security purposes, although product availability and interoperability requirements may lead to adopting hybrid solutions in specific cases
- **RFC 9794** standardizes terminology for hybrid schemes — "composite" (single OID, both-must-verify) vs "non-composite" (parallel independent algorithms); establishes "PQ/T" (Post-Quantum / Traditional) naming
- **Subject key vs. certificate signature**: the subject public-key algorithm and the certificate-signature algorithm are independent. An ML-KEM key cannot sign, so an ML-KEM certificate is always issued by a separate signing-capable CA (ML-DSA, ECDSA, RSA). The ML-KEM subject key performs encapsulation/decapsulation; the issuer key signs the certificate
- **Seven certificate formats in the main comparison** (five signature formats + two KEM formats):
  - **Pure PQC (ML-DSA)** — standard single-algorithm X.509 using ML-DSA signatures; OIDs standardized in RFC 9881; the workshop is tested with OpenSSL 3.6.3
  - **Pure PQC (SLH-DSA)** — hash-based signature X.509 certificates; OIDs in RFC 9909; ANSSI does not recommend systematic hybridisation for hash-based signatures such as SLH-DSA, XMSS and LMS
  - **Composite (dual-algorithm)** — single composite OID identifies the algorithm pair; both signatures must verify; defined in draft-ietf-lamps-pq-composite-sigs-19, approved and in the RFC Editor queue (no RFC number yet)
  - **Alt-Sig / Catalyst** — classical primary cert with PQC key and signature in X.509 extensions (SubjectAltPublicKeyInfo 2.5.29.72, AltSignatureAlgorithm 2.5.29.73, AltSignatureValue 2.5.29.74); legacy verifiers ignore the extensions; defined in ITU-T X.509 (2019) §7.2.2 and §9.8; relying-party policy decides whether one or both signatures are required
  - **Related Certificates (RFC 9763)** — a NEW certificate (Cert B) carries a RelatedCertificate extension holding the hash of the complete final DER of an EXISTING certificate (Cert A); the binding is one-way and Cert A is never modified; the CA issues Cert B only after a relatedCertRequest proves possession of Cert A's key; a protocol may use either certificate or both — RFC 9763 does not require both
  - **Pure PQC KEM (ML-KEM, RFC 9935)** — an ML-KEM public key in X.509; if keyUsage is present, keyEncipherment must be the only bit; the certificate is CA-issued, never self-signed; the key is used e.g. in CMS KEMRecipientInfo (RFC 9629, ML-KEM in CMS: RFC 9936)
  - **Composite KEM** — ML-KEM plus a classical KEM under one OID, ML-KEM first; defined in draft-ietf-lamps-pq-composite-kem-23, approved by the IESG and in the RFC Editor queue since 2026-10-12 (not yet an RFC)
- **Advanced examples (outside the main comparison)**: Certificate Discovery (draft-ietf-lamps-certdiscovery-03, active LAMPS WG draft) lets a primary certificate advertise in subjectInfoAccess where a related secondary certificate can be fetched and which algorithms it uses; a fetched secondary must still pass full path validation; the draft's OIDs are TBD, so the workshop uses documentation-arc placeholders (1.3.6.1.4.1.32473) and its encoding is illustrative. RFC 9925 unsigned certificates use id-alg-unsigned (1.3.6.1.5.5.7.6.36), a zero-length signature and a placeholder issuer (id-rdna-unsigned); they suit keys trusted by other means and are never valid in a certification path
- **Historical design — Chameleon Certificates**: a single cert with a DeltaCertificateDescriptor extension encoding the differences needed to rebuild a paired cert; draft-bonnell-lamps-chameleon-certs-07 is an expired individual draft never adopted by the LAMPS working group; kept for study only and not recommended for new deployments
- **Watchlist**: FN-DSA (planned FIPS 206, not yet final) has an IETF certificate draft, draft-ietf-lamps-fn-dsa-certificates, whose OIDs are still TBD — no deployable FN-DSA certificate exists yet
- **X25519MLKEM768** — the leading hybrid KEM combining Curve25519 ECDH with ML-KEM-768; enabled by default in Chrome 131 (November 2024), protecting most human traffic to Cloudflare by October 2025, and supported on AWS KMS, ACM and Secrets Manager endpoints (non-FIPS, April 2025); its shares and shared secret put the ML-KEM part first (ML-KEM_ss || X25519_ss, RFC 10024 §4.3), unlike SecP256r1MLKEM768 and SecP384r1MLKEM1024, which put ECDHE first
- **Other hybrid KEM variants**: SecP256r1MLKEM768 (P-256 + ML-KEM-768, FIPS-approved classical curve), SecP384r1MLKEM1024 (P-384 + ML-KEM-1024, NIST Level 5)
- **Composite signatures** combine ML-DSA with ECDSA or Ed25519 in a single operation; both must verify; single OID simplifies handling; prevents downgrade attacks
