chunks.title: PQC 101 — scope & keywords
chunks.content:
**Scope.** PQC 101 is the foundational introduction to post-quantum cryptography, covering why current public-key algorithms (RSA, ECC, ECDSA, EdDSA, ECDH, DH) are vulnerable to quantum computers via Shor's algorithm, the three families of NIST-standardized PQC algorithms (lattice-based ML-KEM/ML-DSA, hash-based SLH-DSA/LMS/XMSS, and code-based schemes), and the HNDL (Harvest Now, Decrypt Later) threat model that makes quantum migration urgent regardless of CRQC timeline certainty. The module walks through the 2016–2035 migration timeline from NIST standardization through NSA CNSA 2.0 compliance deadlines, industry-specific urgency levels, and role-based next steps. Out of scope: deep cryptanalysis, detailed algorithm implementations, quantum physics mechanics, and post-quantum signature variants beyond the NIST-selected families.

**Sub-topics keywords:** Shor's algorithm, Grover's algorithm, quantum threat, lattice-based cryptography, hash-based signatures, code-based schemes, NIST FIPS 203 204 205, CNSA 2.0, HNDL attack, HNFL attack, algorithm families, key size comparison, CRQC timeline, quantum threat timeline, classical vs post-quantum.

chunks.title: Quantum Threats — scope & keywords
chunks.content:
**Scope.** This module provides in-depth technical explanation of how quantum computers break cryptography: qubits and superposition, Shor's algorithm solving integer factorization (RSA) and discrete logarithm (ECC/DH) in polynomial time O(n³), Grover's algorithm providing quadratic speedup for symmetric weakening, and CRQC timeline projections from NIST, NSA, Global Risk Institute, BSI, and ANSSI. Covers the HNDL and HNFL attack phases, security level degradation calculator, algorithm vulnerability matrix, and Mosca's Theorem for calculating migration deadlines. Emphasizes quantitative analysis: RSA-2048 requires ~4,098 logical qubits; P-256 ~2,330 qubits; AES-256 remains 128-bit secure under Grover's. Out of scope: quantum physics deeper than superposition/entanglement basics, quantum error correction details, CRQC engineering challenges, and quantum algorithms beyond Shor's and Grover's.

**Sub-topics keywords:** Shor's algorithm, Grover's algorithm, qubits, superposition, entanglement, CRQC cryptographically relevant quantum computer, HNDL harvest now decrypt later, HNFL harvest now forge later, security level degradation, key size, ciphertext size, logical qubit count, RSA vulnerability, ECC vulnerability, AES-256 quantum safety, Mosca's theorem, CRQC timeline, NIST IR 8547.

chunks.title: Hybrid Cryptography — scope & keywords
chunks.content:
**Scope.** Hybrid cryptography combines classical and PQC algorithms for defense-in-depth during the quantum transition: if either component is broken, security holds. Covers why hybrid approaches are mandated (or recommended) by ANSSI and NIST SP 800-227, eight X.509 certificate format approaches — six carrying signatures (pure PQC ML-DSA per RFC 9881, pure PQC SLH-DSA per RFC 9909, composite dual-algorithm under a single OID, alt-sig/catalyst per ITU-T X.509 (2019) §9.8, related certificates per RFC 9763, and chameleon certificates from an expired individual draft) plus two carrying KEM keys (pure PQC ML-KEM per RFC 9935 and composite KEM), and hybrid KEM construction (X25519MLKEM768). Details the fundamental dilemma that PQC algorithms are newer and less battle-tested than classical ones, yet HNDL threats make waiting dangerous. Covers NIST SP 800-227 §4 implementation requirements: implicit rejection, constant-time decapsulation, DRBG quality, side-channel resistance, and domain-separated hybrid combiners. Out of scope: Pure PQC architectures, standalone hash-based signature deployment without hybrid partners, and algorithm replacements for non-KEM key agreement.

**Sub-topics keywords:** Hybrid cryptography, composite signatures, dual-algorithm certificates, X25519MLKEM768, RFC 9794 hybrid terminology, hybrid KEM combiner, ANSSI hybrid mandate, NIST SP 800-227, HKDF HMAC-based extractor, KMAC conditional, domain separation, implicit rejection, constant-time decapsulation, DRBG quality, side-channel resistance, certificate chain size, backward compatibility, related certificates RFC 9763, chameleon certificates, alt-sig catalyst, SubjectAltPublicKeyInfo extension.

chunks.title: Crypto Agility — scope & keywords
chunks.content:
**Scope.** This module teaches designing crypto-agile systems that can rapidly swap cryptographic algorithms, protocols, and implementations without code or infrastructure rewrites. Covers three dimensions of agility (algorithm, protocol, implementation), three architecture patterns (provider model, service mesh, external KMS/HSM), the CBOM (Cryptographic Bill of Materials) concept for discovering all crypto assets, and NIST's recommended 7-phase migration framework (Assessment, Risk Prioritization, Preparation, Testing, Hybrid Migration, Production, Monitoring). Includes real-world case studies from Cloudflare (~4% TLS handshake time increase with hybrid), Google Chrome (X25519MLKEM768 default since Chrome 131), and Apple iMessage (P-256 + Kyber-1024 initial keys, now standardized as ML-KEM-1024/768 per FIPS 203). Out of scope: Protocol-specific implementation details, cryptanalysis of individual algorithms, and hardware-only crypto agility approaches.

**Sub-topics keywords:** Crypto agility, algorithm agility, protocol agility, implementation agility, provider model, service mesh, external KMS HSM, CBOM cryptographic bill of materials, CycloneDX, 7-phase migration framework, assessment inventory, risk prioritization, hybrid migration, production deployment, monitoring, abstraction layer, crypto-agile APIs, JCA OpenSSL providers, configuration-driven algorithm selection, performance overhead, latency budget.

chunks.title: Cryptographic Management Modernization — scope & keywords
chunks.content:
**Scope.** This module teaches the management discipline of Cryptographic Posture Management (CPM) — a continuous, iterative program covering certificates, cryptographic libraries, application software, and key material. Distinct from crypto-agility (a technical capability: "can we change?") and from a Center of Excellence (operating model). CPM answers: "do we know what we have, is it healthy, can we prove it?" Covers five pillars of CPM (Inventory, Governance, Lifecycle/CLM, Observability, Assurance/FIPS), dual-loop iterative process, and ROI justification whether quantum arrives on schedule or never. Addresses three forcing functions: 47-day TLS certificate cadence by 2029 (CA/B Forum), FIPS 140-3 Level 3 self-test drift, and library EoL/CVE cadence (OpenSSL 1.1.1 EoL, OMB M-23-02 mandate). Out of scope: Specific crypto algorithms, detailed cryptanalysis, and FIPS module validation mechanics beyond the CPM governance context.

**Sub-topics keywords:** Cryptographic posture management CPM, CBOM cryptographic bill of materials, certificate lifecycle management CLM, ACME EST enrollment, certificate rotation, 47-day cadence, FIPS 140-3 Level 3, CMVP CAVP validation, library EoL end-of-life, CVE cryptographic vulnerabilities, inventory governance, continuous monitoring, observability metrics, shadow certificate discovery CT logs, root CA rotation, revocation propagation, OMB M-23-02, CNSA 2.0 deadlines.

chunks.title: TLS Basics — scope & keywords
chunks.content:
**Scope.** Deep dive into TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446) and its post-quantum integration: 1-RTT handshake, cipher suite simplification to 5 options (TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 / 128_GCM_SHA256 / CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256 / 128_CCM variants), and key exchange mechanisms (classical ECDH X25519/P-256/P-384, pure PQC ML-KEM, hybrid X25519MLKEM768). Covers TLS 1.3 improvements (mandatory ECDHE forward secrecy, encrypted handshake messages, removed RSA key exchange/CBC/renegotiation), HKDF key schedule (Early Secret, Handshake Secret, Master Secret), and PQC handshakes: classical ~5 KB vs hybrid ~15 KB vs pure PQC ~25 KB. Includes live TLS handshake simulator powered by OpenSSL WASM. Out of scope: TLS 1.2 backward compatibility details, certificate transparency logs, and OCSP stapling mechanics.

**Sub-topics keywords:** TLS 1.3 RFC 8446, handshake 1-RTT, cipher suites, key exchange, ECDHE ephemeral, forward secrecy, HKDF key schedule, ML-KEM, X25519MLKEM768, ClientHello, ServerHello, certificate verification, Finished message, session keys, mutual TLS mTLS, certificate negotiation, cipher suite simplification, removed RSA key exchange, removed CBC modes, removed renegotiation, PQC certificate chain size, hybrid handshake size, performance overhead.

chunks.title: VPN/IPsec & SSH — scope & keywords
chunks.content:
**Scope.** IKEv2 and SSH key exchange with PQC: hybrid ML-KEM integration, WireGuard Rosenpass protocol, and protocol size comparison. Covers IKEv2 (RFC 7296) KEM payload structure with ML-KEM-768 encapsulation (~1,088 bytes ciphertext vs ~256 bytes RSA), RFC 9370 (Multiple Key Exchanges in IKEv2) for hybrid support, OpenSSH KexAlgorithms negotiation (OpenSSH 9.0+ supports mlkem768x25519-sha256), and Rosenpass post-quantum handshake for WireGuard (adds post-quantum rekeying to classical VPN). Covers IKEv2 handshake size growth (classical ~800 bytes → hybrid ~2,200 bytes), SSH handshake growth (classical ~200 bytes → hybrid ~4,500 bytes), and vendor roadmaps (strongSwan, libreswan, OpenVPN). Out of scope: IPsec protocol mechanics beyond key exchange, WireGuard cryptography details, and SSH protocol layers below key exchange.

**Sub-topics keywords:** IKEv2 internet key exchange, IPsec VPN, ML-KEM key encapsulation, RFC 9370 multiple key exchanges, hybrid key exchange, SSH key exchange algorithm, OpenSSH, ml-kem768x25519, WireGuard Rosenpass, post-quantum rekeying, KEM encapsulation, handshake size, CFD data size, strongSwan, libreswan, OpenVPN, X25519, P-256, client authentication, server authentication, perfect forward secrecy.

chunks.title: Email & Document Signing — scope & keywords
chunks.content:
**Scope.** S/MIME and CMS (Cryptographic Message Syntax RFC 5652) for secure email and document signing, focusing on transition from classical to post-quantum cryptography. Covers CMS SignedData and AuthEnvelopedData structures, paradigm shift from RSA key transport to KEM-based encryption (RFC 9629 KEMRecipientInfo), S/MIME certificate requirements (keyUsage digitalSignature, extKeyUsage id-kp-emailProtection), and PQC standards (ML-DSA for signing RFC 9882, ML-KEM for encryption via RFC 9629, RSA-KEM RFC 9690 as transitional, HSS/LMS for long-lived signatures RFC 9708). Covers migration challenges: bidirectional compatibility (both sender and recipient must support same algorithms), dual-algorithm certificates, recipient capability discovery via smimeCapabilities, message size impact (ML-DSA-65 3.3 KB signature vs 72 bytes ECDSA), and email gateway compatibility. Out of scope: PDF signature mechanics, timestamp authorities, and archival validation beyond CMS scope.

**Sub-topics keywords:** S/MIME secure MIME, CMS cryptographic message syntax, RFC 5652, SignedData AuthEnvelopedData, digital signatures, email encryption, KEM-based encryption, KEMRecipientInfo, RFC 9629, ML-DSA signature signing, ML-KEM encryption, RSA key transport, key agreement, recipient certificate, smimeCapabilities, signature size, message size impact, MIME type application/pkcs7-signature, email gateway compatibility, dual-algorithm certificates, bidirectional compatibility, signature verification.

chunks.title: PKI — scope & keywords
chunks.content:
**Scope.** Hands-on public key infrastructure fundamentals through interactive certificate operations: building certificate chains in-browser using OpenSSL WASM. Covers X.509v3 certificate structure (RFC 5280), six workshop steps (Generate CSR, Create Root CA, Certificate Issuance, Parse Certificate, Revocation via CRL, MTC Comparison), trust models (hierarchical, bridge CA, web of trust), digital signature mechanics, and critical challenge of migrating long-lived Root CA certificates to quantum-resistant algorithms. Discusses Merkle Tree Certificates (draft-ietf-plants-merkle-tree-certs, which replaced draft-davidben-tls-merkle-tree-certs) achieving 3–63% size reduction through batch signing vs individual per-certificate signatures. Covers PQC migration challenges: certificate size growth (ML-DSA-87 public keys ~2,592 bytes vs 294 bytes for ECDSA P-256), constrained device support, cross-signed trust chains, and CNSA 2.0 deadline of 2030 for PQC-only PKI. Out of scope: OCSP (Online Certificate Status Protocol) details, CRL distribution points mechanics, and certificate transparency transparency log auditing.

**Sub-topics keywords:** X.509v3 certificates, PKI public key infrastructure, certificate chain, root CA intermediate end-entity, digital signatures, certificate signing request CSR, certificate revocation list CRL, OCSP, trust hierarchy, RFC 5280, PKCS#10, certificate extensions, key usage, extended key usage, subject alternative name, basic constraints, Merkle tree certificates, certificate size, ML-DSA signatures, hybrid certificates, certificate validation, trust model, bridge CA.

chunks.title: KMS & PQC Key Management — scope & keywords
chunks.content:
**Scope.** PQC key management patterns: envelope encryption with ML-KEM, hybrid key wrapping (X25519MLKEM768, P-256+ML-KEM-768, X-Wing), multi-provider rotation planning, and KMIP v2.1 protocol operations. Covers PQC key management fundamentals (algorithm separation, key size explosion from ~32 bytes classical keys to ~1,184 bytes ML-KEM-768 public keys), NIST SP 800-227 KEM guidance for key wrapping, KMS provider landscape (AWS KMS ML-DSA signing keys with hybrid post-quantum TLS but no ML-KEM keys, Google Cloud KMS signing GA and KEMs in Preview, Azure Key Vault, HashiCorp Vault, Thales CipherTrust, Fortanix DSM), and compliance deadlines (CNSA 2.0, NIST IR 8547). Covers envelope encryption demonstration: ML-KEM encaps → KDF → AES-KW wrap, hybrid key wrapping with X25519+ML-KEM-768 combiner, and enterprise multi-cloud patterns. Out of scope: Cloud provider key derivation functions, BYOK/HYOK full implementation details, and HSM-specific vendor APIs beyond KMIP.

**Sub-topics keywords:** KMS key management system, envelope encryption, ML-KEM key encapsulation, key wrapping, hybrid key exchange, X25519MLKEM768, KEM encapsulation decapsulation, HKDF key derivation, AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault, Google Cloud KMS, HashiCorp Vault, KMIP key management interoperability protocol, key hierarchy, DEK data encryption key, KEK key encryption key, key rotation, hybrid key combiner, X-Wing combiner, SP 800-227 recommendations.

chunks.title: HSM & PQC Operations — scope & keywords
chunks.content:
**Scope.** Hardware Security Module operations for PQC: PKCS#11 v3.2 mechanisms (CKM_ML_KEM, CKM_ML_DSA), vendor comparison, firmware migration paths, and FIPS 140-3 validation tracking. Covers HSM architecture for PQC (FIPS 140-3 levels, on-prem vs cloud), deep dive into on-prem vendors (Thales Luna v7.9.2, Entrust nShield v13.8.0, Utimaco Quantum Protect), cloud HSM options (AWS CloudHSM, Azure Dedicated HSM, Google Cloud HSM), side-channel attack surfaces (NTT power analysis, EM emanation, fault injection, ML-DSA hedged signing), firmware migration (upgrade paths, dual-partition strategy, FIPS re-validation), and stateful signature state management (LMS/HSS NVRAM persistence, CNSA 2.0 requirements). Covers FIPS 140-3 validation tiers and CMVP/CAVP PQC validation tracking. Out of scope: Detailed PKCS#11 token initialization, PIN management, and vendor-specific configuration dialects.

**Sub-topics keywords:** HSM hardware security module, PKCS#11 v3.2, CKM ML-KEM ML-DSA mechanisms, FIPS 140-3, Thales Luna, Entrust nShield, Utimaco, AWS CloudHSM, Azure Dedicated HSM, side-channel attacks, power analysis, electromagnetic emanation, fault injection, firmware migration, CMVP CAVP validation, ML-KEM key generation, ML-DSA signing, state management, NVRAM, hardware acceleration, PQC maturity score.

chunks.title: SLH-DSA: Stateless Hash Signatures — scope & keywords
chunks.content:
**Scope.** Master FIPS 205 SLH-DSA: stateless hash-based digital signatures with no per-key state tracking (unlike stateful LMS/XMSS). Covers WOTS+ one-time signatures, FORS few-time signatures, hypertree architecture, twelve parameter sets from FIPS 205 Table 2 at NIST Levels 1/3/5 with SHA-2 and SHAKE variants, context strings for domain separation, deterministic signing mode, and HashSLH-DSA pre-hash variant. Covers the s vs f tradeoff (-s small variants produce smaller signatures but require more hash rounds per layer; -f fast variants use more layers for faster signing at larger signature cost). Signature sizes range from 7,856 bytes (SHA2-128s) to 49,856 bytes (SHAKE-256f). Security rests entirely on hash function properties (SHA-256, SHA-512, SHAKE256), not algebraic hardness. Covers why NSA's CNSA 2.0 FAQ says SLH-DSA is not approved for any use in National Security Systems, where LMS/XMSS are the approved hash-based signatures for firmware signing. Out of scope: WOTS chain-chain details, FORS randomness engineering, and hypertree optimization techniques.

**Sub-topics keywords:** SLH-DSA stateless hash-based signatures, FIPS 205, WOTS plus one-time signatures, FORS few-time signatures, hypertree, Merkle tree, parameter sets, SHA-2 SHAKE, security level, signature size, key size, signing speed, deterministic signing, context strings, domain separation, hash function collision resistance, CNSA 2.0, conservative security, stateless architecture, deployment simplicity.

chunks.title: Stateful Hash Signatures — scope & keywords
chunks.content:
**Scope.** LMS (Leighton-Micali Signature) and XMSS (eXtended Merkle Signature Scheme) — most conservative post-quantum signature schemes standardized in NIST SP 800-208, deriving security solely from hash function properties without new cryptographic hardness assumptions. Covers Merkle tree structure (each leaf contains hash of unique one-time public key, tree root is overall public key, signatures include OTS signature plus authentication path), Winternitz OTS with parameter W controlling size/speed tradeoff (W=1 fastest/largest, W=8 slowest/smallest), and the catastrophic OTS reuse vulnerability (signing two different messages with same leaf enables private key recovery). Covers LMS/HSS (RFC 8554) with tree heights 5–25 (32 to 33M signatures), 56-byte public keys, 1.3–9.3 KB signature sizes, and XMSS/XMSS^MT with bitmask-based tree hash, tighter security proofs, and forward security. State management requirements (atomic updates, non-volatile storage, HSM monotonic counters). Comparison with SLH-DSA: LMS/XMSS offer smaller signatures and faster signing but require state tracking and bounded signature counts; SLH-DSA is stateless with unlimited signatures but larger/slower. Out of scope: Detailed Merkle tree construction, OTS key derivation mechanics, and HSS tree level coordination.

**Sub-topics keywords:** LMS Leighton-Micali Signature, HSS hierarchical signature scheme, XMSS eXtended Merkle signature scheme, XMSS^MT, NIST SP 800-208, Merkle tree, one-time signatures OTS, Winternitz OTS, state management, monotonic counter, signature size, key size, signing speed, forward security, RFC 8554 RFC 8391, bounded signatures, tree height, leaf index advancement, state loss risk, stateful vs stateless comparison.

chunks.title: Digital Assets — scope & keywords
chunks.content:
**Scope.** Cryptographic foundations of Bitcoin, Ethereum, and Solana blockchain networks, exploring quantum threat analysis and institutional custody architecture. Covers key generation and address derivation pipelines (Bitcoin: SHA-256 then RIPEMD-160 then Base58Check; Ethereum: Keccak-256 with EIP-55 checksum; Solana: direct Base58 encoding of Ed25519 public key), digital signature algorithms (ECDSA for Bitcoin and Ethereum, Schnorr (BIP-340) for Bitcoin Taproot spends, EdDSA for Solana), and HD wallet construction (BIP-39 mnemonics, BIP-32 tree derivation, BIP-44 multi-account hierarchy, SLIP-0010 for Solana Ed25519 hardened-only paths). Covers quantum threats (all elliptic curve algorithms secp256k1 ECDSA, Ed25519 EdDSA, ECDH in HD wallets vulnerable to Shor's algorithm), hash function quantum safety (SHA-256, Keccak-256, RIPEMD-160 remain resistant to Grover's), and PQC migration challenges (immutable ledger history, larger post-quantum signatures/keys, consensus protocol changes, backward compatibility). Covers the post-quantum proposals as they stand: Bitcoin's BIP-360 (P2MR, Draft status) includes no post-quantum signature of its own, and its authors intend to offer one as a separate proposal (descriptions of the earlier P2QRH design are out of date); Ethereum's Lean roadmap replaces BLS consensus signatures with the hash-based leanXMSS scheme, targets core post-quantum infrastructure by approximately 2029, and considers EIP-8141 account abstraction for signature agility; Solana's SIMD-0461 Falcon signature-verification syscall was closed by its author on 2026-06-17. Covers custody architecture: hybrid TLS cites RFC 10024, and the HSM reference design assumes a module validated to FIPS 140-3 Level 3 while the Hong Kong SFC and Dubai VARA texts name no certification scheme. Out of scope: Consensus mechanism security, smart contract security, and mining mechanics.

**Sub-topics keywords:** Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana, blockchain, secp256k1, ECDSA, Ed25519, EdDSA, key generation, address derivation, SHA-256, RIPEMD-160, Keccak-256, HD wallet, BIP-39 mnemonic, BIP-32 derivation, BIP-44 multi-account, SLIP-0010, transaction signing, recovery parameter, EIP-55 checksum, post-quantum migration, signature size, address format, ledger immutability, Schnorr BIP-340 Taproot, BIP-360 P2MR, P2QRH, leanXMSS, EIP-8141, SIMD-0461, RFC 10024, custody HSM FIPS 140-3.

chunks.title: 5G Security — scope & keywords
chunks.content:
**Scope.** 3GPP 5G security architecture's three pillars: subscriber privacy (SUCI concealment), mutual authentication (5G-AKA), and SIM provisioning, with detailed focus on post-quantum migration path. Covers SUCI (Subscription Concealed Identifier) encryption to prevent IMSI catcher attacks, classical ECIES-based concealment profiles (Profile A using X25519, Profile B using P-256), and emerging Profile C (ML-KEM/Kyber with quantum resistance). Covers MILENAGE authentication algorithm (AES-128 based, five functions f1–f5 producing MAC-A, XRES, CK, IK, AK; quantum-resistant), 5G key hierarchy (CK/IK → KAUSF → KSEAF → KAMF → KNASint/KNASenc → KgNB), and SIM key provisioning supply chain (K generation in factory HSM, OPc computation, USIM personalization, encrypted transport). Covers differential quantum vulnerability: SUCI concealment (asymmetric ECDH) broken by Shor's algorithm, but MILENAGE/5G-AKA (symmetric AES) and SIM provisioning remain quantum-resistant. Out of scope: 3GPP RAN protocol mechanics, 5G core network architecture, and standalone non-3GPP access.

**Sub-topics keywords:** 3GPP 5G, SUCI subscription concealed identifier, IMSI catcher, ECIES encryption, Profile A B C, X25519, P-256, ML-KEM, 5G-AKA authentication, MILENAGE algorithm, AES-128, CK IK KAUSF KSEAF, SIM provisioning, USIM, K OPc, factory HSM, encrypted transport, HNDL risk, quantum vulnerability differential, Shor's algorithm.

chunks.title: Digital ID — scope & keywords
chunks.content:
**Scope.** EUDI Wallet simulation covering the European Digital Identity ecosystem established by eIDAS 2.0 (Regulation EU 2024/1183), mandating all 27 EU member states provide citizens with at least one EUDI Wallet by late 2026. Covers full credential lifecycle (issuance, presentation, qualified electronic signing) through five-step interactive workshop, credential formats (mso_mdoc ISO 18013-5 CBOR binary for proximity, SD-JWT RFC 9901 for remote), layered trust framework (National Trusted Lists, QTSPs, eIDAS Bridge), and privacy-by-design principles (selective disclosure, unlinkability, data minimization). Covers PID (Person Identification Data), QEAA (Qualified Electronic Attestations), QES (Qualified Electronic Signatures), and post-quantum readiness roadmap (current ECDSA, future ML-DSA/SLH-DSA as FIPS 204/205 replacements). Covers the EU roadmap from the NIS Cooperation Group (it does not name EUDI Wallets) targeting national roadmaps by Dec 2026, high-risk migration by 2030, full PQC transition by 2035. Out of scope: eIDAS regulation compliance details, National Trusted List governance mechanics, and cross-border revocation procedures.

**Sub-topics keywords:** eIDAS 2.0 regulation, EUDI wallet, person identification data PID, qualified electronic attestation QEAA, qualified electronic signature QES, mso_mdoc ISO 18013-5, SD-JWT RFC 9901, selective disclosure, unlinkability, National Trusted Lists, QTSP qualified trust service provider, Architecture Reference Framework ARF, CSC cloud signature consortium, OpenID4VCI OpenID4VP, FIPS 204 ML-DSA, FIPS 205 SLH-DSA, privacy-by-design, credential issuance.

chunks.title: Entropy & Randomness — scope & keywords
chunks.content:
**Scope.** Critical role of entropy and randomness in cryptographic security with emphasis on post-quantum requirements. Covers NIST SP 800-90 framework: SP 800-90A Rev. 1 (DRBG mechanisms: CTR_DRBG, Hash_DRBG, HMAC_DRBG; Rev. 2 is only a pre-draft call for comments, 2025-09-04, announcing a planned SHAKE/XOF-based DRBG with no draft text), SP 800-90B (entropy source validation with continuous health tests and min-entropy estimators), SP 800-90C (RBG constructions combining sources with DRBGs). Covers entropy testing (repetition count test, adaptive proportion test, most common value, collision test, Markov test, compression test), CMVP entropy validation (Entropy Validation Certificates for SP 800-90B sources, Random Bit Generator Validation Certificates for SP 800-90C under IG D.T), TRNG vs QRNG (both judged by the same SP 800-90B requirements; "quantum" is not evidence), and combining sources for PQC defense-in-depth under stated independence conditions. Covers PQC random inputs per FIPS 203/204/205: ML-KEM d, z and m are 32 bytes each with an RBG of at least 128/192/256 bits for ML-KEM-512/768/1024; ML-DSA seed ξ is 32 bytes with an RBG of at least 192 bits (ML-DSA-65), 256 bits (ML-DSA-87), or at least 128 and preferably 192 bits (ML-DSA-44); hedged-signing randomness has no mandatory RBG strength; SLH-DSA key seeds are n bytes with an RBG of at least 8n bits. Out of scope: Detailed statistical test mathematics, hardware RNG implementation details, and QRNG physics.

**Sub-topics keywords:** Entropy randomness DRBG deterministic random bit generator, SP 800-90A 800-90B 800-90C, CTR DRBG Hash DRBG HMAC DRBG, entropy source validation, health tests, min-entropy, TRNG true random number generator, QRNG quantum random number generator, seeding, Debian OpenSSL bug, entropy conditioning, entropy testing, combining sources, Debian 2008 PID seeding, ML-KEM ML-DSA SLH-DSA random inputs RBG security strength, RBG construction.

chunks.title: Merkle Tree Certificates — scope & keywords
chunks.content:
**Scope.** Addresses certificate bloat problem created by PQC signatures: ML-DSA-44 is 2,420 bytes vs ECDSA P-256 64 bytes (37× increase), so a leaf-plus-intermediate ML-DSA-44 chain with its CertificateVerify signature carries about 9.9 KB of keys and signatures. Covers Merkle Tree Certificates (MTCs) solving this through batch signing (SHA-256 Merkle tree leaves = certificate assertions, only root signed with CA's PQC key, each cert holder receives compact inclusion proof ~736 bytes). Discusses MTC architecture: five roles (CA maintains issuance log + builds tree + signs checkpoints, Cosigner signs log view, Authenticating Party presents cert + proof, Relying Party verifies, Monitor watches log). Covers two certificate types: Standalone (inclusion proof + cosignatures, works without pre-sync) and Landmark (no signatures in the certificate, requires pre-synced trusted subtrees; for ML-DSA-44 about 4,668 bytes per handshake vs 10,522 bytes for a leaf-plus-intermediate chain, about 56% smaller, with a standalone certificate about 36% smaller). Covers tradeoffs: Landmark requires periodic pre-sync (not suitable for offline devices), revocation via Revocation by Index, IETF standardization (draft-davidben-tls-merkle-tree-certs adopted by PLANTS WG). Connection to hash-based signatures: SLH-DSA/LMS/XMSS use Merkle trees internally; MTCs apply same principle at infrastructure layer. Out of scope: Tree rebalancing algorithms, cosigner threshold logic, and gossip protocol details for log consistency.

**Sub-topics keywords:** Merkle tree certificates, certificate bloat, PQC signature size, batch signing, inclusion proof, sibling hash chain, hash tree recomputation, domain separation, Merkle tree CA, cosigner attestation, append-only log, standlone certificates, landmark certificates, signatureless proof, revocation by index, draft-ietf-plants-merkle-tree-certs, IETF Hackathon test vectors, size reduction ratio, handshake overhead.

chunks.title: Quantum Key Distribution — scope & keywords
chunks.content:
**Scope.** Quantum Key Distribution methods distributing encryption keys using quantum physics rather than mathematical hardness assumptions, providing information-theoretic security. Covers BB84 protocol (Bennett & Brassard 1984): single photons encoded in two conjugate bases (rectilinear/diagonal), qubit preparation, measurement, basis reconciliation (sifted key ~50% of transmitted bits), eavesdropper detection via QBER threshold (~11%). Covers state of the art: fiber single link (~100 km commercial), fiber with trusted nodes (>2,000 km deployed), satellite (>7,000 km demonstrated: Micius 7,600 km China-Austria 2017), free-space urban (~10 km research). Covers satellite QKD: Micius/QUESS (China), EAGLE-1/EuroQCI (EU), QEYSSat (Canada), SOCRATES (Japan), SpooQy-1 (Singapore), QKDSat (UK). Covers NIST IR 8301 position (does not generally recommend QKD, recommends PQC FIPS 203/204/205, acknowledges niche high-security applications), limitations (~100 km fiber without trusted nodes, trusted node compromise risk, high cost, side-channel vulnerabilities, low key rates, no built-in authentication). Covers QKD+PQC hybrid integration (combines QKD-derived key + ML-KEM shared secret via HKDF) and QKD+HSM integration (PKCS#11 C_UnwrapKey/C_CreateObject). Out of scope: Quantum mechanics derivation, entanglement-based protocols beyond Micius examples, and photon detection engineering.

**Sub-topics keywords:** QKD quantum key distribution, BB84 protocol, qubit superposition, photon measurement, basis reconciliation, sifted key, QBER quantum bit error rate, eavesdropper detection, information-theoretic security, fiber QKD, satellite QKD, trusted-node relay, Micius, EuroQCI, trusted node compromise, key rate, distance, free-space, entanglement-based, NIST IR 8301, QKD vs PQC, hybrid key derivation, HKDF combiner, HSM integration, global deployments.

chunks.title: Code Signing — scope & keywords
chunks.content:
**Scope.** Post-quantum code signing and software supply chain security covering supply chain attacks (SolarWinds, 3CX, Codecov), quantum amplifier for supply chains (quantum computers transform risk from key theft to key forgery via Shor's), and PQC signing algorithms (ML-DSA, SLH-DSA, LMS). Covers classical vs PQC code signing: ECDSA P-256 64 bytes vs ML-DSA-44 2,420 bytes vs ML-DSA-87 4,627 bytes vs SLH-DSA-128s 7,856 bytes — PQC signatures 38–123× larger than ECDSA but acceptable for code signing since verification is per-install. Covers code signing certificate chains (Root CA ML-DSA-87 strongest, Intermediate CA ML-DSA-65, end-entity Code Signing Certificate ML-DSA-44 with keyUsage 1.3.6.1.5.5.7.3.3, 1-year validity). Covers package manager signing (RPM leading with hybrid ML-DSA-87+Ed448 in RHEL 10, most others depend on Sigstore PQC adoption), Sigstore keyless signing (identity-based trust via GitHub/Google auth, short-lived certificates from Fulcio CA, signatures recorded in Rekor transparency log), secure boot/firmware signing (trust chain from immutable root through UEFI Secure Boot to runtime firmware). Covers CNSA 2.0 mandate: LMS/HSS or XMSS for firmware/software signing in NSS, 2025 prefer, 2030 exclusive, 2033–35 full enforcement. Out of scope: Detailed supply chain attack mechanics, GPG/OpenPGP protocol specifics, and SLSA framework implementation.

**Sub-topics keywords:** Code signing, supply chain security, SolarWinds 3CX Codecov attacks, quantum amplifier, signing key recovery, forge signatures, ML-DSA firmware signing, SLH-DSA conservative, LMS stateful, signature size, certificate chain, Sigstore keyless signing, Fulcio CA, Rekor transparency log, cosign, Notation, UEFI Secure Boot, firmware signing, CNSA 2.0 firmware mandate, SLSA framework, SBOM attestation, package signing RPM DEB.

chunks.title: API Security & JWT — scope & keywords
chunks.content:
**Scope.** Migration of JSON Web Token (JWT) infrastructure to post-quantum cryptography covering JWTs as foundation of modern API authentication (OAuth 2.0 access tokens, OpenID Connect ID tokens, DPoP proofs). Covers quantum vulnerability: RS256 (RSA), ES256 (ECDSA P-256), and EdDSA all broken by Shor's algorithm; ECDH-ES key agreement equally vulnerable; HMAC-based algorithms (HS256) remain quantum-safe but require shared secrets. Covers HNDL for JWTs: attackers capture signed JWTs today and forge signatures once quantum computers arrive (especially concerning for long-lived tokens: refresh tokens, long-expiry ID tokens). Covers PQC JWT signing with ML-DSA (IETF draft-ietf-jose-pqc): ML-DSA-44 (NIST Level 2, 2,420 B), ML-DSA-65 (Level 3, 3,309 B recommended), ML-DSA-87 (Level 5, 4,627 B). Covers PQC JWT key agreement with ML-KEM (replaces ECDH-ES in JWE), KEM encapsulation producing ciphertext + shared secret, HKDF derives Content Encryption Key. Covers token size implications: ML-DSA-65 JWT ~4.7 KB vs ~300 B for ES256 (16× increase), challenges with 8 KB HTTP header limits, 4 KB cookie limits. Covers OAuth 2.0/OIDC migration: coordinated changes across authorization servers (JWKS endpoints), resource servers (signature verification, header size limits), client applications (token storage, DPoP proofs). Out of scope: OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow mechanics, OpenID Connect discovery, and client credential grant details.

**Sub-topics keywords:** JWT JSON web token, JWS signing, JWE encryption, RS256 ES256 EdDSA, HMAC-based algorithms, HNDL attack, Shor's algorithm, JWT compact serialization, header payload signature, ML-DSA signing algorithm, ML-KEM key agreement, KEM encapsulation, JWE algorithm ID, token size, HTTP header limits, cookie limits, JOSE JOSE header, alg algorithm ID, OAuth 2.0, OpenID Connect, DPoP demonstrating proof of possession, JWKS endpoint.

chunks.title: Web Gateway PQC — scope & keywords

chunks.title: IoT & Embedded Device PQC — scope & keywords
chunks.content:

chunks.title: PQC Risk Management — scope & keywords
chunks.content:
**Scope.** Identify, quantify, and prioritize quantum computing risks covering CRQC scenario planning (adjustable 2028–2045 timelines), building comprehensive risk registers for quantum-vulnerable cryptographic assets, and generating likelihood-by-impact risk heatmaps (5×5 grid). chunks.title: Confidential Computing & TEEs — scope & keywords

chunks.title: Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) & HSM Key Custody — scope & keywords
chunks.content:
**Scope.** Explore fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) as data-in-use protection that trusts mathematics instead of hardware, covering the contrast with TEEs (root of trust, side channels, speed, integrity of the result), the four schemes in the ISO/IEC 28033 drafts (BGV, BFV, CKKS, TFHE/CGGI with FHEW), noise and bootstrapping. Covers the FHE key set (one small secret key, large public encryption, relinearization, rotation and bootstrapping keys), who runs each operation (client, server, key holder) and how AES data enters FHE through transciphering (Kreyvium, AES-128-CTR in TFHE-rs). Covers FHE against the quantum threat (lattice-based, no known quantum break; the classical parts around the scheme still need a PQC fix). Covers the HSM as FHE key custodian (non-extractable seed, secret key derived inside the HSM, ML-DSA signature over the parameter set, decryption under policy, HSM-to-HSM backup), threshold FHE (OpenFHE, Lattigo), why an HSM must not be a raw decryption oracle, and the open-source implementations (TFHE-rs, OpenFHE, Lattigo, Microsoft SEAL). Out of scope: commercial FHE products, GPU or FPGA acceleration details, and a PKCS#11 or KMIP standard for FHE objects (none exists today).

**Sub-topics keywords:** FHE fully homomorphic encryption, ISO/IEC 28033, BGV, BFV, CKKS, TFHE, CGGI, FHEW, noise, bootstrapping, ciphertext, relinearization key, Galois key, evaluation key, transciphering, Kreyvium, threshold FHE, LWE, RLWE, lattice, HSM key custody, non-extractable seed, decryption oracle, noise flooding, TFHE-rs, OpenFHE, Lattigo, FIPS 203 204, PKCS#11.

chunks.title: Financial Services & Payments PQC — scope & keywords
chunks.content:
**Scope.** The whole payments and banking estate, in three learner paths (Cards & Acceptance, Banking & Settlement, Retail & E-Commerce) so no audience is asked for the full 110 minutes. CARDS: EMV card authentication (SDA static RSA, DDA dynamic RSA per-transaction, CDA combined with application cryptogram, all RSA-2048 quantum-vulnerable), payment networks (Visa, Mastercard, Amex, UnionPay, Discover — 14.7 billion EMV chip cards in circulation at the end of 2024 per EMVCo), transaction flows (online authorization, offline DDA/CDA, contactless, mobile payments), card personalization 5-phase process (Chip OS, Pre-Perso, Personalization, Key Injection, Activation) with RSA certificate chain, FN-DSA-512 (666-byte signatures, ~6.7 KB chain) is smaller than ML-DSA-44 (2,420-byte signatures, ~15.3 KB), the size argument for constrained card NVM (EMVCo's March 2024 position statement names no post-quantum algorithm for EMV cards, the card-side evidence is research such as a 2022 IDEMIA prototype and a Banque de France estimate, cited by Mastercard, of 4 to 6 times more chip RAM, and NIST lists FIPS 206 as in development), tokenization TSP architectures (Visa VTS, Mastercard MDES, Amex EST) and mobile wallets (Apple Pay Google Pay Samsung Pay), POS terminals (5 types: Traditional POS, mPOS, SoftPOS, ATM, Unattended) with DUKPT key management and the Key Injection Facility ceremony as the primary quantum vulnerability (RSA-2048 BDK key transport); the 3DES-to-AES move for PIN encryption is classical modernisation, not a quantum fix. BANKING & SETTLEMENT: interbank rails — Swift messaging (FIN / ISO 20022), domestic RTGS, and correspondent banking chains where the weakest hop sets the security of the whole path and no participant can migrate unilaterally; HNDL exposure driven by how long data stays sensitive rather than by a guessed CRQC date (the Settlement Exposure Modeller applies Mosca's theorem with the migration-time term set to zero, so its result is a floor); bank key management and key blocks, where a key is wrapped together with its usage attributes so it cannot be repurposed, and the current standard is ANSI X9.143 rather than the far more frequently cited X9 TR-31. RETAIL & E-COMMERCE: card-not-present checkout, 3-D Secure 2.x ECDSA challenge signing (PCI SSC lists a separate PCI 3DS Core standard among its standards; this module does not state what it covers or requires), and e-commerce TLS as the fastest migration path in the estate (hybrid ML-KEM TLS is published as RFC 10024, IETF Standards Track, August 2026; the native ML-KEM TLS scheme is still an Internet-Draft). SECTOR REGULATION: nine bodies across six jurisdictions (BIS Project Leap Phase 2, G7 Cyber Expert Group, UK CMORG, Europol Quantum Safe Financial Forum, FS-ISAC, MAS, DORA, the Nacha Payments Innovation Alliance roadmap, which is a recommendation rather than a mandate, and the EU NIS CG Coordinated Implementation Roadmap), none carrying a dated algorithm mandate of the CNSA 2.0 kind — the EU roadmap sets a dated transition expectation (high-risk use cases by end-2030) without naming an algorithm, and otherwise the pressure comes from operational-resilience regulation and HNDL exposure. MIGRATION: 10 payment components mapped by severity and effort, critical path (HSM key wrapping → KIF key injection → Card personalization → Offline auth); the 2030 and 2035 markers on the timeline are NIST IR 8547's trajectory for NIST standards and federal systems, not a payments-sector mandate, and PCI PTS HSM v5.0 (announced 18 May 2026) adds support for post-quantum cryptography considerations, and the PTS listing’s expiry table (HSM v4.x requirements approval June 2027, device models April 2033) gives approval-expiry dates, not post-quantum deadlines. Out of scope: EMV transaction cryptogram verification internals, fraud detection rules, and settlement finality/liquidity mechanics (the module covers settlement rails as a cryptographic migration problem, not the economics of settlement).

**Sub-topics keywords:** EMV chip card, SDA static data authentication, DDA dynamic data authentication, CDA combined data authentication, RSA-2048, tokenization, TSP token service provider, POS point of sale, DUKPT derived unique key per transaction, BDK base derivation key, Key Injection Facility KIF, KIF ceremony, card personalization, NVM non-volatile memory, Visa Mastercard Amex UnionPay Discover, interbank settlement, Swift CSCF, ISO 20022, RTGS real-time gross settlement, correspondent banking, key block, ANSI X9.143, X9 TR-31, EPC 342-08, BIS Project Leap, DORA, CMORG, Europol Quantum Safe Financial Forum, FS-ISAC, MAS, G7 Cyber Expert Group, harvest now decrypt later, card-not-present, 3-D Secure, e-commerce checkout, PCI 3DS Core Security Standard, RFC 10024, EMVCo position statement, FIPS 206, 3DES to AES, Mosca's theorem, Nacha Payments Innovation Alliance, NIS CG roadmap, NIST IR 8547, PCI PTS HSM v5.0.

chunks.title: PQC Candidates & Lifecycle — scope & keywords
chunks.content:
**Scope.** PQC standardisation is a rolling process, not a single event. This module tracks the full algorithm portfolio: NIST-standardised algorithms (FIPS 203 ML-KEM, FIPS 204 ML-DSA, FIPS 205 SLH-DSA); Falcon, selected as the basis for planned FIPS 206 FN-DSA, which remains in development with no published public draft or final standard; and HQC, selected March 2025 as an alternate code-based KEM, plus the signature on-ramp — NIST IR 8528 (Oct 2024) down-selected to 14 second-round candidates and NIST IR 8610 (May 2026) advanced nine to the third round — across four mathematical families. Covers the four candidate families: MPC-in-the-Head (FAEST, MQOM, SDitH — AES-based/combinatorial assumptions, kilobyte signatures), Multivariate (UOV, MAYO, QR-UOV, SNOVA — tiny 96–838 byte signatures, large public keys; 2025 Ran wedge attack broke most UOV/SNOVA parameter sets, reparameterisation to odd-characteristic fields restores security), Isogeny (SQIsign — smallest combined pk+sig of any PQC candidate, 148 bytes at NIST Cat 1, cousin SIKE was broken in 2022), and Lattice (HAWK — integer-only alternative to FN-DSA eliminating floating-point side-channel hazards). Covers validation process (evaluation criteria: security, performance, implementation characteristics, IP; public cryptanalysis rounds; NIST IR status reports), cryptanalysis timeline showing historical attacks, candidate comparator by key/signature sizes across security levels, standardisation lifecycle phases, and future rounds forecaster. Covers worldwide parallel processes: KpqC (Korea, target 2029–2035), CACR/China (OSCCA SM-series extension), CRYPTREC (Japan, monitoring NIST), ISO/IEC SC 27 (ISO 14888 signatures, 18033 KEM — gating step for ISO-pinned jurisdictions), IETF CFRG/pquip/lamps (codepoints, X.509 bindings, hybrid composite), and ETSI QSC (European telecom guidance). Expected on-ramp standardisation window 2027+ for lattice/isogeny/MPCitH winners. Out of scope: Detailed mathematical proofs of security reductions, quantum algorithm resource estimation, and cryptanalysis methodology.

**Sub-topics keywords:** NIST standardisation, FIPS 203 ML-KEM, FIPS 204 ML-DSA, FIPS 205 SLH-DSA, FIPS 206 FN-DSA Falcon, HQC code-based KEM, NIST IR 8528, signature on-ramp candidates, MPC-in-the-Head FAEST MQOM SDitH, multivariate UOV MAYO QR-UOV SNOVA, isogeny SQIsign, lattice HAWK, cryptanalysis timeline, Ran wedge attack, SIKE broken, KpqC Korea, CACR China OSCCA, CRYPTREC Japan, ISO IEC SC27, IETF CFRG, ETSI QSC, algorithm families comparison, key size signature size, worldwide standardisation, on-ramp timeline.

chunks.title: PKI Enrollment Protocols (EST & CMP) — scope & keywords
chunks.content:
**Scope.** EST (RFC 7030) and CMP (RFC 9810, the July 2025 KEM update to RFC 4210) — the two protocols that carry certificate requests from a subscriber to a Certificate Authority and deliver issued certificates back. Covers EST: HTTPS-based enrollment, client POSTs base64-encoded PKCS#10 CSR to `/.well-known/est/simpleenroll`, server returns PKCS#7 SignedData; proof-of-possession is the signed CSR (works for ML-DSA, not for ML-KEM). Covers CMP message structure (PKIMessage = PKIHeader + PKIBody + PKIProtection), CRMF (Certificate Request Message Format RFC 4211) cert templates, PBM-MAC vs signature-based protection, and three proof-of-possession modes: `signature` (sign the request), `encrCert` (CA encapsulates cert under requester's public key for KEM), and `raVerified`. Covers RFC 9810 (KEM-aware POP via encrCert mode for ML-KEM and other non-signing keys), RFC 9881 (ML-DSA OIDs in X.509), RFC 9935 (ML-KEM OIDs in X.509), RFC 9909 (SLH-DSA OIDs in X.509), and the production hybrid PKI pattern (parallel PQC + classical cert chains for the same end-entity, used until composite OIDs in draft-ietf-lamps-pq-composite-sigs stabilize). Workshop drives real in-process CMP exchanges in-browser via OpenSSL 3.6 WASM: six steps covering ML-DSA-65 key generation, CMP Initial Request, EST simpleenroll, CMP KUR with ML-KEM (RFC 9810 encrCert POP), composite enrollment (parallel chains), and certificate inspection. First commercial CA to ship production CMP with ML-DSA and ML-KEM was EJBCA 9.1+ in 2024. Out of scope: OCSP mechanics, certificate transparency log auditing, and ACME certificate lifecycle management (covered in crypto-mgmt-modernization).

**Sub-topics keywords:** EST enrollment over secure transport, RFC 7030, CMP certificate management protocol, RFC 4210, RFC 9810 KEM update, CRMF certificate request message format, RFC 4211, PKIMessage PKIHeader PKIBody, proof-of-possession POP, signed CSR, encrCert KEM POP, PBM-MAC, ML-DSA enrollment, ML-KEM enrollment, composite OIDs LAMPS, parallel cert chains, RFC 9881 ML-DSA X.509, RFC 9935 ML-KEM X.509, RFC 9909 SLH-DSA X.509, EJBCA, OpenSSL 3.6 WASM, certificate inspection.

chunks.title: MLS — Group Messaging — scope & keywords
chunks.content:
**Scope.** Messaging Layer Security (RFC 9420) — the IETF standard for end-to-end encrypted group messaging that scales secure key agreement to groups of thousands of members. Covers TreeKEM: a ratchet tree where each member holds secrets at their leaf and on the path to the root; adding/removing members triggers an Update-Path operation that re-encrypts secrets along the path using HPKE, achieving perfect forward secrecy and post-compromise security in O(log n) messages. Covers HPKE (RFC 9180) as the cryptographic engine for path-update encryption inside MLS (DhKem25519 + SHA-256 + AES-128-GCM baseline ciphersuite), group operations (Welcome, Commit, Proposals: Add, Remove, Update), and the MLS key schedule producing epoch secrets per commit. Covers PQC ciphersuites: draft-ietf-mls-pq-ciphersuites-04 defines ML-KEM + ML-DSA ciphersuites; draft-ietf-mls-combiner-02 defines a classical + PQC hybrid combiner preserving classical security if PQC is broken (defense-in-depth during transition); draft-ietf-mls-extensions-09 covers MLS extensions framework. Covers provider architecture: the OpenMLS provider trait routes `OpenMlsCrypto` operations through PKCS#11 v3.2 against an HSM (CKM_ML_KEM, CKM_ML_DSA, CKM_AES_GCM), keeping signature keys in hardware and persisting private keys only as opaque HSM key handles. Workshop includes TreeKEM visualizer showing live group state after member operations, MLS crypto operations explorer, and provider architecture deep dive. PQC ciphersuites remain in IETF draft stage (Phase 4 of MLS-HSM integration). Out of scope: Signal Protocol double-ratchet comparison, MLS delivery service design, and group governance / moderation policies.

**Sub-topics keywords:** MLS messaging layer security, RFC 9420, TreeKEM ratchet tree, HPKE hybrid public key encryption, RFC 9180, group key agreement, forward secrecy, post-compromise security, epoch secrets, Welcome Commit Proposal, Add Remove Update operations, MLS ciphersuites, draft-ietf-mls-pq-ciphersuites ML-KEM ML-DSA, draft-ietf-mls-combiner hybrid, PKCS#11 v3.2, HSM provider, OpenMLS, opaque key handle, group messaging encryption, end-to-end encryption, O(log n) path update.

chunks.title: CycloneDX Cryptography Registry — scope & keywords
chunks.content:
**Scope.** The Crypto Registry module teaches the CycloneDX v1.7 Cryptography Registry: a standalone, versioned catalog of 96 cryptographic algorithm families (across 14 primitive types — signature, KEM/PKE, key-agreement, block/stream cipher, AEAD, MAC, hash, XOF, KDF, key-wrap, DRBG) and 246 elliptic curves (across 15 standardization categories — NIST, SECG, Brainpool, ANSSI, BLS, GOST, X9.62/X9.63, and more). It solves the "one mechanism, many names" problem: the same algorithm or curve is named differently by an HSM (PKCS#11 mechanism), a certificate (OID), a protocol (code point), a library (config string), and a JOSE/JWT service (`alg` value) — the registry gives every one of these a single canonical resolution target. PQC families (ML-KEM, ML-DSA, SLH-DSA, XMSS, LMS) are registered as first-class entries alongside classical algorithms, not a separate list. The registry is published independently of the CycloneDX specification (own JSON + JSON Schema, own version cadence) and is explicitly designed for use outside CBOM/CycloneDX tooling entirely. chunks.title: AI Security & PQC — In Simple Terms
chunks.content:
### What This Is About

Every AI system relies on an immense data pipeline—from ingestion and storage to training and inference—secured by cryptography. When dealing with billion-parameter model weights and petabytes of training data, securing this intellectual property is paramount. We use TLS for data in transit, AES wrapped with RSA for storage, and ECDSA for signing models to ensure authenticity. Furthermore, as AI agents become autonomous, they require their own machine identities to transact securely.

### Why It Matters

"Harvest Now, Decrypt Later" (HNDL) is an existential risk for AI organizations. Adversaries can steal encrypted proprietary datasets today and decrypt them when a Cryptographically Relevant Quantum Computer (CRQC) becomes available, entirely bypassing current RSA/ECDH protections. Similarly, if classical ECDSA signatures are compromised, malicious actors could seamlessly forge model provenance, inject synthetic data back into the trusted training pipeline (accelerating "model collapse"), or impersonate active AI agents performing automated commerce.

### The Key Takeaway

A holistic Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) strategy must secure the entire AI lifecycle. Migrating to ML-KEM ensures that proprietary training data and model weights remain confidential against HNDL attacks over decades. Adopting ML-DSA guarantees long-term integrity for model signing, content provenance (like C2PA), and agent-to-agent delegation tokens—defending the ecosystem against data poisoning and impersonation.

### What's Happening

AI organizations are beginning to audit their data pipelines for quantum exposure, migrating model signing to ML-DSA for long-term provenance guarantees, and designing quantum-safe authentication protocols for autonomous AI agents entering agentic commerce ecosystems.

chunks.title: API Security & JWT — In Simple Terms
chunks.content:
### What This Is About

Modern API authentication runs on JSON Web Tokens (JWT). These tokens securely pass claims using a header, payload, and a cryptographic signature (JWS) or encryption layer (JWE). Today, signed tokens mostly use classical algorithms like ES256 (ECDSA P-256) or RS256 (RSA), and encrypted ones use classical key agreement like ECDH-ES. The token's header names which algorithm protects it.

### Why It Matters

Shor's algorithm running on a future, cryptographically relevant quantum computer would break these classical mechanisms. For API security, that means an attacker could forge JWT signatures with any key verifiers still trust—impersonating users and minting OAuth 2.0 access tokens. Encrypted API traffic recorded today could be decrypted later (harvest now, decrypt later); signed tokens are not encrypted, so for them the risk is forgery, not decryption. Migrating means moving signing to ML-DSA and encryption to ML-KEM (through HPKE for JWE).

### The Key Takeaway

While the token format doesn't change, the math inside does—and it carries a large size penalty, along with new key formats and verifier policies. An ML-DSA-65 signature is 3,309 bytes compared to a 64-byte ES256 signature, representing a ~51x size increase. This enormous token size can immediately break default 8 KB HTTP headers, exceed 4 KB browser cookie limits, and spike bandwidth requirements for mobile APIs. Engineering teams must overhaul caching and session storage architectures to accommodate this PQC footprint.

### What's Happening

ML-DSA for JWS is now a standard (RFC 9964, May 2026). SLH-DSA, composite signatures and HPKE-based ML-KEM encryption for JWE are still IETF drafts, and engineering teams are prototyping PQC token flows to measure the size impact on their infrastructure.

chunks.title: ACVP Lab Workflow: From Vector Set to Evidence — In Simple Terms
chunks.content:
### What This Is About

Before a cryptographic product can be sold to many governments and regulated buyers, its algorithms are tested by an automated NIST system and the whole product is examined by an accredited laboratory. This module explains, step by step, how that algorithm testing works and what each kind of test result does — and does not — prove.

### Why It Matters

"It passed the NIST tests" can mean very different things: a run against public sample data anyone can download, a run against test data issued to an accredited lab, or an official validation certificate. Mixing them up leads to claims nobody can back.

### The Key Takeaway

Every test result is evidence only for the exact test, settings, software build and machine it ran on. Only NIST publishes validations; running public samples, including on this site, never does.

### What's Happening

The PQC Today owner reviewed and signed off this module on 1 November 2026. No accredited laboratory or certification body has reviewed it. It explains how laboratory testing works; it is not laboratory training material.

chunks.title: Aerospace PQC — In Simple Terms
chunks.content:
### What This Is About

The aerospace sector manages communications across three totally distinct domains: the Ground segment (ATC and airlines), Airborne avionics (in-flight hardware), and the Space segment (satellites). While ground systems can be patched in weeks, airborne and satellite systems rely on certified cryptography (like DO-178C) embedded inside hardware that must operate faultlessly for 20 to 55 years.

### Why It Matters

Aircraft and satellites stay in service for decades, so the classical cryptography they carry (RSA-2048, ECDSA P-256) can span the quantum transition window. The command and telemetry uplinks of a satellite launched around 2028 can be recorded for later decryption ("Harvest Now, Decrypt Later"), and in this module's planning assumptions its hardware cannot be physically upgraded after launch. PQC signatures are also much larger than the messages of legacy aviation links: in the example of IACR ePrint 2024/046 an ECDSA signature of 448 bits is already four times an ADS-B message (112 bits), so a larger PQC signature cannot fit either. Space electronics also face radiation, and the module's single-event-upset (SEU) calculator treats a bit-flip in stored key material as a risk to key refresh intervals.

### The Key Takeaway

Aerospace PQC demands exceptional engineering. Legacy protocols require ground-based "gateway-mediated" wrappers, while only modern networks (like ARINC 664) have the bandwidth for native PQC execution. For ultra-constrained or highly radiated hardware, hash-based algorithms (LMS/XMSS) offer the most resilient solution, relying entirely on public data without the fragile vulnerability of massive lattice matrices.

### What's Happening

Aerospace certification bodies are updating airworthiness standards to accommodate PQC signature sizes, while satellite operators are evaluating hash-based algorithms (LMS/XMSS) for long-duration missions where hardware cannot be physically upgraded post-launch.

chunks.title: Architect Quantum Impact — In Simple Terms
chunks.content:
### Problem

As a Security Architect, your design patterns dictate how cryptography is utilized across the enterprise infrastructure. Currently, most systems hardcode classical algorithms (like RSA-2048 or ECDSA P-256) deeply within application logic, APIs, and microservices. The Post-Quantum transition requires architecting a new "Crypto-Agile" abstraction layer that entirely decouples these algorithms from the business logic.

### Solution

Architectural decisions made today will outlive the quantum transition. Designing a non-agile system now creates massive technical debt, as replacing hardcoded cryptography across an entire microservice mesh takes years. Furthermore, PQC introduces immediate architectural friction: ML-DSA-65 certificates are functionally 50x larger than ECC certificates, immediately straining IoT memory budgets and pushing TLS latency thresholds.

### Strategy

Crypto-agility is a survival requirement, not an optional feature. Architects must immediately map all cryptographic touchpoints and mandate abstraction layers across new deployments. By planning now for the massive footprint of PQC algorithms and establishing strict algorithm-selection governance, you insulate your company's core infrastructure.

### Ecosystem

Enterprise architecture teams are defining crypto-agile reference architectures that mandate abstraction layers for all new deployments, ensuring that cryptographic algorithm swaps can be executed across microservice meshes without requiring application code rewrites.

chunks.title: Automotive PQC — In Simple Terms
chunks.content:
# Automotive PQC — In Simple Terms

## What This Is About

Modern vehicles are essentially massive, high-speed computers on wheels. They have a 15+ year lifespan on the road. The digital cryptography and certificates embedded in the hardware today to secure firmware updates will face catastrophic quantum threats long before the vehicle retires.

## Why It Matters

An attacker equipped with a quantum computer could mathematically forge over-the-air (OTA) update signatures. This would allow them to bypass security checks and push highly malicious, weaponized firmware directly into the engine, brakes, and steering modules of thousands of vehicles simultaneously.

## The Key Takeaway

Automotive manufacturers must engineer their secure boot systems today to embed massive, quantum-safe root certificates (like LMS/HSS or ML-DSA) deeply into the vehicle's engine control units, long before the car ever rolls off the assembly line.

## What's Happening

Automotive standard bodies are racing to update the secure-by-design hardware specifications to handle the significantly larger file sizes of Post-Quantum signatures, ensuring that the heavy math can run smoothly on resource-constrained microcontrollers.

chunks.title: Cryptography Bill of Materials — In Simple Terms
chunks.content:
# Cryptography Bill of Materials — In Simple Terms

## What This Is About

A Cryptography Bill of Materials (CBOM) is a machine-readable list of all the cryptography an organization actually uses — the algorithms, keys, certificates and protocols, and where each one lives. It extends the idea of a Software Bill of Materials (SBOM): the SBOM lists your software, the CBOM lists the cryptography inside it.

## Why It Matters

You cannot migrate to post-quantum cryptography what you cannot find. Most enterprises have a long tail of "ghost" cryptography — forgotten certificates, hardcoded algorithms, crypto buried in cloud services — that never appears in any inventory, and that is exactly where the risk hides. A good CBOM is built by combining the discovery tools you already run with targeted net-new scanning, then normalizing everything into one standard format you can query.

## The Key Takeaway

A CBOM only becomes useful when it is complete, normalized, and machine-verifiable: every cryptographic asset discovered across source code, binaries, the network, infrastructure and the cloud; named consistently despite the many competing standards; tied to a key you can identify and trace; and checkable by policy-as-code so you can prove what is quantum-safe and what is not.

chunks.title: Common Criteria, EUCC & eIDAS Certification — In Simple Terms
chunks.content:
### What This Is About

A closer look at the certificates that matter most in Europe: Common Criteria, the EU's EUCC scheme built on it, and the eIDAS rules for qualified signature and seal devices. It builds on the certification fundamentals module.

### Why It Matters

A Common Criteria grade such as "EAL4+" only means something once you know which extra checks were added. A CC evaluation may support an EUCC certificate or form part of an eIDAS device-assessment chain, while international CCRA recognition remains a separate, conditional question.

### The Key Takeaway

"EAL4+" means nothing until its extra components are named, and EUCC is a legal scheme — not a Protection Profile. Certification engineers must also use the current mandatory CC:2022 errata, not only the base documents.

### What's Happening

As of 24 September 2026, the EU's scheme already lists post-quantum algorithms in its approved cryptography guidance, and says lattice-based algorithms should be combined with a classical one.

The lesson also has two panels that stay closed until you open them. One is an invented example of how three post-quantum requirements could be written in a Security Target. The other is a box on how a laboratory might look at attacks on lattice-based code. No certification scheme or laboratory has reviewed either one.

chunks.title: Code Signing PQC — In Simple Terms
chunks.content:
# Code Signing PQC — In Simple Terms

## What This Is About

Code signing formally guarantees software integrity and publisher authenticity. As software supply chains grow increasingly complex with hundreds of open-source dependencies, verifying who built an update is critical to stopping injected malware.

## Why It Matters

A quantum break of classical algorithms (like RSA or ECDSA) compromises every publisher simultaneously. This means an adversary could forge any signature to impersonate trusted vendors, like Microsoft or Apple, without ever needing to steal a private key.

## The Key Takeaway

Transitioning to massive PQC algorithms (like ML-DSA or SLH-DSA) protects against "harvest now, decrypt later" firmware forgery. While PQC signatures are 38–123x larger than classical counterparts, this tradeoff is generally acceptable since software binaries only need to be verified once during installation.

## What's Happening

Modern open-source tools like Sigstore offer "keyless signing" by cleanly tying short-lived certificates to developer identities. This completely eliminates the need to manage long-term private keys, vastly simplifying the rollout of new PQC standards to developer ecosystems.

chunks.title: Compliance & Regulatory Strategy — In Simple Terms
chunks.content:
### What This Is About

Global governments and standards bodies—including NIST, NSA, ETSI, ANSSI, and BSI—are all publishing direction for the transition to Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC), with different legal force. Organizations operating internationally must reconcile differing priorities: the NSA's CNSA 2.0 requires exclusive PQC by 2030 for certain systems, while European agencies like ANSSI recommend a "Hybrid" phase (mandatory only inside France's regulated perimeter) (running classical and PQC algorithms in parallel) before full migration.

### Why It Matters

Failure to map compliance correctly means missing the dates that actually bind you — for example CNSA 2.0 acquisition milestones from 2027 for U.S. National Security Systems. Organizations cannot simply migrate unilaterally; they are gated by external dependencies such as FIPS 140-3 Cryptographic Module Validation Program (CMVP) queues and sector frameworks such as eIDAS 2.0 and DORA, which do not name PQC but require state-of-the-art cryptography and cryptographic agility. Furthermore, the June 2026 PQC Executive Order (EO 14412) directs CISA to publish guidance on the minimum elements of a Cryptographic Bill of Materials (CBOM), due 19 March 2027 (EO 14306 had earlier removed EO 14144's binding procurement trigger).

### The Key Takeaway

Many jurisdictions follow a two-phase arc — hybrid first, pure PQC later — but not all: CNSA 2.0 targets pure PQC and does not require hybrids. Organizations must construct a Jurisdiction Map to identify their earliest global deadlines, compile a strict CBOM to assess exposure, and prepare Audit Readiness Checklists aligned across all jurisdictions in which they operate.

### What's Happening

Compliance dates are arriving in overlapping waves: CNSA 2.0 sets exclusive-PQC dates for U.S. National Security Systems, ANSSI requires hybrid inside France's regulated perimeter and recommends it elsewhere, and the CMVP certification backlog means vendors must begin validation years in advance.

chunks.title: Confidential Computing & TEEs — In Simple Terms
chunks.content:
### What This Is About

Confidential Computing uses hardware-based Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) to protect Data-in-Use. Unlike standard volume encryption (Data-at-Rest) or TLS (Data-in-Transit), TEE enclaves encrypt data transparently within the processor's DRAM. This hardware isolation provides guarantees that even if the host operating system, hypervisor, or cloud administrator is fully compromised, code and data remain inaccessible from the outside.

### Why It Matters

Quantum computers threaten the TEE trust model in two ways. Grover's algorithm roughly halves the effective strength of symmetric keys (a crude figure): memory encryption with 128-bit AES keys drops to about 64 bits. Shor's algorithm, run on a cryptographically relevant quantum computer, could break the public-key signatures that remote attestation relies on: an attestation report is signed by the TEE's attestation key, and Intel documents ECDSA-based attestation for its SGX processors. An attacker who could forge those signatures could impersonate an enclave and receive secrets provisioned from an HSM.

### The Key Takeaway

All attestation chains are currently quantum-vulnerable. Hardware vendors must rapidly upgrade CPU architectures to support AES-256 for memory encryption, while the ecosystem transitions Remote Attestation protocols to Post-Quantum signatures (ML-DSA) to guarantee trusted TEE-HSM communication.

### What's Happening

Hardware vendors are beginning to evaluate AES-256 upgrades for TEE memory encryption engines and exploring ML-DSA integration into Remote Attestation protocols, as the quantum threat to classical ECDSA attestation signatures across Intel SGX/TDX, AMD SEV-SNP, and ARM CCA becomes increasingly urgent.

chunks.title: Crypto Agility — In Simple Terms
chunks.content:
# Crypto Agility — In Simple Terms

## What This Is About

Crypto agility is the engineering capability to rapidly switch cryptographic algorithms, protocols, and provider implementations without rewriting the underlying application code. Larger keys and signatures, new encodings and new call patterns (a KEM is not an encryption function) still need review and testing.

## Why It Matters

Migrating to new algorithms requires locating every piece of cryptography in an enterprise via a Cryptographic Bill of Materials (CBOM). Without agility patterns—like relying on Provider Models, Service Meshes, or External HSMs—replacing these broken algorithms forces massive, expensive code rewrites.

## The Key Takeaway

The transition demands architectural patterns that completely decouple the cryptographic math from the business application. As algorithms get heavier, these patterns protect the app. For example, when Cloudflare enabled hybrid PQC key exchange, the key size grew from 32 bytes to 1,216 bytes, but the core network routing code remained untouched.

## What's Happening

NIST devotes a white paper, CSWP 39, to crypto agility. Tech giants are already utilizing this agility—Google Chrome and Apple's iMessage have natively enabled hybrid PQC key exchanges through rapid, phased rollouts.

chunks.title: Crypto APIs PQC — In Simple Terms
chunks.content:
# Crypto APIs PQC — In Simple Terms

## What This Is About

Software applications do not build their own cryptography from scratch; they rely on standardized application programming interfaces (APIs) like Java's JCA, OpenSSL, Windows CNG, and PKCS#11 to abstract and execute the complex underlying math safely.

## Why It Matters

These APIs utilize "provider models," meaning the specific algorithm implementations are pluggable. Designing applications around these abstract APIs keeps most of the core application code the same when upgrading to Post-Quantum algorithms. What still changes is the algorithm name, the much larger keys and signatures (and the storage that holds them), how the two sides agree on an algorithm, and what happens when one side does not support it.

## The Key Takeaway

Different APIs have vastly different mechanisms for PQC integration. For example, OpenSSL 3.5 and later include ML-KEM, ML-DSA and SLH-DSA out of the box (older versions needed the `oqsprovider` plug-in), while PKCS#11 requires meticulous session management to communicate with external hardware security modules that are just beginning to support PQC.

## What's Happening

Open-source libraries are actively leading the charge in PQC adoption. Bouncy Castle has provided ML-KEM and ML-DSA since release 1.79 (October 2024). Platform runtimes have caught up: Java (JDK 24+), Go (1.24+ for ML-KEM, 1.27+ for ML-DSA), .NET 10 and Python's cryptography library (48+) now ship them, and Windows CNG has offered ML-KEM and ML-DSA to everyone on Windows 11 24H2 and Windows Server 2025 since November 2025 — though not SLH-DSA.

chunks.title: Cryptographic Management Modernization — quick tour
chunks.content:
# Cryptographic Management Modernization — quick tour

## The one-sentence version

Crypto Management Modernization (CMM) is about running a **continuous program** to know what
crypto you have, keep it healthy, and prove it — across certificates, crypto libraries,
software, and keys.

## Why it matters even if quantum never happens

- Public website (TLS) certificates will last only **47 days** by March 2029. Manually tracking thousands of
  them stops working.
- Every crypto library and HSM has a FIPS 140-3 "driver's license" (a CMVP certificate) that
  can **expire or be revoked**. You have to watch for those notices monthly.
- A **single expired certificate** can cause an outage. This module's cost model uses an
  illustrative assumption of about **$11M** per outage and 86% annual incidence; these are the
  module's own assumptions, not sourced figures.
- Forrester measured a **312% return** on automating certificate lifecycle management — pure
  savings, unrelated to quantum.

## How it's different from "crypto agility"

- **Crypto agility:** can we swap algorithms? (capability)
- **CMM / Posture management:** do we know what we have? (program)
- **CryptoCOE:** who owns it? (operating model)

You need all three, but they are different things.

## Four asset classes to track

1. **Certificates** (TLS, code-signing, internal PKI)
2. **Cryptographic libraries** (OpenSSL, BoringSSL, Bouncy Castle, liboqs, wolfSSL)
3. **Application software** (code that uses crypto — including home-grown)
4. **Key material** (keys and secrets in HSMs and KMS)

## Five pillars

Inventory · Governance · Lifecycle (CLM) · Observability · Assurance (FIPS tracking).

## The iteration loop

Discover → Classify → Score → Remediate → Attest → Reassess. Run this monthly for operations,
then wrap it in an annual Plan-Do-Check-Act cycle for strategy and budget.

## What you'll practice

- Score your own organization on a maturity radar
- Walk sample assets through the 6-stage loop
- Map an SBOM into a crypto-focused CBOM
- Track FIPS 140-3 Level 3 status for both libraries and HSMs
- Model ROI with and without a quantum threat
- Pick the KPIs your board needs to see

chunks.title: Cryptographic Product Certification: Fundamentals — In Simple Terms
chunks.content:
### What This Is About

Security products such as hardware security modules (HSMs) carry certificates: FIPS 140-3 in the US and Canada, Common Criteria internationally, EUCC in the European Union, and PCI approval for payment devices. This module explains what each certificate proves, why you read what a certificate covers before its level, and what happens when a certified product adds post-quantum cryptography. Three follow-on modules go deeper: into FIPS 140-3; into Common Criteria, EUCC and eIDAS; and into PCI.

### Why It Matters

A certificate covers something narrow: a defined product, at a specific version and configuration, checked against one scheme's rules. Adding new algorithms changes the product, and every scheme has its own route for handling that change. Reading a certificate wrongly leads to buying — or selling — protection that was never certified.

### The Key Takeaway

Read what a certificate covers before you read its grade. A deadline to move to post-quantum cryptography makes the work urgent, but it does not make certification faster or skip any step.

### What's Happening

As of 22 October 2026, the FIPS 140-3 standard itself is unchanged, the EU's scheme already lists post-quantum algorithms in its approved cryptography guidance, and PCI's newest HSM standard adds post-quantum definitions without naming a required algorithm or deadline.

chunks.title: CycloneDX Cryptography Registry — In Simple Terms
chunks.content:
# CycloneDX Cryptography Registry — In Simple Terms

## What This Is About

Every tool that looks at your cryptography names it differently. An HSM calls something `CKM_ECDSA_SHA256`. A certificate calls the same thing an OID like `1.2.840.10045.4.3.2`. A login service calls it `ES256`. A network capture calls it `0x0403`. They're all the same signing mechanism — but nothing about the names tells you that.

The CycloneDX Cryptography Registry is a shared dictionary that fixes this: one canonical name for each cryptographic algorithm family (96 of them) and each elliptic curve (246 of them), each backed by a real standard. Once every tool's output is translated into this dictionary, you can finally ask questions like "which of our systems still use something quantum-vulnerable?" and get a real answer — because "ECDSA" means the same thing everywhere, instead of five different strings that happen to describe the same math.

## Why It Matters

Post-quantum readiness starts with knowing what cryptography you actually have. New algorithms like ML-KEM and ML-DSA are registered in this same dictionary right alongside RSA and AES, so checking "is this quantum-safe?" is a lookup, not a research project.

## Try It Yourself

The workshop in this module lets you type in a messy, real-world identifier — the kind a scanner or certificate would actually report — and watch it resolve to its canonical name, plus the standard that defines it.

chunks.title: DNSSEC & Post-Quantum Signatures — In Simple Terms
chunks.content:
### What This Is About

DNSSEC signs DNS answers so resolvers can prove they weren't forged. IANA has assigned DNSSEC algorithm number 18 to ML-DSA-44, with resolver validation of ML-DSA-44 serving as one of the first deployment steps.

### Why It Matters

DNSSEC's PQC problem isn't cryptographic strength, it's size: an ML-DSA-44 signature is 2,420 bytes, about 38x larger than the ECDSA P-256 signatures DNSSEC mostly uses today, and exceeds a common conservative ~1,232-byte UDP payload limit. Responses that large need another transport, normally TCP — a real operational cost that's one of several reasons this remains an individual IETF draft rather than a working-group standard.

### The Key Takeaway

Cloudflare's milestone proves a production resolver CAN validate ML-DSA-44 at scale, against a real signed zone. It does NOT mean any production zone is actually signed with a post-quantum algorithm yet. Resolver-side validation and authoritative-side signing are two different, still-separate steps.

### What's Happening

Cloudflare's own next steps are authoritative-side signing support and registrar DS-record support. Cloudflare's company-wide post-quantum security target is ~2029, but full end-to-end PQ DNSSEC also needs the root and other registries to adopt it — the DNS root zone's own algorithm rollover is a separate, broader estimate of the mid-2030s.

chunks.title: Data & Asset Sensitivity — In Simple Terms
chunks.content:
### What This Is About

The Harvest Now, Decrypt Later (HNDL) threat means adversaries are actively collecting your encrypted data _today_, waiting for a Cryptographically Relevant Quantum Computer (CRQC) to break it. However, you cannot migrate everything to PQC instantly. Data Asset Classification is the process of categorizing your data to answer one critical question: what data is actually worth harvesting, and how urgently must it be protected?

### Why It Matters

Your PQC migration urgency is directly tied to data retention. If a CRQC arrives in 2030, any data that must remain confidential beyond 2030 is already at risk today. Without a structured 4-Tier classification model (Low, Medium, High, Critical), organizations face an impossible blanket migration requirement. Furthermore, GDPR Art. 32 implies using cryptography with consideration for the state of the art, but does not specify algorithms.

### The Key Takeaway

You must immediately inventory all cryptographic assets and classify them by sensitivity and retention. Key material (like root CAs and HSM secrets) must always be classified as Critical. Prioritize your PQC rollout based on a composite score of HNDL exposure risk and regulatory compliance deadlines.

### What's Happening

Regulations like DORA, HIPAA, and GDPR Art. 32 are increasingly being interpreted to require quantum-safe protections for highly sensitive data, making classification and prioritization an immediate compliance requirement rather than a future consideration.

chunks.title: Database Encryption & PQC — In Simple Terms
