chunks.content:
### What This Is About

Database encryption operates in layers: Transparent Data Encryption (TDE) for storage, Column-Level Encryption (CLE) for specific fields, and Queryable Encryption for searching ciphertext. PQC migration for databases does not require changing how the actual data is encrypted, because the underlying AES-256 symmetric encryption is already quantum-safe against Grover's algorithm.

### Why It Matters

The quantum vulnerability in databases lies entirely in the **key wrapping layer**. The Data Encryption Keys (DEKs) and Column Master Keys (CMKs) are currently protected by vulnerable algorithms like RSA-OAEP and ECDH. If an adversary harvests the wrapped keys today, they can decrypt the entire database later. Organizations using Provider-Managed keys are entirely at the mercy of their cloud vendor's timeline, while BYOK and HYOK architectures offer control over when PQC wrapping is enforced.

### The Key Takeaway

Organizations with long-lived data may want to consider HYOK (Hold Your Own Key) architectures and to plan the move of key wrapping to ML-KEM-1024; this is this module's advice, not a regulatory requirement. Because the AES data layer remains unchanged, modern databases (like Oracle and SQL Server) support online TDE re-keying, allowing you to migrate the wrapping keys with zero application downtime.

### What's Happening

Cloud providers and database vendors are rolling out ML-KEM support for key wrapping operations, enabling organizations with BYOK and HYOK architectures to begin migrating their Data Encryption Key protection to quantum-safe algorithms without disrupting the underlying AES data layer.

chunks.title: Developer Quantum Impact — In Simple Terms
chunks.content:
### What This Is About

Cryptography is no longer a set-and-forget implementation detail. Every line of cryptographic code you ship today—from JWT signing to TLS configuration—uses algorithms that quantum computers will break. Understanding Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) is now a core engineering skill, as major libraries like OpenSSL 3.5, BoringSSL, and Go 1.24 are already actively rolling out PQC support.

### Why It Matters

PQC algorithms are not drop-in replacements. ML-KEM public keys are massive (up to 1568 bytes, compared to 32 bytes for an X25519 public value), and ML-DSA signatures are enormous (up to 4627 bytes, compared to 64 bytes for an ECDSA P-256 signature in the JWT format). These size increases can break assumptions baked into your application: HTTP headers will overflow, browser URL limits will be exceeded, TLS client hello messages will fragment and timeout, and your CI/CD pipelines will fail verification.

### The Key Takeaway

Developers must immediately audit their codebases to locate hardcoded algorithms and cipher suites. The critical path forward is building "Crypto Agility"—implementing abstraction layers that allow the application to swap cryptographic algorithms without requiring a total code rewrite.

### What's Happening

Major cryptographic libraries are already shipping PQC support—OpenSSL 3.5, BoringSSL, and Go 1.24 include ML-KEM and ML-DSA implementations—giving developers the tools to begin integrating quantum-safe algorithms into their applications today.

chunks.title: Digital Assets — In Simple Terms
chunks.content:
### What This Is About

Blockchains are fundamentally cryptographic systems. Every transaction is authorized by a digital signature, and every wallet generates its keys from elliptic curve mathematics (like secp256k1 for Bitcoin/Ethereum or Ed25519 for Solana). There is no central authority; cryptography alone establishes ownership.

### Why It Matters

Every elliptic curve algorithm currently protecting blockchain wallets (ECDSA, EdDSA) is entirely vulnerable to Shor's algorithm. Without quantum-resistant cryptography, an adversary with a Cryptographically Relevant Quantum Computer (CRQC) could derive a private key from a public key on the ledger and forge digital signatures. In decentralized finance, forging a signature means irreversibly stealing funds.

### The Key Takeaway

The blockchain ecosystem faces a massive migration challenge. Protocols must transition to hybrid signature schemes and deploy crypto-agile smart contract architectures before quantum actors can drain exposed legacy wallets.

### What's Happening

Blockchain communities are actively researching quantum-resistant signature schemes and crypto-agile smart contract architectures, as the decentralized nature of these protocols makes coordinated algorithm migration exceptionally challenging compared to centralized systems.

chunks.title: Digital Identity — In Simple Terms
chunks.content:
### What This Is About

The eIDAS 2.0 regulation mandates that all 27 EU member states provide citizens with a European Digital Identity (EUDI) Wallet by 2026. These wallets use formats like mdoc and SD-JWT to allow selective disclosure of attributes (e.g., proving age without revealing a birthplace) across a pan-European trust framework.

### Why It Matters

The OpenID4VP and OpenID4VCI specifications use classical ECDSA (P-256) signatures in most of their examples for issuing attestations and binding identities to devices. If an attacker leverages a quantum computer to forge these signatures, they can create perfectly valid but counterfeit credentials, enabling total identity impersonation and fraud across the entire European Union.

### The Key Takeaway

The text of eIDAS 2.0 and of the EUDI wallet Architecture and Reference Framework (ARF) that we checked contains no occurrence of “quantum.” FIPS 204 says ML-DSA is believed to be secure against adversaries with a large-scale quantum computer, and FIPS 205 says SLH-DSA is designed to resist attacks from one.

### What's Happening

The eIDAS 2.0 framework requires all 27 EU member states to deploy EUDI Wallets by 2026. As of October 2026, quantum-safe signatures (ML-DSA and SLH-DSA) are not required, and ETSI says its cryptographic suites specification (TS 119 312 V2.1.1, June 2026) is incomplete for the EUDI Wallet, with an update in preparation.

chunks.title: EMV Payment Systems & PQC — In Simple Terms
chunks.content:
### What This Is About

Payments run on two halves that share cryptography, share vendors and increasingly share deadlines, but are usually migrated by different teams reading different documents. One half is cards: EMV is the global chip standard protecting 14.7 billion cards in circulation at the end of 2024, and when a card is used offline, authentication rests entirely on a chain of RSA certificates. The other half moves money between institutions — Swift messaging, domestic RTGS, correspondent banking chains — plus the bank key management and sector regulation around them.

### Why It Matters

A quantum computer able to break RSA-2048 could forge EMV certificates, letting criminals create counterfeit cards that pass offline terminal checks. Point-of-sale estates face a second exposure at Key Injection Facilities, where an RSA-wrapped Base Derivation Key protects millions of transactions — compromise it and every past and future key derived from it falls with it. On the banking side the threat is different: settlement traffic is long-lived and traverses parties you do not control, so harvest-now-decrypt-later exposure multiplies along a correspondent chain no single institution can migrate alone.

### The Key Takeaway

ML-DSA signatures (2,420 bytes) are large for constrained smart cards, and FN-DSA (Falcon) signatures are much smaller at 666 bytes — but in its March 2024 position statement EMVCo names no post-quantum algorithm for EMV cards, and the card-side evidence is research, such as a 2022 IDEMIA prototype that tried Falcon and Dilithium on a banking card. FIPS 206 is still in preparation, so FN-DSA is not yet deployable. Unlike government, the financial sector has no dated algorithm mandate: the pressure comes from operational-resilience regulation and from how long data stays sensitive. Plan against card replacement cycles — this module assumes roughly 3-5 years per card fleet, an estimate rather than a sourced figure — because cards issued today could still be in wallets at the end of the decade.

### What's Happening

Nine bodies across six jurisdictions now publish financial-sector PQC direction — BIS Project Leap, the G7 Cyber Expert Group, UK CMORG, the Europol Quantum Safe Financial Forum, FS-ISAC, MAS, DORA, the EU NIS Cooperation Group roadmap and a recommended roadmap from Nacha's Payments Innovation Alliance — and which one binds an institution depends on where it is regulated, not where it operates. EMVCo does not expect quantum computing to threaten EMV infrastructure before 2040, and says it may never; it is nevertheless considering mitigations for offline authentication and expects PQC to enter remote-payment protection in due course. Mastercard has published migration guidance and described prototype testing, Visa has published a quantum-readiness sequence for stablecoins and digital payments, and American Express publicly describes an enterprise readiness program. UnionPay and Discover have no network-specific public roadmap in this review, so their likely next steps are labelled as dependency-based inference rather than official commitments.

chunks.title: Email Signing PQC — In Simple Terms
chunks.content:
# Email Signing PQC — In Simple Terms

## What This Is About

Enterprise email security is powered by Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) and S/MIME. It uses digital signatures to definitively prove the sender's identity, and encryption to securely protect the message contents.

## Why It Matters

Classical S/MIME relies on RSA "key transport", which directly encrypts the central message key and is totally vulnerable to Shor's algorithm. To survive quantum threats, PQC replaces this entirely by utilizing a Key Encapsulation Mechanism (KEM) to securely derive a shared secret instead.

## The Key Takeaway

Migrating S/MIME is uniquely difficult because it strictly requires bidirectional compatibility—both the sender and recipient must support the same algorithms simultaneously. Furthermore, new ML-DSA signatures are significantly larger (3.3 KB vs 72 bytes), which heavily impacts mobile clients.

## What's Happening

The IETF LAMPS working group has successfully published RFCs to natively bring PQC into CMS infrastructure, explicitly standardizing ML-DSA for message signing (RFC 9882) and KEM-based combinations for message encryption (RFC 9629).

chunks.title: Entropy & PQC — In Simple Terms
chunks.content:
# Entropy & PQC — In Simple Terms

## What This Is About

Cryptographic security depends on the quality of randomness, known as entropy. A perfectly designed cryptographic algorithm is essentially worthless if the underlying random number generator (RNG) used to pick the keys is predictable.

## Why It Matters

Predictable random seeds lead to total key recovery attacks. The post-quantum standards spell out exactly which random values they draw: ML-KEM (FIPS 203) draws two 32-byte values to make a key pair and a fresh 32-byte value for every encapsulation, and ML-DSA (FIPS 204) draws one 32-byte seed to make a key pair. A 32-byte value is not the same thing as "256 bits of security". What the standards require is an approved random bit generator whose security strength matches the parameter set — for example, at least 192 bits for ML-KEM-768. Furthermore, if random numbers repeat during the generation of Stateful Signatures (like LMS or XMSS), it causes catastrophic tree security failures.

## The Key Takeaway

Hardware random number generators do not depend on math problems that a quantum computer could solve, so a quantum computer does not break them the way it breaks RSA. That does not make them automatically safe. What matters is whether the physical source really delivers the unpredictability claimed, which has to be measured, checked continuously while the device runs, and combined with the rest of the generator correctly.

## What's Happening

NIST's SP 800-90 series explains how to build and test these generators. NIST's Cryptographic Module Validation Program issues Entropy Validation Certificates to entropy sources after an accredited testing lab has shown that they meet SP 800-90B.

chunks.title: Executive Quantum Impact — In Simple Terms
chunks.content:
### What This Is About

The quantum threat is no longer solely an IT problem; it is a corporate governance issue. As an executive, you bear fiduciary responsibility for protecting organizational assets. The decisions made today directly determine whether the organization will safely transition or face catastrophic data exposure.

### Why It Matters

Adversaries are actively executing "Harvest Now, Decrypt Later" (HNDL) attacks—stealing and storing your encrypted communications today in order to decrypt them when quantum computers mature. Simultaneously, regulators are setting binding deadlines: the NSA's CNSA 2.0 suite, which governs U.S. National Security Systems, has an anticipated timetable for software/firmware signing to use CNSA 2.0 exclusively by 2030, with web, cloud, and operating-system use following by 2033.

### The Key Takeaway

Leaders cannot fix what they cannot see. You must immediately demand a comprehensive cryptographic inventory (CBOM) from your security teams to uncover hidden quantum exposure, and formally commission a PQC risk assessment to prioritize system migration.

### What's Happening

Governments are setting binding compliance deadlines—such as the NSA's CNSA 2.0 suite, which requires U.S. National Security Systems to use PQC exclusively for software/firmware signing by 2030 and across web, cloud, and operating systems by 2033—and boards of directors are being held accountable for ensuring their organizations have funded cryptographic inventories and PQC migration programs.

chunks.title: FIPS 140-3 Certification — In Simple Terms
chunks.content:
### What This Is About

A closer look at FIPS 140-3, the US and Canadian standard for cryptographic modules; the validation program behind it, the CMVP, is a joint effort of NIST and the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security. It builds on the certification fundamentals module; payment approval (PCI) has its own module. A hands-on step reads the real algorithm and Security Policy records of two modules, side by side.

### Why It Matters

Passing algorithm tests is only the first step toward FIPS 140-3; the module certificate is a separate result. Adding post-quantum algorithms changes the module, so it needs a new validation route.

### The Key Takeaway

A listing on the Modules In Process list (voluntary, and not every module in review is shown) is a queue position, not a certificate; a module is validated only once NIST and CCCS issue a FIPS 140-3 certificate.

### What's Happening

A US executive order directs the Secretary of Commerce, through NIST's Director, to revise the module validation program's processes within 180 days of the order's date, insofar as appropriate and consistent with applicable law, so that validations of cryptographic modules are accelerated.

chunks.title: 5G Security — In Simple Terms
chunks.content:
# 5G Security — In Simple Terms

## What This Is About

Pre-5G networks exposed subscriber identities to "IMSI catchers." 5G fixes this with SUCI concealment, ensuring privacy over the airwaves. However, the current encryption method (ECIES) is vulnerable to quantum computer attacks.

## Why It Matters

"Harvest now, decrypt later" is the risk: someone could record encrypted cellular traffic today and decrypt it once quantum computers arrive. ATIS describes roaming signalling between operators as exposed to this threat. Without quantum protection, the mobile privacy of 5G subscribers could be stripped retroactively, allowing attackers to track past movements.

## The Key Takeaway

The fix everyone points to is a post-quantum SUCI scheme built on ML-KEM, usually called "Profile C". Be careful with that name: **3GPP has not standardised it.** TS 33.501 Annex C defines exactly three schemes — the null-scheme, Profile A and Profile B — and both real profiles are ECIES. "Profile C" and its 0x3 identifier come from a research proposal, not from the standard.

So the honest position is that the quantum weakness in SUCI concealment is real and the ML-KEM answer is well understood, but there is nothing to comply with yet. Treat Profile C as the shape of the likely fix, not as a specification you can implement against.

## What's Happening

Quantum-safe schemes need heavier processing and larger messages, so operators and equipment makers need to plan how to adopt them without degrading network latency. As of TS 33.501 Release 19 (V19.5.0, February 2026), the guidance comes from bodies such as ATIS and GSMA, and 3GPP has not specified a post-quantum protection scheme for subscriber identities.

chunks.title: Government & Defense PQC — In Simple Terms
chunks.content:
# Government & Defense PQC — In Simple Terms

## What This Is About

Most organisations decide for themselves when to adopt post-quantum cryptography. US government systems do not. A stack of laws, executive orders and policies turns it into a requirement with dates attached — and the dates depend on which kind of system you run. National Security Systems follow one instrument with hard deadlines; federal civilian agencies follow a different set of rules: inventories, reports and migration plans, plus, since June 2026, their own dated deadlines for their most important systems (key exchange moved by the end of 2030, digital signatures by the end of 2031).

## Why It Matters

The deadlines reach much further than government itself. From 1 January 2027, CNSA 2.0 algorithms will be required in all new acquisitions for National Security Systems. Separately, the rules covering Controlled Unclassified Information reach contractors, universities and suppliers who never go near a classified system. A June 2026 executive order also directs a proposed rule that would require covered contractors to comply with NIST's Federal Information Processing Standards, including all applicable ones that cover post-quantum algorithms, by the end of 2030. If you sell to the US government, someone else's deadline has become yours.

## The Key Takeaway

Only the public-key half of the estate is being replaced. The NSA suite swaps out key exchange and digital signatures, but AES-256 encryption and the SHA hash functions carry on essentially unchanged. Budgeting to "replace all our cryptography" overstates the work considerably — the honest first step is finding out which half of your systems is actually affected.

## What's Happening

The dates are set: new purchases must use the new algorithms from January 2027, equipment that cannot be upgraded must be gone by the end of 2030 unless an exception is granted, and, unless otherwise noted, the new algorithms become mandatory at the end of 2031. One practical wrinkle catches people out — the 2022 advisory called the algorithms Kyber and Dilithium, while the October 2026 update calls the same things ML-KEM and ML-DSA. Because the two documents use different names for the same algorithms, searching your own estate for only one set of names will quietly miss half of what you have.

chunks.title: Healthcare PQC — In Simple Terms
chunks.content:
# Healthcare PQC — In Simple Terms

## What This Is About

Unlike a stolen password that can be quickly reset, biometric data (like DNA profiles, fingerprints, and iris scans) is completely permanent. Currently, massive healthcare databases rely on standard encryption to protect these irrevocable lifetime records.

## Why It Matters

State-sponsored adversaries are archiving stolen, encrypted health data today. Because they cannot crack the encryption yet, they just store it in massive server farms. When quantum computers become available, they will perform "Harvest Now, Decrypt Later" attacks, instantly unlocking decades of deeply sensitive, unchangeable health data.

## The Key Takeaway

Healthcare providers must prioritize the Post-Quantum Cryptography transition for permanent, irrevocable biometric datasets immediately. These datasets must be shielded with massive quantum-proof encryption far earlier than easily rotatable systems.

## What's Happening

Medical device manufacturers, genomic research centers, and hospital networks are auditing their longest-term data vaults to build "crypto-agile" architectures capable of wrapping existing records in an impenetrable quantum-safe layer.

chunks.title: Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) — In Simple Terms
chunks.content:
### What This Is About

Fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) lets a server do calculations on data that stays encrypted the whole time. The server returns an encrypted answer that only the data owner can open. Unlike a trusted-hardware enclave, it relies on mathematics instead of trusting a chip.

### Why It Matters

Whoever holds the secret key can open everything, and the public keys that make the computation possible are huge. Where the secret key lives, and who may ask for a decryption, decides whether the scheme protects anything.

### The Key Takeaway

FHE keeps data hidden from the server, but it is much slower than ordinary computing and suits some kinds of data better than others. Its secret key is best kept inside a hardware security module, and whoever is allowed to ask that module to decrypt can, in principle, recover the key from the answers, so who may ask decides how well the data is protected.

### What's Happening

Standardisation of FHE is very active, for example under ISO/IEC 28033, though performance is still a concern for some applications.

chunks.title: HSM & PQC Operations — In Simple Terms
chunks.content:
# HSM & PQC Operations — In Simple Terms

## What This Is About

Hardware Security Modules (HSMs) are physical, highly secure, tamper-resistant devices that protect a network's most sensitive cryptographic keys (meeting standards like FIPS 140-3). PKCS#11 v3.2, an OASIS Standard since June 2026, defines how these devices handle Post-Quantum Cryptography.

## Why It Matters

Classical cryptography used tiny memory buffers. For example, ECDSA uses roughly 64 bytes, while ML-KEM-768 requires 1,184 bytes. If an HSM isn't specifically upgraded to handle PQC, its internal buffers will instantly overflow. Additionally, new stateful signatures (like LMS) require atomic NVRAM writes to track every single signature made, making HSMs the only truly safe platform to run them.

Checking a PQC-capable HSM means checking four different things: NIST's algorithm tests (CAVP), the module's own certificate and its Security Policy (CMVP), the self-tests the module runs on its own algorithms and key pairs, and the submission route a firmware update takes. Passing the algorithm tests does not make a product validated, and firmware that runs ML-KEM or ML-DSA in a non-approved mode does not need the self-tests a validated approved mode needs. Under NIST's CMVP Management Manual, adding PQC to a validated module is an Update only if each category of security change stays under 30%; otherwise it is a full submission.

## The Key Takeaway

The physical hardware upgrades are happening right now. Major on-premise HSM vendors (such as Thales, Entrust, and Utimaco) already ship PQC firmware updates, though the algorithms each one supports differ (Thales's Luna Post Quantum Algorithms page lists ML-KEM, ML-DSA and LMS-HSS, and that page and its v7.9 release post do not list SLH-DSA; Utimaco's Quantum Protect page shows SLH-DSA as in progress; Entrust's nShield release notes describe SLH-DSA), the programming interface can trail the firmware (Entrust's release notes list ML-DSA in its PKCS#11 interface from Security World v13.9.0, ML-KEM from Security World v13.9.3 and SLH-DSA from v13.9.5, after describing ML-KEM and SLH-DSA in v13.9.0 as available only through its native nCore interface), and only some of their FIPS 140 certificates list PQC algorithms yet (Thales Luna T7 certificate #5450 lists ML-KEM, ML-DSA and LMS; Entrust nShield 5s certificates #5329 and #4745 list none). Cloud HSMs are uneven: AWS CloudHSM documents ML-DSA key generation and signing in the cluster. AWS documents ML-DSA as available in FIPS mode on hsm2m.medium clusters from 1 September 2026, while the NIST Security Policy for CMVP certificate #4703, the certificate AWS lists for hsm2m.medium, lists ML-DSA and ML-KEM as non-approved (not allowed in the approved mode of operation) and the certificate lists no PQC algorithm; the two statements have not been reconciled. Google lists its post-quantum algorithms for software keys only, none for HSM keys.

## What's Happening

PKCS#11 v3.2, an OASIS Standard since June 2026, standardizes how applications call HSMs for ML-KEM encapsulation, ML-DSA and SLH-DSA signatures, and stateful hash-based signatures, while vendors add each algorithm to their firmware and then to their programming interface release by release.

chunks.title: Hybrid Cryptography — In Simple Terms
chunks.content:
# Hybrid Cryptography — In Simple Terms

## What This Is About

Transitioning a massive network to brand-new, cutting-edge cryptographic algorithms introduces risk. "Hybrid Cryptography" is the strategy of combining a highly trusted classical algorithm (like X25519) with a new quantum-safe algorithm (like ML-KEM) simultaneously.

## Why It Matters

It is a hedge. If a flaw is found in the new quantum-safe algorithm or in its new code, the classical algorithm still protects the data against today's attackers, provided the two are combined soundly. The hedge has costs: two algorithms to implement, test and negotiate, larger messages, and a second transition later when the classical part is removed. For signatures, every verifier must insist on both signatures, or an attacker can strip one.

## Who Recommends It

Agencies disagree. France (ANSSI), Germany (BSI), the Netherlands and the EU certification group ask for hybrid during the transition. The US NSA, the UK NCSC and the Czech NÚKIB accept post-quantum algorithms on their own, and the NSA warns that hybrids add complexity that can introduce their own flaws. Canada's Cyber Centre recommends the new algorithms without saying either way.

## The Key Takeaway

Whether to use hybrid depends on whose rules apply to you and on what you protect. For key exchange in TLS, hybrid is already the common default on the web. For signatures and certificates the formats are newer and the advice is more divided.

## Hybrid in a Validated Module

A security product certified under FIPS 140-3 can offer a hybrid key exchange as an approved service even though one half, such as X25519, is not an approved algorithm. The NIST/CMVP guidance (IG D.S) sets five conditions: an approved ML-KEM, another key exchange (approved or not), an approved way to combine the two secrets, a fixed list of allowed hybrid pairs that the module enforces itself, and module control over the order in which the secrets are joined. The non-approved half is allowed but "no security claimed": the hybrid's claimed strength comes from ML-KEM. If any condition is missing, the hybrid cannot be an approved service. The guidance says the TLS hybrid groups (X25519MLKEM768, SecP256r1MLKEM768, SecP384r1MLKEM1024) may qualify, while the X-Wing hybrid cannot yet, even though NIST's algorithm-testing page lists X-Wing tests. A separate rule, IG 1.B "Hybrid Modules", is about firmware plus hardware in one module and has nothing to do with hybrid key exchange.

## What's Happening

Major tech companies, including Google and Cloudflare, have already deployed hybrid configurations (now X25519MLKEM768, which replaced the earlier X25519Kyber768Draft00) across Chrome and their web infrastructure, showing that hybrid key exchange runs at scale; Chrome reported about a 4% slower TLS handshake.

chunks.title: Identity & Access Management PQC — In Simple Terms
chunks.content:
# Identity & Access Management PQC — In Simple Terms

## What This Is About

Identity and Access Management (IAM) is built entirely on cryptographic signatures. Every time you log in, protocols like SAML, JWT, or Kerberos use math to assert your identity.

## Why It Matters

Adversaries are actively capturing and storing these secure exchanges today. Kerberos is the highest priority risk: if a quantum computer breaks the initial RSA authentication exchange (PKINIT), the attacker could forge tickets and move laterally across an entire enterprise network, creating a catastrophic "Quantum Golden Ticket."

## The Key Takeaway

All enterprise token signing will soon migrate to the new ML-DSA (FIPS 204) standard. Because ML-DSA comes in different sizes, engineers will calibrate it to the task: ML-DSA-44 for short-lived access tokens, ML-DSA-65 for enterprise SAML logins, and ML-DSA-87 for highly classified government infrastructure.

## What's Happening

Our product catalogue records no post-quantum token signing for most of the identity providers this module lists, so Active Directory teams should plan the Kerberos PKINIT upgrade that prevents the catastrophic "Quantum Golden Ticket" scenario before vendors deliver it.

chunks.title: IoT & Embedded Device PQC — In Simple Terms
chunks.content:
### What This Is About

Smart meters, sensors, wearables and gateways run on tiny chips with a few kilobytes of memory and slow radios. This module looks at how post-quantum cryptography fits on them: which algorithms they can run, how their software updates are signed, and how their networks carry the larger keys.

### Why It Matters

A device sold today may still be working in 15 years. If its update signatures can be forged by a future quantum computer, an attacker could install anything on it — and many devices can only be fixed by replacing them.

### The Key Takeaway

Small devices mostly check signatures rather than make them, and checking is much cheaper. Many post-quantum algorithms fit when built for low memory; signing and heavy handshakes are best left to servers and gateways.

### What's Happening

New laws such as the EU Cyber Resilience Act require secure updates for years after sale, and chip makers have started shipping security chips with post-quantum algorithms built in.

chunks.title: KMS & PQC Key Management — In Simple Terms
chunks.content:
# KMS & PQC Key Management — In Simple Terms

## What This Is About

In classical cryptography, algorithms like RSA served dual purposes—they could handle both encrypting data and signing documents. The post-quantum standards split these roles by algorithm: ML-KEM (FIPS 203) is for key establishment, while ML-DSA (FIPS 204) and SLH-DSA (FIPS 205) are for signatures.

## Why It Matters

In this module's reading, organizations use ML-KEM for key encapsulation (envelope encryption) and ML-DSA for digital signatures, so one key no longer does both jobs as an RSA key could. This fundamentally complicates how large enterprises manage their secret keys.

## The Key Takeaway

Because post-quantum algorithms cannot share one key pair between encryption and signing, organisations that used dual-purpose keys will need more keys, and must upgrade their centralized Key Management Systems (KMS) architecture. This infrastructure must be capable of generating, storing, and transmitting these new, significantly larger quantum-safe keys.

## What's Happening

Cloud providers and Hardware Security Module (HSM) vendors are redesigning their platforms to support the massive throughput required to manage millions of these new, specialized Post-Quantum keys securely.

chunks.title: MLS — Group Messaging (Curious Explorer)
chunks.content:
# MLS — Group Messaging (Curious Explorer)

Signal made one thing famous: end-to-end encrypted chat. But Signal's
ratcheting math only works well for two people. Make it a group of 100,
and every message has to be encrypted 100 times. A group of 1000? Forget
it.

Messaging Layer Security (MLS) is a newer IETF standard (July 2023) that
solves this. Instead of a chain of pairwise locks, MLS arranges members
as leaves of a binary tree. Each branch holds a secret known only to the members below it. When you add a friend, or rotate a key, only the nodes on your path up the tree change, so the work grows with the logarithm of the group size — O(log N) — instead of with the group size.

The next chapter is post-quantum: ML-KEM and ML-DSA suites are in IETF
at draft -06 (July 2026), now submitted to the IESG for publication.

This module covers:

- How TreeKEM gives forward secrecy + post-compromise security at scale
- How HPKE encrypts path updates between members
- How our OpenMLS provider keeps signature keys inside a PKCS#11 v3.2 token
  (softhsmv3 here, an HSM emulation; ML-DSA-ready) — not floating in browser memory

Play with the TreeKEM visualizer in the Workshop tab and see how each
Add / Remove / Update operation lights up only the affected path.

chunks.title: Media, Entertainment & DRM PQC — In Simple Terms
chunks.content:
# Media, Entertainment & DRM PQC — In Simple Terms

## What This Is About

A content-protection system can bind its keys to a particular device and revoke devices that have been compromised. In consumer content protection a compromised device is part of the threat model, so asking whether the system is quantum-safe has to be done link by link. This module reads the actual specifications behind some of those systems — the AACS system, whose specification covers keys held on media and the exchange between a drive and a host, the CI Plus system, which protects content where it leaves a conditional-access module and re-enters the host device, the MovieLabs ECP specification, and the C2PA standard that attaches signed "content credentials" to media — and asks one precise question of each: where does it use public-key cryptography, the kind that a large quantum computer would break?

## Why It Matters

Public-key cryptography does two jobs in these systems: it signs things (a block of keys, a certificate, a media file's credentials) and it lets two devices agree on a shared key. NIST's transition plan says that quantum-vulnerable signature and key-agreement schemes will be deprecated after 2030 and disallowed in NIST standards after 2035. That is NIST's schedule for NIST standards. None of the media specifications read here sets a deadline of its own.

## The Key Takeaway

A specification that does not mention quantum computers is not the same as an organisation that has no plan. The first is a fact about a document; the second would need a different kind of evidence. Reading each link precisely — which kind of cryptography it uses, who can change it, who can revoke a compromised device — is more useful than a general statement that "media is vulnerable".

## What's Happening

In the editions read here, the key tree and the content cipher use symmetric cryptography (AES-128 in AACS; DES-56 or AES-128 in CI Plus), while the signatures and key exchanges use ECDSA, RSA and Diffie-Hellman. The C2PA standard allows ECDSA, RSA and EdDSA signatures for new credentials and lists no post-quantum algorithm; separate IETF documents describe how to carry a post-quantum signature in the same format. For streaming, a hybrid key exchange for the web's encryption layer was published in August 2026 as RFC 10024, while a 2023 research paper reported an absence of post-quantum security in three widely used DRM systems.

chunks.title: Merkle Tree Certificates — In Simple Terms
chunks.content:
### What This Is About

Post-quantum digital signatures are enormously bloated. While an older ECDSA signature is just 64 bytes, a quantum-safe ML-DSA-44 signature is 2,420 bytes. Merkle Tree Certificates (MTCs) solve this "certificate bloat" problem by replacing heavy, per-certificate signatures with a single, highly efficient batch-signing architecture.

### Why It Matters

Massive PQC signatures break constrained internet clients, degrade connection setup times, and drastically increase bandwidth costs for TLS handshakes. Under the MTC architecture, a Certificate Authority (CA) signs a single Merkle Tree root hash covering millions of certificates. Clients receive a compact "inclusion proof" instead of a massive signature.

And because every MTC issuance is recorded in a public, append-only transparency log, a second property emerges: if a server that previously held an MTC-backed PQC certificate suddenly starts presenting only a classical X.509 certificate, monitors can detect that rollback — turning a silent downgrade into an auditable event. This insight, developed by Bas Westerbaan (Cloudflare Research), means MTC adoption strengthens security, not just performance.

### The Key Takeaway

Merkle Tree Certificates cut the authentication data in a PQC handshake — about 36% with standalone ML-DSA-44 certificates and about 56% with landmark certificates, compared with a leaf-plus-intermediate chain (the server still sends its own key and handshake signature). By moving to inclusion proofs and hash recomputation, MTCs provide an approach, described in an IETF PLANTS Internet-Draft, to deploying PQC certificates at internet scale. Chrome's Quantum-Resistant Root Store (CQRS) coexists alongside the existing Web PKI root store, enabling maximum compatibility: PQC for capable browsers, classical fallback for legacy clients, with the MTC log creating the audit trail.

### What's Happening

The IETF PLANTS working group is actively standardizing Merkle Tree Certificates (draft-ietf-plants-merkle-tree-certs). Cloudflare and Chrome have run live production experiments. Bas Westerbaan (Cloudflare Research) has highlighted MTCs as a critical piece of the downgrade detection stack, complementing PQ Lock and PQC Continuity (`draft-sheffer-tls-pqc-continuity`) as the layered defense against quantum rollback attacks during the transition period.

chunks.title: Migration Program Management — In Simple Terms
chunks.content:
### What This Is About

Migrating an enterprise to post-quantum cryptography is not a single IT project—it is a massive, multi-year, cross-functional program encompassing a 7-Phase framework (Discovery, Inventory, Prioritization, Planning, Pilot, Migration, Validation) aligned with official CISA and NIST guidance.

### Why It Matters

A rushed "big-bang" migration is far too risky for core cryptographic infrastructure. The critical path to success is almost always constrained by third-party dependencies; vendor PQC readiness dictates when you can actually transition. Programs fail when they lack executive sponsorship, cross-team coordination, and measurable key performance indicators (KPIs).

### The Key Takeaway

Agencies and enterprises must establish a dedicated migration program today. Success requires building a Cryptographic Bill of Materials (CBOM), securing C-suite authority, and carefully executing phased rollouts to ensure infrastructure remains operational and compliant throughout the transition.

### What's Happening

Government agencies are already executing their PQC migration programs following CISA and NIST guidance, while early adopters in the private sector are completing their Discovery and Inventory phases to establish Cryptographic Bills of Materials as the foundation for phased rollouts.

chunks.title: PQC 101 — In Simple Terms
chunks.content:
### What This Is About

Today's digital world is secured by public-key cryptography (like RSA and ECC), which relies on math problems that are extremely hard for classical computers. A sufficiently large, fault-tolerant quantum computer running Shor's Algorithm could solve these specific problems efficiently, breaking the encryption and signatures that protect banking, defense, and healthcare. No such machine is publicly known to exist today.

### Why It Matters

The risk starts before that machine exists because of "Harvest Now, Decrypt Later" (HNDL): government security agencies, including NSA, CISA and the UK NCSC, warn that adversaries may record encrypted data now to decrypt it later. Likewise, "Harvest Now, Forge Later" matters for long-lived digital signatures on firmware and roots of trust (not sourced in the Library).

### The Key Takeaway

The algorithms are ready. In August 2024, NIST published the first three Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) standards (FIPS 203, 204, 205). Protocols, products and certifications are still catching up, so organizations should begin the transition with a cryptographic inventory and a risk assessment. NIST's transition plan (IR 8547, final since October 2026) deprecates quantum-vulnerable public-key algorithms such as RSA and elliptic-curve cryptography after 2030 and disallows their use under NIST standards and guidelines after 2035.

### What's Happening

Some governments have set dates for specific systems. For example, CNSA 2.0 requires new acquisitions for U.S. National Security Systems to be CNSA 2.0-compliant from January 2027.

chunks.title: Network Security & PQC Migration — In Simple Terms
chunks.content:
### What This Is About

Post-quantum cryptography fundamentally alters network security operations across the entire enterprise stack. Quantum-safe signature certificates (like ML-DSA) are much larger than their classical counterparts: FIPS 204 lists a 1,952-byte public key and a 3,309-byte signature at ML-DSA-65, and in one IETF draft example a two-certificate ML-DSA-65 TLS chain is 11,869 bytes against 2,656 bytes for an RSA chain. Key exchanges also become heavier and more complex.

### Why It Matters

Because PQC artifacts are so large, they severely stress modern firewalls and Deep Packet Inspection (DPI) appliances. Many middleboxes, including firewalls and other inspection devices, have hardcoded buffer sizes or parsing assumptions that break with PQC-sized handshakes and certificates, so each one needs testing. Furthermore, software-only DPI CPU costs increase significantly, and legacy IDS/IPS signatures cannot parse hybrid KEM codepoints.

### The Key Takeaway

In this module's suggested order, Zero Trust Network Access (ZTNA) Identity Providers come first for migration, as a compromised IdP invalidates all access. Network teams should plan for added inspection latency (the module's simulator shows about 35ms for pure PQC, an illustrative setting rather than a measurement) and evaluate vendor PQC roadmaps before deploying hybrid traffic across inline security boundaries.

### What's Happening

Firewall and DPI appliance vendors are releasing firmware updates to handle larger PQC certificate chains, while network teams are testing hybrid TLS deployments and recalibrating inspection latency baselines to accommodate the increased processing overhead of quantum-safe traffic.

chunks.title: OS Cryptography PQC — In Simple Terms
chunks.content:
# OS Cryptography PQC — In Simple Terms

## What This Is About

Modern operating systems have a deep cryptographic stack. When you upgrade the system's foundational TLS configurations (like OpenSSL), those quantum protections automatically cascade to every tool and application running on the OS.

## Why It Matters

System TLS traffic and SSH sessions are actively being recorded today by adversaries for "Harvest Now, Decrypt Later" (HNDL) attacks. If an attacker captures an SSH session today, they could eventually use a quantum computer to break the SSH host key and authenticate as your server in the future.

## The Key Takeaway

While upgrading a system's TLS is as simple as a configuration change (like enabling `X25519MLKEM768`), upgrading OS package managers (like RPM or DEB files) to new ML-DSA signatures is incredibly hard. It requires massive, perfectly coordinated upgrades across the signing server, repository metadata, and end-user client.

## What's Happening

Operating system vendors are adding post-quantum support in stages. Microsoft's November 2025 Windows update added API support for the ML-KEM and ML-DSA algorithms (FIPS 203 and FIPS 204), and its July 14, 2026 update for Windows Server 2025 (KB5099536) added hybrid post-quantum key exchange to TLS 1.3. Microsoft's documentation lists the new key exchange groups as disabled by default, so an administrator turns them on, for example with Group Policy.

chunks.title: OT & Industrial Control Systems PQC — In Simple Terms
chunks.content:
# OT & Industrial Control Systems PQC — In Simple Terms

## What This Is About

Power grids, pipelines, water plants, railways, factories and big buildings are run by industrial computers — controllers that open breakers, move valves and set temperatures. This module is about keeping those systems trustworthy once quantum computers can break today's public-key cryptography.

## Why It Matters

In these systems the scariest quantum attack is not reading old messages. It is forgery: a quantum computer could fake the digital signatures that tell a controller "this software update really came from the manufacturer" or "this command really came from the control room". Controllers stay in service for 20 years or more, so the keys they trust have to be replaced long before that becomes possible.

## How Attackers Get In

There are three ways into these systems. Most attacks start in the company's office network and work their way down into the plant, so protecting the office side protects the plant too. Others come in through remote connections, such as vendor support links and internet-connected sensors, which should all pass through one guarded entry point. The last way is physical: someone on site or nearby, where most of the equipment checks nothing at all about who is sending it commands.

## The Key Takeaway

The fastest messages — like the 3-millisecond trip signals inside a substation — are already protected with symmetric codes that quantum computers don't break, so they stay as they are. The work is in the slower parts around them: the keys that sign firmware and configurations, the certificates that identify devices, and the remote-access links into the plant.

## What's Happening

IEC 62443 is a paid standard, so we could not read it to check whether it addresses post-quantum cryptography, and in the documents we hold we found no quantum-safe option for protocols like OPC UA, BACnet/SC and DNP3. Post-quantum work on the IEC 62351 power-grid security standards has started, but further refinements are needed. Operators are starting with an inventory, moving their signing keys to new schemes such as LMS and ML-DSA, and protecting remote access with hybrid key exchange while the standards catch up.

chunks.title: Ops Quantum Impact — In Simple Terms
chunks.content:
### What This Is About

IT Operations and DevOps teams deploy, monitor, and maintain the cryptography that protects the organization. The PQC migration is fundamentally an operations challenge, encompassing certificate rotation, VPN IPsec tunnels, SSH key management, and CI/CD pipeline deployments.

### Why It Matters

Because PQC signatures and public keys are much larger than today's (GSMA PQ.04 lists an ML-DSA-65 signature of 3,309 bytes against 64 bytes for ECDSA-256), certificates grow too, and automated lifecycle management tools (like cert-manager or ACME) configured for small ECDSA certificates can exceed their size limits and fail silently. Furthermore, the different performance profiles of PQC algorithms will trigger thousands of false-positive latency alerts if monitoring baselines and SLAs are not properly recalibrated.

### The Key Takeaway

Operations teams are on the front line of the quantum transition. They must immediately inventory all cryptographic assets, lab-test PQC protocols (like the hybrid mlkem768x25519-sha256 key exchange, added in OpenSSH 9.9 and the default from OpenSSH 10.0), and update deployment playbooks before executing automated, phased rollovers.

### What's Happening

Operations teams are establishing PQC lab environments to test hybrid protocol deployments—including the hybrid ML-KEM key exchange in OpenSSH 9.9 and later—and recalibrating monitoring baselines to account for the larger certificate sizes and different latency profiles of quantum-safe algorithms.

chunks.title: PKI Enrollment Protocols — In Simple Terms
chunks.content:
# PKI Enrollment Protocols — In Simple Terms

## What This Is About

Before any device, app, or person can use a digital certificate, they need to _get one_ — and a certificate isn't just an X.509 file emailed around. There's a protocol that asks the Certificate Authority "please issue me one," carries the public key safely, proves you actually own the matching private key, and delivers the signed certificate back. Two protocols dominate that conversation: **EST** (Enrollment over Secure Transport, RFC 7030) and **CMP** (Certificate Management Protocol, RFC 4210 + RFC 9810).

## Why It Matters

Post-quantum migration adds two new wrinkles to enrollment. First, the new ML-DSA signatures are roughly 50× larger than classical ECDSA — every CSR, every cert, every protocol envelope balloons. Second, ML-KEM keys cannot sign anything at all, so the standard "sign the request to prove you have the private key" trick stops working. RFC 9810 (published July 2025) solves this by having the CA _encapsulate_ the new certificate under the requester's ML-KEM public key — only the genuine private-key holder can decapsulate it.

## The Key Takeaway

EST is HTTP-friendly and simple, CMP is richer and is where the IETF post-quantum work is happening. Both run real cryptographic message exchanges with proof-of-possession, signature verification, and trust-anchor checks. The same enrollment story that has carried RSA certs for decades now carries ML-DSA and ML-KEM — same shape, different algorithms, same need to get rolled out at industrial scale before quantum computers arrive.

## What's Happening

EJBCA 9.1+ already issues ML-DSA + ML-KEM certificates through CMP today. Bouncy Castle, OpenSSL 3.5+, and the IETF LAMPS working group are filling in the remaining gaps — composite signatures (one cert with both ML-DSA _and_ ECDSA inside) sit in draft form, ready when the operational reality catches up.

chunks.title: PKI Workshop — In Simple Terms
chunks.content:
### What This Is About

Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) manages the digital certificates that build trust across the internet. At its core, it relies on X.509 certificates secured by classical digital signatures like RSA and ECDSA.

### Why It Matters

Because Root Certificate Authorities can live for 20+ years, they are highly vulnerable to "Harvest Now, Forge Later" attacks where a quantum computer could forge signatures and issue rogue certificates. Additionally, moving to quantum-safe replacements like ML-DSA introduces massive certificate bloat (up to a 37x size increase), breaking constrained clients.

### The Key Takeaway

Migration to PQC is urgent: NIST IR 8547 (final, October 2026) deprecates quantum-vulnerable public-key algorithms after 2030 and disallows them after 2035, while NSA's current CNSA 2.0 FAQ requires compliant new **national security system** acquisitions from 2027, phase-out of unsupported equipment and services by 2030, and CNSA 2.0 algorithms by 2031 unless otherwise noted. Organizations should test the certificate profiles appropriate to their authority and interoperability needs, including hybrid or emerging solutions such as Merkle Tree Certificates (MTCs).

### What's Happening

Certificate Authorities and browser vendors are actively testing hybrid and composite certificates, while NIST IR 8547 (final, October 2026) deprecates quantum-vulnerable public-key algorithms after 2030 (disallowed after 2035) and NSA's CNSA 2.0 FAQ version 2.2 records 2027/2030/2031 milestones for national security systems.

chunks.title: PQC Business Case — In Simple Terms
chunks.content:
### What This Is About

Migrating to post-quantum cryptography is not just a technical upgrade; it is a major organizational investment. A well-constructed business case translates technical risk into financial frameworks like Risk-Adjusted ROI and Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) to secure executive buy-in.

### Why It Matters

Without executive sponsorship and dedicated funding, PQC migrations stall. Delaying the transition can increase Harvest-Now-Decrypt-Later exposure, compress delivery work and deepen legacy-system complexity. Whether it raises discounted financial cost depends on the scenario assumptions.

### The Key Takeaway

A useful business case makes direct migration costs, breach-risk assumptions, possible commercial or regulatory consequences, uncertainty and the limits of the evidence visible. It does not turn an industry average into an organization-specific forecast.

### What's Happening

PQC migration cost models can help frame a board decision by comparing start-now and delay scenarios. Their value is in exposing the assumptions and decision trade-off, not in guaranteeing that one precise dollar result will occur.

chunks.title: PQC Candidates — The Curious Take
chunks.content:
# PQC Candidates — The Curious Take

Think of post-quantum cryptography as an Olympic trial that never stops. FN-DSA (FIPS 206) has not been published yet, not even as a draft.

**Why?** Because we don't want all our eggs in one mathematical basket. If clever attackers find a flaw in lattice math (the family most of the first standards use), we need backup algorithms based on completely different math. So NIST opened a second competition just for signatures. In May 2026 it moved nine candidates from four different mathematical worlds to a third round of evaluation (one, HAWK, has since withdrawn). NIST has not said when standards from this round will come.

**The four families, in plain English:**

- **MPC-in-the-Head** — Prove you know a secret by simulating what would happen if a group of people computed something together. The security rests on well-studied building blocks such as AES (the same cipher protecting your wifi). Signatures are pretty big; the security arguments are well understood but, like every candidate, still under review.
- **Multivariate** — Build a giant puzzle of quadratic equations with a hidden shortcut. You can solve it; an attacker can't. Tiny signatures, huge keys. Some parameters got dinged by a clever attack in 2025 — fixes are in progress.
- **Isogeny** — Walk a graph of mathematical curves. Among the smallest signatures in the contest, small enough to fit in a single network packet. But the math is new and one cousin (SIKE) was broken spectacularly in 2022.
- **Lattice (the HAWK variant)** — Same family as the first standards, but uses integers instead of decimal numbers, which makes it easier to implement on small devices. Its team withdrew it in July 2026 after a new attack, so it is no longer in the running.

**The bigger picture.** Korea ran its own competition (KpqC), which picked its winners in January 2025. China is running its own (CACR). The ISO body is turning NIST's standards into international standards. The Internet engineering folks at IETF decide how to actually use them in TLS, SSH and certificates. Lots of parallel work — and your software will eventually need to handle whichever combination your country / industry ends up using.

**What this means for you.** Don't bet on a single algorithm. Build your systems so you can swap crypto modules without rewriting your application. The phrase for this is _crypto-agility_ — and it's why this module exists.

chunks.title: PQC Governance & Policy — In Simple Terms
chunks.content:
### What This Is About

PQC migration touches every system, vendor, and compliance obligation in an enterprise. Formal PQC Governance establishes the policy hierarchy, coordination bodies, and accountability structures required to orchestrate this transformation.

### Why It Matters

Without governance, migration efforts fragment. Different teams may select conflicting algorithms, miss critical deadlines, or operate without clear vendor standards. Utilizing a clear RACI matrix prevents diffusion of responsibility and stalling.

### The Key Takeaway

Most large organizations adopt a Hybrid governance model—centralizing algorithm policy while distributing migration execution to individual business units. Success requires tracking concrete KPIs like policy coverage rate and open exceptions, along with pre-defined escalation paths for conflicts.

### What's Happening

Leading enterprises are establishing dedicated PQC governance boards with formal RACI matrices and KPI dashboards, recognizing that without centralized policy coordination, migration efforts fragment across business units and miss critical deadlines.

chunks.title: PQC Hardware Acceleration — In Simple Terms
chunks.content:
### What This Is About

Post-quantum signatures can be made faster in several ways — wider CPU instructions, built-in hash instructions, graphics cards, custom chips (FPGAs and ASICs) and AI accelerators. This module explains each one with an everyday analogy, and checks the claims against our own measurements across Apple M4 Pro/M5 Max, NXP i.MX95, AMD Kria KV260, Ventuno Q and an AMD AI X1 Pro, plus focused KV260 FPGA experiments.

### Why It Matters

The two main post-quantum signatures spend their time in completely different places. ML-DSA is mostly arithmetic and is already fast; SLH-DSA is mostly hashing and can take seconds on a small chip. So on our KV260 board the FPGA gave only +29% on ML-DSA, but took an SLH-DSA-SHAKE-128s signature from 2.12 seconds on the board's own CPU to 69 milliseconds.

### The Key Takeaway

Speed comes from matching the accelerator to where the time actually goes — and from moving the work cheaply. Moving data to an accelerator and back often costs more than the work itself, one accelerator is shared by all the processor cores, and a chip can own a fast instruction that the software never uses. The X1 tests make this concrete: AVX-512/IFMA helped the measured RSA path, but explicit VAES candidates were correct and slower, so they were not deployed.

### What's Happening

Newer Arm cores (like Apple's M4) add SHA-3 and SHA-512 instructions that older cores lack; x86 has AVX2, AVX-512/IFMA, AES-NI and SHA-NI but no SHA-3 instruction. The common benchmark also measures ML-DSA + ECDSA hybrid signatures and ML-KEM + X25519 hybrid KEMs directly inside the HSM. Chip vendors are adding fixed post-quantum engines to secure elements and roots of trust, while GPU libraries such as NVIDIA cuPQC target very large batches of operations in data centres.

chunks.title: PQC Risk Management — In Simple Terms
chunks.content:
### What This Is About

PQC risk management provides a framework to prepare for the possible arrival of a Cryptographically Relevant Quantum Computer (CRQC). It involves modeling CRQC timelines as scenarios (no one knows when one will exist) and identifying which cryptographic assets (like RSA and ECC) would be exposed.

### Why It Matters

A CRQC could break the asymmetric cryptography that protects most digital communications today. Rating each asset by Likelihood x Impact helps prioritize migration efforts, especially for long-lived secrets exposed to Harvest-Now-Decrypt-Later (HNDL) risk.

### The Key Takeaway

Use the dates that actually apply to you. If you supply U.S. National Security Systems, CNSA 2.0 sets them; otherwise use your regulator's and your customers' dates. The method has three steps: CRQC scenario planning, building a comprehensive risk register, and visualizing exposure on a 5x5 likelihood-impact heatmap to guide executive decision-making. The heatmap ranks your assets against each other; it does not measure when a quantum computer will arrive.

### What's Happening

Organizations are incorporating CRQC scenario planning into their enterprise risk frameworks, using likelihood-impact heatmaps to prioritize which cryptographic systems must migrate first based on HNDL exposure and the deadlines that apply to them.

chunks.title: PQC Network Testing & Validation — In Simple Terms
chunks.content:
### What This Is About

Testing post-quantum cryptography is fundamentally different from classical crypto. Strategies must account for significant performance cliffs (driven by larger certificate sizes and TCP overhead), interoperability fragility during hybrid handshakes, and hardware implementation leakage.

### Why It Matters

A single fixed-versus-random Test Vector Leakage Assessment (TVLA) test is not enough for lattice-based PQC: it flags any input-dependent difference, including leakage of public data such as ciphertexts, so labs add specific tests on the steps that handle secrets. Unmasked PQC implementations are highly vulnerable to power-analysis side-channel attacks, especially during the Number Theoretic Transform (NTT) stage.

### The Key Takeaway

Successful PQC validation requires a layered approach: passive discovery for safe inventorying, active scanning for endpoint readiness, and rigorous hybrid interoperability testing, ensuring that fallback paths don't silently compromise security.

### What's Happening

Testing frameworks are evolving to address PQC-specific challenges like lattice side-channel leakage and hybrid handshake interoperability, with organizations adopting layered validation strategies combining passive discovery, active scanning, and hybrid interoperability testing.

chunks.title: PCI Certification — In Simple Terms
chunks.content:
### What This Is About

A closer look at PCI approval for payment hardware security modules (HSMs), together with the rules for the companies that operate them. It builds on the certification fundamentals module; FIPS 140-3 has its own module.

### Why It Matters

For payment devices, the device approval and the rules for the companies operating it are different things, and both matter. A FIPS 140-3 certificate is not a PCI approval.

### The Key Takeaway

A PCI listing's post-quantum flag only says that support exists — it does not approve a specific algorithm.

### What's Happening

As of 30 October 2026, PCI's newest HSM standard adds post-quantum definitions without naming a required algorithm or deadline.

chunks.title: Platform Engineering & PQC — In Simple Terms
chunks.content:
### What This Is About

CI/CD pipelines heavily rely on classical cryptography, from Git commit signing with ECDSA, to Vault mTLS, to Kubernetes cert-manager deployments. Every layer of the platform engineering stack is exposed to quantum threats.

### Why It Matters

Infrastructure-as-Code (IaC) tools typically default to quantum-vulnerable settings (like RSA-2048). Furthermore, critical supply chain anchors like container image signatures—built on tools like cosign and Notation—must be migrated to algorithms like ML-DSA to prevent complete infrastructure compromise (not sourced in the Library).

### The Key Takeaway

Automation is the only way to manage PQC correctly at scale. Platform teams should use Policy-as-Code via OPA Gatekeeper or Kyverno to block classical algorithms at cluster admission, and employ Prometheus metrics to continuously monitor for algorithmic drift.

### What's Happening

Platform teams are beginning to integrate PQC-aware policies into their CI/CD pipelines, using OPA Gatekeeper and Kyverno to enforce quantum-safe algorithms at cluster admission while migrating container image signing tools like cosign and Notation to ML-DSA.

chunks.title: PQC GRC — In Simple Terms
chunks.content:
### What This Is About

PQC GRC is the governance, risk, and compliance machinery that makes a post-quantum migration measurable and auditable. Where the SOC detects and responds, GRC measures, reports, and governs — turning a multi-year migration into something a board can actually oversee.

### Why It Matters

Quantum risk breaks the standard risk playbook: the timing is uncertain (10 to 30+ years), there are no historical incidents to learn from, and it is at once a technology, compliance, strategic, and operational risk. Logging it as "low likelihood, review annually" is acknowledging the risk, not managing it. The fix is to give quantum risk the same structured treatment as any other top-tier risk.

### The Key Takeaway

Three instruments do most of the work: a Key Risk Indicator cascade that shows the board, the CISO, and operations the right metrics at the right cadence with thresholds that trigger specific action; a risk-appetite statement that lets the program make trade-offs without escalating every one; and a clean GRC-SOC handoff in which the exception register becomes the SOC's suppression list — so genuine cryptographic drift is not lost in alerts from systems that were legitimately deferred.

### What's Happening

Whether your insurer asks about quantum readiness at renewal is a question for your broker, but a documented, governed, measured migration program is easier to explain to an underwriter than a vague intention to migrate later. The organizations that maintain an evidence dossier can answer the attestation surge after any public quantum event with an export, not a project.

chunks.title: Quantum Key Distribution — In Simple Terms
chunks.content:
# Quantum Key Distribution — In Simple Terms

## What This Is About

Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) shares encryption keys using the fundamental laws of quantum physics—specifically the "no-cloning theorem"—rather than relying on difficult mathematical equations.

## Why It Matters

Standard Post-Quantum Cryptography relies on math problems that we _hope_ quantum computers cannot solve. QKD is entirely different: it offers "information-theoretic security" because measuring a quantum state physically disturbs it, immediately exposing any eavesdropper on the network.

## The Key Takeaway

Despite its immense security, QKD has severe physical limitations. Standard fiber optic cables max out at roughly 100 kilometers for QKD transmission. Extending this distance requires "trusted nodes" to relay the signal, but compromising any single node exposes all the keys.

chunks.title: Quantum Threats — In Simple Terms
chunks.content:
# Quantum Threats — In Simple Terms

## What This Is About

Modern encryption relies on math problems (like factoring massive numbers) that are practically impossible for traditional computers to solve. A Cryptographically Relevant Quantum Computer (CRQC) running "Shor's Algorithm" would change that: it could solve the problems behind RSA and ECC far faster than any classical computer. No such machine is publicly known to exist, and expert estimates of when one might arrive range from a few years to a few decades.

## Why It Matters

Government security agencies, including NSA, CISA and the UK NCSC, warn that adversaries may be recording encrypted data today to decrypt it once a powerful enough quantum computer exists ("Harvest Now, Decrypt Later"). Data that must stay secret for many years — health records, state secrets, intellectual property — is therefore at risk now, even though the machine is not.

## The Key Takeaway

Waiting for a quantum computer to appear before reacting would be too late for long-lived secrets. Organizations should identify their most sensitive long-lived data first and plan its migration to NIST's post-quantum standards (FIPS 203, 204, 205) well before a CRQC could exist.

## What's Happening

Several governments have published transition timelines. The U.S. has the most specific ones: CNSA 2.0 for National Security Systems and Executive Order 14412 for federal agencies. Others, such as the UK NCSC and the EU's coordinated roadmap, publish target dates and guidance rather than binding rules for everyone.

chunks.title: Researcher Quantum Impact — In Simple Terms
chunks.content:
### What This Is About

Post-Quantum Cryptography is not a "solved" problem. The global transition requires researchers and academics to actively test, improve, and break these new algorithms. We need minds dedicated to lattice-based cryptanalysis, side-channel attack mitigation, and formal verification.

### Why It Matters

Standardized algorithms (like ML-KEM and ML-DSA) are just the beginning. Without rigorous academic peer-review and continuous cryptanalysis, undiscovered vulnerabilities could compromise future global security infrastructures before they are even fully deployed.

### The Key Takeaway

We need researchers to improve post-quantum cryptography. Experiment with NIST algorithms, hunt for side-channel physical vulnerabilities, collaborate across disciplines, and secure grant funding by advancing the frontier of quantum-safe security.

### What's Happening

The global research community is actively stress-testing NIST's standardized algorithms through cryptanalysis challenges, side-channel evaluations, and formal verification efforts, ensuring that the foundations of post-quantum security remain robust as deployment scales worldwide.

chunks.title: SLH-DSA — In Simple Terms
chunks.content:
# SLH-DSA — In Simple Terms

## What This Is About

SLH-DSA (Stateless Hash-Based Digital Signature Algorithm, **FIPS 205**) is NIST's hash-only signature scheme. It doesn't rely on lattices or elliptic curves: its security relies on the presumed difficulty of finding preimages for hash functions, as well as several related properties of the same hash functions (FIPS 205 section 1.1), and is based on nothing else (BSI TR-02102-1 section 5.3.4). If those hash properties hold, SLH-DSA holds.

## Why It Matters

Hash-based signatures were the first quantum-safe construction anyone trusted, but the early designs (LMS and XMSS, both **stateful**) had a brutal operational catch: the signer has to make sure no one-time key is ever used twice, so it must durably keep track of which keys it has already used. Lose that record, even briefly — accidental reboot, accidental restore-from-backup, accidental clone of a VM — and the whole key is compromised. SLH-DSA fixes that by being **stateless**: every signature is fresh, no counter to track, safe in distributed systems, serverless functions, and multi-instance HSMs. The price is signature size — anywhere from 8 KB to 50 KB depending on the parameter set — which makes SLH-DSA the bulky but conservative option compared with ML-DSA's lattice signatures of 2,420 to 4,627 bytes (FIPS 204 Table 2).

## The Key Takeaway

Reach for SLH-DSA when you want **the longest, most conservative security argument available** and you don't sign often: root CAs that issue once a year, firmware images stamped at the factory, code-signing certificates for ten-year-life embedded devices. (Note: SLH-DSA is not part of CNSA 2.0 — NSA's FAQ says it "is not approved for any use in NSS"; NSA's picks there are LMS/XMSS for firmware signing and ML-DSA-87 for general signing.) Reach for ML-DSA when signature size or throughput actually matters — TLS handshakes, JWTs, anything high-volume.

## What's Happening

FIPS 205 published in August 2024 with twelve parameter sets across NIST Levels 1, 3, and 5 (e.g. `SLH-DSA-SHA2-128s`, `SLH-DSA-SHAKE-256f`). The `-s` variants are smaller signatures / slower signing; the `-f` variants are faster signing / larger signatures. PKCS#11 v3.2 defines the SLH-DSA mechanisms (`CKM_SLH_DSA` and the `CKM_HASH_SLH_DSA` family), and the softhsmv3 build this module drives implements them. Support in other libraries varies by product and release, so check each one's own release notes. Our expectation (no source states it): the size cost makes SLH-DSA impractical at the TLS handshake layer, while it suits root-of-trust artifacts where you sign once and verify for decades.

## How It Is Tested

A validated SLH-DSA module is checked three ways. NIST's algorithm tests (ACVP) cover key generation, signing and verification, and a vendor registers options such as the parameter sets, internal or external interface, pure or pre-hash mode and, for signing, deterministic or hedged mode. The module also runs its own self-tests before first use: signing, verifying and key generation each get one, and if pure and pre-hash modes share the same code, testing one covers both. Finally the algorithm validation is only a prerequisite for the module certificate, not a substitute for it. This module's workshop replays eight published NIST verification cases (valid signatures, and ones NIST says must be rejected) through the in-browser engine; those are reference samples, not an official validation.

chunks.title: Software Bill of Materials — In Simple Terms
chunks.content:
# Software Bill of Materials — In Simple Terms

## What This Is About

A Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) is a machine-readable ingredients list for software: every package and library a product depends on, its version, its supplier, and how the pieces connect. It's the software equivalent of the ingredients label on a food package — except most organizations don't have one yet.

## Why It Matters

When a vulnerability is found in a widely-used library, the first question is always "do we use that, and where?" Without an SBOM, answering that takes days of digging. With one, it's a search. That's also why an SBOM is a required input to a Cryptography Bill of Materials (CBOM): you can't build a complete list of the cryptography inside your software without first knowing what software you're running.

## The Key Takeaway

An SBOM only becomes useful when it lists the right fields consistently (supplier, name, version, and how components depend on each other), is paired with a VEX statement so a listed vulnerability doesn't trigger a false alarm, and is treated as an input other disciplines build on — not a one-off compliance checkbox.

chunks.title: Secrets Management & PQC — In Simple Terms
chunks.content:
### What This Is About

Organizations manage two distinct sets of sensitive materials: functional secrets (API keys, DB credentials) and the cryptographic keys (like KEKs) that wrap them. Their lifetime dictates their quantum vulnerability.

### Why It Matters

Long-lived API keys harvested from a TLS session today could be extracted and exploited by a CRQC years from now. By contrast, migrating the Key Encryption Key (KEK) of a secrets vault to ML-KEM via envelope encryption protects all stored secrets at rest instantly.

### The Key Takeaway

Dynamic secrets (like 8-hour TTL database credentials) eliminate HNDL risk automatically by expiring long before they can be decrypted. For remaining static secrets, modernize your vault's transit engine to support ML-KEM envelope encryption.

### What's Happening

Secrets management platforms are evaluating ML-KEM integration for their transit encryption engines, while organizations are accelerating the shift from long-lived static API keys to short-lived dynamic secrets that naturally resist Harvest Now, Decrypt Later attacks.

chunks.title: Secure Boot & Firmware PQC — In Simple Terms
chunks.content:
### What This Is About

UEFI Secure Boot uses a cryptographic chain of trust (Platform Key, KEK, db) to protect the OS kernel. Currently, every link relies on quantum-vulnerable algorithms like RSA-2048 or ECDSA. The risk to a signature is forgery once a quantum computer exists, not recorded data being read later, so how soon matters depends on how long a device and its trust anchors stay in the field.

### Why It Matters

Migrating to ML-DSA-65 is the standard path, but it introduces a massive size impact. ML-DSA signatures are roughly 13x larger than RSA-2048, which can strain the variable storage a platform sets aside for Secure Boot. That storage is platform-specific, and firmware reports it through QueryVariableInfo() (UEFI 2.11 section 8.2.4). TPM 2.0 Library v185 (published by the Trusted Computing Group in March 2026) adds ML-DSA and ML-KEM, but TPMs built to earlier versions lack them and shipping chips follow the specification.

A firmware signature has two sides that are checked differently. The device checks the signature with code that, for ML-DSA and LMS, can be tested through NIST's algorithm validation program (CAVP); no test specification is published yet for XMSS or HSS. The signer holds the private key: NIST SP 800-208 requires LMS and XMSS key generation and signing to happen inside a hardware module validated to FIPS 140 with Level 3 or higher physical security, and the NSA's CNSA 2.0 FAQ says signers that are National Security Systems must follow SP 800-208 (which means CMVP-validated hardware) or other NSA guidance, while a product that only verifies signatures needs only the CAVP test.

Two other integrity checks sit beside the signature, and they are different kinds of rule. NIST SP 800-193 is a design guideline for platform builders (protect, detect and recover firmware) and names no validation program. The FIPS 140-3 integrity test is a requirement on a cryptographic module: the module checks its own software and firmware before it is used, and the test is run by an accredited laboratory and validated by the CMVP.

### The Key Takeaway

Firmware vendors are at different stages of PQC: Insyde, Dell and HPE state that PQC firmware signing is available, AMI has announced a working implementation, and open-source EDK2 work is in progress. In the interim, organizations must prepare for a dual-signature (RSA + ML-DSA) hybrid transition and immediately audit UEFI NVRAM capacity to accommodate the larger public keys and signatures.

### What's Happening

Firmware vendors are at different stages of PQC-capable UEFI implementations, while organizations are auditing their NVRAM capacity and planning dual-signature (RSA + ML-DSA) hybrid boot chains to maintain backward compatibility during the transition.

chunks.title: Skills & Team Structure — In Simple Terms
chunks.content:
### What This Is About

A post-quantum migration is a multi-year program, and someone has to staff it. This module shows how to build the team: the core roles you need, how big the team should be, what to build in-house versus buy from outside, and how to train everyone.

### Why It Matters

The mix of skills PQC needs — deep cryptography, large-scale program management, and hands-on network/app/OT expertise — almost never sits in one person. Trying to hire a whole team of specialists is unrealistic. Instead, you build a small expert core, upskill the staff you already have, and bring in scarce specialists only where you must.

### The Key Takeaway

Team size follows your cryptographic estate, not your employee count. The rule of thumb is one dedicated person per 500 cryptographic "instances" (certificates, keys, TLS endpoints, HSMs) in the first couple of years, easing to one per 1,000 once tooling matures. A 50,000-person bank with a sprawling crypto estate needs a bigger team than a 200,000-person manufacturer whose crypto is concentrated in one platform.

### What's Happening

Leading programs designate a "crypto champion" on every platform team — web, mobile, data, infrastructure, OT, identity — so the program scales without every developer becoming a cryptographer. Champions sign off on crypto readiness in design reviews and shepherd library upgrades, and after migration they become a permanent network, much like long-running security champion programs.

chunks.title: SOC Implementation for PQC — In Simple Terms
chunks.content:
### What This Is About

PQC migration does not end when the certificates are swapped. The Security Operations Center inherits a permanent new job: making sure migrated systems stay migrated, that hybrid connections are not quietly knocked back to old cryptography, and that the organization is ready for the next algorithm transition after this one.
