This module shows SOC directors and analysts how to build that capability on the SIEM, network monitoring, and certificate tools they already own.

### Why It Matters

There are five things a quantum-aware SOC watches for: a hybrid connection being forced back to classical crypto (a downgrade attack), systems drifting back to old algorithms after migration, suspicious activity around new post-quantum certificates, forged digital signatures (Trust Now, Forge Later), and adversaries quietly harvesting long-lived encrypted data to decrypt once a quantum computer exists (Harvest Now, Decrypt Later). None of it works without one prerequisite: a live, machine-readable registry that records what cryptography each system is supposed to be using. If that registry is a quarterly spreadsheet emailed around, every detection rule falls apart.

### The Key Takeaway

The SOC builds detection on what it already has, then layers on quantum threat intelligence across three time horizons (hours, weeks, years), four incident-response playbooks, and annual tabletop exercises with names like "The Friday Afternoon CVE" and "Signing Key Compromise." The single biggest enabler is the cryptographic posture registry; the single biggest engineering hurdle is teaching the SIEM to recognize post-quantum key exchanges, which are negotiated by codepoints most tools cannot yet parse.

### What's Happening

SOC teams are negotiating SIEM-integrated access to the migration program's cryptographic posture registry, writing custom rules to spot hybrid-downgrade attacks while filtering out their own middleboxes' false alarms, subscribing to the NIST PQC mailing list and IETF working groups for tactical threat intelligence, and running tabletop exercises to pressure-test their quantum incident-response playbooks before a real CVE lands at 16:30 on a Friday.

chunks.title: Software Supply Chain PQC — In Simple Terms
chunks.content:
# Software Supply Chain PQC — In Simple Terms

## What This Is About

When software or a firmware update reaches a device, a digital signature is one of the main ways the receiver can check that what arrived is what was sent. This module reads the documents that govern those signatures, one link at a time, and asks a precise question of each: what does it say about signatures that a large quantum computer could not break, and where is it silent?

## Why It Matters

The documents differ. Some specify post-quantum and hash-based signatures for common formats such as CMS, X.509 and COSE; some are still drafts; one registry marks the post-quantum entries experimental; and two documents that govern signing, the CA/Browser Forum code signing requirements v3.11 and the UEFI Specification Release 2.11, contain no post-quantum term in the editions read here.

## The Key Takeaway

A document that does not mention quantum computers is a fact about that document, not about anyone's plans. Reading each link precisely — which document, which edition, what it says — is more useful than a general statement that the supply chain is vulnerable.

## What's Happening

Update frameworks such as TUF and Uptane spread trust across several roles and keys, and require a threshold of signatures for a role to be trusted. SLSA and in-toto describe provenance and attestations but name no signature algorithm in the pages read here. For a verifier that has already shipped, the documents describe carrying two signatures during a change, combining algorithms, and, for unchangeable boot code, recommending hash-based signatures.

chunks.title: Standards, Certification & Compliance Bodies — In Simple Terms
chunks.content:
### What This Is About

The post-quantum ecosystem involves three distinct roles: Standards bodies (like NIST) write the algorithm specifications, Certification bodies (like CMVP) test the products, and Compliance frameworks (like CNSA 2.0) mandate their use in specific sectors.

### Why It Matters

Confusing these roles is a common source of compliance failure. For example, purchasing a product that merely uses a "NIST algorithm" is insufficient if your framework requires a CMVP FIPS 140-3 validation, which itself involves a long certification queue.

### The Key Takeaway

You comply with a framework, get certified against a standard, and the standard is written by the standard body.

### What's Happening

The CMVP FIPS 140-3 certification backlog is a critical bottleneck for organizations requiring validated PQC modules.

chunks.title: Stateful Signatures — In Simple Terms
chunks.content:
### What This Is About

Stateful hash-based signatures (LMS and XMSS) derive their security only from the security of their underlying hash functions like SHA-256, not from newer mathematical assumptions like lattices or isogenies.

### Why It Matters

Because each One-Time Signature (OTS) key in the Merkle tree can only be used safely once, the signer must track a monotonic state counter. Reusing the same leaf index for two different messages guarantees a catastrophic security failure, allowing an attacker to forge signatures.

### The Key Takeaway

Stateful signatures are among the most conservative post-quantum designs: NIST standardized them in SP 800-208, and NSA's CNSA 2.0 approves LMS and XMSS for signing firmware and software (it prefers LMS with SHA-256/192, and ML-DSA-87 is also allowed for that use). However, they require flawless state management, for which a monotonic counter from some hardware cryptographic modules can help when available.

### What's Happening

LMS and XMSS are already standardized under NIST SP 800-208.

### How It Is Tested

A certificate for a module that signs with LMS or XMSS rests on four checks. NIST publishes an algorithm test for LMS (key generation, signing and verification) but no ACVP specification for XMSS, XMSS^MT or HSS, and the test does not check whether a private key can be exported or a one-time key reused. The module also runs its own self-tests before first use. SP 800-208 requires key generation and signing to stay inside a validated hardware module with Level 3 or higher physical security and no export of private keys; a module that only verifies signatures does not have to meet those hardware rules. For national security systems, NSA's CNSA 2.0 FAQ says a product that only verifies signatures needs algorithm testing (CAVP) alone, while a signer that is itself a national security system must use CMVP-validated hardware, with no waivers. NSA allows LMS and XMSS (all parameters, LMS with SHA-256/192 recommended), not HSS or XMSS^MT, and says SLH-DSA is not approved for any use in national security systems.

In the workshop (Step 4) you can run NIST's published LMS verification samples (16 cases) and the RFC 8554 test cases through the in-browser engine; the page keeps these known-answer checks apart from the functional round trips, which only show that the engine accepts its own output. A match is a reference-sample match, not a validation.

chunks.title: TLS Basics — In Simple Terms
chunks.content:
### What This Is About

TLS 1.3 secured the internet by enforcing modern forward secrecy and 1-RTT handshakes. Upgrading it for PQC involves integrating lattice-based Key Encapsulation Mechanisms (ML-KEM) and signatures (ML-DSA). Running old and new algorithms side by side during the transition also creates a new question: could a connection end up classical-only when both sides support PQC?

### Why It Matters

Post-quantum algorithms demand much larger ciphertexts and keys than classical ECDH (like X25519). Notably, replacing classical certs with ML-DSA certificate chains adds several kilobytes to every handshake, threatening the scalability of billions of daily web connections.

TLS 1.3 signs and MACs the whole handshake, so an attacker who deletes the post-quantum option from the client's message is detected and the connection fails. The real downgrade risks are elsewhere: products that retry without post-quantum after a failed attempt, clients that don't know whether a server supports PQC, and settings that accept a classical-only connection.

### The Key Takeaway

The industry is already deploying "Hybrid" key exchange (X25519MLKEM768) to protect traffic from Harvest-Now-Decrypt-Later attacks. To stop deliberate fallbacks from being abused, clients can remember that a server supported PQC on a previous visit. Browsers do this locally ("PQ Lock"), and PQC Continuity is an individual Internet-Draft (one proposal, not adopted by the TLS working group) for a TLS extension that lets a client cache a server's declared commitment to present PQC or composite certificates for a specified duration. Neither can protect the very first visit.

### What's Happening

Major browsers and CDN providers are already deploying hybrid key exchange (X25519MLKEM768) in production TLS 1.3, and the IETF published it as RFC 10024. Downgrade-memory proposals such as `draft-sheffer-tls-pqc-continuity` are still individual drafts under discussion, while the IETF PLANTS working group develops Merkle Tree Certificates to address certificate bloat.

chunks.title: Talking About PQC Accurately — In Simple Terms
chunks.content:
### What This Is About

You don't need to understand the mathematics to talk about post-quantum cryptography — but you do need to get the facts right. This module is for anyone who has to say something about it at work: in sales, marketing, communications, procurement, policy or the press. It covers what is true today, which deadlines are real and who they apply to, what a security certificate actually proves, and which popular words don't hold up.

### Why It Matters

Customers, buyers and journalists can now check a quantum claim against public records: the standards are published, the government deadlines are written down, and certificate numbers can be looked up. A sentence that overstates a deadline or a certificate costs more trust than it ever wins.

### The Key Takeaway

Say what the record shows, and point to it. Name the standard (for example ML-KEM, FIPS 203), the version of the product, and the evidence — a certificate number or a public roadmap — instead of "quantum-proof" or "fully compliant".

### Try It Yourself

The workshop gives you six real-sounding claims and four customer questions. Pick the most accurate answer and see straight away why it holds up and the others don't.

chunks.title: Trust Services & Signature Longevity — In Simple Terms
chunks.content:
# Trust Services & Signature Longevity — In Simple Terms

## What This Is About

When you sign a mortgage, a will or a land registry entry electronically, that signature has to stay provable for decades. The certificate behind it expires in a year or two. The revocation records that prove it was good at the time disappear after a few more. And eventually the algorithm itself gets broken. This module is about how a signature stays believable long after everything that originally supported it has gone.

## Why It Matters

The answer is timestamping. A trusted authority signs a hash of your document together with the time, which fixes the moment the signature existed. That is what lets a court accept a signature made with a certificate that has since expired, or with an algorithm since broken — because the evidence points at the moment it was made rather than at today.

## The Key Takeaway

The deadline that matters is not the day quantum computers arrive. It is the day by which every signature you have _already_ made must be re-stamped using a quantum-safe algorithm. That work scales with the size of your archive, not with how many new documents you sign — and it has to be planned when the document is signed, because once the supporting evidence has aged out it cannot be recovered.

## What's Happening

Europe's rulebook has already moved. The ETSI cryptographic suites standard was updated in June 2026 to add the new quantum-safe signature algorithms and, importantly, hybrid modes where a classical and a quantum-safe signature must _both_ be valid. That differs from the American position for national security systems, where hybrids are not required. Same algorithms, two authorities, different defaults — which one applies to you depends on where you operate, not on the mathematics.

chunks.title: VPN & SSH PQC — In Simple Terms
chunks.content:
### What This Is About

VPN and SSH protocols are upgrading their key exchanges to Post-Quantum Cryptography using ML-KEM. For instance, recent OpenSSH versions already ship with hybrid modes like `mlkem768x25519-sha256` to secure sessions against future decryption.

### Why It Matters

PQC keys are vastly larger than classical ones. Integrating ML-KEM-768 adds over 1KB per exchange. In highly optimized, lightweight protocols like WireGuard, adding post-quantum protection via Rosenpass (which uses Classic McEliece and the round-3 Kyber, not FIPS 203 ML-KEM) adds four extra Rosenpass messages of 2,464 bytes in total (per the Rosenpass white paper), which raises the risk of UDP IP fragmentation.

### The Key Takeaway

This complex migration strictly targets the "Control Plane" (Key Exchange and Authentication). The "Data Plane" (the actual encrypted tunnel) uses symmetric ciphers like AES-GCM or ChaCha20, which are affected by Grover's algorithm rather than Shor's; per NIST, AES with a minimum key length of 128 bits can continue to be used, and a longer key can be considered for data that must remain secure for many years.

### What's Happening

OpenSSH already ships with hybrid PQC key exchange (mlkem768x25519-sha256) enabled by default, and the IETF drafts for ML-KEM and ML-DSA in IKEv2 are in the RFC Editor queue (October 2026). WireGuard users can add quantum protection through the Rosenpass companion tool.

chunks.title: Vendor & Supply Chain Risk — In Simple Terms
chunks.content:
### What This Is About

Your organization's quantum timeline is limited by your slowest vendor. Third-party software, hardware, and cloud providers handling sensitive data are massive, immediate targets for "Harvest Now, Decrypt Later" campaigns.

### Why It Matters

A commercial product that does not use CNSA 2.0 algorithms cannot be used to protect National Security Systems unless NSA has provided specific written guidance otherwise, and CNSSP 15 states that by 1 January 2027 CNSA 2.0 algorithms will be required in all new NSS acquisitions. NIAP validation is required for commercial products used in NSS and, in the NSA FAQ's words, "will generally require CNSA 2.0 compliance". Where fully certified solutions are not yet available at the end of 2026, the FAQ says a deployment may be accepted on a vendor's contractual commitment to provide a CNSA 2.0 update, combined with a realistic deployment plan that meets the 2030 deadline and is regularly tracked and reported; immediate implementation remains the preferred strategy.

### The Key Takeaway

Organizations can choose to require a Crypto Bill of Materials (CBOM), such as CycloneDX 1.6+, from their vendors — a procurement control, not an external mandate. This standardized inventory reveals all algorithms, allowing automatic scoring of vendor readiness and enabling strict contractual deadlines.

### What's Happening

Some procurement and compliance teams are choosing to ask for Cryptographic Bills of Materials (CBOMs) in vendor contracts, using frameworks like CycloneDX 1.6+ to systematically score third-party PQC readiness before renewal deadlines.

chunks.title: Decommissioning & Program Closure — In Simple Terms
chunks.content:
# Decommissioning & Program Closure — In Simple Terms

## What This Is About

This is the end of a post-quantum migration: turning off the old, quantum-vulnerable cryptography and formally winding the program down. Both steps are surprisingly easy to skip — teams report systems as "done" on a ticket, and programs quietly drift on without ever closing.

## Why It Matters

A migration isn't finished when you add post-quantum cryptography — it's finished when the old RSA/ECC keys are actually gone, on a defensible schedule (under NIST's timeline, the old cryptography is set to be deprecated after 2030 and disallowed after 2035). And you only really know it happened if you can see it in the system's behaviour — for example, capturing the connection handshake and confirming it negotiated a post-quantum algorithm — rather than trusting a change ticket.

## The Key Takeaway

Close deliberately. Verify the highest-value systems completely and sample the rest; remove and then confirm-removed the old cryptography; and hand every ongoing responsibility (the crypto inventory, vendor monitoring, security detections, reporting) to a named permanent owner, accepting any leftover risk on the record. Then the program can formally end instead of fading away.

chunks.title: Web Gateway & PQC — In Simple Terms
chunks.content:
### What This Is About

Web gateways—such as reverse proxies, WAFs, load balancers, and CDNs—are the central nervous system for TLS termination. Deploying PQC at the gateway level instantly shields thousands of backend services without requiring any application code changes.

### Why It Matters

Security appliances like Next-Gen Firewalls (NGFWs) often have strict hardware buffer limits (around ~4 KB) for Deep Packet Inspection. A massive PQC Hybrid handshake (~15+ KB) violently shatters these limits, causing firewalls to blindly drop the connections entirely.

### The Key Takeaway

A phased architecture is critical: deploy classical TLS at your local inspection points (maintaining WAF visibility) while enabling Hybrid PQC (X25519MLKEM768) on the internet-facing edge. This shields the perimeter against quantum harvesting without breaking internal inspection.

### What's Happening

Security vendors are updating their NGFW and WAF firmware to handle larger PQC handshakes, while organizations are testing phased gateway architectures that deploy hybrid PQC (X25519MLKEM768) at the internet edge while maintaining classical TLS at internal inspection points.

Only the symmetric key is wrapped: the ML-KEM-768 ciphertext is 1,088 bytes (FIPS 203). The ML-DSA-65 signature is 3,309 bytes against 64 bytes for ECDSA P-256, about 50 times larger, but the model file is 140 GB, so the overhead of both is negligible.

In the Agent Auth Designer, select "Human-Delegated" agent type and "Trading Bot with Market Data" chain. Examine the 3-hop delegation chain. Calculate the total PQC chain size vs classical.

In the Agentic Commerce Simulator, select "Multi-Agent Negotiation". Enable the quantum overlay. Step through all 6 steps and count how many use quantum-vulnerable signing.
All 6 steps are quantum-vulnerable. The simulator puts the total PQC latency overhead at 10.9% (220 ms to 244 ms), which it labels Moderate — its Acceptable band ends at 5%. chunks.title: AI Security & PQC — Introduction
chunks.content:
Module: AI Security & PQC
Component: Introduction

Every AI system depends on a data pipeline — the flow from raw data ingestion through preprocessing, storage, training, and inference. Each stage involves cryptographic operations that protect data confidentiality and integrity. With the advent of cryptographically relevant quantum computers (CRQCs), these protections face an existential threat.
Adversaries can intercept and store encrypted training data today, then decrypt it when a CRQC becomes available. For proprietary datasets worth millions in curation costs, this is a direct intellectual property theft vector. The data's value outlives the encryption protecting it.
ML-KEM replaces ECDH for key exchange, and ML-DSA replaces ECDSA/RSA for digital signatures.
As AI-generated content floods the internet, a new threat emerges: model collapse. When models are trained on data produced by other AI models, quality degrades with each generation — outputs become repetitive, lose diversity, and drift from reality. Distinguishing authentic human-created data from AI-generated content is now a critical challenge.
Gen 0: 100% Human Data Gen 2: 50% Synthetic Gen 5: 83% Synthetic — Quality Collapse
Content Credentials (C2PA) : Signed metadata embedded in content files — creator identity, creation tool, edit history. Creates a verifiable chain of custody from origin to consumption.
Cryptographic provenance chains: Hash-chain-based data lineage tracking where each transformation appends a signed entry to an append-only log.

chunks.title: AI Security & PQC — Introduction
chunks.content:
Module: AI Security & PQC
Component: Introduction

AI watermark detection: Identifying invisible watermarks embedded by AI generators (SynthID, statistical LLM watermarks) to flag synthetic content.
Provenance signatures must outlive the data they protect — potentially decades. Provenance records signed with ECDSA, RSA-PSS or Ed25519 (the signature algorithms C2PA 2.4 allows) become forgeable post-CRQC, allowing retroactive injection of synthetic data into verified datasets. Migration to ML-DSA signatures ensures long-term provenance trust.
Model weights are the crown jewels of an AI organization — billions of parameters representing multi-million dollar intellectual property (IP). Protecting this IP from Harvest-Now-Decrypt-Later (HNDL) attacks requires ML-KEM wrapping for confidentiality and ML-DSA signing for integrity to ensure long-term protection.
Just as code signing verifies software integrity, model signing uses digital signatures to prove a model has not been tampered with. Frameworks like Sigstore (cosign) and in-toto are adding support for ML-DSA signatures on model artifacts. This creates a provenance record: who trained the model, on what data, when, and with what hyperparameters.
See also: Confidential Computing & TEEs for hardware-enforced model protection during inference.

chunks.title: AI Security & PQC — Introduction
chunks.content:
Module: AI Security & PQC
Component: Introduction

Agentic AI represents a paradigm shift — autonomous agents acting on behalf of users, making decisions, executing transactions, and communicating with other agents without continuous human oversight. This creates entirely new cryptographic challenges: how do you authenticate a machine? How do you delegate authority securely? How do agents trust each other?
AI agents need cryptographic credentials — certificates, tokens, keys — that are not tied to a human session. Unlike a user who logs in once, an agent may operate for hours or days, delegating sub-tasks to other agents, each needing its own verifiable identity.
Each hop in the chain requires a signed delegation token — a cryptographic credential granting limited authority with scope, expiration, and a signature chain back to the original delegating human.
When agents transact on behalf of users — purchasing goods, negotiating contracts, managing subscriptions — every message exchange must be signed for non-repudiation and encrypted for confidentiality. Purchase orders signed with ML-DSA, payment details encrypted with ML-KEM, and delegation chains verified at each hop.

chunks.title: AI Security & PQC — Introduction
chunks.content:
Module: AI Security & PQC
Component: Introduction

Agent communication channels harvested today can be decrypted post-CRQC to reconstruct entire transaction histories, business strategies, and negotiation patterns. Long-lived agent credentials (certificates with 1-year validity) are exposed once a CRQC exists: it could forge the agent's identity and impersonate it. That is a forgery risk, not harvest-now-decrypt-later, which concerns encrypted data (NIST IR 8547).
Related: API Security & JWT for PQC migration patterns for JWT/DPoP tokens.
AI systems operate at a scale that challenges conventional cryptographic approaches — training datasets measured in petabytes, billions of inference requests per day, thousands of models across global deployments. Each data object needs its own encryption key, each API call needs a secure channel, and each model needs integrity verification.
A hierarchical KMS with ML-KEM envelope encryption is essential — root keys wrap intermediate keys, which wrap data encryption keys (DEKs). At enterprise scale, this means managing millions of DEKs with PQC-wrapped key hierarchies.
LLMs and code assistants are increasingly used to accelerate a PQC migration: finding crypto call-sites, drafting CBOM entries, suggesting algorithm swaps, and rewriting config. They are powerful, but cryptographic changes are exactly where a confident-but-wrong suggestion is most dangerous. Treat AI as a drafting tool behind a mandatory human-review gate — never an unattended committer of cryptographic change.

chunks.title: API Security & JWT — APISecurityExercises
chunks.content:
Module: API Security & JWT
Component: APISecurityExercises

Work through these scenarios to understand JWT structure, PQC signing, hybrid tokens, JWE encryption, and size trade-offs. Each exercise pre-configures the Workshop — click "Load & Run" to begin.
Take the PQC quiz to test what you've learned about API security and JWT migration.
1. Decode a JWT and identify the signing algorithm
Paste a JWT into the inspector and examine the JOSE header. Identify the algorithm, token type, and claims. Switch between sample ES256 and ML-DSA-65 tokens to compare signature sizes.
The header is the only part that changes between algorithms. The ES256 signature is ~85 base64url characters while the ML-DSA-65 signature is ~4,412 characters (3,309 × 4 ÷ 3 = 4,412 in base64url).
2. Sign a JWT with ML-DSA-65 and compare with ES256
Select an algorithm, generate a simulated keypair, edit the payload claims, and sign. Compare the resulting JWT sizes between ES256 and ML-DSA-65. Note the verification status display.
The JWT structure is identical for both algorithms. Only the signature length differs dramatically: ~300 bytes total for ES256 vs ~4,700 bytes for ML-DSA-65.
3. Create a hybrid JWT with dual signatures
Explore the two hybrid approaches: nested JWT (inner + outer signatures) and composite headers. Create a hybrid token and examine the nested structure with both ES256 and ML-DSA-65 signatures.
The nested JWT approach wraps the entire ES256-signed JWT as the payload of an ML-DSA-65-signed outer JWT. The total size is roughly the sum of both JWTs.

chunks.title: API Security & JWT — APISecurityExercises
chunks.content:
Module: API Security & JWT
Component: APISecurityExercises

4. Encrypt a JWT payload with HPKE and ML-KEM
Encrypt a JWT payload as an HPKE JWE (draft-ietf-jose-hpke-pq-pqt-01): generate an ML-KEM-768 recipient key, build a protected header with only "alg" and "kid", let HPKE seal the payload, and assemble the five JWE parts. Decrypt it, switch to the HPKE-9 hybrid (ML-KEM-768 + X25519) and compare the sizes, then decrypt the draft's own published example.
JWE keeps its 5 parts (vs 3 for JWS), but in HPKE Integrated Encryption the IV and tag are empty: the Encrypted Key carries the HPKE encapsulated secret (1,088 bytes for ML-KEM-768, 1,120 for the hybrid) and the GCM tag sits inside the ciphertext.
5. Analyze token sizes across 7 algorithms
Edit the JWT payload and observe how total token size changes across all 7 signing algorithms. Note the segmented bar chart showing header, payload, and signature proportions. Identify which algorithms exceed the 8 KB HTTP header limit.
SLH-DSA-SHA2-128s produces the largest signature (7,856 bytes) but the smallest public key (32 bytes). ML-DSA-87 balances key and signature sizes. Only classical algorithms fit comfortably in standard HTTP headers.
Issue a real ML-DSA-65 access token, then try five attacks on it: "alg": "none", edited claims under the original signature, a token minted for another API, an expired token, and an ID token presented as an access token. Compare what a strict RFC 8725 validator and a naive verifier each accept.

chunks.title: API Security & JWT — APISecurityIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: API Security & JWT
Component: APISecurityIntroduction

JSON Web Tokens (JWT) are the foundation of modern API authentication. A JWT is a compact, URL-safe means of representing claims between two parties. The token format is defined in RFC 7519, with signing (JWS, RFC 7515) and encryption ( JWE, RFC 7516) as separate specifications.
BASE64URL(Header) . BASE64URL(Payload) . BASE64URL(Signature)
The header specifies the algorithm (alg) and token type (typ). The payload carries claims. The signature covers both header and payload.
JOSE header with alg (signing algorithm) and typ (token type). Base64url-encoded JSON.
Claims: sub, iss, exp, aud, plus custom claims. Base64url-encoded JSON.
Cryptographic signature over header.payload using the algorithm specified in the header. This is the part PQC replaces — the claims and the encoding stay the same.
The widely deployed asymmetric JWT signature algorithms — RS256 (RSA-PKCS1-v1_5), ES256 (ECDSA P-256), and EdDSA (Ed25519) — rely on mathematical problems that Shor's algorithm would solve efficiently on a cryptographically relevant quantum computer (CRQC). None is broken today; they are vulnerable to a machine that does not yet exist. Key agreement with ECDH-ES is exposed in the same way. HMAC-based JWTs (HS256) are different: they use a shared secret, and Grover's algorithm only reduces their effective strength, so a 256-bit key remains adequate.

chunks.title: API Security & JWT — APISecurityIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: API Security & JWT
Component: APISecurityIntroduction

A signed JWT is not encrypted — anyone holding it can already read its claims, so there is nothing to "decrypt later". The quantum risk is forgery: a CRQC could recover a signing key from its public key and mint new tokens that any verifier still trusting that key accepts. What matters is how long verifiers trust a key (JWKS rotation, pinned keys, signatures kept as long-term evidence), not how long one token lives.
Anything protected by ECDH today — a JWE using ECDH-ES, or the TLS connection that carries a bearer token — can be recorded now and decrypted once a CRQC exists. That is the HNDL threat, and it is why confidentiality migrates first.
RFC 9964 (published May 2026 by the IETF COSE working group) registers JOSE/COSE alg values for ML-DSA-44/65/87 ( FIPS 204), along with a new kty="AKP" (Algorithm Key Pair) key type that carries a 32-byte FIPS 204 seed as the private key. ML-DSA replaces ECDSA and RSA for JWT signing. The rest of the JOSE PQC stack is still in draft: SLH-DSA ( draft-ietf-cose-sphincs-plus-10, two parameter sets), PQ/T composite signatures ( draft-ietf-jose-pq-composite-sigs-06), and ML-KEM encryption for JWE, which now goes through HPKE ( draft-ietf-jose-hpke-encrypt, in the RFC Editor queue, plus the PQ suites in draft-ietf-jose-hpke-pq-pqt), which the workshop's JWE tab implements. An earlier direct-KEM draft for JWE was narrowed to COSE in its revision -06.
Category 3 (≈ AES-192); this module's default example, not a NIST recommendation

chunks.title: API Security & JWT — APISecurityIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: API Security & JWT
Component: APISecurityIntroduction

JWE (JSON Web Encryption) protects token payloads with authenticated encryption. ML-KEM ( FIPS 203) replaces ECDH-ES for key agreement in JWE, using a Key Encapsulation Mechanism instead of Diffie-Hellman key exchange. The standards route is HPKE: ML-KEM (alone or combined with X25519) supplies the KEM, and the HPKE suite fixes the key derivation and AEAD.
In HPKE Integrated Encryption ( draft-ietf-jose-hpke-encrypt) the JWE header carries only "alg", such as HPKE-12 (ML-KEM-768) or HPKE-9 (ML-KEM-768 + X25519, the X-Wing hybrid) from draft-ietf-jose-hpke-pq-pqt. There is no "enc", because HPKE itself encrypts the payload. The JWE Encrypted Key holds the 1,088-byte (or 1,120-byte) encapsulated secret, and the IV and Authentication Tag segments are empty. A recipient must still check that "alg" is one it expects for that key before decrypting.
ECDH falls to Shor's algorithm on a CRQC (discrete log on elliptic curves).
AES-256-GCM-Encrypt(key, payload, AAD = header) → ciphertext
ML-KEM is a lattice-based KEM with no known quantum attack at its standardized parameters.
The token format survives the migration: the JOSE header's alg value changes and the compact serialization does not. That is the easy part. Around it, nearly everything that handles tokens changes too:
Keys: ML-DSA keys use the new kty: "AKP" JWK type (RFC 9964), so every JWKS publisher and consumer must understand it, and each public key is ~1.3–2.6 KB.

chunks.title: API Security & JWT — APISecurityIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: API Security & JWT
Component: APISecurityIntroduction

Verifier policy: each verifier needs an explicit allowlist of algorithms per key (RFC 8725 §3.1) — never "whatever the header says".
Sizes and transport: header, cookie and proxy limits (below).
Libraries: most JOSE libraries do not ship ML-DSA yet; check the JOSE layer, not just the crypto provider underneath.
Rollout: a period where verifiers accept both old and new keys, and a plan to stop accepting the classical ones so the transition can't be used as a downgrade path.
The most significant practical impact of PQC JWTs is token size. ML-DSA-65 signatures are 3,309 bytes vs 64 bytes for ES256 — a 51x increase. This has cascading effects on HTTP headers, cookies, bandwidth, and storage.
OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect use JWTs in several places, but not everywhere: ID tokens are always JWTs; access tokens may be JWTs (RFC 9068) or opaque strings; refresh tokens are usually opaque handles the authorization server looks up, so a quantum computer cannot forge them unless they are themselves signed tokens. DPoP proofs (RFC 9449) are JWTs signed by the client, so PQC changes their key binding and verifier support as well as their size. Migrating requires coordinated changes across authorization servers, resource servers, and client applications.

chunks.title: API Security & JWT — APISecurityIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: API Security & JWT
Component: APISecurityIntroduction

A post-quantum signature protects a token only if the verifier checks the right things. Most real-world JWT breaches come from validation mistakes, and PQC fixes none of them. The rules below come from RFC 8725 (JWT Best Current Practices), RFC 9700 (OAuth 2.0 Security BCP) and RFC 9068 (JWT access tokens).
One PQC-era change helps here: new JOSE registrations such as ML-DSA-65 are fully specified ( RFC 9864 ): the alg value alone names the exact algorithm and parameters, which makes a per-key allowlist straightforward to write.
To see these checks fail on purpose, open the workshop's Attack Lab (Step 7): it aims "alg": "none", edited claims, a token for another API, an expired token and an ID token at a strict validator and at a naive verifier that trusts the header.

chunks.title: API Security & JWT — HybridJWT
chunks.content:
Module: API Security & JWT
Component: HybridJWT

During the PQC transition, a hybrid JWT combines a classical and a PQC signature, so forging a token requires breaking both algorithms, provided the verifier requires both signatures to be valid. Composite mode follows draft-ietf-jose-pq-composite-sigs-06 and verifies against that draft's published examples; it is a work-in-progress Internet-Draft, so treat this tab as experimental.
Sign the claims with ES256 (WebCrypto), then make that compact JWT the payload of an outer ML-DSA-65 JWT with cty: "JWT" (RFC 7519 §5.2). A verifier must check both layers (RFC 8725 §3.3). A classical-only verifier rejects the outer algorithm, so it only reaches the inner token if a gateway or protocol you define unwraps it first.
A single JWT with alg: ML-DSA-65-Ed25519. The signature is the ML-DSA-65 signature followed directly by the Ed25519 signature (no length prefix). Both sign M′, a domain-separated hash of the signing input, and both must verify.

chunks.title: API Security & JWT — JWEEncryption
chunks.content:
Module: API Security & JWT
Component: JWEEncryption

Post-quantum JWE runs through HPKE. draft-ietf-jose-hpke-encrypt (in the RFC Editor queue) defines how HPKE carries a JWE, and draft-ietf-jose-hpke-pq-pqt-01 registers the ML-KEM suites used here. This workshop pins its examples to revision -01; revision -02 adds serialization references and updates recommendation context without changing the HPKE-9 parameters. All operations run real crypto in your browser, and the code is checked against the examples published in that draft. It is still an early working-group draft, so the algorithm names may change — not a format to deploy yet. An earlier direct-KEM design (draft-ietf-jose-pqc-kem) was dropped for JOSE in 2026.
Both use the SHAKE256 KDF and AES-256-GCM. The hybrid keeps a classical X25519 component, so a flaw found in ML-KEM alone would not expose the payload.
Header . Encrypted Key . IV (empty) . Ciphertext . Tag (empty)
1. Generate ${s.kemName} Keypair
The recipient generates a ${s.kemName} keypair and publishes the public key (${s.Npk.toLocaleString()} bytes) as an "AKP" JWK with "alg": "${alg}". The private key is a ${s.Nsk}-byte seed.${ s.kind === 'pq-t-hybrid' ? ' MLKEM768-X25519 is the X-Wing hybrid: an attacker has to break both ML-KEM-768 and X25519.' : '' }

chunks.title: API Security & JWT — JWEEncryption
chunks.content:
Module: API Security & JWT
Component: JWEEncryption

The header names only "alg" (and here "kid"). In Integrated Encryption, "enc" MUST NOT be present — HPKE itself encrypts the payload, so there is no separate content encryption algorithm — and "ek" MUST NOT be present either (draft-ietf-jose-hpke-encrypt-22 §5). The encoded header becomes the AAD.
HPKE runs Encap(pk) to get a shared secret and a ${s.Nenc.toLocaleString()}-byte encapsulated secret, derives the AEAD key and nonce with the single-stage SHAKE256 KDF, and encrypts the payload with AES-256-GCM using AAD = ASCII(BASE64URL(protected header)). The 16-byte GCM tag is part of the HPKE ciphertext.
The five JWE Compact parts: protected header . Encrypted Key (= the HPKE encapsulated secret) . empty IV . HPKE ciphertext . empty Authentication Tag. IV and Tag are empty because HPKE manages its own nonce and tag.
Protected header (alg ${result.alg}, kid — no "enc", no "ek")
Encrypted Key = HPKE encapsulated secret, ${result.encapsulatedKeyBytes} B
Initialization Vector (empty in Integrated Encryption)
Ciphertext (HPKE / AES-256-GCM, ${result.ciphertextBytes} B incl. 16-byte tag)
Authentication Tag (empty — the tag is inside the ciphertext)

The anti-pattern: it reads "alg" from the token and stops at the signature. RFC 8725 §3.1 says to pin the algorithm to the key instead, and to check issuer, audience and expiry on every token.

chunks.title: API Security & JWT — JWTInspector
chunks.content:
Module: API Security & JWT
Component: JWTInspector

Paste a JWT or select a sample token. The decoder splits the three parts and analyzes the algorithm for quantum safety.
The alg header is chosen by whoever made the token, so this describes what the token claims, not what protects it. Nothing here is trustworthy until the signature verifies against a key you already trust and whose algorithm you expect.
Invalid JWT format. A JWT must have exactly 3 base64url-encoded parts separated by dots.
Key takeaway: JWT decoding is purely base64url — no cryptographic keys are needed to read the header and payload. The signature provides integrity, not confidentiality. Anyone with the token can read the claims. Use JWE if payload confidentiality is required.

chunks.content:
Module: API Security & JWT
Component: PQCJWTSigning

Generate a real ML-DSA keypair, sign a JWT over the canonical signing input b64u(header).b64u(payload), and verify the compact JWS — all in your browser. Algorithm codes follow RFC 9964 (ML-DSA for JOSE and COSE, published May 2026). SLH-DSA codes follow draft-ietf-cose-sphincs-plus-10 and composite codes draft-ietf-jose-pq-composite-sigs-06 — both still Internet-Drafts.
Scope note: RFC 9964 §7.2 explicitly excludes HashML-DSA (FIPS 204 §5.4) from JOSE/COSE — this workshop only exposes the pure-mode variants accordingly.
Educational use only. The signing input is b64u(JOSE header).b64u(payload) per RFC 7515 §5.1. Both noble and SoftHSM3 produce byte-identical signatures over the same input — a token signed via one backend verifies under the other, demonstrating that RFC 9964 interoperates across implementations.

JOSE Header (~50 B base64url) Payload (variable, your claims) Signature (varies by algorithm)
Key takeaway: SLH-DSA-SHA2-128s has the smallest key (32 bytes) but the largest signature (~7,856 bytes). ML-DSA-65 is the recommended balance for most API use cases: NIST Level 3 security with a 3,309-byte signature. For APIs with strict header size constraints, consider reference tokens (opaque strings) with server-side introspection instead of self-contained JWTs.

Module: API Security & JWT
Component: XwingEvidence

These checks always run the browser noble implementation, independently of the JWE backend picker. They compare public reference inputs with external expected bytes: 3 X-Wing author KATs (key generation, encapsulation and decapsulation), 32 NIST ML-KEM-768 ACVP component samples, and 1 published X25519 example. Normal encryption uses fresh randomness.
X-Wing author source · SHA-256 409efe19…3e614d. Construction: draft-connolly-cfrg-xwing-kem-11. The draft KATs remain quarantined in the evidence manifest pending independent source/license review. A successful comparison does not promote that evidence or establish certification.
NIST samples @ 975de31e test the ML-KEM component, including modified-ciphertext implicit rejection. The HSM ACVP panel additionally checks valid and invalid keys. These are reference samples, not an ACVTS session for X-Wing.
SoftHSM candidate CKM_HPKE is checked separately against seeded CFRG KATs and published HPKE/JWE examples in the integration suite. The token does not expose its shared secret; direct secret comparisons belong to the engine tests. This panel does not run those tests. The JWE example button below checks the selected backend; a normal round trip is separate functional evidence.

chunks.title: ACVP Lab Workflow: From Vector Set to Evidence — AcvpLabIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: ACVP Lab Workflow: From Vector Set to Evidence
Component: AcvpLabIntroduction

This is the algorithm-testing companion to PQC Network Testing & Validation , whose workshop walks the ACVP workflow at overview level. Here the same workflow is taken apart the way a testing laboratory meets it: what a registration commits you to, what each test type asks the implementation to do, where a PKCS#11 interface cannot follow, and how to state a result without claiming more than the evidence shows. The programme landscape itself (who runs CAVP, CMVP and the testing labs) is covered in Standards, Certification & Compliance Bodies .
The core protocol used here is draft-ietf-acvp-spec-01, an independent draft whose name has stayed the same while NIST has kept revising its protocol sections in the repository (the latest change is dated 16 October 2025); this module pins it by repository commit . What changes is the algorithm JSON specifications, which evolve separately, so evidence must name the exact core draft, algorithm-specification revision, operational environment and vector-set source.
The eight evidence classes and the nine-rung claim ladder in this module are PQC Today’s own scale for describing test results; NIST does not define one. The scale prevents a public ACVP-Server sample, an imported prompt and an ACVTS-issued vector set from being reported as if they were interchangeable.

chunks.title: ACVP Lab Workflow: From Vector Set to Evidence — AcvpLabIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: ACVP Lab Workflow: From Vector Set to Evidence
Component: AcvpLabIntroduction

Two NIST programmes are routinely blurred together. The Cryptographic Algorithm Validation Program (CAVP) validates implementations of approved algorithms and their components; NIST calls algorithm validation “a prerequisite of cryptographic module validation” . The Cryptographic Module Validation Program (CMVP), run jointly by NIST and the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security, validates whole cryptographic modules to FIPS 140-3, using independent NVLAP-accredited Cryptographic and Security Testing (CST) laboratories .
An algorithm implementation, by comparing its outputs with known or expected answers
A defined module against FIPS 140-3’s eleven requirement areas — module specification, interfaces, roles/services/authentication, software/firmware, operating environment, physical, non-invasive, SSP management, self-tests, life-cycle assurance, mitigation of other attacks — at one of four security levels
Approved algorithms; NIST points to SP 800-140C and SP 800-140D for the lists
The approved algorithms the module claims; the lab confirms each complies with all requirements of its standard, including those CAVP tests do not reach
Black-box, through the Automated Cryptographic Validation Testing System (ACVTS): the implementation is never sent to NIST
A CST laboratory tests the module, reviews documentation and source, and submits a report to the CMVP validation authorities
An algorithm validation certificate on the CAVP validation list

chunks.title: ACVP Lab Workflow: From Vector Set to Evidence — AcvpLabIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: ACVP Lab Workflow: From Vector Set to Evidence
Component: AcvpLabIntroduction

A module certificate; its entry links to the CAVP certificates of the algorithms the module uses
The CMVP Management Manual requires the laboratory to confirm compliance with the algorithm standards’ “shall” statements that CAVP testing does not address . The ACVP sub-specifications say the same from the other side: the ML-DSA test types do not test zeroization of intermediate values, DRBG strength, or incorrect-length keys and signatures . The ML-KEM sub-specification carries the same list word for word, including “signatures”, which ML-KEM does not produce: the section was copied from ML-DSA .
Where this Hub stands: it runs neither programme. It executes selected public reference vectors, standards tests, conformance cases and probes, and its results are never an ACVTS verdict or a CAVP/CMVP certificate (see the notice at the top of this page).
The module side (security levels, the Modules In Process queue, and the CMVP routes for adding ML-KEM or ML-DSA to an already-validated module) is taught in FIPS 140-3 Certification .
ACVP testing starts with the client, not the server. A registration is the client’s description of the capabilities of one or more algorithm / mode / revision combinations . ACVTS generates test cases that match those capabilities and hands the inputs to the implementation . Each algorithm in the registration becomes one test vector set (identified by vsId), made of test groups (tgId) that share properties, made of test cases (tcId) .

chunks.title: ACVP Lab Workflow: From Vector Set to Evidence — AcvpLabIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: ACVP Lab Workflow: From Vector Set to Evidence
Component: AcvpLabIntroduction

The registration below is the ML-DSA sigGen example from the ACVP ML-DSA sub-specification, with its hash list shortened. Every array is a promise: the server will generate test groups for combinations of these values, and the implementation has to answer all of them .
deterministic: [true, false] commits the implementation to both signing variants, including hedged groups that carry the server’s randomness .
signatureInterfaces: ["internal"] commits it to answering ML-DSA.Sign_internal on a formatted message, and externalMu: [true] to accepting a message representative μ computed outside the module .
prereqVals names prerequisite algorithm validations (here SHA) .
The revision is part of the identity: the sub-specification lists ML-DSA / sigGen as both FIPS204 and FIPS204-tr1, “a new test revision against the same standard” .
A module may implement hedged signing and still be unable to answer a hedged sigGen test, because the test must inject the randomness. The registration therefore has to match what the test harness can drive, not just what the product does. The Hub’s own ACVP-format prototype makes the same decision in reverse: it accepts only the algorithm / mode / revision triples it pins, and rejects any other with a diagnostic rather than guessing a closest revision.
The ACVP specification’s minimal message flow has six exchanges :

chunks.title: ACVP Lab Workflow: From Vector Set to Evidence — AcvpLabIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: ACVP Lab Workflow: From Vector Set to Evidence
Component: AcvpLabIntroduction

A passed disposition means every test case in the vector set was processed and passed, and indicates the algorithm is ready for validation — it is not itself the validation .
A session created with isSample: true lets the client retrieve the expected results, and its vector sets may be smaller . For a validation authority, vector sets are one-time use: an old vector set can never be reused to obtain a new certificate .
NIST runs two ACVTS environments. Demo is a semi-volatile sandbox for testing implementations and ACVP clients. Prod is restricted to accredited CST laboratories and 17ACVT laboratories; a lab may run an algorithm in Prod only after running it at least once through certification in Demo . Only Prod creates the algorithm validation certificates on the CAVP list .
Map this onto the Hub’s claim ladder and the boundary is exact: generating a response to an issued prompt is rung 7; the disposition is rung 8; a published validation record is rung 9. The Hub’s ACVP-format prototype stops at local import and response export — it has no ACVTS session, credentials, submission or verdict retrieval.
A test type describes the format of a test rather than its intention; several tests of the same type can cover different assurances . The vocabulary is defined per algorithm, in each ACVP sub-specification:
Hash single, multiple and partial blocks of random data — checks chunking and padding

chunks.title: ACVP Lab Workflow: From Vector Set to Evidence — AcvpLabIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: ACVP Lab Workflow: From Vector Set to Evidence
Component: AcvpLabIntroduction

Monte Carlo Test: from one seed, run 100 × 1,000 chained hashes where each digest feeds the next message; aimed at state, allocation and error-handling faults
Large Data Test: hash a multi-gigabyte message described, not transmitted, by the prompt
Generate a key pair from a provided seed (ML-KEM.KeyGen_internal)
Encapsulate with a server-chosen m (ML-KEM.Encaps_internal) and return c and k
Decapsulate valid or modified ciphertexts (ML-KEM.Decaps_internal), or decide whether an encapsulation key (FIPS 203 §7.2) or decapsulation key (§7.3) is valid
Key pair from a seed; signatures compared with the server’s known signature; validity decisions on modified signatures
Key pair from SK.seed, SK.prf and PK.seed; signatures from provided keys and randomness; validity decisions on modified signatures
The sub-specifications fix minimum test counts per combination of capabilities — for example at least 15 ML-DSA sigGen tests and at least 3 ML-DSA sigVer tests per modification type , and at least 13 SLH-DSA sigGen tests . ML-DSA sigGen also requires tests that drive every rejection path of ML-DSA.Sign_internal, and tests that force at least 32 rejections, on the internal, deterministic interface .
A single passing case per parameter set is therefore a sample of an ACVP test type, never its coverage.

chunks.title: ACVP Lab Workflow: From Vector Set to Evidence — AcvpLabIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: ACVP Lab Workflow: From Vector Set to Evidence
Component: AcvpLabIntroduction

FIPS 203, 204 and 205 each split their algorithms into an external interface, which generates its own randomness, and an internal interface that takes the randomness as an input. Tests that must supply the random input use the internal interfaces; the current ACVP ML-DSA specification supports testing both the internal and the external interface . Each standard says they should not be offered to applications other than for testing, because the random values shall be generated by the module .
32-byte m drawn inside the module; Encaps_internal(ek, m) takes it as input
Byte-exact testing needs the internal interface with the server’s m.
Default hedged: rnd from an RBG. Optional deterministic: rnd = 32 zero bytes; that is the only difference
Deterministic signatures can be compared byte for byte; hedged ones only if the test can inject rnd.
Default hedged: opt_rand = addrnd. Deterministic: opt_rand = PK.seed
FIPS 204 treats the variants differently for security, not only for testing: hedged signing helps mitigate side-channel attacks, the deterministic variant “should not be used on platforms where side-channel attacks are a concern and where they cannot be otherwise mitigated”, and implementing the hedged variant alone is sufficient for interoperability .

chunks.title: ACVP Lab Workflow: From Vector Set to Evidence — AcvpLabIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: ACVP Lab Workflow: From Vector Set to Evidence
Component: AcvpLabIntroduction

You are comparing two implementations of ML-DSA, the post-quantum digital-signature algorithm. They sign the same message with the same key, context and settings. In normal hedged signing, each call uses fresh random input, so the signatures can differ without either implementation being wrong. Check that both signatures verify; different bytes alone do not establish a fault.
In an ACVP signature-generation test, however, the test supplies the random input as well as the other inputs. The implementation must use those inputs and produce the expected signature exactly. Successful verification alone is not enough to pass that test .
ACVP talks to an implementation through whatever interface the test harness can reach . For the Hub that interface is PKCS#11 v3.2, on two WASM engines (C++ and Rust). An ACVP test group can only be answered if the interface takes exactly the inputs the group supplies — nothing coerced, nothing defaulted. Where standard PKCS#11 has no field for an input, this HSM accepts it as an optional test input outside the standard, and every result that used one says so.
Import dk, then C_DecapsulateKey with CKM_ML_KEM (ML-KEM.Decaps)
Standard PKCS#11 has no field for m: C_EncapsulateKey takes a public-key handle and a template . This HSM accepts m (32 bytes) as an optional test input, the CKM_ML_KEM mechanism parameter

chunks.title: ACVP Lab Workflow: From Vector Set to Evidence — AcvpLabIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: ACVP Lab Workflow: From Vector Set to Evidence
Component: AcvpLabIntroduction

Executed on both engines in the Playground suite and in Step 3: c and k are byte-compared with NIST’s, and each result is labelled “test input supplied (outside the standard)”. Step 3 first checks that the engine really uses the supplied m (the same m twice gives the same output, a different m a different ciphertext); if not, nothing is answered
None: in the PKCS#11 v3.2 text read for this module the ML-KEM mechanism covers ML-KEM.Encaps and ML-KEM.Decaps , and the FIPS 203 §7.2/§7.3 input checks have no operation of their own
Executed in Step 3 from what these engines do when the key is imported (PKCS#11 itself does not require a key check at import; these engines run one): accepted means valid, refused with exactly CKR_ATTRIBUTE_VALUE_INVALID means invalid, and any other result is an error, never a guess. evidence.json keeps the return code for every key
CKM_ML_DSA (ML-DSA.Verify) or CKM_HASH_ML_DSA_<hash>, context in CK_SIGN_ADDITIONAL_CONTEXT
Executed. SHA2-512/224 and SHA2-512/256 have no CKM_HASH_ML_DSA_<hash> mechanism ; the generic CKM_HASH_ML_DSA takes them as its hash (CKM_SHA512_224 / CKM_SHA512_256) with the caller computing PH(M). Step 3 runs these through that route too, labelled “computed outside the engine”
CKM_ML_DSA implements FIPS 204 Algorithms 2 and 3 on the message M , but the internal interface only ever signs μ = SHAKE256(tr ‖ M′, 64) . The harness computes μ from the public key and M′ and uses the external-μ mechanism below — no extension

chunks.title: ACVP Lab Workflow: From Vector Set to Evidence — AcvpLabIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: ACVP Lab Workflow: From Vector Set to Evidence
Component: AcvpLabIntroduction

Playground suite: executed on both engines (sigGen byte-match and sigVer). Step 3 runs the sigVer groups the same way, labelled “computed outside the engine”
No PKCS#11 v3.2 mechanism. The Hub’s engines use a non-standard mechanism code, 0x403c, for it; FIPS 204 allows μ to be computed in a different module
Executed (Playground suite and ACVP-format prototype) where an engine advertises 0x403c, labelled vendor-defined in evidence.json
Import sk, sign with hedgeVariant CKH_DETERMINISTIC_REQUIRED
Byte-comparable with NIST’s deterministic sigGen sample (Playground suite)
Standard PKCS#11 has no field for rnd: CKH_HEDGE_REQUIRED demands hedging but offers no input for it . This HSM accepts rnd as an optional test input in an extended signing structure: the standard CK_SIGN_ADDITIONAL_CONTEXT fields, then pRandom, ulRandomLen and messageEncoding
Playground suite: byte-comparable with NIST’s hedged sigGen, labelled “test input supplied (outside the standard)”
SLH-DSA sigGen hedged, and sign / verify on the internal interface
Standard PKCS#11 has no field for addrnd and no internal-interface mechanism . This HSM accepts addrnd and messageEncoding = internal (slh_sign_internal / slh_verify_internal) in the same extended structure
Playground suite: executed on both engines, labelled “test input supplied (outside the standard)”
Standard CKM_ECDSA takes no parameter and draws k itself . This HSM accepts k as the optional CKM_ECDSA parameter

chunks.title: ACVP Lab Workflow: From Vector Set to Evidence — AcvpLabIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: ACVP Lab Workflow: From Vector Set to Evidence
Component: AcvpLabIntroduction

Playground suite: r ‖ s byte-compared with NIST’s, labelled “test input supplied (outside the standard)”
CKM_ML_DSA_KEY_PAIR_GEN with the seed ξ supplied as CKA_SEED. The specification lists CKA_SEED among the attributes the mechanism contributes, so accepting a caller’s seed is engine behaviour, not a PKCS#11 requirement
Byte-comparable public key (Playground suite), engine-specific path
Standard PKCS#11 has no field for the random value an operation draws (ML-KEM m, ML-DSA rnd, SLH-DSA addrnd, ECDSA k) or for the SLH-DSA internal interface. This HSM accepts each as an optional test input: left out, the HSM draws the value itself exactly as the standard says, so a caller using only standard PKCS#11 sees no difference.
FIPS 203, 204 and 205 reserve these internal interfaces for testing; outside testing the module must generate the random values itself . A validated module would keep such inputs out of its approved mode. ML-DSA’s internal interface needs no input of this kind: it goes through the external-μ mechanism with a μ the harness computes. A known ECDSA k recovers the private key from one signature, which is why FIPS 186-5 requires k to be protected from disclosure and no real module should accept one outside testing .

chunks.title: ACVP Lab Workflow: From Vector Set to Evidence — AcvpLabIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: ACVP Lab Workflow: From Vector Set to Evidence
Component: AcvpLabIntroduction

For every test case the Hub’s dispatcher produces exactly one of: an answer (e.g. CKR_OK → testPassed: true; CKR_SIGNATURE_INVALID or CKR_SIGNATURE_LEN_RANGE → false), an unsupported record with the reason, or an error (any other return value, which produces no response entry). Unsupported is never counted as a pass, and an API failure is never reported as “signature invalid”.
ACVP builds negative cases into the vector sets. An implementation that answers “valid” to everything fails them:
ML-DSA sigVer: the server modifies a valid signature — modified message, modified commitment, modified z, modified hint — and includes at least 3 tests per modification type .
SLH-DSA sigVer adds modified R, SIGFORS and SIG HT, and signatures that are too long or too short .
ML-KEM VAL: modified ciphertexts must go through implicit rejection and still return a key; invalid encapsulation and decapsulation keys must be detected .
We deliberately give the module a bad signature. If it rejects that signature, the test passes—the module did its job correctly.
A failed internal self-test means something different: the module checked its own cryptographic implementation and that check failed. This does not prove it correctly examined our bad signature.
Therefore, our test must check why the operation failed—not treat every error as a correct rejection.

chunks.title: ACVP Lab Workflow: From Vector Set to Evidence — AcvpLabIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: ACVP Lab Workflow: From Vector Set to Evidence
Component: AcvpLabIntroduction

You are testing a cryptographic implementation’s ML-KEM decapsulation operation: the step that uses the recipient’s private key and the received ciphertext to recover a shared secret. This ACVP test supplies a ciphertext of the correct length that triggers the algorithm’s internal rejection check, with otherwise valid inputs. The expected result is the fallback shared secret prescribed by FIPS 203—not an error and not an arbitrary random secret. The test passes only if the returned secret exactly matches the expected value. This test checks ML-KEM itself; it does not need to encrypt or decrypt application data. A wrong-length ciphertext is a separate input-error case .
Try it. Run the ML-KEM tests in the ACVP suite and compare two results. The row “PKCS#11 boundary · product-authored probe · C_DecapsulateKey with a … (1 short)” gives a ciphertext of the wrong length; the correct result is an input error. A row “Decapsulate · NIST encapDecap VAL … · modified ciphertext → implicit rejection k” gives a correct-length ciphertext that was altered; the correct result is success, with the returned secret equal to NIST’s expected fallback value. Both outcomes are correct: the first input breaks the rules before decapsulation starts, the second passes those checks and is handled by implicit rejection inside the algorithm.

chunks.title: ACVP Lab Workflow: From Vector Set to Evidence — AcvpLabIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: ACVP Lab Workflow: From Vector Set to Evidence
Component: AcvpLabIntroduction

Two kinds of negative testing sit outside ACVP. Requirements ACVP does not test — the sub-specifications list zeroization, DRBG strength and incorrect-length keys and signatures for ML-DSA (the ML-KEM sub-specification repeats the ML-DSA list, a copy error, as it names signatures ). And API behaviour: wrong key type, wrong state, short buffers and other PKCS#11 return codes, which OASIS profile cases and product probes exercise .
Vocabulary the Hub holds itself to: one happy-path case is “sampled”, never “covered”; positive, negative, boundary and error-path coverage are reported separately, so a passing round-trip can never turn a negative-coverage cell green.
The Hub gives every result exactly one of eight evidence classes, each with the only claim a passing result of that class may make . The classes are the Hub’s policy, not a NIST taxonomy:
Public wording stays on the highest rung actually reached. Passing rung 6 does not imply rungs 7–9 .
A result is publishable only with its tested scope attached: algorithm and revision, operation, parameters, positive or negative expectation, vector source with an immutable hash (or oracle name and version), engine and build identity, runner and test ID, actual and expected result, timestamp and known limitations.

chunks.title: ACVP Lab Workflow: From Vector Set to Evidence — AcvpLabIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: ACVP Lab Workflow: From Vector Set to Evidence
Component: AcvpLabIntroduction

The Hub’s public NIST fixtures are pinned by ACVP-Server commit and SHA-256 . Its ACVP-format prototype calls a prompt a public reference sample only when the prompt’s SHA-256 matches one of those pins; any other prompt is recorded as an unverified imported vector set. When a vector is transformed — for example a sigGen output reused as a positive sigVer case — both the upstream and the local operation are recorded.
Running the same case on two implementations or two platforms is valuable — a disagreement is always a finding. Agreement is weaker than it looks:
Shared layers. In the Hub’s ACVP-format prototype, the C++ and Rust engines are driven by one dispatcher and one response builder. A defect in that shared code makes both engines agree and both be wrong, so dual-engine agreement is differential evidence, not independent validation. External expected values — a NIST sample, a published KAT — are what break the tie.
Byte vs semantic equivalence. Hedged signatures differ on every run by design ; the comparison policy must be declared per operation.
Environment identity. ACVP binds testing to an operational environment — “the specific hardware and/or software the client’s cryptographic implementation uses to run” — and certification associates the module with its OE . A result from WebAssembly in a browser says nothing about a native build, a different CPU, or a hardware accelerator until that target runs the same cases and records its own identity.

chunks.title: ACVP Lab Workflow: From Vector Set to Evidence — AcvpLabIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: ACVP Lab Workflow: From Vector Set to Evidence
Component: AcvpLabIntroduction

Confirm the execution path. An “acceleration enabled” setting does not prove that a test used the accelerator. A library may choose different implementations for different operations, or fall back to software. To claim hardware-path coverage, retain evidence showing which implementation handled the tested operation—for example, an implementation-specific execution trace or counter. If that evidence is unavailable, say that the execution path was not confirmed.
Honest statuses. Cross-target reports keep pass, fail, unsupported, not run and not comparable apart; the last three never add up to a pass.
The Hub accepts a new expected-value vector only with its provenance. Every vector file under src/data/acvp/ must have an entry in the vector manifest, and the gate fails until it does. The manifest’s own header documents the procedure:
Generate a skeleton entry with the maintainers’ vector-manifest tool — it records the file’s SHA-256 and one case record per test case.
Fill every TODO: the evidence class; the source (for NIST ACVP-Server material the commit, upstream path, retrieval date and upstream SHA-256); each case’s operation, parameters and positive/negative expectation; and a lineage record for any subset, rename or change of operation.
The maintainers then run the vector-manifest check and regenerate the validation counts.
The source is primary and immutable (a commit, a published document revision).
A licence or redistribution note exists for the copied values.

chunks.title: ACVP Lab Workflow: From Vector Set to Evidence — AcvpLabIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: ACVP Lab Workflow: From Vector Set to Evidence
Component: AcvpLabIntroduction

The expected behaviour is stated, including every negative case.
The Hub’s evidence policy asks for two reviewers — one verifies the source, a different one reviews the implementation — and the author is not the only reviewer.
Nothing issued to a real ACVTS session is committed: issued vector sets may be controlled laboratory data and are processed locally only.
Propose the test with the validation contribution issue template : it asks for the algorithm and parameters, the immutable source, the licence note and the expected behaviour, which is what a reviewer checks above.
Not a coder? Open a Data Suggestion issue with the source URL and the exact case, and the maintainer does the manifest work.
Classify evidence, dissect a public NIST vector set, and produce a response artifact.
The registration lists each algorithm / mode / revision and the options the implementation supports. The server answers with a test session and one vector-set URL per algorithm.
The prompt (the spec also calls it the request) holds test groups (tgId) of test cases (tcId). Exactly one prompt exists per vector set.
The client returns the implementation’s output for every test case, linked to the prompt by vsId.
The server reports a disposition for the vector set and for each test case: passed, fail, incomplete, expired, missing or unreceived. “error” applies to the vector set only, not to individual test cases.

chunks.title: ACVP Lab Workflow: From Vector Set to Evidence — AcvpLabIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: ACVP Lab Workflow: From Vector Set to Evidence
Component: AcvpLabIntroduction

Allowed only when the session is both publishable and passed. The request associates the module and its operational environment (OE) and lists any prerequisite validations.
The certification is a request; once approved it yields the identifier of the validation record.

chunks.title: ACVP Lab Workflow: From Vector Set to Evidence — index
chunks.content:
Module: ACVP Lab Workflow: From Vector Set to Evidence
Component: index

Classify ten test-log observations into the eight evidence classes and see the highest claim each one permits.
Open a public NIST ACVP-Server sample vector set and predict, group by group, what standard PKCS#11 calls can answer. Step 3 then shows what the engines’ test-only inputs add.
Generate response.json and evidence.json on a real engine, compare with NIST’s expected results, and audit the evidence.

chunks.title: ACVP Lab Workflow: From Vector Set to Evidence — EvidenceClassifier
chunks.content:
Module: ACVP Lab Workflow: From Vector Set to Evidence
Component: EvidenceClassifier

Each card is an observation from a test log. Pick the one evidence class it supports — or “Not test evidence” if nothing it describes compares an output with an expected value or behaviour. The answer shows the highest claim-ladder rung and the only wording the observation permits.

chunks.title: ACVP Lab Workflow: From Vector Set to Evidence — ResponseArtifactLab
chunks.content:
Module: ACVP Lab Workflow: From Vector Set to Evidence
Component: ResponseArtifactLab

Reload the module and confirm that browser WASM is enabled. You can still inspect the pinned vector-set structure in Step 2; do not report a response or disposition from this incomplete run.
Pick the vector set, then save its prompt.json exactly as NIST published it.
This is the Hub’s ACVP-format prototype itself — the same panel as in the Playground’s validation workbench . Import the file you saved, choose an engine, run it, then download both response.json and evidence.json. Answers that needed a test-only input, a value computed outside the engine, or what an engine does when a key is imported are counted and labelled separately.
Preflight: this step needs browser WASM and a successfully loaded C++ or Rust engine. Engine identity, prompt/response hashes and unsupported cases belong in evidence.json; loading the panel alone proves nothing.
Load the response.json you downloaded. It is compared, test case by test case, with the expectedResults.json NIST published for the same sample (the vector set chosen in A). This local check exists only because the sample is public: for a vector set issued to an ACVTS session, only the server holds the expected answers.

chunks.title: ACVP Lab Workflow: From Vector Set to Evidence — ResponseArtifactLab
chunks.content:
Module: ACVP Lab Workflow: From Vector Set to Evidence
Component: ResponseArtifactLab

The evidence sidecar is separate from the protocol response: it identifies the prompt and response by SHA-256 only, names the engine, and lists every unsupported case with its reason. Load yours to see the fields a reviewer reads first.
response.json is the answer sheet: only the answers, in the format ACVP defines. The evidence file is the receipt that lets a reviewer ask four questions: what was run, on which engine build, how was each answer obtained, and what was left out. It holds no vector data: no keys, messages, signatures or secrets, only fingerprints (SHA-256) and return codes, so it can be shared.
The edition of the file layout (2: every answer made from the prompt’s own inputs; 3: also labels how each answer was obtained), and what the file is not: it is not a validation, not a verdict from the NIST server, and nothing is sent to NIST.
Whether the prompt is byte-identical to a published NIST sample (nist-acvp-reference-sample) or any other file (unverified-imported-vector-set).
Which code made the file (browser or command line) and the Hub version.
The SHA-256 of the prompt file, where the sample comes from (NIST repository and exact commit), the algorithm, mode and revision, and the pinned specification and schema files the prompt was checked against.
The SHA-256 of response.json. It ties the two files together, so neither can be swapped without the mismatch showing.

How many tests were answered, unsupported and in error. A version 3 file also counts the answers by how they were obtained: from the prompt’s own inputs alone, with NIST’s random value as a test-only input, with a value computed outside the engine, or from the result of importing a key.
One entry per test: its outcome, the mechanism used and whether that mechanism is standard, vendor-defined or relying on a PKCS#11 v3.3 working-draft allowance, how the value was obtained, and the engine’s return code (for a rejected key, the exact code that made it invalid).
Every non-standard mechanism the run used, with its code and source.
What was left out of response.json and why. Nothing is guessed or defaulted to fill a gap.
For a public sample only: how many answers match NIST’s published expected results, and how many differ or are missing. For a prompt issued to a laboratory the expected answers are not supplied: the ACVTS server holds them. A file made in the browser carries no NIST comparison; step C shows the match count instead.

chunks.title: ACVP Lab Workflow: From Vector Set to Evidence — conceptChecks (data)
chunks.content:
Module: ACVP Lab Workflow: From Vector Set to Evidence
Data: conceptChecks

A vendor’s ML-KEM implementation has a CAVP algorithm validation. What does that establish about the cryptographic module that contains it?
CAVP tests algorithm implementations; CMVP validates modules against FIPS 140-3, whose security requirements span eleven areas at four levels. CAVP describes algorithm validation as a prerequisite of module validation, and the CMVP Management Manual requires the lab to confirm algorithm “shall” statements that CAVP testing does not cover.
Every vector set in your ACVTS Demo test session comes back “passed”. What can you now say publicly?
NIST describes Demo as a semi-volatile sandbox for testing implementations and ACVP clients, and Prod as restricted to accredited CST and 17ACVT laboratories and the only way to create algorithm validation certificates.
Why can an application that talks to a token only through PKCS#11 v3.2 C_EncapsulateKey not answer an ML-KEM encapDecap AFT test group?
The ML-KEM sub-specification says the encapDecap AFT tests Algorithm 17 ML-KEM.Encaps_internal(ek, m) with a server-generated m. FIPS 203 keeps that interface for testing only and requires the module to generate the random seeds; the PKCS#11 v3.2 C_EncapsulateKey signature has no input for m. (The Hub’s HSM accepts m as an optional test input outside the standard — something a validated module would keep out of its approved mode.)
An ML-KEM VAL decapsulation test hands the implementation a modified ciphertext. What must the implementation return?
ML-KEM.Decaps_internal performs implicit rejection: on a re-encryption mismatch it returns a key derived from the secret rejection value z and the ciphertext. The ML-KEM sub-specification’s VAL decapsulation test expects k from either the valid path or the implicit-rejection path.
The C++ and Rust engines each sign the same message with the same ML-DSA key using the default (hedged) variant. The signatures differ. What is the right conclusion?
FIPS 204 makes hedged signing the default and uses rnd from an RBG; only the deterministic variant fixes rnd to 32 zero bytes. ACVP sigGen AFTs for non-deterministic signing therefore supply the randomness to the implementation.
The Hub’s two engines agree on 90 cases for which nobody supplied an expected value. Which statement may you publish?
Agreement between two implementations is cross-implementation-differential evidence and its permitted claim is exactly “C++ and Rust agree for this case”. Because both engines are driven by the same adapter code in the Hub, their agreement cannot rule out a common-mode defect.
A vector file you were given carries "isSample": false. Does that make it an ACVTS-issued vector set?
In the ACVP specification isSample is a test-session property that makes the server able to return expected results. It is not a provenance record — the Hub identifies its public samples by SHA-256 against a pinned ACVP-Server commit, not by any flag inside the file.
