In this module’s own test run, the Rust engine decapsulates every ML-KEM decapsulation test in the NIST ACVP-Server ML-KEM-encapDecap-FIPS203 sample prompt (usnistgov/ACVP-Server @ 975de31, SHA-256 pinned), and each shared secret k matches that commit’s expectedResults.json. This is the module’s own result, not a record published by NIST.
The expected values come from the public NIST ACVP-Server repository with an immutable source identity (commit + file hash). That is rung 6 — nothing was issued to an ACVTS session, so rungs 7–9 are not reached.
Calling this “ACVP validated”. A public sample is not an issued vector set and carries no verdict.
A lab downloads vector set vsId 1234567 from its ACVTS test session, runs the prompt through the module without changing it and uploads the response. The disposition has not been retrieved yet.
The prompt was issued to an authorized test session and executed unchanged, so the response is generated (rung 7). Acceptance (rung 8) needs the server disposition, and a validation record (rung 9) needs the certification step and NIST publication.
Reporting “submitted” as “passed”. The ACVP disposition for the vector set is still unknown.
An HMAC implementation reproduces, byte for byte, the expected output printed in a test-vector appendix of the RFC that specifies the construction.
Expected values printed in a cited standard or RFC are a published KAT (rung 5). They are not ACVP material, however authoritative the document is.
Labelling every NIST- or IETF-sourced vector “ACVP”. ACVP is one specific source, not a synonym for “official”.
The C++ engine decapsulates an ML-KEM-768 ciphertext that Node.js’s bundled OpenSSL 3.5.4 produced, and the shared secret equals the one OpenSSL returned.
The expected value came from a separately identified implementation with a recorded version. The permitted claim is “agrees with OpenSSL 3.5.4 for this case” — an oracle can itself be wrong, so this sits below a published KAT.
Dropping the oracle’s name and version, which makes the result impossible to reproduce or re-check.
Both Hub engines import the same ML-KEM decapsulation key, decapsulate the same ciphertext, and return identical shared secrets. No third party supplied an expected value.
Two implementations agree for the same inputs. The Hub’s C++ and Rust engines are driven by the same adapter and dispatch code, so their agreement is a consistency check, not the independent agreement of rung 4: a shared adapter bug would make both agree and both be wrong.
Treating “C++ and Rust agree” as correctness. Agreement is only as independent as the least-shared layer.
A freshly generated ML-DSA-87 key pair signs a message and the same engine verifies the signature (CKR_OK).
Output produced by an implementation is consumed by the same implementation. A signer and verifier that share a bug can agree with each other; the permitted claim is “completes this round-trip” with no external correctness claim.
Counting a round-trip as a KAT.

chunks.title: Aerospace PQC — AerospaceExercises
chunks.content:
Module: Aerospace PQC
Component: AerospaceExercises

Work through these scenarios to explore avionics protocol constraints, satellite link budgets, certification costs, fleet interoperability, export controls, and mission lifecycle planning. Each exercise pre-configures the Workshop — click "Load & Run" to begin.
Take the PQC quiz to test what you've learned about aerospace and space PQC challenges and migration strategies.
1. ACARS Signature Overhead — Evaluate PQC feasibility for air-ground messaging
Select ACARS in the Avionics Protocol Impact Analyzer. Compare ML-DSA-65 and ML-DSA-44 signature sizes against the 220-byte ACARS block limit. Evaluate whether multi-block fragmentation is operationally acceptable.
ML-DSA-65 signatures (3,309 bytes) require 16 ACARS blocks per signed message, increasing VHF channel occupancy by 16x. ML-DSA-44 (2,420 bytes) requires 11 blocks. LMS (H10/W4) signatures (2,512 B per RFC 8554) require 12 blocks — still heavy but the most practical option.
2. GEO Satellite PQC Link Budget — Calculate handshake overhead for geostationary orbit
Configure a GEO satellite with Ka-band, 10 Mbps data rate. Compare ML-KEM-768 hybrid handshake latency against classical X25519 at 600 ms RTT. Set solar activity to maximum and observe SEU impact on key material.

chunks.title: Aerospace PQC — AerospaceExercises
chunks.content:
Module: Aerospace PQC
Component: AerospaceExercises

This tool sets the GEO round trip to 600 ms (GSMA PQ.07 gives about 500 ms for GEO round-trip latency), so a 3-round PQC handshake takes 1.8 seconds minimum. The tool assumes the SEU rate increases 10x at solar maximum, requiring key refresh every 4-8 hours instead of every 24 hours, which means 3-6x more handshakes per day, not a doubling.
3. Flight Management System Recertification — Estimate DO-178C cost for PQC upgrade
Select Flight Management System (FMS) at DAL-A in the Certification Impact Analyzer. Compare the clean-sheet vs retrofit certification timelines and costs.
For a DAL-A FMS the retrofit path comes out longer and costlier than clean-sheet, because PQC changes already-certified software instead of being designed in, and new decision logic must reach MC/DC structural coverage. The months, costs and MC/DC percentage are this tool\u2019s planning assumptions, not published DO-178C benchmarks: compare the paths, not the absolute figures.
4. Mixed-Fleet Gateway Strategy — Plan PQC interoperability across 3 aircraft generations
Build a fleet with a legacy B737-800 (ARINC 429), current A320neo (mixed 429/664), and next-gen A350 (ARINC 664 native). Evaluate the interoperability matrix and determine gateway placement.

chunks.title: Aerospace PQC — AerospaceExercises
chunks.content:
Module: Aerospace PQC
Component: AerospaceExercises

The B737-800 can only communicate via legacy ACARS (no PQC possible). The A320neo supports gateway-mediated PQC for AFDX-connected systems. Only the A350 can run native PQC. At 30% fleet PQC penetration, 70% of air-ground messages still traverse unprotected links.
5. Military UAV Export Classification — Navigate ITAR/EAR for a PQC-equipped UAV
Select UAV Flight Controller and classify it for export to (a) an AUKUS partner (Australia), (b) a NATO ally (Germany), and (c) a non-aligned nation (India). Compare license requirements and sovereign mandates.
AUKUS export is streamlined under bilateral agreement with no individual license. NATO ally requires a DSP-5 license under ITAR Category VIII. Non-aligned nation faces case-by-case review. Germany additionally mandates BSI evaluation of any imported PQC system for Bundeswehr use.
6. End-to-End Mission Lifecycle — Build a 15-year PQC migration plan for a GEO satellite
Configure a GEO communications satellite with 15-year service life. Set CRQC estimate to 2035. Generate a complete crypto lifecycle plan from design through decommission.
A GEO satellite launched in 2028 will operate until 2043 — 8 years past the 2035 CRQC estimate. All crypto must be PQC from launch day. Key provisioning occurs pre-launch only. The lifecycle plan shows crypto algorithm selection must happen in 2026-2027 (design phase) to meet the 2028 launch window.

chunks.title: Aerospace PQC — AerospaceIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Aerospace PQC
Component: AerospaceIntroduction

Aerospace is uniquely vulnerable to the quantum threat because its cryptographic systems must protect data across three segments with fundamentally different upgrade cadences — and because its equipment lifetimes span the entire PQC transition window. A 2025 CEAS Aeronautical Journal paper on post-quantum cryptography in avionics (Varner et al., “Agile, post-quantum secure cryptography in avionics”) states that long development times, certification delay and decades of operation make beginning the migration to post-quantum cryptography a particularly urgent need for avionics.
ATC centers, ground stations, airline ops. Standard TLS/IPsec stack. Patched in weeks. PQC migration via standard IT change management.
Avionics with RSA-2048 / ECDSA P-256 for nav database auth and SATCOM. Crypto libraries certified under DO-178C. Fleet-wide PQC rollout: 5–10 years.
Loadable software: ARINC 835-2 (information report, December 2025) gives guidance on securing loadable software parts with digital signatures and public key infrastructure.
Command/telemetry encrypted with AES + RSA/ECDH key exchange. Satellites cannot be physically accessed post-launch. Crypto must be provisioned pre-launch for 15–20 year GEO missions.

chunks.title: Aerospace PQC — AerospaceIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Aerospace PQC
Component: AerospaceIntroduction

Adversaries can intercept encrypted satellite command uplinks and telemetry downlinks today. With a future CRQC, they could decrypt command sequences and forge authenticated commands — potentially taking control of communications satellites, GPS constellations, or military reconnaissance platforms. A GEO satellite launched in 2028 with RSA-2048 key exchange will still be operating in 2043, which may be after a cryptographically relevant quantum computer exists.
Aviation communication protocols were designed with classical cryptography — or no cryptography at all. PQC signatures and key exchanges are 10–50x larger than their classical counterparts, creating fundamental compatibility problems:
Only ARINC 664/AFDX (modern Ethernet-based avionics bus in A350, B787) can accommodate PQC overhead. Legacy protocols require gateway-mediated PQC: a quantum-safe appliance terminates the legacy session and re-wraps traffic in ML-KEM -protected channels.
Algorithm selection matters enormously: LMS (H10/W4) signatures (2,512 B, RFC 8554) are 24% smaller than ML-DSA-65 (3,309 B): 2,512 ÷ 3,309 = 0.76. For bandwidth-constrained aviation links, hash-based stateful signatures may be the only viable PQC option — but they require secure monotonic counters to prevent state reuse.

chunks.title: Aerospace PQC — AerospaceIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Aerospace PQC
Component: AerospaceIntroduction

Aviation data links today: A 2024 research paper (Dowling and Wimalasiri, IACR ePrint 2024/046) says that at the time of writing all CPDLC communications run over unencrypted and unauthenticated data links. It proposes two quantum-secure hybrid key exchange protocols for aircraft-to-ground links (PQAG-KEM and PQAG-SIG) as a research proposal with an implementation, not a deployed standard. ACARS message security is specified in ARINC 823 Part 1, though the same paper says this approach is rarely adopted by any major airlines. Several research proposals secure CPDLC over LDACS, a newer aeronautical data link.
Satellite links: GSMA PQ.07 (Post Quantum Cryptography for Non-Terrestrial Networks, version 1.0, 4 February 2026) recommends starting the migration of legacy satellite systems with hybrid solutions that combine legacy and PQC keys. It says IPsec and DTLS tunnels for satellite IoT connections should integrate quantum-resistant key exchange such as ML-KEM, and advises watching CCSDS for PQC-related recommendations.
Space electronics face Single-Event Upsets (SEUs) — cosmic ray bit flips that can corrupt cryptographic key material in memory. This is a threat unique to aerospace with no parallel in terrestrial IT.

chunks.title: Aerospace PQC — AerospaceIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Aerospace PQC
Component: AerospaceIntroduction

A bit flip in an ML-DSA private key corrupts all subsequent signatures. A corrupted ML-KEM decapsulation key produces garbage shared secrets. Unlike classical ECDSA (where a bad signature simply fails verification), lattice-based algorithms can produce subtly wrong outputs that may pass basic checks.
Verification relies on SHA-256 hashes computed from public data, not stored private key material. If a signing key buffer is corrupted, the satellite switches to a backup key. Verification of past signatures is unaffected.
Keys are large structured matrices (public keys 1,312–2,592 bytes; private keys 2,560–4,896 bytes). A single bit flip changes the algebraic structure, producing valid-looking but cryptographically incorrect outputs. ECC memory helps but adds 12–25% overhead.
✓ = feasible, ○ = limited (smaller variants only), ✗ = infeasible. Ultra-constrained CubeSat processors (Vorago class) can only run hash-based signatures.
Adding a PQC library to certified avionics software is not a simple dependency update. It triggers a formal DO-178C recertification cycle whose cost scales with the Design Assurance Level (DAL):

chunks.title: Aerospace PQC — AerospaceIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Aerospace PQC
Component: AerospaceIntroduction

EASA’s AMC 20-42 (airworthiness information security risk assessment) recognises three EUROCAE/RTCA document pairs as acceptable means of compliance: ED-202A / DO-326A (Airworthiness Security Process Specification), ED-203A / DO-356 (Airworthiness Security Methods and Considerations) and ED-204 / DO-355 (Information Security Guidance for Continuing Airworthiness, which covers security after the product enters service). Compliance with the AMC is not mandatory: an applicant may use an alternative means of compliance that EASA accepts. The assessment it describes applies to new products and to changes to a product.
Clean-sheet vs. retrofit: A new aircraft program can design PQC in before its product is assessed. PQC added to a product already in service is a change to that product, and the AMC 20-42 assessment above applies to changes as well as to new products. This module gives no cost comparison of the two routes.
Unlike terrestrial IT where NIST-standardized PQC algorithms can be deployed globally, aerospace faces ITAR/EAR export controls that restrict which PQC implementations can be shipped to which countries:
USML Category XI: PQC-enhanced COMSEC modules, crypto key loaders, and military avionics firmware. Requires State Department license for every foreign transfer — even to NATO allies.
ECCN 5A002/5D002: PQC libraries in commercial avionics. License Exception ENC (15 CFR 740.17) covers most civil deployments, but requires BIS classification ruling for novel algorithms.

chunks.title: Aerospace PQC — AerospaceIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Aerospace PQC
Component: AerospaceIntroduction

Sovereignty mandates compound the problem: France (ANSSI) requires national crypto evaluation for military platforms. Germany (BSI) mandates independent validation. An aircraft manufacturer cannot ship a single global PQC firmware build — each destination may require different algorithm configurations, key management regimes, and compliance evidence.
The fundamental crypto challenge: aerospace equipment service lives (20–55 years) span the entire quantum transition. An aircraft delivered in 2025 with RSA-2048 may still be flying in 2055, which may be after a cryptographically relevant quantum computer exists.
Crypto agility in aerospace means planning for algorithm transitions that will happen during equipment service life. Satellites must launch with crypto-agile firmware that can switch algorithms via software-defined radio updates. Aircraft need LRU designs that allow crypto module replacement without re-certifying the entire avionics suite.
Mixed-fleet interoperability: ATC data links must simultaneously serve a 2005 E-175 (ACARS-only, no PQC) and a 2030 A350neo (full PQC). The solution is gateway-mediated PQC: ground-side appliances that bridge legacy sessions into quantum-safe channels, providing crypto protection even for aircraft that will never receive PQC firmware.
Satellite key management is the most extreme cryptographic challenge in aerospace: keys must be provisioned pre-launch and last the entire mission — 15+ years for GEO, with no physical access for rotation.

chunks.title: Aerospace PQC — AerospaceIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Aerospace PQC
Component: AerospaceIntroduction

PQC key pairs generated in ground HSMs and loaded into satellite crypto modules during integration. Multiple backup key sets provisioned for failover. Hash-based signature trees (LMS/XMSS) pre-computed with sufficient leaves for entire mission life.
Software-defined radios allow limited crypto firmware updates. But updating the key exchange algorithm (RSA → ML-KEM) on orbit risks bricking the satellite if the update fails. No rollback possible for hardware crypto.
HNDL timeline pressure (planning example): A satellite’s key exchange is chosen before launch, so the key exchange of a satellite launched in 2028 is fixed during its development. If its command uplinks are recorded now and must stay confidential until a cryptographically relevant quantum computer exists, a classical-only key exchange would not protect them. This module gives no figure for the length of a satellite development cycle; when algorithm selection has to happen depends on the mission.

chunks.title: Aerospace PQC — AerospaceIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Aerospace PQC
Component: AerospaceIntroduction

If the satellite link is part of a National Security System (NSS), NSA CNSA 2.0 applies (CNSA 2.0 FAQ, version 2.2). It replaces RSA and elliptic-curve algorithms with ML-KEM-1024 and ML-DSA-87 — not the ML-KEM-768 and ML-DSA-44/65 used in most examples in this module. CNSA 2.0 algorithms are required in all new NSS acquisitions from 1 January 2027; NSS equipment and services that cannot support them must be phased out by 31 December 2030 unless an exception is granted; and their use is mandated by 31 December 2031, unless otherwise noted.
For the implementation, the same FAQ says quantum-resistant algorithms should be implemented in NSS mission systems as NIAP-validated products, or in accordance with other implementation-specific guidance, and that this typically includes requiring cryptographic modules validated by the NIST Cryptographic Module Validation Program (CMVP).
The aerospace supply chain compounds this: crypto ASICs for military satellites must be fabricated at DMEA-accredited trusted foundries (12–18 month qualification). Counterfeit part detection (SAE AS6171) can leverage PQC-signed component authentication certificates for supply chain integrity.

chunks.title: Automotive PQC — AutomotivePQCExercises
chunks.content:
Module: Automotive PQC
Component: AutomotivePQCExercises

Work through these scenarios to explore zonal architecture crypto audits, sensor signing throughput, V2X channel load, safety-critical timing, OTA campaigns, car key protocols, and vehicle lifecycle planning. Each exercise pre-configures the Workshop — click "Load & Run" to begin.
Deepen your automotive PQC knowledge with these complementary modules.
1. Zonal Architecture Crypto Audit — Map quantum-vulnerable crypto across vehicle zones
Select an autonomous shuttle with zonal architecture in the Vehicle Architecture Mapper. Examine each zone's ECU count, bus protocol, and quantum-vulnerable crypto. Identify which zones need immediate PQC migration.
The ADAS zone runs 12+ ECUs on automotive Ethernet with ECDSA P-256 signing \u2014 highest quantum exposure. The body zone uses CAN 2.0 with AES-CMAC (symmetric, quantum-safe). Zonal architecture consolidates 40% fewer ECUs but concentrates crypto risk in zone controllers.
2. LiDAR Signing Throughput Challenge — Compare PQC signing speed for high-bandwidth sensors
Enable LiDAR (300 MB/s, 20 Hz) in the Sensor Data Integrity Simulator. Compare ML-DSA-44 vs FN-DSA-512 signing throughput. Determine whether per-frame signing meets the 50ms ADAS latency budget.

chunks.title: Automotive PQC — AutomotivePQCExercises
chunks.content:
Module: Automotive PQC
Component: AutomotivePQCExercises

The size trade is the one you can rely on: FN-DSA-512 signatures are 666 bytes against ML-DSA-44’s 2,420, which is what matters on CAN FD, while LiDAR on Ethernet can carry either. The speed trade runs the other way — ML-DSA-44 signs faster than FN-DSA-512 — but per-frame timings depend entirely on the target silicon and whether it has a hardware accelerator, so measure on YOUR ECU against your frame budget rather than trusting a figure from someone else’s board.
2b. V2X Channel Load — How many PQC-signed vehicles fit on one channel?
Scroll to the V2X Channel Load panel in the Sensor Data Integrity Simulator. At the default 100 vehicles, compare ECDSA P-256, FN-DSA-512 and ML-DSA-44 signatures against the 6 Mbps IEEE 802.11p default rate, then move the slider to find where each one fills the channel.
At 10 Hz BSMs, signature bytes alone fill 6 Mbps at about 1,171 vehicles for ECDSA P-256, about 112 for FN-DSA-512 and only about 30 for ML-DSA-44 — 100 vehicles with ML-DSA-44 is 19.36 Mbps. This is a model estimate that ignores the BSM payload, 1609.2 headers, certificate attachment and MAC/PHY/CSMA overhead, so a real channel congests sooner. The US has moved from DSRC to C-V2X (FCC ET Docket 19-138), but the capacity problem carries over.
3. ASIL-D Braking Crypto Verification — Validate PQC timing for safety-critical braking

chunks.title: Automotive PQC — AutomotivePQCExercises
chunks.content:
Module: Automotive PQC
Component: AutomotivePQCExercises

Select Electronic Braking (ASIL-D) in the Safety-Crypto Analyzer. Evaluate whether ML-DSA-44 verification meets the 10ms safety timing deadline. Compare fail-operational design patterns for PQC.
ML-DSA-44 verification (~0.3ms on automotive SoC) easily fits the 10ms budget. However, ASIL-D requires fail-operational mode: if the PQC path stalls, a classical ECDSA backup must maintain braking. This dual-path architecture adds complexity but is mandatory for safety certification.
4. Fleet OTA Campaign with PQC Signatures — Assess signature overhead for mass firmware updates
Configure a 1M-vehicle fleet in the OTA Orchestration Planner. Compare campaign completion time using ECDSA vs ML-DSA-65 firmware signatures. Evaluate the bandwidth impact of larger PQC signatures across the dependency graph.
ML-DSA-65 adds ~3.3 KB (3,309 B, FIPS 204) per signed firmware block (vs 72 bytes for ECDSA). For a 6-ECU campaign with 200 MB total firmware, PQC signature overhead adds <0.01% \u2014 negligible. The critical path is the ADAS ECU (45 min update, A/B partition) which gates all downstream ECUs.
5. NFC Car Key PQC Fragmentation — Analyze ML-KEM fragment behavior over NFC transports
Select NFC transport in the Car Key Protocol Explorer. Switch to PQC mode and observe how ML-KEM-768 public keys and ciphertexts fragment across NFC APDUs. Compare total transaction time vs BLE transport.

chunks.title: Automotive PQC — AutomotivePQCExercises
chunks.content:
Module: Automotive PQC
Component: AutomotivePQCExercises

NFC max APDU is 256 bytes. Exchanging the ML-KEM-768 public key (1,184 B) + ciphertext (1,088 B) requires 9+ APDUs for key agreement alone. Total PQC handshake on NFC takes ~800ms (vs ~120ms classical). BLE handles the same handshake in 1-2 L2CAP frames at ~200ms. UWB ranging is symmetric (quantum-safe).
6. 20-Year Vehicle CRQC Exposure — Plan crypto lifecycle for long-lived vehicles
Configure a 2027 model-year vehicle with 20-year road life in the Lifecycle Migration Roadmap. Set CRQC arrival to 2035. Examine the vulnerability window and planned OTA crypto upgrade windows.
A 2027 vehicle lasts until 2047 \u2014 12 years past the 2035 CRQC estimate. With OTA upgrades every 4 years, there are 5 crypto upgrade opportunities. The first PQC OTA should target 2031 (before CRQC) to protect long-lived root keys. Factory HSMs must dual-provision classical+PQC keys from day one.

chunks.title: Automotive PQC — AutomotivePQCIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Automotive PQC
Component: AutomotivePQCIntroduction

Modern vehicles are among the most complex distributed computing systems in production today. A premium vehicle contains 100–150 Electronic Control Units ( ECUs) communicating over multiple bus technologies; of these, 24–30 are security-relevant — the focus of PQC migration planning. The cryptographic requirements span from real-time safety-critical signing (brake-by-wire commands in <1 ms) to bulk data protection ( OTA firmware packages of several gigabytes).
V2X communication defined by IEEE 1609.2 adds an external attack surface: vehicles broadcast Basic Safety Messages (BSMs) 10 times per second, each signed with ECDSA P-256. A future CRQC could forge BSMs to cause phantom braking or mask real obstacles — a direct safety-of-life threat. Transitioning V2X to PQC signatures is complicated by the size of PQC signatures (2,420 bytes for ML-DSA-44) relative to the ~300-byte BSM payload, and the strict 100 ms end-to-end latency requirement.
The industry is simultaneously migrating from domain architecture (separate ECU clusters for powertrain, chassis, body, infotainment) to zonal architecture (zone controllers aggregating ECUs by physical location). This architectural shift creates a window of opportunity: zonal gateways become natural PQC enforcement points, concentrating cryptographic operations on fewer, more powerful processors.

chunks.title: Automotive PQC — AutomotivePQCIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Automotive PQC
Component: AutomotivePQCIntroduction

ECUs grouped by function: powertrain domain, chassis domain, body domain, infotainment domain. Each domain has a gateway ECU. Crypto is per-domain — 50–70 independent key stores across the vehicle. PQC migration requires touching every domain controller independently.
ECUs grouped by physical location (front-left, front-right, rear). 3–5 high- performance zone controllers run Automotive Ethernet (100BASE-T1 / 1000BASE-T1). Crypto consolidates to zone controllers — ideal for HSM-backed PQC.
In-vehicle bus protocols create hard constraints: CAN 2.0 frames are limited to 8 bytes of payload — impossibly small for any PQC signature. CAN FD extends this to 64 bytes, still insufficient for ML-DSA (3,309 bytes at security level 3). Both require application-layer fragmentation. Automotive Ethernet (1,500-byte MTU) can natively carry ML-KEM payloads (1,088 bytes) without fragmentation, but even Ethernet will require IP fragmentation for ML-DSA-44 or larger signatures.
L0–L2 Driver performs or supervises all driving. L2 controls steering + speed but driver must monitor at all times.
L3 Conditional: system drives in specific conditions (e.g., highway). Driver must respond to takeover requests (~10 s).
L4 High: system drives within a geofenced ODD. No human fallback required. L5 (all conditions) does not yet exist in production.
Higher autonomy levels increase quantum attack surface: more ECDSA-authenticated sensor paths, mandatory V2X, and no human fallback if signatures are forged by a CRQC.

chunks.title: Automotive PQC — AutomotivePQCIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Automotive PQC
Component: AutomotivePQCIntroduction

Autonomous driving systems (SAE Levels 3–5) rely on continuous sensor fusion — combining LiDAR point clouds, radar returns, camera frames, and ultrasonic readings into a unified environmental model updated 20–60 times per second. The integrity of this data pipeline is a safety-of-life concern: a tampered LiDAR stream could cause the vehicle to misidentify obstacles, while a forged HD map update could direct the vehicle onto a wrong route.
The Harvest Now, Decrypt Later (HNDL) threat is especially severe for autonomous driving datasets. Within the projected 10–20 year CRQC arrival window, training data collected today — including detailed 3D maps of military installations, government facilities, and critical infrastructure — could become decryptable. HD map providers (HERE, TomTom, Google) transmit map updates over TLS with ECDH key exchange; a CRQC could decrypt harvested map data exposing sensitive geospatial intelligence. Given OEM data retention of 5–10 years, vehicles shipped 2024–2030 face non-zero HNDL risk.
ML-DSA-44 adds sub-millisecond signing on accelerated silicon (measure your own); within budget
Offline verification; use ML-DSA-65 or SLH-DSA for integrity

chunks.title: Automotive PQC — AutomotivePQCIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Automotive PQC
Component: AutomotivePQCIntroduction

ML model provenance is an emerging concern: autonomous driving neural networks are updated via OTA with models trained on petabytes of driving data. Model signing with ML-DSA ensures that only OEM-authenticated models execute on vehicle hardware. Without PQC model signing, an adversary with a CRQC could forge model updates, replacing safety-critical perception models with adversarially compromised versions.
Autonomous vehicles continuously upload driving telemetry to cloud training pipelines. This data includes centimeter-accurate 3D scans of cities, military bases, and critical infrastructure. Adversaries harvesting this TLS-encrypted traffic today can decrypt it with a future CRQC, gaining a comprehensive geospatial intelligence dataset with no physical surveillance required.
ISO 26262 (Road vehicles — Functional safety) uses the Automotive Safety Integrity Levels (ASIL), and its Part 9 covers ASIL-oriented and safety-oriented analyses. In this module’s design reading, when cryptographic verification becomes part of a safety function — for example, authenticating a steering command or verifying a secure boot chain — the crypto library is treated as carrying the ASIL of that function. PQC algorithms have different timing characteristics than classical ECDSA, and these differences can affect whether a system meets the response deadlines of its safety function.

chunks.title: Automotive PQC — AutomotivePQCIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Automotive PQC
Component: AutomotivePQCIntroduction

The core tension is between fail-safe and fail-operational design. A fail-safe system (ASIL A/B) can enter a safe state when crypto verification fails or times out. A fail-operational system (ASIL C/D) must continue operating safely even during crypto failures — this requires redundant verification paths and strict worst-case timing guarantees that PQC algorithms must satisfy.
For ASIL C/D functions like steer-by-wire and brake-by-wire, PQC verification must complete within a single control loop iteration (typically 5–10 ms). Software-only ML-DSA verification on an automotive-grade ARM Cortex-A72 (2 GHz) takes approximately 2–4 ms; on a more constrained Cortex-R52 (400 MHz) expect 5–15 ms — potentially exceeding the timing budget. Hardware-accelerated PQC (via dedicated crypto coprocessors or FPGA fabric) can reduce this to <0.5 ms but adds BOM cost and silicon area.
Cross-reference the IoT & Embedded Device PQC module for constrained device algorithm selection mechanics, including the tradeoffs between ML-DSA, FN-DSA, and hash-based signatures in resource-limited environments.

chunks.title: Automotive PQC — AutomotivePQCIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Automotive PQC
Component: AutomotivePQCIntroduction

Automotive HSM deployments follow a tiered model: high-assurance HSMs protect the most sensitive keys (V2X root credentials, production signing keys), while lightweight secure elements handle per-ECU operations. Each tier has different PQC readiness — top-tier factory HSMs from established vendors are adding ML-DSA and ML-KEM support first, while constrained SHE (Secure Hardware Extension) modules may never support lattice-based PQC natively.
The vehicle’s cryptographic lifecycle spans three distinct phases, each with different HSM roles and PQC requirements. At production, keys are injected under controlled factory conditions. During road life, HSMs perform millions of real-time signing operations. At end-of-life, all key material must be securely destroyed to prevent harvest-after-disposal attacks.
Rack-mounted HSMs in production plants. Generate and inject root keys into every vehicle. Sign firmware images and V2X enrollment certificates.
Vendors: Thales Luna, Utimaco SecurityServer, Entrust nShield
EU C-ITS Certificate Policy 3.0: Common Criteria, EAL4 or higher (SOG-IS). It does not name FIPS 140
Backend HSMs in the Security Credential Management System. Issue pseudonym certificates, manage butterfly key expansion, and run misbehavior detection. On the vehicle side, the V2X HSM protection profile BSI-CC-PP-0114 (EAL4 augmented with AVA_VAN.4) specifies ECC operations (ECDSA, ECIES) and no post-quantum algorithm.

chunks.title: Automotive PQC — AutomotivePQCIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Automotive PQC
Component: AutomotivePQCIntroduction

chunks.title: Automotive PQC — AutomotivePQCIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Automotive PQC
Component: AutomotivePQCIntroduction

A vehicle sold in 2026 will be on the road until 2041–2046. During that 15– 20 year lifespan, the cryptographic landscape will transform multiple times: post-quantum algorithms will mature, new attacks may weaken initial PQC standards, and hybrid modes will eventually be deprecated in favor of pure PQC. The vehicle’s crypto stack must survive 3–4 complete algorithm generations — a challenge no other consumer product faces.
Crypto agility in automotive requires abstraction at every layer. The AUTOSAR Adaptive Platform provides a Crypto Service Manager (CSM) that decouples application code from specific algorithm implementations. When a new PQC algorithm is standardized or an existing one is deprecated, only the CSM driver needs updating — application ECUs receive the change transparently via OTA updates.
The CRQC vulnerability window concept is critical for automotive planning. If a vehicle’s data has a secrecy requirement of S years, and a CRQC is expected in Q years, then PQC migration must complete within Q − S years. For a vehicle with 20-year data confidentiality requirements and a 10-year CRQC horizon, PQC migration needed to start 10 years ago — illustrating the urgency. Even optimistic CRQC timelines (15–20 years) leave zero margin for vehicles entering production today.

chunks.title: Automotive PQC — AutomotivePQCIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Automotive PQC
Component: AutomotivePQCIntroduction

AUTOSAR Adaptive Platform R23-11 includes the Crypto Service Manager (ara::crypto) which supports algorithm-agnostic key management. AUTOSAR Classic (used in most ECUs) can map its crypto stack onto the SHE (Secure Hardware Extensions) interface, which on SHE-only ECUs has a fixed AES-128 algorithm set with no asymmetric or PQC support. The Classic R23-11 Crypto Driver specification itself defines ECC and RSA algorithm families but no post-quantum family. The Classic-to-Adaptive migration is itself a multi-year effort that must be coordinated with PQC adoption.
Connected vehicles generate 25–40 GB of data per hour, including GPS traces, driving behavior, cabin occupancy, voice commands, and biometric data from driver monitoring systems. This data flows from the vehicle’s Telematics Control Unit (TCU) to OEM cloud backends over LTE/5G connections protected by classical TLS. Under GDPR Article 25 (Data Protection by Design), OEMs must implement cryptographic protections that remain effective for the entire data retention period — which may extend well into the CRQC era.

chunks.title: Automotive PQC — AutomotivePQCIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Automotive PQC
Component: AutomotivePQCIntroduction

V2X pseudonym certificates are the automotive industry’s primary privacy mechanism. IEEE 1609.2 mandates that vehicles rotate through pools of short-lived pseudonym certificates (typically 20–40 active at once) to prevent long-term The butterfly key expansion protocol generates pseudonym keys from a single seed, allowing the SCMS to issue thousands of certificates without knowing the private keys. Transitioning butterfly key expansion from ECDSA to PQC requires careful redesign: ML-DSA public keys are over 20x larger (1,312 bytes vs 64 bytes), and the expansion protocol must be adapted for lattice-based algebra.
GDPR’s right to erasure (Article 17) creates a unique tension with cryptographic audit trails. Immutable logs of V2X certificate issuance and revocation cannot be erased without breaking the chain of trust. The emerging solution is crypto-shredding: encrypting audit entries with per-user keys that can be securely destroyed, making the data unrecoverable without technically deleting the log entries. PQC must be applied to these encryption keys to prevent future quantum decryption of supposedly erased data.
“Quantum Exposure” reflects both retention period and adversarial value. Location data + driving behavior enables complete movement profiling; combined with EV charging records, it reveals home/work patterns with high confidence.

chunks.title: Automotive PQC — AutomotivePQCIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Automotive PQC
Component: AutomotivePQCIntroduction

Vehicles are becoming payment terminals. ISO 15118 Plug & Charge enables automatic authentication between electric vehicles and charging stations using X.509 certificates exchanged over a TLS session. The vehicle presents its contract certificate (issued by the eMobility Service Provider), the charging station verifies it against the Charging Point Operator’s (CPO) trust chain, and charging begins — no RFID card, no app, no user interaction. This entire flow depends on classical RSA/ECDSA certificates that a CRQC would break.
A related demonstration concerns OCPP. A talk abstract at the PKI Consortium PQC Conference 2025 (Kuala Lumpur) reports that TNO, NXP and Infiniot upgraded OCPP with hybrid quantum-safe cryptography (TLS handshake and X.509 certificates) for electric vehicle charging infrastructure, tested on an NXP i.MX 8 board similar to those in real charging stations. The abstract names no algorithm, so treat it as a reported demonstration rather than an established standard.
Beyond EV charging, in-vehicle payment use cases are expanding rapidly: automated tolling (DSRC or GNSS-based), parking payment, fuel purchases, drive-through ordering, and infotainment content purchases. Each payment flow has its own certificate hierarchy and signature requirements, but all share the same quantum vulnerability: classical public-key signatures that authenticate payment authorization.

Validates contract certificate via OCSP/CRL. Authorizes energy delivery. Processes CDR (Charge Detail Record) for billing settlement. PQC upgrade: PQC-signed CDRs for non-repudiation over billing retention period (10+ years).
Cross-reference the EMV Payment PQC module for detailed coverage of payment network PQC migration (Visa, Mastercard, Amex), tokenization frameworks, and the role of FN-DSA-512 in constrained payment terminals.
ISO 15118 Plug & Charge PQC migration requires synchronized upgrades across the entire ecosystem: vehicle OEMs, charging station manufacturers, CPO backend systems, eMobility Service Providers, and the V2G root CA. Any single participant using classical-only certificates creates a weak link. The ISO 15118-20 revision process must include PQC algorithm profiles.

The Car Connectivity Consortium (CCC) Digital Key 3.0 specification enables smartphones and wearables to unlock and start vehicles using NFC, BLE, and UWB (Ultra-Wideband) transports. The protocol uses ECDH P-256 for key agreement and ECDSA P-256 for authentication — both quantum-vulnerable. A PQC migration of CCC Digital Key would reach every vehicle, phone and wearable that implements the standard.

chunks.title: Automotive PQC — AutomotivePQCIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Automotive PQC
Component: AutomotivePQCIntroduction

The NFC APDU fragmentation problem is the most acute PQC challenge for digital car keys. Short APDUs (Application Protocol Data Units) carry about 256 bytes. An ML-KEM-768 public key is 1,184 bytes, and the resulting ciphertext requires another 1,088 bytes. A car and phone that support only short APDUs need at least 5 exchanges for the key alone and at least 9 for the key and ciphertext together; APDUs with extended length fields (which ICAO Doc 9303-11 requires for large cryptographic objects) avoid the split where both sides support them. Each exchange adds ~50 ms of round-trip latency, potentially pushing the total NFC transaction time beyond the 500 ms user experience threshold that CCC requires for “tap and go” unlock. Solutions under investigation include extended-length APDUs (supported by some NFC controllers but not all smartphones), pre-cached key material, and hybrid protocols where NFC bootstraps a BLE connection for the PQC handshake.
Owner initiates share — OEM app generates a sharing invitation containing the vehicle’s public key and access policy (time window, geofence, feature restrictions).
Friend’s device enrolls — Friend’s phone generates an ephemeral key pair, signs an enrollment request, and sends it to the OEM key server. The server issues a time-limited digital key credential signed by the OEM CA.

chunks.title: Automotive PQC — AutomotivePQCIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Automotive PQC
Component: AutomotivePQCIntroduction

Vehicle verifies credential — On first NFC/BLE tap, the vehicle verifies the friend’s credential against the OEM CA chain and the owner’s access policy. All signatures must be PQC to prevent a CRQC from forging shared keys after the fact.
Revocation — Owner revokes access via the OEM app. Vehicle receives revocation update via OTA or at next cloud sync. PQC-signed revocation lists prevent forgery of “keep access” messages.
The automotive supply chain operates as a deep hierarchy: OEMs (BMW, Toyota, Volkswagen) set cryptographic requirements that cascade through Tier-1 suppliers (Bosch, Continental, Denso), who pass them to Tier-2 suppliers (specialized chip vendors, firmware houses), who may further subcontract to Tier-3 and beyond. PQC readiness at the OEM level is meaningless if a Tier-2 supplier ships an ECU with hardcoded RSA-2048 keys and no firmware update capability.
The regulatory backdrop is UNECE WP.29 R155 / R156: since July 2024 vehicle types need a valid Cyber Security Management System (CSMS) certificate under R155 (and a Software Update Management System certificate under R156). R155 section 7.3.8 requires cryptographic modules to follow consensus standards; it does not mention post-quantum cryptography.

TISAX (Trusted Information Security Assessment Exchange), managed by the VDA (Verband der Automobilindustrie), is the automotive industry’s standard information security assessment framework. TISAX assessment labels (AL 1–3) are required for suppliers handling confidential OEM data. As PQC becomes a regulatory requirement, TISAX assessment scope is expanding to include quantum-readiness criteria: cryptographic inventory documentation, PQC migration timelines, and evidence of crypto-agility in delivered components.
Defines PQC policy and algorithm requirements. Mandates hybrid mode for all new platforms from 2027+. Requires TISAX AL2+ with PQC addendum from all Tier-1 suppliers.
Implements PQC in ECU firmware and gateway modules. Provides crypto-agile hardware (HSM with PQC firmware update path). Cascades requirements to Tier-2 component vendors.
Delivers chips, secure elements, and firmware libraries. Must ensure hardware supports PQC key sizes and computation. Longest lead time (18–36 months for silicon respins).
Used in most automotive ECUs. The Crypto Stack (Csm + CryIf + Crypto Driver) can map onto SHE hardware: fixed AES-128 + CMAC, no asymmetric crypto on SHE-only ECUs. The R23-11 Crypto Driver specification itself defines ECDSA, ECDH and RSA algorithm families, so the Classic specification accommodates ECC, but it defines no post-quantum family. Secure boot on SHE-only ECUs uses AES-CMAC chains, not digital signatures.

A single Tier-3 supplier shipping a sensor ECU with non-upgradeable classical crypto creates a permanent vulnerability in every vehicle that ECU is installed in. OEMs must enforce PQC readiness requirements at every tier of the supply chain and require contractual guarantees of firmware-updateable cryptographic implementations. TISAX assessments must verify actual crypto-agility, not just policy documentation.

Model limits: only signature bytes are counted. The BSM payload, IEEE 1609.2 headers, the certificate or certificate digest attached to messages, and MAC/PHY/CSMA contention overhead are all ignored — so a real channel congests well below the point flagged here.
DSRC vs C-V2X: 6 Mbps is the 802.11p (DSRC / ITS-G5) default rate. In the US the FCC moved the 5.9 GHz ITS band from DSRC to C-V2X (ET Docket 19-138: 2020 order, finalized in the November 2024 order). C-V2X sidelink has a different PHY and capacity, but the conclusion carries over: kilobyte-scale PQC signatures on every 10 Hz safety message do not fit a shared broadcast channel, which is why designs look at compact signatures, attaching certificates less often, or symmetric and hybrid schemes.

chunks.title: Cryptography Bill of Materials (CBOM) — CbomIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Cryptography Bill of Materials (CBOM)
Component: CbomIntroduction

A Cryptography Bill of Materials (CBOM) is a machine-readable inventory of every cryptographic asset — algorithms, keys, certificates, protocols and their configurations — and how they relate to software components. It extends the SBOM: the SBOM lists your software, the CBOM lists the cryptography inside it.
In the migration lifecycle it is Phase 2: discovery (Phase 1) feeds the CBOM, and risk scoring (Phase 3) consumes it. A bare list of algorithms isn't enough — the value is a CBOM you can query and rank.
Start with a Minimum Viable CBOM: capture the fields you need to prioritise (algorithm, where it's used, what it protects, owner), not a perfect catalogue. Regulators are converging on the same expectation: the EU's NIS Cooperation Group roadmap (v1.1, 11 Jun 2025) sets an end-2026 milestone for Member States whose first steps include mature cryptographic asset management, saying they “should promote and support that useful cryptographic inventories are being created and maintained” and naming CBOM as a recommended format. It is guidance to Member States rather than a direct obligation on you — but it is what national rules will be built from.
Two BOM standards compete, with different stewards: CycloneDX (OWASP; standardized as ECMA-424, current spec v1.7) and SPDX (Linux Foundation; ISO/IEC 5962; v3.0.1).

chunks.title: Cryptography Bill of Materials (CBOM) — CbomIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Cryptography Bill of Materials (CBOM)
Component: CbomIntroduction

The decider for a CBOM: SPDX 3.0.1 has no dedicated cryptography object model yet, so CycloneDX is the practical choice today. CycloneDX 1.7 adds a Cryptography Registry (consistent algorithm-family and curve naming) built for PQC-readiness reviews.
The PKI Consortium CBOM-Profiles Working Group (launched 8 Jun 2026) is building a neutral methodology so a CBOM profile maps onto both formats — the format-neutral future.
“Ghost” crypto is every cryptographic use that isn't in any inventory — shadow-IT services, forgotten-but-live certs, hardcoded algorithms, embedded/OT crypto, default library crypto. A CBOM built only from known systems is falsely reassuring. You can't migrate what you can't find.
Reuse before you deploy. A new agent rollout is usually the real blocker. Pull from tools you already run as discovery sources — Qualys / Tenable / Rapid7 and on-host agents (which surface TLS endpoints, ciphers and certs), Venafi / Keyfactor / DigiCert for certificates — and scan net-new only where you are blind.
No single method finds it all — layer five: source code (sonar-cryptography / CBOMkit, IBM Quantum Safe Explorer), binary / container (CBOMkit-theia), network / traffic (passive handshake capture + active scanning), infrastructure / runtime (HSM/KMS, CLM, CT logs), and cloud (KMS/cert APIs + CSPM — no host to scan, provider-managed crypto, shared responsibility). Coverage = the union.

chunks.title: Cryptography Bill of Materials (CBOM) — CbomIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Cryptography Bill of Materials (CBOM)
Component: CbomIntroduction

Framework v2.1 Activity 1.3 defines 13 mandatory fields per cryptographic instance. Recording them consistently is what turns a raw discovery export into a queryable, risk-rankable backlog that Phase 3 can score and Phase 4 can sequence.
Minimum Viable CBOM shortcut: if full capture is too slow, start with Algorithm + Key Size + Owner + Control Posture. Those four fields alone let you produce a prioritized remediation queue and unblock Phase 3 scoring for your highest-risk systems.
Discovery finds artifacts; risk needs context. Attach to each key what it protects (+ confidentiality horizon = the HNDL input), its purpose (Track A vs B), location, owner, vendor-dependency, and active-vs-dormant. That enrichment turns an inventory into a risk-rankable backlog.
Two kinds of identifier. Assigned ids are local and don't correlate (PKCS#11 CKA_ID, KMIP Unique Identifier, KMS key-id, JWK kid). Content-derived ids do: the X.509 SKI / SPKI hash, KMIP Digest, JWK Thumbprint (RFC 7638), KCV for symmetric keys. Correlate “same key across HSM / cert / code / wire” on the SPKI fingerprint.
Attestation proves a key's origin (generated in hardware, non-exportable) — HSM/TPM attestation, Android Key Attestation, FIDO2/WebAuthn; for PQC, attest generation in a FIPS 140-3-validated module. And record where the key is managed — software (exportable, sprawl-prone), HSM (non-exportable, attestable), or cloud KMS (API-mediated, envelope encryption) — it drives risk and migration feasibility.

chunks.title: Cryptography Bill of Materials (CBOM) — CbomIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Cryptography Bill of Materials (CBOM)
Component: CbomIntroduction

One mechanism has many names. ECDSA-P256-SHA256 is CKM_ECDSA_SHA256 to an HSM, OID 1.2.840.10045.4.3.2 to a certificate, ES256 to a JWT, and 0x0403 to TLS 1.3 — and the curve alone is P-256 = secp256r1 = prime256v1. Six codification layers (spec, OID, protocol code point, key-mgmt enum, library string, CBOM) with no shared key.
PQC makes it worse. Each parameter set is its own algorithm: ML-DSA chose one OID per parameter set, parameters absent (id-ml-dsa-44/65/87, RFC 9881), so OIDs proliferate. Hybrid KEMs (X25519MLKEM768) and composite signatures each get their own identifier — combination × nomenclature.
The answer is to map every source onto a canonical model (the CycloneDX Cryptography Registry) while never over-collapsing security-relevant parameters (mode, padding, curve, hash). The PKIC CBOM-Profiles WG is the neutral venue maintaining this as registries keep moving.
For the full family/curve reference and a hands-on normalizer, see the dedicated CycloneDX Cryptography Registry module.
Machine-verifiable in practice = policy-as-code. CBOMkit runs an OPA/Rego check classifying each asset quantum-safe / quantum-vulnerable / na / unknown, queryable over a REST API. Normalized names (above) are what make the rules match reliably.
Secure the CBOM. The CBOM plus the risk backlog is a map of your weakest cryptography — an attacker's shopping list. Protect it with access control and integrity, the way you would any sensitive asset inventory.

Module: Common Criteria, EUCC & eIDAS Certification
Component: CcEuSections

Common Criteria (CC) is a framework for writing down security claims about an IT product and having an accredited laboratory check them. The criteria are published by the Common Criteria Recognition Arrangement (CCRA) participants as CC:2022, and by ISO/IEC as ISO/IEC 15408:2022. The evaluator follows the Common Evaluation Methodology, CEM:2022 (ISO/IEC 18045:2022). A certification scheme — for example France’s ANSSI or Singapore’s CSA — oversees the laboratory and issues the certificate. The CCRA then decides which certificates its member countries accept from one another.
Under EUCC: in the EU, certificates are issued under the EUCC scheme, which adds its own rules on top of Common Criteria (see the EUCC path).
A current evaluation baseline is not the five CC:2022 R1 documents alone. The Common Criteria portal marks the applicable CC:2022 and CEM errata and interpretations as mandatory; this module was checked against the portal's v1.2 package on 16 October 2026. Record that errata version in the evaluation baseline and re-check it before starting or changing an evaluation.

chunks.title: Common Criteria, EUCC & eIDAS Certification — CcEuSections
chunks.content:
Module: Common Criteria, EUCC & eIDAS Certification
Component: CcEuSections

Does this defined Target of Evaluation (TOE) meet the security functional and assurance claims in its Security Target — possibly while conforming to a Protection Profile?
Common Criteria does not say what a product must do. The Security Target does. CC supplies the vocabulary for writing those claims and the method for checking them.
, , ], [ 'Security Assurance Requirements (SARs)', 'How much evidence and evaluator work backs the claims — classes ADV, AGD, ALC, ASE, ATE, AVA', , ], [ 'Packages, including the EALs', 'Predefined sets of requirements; EAL1–EAL7 are assurance packages', , ], [ 'Evaluation methods and activities', 'Product-class-specific tests; collaborative PPs (cPPs) define their own', , ], [ 'ITSEF, certification body (CB), ETR', 'The lab evaluates and writes the Evaluation Technical Report (not public); the CB reviews it and issues the certificate and a public certification report', 'The scheme’s rules', ], ]} />
The ST states the threats and objectives, the SFRs the TOE meets, the SARs it was evaluated against, and a TOE summary specification saying how each SFR is implemented. The evaluator works through the CEM work units for each SAR, using the developer’s evidence and their own testing. The certificate then says one narrow thing: this TOE, in this configuration, meets this ST at this assurance.
This certificate applies only to this specific version of the product in its evaluated configuration.

chunks.title: Common Criteria, EUCC & eIDAS Certification — CcEuSections
chunks.content:
Module: Common Criteria, EUCC & eIDAS Certification
Component: CcEuSections

CC has no list of approved algorithms. Cryptography appears as SFRs from class FCS — mainly
(cryptographic operation) — iterated once per algorithm or operation. A PP can constrain them. The EN 419221-5 HSM PP, for example, requires algorithms “approved for the identified purpose” and tells the ST author to consult the relevant national body. Schemes add their own rules: ANSSI, for example, analysed TrustWay Proteccio’s mechanisms against its own cryptographic guide. Under EUCC: the ECCG Agreed Cryptographic Mechanisms play this role (see the EUCC path).
iterations and the certification report. An assurance level never answers that question. A product can hold a high-assurance certificate for a version with no post-quantum algorithm at all — TrustWay Proteccio’s ST lists none .
For a worked example of how three post-quantum requirements could be written in a Security Target, see the section
An ST that claims a PP must meet it in the way the PP demands. Both PPs studied in this module require strict conformance: the ST may add to the PP’s requirements but may not weaken or omit any of them. Some PPs require exact conformance, where the ST must reproduce the PP’s requirements. CC:2022 Part 5 notes that an ST claiming exact conformance cannot augment its EAL at all.

chunks.title: Common Criteria, EUCC & eIDAS Certification — CcEuSections
chunks.content:
Module: Common Criteria, EUCC & eIDAS Certification
Component: CcEuSections

, , , , , ; Common Criteria portal mandatory CC:2022/CEM errata and interpretations v1.2; ; ANSSI certificate and report ANSSI-CC-2025/09 and CSA report CSA_CC_23004 (links in the Decode the certificate claim workshop step).
An Evaluation Assurance Level (EAL) is a predefined assurance package: a fixed set of assurance components from CC Part 3. The seven EALs are ordered — each contains more, or more rigorous, components than the one below. That is all an EAL measures: how much design evidence the developer provided and how hard the evaluator looked. It is not a rating of cryptographic strength, of resistance to quantum attack, or of whether a product is “more secure” than a product of another type.
An EAL is not a FIPS 140-3 security level, and there is no mapping between the two. FIPS 140-3 levels come from one fixed set of cryptographic-module requirements. EALs grade the assurance behind whatever SFRs an ST chooses to claim.
Notice that an EAL4 evaluation “augmented with AVA_VAN.5” reaches the same vulnerability component as EAL6 while keeping EAL4’s design and development evidence. HSM and chip PPs use exactly that pattern — which is why a component list, not the EAL number, tells you what was tested.
CC:2022 Part 5 describes EAL4 as “methodically designed, tested and reviewed”, and as the highest level at which it is likely to be economically feasible to retrofit an existing product line. Its components include:

chunks.title: Common Criteria, EUCC & eIDAS Certification — CcEuSections
chunks.content:
Module: Common Criteria, EUCC & eIDAS Certification
Component: CcEuSections

}> The notion of “augmentation” allows the addition of assurance components (from assurance families not already included in the EAL) or the substitution of assurance components (with another hierarchically higher assurance component in the same assurance family) to an EAL.
Listings shorten “EAL4 augmented” to “EAL4+”. The plus sign tells you something was added; it does not tell you what. The same headline can stand for one extra component or for five. A bare “EAL4+” is therefore incomplete — the claim only means something with its component list, as in “EAL4 augmented with ALC_DVS.2, ALC_FLR.2 and AVA_VAN.5”.
The AVA_VAN component matters most for devices that hold keys: it sets the attack potential the evaluator’s penetration testing assumes — Basic for AVA_VAN.1–2, Enhanced-Basic for .3, Moderate for .4 and High for .5. Under EUCC: the ‘substantial’ and ‘high’ assurance levels are defined by this component (see the EUCC path).
The TrustWay Proteccio network HSM holds ANSSI certificate ANSSI-CC-2025/09 (31 March 2025). One list shows it as “EAL4+”. The certificate says:
EAL4 augmented (ADV_IMP.2, ALC_CMC.5, ALC_DVS.2, ALC_FLR.3, AVA_VAN.5), conformant to the protection profile NF EN 419221-5:2018 … Within the CCRA, this certificate is recognised at the level EAL2 augmented with FLR.3.

Collaborative PPs (cPPs) replace the EAL ladder with evaluation activities written for one product class. A cPP evaluation can carry a nominal “EAL1 augmented with ALC_FLR.2 and ASE_SPD.1” and still involve demanding, class-specific testing. ASE_SPD.1 is an augmentation there only because EAL1 lacks the security problem definition that EAL2 and above include. Comparing that certificate with an HSM’s EAL4 augmented certificate tells you nothing about which product is “more secure”: they are different TOEs with different SFRs, PPs and environments.
the EAL and every augmentation component, e.g. EAL4 augmented with ALC_FLR.2 and AVA_VAN.5;
who recognises it (the CCRA or another arrangement) and at what level; for an EUCC certificate, also its EUCC assurance level.

Choose a PP or write a product-specific ST. A PP brings fixed threats, objectives and requirements; strict conformance lets you add but not weaken.
Write the security problem, objectives, SFRs and SARs. Cryptographic services become

Produce the evidence the SARs call for: architecture, functional specification, design, implementation representation, life-cycle and development-security documentation, tests and guidance.
The ITSEF evaluates: documentary checks, independent functional testing, vulnerability analysis and penetration testing at the AVA_VAN level claimed.
The certification body reviews the Evaluation Technical Report and issues the certificate and a public certification report.
Publication: the sanitised ST, certificate and report appear on the scheme’s site and the CC portal.
Life after certification: flaw remediation, vulnerability handling, and assurance continuity for every change — maintenance, re-evaluation or re-assessment.
Each scheme sets a validity period. The three real certificates in this path’s workshop all run five years: ANSSI’s report gives five years from the signature date, Singapore’s CSA gives a fixed end date, and the EUCC certificate follows EUCC’s own limit (see the EUCC path). Validity does not freeze the threat landscape — that is what re-assessment is for.
CC:2022 Release 1 (November 2022) replaced CC 3.1 Revision 5. The CCRA transition policy, (20 April 2023), sets the dates:

Module: Common Criteria, EUCC & eIDAS Certification
Component: CcEuSections

The same policy lets a CC:2022 certification reuse CC 3.1 R5 life-cycle (ALC) results and CC 3.1 R5 platform certificates in a composite evaluation. PP maintainers must move their PPs to CC:2022; new or updated PPs published after 30 June 2024 must use CC:2022. All three certificates in this path’s workshop use CC 3.1 R5. Under EUCC: a separate EUCC rule allows CC 3.1 R5 certificates until 31 December 2027 (see the EUCC path).
Under EUCC: in the EU, EUCC replaced the national schemes from 27 February 2025, and EUCC certificates carry the CCRA mark only through a separate process (see the EUCC path).
Under Common Criteria: Adding ML-KEM or ML-DSA to a certified product means new
iterations in the ST — a change to the claimed SFRs, which CCDB-015 lists as a typical major change. Expect the certification body to classify it as major and require a re-evaluation, and plan that re-evaluation on CC:2022. If your PP is still CC 3.1, the CCRA transition policy allows claiming it only until 31 December 2027.

chunks.title: Common Criteria, EUCC & eIDAS Certification — CcEuSections
chunks.content:
Module: Common Criteria, EUCC & eIDAS Certification
Component: CcEuSections

Under EUCC: The EUCC cryptography guidelines say evaluators should verify that protection profiles and products preferably rely on the agreed cryptographic mechanisms in the ECCG ACM (ACM v2), which lists post-quantum mechanisms; the ACM is a guideline rather than a legal list. CIR 2025/2462 defines minor and major changes, and the certification body decides which applies. An EUCC carve-out keeps older protection profiles (CC 3.1 revisions 1–4) usable where eIDAS, Decision 2016/650 or the tachograph rules require them, with no end date (see the EUCC path).
Assurance continuity is how a certified product changes without losing its certificate — or learns that it must be evaluated again. The CCRA minimum rules are in (29 February 2024). Schemes may add to them. Under EUCC: EUCC sets its own change rules in law (see the EUCC path).
The developer proposes; the certification body decides. CCDB-015 gives typical cases:
Typically minor: editorial changes; changes that do not affect the assurance evidence; a new product name in the ST front matter; development-environment changes shown to have no follow-on effect.
Typically major: changes to the claimed assurance requirements (except adding ALC_FLR); changes to confidentiality or integrity controls of the development environment; “changes to the set of claimed functional requirements”; and “a set of minor changes that together have a major impact upon the security”.

chunks.title: Common Criteria, EUCC & eIDAS Certification — CcEuSections
chunks.content:
Module: Common Criteria, EUCC & eIDAS Certification
Component: CcEuSections

A bug fix can be either, CCDB-015 notes, because its extent cannot be predicted. And a PP requiring exact conformance makes even an editorial change to the ST’s objectives major.
Optional history: why EN 419221-5 appears as both v0.15 and v1.0
In this example, ANSSI assessed a Protection Profile—the document describing requirements for a class of cryptographic modules—not a particular HSM product.
16 December 2016: ANSSI certified the draft Protection Profile, prEN 419221-5 v0.15, under reference ANSSI-CC-PP-2016/05.
18 May 2020: its maintenance report identified the published EN 419221-5:2018 E v1.0 as the maintained profile. The report describes standardisation edits, editorial fixes and replacing “must” with “shall”. ANSSI judged their impact minor.
The lesson: different version labels need an explanation, not an assumption that the documents are unrelated or interchangeable. Check the exact profile claimed and the maintenance report connecting the versions. The Hub quotes the public v0.15 text; it does not claim to have independently compared every line of the published CEN edition.
The limit: this report does not establish that adding PQC to an HSM is a minor change. It assesses changes to the requirements document, not new cryptographic code, services or security claims in a product. It also does not establish a product certificate’s current validity.

Assess those actual changes under the issuing scheme’s rules; the certification body determines the route. The editorial PP update above is not evidence that this product change qualifies for maintenance.
The European Common Criteria-based cybersecurity certification scheme (EUCC) is EU law adopted under the Cybersecurity Act (Regulation (EU) 2019/881). It says how CC evaluations are run and how certificates are issued under EUCC. It is not another name for Common Criteria, and its rules must not be applied indiscriminately to other CC certification schemes. The security requirements still come from a Security Target and, where claimed, a Protection Profile.
An EUCC evaluation is a Common Criteria evaluation run under EU law.

CIR 2025/2462 defines a minor change as one “that does not adversely impact the assurance expressed in the EUCC certificate”, and a major change as one that “may adversely impact” it. The holder sends an impact analysis report; the CB decides.
} > Where the changes have been confirmed by the certification body to be minor, no new certificate shall be issued for the modified ICT product … and a maintenance report to the initial certification report shall be established.
Minor → maintenance report, published by ENISA; the certificate stands. The CB may ask for a subset evaluation and partial ETR first.
Major → re-evaluation, reusing results that still apply → new ETR and, where applicable, a new certificate and certification report.
Re-assessment (unchanged product, changed threats) → if successful, the CB confirms the certificate or issues a new one with an extended validity.
Product series → a CB may certify a set of products built on the same functional basis (Art 5(3)). ENISA’s guideline has one certificate cover a reference TOE and the declared variants.

eIDAS is a regulation. It defines roles — qualified trust service providers (QTSPs), qualified signature and seal creation devices (QSCDs) — and obliges QSCDs to be certified. Where CC is used, the applicable Protection Profile and Security Target describe the technical claims to be evaluated.

An HSM component certificate is not automatically certification of the complete QSCD. Check the device configuration and certification report, then assess the trust service separately. The Commission publishes notified alternative assessment processes ; do not assume that every eIDAS device certificate must be an EUCC certificate.
Decision 2016/650 is still in force. It lists ISO/IEC 15408 (2008/2009 editions), ISO/IEC 18045:2008 and the EN 419211 PPs for devices where the signature creation data is held in an entirely — but not necessarily exclusively — user-managed environment. For devices a QTSP manages remotely, it only provided an interim route: a process with comparable security levels, notified to the Commission, until a list of standards exists. EUCC’s Annex II now lists EN 419241-2 and EN 419221-5 for remote QSCDs.
CIR 2025/1570 governs notification of certified QSCDs. It does not itself establish an algorithm profile or Protection Profile. The applicable technical chain must still be established from the device type, Article 30 assessment basis, EUCC Annexes, the selected PP and the scheme's current cryptographic guidance.

The PP is deliberately generic: the TOE is “a set of configured software and hardware” — for example a PCIe card inside a server, or a dedicated module that client applications reach over a network — and client applications are always outside it. The TOE supports signing and sealing, certificate issuance and revocation, time stamping and authentication, and may support key backup. It is not, in general, aware of the context in which a function is used — enforcing sole control of a signing key is the client application’s job, with the TOE’s authorisation mechanisms.
} > Only algorithms and algorithm parameters (e.g. key length) approved for the identified purpose shall be used by the TOE to carry out cryptographic operations for trust services.
The PP names no algorithms. The ST author consults the relevant national body; the PP points to ETSI TS 119 312 and the SOG-IS crypto catalogue as examples. Under EUCC today that role falls to the ECCG Agreed Cryptographic Mechanisms (next section).

This PP covers the security IC — the chip and its dedicated support software — on which a smart card, secure element or embedded root of trust is built. The final product is a composite: the application is evaluated on top of the certified chip, reusing the chip’s certificate. That is the opposite of EN 419221-5, which covers a complete cryptographic module used by a trust service.
Beyond the core PP, five optional functional packages can be claimed in any combination: Authentication of the Security IC, Loader 1 (secured environment only), Loader 2 (authorised users only), Cryptographic Services, and Address-based Access Control.
The Cryptographic Services package defines generic SFRs for services the chip offers to the embedded software, and the ST author “shall iterate the SFRs as necessary to cover all the cryptographic services in the scope of the evaluation”. This invented excerpt shows how a Security Target for the fictional Orrin N7 could word three post-quantum requirements: ML-KEM-768 key generation, ML-DSA-65 signing and a hybrid key derivation. It follows CC:2022 Part 2 with the mandatory errata applied and ends with the dependencies each requirement pulls in. No scheme or laboratory has reviewed it.
Earlier sections say that adding ML-KEM or ML-DSA means new FCS_CKM and FCS_COP iterations in the Security Target. This example shows what three of them look like. The product is the fictional Orrin N7 at firmware 5.0.0. The excerpt is invented. It is not taken from a real Security Target, and no scheme or laboratory has reviewed it.
The wording follows CC:2022 Part 2 with the mandatory errata applied (version 1.2, 15 October 2025). Completed assignments are in bold. Each iteration has its own label in brackets, because CC:2022 Part 1 says different iterations must be uniquely identified. Some profiles write the label after a slash instead, for example FMT_MSA.1/GenKeys in EN 419 221-5.

chunks.title: Common Criteria, EUCC & eIDAS Certification — CcEuSections
chunks.content:
Module: Common Criteria, EUCC & eIDAS Certification

FCS_CKM.1.1(ML-KEM-768) The TSF shall generate cryptographic keys in accordance with a specified cryptographic key generation algorithm ML-KEM.KeyGen with the parameter set ML-KEM-768 and specified cryptographic key sizes encapsulation key 1184 bytes and decapsulation key 2400 bytes that meet the following: FIPS 203, Section 7.1 (Algorithm 19, ML-KEM.KeyGen).
Name the parameter set. FIPS 203 defines three, and their key sizes differ: for ML-KEM-768 the encapsulation key is 1184 bytes and the decapsulation key is 2400 bytes. A claim that says only “ML-KEM” does not tell the laboratory which parameter set to test.
FCS_CKM.1 has three assignments and no selection. An ST author must complete every assignment.
One iteration is enough for one method, even with several key sizes. A later ML-KEM-1024 could be handled in two ways: the author can list both parameter sets and their key sizes in the assignments of this iteration, or write a second iteration. CC:2022 Part 1 leaves the choice to the author, who weighs whether one rationale covers the whole list or each value needs its own rationale and trace.
Key generation uses random bytes. FIPS 203 requires an approved random bit generator with at least 192 bits of security strength for ML-KEM-768. In CC terms that is the dependency of FCS_CKM.1 on FCS_RBG.1 or FCS_RNG.1, which the errata keep.

chunks.title: Common Criteria, EUCC & eIDAS Certification — CcEuSections

FCS_COP.1.1(ML-DSA-65 sign) The TSF shall perform digital signature generation in accordance with a specified cryptographic algorithm ML-DSA.Sign, hedged variant, parameter set ML-DSA-65 and cryptographic key sizes private key 4032 bytes that meet the following: FIPS 204, Section 5.2 (Algorithm 2, ML-DSA.Sign).
Put “hedged” in the algorithm assignment. FIPS 204 signs with fresh randomness by default and also allows a deterministic variant. The two variants differ in one step. A product that offers both can name both variants in the assignments of one iteration or write one iteration per variant. CC:2022 Part 1 requires every iteration to differ from the others in its completed assignments, selections or refinements, and leaves the choice between a list of values and separate iterations to the author.
FIPS 204 says the deterministic variant should not be used where side-channel attacks are a concern and cannot be otherwise mitigated. So offering the deterministic variant adds a question for the vulnerability analysis.

The hedged variant uses a fresh 32-byte random value, which FIPS 204 says should ideally be generated by an approved random bit generator. The errata say that random bits generated inside an operation should be covered by FCS_RBG.1 or FCS_RNG.1, through a dependency added to the operation or, where it applies, through the operation’s dependency on key generation, which itself depends on one of them. Here the second route applies, through the ML-DSA-65 key generation iteration that this excerpt leaves out.
This iteration covers signature generation only. Checking a signature, for example on a firmware update, is a different operation. CC:2022 Part 2 would let one iteration list both operations; this example gives checking its own iteration because it uses a different key (the public key) and a different algorithm entry (ML-DSA.Verify). EN 419 221-5 requires that, if the TOE supports updates, the iterations cover the operations that check update signatures.
The classical half keeps its existing ECDSA or RSA iteration. ACM v2 says lattice mechanisms should be combined with a classical one, and that a hybrid signature can be a concatenation of signatures that must all verify. The excerpt does not show how the hybrid signature itself is claimed; see the note after the two panels.

FCS_CKM.5.1(Hybrid) The TSF shall derive cryptographic keys 256-bit AES session keys from the concatenation of the ML-KEM-768 shared secret and the ECDH P-256 shared secret in the fixed order of the combination; a salt; and a FixedInfo string that holds the name of the combination, the ML-KEM-768 encapsulation key and ciphertext, and both ECDH public values in accordance with a specified key derivation algorithm two-step key derivation, with HMAC-SHA-256 for randomness extraction and HMAC-SHA-256 for key expansion (the HKDF construction of RFC 5869) and specified cryptographic key sizes 256 bits that meet the following: NIST SP 800-56C Rev. 2, Sections 2 and 5; NIST SP 800-227, Section 4.6.2; RFC 5869 .
CC:2022 has a component for this step. FCS_CKM.5 is the key derivation component. It requires that the methods, standards and parameters for key derivation are specified. A CC 3.1 profile such as EN 419 221-5 has no such component. Its cryptographic support section lists FCS_CKM.1, FCS_CKM.4, FCS_COP.1 and FCS_RNG.1.
FCS_CKM.5 has five assignments: key type, input parameters, key derivation algorithm, key sizes and standards. The errata add the missing application notes for all five. The input parameters are where the design shows: which secrets go in, in what order, and what context is bound to the result.

chunks.title: Common Criteria, EUCC & eIDAS Certification — CcEuSections
chunks.content:
Module: Common Criteria, EUCC & eIDAS Certification

NIST SP 800-56C Rev. 2 allows a hybrid shared secret, which is the concatenation of a standard shared secret and a second secret. SP 800-227 approves applying SP 800-56C key-derivation methods to the shared secret of an approved KEM, and approves a key combiner built on them when at least one of the shared secrets comes from SP 800-56A, SP 800-56B or an approved KEM. With the two-step method, extraction is done on all the shared secrets together. HKDF, defined in RFC 5869, is a version of that two-step method that uses HMAC for both steps.
FIPS 203 itself says that further key derivation from the ML-KEM shared secret shall be done in an approved manner, as specified in SP 800-108 and SP 800-56C. Inside SP 800-56C, the functions of SP 800-108 are used in the key-expansion step of the two-step method. That is why the example lists SP 800-56C and not SP 800-108.
SP 800-227 says that a combiner that uses only the two shared secrets does not preserve IND-CCA security when only one of the two schemes is IND-CCA. It encourages combiners that preserve IND-CCA security, and its example also takes the ciphertexts, the encapsulation keys and a domain separator. SP 800-227 says that the FixedInfo input of SP 800-56C can carry such inputs, which is why the excerpt lists them.
The FIPS 140-3 route asks for two related design choices: a fixed set of combinations and module control of the order in which the secrets are joined. There the step is called the key combiner.

What this excerpt leaves out: FCS_CKM.1 for ML-DSA-65 and for ECDH P-256, FCS_CKM.2 for ML-KEM-768 and for ECDH P-256, FCS_RBG.1 and FCS_CKM.6, and everything else a Security Target holds: the threats, the objectives, the other requirements and the TOE summary specification. Module: Common Criteria, EUCC & eIDAS Certification

What AVA_VAN.5 asks. The evaluator tests as an attacker with High attack potential. The evaluator also searches public sources for known weaknesses in the TOE and in its third-party components. The CEM names research papers and conference proceedings among the publicly available sources an evaluator examines, and says the search should focus on sources that refer to the technologies used in the product. For a lattice-based implementation, the published side-channel and fault papers on lattice-based key encapsulation and signatures can therefore belong to that public record. Lattice code from a third party goes on the third-party list.
How High is counted. The CEM scores an attack on five factors: elapsed time, expertise, knowledge of the TOE, window of opportunity and equipment. The CEM example table is read by the attack potential an attack needed: 20 to 24 points is High and 25 or more is beyond High, and the CEM’s own worked case says an attack scenario of 21 points that breaks the TOE fails AVA_VAN.5. The CEM says its values may need to be adjusted for the technology type, and that the evaluator should seek guidance from the evaluation authority. For AVA_VAN.5 it also points to guidance for special technical areas that is relevant for the national scheme.
Which document rates it, by domain. Under EUCC, Annex I lists one attack-potential document for each of two technical domains at AVA_VAN level 4 or 5. Both replace the CEM table for their domain.
