The CEM table says what attack potential an attack needed. The two domain tables say which attacker the TOE resists. In the CEM, AVA_VAN.5 stands for a TOE resistant to attackers with High attack potential, whose residual vulnerabilities can only be exploited by attackers with beyond-High potential. The three top rows therefore describe different things and are not three starting points of one scale.

chunks.content:
Module: Common Criteria, EUCC & eIDAS Certification
Component: CcEuSections

Annex I lists the EN 419 221-5 HSM interpretation under the security-box domain, and the security-box document has an annex with rating advice for hardware security modules. An HSM that claims EN 419 221-5, such as the Orrin N7, would therefore normally be assessed in that domain; the certification body confirms the domain for a given product. The same attack path can get different points under the CEM, the security-box document and the smart-card document, because the factor values differ: for a difficult window of opportunity the CEM table gives 10 points, and the security-box document gives 4 for identification and 5 for exploitation. A total is read on the table of the domain that applies and is not carried to another table. The security-box document scores the effort to find an attack (identification) and the effort to repeat it (exploitation) separately, then adds them.

chunks.title: Common Criteria, EUCC & eIDAS Certification — CcEuSections
chunks.content:
Module: Common Criteria, EUCC & eIDAS Certification
Component: CcEuSections

Neither document names a post-quantum algorithm. The security-box document says rating advice for software attacks and random number generator attacks will be added in further revisions. The smart-card document already has a section on attacks on random number generators, and it lists changing the characteristics of the random numbers generated among the effects of perturbation. The documents give no separate table for post-quantum attacks, so the general factor tables of the domain are what is available. The smart-card document adds that where cryptography is involved the certification body should be consulted. The attack types the documents already name are the ones behind the targets below: perturbation, power consumption, emanation and timing (security boxes); perturbation, key retrieval by fault analysis and side-channel attacks (smart cards).

chunks.title: Common Criteria, EUCC & eIDAS Certification — CcEuSections
chunks.content:
Module: Common Criteria, EUCC & eIDAS Certification
Component: CcEuSections

Scope check before planning tests. Before rating an attack path, the evaluator determines whether it is applicable and reachable under the TOE boundary, the interfaces, the assumptions and the operational environment. EN 419 221-5 assumes a protected environment that limits physical access to authorised administrators. Its OE.Env also lists inspections that detect attempts to reach side-channels, and protection against emanation attacks. The profile’s refinement of AVA_VAN.5 says that the protection which FPT_PHP.1 and FPT_PHP.3 must give against physical attacks is equivalent to the assessment in ISO/IEC 19790 at Security Level 3. Its rationale for AVA_VAN.5 (section 7.2.4) adds that, while the environment is meant to protect against physical attacks, a high level of protection against logical attacks, especially remote ones, is also necessary, and that this is why the vulnerability analysis is augmented to High attack potential. ENISA’s interpretation adds that physical attacks by other persons are not applicable, that no additional vulnerability analysis for physical attacks is needed, and that all kinds of administrator access must be taken into account, including logical access through interfaces that only administrators can reach. The security-box document describes power-consumption analysis as done through an external interface of the TOE, emanation analysis as done with an antenna outside the security-box boundary, and timing analysis as usually possible through the external interfaces. For an HSM under that profile, logical attacks reachable through interfaces, including timing and error behaviour seen from outside, therefore remain relevant. A profile that names power, emanation or fault attacks as threats puts them in scope: the Security IC Platform profile, for example, names inherent and forced information leakage as threats. The texts do not say how these rules combine for new cryptographic code in an HSM; see the note after the two panels.

chunks.title: Common Criteria, EUCC & eIDAS Certification — CcEuSections
chunks.content:
Module: Common Criteria, EUCC & eIDAS Certification
Component: CcEuSections

Three typical test targets. Most of the published attacks below were shown on Kyber or Dilithium implementations. ML-KEM and ML-DSA are derived from those designs, and the standards list the differences in an appendix. NIST notes that exposure to side-channel attacks varies by application, so universal guidelines are unlikely to help.
Primas, Pessl and Mangard showed a single-trace attack on a lattice-based encryption scheme that uses leakage from the number-theoretic transform and can also attack masked implementations; they note that the attack can be adapted to other lattice-based constructions (CHES 2017).
Hamburg and co-authors attacked CCA2-secure Kyber with chosen ciphertexts, also against masked implementations, in a noisy leakage setting (TCHES 2021, issue 4).
Bos and co-authors built the first completely masked Kyber, with first-order masked decapsulation costing 3.1 million cycles on an Arm Cortex-M4F (TCHES 2021, issue 4).
Hermelink, Pessl and Pöppelmann combined a modified ciphertext with a fault that restores it during decapsulation, and say shuffling and Boolean masking do not stop the attack (INDOCRYPT 2021).
Bernstein and co-authors found that a division on secret data takes input-dependent time (KyberSlash), and recovered Kyber secret keys within minutes to a few hours on a Raspberry Pi 2 and an Arm Cortex-M4 (TCHES 2025, issue 2).

chunks.title: Common Criteria, EUCC & eIDAS Certification — CcEuSections
chunks.content:
Module: Common Criteria, EUCC & eIDAS Certification
Component: CcEuSections

NIST SP 800-227 says KEM modules should have countermeasures against side-channel attacks, including constant-time code and protection of memory from leakage.
ML-DSA signing repeats a loop until the checks pass, and FIPS 204 says each pass either produces a valid signature or an invalid one whose release would leak information about the private key.
Zhou and co-authors showed that leakage from rejected signing attempts gives the challenge and response of those attempts, from which an integer-programming step recovered Dilithium-2, -3 and -5 private keys in seconds or minutes; they measured the leakage as power consumption on an Arm Cortex-M4 (TCHES 2025, issue 4).
Zhao and co-authors used power traces from both rejected and final attempts, and report that the attack also works in the hedged mode (DATE 2026). Both attacks use power measurements.
FIPS 204 notes that deterministic signing leaks information about the message, not the private key, through timing, and advises hedged signing if the message must stay hidden.
Azouaoui and co-authors classify the steps of Dilithium signing by the protection they need, and report that the randomized variant can be much cheaper to protect than the deterministic one (TCHES 2023, issue 4).
Signature verification takes only a public key, a message and a signature. Fault analysis that retrieves a key works from the difference between correct and faulty cryptographic outputs. So the fault target for key recovery is signing, not verification.

chunks.title: Common Criteria, EUCC & eIDAS Certification — CcEuSections
chunks.content:
Module: Common Criteria, EUCC & eIDAS Certification
Component: CcEuSections

Bruinderink and Pessl showed that single random faults in deterministic Dilithium can cause nonce reuse and key recovery; with clock glitching on an Arm Cortex-M4, up to 65.2% of the execution time of Dilithium was vulnerable to an unprofiled attack that injects a random fault anywhere during signing (TCHES 2018, issue 3). FIPS 204 cites this paper among the reasons for the hedged default.
Ravi and co-authors injected electromagnetic faults into the deterministic Dilithium code of the pqm4 library and recovered an important portion of the secret key (AsiaCCS 2019).
Krahmer and co-authors showed key-recovery faults against hedged (randomized) Dilithium too: as few as 1024 and 512 faulty signatures for Dilithium2 in their two attacks, one of which faults the public matrix A (TCHES 2024, issue 3).
Azevedo-Oliveira and co-authors build a key-recovery attack on Dilithium for the case where the rejection step is weakened, and note that physically preventing one of the rejection tests gives two fault attacks (PKC 2025).
FIPS 204 says the missing randomness makes fault attacks on the deterministic variant harder to mitigate. So hedging makes fault attacks easier to mitigate, but published work shows it does not stop them.

chunks.title: Common Criteria, EUCC & eIDAS Certification — CcEuSections
chunks.content:
Module: Common Criteria, EUCC & eIDAS Certification
Component: CcEuSections

A fault in verification does not recover a key, but it can change an accept or reject result: the smart-card document lists changing “the results of validation such as authentication” among the goals of faults. Calle Viera, Berzati and Heydemann examined the verification of the Dilithium reference implementation under randomizing, zeroizing and skipping faults, and describe how to forge signatures without the secret key by using faults in verification together with properties of the public parameters (CARDIS 2023). EN 419 221-5 has the evaluator test that only validly signed updates can be installed, so for a product with signed updates the check itself is a target.
This list is not complete. A laboratory may test other targets.

Where ML-KEM encapsulation is written. Three NIAP profiles list ML-KEM encapsulation and decapsulation in an FCS_COP.1 iteration that FCS_CKM.2 selects, while the NIAP VPN Client module names ML-KEM-1024 directly in FCS_CKM.2. CC:2022 Part 2 lists key agreement among the typical FCS_COP.1 operations. The choice changes what else the Security Target must hold, because the corrected dependency lists differ: FCS_COP.1 depends on FCS_CKM.6, and FCS_CKM.2 does not. No text read says which of the two a given scheme expects for ML-KEM, so the example shows FCS_CKM.2 and does not decide.
How a hybrid signature is claimed. ACM v2 describes a hybrid signature as signatures from different schemes that must all verify. CC:2022 Part 2, the errata, the CEM and the NIAP profiles read contain no rule for writing that as requirements (for example two FCS_COP.1 iterations, or one iteration with a refinement), or for what certification bodies accept.
Whether HMAC and SHA-256 inside the key derivation need their own iterations. CC:2022 Part 2 does not say. NIAP’s cPP for Dedicated Security Component v2.1 refers to its hash and keyed-hash iterations for its one-step derivation methods, and names the MAC and PRF inside FCS_CKM.5 for its two-step method.

chunks.content:
Module: Common Criteria, EUCC & eIDAS Certification
Component: CcEuSections

Claiming EN 419 221-5 from a CC:2022 Security Target. CC:2022 Part 1 says a Security Target that claims strict conformance may add SFRs to those of the profile. The transition policy lets a CC:2022 Security Target claim a CC 3.1 profile until 31 December 2027 and says changed components should be replaced by their CC:2022 counterparts. No text read says how a certification body handles FCS_CKM.5 and FCS_CKM.6 beside the profile’s own FCS_CKM.1, FCS_CKM.4 and FCS_COP.1, or whether they must trace to the profile’s objectives and its policy P.Algorithms. The profile text used here is version 0.15, the version that EUCC Annex II lists; the paid CEN edition was not checked.
Whether physical attacks on the new code are in scope under that profile. ENISA’s interpretation says physical attacks by other persons are not applicable, that no additional vulnerability analysis for physical attacks is needed, and that logical access through interfaces, including administrator-only interfaces, must be taken into account. The security-box document describes power and emanation analysis as done from outside the security box. The texts do not say whether power, electromagnetic and fault attacks on the new cryptographic code are tested under AVA_VAN.5, under the Level 3 physical testing, or not at all.

How a fault on the random input of hedged signing is rated, and how published attacks carry over. The security-box document says rating advice for random number generator attacks will be added. The smart-card document has a section on such attacks and says the certification body should be consulted where cryptography is involved. The CEM lists research papers and conference proceedings as sources. No text read says how an attack published on the earlier Kyber or Dilithium design is treated for ML-KEM or ML-DSA, or how a fault on the randomness input is rated today.
EUCC cryptographic guidance helps developers and evaluators select mechanisms for an EUCC evaluation. It does not establish a universal rule for all CC evaluations or eIDAS assessments. The ENISA guidance recommends preferred mechanisms; distinguish those recommendations from requirements in the applicable scheme rules, Protection Profile and Security Target.
(the document is dated April 2025) and the EUCC Guidelines on Cryptography v2; ENISA’s page lists both with the date 6 May 2025:
Key establishment: ML-KEM (FIPS 203) and FrodoKEM are agreed. Recommended parameters: “the highest possible standardised parameter size, either ML-KEM-1024 or ML-KEM-768” (FrodoKEM-1344 or -976).
Signatures: ML-DSA (FIPS 204), SLH-DSA (FIPS 205), XMSS and LMS (SP 800-208) are agreed. ML-DSA: “either ML-DSA-87 or ML-DSA-65”. SLH-DSA: the parameter sets at security levels 3 and 5.

Hybridisation of lattice schemes: “LWE or MLWE based cryptographic mechanisms shouldn’t be used in a standalone way to provide the intended security functionality, but should be combined with a well established classical cryptomechanism.” (ACM v2.0, Note 40) For signatures, concatenating signatures that must all verify is acceptable.
Hash-based signatures: hybridisation optional — they “may however also be used in a standalone way”. The state of LMS/XMSS is critical data to protect against replay.
Classical asymmetric: where quantum resistance is required, RSA and discrete-log mechanisms “shall not be used without being combined with a quantum resistant mechanism”.
These rows compare selected mechanisms with cited guidance; they are not certification verdicts. The evaluator must also examine the construction, implementation, applicable PP and Security Target. The certification body classifies a product change under the applicable EUCC continuity rules. Following an ACM recommendation alone does not establish conformity.
iterations naming the mechanism and parameter set, and updated TOE summary specification.
The hybrid construction itself: ACM v2 says hybrid modes “shall ensure that all combined pre or post-quantum cryptographic mechanisms need to be broken simultaneously for the hybrid mode to be broken” — so the combiner is part of what is examined, not just the two algorithms.

Module: Common Criteria, EUCC & eIDAS Certification

Common Criteria is one standard (ISO/IEC 15408, with ISO/IEC 18045 for the evaluation method), but nobody is certified by “Common Criteria”. A certificate is issued under a certification scheme: a national scheme or, in the EU, the EUCC set out in Regulation (EU) 2024/482. What it is worth elsewhere depends on a recognition arrangement. Every scheme starts from the same criteria and then adds its own requirements on top.
CCRA (worldwide): mutual recognition only for a collaborative PP, or up to EAL2 + ALC_FLR. EUCC (EU law): ‘substantial’ and ‘high’; AVA_VAN 4 or 5 where the product is covered by an Annex I technical domain or by a certified protection profile listed in Annex II (Art 7(3)).

chunks.title: Common Criteria, EUCC & eIDAS Certification — CcEuSections
chunks.content:
Module: Common Criteria, EUCC & eIDAS Certification
Component: CcEuSections

The 2014 arrangement says collaborative PPs “shall not contain requirements that have a dependency on national conformity assessment schemes” and should allow “other national approved primitives/protocols so nations can provide their own refinements”. Schemes in this module add their own cryptographic requirements on top: the US asks for a CAVP certificate, Canada for Cyber Centre-approved cryptography, Korea for KCMVP on the product types it lists, Malaysia for MyCV, and in the EU the cryptography guidelines point evaluators to the ECCG Agreed Cryptographic Mechanisms (a guideline, not a validation). Post-quantum requirements enter through these scheme-level rules.
36 countries take part in the CCRA: 18 issue certificates and 18 only recognise them. EU member states are bound by EUCC whatever their CCRA role. China, Russia and Kazakhstan use the Common Criteria text in their own national standards, outside the arrangement.
Four patterns repeat: a PP policy (NIAP evaluates only against its own approved PPs; Singapore and Korea add national PPs), cryptography rules (validation or an approved-mechanism list), a lighter national method (France’s CSPN, Germany’s BSZ, Spain’s LINCE, Japan’s ST confirmation), and a procurement or legal mandate that turns a certificate into a condition of sale (NIAP’s Product Compliant List, Australia’s ISM, Spain’s CPSTIC catalogue; the EUCC scheme itself is voluntary-based, per ENISA).

chunks.title: Common Criteria, EUCC & eIDAS Certification — CcEuSections
chunks.content:
Module: Common Criteria, EUCC & eIDAS Certification
Component: CcEuSections

Post-quantum positions — where a scheme or its government has published one
NIAP Policy #33 applies to products “certified by either NIAP or a CCRA partner”. From 1 January 2028 a product that does not meet CNSA 2.0 for every cryptographic function is not accepted into NIAP evaluation, and from 1 January 2029 it is not posted to the Product Compliant List — so a certificate from any CCRA scheme stops opening the US national-security market unless its cryptography is CNSA 2.0. The policy states one exception: AES-128 for Bluetooth is exempt until the Bluetooth standard is updated. The same policy sets earlier cut-offs for products that do not meet CNSA 1.0 minimum requirements: they can no longer extend a certificate through Assurance Maintenance or hold one for more than two years, are not accepted into NIAP evaluation from 1 January 2027, and are not posted to the Product Compliant List from 1 July 2027.
The same criteria, no mutual recognition: a certificate from these schemes is not recognised by CCRA members, and a CCRA certificate does not replace their national certification.
Some countries have adopted the Common Criteria text as a national standard (for example Belarus, Vietnam and Taiwan) without an official source confirming a certification scheme; they are left off the map. Korea’s national PQC migration year is reported in the press but not yet in an official document.

How it works. NIAP is the US scheme for Common Criteria and is part of the NSA ( ). A lab evaluates the product. It reaches the Product Compliant List only if it was evaluated against a NIAP-approved protection profile, and conformance is exact, so the profile fixes the tests, with fixed Evaluation Activities in the profile or its Supporting Document. Which profile fits an HSM-type product is for the vendor, the lab and NIAP to decide. We did not find a NIAP profile written for HSMs: “not found”, not “does not exist”. Our Library’s HSM profiles (
NIAP, run by the NSA, issues the Common Criteria certificate. NIST is a different agency with two programs: CAVP tests an algorithm and gives an algorithm certificate; CMVP validates a whole module and gives a module certificate. NIAP Policy #5 ties them together: “At a minimum an appropriate NIST CAVP certificate is required before a NIAP CC Certificate will be awarded.” ( )
First example: the Dedicated Security Component cPP, version 2.1 (17 November 2025). Its revision history says “post-quantum cryptography”. It describes a component that serves “the encompassing platform”. Its authors “designed the DSC cPP as a standalone PP” (a base profile, evaluated once and reused across devices)

Whether an HSM design fits that embedded boundary is for the vendor, the lab and NIAP to decide. The profile lists post-quantum algorithms as allowed choices beside the classical ones, including ML-KEM (512, 768, 1024) and ML-DSA (44, 65, 87). The profile text offers them as selections and has no CNSA wording.
NIAP adds the CNSA rule by Technical Decision TD1011, published 26 March 2026. NIAP endorsed CPP_DSC_V2.1 on that date, and the older CPP_DSC_V1.0E “will sunset effective 26 September 2026” ( ). TD1011 says: “In order to be listed on the NIAP PCL, evaluations against CPP_DSC_V2.1 must meet the following requirements:” and “Each applicable Cryptographic SFR (FCS_) must include at least one selection conforming to Commercial National Security Algorithm (CNSA) Suite V1.0 or V2.0;”. Its list includes “ML-KEM-1024”, “ML-DSA-87” and “LMS or XMSS (LMS 256-192 preferred) for soft/firmware signature”, next to “ECDH 384”, “ECDSA 384” and “RSA with minimum 3072-bit modulus”; and “Evaluations certified by NIAP must only make CNSA-compliant selections.” ( ) So post-quantum is one allowed route, not the only one: CNSA 1.0 selections such as ECDSA 384 and RSA 3072 also count.

Contrast: Application Software, version 2.0 (16 June 2025). It is here because it shows explicit CNSA 1.0 and CNSA 2.0 branches in one US profile. Its CNSA 2.0 branch sits next to a CNSA 1.0 branch (RSA of 3072 bits or more, P-384 and P-521, safe-prime groups). The profile says: “ML-DSA and ML-KEM are not usable in any functions at the time of initial publication, they are added to this requirement in support of future protocol updates. As support is expanded for CNSA 2.0, CNSA 1.0 will be removed as an selection in a future update.” It prepares for the move and does not force it. ( )
As of 23 October 2026, 11 NIAP documents we checked (8 profiles and 3 profile modules) list post-quantum choices such as ML-KEM, ML-DSA, LMS and XMSS. All 11 refer to CC:2022 in their own text. In all 11, classical algorithms remain in the cryptographic requirements alongside the post-quantum entries, though some key-encapsulation tables list only ML-KEM-1024. None of the 11 requires post-quantum cryptography, and none has removed the classical (CNSA 1.0) choices; three of them (Application Software 2.0 and Full Drive Encryption Authorization Acquisition 3.0 and Encryption Engine 3.0) say that will happen “in a future update”. The checks cover only these 11 documents. NIAP’s table of approved protection profiles lists 58 on 23 October 2026: the 15 documents below are listed as reported and not yet read, and the other 32 (26 of them still on Common Criteria 3.1) are neither read nor listed here.

“Date in document” is the one the document itself shows; “NIAP approved” is the approval date as listed on (read 23 October 2026), which lists all 11 as CC:2022. Algorithm lists are written as the profile lists them. Source pages: the and the .
Three of the profiles (Dedicated Security Component, Network Devices and Hardcopy Devices) are international collaborative profiles whose text lists classical algorithms below CNSA 1.0, such as RSA 2048 and P-256 (and KCDSA in Hardcopy Devices). NIAP restricts what can be posted to the Product Compliant List by endorsement Technical Decisions that all say the same: each applicable cryptographic requirement must include at least one selection conforming to CNSA 1.0 or 2.0, and an evaluation in another scheme may select other algorithms if the product can be configured not to use them. These are for Dedicated Security Component, for Network Devices, and for Full Drive Encryption 3.0 (Authorization Acquisition and Encryption Engine), and for Hardcopy Devices version 1.1 only. NIAP’s page for Hardcopy Devices 2.0 lists no Technical Decision (read 23 October 2026), and we found no such decision for version 2.0. For the Functional Package for TLS 2.1 (a package, not a profile), (1 April 2026) says the same for (D)TLS servers.

“Listed” means a selectable entry in an allowed-choices table or a selection list. In the tables we read, post-quantum entries are options; we did not find a function where only a post-quantum entry is available. Some key-encapsulation tables list only ML-KEM-1024 (the Network Devices cPP, Table 14, and Virtualization, Table 18); in others (Dedicated Security Component, General-Purpose Computing Platforms, Full Drive Encryption) RSA entries sit in the same table. Where a table has a single entry, the requirement itself applies only if the Security Target selects ML-KEM.
In two profiles, Application Software 2.0 and Full Drive Encryption Encryption Engine 3.0, ML-KEM and ML-DSA are present as selections that the profile says cannot yet be used in any function (see the quotes above).
“LMS and XMSS for verification” and “only” in the table state what we did not find in the other tables of the same profile, from a search of the text; for example, Virtualization has no LMS or XMSS entry in its signature-generation table.
The two File Encryption modules define a hybrid key-transport requirement (FCS_COP.1/KT) that uses ML-KEM as specified in the base profile’s FCS_CKM.2, with a key wrapping algorithm; their text has no match for ML-DSA, LMS or XMSS.

NIAP’s approval dates differ from the dates inside the documents. The 25 March 2026 announcement names Hardcopy Devices version 1.1, not 2.0; the Hardcopy Devices 2.0 document is dated 31 July 2026 and NIAP’s table lists it approved 23 September 2026.
Virtualization and General-Purpose Computing Platforms: NIAP’s announcement says each “supports CNSA 2.0 updates”, yet the revision history in the document does not mention post-quantum cryptography, although the requirement tables carry post-quantum selections. The tables are what we used.
The VPN Client module’s revision history, dated 2025-09-30 in the document, says “limitation of cryptographic algorithms to CNSA 1.0”, while the same module text carries the CNSA 2.0 selections and, in the Mobile Device Fundamentals configuration, still lists Curve25519 as a “Non-CNSA Algorithm”. 1. Generate a ML-DSA-65 keypair and sign a binary hash
Select ML-DSA-65 in the Workshop, generate a keypair, enter text to sign, and step through the signing and verification process. Compare the signature size against classical algorithms in the side-by-side panel.
The ML-DSA-65 signature is 3,309 bytes compared to 64 bytes for ECDSA P-256 — a 51x increase. However, signing and verification remain fast because lattice operations are computationally efficient.

Click "Build Chain" in the Certificate Chain workshop to generate a Root CA (ML-DSA-87), Intermediate CA (ML-DSA-65), and Code Signing certificate (ML-DSA-44). Examine the ASN.1-style info for each certificate in the chain.

chunks.title: Code Signing — CodeSigningExercises
chunks.content:
Module: Code Signing
Component: CodeSigningExercises

In the Package Signing workshop, toggle between Classical (RSA-4096), PQC (ML-DSA-87), and Hybrid (ML-DSA-87+Ed448) modes. Compare the RPM signature header sizes and observe the size of the hybrid signature that RPM 6 adds alongside the RSA signature.
Hybrid mode produces a signature of ~4,741 bytes (4,627 B ML-DSA-87 + 114 B Ed448 = 4,741 B). Red Hat keeps the RSA signature in the package as well: systems that understand the RPM 6 header format verify both signatures, and older systems validate only the RSA signature.
4. Trace a Sigstore verification from log entry to identity
Step through all 7 stages of the Sigstore keyless signing flow. Pay attention to how the ephemeral key is created and destroyed, and how the transparency log provides a permanent, immutable record of the signing event.
The key advantage of Sigstore is that no long-term private keys exist. The ephemeral keypair — ECDSA P-256 in Fulcio today, with ML-DSA-65 as the post-quantum upgrade — lives for ~20 minutes, and the transparency log (Rekor) serves as the permanent verification anchor.
5. Walk through the secure boot trust chain and compare firmware signing algorithms
In the Secure Boot Chain workshop, step through all 4 stages of the boot trust chain. Toggle between LMS, XMSS, and ML-DSA to see how signature sizes and state management requirements differ. Run the firmware signing simulation and observe the state counter behavior for stateful algorithms.

LMS signatures (2,512 bytes per RFC 8554) are smaller than ML-DSA (3,309 bytes), but require a monotonic state counter that must never be reset or cloned. CNSA 2.0 lists LMS and XMSS for firmware signing in national security systems and expects exclusive CNSA 2.0 use for software and firmware signing by 2030; its FAQ says NSA wants LMS and XMSS used whenever possible, while ML-DSA is also approved for all signing use cases, so the state management burden is the price of that preference.

chunks.title: Code Signing — CodeSigningIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Code Signing
Component: CodeSigningIntroduction

Code signing is the cryptographic mechanism that guarantees software integrity and publisher authenticity. Every operating system, package manager, and app store relies on digital signatures to ensure that binaries have not been tampered with after publication.
A compromised signing key is a skeleton key to every machine that trusts it.
These attacks exploited trust in code signing infrastructure. Post-quantum code signing must protect not only against today's threats but also against harvest-now-decrypt-later attacks where adversaries collect signed artifacts to forge signatures once quantum computers become available.
The attacks above are symptoms of deeper structural problems in modern software supply chains. As software composition grows more complex, the attack surface expands — and quantum computing threatens to break the cryptographic foundations that hold it together.
“Today, a supply chain attacker must steal a signing key. Tomorrow, a quantum-capable adversary can forge any signature without stealing anything.”
Today's supply chain attacks require compromising a specific publisher's signing key. A quantum attacker running Shor's algorithm could derive any publisher's private key from their public certificate — no infiltration, no social engineering, no insider threat required.

chunks.title: Code Signing — CodeSigningIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Code Signing
Component: CodeSigningIntroduction

Adversaries can harvest signed binaries and code signing certificates today. Once quantum computers arrive, they could forge new signatures that chain to existing certificates, or create fake artifacts that appear legitimately signed by any publisher. This is the harvest-now-decrypt-later threat applied to code integrity.
A quantum-compromised Root CA key would let an attacker sign software as any publisher in that CA's trust hierarchy. Unlike a stolen intermediate key (scoped to one publisher), breaking the Root CA's algorithm affects the entire ecosystem simultaneously.
A stolen signing key compromises one publisher. A quantum break of ECDSA or RSA compromises every publisher simultaneously — every code signing certificate using that algorithm becomes forgeable. This is a systemic, not isolated, risk.
SCADA controllers, medical devices, avionics, and industrial infrastructure deployed today with classical signatures will still be operating 15–25 years from now. These systems cannot be easily patched and will be running in a post-quantum threat environment. Their classical signatures will offer zero protection against firmware forgery.
This is why PQC migration for code signing is not just about upgrading algorithms — it requires rethinking the entire supply chain trust model, from build provenance to signature verification to certificate chain management.

chunks.title: Code Signing — CodeSigningIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Code Signing
Component: CodeSigningIntroduction

Classical code signing relies on RSA and ECDSA, both of which are vulnerable to Shor's algorithm on a cryptographically relevant quantum computer. NIST has standardized ML-DSA ( FIPS 204) and SLH-DSA ( FIPS 205) as PQC replacements for digital signatures.
PQC signatures are 38–123x larger than ECDSA. For code signing this is acceptable — signatures are verified once per install, and bandwidth is not the primary constraint.
Code signing certificates form a trust chain from a Root CA down to the signing certificate. The chain establishes that a trusted authority vouches for the identity of the software publisher.
Code signing certificates expire, but signed software must remain valid long after. Timestamping (RFC 3161) proves the signature was created while the certificate was still valid. PQC timestamping requires PQC-capable Time Stamping Authorities (TSAs) — a critical dependency for migration.
Every major package manager uses code signing to verify package authenticity. Migration to PQC varies widely — RPM is leading with hybrid ML-DSA-87+Ed448 support in RHEL 10.1, while npm and PyPI sign through Sigstore, whose ML-DSA support is listed as experimental.
Hybrid signing (also called composite signing) attaches both a classical and PQC signature to the same artifact. This provides backward compatibility — older tools verify the classical signature, while PQC-aware tools verify both. Red Hat's RPM PQC signing uses OpenPGP v6 (RFC 9580, via Sequoia) with the RPM v6 package format.

chunks.title: Code Signing — CodeSigningIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Code Signing
Component: CodeSigningIntroduction

Sigstore is an open-source project that eliminates the need for long-term signing key management. Instead of distributing and protecting private keys, developers authenticate with their existing identity (GitHub, Google) and receive short-lived certificates. All signatures are recorded in a public transparency log.
No long-term private keys to manage, rotate, or protect. Identity-based trust replaces key-based trust. This dramatically simplifies PQC migration — only the Sigstore infrastructure needs to upgrade, not every individual developer.
Sigstore's architecture centralizes cryptographic operations in Fulcio (CA) and Rekor (transparency log). Upgrading these two services to ML-DSA automatically provides PQC protection to all downstream consumers (npm, PyPI, etc.).
Every platform depends on a chain of trust that starts at an immutable root of trust and extends through bootloaders, the OS kernel, and runtime firmware. Each link in the chain verifies a cryptographic signature before passing execution to the next stage. If any signature fails, the boot process halts.
Firmware signing is a critical PQC migration target because firmware keys have 10–20 year lifetimes, and devices deployed today will still be in the field when cryptographically relevant quantum computers arrive. An attacker who harvests firmware update signatures today could forge malicious firmware updates in the future.

chunks.title: Code Signing — CodeSigningIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Code Signing
Component: CodeSigningIntroduction

The NSA's CNSA 2.0 guidance lists stateful hash-based signatures (LMS or XMSS) for firmware and software signing in National Security Systems, and its FAQ says NSA wants them used whenever possible rather than waiting for ML-DSA, which is also approved for all signing use cases.
Compact signatures (2,512 B, about 2.5 KB) and tiny public keys (56 bytes), per RFC 8554 — ideal for hardware-constrained boot ROM. Fast verification (~0.1 ms). CNSA 2.0 compliant. Security derives solely from hash functions (minimal cryptographic assumptions). Trade-off: requires a monotonic state counter managed in an HSM or TPM.
Fully stateless — no counter, no state management burden. Simpler operations for environments where maintaining state is impractical (distributed build systems, CI/CD pipelines). Trade-off: larger signatures (3,309 B, about 3.3 KB) and public keys (1,952 B, about 1.9 KB) per FIPS 204. Not mandated by CNSA 2.0 for firmware signing.
For a deep dive into LMS/XMSS parameter selection, Merkle tree mechanics, and the state management challenge, see the Stateful Hash Signatures module .

chunks.title: Code Signing — SigstoreFlow
chunks.content:
Module: Code Signing
Component: SigstoreFlow

Step through the 7 stages of Sigstore keyless signing. Compare how classical ECDSA and PQC ML-DSA-65 differ at each stage.
The primary impact is on Rekor log storage (each entry grows ~18x). For individual developers, the difference is negligible — signing and verification remain sub-second.
Traditional code signing: Every developer manages long-term private keys. PQC migration requires every developer to generate new PQC keys, update signing configurations, and distribute new public keys.
Sigstore keyless signing: Only Fulcio (CA) and Rekor (log) need to upgrade to PQC. Developers get PQC protection automatically through ephemeral certificates — zero configuration changes needed.
Note: This walkthrough simulates the Sigstore keyless signing flow with realistic data structures. Sigstore is a Linux Foundation project used by npm, PyPI, Kubernetes, and many other ecosystems. PQC support in Sigstore is under active development. The transparency log entries shown are for educational purposes only.
The developer logs in via GitHub/Google/Microsoft OIDC. The identity provider issues a JWT that Fulcio uses to bind an identity to a certificate. This step is algorithm-agnostic.
A short-lived keypair is generated locally. The private key never leaves the developer's machine and is automatically destroyed after signing. Private key: ECDSA P-256 = 32 bytes, ML-DSA-65 = 4,032 bytes. The ML-DSA-65 public key is 1,952 bytes.

chunks.title: Code Signing — SigstoreFlow
chunks.content:
Module: Code Signing
Component: SigstoreFlow

Fulcio issues a certificate binding the OIDC identity (e.g., "user@github.com") to the ephemeral public key. The cert is short-lived (~20 minutes) and logged in a Certificate Transparency log.
The artifact (e.g., container image, npm package) is hashed (SHA-256) and the hash is signed with the ephemeral private key. This is the core signing operation.
The signature, certificate, and artifact hash are recorded in Rekor, an immutable, append-only transparency log. Each entry gets a unique log index and UUID. Once recorded, the entry cannot be modified or deleted.
The ephemeral private key is destroyed immediately after signing. There is no long-term key to protect, rotate, or revoke. The transparency log serves as the permanent proof that the signature was valid at the time of signing.
Verification checks three things: (1) the signature is valid for the artifact hash, (2) the certificate chains to Fulcio's root CA, and (3) the Rekor log contains a matching entry. No public keys need to be distributed.

chunks.title: Compliance & Regulatory Strategy — Introduction
chunks.content:
Module: Compliance & Regulatory Strategy
Component: Introduction

Governments and standards bodies worldwide are establishing requirements for the transition to post-quantum cryptography. For organizations operating across borders, navigating these overlapping and sometimes conflicting requirements is a critical challenge.
“A quantum computer of sufficient size and sophistication — also known as a cryptanalytically relevant quantum computer — will be capable of breaking much of the public-key cryptography used on digital systems across the United States and around the world.”
— Executive Order 14306, Sustaining Select Efforts to Strengthen the Nation's Cybersecurity (June 6, 2025)
NIST, NSA, ETSI, ANSSI, and BSI are all publishing PQC transition guidance with concrete deadlines.
Some sector frameworks now mention quantum computing. The 2025 HHS proposal to update the HIPAA Security Rule would expect a regulated entity, as part of its risk analysis, to consider whether quantum computing poses a reasonably anticipated threat to the confidentiality, integrity, or availability of its ePHI, and PCI SSC's May 2026 announcement of PTS HSM v5.0 says that update addresses emerging threats such as post-quantum risks.
Organizations operating in multiple jurisdictions must reconcile different algorithm preferences, timelines, and certification requirements.
Understanding the major compliance frameworks driving PQC adoption is essential for building a multi-jurisdiction strategy.

chunks.title: Compliance & Regulatory Strategy — Introduction
chunks.content:
Module: Compliance & Regulatory Strategy
Component: Introduction

The Commercial National Security Algorithm Suite 2.0 mandates PQC adoption for National Security Systems. Key deadlines: software/firmware signing preferred by 2025, exclusive by 2030 (with traditional networking); operating-system support by 2027; web/cloud/servers and operating systems by 2033 (NSM-10 targets all NSS quantum-resistant by 2035). Requires ML-KEM -1024 (FIPS 203) and ML-DSA-87 (FIPS 204) as minimum security levels.
NIST's transition guidance for post-quantum cryptography standards (final, October 2026; it replaced the November 2024 draft). Deprecates RSA, ECC, and other quantum-vulnerable public-key algorithms after 2030 and disallows them under NIST standards and guidelines after 2035. Emphasizes cryptographic agility and hybrid approaches during the transition period.
European bodies have published PQC migration guidance. ANSSI recommends hybrid cryptography combining classical and PQC algorithms, and makes it mandatory inside the French regulated perimeter (classified and Diffusion Restreinte data, vital information systems, ANSSI-certified or qualified products). BSI's TR-02102-1 currently recommends PQC in hybrid form, except that hash-based signatures may in principle be used alone, provided their implementation security is carefully considered, and endorses ML-KEM (FIPS 203) and ML-DSA (FIPS 204) with specific parameter recommendations. ETSI provides interoperability guidance for hybrid key exchanges.

chunks.title: Compliance & Regulatory Strategy — Introduction
chunks.content:
Module: Compliance & Regulatory Strategy
Component: Introduction

Hybrid or Pure PQC: It Depends on the Authority and the System
Authorities do not agree on hybrid deployment, and the answer depends on which systems are in scope. ANSSI makes hybrid mandatory inside the French regulated perimeter and recommends it everywhere else, except that it does not recommend systematic hybridisation for hash-based signatures (SLH-DSA, XMSS, LMS). BSI's TR-02102-1 currently recommends PQC in hybrid form, except that hash-based signatures may in principle be used alone, provided their implementation security is carefully considered. ETSI TS 119 312 specifies hybrid signatures for trust services. NSA does not require hybrids for National Security Systems: CNSA 2.0 sets pure ML-KEM-1024 and ML-DSA-87 as the end state, and counts only the hybrids it has specifically identified. Many programs therefore deploy hybrid now and plan pure PQC later, but that is a common migration pattern, not a rule every framework imposes.
Planning rule of thumb: Start hybrid deployments now. Plan your transition to pure PQC to meet your earliest jurisdiction deadline — which you will identify in the Jurisdiction Mapper workshop below.
Organizations typically approach PQC migration from one of two angles. The optimal strategy often combines both, using compliance deadlines as hard constraints and risk scoring to prioritize within those constraints.
• Driven by regulatory deadlines and audit requirements
• Risk: may miss high-risk systems outside compliance scope

• Best for: regulated industries (finance, government, healthcare)

Key deadlines are converging across jurisdictions, creating a narrow window for organizations to complete their PQC migration.
Individual countries are setting their own PQC transition deadlines, and they do not line up. Organizations operating internationally must track every jurisdiction they touch — the binding date is the earliest one, not the average.
Two parallel clocks. Federal agencies, excluding National Security Systems: EO 14412 (22 June 2026) requires High Value Assets and high-impact systems to use PQC for key establishment by 31 December 2030 and for digital signatures by 31 December 2031, implemented by OMB M-26-15; it also directs a proposed FAR rule that would require covered contractors to comply with NIST’s FIPS by 31 December 2030. National security systems: CNSA 2.0 — software/firmware signing and traditional networking exclusive by 2030; web browsers/servers, cloud and operating systems by 2033; NSS transition complete by 2035 per NSM-10.

ASD recommends ceasing the use of traditional asymmetric cryptography by the end of 2030; the EU roadmap recommends that high-risk use cases be transitioned as soon as possible and no later than the end of 2030, and that the transition be completed for as many systems as practically feasible by 2035.
Several cross-cutting compliance requirements affect PQC migration timelines regardless of jurisdiction.

chunks.title: Compliance & Regulatory Strategy — Introduction
chunks.content:
Module: Compliance & Regulatory Strategy
Component: Introduction

The Cryptographic Module Validation Program certifies cryptographic implementations for government use. PQC algorithm implementations (FIPS 203/204/205) must undergo CMVP validation before deployment in federal systems. These are separate assurance programs, not points on one scale. CAVP validates an algorithm implementation. CMVP validates a cryptographic module (FIPS 140-3), and a module “in process” is not yet validated. “FIPS mode” is a vendor configuration claim unless a CMVP certificate covers that exact module and version. FedRAMP authorizes a cloud service, and WebTrust audits a certificate authority; neither validates cryptography. This certification backlog is a key dependency in migration timelines.
The updated EU regulation for electronic identification requires each Member State to provide at least one European Digital Identity (EUDI) wallet within 24 months of the entry into force of the wallet implementing acts (Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2981 was published on 4 December 2024). The regulation text and the EUDI Wallet architecture and reference framework (ARF) we checked do not mention quantum computing; the SD-JWT standard (RFC 9901) leaves the choice of signature algorithm to the application, including post-quantum algorithms “when they are ready”.

chunks.title: Compliance & Regulatory Strategy — Introduction
chunks.content:

EO 14306 (June 6, 2025) — “Sustaining Select Efforts to Strengthen the Nation's Cybersecurity” — directs CISA, in consultation with NSA, to publish and maintain a list of product categories in which PQC-capable products are widely available (initial list due December 1, 2025). CISA subsequently issued advisory procurement guidance recommending that agencies acquire PQC capabilities in new federal product and service acquisitions (EO 14306 removed EO 14144's binding solicitation requirement), encouraging market demand for PQC-capable solutions.
Executive Order 14412 & OMB M-26-15 — the binding federal civilian mandate

chunks.title: Compliance & Regulatory Strategy — Introduction
chunks.content:
Module: Compliance & Regulatory Strategy
Component: Introduction

EO 14412 (signed June 22, 2026) — “Securing the Nation Against Advanced Cryptographic Attacks” — is the order that actually sets dates. Federal agencies’ High Value Assets and high-impact systems (National Security Systems excluded) must use PQC for key establishment by December 31, 2030 and for digital signatures by December 31, 2031. The function split is deliberate: key establishment carries harvest-now-decrypt-later exposure, so it moves first. It further directs the FAR Council to publish a proposed rule (due 19 December 2026, 180 days after EO 14412) that would require covered contractors to comply by 31 December 2030 with NIST’s FIPS, including all applicable FIPS incorporating PQC-compliant algorithms; the order directs that proposed rule, it is not itself the rule. It also directs CISA guidance on minimum CBOM elements (due 19 March 2027, 270 days after EO 14412). OMB Memorandum M-26-15 (June 24, 2026) is the implementing guidance: a five-phase agency schedule and PQC migration plans filed with OMB. National security systems are out of scope — they remain under CNSA 2.0.
The EU's Digital Operational Resilience Act (enforcement January 2025) requires financial institutions to implement robust ICT risk management including cryptographic controls. While not PQC-specific yet, organizations subject to DORA must demonstrate encryption resilience planning that will inevitably encompass quantum threats.

A CBOM is your foundational compliance artifact — you cannot migrate what you haven't inventoried, and in most organizations the inventory does not yet exist in any auditable form. For the full CBOM framework, including CycloneDX format requirements and vendor contract language, see Vendor & Supply Chain Risk .

chunks.title: Confidential Computing & TEEs — ConfidentialComputingExercises
chunks.content:
Module: Confidential Computing & TEEs
Component: ConfidentialComputingExercises

Work through these scenarios to explore TEE architectures, attestation flows, memory encryption, TEE-HSM integration, and quantum threat migration. Each exercise pre-configures the Workshop — click "Load & Run" to begin.
Take the PQC quiz to test what you've learned about confidential computing and TEE security.
1. TEE Architecture Selection — Choose the right TEE for ML model inference at a bank
In the TEE Architecture Explorer, compare Intel SGX (process-level isolation; ~256 MB EPC on legacy client parts, hundreds of GB on recent Xeon) against AMD SEV-SNP (full VM encryption) for protecting ML model inference with customer data. Consider TCB size, memory limits, cloud availability, and PQC readiness.
SGX has a smaller TCB (CPU + enclave only); legacy client SGX was capped at ~256 MB EPC (too small for large ML models without partitioning), though recent Xeon server parts raise this to hundreds of GB. SEV-SNP encrypts the full VM including guest OS, which results in a larger TCB. Both are available on Azure; we found no published PQC attestation roadmap for either.
2. Attestation Flow Analysis — Identify quantum-vulnerable steps in Intel DCAP
Open the Attestation Workshop and select the Intel DCAP flow. Step through all 5 stages. Identify which steps use ECDSA P-256 and are therefore quantum-vulnerable. Count the total number of vulnerable steps.

chunks.title: Confidential Computing & TEEs — ConfidentialComputingExercises
chunks.content:
Module: Confidential Computing & TEEs
Component: ConfidentialComputingExercises

Three of five DCAP steps are quantum-vulnerable: Quote signing (step 2, ECDSA P-256), Quote verification (step 4, ECDSA P-256), and TCB Info verification (step 5, ECDSA P-256). A CRQC could forge attestation quotes, allowing enclave impersonation and bypassing all trust decisions.
3. Memory Encryption Grover Impact — Calculate post-quantum security of AES-128
In the Encryption Mechanisms workshop, examine the Intel TME-MK and AMD SME/SEV engines. Both use AES-XTS-128. Use the Grover impact calculator to determine the effective post-quantum security level.
The Grover calculator shows AES-128 brute-force search dropping from 2^128 to ~2^64 operations — the theoretical quadratic speedup. In practice that speedup is far less useful (Grover has enormous circuit depth and barely parallelizes), which is why NIST still rates AES-128 at security category 1. AES-256, used by ARM TrustZone and AWS Nitro, keeps a large margin and is the recommended choice for long-term (HNDL) confidentiality. Upgrade path: AES-XTS-256 in next-gen Intel/AMD CPUs.
4. TEE-HSM Integration Design — Build a PQC channel between SGX and Luna HSM
In the TEE-HSM Trusted Channel workshop, select Intel SGX as the TEE and Thales Luna 7 as the HSM. Toggle between classical and PQC modes to compare key exchange sizes. Walk through the 4-step key provisioning simulation.

chunks.title: Confidential Computing & TEEs — ConfidentialComputingExercises
chunks.content:
Module: Confidential Computing & TEEs
Component: ConfidentialComputingExercises

The PQC channel replaces ECDSA P-256 with ML-DSA-65 for attestation and ECDH P-256 with ML-KEM-768 for key exchange. ML-KEM-768 ciphertext (1,088 bytes) is ~33x larger than ECDH P-256 (33 bytes). Migration requires both Intel DCAP PQC update and Luna firmware v7.9.2+.
5. Quantum Migration Prioritization — Rank 5 threat vectors by severity and effort
In the Quantum Threat Migration workshop, examine the threat vector table and priority matrix. Identify which threats have HNDL exposure (recorded data at risk). Determine the correct migration order based on severity and effort.
Two vectors are critical: ECDSA attestation chain forgery and TLS channel key exchange compromise. Only the TLS channel has HNDL exposure (recorded data at risk); attestation forgery is a signature risk, and NIST IR 8547 says the authentication algorithm "may be transitioned at a different time". Both are migrated first because of their severity. Memory encryption (medium severity) is lower priority because Grover only halves key strength and real-time quantum attack on AES-128 is unlikely. Sealing key and firmware vectors require silicon refresh (highest effort).
6. End-to-End PQC Readiness — Assess Nitro + CloudHSM for healthcare

chunks.title: Confidential Computing & TEEs — ConfidentialComputingExercises
chunks.content:
Module: Confidential Computing & TEEs
Component: ConfidentialComputingExercises

For a healthcare organization using AWS Nitro Enclaves with CloudHSM to process patient records, assess PQC readiness across all 5 layers: TEE architecture, attestation, memory encryption, HSM integration, and quantum threats. Use the Quantum Threat Migration workshop to build the complete picture.
Nitro attestation uses ECDSA P-384 (quantum-vulnerable). AWS documents ML-DSA key generation and signing inside CloudHSM, in FIPS mode on hsm2m.medium clusters from 1 September 2026, but no ML-KEM, and the HSM\u2019s CMVP certificate does not list ML-DSA yet (checked October 2026). These details move faster than any catalogue, so confirm them in AWS documentation before you design around them. AES-256 memory encryption is Grover-resilient. Patient records can have long retention: state law generally governs how long medical records are retained (the HIPAA Privacy Rule has no medical-record retention requirement), while HIPAA requires covered entities to retain required compliance documentation for 6 years, making HNDL exposure critical for long-lived records. Overall: 3 of 5 layers need PQC migration, with attestation and TLS channel as highest priority.

chunks.title: Confidential Computing & TEEs — Introduction
chunks.content:
Module: Confidential Computing & TEEs
Component: Introduction

A Trusted Execution Environment (TEE) is a hardware-isolated region of a processor that guarantees confidentiality and integrity of code and data loaded inside it. Unlike traditional OS-level isolation, TEEs protect workloads even when the operating system, hypervisor, or firmware has been fully compromised.
Code running inside a TEE operates within an enclave — a protected memory region where the processor enforces access control in hardware. Data inside the enclave is encrypted in DRAM, decrypted only within the CPU cache, and inaccessible to any software outside the enclave boundary.
The TCB is the set of all hardware, firmware, and software components that must function correctly for the security guarantees to hold. A smaller TCB means fewer components can undermine security. Process-level TEEs (SGX) have the smallest TCB — just the CPU and enclave code. VM-level TEEs (TDX, SEV-SNP) include the guest OS, resulting in a larger but more practical TCB.
Encrypted on disk via AES-XTS or similar. Protected by volume encryption (LUKS, BitLocker) or database-level TDE.
Encrypted over the network via TLS 1.3, IPsec, or WireGuard. Protects against eavesdropping and tampering during transmission.
Encrypted in memory while being processed. TEEs provide hardware-enforced isolation so data remains protected during computation.
Seven major TEE architectures span the ecosystem, each with distinct isolation scopes, deployment models, and PQC readiness levels.

chunks.title: Confidential Computing & TEEs — Introduction
chunks.content:
Module: Confidential Computing & TEEs
Component: Introduction

Remote attestation is the process by which a TEE proves its identity and integrity to a remote verifier. The enclave generates a cryptographically signed report of its code measurement, platform state, and configuration — enabling a relying party to verify that it is communicating with genuine, untampered hardware before releasing sensitive data.
Without attestation , a TEE is just an opaque box — the relying party has no assurance that the enclave is running the expected code on legitimate hardware. Attestation is the foundation of trust in confidential computing.
Every current attestation implementation — Intel DCAP, ARM CCA, AMD SEV-SNP, and AWS Nitro — uses ECDSA P-256 or P-384 for signing attestation reports. Shor's algorithm can break these signatures in polynomial time on a cryptographically relevant quantum computer (CRQC). An attacker who can forge attestation quotes can impersonate a legitimate enclave, completely undermining the trust model of confidential computing.
TEEs protect data in use through hardware memory encryption engines that encrypt DRAM contents transparently. Each vendor implements this differently, with varying key widths, granularities, and integrity protection mechanisms.

chunks.title: Confidential Computing & TEEs — Introduction
chunks.content:
Module: Confidential Computing & TEEs
Component: Introduction

A sealing key is a symmetric key derived from the platform's hardware root of trust, bound to the enclave's identity (code measurement and/or signer identity). Enclaves use sealing keys to encrypt data that persists across restarts — only an enclave with the same identity on the same physical platform can unseal the data. The key derivation chain typically flows: CPU Root Key → CPU SVN → Enclave Identity → Sealing Key . If any component in the chain changes (firmware update, different enclave version), the derived sealing key changes and previously sealed data becomes inaccessible without a migration protocol.
Intel TME-MK and AMD SME/SEV use AES-XTS-128 for memory encryption. AES-128 sits in NIST security Category 1, and Grover's algorithm reduces its effective key strength from 128-bit to 64-bit. While real-time brute-forcing of memory encryption keys remains impractical even with a CRQC, this weakened margin erodes the security guarantee. Next-generation CPUs are expected to upgrade to AES-XTS-256 (NIST Category 5; 128-bit effective post-quantum security).
In production deployments, TEEs rarely operate in isolation — they need access to long-lived cryptographic keys stored in Hardware Security Modules (HSMs). The communication channel between a TEE and an HSM must itself be trustworthy, creating a mutual trust requirement: the TEE must verify it is talking to a genuine HSM, and the HSM must verify the TEE is running expected code on legitimate hardware.

chunks.title: Confidential Computing & TEEs — Introduction
chunks.content:
Module: Confidential Computing & TEEs
Component: Introduction

The TEE presents its attestation report (e.g., SGX Quote, SEV-SNP Report) as evidence. NIST IR 8320E (initial public draft) has the evidence go to a key management or attestation service, which compares it against predefined trust policies set by the data owner or a relying party. In this workshop's modelled design the HSM plays that role: it verifies the report against the vendor's root CA, checks the code measurement, and validates the TCB level before releasing any key material.
In reverse, the TEE verifies the HSM's PKCS#11 or KMIP endpoint certificate against a pinned CA to prevent man-in-the-middle attacks.
The HSM & PQC module includes an interactive PKCS#11 simulator where you can step through ML-KEM encapsulation, ML-DSA signing, and key provisioning operations — the same operations used in TEE-HSM key provisioning flows.
Quantum computers threaten multiple layers of the confidential computing stack — from attestation signatures to memory encryption to TEE-HSM communication channels. The severity and migration urgency varies by component.
Vendor PQC Attestation Timeline (the module's expectation; no vendor has published these dates)
A TEE asks you to trust the chip vendor and an attestation chain. Fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) trusts the mathematics instead: the server computes on ciphertexts and never sees the data, at the cost of speed. It has its own module, including how an HSM holds the FHE keys.

Forgery Warning: Attestation flows using ECDSA signatures are quantum vulnerable. This is a signature-forgery risk, not harvest-now-decrypt-later, which concerns encrypted data (NIST IR 8547).
Note: Attestation flows are simplified for educational purposes. Real implementations include additional error handling, retry logic, certificate caching, and collateral management. PQC replacements are based on vendor roadmaps and NIST FIPS 203/204 standards.

chunks.content:

Grover's algorithm provides a quadratic speedup for brute-force key search, effectively halving the security level of symmetric ciphers. Adjust the AES key width to see the post-quantum impact.
What each memory encryption engine protects at the hardware level.
Each engine derives sealing keys through a chain from the platform root of trust to the final workload-specific key. Understanding this chain is critical for PQC migration planning.
Note: Memory encryption implementations vary by CPU generation and firmware version. Grover's algorithm impact assumes a fault-tolerant quantum computer with sufficient logical qubits. Real-world quantum attacks on AES would require sustained quantum computation over extended periods. This calculator is for educational assessment only.
AES-256-class strength — the highest NIST post-quantum security category. Retains a 128-bit effective margin even under Grover.
AES-192-class strength (NIST Category 3). Grover reduces the effective margin to ~96 bits.
AES-128-class strength (NIST Category 1). Grover reduces the effective margin to ~64 bits — prefer AES-256 for long-lived data.
Below all NIST post-quantum security categories. Immediate upgrade to AES-256 or larger keys required.

Mutual attestation means both sides prove their identity cryptographically before any key material is exchanged. Without it, a rogue process could impersonate a TEE or HSM and receive provisioned keys.
The TEE generates a hardware-signed attestation quote (e.g., SGX DCAP Quote, SEV-SNP Report). In this simulation the HSM verifies the quote signature against the vendor root CA to confirm it is talking to a genuine, unmodified enclave.
In this demo, the HSM presents its own certificate chain (for example a vendor device certificate). The TEE validates this chain to confirm it is provisioning keys into a genuine, tamper-resistant HSM — not a software mock.
The attestation evidence is cryptographically bound to the TLS session (e.g., via a nonce or public key hash in the attestation payload). This prevents a man-in-the-middle from replaying a valid quote from a legitimate enclave over a different TLS session.

Module: Crypto Agility
Component: CryptoAgilityExercises

Work through these scenarios to understand crypto agility, CBOM scanning, and PQC migration planning. Each exercise pre-configures the Workshop — click "Load & Run" to begin.
1. RSA to Hybrid: What Changes, What Does Not
Start with the RSA-2048 backend, then switch to X25519MLKEM768. Notice that the encrypt()/keyExchange() call sites stay the same — the configuration selects the algorithm. Then look at what the abstraction cannot hide: the key and ciphertext sizes.
The encrypt()/keyExchange() calls never change: the abstraction layer maps the same API to different algorithm implementations. What still changes around them is the algorithm identifier, key and ciphertext sizes (buffers, storage and message formats), key encodings, negotiation with peers, and the error path when a peer does not support the new algorithm.
Review the four common anti-patterns that block crypto agility: hardcoded algorithms, hardcoded buffer sizes, missing inventory, and single provider lock-in. Compare with the abstraction layer approach.
Each anti-pattern would require code changes across multiple services to migrate. The provider model centralizes the algorithm choice in configuration.
Examine the sample CBOM of a typical enterprise. Filter by "Vulnerable" to see which algorithms need migration. Check the CycloneDX JSON format.

The majority of asymmetric algorithms (RSA, ECDSA, ECDH, Ed25519) are quantum-vulnerable. Symmetric algorithms (AES-256) and hashes (SHA-256) are generally safe. This is typical — most enterprises have 60-70% vulnerable assets (our estimate, not a survey figure).
4. Migration Phase 1: Assessment
Walk through Phase 1 of the 7-phase migration framework. Understand the tasks, framework alignment, and how it connects to the Assessment tool in this app.
Phase 1 (Assessment) produces a CBOM — the same artifact you explored in Exercise 3. Each subsequent phase builds on this inventory to prioritize, plan, test, and deploy.
5. Complete Migration Walkthrough
Walk through all 7 phases of the migration framework. Mark each phase complete as you go. Notice how the phases align with NIST IR 8547 and NSA CNSA 2.0 timelines.
The framework spans from discovery through monitoring. NSA CNSA 2.0 (which applies to U.S. national security systems) sets phased deadlines: software/firmware signing and traditional networking reach exclusive PQC by 2030, while web browsers, cloud services, and operating systems follow by 2033.

chunks.title: Crypto Agility — CryptoAgilityIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Crypto Agility
Component: CryptoAgilityIntroduction

Crypto agility is the ability to switch cryptographic algorithms, protocols, and implementations without rewriting the applications that use them. It is a design goal, not a switch: callers can be insulated from the primitive, but credentials, encodings, key and signature sizes, negotiation, storage, rollback and tests still change with each algorithm. NIST devotes a white paper, CSWP 39, to it.
“Cryptographic (crypto) agility refers to the capabilities needed to replace and adapt cryptographic algorithms in protocols, applications, software, hardware, firmware, and infrastructures while preserving security and ongoing operations.”
— NIST CSWP 39upd1, Considerations for Achieving Crypto Agility (December 2025, updated June 2026)
Swap algorithms (RSA → ML-KEM) in configuration rather than hard-coded calls. A KEM cannot encrypt data directly (NIST SP 800-227), so RSA encryption call patterns and buffer sizes still change.
Support multiple protocol versions simultaneously ( TLS 1.2/1.3, hybrid key exchange).
Switch between crypto providers (OpenSSL, BoringSSL, AWS-LC) without application changes.
Crypto agility isn't just about code — it's an architectural decision. Organizations typically use one or more of these three macro-patterns to achieve agility:
Applications link to a crypto library through an abstraction API (like JCA or OpenSSL Providers). The algorithm is selected in config, one application at a time.

chunks.title: Crypto Agility — CryptoAgilityIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Crypto Agility
Component: CryptoAgilityIntroduction

Cryptography for data-in-transit (mTLS) is completely offloaded to an infrastructure proxy (Envoy, Istio). The application behind the proxy needs no crypto code changes.
Crypto operations are outsourced over the network to a central service (AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault). Callers are insulated from the primitive, but each one still adopts new key types, handles larger outputs and is re-tested; upgrading the service is not instant enterprise-wide migration.
Before you can migrate, you need to find every cryptographic algorithm in your organization. A CBOM provides this visibility using the CycloneDX standard.
PQC migration follows a structured framework aligned with NIST IR 8547, CISA guidance, and NSA CNSA 2.0 timelines. Each phase builds on the previous.
Enabled hybrid PQC key exchange (X25519Kyber768, later X25519MLKEM768) across its network in 2024. TLS handshake times increased ~4%; hybrid client key share is 1,216 bytes vs 32 bytes for X25519 alone.
Enabled hybrid PQC key exchange (X25519Kyber768) by default in Chrome 124 (April 2024); upgraded to standardized X25519MLKEM768 in Chrome 131 (November 2024).
iMessage adopted PQ3 protocol (P-256 ECDH + Kyber-1024 initial keys, Kyber-768 rekeying ratchet — both now standardized as ML-KEM-1024 / ML-KEM-768 per FIPS 203) in iOS 17.4. Phased rollout leveraging protocol agility.
Explore abstraction layers, scan a sample CBOM, and plan a PQC migration.

Can you select cryptographic algorithms in configuration, and absorb the size, encoding and call-pattern changes that come with them?
Algorithm choices are externalized — stored in config files, environment variables, or a feature flag system rather than hardcoded in application source code.
Your systems can run multiple algorithm variants simultaneously (e.g., RSA-2048 alongside ML-KEM-768) — useful for gradual rollout and rollback.
Key material storage and transmission buffers are not hard-capped to classical sizes (e.g., no VARCHAR(256) for public keys, no fixed 32-byte shared secret assumptions).
Can your services negotiate and serve multiple protocol versions at once?
TLS endpoints are configured to offer both classical and hybrid cipher suites (e.g., X25519MLKEM768 alongside X25519), letting clients negotiate based on capability.
Adding a new protocol version or cipher suite to production does not require service downtime — configuration reload or feature-flag toggle is sufficient.

chunks.title: Crypto Agility — architecturePatterns (data)
chunks.content:
Module: Crypto Agility
Data: architecturePatterns

Business logic calls a generic crypto API. No algorithm-specific code.
Unified interface: encrypt(), sign(), verify(), keyExchange(). Algorithm-agnostic.
Configurable backend selects the actual algorithm. Changed via config, not code.
The actual cryptographic primitive: RSA, ML-KEM, X25519MLKEM768, etc.
Applications statically or dynamically link to a cryptography library (like OpenSSL or BouncyCastle) through an abstraction layer (like JCA). The design goal is that the algorithm is selected in configuration, so call sites do not change. It must still be done per application, and key and signature sizes, encodings, storage and tests still change with the algorithm.
Cryptographic operations for data-in-transit (e.g., mTLS) are completely offloaded to an infrastructure layer proxy (like Envoy or Istio). Applications speak plaintext to the proxy, so the proxy TLS configuration changes rather than application code. Certificates, peer support for the new key exchange, and anything the application does with crypto outside the mesh still need their own migration.
Cryptography is outsourced over the network to a centralized service (like AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault, or an on-prem HSM cluster). Callers are insulated from the primitive, so the change is made once in the service rather than in every application. It is not instant: callers still choose new key types, handle larger keys, signatures and ciphertexts, store them, and switch from encrypt calls to KEM encapsulate/decapsulate where a KEM replaces RSA encryption (a KEM cannot encrypt data directly — NIST SP 800-227). Rollback and testing remain per application.

chunks.content:
Module: Cryptographic APIs & Developer Languages
Component: CryptoDevAPIsExercises

Each exercise guides you through a realistic scenario using the interactive workshop steps. Work through them in order for the best learning progression, or jump to the scenario most relevant to your current project.
1. API Selection — Choose the right crypto API for a PQC-enabled payment gateway
In the API Architecture Explorer (Step 1), compare JCA/JCE and OpenSSL EVP APIs. Your payment gateway needs: cross-platform support, PKCS#11 HSM integration, and ML-DSA signing for transaction authorization. Which API scores higher for HSM integration? Which has better PQC readiness?
JCA/JCE via JCProv and OpenSSL via PKCS#11 engine both achieve HSM integration, but through different paths. OpenSSL scores higher on PQC readiness (native ML-KEM/ML-DSA/SLH-DSA since OpenSSL 3.5), while JCA/JCE has broader Java ecosystem integration. For a Java-native stack, JCA+JCProv+BouncyCastle is optimal. For a C/C++ gateway, OpenSSL 3.5+ is the clear winner.
2. Language Choice — Select the safest language for a cryptographic key management service
Open the Language Ecosystem Comparator (Step 2). You are building a key management service that handles ML-KEM key generation, wrapping, and distribution. Compare Rust, Java, and Go on: memory safety, crypto ecosystem, FFI capability, and compile-time guarantees. Which language minimizes the risk of key material exposure?

chunks.title: Cryptographic APIs & Developer Languages — CryptoDevAPIsExercises
chunks.content:
Module: Cryptographic APIs & Developer Languages
Component: CryptoDevAPIsExercises

Rust's ownership model and borrow checker prevent use-after-free on key buffers at compile time; the pqcrypto and aws-lc-rs crates provide PQC support. In Java, the JVM's garbage collector means key material may persist in memory longer before collection, though Bouncy Castle's zero-copy APIs reduce exposure. Go's garbage collector is non-deterministic for key cleanup, and compile-time memory guarantees are not provided by the language.
3. Provider Pattern — Implement algorithm-agile signing across 3 APIs
In the Provider Pattern Workshop (Step 3), select the "Sign" operation. Compare how JCA/JCE, OpenSSL, and PKCS#11 all implement ML-DSA-65 signing. Note how the provider registration pattern differs in each. What is the common abstraction that enables algorithm-agile code?
All three APIs use a two-phase pattern: (1) register/configure the provider at startup, (2) use algorithm-agnostic operations at runtime. JCA uses Security.addProvider() + Signature.getInstance("ML-DSA-65", "BC"). OpenSSL uses OSSL_PROVIDER_load() + EVP_PKEY_sign(). PKCS#11 v3.2 uses C_Initialize() + CK_MECHANISM {CKM_ML_DSA, NULL, 0} (the parameter set such as ML-DSA-65 is selected via the CKA_PARAMETER_SET key attribute). In all cases, the business logic (sign this buffer) is identical — only initialization differs.
4. PQC Library — Choose the right open-source PQC library for a regulated fintech app

chunks.title: Cryptographic APIs & Developer Languages — CryptoDevAPIsExercises
chunks.content:
Module: Cryptographic APIs & Developer Languages
Component: CryptoDevAPIsExercises

In the PQC Library Explorer (Step 5), filter by FIPS Status: "Validated". Your fintech app processes payment card data (PCI DSS), needs ML-KEM and ML-DSA support, and must be FIPS 140-3 validated. Compare the available options. Which library best satisfies all three constraints?
As of October 2026, AWS-LC (Amazon's fork of BoringSSL) is the closest fit: its AWS-LC 3 FIPS 140-3 certificates (CMVP #5298, #5314) list ML-KEM as an approved algorithm, but not ML-DSA — so ML-DSA signing would sit outside the validated boundary. Java applications reach AWS-LC through the Amazon Corretto Crypto Provider. wolfSSL has a FIPS 140-3 module and ML-KEM support, but its certificate (#4718) lists no PQC algorithm. BoringSSL's "BoringCrypto" FIPS module is validated but limited to Google's internal use case. FIPS and PQC support move quickly, so confirm each option against the PQC Library Explorer and current CMVP listings.
5. Support Matrix — Identify PQC gaps for a cross-vendor PKI migration
In the PQC Support Matrix (Step 6), open the KSP / CNG row. Your PKI uses Windows CNG for CA signing and PKCS#11 for HSM key storage. You need ML-DSA for CA signing and ML-KEM for key transport, and policy asks for an SLH-DSA root as a hedge against lattice breaks. Which of the three FIPS algorithms does the default CNG provider NOT implement, and what are your options for it? Click the cell to see the source and check date.

chunks.content:
Module: Cryptographic APIs & Developer Languages
Component: CryptoDevAPIsExercises

CNG shows ML-KEM and ML-DSA as Stable (generally available since November 2025 on Windows 11 24H2+ and Windows Server 2025), so the CA signing and key transport needs are covered on current Windows builds. SLH-DSA shows "Not implemented": BCRYPT_SLHDSA_ALGORITHM is defined, but Microsoft documents it as not currently implemented by the default CNG provider. Options for the SLH-DSA root: (1) sign it with OpenSSL 3.5+ or Bouncy Castle, which implement SLH-DSA natively; (2) generate it in an HSM through PKCS#11 v3.2 (CKM_SLH_DSA); Thales documents ML-DSA and ML-KEM from Luna firmware 7.9.0 (LMS-HSS from 7.8.9), and Utimaco’s Quantum Protect page lists SLH-DSA as "in progress" and PKCS #11 "Vendor Defined Mechanisms"; (3) use a third-party CNG key storage provider that adds SLH-DSA. Also note what the matrix separates: a CNG primitive being available does not mean Schannel negotiates it in TLS.

In the Migration Decision Lab (Step 8), use the Decision Wizard. Select: Java/Kotlin → JCA/JCE → No HSM required → Compliance: SOC 2 → Timeline: 12 months. Follow the wizard to your recommended migration path. Then click "Migration Paths" and examine the before/after code examples.
