chunks.title: Cryptographic APIs & Developer Languages — CryptoDevAPIsIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Cryptographic APIs & Developer Languages
Component: CryptoDevAPIsIntroduction

Cryptographic APIs have grown organically over decades. Each emerged from a specific need: PKCS#11 was created by RSA Laboratories in the mid-1990s to provide a vendor-neutral interface to hardware security modules. JCA/JCE debuted in the late 1990s as Sun Microsystems built cryptography into the Java platform with a pluggable provider model. CNG replaced the legacy CryptoAPI in Windows Vista, separating key storage providers from algorithm providers. OpenSSL's EVP API evolved to abstract over multiple algorithm implementations, with v3.x adding a loadable provider system.
These APIs are not interchangeable — they reflect different design philosophies, security models, and deployment targets. Understanding their relationships helps you choose correctly and design for crypto agility.
Despite their differences, all crypto APIs share a common set of abstractions:
The Java Cryptography Architecture / Extension is the standard Java cryptographic framework. Engine classes ( KeyPairGenerator, Cipher, Signature) delegate to pluggable Provider implementations registered at startup.
Open-source Java/.NET crypto library plays a dual role: as a JCA provider ( new BouncyCastleProvider() registered via Security.addProvider()), and as a standalone lightweight API for environments where JCA overhead is undesirable. BC has offered ML-KEM, ML-DSA and SLH-DSA (FIPS 203, 204, 205) since release 1.79 (October 2024).

chunks.title: Cryptographic APIs & Developer Languages — CryptoDevAPIsIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Cryptographic APIs & Developer Languages
Component: CryptoDevAPIsIntroduction

SafeNet/Thales Java PKCS#11 wrapper bridges JCA and PKCS#11 — once registered, standard JCA calls transparently hit the HSM. This is the recommended pattern for enterprise Java apps that need HSM-backed keys.
OpenSSL's EVP API (Envelope) is the high-level, algorithm-agnostic layer. Use EVP_PKEY for key objects, EVP_MD_CTX for hashing, and EVP_CIPHER_CTX for encryption. Never use the deprecated low-level APIs ( RSA_*, EC_*).
OpenSSL 3.5+ (April 2025) ships native ML-KEM, ML-DSA, and SLH-DSA in the default provider — no plugin needed. On OpenSSL before 3.5, or for algorithms that are not standardised, OSSL_PROVIDER_load(NULL, "oqsprovider") loads PQC algorithm support at runtime via the OpenSSL provider for PQC algorithms (liboqs) . Either way, the EVP call pattern stays the same when you switch to PQC. What still changes: the algorithm identifier, key, signature and ciphertext sizes (and the buffers and storage that hold them), key encodings, TLS group and signature negotiation, and the error paths for peers or builds that lack the algorithm.
PKCS#11 is a C API standard for communicating with cryptographic tokens (HSMs, smart cards, TPMs). The key objects are Slots, Tokens, and Sessions. Operations follow the pattern: C_Initialize → C_GetSlotList → C_OpenSession → C_Login → C_GenerateKeyPair → C_Sign.

chunks.title: Cryptographic APIs & Developer Languages — CryptoDevAPIsIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Cryptographic APIs & Developer Languages
Component: CryptoDevAPIsIntroduction

PKCS#11 v3.2 (OASIS Standard, 3 June 2026) adds PQC mechanisms: CKM_ML_KEM_*, CKM_ML_DSA_*, CKM_SLH_DSA_*. Hardware tokens are beginning to implement these — Thales Luna (Firmware 7.9.0+, Client 10.9.0+) and Utimaco (Quantum Protect application package) both ship it now.
PKCS#11 sessions are mandatory — unlike JCA or OpenSSL, every operation requires an open session. Session management is the #1 source of bugs in PKCS#11 implementations.
Cryptography Next Generation (Windows API) separates algorithm providers ( BCryptOpenAlgorithmProvider) from key storage providers ( NCryptOpenStorageProvider). The Key Storage Provider manages key isolation — private keys can live in software, TPM, or HSM without changing application code.
CNG integrates with the Windows certificate store and is the foundation for Windows FIPS mode. ML-KEM and ML-DSA became generally available in November 2025 on Windows 11 24H2+ and Windows Server 2025 (and .NET 10 uses them). SLH-DSA has an identifier (BCRYPT_SLHDSA_ALGORITHM) but is not currently implemented by the default CNG provider. Microsoft’s CNG identifiers page (updated 30 May 2026) still marks the composite identifiers as Insider Preview, while Microsoft’s blog (14 July 2026 update) says composite algorithms are available in Windows 11 update KB5095093 and Windows Server 2025 update KB5099536; confirm on your build.
Choosing your crypto library source is a strategic decision with long-term implications:

chunks.content:
Module: Cryptographic APIs & Developer Languages
Data: agilityPatternsData

Use the built-in provider/plugin mechanism of your crypto API to swap algorithms at configuration time. JCA providers, OpenSSL providers, and PKCS#11 modules all support this pattern natively.
Call sites stay the same when switching algorithms; the algorithm identifier, key/signature sizes, encodings, storage and error paths still need review
Limited to algorithms your provider supports
Provider selection can be driven by configuration files
Provider ordering and priority can be confusing
Well-understood pattern with decades of use
Not all APIs support pluggable providers (e.g., CNG is limited)
// Switch algorithm and provider via configuration // config.properties: crypto.sig=ML-DSA crypto.provider=SUN String alg = config.get("crypto.sig"); String providerName = config.get("crypto.provider"); Signature sig = Signature.getInstance(alg, providerName);
The Signature calls stay the same for RSA, ECDSA or ML-DSA. Still review what changes around them: key and signature sizes (ML-DSA-65 signatures are ~3.3 KB), key encodings and storage, and the exceptions a missing algorithm raises.
// Load PQC provider at startup const char *provName = getenv("CRYPTO_PROVIDER"); OSSL_PROVIDER_load(NULL, provName ? provName : "default"); // All EVP calls now use the configured provider
Environment variable or config file drives provider selection.
Algorithm selection is driven by external configuration (YAML, JSON, environment variables) rather than hardcoded in source code. A thin abstraction layer maps config keys to API calls.
Swapping between algorithms the code already supports is a config change, not a code deploy (a new algorithm family, with new sizes or call patterns, still needs code)
Need to validate config at startup to catch typos
Configuration complexity increases with more algorithms
Same binary works in FIPS and non-FIPS environments
Runtime errors if configured algorithm is unavailable

Module: Cryptographic APIs & Developer Languages
Data: apiData

Java Cryptography Architecture / Extension
The standard Java cryptographic framework providing a pluggable provider architecture. JCA covers signatures, message digests, and key management; JCE extends it with ciphers, key agreement, and MAC operations.
Engine classes (KeyPairGenerator, Cipher, Signature, MessageDigest, KeyStore) delegate to pluggable Provider implementations. Algorithm selection is string-based ("ML-DSA-65"). Provider priority order determines default implementation.
Digital signature generation/verification
Cryptographically strong random number generator
Stateless engine instances. Each Cipher/Signature instance maintains internal state through init → update → final lifecycle. Thread safety depends on provider implementation.
Java checked exceptions: NoSuchAlgorithmException, InvalidKeyException, SignatureException, NoSuchProviderException. Provider-not-found errors are compile-time catchable.
KeyPairGenerator kpg = KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("ML-DSA"); // JDK 24+ built-in // or a third-party provider: Security.addProvider(new BouncyCastleProvider()); KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("ML-DSA-65", "BC");
Built-in JDK support — …. JDK 24+ adds native ML-KEM (JEP 496) and ML-DSA (JEP 497); JDK 25 LTS has them, and Oracle backported them to Oracle JDK 21.0.13 and 17.0.21 in October 2026 (JDK 11 and 8 planned for the second half of 2027). The javax.crypto.KEM API arrived in JDK 21 (JEP 452). Bouncy Castle adds SLH-DSA (and Falcon) on any JDK and ML-KEM/ML-DSA on older JDKs. JCProv (Thales) adds PKCS#11-backed PQC when HSM firmware supports it.
A commercial Java wrapper around the PKCS#11 C API, providing Java-native access to HSM operations. Bridges the JCA provider model with hardware security modules through the Cryptoki interface.
Wraps PKCS#11 C_* functions in Java classes. Can register as a JCA provider (transparent to application code) or be used directly via its own API for fine-grained HSM control. Sessions map to PKCS#11 sessions.

Multi-paradigm (OOP, generic, procedural)

Compile-time ownership and borrowing system eliminates use-after-free, double-free, and data races. unsafe blocks required for raw pointer operations (clearly marked for audit).

The ownership system catches memory bugs that plague C code, and the type system can encode invariants like "this key is only usable for signing." The pqcrypto crate provides immediate PQC access. The main gap is FIPS certification — aws-lc-rs is closing this.

No garbage collector, no hidden control flow. comptime evaluation enables compile-time algorithm verification. Runtime safety checks (bounds checking, null detection) can be toggled. Explicit allocator passing.

However, the ecosystem is nascent — you will write C interop wrappers. Best suited for teams with existing C crypto expertise who want better tooling.
Garbage collected — no manual memory management. No buffer overflows or use-after-free. However, sensitive key material may linger in memory until GC collects it (use char[] and explicit zeroing).

What is your primary development language?

JCProv / Luna: PQC through the HSM firmware

JCProv is a Java wrapper over the PKCS#11 C API, so PQC arrives when the HSM firmware exposes the ML-KEM and ML-DSA mechanisms. Keys stay in hardware; your JCA calls change only in the algorithm names.
Botan 3.x (classical + ML-KEM, ML-DSA, SLH-DSA)
Botan 3.x ships ML-KEM, ML-DSA and SLH-DSA natively, so no extra provider or FFI layer is needed. The cost is the 2.x to 3.x API changes, not the PQC itself.
wolfSSL: Enable the PQC algorithms in your build
wolfSSL supports PQC and is FIPS validated, which makes it one of the two libraries this module lists with FIPS-certified PQC. The work is a rebuild with the PQC options on, then enabling the hybrid TLS groups.
aws-lc-rs (classical + ML-KEM, FIPS-validated backend)

chunks.title: Cryptographic Management & Modernization — Introduction
chunks.content:
Module: Cryptographic Management & Modernization
Component: Introduction

Quantum-safe migration gets the headlines, but four compounding forcing functions — one per crypto asset class — already bite every enterprise, whether a cryptographically relevant quantum computer arrives in 2030 or never. Certificates, libraries, application software, and key material each have their own deadline; managing one without the others leaves the chain weakest at the unmanaged class.
Inventory the use of cryptography for data protection across the organization by adopting an assets-centric approach … to identify the organization’s use cases and most valuable assets, such as application codes, libraries, software, hardware, firmware, user-generated content, communication protocols, enterprise services, and systems.
The four classes compound. A pristine certificate inventory does not save you when the underlying library is stuck in the CMVP queue; an upgraded library does not help if the application still calls a deprecated API; a clean codebase still fails audit if the keys it consumes live in an HSM that cannot rotate fast enough. Each driver below is already in force today.
Certificates & PKI — Organizations manage an average of 114,591 internal certificates (Ponemon Institute, Trends in PKI Security: A Global Study, sponsored by CyberArk, February 2026).

chunks.title: Cryptographic Management & Modernization — Introduction
chunks.content:
Module: Cryptographic Management & Modernization
Component: Introduction

Crypto Libraries — a module on the NIST CMVP Modules-in-Process list has a status, not a completion date, and the FIPS 140-3 Implementation Guidance added self-test requirements for FIPS 203/204/205 in August 2024 and, in September 2025, let their key-generation tests check against the private key only. You cannot “audit once” and walk away.
Application Software — OMB Memorandum M-23-02 mandates annual cryptographic-inventory submissions for US federal agencies through 2035, and EU DORA (Art. 9 — ICT risk management) and NIS2 (Art. 21 — cybersecurity measures) demand demonstrable cryptographic governance across the entire application portfolio — not just the TLS edge.
Key Material — CNSA 2.0 forces HSM and KMS roadmaps now (2030 for software/firmware signing); NIST SP 800-57 Pt 1 Rev 5 key-validity periods drive rekey cadence (Rev 6 is an initial public draft, not yet final); and orphaned keys, secrets-in-repo, and unrotated service credentials remain a top breach vector.
NIST CSWP.39 (December 2025, updated June 2026, Considerations for Achieving Crypto Agility) defines the Crypto Agility Strategic Plan as a continuously repeated five-step process. CPM is the organisational discipline that executes this loop.
Govern — embed crypto policy into standards, mandates, technology supply chains, threats, processes, business requirements, partner ecosystem, stakeholders, crypto policies, and crypto architecture.

See the Visual tab for an interactive diagram of the full CSWP.39 Fig. 3 framework — click any zone to see what belongs there, which CPM pillar it maps to, and the relevant CSWP.39 section.
CSWP.39 places a Management Tools layer between the asset inventory and the Risk Analysis Engine. Without automation at this layer, the Information Repository is populated manually and the risk engine operates on incomplete, stale data.
CSWP.39 §6.5 defines a 4-tier maturity model derived from the NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF). The Workshop's Maturity Self-Assessment maps your CPM score to the corresponding CSWP.39 tier automatically.

Module: Cryptographic Management & Modernization

Crypto agility formally integrated into risk management; roles defined; automated discovery and remediation tools deployed; agility practices tested.
Crypto agility measured and reported to executives; linked to financial and mission objectives; policies updated in near-real-time as standards and threats evolve.
Vendors and analysts routinely conflate three distinct layers. The module carves them out up front so your next conversation with a product, a consultant, or your board is unambiguous.
Technical capability: abstraction layers, protocol/provider swapping
Program: inventory · governance · lifecycle · observability · assurance
This module's view: an organization that stands up a Cryptographic Center of Excellence and a formal posture management program is in a better position to run PQC migration as a managed program than one that treats it as a one-off project. The module gives no cost figure for this.
A CPM program treats cryptography as four tightly-linked asset classes, each with its own discovery technique but rolled up under a single CBOM.

chunks.title: Cryptographic Management & Modernization — Introduction
chunks.content:
Module: Cryptographic Management & Modernization
Component: Introduction

A FIPS 140-3 algorithm certificate and an SP 800-90B Entropy Source Validation (ESV) certificate are two separate CMVP submissions. A library or HSM can hold a valid FIPS 140-3 certificate while its entropy source has never been independently validated. In this module's reading, PQC migration is the natural moment to close this gap: PQC algorithms (ML-KEM, ML-DSA) require higher-quality randomness and demand an auditable chain from validated entropy source through conditioning to the approved DRBG. Infrastructure migrations — cloud lift-and-shift, containerization, VM consolidation — are also ESV re-evaluation triggers, since they alter the entropy pool available to the OS and can silently degrade seed quality. The Assurance pillar CBOM should carry an ESV status field alongside the FIPS 140-3 validation field, and the remediation workflow must distinguish algorithm re-validation from entropy source re-validation, as timelines and responsible vendors differ.
The same CMVP change-notice subscription that tracks FIPS 140-3 Implementation Guidance updates must also track SP 800-90A/B/C revision publications and their effective dates. When a revision is issued, the CBOM workflow should trigger an impact assessment: which validated entropy sources are bound to the superseded revision, which require re-testing under the new thresholds, and which vendor roadmaps commit to updated ESV submissions.

chunks.title: Cryptographic Management & Modernization — Introduction
chunks.content:
Module: Cryptographic Management & Modernization
Component: Introduction

Entropy & Randomness (LM-009) covers the technical depth; the CMM process obligation is to track and close the status gap.
Protocol standards and cipher deprecation — a continuous tracking obligation
The cryptographic posture of an organization is not defined by libraries and certificates alone. Every protocol version and cipher suite negotiated on the wire is a posture element: TLS 1.0/1.1 deprecated by (IETF) RFC 8996, 3DES sunset by (NIST) SP 800-131A Rev 2, SHA-1 code-signing banned by CA/B Forum, RSA-1024 below NIST minimum-security thresholds, RC4 prohibited by (IETF) RFC 7465. Each of these was a standards-body decision published on a specific date with a specific effective date — and organizations that had no process to track standards-body publications discovered the gap only when auditors or scanners flagged live endpoints still negotiating deprecated suites.

chunks.title: Cryptographic Management & Modernization — Introduction
chunks.content:
Module: Cryptographic Management & Modernization
Component: Introduction

The CMM Assurance pillar must maintain a standards-watch subscription across the relevant bodies: IETF RFC Obsoletes/Updates, NIST SP 800-131A revision cycle, NSA CNSA suite announcements, CA/B Forum ballot outcomes, ETSI TS 119 312, BSI TR-02102, and ANSSI RGS. When a deprecation notice is published, the CBOM classification rules must be updated to flag the newly prohibited primitive, and the operational loop must trigger a discovery scan for affected endpoints, libraries, and application cipher-suite configurations. Remediation is not limited to patching a library version — it includes reconfiguring cipher-suite preference lists in TLS termination points, SSH server policies, IKEv2 proposals, and code-signing pipeline configurations, each of which may have separate ownership and change-management tracks.
The Observability pillar closes the loop: continuous protocol-version and cipher-suite scanning (passive TLS inspection, SSH banner collection, IKE proposal enumeration) ensures that deprecated primitives do not re-appear after routine infrastructure refreshes. A deprecation remediation that is not covered by ongoing detection is not a remediation — it is a point-in-time fix waiting to regress.
CVE management for crypto resources — three compounding constraints

chunks.title: Cryptographic Management & Modernization — Introduction
chunks.content:
Module: Cryptographic Management & Modernization
Component: Introduction

Crypto library CVEs introduce a constraint that generic vulnerability management does not encounter: patch-then-revalidate bind. Patching the library can leave the validated FIPS provider unchanged: the OpenSSL project lists validated provider versions 3.1.2, 3.0.9, 3.0.8 and 3.0.0 and says other OpenSSL releases “MAY use the validated FIPS provider”. Which provider build is in use, and whether it is on the validated list, therefore has to be tracked separately from the library version. The remediation workflow must treat the CVE fix and the validation status as two separate work items with separate timelines, and the CBOM must carry a “patch applied, revalidation in progress” state that is distinct from both “vulnerable” and “validated.”
For HSM firmware CVEs, the constraint is even harder: the validated firmware revision is chosen by the vendor, not the customer. There is no published timeline from CVE disclosure to a re-validated firmware release appearing on the CMVP active list: the Modules-in-Process list shows a resubmission's status and status date, not when it will finish (NIST CMVP Modules-in-Process list, checked 24 Sep 2026) . During that window, the organization's options are limited to residual-risk acceptance, compensating controls, or emergency procurement of an alternate validated module. This window must be tracked explicitly in the Assurance pillar, not assumed away because the vendor has acknowledged the CVE.

chunks.title: Cryptographic Product Certification: Fundamentals — CertificationContexts
chunks.content:
Module: Cryptographic Product Certification: Fundamentals
Component: CertificationContexts

FIPS 140-3, Common Criteria and EUCC are not interchangeable
CMVP validates a defined cryptographic module against FIPS 140-3. When adding PQC, check the module’s approved services, algorithm validations and applicable CMVP change requirements.
CC provides criteria for evaluating a defined product (the TOE) against its Security Target and any claimed Protection Profile. When adding PQC, check which security claims, requirements and evaluation evidence change. Identify the certification scheme separately.
For an EUCC evaluation, apply CC together with EUCC’s scheme-specific rules and applicable cryptographic guidance. EUCC rules are not automatically requirements for every CC evaluation. eIDAS is a separate legal context, relevant only where its requirements apply.
A passing algorithm test does not establish module validation or product certification. Evidence accepted in one context does not automatically satisfy another.
Sources: NIST FIPS 140-3 ; CC:2022 Part 1 ; ENISA EUCC overview .
FIPS 140-3, Common Criteria and EUCC answer different questions, and evidence accepted in one does not automatically satisfy another. The side-by-side comparison is in Cryptographic Product Certification: Fundamentals .

chunks.title: Cryptographic Product Certification: Fundamentals — PqcParameterComparison
chunks.content:
Module: Cryptographic Product Certification: Fundamentals
Component: PqcParameterComparison

“ML-DSA passed” is incomplete. Which parameter set, operation and signing mode passed? Compare three lists: what the standard defines, what this product supports, and what the report actually tested. They are not necessarily the same.
Example: a passing ML-DSA-65 pure, deterministic signing test does not by itself establish coverage of ML-DSA-87, hedged signing or HashML-DSA. Look for evidence covering the combinations the product claims to support, including whether tests exercise an internal algorithm function or the application-facing interface. This is a review aid, not a new universal certification checklist; the applicable validation or evaluation rules determine required coverage. NIST security categories are not CC assurance levels or EUCC assurance levels.
Also identify the software version and execution environment. For key import, export or wrapping, name the key representation: a regeneration seed and an expanded private key are not interchangeable byte strings. A correct signing result alone does not test backup and restore. Keep measured speed and memory use separate from correctness and certification claims.
Explore the existing SLH-DSA parameter and signing exercises . For LMS or XMSS, use the state-management exercise and review guide : a signature can verify even when unsafe reuse of a one-time signing key has occurred. These Hub exercises are learning tools, not product certification evidence.

chunks.title: Cryptographic Product Certification: Fundamentals — CoreSections
chunks.content:
Module: Cryptographic Product Certification: Fundamentals
Component: CoreSections

FIPS 140-3 specifies cryptographic-module requirements. Common Criteria provides product evaluation criteria; EUCC is one certification scheme that uses those criteria. PCI PTS HSM addresses payment HSMs. These are not four interchangeable standards. A certificate applies only to the named version, configuration, security boundary or TOE, claims and conditions shown in its official record.
Most confusion about certification starts with one sentence: “our HSM is certified.” Certified by whom, for what, and which part of it? This module distinguishes evaluation criteria from certification schemes and asks what each certificate actually covers. Once you know the scope, you also know which questions a certificate leaves open — and those are the ones a buyer, an evaluator or an auditor will ask next.
Notice what the table does not contain: a column that ranks the schemes. There is no exchange rate between a FIPS level, an EAL and a PCI approval, because they measure different things about different objects. A FIPS 140-3 validation says a defined module meets FIPS requirements (, as modified by SP 800-140A–F). A Common Criteria certificate says a TOE met the claims in its Security Target, to the depth of a named assurance package ( ). EUCC does the same under EU law ( ), with two assurance levels: substantial (AVA_VAN 1–2) and high (AVA_VAN 3–5). PCI SSC approves a payment device, and separately its standards assess the entities that run payment operations.

chunks.title: Cryptographic Product Certification: Fundamentals — CoreSections
chunks.content:
Module: Cryptographic Product Certification: Fundamentals
Component: CoreSections

A FIPS 140-3 Level 3 HSM does not obtain PTS HSM approval: that is a separate device approval by a PCI-recognized lab, assigned and listed by PCI SSC ( ). Whether a PCI operational standard (PIN Security, P2PE) accepts a FIPS certificate in place of a PTS approval is set in that standard’s own requirement text, which this module does not state — read the current standard. For the device approval, a FIPS validation never is enough.
Each of these sentences appears in real marketing, procurement and even training material. Each is false. Learn the correct statement beside it; the capstone checks your claims against this list.
Three more shortcuts concern timing and process — a market deadline treated as a certification route, SP 1800-40 read as vendor self-certification, and Executive Order 14412 treated as if it had already changed the CMVP. They are taught in the deadlines section.
US federal agency: the answer to its question — if the validated module version and approved mode are the ones it will run. Scope is the next question.
EU qualified trust service provider: nothing about the Protection Profile its eIDAS assessment expects. Identify the device, its Article 30 assessment basis and the designated certification body. EUCC evidence may be relevant where that scheme is used; a FIPS certificate alone does not establish QSCD certification or qualified-service status.

chunks.title: Cryptographic Product Certification: Fundamentals — CoreSections
chunks.content:
Module: Cryptographic Product Certification: Fundamentals
Component: CoreSections

Secure-element manufacturer: possibly useful evidence about a tool in its production site — whether its evaluator accepts it is a question to ask.
Payment processor: not device approval. Possibly enough for its PIN or P2PE HSM requirement. Its own operations still need their own assessment.
One true sentence; four different amounts of information. The Which scheme answers the question? workshop step lets you practise this with real procurement claims.
Go deeper, one scheme at a time: FIPS 140-3 Certification , Common Criteria, EUCC & eIDAS Certification and PCI Certification .

“Level 3”, “EAL4+”, “high”, “approved”: every scheme has a word that sounds like a grade. None of them means anything until you know what it is the level of. A level describes a defined boundary or TOE, at a version, in a configuration. Change any of those and the level no longer describes what you have. That is why this module teaches scope before level: read the object first, the grade second.
Before comparing any two certificates — or making any claim about your own — answer these from the official record, never from a datasheet:

chunks.title: Cryptographic Product Certification: Fundamentals — CoreSections
chunks.content:
Module: Cryptographic Product Certification: Fundamentals
Component: CoreSections

For FIPS 140-3 the Security Policy is the richest single document: it follows the SP 800-140B format ( ), names the module and its versions, lists the approved services and algorithms with their algorithm-certificate numbers, and gives the security level for each requirement area as well as the overall level. The validated-modules search is the authoritative record ( ). For Common Criteria and EUCC, read the certification report and the Security Target together: the ST says what was claimed, the report says what was evaluated and under which conditions. For PCI, the listing names the device version and its approval class, and the device Security Policy carries the algorithm detail (not sourced in the Library).
The anchor product has six components. Where each one runs decides which boundaries it can sit inside.

chunks.title: Cryptographic Product Certification: Fundamentals — CoreSections
chunks.content:
Module: Cryptographic Product Certification: Fundamentals
Component: CoreSections

Now draw the three boundaries. For Orrin N7 the FIPS 140-3 module is bounded by its tamper-responsive enclosure: appliance hardware, firmware, the crypto library compiled into it, and the firmware-enforced tenant partitions. The client SDK runs on customer hosts and the cloud front end runs on the provider’s servers, so both normally stay outside — and the validation then says nothing about them. A Common Criteria TOE is whatever the Security Target defines; it could be drawn larger (claiming the administration interfaces, for example) or smaller, and a Protection Profile may constrain it. A PCI PTS HSM approval names the device — model, hardware and firmware version — up to initial deployment; the way a processor then operates it is assessed separately.
Every scheme has a rule for this. The CMVP’s Management Manual defines the revalidation routes for a changed module ( ). Common Criteria and EUCC use assurance continuity. PCI uses delta evaluations of an approved device. None of them lets a changed product inherit the old result silently; the agility and deadlines sections show how to plan around that.
FIPS 140-3 has four security levels, with an overall level and a level per requirement area. Level 1 is not “software-only”, and the level you need follows from the threat and the environment — not from “highest available”.

chunks.title: Cryptographic Product Certification: Fundamentals — CoreSections
chunks.content:
Module: Cryptographic Product Certification: Fundamentals
Component: CoreSections

Common Criteria expresses depth as an EAL plus named augmentations — for example the EN 419221-5 Protection Profile requires EAL4 augmented with AVA_VAN.5 ( ), and the Security IC Platform PP requires EAL4 augmented with ALC_DVS.2, ALC_FLR.2 and AVA_VAN.5 ( ). “EAL4+” alone tells you nothing.
PCI PTS HSM has no levels. The listing marks an approval restricted (valid only in a controlled environment) or unrestricted.

chunks.title: Cryptographic Product Certification: Fundamentals — SharedSections
chunks.content:
Module: Cryptographic Product Certification: Fundamentals
Component: SharedSections

The algorithms themselves are standardised: ML-KEM in , ML-DSA in and SLH-DSA in . A standard tells you what an algorithm is. It tells you nothing about whether a particular product implements it correctly, protects its keys, tests itself, resists side channels, or was evaluated by anyone. That is the certification schemes’ job — and it is why “we support ML-KEM” and “our ML-KEM is certified” are different sentences.
The Implementation Guidance items named above are from the current FIPS 140-3 IG ( , last updated 19 August 2026). For an HSM the hardware list is often the harder half: side-channel and fault analysis for lattice arithmetic is new work for most labs and most vendors, and the evidence for it cannot be copied from the RSA era.
Keep two columns apart: what applies today, and what is only a planning implication. Mixing them is the most common PQC certification error — a draft taught as a requirement, or a requirement dismissed as a draft.

chunks.title: Cryptographic Product Certification: Fundamentals — SharedSections
chunks.content:
Module: Cryptographic Product Certification: Fundamentals
Component: SharedSections

Three distinct observations matter here. First, EUCC has PQC guidance: the applicable ECCG ACM v2 () already names the PQC mechanisms and parameter sets (its hybrid rules are in the table below). Do not turn that guidance into a blanket legal requirement; check the applicable scheme rules, PP and Security Target. Second, FIPS 140-3 certificates with PQC already exist: four active Level 3 HSM certificates approve ML-KEM and ML-DSA, so “no validated PQC module exists” is false ( ). Third, PCI names no PQC algorithm or date in its standards: the listing notation says only that PQC support exists ( ), and the public PCI DSS v4.0.1 announcement states no PQC algorithm, parameter set or deadline for the standard ( ). PCI SSC’s blog does host guest posts in which HSM vendors discuss ML-KEM and ML-DSA ( , , September and October 2026); these are vendor views, not PCI requirements.
Executive Order 14412 has not changed the CMVP: §6(b) gives NIST 180 days to revise the program’s processes, which falls around 19 December 2026 ( The standard itself is unchanged: NIST's CMVP page lists FIPS 140-3 as published in March 2019, and the order concerns the validation process, which it directs NIST to speed up.

chunks.title: Cryptographic Product Certification: Fundamentals — SharedSections
chunks.content:
Module: Cryptographic Product Certification: Fundamentals
Component: SharedSections

What this means for a certification engineer: a product sold into both the US and the EU should be designed with hybrid in mind. Standalone ML-KEM or ML-DSA can be fine for a FIPS 140-3 validation but falls short of the EUCC guidance and the German and French positions. If the product offers a hybrid, check that its FIPS module meets the IG D.S conditions — a hybrid the module does not enforce cannot be claimed as an approved service. Hash-based signatures are the exception almost everywhere: they may stand alone.
How to build a hybrid signature is being standardised now: IETF Composite ML-DSA (ML-DSA paired with RSA, ECDSA, Ed25519 or Ed448) is approved and awaiting RFC publication ( ; tracked in ENISA’s ). Neither the FIPS 140-3 Implementation Guidance nor the ECCG mechanisms (v2 or the v3 draft) names it yet. Re-check before relying on this table.
Every statement about PQC and certification belongs to exactly one of these tiers. Label it, and most errors disappear.
When a datasheet says “FIPS 140-3 validated with ML-KEM”, open the Security Policy and check, in order:
Is the algorithm in the approved algorithm table, with an algorithm (CAVP) certificate number — or only mentioned elsewhere in the document?
Which services use it in approved mode — key generation, encapsulation, signing, verification — and which roles may call them?

chunks.title: Cryptographic Product Certification: Fundamentals — SharedSections
chunks.content:
Module: Cryptographic Product Certification: Fundamentals
Component: SharedSections

For a PCI listing, the PQC notation answers only the first half of question 1 (“support exists”); the rest is in the device’s Security Policy. For CC and EUCC, the answers are in the Security Target’s cryptographic SFRs and the certification report.
FIPS 140-3: new approved services, SSPs and self-tests; ML-KEM and ML-DSA algorithm testing; an updated Security Policy; a revalidation route the lab proposes and the CMVP decides.
Common Criteria: new cryptographic SFRs in the Security Target; an impact analysis; very likely re-evaluation of the affected claims.
EUCC: review the applicable scheme rules and cryptographic guidance. ACM v2 recommends mechanisms, parameter choices and hybridisation for ML-KEM; the mechanism name alone does not determine acceptance of an implementation.
PCI: a new firmware version to scope with a recognized lab; the Security Policy’s algorithm tables change; the listing notation, if set, still means only “PQC support exists”.
Nothing in that list is covered by the baseline’s certificates. The next section is about introducing PQC anyway, promptly, without breaking what is certified.
A CAVP certificate for “ML-KEM EncapDecap” for each implemented parameter set (512, 768, 1024), with “Decapsulation Key Check” and “Encapsulation Key Check” under Functions, unless the lab shows “assurance that these checks have been performed […] through other means”; “ML-KEM KeyGen” if the module generates key pairs

chunks.title: Cryptographic Product Certification: Fundamentals — SharedSections
chunks.content:
Module: Cryptographic Product Certification: Fundamentals
Component: SharedSections

If approved: key-agreement testing under IG D.F. If not (X25519, X448): the Security Policy lists it as a “non-approved but allowed algorithm with no security claimed”
SP 800-56C key derivation (“KDA HKDF” counts), or an SP 800-133 §6.3 method. The SP 800-133 method “cannot combine shared secrets that are NOT already keys (e.g., cannot operate on the Z value computed via SP 800-56A or SP 800-56B methods) nor can it incorporate non-approved schemes”, so a non-approved classical half such as X25519 needs the SP 800-56C route.
Algorithm test vectors for the KDF (“KDA HKDF” for HKDF); for SP 800-133, HMAC testing if HMAC is used for key extraction, plus a key-generation claim that is not CAVP-testable
The fixed set of combinations and the order the secrets are joined (for example SecP256r1MLKEM768, X25519MLKEM768, SecP384r1MLKEM1024)
The Security Policy’s hybrid entries and the lab’s compliance demonstration
Not an algorithm test: the lab checks it “via source code review and/or functional testing”
“There is currently no separate self-test requirement for the approved key combiner”, but approved algorithms used for the key combiner (for example an SP 800-56C KDF or HMAC) “must still meet applicable self-test requirements per IG 10.3.A”
A hybrid key establishment is not one line on a certificate. IG D.S sets five conditions, and they are evidenced in different places: CAVP certificates, the Security Policy and the lab’s own review. Several of them no algorithm test can show.

chunks.title: Cryptographic Product Certification: Fundamentals — SharedSections
chunks.content:
Module: Cryptographic Product Certification: Fundamentals
Component: SharedSections

The FIPS 140-3 Implementation Guidance ( ) says a module claims a hybrid only if it has an approved ML-KEM, one or more other key-establishment schemes, an approved key combiner, a fixed set of combinations, and control of how the secrets are joined. The Security Policy records the claim as “KEM-Hybrid” or “KEM-Hybrid-Full” in its security-function table (for the “Full” variants the key-establishment method must also be listed under AS09.10), and the lab shows compliance for each hybrid set the module implements.
Where each part of a hybrid key establishment shows on paper, and what “tested” means for it
An approved ML-KEM is not a hybrid claim. If the module lacks any of the five items, “Scenario 2 of this IG shall not be claimed”, and a non-approved classical scheme must stay in the non-approved mode.
The module must enforce it. A non-approved classical half such as X25519 is allowed in the approved mode only inside an approved hybrid, and the module has to enforce that: “It cannot be enforced by operator guidance within the Security Policy.” (An approved classical scheme, such as P-256 under IG D.F, can also be used on its own.)
A named hybrid is not automatic. The IG says the TLS 1.3 hybrid sets “may meet” Scenario 2 and that the X-Wing hybrid KEM “cannot yet meet” it; it adds that the specifications “may still be in draft form and thus subject to change”. Check the date of the guidance you rely on.

chunks.title: Cryptographic Product Certification: Fundamentals — SharedSections
chunks.content:
Module: Cryptographic Product Certification: Fundamentals
Component: SharedSections

There is no end-to-end hybrid test yet. The IG leaves room for one “if available within CAVP” and says it will be updated when it is. Until then, each part is evidenced separately.
In a Common Criteria or EUCC certificate the algorithm claims sit in the Security Target’s cryptographic requirements, not in the assurance level. The EU’s agreed cryptographic mechanisms ( ) say LWE- or MLWE-based mechanisms “shouldn’t be used in a standalone way to provide the intended security functionality, but should be combined with a well established classical cryptomechanism”, and ENISA’s states that its alignment tables are “indicative, not recommendations”. Ask whether the Security Target lists the combined construction or only its components, and what the evaluator’s cryptographic assessment covered.
The five conditions in full: Hybrid Cryptography, Hybrid in a validated module (IG D.S)
The two meanings of “hybrid” in FIPS 140-3: FIPS 140-3 Certification, Today’s landscape and the 2026 horizon
Where to read a real certificate’s Approved Algorithms: Compliance, Product Records
What the algorithm test covers: Validation Workbench , run the ML-KEM cases

chunks.title: Cryptographic Product Certification: Fundamentals — SharedSections
chunks.content:
Module: Cryptographic Product Certification: Fundamentals
Component: SharedSections

Crypto agility means being able to replace or add algorithms, parameters, implementations, providers, accelerators, protocols, keys and operational environments without redesigning the product. Certification establishes assurance for a precisely identified version, boundary or TOE, configuration and evidence set at a point in time. The two are not contradictory — but a cryptographic change can alter exactly what was evaluated.
The three run at different speeds and nobody controls all of them. The engineering goal is not “certification-free agility”. It is stable boundaries, reusable evidence, controlled variants, automated tests and pre-agreed change classifications, so that each change triggers only the reassessment it really needs.
Preserve validity: never silently mutate the certified artifact or its claimed configuration.
Minimise recertification scope: stable boundaries, evidence reuse and the scheme’s legitimate change path.
Introduce PQC promptly: develop and test the candidate in parallel, but activate certification-dependent claims only when official coverage exists.
Where a product must expose PQC before certification finishes, say precisely that the feature is experimental, non-approved-mode or outside the certified configuration — and only if the scheme and the architecture allow that separation. Never weaken approved-mode enforcement, and never use a disclaimer to escape the certified boundary.

chunks.title: Cryptographic Product Certification: Fundamentals — SharedSections
chunks.content:
Module: Cryptographic Product Certification: Fundamentals
Component: SharedSections

Each scheme has its own way to handle a change. You do not need the full route tables to plan — you need the questions that decide which route is even possible. The lab proposes; the authority decides.
Route definitions: CMVP Management Manual v2.7 (9 April 2026) §7.1; CCDB-015 v3.1 (29 February 2024); CIR (EU) 2025/2462. Link to the live documents rather than memorising the tables — they change.
Recent improvements reduce avoidable friction for the card-payment device program: minor changes that do not affect security can be handled by submitting documentation to the lab, while changes that do affect security requirements still need another evaluation. NIST describes its CMVP automation work as in progress.
So the goal is not “the certificate never changes”. It is continuous, truthful coverage: at every release, anyone can tell which artifact and which mechanisms are covered, which are being evaluated, and which are outside scope.
The vendor “bears all responsibility”. “The CMVP makes no statement as to the correct operation of the module or the security strengths of the generated keys” in an environment not listed on the certificate, and the Security Policy must say so. “This shall require CAVP-testing the algorithm validations on the new/modified OEs”, entropy-source validation covering the new environments where applicable, and the full regression test. Code changes only if non-security-relevant and needed to run there. The CMVP then “provides the same assurance as the original OE(s)”.
“This is not porting or vendor affirming the OE” but putting the new environment onto the certificate as part of a changed module.
A validation is a statement about one module on the environments it was tested on. Move the module, and the statement stops where the testing stopped.
Why the environment is part of the claim. The FIPS 140-3 Implementation Guidance ( ) puts it plainly: “The validation certificate serves as a benchmark for the configuration and operational environment used during the validation testing.” The rule reaches down to the algorithm certificates the module uses. If an implementation was tested on a 32-bit processor, “a claim cannot be made that the implementation also runs on different bit size processors”, and likewise for another operating system. For a software module, the algorithm implementation “must have been tested on every operating environment claimed by the software module.”

The Common Criteria view. ENISA’s assurance-continuity guidance ( ) sorts a platform change by what the Security Target says about the platform. If the new platform does not meet the stated assumptions, the change is “Always major regardless of the assurance level – requires re-evaluation”. A move between near-identical operating system releases is rated Minor; a change from Intel to Arm hardware is rated Major because of “Changes in boot chain, memory model, crypto acceleration”. And a migration that causes “measurable changes to timing or resource behaviour” is “Always major at AVA_VAN.4 and 5, due to side-channel attacks”; at lower assurance levels it “may be minor if no impact is shown”.
What to ask a vendor who says “it runs the same on our new hardware”. Is the new platform on the certificate, or only affirmed by the vendor? Which route was used? Was the accelerated path tested, and is it a known accelerator? Were the algorithm certificates re-tested on that platform, and the entropy source? If a Common Criteria certificate exists, does the Security Target’s platform assumption still hold?

The first clock has already struck: on 21/22 September 2026 every FIPS 140-2 certificate moved to the Historical list. Those modules may still be bought and used for existing systems, but NIST says Federal Agencies should not include them in new systems. That is what a scheme transition looks like from the inside. It is not a TRNS event either: the CMVP’s TRNS route exists only for published CMVP algorithm transitions (for example the 2024 non-SP 800-56Brev2 RSA key-encapsulation transition, Management Manual §7.1.12).
Three more shortcuts belong here. SP 1800-40 does not let vendors self-certify: its Volume B draft demonstrates an accredited lab making a first submission to the CMVP ( ). Executive Order 14412 has not already changed the CMVP; its process revision is due around 19 December 2026. And a deadline is never certification evidence — neither is a Modules-in-Process entry, nor a PCI PQC flag.
The plan that works is the two-lane release: the certified lane stays valid while the PQC lane moves through each scheme’s real route, and the timing question becomes “when must the PQC lane start?” rather than “which rule can we bend?”.

The Management Manual v2.7 (, 9 April 2026, §7.1) defines the submission scenarios; the full table is in CMVP submission routes in the FIPS 140-3 Certification module. For a PQC addition, five are decisive:
ALG — only for “a previously vendor affirmed or allowed algorithm that was available in the approved mode now has CAVP testing available and already meets the algorithm requirements (e.g., self-tests) and module requirements (e.g., approved service indicator)”. “Code or configuration changes are not permitted.”
UPDT — “less than 30% of security changes”, assessed separately in each of five categories: functions / algorithms, SSPs, services, self-tests, FSM states. The CMVP may decide the change is a Full Submission.
CVE — vulnerability and security-relevant maintenance fixes; changes “shall not introduce new features or cryptography”.
TRNS — only for changes made solely in response to a published CMVP algorithm transition (§7.1.12). A “soft” transition permits no changes.
FS — a Full Submission, including the INTU sub-type (“Br1 Update to Interim”) that follows an interim validation.
Under CCDB-015 v3.1 ( ), the developer proposes and documents the impact in an Impact Analysis Report; the certification body classifies it.
Maintenance (minor change): an optional subset evaluation and partial ETR, a maintenance addendum — with “no implied issuance of an updated certificate” — and a published Maintenance Report.

Watch for “a set of minor changes that together have a major impact”: shipping PQC as five small releases does not make it minor.
EUCC uses CC evaluation evidence but sets its own continuity rules in EU law. Under CIR 2025/2462 ( ), a minor change leads to a maintenance report, and “no new certificate shall be issued”; when the assurance measures of the development environment change, the certification body may request a subset evaluation and a partial ETR. After a successful re-assessment, the certification body should confirm the certificate or issue a new certificate with an extended expiry date. the change-scenarios guideline, v1, October 2025, focused on AVA work

Test-vector protocol. ACVP exchanges machine-readable algorithm capabilities, vectors, responses and verdicts ( ). It speeds up algorithm testing, not module validation.

Specialised validation API. The ESV server accepts entropy-source and RBG submissions through a protocol “based on ACVP” ( ). A reusable entropy validation avoids repeating that work in every module submission.
Structured submission record. The CMVP “uses JSON as the submission format” for the Module Information Structure, to automate verification and processing and to populate parts of the Security Policy from one source.
Broader evidence exchange (draft). SP 1800-40B, an Initial Public Draft of 15 April 2026, demonstrates JSON-schema certificate requests and evidence catalogues sent by an accredited lab ( ). It covers first (full) submissions only; CVE and added-OE submissions are named as future phases. Comments closed on 1 June 2026.
Machine-readable evidence can reduce transcription, completeness errors, duplicate data and review handling time. It does not prove the evidence is sufficient, remove evaluator judgement, expand a certificate’s scope, or turn a draft protocol into an approved validation.
Vendors already produce most of the raw material: the implementation inventory, Security Policy inputs, source and build evidence, design documents, change-impact analysis, test access and remediation responses. But the accredited lab tests and submits, and the evidence catalogues in the SP 1800-40B demonstration are lab submissions. Vendor evidence can be structured; the lab still verifies it and stays in the assurance chain.

Module: CycloneDX Cryptography Registry
Component: CryptoRegistryIntroduction

f.variant.map((v) => v.primitive))) .size export const CryptoRegistryIntroduction: FC
The same cryptographic mechanism gets a different name from every angle you look at it — CKM_ECDSA_SHA256 to an HSM, OID 1.2.840.10045.4.3.2 to a certificate, ES256 to a JWT, code point 0x0403 to TLS 1.3. A CBOM (or any inventory) built from several discovery tools inherits all of these inconsistent names — and nothing lines up until you normalize them.
CycloneDX v1.7 answers this with the Cryptography Registry: one versioned, machine-readable list of canonical algorithm-family and elliptic-curve names, each backed by its standardization reference (RFC, FIPS, IEEE, ISO).
ML-KEM, ML-DSA, SLH-DSA, XMSS and LMS are registered algorithm families alongside RSA, ECDSA and AES — not a separate or bolted-on list. For a PQC-readiness review, that means one place to check whether a mechanism a scanner found is quantum-safe, quantum-vulnerable, or a stateful hash-based signature that needs its own state-management scrutiny.
PQC makes normalization harder, not easier: ML-DSA registers one OID per parameter set (RFC 9881's id-ml-dsa-44/65/87), so a single family fans out into several distinct identifiers a tool must still resolve back to “ML-DSA”.
The registry ships as its own versioned JSON + JSON Schema, decoupled from the CycloneDX specification release cycle — it can add a new algorithm family without waiting for the next CycloneDX version.

chunks.title: DNSSEC & Post-Quantum Signatures — DNSSECExercises
chunks.content:
Module: DNSSEC & Post-Quantum Signatures
Component: DNSSECExercises

Work through these scenarios to see exactly why DNSSEC’s PQC transition is constrained by message size, and where the real Cloudflare deployment sits in the bigger migration picture. Each exercise pre-configures the Workshop — click "Load & Run" to begin.
Take the PQC quiz to test what you've learned about DNSSEC and post-quantum signatures.
1. Compare Signature Sizes Against the DNS UDP Ceiling
Step through RSA-2048, ECDSA P-256, Ed25519, ML-DSA-44, and SLH-DSA-SHA2-128s signature sizes against DNS’s practical ~1,232-byte UDP response limit.
ML-DSA-44 (2,420 B) alone exceeds the UDP ceiling by roughly 2x; SLH-DSA-SHA2-128s (7,856 B) exceeds it by more than 6x. Every classical algorithm shown fits comfortably under it.
2. Walk the PQ Validation Chain
Step through the root → TLD → domain DS/DNSKEY/RRSIG trust chain and see exactly where algorithm 18 sits today versus where it would need to sit for full deployment.
In this simplified illustration, algorithm 18 exists only at the leaf (dnstest.dev’s own zone). Every level above it — the .dev TLD and the DNS root — still delegates classically, so the chain of trust as a whole is not yet post-quantum.
3. Track the Deployment Roadmap
Review Cloudflare's own roadmap from resolver validation through authoritative signing and registrar DS support, and see how it compares to the DNS root's separate rollover estimate.

chunks.title: DNSSEC & Post-Quantum Signatures — DNSSECIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: DNSSEC & Post-Quantum Signatures
Component: DNSSECIntroduction

DNSSEC (DNS Security Extensions, RFC 4034, consolidated in RFC 9364/BCP 237) adds cryptographic signatures to DNS answers. A resolver that validates DNSSEC can prove a DNS record came from the zone's real owner and was not altered or forged in transit — it chains trust from the DNS root, through each delegated zone's DS record, down to the DNSKEY/RRSIG pair that signs the actual answer.
DNSSEC is signature-only — it protects authenticity and integrity, not confidentiality. There is no ciphertext to harvest today and decrypt later. The quantum threat here is that a cryptographically relevant quantum computer would let an attacker forge a DNSSEC signature on any RSA- or ECDSA-signed zone, right now, the day such a computer exists — not retroactively.
Today's most widely deployed DNSSEC signature algorithms are RSA and ECDSA (RFC 6605). Both rely on integer factorization or elliptic-curve discrete logarithm hardness — exactly the problems Shor's algorithm breaks.
draft-westerbaan-dnssec-mldsa (Westerbaan/Cloudflare, Schmieg/Google) specifies DNSSEC's DS, DNSKEY, and RRSIG resource records for ML-DSA-44 — the smallest of FIPS 204's three parameter sets (44 / 65 / 87), chosen specifically to minimize DNS message size. IANA has assigned it DNSSEC algorithm number 18 (mnemonic MLDSA44).

chunks.title: DNSSEC & Post-Quantum Signatures — DNSSECIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: DNSSEC & Post-Quantum Signatures
Component: DNSSECIntroduction

An RRSIG carrying a 2,420-byte ML-DSA-44 signature dwarfs 1,232 bytes — a common conservative UDP payload limit (RFC 9715 recommends up to 1,400 bytes). Responses over that limit need another transport, normally TCP — a real operational cost, not just a theoretical one. Signature size is one of several open migration challenges alongside compatibility and downgrade protection; the specification remains an individual draft rather than a working-group-adopted standard.
RFC 6840 recommends lenient validators accept any single valid signature path. If a zone is signed with both ML-DSA-44 and a quantum-vulnerable algorithm, a future quantum attacker could strip the ML-DSA-44 RRSIG and have a lenient validator accept the forged classical one instead. The draft's own fix: a validator that requires ML-DSA-44 whenever the zone's DS record advertises it avoids the downgrade.
On 2026-09-10, Cloudflare announced that ML-DSA-44 (algorithm 18) DNSSEC validation is enabled by default on the 1.1.1.1 public resolver, alongside dnstest.dev, a live ML-DSA-44-signed test zone resolvers can validate against. This is a real production deployment of ML-DSA-44 validation on Cloudflare's resolver — not just a draft.
A production DNS resolver can validate ML-DSA-44 signatures by default, at Cloudflare's scale, against a real signed zone.

chunks.title: DNSSEC & Post-Quantum Signatures — DNSSECIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: DNSSEC & Post-Quantum Signatures
Component: DNSSECIntroduction

No production zone — not dnstest.dev's own real-world siblings, not a registry, not a registrar, not the DNS root — has been signed with a PQ algorithm. This is resolver-side validation of one test zone, not authoritative-side signing.
See the Protocol Support matrix's DNSSEC row for the full, continuously-tracked deployment record behind this claim.
Cloudflare's own roadmap names two concrete steps still ahead before PQ DNSSEC can run end-to-end in production:
Done (pilot) Resolver-side validation of ML-DSA-44 (1.1.1.1, by default)
Next Authoritative-side signing support — zones need to be signable with ML-DSA, not just validatable
And Registrar DS-record support — parent-zone delegation needs algorithm-18 DS records for the chain of trust to reach a signed zone
Cloudflare's own company-wide post-quantum security target is ~2029 — the blog post doesn't give a separate, DNSSEC-specific completion date, and delivering Cloudflare's own two features above is not the same as full end-to-end PQ DNSSEC: that also needs the root to become a trusted PQ anchor and other registries/registrars to adopt algorithm 18. Keep that distinct from the DNS root zone's own algorithm rollover, which Verisign estimates at the mid-2030s — every level of the chain needs PQ support before the downgrade-safety design above is fully post-quantum-secure, though the order in which levels migrate isn't prescribed. Keep the two numbers separate: one vendor's roadmap, one global infrastructure migration.

chunks.title: DNSSEC & Post-Quantum Signatures — DNSSECIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: DNSSEC & Post-Quantum Signatures
Component: DNSSECIntroduction

Two parallel efforts attack the same signature-size problem differently: draft-sheth-pqc-dnssec-strategy surveys SLH-DSA-MTL, Falcon, XMSS, and LMS as DNSSEC candidates, while draft-fregly-dnsop-slh-dsa-mtl-dnssec and draft-kaizer-dnsop-ml-dsa-mtl-dnssec both apply Merkle Tree Ladder mode — to SLH-DSA and ML-DSA respectively — to shrink the per-query signature cost. None of these has IETF working-group status yet.

Work through these real-world scenarios to apply data classification, compliance mapping, risk methodology comparison, and sensitivity scoring. Each exercise pre-configures the Workshop to the relevant step — click "Load & Run" to begin.
Take the PQC quiz to check your understanding of data classification, compliance frameworks, and risk management methodologies.
1. Healthcare HNDL Classification Challenge
A regional hospital system stores electronic health records (ePHI) under HIPAA. The regulation requires 6-year minimum retention from last patient encounter — but records are routinely kept 30+ years in practice. Using the Asset Inventory Builder, create an asset entry for this ePHI database: Asset Type = Data Store, Sensitivity = High, Retention = 25+ years, Industry = Healthcare. Then check the HNDL Risk Year column.
With a 30-year retention period and High sensitivity, the HNDL risk year is 2034 − 30 = 2004. In effect, data collected as far back as 2004 (the CRQC year minus the retention period) is already in adversary archives. When you run this asset through the Sensitivity Scoring Engine (Step 4), the composite score will be ≥ 85 — placing it in the Critical urgency band. HIPAA + NIST IR 8547 compliance flags add further urgency.
2. Multi-Jurisdiction Financial Institution

chunks.title: Data & Asset Sensitivity — DataAssetExercises
chunks.content:
Module: Data & Asset Sensitivity
Component: DataAssetExercises

Your bank operates across the US, EU, and Australia. In the Compliance Matrix (Step 2), select "Finance & Banking" as your industry. Identify which compliance frameworks apply. Your TLS server certificates (ECDSA P-256) rotate every 90 days. In the Risk Methodology Explorer (Step 3), apply the DORA/NIS2 tab to a communication channel asset. Is the ECDSA P-256 encryption compliant with "state-of-the-art" requirements? What does the FAIR model say about the ALE for non-migration?
Finance & Banking maps to DORA, GDPR, PCI DSS, NIST IR 8547, ISO 27001, and FIPS 140-3. The DORA/NIS2 tab will flag ECDSA P-256 as a potential "Protect" gap — "state-of-the-art" is a living standard that increasingly implies PQC planning. Short-lived TLS certs (under-1y retention) have low HNDL risk individually, but the FAIR ALE for non-migration is dominated by DORA periodic-penalty risk (a share of average daily worldwide turnover, for critical ICT third-party providers), easily outweighing migration costs.
3. Root CA Migration — Methodology Comparison
Your organization's offline Root CA (RSA-4096, 25-year lifespan, CNSA 2.0 scope) needs PQC migration. In the Risk Methodology Explorer (Step 3), select the Root CA Signing Key asset and apply all four tabs: NIST RMF, ISO 27005, FAIR, and DORA/NIS2. Compare how each methodology assesses urgency. Which produces the highest urgency score? Then jump to Step 5 (Priority Map) to see the recommended PQC algorithm.

chunks.title: Data & Asset Sensitivity — DataAssetExercises
chunks.content:
Module: Data & Asset Sensitivity

NIST RMF categorizes the root CA as FIPS 199 "High" impact — for national security systems, CNSA 2.0 specifies CRYSTALS-Dilithium with Level V parameters for signing (with LMS/XMSS for software/firmware signing); software and firmware signing should transition to exclusive CNSA 2.0 use by 2030, while large PKI systems should support and favor CNSA 2.0 by 2030, moving to exclusive use by 2033. ISO 27005 scores it Critical risk (Likelihood 3 × Consequence 5 = 15) — treatment: Mitigate, immediate. FAIR ALE is highest for this asset because root CA compromise enables forging all certificates — catastrophic loss magnitude drives ALE into the tens of millions. DORA/NIS2 Protect pillar fails because RSA-4096 will no longer meet "state-of-the-art." For a CNSA 2.0-scoped CA, the compliant choice is ML-DSA-87; where CNSA compliance is not required, the Priority Map highlights SLH-DSA (stateless hash-based) as the most conservative long-term option for key material with indefinite validity periods.
4. Build Your Own Priority Map

chunks.title: Data & Asset Sensitivity — DataAssetIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Data & Asset Sensitivity
Component: DataAssetIntroduction

The Harvest Now, Decrypt Later (HNDL) threat means adversaries are collecting encrypted data today — storing it until a Cryptographically Relevant Quantum Computer (CRQC) arrives to break it. The critical question is: which of your data is worth harvesting?
The answer depends on how sensitive the data is and how long it needs to remain confidential. You cannot prioritize your PQC migration without first knowing what data assets you hold, how sensitive they are, and what compliance frameworks govern their protection.
In NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, RMF step 1 is Prepare and step 2 is Categorize. Our view: data classification is not optional; it is the foundation of any risk-based approach to cryptographic migration.
The app uses a four-tier sensitivity model aligned with NIST FIPS 199 impact levels and common enterprise data governance frameworks. Each tier carries a distinct HNDL risk level and PQC migration urgency.
Asset type also matters: Key material (root CA keys, HSM-protected secrets) should always be classified Critical regardless of sensitivity tier — even if the data it protects is Medium. Keys are the root of trust for everything above them.
Cross-reference: The PQC Risk Management module has a CRQC Scenario Planner where you can adjust the CRQC arrival year and model your organizational risk profile in detail.

chunks.title: Data & Asset Sensitivity — DataAssetIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Data & Asset Sensitivity
Component: DataAssetIntroduction

Ten major data protection laws govern how organizations must protect data — and all of them require cryptographic measures that will be affected by the transition to PQC. The table below summarizes each law's PQC relevance and current mandate status.
Conflicting requirements: PIPL's GM algorithm mandate (SM2, SM3, SM4) conflicts with NIST-aligned PQC standards for cross-border data controllers. Organizations operating in both China and the EU or US should seek legal guidance on the applicable encryption standard per data flow direction.
Four methodologies are available to assess the risk of your data assets from a PQC perspective. This section gives you the conceptual foundation; the PQC Risk Management module applies all four hands-on.
Which to use? Most organizations use NIST RMF if they are US federal contractors, ISO 27005 if they hold ISO 27001 certification, FAIR if they need board-level financial justification, and DORA/NIS2 if they are in scope for EU regulation. For a hands-on deep dive applying all four frameworks to your assets, see the PQC Risk Management module.
The 5-step workshop takes you through a complete data governance workflow — from cataloging your assets to generating a prioritized PQC migration list. By the end, you'll have a structured output you can take to your security team.
Or explore related: PQC Risk Management · Compliance Strategy · Assessment Wizard

chunks.title: Database Encryption & PQC — DatabaseEncryptionIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Database Encryption & PQC
Component: DatabaseEncryptionIntroduction

Not all data-at-rest needs the same treatment. Describe the dataset and this chooser recommends a migration strategy — from cheapest (key-wrap) to most expensive (re-encrypt), or crypto-shred when migration isn't worth it.
Source: Applied Quantum PQC Migration Framework §5.6 (Data-at-rest strategy).
Database encryption is not a single switch — it is a layered architecture. Each layer addresses a different threat model. From outermost to innermost:
TDE encrypts database files on disk (data pages, log files, backups) using AES-256. It protects against physical theft of storage media or backup exfiltration — but provides no protection against a privileged DBA who has direct database access. The database engine decrypts data transparently on read.
Threat covered: stolen backup tapes, cloud storage breach, decommissioned disks
Threat NOT covered: DBA with SELECT privilege, memory scraping, SQL injection
CLE encrypts specific columns (PAN, SSN, date-of-birth) using per-column keys. In Always Encrypted (SQL Server), the Column Master Key (CMK) lives in Azure Key Vault or an HSM — the database engine never sees the plaintext CMK, only the Column Encryption Key (CEK) wrapped by it. A DBA querying the column sees only ciphertext.

chunks.title: Database Encryption & PQC — DatabaseEncryptionIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Database Encryption & PQC
Component: DatabaseEncryptionIntroduction

FLE is performed by the application before data reaches the database wire. MongoDB FLE 1.0/2.0 encrypts document fields client-side; the server stores only ciphertext. Key material never leaves the application, so the server stores only ciphertext. This architecture limits server-side query capabilities.
Queryable Encryption (MongoDB FLE 2.0, SQL Server Always Encrypted with secure enclaves) allows specific query types (equality, range) to execute on encrypted data without full decryption. MongoDB uses HMAC-SHA-256 equality tokens and structured encryption over fully randomized ciphertext for range queries. SQL Server uses secure enclaves (VBS or SGX) to execute queries on plaintext inside a trusted execution environment.
AES-256 symmetric encryption used at every layer is already quantum-safe (Grover's algorithm reduces effective security to 128 bits — still above the 112-bit minimum).
Key ownership architecture determines who can access plaintext key material — and therefore who can decrypt your database. Three models exist, with dramatically different PQC readiness:
Cloud provider generates and stores all key material. PQC migration timeline is entirely at the provider's discretion. No customer control over ML-KEM adoption date.

chunks.title: Database Encryption & PQC — DatabaseEncryptionIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Database Encryption & PQC
Component: DatabaseEncryptionIntroduction

HYOK with on-prem CMK custody is one design for keeping key custody under your own control; it is not named as a requirement. DORA's ICT risk-management technical standard (Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/1774) requires financial entities to have a policy on encryption and cryptographic controls that covers “the cryptographic key management referred to in Article 7, laying down rules on the correct use, protection, and lifecycle of cryptographic keys”, and Article 7 requires controls to protect keys through their whole lifecycle. How long RSA-2048 wrapped CMKs stay exposed to harvest-now-decrypt-later depends on how long the wrapped data must stay confidential; this module gives no figure. A database whose HYOK HSM supports ML-KEM-1024 can move its key wrapping to ML-KEM once that HSM is upgraded.
The good news for database PQC migration: AES-256, used to encrypt actual data files, is already quantum-safe. The migration effort targets only the DEK wrapping algorithm. Oracle and SQL Server both support online TDE re-keying with zero application downtime.
• MySQL InnoDB: requires ALTER TABLE for each encrypted table
• Typical maintenance window: 2–8 hours for 1TB database
The ML-KEM ciphertext (stored in KMS metadata per DEK) increases from 256 bytes to 1,568 bytes — a 6× increase in key metadata storage, not data file size. This overhead is negligible relative to multi-TB database sizes.

chunks.title: Database Encryption & PQC — DatabaseEncryptionIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Database Encryption & PQC
Component: DatabaseEncryptionIntroduction

The actual data encryption layer uses AES-256-XTS or AES-256-GCM regardless of classical or PQC key wrapping. Only the KEM ciphertext stored in KMS metadata grows. Performance overhead on OLTP query paths is zero after the re-encryption window.
Standard encryption prevents queries on ciphertext — you cannot WHERE encrypted_ssn = :value if the field is randomly encrypted. Queryable encryption solves this by using structured encryption schemes that preserve query semantics while hiding plaintext values from the server.
For equality queries, FLE 2.0 stores an HMAC-SHA-256 token of the plaintext alongside the ciphertext. The server compares tokens without seeing plaintext. For range queries, a structured encryption scheme over fully randomized ciphertext is used for the index — the server matches encrypted index tokens without learning plaintext order.
PQC Impact: HMAC-SHA-256 is quantum-safe. Range indexes use symmetric primitives (quantum-safe). DEK wrapping upgrade path: RSA-OAEP → ML-KEM-1024 (this module's projection, not a MongoDB statement).
Secure enclaves (VBS/SGX) execute a defined set of operations on plaintext decrypted inside the enclave: comparisons, range queries, LIKE pattern matching, DISTINCT, joins and, in SQL Server 2022 and Azure SQL, ORDER BY and GROUP BY on randomized-encryption columns. The database engine never sees plaintext outside the enclave boundary.

chunks.title: Database Encryption & PQC — DatabaseEncryptionIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Database Encryption & PQC
Component: DatabaseEncryptionIntroduction

In this module's reading, equality queries are straightforward to make PQC-safe: HMAC-SHA-256 tokens are quantum-safe, and DEK wrapping upgrades are independent. Range query encryption is harder: structured encryption range schemes (MongoDB uses fully randomized ciphertext, not order-preserving encryption) are not yet standardized for PQC; this module cites no standard or date for PQC-compatible queryable encryption.
Several regulatory frameworks require protection of sensitive data. GDPR Article 32(1) lists “the state of the art” among the factors for choosing appropriate technical and organisational measures, and DORA's technical standard requires provisions for “updating or changing, where necessary, the cryptographic technology on the basis of developments in cryptanalysis”; neither names a post-quantum algorithm or a date.
Exposure depends on how long the data must stay confidential, not on how long it is retained: a database with RSA-2048 wrapped DEKs and records that must stay confidential for 15 years has up to 15 years of exposure. If a CRQC arrives in 2030, data collected today could be decrypted by 2030 via harvested ciphertext. Using BYOK or HYOK with ML-KEM wrapping protects keys wrapped from now on; ciphertext and old key envelopes that an adversary has already taken remain exposed, and re-encrypting the data protects only the copies the adversary has not yet taken.
Algorithm-agnostic encryption layers for future-proof databases

chunks.title: Digital Assets — BlockchainCryptoIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Digital Assets
Component: BlockchainCryptoIntroduction

Blockchains are fundamentally cryptographic systems. Every transaction is authorized by a digital signature, every address is derived from a public key through hash functions, and every wallet generates its keys from elliptic curve mathematics. There is no central authority — cryptography alone establishes ownership and prevents fraud.
Blockchain private keys are random 256-bit numbers. The corresponding public key is derived via scalar multiplication on an elliptic curve — a one-way trapdoor function that is easy to compute forward but computationally infeasible to reverse. Two curves dominate:
Used by Bitcoin and Ethereum. Defined in SEC 2 (Certicom, 2010). 128-bit security level. Public keys are 33 bytes (compressed) or 65 bytes (uncompressed). Signatures use ; Bitcoin Taproot (P2TR) spends use Schnorr signatures (BIP-340) on the same curve.
Used by Solana. Defined in RFC 8032. Twisted Edwards curve with 128-bit security. 32-byte public keys. Signatures use with deterministic nonces — immune to nonce-reuse attacks.
secp256k1 ECDSA uses a random nonce per signature (nonce reuse leaks the private key). Ed25519 EdDSA derives the nonce deterministically from the message, eliminating this class of vulnerability entirely.
The same mathematical operation (private key × generator point = public key) is just the first step. Each blockchain then applies a different hashing and encoding pipeline to derive the final address:

chunks.title: Digital Assets — BlockchainCryptoIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Digital Assets
Component: BlockchainCryptoIntroduction

Ethereum PubKey (uncompressed, 64B) → → Last 20 bytes → → 0x...
Solana PubKey (32B) → encoding → Address = public key itself
Bitcoin uses a double-hash (SHA-256 then RIPEMD-160) to produce a 20-byte hash before encoding. Ethereum uses Keccak-256 (note: this is the original Keccak submission, not the NIST SHA3-256 standard — they differ in padding). Solana is the simplest: the 32-byte Ed25519 public key is directly Base58-encoded as the address.
Digital signatures prove that a transaction was authorized by the holder of a private key without revealing the key itself. Each chain uses a different signature scheme with different trade-offs:
1. Hash the message — Bitcoin: double SHA-256. Ethereum: Keccak-256. Solana (Ed25519): the message is signed directly (hashing is internal to EdDSA).
2. Sign with private key — produces (r, s) using a random nonce k. produces (R, s) using a deterministic nonce derived from the private key and message — no random number generator needed.
3. Verify with public key — Anyone can verify the signature using the signer's public key + the original message + the signature. This is the foundation of trustless transaction validation.
4. Ethereum special case — ECDSA signatures include a (v) per EIP-155, allowing the signer's public key (and therefore address) to be recovered from the signature itself. This is why Ethereum transactions don't need to include the sender's public key.

Rather than managing separate private keys for each address, Hierarchical Deterministic (HD) wallets derive an unlimited number of keys from a single seed. The standard converts random entropy into a 24-word mnemonic phrase for human-readable backup. defines the tree derivation, and standardizes the path structure across chains.
All segments hardened — Ed25519 does not support non-hardened derivation
Every cryptographic algorithm covered above — (ECDSA), (EdDSA), and the elliptic curves underlying HD wallets — is vulnerable to . Understanding these threats is essential before working with blockchain cryptography hands-on.
