chunks.title: Digital Assets — BlockchainExercises
chunks.content:
Module: Digital Assets
Component: BlockchainExercises

Work through these scenarios in order to compare the cryptographic primitives across Bitcoin, Ethereum, and Solana. Each exercise loads the corresponding workshop flow — click "Load & Run" to start.
Take the quiz to test what you've learned about blockchain cryptography.
1. Bitcoin Key-to-Address Pipeline
Generate a Bitcoin private key with OpenSSL, derive the public key, and trace the full SHA-256 + RIPEMD-160 + Base58Check address derivation pipeline.
Watch how a 256-bit private key becomes a 33-byte compressed public key, gets double-hashed into a 20-byte hash, and finally encodes into a human-readable "1..." address with a 4-byte checksum.
2. Ethereum vs Bitcoin: Same Curve, Different Address
Both Bitcoin and Ethereum use secp256k1, but their address derivation is completely different. Run the Ethereum flow and compare address formats with Bitcoin.
Ethereum uses the uncompressed public key (64 bytes, no prefix), hashes with Keccak-256 (NOT NIST SHA3-256), takes only the last 20 bytes, and applies EIP-55 mixed-case checksum. Compare with Bitcoin's double-hash approach.
Solana uses Ed25519 instead of secp256k1. The public key IS the address (Base58-encoded). Run the Solana flow and compare the signing process with ECDSA chains.
Notice the deterministic nonce in EdDSA — no random number generator needed, unlike ECDSA. The address is simpler: just the Base58-encoded 32-byte public key. EdDSA signs the raw message (hashing is internal).
4. HD Wallet: One Seed, Three Chains

chunks.title: Digital Assets — BlockchainExercises
chunks.content:
Module: Digital Assets
Component: BlockchainExercises

Generate a single BIP-39 mnemonic phrase and derive addresses for Bitcoin, Ethereum, and Solana from the same seed. Understand how BIP-44 derivation paths separate keys across chains.
All three addresses derive from the same 24-word mnemonic. Bitcoin and Ethereum use BIP-32 (HMAC-SHA512), while Solana uses SLIP-0010 for Ed25519. Different paths (m/44'/0'/..., m/44'/60'/..., m/44'/501'/...) produce completely different keys.
5. The Quantum Threat: What Breaks?
After completing any chain flow, review how quantum computers threaten the exact cryptographic operations you just performed. Both secp256k1 (ECDSA) and Ed25519 (EdDSA) are vulnerable to Shor's algorithm.
Every signature you created relies on the elliptic curve discrete logarithm problem. A quantum computer could reverse the public key derivation to recover the private key. Bitcoin's HNFL risk is particularly severe because on-chain data is immutable — exposed public keys cannot be retroactively protected.

chunks.title: Digital Assets — PQCThreatSummary
chunks.content:
Module: Digital Assets
Component: PQCThreatSummary

Every cryptographic algorithm you used in this module — secp256k1 (ECDSA), Ed25519 (EdDSA), and the elliptic curves underlying HD wallets — is vulnerable to . A sufficiently powerful quantum computer ( ) could derive private keys from public keys, breaking the security of all three blockchains.
Shor's algorithm breaks ECDLP, and with it both ECDSA and Schnorr signatures. A large share of early P2PK outputs sits in addresses with exposed public keys.
New output type via soft fork; no post-quantum signature yet
All accounts that have transacted expose public keys. Validator BLS signatures also vulnerable.
PQC signing available today via Account Abstraction; EF PQC team funded
Shor's algorithm breaks Ed25519. All account public keys are the address itself (always exposed).
On-chain data is immutable — unlike traditional systems where you can rotate keys, blockchain transaction history is permanent. Public keys exposed in past transactions remain harvestable indefinitely. When cryptographically relevant quantum computers arrive, every previously exposed public key becomes a target. This makes the HNFL threat particularly severe for blockchains: there is no retroactive fix for exposed keys.
The proposal introduces a new SegWit v2 output type ( bc1z…) that works like Taproot with the quantum-vulnerable key-spend path removed. Requires a soft fork. It contains no post-quantum signature: its authors say they intend to offer a separate proposal for that upon further research.

chunks.title: Digital Assets — PQCThreatSummary
chunks.content:
Module: Digital Assets
Component: PQCThreatSummary

Two complementary paths: EIP-4337 Account Abstraction (live) lets smart-contract wallets verify PQC signatures today. EIP-7702 (Pectra) allows EOAs to delegate to contract code, enabling PQC signing without a full migration. The Ethereum Foundation's Lean Ethereum roadmap proposes replacing validator BLS signatures with the hash-based leanXMSS scheme and using EIP-8141 account abstraction (considered for Hegotá in the second half of 2026) to give accounts signature agility, targeting core post-quantum infrastructure by approximately 2029. STARK-based and lattice-based commitments are the two leading candidates to replace KZG commitments.
SIMD-0461 (Solana Improvement Document), a proposed Falcon signature-verification syscall, was closed by its author on 2026-06-17. The core challenge is structural: Solana addresses are Ed25519 public keys — there is no hash layer to hide behind. Community proposals explore new PQC-keyed account types requiring users to explicitly migrate all assets and positions.

chunks.title: Digital Assets — BitcoinFlow
chunks.content:
Module: Digital Assets
Component: BitcoinFlow

Generate a key pair for the sender inside SoftHSMv3 (PKCS#11 via WebAssembly). The private key is a 256-bit scalar (32 bytes) generated by the HSM's internal CSPRNG and never leaves the token. Note: breaks secp256k1 — this algorithm will require migration when a cryptographically relevant quantum computer (CRQC) arrives.
Extract the sender's public key from the HSM token via C_GetAttributeValue(CKA_PUBLIC_KEY_INFO) . This returns the SPKI DER blob; the raw EC point is parsed out and compressed to 33 bytes. The private key is not involved and never leaves the token. HNFL attack point. Once this public key appears on-chain it becomes a permanent target — a future quantum computer running can derive the private key and forge any signature. Addresses that have never spent funds (public key not yet revealed) are safer, but re-use or spending exposes the key irreversibly. See .
Hash the sender's public key ( + ) and encode with to create a address. The leading byte 0x00 is the mainnet P2PKH version prefix; testnet uses 0x6f. Address format note: P2PKH (1xxx, Base58Check) is the legacy format. Modern Bitcoin wallets use SegWit P2WPKH ( BIP-141 , bc1q... bech32 addresses) or Taproot P2TR ( BIP-341 /BIP-350, bc1p... bech32m addresses). This demo uses P2PKH for clarity — it avoids the witness data structures that SegWit and Taproot require.

chunks.content:
Module: Digital Assets

Generate a key pair for the recipient using the same process as step 1. Each participant needs their own independent key pair — the private key is generated inside the HSM and never exposed.
Extract the recipient's public key from the HSM token, then derive their address using the same → → pipeline as step 3.
Define the transaction details including amount, fee, and addresses. Bitcoin uses the UTXO model: transactions consume entire previous outputs; any amount above the recipient payment must be explicitly returned to the sender as a change output (minus the miner fee) — unaccounted value becomes an implicit fee. Verify the recipient address carefully — a wrong address means permanent loss of funds.

Module: Digital Assets

Seed derivation is symmetric. Your 24-word mnemonic and the derived 512-bit seed remain safe. The risk is in the asymmetric keys derived FROM the seed.

Solana's quantum vulnerability is architecturally different from Bitcoin and Ethereum. Its design decision — making addresses equal to Ed25519 public keys — creates a uniquely difficult migration problem.
In Bitcoin and Ethereum, addresses are derived from public keys via hash functions. The hash hides the public key until a transaction is signed. In Solana, the 32-byte Ed25519 public key is Base58-encoded and used directly as the account address. From the moment an account is created, its public key is permanently visible on-chain — there is no hash layer to provide partial protection.
Solana protocol changes go through Solana Improvement Documents (SIMDs) — a process similar to Bitcoin's BIPs and Ethereum's EIPs. A concrete proposal, SIMD-0461, would have added a Falcon (FN-DSA) signature-verification syscall as an exploratory, verification-only addition that would not replace Ed25519. Its author closed the pull request on 2026-06-17 and said it would be reopened if there is more demand, pointing to an existing Falcon implementation that runs as an on-chain (SBF) programme. A commenter in the thread says Falcon-512 and Hawk-512 verifiers already exist as on-chain programmes and work without protocol changes, and that a Keccak-p1600 syscall (#563) is planned instead to speed up many such signature schemes. Approaches that have been discussed include:

Programme-level PQC verification: Using Solana's native programs to verify PQC signatures, similar to how Ethereum's EIP-4337 uses smart contracts — but with Solana's programme model. A comment in the SIMD-0461 thread cites a Falcon implementation in SBF at under 170,000 compute units.
Reported: Falcon-512 and Hawk-512 verifiers run as on-chain programmes without protocol changes (SIMD-0461 thread)
SIMD-0461 (Falcon verification syscall) closed by its author in June 2026
Key takeaway: Solana's quantum risk is structurally higher than Ethereum's. Every account's public key is permanently and irrevocably on-chain from the moment of first use. Without protocol-level PQC support and broad wallet support, the window to migrate safely is shrinking with each passing year.

Generate an Ed25519 private key for the sender. Solana uses Ed25519 for high-performance, deterministic signatures with strong security guarantees.
Why Ed25519? Unlike Bitcoin's secp256k1 (ECDSA), Ed25519 uses EdDSA which is faster, more secure against side-channel attacks, and produces deterministic signatures (no random k value needed).
Demo vs Production Key Generation: This demo generates a raw Ed25519 seed directly via SoftHSMv3 C_GenerateKeyPair. Real Solana wallets (Phantom, Solflare, etc.) use a different flow:
2. PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA512 derives a 64-byte root seed from the mnemonic + optional passphrase
3. derives the Ed25519 child key via path m/44'/501'/0'/0' using HMAC-SHA512 (hardened derivation only — standard BIP-32 does not support Ed25519)
The final 32-byte value is the same Ed25519 seed this demo generates directly. The cryptographic operations from step 2 onward are identical regardless of how the seed was derived. → For the full BIP-32/39/44 + SLIP-0010 derivation walkthrough, pick HD Wallet from the chain selector in this workshop.
Derive the public key from the private key using Ed25519 scalar multiplication on the Edwards curve. This is a one-way function — you cannot derive the private key from the public key.
Ed25519 Public Key Derivation: Unlike ECDSA which uses point multiplication on a Weierstrass curve, Ed25519 uses the twisted Edwards curve for faster computation. The public key is exactly 32 bytes (256 bits).

chunks.content:
Module: Digital Assets
Component: SolanaFlow

PKCS#11 Attribute Used — CKA_PUBLIC_KEY_INFO: The HSM returns the public key as a DER-encoded SubjectPublicKeyInfo (SPKI) structure, not raw bytes. SPKI wraps the 32-byte Ed25519 point in an ASN.1 envelope: SEQUENCE { AlgorithmIdentifier, BIT STRING { pubkey } } . The raw 32-byte public key is extracted from the last 32 bytes of this structure. CKA_VALUE is a different attribute (raw key material) — for Ed25519 public keys, PKCS#11 v3.2 mandates CKA_PUBLIC_KEY_INFO for portability across HSM vendors.
The Solana address is simply the Base58 encoding of the 32-byte public key. Unlike Bitcoin (which hashes the public key) or Ethereum (which hashes and takes last 20 bytes), Solana uses the raw public key directly.
Why Direct Encoding? Solana prioritizes performance and simplicity. The 32-byte Ed25519 public key is already compact and secure, so no additional hashing is needed.
Wallet vs PDA: This address is a wallet address — an on-curve Ed25519 public key with a corresponding private key. Solana also has (Program-Derived Addresses) which are off-curve and have no private key; they are controlled exclusively by programs, not users.

Module: Digital Assets
Component: SolanaFlow

HNFL Attack Point Unlike Bitcoin and Ethereum, which hash addresses and only expose the public key when spending, Solana exposes the raw Ed25519 public key as the address itself — it is visible on-chain from the moment the account is created. This makes every Solana wallet a permanent target for (Harvest Now, Forge Later) attacks. A sufficiently powerful quantum computer running could recover the private key from the on-chain public key and forge signatures — even for accounts that have never signed a transaction.
Generate an Ed25519 keypair for the recipient to receive funds. This follows the same process as step 1.
Why show recipient keygen? In a real transaction you would only receive the recipient's public address — they generate their own keypair privately and never share the private key. This step simulates the recipient's side of the exchange so you can see the full lifecycle in one flow. The recipient private key generated here is used only to produce the address in step 5; it plays no further role in the transaction.
Key Security: In production, the recipient would generate their own keys on their own device. Never share private keys!
Derive the recipient's address from their public key using Base58 encoding.
Address Verification: Always verify the recipient address before sending funds. Solana addresses are case-sensitive and 43–44 characters long (32 bytes of Ed25519 public key Base58-encoded — never as short as 32 characters).

Define the transaction details including recent blockhash and instructions. Verify the recipient address carefully!
Transaction Structure: Solana transactions contain a recent blockhash (for deduplication/expiration) and one or more instructions. Each instruction specifies a program to call, accounts to use, and data to pass.
Lamports: The amount is specified in (1 SOL = 1 billion lamports). This transaction sends 0.5 SOL (500,000,000 lamports = 0x1DCD6500 little-endian → bytes 00 65 cd 1d 00 00 00 00 ).
Fee Payer : The source account (index 0 in account keys) is both the signer and the fee payer. Solana deducts the base fee (~5,000 lamports) from the fee payer before executing instructions.
Address Verification: The recipient address below is decoded back to raw bytes and compared against the generated public key. A mismatch means the funds would go to a different account — always verify!
⚠️ Address modified — the signed transaction will commit to this recipient, not the generated one.
Ordered array of 32-byte addresses. Index 0 is the fee payer and must sign. Index 1 (recipient) is writable so its lamport balance can increase. Index 2 is the System Program — the native program that executes SOL transfers. HNFL Attack Point All three addresses are visible on-chain permanently. The Ed25519 public keys at [0] and [1] can be harvested now and attacked after Q-Day.

Sign the serialized message using the source private key with (EdDSA). Unlike ECDSA, no random nonce is needed — the nonce is deterministically derived from the key and message, eliminating nonce-reuse vulnerabilities.
Demo vs Production — What Gets Signed: This demo signs the JSON representation of the message (UTF-8 bytes). In production, Solana wallets sign the compact binary wire format shown in step 7 — the same byte sequence that validators receive over the network. The JSON is used here for readability; the EdDSA algorithm and key material are identical either way, but the signed bytes differ. The SHA-256 integrity fingerprint from step 7 proves the demo signs exactly the bytes that were visualized, maintaining internal consistency.
1. Expand the 32-byte seed with SHA-512 → scalar s + nonce prefix
Verify the Ed25519 signature using the source public key. This ensures the message was signed by the holder of the corresponding private key.
What this step proves: Signature verification confirms authenticity (the source key signed this exact message) and integrity (the message was not modified after signing). It does not prove authorization — on-chain, the Solana runtime also checks that the account actually owns the funds and that all account access flags (writable/signer) match the instruction.

chunks.content:
Module: Digital Assets

Local vs On-Chain: This verification runs offline in your browser (SoftHSMv3 WASM or JS fallback). In production, the Solana validator performs the same Ed25519 verification on-chain during transaction execution — if it fails, the entire transaction is rejected atomically. Clients can also pre-verify locally to catch errors before paying network fees.
Security: Ed25519 verification is faster than ECDSA and provides strong protection against signature malleability attacks.
Quantum Threat: can break Ed25519 on a sufficiently powerful quantum computer (CRQC). All Solana wallet public keys are visible on-chain from account creation, making them permanent targets for attacks — adversaries harvest public keys today and forge signatures after . Post-quantum signature standards (Falcon, ML-DSA/FIPS 204) are being standardized as replacements for Ed25519; any Ed25519-based blockchain will require a coordinated protocol migration.
When enabled, a byte of the signature is flipped before verification — Step 9 will show ❌ INVALID.
View the Solana Message structure that will be serialized and signed. This demo uses a simplified JSON representation for readability; production Solana transactions use a compact binary wire format (shown in the table below). The JSON and binary represent the same logical message — the cryptographic operations in steps 8–9 are identical either way.

chunks.content:
Module: Digital Assets
Component: SolanaFlow

Three bytes encoding account access control. numRequiredSignatures=1 means only the source must sign. numReadonlyUnsignedAccounts=1 marks the System Program (index 2) as read-only — it cannot be debited. The recipient (index 1) is writable by default, allowing its balance to increase.
A recent blockhash (max 150 blocks ≈ 60 seconds at ~400ms/block). Prevents replay attacks — a transaction with a stale blockhash is rejected. In durable nonce transactions, a nonce account replaces this field for offline signing workflows.
programIdIndex: 2 points to the System Program. accounts: [0,1] are the source and destination indices. data encodes the System Program Transfer instruction: 4-byte type (02000000 LE = 2) + 8-byte amount (0065cd1d00000000 LE = 500,000,000 lamports). This is the native System Program format — Anchor programs use an 8-byte SHA-256 discriminator prefix instead.
The native Solana program at address 32 zero bytes (Base58: all 1s). It is the only program that can debit a user-owned account and transfer SOL. Instruction type 2 (Transfer) moves lamports from accounts[0] to accounts[1]. Other System Program instructions: 0=CreateAccount, 1=Assign, 3=CreateAccountWithSeed, 9=AdvanceNonceAccount.

chunks.title: Digital Assets — SolanaFlow
chunks.content:
Module: Digital Assets
Component: SolanaFlow

Production Solana messages use compact binary, not JSON. compact-u16 is Solana's variable-length encoding: small values fit in one byte and larger ones in two or three, with a continuation bit. Each instruction is: 1-byte programIdIndex | compact-u16 account count | account indices | compact-u16 data length | raw data. The full serialized message is base58- or base64-encoded for transmission.
Breakdown: 01=1 required sig | 00=0 readonly signed | 01=1 readonly unsigned | 03=3 account keys | [3×32B keys] | [32B blockhash] | 01=1 instruction | programIdx=02 | 02 account indices=[00,01] | 0C=12 bytes data | 02000000 0065cd1d00000000. The signed transaction prepends [1 sig slot (64B)] before the message.
This demo uses the legacy transaction format. Modern Solana adds: (1) Versioned transactions (v0) — a new message format that supports Address Lookup Tables (ALTs), expanding the account limit from ~20 to ~250 per transaction. (2) Compute Units — every transaction declares a compute budget; exceeding it causes failure. (3) Priority Fees — lamports-per-compute-unit tip to validators for faster inclusion during congestion. (4) Transaction Simulation — wallets call simulateTransaction (a dry-run RPC call) before signing to detect failures without paying fees. These features do not change the Ed25519 signing or verification mechanics — steps 8 and 9 apply to both legacy and versioned formats.

After signing (step 8), the serialized transaction is base58- or base64-encoded and submitted to an RPC node via sendTransaction. The validator simulates the transaction to check pre-conditions (balances, access flags, compute budget). If simulation passes, the transaction enters the leader's queue. Once included in a block, it is optimistically confirmed (~400ms). Finalization (irreversibility) occurs after 31 additional blocks (~12 seconds) via the Tower BFT consensus mechanism.

chunks.content:

Generate a secp256k1 private key for the sender using OpenSSL.Ethereum uses the same elliptic curve as Bitcoin for ECDSA signatures.
Why secp256k1 ? This curve offers a good balance of security (128-bit) and performance. It's battle-tested across Bitcoin and Ethereum ecosystems.
Derive the uncompressed public key(65 bytes) from the private key using elliptic curve point multiplication.This is a one - way trapdoor function - you cannot reverse it to get the private key.
ECDSA Public Key: The public key is a point (x, y) on the secp256k1 curve. Uncompressed format: 0x04 || x || y (65 bytes total).
Compute the Keccak - 256 hash of the public key(excluding the 0x04 prefix) and take the last 20 bytes.Then apply EIP - 55 checksum for error detection.
Why Keccak - 256 ? Ethereum uses the original Keccak submission, NOT the final NIST SHA3-256 standard. They differ in padding.

Generate a secp256k1 keypair for the recipient.This follows the same process as step 1.

Derive the recipient's address using Keccak-256 and EIP-55 checksum, same as step 3.
Address Verification: Always verify the recipient address before sending funds. Ethereum addresses are case-sensitive (due to EIP-55) and exactly 42 characters (0x + 40 hex).

Sign the transaction hash using OpenSSL's standard ECDSA implementation.
The Challenge: Standard ECDSA signatures (like those from OpenSSL) only produce r and s. Ethereum requires a third parameter, v (recovery ID).
The Solution: We compute v as a post-processing step. We test recovery IDs (0 and 1) to find the correct one, then encode it.

View the transaction fields that will be hashed with Keccak-256 and signed. In production Ethereum, these fields are serialized using RLP (Recursive Length Prefix) binary encoding before hashing. This demo uses a simplified JSON representation for readability.
7. Visualize Transaction Fields
Counter to prevent replay attacks. Starts at 0 for new accounts.
Price per unit of gas (in Wei) the sender is willing to pay.
Maximum gas allowed for the transaction (21000 is standard for transfers).
The destination address (20 bytes).
Amount of Ether to transfer (in Wei).

chunks.title: Digital Identity — DigitalIDExercises
chunks.content:
Module: Digital Identity
Component: DigitalIDExercises

Work through these scenarios to master the EUDI Wallet ecosystem: audit wallet keys, trace PID issuance trust chains, explore selective disclosure privacy, evaluate QTSP requirements, and map the EU PQC migration roadmap. Each exercise navigates directly to the relevant workshop step — click "Load & Run" to begin.
Take the PQC quiz to check what you've learned about digital identity and eIDAS 2.0.
1. Wallet Cryptographic Key Audit
Open the EUDI Wallet (Step 1) and examine the key store. How many keys does María hold? Identify the key algorithm and purpose for each key slot. Consider: which keys are used for credential binding vs. device authentication, and what PQC replacements exist for each.
The wallet uses ECDSA P-256 for credential binding — the same key is used to sign presentation proofs sent to relying parties. Under a CRQC threat, harvested presentations could be used to forge proofs. ML-DSA-65 (FIPS 204) is the parameter set this module standardises on for wallet device keys: BSI TR-02102-1 recommends the hedged variant of ML-DSA with all parameter sets at NIST security categories 3 and 5.
2. PID Issuance and Trust Chain

chunks.title: Digital Identity — DigitalIDExercises
chunks.content:
Module: Digital Identity
Component: DigitalIDExercises

Use the PID Issuer (Step 2) to issue a Person Identification Data credential. After issuance, answer: What format is the PID (mso_mdoc or SD-JWT VC)? Who signed it? Where is the issuer certificate anchored? What does the EU Coordinated Implementation Roadmap for PQC ask of high-risk use cases, and does the EUDI ARF set a PQC deadline for national PID issuers?
The PID is issued in mso_mdoc format (ISO 18013-5), signed by the national PID Issuer using ECDSA P-256. The issuer certificate is anchored to the national Trusted List. The EU Coordinated Implementation Roadmap for PQC recommends national PQC roadmaps by 2026 and migration of high-risk use cases by 2030 — a policy recommendation rather than a binding EUDI ARF mandate.
3. Selective Disclosure at the Bank
Navigate to the Bank (Relying Party, Step 4). The bank asks for your name, your degree, and age_over_18 — note it does NOT ask for birth_date. At the disclosure step you choose what to share. First run it as offered and read the log: which PID element's digest is verified, and which one never leaves the wallet? Then run it again and untick age_over_18 — what does the bank do, and is the proof itself still valid? Finally: what's the risk if the presentation proof's signature algorithm is broken by a CRQC?

chunks.title: Digital Identity — DigitalIDExercises
chunks.content:
Module: Digital Identity
Component: DigitalIDExercises

age_over_18 is disclosed and its digest is checked against the issuer-signed Mobile Security Object, while birth_date is absent from the payload entirely — not hidden from view, never transmitted. That is ISO 18013-5 selective disclosure: the issuer signs the digests, so withholding an element costs nothing cryptographically, and the bank learns you are eligible without learning when you were born. Untick age_over_18 and the bank refuses — the proof stays cryptographically valid, it simply no longer answers the question asked, which is the honest cost of withholding. The key binding proof is still ECDSA, though: a CRQC could forge it and impersonate you. ML-DSA-65 would fix that.
4. QTSP Selection for QES Signing
Use the QTSP provider (Step 5) to sign a document with a Qualified Electronic Signature. Note which algorithms the QTSP uses for signature creation. Then evaluate: why does QES require SCAL2 (Sole Control Assurance Level 2), and what makes a QTSP 'qualified' under eIDAS 2.0? Which ETSI standard governs QTSP requirements?

chunks.title: Digital Identity — DigitalIDExercises
chunks.content:
Module: Digital Identity
Component: DigitalIDExercises

QES requires SCAL2 because the signing key must be under the sole control of the signatory — the QTSP must ensure no third party (including the QTSP itself) can sign on the user's behalf without their active authorisation. QTSPs that issue qualified certificates follow ETSI EN 319 411, while remote QES signing with SCAL2 is governed by the CEN standards for server signing (the remote QSCD combines a signature activation module under the CEN protection profile EN 419 241-2 with a cryptographic module certified against EN 419 221-5 — those standards come from CEN/TC 224, not ETSI); QTSPs are listed on National Trusted Lists. The CSC API v2 (Cloud Signature Consortium) standardises the remote signing protocol.
5. EUDI Wallet PQC Migration Timeline
Review the full wallet workflow (all 5 steps). Then map the three-phase EU PQC migration roadmap for digital identity systems: end of 2026 (national strategies), end of 2030 (high-risk use cases), 2035 (transition complete). For each of the five workshop actors (Wallet, PID Issuer, University, Bank, QTSP), identify which phase applies and which algorithm they'd migrate first.

chunks.title: Digital Identity — DigitalIDExercises
chunks.content:
Module: Digital Identity
Component: DigitalIDExercises

PID Issuers and QTSPs sign the PIDs, attestations and qualified certificates that relying parties verify, so placing them in Phase 2 (2030) or earlier is a planning judgement rather than a requirement: the NIS Cooperation Group roadmap asks for high-risk use cases to be migrated by the end of 2030 and does not name PID Issuers. The wallet device key is the key a Wallet Unit uses to sign data from the relying party when it proves that a PID or device-bound attestation is bound to it, and relying parties also verify the signature of the PID Provider or Attestation Provider on the credential, so both kinds of key matter for a post-quantum migration. A university attestation issuer also signs credentials that relying parties verify, and a bank, as a relying party, verifies the signatures on the credentials it receives; the roadmap does not rank these actors, so their order is a planning choice too.

chunks.title: Digital Identity — OverviewComponent
chunks.content:
Module: Digital Identity
Component: OverviewComponent

The European Digital Identity Regulation ( eIDAS 2.0, Regulation EU 2024/1183) entered into force on 20 May 2024 and mandates that all 27 EU member states provide citizens and residents with at least one EUDI Wallet by late 2026. Unlike eIDAS 1.0 where national eID notification was voluntary, eIDAS 2.0 makes digital identity wallets mandatory — creating a pan-European trust framework for identity, attestations, and qualified electronic signatures.
Nov 2024: Five implementing regulations adopted (published 4 Dec)
The EUDI Architecture Reference Framework (ARF) makes two attestation formats mandatory, and adds W3C Verifiable Credentials Data Model v2.0 as an optional third. Both mandatory formats enable selective disclosure, but serve different use cases.
Optimized for: Proximity — NFC, BLE (in-person verification)
Device proof: a device signature (for example ECDSA) or a MAC (HMAC 256/256 over an ECDH-derived key)
EUDI establishes a layered trust chain. Relying Parties can verify credential authenticity without contacting the issuer, using public trust infrastructure.
National Trusted Lists Each member state publishes a machine-readable list of Qualified Trust Service Providers (QTSPs).
QTSPs (Qualified Trust Service Providers) Certified organizations that issue qualified attestations (QEAA) and provide qualified signatures ( QES).
eIDAS Trust Framework (Bridge) Cross-border mechanism ensuring mutual recognition of wallets, PIDs, and attestations across all 27 member states.

chunks.content:

The EUDI Wallet enforces strong privacy guarantees aligned with GDPR.
Only requested attributes are revealed. All other claims remain cryptographically hidden from the verifier.
Different presentations to different Relying Parties should not be correlatable. The ARF addresses this through batch-issued credentials and pseudonymous identifiers.
GDPR Art. 5(1)(c) compliance. The wallet enforces sharing only the minimum data necessary for a specific purpose.
The OpenID4VP and OpenID4VCI specifications use classical ECDSA (for example ECDSA with SHA-256 on a P-256 key) in most of their examples. The eIDAS 2.0 regulation text and the ARF text we checked do not mention quantum computing. The SD-JWT standard (RFC 9901) leaves the choice of signature algorithm to the application, including post-quantum algorithms “when they are ready”. NIST has standardised ML-DSA and SLH-DSA as post-quantum signatures.
NIS Cooperation Group Coordinated Implementation Roadmap (June 2025)
This simulation uses classical algorithms such as ECDSA. ETSI says its cryptographic suites specification (TS 119 312 V2.1.1) is incomplete for the EUDI Wallet, with an update in preparation.
The EU funded four Large-Scale Pilots (LSPs) testing EUDI wallets across 26+ countries, followed by a second wave in 2025.

In a production EUDI Wallet, activation begins with the Wallet Provider issuing a WUA. This process: (1) generates a key pair in the Wallet Secure Cryptographic Device (WSCD), (2) binds the wallet instance to the user's device, and (3) proves to PID Providers and Attestation Providers that the wallet is genuine, unmodified, and running on certified hardware. Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2981 requires the WSCD to be assessed against assurance level high as a prerequisite to certification under national schemes. When that hardware is provided, directly or indirectly, by the wallet solution and is needed to meet the desired level of assurance, the evaluation also includes a Common Criteria AVA_VAN.5 vulnerability assessment, unless it is duly justified to the certification body that the security characteristics of the wallet secure cryptographic application (WSCA) make a lower assessment level possible while the overall assurance level stays high. Without a valid WUA, no PID Provider will issue credentials. This simulation starts from PID issuance for simplicity.
Following the EUDI ARF, your PID will natively be constructed as a binary mso_mdoc payload utilizing strict CBOR (Concise Binary Object Representation) encoding, cryptographically securing your attributes within a COSE_Sign1 signature container signed by the remote HSM.

chunks.title: EMV Payment Systems & PQC — EMVPaymentExercises
chunks.content:
Module: EMV Payment Systems & PQC
Component: EMVPaymentExercises

Work through these scenarios to explore payment network comparisons, EMV transaction flows, card provisioning, tokenization, DUKPT key management, and PQC migration planning. Each exercise pre-configures the Workshop — click "Load & Run" to begin.
Take the PQC quiz to test what you've learned about EMV payment systems and quantum-safe migration.
1. Network PQC Readiness Assessment \u2014 Compare Visa and UnionPay quantum exposure
In the Network Comparator, compare Visa and UnionPay side by side. Identify which network has the larger offline authentication exposure and which has a more advanced PQC posture. Calculate the total cards at risk across both networks.
Visa has billions of cards in circulation with active PQC research (quantum lab since 2022), while UnionPay has 9.4B cards tied to China\u2019s pending GB/T standards. UnionPay\u2019s scale makes it the single largest quantum-vulnerable payment ecosystem. Note the two card counts are not subsets of the 14.7 billion EMV figure: network totals count every card a network has in circulation, including non-EMV and multi-badged cards, so they cannot be added up against it.
2. Offline vs Online Quantum Attack Surface \u2014 Compare quantum-vulnerable steps
In the Transaction Simulator, compare Online mode with Offline CDA mode. Toggle the quantum exposure overlay for both. Count the quantum-vulnerable steps in each. Identify which mode has higher HNDL exposure.

chunks.title: EMV Payment Systems & PQC — EMVPaymentExercises
chunks.content:
Module: EMV Payment Systems & PQC
Component: EMVPaymentExercises

Online mode has 2 quantum-vulnerable steps: the ICC certificate-chain verification during card authentication, and the TLS key exchange from terminal to acquirer. Issuer ARQC verification is NOT one of them — it is symmetric end to end. Offline CDA has 3 (ICC certificate verification, the combined AC+SSAD signature, and the combined-signature verification). Offline CDA is more dangerous because forged certificates enable counterfeit acceptance at any terminal without network connectivity. Online mode mitigates risk through real-time issuer authorization.
3. EMV Certificate Chain Size Impact \u2014 Compare RSA vs ML-DSA vs FN-DSA
In the Card Provisioning Visualizer, toggle between RSA-2048, ML-DSA-44, and FN-DSA-512 certificate chains. Compare the total chain size for the 3 levels (payment-system CA \u2192 Issuer \u2192 ICC); the terminal holds the payment-system CA public key, so the card itself carries the issuer and ICC certificates. Assess whether FN-DSA-512 fits within typical EMV card NVM constraints (32-64 KB).

chunks.title: EMV Payment Systems & PQC — EMVPaymentExercises
chunks.content:
Module: EMV Payment Systems & PQC
Component: EMVPaymentExercises

RSA-2048 chain: ~1.2 KB (3 \u00d7 384 bytes). ML-DSA-44 chain: ~11.5 KB (3 \u00d7 3,832 bytes, each a 2,420 B signature + 1,312 B key + ~100 B of fields). FN-DSA-512: ~5.1 KB (3 \u00d7 1,687 bytes, each a 666 B signature + 897 B key + ~124 B of fields). The card itself carries only the issuer and ICC certificates (about 0.8 KB for RSA, 7.7 KB for ML-DSA-44, 3.4 KB for FN-DSA-512). FN-DSA is ~2.3\u00d7 smaller than ML-DSA but 4.4\u00d7 larger than RSA. At 5.1 KB, FN-DSA is smaller than ML-DSA at 11.5 KB; whether either fits depends on the chip and the application profile (the 32-64 KB card NVM range is this module\u2019s assumption). FIPS 206 standardization for FN-DSA (Falcon) is still pending, so it is not yet a deployable option.
4. Mobile Wallet Quantum Exposure \u2014 Identify ECDSA vs AES steps in Apple Pay
In the Tokenization Explorer, select Visa VTS as the TSP and Apple Pay as the wallet. Walk through the 6-step provisioning flow. Identify which steps use quantum-vulnerable asymmetric crypto (ECDSA/RSA) and which use quantum-safe symmetric crypto (AES). Count the total vulnerable points.
In this module's illustration, most provisioning steps use quantum-vulnerable asymmetric cryptography (ECDSA or RSA); only the activation confirmation relies on symmetric cryptography. This module's advice: migrate TSP TLS and device attestation first.
5. DUKPT Quantum Attack Analysis \u2014 Find the RSA vulnerability in key injection

chunks.title: EMV Payment Systems & PQC — EMVPaymentExercises
chunks.content:
Module: EMV Payment Systems & PQC
Component: EMVPaymentExercises

In the POS Crypto Analyzer, select Traditional POS and explore the Key Injection Ceremony. Step through all 4 phases. Identify the exact point where quantum computers create risk. Toggle between Classical and PQC modes to see the difference.
DUKPT per-transaction key derivation uses symmetric crypto (quantum-safe). The quantum exposure spans TWO steps, not one: Step 2 wraps the BDK under an RSA-2048 key transport key, and Step 3 transports it — RSA-2048 decryption at the injection station plus TLS. Compromising either exposes the BDK, which can derive ALL past and future transaction keys. ML-KEM-768 key encapsulation replaces RSA at both. Steps 1 (BDK generation) and 4 (terminal derivation) are symmetric and need no change.
6. End-to-End Migration Priority \u2014 Identify the critical-path dependency chain
In the Migration Risk Matrix, examine the dependency graph. Identify the critical-path migration sequence. Which 3 components must migrate first? What is the dependency chain that sets the order of the migration?

chunks.title: EMV Payment Systems & PQC — EMVPaymentExercises
chunks.content:
Module: EMV Payment Systems & PQC
Component: EMVPaymentExercises

Critical path: (1) Payment HSM key wrapping must migrate to ML-KEM first (enables all downstream changes), (2) Key injection ceremonies at KIFs must switch to ML-KEM key transport (unblocks terminal re-keying), (3) Card personalization must generate PQC certificates (unblocks offline auth). Dependency chain: HSM \u2192 KIF \u2192 Card Personalization \u2192 Offline Auth. The chain sets the order of work; how long it takes depends on card and terminal replacement cycles, and this module\u2019s assumed 3-5 year card cycle is an estimate, not a sourced figure.

chunks.title: EMV Payment Systems & PQC — EMVPaymentIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: EMV Payment Systems & PQC
Component: EMVPaymentIntroduction

EMV (Europay, Mastercard, Visa) is the global standard for chip-based payment card authentication. Originally developed in the 1990s, EMV is now managed by EMVCo, jointly owned by the six major payment networks. With 14.7 billion EMV cards in circulation at the end of 2024 — EMVCo’s own figure, reported at the 2025 EMV User Meeting, and still growing — it is the largest deployed PKI ecosystem in the world.
Five of EMVCo’s six owners are profiled below. JCB, the sixth, is not — its published PQC position and card-fleet figures are not sourced to the standard the other five rows meet, and this module does not assert what it cannot cite.
Every transaction traverses this chain. Cryptography protects each link.
EMV defines three offline authentication methods, all based on RSA signatures. The card carries the issuer certificate and its own ICC certificate; the terminal holds the payment-system (scheme) CA public key and verifies the chain up to it, so it can authenticate the card without contacting the issuer.
Key insight: All three EMV authentication methods rely on RSA. A quantum computer capable of running Shor's algorithm could forge ICC certificates, enabling counterfeit cards to pass offline terminal verification.

chunks.title: EMV Payment Systems & PQC — EMVPaymentIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: EMV Payment Systems & PQC
Component: EMVPaymentIntroduction

Every online EMV transaction follows a precise authorization flow. The card generates an ARQC (Authorization Request Cryptogram) using symmetric keys, which travels through the acquirer and network to the issuer. The issuer verifies and responds with an ARPC .
Card → Terminal RSA-2048 certificate chain verification (offline auth) + 3DES/AES ARQC generation (symmetric)
Terminal → Acquirer TLS 1.2/1.3 with RSA/ECDSA key exchange + AES-GCM payload encryption
Acquirer → Network TLS (network-to-network) + ISO 8583 MAC (3DES/AES symmetric)
Network → Issuer ARQC verification in issuer HSM (symmetric) + HSM key wrapping (RSA-2048)
Online vs Offline: Online transactions get real-time issuer authorization, providing a second layer of defense. Offline transactions rely entirely on the RSA certificate chain — the quantum attack surface is larger.
Payment tokenization replaces the real PAN with a surrogate token managed by a Token Service Provider (TSP) . Each major network operates its own TSP: Visa Token Service (VTS), Mastercard MDES, and Amex EST.
Key insight: Per-transaction cryptograms (AES-256) are quantum-safe. The quantum vulnerability is in the provisioning phase — RSA/ECDSA device attestation and TLS key exchange to the TSP.

chunks.title: EMV Payment Systems & PQC — EMVPaymentIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: EMV Payment Systems & PQC
Component: EMVPaymentIntroduction

Card-not-present (CNP) transactions transmit card data over TLS to payment gateways. 3-D Secure 2.0 (Visa Secure, Mastercard Identity Check) adds cardholder authentication using ECDSA challenge signing and device binding. PCI SSC lists a separate PCI 3DS Core standard among its standards; this module does not state what it covers or requires.
TLS key exchange: RSA/ECDSA vulnerable to Shor's algorithm — HNDL risk on payment data in transit
3DS challenge signing: ECDSA P-256 signatures can be forged, enabling unauthorized authentication
Payment gateway certificates: X.509 certificates with RSA/ECDSA keys
E-commerce TLS is the fastest migration path — hybrid ML-KEM TLS 1.3 is already supported by major CDN providers and browsers.
Payment terminals range from powerful ATMs to constrained mPOS dongles. DUKPT (Derived Unique Key Per Transaction) ensures each transaction uses a unique symmetric key derived from a Base Derivation Key (BDK) .
Critical vulnerability: The DUKPT symmetric derivation chain is quantum-safe. The quantum attack point is RSA-2048 key transport at Key Injection Facilities . Compromising the BDK allows deriving ALL past and future transaction keys.

What certifies the device. PCI SSC assigns and lists PTS approvals for HSMs and for POI devices ( PTS listing definitions ). Whether a PCI operational standard accepts a FIPS certificate in place of a PTS HSM approval is set in that standard's own requirement text, which this module does not state. Check any post-quantum change to key transport or terminal firmware against these approval regimes, not only against the algorithm.
Cards are only one half of the payments estate. The other half moves money between institutions — and it has a different threat profile, because settlement traffic is long-lived, highly structured, and traverses parties you do not control.
The correspondent chain is the structural problem: a payment crosses several institutions, each retaining its own records, and no participant can migrate the chain unilaterally. This is why the sector publishes jointly rather than per-bank.
Where payments cryptography stands, in the sector’s own words
Source: EPC 342-08 v16.0.1, 24 June 2026 — open in the Library .
No single authority sets the financial sector’s post-quantum timetable. The nine bodies below publish across six jurisdictions, and which of them binds a given institution depends on where it is regulated — not on where it operates.

Module: EMV Payment Systems & PQC
Component: EMVPaymentIntroduction

Unlike Government & Defense, none of these carries a dated algorithm mandate of the CNSA 2.0 kind — nothing here names a specific algorithm and a date it must be running by. The EU NIS CG Coordinated Implementation Roadmap (above) is the closest exception: it sets a dated transition expectation for EU Member States — high-risk use cases transitioned by end-2030 — that reaches EU-regulated banks indirectly through NIS2 and DORA’s state-of-the-art-cryptography requirements. It is a Commission Recommendation, not a law, and it names no algorithm. The Nacha roadmap (above) is a recommendation, not a mandate: an industry alliance project team recommends that all requests for information and proposals require vendors to be quantum-safe by 2030. Otherwise, the sector’s pressure comes from operational-resilience regulation and from harvest-now-decrypt-later exposure, not from a compliance cliff.
Out of scope. This module covers card payments, interbank rails, and — as of the next section — open banking APIs and PSD2 Strong Customer Authentication. Instant-payment schemes (SEPA Instant, FedNow) and central bank digital currencies raise their own post-quantum questions — different threat models, different standards bodies — that this module does not address. They are not covered here because the library does not yet hold a substantive PQC source for either; this note will be narrowed further once one is acquired, not expanded from general knowledge.

Module: EMV Payment Systems & PQC
Component: EMVPaymentIntroduction

Open banking gives account information service providers (AISPs) and payment initiation service providers (PISPs) — often fintechs, not banks — programmatic access to a customer’s account at their bank. In the EU this is not a voluntary API program; it is a legal right created by PSD2 Article 97, which requires two-factor strong customer authentication (knowledge, possession, and inherence — at least two of the three) for online account access, remote payment initiation, and any action carrying fraud risk, with the authentication code dynamically linked to the exact amount and payee of the transaction.
The RTS on SCA (Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2018/389)
PSD2 sets the legal requirement; the RTS is where the technical shape of it lives — and where the cryptography actually shows up.
Dedicated interface (Art. 30). Every bank offering online-accessible accounts must expose an interface AISPs and PISPs can use to identify themselves, request account data, and initiate payments — the legal basis for every open-banking API in the EU.
Mandatory fallback (Art. 33). If a bank’s dedicated interface is unavailable or under-performing, third-party providers must be able to fall back to the interface the bank’s own customers use — unless the bank’s interface has passed three months of problem-free operation under independent testing.

eIDAS qualified certificates (Art. 34). AISPs, PISPs, and banks identify themselves to each other using qualified certificates for website authentication (QWAC) or electronic seals (QSealC) under eIDAS — the same certificate framework the Digital ID module covers for the EUDI Wallet.
Channel encryption (Art. 35). The regulation requires “strong and widely recognised encryption techniques” for the communication channel — it names no algorithm and no TLS version. That wording is deliberately technology-neutral: migrating a dedicated interface to hybrid ML-KEM TLS needs no legislative change, only an implementation one.
Sources: Directive (EU) 2015/2366, Art. 97 ; Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2018/389, Art. 4, 5, 30, 33, 34, 35 .
Continental Europe’s dominant technical implementation of the Article 30 dedicated interface is the Berlin Group’s NextGenPSD2 Framework, adopted by most large EU banking groups. Its site was unreachable while researching this section, so this module names it without citing specifics from its own spec — the same discipline applied everywhere else here.
The payment ecosystem faces multiple quantum threat vectors, from offline card authentication to key injection infrastructure. The scale is unprecedented — 14.7 billion EMV cards (end of 2024) cannot be replaced overnight.

Module: EMV Payment Systems & PQC

The payment industry is at an inflection point. EMVCo does not expect quantum computing to threaten EMV infrastructure before 2040 — and says it may never — while the G7 Cyber Expert Group points to the early 2030s for the most critical financial systems, against a broader 2035 horizon. The G7 CEG is explicit that this is not a deadline: the period “is reflective of the variety of envisaged approaches taken across G7 jurisdictions”, and the statement “does not set guidance or regulatory expectations”. Among the card networks, Mastercard has published financial-sector migration guidance and described prototype testing; Visa has published quantum-readiness steps for stablecoins and digital payments; and American Express publicly describes an enterprise PQC-readiness and crypto-agility program. UnionPay and Discover have no network-specific public roadmap located in this review, so their rows show the shared EMVCo work separately from a clearly labelled tentative dependency plan.
FN-DSA (Falcon, FIPS 206 in development): Compact signatures (666 bytes, a fixed padded size, vs ML-DSA's 2,420 bytes) make it attractive for constrained card chips on size alone. In its March 2024 position statement, EMVCo names no post-quantum algorithm for EMV cards; the card-side evidence is research, such as a 2022 IDEMIA prototype that tried Falcon and Dilithium on a banking card

chunks.content:

Cross-border instruction messaging between correspondent institutions. Not itself a settlement system — it moves the instruction, not the money.
TLS + PKI-based message authentication; controls 2.1/2.4/2.5A/2.6 of the CSCF
Instruction metadata is commercially sensitive for years; sanctions and AML records are retained far longer.
The CSCF v2026 points these controls at Swift’s cryptography guidance, which Swift states will be updated in line with its post-quantum strategy. No dated mandate yet.
Real-time gross settlement operated by a central bank — the leg where finality actually happens.
HSM-backed signing, national PKI, TLS between participants
Individual payments are short-lived, but participant identity keys and the audit trail are long-lived.
BIS Project Leap Phase 2 is the reference experiment: in it, the RSA signature on the Business Application Header of the payment messages was replaced by a CRYSTALS-Dilithium post-quantum signature (the pre-standard version of what is now ML-DSA; BIS says it could not test the more recent ML-DSA version).
A payment may traverse several institutions. Security is only as good as the weakest hop, and no single party sees the whole chain.
Bilateral TLS + message authentication at each hop
Each hop retains records independently — HNDL exposure multiplies along the chain.
The hardest coordination problem in the sector: migration cannot be unilateral, which is why the sector bodies below publish jointly.
A key block wraps a cryptographic key together with its usage attributes, so a key issued for one purpose cannot be repurposed. The attribute binding is the security property — not the encryption alone.
Sometimes called a key control vector (CV): every operation outside the declared usage fails. EPC 342-08 notes this only works if all parties use compatible CVs with the same certified TRSMs enforcing the policy.
EPC 342-08 v16.0.1 describes ISO 20038 as "based on ANSI TR31" and cites X9.143 as the standard for key wrapping using AES and Triple DES. Material still teaching TR-31 as current is out of date — X9.143 is the live specification.
X9.143, X9.24-1/-2 and TR-31 are all ANSI-webstore purchases. This module teaches the concepts from EPC 342-08 (freely downloadable and mechanism-naming) and cites the X9 documents as normative but unobtainable, rather than paraphrasing standards nobody on the team has read.
The PCI PIN Security Standard requires implementation of Key Blocks (Requirement 18-3); PIN Security v3.1 incorporated the revised effective dates announced in July 2020 (v3.1 announcement).
NIST standardised the first PQC algorithms in August 2024: CRYSTALS-Kyber became ML-KEM (FIPS 203), CRYSTALS-Dilithium became ML-DSA (FIPS 204), SPHINCS+ became SLH-DSA (FIPS 205).
A further signature standard based on FALCON is in preparation, renamed FN-DSA (FIPS 206).

chunks.content:
Module: EMV Payment Systems & PQC
Data: cardCryptoData

The simplest offline authentication method. Card data is signed once at personalization by the issuer. The terminal verifies this static signature but cannot detect cloned cards because any copy has the same valid signature.
Replace RSA static signatures with ML-DSA-44 or FN-DSA-512. However, SDA is being phased out in favor of CDA regardless of PQC migration.
~5% of active EMV cards (legacy, declining)
Each transaction generates a unique RSA signature using the card\u2019s own ICC private key. The terminal sends a random challenge; the card signs it. This proves the card possesses the private key and prevents cloning.
FN-DSA-512 (Falcon, FIPS 206 in development) produces compact signatures (~666 bytes, fixed padded size) that are easier to fit in constrained card NVM. ML-DSA-44 signatures are ~2,420 bytes. FIPS 206 standardization for FN-DSA is pending.
Combined DDA/Application Cryptogram Generation
CDA (Combined DDA/Application Cryptogram Generation) combines dynamic card authentication with the Application Cryptogram (AC), binding card identity to the specific transaction. The card signs both its challenge response AND the transaction authorization data in a single RSA signature, providing both card authentication and transaction integrity.
This module's advice: Hybrid approach recommended: RSA-2048 + FN-DSA-512 dual signatures during transition. Long-term: pure FN-DSA-512 CDA when card chip capacity and terminal software support it.
~60% of active EMV cards (majority of new issuance)
Silicon vendor loads the chip operating system (Java Card, MULTOS, or proprietary OS) onto the IC. The OS provides the cryptographic runtime environment.
Card bureau loads the payment applet (Visa VIS, MC M/Chip, etc.) and initializes the file structure. Transport keys protect the card during manufacturing.
Issuer-specific data is written to the card: PAN, expiry, cardholder name, card risk management data. Issuer and network CA certificates are loaded for offline authentication.
The most security-critical step. ICC key pair is generated (on-card or injected), card master keys are loaded, and the ICC public key certificate is created and signed by the Issuer CA using RSA-2048.
FN-DSA-512 ICC key pair + ML-DSA-44 Issuer CA signature + ML-KEM-768 key transport
Card is tested for correct personalization, offline authentication capability, and online authorization. Transport keys are revoked and production keys activated.
The current EMV standard. RSA-2048 provides 112-bit classical security but zero post-quantum security.
FIPS 186-5 (approved, but quantum-vulnerable)
Payment-system (scheme) CA — public key held by the terminal
NIST FIPS 204 standard. Provides NIST Level 2 post-quantum security. Larger keys and signatures than RSA, but a standardised design based on the Module Learning With Errors problem and believed to be secure even against quantum adversaries (FIPS 204), with a claimed category-2 security strength.

chunks.title: EMV Payment Systems & PQC — migrationRiskData (data)
chunks.content:
Module: EMV Payment Systems & PQC
Data: migrationRiskData

HSMs use RSA-2048 to wrap and transport master keys between HSM clusters and to downstream systems. Quantum computers can recover wrapped keys, exposing the entire key hierarchy.
All payment HSMs globally (~100,000+ devices)
DUKPT Base Derivation Keys are wrapped with RSA-2048 for transport to terminals. Recovering the BDK compromises all past and future transactions for terminals sharing that BDK.
Card Personalization & Certificate Issuance
New cards issued with RSA-2048 ICC keys are quantum-vulnerable from day one. On an assumed 3-5 year card replacement cycle (this module’s estimate, not a sourced figure), cards issued today could stay in circulation until about 2029-2031.
Offline authentication relies on RSA (or ECC) signatures. A cryptographically relevant quantum computer breaking an issuer or payment-system key could let forged cards pass offline checks; breaking one card key only clones that card. Up to 14.7 billion EMV cards (EMVCo, Q4 2024) carry such keys, and EMVCo says that on current projections a realised quantum threat is unlikely prior to 2040.
14.7 billion EMV cards globally (EMVCo, end of 2024)
TLS connections between terminals, acquirers, networks, and issuers use RSA/ECDSA key exchange. Quantum computers can break these key exchanges, enabling man-in-the-middle attacks on authorization messages.
All online card transactions — ~$46.6 trillion a year across the five networks in the Network Comparator
Moving PIN encryption from 3DES to AES is classical modernisation, not a quantum fix: EMVCo states that the choice of symmetric algorithm and key size is driven by classical attack feasibility rather than by Grover\u2019s algorithm, and that even 2-key Triple DES keeps a significant security margin against a Grover attack. Millions of terminals still use 3DES DUKPT. The quantum-exposed link is the RSA wrapping of the BDK at key injection.
Token provisioning uses RSA/ECDH for key transport and ECDSA for device attestation. The token vault itself uses AES-256 (quantum-safe), but token-PAN mappings could be exposed via HNDL on TLS channels.
Billions of tokenized credentials across Apple/Google/Samsung Pay
Card-not-present transactions transmit PAN + CVV over TLS. HNDL attacks can harvest encrypted payment data for future decryption.
$6+ trillion annual e-commerce transactions
3DS 2.x uses ECDSA for challenge-response signing and device binding. Quantum computers can forge 3DS authentication, enabling unauthorized card-not-present transactions.
All 3DS-enabled merchants and issuers globally
Device attestation uses ECDSA certificates. Quantum computers could forge device attestation, allowing unauthorized devices to receive payment tokens.
Billions of active mobile wallet installations

chunks.content:
Module: EMV Payment Systems & PQC
Data: posCryptoData

Smartphone SoC (Snapdragon / Exynos / A-series)
Unattended Terminal (Vending, Parking, Transit)
Standard Key Injection Facility (KIF) Ceremony
A secure, audited process where cryptographic keys are loaded into payment terminals. The KIF is a physically secured room with dual-control, split-knowledge procedures. This is the primary quantum-vulnerable point in the DUKPT key management chain.
The Base Derivation Key (BDK) is generated inside a payment HSM (for example a PCI-approved PTS HSM). The BDK never leaves the HSM in cleartext. Dual custody is required (two key custodians each contribute key components).
No change needed \u2014 symmetric key generation is quantum-safe
The BDK is encrypted (wrapped) using an RSA-2048 key transport key for secure transfer to the terminal injection station. THIS IS THE PRIMARY QUANTUM VULNERABILITY: a quantum computer could recover the BDK from the RSA-wrapped ciphertext.
RSA-2048 key transport (PKCS#1 v1.5 or OAEP)
The RSA-wrapped BDK is transferred to the injection station via secure channel (TLS or dedicated HSM-to-HSM link). The injection station decrypts using its RSA private key.
ML-KEM-768 decapsulation + Hybrid ML-KEM TLS
The injection facility derives the Initial PIN Encryption Key (IPEK) from the BDK using the terminal\u2019s unique Key Serial Number (KSN), and only the derived key is loaded into the terminal\u2019s tamper-resistant security module; the BDK itself stays with the injection facility. All subsequent per-transaction keys are derived from the IPEK using symmetric DUKPT derivation.
3DES/AES DUKPT key derivation (symmetric)
No change needed \u2014 symmetric DUKPT derivation is quantum-safe
DUKPT (Derived Unique Key Per Transaction) generates a unique symmetric key for every transaction from a Base Derivation Key. The symmetric derivation chain is quantum-safe; only the initial key injection uses RSA (quantum-vulnerable).
Master key stored in payment HSM. Never exported in cleartext.
Derived from BDK + terminal Key Serial Number (KSN). Unique per terminal.
Binary tree of 21 future keys derived from IPEK. Each transaction consumes one key and derives the next.
Unique key for each transaction. Used for PIN block encryption (EP) and data encryption (DE). Discarded after use.
RSA-2048 key transport of BDK at Key Injection Facility (KIF). Compromising the BDK allows derivation of ALL past and future transaction keys for terminals sharing that BDK.

chunks.content:
Module: EMV Payment Systems & PQC
Data: tokenizationData

Visa\u2019s Token Service Provider replaces the real PAN with a Visa token for use in mobile wallets, e-commerce, and IoT payments. Token lifecycle managed by Visa\u2019s token vault.
Cardholder enters card details or scans card. Wallet app collects PAN, expiry, and device information, then sends enrollment request to Visa.
Visa routes the request to the card issuer for identity verification. Issuer may use SMS OTP, in-app push, or call center verification.
Visa generates a payment token (16-digit surrogate PAN) and creates a mapping entry in the token vault. Token is assigned a domain restriction (e.g., mobile NFC only).
A unique per-device token cryptographic key (LUK \u2014 Limited Use Key) is generated and encrypted for transport to the device Secure Element.
ML-KEM-768 key agreement + AES-256 wrapping
Token and LUK are installed into the device Secure Element (Apple SEP, Android StrongBox, Samsung Knox). Device attestation confirms the SE integrity.
Token is activated in the vault. Cardholder receives confirmation. Token is now ready for contactless or in-app payments.
Mastercard Digital Enablement Service (MDES)
Mastercard\u2019s tokenization platform provides lifecycle management for digitized credentials. Supports cloud-based payments (HCE) and Secure Element-based wallets.
Wallet provider submits a digitization request with encrypted card data. MDES validates the request format and routes to the issuer.
Issuer performs risk assessment and identity verification. May require additional authentication (step-up) via SMS, app push, or email.
MDES generates the token PAN and associated credentials. For HCE (cloud), generates cloud-based payment credentials. For SE, generates SE-targeted credentials.
Encrypted credentials delivered to the wallet provider for installation on the device. Uses Mastercard\u2019s secure credential delivery protocol.
Wallet app installs credentials in Secure Element or cloud-based TEE. Device attestation verifies platform integrity.
Token activated in MDES vault. For HCE tokens, replenishment keys are provisioned for dynamic credential refresh.
Amex\u2019s three-domain model tokenization service. Amex is unique as both the network and issuer for most cards, simplifying the token lifecycle.
Wallet sends a token request with encrypted card data to Amex. As both network and issuer, Amex handles the full lifecycle internally.
Hybrid ML-KEM TLS + ML-KEM payload encryption
Amex performs internal identity verification. Since Amex is typically both network and issuer, there is no inter-party routing.
Token and associated cryptographic material generated in Amex HSMs. Token mapped to the card account in the internal vault.
Encrypted token and LUK delivered to wallet provider for device provisioning.
Credentials installed in the device Secure Element with device attestation.
Token activated. Amex\u2019s closed-loop model means the token vault lookup during transactions is internal, reducing latency.

chunks.title: EMV Payment Systems & PQC — transactionFlowData (data)
chunks.content:
Module: EMV Payment Systems & PQC
Data: transactionFlowData

Standard EMV chip transaction with real-time issuer authorization. The card generates an ARQC cryptogram using symmetric keys, sent through the acquirer and network to the issuer for verification.
Terminal reads card AID list and selects payment application. No cryptographic operations at this stage.
Terminal verifies the ICC certificate chain: payment-system (scheme) CA public key held in the terminal \u2192 Issuer certificate \u2192 ICC certificate. All signatures are RSA.
ML-DSA-44 or FN-DSA-512 certificate chain
~0.8 KB (issuer and ICC certificates from the card)
Card generates Authorization Request Cryptogram (ARQC) using 3DES/AES session key derived from card master key. Includes transaction amount, terminal data, and unpredictable number.
Terminal sends authorization request with ARQC to acquirer processor over TLS-encrypted connection.
Acquirer routes the authorization message (ISO 8583) to the appropriate card network switch. Network applies fraud rules and forwards to issuer.
Issuer ARQC Verification & ARPC Generation
Issuer HSM verifies the ARQC using the card master key (symmetric), checks balance/fraud. Generates ARPC (Authorization Response Cryptogram) for the card. The card master key lives in the HSM under a symmetric Local Master Key, so nothing in this step is quantum-vulnerable — the RSA exposure in issuer key management is in key DISTRIBUTION between institutions, modelled separately as the hsm-key-wrapping and key-injection vectors.
Issuer sends approve/decline with ARPC back through the network and acquirer to the terminal. Card verifies ARPC to authenticate the issuer.
Dynamic Data Authentication: the card proves its authenticity by generating a unique RSA signature per transaction. No network connection required \u2014 the terminal verifies locally using the certificate chain.
Terminal reads card AID and selects payment application.
Terminal recovers and verifies the ICC public key from the chain: payment-system CA public key (in the terminal) \u2192 Issuer certificate \u2192 ICC certificate. All RSA.
FN-DSA-512 certificate chain (compact signatures)
Card signs a challenge (terminal unpredictable number + card data) with its ICC private key. This proves the card has the private key and is not a clone.
Terminal verifies the dynamic signature using the recovered ICC public key. If valid, card is authenticated as genuine.
Terminal approves transaction based on offline floor limits and risk management. Transaction log stored for later batch upload.
Combined Data Authentication (CDA): the card signs the Application Cryptogram (AC) together with dynamic transaction data, combining card authentication and transaction integrity in a single signature. Requires the terminal to verify the card signature offline.
Terminal verifies the ICC public key certificate chain. Same 3-level RSA chain as DDA.
AC + SSAD Generation (Combined Signature)
Card generates Application Cryptogram (AC) using symmetric key AND signs it together with dynami
...(truncated)

Work through these scenarios to understand S/MIME certificate structure, CMS signing, and KEM-based encryption. Each exercise pre-configures the Workshop — click "Load & Run" to begin.
Take the PQC quiz to test what you've learned about email and document signing.
1. RSA vs ML-DSA Certificate Fields
Examine an S/MIME signing certificate side by side: RSA-2048 vs ML-DSA-65. Compare the public key sizes, signature sizes, and total certificate footprint. Note which fields are identical and which change.
The X.509 extensions (keyUsage, extKeyUsage, subjectAltName) are identical for both algorithms. Only the algorithm OID, key size (256 vs 1,952 bytes), and signature size (256 vs 3,309 bytes) differ.
Walk through the four-stage signing pipeline: content preparation, SHA-256 hashing, signature generation, and CMS wrapping. Step through each stage and observe how the ASN.1 tree builds up.
The CMS SignedData structure is algorithm-agnostic by design. The signer info contains the algorithm OID and signature bytes, but the overall structure is the same for ECDSA and ML-DSA.
Toggle between RSA key transport and ML-KEM encryption modes. Compare how the CEK is delivered to the recipient in each case. Pay attention to the extra KDF and key-wrap steps in the KEM flow.
RSA directly encrypts the CEK (one step). ML-KEM requires three steps: encapsulation, key derivation (HKDF), and key wrapping (AES-WRAP). Despite the extra complexity, KEM is quantum-safe.

5. Dual-Algorithm Migration Strategy

chunks.title: Email Signing — EmailSigningIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Email Signing
Component: EmailSigningIntroduction

Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) , defined in RFC 5652, is the foundational format for digitally signing and encrypting arbitrary data. It powers S/MIME (Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions), the standard for end-to-end email security used by enterprises, governments, and military organizations worldwide.
“CMS is used to digitally sign, digest, authenticate, or encrypt arbitrary message content.”
Creates a CMS SignedData structure: the sender's private key signs a hash of the message, and recipients verify using the sender's certificate.
Creates a CMS AuthEnvelopedData structure (RFC 5083): the message is AEAD-encrypted ( AES -GCM) with a random content-encryption key (CEK), which is then wrapped for each recipient.
• Email (S/MIME) • Document signing • Code signing • Timestamping • PDF signatures • SCEP / EST • Firmware updates • eIDAS signatures
The IETF LAMPS working group has published a series of RFCs that bring post-quantum cryptography into CMS. These standards define how PQC algorithms integrate with existing S/MIME infrastructure.
In this module's reading, together, these RFCs provide a complete PQC story for CMS: ML-DSA for signing (RFC 9882), KEM-based encryption via KEMRecipientInfo (RFC 9629), RSA-KEM as a transitional KEM option (RFC 9690), and HSS/LMS for hash-based firmware and long-lived signatures (RFC 9708). See the References tab for full details on each standard.

chunks.title: Email Signing — EmailSigningIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Email Signing
Component: EmailSigningIntroduction

Classical S/MIME encryption uses RSA key transport : the sender encrypts the CEK directly with the recipient's RSA public key. PQC replaces this with a Key Encapsulation Mechanism (KEM) — a fundamentally different approach.
The CEK is directly encrypted — vulnerable to Shor's algorithm.
No direct encryption of CEK — quantum-resistant shared secret derivation.
Post-quantum public-key encryption (like lattice-based encryption) is less efficient and harder to standardize than KEM + symmetric key wrap. NIST standardized ML-KEM ( FIPS 203) as a KEM primitive, not a public-key encryption scheme. RFC 9629 bridges this gap by defining KEMRecipientInfo, a new CMS structure that replaces KeyTransRecipientInfo.
S/MIME certificates carry specific extensions that bind an email address to a key pair and declare the permitted operations (signing vs encryption). PQC introduces new considerations for key usage and algorithm negotiation.
• keyUsage: keyEncipherment (RSA) or keyAgreement ( ECDH). For ML-KEM certificates keyEncipherment is the only key usage set when keyUsage is present (RFC 9935 §5)
In practice, users often have separate key pairs for signing and encryption. This is especially true for PQC migration, where signing keys (ML-DSA) and encryption keys (ML-KEM) use fundamentally different algorithms. The smimeCapabilities attribute in signed messages advertises supported algorithms, enabling gradual PQC rollout.

chunks.title: Email Signing — EmailSigningIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Email Signing
Component: EmailSigningIntroduction

S/MIME is not the only way mail and files get signed and encrypted. OpenPGP (RFC 9580, the 2024 revision that introduced version 6 keys) has no X.509 certificates and no CA: keys carry their own identities and are trusted through signatures from other keys. Its PQC migration therefore arrives as new algorithm IDs inside keys and packets, not as new certificate profiles — and it is already a Proposed Standard: RFC 9980, Post-Quantum Cryptography in OpenPGP.
RFC 9980 takes a different line from the CMS RFCs above. Because lattice schemes are new, ML-KEM and ML-DSA are used only as PQ/T composites — each one is bound to an elliptic-curve partner so that, in the RFC's words, security is retained even if all schemes but one in the combination are broken. The one exception is SLH-DSA, whose hash-based security assumptions the RFC considers well enough understood to stand alone.
A conformant implementation MUST implement ML-DSA-65+Ed25519 and ML-KEM-768+X25519; the 1024/448 pair is SHOULD. Deployment detail that bites: the PQ algorithms are for v6 keys only, with one exception — ML-KEM-768+X25519 (ID 35) is also allowed in v4 encryption-capable subkeys, so an existing v4 key can gain a post-quantum encryption subkey without a full key rollover, while PQ signing waits for a v6 primary key.

chunks.title: Email Signing — EmailSigningIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Email Signing
Component: EmailSigningIntroduction

Compare with S/MIME: same primitives (ML-KEM, ML-DSA, SLH-DSA), same key-exchange → signature split, but OpenPGP mandates the hybrid pairing that LAMPS leaves to the deployment, and it has no certificate-profile work to do because it never had certificates. The Industry Landscape tracks this as the cross-industry use case “OpenPGP email & file encryption”.
Migrating email security to PQC is uniquely challenging because S/MIME requires bidirectional compatibility — both sender and recipient must support the same algorithms. This creates a chicken-and-egg problem that doesn't exist in TLS (where servers can unilaterally upgrade).
Explore S/MIME certificates, CMS signing structures, and KEM-based encryption.

Visual checks describe these 64 bytes only and give no security verdict. The health tests treat each byte as a raw noise-source sample at an assumed H = 8 bits/sample; on browser output they are a demonstration only.
Use "Flip 10%" a few times: random flips on random data leave random-looking data, so the checks rarely react.
