chunks.title: Entropy & Randomness — EntropyExercises
chunks.content:
Module: Entropy & Randomness
Component: EntropyExercises

These exercises guide you through practical entropy analysis scenarios. Each exercise opens the Workshop tab with pre-configured settings.
Ready to test what you've learned about entropy and randomness?
1. A Stuck Source: Which Check Belongs in the Device?
Load All Zeros (a stuck-at failure) and run the checks. Every result turns red. Decide which of them an entropy source has to run on its own raw samples while it operates, and why the others cannot stand in for it.
Every visual check lands outside range and both health tests signal a failure (Repetition Count sees a run of 64 against a cutoff of 4 at the assumed H = 8 bits/sample). Only the health tests belong in the device: SP 800-90B §4.3 says the health tests "shall include both continuous and start-up tests", and the Repetition Count Test is there "to quickly detect catastrophic failures that cause the noise source to become “stuck”" (§4.4.1). The visual checks describe one buffer after the fact.
2. Repeating Pattern: Stuck or Biased?
Load Repeating Pattern (0xDEADBEEF over and over) and run the checks. Before reading the health-test group, predict which of the two SP 800-90B health tests catches a source that never repeats a byte back-to-back but keeps returning to the same few values.

chunks.title: Entropy & Randomness — EntropyExercises
chunks.content:
Module: Entropy & Randomness
Component: EntropyExercises

Repetition Count signals nothing, because no byte repeats consecutively. Adaptive Proportion signals a failure: in each of the two 512-sample windows 0xDE recurs 128 times, against a cutoff of 13 (SP 800-90B Table 2: H = 8, W = 512, alpha = 2^-20). That is the split SP 800-90B describes — Repetition Count for a source stuck on one value (§4.4.1), Adaptive Proportion to detect "when some value begins to occur much more frequently than expected" (§4.4.2). This sample is 1,024 bytes, so the window is the full W = 512 that §4.4.2 specifies for 8-bit samples and the 1,024-sample startup minimum of §4.3 item 4 is met; the shorter 64-byte samples on this page only run a partial window.
3. DRBG State Machine: What Does a Known-Answer Match Prove?
Instantiate HMAC_DRBG, press Generate until it refuses, then Reseed. Run the known-answer check. Decide: if all 16 NIST vectors match byte for byte, what have you learned about the entropy input on this page?

chunks.title: Entropy & Randomness — EntropyExercises
chunks.content:
Module: Entropy & Randomness
Component: EntropyExercises

Generate refuses once reseed_counter exceeds the demo interval of 10 (SP 800-90A Rev. 1 §10.1.2.5 step 1; Table 2 allows HMAC_DRBG up to 2^48 requests between reseeds), and Reseed takes fresh entropy input and sets the counter back to 1 (§10.1.2.4). The vectors match because HMAC_DRBG is deterministic: the same entropy input, nonce and personalization string always give the same output, and one flipped entropy-input bit gives a different one. So a match shows the mechanism is computed correctly — and nothing about the entropy input. The output is only as unpredictable as the seed, which is why SP 800-90C §2.6 has validated SP 800-90B entropy sources provide the seed material.
4. One Source Compromised: Does the Other Save You?
In Step 6, load the "Stuck source, detected" counterexample, then "Malicious cancellation". In both, Source A is compromised and Source B is healthy. For each, decide before reading the verdict whether Source B justifies the construction.

chunks.title: Entropy & Randomness — EntropyExercises
chunks.content:
Module: Entropy & Randomness
Component: EntropyExercises

Stuck source: the raw-sample health tests catch Source A and its samples are excluded (SP 800-90C §3.1 item 4.a.1), so only Source B’s 256 declared bits are credited — fewer than the 384 bits (3s/2 for s = 256, §2.6 item 11) needed to instantiate the DRBG — and the sources are not validated: "Not enough evidence". Malicious cancellation: an attacker who controls A and can see B sets A = B, and A ⊕ B is all zeros: "Construction is unsafe". Whether the surviving source protects you depends on independence, the adversary’s control and the entropy you can credit — not on the combining function.
5. Where Must the Health Test Sit?
Load the "Conditioned output from a failed source" counterexample: Source A is biased toward 0x5A and the design conditions its samples anyway. Walk the pipeline to Step 5 and run the output diagnostics. Decide: could any check on the final output have caught this failure?
In Step 2 only Adaptive Proportion signals Source A’s failure — 0x5A is every fourth sample but never repeats back-to-back, so Repetition Count stays quiet. After conditioning and the HKDF expansion, the output diagnostics usually land within range. No output check could have caught it: SP 800-90B §4.3 item 6 says "Health tests shall be performed on the noise source samples before any conditioning is done." The verdict is "Construction is unsafe" — entropy collected by a failed source shall not be used (SP 800-90C §3.1 item 4.a.1).
6. A Counter Passes the Health Tests

chunks.title: Entropy & Randomness — EntropyExercises
chunks.content:
Module: Entropy & Randomness
Component: EntropyExercises

Load Incrementing (bytes 0x00, 0x01, 0x02, …) and run the checks, then look at the Bit Matrix and the lag plot. The sequence is completely predictable. Decide why both SP 800-90B health tests stay quiet, and what that tells you about what health tests are for.
No byte repeats and no value recurs in the window, so Repetition Count and Adaptive Proportion signal nothing; the monobit and chi-squared checks and the straight line in the lag plot give the pattern away. Health tests are not an entropy assessment: SP 800-90B §4.2 says continuous tests "are usually designed so that only gross failures are likely to be detected". Whether a source is predictable is a question for the SP 800-90B entropy assessment of at least 1,000,000 raw noise-source samples (§3.1.1), not for any check on 64 bytes.
Enable all four sources (Web Crypto, OpenSSL, Math.random, Timestamp LCG), generate, and use Predict Next 4 Bytes to show the LCG is fully predictable. Then press Compare All Tests. Decide what verdict about a generator the visual-check group can support.

chunks.title: Entropy & Randomness — EntropyExercises
chunks.content:
Module: Entropy & Randomness
Component: EntropyExercises

The prediction matches the LCG’s next bytes exactly, yet Math.random() and the LCG usually land within range on the visual checks and signal nothing on the health tests. That is the expected lesson: output statistics cannot tell a predictable generator from an unpredictable one, so the visual group supports no secure or insecure verdict. What separates the sources is both the mechanism and its seed: each LCG state is a fixed linear function of the previous one, so whoever learns the state knows every later output however good the seed was, and here it is seeded from the clock; Web Crypto and OpenSSL run cryptographic generators seeded from the operating system’s entropy source.
8. Corruption Without Structure
Switch to Bit Flipper mode. Press Flip 10% a few times, then All Zeros. Decide why the checks barely react to random flips but all react to All Zeros, and what that means for spotting a degraded or tampered source from its output.
Flipping random bits of random data leaves random-looking data, so the visual checks mostly stay within range and the health tests stay quiet; All Zeros sends every visual check outside range and trips both health tests. Output checks only see structure. A degraded source that still emits unstructured output — or a generator seeded with a guessable value — looks the same as a healthy one, which is why assurance comes from assessing the noise source, not from checking its output.
9. Live Degradation: Which Health Test Fires?

chunks.title: Entropy & Randomness — EntropyExercises
chunks.content:
Module: Entropy & Randomness
Component: EntropyExercises

Switch to Live Monitor. Stream Web Crypto, then switch to All Zeros, then to Repeating 0xDEADBEEF. For each bad source, predict which SP 800-90B health test fires before you look.
All Zeros trips Repetition Count in the first batch — a stuck source is the failure it exists for (SP 800-90B §4.4.1). The repeating pattern never repeats a byte back-to-back, so Repetition Count stays quiet and Adaptive Proportion fires instead (§4.4.2, here on a 64-sample partial window). Continuous tests run on the noise-source output while it operates, to detect failures (§4.2), and SP 800-90B requires them (§4.3). These gauges run on 64-byte batches of browser output, so they demonstrate the idea; they are not an entropy-source health test.

chunks.title: Entropy & Randomness — EntropyIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Entropy & Randomness
Component: EntropyIntroduction

Cryptographic key generation and randomized operations depend on the quality of randomness used for keys, nonces, and initialization vectors. A perfectly designed algorithm cannot provide its claimed security strength when its random generator is predictable. The difference between "secure" and "broken" often comes down to entropy — the measure of true unpredictability in the bits that seed your cryptographic operations.
Debian OpenSSL bug (2008): PID-only seeding left ~32,767 possible keys per key type, size and CPU architecture
Stateful Signatures (LMS/XMSS): Repeated key-generation material can duplicate signing state; catastrophic failure occurs if cloned or rolled-back state reuses a one-time key or leaf index.
Processor RNG instructions: Intel RDRAND and Arm RNDR return DRBG output, Intel RDSEED returns conditioned seed values from the on-chip TRNG — none is raw noise
Use additional sources only with justified independence and threat assumptions
Use the CMVP Entropy Source Validation process when validation is required
NIST's SP 800-90 series provides a complete framework for random number generation, from raw entropy sources to fully constructed Random Bit Generators (RBGs).
DRBG Mechanisms: Defines CTR_DRBG, Hash_DRBG, and HMAC_DRBG for stretching seed entropy into arbitrary-length random streams.
Entropy Sources: Methods for validating that physical noise sources provide sufficient entropy. Includes health tests and min-entropy estimation.

chunks.title: Entropy & Randomness — EntropyIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Entropy & Randomness
Component: EntropyIntroduction

RBG Constructions: How to combine entropy sources with DRBGs into complete Random Bit Generators. Defines RBG1, RBG2, RBG3, and RBGC classes.
SP 800-90A defines approved DRBG mechanisms built on symmetric primitives: hash functions, HMAC and block ciphers. Engineering judgment, not a NIST statement: Shor's algorithm does not apply to these primitives, so a DRBG's resistance to quantum attack depends on the primitive and security strength chosen — Rev. 1 CTR_DRBG still allows three-key TDEA alongside AES.
Note: SP 800-90A Rev. 1 (June 2015) is the current final version. It specifies Hash_DRBG and HMAC_DRBG (§10.1) and CTR_DRBG (§10.2).
SP 800-90B (2018) provides methods for validating that entropy sources produce sufficient randomness. Tests fall into two categories: continuous health tests that run during operation, and min-entropy estimators used during formal validation.
Detects a noise source that gets stuck on one value (SP 800-90B §4.4.1). The test signals a failure if a sample is repeated C or more times in a row, where the cutoff C follows from the assessed min-entropy H and the false-positive probability α.
Detects a large loss of entropy (SP 800-90B §4.4.2). It takes one sample, counts how many times that same value occurs within the next W−1 samples, and signals a failure if the count reaches the cutoff C; then it starts a new window with the next sample. W is 1,024 for a binary noise source and 512 otherwise.

chunks.title: Entropy & Randomness — EntropyIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Entropy & Randomness
Component: EntropyIntroduction

Tool: NIST provides an open-source C++ implementation (SP800-90B_EntropyAssessment) for running these tests on raw noise samples.
Errata status: Two errata for SP 800-90B have been identified by NIST. Review the current publication status .
SP 800-90B sets the requirements an entropy source must meet. The certificate comes from NIST's Cryptographic Module Validation Program (CMVP): a testing lab accredited for entropy validation submits the source's SP 800-90B conformance justification, and CMVP issues an Entropy Validation Certificate.
Separate from a FIPS 140-3 module certificate. Since 7 November 2020 CMVP has required module submissions to include documentation justifying SP 800-90B conformance where applicable.
Reusing an entropy-validation certificate: this means relying on existing validation evidence in another cryptographic module’s certification, not simply using the vendor’s software. “Reuse restricted to vendor” allows the same vendor to reuse the certificate when the entropy source meets the Public Use Document’s portability conditions, such as the environment and configuration. Another vendor needs written, signed permission from the certificate vendor’s named contact, and must still meet the applicable technical conditions. “Open for reuse” removes that specific permission requirement; it does not remove the technical conditions or allow another vendor to rebrand the validation as its own. NIST CMVP Management Manual, §4.8.1

chunks.title: Entropy & Randomness — EntropyIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Entropy & Randomness
Component: EntropyIntroduction

RBG constructions are a separate step: CMVP also issues Random Bit Generator Validation Certificates for SP 800-90C conformance; the CMVP Entropy Validations page names IG D.T as the guidance, and D.T is not in the 19 August 2026 edition of the Implementation Guidance.
NIST publishes no review duration. Do not plan around a fixed number of weeks.
Start with these four sections of the FIPS 140-3 Implementation Guidance (IG), edition of 19 August 2026.
Does my module need an entropy estimate? Which certificate caveat applies? IG 9.3.A, Entropy Caveats (last changed July 2024). It also says which module designs need an ESV certificate.
How does a lab test a source? What must the certificate show? IG D.J, Entropy Estimation and Compliance with SP 800-90B (last changed November 2021).
How does the CMVP read a particular SP 800-90B requirement? IG D.K, Interpretation of SP 800-90B Requirements (last changed April 2026).
How is entropy counted when several sources seed one DRBG? IG D.O, Combining Entropy from Multiple Sources (last changed May 2021).
A lab submits a source through the ESV Server to receive an Entropy Validation Certificate. Validated sources are listed in the CMVP Entropy Source Validation search. The older ENT entries are legacy. Where D.J applies, new submissions need ESV.

chunks.title: Entropy & Randomness — EntropyIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Entropy & Randomness
Component: EntropyIntroduction

"Quantum" describes a noise source; it is not evidence. A QRNG is judged by the same SP 800-90B requirements as any other entropy source, and SP 800-90B calls the noise source "the root of security for the entropy source and for the RBG as a whole". What matters for either kind is the assessed min-entropy of its raw data and health tests that catch it failing.
A certificate covers the implementation and versions it lists, not a vendor's whole product line.
A hardware noise source does not rest on a computational hardness assumption, so a quantum computer does not break it the way it breaks RSA or elliptic-curve keys. That does not make it secure: it is only as good as the entropy it actually delivers, and that has to be assessed and monitored.
Combining sources can add assurance, but only under stated conditions:
Defense-in-depth: A second source helps only if it is independent of the first. If one fails or is compromised, what is left is the entropy the other source actually delivers.
SP 800-90C: Specifies the RBG1, RBG2, RBG3 and RBGC constructions, which build RBGs from SP 800-90A DRBG mechanisms and SP 800-90B entropy sources

chunks.title: Entropy & Randomness — EntropyIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Entropy & Randomness
Component: EntropyIntroduction

XOR combination: XOR of two independent inputs is at least as unpredictable as the stronger one. If the inputs are correlated, or an attacker can influence one of them, that guarantee is gone. For a CMVP certificate, IG D.O says entropy sources can be combined only by concatenating their output strings, and IG D.K treats XOR of copies of a noise source as a digitization step that needs extra justification.
Conditioning: HMAC or hash conditioning can raise the entropy rate of its output, but it cannot add entropy. SP 800-90B assesses conditioned output from the entropy that went in.
Random-input length is not security strength. A 32-byte input does not by itself mean 256 bits of entropy or a 256-bit RBG requirement: each standard sets the minimum RBG security strength per parameter set. Only the additional randomness used for hedged signing has no mandatory minimum strength; key generation does.
Example. ML-KEM-768 encapsulation uses a 32-byte random input, but the length alone does not tell you whether the generator is suitable. FIPS 203 requires an approved random bit generator with at least 192-bit security strength for ML-KEM-768. Read the generator’s documented strength and approval evidence rather than infer them from the output length. An algorithm test matching the expected output does not, by itself, establish that the randomness source meets its requirements.

chunks.title: Entropy & Randomness — EntropyIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Entropy & Randomness
Component: EntropyIntroduction

ML-DSA uses randomness for two different purposes. Creating the key pair uses a fresh 32-byte seed (ξ) that must come from an approved random bit generator — for example, at least 192-bit strength for ML-DSA-65 (FIPS 204 §3.6.1). Signing in the default hedged mode uses an additional fresh 32-byte value (rnd) that helps protect against side-channel and fault attacks. An approved generator is recommended, but other methods of generating fresh random values are allowed, with no numerical minimum strength; it must be generated inside the signing module (§5.4). Both inputs are 32 bytes long, but their generator requirements are not the same. The flexibility allowed for the signing input does not apply to key generation. The table below gives the rule for every parameter set.

All Zeros trips the Repetition Count health test in the first batch; the repeating pattern never repeats a byte back-to-back, so the Adaptive Proportion test fires instead. chunks.title: Entropy & Randomness — DrbgArchitectureDemo
chunks.content:
Module: Entropy & Randomness
Component: DrbgArchitectureDemo

Explore the internal lifecycle of a Deterministic Random Bit Generator. This is HMAC_DRBG with SHA-256 as specified in SP 800-90A Rev. 1 §10.1.2: the working state is the Key and V values plus a reseed counter, and every step updates them with HMAC-SHA-256.
The steps shown here are the HMAC_DRBG algorithms for Instantiate (§10.1.2.3), Generate (§10.1.2.5) and Reseed (§10.1.2.4).
A DRBG is not an entropy source: its output is only as unpredictable as the entropy input it was seeded with. Here the entropy input comes from the browser’s crypto.getRandomValues() as a stand-in. In SP 800-90C (section 2.2, Table 1) an RBG2 or RBG3 seeds its DRBG from entropy sources validated under SP 800-90B; an RBG1 is seeded once by another RBG (an RBG2(P), an RBG3 or a root RBGC).
Instantiate the DRBG first; Generate and Reseed unlock once it has a state.
The reseed interval is reached: press Reseed before generating again.

chunks.title: Entropy & Randomness — DrbgArchitectureDemo
chunks.content:
Module: Entropy & Randomness
Component: DrbgArchitectureDemo

Runs the same HMAC_DRBG code used above on 16 pinned SHA-256 vectors — 4 from NIST’s ACVP-Server hmacDRBG-1.0 sample set and 12 from the NIST CAVP HMAC_DRBG.rsp files. They cover prediction resistance on and off, reseed, and empty or non-empty personalization strings and additional input. Each output must equal the published answer byte for byte. The check then flips one bit in each input of two vectors — entropy input, nonce, personalization string, additional input, reseed entropy and additional input, and prediction-resistance entropy; every one of those runs must not match.
What a pass shows: this browser code computes the SP 800-90A Rev. 1 HMAC_DRBG mechanism correctly for these inputs. What it does not show: it is not a CAVP/ACVP algorithm validation, it is not an entropy-source test, and it says nothing about the quality of any entropy input.

chunks.title: Entropy & Randomness — ESVWalkthroughDemo
chunks.content:
Module: Entropy & Randomness
Component: ESVWalkthroughDemo

The first step is to formally describe the entropy source. The fields below are illustrative example values, not taken from a real submission.
Temperature: -40 to +85 C | Voltage: 1.0V - 1.2V | Sampling rate: 100 MHz
(example submitter estimate per 8-bit sample — Hsubmitter, SP 800-90B §3.1.3)
The noise source model describes the full pipeline from physical randomness to digital output. Each block must be documented and justified.
Key requirement: The model must include a stochastic analysis showing how physical randomness propagates through each stage. Failure modes (e.g., bias under temperature extremes, stuck-at faults) must be documented with mitigations.
The ESV Server runs the SP 800-90B Entropy Assessment Tool on outputs provided by the entropy source. The estimate is made from raw samples taken directly from the noise source, before any conditioning.
1,000,000 sequential raw samples, at least (SP 800-90B §3.1.1 item 1)
1,000 × 1,000 restart matrix: 1,000 restarts, 1,000 samples each (§3.1.1 item 3)
≤ 256 symbols: larger alphabets are reduced before estimation (§3.1.3, §6.4)
Must be unconditioned (raw noise) -- no hashing, no compression, no whitening.

chunks.title: Entropy & Randomness — ESVWalkthroughDemo
chunks.content:
Module: Entropy & Randomness
Component: ESVWalkthroughDemo

Health tests run on the raw noise-source samples, before any conditioning (SP 800-90B §4.3 item 6). §4.4 provides two approved continuous tests; if both are included, no other continuous tests are required. Startup tests run the continuous tests over at least 1,024 consecutive samples (§4.3 item 4), and the source must also support on-demand testing (§4.3 item 5).
C = cutoff value (consecutive identical samples before alarm)
W = window size: 1,024 for a binary noise source, 512 for a non-binary one (§4.4.2)
C = cutoff: the test takes the window’s first sample and counts how often that value occurs in the next W−1 samples; reaching C signals a failure. C is chosen so that a healthy source reaches it with probability at most α (§4.4.2).
Detects a large loss of entropy, such as one value becoming much more common than the assessed entropy allows.
Example: SP 800-90B Table 2 (α = 2-20): a non-binary source assessed at H = 8 bits/sample has W = 512 and C = 13. If the window’s first sample value occurs 13 or more times in those 512 samples, the test signals a failure.
The conditioning component is optional. It can concentrate entropy into fewer bits, but it cannot create entropy: because it is deterministic, the entropy of its output is at most the entropy of its input (SP 800-90B §3.1.5).

chunks.title: Entropy & Randomness — ESVWalkthroughDemo
chunks.content:
Module: Entropy & Randomness
Component: ESVWalkthroughDemo

When is the output full entropy? A vetted conditioning component may claim full-entropy output (SP 800-90B §3.1.5.1.2), but only when its input carries enough entropy. SP 800-90C §3.2.2.2 requires output_len + 64 bits of entropy for each use of the conditioning function that produces output_len full-entropy bits. With less input entropy, the output has less than full entropy however random it looks.
Raw samples: hin bits of entropy Conditioning Function Output: hout ≤ hin; full entropy only if hin ≥ output_len + 64
Through the Entropy Validation Server (ESV), an accredited lab submits an entropy source to the CMVP. The server runs the SP 800-90B Entropy Assessment Tool on the source’s outputs; the rest of SP 800-90B is covered by documentation, and a CMVP reviewer decides whether the justification is sufficient before an Entropy Validation Certificate is issued. Since 7 November 2020 the CMVP has required FIPS 140-2 and FIPS 140-3 module submissions to include documentation justifying SP 800-90B conformance, if applicable.
The same server accepts SP 800-90C random bit generator submissions (the CMVP Entropy Validations page names IG D.T for them; D.T is not in the 19 August 2026 edition of the Implementation Guidance), which lead to a separate Random Bit Generator Validation Certificate. Neither certificate is a FIPS 140-3 module certificate.

chunks.title: Entropy & Randomness — EntropyTestingDemo
chunks.content:
Module: Entropy & Randomness
Component: EntropyTestingDemo

This mode shows the visual checks and the SP 800-90B health tests side by side. Read them as separate groups: a count of passing checks is not an entropy verdict, and the health tests only mean something on raw noise-source samples.
Load a data sample and run the checks. Results appear in four separate groups: visual checks, SP 800-90B health tests, SP 800-90B entropy estimators (not run here) and primitive self-checks. None of them, alone or added up, tells you whether a source is unpredictable.
Samples are 64 bytes, except Repeating Pattern: it is 1,024 bytes, so the Adaptive Proportion test runs on full 512-sample windows as SP 800-90B §4.4.2 specifies and the 1,024-sample startup minimum (§4.3 item 4) is met.
The primitive self-checks for SHA-256 and HMAC are below; the HMAC_DRBG known-answer check is in the DRBG State Machine step. They show an algorithm is computed correctly and say nothing about entropy.
Byte value range (hex) — a flat histogram is consistent with uniform output; it does not show the source is unpredictable
These are simplified educational implementations. An SP 800-90B entropy assessment uses the NIST SP 800-90B EntropyAssessment tool ( github.com/usnistgov/SP800-90B_EntropyAssessment ) on at least 1,000,000 raw noise-source samples plus restart data (SP 800-90B §3.1.1).

chunks.title: Entropy & Randomness — EntropyTestingDemo
chunks.content:
Module: Entropy & Randomness
Component: EntropyTestingDemo

Hardware entropy sources and HSMs that provide NIST-validated entropy for production use are tracked in the Migrate catalog → Hardware Security Modules . NIST entropy source validation certificates are listed under Compliance, Entropy (ESV) . No standalone entropy-source products are currently cataloged; contributions welcome via the issue tracker .
Repeating Pattern (1,024 bytes)

chunks.title: Entropy & Randomness — QRNGDemo
chunks.content:
Module: Entropy & Randomness
Component: QRNGDemo

Simulation — no QRNG hardware involved. The “QRNG” sample below is generated on load (and on Try Another Sample) by the browser’s crypto.getRandomValues() — the same classical CSPRNG call the “CSPRNG” panel uses. It stands in for QRNG output so you can see the data flow and the tests; nothing here comes from a quantum device.
This tool compares three samples side by side: a simulated “QRNG” sample, a fresh sample from your browser's CSPRNG (Web Crypto API), and a deliberately broken weak PRNG. The first two are the same kind of output, so any difference in their results is sampling noise. The weak PRNG should visibly fail several tests, which shows what the tests can catch.
Simple statistical tests catch grossly broken output, like the weak PRNG's.
Good output from different generators looks the same to these tests.
How much entropy any source has. SP 800-90B estimates entropy from at least 1,000,000 raw noise-source samples, not from 64 or 128 bytes of final output.
A working CSPRNG and a working QRNG both produce output that passes standard statistical tests, so tests on output cannot tell them apart. Passing is the floor, not the differentiator.

chunks.title: Entropy & Randomness — QRNGDemo
chunks.content:
Module: Entropy & Randomness
Component: QRNGDemo

The difference is the noise source, which SP 800-90B calls “the root of security for the entropy source and for the RBG as a whole”. A QRNG's noise source is a quantum process. Whether a particular device actually delivers its claimed entropy is established the same way as for any other source: an SP 800-90B assessment of its raw data, plus health tests that detect failures in operation. The word “quantum” is not evidence.
SP 800-90B specifies the requirements and validation tests for entropy sources; it does not certify anything. CMVP issues Entropy Validation Certificates after an accredited testing lab submits the source's SP 800-90B conformance justification. Statistical tests on output are not that evidence.
Read each group on its own. Visual checks describe these bytes and give no security verdict. The health tests are defined on raw noise-source samples before conditioning (SP 800-90B §4.3 item 6); on these generator outputs they are a demonstration only.

Weak PRNG only ever emits values 0–15 (the high nibble is forced to zero), so its histogram is lopsided and the visual checks land outside range. The health tests, whose cutoffs assume H = 8 bits/sample, may signal a failure too. Gross structure like this is what output checks can catch.

chunks.title: Entropy & Randomness — QRNGDemo
chunks.content:
Module: Entropy & Randomness
Component: QRNGDemo

Simulated QRNG and CSPRNG usually get the same results because they are the same kind of output — the simulated QRNG sample is CSPRNG output. At 64 or 128 bytes a single check can land outside range for either by chance; that is a small-sample effect, not a finding about the source.
Statistical tests measure output patterns, not source security. A CSPRNG seeded with a compromised value can produce output that passes every test while being predictable to whoever knows the seed. Choosing a QRNG is a decision about the noise source; it still needs SP 800-90B validation and an SP 800-90C construction like any other source.
CMVP Entropy Validation Certificates for products marketed as quantum entropy sources
NIST SP 800-90B — Entropy Source Requirements NIST SP 800-90A — DRBG Mechanisms NIST SP 800-90C — RBG Constructions NIST SP 800-22 — Statistical Test Suite BSI AIS 20/31 — Functionality Classes for RNGs

chunks.title: Entropy & Randomness — RandomGenerationDemo
chunks.content:
Module: Entropy & Randomness
Component: RandomGenerationDemo

Compare cryptographically secure and insecure random sources side by side, and see why output that looks random can still be fully predictable.
Commit to a prediction before generating. You will test whether appearance reveals predictability.
Optional extensions; the guided comparison uses Web Crypto and the timestamp LCG.
src.id === 'openssl' || src.id === 'mathrandom').map( (src) => (
Visual similarity is not security. First recover the timestamp seed from four observed bytes, then continue the exposed state to predict future output.
This browser demonstration searches around the known generation time; a real attacker estimates that time from surrounding events.
Numerical Recipes parameters (Knuth, The Art of Computer Programming, Volume 2 — Seminumerical Algorithms, 3rd ed., 1997)
NIST SP 800-90A Rev. 1 §10 specifies three DRBG mechanisms: Hash_DRBG, HMAC_DRBG and CTR_DRBG. An LCG is not one of them, so it is not an approved DRBG. Each state is a fixed linear function of the previous one, so anyone who learns the state can compute every later output.
Date.now() has ~1ms resolution — an attacker who knows the approximate generation time can enumerate ≤ 86,400,000 candidates per day, making brute-force trivial on any modern CPU.
Exact match: continuing from the same exposed state produced these four bytes.

chunks.title: Entropy & Randomness — RandomGenerationDemo
chunks.content:
Module: Entropy & Randomness
Component: RandomGenerationDemo

An LCG is deterministic: knowing its state determines every later output. Generate starts a new timestamp-seeded run; verification above continues this run instead. LCGs must never be used for cryptographic key generation.
Each bar counts bytes in a 16-value range. Every chart uses the same vertical scale; this small sample can describe output, but cannot establish entropy or security.
Plots (byte[i], byte[i+k]) pairs. Random data fills the square uniformly; patterns create lines, clusters, or voids that reveal sequential correlations.
Products marketed as entropy sources for DRBGs and HSMs. Where a CMVP Entropy Validation Certificate exists it is named (checked 2026-09-24); a certificate covers the listed versions only, and none of this is demonstrated by this workshop.
Secure sources (Web Crypto, OpenSSL) draw from the operating system's entropy pool (e.g., /dev/urandom). Insecure sources (Math.random, LCG) use deterministic algorithms with predictable seeds — their output looks random but is fully reproducible. An SP 800-90A DRBG is deterministic too: its output is only as unpredictable as its seed, which SP 800-90C expects to come from validated SP 800-90B entropy sources.
Browser CSPRNG backed by OS entropy
OpenSSL DRBG seeded from OS entropy
Browser PRNG — NOT cryptographically secure
Linear Congruential Generator seeded from Date.now()

chunks.title: Entropy & Randomness — RbgConstructionPanel
chunks.content:
Module: Entropy & Randomness
Component: RbgConstructionPanel

SP 800-90C defines four classes of Random Bit Generator construction — RBG1, RBG2, RBG3 and RBGC — and every one includes an SP 800-90A DRBG (§2.2). The source combining pipeline demonstrated below implements the source assembly (§3.1) and external conditioning (§3.2) component of these architectures. A complete RBG construction would additionally include an SP 800-90A DRBG for pseudorandom bit generation.
DRBG seeded once from another RBG
A DRBG with no entropy source of its own. SP 800-90C §2.2: it "does not have access to a randomness source after instantiation"; it is instantiated once over a physically secure channel from an external RBG2(P), RBG3 or root RBGC construction, does not support reseeding, cannot provide prediction resistance and cannot provide full-entropy output. It can seed subordinate DRBGs (sub-DRBGs).
DRBG with its own entropy sources
One or more entropy sources instantiate the DRBG and may reseed it; prediction resistance is available when a reseed is performed. RBG2(P) uses a physical entropy source, RBG2(NP) a non-physical one. An RBG2 construction cannot provide full-entropy output.
Full-entropy output from physical entropy sources

chunks.title: Entropy & Randomness — RbgConstructionPanel
chunks.content:
Module: Entropy & Randomness
Component: RbgConstructionPanel

Includes one or more physical entropy sources and produces outputs with full entropy; prediction resistance is provided for all outputs. RBG3(XOR) XORs validated entropy-source output with the output of an instantiated, approved DRBG (§6.4). RBG3(RS) uses the entropy sources to provide seed material for the DRBG by continuously reseeding (§6.5).
Allows a tree of RBGs that consists only of RBGC constructions on the same computing platform. The root RBGC accesses an initial randomness source for instantiation and reseeding; a non-root RBGC obtains its seed material from its parent RBGC. Prediction resistance may be provided for the root, not for non-root RBGC constructions.

chunks.title: Entropy & Randomness — SourceCombiningDemo
chunks.content:
Module: Entropy & Randomness
Component: SourceCombiningDemo

ML-KEM and ML-DSA key generation consume random seeds. If the entropy behind the RBG is weak or a failed source goes unnoticed, a post-quantum key is as guessable as an RSA or ECDSA one.
SP 800-90B §4.3 item 6: “Health tests shall be performed on the noise source samples before any conditioning is done.” This workshop simulates the first five boxes. Its last stage is an HKDF expansion used as a stand-in; it is not an SP 800-90A DRBG, and nothing here is an SP 800-90C construction.
Step 2: Health tests on the raw samples — before conditioning
Counterexample active: the failed source’s samples are fed to the conditioner anyway. Watch the output diagnostics below stay within range.
Every source signalled a failure, so there is nothing to assemble: with Method 1 counting, SP 800-90C §3.1 (item 4.a.3) says the RBG operation shall be terminated when all physical entropy sources report failures.
Only one source is in use, so its request samples are the whole input.
HKDF-Expand (RFC 5869) stretches the block to 64 bytes so the diagnostics have something to look at. HKDF is not an SP 800-90A DRBG, and this pipeline is not an SP 800-90C RBG construction. In a real design the conditioned entropy seeds an approved DRBG — see the DRBG State Machine step.

chunks.title: Entropy & Randomness — EntropyEvidenceLab
chunks.content:
Module: Entropy & Randomness
Component: EntropyEvidenceLab

An ML-KEM or ML-DSA implementation can produce the correct test results without those tests establishing that its random generator meets the algorithm’s requirements.
This lab teaches you how to read the separate evidence about randomness. If your PQC migration also changes the hardware, operating system or random generator, check whether the existing evidence still applies.
Assess real CPU-jitter recordings from a KV260, an i.MX 95 and a Mac with the NIST SP 800-90B estimator tool, compiled to WebAssembly and run in your browser. Every result is estimator output for one dataset under its recorded conditions — nothing here validates or certifies a device.
Health tests run on the raw noise-source samples (SP 800-90B §4.4). Cutoffs derived from an estimate of conditioned output would be applied to the wrong stream, so none are derived for this dataset.

chunks.title: Entropy & Randomness — EvidenceLabScreens
chunks.content:
Module: Entropy & Randomness
Component: EvidenceLabScreens

Choose one stored dataset to examine. This does not activate a live entropy source or run an estimator. It prepares the selected bytes so the next screen can show their provenance, collection conditions and SHA-256 before you choose an assessment track.
The bytes are being prepared now. Select Next to inspect their identity and conditions; no entropy estimate exists until you choose a track and run the NIST tool on screen 4. Choosing another dataset clears any results from the previous choice.
in your browser. It is not a measurement of any device or noise source.
The browser analyses these generated values when you run the test. It does not contact a board or measure a live source.
The browser loads this saved recording and analyses it when you run the test. It does not contact the device or collect new samples. The collection conditions and dates are listed below.
The paired restart recording was collected by recreating the software collector 1,000 times and recording 1,000 samples each time. The board was not rebooted or power-cycled between rows.
Processed output — not raw noise. These bytes have already been processed by the operating system’s random generator. A high estimate on this file does not tell us how much unpredictable noise originally entered that generator. We need evidence about the underlying source too. This comparison checks whether the browser reproduces the stored native-tool results for the same dataset and settings. A match supports reproducibility, not the security of the source or certification. A mismatch needs investigation before relying on the result.
These observations compare our saved CPU-timing recordings from the i.MX95, KV260 and Mac. They are not new measurements from your current run. Some comparison datasets are not shipped in the Hub; their results were calculated previously with the native NIST tool.
1. A recording can look fine until you check what happens after restarting.
The Mac’s Linux VM, under added load, produced a long recording with no obvious problem in its entropy estimate. But a separate recording—made by repeatedly restarting the collection software—failed a check for excessive repetition.
The lesson: looking only at one continuous recording can miss a problem around startup. We have not established what caused this failure.
Here, “restart” means recreating the software collector, not rebooting the machine.
2. Making the machine busier did not consistently improve the results.
When we added work, the estimate went up on the i.MX95, KV260 and Linux VM, but down on native macOS.
The lesson: “more activity means more randomness” is not a safe assumption. We need measurements under the conditions in which the system will actually run.

chunks.title: Entropy & Randomness — EvidenceLabScreens

The Mac baseline was already busy with other work; it was not truly idle. These observations do not show that load alone caused the differences.
3. The same physical computer gave different results under different software environments.
The Mac running the collector directly in macOS produced different estimates from the collector running inside its Linux VM.
The lesson: the processor alone does not determine the result. The operating system and virtual-machine environment can affect timing measurements. These recordings do not isolate which factor caused the difference.
4. OS output scored higher, but we have not traced where its entropy came from.
Our OS random-output recordings received higher statistical estimates than our CPU-timing recordings on the i.MX95, KV260 and Mac environments. The recordings were collected separately, not as paired input and output from one generator.
The lesson: a higher output score does not show that the OS created extra entropy or improved the particular timing source we measured.
The limit: we have not checked the OS documentation and configuration to establish whether the measured timing source feeds those generators. These are separate recordings—not a demonstrated “before and after” comparison.
These are observations for particular recordings and conditions—not a ranking of hardware security, proof that a device is insecure, or an entropy validation. The expandable results below show the other recorded conditions for the selected device.

These estimators ask how easily the next sample could be guessed from bias or patterns. They return an entropy estimate, not a pass/fail score. A lower number means less unpredictability is credited per sample. Use the lowest applicable estimate, not the average or the most favourable result. A high number alone does not prove a secure source.
“Samples” means the original values; “bit string” means those values unpacked into bits. The table converts both to bits of entropy per sample so they can be compared. A dash means no value was reported, not zero entropy or a passed test.

IID assumes samples do not depend on earlier samples and their probabilities stay the same over time. It does not require all values to be equally likely.
Check for dependence between samples and changes in value frequencies across parts of the file. Rejection means the IID assumption is not supported; use the non-IID track.
Checks whether a repeated sequence is unusually long for the observed value frequencies under the IID assumption. Rejection means the IID assumption is not supported; use the non-IID track.
Compare the original order with shuffled copies, looking at trends, runs, repeats, periodicity, relationships between separated samples and compressibility. Unusual results in the original order can reveal dependence. Rejection means use the non-IID track.

chunks.content:
Module: Entropy & Randomness
Component: TestExplanations

Not rejecting IID means these checks found no reason to reject it in these samples. It does not prove independence: a source-design justification is also needed. Missing results or a tool error are not a pass.
A tool error means the assessment needs investigation. Read the diagnostic: failure to finish is not, by itself, proof of zero entropy.
A source can look healthy during a long run but repeat predictable behaviour whenever it starts again. Each row contains samples from one restart; each column compares the same sample position across restarts.
Sanity check: looks for a value occurring too often in any row or column, given the initial estimate. Failure means the restart data do not support that estimate; no entropy estimate is awarded by this assessment.
Row and column estimates: repeat entropy estimation in both arrangements. If either estimate is below half the initial estimate, the restart assessment fails. Otherwise, keep the lowest of the initial, row and column estimates. Passing can still reduce the amount of entropy credited.
What a pass means: these restart data passed these checks, not that every startup condition is safe. Here, device collection restarts the software collector, not the board power supply. An error or an unrun test leaves the assessment incomplete; it is not a pass.

chunks.title: Executive Quantum Impact — Introduction
chunks.content:
Module: Executive Quantum Impact
Component: Introduction

The quantum computing revolution is not a distant possibility — it is an active threat requiring executive action today. Harvest Now, Decrypt Later attacks mean that data intercepted today can be decrypted once quantum computers mature, potentially exposing strategic plans, financial data, and intellectual property years from now.
As an executive or GRC leader, the quantum threat impacts you differently than it does engineers or architects. Your responsibility is not to implement cryptographic changes — it is to ensure the organization is prepared, funded, governed, and accountable for a multi-year cryptographic transition.
Boards oversee material cyber risk. Quantum risk is now publicly documented, so it belongs in that oversight; what it means for directors legally depends on jurisdiction.
CNSA 2.0 (US national security systems) and EO 14412 (US federal civilian systems) set dated PQC milestones; the EU PQC roadmap targets 2030 and 2035. NIS2 and DORA add cyber risk-management duties, not PQC deadlines.
Competitors gaining PQC readiness first may win contracts, customer trust, and regulatory standing.
The timeline is tighter than most executives realize. NIST finalized its first post-quantum standards in August 2024, and regulatory bodies worldwide are already setting compliance deadlines:

chunks.title: Executive Quantum Impact — Introduction
chunks.content:
Module: Executive Quantum Impact
Component: Introduction

PQC Today summary: migration takes years, while long-lived encrypted data may be collected now for future decryption. Planning therefore needs to begin before a cryptographically relevant quantum computer exists.
Source: NIST IR 8547, Transition to Post-Quantum Cryptography Standards (final, October 2026).
Two separate US clocks run in parallel, and boards routinely conflate them. CNSA 2.0 governs National Security Systems. Executive Order 14412, “Securing the Nation Against Advanced Cryptographic Attacks” (signed 22 June 2026), governs federal civilian systems and the contractors that serve them — with OMB Memorandum M-26-15 (24 June 2026) as its implementing guidance. If you sell to the US government, the second clock is the one that reaches you.
Dec 2026 (180 days after EO 14412): the order directs the FAR Council to publish a proposed rule requiring covered federal contractors to meet NIST FIPS standards—including all applicable FIPS that incorporate PQC-compliant algorithms—by December 31, 2030. M-26-15 required agency PQC migration plans at OMB within 120 days of issue
2030: EO 14412 — federal High Value Assets and high-impact systems, and covered contractors, on PQC for key establishment (ML-KEM, FIPS 203) by 31 December 2030
2031: EO 14412 — the same systems on PQC for digital signatures by 31 December 2031. The split is deliberate: key establishment carries the harvest-now-decrypt-later risk, so it moves first

chunks.title: FIPS 140-3 Certification — FipsSections
chunks.content:
Module: FIPS 140-3 Certification
Component: FipsSections

, Security Requirements for Cryptographic Modules, was approved on 22 March 2019, took effect on 22 September 2019 and replaced FIPS 140-2. It is “applicable to all Federal agencies that use cryptography-based security systems to protect sensitive information in computer and telecommunication systems”, and it “provides four increasing, qualitative levels of security”. Canada accepts the same validations for its federal agencies.
The standard itself is short. Its §2 says FIPS 140-3 “is based on ISO/IEC 19790:2012/Cor.1:2015(E) and ISO/IEC 24759:2017(E)”, and the SP 800-140 series lists what NIST supersedes or modifies. ISO published 2025 editions of both documents (
still lists only the 19790:2012 and 24759:2017 editions, and the August 2026
still cites 19790:2012 throughout. Yet one IG note (IG 4.4.B) says the IG “is consistent with ISO/IEC 19790:2025”. The sources cited here contain no CMVP statement that adopts the 2025 editions or sets a transition date (checked 23 October 2026), so ask the laboratory which edition applies to a submission. Both ISO documents are paid, so this module does not reproduce them. It teaches from public NIST documents and real Security Policies instead.
Versions . The Manual and IG change several times a year; open the live documents before relying on a section number.
The CMVP is “a joint effort between the National Institute of Standards and Technology and the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security” (FIPS 140-3).

chunks.title: FIPS 140-3 Certification — FipsSections
chunks.content:
Module: FIPS 140-3 Certification
Component: FipsSections

Accredited CST laboratories test. Vendors “use independent, accredited Cryptographic and Security Testing (CST) laboratories to have their modules tested”.
The vendor contracts the lab, supplies the module and documents, and fixes what the lab finds.
The CMVP reviews the lab’s submission. If it passes, the validation authorities issue a certificate number (
A certificate covers a cryptographic module: a defined boundary, at named versions, in tested operational environments, used in its approved mode. Two real Security Policies show how narrow that can be:
AWS-LC 3 (, software): “The cryptographic boundary is defined as … a cryptographic library consisting of the bcm.o file”. The application that links it is outside, and the computer is only the “Tested Operational Environment’s Physical Perimeter”.
QASM (, HSM): the certificate covers the QASM module. The appliances it goes into add an x86 single-board computer running hardened Linux, which the Security Policy describes as a separate part of the product.
— one of the four Level 3 HSMs whose certificates approve ML-KEM and ML-DSA — reads like this :
A certificate snapshot for reading practice. Open the live page before quoting it: dates, versions and algorithms change with every revalidation.

chunks.title: FIPS 140-3 Certification — FipsSections
chunks.content:
Module: FIPS 140-3 Certification
Component: FipsSections

FIPS 140-3 names eleven areas: cryptographic module specification; interfaces; roles, services, and authentication; software/firmware security; operating environment; physical security; non-invasive security; sensitive security parameter (SSP) management; self-tests; life-cycle assurance; and mitigation of other attacks. Security Policies call the fifth area “operational environment”.
FIPS validation includes requirements for protecting keys and controlling their entry and output. It does not mean every validated module forbids every plaintext export: the applicable requirements depend on the security level, module type and transfer method. See
In a PKCS#11 interface, a key can be configured to refuse plaintext reads while permitting encrypted backup. Check the module’s Security Policy to understand which services and protections its validation covers. The linked Hub exercise demonstrates this selected key policy; it does not establish FIPS validation.
Open the PKCS#11 Learn exercises — choose Foundations → “Key wrap & the extraction question” for the AES demonstration.
A module is not rated once. Each published Security Policy opens with a Security Levels table, in the format
requires. It gives every area a level from 1 to 4, or N/A, and then the overall level. The requirements behind each cell are in ISO/IEC 19790, which is paid. The tables themselves are public, so we read four of them.

chunks.title: FIPS 140-3 Certification — FipsSections
chunks.content:
Module: FIPS 140-3 Certification
Component: FipsSections

Sources: the non-proprietary Security Policies of CMVP certificates (Crypto4A QASM), (Thales Luna T7), (Juniper EX2300/EX3400 switches) and (AWS-LC 3), each linked from its certificate page.
N/A is a real answer. AWS-LC’s Security Policy says of physical security: “The module is comprised of software only and therefore this section is not applicable.” None of the four rates non-invasive security.
Same overall level, different profile. QASM and Luna T7 are both Level 3, but only Luna T7 rates “mitigation of other attacks” (at 3). “Level 3” alone does not tell you which areas were claimed.
One area can exceed the overall level. The Juniper switches rate roles, services, and authentication at 3 and are overall Level 1. The certificate page lists that area under “Security Level Exceptions”.
The overall level matches the lowest rated area in all four tables. That is an observation from these documents, not a rule quoted here; the rule is in the standard.
Don’t infer a rating from a label. QASM and the Juniper switches both describe their operational environment as “Limited”. QASM rates that area N/A; Juniper rates it 1. Read the table.

chunks.title: FIPS 140-3 Certification — FipsSections
chunks.content:
Module: FIPS 140-3 Certification
Component: FipsSections

The Security Policy follows the same numbering, so the table doubles as a map. In the AWS-LC document, for example, §2 holds the boundary, the approved algorithms and key establishment; §4 the roles and the approved and non-approved services; §9 where keys are stored and how they are zeroised; §10 the self-tests; and §11 the installation and initialisation steps that the certificate’s caveat points to.
Adding ML-KEM or ML-DSA is not “one more algorithm”. It touches the approved security functions (new approved algorithms), SSP management (new key types and seeds), services (new approved services and their indicator) and self-tests (the IG 10.3.A tests for each PQC algorithm). Those are four of the five categories the Manual lists for an Update (UPDT),
: “approved / allowed security functions/algorithms, SSPs, approved security services, self-tests, and security states within the FSM”, each of which may not exceed 30% of changes. The Manual does not say how a PQC addition is treated; that part is our reasoning: expect it to be treated as a significant change, with the lab assessing it and proposing the submission route, and the CMVP free to decide that the changes exceed 30% and require a full submission (see the optional route table).

chunks.title: FIPS 140-3 Certification — FipsSections
chunks.content:
Module: FIPS 140-3 Certification
Component: FipsSections

FIPS 140-3 “provides four increasing, qualitative levels of security: Level 1, Level 2, Level 3, and Level 4. These levels are intended to cover the wide range of potential applications and environments in which cryptographic modules may be employed.” Read that carefully: increasing assurance for different environments, not a score where higher is always better.
Level 1 is not “software-only”. The Juniper EX2300/EX3400 switches ( ) are a hardware module at overall Level 1. Their Security Policy rates physical security at 1 and describes “a multi-chip standalone meeting Level 1 Physical Security requirements … completely enclosed in a … steel … enclosure”.
Level 1 is a real validation. AWS-LC 3 () is a Level 1 software module with a full certificate, tested platforms, self-tests and a Security Policy. Its certificate even approves ML-KEM.
The overall level is a summary. If your worry is physical attack, read the physical-security row. If it is operator authentication, read that row: the Juniper switches reach Level 3 there.
We don’t paraphrase the level-by-level requirements; they are in ISO/IEC 19790 as modified by the SP 800-140 series. The Security Policies do show what the evidence looks like:
Juniper, Level 1 physical: “No actions are required by the operator to ensure that physical security is maintained.”

chunks.title: FIPS 140-3 Certification — FipsSections
chunks.content:
Module: FIPS 140-3 Certification
Component: FipsSections

QASM, Level 3 physical: tamper labels the Crypto Officer inspects, and environmental failure protection — outside −10 °C to 70 °C, or outside the listed voltages, the module shuts down.
1.B: “At this time, the CMVP will only accept Overall Level 1 and Level 2 for sub-chip hybrid validations.”
§7.1.15: raising any section’s level, or changing the embodiment, makes it a new module that needs a Full Submission. Lowering a level is security-relevant: it may go through an Update (UPDT) with full testing of the sections lowered or affected.
So the level is a design decision you make once, early, from the threat model and what your buyers must show — not a label you upgrade later.
A normative requirement comes from FIPS 140-3, ISO/IEC 19790 as modified by the SP 800-140 series, the current IG and programme rules. A published certificate is evidence that one named module met its stated profile. A planning recommendation applies those requirements to declared threats and assumptions. Do not turn today's market pattern into a rule.
Level 2 is a real level too. The planner accepts it when the learner states the operational environment and confirms the applicable requirement-area evidence; embodiment alone never rules it out.
A FIPS 140-3 Level 3 HSM does not thereby have PCI PTS HSM approval — that is a separate device approval by a PCI-recognised lab, assigned and listed by PCI SSC (

chunks.content:
Module: FIPS 140-3 Certification

And a FIPS level is not an EAL: “FIPS Level 4 = EAL4+” compares two different schemes’ answers to different questions.
Area N/A by default; a publicly documented countermeasure must be addressed under “Mitigation of other attacks”
analysis and penetration testing at the level’s attack potential, if such attacks are within the Security Target’s scope

A FIPS 140-3 certificate tells you the module met the requirements the CMVP can test. Resistance to side-channel and fault attacks is, today, mostly not among them. The nearest tested feature is physical security: at Level 3 and above the lab tests environmental failure protection or testing, with “EFP temperature or voltage response parameters” (IG 7.A and 9.7.B).
The standard has an area for it; the program has no test metrics for it.
names non-invasive security as the major change from FIPS 140-2: “Major changes in FIPS 140-3 are limited to the introduction of non-invasive physical requirements.” But the publication that would say how a lab measures it,

chunks.title: FIPS 140-3 Certification — FipsSections

Module: FIPS 140-3 Certification

treats the area as not applicable by default: “Section 6.8, Non-invasive security is N/A by default as there are currently no requirements in SP 800-140F.”
That leaves a gap you can read straight off the Security Policy. With no approved metric, there is no CMVP-set leakage limit that a PQC implementation has to meet.
What a lab does check. Until SP 800-140F defines requirements, non-invasive mechanisms fall under “Mitigation of other attacks” (
Why it matters for ML-KEM and ML-DSA. Published research shows attacks on lattice implementations that have no countermeasures, and on some that do. A
concludes that “Variety of FIA are possible on unprotected Kyber and Dilithium”. A
covers side-channel and fault attacks on software implementations of ML-KEM and ML-DSA and reports that “Implementations protected by both masking and shuffling, or higher-order masking, may also be vulnerable”. These are research findings, not certification requirements. They explain why the question is worth asking a vendor.
Where attack testing does exist: Common Criteria. In a CC or EUCC evaluation, the

chunks.title: FIPS 140-3 Certification — FipsSections
chunks.content:
Module: FIPS 140-3 Certification
Component: FipsSections

family has the evaluator look for vulnerabilities and test them by penetration testing. The levels rise with “an increasing rigour of vulnerability analysis by the evaluator and increased levels of attack potential”: Basic (AVA_VAN.1 and .2), Enhanced-Basic (.3), Moderate (.4), High (.5). At AVA_VAN.5 “penetration testing is performed by the evaluator assuming an attack potential of High”. The limit is scope: the analysis asks whether vulnerabilities “can allow attackers to violate the SFRs”, so it covers what the Security Target claims, under the Security Target’s assumptions. The

What a FIPS 140-3 certificate and a CC or EUCC certificate show about side-channel, fault, random-number and implementation risks

Is there a CC or EUCC certificate for the same product, at which AVA_VAN level, with which assumptions? Which build and platform was tested? And what changed since?

The algorithm validation and the Security Policy, side by side
A certificate for a module and a certificate for its algorithms are different records. Practise reading both for the same operation.
A CMVP certificate lists algorithms, and each entry carries a reference such as A5631. That reference is a separate record, a CAVP algorithm validation. It lists what was tested for one implementation, including parameter sets and options.
A module's Security Policy, called the Policy below, has its own tables. Two of them matter in this step. The Approved Algorithms table names each validation number and prints its options. chunks.title: 5G Security — FiveGExercises
chunks.content:
Module: 5G Security
Component: FiveGExercises

Run these scenarios to compare classical, NIST-compliant, and post-quantum 5G security configurations. Each exercise pre-configures the simulator — click "Load & Run" to apply the settings and switch to the Simulate tab.
Take the Protocol Integration quiz to test what you've learned.
1. Profile A: Classical SUCI (X25519)
Run the full SUCI concealment flow using Profile A — Curve25519 (X25519) key exchange with AES-128-CTR encryption. This is the most common 5G privacy scheme deployed today.
Observe the 32-byte X25519 public keys, ECDH shared secret derivation, and the compact SUCI structure. Note the baseline handshake size for comparison with other profiles.
2. Profile B: NIST-Compliant SUCI (P-256)
Switch to Profile B — NIST P-256 (secp256r1) curve. This profile is common in legacy-compliant deployments and US federal 5G networks requiring FIPS-approved algorithms.
Compare the 33-byte compressed P-256 ephemeral public key in the Profile B scheme output with Profile A's 32-byte X25519 key. The SUCI structure is one byte larger because of the compression prefix.
3. Profile C: Post-Quantum SUCI (Hybrid)
Use Profile C in hybrid mode — combining X25519 classical ECDH with ML-KEM-768 lattice-based KEM. The shared secret is derived from both algorithms, providing quantum resistance with a classical fallback.

chunks.title: 5G Security — FiveGExercises
chunks.content:
Module: 5G Security
Component: FiveGExercises

Notice the 1,184-byte ML-KEM public key and the dual shared secret derivation (Z_ecdh + Z_kem). The SUCI is significantly larger than Profile A/B due to the KEM ciphertext (~1,088 bytes).
4. Profile C: Post-Quantum SUCI (Pure)
Use Profile C in pure PQC mode — ML-KEM-768 only, with no classical component. This is the target end-state for quantum-resistant subscriber privacy, using AES-256-CTR and HMAC-SHA3-256.
Compare with hybrid mode: no X25519 ephemeral key, only ML-KEM encapsulation. Notice AES-256 (vs AES-128 in Profile A/B) and SHA3-256 (vs SHA-256), chosen here for added resilience.
5. 5G-AKA: Mutual Authentication
Run the full 5G-AKA authentication flow: credential retrieval, RAND generation, MILENAGE computation (f1-f5), AUTN construction, and KAUSF derivation. See how the network and subscriber mutually prove their identity.
Watch the MILENAGE algorithm compute all five functions (MAC-A, XRES, CK, IK, AK) from K, OPc, and RAND. Note that MILENAGE uses AES-128 — a symmetric algorithm that Shor’s algorithm does not break, so it needs no PQC key-exchange or signature upgrade.
6. SIM Key Provisioning Supply Chain
Walk through the factory-to-operator K lifecycle: generate K in a factory HSM using TRNG, compute OPc (unique per SIM), personalize the USIM secure element, encrypt K for transport (eK), and import it into the operator's encrypted subscriber database.

chunks.title: 5G Security — FiveGIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: 5G Security
Component: FiveGIntroduction

3GPP TS 33.501 defines the security architecture for 5G systems, introducing fundamental improvements over previous generations. In 2G/3G/4G networks, the subscriber's permanent identity (IMSI) was transmitted in cleartext over the air interface, enabling "IMSI catchers" — rogue base stations that intercept and track mobile users. 5G addresses this with SUCI (Subscription Concealed Identifier), encrypting the subscriber identity before it ever leaves the device.
5G security rests on three pillars that work together to protect subscribers from identity theft, network impersonation, and supply chain attacks. Each pillar addresses a different phase of the subscriber lifecycle.
The USIM encrypts the subscriber's permanent identity ( SUPI) into a concealed identifier (SUCI) using ECIES or KEM. Only the Home Network can de-conceal it.
Mutual authentication ensures both the network and subscriber prove their identity. Uses the MILENAGE algorithm (AES-128 based) and a 5G-specific key hierarchy.
Secure SIM manufacturing and key distribution. Subscriber keys (K) are generated in HSMs, encrypted for transport, and stored in the operator's encrypted subscriber database.
3GPP defines multiple protection schemes for SUCI concealment. Each scheme uses a different asymmetric algorithm for key agreement, but all follow the same ECIES pattern: generate an ephemeral key, derive a shared secret, encrypt the MSIN, and compute a MAC tag.

chunks.title: 5G Security — FiveGIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: 5G Security
Component: FiveGIntroduction

33-byte compressed ephemeral public key (point compression is mandatory)
Profile C is not a 3GPP profile: TS 33.501 Annex C defines Profiles A and B and stops there. The name comes from a research proposal (Khan, Purification & Chang, Information 2025, 16, 617), which uses ML-KEM (Kyber-512). The parameters on this card, including ML-KEM-768, and the hybrid (X25519 + ML-KEM) mode that this playground adds, are the playground's own, not the proposal's and not 3GPP's.
TS 33.501 caps the output of a proprietary protection scheme at 3000 octets plus the size of the input. A note to that limit says it was chosen to allow the introduction of quantum-resistant protection schemes, but the specification defines none. ATIS, in its analysis "Preparing 5G for the Quantum Era", recommends that 3GPP specify quantum-resistant key encapsulation (for example ML-KEM) for SUPI protection, with optional support for hybrid cryptography (for example ECIES with ML-KEM).
5G-AKA (Authentication and Key Agreement) provides mutual authentication between the subscriber and the network. At its core is the MILENAGE algorithm, which uses AES-128 to compute five cryptographic functions from the subscriber key (K) and a random challenge (RAND):
f1 MAC-A — Network authentication token (USIM verifies the network is genuine)
f2 XRES — Expected response (network verifies the USIM is genuine)
f5 AK — Anonymity Key (conceals the sequence number in AUTN)

chunks.title: 5G Security — FiveGIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: 5G Security
Component: FiveGIntroduction

Before a subscriber can connect, their keys must be securely generated, written to the USIM, and delivered to the mobile operator. This supply chain is a critical trust boundary — if keys are leaked during manufacturing or transport, all subsequent security is compromised.
1. Generate K — 128-bit subscriber key created in the factory HSM (TRNG)
2. Compute OPc — Derived operator key (AES(K, OP) XOR OP), unique per SIM
3. Personalize USIM — Write K, OPc, and IMSI to the secure element
4. Encrypt for Transport — K encrypted with a pre-agreed Transport Key (eK)
5. Import at Operator — HSM decrypts eK; K stored encrypted in subscriber database for authentication
For consumer eSIMs that declare compliance with GSMA SGP.24, the eUICC itself is subject to product security requirements. GSMA SGP.24 says the IC/hardware platform on which the eUICC is based shall be certified to Common Criteria protection profile PP-0084 or PP-0035. It also says eUICC security evaluations are expected to include the complete Target of Evaluation defined in GSMA SGP.25, the protection profile for eUICC software that BSI registers as BSI-CC-PP-0100.

chunks.title: 5G Security — FiveGIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: 5G Security
Component: FiveGIntroduction

Not all parts of 5G security are equally vulnerable to quantum computers. SUCI concealment relies on asymmetric cryptography (ECDH in Profile A/B), which a large-scale quantum computer running Shor's algorithm could break. However, 5G-AKA authentication uses an algorithm set such as MILENAGE (built on AES-128) or TUAK — symmetric algorithms that Shor's algorithm does not break. Grover's algorithm can only erode the effective key length of a symmetric cipher. The 128-NEA and 128-NIA ciphering and integrity algorithms used on the air interface are symmetric too, so none of them carries a post-quantum key exchange or signature.
Profile C is a proposed migration path to quantum-resistant subscriber privacy. The research proposal replaces ECDH key agreement with ML-KEM (Kyber-512) encapsulation; this playground implements ML-KEM-768 and adds a hybrid transition mode (X25519 + ML-KEM-768) next to a pure PQC target mode, and the ML-KEM-768 parameter set and the hybrid mode are the playground's own, not the proposal's and not 3GPP's.

chunks.title: 5G Security — FiveGIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: 5G Security
Component: FiveGIntroduction

Telecom bodies have published post-quantum guidance and specifications, although TS 33.501 (Release 19, V19.5.0, February 2026) defines no post-quantum protection scheme for subscriber identities. GSMA's PQ.03 guidelines for telecom use cases present a phased approach to migration, and ETSI TS 103 744 covers quantum-safe hybrid key establishment. 3GPP's SA3 security group has started a study of the transition to post-quantum cryptography (TR 33.703); this is separate from TR 33.938, which is an inventory of the cryptography used in the 3GPP specifications for the 5G System in standalone mode.
SHA-256 binds both secrets so that breaking either classical or PQC alone is insufficient to recover Z. SHA3-256 is applied separately inside the ANSI X9.63 KDF. Pure mode sets Z = Z_kem directly (no combination needed).
