Government & Defense PQC — GovernmentDefenseIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Government & Defense PQC
Component: GovernmentDefenseIntroduction

The Commercial National Security Algorithm Suite is the algorithm list National Security Systems are required to use. CNSA 1.0 is the classical suite carried in CNSSP 15 Annex B; CNSA 2.0 replaces every public-key line in it. Reading the two side by side is the clearest illustration of crypto agility available in a real standard — the symmetric rows barely move, and the asymmetric rows are replaced wholesale.
This matters operationally: an estate search for “Kyber” will not find anything written after standardisation, and a search for “ML-KEM” will not find anything written before it. Inventory tooling has to know both.
NSA’s stated objections, which are worth knowing because other bodies recommend or require hybrids (for example BSI, ANSSI and ETSI TS 119 312) — see Hybrid Cryptography :
These dates are what separates this sector from every other one in this track. They come from CNSSP 15 as stated in the October 2026 CNSA 2.0 FAQ (Ver. 2.2) — not from the 2022 advisory, which carried a different, per-equipment-type timetable running from 2025 to 2033.

chunks.title: Government & Defense PQC — GovernmentDefenseIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Government & Defense PQC
Component: GovernmentDefenseIntroduction

The binding date for most vendors is the earliest one. From 1 January 2027 new NSS acquisitions are required to use CNSA 2.0 algorithms, regardless of how long the rest of the transition runs. That does not make every other product automatically unbuyable: NSA’s FAQ (version 2.2, October 2026) says that where no CNSA 2.0 compliant product meeting the need is available on 1 January 2027, a deployment may, if needed, be accepted on a vendor’s contractual commitment to provide a CNSA 2.0 update, combined with a realistic deployment plan that prioritises partial quantum resistance and meets the 2030 deadline for full quantum resistance, and NIAP Policy Letter #33 says that from 1 January 2027 government contracts must include language requiring products used in NSS to implement PQC or be updateable to implement PQC.

chunks.title: Government & Defense PQC — GovernmentDefenseIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Government & Defense PQC
Component: GovernmentDefenseIntroduction

Which deadline applies to a system depends on whether it is a National Security System. NSS follow CNSSP 15 and the CNSA dates. Federal civilian systems follow the OMB memoranda under the Quantum Computing Cybersecurity Preparedness Act and Executive Order 14412 (22 June 2026), which directs OMB to require agencies to move their high value assets and high impact systems to post-quantum cryptography for key establishment by 31 December 2030 and for digital signatures by 31 December 2031. Those deadlines are separate from the CNSA ones: National Security Systems are excluded from them and follow CNSSP 15, whose requirements and timelines NSA describes as comparable. Confusing the two is a planning error to avoid in this sector.
Commercial Solutions for Classified (CSfC) layers two independent commercial encryption implementations to protect classified data without government-furnished cryptography. Its PQC guidance addendum is the document that tells integrators how the layers change under CNSA 2.0 — but the April 2025 edition (version 1.0 draft .5) is a draft whose planned timeline, subject to change, aims for all CSfC solutions to implement post-quantum cryptography by 2030. And because a CSfC solution composes two implementations, it inherits the migration problem twice.

chunks.title: Government & Defense PQC — GovernmentDefenseIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Government & Defense PQC
Component: GovernmentDefenseIntroduction

Systems validated against a NIAP or CSfC profile can stay in use while the transition runs, but any reliance on non-CNSA-2.0 algorithms becomes reportable under NSM-10. NSA expects that reporting to continue for many customers through 31 December 2031. NSA also says that NIAP will begin archiving the certificates of partially quantum-resistant and quantum-vulnerable products generally within a year of fully quantum-resistant products coming on the market, that it expects this archiving to start in late 2027, and that products with archived certificates will not comply with CNSSP 11 and will not be appropriate for NSS.
The Federal PKI issues the certificates behind PIV cards, federal employee authentication, and document signing. Its certificate profiles are maintained by the Federal PKI Policy Authority — and there are currently two, which is exactly what crypto agility looks like as a document lifecycle rather than a slogan.
The PQC profile is a draft for CITE testing. It shows the direction and the intended algorithms, and it is not something to hold a supplier to yet. This module cites it as a draft deliberately.

chunks.title: Government & Defense PQC — GovernmentDefenseIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Government & Defense PQC
Component: GovernmentDefenseIntroduction

Two further details from the Federal PKI. The Federal PKI page announced that the Federal Bridge Certification Authority (FBCA) G4 would be replaced by the FBCA G5 starting 27 August 2026, to meet federal cryptographic-strength requirements, and that applications may need to update their trust stores with new intermediate CA certificates. And under the Common Policy, CA private keys must be held in cryptographic modules validated to at least FIPS 140 Level 3.
For X.509 and certificate-chain fundamentals this section deliberately does not repeat, see PKI .
Most organisations meet CNSA 2.0 not as a cryptography project but as a procurement constraint: from 1 January 2027 new NSS acquisitions must be CNSA 2.0 compliant, so the requirement propagates to every supplier in the chain.
CISA maintains a product-category list for PQC technologies, which is the practical starting point for working out which parts of an estate are in scope. It names ML-KEM (FIPS 203), ML-DSA (FIPS 204), SLH-DSA (FIPS 205) and the stateful hash-based signatures of SP 800-208, and it says that organizations should acquire only PQC-capable products in the categories it lists as widely available. The list is broader than the CNSA 2.0 algorithm set: NSA does not approve SLH-DSA, HSS or XMSS^MT for National Security Systems.

chunks.title: Government & Defense PQC — GovernmentDefenseIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Government & Defense PQC
Component: GovernmentDefenseIntroduction

NIST SP 800-171 Rev. 3 reaches further still — it applies to nonfederal systems handling Controlled Unclassified Information, which pulls contractors, universities and suppliers into the same conversation even when they never touch a National Security System. For defence contractors, DoD’s CMMC briefing (cleared for open publication on 21 January 2025) says assessments remain against Rev. 2 until DoD formally adopts Rev. 3 through rulemaking. Executive Order 14412 goes a step further for contractors: it directs a proposed Federal Acquisition Regulation rule that would require covered contractors to comply by 31 December 2030 with NIST’s FIPS, including all applicable FIPS incorporating PQC-compliant algorithms. The order directs that proposed rule; it is not itself the rule.
Algorithm support is only one gate. CNSSP 11 requires commercial IA and IA-enabled IT products bought to protect information on NSS to comply with the NIAP program, with agencies selecting evaluated products from the NIAP Product Compliant List, and, where applicable, with the FIPS cryptographic validation programs. NSA’s CNSA 2.0 FAQ (version 2.2, October 2026) says NIAP and FIPS validation are required in most circumstances, so in most cases a product needs NIAP evaluation and FIPS validation as well as CNSA 2.0 algorithm support.
CISA PQC Product Category List NIST SP 800-171 Rev. 3 CMMC 2.0 Executive Order 14412 CNSSP 11

It is strong evidence of direction and of the algorithms the Federal PKI intends to profile, and it is not something to write into a supplier contract yet. Treating a draft as a requirement is one of the more common ways migration programmes acquire commitments they cannot enforce.

chunks.content:

Which instruments bind a system, and whether it has a dated deadline at all.
The CNSA 2.0 dates do not apply here. The obligations are the instruments listed above: for federal civilian systems, inventory, reporting and migration planning plus the Executive Order 14412 deadlines for high value assets and high impact systems; for nonfederal systems, NIST SP 800-171 Rev. 3, with Executive Order 14412 only directing a proposed rule (not sourced in the Library). Programmes in this category often adopt the CNSA 2.0 dates voluntarily as a planning anchor — which is reasonable, as long as it is not described to auditors as a requirement.
Nonfederal system handling CUI

chunks.title: Government & Defense PQC — cnsaData (data)
chunks.content:
Module: Government & Defense PQC
Data: cnsaData

LMS or XMSS (NIST SP 800-208); ML-DSA-87 also approved
NSA moved this use case first, for three stated reasons: NIST had already standardised the algorithms, the use case is more urgent than others, and stateful hash-based signatures have the longest cryptanalytic history — their performance costs matter least here. LMS and XMSS are the approved SP 800-208 schemes (all parameter sets; NSA recommends LMS with SHA-256/192); the multi-tree variants HSS and XMSS^MT are not allowed. Validated ML-DSA-87 is also approved for software and firmware signing, but NSA wants LMS and XMSS adopted now where possible because validated implementations have been available longer. ML-DSA can make sense when a signing strategy needs more signatures than a single LMS or XMSS key can reasonably provide, or in distributed signing environments.
Level-5 parameters only. CNSA 2.0 does not offer the lower ML-KEM parameter sets that FIPS 203 defines — an NSS-specific narrowing of the standard.
Again level-5 only. ML-DSA-44 and ML-DSA-65 are FIPS-approved but not CNSA 2.0-approved. ML-DSA-87 is approved for any signing use case, including software and firmware.
Unchanged. Grover gives at most a quadratic speed-up, so a 256-bit key retains a 128-bit security margin. The advisory describes this section as only a modest change from CNSA 1.0, allowing a little more flexibility.
Symmetric primitives survive the transition. This is the part of the estate that does not need replacing — worth knowing before budgeting to replace it.
CNSA 2.0 algorithms will be required in all new acquisitions for NSS.
CNSSP 15, as stated in CNSA 2.0 FAQ Ver 2.2 (October 2026)
All NSS equipment and services that cannot support CNSA 2.0 must be phased out unless otherwise granted an exception. NSA also expects encryption to be broadly quantum resistant by default by this date.
CNSA 2.0 algorithms are mandated for use, unless otherwise noted, to achieve full quantum resistance for NSS.
The goal set in NSM-10 for achieving quantum resistance. NSA intends that all NSS will be quantum-resistant well ahead of 2035.
NSM-10, as described in CNSA 2.0 FAQ Ver 2.2 (October 2026)
The advisory predates FIPS 203/204 final. The two documents name the same algorithms differently.

chunks.content:
Module: Government & Defense PQC

Quantum Computing Cybersecurity Preparedness Act
Federal civilian executive-branch agencies
Requires agencies to inventory cryptographic systems vulnerable to a CRQC and to migrate them, with OMB reporting. The statute is what makes the rest of the stack enforceable rather than advisory.
OMB M-23-02 — Migrating to Post-Quantum Cryptography
To comply with NSM-10, directs agencies to submit a prioritised inventory of CRQC-vulnerable cryptographic systems (excluding National Security Systems) by 4 May 2023 and annually thereafter until 2035, or as directed by superseding guidance.
OMB M-26-15 — Execution of the Migration to Post-Quantum Cryptography
Implements the accelerated migration set by Executive Order 14412 (22 June 2026), and fulfils OMB’s responsibility under the QCCPA to issue guidance directing each agency to prioritise critical IT for migration to PQC and to plan that migration. Each agency submits a PQC migration plan within 120 days, phased from discovery (2026–2027) through pilots (2027–2028), prioritised key-establishment migration (2028–2030) and signature migration (2031) to full migration (2035). It does not apply to National Security Systems.
Sustains and amends prior federal cybersecurity direction, including the PQC provisions that drive the CISA product-category work.
Executive Order 14412 — Securing the Nation Against Advanced Cryptographic Attacks
Federal agencies (high value assets and high impact systems, not National Security Systems); covered contractors through a directed FAR rule
Section 4(b) directs OMB to require agencies to move all high value assets and high impact systems to post-quantum cryptography for key establishment by 31 December 2030 and for digital signatures by 31 December 2031. Section 6(c) directs the FAR Council to publish, within 180 days, a proposed rule requiring covered contractors to comply by 31 December 2030 with NIST FIPS, including all applicable FIPS incorporating PQC-compliant algorithms. The order directs a proposed rule; it is not itself that rule.
The instrument that actually carries the CNSA 2.0 dates. NSS follow this, not the OMB memoranda — a distinction that decides which deadline applies to a given system.

chunks.content:
Module: Healthcare PQC
Component: HealthcarePQCExercises

Work through these scenarios to explore biometric threat assessment, pharmaceutical IP exposure, patient privacy mapping, medical device safety, and hospital migration planning. Each exercise pre-configures the Workshop — click "Load & Run" to begin.
Take the PQC quiz to test what you've learned about healthcare PQC challenges and migration strategies.
1. Biometric Permanence Assessment — Compare HNDL exposure across biometric types
Select DNA SNP Profile in the Biometric Vault Assessor. Compare its HNDL exposure against a fingerprint template. Note the template size difference and the implications for multi-generational privacy.
DNA SNP profiles are 5 MB vs 512 bytes for fingerprints, but both are permanently compromised. DNA data additionally affects biological relatives, making it the highest-priority biometric type for PQC migration.
2. Pharma Pipeline Financial Exposure — Calculate HNDL risk for a discovery compound
In the Pharma IP Calculator, add a Discovery-phase compound worth $800M encrypted with RSA-2048. Set CRQC year to 2033. Calculate the HNDL exposure.
Discovery-phase compounds have 20 years to patent expiry. With CRQC at 2033, the entire commercial value is at risk. A competitor decrypting this data skips 15+ years of R&D.
3. Pediatric Privacy Timeline — Map HNDL windows for pediatric and genomic data
In the Patient Privacy Mapper, select Pediatric EHR and Genomic data. Set CRQC to 2035. Compare the HNDL window for each category.

chunks.title: Healthcare PQC — HealthcarePQCExercises
chunks.content:
Module: Healthcare PQC
Component: HealthcarePQCExercises

Pediatric records have 25-year true retention. Genomic data is effectively lifetime (100+ years). Both exceed the CRQC timeline, making them immediate HNDL targets.
4. Pacemaker Attack Simulation — Evaluate PQC feasibility on constrained medical devices
Select the Cardiac Pacemaker in the Device Safety Simulator. Review the Command Injection attack scenario. Check which PQC algorithms are feasible on Cortex-M0+.
In this exercise's model, ML-DSA-44 needs more RAM than the 32 KB available, while LMS (H5/W8) and XMSS (H10) verification is assumed to fit, so they are feasible for firmware signing. The RAM figures are this module's planning assumptions, not measurements.

6. End-to-End Healthcare Assessment — Full hospital PQC posture with compliance alignment
Configure all 7 hospital layers with realistic PQC postures. Compare the auto-calculated priority matrix against the compliance milestone timeline.

chunks.title: Healthcare PQC — HealthcarePQCExercises
chunks.content:
Module: Healthcare PQC
Component: HealthcarePQCExercises

The priority matrix ranks Medical Devices and Research/Genomics highest due to critical data sensitivity and HNDL exposure. On the regulatory side, the FDA's premarket cybersecurity guidance is already final (first issued September 2023, current edition February 2026), while the HIPAA Security Rule in force names no encryption algorithm and sets no post-quantum date, and HHS lists OCR's proposed rewrite of it separately from the rule in effect (HHS page last reviewed 7 August 2026) \u2014 so plan migration phases against your own risk, and treat any specific HIPAA year you see quoted as a guess.

chunks.title: Healthcare PQC — HealthcarePQCIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Healthcare PQC
Component: HealthcarePQCIntroduction

Healthcare organizations are custodians of the most sensitive category of personal data: biometrics. Unlike passwords, API keys, or even Social Security numbers, biometric identifiers — fingerprints, iris scans, facial geometry, and DNA profiles — are permanently bound to an individual. They cannot be rotated, revoked, or reissued after a breach.
The Harvest Now, Decrypt Later (HNDL) threat makes biometric databases an extraordinarily high-value target for adversaries with long time horizons. Nation-state actors can intercept and store encrypted biometric data today, knowing that a future cryptographically relevant quantum computer (CRQC) will allow them to decrypt the entire archive.
The U.S. Office of Personnel Management breach exposed 5.6 million fingerprint records alongside 21.5 million background investigation files. Over a decade later, every affected individual's fingerprints remain compromised — and will remain so for life. Had genomic or iris data been included, the damage would extend across generations.
A quantum computer decrypting a biometric database doesn't just breach data — it permanently compromises every identity in that database. Unlike a password breach where users can reset credentials, a biometric breach is irreversible. This makes pre-quantum encryption of biometric data stores one of the highest-priority PQC migration targets in healthcare.

chunks.title: Healthcare PQC — HealthcarePQCIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Healthcare PQC
Component: HealthcarePQCIntroduction

Bringing a new drug to market costs billions of dollars and takes 10–15 years from discovery to FDA approval. Every stage of this pipeline generates data that represents billions of dollars in competitive advantage — from molecular structures and synthesis routes to clinical trial results and regulatory submissions.
Applying the Mosca Inequality to pharmaceutical data reveals why the industry must act now. If the security shelf life of a compound's data (typically 20+ years until patent expiry) plus the migration time to PQC (estimated 5–10 years for pharmaceutical IT) exceeds the time until a CRQC arrives, then the data is already at risk of HNDL harvesting.
FDA 21 CFR Part 11 establishes requirements for electronic records and electronic signatures in pharmaceutical manufacturing and clinical trials. It mandates that electronic records must be trustworthy, reliable, and equivalent to paper records. Part 11 names no signature algorithm, but the electronic signatures deployed today typically use RSA or ECDSA — both quantum-vulnerable. A CRQC could forge signatures on regulatory submissions, batch release records, or clinical trial data, undermining the chain of trust that supports drug safety. How long those records must be kept comes from the applicable predicate rule (for example 21 CFR 312.62(c)), not from Part 11 itself.

chunks.title: Healthcare PQC — HealthcarePQCIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Healthcare PQC
Component: HealthcarePQCIntroduction

A drug in Phase I trials today will have data requiring protection for 20+ years (patent life + data exclusivity). If PQC migration takes 7 years and CRQC arrives in 2035, the Mosca window has already closed: 20 + 7 > 9. Competitors or nation-state actors harvesting encrypted trial data today could decrypt it before the drug's patent expires, stealing billions in R&D investment.
Patient privacy extends far beyond HIPAA. A comprehensive healthcare privacy framework must account for multiple overlapping regulatory regimes, each protecting different categories of sensitive health data with varying retention requirements and disclosure restrictions.
The Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act (GINA) prohibits the use of genetic information in employment and health insurance decisions. Separately, 42 CFR Part 2 imposes even stricter protections than HIPAA on substance use disorder treatment records, requiring patient consent for virtually any disclosure — including to other treating physicians.
Certain health data categories — substance abuse treatment, mental health diagnoses, HIV status, reproductive decisions — carry significant social stigma. A quantum-enabled breach of these records doesn't just violate privacy; it can destroy careers, relationships, and lives. The harm is amplified because health stigma data, once exposed, cannot be "un-known" by those who see it. This makes long-retention stigma data the highest-priority category for PQC migration in healthcare.

chunks.title: Healthcare PQC — HealthcarePQCIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Healthcare PQC
Component: HealthcarePQCIntroduction

Genomic data is unique because it is both lifetime-persistent (your genome never changes) and generational (it reveals information about parents, children, and siblings). A pediatric patient's genomic sequence collected today must remain confidential for 100+ years — well beyond any reasonable CRQC timeline. This data is an immediate HNDL target and requires PQC protection now, not after a regulatory mandate.
In healthcare, cryptographic failure is not just a data breach — it can be a patient safety event. The Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) encompasses insulin pumps, cardiac pacemakers, infusion controllers, and surgical robots — devices where a forged firmware update or injected command could directly harm or kill a patient.
Many implantable and wearable medical devices operate on severely resource-constrained processors. For illustration, this module models a pacemaker-class device as an ARM Cortex-M0+ with only 32 KB of RAM and a 48 MHz clock. This module assumes that ML-DSA-44, the smallest ML-DSA parameter set, needs more RAM than the whole 32 KB (a planning assumption, not a measurement).
For these constrained devices, hash-based signatures like LMS (H5/W8) and XMSS (H10) are assumed here to be the only feasible PQC options, with verification fitting in a few KB of RAM (also a planning assumption). However, they are stateful — the device must track which one-time keys have been used, adding complexity to firmware update mechanisms.

chunks.title: Healthcare PQC — HealthcarePQCIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Healthcare PQC
Component: HealthcarePQCIntroduction

• Abbott (formerly St. Jude Medical) pacemaker vulnerabilities (2017, FDA safety communication and ICS Medical Advisory ICSMA-17-241-01) — the advisory says a nearby attacker could gain unauthorized access to an affected pacemaker and issue commands, change settings, or otherwise interfere with its intended function. The pacemaker's authentication algorithm could be compromised or bypassed, and the devices did not limit “RF wake-up” commands, which could be sent repeatedly to reduce battery life. Abbott's mitigation was a firmware update applied by a healthcare provider.
• MedJack attacks — attackers compromise medical devices (infusion pumps, X-ray systems, blood gas analyzers) to establish persistent network footholds within hospital networks. These devices often run outdated operating systems with no crypto agility.
• Insulin pump vulnerabilities — researchers demonstrated remote command injection on insulin pumps, capable of delivering lethal doses. Firmware integrity verification relied on RSA-1024 signatures.
For general IoT/OT PQC challenges including constrained device cryptography, OTA update signing, and industrial control system migration, see the IoT & Embedded Device PQC module.
Healthcare PQC migration is uniquely complex because hospitals operate a deeply interconnected technology stack where every layer has distinct cryptographic dependencies, vendor constraints, and regulatory approval requirements.

chunks.title: Healthcare PQC — HealthcarePQCIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Healthcare PQC
Component: HealthcarePQCIntroduction

Healthcare data exchange relies on standards that were designed decades before PQC was a consideration. HL7 v2 messages often travel over MLLP (Minimal Lower Layer Protocol) with no encryption at all. The SMART App Launch v2.2.0 launch-and-authorization page requires apps to send authentication secrets, authorization codes, and tokens only to authenticated servers over TLS-secured channels. DICOM supports TLS for image transfer but has no PQC cipher suite definitions.
For the transport itself, TLS 1.3 is specified in RFC 9846, and RFC 10024 defines three ML-KEM hybrid key agreement mechanisms for TLS 1.3 (X25519MLKEM768, SecP256r1MLKEM768 and SecP384r1MLKEM1024) — the building blocks for telehealth sessions and FHIR API traffic. On the US certification side, the ONC criteria for certified EHR software (§ 170.315(d)(7)–(d)(9): end-user device encryption, integrity and trusted connection) refer to NIST-approved encryption and SHA-2 or stronger hashing, and they name no post-quantum algorithm.
Migrating these protocols to PQC requires coordinated updates across hundreds of vendors, thousands of implementations, and multiple standards bodies (HL7 International, IHE, DICOM Committee). No single hospital can migrate in isolation.

chunks.title: Healthcare PQC — HealthcarePQCIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Healthcare PQC
Component: HealthcarePQCIntroduction

Any change to a medical device's cryptographic subsystem may require a new 510(k) premarket notification or even a full PMA (Premarket Approval). The FDA review process takes 3–12 months, during which the device cannot ship with the update. For Class III devices (pacemakers, defibrillators), the approval timeline can extend to 18+ months.
Medical devices have operational lifetimes of 15–20 years, with some MRI machines and radiation therapy systems lasting 25+ years. Many of these devices cannot be remotely updated and will never receive PQC firmware. The migration strategy for these legacy devices must focus on network segmentation and cryptographic gateways rather than device-level upgrades. FDA's premarket cybersecurity guidance recommends cryptography that is expected to stay cryptographically strong throughout the service life of the device, which is why these long lifetimes matter for the algorithms chosen today.
The Health Sector Coordinating Council (HSCC) and the Health Information Sharing and Analysis Center (H-ISAC) are the primary coordinating bodies for healthcare cybersecurity in the United States. HSCC publishes the Health Industry Cybersecurity Practices (HICP) guidelines, while H-ISAC provides threat intelligence and incident response coordination. Both organizations are actively developing PQC transition guidance for the healthcare sector, including recommended migration timelines and priority frameworks.

chunks.title: Healthcare PQC — DeviceSafetySimulator
chunks.content:
Module: Healthcare PQC
Component: DeviceSafetySimulator

Cryptographic inventory documented
All cryptographic algorithms, key sizes, protocols, and libraries used in the device are catalogued in a Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) with crypto annotations.
PQC algorithm selection justified
The choice of PQC algorithm (e.g., ML-KEM, ML-DSA, LMS) is justified based on device resource constraints, security level requirements, and NIST FIPS standards.
Key management plan covers device lifetime
Key provisioning, rotation, and revocation procedures address the full expected device lifetime, including post-market firmware updates for algorithm transitions.
Firmware update mechanism supports PQC signatures
The secure boot chain and firmware update verification can validate PQC signatures (e.g., ML-DSA or LMS) in addition to or replacing classical signatures.
Post-market surveillance for crypto vulnerabilities
The post-market cybersecurity plan includes monitoring for cryptographic algorithm deprecations, new quantum computing milestones, and NIST advisory updates.
SBOM includes cryptographic dependencies
The SBOM (required for cyber devices by section 524B of the FD&C Act) explicitly enumerates cryptographic libraries, their versions, and the specific algorithms/key sizes used by each component.
Hybrid mode transition plan documented
A phased migration plan from classical-only to hybrid (classical + PQC) to PQC-only is documented, with rollback procedures for each transition stage.

chunks.title: Healthcare PQC — HospitalMigrationPlanner
chunks.content:
Module: Healthcare PQC
Component: HospitalMigrationPlanner

Configure the 7 layers of a hospital network architecture to generate a prioritized PQC migration roadmap with compliance milestones and budget estimates. Adjust crypto posture and endpoint counts to see how migration priority and costs change.
All layers are set to “No Change.” Select a crypto posture above to generate budget estimates.
Hospital networks carry some of the longest data retention requirements of any sector. Patient records, genomic data, and biometric identifiers must be protected for decades to a lifetime. Encrypted healthcare data captured today by harvest-now-decrypt-later adversaries could be decrypted when cryptographically relevant quantum computers arrive, exposing irreplaceable patient information. Internet-facing layers (patient portals, research infrastructure) and high-sensitivity internal systems (medical devices, EHR) should be prioritized for immediate PQC migration planning.
Phase 1: Critical Priority (2023\u20132027)
Internet-facing and highest-sensitivity layers. Deploy PQC hybrid TLS on patient portals, begin medical device firmware signing migration, and protect genomic research infrastructure.
Phase 2: High Priority (2027\u20132029)
Internal clinical systems with significant data sensitivity. Upgrade EHR workstations, medical imaging PACS, and laboratory systems during planned maintenance cycles.
Phase 3: Standard Priority (2029\u20132031)

chunks.title: Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) — FheContextSections
chunks.content:
Module: Homomorphic Encryption (FHE)
Component: FheContextSections

Gentry proposed a fully homomorphic encryption scheme, “a scheme that allows one to evaluate circuits over encrypted data without being able to decrypt” (Gentry, STOC 2009). “Fully” means there is no limit on which circuit can be evaluated: with bootstrapping, additions and multiplications can be chained without end. It is a statement about what is possible, not about precision, speed, integrity or who sees the result. The name invites expectations that the sources qualify:
CKKS was built as “a homomorphic encryption scheme for approximate arithmetic” (Cheon, Kim, Kim & Song 2017). A real value is multiplied by a scaling factor and rounded to an integer polynomial before encryption, which preserves its precision despite the rounding. Values must stay small compared with the ciphertext modulus, and the last bits of every result carry error.
Costs are as reported by each source, on its own hardware and baseline; they are not comparable across rows. Sources are in the References list at the end of this tab.
AI inference and training. Encrypted inference is well studied: CryptoNets (2016) classified handwritten digits at 99% accuracy. Encrypted training has been shown for small models and takes hours (logistic regression on 422,108 samples in about 17 hours, Han et al. 2019). TFHE-based tools work on small integers: Concrete ML's documentation states that “FHE requires all inputs, constants, and intermediate values to be integers of maximum 16 bits” (not sourced in the Library).

A pattern runs through the deployments above, offered as a reading of the sources rather than a rule. The query or computation is small or simple (a lookup, a match, a count, a linear model). A response in seconds to hours is acceptable: Mastercard notes that “for now, FHE is more suited to needs requiring a response measured in seconds rather than milliseconds”. And a legal or trust barrier keeps the data from being shared in the clear, such as cross-border rules on financial data or a service that must not learn what a user looks up. The UK NCSC advises organisations to “first consider whether traditional cryptography will solve your data processing problem”.
These claims circulate online; we could not confirm them from a primary source, so this module does not repeat them:
The figures differ by orders of magnitude because they describe different workloads, schemes and years. Beyond computation, the UN PET Guide lists “message expansion, computational cost, and engineering cost”: ciphertexts and keys are much larger than the data they protect.
Each technique has a different cost and asks you to trust something different. They are often combined.
Reading these numbers: each speedup is measured against that paper's own baseline, often a single CPU thread, so the figures cannot be compared with each other or multiplied together. DARPA's DPRIVE programme set the goal of bringing FHE “within a factor of ten of unencrypted computations”; none of the sources above shows that goal met.

Single runs with Lattigo v6.2.0's default bootstrappable parameter set (N = 2^16, 51 evaluation keys) and the educational software token from this workshop, one CPU core each unless noted. They show where the cost sits for one deployment, not a general benchmark.
The one-time key setup is the heaviest step here, minutes on a small board core; each bootstrap then costs seconds on one laptop-class CPU core.
Each scheme has a small set of native operations. Only decryption (and key generation) needs the secret key; the server runs everything else with public evaluation keys. Whatever is not native has to be built from these operations.
FHE computes on polynomials with integer coefficients, so every input is encoded before encryption and every result decoded after decryption. The encoding sets the precision and what happens when a value grows too large.
How to read a noisy CKKS result, and when rounding is enough, is in Decryption results are noisy below.
An FHE program is a circuit: a fixed sequence of the native operations above, the same for every input. The SoK on FHE compilers describes it as “gates (or operations) connected by wires, where the execution follows the same steps, no matter what values the input has”. Writing one means following a few rules.
The workshop step “FHE concepts, hands-on” lets you try these rules on small examples.

chunks.title: Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) — FheExercises
chunks.content:
Module: Homomorphic Encryption (FHE)
Component: FheExercises

Predict the outcome first, try the linked interaction or Learn section, then reveal the explanation. The foundations path focuses on noise, scheme choice and assurance claims; the advanced path adds custody, threshold operation and transciphering.
Take the PQC quiz to test what you've learned about homomorphic encryption and HSM key custody.
1. CKKS single-HSM custody — find the heaviest step and what limits it
In FHE + HSM Flows, select "CKKS single-HSM custody". Walk the steps until you reach the one titled "Stream the evaluation keys: the heaviest step", open its details and evidence, then read the scenario's scaling note.
The relinearization, rotation and bootstrapping keys are public, but each one encrypts something derived from the secret key, so only the HSM can make them. A bootstrappable CKKS set is 7.87 GB, 3.94 GB as exported (measured): too large for an HSM to hold, so it streams the set out in 1,001 bounded PKCS#11 calls with a token peak of about 16 MiB. What limits the step is CPU time, not memory or the PKCS#11 interface: 473 s on one MX95 Cortex-A55 core, 42–44 s on one Mac core, with the network adding about 5 %. Letting the token cache work between calls cuts it to 214 s on one MX95 core and 72–84 s on six MX95 Pro cores, at the cost of more token memory (65–124 MiB). It is a one-time cost per key set, paid again on rotation or recovery.
2. Why TFHE custody fits an HSM — compare key sizes with the CKKS scenario

chunks.title: Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) — FheExercises
chunks.content:
Module: Homomorphic Encryption (FHE)
Component: FheExercises

Select "TFHE single-HSM custody" and compare what the HSM creates and exports at each step with the CKKS scenario. Note which keys stay inside the HSM and which are published.
Every key the HSM creates is kilobytes to tens of megabytes: the secret is a few hundred bytes of key bits (tens of KB as stored), the server key is tens of MB compressed and generated in seconds, and decryption is a dot product. The trade-off is that TFHE computes on bits and small integers, so heavy numeric workloads run slower than with CKKS.
3. Threshold FHE — no single party can decrypt
Open "Threshold: OpenFHE BFV (3-of-3)" and then "Threshold: Lattigo BGV (2-of-3)". For each, note how the key is generated, who must contribute to a decryption, and what replaces bootstrapping keys.
OpenFHE's threshold extension with BFV uses additive key shares and chained key generation, and every party must contribute a partial decryption. Lattigo's multiparty protocols with BGV use t-of-N shares and collective key generation, with an interactive refresh among the key holders instead of bootstrapping keys, so no GB-scale bootstrapping keys are generated. Each party still produces a full-size share of every Galois key the application needs.
4. What can run in the HSM? — which FHE operations fit?
Select "What can run in the HSM?" and note, for each FHE operation, whether it fits inside an HSM, fits only when streamed, or does not fit.

chunks.title: Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) — FheExercises
chunks.content:
Module: Homomorphic Encryption (FHE)
Component: FheExercises

Seed and secret-key generation and decryption fit: small inputs and milliseconds of compute. Evaluation-key generation fits when streamed: a TFHE server key of about 30 MB fits in one piece, and a CKKS bootstrapping key set (3.94 GB exported) streams out in bounded pieces, taking minutes on a small board core. Homomorphic evaluation and bootstrapping do not run in the HSM: they need gigabytes of keys in memory plus GPU or FPGA acceleration, and they need no secret, so running them in the HSM would add nothing but load.
5. Transciphering with Kreyvium — why upload the stream cipher, not FHE ciphertexts
Select "Transciphering: TFHE-rs Kreyvium". Follow the data from the client to the server and note what the client uploads, what the server runs, and what it gets back.
The client uploads data encrypted with the Kreyvium stream cipher, plus its Kreyvium key encrypted under FHE once. The server runs the keystream inside FHE and ends with FHE ciphertexts it never saw in the clear. Uploads stay at plaintext size instead of FHE size, which can be a thousand times larger or more. Use Kreyvium's 128-bit key: Trivium's 80-bit key falls below the federal minimum of 112 bits of security strength for applying cryptographic protection before Grover.
6. Read a noisy CKKS result — decide what precision to report

chunks.title: Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) — FheExercises
chunks.content:
Module: Homomorphic Encryption (FHE)
Component: FheExercises

In the Learn tab, open "Schemes, Data Types and Noisy Results" and find the illustration under "Reading a noisy CKKS result: rounding". The encrypted input was 3.14159265 and decryption returned 3.1415926481. Decide how many digits you would report, and what changes if the result goes to someone other than the key owner.
The last digits of a CKKS result are noise, so report it rounded to a precision you trust: rounded to 20 bits (multiples of 2^-20 ≈ 0.00000095) it reads 3.141593 to six decimals. Rounding removes low-order noise bits but cannot recover bits the noise has already destroyed. If the result goes to others, rounding alone is not enough: decrypted CKKS results seen by others can lead to key recovery, and the research countermeasure, noise flooding, costs further precision. At the default parameters flooding for third parties leaves no correct bits (−12.8 bits in the noise-study emulation, and the token refuses the release); a second parameter set with higher-precision bootstrapping keeps 11.1–11.4 bits against a bar of 10 bits, measured with the corrected flood width on a Mac and with the token on both MX95 boards: a thin margin, set by the published sizing.
7. Pick a scheme for three use cases

chunks.title: Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) — FheExercises
chunks.content:
Module: Homomorphic Encryption (FHE)
Component: FheExercises

Using "Which scheme for which data" in the Learn tab, pick a scheme for each: (a) counting how many encrypted records match a condition, exactly; (b) running a machine-learning model on encrypted real-valued measurements; (c) comparing encrypted values and branching on the result, or evaluating a lookup table.
(a) BFV or BGV: exact integer arithmetic; Microsoft SEAL notes that where exact values are necessary these schemes are more suitable. (b) CKKS: approximate arithmetic on real numbers, suited to evaluating machine-learning models; read the results to a trusted precision. (c) TFHE: it evaluates functions through lookup tables during bootstrapping, while with BFV, BGV and CKKS encrypted comparison is in most cases not feasible.
8. Check a compliance claim — “our FHE service is FIPS 140-3 validated”
A vendor writes: "Our FHE service is FIPS 140-3 validated." Using "Standards and Compliance" in the Learn tab, decide what part of that claim can be true and what question you would ask the vendor.
Only the conventional cryptography around the service can be validated: TLS, AES, key wrapping, signatures and random number generation in a FIPS 140-3 module. FHE is not among the approved security functions (NIST SP 800-140C), and a non-approved function does not run in a module’s approved mode. Ask for the CMVP certificate number and check which algorithms it lists: the certificate of an FHE-related product (#5175) lists only conventional algorithms.

chunks.title: Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) — FheSections
chunks.content:
Module: Homomorphic Encryption (FHE)
Component: FheSections

A TEE protects data in use by trusting hardware. Fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) takes the other route: it trusts mathematics. The server computes directly on ciphertexts and returns an encrypted result. It never sees the input or the output, and there is no enclave to attest. The cost is speed: FHE is orders of magnitude slower than computing in the clear.
FHE primarily hides plaintext from the evaluator. It does not automatically prove that the evaluator ran the right circuit, authenticate ciphertexts, hide request timing or size, conceal every access pattern, protect a compromised client, or authorize who may receive a decrypted result. Record the evaluator, client, custodian and result recipient separately, then state which may be malicious or collude.
If correctness against a malicious evaluator matters, add an integrity mechanism such as a verifiable-computation proof or an application-specific check. Circuit privacy and model privacy are separate requirements from input confidentiality.
Every ciphertext carries a small random error (“noise”). Additions grow it a little and multiplications grow it a lot. Once it is too large, decryption fails. Bootstrapping refreshes the noise by running decryption homomorphically under an encrypted copy of the key. All four schemes are being standardized in ISO/IEC 28033, which the Library records as under development; the current stage of each part is not sourced in the Library (see section 7).

Decryption results are noisy: what that means and how to read them
Every FHE ciphertext carries a small random error, called noise, that grows as you compute. What that noise does to a decrypted result depends on the scheme.
Read the result to the precision you trust and discard the rest, by rounding it to a chosen number of bits. Lattigo provides this as DecodePublic, which takes the desired bit precision and rounds each value as y = ⌊x/ε⌉·ε. Its documentation says values shared with external parties should be decoded with DecodePublic instead of the usual Decode, and that “the Lattigo API does not provide automatic IND-CPA-D security”.

Decrypted CKKS results seen by others can lead to complete key recovery (Li & Micciancio 2021). The research countermeasure is noise flooding: “adding Gaussian noise to the output of CKKS decryption suffices to achieve IND-CPA^D security” (Li, Micciancio, Schultz & Sorrell 2022). OpenFHE exposes it as the NOISE_FLOODING_DECRYPT decryption mode, which its example marks experimental and not yet recommended for production; the example runs the computation twice, first to estimate the noise, and with 128-bit arithmetic chooses the scaling modulus size from that estimate.

chunks.content:
Module: Homomorphic Encryption (FHE)
Component: FheSections

Sizes depend heavily on the parameter set; measured values are marked. The public evaluation keys don't need to be secret, but they encrypt functions of the secret key, so they need integrity. There is no standard encoding yet: no PKCS#11 or KMIP object type and no X.509 OID. Each library serializes keys its own way, and a key is meaningless without its exact parameter set.
No standard defines an FHE mechanism either. This lab's HSM therefore serves FHE key custody as vendor-defined PKCS#11 mechanisms, for key generation, public-key derivation and decryption, listed in its mechanism list and carried over KMIP's PKCS_11 operation. It offers no FHE encryption mechanism: the data owner encrypts under the public key itself (
Which operation needs which of these keys, and who runs it, is listed per scheme in section 2, “Operations each scheme supports”.
Not directly. You can only compute on ciphertexts from a homomorphic scheme. An AES-GCM ciphertext has no structure a server can exploit, so you can't add two of them. The bridge is transciphering: the server runs the symmetric cipher's decryption inside FHE. TFHE-rs ships it for Kreyvium and AES-128-CTR (tfhe::transciphering); this workshop shows Kreyvium because it is cheaper:
This keeps uploads at plaintext size instead of FHE size. Use Kreyvium's 128-bit key: Trivium's 80-bit key falls below the federal minimum of 112 bits of security strength for applying cryptographic protection, before Grover.

chunks.title: Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) — FheSections
chunks.content:
Module: Homomorphic Encryption (FHE)
Component: FheSections

Lattice FHE has no known quantum break. It rests on the (Ring-)Learning With Errors family behind ML-KEM; for a stated post-quantum level, pick parameters from the HE Standard's quantum tables (common defaults target classical 128-bit security) (not sourced in the Library). FHE schemes themselves are not NIST-standardized. An FHE deployment is a different matter, because the parts around the scheme are usually still classical:
The UK ICO says the security of most HE schemes rests on hard mathematical problems “that are currently considered to be secure even against quantum computers”. NIST and the NSA make no such statement: the NSA's CNSA 2.0 FAQ says that neither NSA nor NIST has produced standards for these areas, and it lists homomorphic encryption among areas with “no generally approved solutions” (in its “Future cryptographic algorithms” section).
Deployment pattern: our composition of standard HSM functions around library calls. No FHE library or paper defines an HSM role.
Generate a 32-byte seed inside the HSM as a non-extractable key: ordinary key wrapping refuses it
Derive the secret key from it inside the HSM; stream the public and evaluation keys out
Sign the parameter set and evaluation-key hashes with ML-DSA

chunks.title: Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) — FheSections
chunks.content:
Module: Homomorphic Encryption (FHE)
Component: FheSections

Target architecture: back up the seed (not GBs of keys) only HSM to HSM: a live clone to an authenticated peer, or an offline package that only an enrolled backup HSM can restore. Each HSM proves itself with a manufacturing → device → function certificate chain and fresh attestation evidence (draft-ietf-rats-pkix-key-attestation). The package is pure post-quantum at NIST Category 3: sealed to the recipient’s FIPS 203 ML-KEM-768 certificate and signed with FIPS 204 ML-DSA-65, with no classical or hybrid fallback.
Alternative: threshold FHE. Split the key across several parties (each ideally holding its share in its own HSM), so no single decryptor exists. OpenFHE (BFV, N-of-N) and Lattigo (BGV, t-of-N) both implement it; the workshop shows both.
Yes: seed and secret-key generation, decryption. Both are small inputs and milliseconds of compute.
Yes, streamed: evaluation-key generation. TFHE's 30 MB server key fits in one piece. A CKKS bootstrappable set (3.94 GB exported, measured) is too large to hold, so the HSM produces it as a stream of bounded calls with a token peak of 15–17 MiB, or up to 124 MiB when the token caches work between calls to go faster (below).
No: homomorphic evaluation and bootstrapping. They need GBs of keys in memory plus GPU or FPGA acceleration. They need no secret, so running them in the HSM would add nothing but load.

chunks.title: Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) — FheSections
chunks.content:
Module: Homomorphic Encryption (FHE)
Component: FheSections

No standard PKCS#11 mechanism exists for any of this today, so this lab's HSM uses vendor-defined mechanisms, also reachable over KMIP (section 5).
Roles: FHE keys follow the normal PKCS#11 user and security-officer roles. Key generation, public-key derivation, attribute reads and decryption are user operations; there is no FHE-specific role, and so no separate decrypt role as the controls below recommend.
Destroying a seed: FHE seeds are created with CKA_DESTROYABLE = FALSE, so only the security officer can destroy one, through a signed administrative request.
Decryption budget: each decryption spends one unit of a counter fixed by the officer's enrolled decryption policy. A request refused after the role and key checks (a malformed ciphertext, a failed check on the result) spends a unit too; a wrong role or an unknown recipient is refused before the counter, and the size query spends none.
Decryption calls: PKCS#11 single-part, C_DecryptInit, a size query, then C_Decrypt. Over KMIP each output took a median of 24.8 ms (
A CKKS evaluation key is a set of polynomials in residue (RNS) form. One limb is one residue polynomial: 2^16 coefficients of 8 bytes, 512 KB. A full-size key in Lattigo's default bootstrappable set has 5 digits of 30 limbs, so the 51 keys hold 7,502 limbs of their b half (

chunks.title: Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) — FheSections
chunks.content:
Module: Homomorphic Encryption (FHE)
Component: FheSections

One chunk, one call: each PKCS#11 call derives a range of limbs of one key digit (8 limbs, 4 MB, by default) as a public session object; the host reads it and destroys it, then asks for the next. The whole set takes 1,001 calls. No new PKCS#11 functions are needed: a vendor mechanism and ordinary object reads, each object bounded.
Bounded memory: the token holds one chunk at a time, so its peak stayed at 15–17 MiB on every device, against 17.2 GB for Lattigo generating and holding the whole set in one process. The faster version below also keeps caches, so its peak is 64.5–123.6 MiB; it stays bounded whatever the size of the set.
Determinism: each chunk depends only on the seed and on which key, digit and limbs were asked for, so any order, core or replica gives the same bytes. Every limb matched the reference spec, and the MX95 and MX95 Pro, loaded with the same test seed, produced identical key material (1,003 of 1,003 manifest entries; only the descriptor differs, by an identifier each token draws at random).
Integrity: each chunk's SHA-256 goes into a manifest signed with the token's key. The receiver can check that it got the pieces the token signed; only a test decryption shows the keys encrypt the right secret.

chunks.title: Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) — FheSections
chunks.content:
Module: Homomorphic Encryption (FHE)
Component: FheSections

Montgomery arithmetic: the products of two variables (the random a times the secret in NTT form, the secret squared for relinearization, and c1·s in decryption) use Montgomery multiplication: values are kept as x·2^64 mod q, so each reduction is multiplications and a shift, with no division and no branch on secret data. The output stays in Montgomery and NTT form, which is Lattigo's own wire form, so the receiver uses the limbs as they arrive.

In the pqctoday HSM simulation (an educational engine), the security officer enrolls an immutable FHE decryption policy bound to each FHE key seed. Version 1 is for TFHE; version 2 adds a CKKS block.

chunks.title: Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) — FheSections
chunks.content:
Module: Homomorphic Encryption (FHE)
Component: FheSections

CKKS: the release is decoded inside the token and rounded. With at most maxValues slots, each with a real and an imaginary part, a crafted request can learn at most about maxValues × 2 × (precisionBits + valueBoundLog2 + 1) bits per release. This is how the policy bounds what one release reveals, not a security proof.
TFHE: the policy has no noise setting, because decryption is exact; it limits what is released, to whom and how often.
Replication: when a key is replicated to another HSM, its policy can only be narrowed, never widened, and flooding cannot be switched off. A copy of a CKKS key must also keep the same replica limit as its source, so every copy computes the same flood width.
Decryption computes c0 + c1·s on whatever ciphertext it receives, and it cannot tell a genuine result from a crafted input. So an unrestricted or insufficiently checked decryption interface can become a key-recovery oracle . In CKKS one crafted request is enough: c0 = 0, c1 = Δ returns Δ·s. In exact schemes such as TFHE, BFV and BGV the key comes out bit by bit over many requests (Loftus et al. 2010; Chenal & Tang 2014). A crafted input need not look odd: a fresh encryption of a known value plus a small, shaped change looks uniform and in range.
Crafted inputs (chosen-ciphertext): inherent to FHE, which is malleable by design. The token decrypts what it is given.

chunks.title: Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) — FheSections
chunks.content:
Module: Homomorphic Encryption (FHE)
Component: FheSections

Passive: decrypted CKKS results leak the key even when every computation was honest, if people other than the key owner see them (Li & Micciancio 2021). Exact schemes leak the same way through decryption failures when the failure probability is not negligible (Cheon et al. 2024; Checri et al. 2024).
The FHE server: it computes on ciphertexts but has no token session.
Someone who steals the token's storage, without a session on the token.
Any caller allowed to decrypt: the owner's application, or whoever compromises it.
For the passive variant: anyone who sees unprotected CKKS results.
Detection catches only careless attempts: a constant or low-entropy c1, out-of-range values, near-duplicate inputs, unusual request rates. A careful crafted request looks exactly like a genuine one, so detection is an audit alarm, not the protection. Only cryptographic provenance of the input can tell the two apart (see the research mitigations below).
Single-HSM decryption, the default in this module, trusts every caller allowed to decrypt. The token protects the key from the FHE server and from theft of its storage, not from an authorized caller, so the key is only as protected as every path that can submit a decryption request. A deployment therefore adds compensating logical and physical controls; they are part of the security model.
The educational software token used in the workshop has no tamper resistance, so on a board these controls have to cover the host it runs on as well.

Rounding released CKKS values to a fixed precision removes the low-order bits that carry the leak (listed as a countermeasure by Li & Micciancio 2021).
Noise flooding before a CKKS result is released (Li, Micciancio, Schultz & Sorrell 2022; OpenFHE NOISE_FLOODING_DECRYPT ), sized from noise estimates such as Bossuat et al. 2024. It costs precision.
Negligible decryption-failure probability for exact schemes (BFV, BGV, TFHE), rather than heuristic correctness (Cheon et al. 2024).
Threshold decryption: no single token can decrypt (see below).
Zero-knowledge proofs that inputs are well formed, as in Zama's fhEVM, and verifiable FHE (Manulis & Nguyen 2024): research directions that would let each HSM refuse ciphertexts it cannot verify.
Rounding and flooding reduce and bound what each release reveals; repeated crafted requests from an allowed caller can still add up, which is why the controls above stay in place.
After an incident the response is to stop decryption and move to a new key. Decrypting every stored ciphertext and encrypting it again would send the data through the path under suspicion. Instead the token streams one key-switching key from the old secret to the new one, and the FHE server applies it to each stored ciphertext; no plaintext appears.
Size: stored ciphertexts sit at the lower levels left after bootstrapping, so the key is 31.5 MB (15.7 MB streamed, 4 calls), not the 157 MB of a bootstrapping-level key. Its bytes matched Lattigo's own rebuild.

Module: Homomorphic Encryption (FHE)

Any computation can run on encrypted data
In principle yes, but each scheme favours a data type. Microsoft SEAL: “For applications where exact values are necessary, the BFV and BGV schemes are more suitable”, CKKS suits real numbers, and with these schemes “encrypted comparison, sorting, or regular expressions, are in most cases not feasible”. TFHE handles comparisons and lookup logic, on small integers.
Depends on the scheme. CKKS is “a homomorphic encryption scheme for approximate arithmetic” (Cheon, Kim, Kim & Song 2017): results are close to the true value, correct to a number of bits. BFV, BGV and TFHE return exact integers as long as the noise stays within bounds.
Whoever holds the secret key, or may ask for decryptions, decides who sees results (section 8).
At a cost. The ICO describes HE as “several thousand times slower than processing plaintext”; DARPA estimated in 2021 that it was “about a million times slower” to compute in the FHE world; NIST SP 800-226 says that in most cases secure computation “is several orders of magnitude slower than native execution” and that “its performance is improving quickly” (section 4) (not sourced in the Library).
Not without care. Decrypted CKKS results seen by others can lead to key recovery (Li & Micciancio 2021); the countermeasure, noise flooding, costs precision (Li, Micciancio, Schultz & Sorrell 2022). Exact schemes need a negligible decryption-failure probability (Cheon et al. 2024).
Exact integers: counting, matching, private lookups

Comparisons, branching, lookup-table logic
With BFV, BGV and CKKS, “encrypted comparison, sorting, or regular expressions, are in most cases not feasible” (SEAL README). TFHE evaluates functions through lookup tables during bootstrapping, on bits and small integers.

Move stored ciphertexts to a new key without decrypting them: the security officer, the token and the server, and what the token refuses.
A rotation key is one key-switching key at the lower levels stored ciphertexts use: 31.5 MB (15.7 MB streamed in 4 calls of 8 limbs, token peak 51.4 MiB), not the 157 MB of a bootstrapping-level key and not the 3.94 GB key set. Changing the lock on a warehouse without opening the sealed crates: a one-way adapter converts each crate’s seal from the old lock to the new one, and nobody reads what is inside.
Decrypting every stored ciphertext and encrypting it again would send the data through the very path that is under suspicion after an incident. Here the token produces one small key and the server does the conversion on ciphertexts.
The adapter has a price: whoever holds the new secret and the adapter can compute the old secret, so it is used once and deleted. Whether someone who holds the old secret can read a converted ciphertext without having kept the original is not established.

chunks.title: HSM & PQC Operations — HsmPqcExercises
chunks.content:
Module: HSM & PQC Operations
Component: HsmPqcExercises

Work through these scenarios to understand PKCS#11 PQC operations, HSM vendor selection, firmware migration planning, and FIPS validation. Each exercise pre-configures the Workshop — click "Load & Run" to begin.
Take the PQC quiz to test what you've learned about HSM operations and PQC integration.
1. PKCS#11 Key Generation — Generate ML-KEM-768 keypair and compare buffer sizes
In the PKCS#11 Simulator workshop, step through the key generation operation. Observe the C_GenerateKeyPair call with CKM_ML_KEM_KEY_PAIR_GEN mechanism. Compare the 1,184-byte ML-KEM-768 public key against the 256-byte RSA-2048 public key in the classical comparison section.
The ML-KEM-768 public key (1,184 bytes) is 4.6x larger than RSA-2048 (256 bytes). Applications using fixed-size buffers will need updating. The private key never leaves the HSM boundary — CKA_SENSITIVE=TRUE and CKA_EXTRACTABLE=FALSE are enforced.
2. ML-DSA Signing in HSM — Sign and verify with ML-DSA-65
Continue through the PKCS#11 Simulator to the signing operations (Steps 5-6). Observe the message-based signing calls (C_MessageSignInit / C_SignMessage and C_MessageVerifyInit / C_VerifyMessage) using CKM_ML_DSA. Note the hedged signing output and the 3,309-byte signature size. Expand the on-prem vs cloud notes to see vendor support status.

chunks.title: HSM & PQC Operations — HsmPqcExercises
chunks.content:
Module: HSM & PQC Operations
Component: HsmPqcExercises

ML-DSA-65 signatures are 3,309 bytes (vs 64 bytes for ECDSA P-256 — a 51x increase). Hedged signing (rnd drawn from a random source instead of all zero) is the default variant in FIPS 204 section 3.4, which says the deterministic variant "should not be used on platforms where side-channel attacks are a concern and where they cannot be otherwise mitigated". PKCS#11 v3.2 lets the caller choose (CKH_HEDGE_PREFERRED, CKH_HEDGE_REQUIRED or CKH_DETERMINISTIC_REQUIRED), so which variant a given HSM uses by default is a product property: look for it in the module documentation and Security Policy rather than assuming it.
3. Vendor Selection — Given requirements, identify matching vendors
Open the Vendor Comparison workshop. Filter vendors by "production" status. For a regulated financial institution requiring FIPS 140-3 Level 3 and ML-KEM + ML-DSA support, identify which vendors meet those criteria. Expand each vendor row to check hybrid support and side-channel countermeasures.

chunks.title: HSM & PQC Operations — HsmPqcExercises
chunks.content:
Module: HSM & PQC Operations
Component: HsmPqcExercises

Thales Luna 7 and Entrust nShield 5 both offer ML-KEM and ML-DSA in firmware on FIPS 140-3 Level 3 hardware, but the module certificates differ: Luna T7 #5450 lists ML-KEM, ML-DSA and LMS among its approved algorithms, while the nShield 5s certificates #5329 and #4745 list no PQC algorithm. Crypto4A #5497 lists ML-KEM, ML-DSA, SLH-DSA and LMS. The interface also differs by version. On nShield, ML-DSA reached the PKCS#11 interface in Security World v13.9.0, ML-KEM in v13.9.3 and SLH-DSA (12 parameter sets) in v13.9.5; in v13.9.0 ML-KEM and SLH-DSA were nCore-only, so check the release notes for the version you run. SLH-DSA support does not help with CNSA 2.0 firmware signing: the NSA FAQ approves LMS and XMSS (not HSS or XMSS^MT) and says SLH-DSA "is not part of CNSA and is not approved for any use in NSS". LMS for nShield has a CAVP certificate (A7990, PQSDK); we found no Entrust page describing XMSS.
4. On-Prem vs Cloud HSM — Compare deployment for a regulated institution
In the Vendor Comparison workshop, filter to show all vendors and compare on-prem vs cloud types. Examine which cloud HSMs support native PKCS#11 PQC mechanisms versus SDK-only access. Consider a scenario where the institution needs ML-KEM encapsulation for TLS key exchange.

chunks.title: HSM & PQC Operations — HsmPqcExercises
chunks.content:
Module: HSM & PQC Operations
Component: HsmPqcExercises

Cloud HSM PQC support is uneven rather than absent, and the interface differs from the standard one. AWS CloudHSM documents ML-DSA only, through vendor-defined mechanisms (CKM_CLOUDHSM_ML_DSA_KEY_PAIR_GEN, CKM_CLOUDHSM_ML_DSA) rather than the standard CKM_ML_DSA, and no ML-KEM mechanism; Google Cloud KMS lists its PQC algorithms at the software protection level only, with none for HSM keys. Keep three statements apart for AWS: ML-DSA works in the HSM; AWS says it is available in FIPS mode on hsm2m.medium from 1 September 2026; and the NIST Security Policy for the same module (CMVP #4703) lists ML-DSA and ML-KEM as non-approved services, with no PQC algorithm on the certificate. We have not found a document that reconciles the last two, so ask the vendor which applies to your cluster. For ML-KEM key exchange, also check which interface exposes it in the exact firmware or release you run: nShield, for example, added ML-KEM to PKCS#11 only in Security World v13.9.3.
5. Firmware Migration Planning — Plan upgrade for 10 HSMs with zero downtime
Open the Migration Planner workshop. Select Thales Luna 7 as your vendor. Walk through all 4 phases: Assessment, Firmware Planning, Key Migration, and Validation. For a fleet of 10 HSMs, calculate total migration time using the dual-partition strategy where classical and PQC partitions run in parallel.

chunks.title: HSM & PQC Operations — HsmPqcExercises
chunks.content:
Module: HSM & PQC Operations
Component: HsmPqcExercises

With Thales Luna 7 (low complexity, 30-60 min/HSM), a rolling upgrade of 10 HSMs takes approximately 5-10 hours. The dual-partition strategy allows classical operations to continue during migration. Note that adding PQC algorithms in new firmware needs CAVP algorithm validations and a module revalidation — the existing certificate does not cover the new firmware, so budget for the CMVP timeline. Under the CMVP Management Manual (version 2.7, 9 April 2026) the route is an Update (UPDT) only if each category of security change (approved algorithms, SSPs, approved services, self-tests, FSM states) stays under 30%; otherwise the module goes through a Full Submission (FS). The Learn tab panel "What the lab tests" quotes the sources.
6. FIPS 140-3 Readiness Check — Walk through CMVP validation checklist
Open the FIPS Validation Tracker workshop. Filter by "Active" status to see which vendors have achieved PQC validation. Compare CAVP algorithm-level certifications vs FIPS 140-3 module-level certifications. Check which algorithms have the most validations across vendors.

chunks.content:
Module: HSM & PQC Operations
Component: HsmPqcExercises

ML-KEM and ML-DSA carry the most validations in the tracker, across both algorithm (CAVP) and module (CMVP) certificates. Several Level 3 HSM module certificates list ML-KEM and ML-DSA as approved (Thales Luna T7 #5450, Kryptus #5282, Crypto4A #5497, Sansec #5503), while others from the same vendors list none (Luna K7 #4684, nShield 5s #5329 and #4745; Luna M7 #5300 lists only LMS). Read the approved-algorithm list of the exact certificate rather than a vendor name — that is the point of the exercise. An algorithm certificate is a prerequisite for listing an approved algorithm on a module certificate, but it is not a module certificate.

A Hardware Security Module (HSM) is a tamper-resistant physical device that performs cryptographic operations and protects keys within a certified security boundary. The FIPS 140-3 standard defines four increasing, qualitative security levels. A module's certificate states one overall level; its Security Policy lists the level reached in each requirement area.
• Entrust nShield 5 (FIPS 140-3 L3 certificates #5329 and #4745 cover the nShield 5s module)
• Utimaco SecurityServer (PCIe, FIPS 140-2 L3, certificate now Historical)
PQC firmware is shipping. Algorithm sets, APIs and validated configurations differ by vendor — see the vendor deep dive below.
• AWS CloudHSM (ML-DSA keys in the HSM; whether ML-DSA counts as FIPS-approved is unreconciled, see the Cloud HSM deep dive)
• Azure Dedicated HSM (Thales Luna 7; PQC needs a customer-administered firmware upgrade; retiring)
• Google Cloud HSM (Cloud KMS lists no PQC algorithm for HSM keys)
Cloud PQC support is uneven: check each service's own documentation (checked 15 Oct 2026)
PKCS#11 v3.2 (OASIS Standard, 3 June 2026) introduces new mechanism types for post-quantum cryptography. These define how applications interact with PQC keys inside HSMs via the standard Cryptoki API.

Key insight: On-prem HSMs (Thales, Entrust, Utimaco, Crypto4A) ship PQC firmware, with different algorithm sets (Thales's Luna Post Quantum Algorithms page lists ML-KEM, ML-DSA and LMS-HSS, and that page and its v7.9 release post do not list SLH-DSA; Utimaco's Quantum Protect page shows SLH-DSA as in progress) and different FIPS 140 coverage: some module certificates list PQC algorithms (Crypto4A #5497, Thales Luna T7 #5450), others do not (Entrust nShield 5s #5329 and #4745, Thales Luna K7 #4684). Cloud HSMs are uneven: AWS CloudHSM generates and uses ML-DSA keys inside the HSM through vendor-defined PKCS#11 mechanisms. AWS documents ML-DSA as available in FIPS mode on hsm2m.medium clusters from 1 September 2026, while the NIST Security Policy for the same module (CMVP #4703) lists ML-DSA and ML-KEM as non-approved services and the certificate lists no PQC algorithm among its approved ones; we have not found a document that reconciles the two (see the AWS CloudHSM card). Azure Dedicated HSM is a Thales Luna 7 appliance: Azure lists no PQC algorithm, and ML-KEM and ML-DSA come with Luna firmware 7.9 if the customer upgrades, after consulting Thales Support (the service is retiring — no new customer onboardings); Google Cloud KMS lists its PQC algorithms at the software protection level only, with none for HSM keys (AWS and Google statements checked 23 Oct 2026; the Azure statements checked 29 Oct 2026).

AWS-LC has its own CMVP certificates as a Level 1 software module (AWS-LC 3, #5298/#5314, approve ML-KEM but not ML-DSA); they do not change the HSM's Level 3 certificate. Checked 23 Oct 2026.
“Available in FIPS mode” and “listed on the certificate” are different claims. FIPS mode is an AWS cluster setting; the certificate and its Security Policy are NIST CMVP documents, which speak of an “approved mode of operation”. The AWS pages we read do not say the two are the same. We show both statements and prefer neither.
Starting September 1, 2026, ML-DSA is available in FIPS mode for hsm2m.medium clusters.
In FIPS mode, only Federal Information Processing Standard (FIPS) validated keys and algorithms can be used.
The NIST Security Policy for the same module says (CMVP #4703, Marvell LS2 HSM Family, policy dated January 29, 2026; NIST's certificate page shows its latest update on 26 February 2026):
