Hardware HSM backing for Cloud KMS keys. Google's Cloud KMS algorithms page lists its PQC signing algorithms (ML-DSA-44/65/87, including external-mu, and SLH-DSA-SHA2-128S) and its key encapsulation algorithms (ML-KEM-768, ML-KEM-1024 and X-Wing) for the software protection level; its tables for the HSM and single-tenant HSM protection levels list none (page read 23 Oct 2026).
Hardware: Google's Cloud HSM architecture page says Cloud HSM uses Marvell LiquidSecurity HSMs (certificate #4399) in FIPS 140-2 Level 3 certified hardware security modules.

chunks.title: HSM & PQC Operations — HsmPqcIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: HSM & PQC Operations
Component: HsmPqcIntroduction

PQC algorithms introduce new side-channel attack surfaces. An attacker with physical access to a module, or one who can observe its timing, power draw, electromagnetic emissions or the effect of injected faults, may learn about secret values from how a computation runs rather than from its output. HSM designs use countermeasures for lattice-based and hash-based operations that differ from classical protections.
Check the module's Security Policy, not the technique's name. The cards below describe attack classes and the countermeasure techniques discussed for them. Whether a given HSM implements a technique is stated, if at all, in the vendor's documentation and in the module's Security Policy; the existence of a technique does not show that a product uses it. On the validation side, CMVP has no approved non-invasive test metrics today:
If a vendor has publicly documented that a module mitigates a specific attack, FIPS 140-3 IG 12.A makes the lab address that claim:
If a cryptographic module has been purposely designed, built and publicly documented to mitigate one or more specific attacks, this section is applicable and AS12.01 through AS12.04 (as applicable) shall be addressed regardless if the vendor of the module wishes to address the claim or not.

chunks.title: HSM & PQC Operations — HsmPqcIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: HSM & PQC Operations
Component: HsmPqcIntroduction

ML-DSA supports a "hedged" signing mode where the rnd parameter is set to a random value rather than zero. FIPS 204 §3.4 makes hedged signing the default variant and says “The use of fresh randomness during signing helps mitigate side-channel attacks”. It also permits a deterministic variant, and says that this variant “should not be used on platforms where side-channel attacks are a concern and where they cannot be otherwise mitigated”. PKCS#11 v3.2 lets the caller choose the variant (CKH_HEDGE_PREFERRED, CKH_HEDGE_REQUIRED or CKH_DETERMINISTIC_REQUIRED), so which variant a given HSM uses unless told otherwise is a property of that product. Look for it in the module's documentation and Security Policy rather than assuming it.
Upgrading HSM firmware to support PQC algorithms requires careful planning. Each vendor has a different upgrade path, complexity, and recertification timeline.
Note: Recertification time varies by module and queue; the CMVP Modules in Process list shows where each submission is. Until a certificate listing the PQC algorithms is issued, the firmware may run PQC algorithms, but the module certificate does not cover them.

chunks.title: HSM & PQC Operations — HsmPqcIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: HSM & PQC Operations
Component: HsmPqcIntroduction

A PQC-capable HSM is checked in four separate places, and the single word “Required” in the FIPS Recert column above covers all of them. CAVP is NIST's algorithm validation program (its tests are specified in ACVP documents). CMVP is NIST's cryptographic module validation program; a module's certificate lists its approved algorithms, and the Security Policy published with it lists its services. A CAST is a cryptographic algorithm self-test that a validated module runs on its own algorithms, and a PCT is a pairwise consistency test on a generated key pair. A CSTL is an accredited testing laboratory. In the quotations, IUT means implementation under test, OTS means one-time signature, and FS means full submission. Every quotation below is verbatim from the document named after it, with footnote and reference-number markers left out.
NIST's ACVP specification drafts (all dated 2 October 2026) cover ML-KEM (keyGen and encapDecap), ML-DSA (keyGen, sigGen, sigVer), SLH-DSA (keyGen, sigGen, sigVer) and LMS (keyGen, sigGen, sigVer). The CAVP overview page says what such a certificate is for, and how it is tested:
Cryptographic algorithm validation is a prerequisite of cryptographic module validation.
Due to this structure, ACVTS testing is entirely black-box. The implementation is never provided to NIST or the CAVP in order to receive a validation certificate.
For ML-KEM the ACVP draft includes checks that an HSM rejects bad keys:

chunks.title: HSM & PQC Operations — HsmPqcIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: HSM & PQC Operations
Component: HsmPqcIntroduction

For the encapsulation key check, the server will generate a potentially valid or invalid encapsulation key ek. The IUT SHALL determine if the provided ek is valid based on [FIPS203] Section 7.2.
What the algorithm tests leave out, in the specifications' own words:
An ACVP server will not test the zeroization of intermediate values, security strength of the deterministic random bit generators (DRBGs), or incorrect length signatures or public keys.
ACVP does not test the inability of an implementation to export a private key. ACVP does not provide any guarantees on the inability to reuse private OTS pairs of an implementation.
Of the SP 800-208 schemes only LMS has an ACVP specification; none is published for XMSS, XMSS^MT or HSS (NIST's ACVP specification list, October 2026). The FIPS 140-3 Implementation Guidance (IG) C.N, last modified September 2024, says the same:
CAVP tests are undergoing development with testing available for LMS but not yet for XMSS, HSS, or XMSSMT.
An algorithm certificate does not make a product validated. The CAVP overview page states the relationship:

chunks.title: HSM & PQC Operations — HsmPqcIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: HSM & PQC Operations
Component: HsmPqcIntroduction

For an algorithm implementation to be listed on a cryptographic module validation certificate as an Approved security function, the algorithm implementation must meet all the requirements of FIPS 140 and must successfully complete the cryptographic algorithm validation process. However, a product or implementation does not meet the FIPS 140 module validation requirements by simply implementing an Approved security function and acquiring validations for each of the implemented algorithms.
A Security Policy keeps approved and non-approved items apart. The Security Policy of CMVP certificate #4703 (an HSM), for example, has “Table 10 Approved Services” and “Table 11 Non-Approved Services”, and lists the non-approved algorithms the module also offers in its Tables 4, 5 and 6. For algorithms that are allowed with no security claimed, the IG says:
the algorithm shall be included in the Security Policy's list of non-approved algorithms allowed in the approved mode of operation with no security claimed (see SP 800-140B). However, the module's certificate shall not include these algorithms as they do not claim any security and are not used to meet any requirement of FIPS 140-3.
So the question to put to a certificate is not “does the vendor sell ML-DSA?” but “is ML-DSA among the approved algorithms of this certificate, and which approved services use it?”

chunks.title: HSM & PQC Operations — HsmPqcIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: HSM & PQC Operations
Component: HsmPqcIntroduction

IG 10.3.A (last modified 19 August 2026) sets when the self-tests run and what they must cover. Timing, and what happens outside the approved mode:
The requirements of this IG apply prior to the first operational use of the cryptographic algorithm.
GeneralNote8: For all algorithms that require a CAST (e.g., approved algorithms, allowed algorithms with a claim of security as permitted by an IG, and legacy algorithms per IG C.M), a CAST shall be performed prior to first time algorithm execution in the approved mode; but CASTs are NOT required (but are certainly permissible) prior to first time algorithm execution in the non-approved mode.
So firmware that runs ML-KEM or ML-DSA in a non-approved mode need not carry the CASTs that a validated approved mode needs. For ML-KEM:
if the module implements ML-KEM encapsulation, the module shall have a CAST for the ML-KEM encapsulation mechanism.
The ML-KEM decapsulation CASTs shall cover both the implicit rejection and (unnamed) non-rejection paths.
For ML-DSA signing, the CAST may use either variant from the hedged-signing section above:
if the module implements digital signature generation, the module shall have an ML-DSA digital signature generation CAST for either the ‘hedged’ or ‘deterministic’ algorithm (per FIPS 204 Section 5.2).
If the module implements LMS signature generation then it shall also implement key generation and shall have CASTs for both LMS signature generation and key generation.

chunks.title: HSM & PQC Operations — HsmPqcIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: HSM & PQC Operations
Component: HsmPqcIntroduction

A key pair the HSM generates is also tested once, by a PCT, which is not a CAST:
Though not a CAST, a pairwise consistency test (PCT) shall be conducted for every generated public and private key pair for the applicable approved algorithm (per ISO/IEC 19790:2012 Section 7.10.3.3).
For key pairs generated for use with approved KEMs in FIPS 203, the PCT (described by the tester in TE10.35.01) shall consist of applying the encapsulation key ek to encapsulate a shared secret K leading to ciphertext c, and then applying decapsulation key dk to retrieve the same shared secret K. The PCT passes if the two shared secret K values are equal.
An HSM that stores a seed and rebuilds the key pair from it later is covered by a separate sentence:
For key pairs generated from stored seeds per FIPS 203 (section 3.3) or FIPS 204 (section 3.6.3), a PCT is only required to be performed on the key pair prior to the first exportation of the seed or key pair or prior to the first operational use of the key pair after the seed has been generated within the module.
For an approved ML-KEM, IG D.S (last modified 9 April 2026) ties the algorithm certificate to the module checks:
ML-KEM shall be CAVP tested via ‘ML-KEM EncapDecap’ for all implemented parameter sets (ML-KEM-1024, ML-KEM-512, ML-KEM-768) and functions (Decapsulation, Encapsulation). The module shall implement the encapsulation and decapsulation key checks specified in FIPS 203 Sections 7.2 and 7.3

chunks.title: HSM & PQC Operations — HsmPqcIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: HSM & PQC Operations
Component: HsmPqcIntroduction

The FIPS 140-3 CMVP Management Manual (version 2.7, 9 April 2026) decides how a changed module is submitted. It lists twelve submission scenarios (section 7.1), among them the full submission (FS) and several revalidation routes. The starting point:
An updated version of a previously validated cryptographic module can be considered for a revalidation rather than a full validation depending on the extent of the modifications from the previously validated version of the module.
If no revalidation scenario fits, the module is treated as new:
If modifications are made to hardware, software, or firmware components that do not meet any of the below revalidation criteria, then the cryptographic module shall be considered a new module and shall undergo a full validation testing by a CSTL and submitted as a FS.
Some revalidation scenarios cannot carry new cryptography. Algorithm Update (ALG) is for algorithms that became CAVP-testable after validation, and Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) is for security fixes:
Code or configuration changes are not permitted under this revalidation scenario.
The scenario that allows security-relevant changes is Update (UPDT), up to a limit:

chunks.title: HSM & PQC Operations — HsmPqcIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: HSM & PQC Operations
Component: HsmPqcIntroduction

An updated cryptographic module can be considered in this scenario if less than a 30% of security changes were made to the module. Security changes include impacts to: approved / allowed security functions/algorithms, SSPs, approved security services, self-tests, and security states within the FSM. None of these, assessed individually, can exceed 30% of changes.
The CMVP upon review, may determine that the changes are >30% and shall be submitted as an FS.
The Manual's summary table (section 7.1.14, p. 65) gives UPDT a new certificate and a new sunset date, requires the latest guidance, and requires CAVP testing and, where IG 9.3.A applies, entropy source validation (ESV) testing (not sourced in the Library). Adding ML-KEM, ML-DSA or SLH-DSA changes the approved algorithms, the approved services and the self-tests, which are categories the Manual counts toward the 30% limit; whether a particular firmware release is an UPDT or an FS is decided by the CMVP on the lab's submission, not something this page can state in advance.
Related: how the ACVP tests are run in ACVP Lab Workflow , how the signing state is managed in Stateful Hash-Based Signatures , and how a module is validated in FIPS 140-3 Certification .
LMS/HSS and XMSS are stateful hash-based signature schemes — each leaf in the Merkle tree can only be used to sign once. Reusing a leaf completely compromises the signing key.

chunks.title: HSM & PQC Operations — HsmPqcIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: HSM & PQC Operations
Component: HsmPqcIntroduction

For every signing request, the HSM must write the updated state counter to NVRAM before the signature leaves the module. A power failure around this write can result in state loss, causing the same leaf to be used twice. NIST SP 800-208 §8.1 requires that LMS/XMSS key and signature generation “shall only be validated for use within hardware cryptographic modules” at FIPS 140-2 or FIPS 140-3 Level 3 or higher physical security (see also FIPS 140-3 IG C.N, Requirements for SP 800-208 Schemes). HSMs meet it with atomic NVRAM writes, write-ahead logging, and pre-reservation of signature indices.
• Write-ahead logging prevents partial state corruption
• Pre-reservation of signature indices (batch allocation)
• LMS or XMSS (single-tree only; HSS and XMSS^MT are not allowed in NSS) preferred to start firmware signing now; validated ML-DSA-87 is also approved
• Software and firmware signing: CNSA 2.0 exclusively by 2030
• CNSA 2.0 mandated for National Security Systems by 31 Dec 2031
• HSS (multi-tree) extends the signature count, for commercial (non-NSS) use only
Power failure recovery: the standard fixes the order of operations, not the recovery procedure. How a particular product behaves when it finds incomplete state after a power loss, for example whether it refuses to sign with that key until an operator checks it, is product behaviour: read its Security Policy and administrator guide. NIST SP 800-208 section 8.1 says:

chunks.title: HSM & PQC Operations — HsmPqcIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: HSM & PQC Operations
Component: HsmPqcIntroduction

In order to prevent the possible reuse of an OTS key, when the cryptographic module accepts a request to sign a message, the cryptographic module shall increment the leaf index of the private key (q in LMS, idx in XMSS, idx_sig in XMSSMT) and shall store the incremented leaf index value in nonvolatile storage before exporting a signature value or accepting another request to sign a message.
FIPS 140-3 IG C.N Resolution 12 has the lab check it: “the tester shall confirm that the state information for the key (at minimum the leaf index value) is updated in the non-volatile memory before exporting a signature value or accepting a request to sign another message.”

chunks.title: Hybrid Cryptography — CombinerComparison
chunks.content:
Module: Hybrid Cryptography
Component: CombinerComparison

Every hybrid KEM merges two shared secrets, but designs differ in what else goes into the final key. Hashing the exchanged values (ciphertexts, public keys) ties the key to this exchange; TLS gets the same effect from its transcript.
It omits the ML-KEM ciphertext and key. The draft explains that X-Wing's security relies on the specifics of ML-KEM-768's Fujisaki-Okamoto transform, and warns that the combiner “cannot be assumed to be secure, when used with different KEMs”: it is “not known to be safe to leave out the post-quantum ciphertext from the combiner in the general case”.
Its security claim. If SHA3-256, SHA3-512 and SHAKE-256 are modelled as random oracles, X-Wing's IND-CCA security is bounded by that of ML-KEM-768 and the gap-CDH security of Curve25519.
Binding. The draft states that X-Wing binds the shared key to the public key and to the ciphertext (MAL-BIND-K-PK and MAL-BIND-K-CT), properties ML-KEM on its own does not achieve.
One fixed KEM with a seed key. X-Wing pairs only ML-KEM-768 with X25519. Its private key is a 32-byte seed that SHAKE256 expands into both component keys; the public key is 1,216 bytes, the ciphertext 1,120 bytes and the shared secret 32 bytes. That seed expansion is why the FIPS 140-3 guidance says X-Wing cannot yet be an approved hybrid service (see Implementation & Validation).

chunks.title: Hybrid Cryptography — CombinerComparison
chunks.content:
Module: Hybrid Cryptography
Component: CombinerComparison

The same construction, standardized elsewhere. The CFRG's concrete MLKEM768-X25519 is stated to be identical to X-Wing. The composite ML-KEM draft calls X-Wing and its MLKEM768-X25519 entry “largely interchangeable”: the one difference is that X-Wing generates both private keys from the same seed, while composite ML-KEM assumes independently generated components, for example separately validated ones. An X-Wing implementation counts as compliant composite ML-KEM, but not the other way round.

chunks.title: Hybrid Cryptography — HybridCryptoExercises
chunks.content:
Module: Hybrid Cryptography
Component: HybridCryptoExercises

Work through these scenarios to understand hybrid cryptography in practice. Each exercise pre-configures the Workshop — click "Load & Run" to begin.
Take the Hybrid Cryptography quiz to test what you've learned.
Generate X25519, ML-KEM-768, and X25519MLKEM768 key pairs side-by-side. Compare their public key sizes to see how much overhead the hybrid approach adds.
X25519MLKEM768 public key (1,216 bytes) is roughly X25519 (32 bytes) + ML-KEM-768 (1,184 bytes). The hybrid overhead is minimal compared to the PQC component alone.
Switch to signature mode and generate ECDSA P-256 and ML-DSA-65 key pairs. See the dramatic difference in key and signature sizes between classical and PQC.
ML-DSA-65 private keys (4,032 bytes) are 126x larger than ECDSA P-256 (32 bytes). Signatures are 3,309 bytes vs 64 bytes (raw ECDSA; ~72 bytes when DER-encoded). This is the main PQC migration challenge for bandwidth-constrained systems.
Run the full encap/decap workflow with both ML-KEM-768 and X25519MLKEM768. Verify that encapsulated and decapsulated shared secrets match — proving correctness.
Both algorithms produce matching shared secrets. The hybrid X25519MLKEM768 takes slightly longer due to running both X25519 and ML-KEM internally, but the security benefit is significant.
In Step 1, open the signature view and run the test panel under the key table: it signs and verifies with ECDSA P-256 and with ML-DSA-65. Compare the run times with the signature sizes in the key table.

chunks.title: Hybrid Cryptography — HybridCryptoExercises
chunks.content:
Module: Hybrid Cryptography
Component: HybridCryptoExercises

ECDSA is faster for individual operations, but ML-DSA-65 provides quantum resistance. In a composite scheme, both signatures would be generated and verified together.
Generate self-signed certificates with both ECDSA P-256 and ML-DSA-65. Inspect the certificate fields to see how PQC algorithm OIDs differ from classical ones.
The ML-DSA-65 certificate is significantly larger than ECDSA. The parsed output shows different algorithm OIDs and much larger public key and signature fields embedded in the certificate structure.

chunks.title: Hybrid Cryptography — HybridCryptoIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Hybrid Cryptography
Component: HybridCryptoIntroduction

The transition to post-quantum cryptography faces a fundamental dilemma: PQC algorithms are newer and less battle-tested than classical algorithms, yet the “ Harvest Now, Decrypt Later ” (HNDL) threat means waiting is dangerous. Hybrid cryptography solves this by combining classical and PQC algorithms together.
A classical key exchange (for example X25519) and a post-quantum KEM (ML-KEM) run side by side, and a key combiner merges the two shared secrets. The session key stays secret as long as either component is unbroken, provided the combiner is a sound one (for example the TLS hybrid design or X-Wing).
A message carries a classical and a post-quantum signature. A forgery requires breaking both algorithms, provided the verifier requires both signatures to be valid. A verifier that accepts either one lets an attacker strip the other.
Hybrid is a trade-off rather than a free upgrade. The next two sections set out what it risks compared with pure PQC, for key establishment and for signatures, and how national agencies, standards bodies and industry have decided. The rest of the lesson then builds from the primitives up: hybrid KEMs, hybrid signatures, and finally the certificates that carry them.
RFC 9794 standardizes terminology for hybrid schemes — distinguishing “composite” (single OID, both-must-verify) from “non-composite” (parallel independent algorithms) and establishing naming conventions such as “PQ/T” (Post-Quantum / Traditional).

chunks.title: Hybrid Cryptography — HybridCryptoIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Hybrid Cryptography
Component: HybridCryptoIntroduction

X25519MLKEM768 is the leading hybrid KEM, combining Curve25519 ECDH with ML-KEM-768. Chrome enabled it by default in version 131 (November 2024, Google ); by October 2025 it protected most human traffic to Cloudflare ( Cloudflare ); and AWS KMS, ACM and Secrets Manager endpoints support it (non-FIPS endpoints, April 2025, AWS ).
1. Key Generation: Generate both X25519 key pair and ML-KEM-768 key pair
2. Encapsulation: Sender performs X25519 ECDH + ML-KEM-768 encap → produces combined ciphertext
3. Decapsulation: Recipient performs X25519 ECDH + ML-KEM-768 decap → recovers combined shared secret
4. Key Derivation: Combined shared secret = KDF(both shared secrets, concatenated in the order the group defines) → session key
Even if ML-KEM-768 is broken in the future, X25519 still provides classical security. Even if X25519 is broken by a quantum computer, ML-KEM-768 provides quantum resistance.
FIPS 203 (§8) approves three ML-KEM parameter sets, each mapped to a NIST security category matching the strength of a given AES key size. Pick the set by threat model, not by default.
This module's advice: HNDL risk + data-retention window should drive the choice. If harvested ciphertext must remain secret past ~2035, prefer Cat 3 or Cat 5 over Cat 1.
SecP256r1MLKEM768 — P-256 + ML-KEM-768. Important for organizations requiring FIPS-approved classical curves (X25519 is not FIPS-approved).

chunks.title: Hybrid Cryptography — HybridCryptoIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Hybrid Cryptography
Component: HybridCryptoIntroduction

SecP384r1MLKEM1024 — P-384 + ML-KEM-1024. Provides NIST Level 5 security for high-assurance environments.
The high-level “KDF(both shared secrets)” above hides three real requirements that SP 800-227 defers to SP 800-56C-Rev2:
Concatenation order is fixed per group. In TLS 1.3 (RFC 10024 §4.3), X25519MLKEM768 concatenates ML-KEM_ss || X25519_ss, while SecP256r1MLKEM768 and SecP384r1MLKEM1024 concatenate ECDHE_ss || ML-KEM_ss; the result enters the TLS key schedule as its shared-secret input. SP 800-56C-Rev2 approves this when the first secret comes from a FIPS-approved scheme, so X25519MLKEM768 puts ML-KEM first (X25519 is not approved), while the NIST-curve groups put ECDHE first because certified P-256 and P-384 implementations are more widely available (RFC 10024 §5). SP 800-227 §4.6.2 (September 2025) relaxes the ordering rule: its key combiner is approved when at least one shared secret, in any position, comes from an approved scheme. Swapping order silently breaks interop. Order does not add security, but binding to a known order prevents cross-protocol confusion.
HKDF vs KMAC. SP 800-56C permits either an HMAC-based extractor (HKDF-SHA-256/384/512) or KMAC128/256. TLS 1.3 uses HKDF through its key schedule; KMAC is available for KEM-only protocols that want a single primitive.

chunks.title: Hybrid Cryptography — HybridCryptoIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Hybrid Cryptography
Component: HybridCryptoIntroduction

Dual-PRF assumption. The combined secret stays safe as long as either input looks uniform to the attacker — so a future break of ML-KEM or of X25519 alone does not break the session key. This is why the classical half is kept during the transition.
Domain separation is strongly recommended. SP 800-227 §4.6.3 says a domain separator should be used to uniquely identify the composite scheme in use (for example the component schemes, order of composition, choice of parameter set, key combiner, KDF).
X-Wing and composite ML-KEM build the combiner into the KEM itself; TLS 1.3 relies on its own HKDF key schedule. The comparison below shows how they differ.
— generate X25519 and ML-KEM-768 keys, run the encapsulation, then compare the HKDF, X-Wing and concatenation-only combiners on the same two secrets.
In TLS 1.3 (RFC 9846), hybrid KEMs integrate into the handshake via the key_share extension. The client and server exchange hybrid key material just as they would for classical ECDH — but with larger payloads:
Client → ClientHello supported_groups: [X25519MLKEM768, X25519]
key_share: ML-KEM-768 encapsulation key || X25519 public key (1,184 + 32 = 1,216 bytes)
key_share: ML-KEM-768 ciphertext || X25519 public key (1,088 + 32 = 1,120 bytes)
Both → Shared secret = ML-KEM_ss || X25519_ss → 64 bytes (32 bytes each) (RFC 10024 §4.3)

chunks.title: Hybrid Cryptography — HybridCryptoIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Hybrid Cryptography
Component: HybridCryptoIntroduction

Classical X25519 ClientHello key_share is 32 bytes. X25519MLKEM768 is 1,216 bytes (1,184 for ML-KEM plus 32 for X25519) — a 38× increase in the key share. Cloudflare notes that the ClientHello used to almost always fit within a single network packet; with a 1,216-byte key share it may now span more than one. RFC 6928 (Experimental) proposes an upper bound of 10 segments for TCP’s initial window (min (10*MSS, max (2*MSS, 14600))) in the first round-trip time, and a sender MAY start smaller.
The dominant cost is the larger key_share payload, not computation. Chrome reported about a 4% slowdown in TLS handshake time, larger on slow connections (as cited by Cloudflare, October 2025). AWS measured a 0.05% throughput drop for KMS calls that reuse connections, and 2.3% when every request opens a new handshake (April 2025).
For a full interactive TLS 1.3 handshake simulation with hybrid KEM negotiation, see the TLS Basics module.

chunks.title: Hybrid Cryptography — HybridCryptoIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Hybrid Cryptography
Component: HybridCryptoIntroduction

A compliant ML-KEM deployment is more than “call the library.” SP 800-227 §3.2 covers the required input checks, and FIPS 203 specifies implicit rejection: if the re-encrypted ciphertext does not match the one received, decapsulation returns a key derived from the ciphertext and a secret value stored in the decapsulation key (Algorithm 18) instead of reporting an error. SP 800-227 §3.3 says KEM modules should be designed with appropriate countermeasures against side-channel attacks, including constant-time implementations and protecting memory from leakage.
ML-KEM is the key-encapsulation algorithm defined in FIPS 203. Alice uses Bob's public encapsulation key to produce a shared secret and a ciphertext. Bob uses his private decapsulation key and that ciphertext to recover the same secret. A protocol can then derive encryption and authentication keys from it.
Input checks can fail. For example, an ML-KEM-768 ciphertext must be 1,088 bytes long. A 1,087-byte ciphertext fails the length check, and decapsulation must not run. FIPS 203 also requires checks on the decapsulation key. Normal library argument and operational errors still apply.

chunks.title: Hybrid Cryptography — HybridCryptoIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Hybrid Cryptography
Component: HybridCryptoIntroduction

An internal mismatch is different. For inputs that pass those checks, ML-KEM decrypts and re-encrypts internally, then compares the reconstructed ciphertext with the received one. If they differ, it selects a fallback shared secret derived from the secret rejection value z and the received ciphertext. The implementation returns that secret without exposing the mismatch as an error or through timing. This is implicit rejection.
What happens to the encrypted data? Suppose an attacker changes Alice's ciphertext without changing its length and triggers implicit rejection. Bob obtains a different secret. If the protocol derives an AES-GCM key from it, authentication of Alice's encrypted message fails, and the receiver rejects the message without releasing unauthenticated plaintext. Successful decapsulation alone does not confirm that both parties share a key; the protocol needs authentication or key confirmation.
Why hide the mismatch if authentication fails later? A specific decapsulation error would answer an attacker's repeated queries about the internal ciphertext check, creating a validity oracle. Implicit rejection conceals that answer. A later authentication failure only says that the message did not authenticate with the resulting key; a wrong tag can cause the same failure even after valid decapsulation. The protocol must preserve this distinction in its error handling and timing.

chunks.title: Hybrid Cryptography — HybridCryptoIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Hybrid Cryptography
Component: HybridCryptoIntroduction

Correct results alone do not show that an implementation protects its secrets. Attackers may learn information by measuring execution time or observing memory access. Constant-time techniques help prevent these behaviours from revealing secret values; they do not mean every call takes exactly the same number of milliseconds. NIST recommends appropriate protections against these attacks. Their effectiveness depends on the implementation and the device running it.
ML-KEM encapsulation requires fresh, unpredictable random input (the 32-byte m). If an attacker knows that input, they can reproduce the encapsulation using the recipient’s public key and recover the same shared secret. FIPS 203 specifies the randomness requirements (§3.3), including use of an approved DRBG.
Consider X25519 and ML-KEM combined to derive a session key. If a leak exposes only the X25519 shared secret, a suitable combiner can still protect the session key through the uncompromised ML-KEM secret. If the leak exposes both secrets or the final session key, that protection is lost. Assess what information the implementation leaks, including during combination and key handling.
For an HSM, TPM or other hardware device, check the manufacturer’s documentation to understand which protections are provided, which settings affect them, and which attacks they address. Do not assume every device has a switch to enable PQC protections.

chunks.title: Hybrid Cryptography — HybridCryptoIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Hybrid Cryptography
Component: HybridCryptoIntroduction

Everything above is about how a hybrid KEM works. Whether a FIPS 140-3 validated module may offer it as an approved service is a separate question, answered by CMVP Implementation Guidance (IG) D.S, Key Encapsulation Mechanisms (last modified 9 April 2026). The IG calls an approved ML-KEM combined with one or more non-ML-KEM schemes “Scenario 2”. The non-ML-KEM part may be approved or non-approved (the IG's examples are X25519 and X448).
The five conditions: a module must implement, at a minimum, all of them
An approved key combiner: the shared secrets concatenated and fed into an SP 800-56C key-derivation function (HKDF counts), or combined by an SP 800-133 §6.3 method (concatenation, XOR, or key extraction using HMAC). The IG describes the SP 800-133 §6.3 route only for combining ML-KEM shared secrets with those of approved key-agreement schemes (IG D.F Scenario 1 or 2).
The module does not offer arbitrary hybrid combinations. It enforces a pre-defined set of hybrid schemes, for example SecP256r1MLKEM768, X25519MLKEM768 and SecP384r1MLKEM1024.
For each of those sets, the module controls at least how the shared secrets are sequenced, for example the concatenation order.

chunks.title: Hybrid Cryptography — HybridCryptoIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Hybrid Cryptography
Component: HybridCryptoIntroduction

If any one is missing, Scenario 2 cannot be claimed, and any non-approved scheme the module offers must be restricted to the non-approved mode only. The IG's own examples: a software library with an approved ML-KEM and X25519 but no approved key combiner, or a library with the first three items that does not enforce a specific set of combinations or control the sequencing.
The non-approved half. A non-approved component such as X25519 is classified as a “non-approved but allowed algorithm with no security claimed” (IG 2.4.A): it is listed in the Security Policy, not on the certificate. It may be used only inside the approved hybrid, and the module itself must enforce that. It cannot be used for other purposes in the approved mode or offered as an independent approved service, such as a separate API call in a software library, and operator guidance in the Security Policy cannot stand in for that enforcement. The hybrid's claimed security strength comes from the ML-KEM, and the hybrid service is then treated as an approved security service.

chunks.title: Hybrid Cryptography — HybridCryptoIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Hybrid Cryptography
Component: HybridCryptoIntroduction

Which real hybrids qualify. The IG says the TLS 1.3 hybrid key exchange (the IG cites an early version of the IETF draft that was later published as RFC 10024) may meet Scenario 2 with the SP 800-56C HKDF as the approved combiner, if one of SecP256r1MLKEM768, X25519MLKEM768 or SecP384r1MLKEM1024 is used, and notes that these specifications may still be in draft form. It also says the X-Wing hybrid KEM “cannot yet meet the requirements of Scenario 2” even though it uses an SP 800-56C one-step KDF as its combiner: at a minimum, SP 800-133 needs an update to approve X-Wing's seed generation, because seed expansion using SHAKE to generate the key pairs is not currently in SP 800-133. Separately, the CAVP prerequisites page (updated 22 September 2026) lists X-Wing keyGen and encapDecap tests. Both statements are published; CAVP itself says that acquiring a validation for each implemented algorithm does not by itself meet the FIPS 140 module requirements.

chunks.title: Hybrid Cryptography — HybridCryptoIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Hybrid Cryptography
Component: HybridCryptoIntroduction

What the Security Policy shows. The module records the claim in the Security Function Implementation table as “KEM-Hybrid” or “KEM-Hybrid-Full”, with entry names such as “KEM-Hybrid X25519MLKEM768”. The non-approved half is listed separately with the caveat “no security claimed”, citing IG D.S Scenario 2 and IG 2.4.A. Per the CMVP's supplemental guidance (last updated 8 April 2026), “KEM-Hybrid” applies to a module that meets items 1 to 5 but not the extra conditions for “KEM-Hybrid-Full”, and it can still be an approved service, even for a software library offering the hybrid KEM to a calling application.
Self-tests. Every approved scheme in the hybrid must be self-tested individually under IG 10.3.A. For the ML-KEM part that means known-answer self-tests for each ML-KEM function the module implements (encapsulation, decapsulation and key generation), with the decapsulation tests covering both the implicit-rejection and the non-rejection path, on at least one of ML-KEM-512, ML-KEM-768 or ML-KEM-1024 as implemented in approved mode. The IG currently has no separate self-test for the approved key combiner or for the non-approved half, beyond self-testing any approved algorithms used within, such as KDFs.

chunks.title: Hybrid Cryptography — HybridCryptoIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Hybrid Cryptography
Component: HybridCryptoIntroduction

Algorithm testing (CAVP). The IG lets the approved pieces be tested separately (the ML-KEM and, with a non-approved other half, the approved algorithms beneath it, such as KDFs). Its other option is end-to-end tests of the full hybrid scheme, “if available within CAVP”; it says it will be updated with the specific tests after they become available. No hybrid-KEM specification appears in the ACVP specification index (pages.nist.gov/ACVP) as of 23 October 2026.
Not to be confused with IG 1.B, “Hybrid Modules” (new 19 August 2026): that is about a module whose boundary combines a software or firmware component with a disjoint hardware component. It has nothing to do with hybrid key exchange.
FIPS 140-3 Certification module FIPS 140-3 Implementation Guidance (Library)
In short: SP 800-227 sets out certain requirements and recommendations for KEM implementation and use in FIPS 140-validated modules, and gives guidance to vendors that choose to combine keying material securely.

chunks.title: Hybrid Cryptography — HybridCryptoIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Hybrid Cryptography
Component: HybridCryptoIntroduction

HPKE is a public-key encryption scheme built from three swappable components — a KEM, a KDF, and an AEAD — combined through a standard KeySchedule so any KEM/KDF/AEAD triple, plus one of four modes (Base, PSK, Auth, AuthPSK), yields an interoperable construction. "Hybrid" in HPKE's own name refers to this KEM+KDF+AEAD composition, not to a PQC+classical pairing — that is a separate, additional meaning layered on top by draft-ietf-hpke-pq (below), and easy to conflate with the certificate-level hybrid formats covered earlier on this page.
A KEM’s Encaps takes the recipient’s public key (plus a parameter set) and returns both a shared secret and the ciphertext; the sender does not hand it a key of its own choosing, whereas in key transport (for example RSA-OAEP) one party selects the key and transmits it. HPKE’s Encap is a randomized algorithm that generates an ephemeral shared secret and its encapsulation. Needing only the recipient’s public key is why it shows up wherever a protocol needs one-shot public-key encryption rather than an interactive handshake:
MLS uses HPKE for TreeKEM path updates (see the MLS Group Messaging module).
TLS 1.3 Encrypted Client Hello (ECH) uses it to encrypt the ClientHello.
JOSE and COSE extend it to wrap a JWT or CWT payload the same way.

chunks.title: Hybrid Cryptography — HybridCryptoIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Hybrid Cryptography
Component: HybridCryptoIntroduction

RFC 9180 itself registers only classical KEMs. The PQC angle comes from draft-ietf-hpke-pq — still an Internet-Draft, not yet an RFC — which registers pure ML-KEM and PQ/T hybrid KEM IDs that plug into the same KeySchedule and Seal/Open.
ML-KEM-512/768/1024; MLKEM768-X25519, MLKEM768-P256, MLKEM1024-P384
Independently of the KEM/KDF/AEAD choice, RFC 9180 defines four modes : Base (unauthenticated), PSK (pre-shared key), Auth (sender authenticated via its own KEM keypair), and AuthPSK (both). Auth and AuthPSK stay classical-only: draft-ietf-hpke-pq's ML-KEM and PQ/T hybrid KEM entries mark the Auth column "no", since ML-KEM has no AuthEncap/AuthDecap interface.
The MLKEM768-X25519/P256 and MLKEM1024-P384 hybrid KEMs are not defined by draft-ietf-hpke-pq itself — it delegates to the CFRG's generic hybrid-KEM combiner ( draft-irtf-cfrg-hybrid-kems ), instantiated concretely in draft-irtf-cfrg-concrete-hybrid-kems : PQ-component-first concatenation, SHA3-256 as the combiner over concat(ss_PQ, ss_T, ct_T, ek_T, Label).
PKCS#11 v3.2 has no CKM_HPKE mechanism — checked against the canonical v3.2 header, no HPKE entry exists at all. A real HSM deployment composes it from mechanisms the spec does define: CKM_ECDH1_DERIVE / CKM_ML_KEM for the KEM leg, CKM_HKDF_DERIVE plus HMAC signing for LabeledExtract/LabeledExpand, and AES-GCM / ChaCha20-Poly1305 for Seal/Open.

chunks.title: Hybrid Cryptography — HybridCryptoIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Hybrid Cryptography
Component: HybridCryptoIntroduction

— every KEM/KDF/AEAD/mode combination above is selectable, and the classical DHKEM path is cross-checked byte-for-byte against RFC 9180 Appendix A.
Signing with both a classical and a PQC algorithm at the same time. The key design question: can either component be stripped and verified alone?
RFC 9955: Hybrid Signature Spectrums (Informational, July 2026)
Defines the taxonomy of hybrid signature constructions and a non-separability spectrum. Basis for evaluating all hybrid signature proposals including Silithium.
Devevey, Guerreau, Roméas · ePrint 2025/2059 · November 2025
Silithium adapts the Fiat-Shamir transform to produce a fused hybrid signature from EC-Schnorr (classical, secp256k1) and ML-DSA-65 (FIPS 204). Both components share a single challenge μ derived from both public keys, the EC commitment R, and the message. Neither component verifies on its own with the standard challenge. The paper targets Strong Non-Separability (SNS) and reports no separability issues for its construction; this page demonstrates the idea and does not prove the property.

chunks.title: Hybrid Cryptography — HybridCryptoIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Hybrid Cryptography
Component: HybridCryptoIntroduction

IG D.S covers key encapsulation only. The IG (last updated 19 August 2026) has no section on composite or hybrid signatures. It does name one hybrid key-establishment scheme that uses ML-KEM (IG D.S, “Hybrid scheme that uses an approved ML-KEM”); a hybrid module (IG 1.B) is a different thing, about how a module is built, not about combining algorithms. What the IG does say applies to each algorithm on its own: a module that implements ML-DSA signing or verification needs the self-tests of IG 10.3.A. Whether a composite signature can be offered as an approved service is not answered in the published guidance; ask the lab.
Seven X.509 certificate formats make up the workshop's main comparison: five carry signature keys and two carry KEM (encryption) keys. One rule underlies all of them: the subject public key and the certificate signature are independent. The subject key is what the certificate is about; the signature comes from the issuer's key.
Standard single-algorithm X.509 using a lattice-based PQC signature. ML-DSA OIDs are standardized in RFC 9881. Quantum-safe but requires all verifiers to support ML-DSA.

chunks.title: Hybrid Cryptography — HybridCryptoIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Hybrid Cryptography
Component: HybridCryptoIntroduction

Hash-based signature (SPHINCS+) with no lattice assumptions. OIDs in RFC 9909. ANSSI does not recommend systematic hybridisation for hash-based signatures such as SLH-DSA, XMSS and LMS, because it considers their underlying problem well studied (its 2022 position paper also notes their limited range of application). Larger signatures (7,856 B, about 7.9 KB, for SLH-DSA-SHA2-128s per FIPS 205) are the trade-off.
A single composite OID identifies the algorithm pair. Both signatures must verify. Defined in draft-ietf-lamps-pq-composite-sigs-19, approved and in the RFC Editor queue (no RFC number yet). Strongest binding — the signatures are tied to the composite algorithm: a split-off ML-DSA signature fails on its own, but the traditional signature still verifies (draft §9.2.3). Not backward-compatible with legacy validators.
A single classical cert with PQC key and signature in X.509 extensions. Legacy verifiers ignore the extensions; PQC-aware verifiers can check the alternative signature too, and their policy decides whether one or both must verify. Defined in ITU-T X.509 (2019) §7.2.2 and §9.8.
A new certificate carries a RelatedCertificate extension holding the hash of an existing one. The link is one-way: Cert A is never modified. The CA issues Cert B only after the requester proves it holds Cert A's key. Legacy systems use the classical cert; a protocol may ask for either certificate or both — RFC 9763 does not require both.

chunks.title: Hybrid Cryptography — HybridCryptoIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Hybrid Cryptography
Component: HybridCryptoIntroduction

KEM certificates — the subject key encrypts, the issuer signs
RFC 9935 defines ML-KEM public keys in X.509. An ML-KEM key cannot sign, so its certificate is always issued by a separate signing-capable CA (ML-DSA, ECDSA, RSA, …). If keyUsage is present, keyEncipherment must be the only bit. Because the CA cannot check a self-signature from a KEM key, proof of possession uses a KEM-based exchange instead. The key is then used, for example, in CMS KEMRecipientInfo (RFC 9629, ML-KEM in RFC 9936).
draft-ietf-lamps-pq-composite-kem-23 puts an ML-KEM key and a classical KEM key (X25519, ECDH, RSA) under one OID, ML-KEM component first. Encapsulation runs both and combines the shared secrets. Approved by the IESG and awaiting publication as an RFC; not backward compatible.
draft-ietf-lamps-certdiscovery-03 lets a certificate tell PQC-capable relying parties where to fetch a related certificate, through a subjectInfoAccess entry. A fetched certificate must still pass full path validation. The OIDs are not assigned yet, so the workshop's encoding is illustrative.
RFC 9925 defines id-alg-unsigned for a certificate with no signature at all — a container for a key that is trusted by other means, such as a trust anchor. It is never valid in a certification path.

chunks.title: Hybrid Cryptography — HybridCryptoIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Hybrid Cryptography
Component: HybridCryptoIntroduction

One certificate with a DeltaCertificateDescriptor extension encoding the differences needed to rebuild a paired certificate. The proposal, draft-bonnell-lamps-chameleon-certs-07, is an expired individual draft that the LAMPS working group never adopted. It is shown for study only and is not recommended for new deployments.
Deployment guidance: This module's advice: Pure PQC (ML-DSA) is ready today (RFC 9881; the workshop is tested with OpenSSL 3.6.3). Pure SLH-DSA is also ready (RFC 9909). Composite requires both parties to support the draft spec — best suited to closed PKI. Alt-Sig works with legacy verifiers via extensions. Related Certs (RFC 9763) keeps the classical certificate fully usable on its own. Watchlist: FN-DSA (planned FIPS 206, not yet final) has an IETF certificate draft whose OIDs are still TBD; composite KEM will enable hybrid key encapsulation in S/MIME once published.
Interactive TLS 1.3 handshake simulator with hybrid KEM negotiation
Physical-layer key exchange complementing hybrid PQC schemes
Generate hybrid keys, run KEM operations, and inspect composite certificates.
Adversary strips the PQC component and presents only the classical signature. Verifiers that accept classical-only sigs are fooled. Prevented by SNS.
Adversary combines a legitimate EC sig with a different ML-DSA sig (or vice versa) to forge a hybrid signature. Prevented because μ ties both to the same R.

chunks.title: Hybrid Cryptography — HybridInCryptoApis
chunks.content:
Module: Hybrid Cryptography
Component: HybridInCryptoApis

An application gets a hybrid in one of two ways. It can compose it: call a classical API and a pure-PQC API separately, then combine the results itself. Or the library or token offers the hybrid as one algorithm: a TLS named group, a composite KEM such as X-Wing or composite ML-KEM, or a composite signature. Today most libraries offer hybrid key exchange only inside TLS, so any hybrid outside TLS is usually composed by the application.
Key establishment in Java: an X25519 KeyAgreement, an ML-KEM KEM and the KDF API's HKDF, fed both secrets in an order the application fixes. JEP 527 notes the platform “already contains the building blocks”, but adds hybrid itself only for TLS 1.3; Bouncy Castle's guidance is that “the order is part of the protocol and must be fixed by both parties in advance”.
Key establishment on an HSM (PKCS#11 v3.2): CKM_ECDH1_DERIVE for the classical secret, C_EncapsulateKey / C_DecapsulateKey with CKM_ML_KEM for the post-quantum one, then the application either reads both out and combines them, or chains CKM_CONCATENATE_BASE_AND_KEY, CKM_CONCATENATE_BASE_AND_DATA and CKM_SHA3_256_KEY_DERIVATION inside the token, as this module's HPKE step does.
Signatures: two separate signatures, one classical and one ML-DSA, each with its own key, and a verification policy in the application that requires both. Microsoft's 2025 guidance still recommended this kind of combination with existing algorithms before its composites shipped.

The PKCS#11 v3.3 working draft adds key types CKK_COMP_KEM and CKK_COMP_SIG and five mechanisms: CKM_COMP_KEM_KEY_PAIR_GEN and CKM_COMP_KEM (run through C_EncapsulateKey / C_DecapsulateKey, returning the combined secret as a key handle), and CKM_COMP_SIG_KEY_PAIR_GEN, CKM_COMP_SIG and CKM_COMP_SIG_EXTERNAL_HASH (one C_Sign call for one composite signature from one key object holding both halves). The combiner then runs inside the token, as the composite ML-KEM and ML-DSA drafts define it. The OASIS PKCS 11 TC approved these identifiers in October 2026; no v3.3 specification has been published, and an X-Wing or HPKE mechanism is still an open discussion.
Try both mechanisms in the Hub's PKCS#11 engine: composite ML-KEM and composite ML-DSA in the PKCS#11 workshop's v3.3 tab. A single mechanism is not automatically an approved FIPS 140-3 service: the published guidance has no section on composite signatures (see Implementation & Validation).
“Not offered” means the project's release notes and documentation list no such algorithm as of 1 November 2026. The TLS groups are those of RFC 10024: X25519MLKEM768, SecP256r1MLKEM768 and SecP384r1MLKEM1024. The Migrate catalog shows the same information per product.

A counter-example, not a design. Each half of the key is also simply one raw component secret.

Two quantum risks reach certificates differently. "Harvest now, decrypt later" is a confidentiality risk: traffic recorded today can be decrypted once a cryptographically-relevant quantum computer can break the classical key exchange, so key establishment must move to PQC first. Signatures are different: a future quantum computer could forge new RSA/ECDSA signatures, but it cannot reach back and undo authentication that already happened. Certificates need PQC signatures before that computer exists, and relying parties upgrade at different speeds.

A Key Encapsulation Mechanism (KEM) is a one-sided primitive: the sender gives Encaps the receiver's public key and gets back a shared secret and a ciphertext, rather than supplying a key of its own choosing.
Combining X25519 ECDH with ML-KEM-768 via HKDF provides defense-in-depth:
If a cryptographically-relevant quantum computer (CRQC) breaks X25519 via Shor's algorithm, the ML-KEM shared secret remains secret.
If ML-KEM-768 has an unforeseen algebraic weakness, the X25519 shared secret remains secret.
What this construction does and does not do: its combiner has the form CMVP IG D.S accepts (both secrets concatenated and fed into an SP 800-56C KDF, HKDF included), but it mixes in only the two secrets and a fixed label, not the exchanged key shares or public keys. Deployed combiners bind those too (X-Wing hashes the X25519 key share and public key into its output; TLS 1.3 feeds the whole handshake transcript into its key schedule). A validated module must also enforce a fixed set of hybrid schemes and control the concatenation order itself, which this demo does not, so treat it as the idea, not a design to copy.

Generate classical, PQC, and hybrid key pairs side-by-side. Compare key sizes, generation times, and PEM output to understand the trade-offs.
Key observation: Hybrid keys (X25519MLKEM768) combine X25519 (32 bytes) + ML-KEM-768 (1,184 bytes) into a single key pair. The total size is roughly the sum of both components. This provides quantum resistance via ML-KEM while maintaining classical security through X25519 — even if one algorithm is broken, the other provides protection.
Key observation: ML-DSA-65 public keys (1,952 bytes) are ~30x larger than ECDSA P-256 keys (65 bytes), and signatures (3,309 bytes) are ~46x larger. This size increase is the main trade-off for quantum resistance. Composite signature standards (draft-ietf-lamps-pq-composite-sigs) would combine both.
About these checks: a row tagged “Functional” is a round trip (the engine makes a key, uses it, and accepts its own output), so it shows the engine is self-consistent but has no published expected value. Rows tagged “NIST ACVP sample” or “Standard KAT” compare the engine with an answer someone else published. Neither a round trip nor a sample run establishes a validation. No published test vector for a hybrid key exchange (X25519MLKEM768 or X-Wing) is run here: the CAVP prerequisites page (updated 22 September 2026) lists X-Wing keyGen and encapDecap tests but no test for X25519MLKEM768, and the ML-KEM checks use NIST’s published samples.

During the PQC transition, systems must support verifiers that understand only classical algorithms (legacy) and verifiers that require post-quantum algorithms (future-safe). Hybrid signatures let one signed artifact satisfy both.
The critical security question is: what prevents an attacker from stripping the PQC component? If they can, the document is no longer quantum-safe — it degrades silently to classical security. This is the non-separability problem this tool demonstrates.
Standards: IETF draft-ietf-lamps-pq-composite-sigs (a labelled concatenation, not the bare form shown here); RFC 9955, Hybrid Signature Spectrums (the concatenation, nesting and fused categories); ePrint 2025/2059 (Silithium).
μ = H(R ‖ pk_ec ‖ pk_ml ‖ msg) — both components are bound to this value

chunks.title: Hybrid Cryptography — HybridSignatures
chunks.content:
Module: Hybrid Cryptography
Component: HybridSignatures

The EC component verified independently. An adversary could strip the ML-DSA component and present just the EC signature — the verifier would accept it if it only checks EC. This is the separability attack.
The EC component still verifies alone (the outer ML-DSA layer doesn't prevent extraction). However, swapping the EC signature for a different one would invalidate the outer ML-DSA sig. This is Weak Non-Separability.
The EC-Schnorr component cannot be verified with the standard challenge H(R ‖ pk ‖ msg). The signer used the fused challenge μ that also incorporates pk_ml — so any attempt to verify just the EC part with the wrong challenge fails. This is the property RFC 9955 §1.3.4 calls Strong Non-Separability (SNS), shown here with a simplified Silithium (see the note under the shared challenge above); the security argument for the full scheme is in the paper (ePrint 2025/2059), not in this demo.
An attacker generates a fresh Silithium key pair and signs the same message. They then splice the legitimate EC component (R, s) with their own ML-DSA component (z) and attempt to verify against their own public keys.
The attack fails because μ = H(R ‖ pk_ec ‖ pk_ml ‖ msg) binds both public keys. Substituting the attacker's ML-DSA component requires their pk_ml, which changes μ, making the legitimate EC response s invalid for the new challenge.

RFC 9955 (section 1.3.4) notes that concatenation with a label in the message gives weak non-separability; Composite ML-DSA (draft-ietf-lamps-pq-composite-sigs section 9.2.3) works that way.
The outer ML-DSA signature covers msg ‖ ecSig, binding the EC component. Swapping the EC signature invalidates the outer layer, but the EC component still verifies alone on the original message.
Fused Fiat-Shamir: both components share a single challenge μ that includes the EC commitment R. Neither component verifies without the shared μ. Targets Strong Non-Separability; the paper reports no separability issues for its construction.

chunks.title: Identity & Access Management with PQC — IAMPQCIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Identity & Access Management with PQC
Component: IAMPQCIntroduction

Identity and Access Management relies on cryptography at every layer. From JWT and SAML token signing to TLS channels and PKI certificates, a quantum computer running Shor’s Algorithm can break the RSA and ECDSA signatures that protect every identity assertion in your enterprise.
Adversaries are recording encrypted network traffic today. When a Cryptographically Relevant Quantum Computer (CRQC) becomes available, they can decrypt captured Kerberos PKINIT exchanges and the TLS sessions that carry identity traffic. Signed tokens (JWT, SAML, OIDC) are signed, not encrypted: breaking a signing key later reveals nothing that was hidden. The risk is that a broken signing key lets an attacker forge tokens. NIST IR 8547 ties harvest now, decrypt later to encrypted data and says the authentication algorithm may be transitioned at a different time.
ML-DSA (FIPS 204, formerly CRYSTALS-Dilithium) is the primary NIST-standardized replacement for RSA and ECDSA in all token signing operations. Its three parameter sets (ML-DSA-44, ML-DSA-65, ML-DSA-87) allow calibrating security level against signature size.
Enterprise directory services — Active Directory, LDAP, and Kerberos — all rely on classical cryptography for key exchange, authentication, and session establishment. Kerberos PKINIT uses RSA for initial authentication; LDAP channels use TLS with classical ciphers.
• PKINIT (RFC 4556) uses RSA to encrypt the initial authentication exchange

A CRQC decrypts captured Kerberos PKINIT handshakes from network recordings. The RSA-encrypted pre-authentication data reveals the session key, enabling ticket forgery and full domain compromise without any credentials.
NTLM challenge-response uses MD4 hashing with no forward secrecy. Captured NTLM exchanges and rainbow table attacks combined with quantum computation expose domain credentials.
Golden Ticket via KRBTGT Exposure
If the KRBTGT account password hash is compromised and later quantum-decrypted, attackers can forge Ticket Granting Tickets (Golden Tickets) for any user, including Domain Admins.
All LDAP directory queries, including user enumeration and attribute reads, travel over TLS. A CRQC decrypting captured LDAPS sessions exposes all directory data including group memberships, email addresses, and organizational structure.
Simple Bind Credential Exposure
LDAP simple bind sends credentials (Base64-encoded username:password) over the TLS channel. If TLS is quantum-decrypted, all bind credentials are exposed.
JWT Token Forgery via RSA Key Recovery
A CRQC could derive a private signing key from the published public key material and forge identity tokens.

chunks.title: IoT & Embedded Device PQC — IoTPQCExercises
chunks.content:
Module: IoT & Embedded Device PQC
Component: IoTPQCExercises

Each exercise opens one workshop step with its settings loaded. The expected observations are the numbers that step computes — benchmark-based fits and model estimates, labelled as such in the workshop.
Take the PQC quiz on constrained-device PQC, firmware signing and IoT protocols.
1. What can a Class 1 device verify — and sign?
The Algorithm Explorer opens on Class 1, "Device verifies signatures", stack-optimised builds. Read the summary, then switch the build to speed-optimised, then switch the role to "Device signs".
Verifying with stack builds: ECDSA, LMS and FN-DSA-512 fit; XMSS and all three ML-DSA sets are tight (ML-DSA-44 peaks at 6,444 B, 63% of 10 KiB). With speed builds every ML-DSA set is too large (ML-DSA-44 needs 12,644 B). Signing: FN-DSA-512 turns red — 41,952 B of stack and ~104 KB of code — while ML-DSA-44 is still tight. Devices verify; signing belongs on a server.
2. Sign a smart-meter update with LMS, then with ML-DSA
Firmware Signing opens with the smart meter and LMS. Once the live HSM is ready, sign and verify the manifest. Then pick ML-DSA-44 and sign again. Read the CNSA 2.0 line and the verification ranking.

chunks.title: IoT & Embedded Device PQC — IoTPQCExercises
chunks.content:
Module: IoT & Embedded Device PQC
Component: IoTPQCExercises

LMS produces a 2,512-byte signature that verifies, the one-bit-tampered manifest is rejected, and the token’s remaining-signature counter (where the engine publishes one) reads one less than 1,024. Signature plus SUIT/COSE is about 0.97% of the 256 KiB update (≈0.8 s of NB-IoT downlink). ML-DSA-44 gives 2,420 bytes and is not accepted by CNSA 2.0 (only ML-DSA-87 or LMS/XMSS are). In the ranking LMS is fifth: FN-DSA-512, ECDSA, ML-DSA-44 and ML-DSA-65 verify in fewer cycles.
3. DTLS 1.3 or EDHOC over a 6LoWPAN mesh
Constrained Handshake opens on ML-KEM-768 with ML-DSA-44. Compare the two panels, then switch to X25519 + ECDSA P-256 for the classical baseline.
DTLS 1.3 with an ML-DSA-44 chain is about 13,146 B: 13 IPv6 datagrams and 171 IEEE 802.15.4 frames, 9.6× the 1,374 B classical handshake. EDHOC with credentials by reference needs about 7,141 B (92 frames) because no certificate chain is sent. Classically EDHOC is about 216 B against 1,374 B. Tick "send credentials by value" to see EDHOC lose that advantage.
4. Fit an ML-DSA-65 chain on a 10 KiB device
Certificate Chain opens with all three levels on ML-DSA-65 and a 10 KiB RAM budget. Then try each delivery mode. Finally set the root to ML-DSA-87 and the other two to ML-DSA-44.

chunks.title: IoT & Embedded Device PQC — IoTPQCExercises
chunks.content:
Module: IoT & Embedded Device PQC
Component: IoTPQCExercises

The full chain sends 11,122 B (leaf + intermediate; the root stays on the device) — more than the 10 KiB budget. Compression saves only 300 B (PQC keys and signatures are high-entropy, which limits how much compression can help) and C509 320 B. A raw public key needs 1,982 B, an MTC with a 20-level proof 2,892 B — each with its own trust caveat — and resumption sends nothing. With an ML-DSA-87 root the intermediate grows to 6,239 B, because it carries the root’s 4,627-byte signature.
5. Provision a BLE Mesh node and commission a Matter device with PQC keys
Constrained Handshake opens on the BLE Mesh & Matter provisioning view with ML-KEM-768 and ML-DSA-44. Compare with X25519 + ECDSA P-256, and try the X25519MLKEM768 hybrid.
Today a P-256 provisioning key is 3 PB-ADV segments. An ML-KEM-768 public key would take 52 segments and its ciphertext 48 (the hybrid: 54 and 49), close to the 64-segment, 1,469-byte transaction limit — and no PQC provisioning algorithm is defined in Mesh Protocol 1.1. For Matter, an ML-DSA-44 DAC + PAI chain is 8,064 B (about 7 IPv6-MTU messages) versus 856 B with ECDSA. Out-of-band bootstrap (NFC, QR) or a larger GATT MTU is the practical path.
6. Find the bottleneck in a 2-million-meter key rotation
The Fleet Key Manager opens on its default fleet: 2M smart meters, 1,000 per collector, G3-PLC, ML-KEM-768, standard HSM. Then switch the HSM to high-throughput, the baseline to Suite 0, and the link to LoRaWAN.

chunks.title: IoT & Embedded Device PQC — IoTPQCExercises
chunks.content:
Module: IoT & Embedded Device PQC
Component: IoTPQCExercises

Each collector finishes its radio exchanges in about 16 minutes (2,472 B per meter, 7.5× today’s 328 B), but the head-end HSM needs about 1.1 hours for 4 million operations — the HSM is the bottleneck. A high-throughput HSM moves the bottleneck back to the network. Suite 0 has no public-key exchange to break. LoRaWAN raises the warning that its air interface has no public-key key establishment at all.
7. Is PQC what overloads the cell?
LPWAN Airtime opens on NB-IoT, a 150 KiB image signed with ML-DSA-87, 2,000 devices, unicast. Read the signature share and the window verdict, then tick multicast.
The ML-DSA-87 signature is 2.9% of the update. Unicast needs about 45 hours of downlink and misses the 24-hour window — but the same update signed with ECDSA needs about 44 hours and misses it too. Multicast delivers it in under 2 minutes. The image and the delivery mode decide this, not the PQC signature.

chunks.title: IoT & Embedded Device PQC — IoTPQCIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: IoT & Embedded Device PQC
Component: IoTPQCIntroduction

A constrained device cannot borrow more memory for a bigger signature, often cannot be reached for an update, and may stay in service for 10–20 years. Devices shipped now will still be verifying firmware and opening sessions when a cryptographically relevant quantum computer may exist — so the choice of algorithm, protocol and hardware is made today and lived with for a decade.
AES and SHA-2 stay; a quantum computer weakens them only modestly. For devices too small for AES-GCM, NIST standardised the lightweight Ascon family in SP 800-232 (final, August 2025). In this module's reading, PQC replaces the public-key parts: key establishment and signatures.
Industrial IoT sensors and gateways often sit at the bottom of a plant network but send their data to the cloud. In NIST’s reference architecture, communication from the IIoT platform tier is routed through the industrial DMZ border firewall (level 3.5 of the plant network;
§5.4.2). A device that connects straight to the cloud skips that boundary. How this fits into the three paths attackers use to reach OT is covered in
Industrial control systems (SCADA, PLCs, zones and conduits) are covered in
Most devices verify far more than they sign: they check firmware and server certificates, while signing happens on a build server or HSM. The two operations have very different costs, so "does FN-DSA fit on a sensor?" has two answers.
Stack RAM on an Arm Cortex-M4 (benchmark; varies by implementation)

Module: IoT & Embedded Device PQC
Component: IoTPQCIntroduction

A forged firmware image is the worst outcome for a device fleet, and the update signature must stay unforgeable for the device's whole life. Three families are standardised for it:
Firmware and software signing should prefer CNSA 2.0 algorithms from 2025 and use them exclusively by 2030.
SUIT is three documents: RFC 9019 is the update architecture, RFC 9124 the manifest information model, and draft-ietf-suit-manifest the CBOR manifest format itself. chunks.content:
Module: KMS & PQC Key Management
Component: KmsPqcIntroduction

Post-quantum cryptography fundamentally changes how organizations manage keys. NIST SP 800-227 establishes that ML-KEM is a Key Encapsulation Mechanism only — it cannot sign. Similarly, ML-DSA is for signatures only — it cannot encapsulate. This strict algorithm separation replaces the dual-use nature of RSA, which could both encrypt and sign.
“A KEM can be combined with a symmetric-key encryption scheme to yield very efficient public-key encryption. This is sometimes referred to as the KEM-DEM paradigm for PKE”
— NIST SP 800-227, Recommendations for Key-Encapsulation Mechanisms, Sec. 5.2.1
• One RSA key pair can do both, but should not (NIST SP 800-57)
• Separate key pairs are mandatory, not just good practice
PQC keys are significantly larger than classical equivalents — 4–10× vs RSA baselines, and up to 40× vs ECDSA P-256 — impacting HSM storage, certificate sizes, and network bandwidth during key distribution.
Because ML-KEM produces a random shared secret (not a direct encryption), envelope encryption uses a different pattern from RSA-OAEP, which wraps the DEK in one step. In this module's design, ML-KEM encapsulates → derives a wrapping key via HKDF → wraps the DEK with AES-KW. The shared secret key from ML-KEM does not itself require further key derivation (NIST PQC FAQ); the HKDF step binds the wrapping key to this protocol and version.

The Messaging Layer Security protocol (RFC 9420) provides asynchronous group key establishment with forward secrecy and post-compromise security for groups from two to thousands. Our openmls_pqctoday_crypto Rust provider wires the OpenMLS reference implementation to PKCS#11 v3.2 so signature keys live in an HSM and HPKE runs end-to-end inside the token.
Asynchronous group key agreement via TreeKEM. Forward secrecy + post-compromise security with O(log N) Commit cost.
draft-ietf-mls-pq-ciphersuites-06 (21 July 2026) registers eleven ML-KEM cipher suites, hybrid and pure. On 30 October 2026 its datatracker page shows WG state “Submitted to IESG for Publication” and IESG state “Publication Requested”.
Our PKCS#11 provider holds signature keys as token objects with CKA_SENSITIVE=TRUE. OpenMLS sees opaque handles, never raw bytes.

chunks.title: MLS — Group Messaging — MLSGroupMessagingPlayground
chunks.content:
Module: MLS — Group Messaging
Component: MLSGroupMessagingPlayground

Signal's Double Ratchet provides per-message forward secrecy and post-compromise security (PCS) for two parties: after a key compromise, the next message from the honest party re-seeds the ratchet and the attacker loses access. TreeKEM (RFC 9420, MLS) extends this to groups using a binary Merkle tree of Diffie-Hellman key pairs.
On a Commit operation, the committer generates a fresh leaf key pair, then re-encrypts path secrets up to the root — updating the nodes in the filtered direct path. Only group members who are co-path children receive the new secrets. Members who were compromised before the Commit lose access to all future epochs: this is group PCS.
In a PQC MLS deployment, each leaf key pair uses ML-KEM-768 for encapsulation (path secrets are encrypted to the next node's public KEM key) and ML-DSA-65 for signing leaf credential bindings — making both the secrecy and authentication paths quantum-resistant.

chunks.title: MLS — Group Messaging — ProviderArchitecture
chunks.content:
Module: MLS — Group Messaging
Component: ProviderArchitecture

OpenMLS expects a single OpenMlsProvider trait combining crypto, randomness, and storage. Our provider routes each crypto trait method through PKCS#11 v3.2 against softhsmv3. The table below reflects the v0.2 implementation (Phase 1 + Phase 2 of the provider roadmap).
What this table describes: the real openmls_pqctoday_crypto Rust crate, which runs server-side. The workshop in this module is a JavaScript reimplementation of the same PKCS#11 calls against the same softhsmv3 engine — the crypto is genuinely HSM-backed either way, but the steps you run here are not literally this crate executing.
When OpenMLS calls signature_key_gen(), our provider runs C_GenerateKeyPair with CKA_SENSITIVE=TRUE and CKA_EXTRACTABLE=FALSE. What we return to OpenMLS as the "private key" is an opaque, versioned handle blob.
On every sign() call, the provider decodes the handle, looks up the token object via C_FindObjects{ CKA_CLASS=PRIVATE_KEY, CKA_ID=… }, and runs C_SignInit + C_Sign inside the HSM. Real key bytes never exist in process memory.

In consumer content protection a compromised device is part of the threat model, so “is it quantum-safe?” has to be asked link by link: which secret does the system rely on, and which signature does it rely on.
This edition of ECP (v1.4) does not mention quantum computing. That is a statement about one document. It does not say that anyone has or has not planned a migration, and it does not describe other editions.
The ladder below runs from the secret keys a device is given at manufacture to the key exchange between a drive and a host. For each rung the lesson shows the primitive the specification names, and, for the public-key rungs, which NIST IR 8547 table lists that kind of primitive. The pairing with NIST is this lesson’s, not the specification’s.
All digital signatures in AACS use the ECDSA digital signature scheme defined in ANSI X9.62 and FIPS 186-2. The Media Key Block signature and the drive and host signatures in the Bus Key exchange all rest on that one scheme.
Table 2-1 of the book gives the curve. By this lesson’s own count the prime is 160 bits and the order of the base point is also 160 bits. NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 Revision 5, Table 2, places elliptic-curve keys with f = 160 to 223 at a security strength of at most 80 bits, while NIST IR 8547 Table 2 lists ECDSA at 112 bits of classical security strength or more. The two facts are set side by side here; the lesson draws no further conclusion from them.

chunks.content:

The Device Key tree, the Processing Keys and the Media Key are built from AES-128. The public-key operations in this edition are the ECDSA signatures and the Bus Key exchange. Forging a Media Key Block signature would need the AACS LA signing key, so an attacker who could derive an ECDSA key from a public key could do that. The lesson draws no conclusion about the effect of a quantum computer on AES.
The text of this edition does not mention quantum computing.
The specification distinguishes three mechanisms of revocation for host devices whose security has been compromised: Host Service Shunning, revocation by the CA system, and Host Revocation. Revocation by the CA system is defined by a particular CA system and is out of scope for the specification.
Host Revocation is revocation by denial of service: the CICAM stops CI Plus operation, withholding Content Control services from the host. Revoked hosts are listed in a Service Operator Certificate Revocation List (SOCRL), and a Service Operator Certificate White List (SOCWL) undoes a revocation. A SOCRL is created by the Root-of-Trust on request of a Service Operator for its own operation, so a host can be revoked for one operator and still work for others. The exact rules are set by the CI Plus license.

ECP describes ripping software as enabled by two “hack one, hack all” scenarios. Breaking protection on one device, for example a PC and drive combination or a mobile streaming device, breaks it on a wide class of devices.

DRM System Specifications, “Revocation & Renewal”

Each compliant device is given a set of secret Device Keys when it is manufactured. The keys come from AACS LA and are 128 bits each.
Subsidiary Device Keys and Processing Keys
A device calculates subsidiary Device Keys and Processing Keys from its Device Keys with the AES-G3 function, which is built from AES-128.
AACS LA generates the Media Key Block. A device decrypts one or more elements of it with its Device Keys to extract the 128-bit Media Key: AES-128D of the encrypted key data under a Processing Key, combined by XOR with a mask built from the uv number. The encrypted key data is in the Media Key Data Record of the block.
3.2 Media Key Block; Km equation in 3.2.4
If a set of Device Keys is compromised, an updated Media Key Block can be released that stops devices with those Device Keys from calculating the correct Media Key. The block of a subset-difference tree system is of the same order in size as a public-key certificate revocation list, which the document says makes it equivalent in revocation power to a public-key system (an informative section).
Devices are required to check the signature on the Media Key Block. The End of Media Key Block record carries the AACS LA signature on the data in the block.
