chunks.title: Merkle Tree Certificates — MTCExercises
chunks.content:
Module: Merkle Tree Certificates
Component: MTCExercises

Work through these exercises in order to understand how Merkle Tree Certificates work. Each exercise guides you through a specific Workshop step — click “Start Exercise” to jump to the right step.
Explore the PKI Workshop for hands-on certificate chain building, or the Stateful Hash Signatures module to see how Merkle trees are used in LMS/XMSS.
1. Build a Merkle Tree with 8 Certificates
Add 8 certificate leaves to the tree builder — use a mix of ML-DSA-44, ML-DSA-65, and ML-DSA-87 algorithms. Build the tree and examine how the SHA-256 hashes propagate from leaves to root.
Note that changing any single certificate leaf (even one character in the subject) completely changes the root hash. This is the avalanche effect — the foundation of Merkle tree security. Also notice how padding works when the number of leaves is not a power of two.
2. Generate and Examine an Inclusion Proof
Build a tree with the sample certificates, then click different leaves to generate their inclusion proofs. Compare the authentication paths for leaves at different positions in the tree.
Each proof contains exactly log2(N) sibling hashes, where N is the number of leaves. For 8 leaves, every proof has 3 siblings. Notice that the proof size is the same regardless of which leaf you select — the path length is always equal to the tree height.
3. Tamper with a Proof and Observe Failure

chunks.title: Merkle Tree Certificates — MTCExercises
chunks.content:
Module: Merkle Tree Certificates
Component: MTCExercises

First verify a valid proof to see the step-by-step hash recomputation succeed. Then verify the tampered proof to see how a single flipped bit causes complete verification failure.
The tampered proof flips just one hex character in the first sibling hash. Despite this tiny change, the computed root hash is entirely different from the expected root — demonstrating that Merkle proofs are computationally infeasible to forge without knowing the correct sibling hashes.
4. Compare Handshake Sizes Across Algorithm Families
Toggle between ECDSA, ML-DSA-44, ML-DSA-65, ML-DSA-87, and SLH-DSA-128s in the size comparison dashboard. Analyze how the MTC size advantage scales with signature size.

chunks.title: Merkle Tree Certificates — MTCExercises
chunks.content:
Module: Merkle Tree Certificates
Component: MTCExercises

An inclusion proof depends only on how large its subtree is, never on the signature algorithm: ~96 bytes for this 8-leaf demo, 384 bytes for a standalone certificate reaching the latest checkpoint (~3,000 entries), 736 bytes for a landmark subtree of ~5.4M — the two figures the draft projects in §6.5. Every column also carries the server's public key and its CertificateVerify signature, and the traditional column is a leaf-plus-intermediate chain (the root is in the trust store). Because the proof is a fixed cost and the signatures it replaces are not, MTC savings scale with signature size: ECDSA (64 B sig) saves 183 bytes standalone, ~19%; ML-DSA-44 (2,420 B sig) saves 3,786 bytes, ~36% standalone (one CA cosignature) and 5,854 bytes, ~56% landmark; SLH-DSA-128s (7,856 B sig) saves 7,942 bytes, ~33% standalone and 15,446 bytes, ~64% landmark. Watch what landmark mode does to ECDSA: at 1,065 bytes it is LARGER than the 960-byte traditional chain, because a 736 B landmark proof costs more than the two certificate signatures it replaces. MTCs are built for PQC migration — for compact classical algorithms the saving is a few hundred bytes at most, and landmark mode is a net loss.

chunks.title: Merkle Tree Certificates — MTCIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Merkle Tree Certificates
Component: MTCIntroduction

Post-quantum digital signatures are dramatically larger than their classical counterparts. While an ECDSA P-256 signature is just 64 bytes, an ML-DSA-44 signature is 2,420 bytes — a 37× increase. In a typical TLS handshake the server sends a leaf and one intermediate certificate (two public keys and two certificate signatures; the root is already in the client's trust store), signs the handshake once more in CertificateVerify, and usually adds Certificate Transparency SCTs.
ML-DSA-44 keys + signatures per handshake (7,260 B of authentication overhead from two SCTs and a leaf certificate signature with a directly-trusted intermediate; 9,927 B with ML-DSA-65)
This “certificate bloat” breaks constrained clients that reject chains larger than 10 KB (not sourced in the Library), degrades connection setup times (especially on mobile networks), and increases bandwidth costs for high-traffic servers handling millions of TLS handshakes per second.
Merkle Tree Certificates (MTCs) solve certificate bloat by replacing individual per-certificate signatures with a batch-signing approach using Merkle trees:
The Merkle Tree CA collects thousands of certificate assertions and places them as leaves in a binary hash tree. Each leaf is SHA-256(0x00 || cert data); internal nodes use SHA-256(0x01 || left || right). The domain-separation prefixes (0x00 / 0x01) prevent leaf hashes from ever being confused with internal node hashes.

chunks.title: Merkle Tree Certificates — MTCIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Merkle Tree Certificates
Component: MTCIntroduction

One CA signing operation covers the entire batch — potentially millions of certificates. Depending on the relying party's cosigner policy, additional external witnesses may also co-sign the subtree to guarantee public transparency. For signatureless certificates, no embedded signatures are needed at all (relying parties use predistributed trusted subtrees instead).
Each certificate holder receives a compact inclusion proof: the chain of sibling hashes from their leaf up to the root. Its size depends only on how large the subtree is: 384 bytes for a standalone certificate's subtree of around 2,500 certificates (12 hashes × 32 bytes).
The relying party hashes the certificate, then combines it with each proof sibling up the tree. If the computed root matches the signed root, the certificate is authenticated — no per-certificate signature verification needed.
Cert 1  Cert 2    Cert 3  Cert 4
To prove Cert 3 belongs to the batch, provide: H(Cert 4) + H(0,1) → recompute up to root
The MTC ecosystem defines five key roles (per draft-ietf-plants-merkle-tree-certs Section 2.1), redesigned from Certificate Transparency for batch efficiency:
Maintains the issuance log, builds the Merkle tree, signs checkpoints and subtrees, requests cosignatures, and assembles certificates with inclusion proofs. The CA certifies information by logging it, inverting the CT model.

chunks.title: Merkle Tree Certificates — MTCIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Merkle Tree Certificates
Component: MTCIntroduction

Signs views of the issuance log to assert correct operation. Cosigners verify the log is append-only, optionally mirror its contents, and cosign checkpoints and subtrees. One cosigner signature covers a subtree of millions of entries.
TLS servers that receive their certificate assertion + inclusion proof from the CA and present them during the TLS handshake. Sends the Certificate and CertificateVerify messages.
The client that verifies certificates. Maintains trusted subtrees, cosigner requirements, and revoked index ranges. For landmark certificates, relying parties pre-sync trusted subtrees in the background.
Watches the issuance log for certificates of interest, analogous to CT monitors. Ensures the CA is operated correctly and entries are publicly visible.
The spec defines two certificate types. Authenticating parties SHOULD deploy both and select based on client capabilities:
Contains an inclusion proof plus cosignatures from the CA and external cosigners. Works without any predistributed state — the relying party verifies signatures at connection time. Can be issued with minimal processing delay.
Contains an inclusion proof to a predistributed landmark subtree and no signatures. Relying parties pre-sync trusted landmark subtrees in the background. Maximal size savings but requires an up-to-date client.
• Massive size reduction (63–65% standalone, 92–96% landmark for ML-DSA) (not sourced in the Library)
• Single CA signing operation covers millions of certificates

chunks.title: Merkle Tree Certificates — MTCIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Merkle Tree Certificates
Component: MTCIntroduction

• Inclusion proof is pure hash computation — fast to verify
• Inherent certificate transparency (issuance log = public record)
• Landmark only: clients must pre-sync trusted subtrees periodically; not suitable for offline or intermittently-connected devices
• Revocation uses Revocation by Index (Section 7.5): relying parties maintain revoked ranges of indices checked at verification time
• Trust requires meeting cosigner requirements — relying parties accept a subtree only after a configured set of cosigners have signed it, preventing a compromised CA from silently misissu­ing
• Standalone only: certificates carry multiple cosignatures, adding some bytes beyond the inclusion proof
Landmark certificates carry zero embedded signatures. Instead of embedding cosignatures, relying parties periodically pre-sync “landmark” subtrees out-of-band (the spec suggests allocating landmarks at regular intervals, e.g. every hour), then verify inclusion proofs against their cached landmark root — the certificate carries no CA signature at all. The server still signs the handshake itself (CertificateVerify), so that signature and the server's public key remain in the handshake.
Periodically (e.g., every hour), the CA designates its latest checkpoint tree size as a landmark. With projected short-lived certificate issuance rates (~5.4M certs/hour for a large CA), each landmark subtree spans millions of entries.

chunks.title: Merkle Tree Certificates — MTCIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Merkle Tree Certificates
Component: MTCIntroduction

Browsers and OS clients periodically download and cache trusted landmark subtrees, with cosignatures checked against relying party requirements — similar to certificate revocation syncs today. No online step required during the TLS handshake.
The TLS server presents its certificate (including its 1,312 B public key) with a 23-hash inclusion proof (736 B), then signs the handshake (2,420 B CertificateVerify). The client verifies the proof against its cached landmark root.
Same scenario in every row: a leaf-plus-intermediate chain, the root already in the client's trust store. Traditional: 3 sigs (7,260 B: leaf cert, intermediate cert, CertificateVerify) + 2 keys (2,624 B) + 2 SCTs (238 B) + metadata (400 B). Standalone: server key (1,312 B) + CertificateVerify (2,420 B) + 1 CA cosignature (2,420 B, the minimum) + 384 B proof + 200 B metadata. Landmark: server key + CertificateVerify + 736 B proof + 200 B metadata; no cosignature because the client has the trusted subtree cached. The two proofs differ because they reach different subtrees: a standalone proof stops at the latest checkpoint (~3,000 entries), a landmark proof at the last landmark (~5.4M). The number of cosignatures is relying party policy; each extra one adds a signature.

chunks.title: Merkle Tree Certificates — MTCIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Merkle Tree Certificates
Component: MTCIntroduction

Tradeoff: Landmark certificates require relying parties to pre-sync landmark subtrees regularly (e.g., every few hours). Clients that miss a sync window cannot verify newer certificates without an update — acceptable for always-online clients (browsers, mobile) but unsuitable for air-gapped or intermittently-connected devices.
Merkle Tree Certificates originated as draft-davidben-tls-merkle-tree-certs (reaching draft-10 in 2026) and have since been adopted by the IETF PLANTS working group as draft-ietf-plants-merkle-tree-certs. The draft has five co-equal authors across Google, Cloudflare, and Geomys. Draft — not yet an RFC
• October 2025: Cloudflare + Chrome experiment announced
• 2026: draft-davidben-tls-merkle-tree-certs-10 submitted; adopted by IETF PLANTS WG as draft-ietf-plants-merkle-tree-certs-00

• Status: Active IETF draft — not yet standardized as an RFC. This module's advice: Not recommended for production deployment without vendor support.
• Radboud University (independent implementation analysis, 2025)

chunks.title: Merkle Tree Certificates — MTCIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Merkle Tree Certificates
Component: MTCIntroduction

Merkle trees are fundamental to post-quantum cryptography beyond MTCs. SLH-DSA (SPHINCS+, FIPS 205) uses nested Merkle trees internally for quantum-resistant signatures. Stateful hash-based schemes like LMS and XMSS use Merkle trees to organize pools of one-time signing keys. MTCs apply the same principle at the infrastructure level to solve the certificate size problem PQ signatures create.

Monitor role: An independent CT monitor continuously downloads each signed batch and compares the CA's published root against its own recomputation. Because the STH is public , any monitor in the world can detect and report the discrepancy, making undetected misissuance computationally infeasible.

chunks.title: Migration Program Management — Introduction
chunks.content:
Module: Migration Program Management
Component: Introduction

Migrating an enterprise to post-quantum cryptography is not a single project — it is a multi-year, cross-functional program that spans every system, vendor, and team that touches cryptography. Success requires structured planning, executive sponsorship, and continuous stakeholder alignment.
Migrating to post-quantum cryptography is as much an organizational challenge as it is a technical one. Agencies and enterprises should establish a dedicated migration program with clear governance, milestones, and reporting structures.
Aligned with CISA Post-Quantum Cryptography Initiative guidance (cisa.gov/pqc)
A project delivers a specific output; a program coordinates multiple interdependent projects toward a strategic goal — full PQC readiness.
The longest sequence of dependent tasks determines your minimum migration timeline. Vendor PQC readiness is often the binding constraint.
Without C-suite commitment, PQC migration stalls. Budget, priority, and cross-department coordination require top-down authority.
Aligned with CISA and NIST migration guidance, this structured framework serves as the foundation for enterprise PQC migration programs. Each phase builds on the previous and has clear deliverables.
Enterprise PQC migration programs that succeed share common characteristics. These success factors are drawn from early adopters and regulatory guidance.

chunks.title: Migration Program Management — RoadmapBuilder
chunks.content:
Module: Migration Program Management
Component: RoadmapBuilder

A PQC migration runs as two parallel tracks on the framework's phase spine, not one linear list:
Track A (Confidentiality / KEM) — urgent now because of Harvest-Now-Decrypt-Later (HNDL).
Track B (Integrity / Signatures & PKI) — not urgent today but the longest lead time, so it must start early because of Trust-Now-Forge-Later (TNFL): forged signatures only matter once a quantum computer can forge them, but replacing signing keys and trust anchors takes years.
Gates G0→G3 (mandate → inventory → CBOM → risk scoring) are a shared governance spine both tracks pass through together, producing the prioritized backlog and approved roadmap (G4) they then execute against. From there the same phase/gate structure runs independently and in parallel per track, because the two tracks don't share deadlines or dependencies once execution begins. The illustrative milestones below show one example: Track A piloting hybrid key exchange (G5) while Track B first migrates code-signing algorithms (also G5) before later re-issuing PKI root/intermediate CAs (G6) — infrastructure work that only shows up once a roadmap actually reaches that stage.
US federal deadlines below derive from Executive Order 14412, “Securing the Nation Against Advanced Cryptographic Attacks” (June 22, 2026): High Value Assets and high-impact federal systems transition to PQC for key establishment by December 31, 2030, and digital signatures by December 31, 2031.

chunks.title: Migration Program Management — TwoTrackSequencing
chunks.content:
Module: Migration Program Management
Component: TwoTrackSequencing

A PQC migration is not one cutover. It is two parallel workstreams with different drivers, different clocks, and different standards readiness. Confusing them leads programs either to over-invest early in signatures (where the threat is gated on a CRQC that does not yet exist) or to under-prioritise confidentiality (where the Harvest-Now-Decrypt-Later clock is already running).
Rule of thumb: lead with KEM ordered by data secrecy-lifetime, run signatures in parallel gated on PKI readiness, and never block the confidentiality track waiting on signature-standard finalisation.
Source: Applied Quantum PQC Migration Framework §5 (Migration Execution).

chunks.title: PQC 101 — AlgorithmComparisonTable
chunks.content:
Module: PQC 101
Component: AlgorithmComparisonTable

Compare key sizes, output sizes, and quantum resilience across the major algorithm families.
ML-KEM is built on the Module Learning With Errors (M-LWE) problem. RSA relies on integer factorisation — solvable by Shor's Algorithm on a quantum computer. ECC relies on the discrete logarithm — same problem. M-LWE is fundamentally different: no known algorithm (quantum or classical) solves it efficiently. This is why NIST chose lattice-based cryptography as the primary PQC standard.
Broken by Shor's Algorithm on a sufficiently large quantum computer.
Broken by Shor's Algorithm. Widely used today in TLS, SSH, and code signing.
Based on Module-LWE. No known quantum or classical algorithm breaks it efficiently.
Lattice-based signature. Replaces ECDSA in certificates and code signing; keys and signatures are much larger, so certificate chains, storage and protocols must allow for them.
Hash-based. Tiny keys but large signatures. Stateless and conservative security assumption.

Three families of math problems protect the post-quantum world. Each relies on a problem that no known quantum algorithm can efficiently solve — unlike RSA and ECC which Shor's Algorithm breaks completely. Explore each family below to build intuition for why they resist quantum attack.

chunks.content:

Component: KeyGenWorkshop

Why are PQC keys larger? Quantum-resistant algorithms are based on harder mathematical problems — lattices or hash functions instead of integer factoring or elliptic curves. Representing these harder problems requires more bytes, but that extra size is exactly what makes them safe against quantum computers running Shor's algorithm.

chunks.title: PQC 101 — PQC101Module
chunks.content:
Module: PQC 101
Component: PQC101Module

Today's most widely used encryption — RSA and ECC — relies on math problems that are extremely hard for classical computers. But quantum computers using an algorithm called Shor's Algorithm can solve these problems exponentially faster.
Government & military secrets — classified data encrypted with RSA
Medical records & personal data — long-lived data at risk from “Harvest Now, Decrypt Later”
Digital signatures & code signing — firmware and software updates (HNFL risk)
“ Harvest Now, Decrypt Later ” (HNDL) is an attack strategy where adversaries collect encrypted data today and store it until quantum computers can break the encryption.
This means data encrypted now with RSA or ECC could be readable in the future. For sensitive data with long lifespans (health records, state secrets), migration must start before quantum computers arrive.
“ Harvest Now, Forge Later ” (HNFL) is the signature counterpart to HNDL. Adversaries capture signed artifacts today — firmware images, certificate chains, code-signing blobs — and store them. Once a quantum computer exists, they can forge or repudiate those signatures retroactively.
Unlike HNDL (which targets confidentiality), HNFL targets authenticity and integrity. Long-lived credentials — PKI hierarchies, firmware signing keys, code-signing certificates — must migrate to PQC signing algorithms (ML-DSA, SLH-DSA) before quantum computers mature.

chunks.title: PQC 101 — scenarioQuestions (data)
chunks.content:
Module: PQC 101
Data: scenarioQuestions

A hospital encrypts patient records with RSA-2048 and stores them for 50 years per regulation. A CRQC (cryptographically relevant quantum computer) is projected to exist within 10–15 years.
Should the hospital migrate its archive encryption now, or wait until quantum computers actually exist?
Migrate now. The data has a 50-year sensitivity window, meaning records encrypted today will still need to be secret in 2075. With a CRQC projected in 10–15 years, adversaries may already be running HNDL attacks — collecting ciphertext today to decrypt later. RSA-2048 must be replaced with a quantum-safe scheme (e.g., AES-256 for symmetric data encryption at rest) before the CRQC window closes.
A device manufacturer signs firmware updates for embedded IoT sensors using ECDSA P-256. The sensors have a 15-year field lifetime and cannot receive key-exchange algorithm updates — only firmware signature verification logic can be patched via OTA.
Which PQC signing algorithm should the manufacturer adopt for new firmware releases, and why?
SLH-DSA (FIPS 205) is the safest choice for firmware signing due to its minimal and conservative security assumptions — security relies only on hash function properties (BSI TR-02102-1 section 5.3.4; FIPS 205 section 1.1), not on lattice problems. ML-DSA (FIPS 204) is also acceptable and produces smaller signatures. Floating-point arithmetic in FN-DSA is a challenge: it is hard to make constant-time and resistant to power analysis, as side-channel attacks on existing implementations illustrate. Since sensors cannot update their key-exchange mechanism, the HNFL threat (forge firmware signatures post-quantum) is the primary concern — making signing algorithm choice the critical decision.
A private CA issues X.509 certificates with 2-year validity for internal services. The CA root has a 20-year validity. The security team is planning its PQC migration roadmap.
Which component — the CA root certificate, intermediate CA certificates, or end-entity certificates — is most urgent to migrate to PQC signing, and why?
The CA root certificate is most urgent. It has a 20-year validity window, meaning a root signed today with classical ECDSA could be forged post-quantum before it expires. This module's advice: Intermediate CAs (typically 5–10 years) are next. End-entity leaf certificates with 2-year validity are least urgent by timeline alone. However, all three should be on the migration roadmap: the root and intermediates to ML-DSA (FIPS 204) immediately, and end-entity certificates as part of the rollout. The CA's key-encapsulation (TLS handshake) should also migrate to ML-KEM (FIPS 203) for forward secrecy.
A government agency encrypted 10 years of classified intelligence reports with RSA-4096 and stores them air-gapped. An adversary nation-state is known to be collecting encrypted government traffic (HNDL program).
RSA-4096 is much larger than RSA-2048. Does this buy meaningful extra time against a CRQC?
No. Shor's Algorithm breaks RSA re

} title="How PQC Changes Network Security Operations" defaultOpen >
Post-quantum cryptography introduces fundamental changes to network security operations that go beyond algorithm upgrades. Larger ML-DSA certificates (at ML-DSA-65, FIPS 204 lists a 1,952-byte public key and a 3,309-byte signature), heavier TLS handshakes, and new key exchange patterns challenge every component of a modern network security stack — from perimeter firewalls to inline DPI appliances.
One ML-DSA-65 certificate holds a 1,952-byte public key and a 3,309-byte signature (FIPS 204 Table 2), before any other certificate field.
Illustrative values from this module's TLS Inspection Lab, not measurements: classical (9 ms), hybrid (28 ms), and pure PQC (35 ms) inspected handshake.
In an IETF C509 draft example, a two-certificate ML-DSA-65 TLS chain is 11,869 bytes against 2,656 bytes for an RSA chain.
} title="TLS Inspection & Deep Packet Inspection Challenges" >
TLS inspection (SSL interception) is central to NGFW security operations. PQC migrations stress every assumption in inspection pipelines: buffer sizes, certificate parsing logic, hardware offload capacity, and session reassembly.
} title="IDS/IPS: Signature Updates & Algorithm Visibility" >
Intrusion detection and prevention systems must evolve to recognize hybrid PQC traffic patterns, detect certificate size anomalies, and identify downgrade attacks targeting the classical component of hybrid key exchanges.

chunks.title: Network Security & PQC Migration — NetworkSecurityIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Network Security & PQC Migration
Component: NetworkSecurityIntroduction

} title="Cisco, Palo Alto, Fortinet, Juniper Migration Timelines" >
The four dominant enterprise NGFW vendors are at varying stages of PQC adoption. Planning infrastructure upgrades requires understanding not just current capabilities but the firmware and hardware upgrade paths required for full PQC TLS inspection support.
Zero Trust architecture assumes no implicit trust based on network location. Every connection is authenticated, authorized, and encrypted. ZTNA components that rely on classical PKI for authentication are vulnerable to harvest-now-decrypt-later (HNDL) attacks — making quantum-safe migration a priority for zero trust frameworks.
NIST SP 800-207 (Zero Trust Architecture, 2020) predates PQC guidance and says nothing about it — its full text contains no mention of quantum, key encapsulation, or NIST SP 800-227 (2025), which covers KEMs generally rather than ZTNA. Read them together, not as one citing the other. Organizations implementing zero trust should plan PQC adoption in their ZTNA architecture against the authority that actually applies. For NSS, CNSA 2.0 FAQ version 2.2 records 2027, 2030 and 2031 milestones; the separate 2035 date is the broader NSM-10 objective. CNSA 2.0 does not generally require hybrid constructions.

chunks.title: Operating System & Platform Crypto PQC — OSPQCIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Operating System & Platform Crypto PQC
Component: OSPQCIntroduction

Modern operating systems rely on a layered cryptographic stack that spans from the kernel to user applications. Understanding where each layer sits is essential for a complete PQC migration. Unlike application-layer cryptography (where you control the library), OS-level crypto changes affect every service running on the system.
PQC migration touches every layer. System TLS configuration cascades to all applications that use system OpenSSL. SSH host key migration requires new key types. Package signing requires coordinated infrastructure upgrades.
System TLS traffic (HTTPS, API calls, database connections) and SSH sessions are being recorded today for future decryption. Every TLS 1.3 session using only classical key exchange is a potential HNDL target. Hybrid X25519MLKEM768 eliminates this risk with a single config change.
Shipping ML-KEM and ML-DSA in an operating system is a separate step from having them listed on a FIPS 140-3 certificate, so check each platform against the CMVP listings.
The most impactful PQC change for any OS is enabling hybrid TLS key exchange at the system level. When you configure X25519MLKEM768 as a TLS 1.3 KEM group, every application that uses the system OpenSSL or CNG library benefits automatically.

Many Linux services use GnuTLS rather than OpenSSL — including curl on Debian/Ubuntu, wget, NetworkManager, and systemd-networkd. GnuTLS 3.8.3+ supports X25519MLKEM768 hybrid groups configured via GNUTLS_SYSTEM_PRIORITY_FILE or priority string SECURE128:+X25519MLKEM768.
SSH host keys are a prime target for Harvest Now, Decrypt Later attacks. An attacker recording SSH sessions today could authenticate as your server in the future once they break the host key with a quantum computer. Migrating to ssh-mldsa65 eliminates this risk.
Protects session encryption. OpenSSH 8.5+ supports sntrup761x25519-sha512 hybrid KEX (the default from 9.0). OpenSSH 9.9 adds mlkem768x25519-sha256, enabled by default, and OpenSSH 10.0 makes it the default KEX. Addresses HNDL for session contents.
Verifies server identity via host key signature. ML-DSA host key types are described in the Internet-Draft draft-sfluhrer-ssh-mldsa-06, which writes the names as ssh-mldsa-44, ssh-mldsa-65 and ssh-mldsa-87; this lesson uses ssh-mldsa65 as shorthand. An Internet-Draft is a work in progress, not a standard. The composite ssh-mldsa44-ed25519 algorithm is specified in the SSHM working group draft draft-ietf-sshm-composite-sigs-00, and OpenSSH 10.6 enables it.

Component: OSPQCIntroduction

Package signing is a supply chain integrity mechanism — it proves that the package you install came from the expected vendor and has not been tampered with. Today, RPM and DEB packages use GPG signatures (RSA-4096 or Ed25519). PQC migration requires coordinating upgrades across the signing server, repository metadata, and all client package managers.
Package signing requires coordinated ecosystem upgrades. The signing infrastructure, repository metadata format, package manager client, and end-user systems must ALL support the new algorithm before migration. This is significantly harder than a server-side TLS config change. Sigstore-style transparency logs with ML-DSA detached signatures are a promising intermediate solution.
FIPS 140-3 compliance creates a significant challenge for PQC migration: most current FIPS modules were certified before ML-KEM and ML-DSA were standardized. Organizations in regulated industries (government, finance, healthcare) face a temporary conflict between FIPS compliance and PQC deployment.
Until PQC algorithms appear in FIPS-certified modules, use a dual approach:
Existing regulated services continue using the FIPS 140-3 module (classical crypto only). No disruption to compliance posture.
New services use the default OpenSSL provider + oqsprovider. Document the non-FIPS status and include it in compliance assessment until new FIPS certs are issued.

chunks.title: OT & Industrial Control Systems PQC — OTPQCExercises
chunks.content:
Module: OT & Industrial Control Systems PQC
Component: OTPQCExercises

Six scenarios, one per workshop step. Each pre-configures its step — click "Load & Run" — and every number in "What to observe" is what that step computes.
Take the PQC quiz on OT protocols, IEC 62443, safety-critical timing and OT regulations.
1. Find where the quantum exposure really is in DNP3 and GOOSE
In the Protocol Analyzer, open DNP3 Secure Authentication v5 and IEC 61850 GOOSE. Count the symmetric layers and find the single layer in each that a quantum computer could attack. Then run the KAT panel.
DNP3 SAv5 has three symmetric layers (HMAC challenge-response, AES key wrap of session keys, and the default symmetric update-key change). Only the optional asymmetric update-key change is exposed. GOOSE authenticates each frame with HMAC or GMAC; its exposure is the GDOI key-distribution channel (IEC 62351-9 / RFC 8052), not the frame. The KAT panel checks HMAC-SHA-256 against a NIST ACVP vector and AES-256 key wrap against RFC 3394.
2. Where attacks start vs where they hurt
Open the Zone & Conduit Planner with its defaults. Filter the conduits by path A, then path B, and note which zones they start from. Compare the drivers of the top zones with those of Basic control and the SIS, and read the gap flagged on Basic control. Then set Basic control's firmware signing to "ML-DSA / LMS".

chunks.title: OT & Industrial Control Systems PQC — OTPQCExercises
chunks.content:
Module: OT & Industrial Control Systems PQC
Component: OTPQCExercises

IIoT & cloud connectors, Remote & vendor access and the Industrial DMZ rank first at ${zone('iiot-connectors').priority}, all driven by HNDL: path B comes in there, and path A starts in the Enterprise zone (${zone('enterprise').priority}) and crosses the DMZ. Basic control and the SIS come next at ${zone('control').priority}, driven by forgery: that is where the consequences land. Their commands are flagged as unauthenticated today, a gap to close with classical authentication now. Switching Basic control's firmware signing to a PQC scheme drops its forgery score to 0: the signing root, not the traffic, was the quantum exposure. Both ends need migrating.
3. Prioritise a high-impact transmission substation
The Substation Planner opens with a transmission substation: 80 IEDs, utility fibre, IEC 62351 Parts 3/4/6/8/9, High impact. Which zone is first, and where does the process bus land?
WAN / control-centre links come first (${sub('wan-iccp').priority}), then the station bus (${sub('station-bus').priority}) and engineering access (${sub('engineering').priority}). The process bus scores only ${sub('process-bus').priority}: GOOSE and SV keep their symmetric MAC, so only the GDOI key channel needs work — even though it is the highest-complexity zone. The trip-message budget shows 3 ms (TT6).
4. What PQC firmware signing does to a pipeline score

chunks.title: OT & Industrial Control Systems PQC — OTPQCExercises
chunks.content:
Module: OT & Industrial Control Systems PQC
Component: OTPQCExercises

In the Safety & Consequence Scorer, open the gas pipeline compressor station. Note the score, then change Controller firmware to "LMS / ML-DSA signed". Compare with the hydro dam spillway.
The pipeline starts at ${consequenceDefaults['gas-pipeline'].compound} (${consequenceDefaults['gas-pipeline'].riskLevel}): its DNP3 SAv5 commands are symmetric, so the exposure is firmware signing. With PQC firmware it falls to ${gasWithPqcFirmware.compound} (${gasWithPqcFirmware.riskLevel}). The spillway scores ${consequenceDefaults['hydro-spillway'].compound} (${consequenceDefaults['hydro-spillway'].riskLevel}) because no independent safety layer bounds the outcome.
5. When site count, not technology, sets the finish date
Open the Sector Roadmap with its defaults (energy, medium programme, 50 sites, US, planning year 2033), then raise the number of sites to 400.
With 50 sites the programme takes ${roadmapDefault.totalMonths} months and ends in ${roadmapDefault.finishYear}, with signing roots done by ${roadmapDefault.signingRootsFinish}. At 400 sites the site rollout alone runs ${roadmapLargeFleet.phases.find((p) => p.id === 'site-rollout')!.durationMonths} months and the programme ends in ${roadmapLargeFleet.finishYear} — ${roadmapLargeFleet.lateCount} phase lands after the 2033 planning year. Signing roots still finish in ${roadmapLargeFleet.signingRootsFinish}, which is why they are scheduled early.
6. Why project signing should not use a small LMS tree

chunks.title: OT & Industrial Control Systems PQC — OTPQCExercises
chunks.content:
Module: OT & Industrial Control Systems PQC
Component: OTPQCExercises

In the Firmware & Project Signing Lab, choose LMS H10/W8, "PLC project / logic downloads", 5,000 signatures a year, 1 HSM, 15 years. Then switch the scheme to ML-DSA-87.
An H10 tree holds 1,024 signatures, so at 5,000 a year the key is exhausted after ${signingProjectLms.yearsToExhaustion} years, and the lab warns that keeping a counter consistent across engineering workstations is hard. ML-DSA-87 is stateless — no counter, no exhaustion — at the cost of a 4,627-byte signature. Keep LMS for rare, central vendor firmware releases.

Operational technology (OT) runs physical processes: grids, pipelines, water plants, railways, factories and buildings. IT security usually ranks confidentiality first. OT turns the order around: safety, then availability, then integrity, then confidentiality. A control system that leaks data is a problem; one that accepts a forged command can hurt people.
That changes what the quantum threat means here. In IT the headline risk is harvest now, decrypt later. In OT the bigger risk is authenticity: a cryptographically relevant quantum computer could forge the RSA or ECDSA signatures that controllers use to accept firmware, project downloads, certificates and commands. Forgery needs no harvesting — it starts the day such a machine exists — and the devices that trust the old keys stay in service for decades.
Signing roots (vendor firmware keys, engineering-tool keys, device CAs) are the first thing to migrate. Step 2 of the workshop scores this as its own axis.
Still real at the boundary: remote-access sessions, inter-site links and vendor VPNs carry credentials, topology and settings worth recording now.
says the lifespan of an OT system can exceed 20 years. On the typical lives in the table below, a relay or PLC installed today may still run in the 2040s; substation primary plant lasts longer still.

chunks.title: OT & Industrial Control Systems PQC — OTPQCIntroduction

Module: OT & Industrial Control Systems PQC
Component: OTPQCIntroduction

Changing crypto in a safety-related device can mean re-testing a protection scheme, re-running a SIL assessment or re-opening a rail safety case — far more than a software update.
The typical lives above are this module's illustrative figures, not values from a standard. For comparison, the Applied Quantum PQC Migration Framework (version 2.1, June 2026) says OT systems (SCADA, PLCs, RTUs) often have 15–25 year lifecycles.
Smart meters, AMI head-ends and RF-mesh networks are covered in IoT & Embedded Device PQC , which deals with fleets of constrained devices.
The Purdue model stacks an industrial network into levels — field devices (L0), controllers (L1), supervisory systems (L2), site operations (L3), an industrial DMZ (L3.5) and the enterprise (L4–5). IEC 62443 turns that picture into something you can secure: assets with the same security needs form a zone, and every communication path between zones is a conduit with its own controls.
SL-T (target) — what the zone needs, from the risk assessment.
Zones say what is at stake; they do not say how an attacker gets there. OT is reached along three paths, and each needs a different fix. Step 2 of the workshop tags every conduit with its path.

The most common way in starts on the business network: a phished laptop, stolen credentials, then a pivot through the DMZ into site operations and supervisory control. CISA notes that OT may be exposed to a quantum computer precisely “due to connectivity or association with IT platforms” and their identity and access management (
Vendor VPNs, jump hosts and IIoT platforms that send plant data to the cloud. In NIST’s reference architecture, communication from the IIoT platform tier is routed through the DMZ border firewall; IIoT that connects straight to the cloud from L1 or L2 changes the boundaries the zone model relies on (
Sometimes called close access: someone on site or nearby, on a field network, serial link or wireless segment. CISA concludes that secure versions of industrial protocols remain underutilized in OT environments, and found that “many OT systems built in 2026 still rely on protocol implementations designed decades ago, leaving their networks fully trusting anyone with access” (
Most OT protocols already protect their real-time messages with symmetric crypto — HMAC, GMAC, AES key wrap — which a quantum computer does not break. The exposure sits in the public-key parts around them: certificates, key distribution and TLS handshakes.

DNP3 Secure Authentication v5 uses an HMAC challenge-response and wraps session keys with AES key wrap. Update keys are pre-shared by default; where they are changed remotely, the 2011 IEEE 1815 working draft makes the symmetric method (AES-256 key wrap plus HMAC-SHA-256) the default and the asymmetric methods, which use RSA and DSA, optional. IEEE SA lists IEEE 1815-2012 as an Inactive-Reserved standard (inactivated 30 March 2023) and lists a P1815 project that would supersede it; the documents we hold describe no revision named “SAv6”. IEC 104 uses IEC 62351-3 TLS and IEC 62351-5 authentication.
SecurityPolicies use RSA (e.g. Basic256Sha256) or ECC (nistP256, nistP384, brainpool, curve25519) for certificates and key establishment (

Modbus/TCP Security wraps Modbus in mutual TLS; plain Modbus has no security at all.

Two kinds of signature decide what a controller runs. Firmware is signed by the vendor and checked by the device’s bootloader or update agent. Projects — the logic, configuration and settings an engineer downloads from a workstation — are increasingly signed too. Both are forgeable once RSA and ECDSA fall.
NERC CIP-010-4 R1.6 requires verifying the software source and integrity before a baseline change on high and medium impact systems (
IEC 62443-4-1 (secure development lifecycle) covers how vendors sign and deliver updates; IEC 62443-4-2 CR 3.4 requires software and information integrity in the component.

Small public key, fast verification, conservative hash-only security — but every signature uses a one-time key from a fixed budget, and the counter must never repeat. SP 800-208 requires signing in hardware modules that do not let the state be cloned.
The boundary is where HNDL matters most in OT. Remote sessions carry credentials and engineering traffic, and they cross networks an adversary can record.
Industrial DMZ (L3.5) — no direct path from enterprise to control; data is brokered through replicas and file-transfer services.
Jump hosts — interactive sessions terminate on an intermediate system with MFA before reaching anything in L1–L2. Hybrid ML-KEM on the VPN or SSH in front of them protects the recorded session.
IPsec / IKEv2 VPNs — two IETF routes protect the key exchange of a recorded session. RFC 8784 (Standards Track) stirs an additional shared secret into the IKEv2 key derivation, so that, where the two ends share a long secret key, the exchange is quantum secure without waiting for new key-exchange algorithms. RFC 9370 lets IKEv2 add a post-quantum key exchange alongside the classical (EC)DH one. As of 21 August 2026 (version 12), post-quantum signature authentication for IKEv2 was specified in an IETF Internet-Draft, draft-ietf-ipsecme-ikev2-pqc-auth.

Controllers rarely carry secrets worth harvesting, so an HNDL-only view ranks them last. But they accept firmware and project downloads signed with RSA or ECDSA. The day a quantum computer can forge those signatures, every controller that still trusts the old key will accept the attacker’s code — and controllers stay in service for decades, so the signing roots have to move years before that day.
Their command traffic is a different story: most installed field protocols still trust anyone with network or physical access, so the planner defaults L0–L1 commands to “none” and flags them as a present-day gap. That is fixed with classical authentication or an authenticating gateway, not with PQC.

chunks.title: PKI Enrollment Protocols (EST & CMP) — EnrollmentIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: PKI Enrollment Protocols (EST & CMP)
Component: EnrollmentIntroduction

When an end-entity needs an X.509 certificate, it doesn't just hand a self-signed key to the CA — the request is wrapped in a structured enrollment protocol that carries the public key, attribute requests, proof-of-possession, and authentication. Two enrollment protocols matter for post-quantum PKI: EST (RFC 7030) and CMP (RFC 9810, July 2025, which obsoleted RFC 4210 and added certificate management for KEM keys).
Enrollment over Secure Transport — HTTPS-based, designed to be simple. Client POSTs a base64-encoded PKCS#10 CSR to /.well-known/est/simpleenroll; server returns a base64-encoded PKCS#7 degenerate SignedData containing the issued cert.
2013 standard; PQC-aware only via inherited X.509 OIDs (no PQC-specific update)
Certificate Management Protocol — richer state machine, supports initial request (ir), cert request (cr), key update (kur ), revocation (rr), and more. RFC 9810 added support for KEM keys for proof-of-possession (POP) and message protection.
Transport: HTTP (application/pkixcmp, RFC 9811, obsoletes RFC 6712)
Active IETF track — EJBCA 9.1+ ships ML-DSA + ML-KEM via CMP
ML-DSA support. The CSR / CRMF must carry the new ML-DSA OIDs (RFC 9881) and the request must be signed under the new algorithm.

chunks.title: PKI Enrollment Protocols (EST & CMP) — EnrollmentIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: PKI Enrollment Protocols (EST & CMP)
Component: EnrollmentIntroduction

ML-KEM enrollment. KEM keys can't sign the request, so signature-POP doesn't apply. RFC 9810 introduces encrCert POP: the CA encapsulates the new cert under the EE's KEM pubkey; the EE proves possession by decapsulating. EST has no KEM-aware update yet. (Checked 2026-08-22 against the three RFCs that update RFC 7030 — 8951, 8996 and 9908. RFC 9908, the most recent, clarifies CSR Attributes Response encoding and contains no mention of KEMs at all, so this still holds.)
Composite enrollment. Hybrid PKI (one cert carrying both classical and PQC pubkeys) is currently a draft track — draft-ietf-lamps-pq-composite-sigs-19 and draft-ietf-lamps-pq-composite-kem. Both EST and CMP can carry composite requests once the OIDs stabilize.
The Workshop tab drives real cryptographic operations in your browser using OpenSSL 3.6 WASM and our softHSM v3 (PKCS#11 v3.2). You'll:
Generate an ML-DSA-65 keypair (or ML-KEM-768) via OpenSSL genpkey

Exercise ML-KEM encapsulation/decapsulation for the RFC 9810 KUR POP

chunks.content:
Module: PKI Enrollment Protocols (EST & CMP)
Component: CmpKemKeyUpdate

RFC 9810 — Certificate Management Protocol (adds support for KEM keys, including encrCert proof-of-possession)
ML-KEM keys can't sign, so signature-POP doesn't apply. The CA encapsulates the issued cert under the new ML-KEM public key; the EE proves possession by decapsulating. This step runs the full flow: CMP IR enrolls an ML-KEM-768 cert (CA signs with its ML-DSA-65 key), then encap → decap proves the EE holds the matching private key. If the two derived shared secrets match, POP succeeded.
The cert this step issues is fully spec-conformant — every byte traces to a published standard:
encrCert POP successful. CA-encapsulated secret matches EE-decapsulated secret byte-for-byte — the EE possesses the ML-KEM private key.

chunks.content:

Parallel-certs hybrid PKI (the pattern actually shipping in 2026)
True composite signatures (one cert, one OID, one signature blob containing both ML-DSA + ECDSA outputs per draft-ietf-lamps-pq-composite-sigs-19 ) need composite OIDs in an OpenSSL provider that OpenSSL 3.6 doesn't ship. Until those land, the production hybrid pattern is parallel certs: two EE certificates for the same identity, one PQC, one classical, both anchored at the same CA. This step issues both through the same CMP server you used in Step 2 — same protocol, same trust anchor, different leaf algorithms.
Run Step 2 (CMP Initial Request) first to also see the ML-DSA-65 leg side-by-side. The ECDSA leg works standalone.

chunks.content:
Module: PKI Workshop
Component: CertCapacityCalculator

Educational estimates for entirely classical or entirely PQC chains. Each example uses one algorithm and parameter set throughout.
TLS sends two certificates: intermediate + leaf. The root is excluded. The PQC example is a size comparison, not a claim of deployment support.
The PQC rows cover the ML-DSA signature family; each parameter set is shown separately because its public-key and signature sizes differ.
The overhead allowance excludes the encoded public key and signature. Resumed connections are excluded from the full-handshake input. Annual storage models leaf issuance in steady state; initial issuance, CA renewals, backups and retained historical archives are additional.
Certificate = raw public key + public-key encoding allowance + issuer signature + template overhead.
Sent chain = two certificates. Certificate-related payload = sent chain + one server CertificateVerify signature contribution.
Annual leaf issuance storage = leaf count × certificate bytes × (365 ÷ renewal days).
TLS framing, key shares, other handshake messages, optional OCSP/SCT additions and client authentication are excluded. This is not total handshake bandwidth or a latency estimate. Signing and key exchange are separate: PQC certificates can accompany hybrid key exchange.
ECDSA DER signatures vary in length; this example uses a 72-byte upper bound. The template allowance is illustrative, not a measured certificate size.

chunks.title: PKI Workshop — PKIExercises
chunks.content:
Module: PKI Workshop
Component: PKIExercises

Work through these exercises in order to explore classical and post-quantum PKI workflows. Each exercise guides you through the Workshop tab — click "Start Exercise" to jump to the right step. Compare your results across exercises to understand the trade-offs between algorithm families.
Take the PQC quiz to test what you've learned about PKI and post-quantum cryptography.
1. Build a Classical PKI Chain (RSA)
Generate an RSA-4096 Root CA, create an RSA-2048 CSR for a server certificate, sign it with the Root CA, then parse and verify the full chain.
Note the RSA key sizes (4096-bit for Root CA, 2048-bit for end entity), the sha256WithRSAEncryption signature algorithm, Basic Constraints (CA:TRUE vs CA:FALSE), and Key Usage extensions in the parsed output.
2. PQC Certificate Chain (ML-DSA)
Create a full post-quantum PKI chain using ML-DSA-87 for the Root CA and ML-DSA-44 for the end-entity certificate. Compare signature and key sizes with the RSA chain from Exercise 1.
ML-DSA-87 signatures are ~4,627 bytes vs ~512 bytes for RSA-4096. Public keys are ~2,592 bytes. Check the OID values in the parsed output — you will see ml-dsa-87 instead of rsaEncryption (not sourced in the Library).
3. Hash-Based Signatures (SLH-DSA)
Generate a Root CA using SLH-DSA-SHA2-128s (SPHINCS+) and compare its signature and key sizes with ML-DSA. Understand the trade-off between lattice-based and hash-based post-quantum signatures.

chunks.title: PKI Workshop — PKIExercises
chunks.content:

SLH-DSA-SHA2-128s signatures are ~7,856 bytes (larger than ML-DSA) but rely only on hash-function properties (BSI TR-02102-1 section 5.3.4; FIPS 205 section 1.1). Notice the longer signing time compared to ML-DSA — the trade-off is conservative security assumptions vs performance.
4. Cross-Algorithm Chain Verification
Create a Root CA with one algorithm (e.g., ML-DSA-87) and sign an end-entity CSR that was generated with a different algorithm (e.g., RSA-2048). Parse the signed certificate and verify the chain.
The signature algorithm field in the signed certificate reflects the CA key (ML-DSA-87), not the subject key (RSA). The Subject Public Key Info still shows the original RSA key. Use the "Verify Chain" button in Step 4 to confirm the chain is valid.
5. Industry Profile Comparison
Generate CSRs using different industry certificate profiles — Financial (ETSI EN 319 412-2), General IT (CA/Browser Forum TLS BR), and Telecom (3GPP TS 33.310) — and compare the required X.509 attributes and extensions.
Each profile requires different mandatory Subject DN fields and certificate extensions. Financial profiles require organizationIdentifier; Telecom profiles add NF Type extensions. Click the "Info" button next to each profile to read the full standard documentation.

Module: PKI Workshop

Compare the TLS handshake authentication size using traditional X.509 certificate chains versus Merkle Tree Certificates (MTCs). Toggle between ECDSA, ML-DSA-44, ML-DSA-87, and SLH-DSA to see how post-quantum signature bloat is addressed.
With ML-DSA-44, the tool shows ~10.3 KB for the traditional chain: what a server sends (leaf and intermediate keys, two certificate signatures and the CertificateVerify signature, 9,884 B, as in the Introduction) plus 2 SCTs and metadata for two certificates (10,522 B in all; the root is in the client's trust store and is not sent). A standalone MTC is ~6.6 KB (server key, CertificateVerify signature, one CA cosignature, 384 B inclusion proof, metadata: 6,736 B), about 36% smaller. The reduction in bytes grows with SLH-DSA, whose signatures are larger. Note the tradeoff: standalone MTCs need relying parties to meet cosigner requirements, and landmark certificates need clients to synchronize trusted subtrees periodically.

chunks.title: PKI Workshop — PKIIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: PKI Workshop
Component: PKIIntroduction

Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) is a framework of policies, hardware, software, and procedures for creating, managing, distributing, and revoking digital certificates. Defined by ITU-T X.509 and profiled for the internet in RFC 5280, PKI enables entities to establish trust through a hierarchy of Certificate Authorities (CAs) that vouch for the binding between a public key and an identity (not sourced in the Library).
Every X.509 certificate follows a defined lifecycle from key generation through revocation. RFC 5280 Section 3 presents an architectural model, while RFC 6960 ( OCSP) and RFC 5280 Section 5 ( CRLs) define the revocation checking mechanisms that relying parties use to verify certificate validity in real time.
An X.509v3 certificate (RFC 5280 Section 4.1) contains three main parts: the TBSCertificate (to-be-signed data), the signature algorithm identifier, and the digital signature value. The TBSCertificate holds all the fields that get signed by the CA:
Serial Number Unique per CA — MUST be positive integer (RFC 5280 Section 4.1.2.2)
Signature Algorithm sha256WithRSAEncryption, ml-dsa-65, slh-dsa-sha2-128s, etc.
Validity Not Before / Not After — defines certificate lifetime
Extensions Key Usage, Basic Constraints, SAN, CRL Distribution Points (RFC 5280 Section 4.2)

chunks.title: PKI Workshop — PKIIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: PKI Workshop
Component: PKIIntroduction

Certificate issuance and verification rely on digital signatures as defined in RFC 5280 Section 4.1.1.2. The CA signs the TBSCertificate using its private key, and any relying party can verify the signature using the CA's public key from a trusted root store.
Traditional PKI relies on RSA and ECDSA signatures, both vulnerable to Shor's algorithm on a cryptographically relevant quantum computer. NIST has standardized post-quantum replacements: ML-DSA (FIPS 204) for lattice-based signatures and SLH-DSA (FIPS 205) for stateless hash-based signatures.
Proven, widely deployed. Small signatures (256-512 bytes). Vulnerable to quantum computers running Shor's algorithm.
Quantum-resistant. ML-DSA-65 signatures ~3,309 bytes, SLH-DSA-SHA2-128s ~7,856 bytes (FIPS 204, FIPS 205). Larger but quantum-safe.
A composite certificate puts classical + PQC keys and signatures under one composite OID. Only relying parties that understand that OID can validate it, so it is not backward compatible.

chunks.title: PKI Workshop — PKIIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: PKI Workshop
Component: PKIIntroduction

Root CA certificates can have lifetimes of 20+ years. While data encryption is vulnerable to " harvest now, decrypt later " attacks, long-lived CAs are vulnerable to "forge later" attacks, where a cryptographically relevant quantum computer could forge signatures and issue rogue certificates. NIST IR 8547 recommends beginning the transition to post-quantum algorithms immediately, with CNSA 2.0 (NSA) requiring exclusive PQC use in national security systems by 2033 for large PKI systems (2030 for software/firmware signing and networking equipment).
Key migration challenges include certificate size growth (ML-DSA-87 public keys are ~2,592 bytes), constrained device support, and maintaining cross-signed trust chains during the transition period. NIST SP 800-131A Rev 2 provides guidance on algorithm deprecation timelines.
Post-quantum signatures are dramatically larger than their classical counterparts: ML-DSA-44 signatures are 2,420 bytes compared to just 64 bytes for ECDSA P-256 — a 37× increase. A TLS server using ML-DSA-44 throughout sends its leaf and one intermediate certificate (two public keys and two certificate signatures) and signs the handshake once more in CertificateVerify. That is 9,884 bytes (~9.9 KB) of keys and signatures in every full handshake, which can break constrained clients and degrade performance. The figure grows with the algorithm and the chain length: the same chain needs 13,831 B with ML-DSA-65 and 19,065 B with ML-DSA-87.

chunks.title: PKI Workshop — PKIIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: PKI Workshop
Component: PKIIntroduction

Merkle Tree Certificates (MTCs), specified in draft-ietf-plants-merkle-tree-certs in the IETF PLANTS working group (it replaced draft-davidben-tls-merkle-tree-certs; latest version -07, 7 October 2026; still an Internet-Draft, not yet proposed for publication), offer an elegant solution: instead of signing each certificate individually, a Merkle Tree CA (MTCA) batches thousands of certificates as leaves in a Merkle tree, signs only the root hash, and distributes compact inclusion proofs (384–736 bytes in the draft's estimates) that let any relying party verify a certificate belongs to the signed batch. In landmark mode, the certificate carries no signatures at all: an inclusion proof to a landmark subtree, which the client already trusts through predistributed log information, takes their place. It is an optional size optimization that only works with an up-to-date client.
3 ML-DSA-44 signatures (intermediate cert, leaf cert, CertificateVerify) — 3 × 2,420 B = 7,260 B
Total: 7,260 + 2,624 B, which gives 9,884 B (~9.9 KB) per handshake

chunks.title: PKI Workshop — PKIIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: PKI Workshop
Component: PKIIntroduction

Assumptions: ML-DSA-44 everywhere (FIPS 204: 1,312 B public key, 2,420 B signature); the server sends a leaf and one intermediate, not the root, whose key is already in the client's trust store; no Certificate Transparency SCTs; certificate names, extensions and other encoding overhead are not counted. A standalone MTC (no pre-synced landmark) also carries CA and cosigner signatures. The MTC Size Analysis tool uses a different model (it also counts the root key, SCTs and certificate metadata, but not the CertificateVerify signature), so its figures differ.
Tradeoff: MTC clients must periodically fetch transparency service updates (similar to CRLite). This trades per-handshake size for background data synchronization — a favorable tradeoff for high-traffic servers and constrained IoT devices.

chunks.content:
Module: PQC Business Case

Everything above models confidentiality risk — data harvested today, decrypted later. Quantum computing threatens a second, independent property: authenticity. Once a CRQC can break a signature scheme, it can forge NEW signatures going forward — but it cannot forge a signature that was already validly created in the past.
Data is being harvested today. Every year of delay adds another year of exposed historical data — there is no "catching up" later.

This split is what the US federal PQC executive order sets for federal high value assets and high-impact systems (national security systems are excluded): post-quantum key establishment by 31 December 2030, post-quantum digital signatures by 31 December 2031 ( Executive Order 14412, June 2026 ).

chunks.title: PQC Business Case — Introduction
chunks.content:
Module: PQC Business Case
Component: Introduction

Post-quantum cryptography migration is not just a technical initiative — it requires significant organizational investment. A well-constructed business case translates technical risk into financial language that executives and boards understand.
Delay tends to compound cost: more data exposed to harvest-now-decrypt-later collection, more legacy cryptography to unwind, and less time before published transition dates.
Our summary. Sources for the dates: NIST IR 8547 (final, October 2026) deprecates RSA and elliptic-curve algorithms after 2030 and disallows them after 2035; the joint CISA, NSA and NIST quantum-readiness factsheet (2023) urges organizations to start inventories and roadmaps now.
Without executive buy-in and adequate funding, PQC migration stalls. The business case bridges the gap between technical teams who understand the urgency and decision-makers who control budgets.
A credible business case names two distinct, already-running risks — not one. They hit different systems, on different clocks, and they map to the two parallel migration tracks a program runs. Framing only the data-confidentiality risk leaves the signature-forgery half of the estate — and whole sectors like OT, PKI operators, and code-signing shops — out of the argument.
Adversaries capture encrypted traffic today and store it to decrypt once a quantum computer exists. The risk is active now — any data whose confidentiality must outlast the quantum threat horizon is already exposed.

chunks.title: PQC Business Case — Introduction
chunks.content:
Module: PQC Business Case
Component: Introduction

Drives urgency on: long-lived secrets (trade secrets, M&A, health records, attorney-client) and internet-exposed key exchange.
Migration Track A: key exchange & confidentiality (TLS, VPN, data-at-rest).
Long-lived signatures and trust anchors signed today stay trusted for years. Once a quantum computer can forge them, an attacker can mint trusted software updates, certificates, or firmware. Signature migration has the longest lead times (PKI, toolchains, HSMs), so it must start in parallel — not after HNDL.
Drives urgency on: PKI roots (20+ yr), code- & firmware-signing keys, OT safety certificates, long-validity document signatures.
The decision point: data with a 10+ year confidentiality requirement in a regulated industry means HNDL alone justifies immediate action; where signature integrity is the primary risk (OT/ICS, PKI operators), TNFL drives the urgency on a different set of systems. Most enterprises carry both and therefore run both tracks at once.
Building a compelling case requires fluency in three financial frameworks that executives use to evaluate technology investments:
The complete cost of migration including software, hardware, training, consulting, downtime, and ongoing operational changes over the full lifecycle.
Return on investment weighted by the probability and magnitude of quantum-enabled breaches, regulatory fines, and competitive disadvantage from inaction.

chunks.title: PQC Business Case — Introduction
chunks.content:
Module: PQC Business Case
Component: Introduction

Translating technical quantum risk into business language: revenue impact, market position, regulatory exposure, and fiduciary responsibility.
PQC migration costs span four major categories. Each must be estimated and presented alongside the cost of not migrating:
• Mandate dates (CNSA 2.0, ANSSI), which are binding for national security systems in the case of CNSA 2.0 and mandatory in some certification contexts in the case of ANSSI
Don't wait for precise numbers — estimate each cost driver separately and refine as discovery matures. A multi-year PQC budget breaks into eight categories:
Combine independently justified investments — PKI automation for short certificate lifetimes, FIPS 140-3 upgrades for the FIPS 140-2 sunset, HSM refresh for end-of-life hardware, library upgrades for CVEs — into a single “cryptographic infrastructure modernization” program. In this module's reading, positioning PQC as the organizing wrapper for overdue security modernization avoids a big-bang budget spike and aligns spend to already-funded refresh cycles.
• The major PQC migration cost figure published by an accountable body is the U.S. federal civilian estimate: $7.1B for 2025–2035 (OMB, Report to Congress). It was built bottom-up from agency cryptographic inventories — which is why it is quotable and most vendor figures are not.

chunks.title: PQC Business Case — Introduction
chunks.content:
Module: PQC Business Case
Component: Introduction

• Beware round numbers with no owner. Per-organization PQC program costs circulate widely (“$2–5M for discovery”, “$300–500M for a global telco”) and almost none of them trace to a published methodology. If you cannot name whose board approved a number, do not put it in front of yours.
• Derive your own instead: count the assets you actually have (certificates, HSMs, applications, third-party integrations), price one representative unit of each with your own vendors, and multiply. The Cost Model Explorer in Step 1 does this across six model families so you can see the spread rather than a single number.
Present gross program cost and net incremental cost separately — much of the spend is modernization you needed anyway. And state which method produced each figure; a board can challenge a method, but it cannot challenge a number from nowhere.
No published methodology yet gives a reliable top-down total for a full PQC migration — the field has too few completed programs to calibrate against. The defensible move is to estimate the same program in more than one way and treat agreement between methods as confidence, and divergence as a signal to dig deeper. Six model families are in use — the workshop's Cost Model Explorer (Step 1) lets you watch them diverge on one scenario:

Component: Introduction

Under deep uncertainty, cross-checking a bottom-up buildup against an independent second estimate is stronger than precision within any single method. The workshop's ROI Calculator does this for you: it reconciles your per-product estimate against an independent assessment-derived one and flags when the two disagree — still pair the result with your finance team's discounted-cash-flow model before committing capital.
Timeline & urgency anchors (one published planning scenario)
• Full migration runs 5–7 years (small), 8–12 (medium), and 12–15+ (large enterprises) — against a fault-tolerant quantum window of 2028–2033 (Campbell, Computers 2026, 15(1):9, peer-reviewed). This is one paper's planning scenario, not an official forecast — test your plan against earlier and later quantum dates too.

• The hardest cost driver is legacy systems with cryptography hardwired in hardware or firmware — the OMB report attributes a significant share of the federal total to replacing exactly those.

chunks.title: PQC Candidates & Standardisation Lifecycle — CandidatesExercises
chunks.content:
Module: PQC Candidates & Standardisation Lifecycle
Component: CandidatesExercises

Each exercise pre-configures a workshop step and tells you what to look for. Open one, then come back and try the next.
1. UOV under the 2025 wedge attack
Open the Lifecycle Simulator and advance UOV through Round 2. Watch the Ran wedge-attack event fire and see three of four parameter sets drop below their security target.
UOV-Ip, UOV-III, and UOV-V all lose security in characteristic-2 fields. QR-UOV (odd characteristic) is untouched — this is exactly why algorithmic diversity within a family matters.
2. SQIsign vs FAEST — bandwidth vs CPU
Open the Candidate Comparator and select SQIsign (148 B signatures, slow signing) and FAEST (6.3 KB signatures, AES-grade trust). See where each one fits.
SQIsign wins for bandwidth-constrained protocols (IoT, certs). FAEST wins where AES-grade security trust is more important than wire cost. Same problem, opposite Pareto corners — that's why NIST keeps both.
3. Family math — what makes each one tick
Open the Family Math Explainer and step through MPCitH → multivariate → isogeny → lattice. Each panel shows the core construction in an animated visual.
Notice how different the underlying assumptions are. A lattice break does not threaten an isogeny scheme, and vice versa — this is exactly the diversity NIST wants in the standardisation portfolio.
4. HAWK as the integer-only Falcon alternative
Open the Comparator and contrast HAWK against FN-DSA's deployment story. FN-DSA needs constant-time floating-point Gaussian sampling. HAWK doesn't.

HAWK at NIST Cat 1 is 555 B — smaller than both FN-DSA and ML-DSA — and uses integer-only arithmetic on a rank-2 module lattice. That eliminates a whole class of constant-time bugs that have plagued Falcon implementations.
5. Where the worldwide tracks intersect
Open the Worldwide Standardisation Map and find where KpqC, CACR, and ISO/IEC overlap with NIST. Look at which bodies have a parallel process vs an aligned process.
KpqC and CACR run parallel selections — they may pick algorithms NIST didn't. ISO/IEC aligns with NIST output, gating procurement in countries that pin to ISO. Your migration plan needs to know which mode applies in your jurisdiction.

Post-quantum cryptography is not a single 2024 event. NIST has already published one KEM (FIPS 203 ML-KEM) and two signatures (FIPS 204 ML-DSA, FIPS 205 SLH-DSA) — with a third, FN-DSA (FIPS 206), still in development — picked an alternate KEM, and is mid-flight on a signature on-ramp. Korea, China, and Japan each run parallel national tracks. International bodies (ISO/IEC, IETF, ETSI) layer compatibility and protocol bindings on top. New candidates will keep arriving — the operational question is not which algorithm wins but how fast your stack can absorb the next one.
…and counting. The cryptanalysis timeline workshop step shows every event including the 2025 wedge attack and ongoing reparameterisations.
NIST evaluates submissions on four axes — security, performance, implementation characteristics, and intellectual property — then opens each round to public cryptanalysis. Attacks are not a failure of the process; they are the point. The 2022 SIKE break, the 2022 Rainbow break, the 2025 Ran wedge attack on UOV-family schemes — each event reshaped the field, eliminated some candidates, and forced others to reparameterise.

When the Ran wedge attack revealed an exterior-product weakness in characteristic-2 UOV parameter sets, three of UOV's four parameter sets fell below their security target, MAYO-2 lost ~30 bits, and most SNOVA parameter sets broke. The process worked: NIST surfaced the attack, teams proposed odd-characteristic reparameterisations, the surviving constructions are now better-understood.
The nine third-round candidates (NIST IR 8610, May 2026) break down into four mathematical families. One has since left: the HAWK team withdrew it on 29 July 2026 after a new key- recovery attack (NIST Round 3 page), leaving eight. Diversity across families is the entire point — if lattice math falls, the portfolio survives. The workshop's Family Math Explainer step shows animated visualisations of each construction.
NIST is not the only show. Korea, China, and Japan each run national tracks; international bodies (ISO/IEC, IETF, ETSI) layer compatibility and protocol bindings on top; and regional regulators (BSI, ANSSI) overlay deployment guidance. Different jurisdictions will ship different combinations of these outputs — your migration plan needs to know which ones apply to you.

Simulate N parties locally · commit to each · Fiat-Shamir reveals N−1 · keep 1 hidden
Signing simulates all N parties locally and commits to each computation. The Fiat-Shamir challenge then chooses which N−1 to open; the unopened party hides the secret. Verifier replays the opened parties and checks every commitment. Security reduces to the symmetric primitives that drive the simulated parties (AES for FAEST, hash-based for SDitH).
Public map P : Fn → Fm looks random — secret is the hidden oil subspace
⚠ 2025 Ran wedge attack: exterior products expose the oil subspace in characteristic-2 fields
The verifier sees only the public map P — designed to look random. The signer knows where the oil subspace sits inside the variable space; substituting random vinegar collapses the quadratic system to a linear one in the oil coordinates, which Gaussian elimination solves in milliseconds. Wedge attacks broke that secrecy in some characteristic-2 instances, driving the move to odd-characteristic fields (QR-UOV survived unscathed).

chunks.content:
Module: PQC Candidates & Standardisation Lifecycle
Component: FamilyMathExplainer

Knowing the isogeny φ : E₀ → E_pub is hard. The signature compactly proves you know it.
toy graph shown — real supersingular isogeny graph has ~p/12 ≈ 2²⁵⁶ nodes
The signer knows a secret isogeny φ from E₀ to E_pub — equivalently, a path through the supersingular graph. The signature is a compact algebraic representation of that morphism (an ideal in a quaternion order, not a literal node list), so it stays at 148 B even though the underlying graph has astronomic size. SQIsign avoids SIKE's pitfall by not revealing auxiliary torsion points to the verifier.
Both schemes sample a short vector — Falcon needs floats, HAWK uses integers only
Both schemes solve the same problem — produce a short vector in a coset defined by a hash of the message. Falcon (FN-DSA) samples from a continuous Gaussian distribution and rounds to the lattice, which needs floating-point arithmetic that's notoriously hard to make constant-time. HAWK reformulates the problem on a rank-2 module lattice with a Gram matrix as the public key, and uses integer-only Babai-style rounding — 555 B signatures at security category 1, and, per NIST IR 8610, a primary advantage over Falcon in its reliance on integer-only arithmetic.

chunks.title: PQC Candidates & Standardisation Lifecycle — families (data)
chunks.content:
Module: PQC Candidates & Standardisation Lifecycle
Data: families

Prove knowledge by simulating a multi-party computation inside a hash transcript.
Security reduces to symmetric primitives (AES, hash functions) or well-studied combinatorial problems (syndrome decoding, MQ). No novel number-theoretic assumptions required.
Three candidates kept to cover the strongest security foundations: FAEST (AES), SDitH (coding theory, studied since 1970s), MQOM (MQ, best performance of MPCitH category).
Signatures are inherently large (kilobytes) because they encode a simulated-computation transcript. MQOM still needs further QROM proof maturation.
Imagine you want to prove you know a secret password without ever saying it out loud. You split the password into four pieces, hand each piece to a different friend, ask each of them to do a calculation, and have them seal their answers in envelopes. A random challenge then picks three of the four envelopes to open. If the opened answers are consistent with each other, I'm convinced you know the real password — and the one envelope I never opened keeps the secret safe.
This family is built entirely from cryptographic tools we already trust deeply — AES (the same cipher protecting your Wi-Fi) and hash functions. No exotic new math, just clever use of old reliable bricks. That makes it the most conservative bet of the four families: if these schemes break, a lot of other cryptography breaks first.
Signatures are pretty chunky — kilobytes, not bytes — because you have to send all those envelope contents along. Fine for desktops and servers; awkward for tiny sensors where every byte costs battery.
Hidden-structure quadratic systems — tiny signatures, big public keys.
Inverting a system of multivariate quadratic polynomials with a trapdoor (Oil and Vinegar, introduced 1999). Hardness rests on the MQ problem and the secrecy of the oil/vinegar partition.
Potentially smallest signatures of any PQC family. SNOVA odd-characteristic reparameterisation reaches sub-FN-DSA combined sizes. No attack has broken the underlying UOV construction itself.
The 2025 Ran wedge attack and the Furue–Ikematsu small-field attack each pushed 3 of UOV's 4 parameter sets below their security targets, hit MAYO-2 by ~30 bits, and broke most SNOVA parameter sets. QR-UOV (odd characteristic) survived unscathed.
Imagine a giant puzzle made of quadratic equations. To anyone without the secret shortcut, solving it would take longer than the universe has existed. But the signer knows a hidden trick: pick random values for half the puzzle (called the "vinegar"), and the other half (the "oil") collapses into simple linear math you can solve in milliseconds. The verifier sees only the public puzzle template — which looks impenetrably random — and has no idea where the shortcut hides.

CRYSTALS-Kyber selected in 2022; published as ML-KEM under FIPS 203 in August 2024. The primary PQC KEM.

A classical attack on the Rainbow multivariate signature scheme breaks all parameter sets. Rainbow eliminated. UOV (Rainbow's ancestor) was re-submitted in the on-ramp call.
NIST selects Kyber, CRYSTALS-Dilithium, Falcon and SPHINCS+ for standardization
Kyber, CRYSTALS-Dilithium, Falcon and SPHINCS+ were selected for standardization. ML-KEM (FIPS 203) is derived from CRYSTALS-Kyber, ML-DSA (FIPS 204) from CRYSTALS-Dilithium, and SLH-DSA (FIPS 205) is a variant of SPHINCS+; Falcon is to be published in FIPS 206 (in development).
Recognising lattice over-concentration in the signature selections, NIST opens a parallel "on-ramp" call for additional digital signature schemes.
40 submissions accepted for evaluation. First public cryptanalysis period opens.
ML-KEM (FIPS 203), ML-DSA (FIPS 204), SLH-DSA (FIPS 205) become final federal standards.
14 of 40 first-round submissions advance to Round 2: CROSS, FAEST, HAWK, LESS, MAYO, Mirath, MQOM, PERK, QR-UOV, RYDE, SDitH, SNOVA, SQIsign, UOV. NIST cites security, performance, implementation characteristics, and IP as the four evaluation axes.
Exterior-product attack exposes hidden oil subspace in characteristic-2 UOV instances. 3 of 4 UOV parameter sets fall below security target; MAYO-2 loses ~30 bits; most SNOVA parameter sets broken.
Independent attack exploiting small-field characteristics in UOV pushes uov-Ip, uov-III, uov-V further below their advertised security strengths.
NIST announces it will create a draft standard based on HQC for public comment, with a final version expected in approximately two years after the comments are adjudicated.
SNOVA team proposes modified parameters using odd-characteristic fields. Resulting Category-1 PK and signature are both smaller than FN-DSA.
HAWK team addresses an omSVP-definition discrepancy with a refined formulation. smLIP advances do not currently apply to HAWK's cyclotomic number fields.
Nine third-round candidates advance: FAEST, MQOM, SDitH (MPCitH); UOV, MAYO, QR-UOV, SNOVA (Multivariate); SQIsign (Isogeny); HAWK (Lattice). Five Round-2 schemes did not advance (CROSS, LESS, Mirath, PERK, RYDE).
The HAWK submission team withdraws it from the additional signatures process after a new attack roughly halves the lattice-reduction block size needed for key recovery. Eight third-round candidates remain. NIST has set no standardisation year.
