chunks.title: PQC Governance & Policy — Introduction
chunks.content:
Module: PQC Governance & Policy
Component: Introduction

The transition to post-quantum cryptography is not just a technical upgrade — it's an enterprise-wide transformation that touches every system, vendor, and compliance obligation. Without formal governance, organizations risk fragmented migration efforts, missed deadlines, and security gaps.
OMB Memorandum M-23-02 directs federal agencies to establish governance structures with clear roles, responsibilities, and executive sponsorship for their cryptographic transition to post-quantum algorithms — a model that applies equally to private-sector organizations managing complex PQC migrations.
— OMB M-23-02, Migrating to Post-Quantum Cryptography (2022)
Align security, engineering, compliance, and procurement teams on a unified migration roadmap.
Clear ownership of decisions — who selects algorithms, who approves exceptions, who tracks compliance.
Enterprise-wide cryptographic standards prevent teams from making conflicting algorithm and library choices.
A RACI matrix (Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed) is the standard tool for mapping governance roles to migration activities. Every PQC program needs clarity on who does the work, who owns the decision, who provides input, and who needs to know.
Key rule: Each activity should have exactly one "A" (Accountable) to avoid diffusion of responsibility. Multiple "R" and "C" assignments are common for cross-functional work.

chunks.title: PQC Governance & Policy — Introduction
chunks.content:
Module: PQC Governance & Policy
Component: Introduction

PQC governance requires a layered policy framework. Each layer provides increasing specificity, from enterprise-wide principles to team-level procedures.
The charter is the founding authority document for the entire program. Without it, the Quantum Readiness Program Manager (QRPM) has no formal power to compel other business units, and budget requests get re-litigated at every phase gate. Framework 2.1 identifies insufficient mandate scope as the most common reason Phase 0 programs stall before Phase 1.
Framework 2.1 common failure: organizations reach Gate G1 with a signed email thread instead of a formal charter. The SteerCo has no documented authority, budget re-approval is required at each phase, and the first procurement dispute stalls the program for months.
A single crypto governance team sets all policies, selects algorithms, and manages migration. Best for smaller organizations or those with a strong central security function.
Each business unit or region manages its own PQC transition within guardrails. Governance board sets boundaries but delegates execution. Common in regulated multi-nationals.
Central team owns algorithm policy and compliance mapping. Business units own migration execution and testing. Most common model for large enterprises migrating to PQC.

chunks.title: PQC Hardware Acceleration — AccelerationExercises
chunks.content:
Module: PQC Hardware Acceleration
Component: AccelerationExercises

Each exercise opens the right Workshop step. Predict the answer first, then check it against the diagram or our measurements.
Take the PQC quiz to test what you've learned about PQC hardware acceleration.
Open the GPU model, read the plain-English analogy, then compare the “1 signature” and “4,096 signatures” rows of the diagram.
With one signature a single lane works while the launch cost is paid in full, so the CPU finishes first. With thousands the launch cost is shared and every lane is busy. That is why GPU PQC figures are always quoted at large batches.
2. Why the AI Accelerator Cannot Help
Open the NPU model and check each ✗ against what the “Building blocks” step says Keccak and the NTT need.
The NPU does rounded 8-bit multiply-adds. ML-DSA needs exact 23-bit modular arithmetic, and Keccak has no multiplication at all — the mismatch is structural, not a matter of speed.
3. Check Montgomery Reduction by Hand
In “Building blocks”, follow the decimal example 4321 → 5000 → 50 with N = 97 and R = 100. Verify that 50 × 100 ≡ 4321 (mod 97).
50 × 100 = 5000 = 51 × 97 + 53, and 4321 = 44 × 97 + 53 — the same remainder. The only “division” was dropping two zeros, which in binary is a free shift.
4. Same Scheme, Opposite Winner
In “Our measurements”, compare SLH-DSA-SHA2-128s with SLH-DSA-SHAKE-128s on each platform, then look at each platform’s instruction badges.

chunks.title: PQC Hardware Acceleration — AccelerationExercises
chunks.content:
Module: PQC Hardware Acceleration
Component: AccelerationExercises

On the Cortex-A55 and A53, which have SHA-256 instructions and no SHA-3 ones, the SHA-2 variant signs about 11× faster on today’s engine — only the KV260, whose FPGA does SHAKE, reverses it. The hardware you have, not the algorithm, decides which variant to deploy on a given chip.
5. When Software Beat Our FPGA
In “Our measurements”, read the “Same boards, two days later” table, then compare the KV260’s new ML-DSA-65 figure with the +29% FPGA result in step 4.
NEON assembly on the A53 alone reached about five times the FPGA-assisted ML-DSA rate. Meanwhile the FPGA made the KV260 13× faster than the i.MX 95 on SLH-DSA-SHAKE-128s. Accelerate the workload that is actually stuck.
In “FPGA limits”, move the clock slider from 200 to 260 MHz and watch where the clock period crosses the 4-lane engine’s critical path.
At 250 MHz the period is 4.000 ns and our routed path was 4.010 ns — 10 picoseconds too long. Shipping at 240 MHz (4.167 ns) cost 4% throughput; the alternative was a redesign.
7. Can Any Batch Pay Back the Trip?
In “Offload, sharing and batching”, keep our measured costs and move the batch slider to 500. Then lower the per-job cost below 12 µs.
At 58.7 µs per job the accelerator is slower than the A53 for every batch size — the fixed cost can never be earned back. Only when the per-job cost drops below the CPU’s does a break-even batch size appear.
8. Read a Hybrid Result Correctly

The hybrid rows are direct PKCS#11 v3.3 HSM operations: component secrets are combined inside the HSM. Do not add separate classical and PQC TPS values, and use one-worker versus whole-platform views to see the measured scaling.

chunks.title: PQC Hardware Acceleration — AccelerationIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: PQC Hardware Acceleration
Component: AccelerationIntroduction

“Accelerating PQC” is not one problem. Each algorithm spends its time in a different place, and an accelerator only helps if it speeds up that place — and if moving the work there costs less than it saves.
Polynomial arithmetic mod 8,380,417 via the NTT, plus a lot of SHAKE to grow the public matrix and sample secrets, inside a retry loop that runs about 4–5 times per signature on average. Already fast: milliseconds on a small core.
Almost nothing but hashing — about two million Keccak permutations for one SHAKE-128s signature — built into large Merkle trees. Slow: seconds on a small core for the compact “s” parameter sets.
Big-integer multiplication with Montgomery reduction. Still in every hybrid deployment during the migration, so still worth accelerating.
Hardware rarely accelerates “an algorithm”. It accelerates the primitives underneath:
Montgomery reduction — computes “mod N” with multiplications and a shift instead of a slow division (Montgomery, 1985; FIPS 204 Appendix A). Inside RSA, ECC and every ML-DSA coefficient multiply.
NTT (Number-Theoretic Transform) — turns polynomial multiplication from 65,536 products into about 3,300 for 256 coefficients. ML-DSA runs a full 8-layer NTT; ML-KEM’s modulus 3,329 only allows 7 layers.
Keccak-f[1600] — a 24-round shuffle of a 1,600-bit state using only XOR, AND, NOT and rotate (FIPS 202). Constant-time by nature and cheap in hardware.

chunks.title: PQC Hardware Acceleration — AccelerationIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: PQC Hardware Acceleration
Component: AccelerationIntroduction

SHA-3 — Keccak in a “sponge”: absorb the message into the 1,088-bit rate, keep a 512-bit capacity sealed, output a fixed 256 bits (SHA3-256).
SHAKE — the same sponge with an output tap you can leave open. SHAKE128 (capacity 256) grows ML-DSA’s and ML-KEM’s matrices; SHAKE256 is every hash in SLH-DSA-SHAKE.
Workshop step 2 explains each one in plain English, with a worked Montgomery example you can check by hand and an animated NTT butterfly network.
From closest-to-the-CPU to furthest away: scalar code; SIMD vector units (Arm NEON/SVE, x86 AVX2/AVX-512); dedicated crypto instructions (AES, SHA-256, SHA-512, SHA-3); GPUs; FPGAs; ASICs and secure elements; and NPUs. The further from the CPU, the more raw speed is available — and the more you pay to move data there and back.
Instruction availability per Arm’s feature list and core manuals, Intel’s SHA Extensions note and LLVM’s CPU definitions. Note the asymmetry for PQC: x86 has no SHA-3/Keccak instruction at all, and hardware SHA-512 reached x86 only with Arrow Lake-S and Lunar Lake (2024); Arm has had optional SHA-3 and SHA-512 instructions since the Armv8.2 extension — but the Cortex-A53 and A55 do not implement them.

chunks.title: PQC Hardware Acceleration — AccelerationIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: PQC Hardware Acceleration
Component: AccelerationIntroduction

We run the same Rust PKCS#11 engine on several Arm platforms: an Apple M4 Pro laptop (Armv9.2-A, with SHA-3, SHA-512 and SME2), an NXP i.MX 95 appliance (6× Cortex-A55, Armv8.2-A) and an AMD Kria KV260 appliance (4× Cortex-A53, Armv8.0-A, plus FPGA fabric), plus the Ventuno Q (Qualcomm QCS8275: 4× Cortex-A78C and 4× Cortex-A55). The A55 and A53 both have AES and SHA-256 instructions and neither has SHA-3 or SHA-512. The Ventuno mixes faster A78C cores with A55 cores, so its whole-board result is not eight identical per-core results.
Newer is not simply “more of the same”. The M4 Pro has 10 big cores and 4 small efficiency cores. The M5 Max drops the efficiency cores: it has 6 top-tier “super cores” and 12 new mid-tier performance cores. A single signature runs on one core, so its speed depends on which kind of core it lands on; a batch spread over all cores depends on how many cores of each kind there are.
Workshop step 3 lets you compare the current classical, pure-PQC and hybrid mechanisms across all seven platforms, then inspect the older focused Arm/FPGA experiments.
The AI X1 Pro benchmark environment exposes 12 AMD64 virtual CPUs on a Ryzen AI 9 HX 370 host. They advertise AVX2, AVX-512F, IFMA, VAES, AES-NI and SHA-NI. That only tells us what the CPU can execute; each mechanism still needs a compatible implementation, runtime dispatch and a measurement.
We tested the actual release build and candidates rather than inferring a gain from the instruction flags.

chunks.title: PQC Hardware Acceleration — AccelerationIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: PQC Hardware Acceleration
Component: AccelerationIntroduction

The current comparison is CPU-only. Radeon 890M and XDNA/NPU results are deliberately not implied by these CPU numbers and need their own workload and evidence.
The Arm rows below are measured before → after changes in our engine or appliance images. The deployment cards then show the same current PKCS#11 workload on Ventuno Q and AI X1 Pro. The coloured tag says which acceleration model is involved — and many of the largest wins are software dispatch and implementation work, not a new chip.
This is CPU acceleration through the Arm cores and software implementation; no GPU or NPU acceleration is claimed or measured.
Its instruction-set evidence is separate: AES-NI/SHA-NI dispatch is verified, RSA uses a measured AVX-512 IFMA path, and the tested VAES variants were rejected because they were slower.
A hybrid signature pairs ML-DSA-65 with ECDSA P-256. A hybrid KEM pairs ML-KEM-768 with X25519. In the PKCS#11 v3.3 mechanisms we measured, the component secrets are combined inside the HSM. The hybrid result is therefore a direct operation measurement, not a total made by adding two independent benchmark rows.
The Workshop lets you compare these direct hybrid rows with their ML-DSA/ML-KEM and ECDSA/X25519 controls at one worker and whole-platform scale. That exposes whether the classical component, the PQC component, or worker contention is dominating.

chunks.title: PQC Hardware Acceleration — AccelerationIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: PQC Hardware Acceleration
Component: AccelerationIntroduction

256 coefficients all get the same treatment, which is exactly what SIMD does best, inside the CPU with no transfer cost. Offload is hard: the retry loop, key decoding and SHAKE sampling all bounce between stages.
Millions of small, independent hash calls. Hash instructions help directly (if the variant matches the core’s hash), SIMD can run several tree paths side by side, and a hash engine that takes a whole signature per call can shine.
Area. Our ML-DSA design used 81% of the LUTs and 95% of the block RAM. Each SLH-DSA Keccak lane cost about 14k LUTs after a redesign, so eight lanes (~130k) would not fit on the whole chip.
Clock. The clock can tick only as fast as the longest logic path allows, and that path grows as the design grows. Our 4-lane engine missed 250 MHz by 10 picoseconds and ships at 240 MHz.
Where the FPGA wins: SLH-DSA-SHAKE signing, today’s engine on every platform
Reprogramming. Unlike an ASIC, the fabric can be rewritten in the field. Our KV260 ships one complete image; we also tested swapping whole images at runtime (“profiles”: ML-DSA signers ⇄ SLH-DSA hash engine, live on the board, with the crypto services restarting). AMD’s modular alternative — partial reconfiguration, which swaps one slot while the rest keeps running — we documented but did not use.

chunks.title: PQC Hardware Acceleration — AccelerationIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: PQC Hardware Acceleration
Component: AccelerationIntroduction

A real system never runs one algorithm. It runs ML-KEM and ML-DSA for new sessions, SLH-DSA for long-lived signatures, RSA and ECC for everything not yet migrated, and AES and SHA-2 for the traffic — and the list will change as standards evolve. Acceleration has to follow that list without being rebuilt every time.
So the KV260 carries two profiles and loads one at a time: mldsa (two whole-signature ML-DSA-65 signers) or hashsig (a 4-lane Keccak engine for SLH-DSA-SHAKE), both with the same behaviour monitor. One command switches them live — the crypto services stop, the image is checked and loaded, the services restart. Whatever the loaded profile does not cover runs on the ARM cores.
GPUs win on throughput, not latency. Every launch has a fixed cost, lanes run in lock-step groups, and memory delays are hidden only when thousands of independent operations are in flight — perfect for signing 50,000 certificates, poor for one TLS handshake.
ASICs share the FPGA’s limits — bus transfers, one engine shared by many cores, a fixed area budget — and add their own: the design is frozen at tape-out, takes years and a large up-front investment, and cannot follow a new parameter set or a revised standard. Their reward is the highest clock and lowest power of any option.

chunks.title: PQC Hardware Acceleration — AccelerationIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: PQC Hardware Acceleration
Component: AccelerationIntroduction

Read the two tables together. A complete, side-channel-protected ML-DSA + ML-KEM engine fits in about a tenth of a square millimetre of 5 nm silicon, and lattice ASICs run in milliwatts or less. The same engines in an FPGA need a mid-sized part like our K26 — far more silicon and power — because programmable logic pays for its flexibility:
Buying it instead of building it: commercial PQC hardware IP
Constant-time means the circuit takes exactly the same time and follows the same steps whatever the secret key is, so a stopwatch learns nothing. It is cheap. Masking goes further: every secret value is split into random pieces (“shares”) that are processed separately and only recombine at the end, so the power drawn or radio noise emitted at any moment is unrelated to the key. It defeats power and electromagnetic analysis — but every share has to be carried, refreshed with fresh randomness and recombined carefully, which costs extra area, randomness and time, and the cost grows with the number of shares.
Published, not measured by us. Our own KV260 engines were built for speed and have not yet been evaluated against power or electromagnetic analysis — a planned later phase.
Can an ASIC be reprogrammed? Partly — it depends where the “recipe” lives

chunks.title: PQC Hardware Acceleration — AccelerationIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: PQC Hardware Acceleration
Component: AccelerationIntroduction

Many crypto engines are microcoded: fixed hardware (multipliers, Keccak, memories) follows a stored list of steps, like a kitchen following a recipe card. If that card is in writable memory, a signed update can change the step order, the parameter sets or fix a bug — but never add hardware the chip lacks. If the card is burned into ROM, nothing changes after manufacture. Adams Bridge is microcoded, and its microcode is in ROM.
The practical middle path for crypto agility in silicon: put the stable building blocks (Keccak, NTT, modular multiply) in hardware and keep each scheme’s steps in updatable firmware — most of the ASIC’s efficiency, much of the FPGA’s flexibility.
NPUs are arrays of 8-bit multiply-accumulate units fed a pre-compiled neural-network graph, designed to tolerate rounding. PQC needs exact arithmetic on 23-bit (ML-DSA) and 12-bit (ML-KEM) numbers, and Keccak is bitwise logic with no multiplication at all.
We evaluated the i.MX 95’s eIQ Neutron NPU for PQC and ruled it out on paper (not prototyped): it is reached only through compiled model graphs, its int8 quantisation is lossy, every NTT stage would need a round trip back to the CPU, and the dominant cost in our traces is Keccak, which no multiply-accumulate array can express. We use the NPU to monitor the appliance’s crypto behaviour instead.

chunks.title: PQC Hardware Acceleration — FpgaLimitsLab
chunks.content:
Module: PQC Hardware Acceleration
Component: FpgaLimitsLab

An assembly line moves one step every time the bell rings. Between two bells, every station must finish its piece of work — so the bell can ring only as fast as the slowest station allows. On an FPGA the bell is the clock, and the slowest station is the critical path: the longest chain of LUTs and wires between two registers.
A CPU’s clock is fixed by the chip designer. An FPGA’s clock is whatever your own design can manage — add more lanes and the wires get longer and more crowded, the critical path grows, and the clock you can run drops. You can split a slow station into two (pipelining), but that costs registers, area and an extra cycle of latency.
The fabric could sign ~2.5× faster than we can feed it. The limit is on the ARM side — Amdahl’s law: speeding up part of a job can never beat the part you left alone.

GPUs trade latency for throughput: each launch costs a fixed start-up time, and memory delays are hidden only when many independent operations are in flight. That is why GPU PQC results are quoted at batches of thousands.
The fabric is fast — but data must travel CPU → fabric → CPU, and the CPU keeps its share
One signature, not to scale: ARM work · transfer · fabric work
Amdahl’s law: if the fabric only takes over part of each operation, the rest caps the gain.
ML-DSA keeps key decoding, ExpandA, copying and PKCS#11 on the ARM cores for every signature.
SLH-DSA is almost pure hashing, so nearly the whole operation moves into the fabric.
Same board, same fabric, opposite results: that is the FPGA lesson in one picture. The “FPGA limits” step shows the area, clock and sharing limits behind it.
Hard-wired and efficient — but fixed at tape-out, and still one engine behind a shared bus
Every core that wants a signature waits its turn for the single engine — the same sharing problem as an FPGA.
A new parameter set, a revised standard or an algorithm broken after tape-out means new silicon. That is why many chips pair a fixed Keccak or NTT block with firmware, rather than hard-wiring a whole algorithm.
A giant grid of 8-bit multiply-add units — PQC needs exact 23-bit arithmetic and bit shuffling

Module: PQC Hardware Acceleration
Component: ModelVisuals

The contrast with GPUs is instructive: NVIDIA cuPQC runs on the GPU’s general-purpose CUDA cores, which do exact integer arithmetic. Even research that does push lattice-style math onto 8-bit tensor units (TensorFHE) splits every 32-bit number into four 8-bit pieces and relies on those neighbouring general-purpose cores to put them back together. A fixed-function NPU has no such neighbour.
fabric: millions of Keccak calls
ML-DSA numbers are mod q = 8,380,417 (23 bits) — they do not fit in 8 bits
Results must be exact; NPU quantisation rounds by design
Keccak/SHAKE is XOR, AND, NOT and rotate — no multiplication at all
Each NTT stage would need a round trip back to the CPU
What we use it for instead: watching the appliance’s behaviour

chunks.title: PQC Hardware Acceleration — OffloadLab
chunks.content:
Module: PQC Hardware Acceleration
Component: OffloadLab

Every offload is a delivery run: pack the data, hand it over the bus (DMA), flush the caches so both sides see the same memory, wait for the accelerator, then unpack the answer. That costs roughly the same whether the truck carries one box or thirty — so an accelerator only wins if it is so much faster per box that it earns back the trip.
A CPU has several cores, but an accelerator block is usually one shared machine — like one espresso machine in an office. Four people queuing does not make four coffees at once. Worse, if the people who find it busy go and make instant coffee instead, they are served faster than waiting would take, but with a much worse result.
C · The school bus: batch throughput vs single-operation latency
A GPU is built to finish a mountain of identical work, not to finish one piece quickly. Each launch has a fixed start-up cost; its thousands of lanes run in lock-step groups; and it hides slow memory by switching to other work while waiting. All three only pay off when there are thousands of independent operations in flight.
One signature can use a handful of lanes and still pays the full launch cost — the CPU, built for low latency, finishes first. And ML-DSA’s retry loop means a batch is only as fast as its unluckiest signature.

chunks.title: PQC Hardware Acceleration — PlatformExplorer
chunks.content:
Module: PQC Hardware Acceleration
Component: PlatformExplorer

Step 3A above is the current seven-platform matrix: use it for common classical, pure PQC and hybrid comparisons. These 2026-09 experiments isolate software and KV260 FPGA changes on a different signature-focused workload. They teach causality and must not be read as that common CPU ranking.
Between the two runs our engine moved ML-DSA onto hand-written NEON (SIMD) assembly, reworked SLH-DSA’s hashing, and the KV260 loaded its SLH-DSA hash-engine bitstream. Nothing about the silicon changed.
Ed25519 was not touched by the update and still moved ~16% on the i.MX 95 — the size of ordinary run-to-run and load differences. Read the 5–45× changes as real; ignore differences of a few tens of percent between runs.
The cleanest way to credit an acceleration: same machine, same engine, one feature on or off, runs alternated. Left: letting SLH-DSA’s SHAKE use the M4’s SHA-3 instructions. Right: running ML-DSA/ML-KEM on AWS-LC’s hand-written NEON code instead of portable Rust.
SHA-3 instructions: +17–21%. Real, but small next to AES’s 7–13× — the M4’s wide cores already run the software Keccak well. Even with it, SLH-DSA-SHA2 still signs about 7× faster than SLH-DSA-SHAKE on this chip.
AWS-LC NEON: about 4× for ML-DSA signing and verifying, 7–8× for key generation. Hand-scheduled SIMD code is the biggest single CPU win we measured for lattice signatures. ML-KEM encapsulation and key generation stay on Rust in our build, which is why they show no change.

Accelerate shared building blocks, not whole algorithms
One Keccak engine serves ML-KEM, ML-DSA and SLH-DSA-SHAKE; one NTT engine serves both lattice schemes. A new algorithm built from the same blocks gets faster for free.
Our first plan did exactly this — but a per-hash Keccak engine lost to the CPU (1,481 µs fixed cost per call). Building blocks only pay off when each call carries a lot of work.
Offload whole operations only where the win is decisive
A whole-signature engine avoids the round trip and can be many times faster — but it only knows one algorithm and a few parameter sets.
Our SLH-DSA engine signs the SHAKE “s” sets 26–31× faster on the same board, and does nothing for the SHA-2 or “f” sets.
Always keep a software path for every algorithm
Hardware is an optimisation, never the only implementation: if the accelerator is missing, busy or does not know the parameter set, the CPU does the work.
Our engine falls back to ARM when the FPGA is busy or absent, and verification always stays on ARM. Every accelerated result is checked against the software path.
Route by configuration, not by code change
A routing table decides which algorithm goes to which accelerator, so a new standard or a broken parameter set is a configuration change.
Our engine prints its routing at start-up, e.g. “shake=Fpga sha2=Cpu”, and can be told to ignore the hardware entirely (a switch we use for on/off measurements).
Reprogram the hardware when the workload changes
An FPGA can swap whole images (profiles) or single slots (partial reconfiguration). An ASIC cannot — which is why ASIC PQC engines fix their parameter sets up front.
We swap ML-DSA and SLH-DSA profiles live on the KV260; Caliptra’s Adams Bridge ASIC supports ML-DSA-87 and ML-KEM-1024 only.
Prefer general instructions over fixed engines on the CPU
A SHA-3 or SIMD instruction helps every algorithm that uses the primitive, now and later — the most agile acceleration there is.

chunks.content:
Module: PQC Hardware Acceleration
Data: circuits

ML-DSA-65 matrix × vector (NTT + multiply)
The A·y step: 5 forward NTTs, 6×5 pointwise products, 6 inverse NTTs
One Keccak-f[1600], 53 cycles per permutation
Permutation core + batching and host interface (the engine that lost to the CPU)

Watches the appliance’s crypto activity; present in both profiles
Control + DMA + interconnect (ML-DSA image)
Register control, two DMA engines, crossbars — the “plumbing”
Put N copies of the engine on the chip so N cores can use one each at the same time. Throughput grows with N — until the chip is full or something else becomes the bottleneck.
Our ML-DSA profile has two whole signers (24.4k LUTs each). Result: 404 → 523 signatures/s at 4 workers — but an earlier single-signer build had already reached 535/s (a different build and clock, so not a clean comparison) — the ARM-side work, not the signers, was the limit. Duplicating a circuit only helps if the circuit is the bottleneck.
Make one engine faster by giving it internal lanes that work on the same operation at once. Every request gets the speed-up, but requests still go one at a time.
Our SLH-DSA engine has 4 Keccak lanes working on one signature: co-simulation went from 218 ms (1 lane) to 114 ms (2) to 60 ms (4). Eight lanes would not fit on the chip.
Share one engine with a queue — and fall back
All cores send requests to one engine; a scheduler queues them (or sends overflow back to the CPU). Cheap in area, but the engine becomes a shared resource.
Our engine routes a request to the FPGA when it is free and to the ARM cores when it is busy. Four signing threads got the same 14.3/s as one, and the overflow on ARM (~30× slower) pushed p99 latency to 2.7 s — a queue in front of the engine is the planned fix.
Match the design to the bottleneck: duplicate when the engine is saturated and area allows; add lanes when single-request latency matters; queue when requests are bursty and area is tight — and always keep the CPU as the overflow path.

chunks.content:
Module: PQC Hardware Acceleration
Data: models

The baseline: one instruction works on one 64-bit number at a time.
Portable C / Rust reference code on any core
One cook, one pan. Every onion is chopped one at a time, by hand, in order. It always works and it runs on any kitchen, but the speed is set by how fast one pair of hands can go.
This is what this module measures every other model against. The pseudocode in FIPS 204 and FIPS 205 is written as one step after another, and both standards permit any mathematically equivalent procedure.
A post-quantum signature is thousands to millions of small, repetitive steps. Doing them one at a time wastes most of what a modern chip can do in parallel.
Our boards before tuning: SLH-DSA-SHAKE-128s took 12.3 s per signature on the KV260 Cortex-A53.
One instruction, many numbers: Arm NEON/SVE, Intel/AMD AVX2 and AVX-512.
Arm NEON (128-bit), SVE/SME; x86 AVX2 (256-bit), AVX-512 (512-bit) and AVX-512 IFMA
The same cook now uses a wide blade that chops four or eight onions in one stroke. Nothing about the recipe changes — the cook simply does the same motion on a whole row at once.
Lattice schemes are a perfect match: an ML-DSA polynomial is 256 small numbers that all get the same treatment, so a 128-bit NEON register handles 4 at once and a 512-bit AVX-512 register handles 16. AVX-512 IFMA is a related x86 feature that speeds selected large-integer multiply-accumulate work. All of this stays inside the CPU, so there is no transfer cost at all.
It only helps when the program actually dispatches to a matching vector implementation. Hash-heavy SLH-DSA is one long chain of dependent hashes per tree path, so it needs a different trick (hashing several independent paths side by side). CPU flags alone do not prove that ML-DSA, ML-KEM, ECDSA or X25519 is using AVX-512.
Our engine routes native ML-DSA/ML-KEM through AWS-LC’s hand-written AArch64 NEON code. On the AI X1 Pro, AVX-512F/IFMA is exposed and AWS-LC RSA-PSS-2048 signing measured 2.08× faster at one worker (1.99× whole-platform) than its masked control. The tested additional AVX2 ML-KEM candidate did not improve saturated whole-platform throughput; do not infer an AVX-512 PQC path from CPU flags.
Dedicated instructions that do a whole hash or cipher round in one step.
Arm: AES, PMULL, SHA-256, SHA-512, SHA-3 (EOR3/RAX1/XAR/BCAX). x86: AES-NI, PCLMULQDQ, SHA-NI
A kitchen gadget built for one job — an apple corer. For that one job it beats any knife by a mile. For anything else it is useless, and if your kitchen doesn’t own one you are back to the knife.
This is why the SAME algorithm runs at very different speeds on cores of different generations. Which hash an SLH-DSA variant uses (SHA-2 or SHAKE) decides whether the core’s gadget helps at all.
Owning the gadget is not the same as using it: our AES ran in software on every board until a build flag was set. And a gadget is not always a big win — switching on the M4 Pro’s SHA-3 instructions sped SHAKE up by only about 20%.

chunks.title: PQC Risk Management — Introduction
chunks.content:
Module: PQC Risk Management
Component: Introduction

Quantum computers exploit quantum mechanical properties to solve certain mathematical problems exponentially faster than classical computers. Most critically, Shor's algorithm — running on a sufficiently powerful quantum computer — can factor large integers and solve discrete logarithm problems in polynomial time, which would break RSA, Diffie-Hellman, and elliptic curve cryptography that protect virtually all internet communications today.
The arrival of a cryptographically relevant quantum computer (CRQC) will break the asymmetric cryptography that protects virtually all digital communications. Risk management provides the framework for understanding when this threat becomes real, what assets are exposed, and how to prioritize migration efforts.
“This means that even if quantum computers are a decade away, organizations must begin the migration to post-quantum cryptography today to avoid having their cryptographically protected data exposed once quantum computers become operational in the future.”
— NIST IR 8547, Transition to Post-Quantum Cryptography Standards (final, October 2026).
Discover every cryptographic asset in your organization and map quantum vulnerability exposure.
Assign likelihood and impact scores to each risk, calculate composite risk levels, and estimate exposure windows.
Rank risks by severity, align with compliance deadlines, and allocate migration resources where they matter most.

chunks.title: PQC Risk Management — Introduction
chunks.content:
Module: PQC Risk Management
Component: Introduction

PQC risk management introduces several concepts specific to quantum-era threats. Understanding these is essential for building an effective risk register.
A Cryptographically Relevant Quantum Computer is one powerful enough to break RSA, ECC, and Diffie-Hellman key exchange. Quantum computers already exist; none published to date is cryptographically relevant, and the gap between the two is large. Published expert estimates for CRQC arrival vary widely — commonly spanning the 2030s and beyond — and they are opinion surveys, not measurements, so treat any single date as a planning assumption you choose rather than a forecast. Plan against the date you would regret being wrong about.
HNDL attacks involve adversaries capturing encrypted data today with the intent to decrypt it once quantum computers become available. Data with long confidentiality requirements (healthcare records, classified information, financial data) is already at risk even though quantum computers don't yet exist.
Quantum risk is quantified as Likelihood x Impact on a 1–5 scale for each dimension, producing a risk score from 1 to 25. Likelihood considers the probability that the asset's algorithm will be broken within its required protection lifetime. Impact considers the business, regulatory, and reputational consequences of a breach.

chunks.title: PQC Risk Management — Introduction
chunks.content:
Module: PQC Risk Management
Component: Introduction

A common scoring mistake is to rank likelihood by an algorithm's classical strength. Against a CRQC that ranking inverts. Under Shor's algorithm, what matters is the public-key size and math family relative to the quantum resources needed to break it — not how many years a classical attacker would need.
ECC-256 is as urgent as RSA-2048. Classically, a 256-bit elliptic curve looks far stronger than a 2048-bit RSA modulus. But Shor solves the elliptic-curve discrete-log problem with fewer logical qubits than it needs to factor RSA-2048 — so a CRQC reaches ECC-256 at least as early (not sourced in the Library). Both belong in the same top-urgency band.
Scoring rule: weight likelihood by Shor-breakability and key size, not classical key-strength. Asymmetric public-key algorithms (RSA, ECC, DH) share the same critical band; symmetric ciphers and hashes are only weakened (Grover), so doubling key length restores their margin. Source: Applied Quantum PQC Migration Framework §3 (Risk Scoring).
This workshop walks you through a structured three-step quantum risk management process:
For CISOs and security leaders, quantum risk management is not a future concern — it's a present-day requirement. Regulatory bodies worldwide are setting migration deadlines, and the HNDL threat means sensitive data is already at risk.
• NIST IR 8547 (final, October 2026): quantum-vulnerable digital signature algorithms deprecated after 2030, disallowed under NIST standards and guidelines after 2035

chunks.content:
Module: PQC Network Testing & Validation
Component: PQCTestingExercises

Your OT/SCADA network includes Modbus TCP, DNP3, and TLS-protected historian connections. You cannot perform active scanning — any injected packets risk disrupting safety systems. Use passive discovery to classify traffic and identify which connections are plaintext, classically encrypted, or quantum-safe. Produce a risk-ranked inventory.
Modbus TCP appears as plaintext (no encryption at all) — highest risk. TLS 1.2 with CBC mode is present on the historian. DNP3 uses HMAC-SHA-256 (authentication only, no confidentiality). Only one segment uses hybrid TLS. Critical finding: three connections transmitting operational data with zero cryptographic protection.
VPN Gateway Pre-Migration Scan
Before upgrading your VPN headend to support IKEv2 with ML-KEM, scan all VPN-adjacent endpoints to understand the current state. Identify which branch offices use legacy IKEv2 configurations, which use modern DH groups, and which could already negotiate hybrid PQC if the headend supported it.
VPN gateway shows DH Group 14 (2048-bit) — quantum-vulnerable and scheduled for NIST deprecation after 2030. RSA-2048 certificate also flags for replacement. SSH bastion uses legacy curve25519 key exchange without hybrid. The cloud proxy is already using X25519+ML-KEM-768 hybrid TLS — ahead of the VPN.
Satellite Link Performance Impact

chunks.title: PQC Network Testing & Validation — PQCTestingExercises
chunks.content:
Module: PQC Network Testing & Validation
Component: PQCTestingExercises

Your organization has remote sites connected via VSAT satellite links with 600ms RTT. Before mandating pure PQC for all VPN tunnels, benchmark the performance impact. Test classical, hybrid, and pure-PQC configurations to determine which meets your latency SLA (<2 second VPN setup time).
Satellite link results are stark: classical IKEv2 SA setup is 4.8 seconds (already at SLA limit). In this scenario, hybrid PQC increases this to 7.2 seconds (+50%). Pure PQC with ML-KEM-768 reaches 95 seconds — completely unusable for interactive applications. Recommendation: satellite sites require hybrid PQC only; pure PQC mandate must include WAN latency exemptions.
Legacy Server Interop Failure Analysis
After enabling hybrid PQC on your corporate clients (Chrome 130+), help desk tickets spike. Users report intermittent TLS connection failures to internal applications. Use the interoperability matrix to diagnose which server configurations reject the hybrid ClientHello and why.
Chrome sends an oversized hybrid ClientHello (it adds about 1.2 KB: a 1,216-byte key share vs 32 bytes). Legacy TLS 1.2 servers with small receive buffers reject the connection. Servers with default TLS 1.3 settings work correctly because the client can fall back to a classical key exchange the server supports. Root cause: 3 internal applications still on TLS 1.2 with default buffer sizes. Fix: update TLS 1.2 configurations or accelerate those apps to TLS 1.3.

chunks.title: PQC Network Testing & Validation — PQCTestingExercises

Your IoT device vendor claims their ML-KEM implementation is "quantum-safe." Before deploying 50,000 field devices with this firmware, conduct a TVLA assessment. Identify whether the implementation uses masking and whether the NTT stage leaks key material under power analysis.
The unmasked reference implementation leaks at the NTT stage — t-test values well above the 4.5-sigma threshold. The Key Load and Polynomial Multiplication stages also show statistically significant leakage. The vendor's claimed "quantum-safe" status refers only to algorithm selection, not implementation security. Require first-order masking countermeasures before production deployment.
EU 2026 Inventory Milestone Strategy

chunks.title: PQC Network Testing & Validation — PQCTestingExercises
chunks.content:
Module: PQC Network Testing & Validation

For enterprise IT in inventory phase against the EU 2026 milestone, one workable order is passive network discovery, then active endpoint scanning, then certificate inventory via a CLM platform. The durations (about 1-2 weeks, 1 week and 2-3 days) and the example tools (CryptoNext COMPASS for passive discovery, pqcscan for active scanning, Keyfactor AgileSec for certificate inventory) are an illustration from this module, not sourced figures or recommendations. CryptoNext Security is listed as a technology collaborator in the NCCoE Migration to Post-Quantum Cryptography project, and NIST SP 1800-38B states that naming a product is not intended to imply recommendation or endorsement by NIST or NCCoE. For the COBOL systems, SP 1800-38B describes IBM Application Discovery and Delivery Intelligence (ADDI) as a static analysis tool that analyzes COBOL application source files; scope the COBOL systems as their own work item.

chunks.title: PQC Network Testing & Validation — PQCTestingIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: PQC Network Testing & Validation
Component: PQCTestingIntroduction

Testing post-quantum cryptography deployments is fundamentally different from classical crypto testing. Three forces make it uniquely challenging:
In GSMA PQ.06 (27 May 2026), enabling hybrid key negotiation with seven additional ML-KEM-1024 exchanges raised the average time to establish one IKE SA from 140 ms to 335 ms. Certificates add a second kind of cost: a pure PQC certificate CHAIN reaches ~17KB by this module's arithmetic, more than the 14,600-byte initial window of 10 segments (RFC 6928), so that flight takes more than one round trip. (One ML-DSA-65 certificate is ~5-6KB: a 1,952-byte public key plus a 3,309-byte signature plus X.509 overhead. It is the chain that breaks the budget.)
A hybrid ClientHello adds about 1.2 KB (the X25519MLKEM768 key share is 1,216 bytes against 32 bytes for X25519 alone; RFC 10024 §4.1). Faulty server implementations silently reject the larger message. Pure PQC clients fail on servers that accept only hybrid key exchange.
ML-KEM and ML-DSA reference implementations leak key material via power analysis at the NTT stage. A fixed-vs-random TVLA test alone is not enough for lattice crypto: it also flags public-data leakage, so labs add specific tests on the secret-handling stages.
Classical crypto testing assumed algorithms were computationally secure if implemented correctly. PQC testing adds a third dimension: are implementations physically secure against side-channel attacks on the new mathematical structures?

chunks.title: PQC Network Testing & Validation — PQCTestingIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: PQC Network Testing & Validation
Component: PQCTestingIntroduction

A TCP connection costs one round trip before application data can flow (RFC 9293 section 3.5), and a TLS 1.3 handshake costs one more (RFC 8446 section 2). On high-latency links (satellite, WAN) every round trip costs more. NIST SP 1800-38C's TLS 1.3 tests, at a simulated 133 ms round-trip time with an ECDSA P256 server certificate, found “essentially minimal impact on the handshake time”: the hybrid key exchange even with Kyber-1024 was “just a few milliseconds slower” than P256. The extra round trips NIST reported came from other causes: a 3% loss probability led to “almost an extra round-trip’s delay”, and in the QUIC tests Dilithium authentication data from the server above the initial congestion window (~14 KB) or the amplification window (~3.6 KB) can add one. This changes where you need to optimize.
Two complementary approaches cover different parts of the crypto inventory problem:
A network tap or SPAN port feeds traffic to a passive probe. The probe inspects TLS/SSH/IKEv2 handshakes in-flight — classifying cipher suites, detecting hybrid algorithm negotiation, and flagging quantum-vulnerable connections — without injecting any packets.
An active scanner initiates connections to target endpoints, probing for PQC algorithm support, TLS version, cipher suites, and certificate details. Results reveal what each server can negotiate, not just what it currently does.

chunks.title: PQC Network Testing & Validation — PQCTestingIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: PQC Network Testing & Validation
Component: PQCTestingIntroduction

Best practice: run passive discovery first to build the full inventory, then use active scanning to validate PQC readiness endpoint-by-endpoint before cutover.
Performance testing for PQC requires a layered methodology — because the bottleneck is rarely where you expect.
Measure current TLS handshake latency, IPSec SA setup time, and throughput under realistic load. Document hardware specs — CPU, NIC offload capabilities, available RAM.
X25519+ML-KEM-768 adds about 1.2 KB to ClientHello (1,216-byte key share vs 32 bytes) but minimal compute overhead on modern hardware. The real latency impact is path-, MTU-, and middlebox-dependent, so test the actual network paths.
A pure ML-DSA-65 certificate chain (~17KB, this module's planning assumption, not a measurement) exceeds the largest initial window that RFC 6928 permits, 10 segments (at most 14,600 B), and a sender may start with a smaller one. On high-latency links, this forces extra round-trips. Measure the whole chain your server actually sends, not one leaf certificate, and test against your worst-case latency links.
Emulate realistic concurrent user counts with application-layer traffic (video, collaboration). VIAVI TeraVM and Keysight CyPerf simulate this at scale; PQC-LEO (open source) provides lab-grade benchmarking on x86 and ARM without commercial licensing. CPU utilization on VPN headends can spike dramatically without hardware offload.

chunks.title: PQC Network Testing & Validation — PQCTestingIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: PQC Network Testing & Validation
Component: PQCTestingIntroduction

Lab benchmarks measure clean-path overhead, but enterprise networks have middleboxes, hardware constraints, and bursty traffic that amplify PQC costs far beyond what simple protocol testing reveals.
Enterprise traffic flows through Next-Generation Firewalls (NGFWs) and Secure Web Gateways (SGWs) that decrypt, inspect, and re-encrypt every TLS session. Each inspection point must complete a full PQC handshake with both the client and the destination server — effectively doubling the cryptographic workload per hop.
A typical enterprise proxy chain (NGFW → SGW → DLP) means each connection pays the PQC handshake cost three times. Where VIAVI's white paper Testing, Measuring and Managing PQC Migration reports a sharp drop in connection rate on a clean path, enterprises with inspection chains should expect a much larger one (our estimate).
Most network security appliances rely on dedicated silicon for RSA and ECC acceleration. These chips cannot accelerate ML-KEM or PQ signature algorithms — devices fall back to general-purpose CPUs under PQC workloads.
Under high connection rates, this can reduce appliance capacity by 50-90% (our estimate) compared to hardware-accelerated classical crypto. Vendors acknowledge that many existing deployments will require new hardware for PQC at scale.

chunks.title: PQC Network Testing & Validation — PQCTestingIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: PQC Network Testing & Validation
Component: PQCTestingIntroduction

PQC overhead hits hardest in environments with short-lived, bursty connections. Login storms (morning surges, post-outage reconnections), API spikes, and microservice authentication chatter all pay the full PQC handshake cost per connection.
Unlike persistent VPN tunnels that amortize setup cost over hours, bursty workloads continuously create new TLS sessions. VIAVI testing showed web pages loading 48× slower with PQC — a metric driven by repeated short connections, not raw crypto speed.
TLS session resumption allows returning clients to reuse previously negotiated parameters via Pre-Shared Keys (PSK), skipping the expensive PQC key exchange entirely. VIAVI's white paper says this eliminates 80-90% of the PQC performance impact for returning users.
Combined with hardware acceleration (AVX2/AVX-512 or FPGA accelerators for lattice operations) and hybrid mode (PQC + classical), organizations can reduce the production impact to manageable levels. The key is measuring these mitigations under realistic conditions — not assuming lab results translate to production.

chunks.title: PQC Network Testing & Validation — PQCTestingIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: PQC Network Testing & Validation
Component: PQCTestingIntroduction

VIAVI's white paper Testing, Measuring and Managing PQC Migration reports testing on Dell R6625 hardware with HAProxy (TLS) and Strongswan (IKEv2) against more than a million emulated users: markedly fewer connections per second, lower throughput, client response times an order of magnitude higher, and VPN tunnel setup rates cut to a fraction. The paper sits behind a registration wall, so its other figures are not reproduced here. Those results represent the floor — enterprise middlebox chains multiply them further.
RFC 9794 (Informational, June 2025) defines the terminology for post-quantum/traditional hybrid schemes; it does not set protocol rules. The two rules below are this module's test practice, not RFC requirements:
At least one component algorithm must be supported by both parties. A pure-PQC client cannot connect to a classical-only server and vice versa — there's no shared algorithm to fall back to.
For confidentiality, all hybrid components must execute successfully. A hybrid where only the classical component works provides no quantum protection — the session must fail or fall back, not silently degrade.

chunks.title: PQC Network Testing & Validation — PQCTestingIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: PQC Network Testing & Validation
Component: PQCTestingIntroduction

The mechanism itself is in the protocol document, not in RFC 9794. For TLS 1.3 the hybrid key exchange construction (draft-ietf-tls-hybrid-design, published as RFC 9954, Informational, July 2026) concatenates the two component shared secrets and uses the result in the key schedule in place of the (EC)DHE secret, so a session only gets a hybrid secret if both components completed. It describes a non-hybrid result as the expected outcome only when the hybrid-aware endpoint is willing to downgrade (§1.4), so a test should confirm that any fallback is a visible, intended outcome.
Test coverage must include: hybrid client → hybrid server, hybrid client → classical-only server (fallback path), and pure-PQC client → hybrid server (should fail per policy at most enterprises). The Open Quantum Safe test server at test.openquantumsafe.org provides a reference endpoint for each algorithm combination.
Test Vector Leakage Assessment is a widely used method for detecting side-channel leakage in cryptographic implementations. Its non-specific test compares fixed-input and random-input trace groups; its specific tests target chosen intermediate values.
A non-specific fixed-vs-random test flags any input-dependent difference, including leakage of public data such as ciphertexts, so a failing result does not by itself show that secret data leaks. PQC labs therefore add specific tests on the operations that handle secrets: the NTT, sampling and, in ML-KEM, the Fujisaki–Okamoto re-encryption.

chunks.title: PQC Network Testing & Validation — PQCTestingIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: PQC Network Testing & Validation
Component: PQCTestingIntroduction

The adapted TVLA approach for lattice crypto targets specific operations:
The NTT (Number Theoretic Transform) is the core of lattice operations. Unmasked implementations consistently leak at this stage. First-order masking mitigates single-trace attacks but higher-order leakage can persist — requiring additional analysis rounds.
Tools: Keysight Inspector Crypto 3 (commercial leakage testing), ChipWhisperer (open source, power analysis + fault injection). CMVP has no approved non-invasive attack test metrics yet: SP 800-140F §6.2 says “No additional requirements at this time”.
What the standard is. ISO/IEC 17825 sets non-invasive attack mitigation test metrics for checking conformance with ISO/IEC 19790 at Security Levels 3 and 4. ISO lists the 2016 edition as withdrawn on 19 January 2024 ; ISO/IEC 17825:2024 is the current edition.
What CMVP has defined. NIST SP 800-140F (March 2020) replaces ISO/IEC 19790 Annex F, and its §6.2 “Approved non-invasive attack mitigation test metrics” reads “No additional requirements at this time”. ISO/IEC 17825 is named only in the August 2021 draft of SP 800-140F Rev. 1 (with ISO/IEC 20085-1 and -2), which NIST still lists as a draft.

Where side channels land in a validation today. CMVP Implementation Guidance 12.A says: “Until requirements of SP 800-140F are defined, non-invasive mechanisms fall under ISO/IEC 19790:2012 Section 7.12 Mitigation of other attacks.” If a module was purposely designed, built and publicly documented to mitigate specific attacks, that section applies and its assertions (AS12.01 to AS12.04, as applicable) must be addressed.
Not found. No CMVP statement says that ISO/IEC 17825 testing is required or accepted for a certificate, and SP 800-140F defines no approved metric, so a TVLA result is not an approved CMVP test metric.
For how a Common Criteria or EUCC evaluation looks at side-channel attacks on post-quantum code (AVA_VAN.5), see Common Criteria, EUCC & eIDAS Certification .
Sources: ISO catalogue pages above; NIST SP 800-140F (March 2020) abstract and §6.2; SP 800-140F Rev. 1 draft (August 2021) §6.2; FIPS 140-3 Implementation Guidance (last update 19 August 2026) IG 12.A, Additional Comments and Resolution.
Before performance testing, interoperability, or TVLA, a cryptographic implementation must be functionally correct. NIST's Cryptographic Algorithm Validation Program (CAVP) checks this: the implementation is tested through the Automated Cryptographic Validation Protocol and, if it passes, receives an algorithm certificate. That is not a module certificate.

chunks.title: PQC Network Testing & Validation — PQCTestingIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: PQC Network Testing & Validation
Component: PQCTestingIntroduction

A FIPS 140-3 certificate comes from a separate program, the Cryptographic Module Validation Program (CMVP), which validates the whole module. The module certificate lists its approved algorithms, which (apart from a few vendor-affirmed functions) are backed by algorithm certificates. Where a law, policy or contract requires FIPS 140-3 validated modules — US federal systems, for example — algorithm validation is one prerequisite, not the whole requirement.
ACVP messages are JSON exchanged over HTTPS . The client registers the algorithm capabilities it implements, the server generates matching test vector sets (the prompt), the implementation computes its answers and uploads them (the response), and the server returns a disposition for each vector set . A vector set passes only when every test case in it passes, and even then the pass is not itself the validation . The .req/.rsp request and response files often associated with NIST test vectors belong to ACVP's predecessor, the CAVS tool (e.g. SHAVS §6.2.1 ), which the CAVP page lists as deprecated by ACVTS .

chunks.title: PQC Network Testing & Validation — PQCTestingIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: PQC Network Testing & Validation
Component: PQCTestingIntroduction

For PQC algorithms like ML-KEM and ML-DSA, the ACVP sub-specifications define test types for key generation, encapsulation and decapsulation, and signature generation and verification . FIPS 203 and FIPS 204 expose internal interfaces that take the randomness as an input, which is what lets a test vector fix it . ACVP testing does not cover everything: the same sub-specifications leave out zeroization of intermediate values, DRBG strength, and incorrect-length keys and signatures.
PQC is not free at scale. Larger keys and signatures, plus heavier key generation, change the load profile of every endpoint that terminates a handshake. Before a wave cutover, size the infrastructure: model the per-handshake cost increase against peak connections-per-second, not just average load.
A completed hybrid or pure-PQC handshake is positive proof: both endpoints negotiated, exchanged, and verified post-quantum material end to end. It is the cheapest, most trustworthy verification signal you have — far stronger than a config flag or an inventory record. Instrument your edge to count negotiated PQC handshakes as a live migration KPI: the curve climbing toward the 100% target is your real cutover evidence, and a stalled curve surfaces silent interop failures the inventory can't see.
Sources: Applied Quantum PQC Migration Framework §6 (Infrastructure & Performance) and §7 (Validation).

Pure PQC clients send ClientHello messages up to 1,536 bytes. When a server's TCP MSS is 1,460 bytes (standard Ethernet), the ClientHello spans 2 TCP segments, which is inside the initial window of up to 10 segments that RFC 6928 applies. Cloudflare reported that some middleboxes assume the ClientHello fits in one packet, which can cause silent failures. Use pqcscan to probe affected endpoints and verify they handle oversized ClientHellos correctly.

chunks.title: PCI Certification — PciSections
chunks.content:
Module: PCI Certification
Component: PciSections

This lesson covers four PCI programmes: PTS HSM, PIN Security, P2PE and key management operations. It does not cover PTS POI, card production and provisioning, 3-D Secure, or MPoC and CPoC.
PCI has two very different kinds of evidence, and most mistakes about payment HSMs come from mixing them up. Device approval says a product model was designed and evaluated to PCI’s device requirements. Entity assessment says an organisation runs its payment operations — PIN processing, encryption, key management — to PCI’s operational requirements. This section is about the first: PCI PIN Transaction Security (PTS) Hardware Security Module (HSM) approval.
Everything PCI-specific in this lesson comes from public PCI SSC pages, which are cited next to each statement. Where a sentence is this module’s own reading or advice, it says so. Documents in the PCI Document Library are named by title and date only; their content is not used here.
PCI SSC describes the PTS HSM standard as providing guidance for designing HSMs to meet the security needs of the financial payments industry, “and for protecting those HSMs up to the point of initial deployment. Other security requirements apply at the point of deployment for the management of HSMs involved with the financial payments industry.”
That sentence sets the boundary. An approval tells you about:
a device model, at the hardware and firmware versions named on its listing;
evaluated against one major version of the PTS HSM requirements (v3.x, v4.x, v5.x);

chunks.title: PCI Certification — PciSections
chunks.content:
Module: PCI Certification
Component: PciSections

by an independent PCI-recognized laboratory: “Independent PCI-Recognized Laboratories evaluate HSMs against PTS HSM security requirements. PCI SSC reviews evaluation reports, approves PTS HSM devices, and provides a listing of approved devices.”
This module reads the page’s “other security requirements” at deployment as entity questions — how a bank, processor or cloud operator installs, administers or keys the device — answered by PIN, P2PE or KMO assessments (the boundary lesson below). That mapping is the module’s own reading. PCI says who must validate, or use a listed product, is not its call: “Compliance programs for all PCI SSC standards are managed by the payment brands.”
The listing’s field definitions say: “Version refers to the version of the security requirements the device has been evaluated against. Each approval class may follow its own version release schedule.” They also say: “Approval numbers are assigned by PCI SSC at the time of approval and remain the same for the life of the device’s approval.” So read a listing as a pair: the approval number and the requirements version behind it. This module’s own advice, not a PCI requirement: when you rely on a listed device, compare the vendor, model, hardware and firmware versions and the approval number you deploy with the listing.

chunks.title: PCI Certification — PciSections
chunks.content:
Module: PCI Certification
Component: PciSections

PCI’s Device Testing and Approval Program Guide is listed in the Document Library on 18 May 2026; the feed gives its title and date and no version number. Its content is not used in this module.
An HSM approval can be restricted: “Approval is valid only when deployed in an environment meeting at least the security requirements of a Controlled Environment as defined in the Key Management Operations Security and Test Requirements and in the device’s PCI HSM Security Policy.” Unrestricted approval “is valid in any operational environment.” The listing states which, under Additional Information. Two real listings, read on 30 October 2026, show both: payShield 10K (4-40266) reads “Approved usage: Restricted” and Atalla HSM AT1000 (4-70041) reads “Approved usage: Unrestricted” . This module’s reading: a restricted approval moves a question to the deployment, to be answered where the device is installed.
These are scheme clocks — what PCI’s device programme is doing. They are not market PQC deadlines, which this module never types into prose. The dates in the listing’s expiry table say when device approvals expire; no PCI page used here ties them to quantum.

chunks.title: PCI Certification — PciSections
chunks.content:
Module: PCI Certification
Component: PciSections

“A FIPS 140-3 Level 3 HSM is PCI PTS HSM approved.” It is not: PCI SSC says laboratories evaluate HSMs against the PTS HSM requirements, and PCI SSC reviews the reports, approves the devices and lists them. Whether another PCI programme accepts a FIPS certificate in place of a PTS approval is set in that programme’s own requirement text, which this module does not state.
[c.area, c.blogSays, c.forTheAnchor])} strongFirstColumn testId="pci-v5-changes" />
The cloud is now structural. The HSM standard page says the standard “has been expanded to include Multi-tenant HSMs, which are HSMs intended for concurrent usage by multiple organizations at a cloud services provider”. The v5.0 announcement says the multi-tenant requirements “have been consolidated and expanded” and adds modules for Key-Transfer Functionality, Remote Administration and “HSM Solution Security”. The listing’s function types already include “HSM Solution (v5 only)” and “Multi-tenant HSM (v4 only)”.
Device-security cryptography got stricter. The announcement says device-security keys need an effective key strength of at least 128 bits, TDES is no longer permitted for device security purposes, and weak methods such as CBC-MAC are prohibited for firmware or application authentication. These are about protecting the HSM itself. The same announcement says the update includes “support for post-quantum cryptography considerations”, and it names no post-quantum algorithm and no deadline.

The announcement says several legacy sections (key-loading devices, logical security and specific functionality-based sections) “have been removed or restructured”, with responsibilities redistributed across new modular evaluation areas or aligned with the PCI Key Management and Operations (KMO) framework. This module’s reading: a vendor cannot assume that a control evaluated under v4 is still evaluated at the device under v5 — some of it may now be the operator’s to show.
Hardware Security Module (HSM) Modular Security Requirements · HSM Security Requirements Modifications: Summary of Changes · Device Testing and Approval Program Guide (all listed 18 May 2026) · PTS HSM Technical Frequently Asked Questions (listed 28 October 2026).
Vendors, buyers and assessors all ask the same question: what does PCI require for post-quantum cryptography? The honest answer from PCI SSC’s standard announcements and listing definitions used for this module, , is short: they name no PQC algorithm, no parameter set and no PQC deadline. What exists there is a listing notation and post-quantum wording in the v5.0 announcement. PCI SSC’s Quantum Leap interviews are awareness material in which the interviewees, not PCI SSC, name algorithms such as ML-KEM and ML-DSA. Each is read below, with what it does not say.

chunks.content:
Module: PCI Certification
Component: PciSections

The listing’s field definitions explain the notation in full. For v3-and-higher HSMs, “the HSM has been evaluated to determine if it supports PQC. Specifically, the support in the API and/or processing of the device of cryptographic algorithms that are considered secure against a cryptanalytic attack by a quantum computer. The details of the PQC implementation are stated in the security policy … This notation is for the existence of PQC support. Details of the degree of post-quantum readiness can be obtained from the device vendor.”
the Security Policy states the details, including all cryptography and its CSPs.
how far the product is “post-quantum ready” — ask the vendor.
The absence of a notation is just as narrow. None of the three real HSM listings read for the workshop shows one on 30 October 2026 (4-40266, 4-70041 and 4-40069). The 4-40069 listing is v1.x, which the PQC field’s “v3 and higher” scope does not cover. That describes the listed firmware, not the vendor’s roadmap.
This part is the module’s own reasoning, not a PCI statement. Symmetric keys (TDES, AES) are not where a quantum computer helps most; the most exposed links are the public-key ones, wherever a symmetric key is distributed or a message is signed with RSA or elliptic-curve cryptography. Two things in the public PCI pages bear on that:

chunks.title: PCI Certification — PciSections
chunks.content:
Module: PCI Certification
Component: PciSections

Key blocks. PCI’s Key Blocks 101 post calls Key Blocks “a standard way of protecting the integrity of cryptographic keys and of associating them with their intended use”, for both TDEA and AES keys. A Utimaco cryptographer says in the Quantum Leap interview: “We currently lack standards for key management, asymmetric key blocks, and other protocols.” That is Utimaco’s view, not a PCI requirement.
Firmware and certificate signatures inside the device and the vendor PKI. The v5.0 announcement says device-security keys such as firmware authentication keys need an effective strength of at least 128 bits and prohibits weak methods such as CBC-MAC for firmware or application authentication; it names EC-SDSA for certain use cases and no post-quantum signature algorithm.
The PCI DSS v4.0.1 announcement does not mention post-quantum cryptography. It describes a limited revision with “no additional or deleted requirements”, says PCI DSS v4.0 would retire on 31 December 2024 so that v4.0.1 is “the only active version” of the standard, and says the 31 March 2025 effective date for the new requirements did not change. The requirement text of the standard itself is not reproduced in this module.

chunks.title: PCI Certification — PciSections
chunks.content:
Module: PCI Certification
Component: PciSections

“A PCI listing’s PQC flag means a specific PQC algorithm or parameter set is approved.” The flag means support exists. The “Quantum Leap” interview series on PCI SSC’s blog is described as “a resource for payment security industry stakeholders to share information about how they are taking steps to ensure their systems are crypto-agile into the future”: awareness material, in which the interviewees’ statements are their own, not PCI requirements.

After “FIPS Level 3 is not PTS approval”, many people ask whether FIPS certificates count anywhere in PCI. Whether a PCI operational standard accepts a FIPS 140-2 or 140-3 certificate in place of a PTS HSM approval — and what it requires the listing or certificate to match — is set in that standard’s own requirement text. That text is not a public PCI SSC page, so this module does not state it. Read it in the current standard, and check which version applies.
One fact that is not PCI’s may matter when you do: NIST’s CMVP schedule moves all FIPS 140-2 certificates to the Historical List on 21/22 September 2026.
P2PE has a version rule of its own: v3.2 replaced v3.1 for new submissions and reassessments on 1 January 2026, and existing v3.1 validations are unaffected.

chunks.title: PCI Certification — PciSections
chunks.content:
Module: PCI Certification
Component: PciSections

The PCI PIN Security Standard “provides requirements and testing procedures for the secure management, processing, and transmission of PIN data at ATMs and attended and unattended point-of-sale (POS) terminals”. Version 3.1 was released on 12 March 2021 as a minor revision. The Document Library lists the PIN Security Requirements and Testing Procedures with the date 11 March 2021.
This section uses only what public PCI SSC pages say about PIN Security: the v3.1 announcement, the Key Blocks 101 post and the PTS listing definitions. The requirement text itself is not a public PCI SSC page and is not used here.
Requirements and testing procedures for the secure management, processing and transmission of PIN data at ATMs and attended and unattended POS terminals.
The v3.1 announcement clarifies that a PCI-approved HSM’s approval “may be contingent on being deployed in controlled environments or more robust (e.g., secure) environments as defined in ISO 13491-2 and in the device’s PCI HSM Security Policy”, and that this is noted in the Additional Information column of approved PTS devices.

chunks.title: PCI Certification — PciSections
chunks.content:
Module: PCI Certification
Component: PciSections

The Standard requires implementation of Key Blocks, “a standard way of protecting the integrity of cryptographic keys and of associating them with their intended use”, usable for both TDEA and AES keys. v3.1 incorporated revised effective dates for key block implementations, announced in July 2020 in response to stakeholder feedback about the impact of COVID-19; take dates from the current Standard and PCI’s bulletin “Revisions to the Implementation Date for PCI PIN Security Requirement 18-3”, not from this table.
v3.1 incorporated the earlier-announced revisions to the dates and scope for implementing encrypted key injection: the dates were deferred three years and the applicability changed from POI v3 and higher devices to POI v5 and higher devices (the change was announced in November 2020).
v3.1 suspended the effective dates for entities to support ISO Format 4 PIN blocks (announced March 2021), to be reevaluated for the migration from TDEA to AES. The PTS listing definitions say HSM v4 and higher devices supporting PIN processing “are required to support ISO PIN Block Format 4” (AES).
Normative Annex C is titled “Minimum and Equivalent Key Sizes and Strengths for Approved Algorithms”; v3.1 rewrote it for clarity and to align with the nomenclature used in NIST publications. This module states nothing about the annex’s content.

chunks.title: PCI Certification — PciSections

Module: PCI Certification
Component: PciSections

PQC: none of the public PIN Security pages used here (the v3.1 announcement and Key Blocks 101) mentions post-quantum cryptography. The listing’s PQC notation (see the PQC lesson) records only that PQC support exists.
P2PE requirements are intended “to protect payment account data via encryption from the point it is captured in the merchant’s payment device to the point it is decrypted in a solution or component provider’s environment”. Merchants using PCI-listed P2PE solutions have fewer applicable PCI DSS requirements. P2PE Assessors “are qualified and trained by PCI SSC to perform independent assessments of P2PE solutions, components, and applications”.
P2PE v3.2 is current: PCI SSC announced it on 30 June 2025 as a minor revision, and the Council is developing P2PE v4.0. The Document Library lists the P2PE Standard and its Summary of Changes on 30 June 2025. v3.1 submissions were accepted through 31 December 2025 and had to complete quality review by 31 March 2026; from 1 January 2026 all new submissions and reassessments must comply with v3.2, and existing v3.1 validations are unaffected. The P2PE standard documents are not public PCI SSC pages, so this module does not describe their structure or requirement numbers: check the current version.
The public P2PE pages used here (the program page and the v3.2 announcement) do not mention post-quantum cryptography. This module therefore states no P2PE algorithm requirement and no deadline.

chunks.content:
Module: PCI Certification
Component: PciSections

The PCI Key Management and Operations (KMO) Standard v1.0 was published on 14 September 2026, together with the KMO Program Guide. It “defines security requirements, test requirements, and guidance for entities involved in the operation and management of systems that use cryptographic keys for the security of account data”, across the whole key lifecycle “from generation through to destruction”.
Scope: initially PIN and P2PE keys — “consolidating, aligning, and updating those requirements”. Future revisions “may address additional specific needs of other data types such as those covered by the PCI Card Production Standards”.
One assessment, two key types: “a single PCI KMO assessment to validate the security for both key types, with the resultant KMO Listing able to be referenced by a PCI P2PE implementation (where appropriate).”
Cloud and remote HSMs: KMO “directly addresses the use of cloud-based and remote HSMs and has been created in alignment with the recently published PCI HSM v5 requirements.”
Design: modular, “a single source for requirements covering key management operations”, and “assess-once-use-many”.
Who: “Entities involved in the management of cryptographic keys that are intended for use with PIN or P2PE data. This includes entities operating HSM-as-a-Service systems which may operate on those keys.”

The KMO standard document is not a public PCI SSC page and is not used here. The announcement’s consolidation language does not by itself say what becomes of the existing PIN and P2PE key-management requirements, and the KMO page leaves the question of who must validate to “organizations that manage compliance programs, such as a payment brand, acquirer, or other entity”.
