chunks.title: Platform Engineering & PQC — Introduction
chunks.content:
Module: Platform Engineering & PQC
Component: Introduction

In this module's illustration, every layer of the software delivery pipeline embeds classical cryptography: ECDSA P-256 signing keys for container images, RSA-2048 certificates for TLS sessions to Vault and the Kubernetes API server, and HMAC-SHA-256 for webhook secrets. A cryptographically relevant quantum computer (CRQC) running Shor's algorithm breaks all public-key schemes currently used in CI/CD infrastructure.
Adversaries are recording encrypted TLS sessions today — Vault mTLS, kube-apiserver traffic, registry pulls — and storing them for decryption once a CRQC is available. Even if your certificates expire in 90 days, the data they protected may remain sensitive for 10–20 years. This makes TLS key exchange (ECDHE) the most critical asset to migrate, ahead of signing keys.
Before migration, you must know what to migrate. CI/CD pipelines embed cryptographic primitives at every stage — many invisible to standard security scanners because they live inside tool configuration rather than source code.
Use a Cryptographic Bill of Materials (CBOM) scanner (Syft, OCI manifest scan, or custom Prometheus queries) to produce a machine-readable inventory of every algorithm OID in your running cluster.
Container image signatures anchor the entire supply chain trust model. If the signing key is broken, every image in your registry can be forged. Current tools — cosign and Notation — use ECDSA P-256, which Shor's algorithm breaks in polynomial time.

chunks.title: Platform Engineering & PQC — Introduction
chunks.content:
Module: Platform Engineering & PQC
Component: Introduction

Notation — we found no vendor documentation that Notation or its AWS Signer plugin supports ML-DSA, so treat any ML-DSA support as unconfirmed.
cosign / Sigstore — Sigstore says (June 2025) it wants to enable post-quantum signing as soon as possible and has added ML-DSA to its protocol specification for client experiments; its services will adopt post-quantum algorithms once vetted implementations are in the Go ecosystem. No date is given, the post does not mention cosign, and the Rekor transparency log must also be migrated.
SLH-DSA for SBOMs — stateless hash-based signatures preferred for long-lived attestation documents (20+ year validity). See the SBOM module for what those attestation documents actually contain.
Docker Content Trust (DCT) — being fully retired with the Notary v1 service (full shutdown 8 December 2026; the upstream Notary v1 codebase is no longer maintained). Docker names Sigstore/Cosign and Notation as the alternatives; its guidance says nothing about post-quantum signatures.
Infrastructure-as-Code tools bake classical cryptography into defaults that persist for years without active change. Terraform, Helm, and cert-manager all default to RSA-2048 or ECDSA P-256 — every resource provisioned without explicit PQC configuration is a quantum-vulnerable asset.

chunks.title: Platform Engineering & PQC — Introduction
chunks.content:
Module: Platform Engineering & PQC
Component: Introduction

Policy-as-Code ensures that quantum-vulnerable algorithm choices are caught at admission time — before resources enter the cluster. Both OPA Gatekeeper and Kyverno can block RSA/ECDSA algorithm OIDs in cert-manager Certificate resources, Ingress TLS annotations, and image signature attestations.
OPA Gatekeeper ConstraintTemplate — evaluates cert-manager Certificate.spec.privateKey.algorithm; rejects anything that doesn't start with "ml" or "slh".
Kyverno ClusterPolicy — verifyImages rule requires ML-DSA-65 cosign or Notation signature on all Pods in production namespace. Blocks unsigned or ECDSA-only images.
SLSA Build L3 (this module's projected PQC rule) — ML-DSA or SLH-DSA signature on build provenance; SLSA itself names no signature algorithm. Enforce via OPA Deployment annotation check.
Rollout strategy — deploy in Audit mode first (validationFailureAction: Audit), baseline violations for 2 weeks, then switch to Enforce after remediation window.
Continuous monitoring detects algorithm drift — when classical certs re-enter the cluster through CA fallback, manual issuance, or operator error. Four Prometheus-based exporters cover the full platform crypto surface.
SIEM integration (Splunk, Elastic, Datadog, Microsoft Sentinel) extends monitoring to cross-platform detection — catching algorithm-downgrade events, CI/CD OIDC token algorithm drift, and TLS cipher negotiation without ML-KEM.

chunks.title: Platform Engineering & PQC — Introduction
chunks.content:
Module: Platform Engineering & PQC
Component: Introduction

A phased migration protects against rollback failures and ensures compatibility with clients that haven't yet updated. The six phases progress from inventory to complete cut-over, with explicit rollback procedures at each step.
Key insight: Phases 1 and 2 (Root CA + TLS Key Exchange) address HNDL directly and should begin immediately, regardless of your CRQC timeline estimate. Even if a CRQC is 15 years away, encrypted traffic recorded today will be decryptable in 2039.
Inventory your CI/CD pipeline crypto assets, migrate container signing to ML-DSA, and enforce PQC policy across your Kubernetes cluster in the interactive workshop.
Sigstore and Notation migration to ML-DSA in CI/CD pipelines
TLS Key Exchange (X25519MLKEM768 hybrid)

chunks.title: Platform Engineering & PQC — PlatformEngExercises
chunks.content:
Module: Platform Engineering & PQC
Component: PlatformEngExercises

Six exercises map to the six workshop steps. Each exercise gives you a specific task to investigate in the interactive tool, then reveals the expected findings. Work through them in order — later exercises build on the crypto asset inventory you'll create in the first exercise.
1. HNDL Exposure Audit — Identify your highest-risk pipeline stage
In the Pipeline Crypto Inventory (Step 1), filter by HNDL Exposure: High and Migration Priority: Critical. Review the three assets in the Build stage. Which single asset poses the greatest harvest-now-decrypt-later risk and why?
The Vault mTLS session (build-vault-mtls) is the highest-risk asset. It uses ECDH P-256 key exchange, has an exposure window of 10+ years (secrets fetched by the pipeline may remain sensitive long after the session ends), and is classified as HNDL: High. An adversary recording Vault mTLS traffic today can decrypt every secret the pipeline fetched post-CRQC. The PQC replacement is X25519MLKEM768 hybrid TLS.
2. CRQC Countdown — Model your pipeline exposure under different threat scenarios
In the Quantum Threat Timeline (Step 2), select CRQC Year: 2030. Count how many pipeline assets have a data expiry year beyond 2030 — meaning data protected by them will still be sensitive when a CRQC arrives. Then switch to CRQC Year: 2035 and compare.

chunks.title: Platform Engineering & PQC — PlatformEngExercises
chunks.content:
Module: Platform Engineering & PQC
Component: PlatformEngExercises

Under a 2030 CRQC scenario, all 14 quantum-vulnerable assets are at risk because their exposure windows extend beyond 2030. Under 2035, the same 14 assets remain at risk — signature and certificate lifetimes are measured in decades, not years. For encrypted data this is the harvest-now-decrypt-later threat, which is independent of CRQC timeline because the exposure window starts when the data is captured (NIST IR 8547); for signatures the concern is forgery once a CRQC exists, which is not HNDL.
3. Signing Tool Comparison — Choose the right migration path for container signing
In the Container Signing Migration (Step 3), enter Compare mode and select Notation and cosign. Compare their PQC Readiness status and estimated PQC year. What does each tool's documentation let you conclude about ML-DSA support?
We found no vendor documentation that confirms ML-DSA support in Notation, and the Sigstore post (June 2025) does not mention cosign, so both are shown as unconfirmed; the post says it wants to enable post-quantum signing as soon as possible, has added ML-DSA to its protocol specification for client experiments, and gives no production date. Vendor timelines move quickly, so confirm current status before choosing a tool. Docker Content Trust (DCT) should be migrated immediately — Docker is fully retiring DCT and the Notary v1 service (full shutdown 8 December 2026), and the upstream Notary v1 codebase is no longer maintained.

chunks.title: Platform Engineering & PQC — PlatformEngExercises
chunks.content:
Module: Platform Engineering & PQC
Component: PlatformEngExercises

4. Policy Design — Write a cert-manager algorithm enforcement policy
In the Policy-as-Code Enforcer (Step 4), expand the "Block Non-PQC Certificate Algorithms" OPA rule. Study the Rego code. Then explain: (a) what trigger causes the violation, and (b) which string prefixes are used to identify PQC algorithms.
The violation fires when: (a) the resource is a cert-manager Certificate, and (b) the spec.privateKey.algorithm does not start with "ml" (ML-DSA family) or "slh" (SLH-DSA family). The string prefix check (startswith(lower(algo), "ml") / startswith(lower(algo), "slh")) is algorithm-agnostic for the ML-DSA parameter set — it matches MLDSA44, MLDSA65, and MLDSA87 without listing each variant explicitly.
5. Capacity Planning — Calculate TLS cert storage growth for a 500-cert cluster
In the Crypto Posture Monitor (Step 5), navigate to the Capacity Planner tab. Set TLS Certificates in Cluster to 500. Compare the etcd storage consumption between Classical and PQC. What is the storage multiplier and should this affect your migration decision?

chunks.title: Platform Engineering & PQC — PlatformEngExercises
chunks.content:
Module: Platform Engineering & PQC
Component: PlatformEngExercises

With 500 certs, etcd storage grows from ~1.5 MB (classical RSA-2048 key+cert at 3KB each) to ~7 MB (ML-DSA-65 at 14KB each) — approximately a 4.7× increase (this module's planning assumption, not a measurement). For most clusters, this is negligible relative to total etcd capacity (default 8 GB). The storage impact is NOT a reason to delay migration. The TLS handshake latency increase (12ms → 28ms, +133%) warrants more attention in high-throughput microservice environments.
6. Rollback Simulation — Navigate the rollback decision tree for a TLS failure
In the Platform Migration Planner (Step 6), expand the Rollback Decision Tree. Walk through this scenario: clients are reporting TLS handshake failures, the failure is on key exchange (not certificate validation), and affected clients do support TLS 1.3. What is the recommended rollback action?
The decision path leads to: "Revert ssl-ecdh-curve to X25519:P-256. The X25519MLKEM768 group is additive — removing it is non-breaking. File bug with client vendor for ML-KEM support." This is the correct approach because X25519MLKEM768 (ML-KEM-768 + X25519) is a hybrid — removing the ML-KEM component is safe for compatibility and does not break existing sessions. The classical X25519 continues to provide forward secrecy.

chunks.title: Platform Engineering & PQC — ContainerSigningMigration
chunks.content:
Module: Platform Engineering & PQC
Component: ContainerSigningMigration

Compare OCI artifact signing tools by PQC readiness, signature format, and migration path. Current tools use ECDSA P-256 — quantum-vulnerable signatures that must be migrated to ML-DSA before CRQC arrival.
Recommendation: Do not plan around Notation or cosign for ML-DSA signing yet: we found no vendor documentation that either supports ML-DSA, and Sigstore (June 2025) gives no production date for its services. For new deployments choose an OCI-native tool (Notation or cosign) and keep the signing key in a place where the algorithm can be swapped later. Avoid DCT (Docker Content Trust): it and the Notary v1 service are being retired, with full shutdown on 8 December 2026.

chunks.title: Platform Engineering & PQC — CryptoPostureMonitor
chunks.content:
Module: Platform Engineering & PQC
Component: CryptoPostureMonitor

Four Prometheus-compatible exporters cover the entire platform crypto surface. Each tool exposes key algorithm labels — enabling alert rules that fire when classical crypto is still active after your migration deadline.
Pre-built SIEM queries for detecting quantum-vulnerable cryptographic operations in your pipeline. Covers Vault signing key usage, cert-manager RSA issuance, CI/CD OIDC token algorithm, and TLS cipher negotiation.
Integration workflow: Enable these queries in Audit mode first to baseline volumes. Tune thresholds over 2 weeks before enabling alerting. Map alerts to your on-call rotation with 48-hour SLA for CRITICAL findings. Weekly SIEM digest reports should track percentage of operations using PQC algorithms — target 100% by your mandated migration deadline.
Quantify the infrastructure impact of migrating from ECDSA to ML-DSA and from X25519 to ML-KEM. Calculate storage growth, bandwidth increase, and latency overhead before your migration window.
Adjust your deployment parameters to estimate the storage and bandwidth impact of PQC migration.
The ACME certificate lifecycle with PQC overlay. Each step shows the current state (classical / hybrid / PQC-ready / algorithm-agnostic) and what changes are needed for a quantum-safe issuance pipeline via cert-manager with an ML-DSA-capable issuer.

chunks.title: Platform Engineering & PQC — CryptoPostureMonitor
chunks.content:
Module: Platform Engineering & PQC
Component: CryptoPostureMonitor

Let's Encrypt is targeting late 2026 for a staging environment that issues Merkle Tree Certificates (MTCs) and 2027 for a production-ready environment, and it is tracking ML-DSA in X.509 (RFC 9881) and TLS. Its post says the transition will take time. This module's advice: until post-quantum certificates are available from Let's Encrypt, use internal CAs (Vault PKI, EJBCA) for ML-DSA certificate issuance in production environments.

Use this decision tree when a post-migration incident occurs. Follow the questions to identify the root cause and the correct rollback action.
Timeline guidance: Phases 1 and 2 (Root CA + TLS Key Exchange) address the most critical HNDL exposure and should be completed first, regardless of CRQC timeline uncertainty. For each quantum-vulnerable crypto asset in your pipeline, calculate whether the data it protects will still need to be kept secret when a CRQC arrives. Assets whose data lifetime extends past the CRQC horizon are harvest-now-decrypt-later (HNDL) risks today.

Why Short-Lived Certificates Don't Protect a Recorded TLS Session
A Vault mTLS session using ECDH with a 1-hour certificate is still an HNDL target. The cert lifetime doesn't matter — what matters is how long the data transmitted in that TLS session must remain secret. A pipeline that fetches an API key valid for 10 years creates a 10-year HNDL window, regardless of the cert TTL.

chunks.title: PQC GRC — Introduction
chunks.content:
Module: PQC GRC
Component: Introduction

Where the SOC detects and responds, the GRC function measures, reports, and governs. It produces the instruments the board uses to oversee the program, the CISO uses to manage it, and internal audit uses to verify it.
Standard enterprise risk management assumes observable precursors, historical frequency, and bounded timelines. Quantum risk has none: CRQC estimates span 10 to 30+ years, there are no historical incidents to calibrate against, and the risk straddles technology, compliance, strategic, and operational categories at once. Logging it as "Low likelihood / High impact, review annually" is risk acknowledgment, not risk management.
The fix is not a separate quantum-risk framework. It is adapting the existing ERM framework so quantum risk receives the same structured treatment — risk-appetite statement, KRIs, escalation thresholds, board cadence — as every other top-tier risk.
Key Risk Indicators make governance operational. For PQC migration they cascade across three organizational levels — each serving a different audience at a different cadence. Every KRI carries a threshold that triggers a specific action; an indicator with no trigger is a chart, not a control.

chunks.title: PQC GRC — Introduction
chunks.content:
Module: PQC GRC
Component: Introduction

A quantum risk-appetite statement translates the board's intent into decision criteria the program can act on. Without it, every trade-off between migrating a costly legacy system and deferring it must be escalated, because no instrument defines which choice aligns with the board's intent. The statement operates at two levels.
These thresholds are illustrative — the right values depend on sector, regulatory environment, data profile, and risk culture. The requirement is that they exist, are specific enough to drive decisions, and are reviewed annually at board level.
PQC regulation is moving faster than most GRC teams appreciate. Annual review is too infrequent; quarterly is the minimum, and monthly is more appropriate in regulated sectors. The output is a quarterly Regulatory Horizon Report to the Steering Committee and risk committee, listing each development's jurisdiction, effective date, migration-plan implications, and required action.
The SOC's detection use cases depend on a queryable cryptographic-posture registry — which is a GRC asset. Beyond that registry, GRC produces four outputs the SOC consumes. The relationship is symbiotic, but only if both sides make their outputs consumable by the other; designing these data flows is a Phase 0 governance decision.

chunks.title: PQC GRC — Introduction
chunks.content:
Module: PQC GRC
Component: Introduction

The exception register as a suppression list. The SOC must ingest the exception and deferral register as a dynamic suppression list. Without it, cryptographic-drift detection rules generate constant alerts from legacy systems that are legitimately deferred — drowning out the genuine regressions the rules exist to catch.
An organization can migrate its own cryptography flawlessly and still be exposed through its vendors. GRC tiers third parties by how their readiness affects the migration.
For Tier 1 vendors, consider making a machine-readable CBOM (for example CycloneDX 1.6+) a procurement requirement — a control you choose, not an external mandate. A vendor who cannot produce one has a level of cryptographic visibility that should itself concern the organization. Maintain a documented substitution assessment for each — concentration on a single HSM vendor, CA, or crypto library is its own risk.
A multi-year transformation with significant budget and risk should face the same audit oversight as any comparable enterprise program. The key audit question is whether systems are actually migrated or only marked migrated — evidenced through an auditable artifact set (inventory database with timestamps, quarterly CBOM snapshots, SteerCo minutes, the board-approved risk-appetite statement, Regulatory Horizon Reports, vendor records, and the exception register).

chunks.title: PQC GRC — Introduction
chunks.content:
Module: PQC GRC
Component: Introduction

Insurance. Ask your broker whether your insurer's renewal questionnaire covers cryptographic inventories, migration plans or crypto-agility, and how the policy's cyber wording and any state-backed attack exclusion would treat a quantum-enabled attack. Keep the program's documentation presentable to underwriters either way: a documented, governed, measured program is easier to explain at renewal than an intention to "migrate when standards are ready."
A quantum cryptographic event is a confidence crisis before it is a technical incident: operational damage may take days, but trust damage begins with the first headline. The SOC playbooks own the technical response; GRC owns the external one — and it cannot be drafted during the event. Maintain pre-drafted templates, name the spokesperson and approval chain in advance, and exercise the communications leg in the same tabletop exercises that test the technical playbooks.
Expect an attestation surge after any public quantum event — counterparties and customers demand evidence of migration status. Maintain the evidence dossier so that answering is an export, not a project.

Notice the ~25% QBER when Eve intercepts every qubit (a wrong basis half the time, then a wrong bit half of those: 1/2 × 1/2 = 25%). Compare this with the ~0% QBER in the simulated clean channel.
Run BB84 without an eavesdropper using 16 qubits, then follow through to post-processing to see the complete key establishment pipeline.

Both the QKD secret and ML-KEM secret contribute entropy. The HKDF output is secure even if one source is compromised.

chunks.title: Quantum Key Distribution — QKDIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Quantum Key Distribution
Component: QKDIntroduction

Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) is a method of distributing encryption keys using the laws of quantum physics rather than mathematical hardness assumptions. Unlike PQC, which relies on computationally hard problems, QKD derives its security from the no-cloning theorem and the principle that measuring a quantum state inevitably disturbs it — providing information-theoretic security.
BB84, proposed by Bennett and Brassard in 1984, was the first QKD protocol. It uses single photons encoded in two conjugate bases to establish a shared secret key between two parties (Alice and Bob) while detecting any eavesdropper (Eve).
Alice generates random bits and encodes each in a randomly chosen basis: rectilinear (+) with states ↕/↔, or diagonal (x) with states ⤢/⤡. She sends the photons to Bob over a quantum channel.
Bob independently chooses a random basis (+ or x) for each photon and measures it. When his basis matches Alice's, the result is deterministic. When it doesn't, the result is random.
Alice and Bob publicly compare which basis they used for each position (without revealing the bit values). They keep only the positions where both used the same basis — the sifted key (~50% of transmitted bits).
They sacrifice a random sample of the sifted key to check for errors. If the QBER (Quantum Bit Error Rate) exceeds ~11%, eavesdropping is detected and the key is discarded.

chunks.title: Quantum Key Distribution — QKDIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Quantum Key Distribution
Component: QKDIntroduction

QKD technology has matured significantly since the first demonstration in 1989 (IBM Research, The early days of experimental quantum cryptography). Today, commercial systems are deployed by governments and telecom operators worldwide, though significant constraints remain.
Notable milestones: Micius satellite (China, 2016), Beijing-Shanghai 2,000 km backbone (2017), BT/Toshiba commercial metro network (UK, 2022).
Fiber-based QKD is limited to roughly 100 km per link due to exponential photon loss in optical fiber. Trusted node chains can extend range, but each relay is a potential point of compromise. Satellite QKD bypasses this fundamental constraint: free-space optical links through vacuum suffer no fiber absorption, and the atmosphere is thin (~10–20 km), meaning a low-Earth-orbit satellite pass traverses a relatively short atmospheric path. This makes satellites the leading approach for intercontinental and trans-oceanic quantum key distribution — including Earth-to-satellite, satellite-to-ground, and inter-satellite links.
Satellite acts as a moving trusted node between ground stations
Generates separate keys with each ground station, then relays
Demonstrated by Micius (China–Austria, 7,600 km; Liao et al., Satellite-Relayed Intercontinental Quantum Network)
Satellite must be physically secured (compromise exposes keys)
Satellite distributes entangled photon pairs to two ground stations
More technically demanding; requires high-fidelity photon sources

chunks.title: Quantum Key Distribution — QKDIntroduction

Microsatellite; space-to-ground quantum communication (2016)
Explore all satellite and terrestrial deployments interactively in the Workshop tab (Part 3: Global Deployments).
While QKD offers unique theoretical security guarantees, it faces significant practical limitations. NIST has expressed skepticism about QKD as a general-purpose solution, recommending PQC for most use cases.
Information-theoretic security (not based on computational assumptions)
Forward secrecy — past keys remain secure even if future technology advances
Cost: dedicated fiber, cryogenic detectors, specialized hardware
Side channels: real devices have implementation vulnerabilities
"NSA does not recommend the usage of quantum key distribution and quantum cryptography for securing the transmission of data in National Security Systems …" QKD addresses only the key distribution problem, requires special-purpose equipment, and is only proven secure under theoretical models that may not match real-world implementations.
NSA instead considers mathematically based cryptography a better alternative for protecting National Security Systems from future quantum computing developments.
In practice, QKD is most valuable when combined with PQC key encapsulation mechanisms. A hybrid approach uses both a QKD-derived key and an ML-KEM shared secret, combining them via HKDF so that security holds even if one source is compromised.

The combined key is secure as long as either the QKD channel OR the ML-KEM exchange remains unbroken — defense in depth.
Hardware Security Modules (HSMs) play a critical role in QKD deployments by providing tamper-resistant storage for QKD-derived keys and managing the key lifecycle. The integration follows standard PKCS#11 patterns.
Key Generation: QKD hardware generates shared secret via BB84 or similar protocol between endpoints.
HSM Import: QKD-derived key material is imported into the HSM via secure key injection (C_UnwrapKey or C_CreateObject).
Key Usage: Applications access QKD-derived keys through the HSM PKCS#11 API for encryption, MAC generation, or further key derivation.
Key Rotation: QKD continuously generates fresh keys; the HSM manages rotation and lifecycle (expiry, destruction).
Learn more about HSM operations and PKCS#11 workflows in the HSM & PQC Operations module .
QKD is being adopted primarily by governments and telecom operators who need the highest levels of communication security. China leads with the world's largest QKD infrastructure, while Europe is building a pan-continental network through the EuroQCI initiative.

chunks.title: Quantum Key Distribution — HSMKeyDerivationDemo
chunks.content:
Module: Quantum Key Distribution
Component: HSMKeyDerivationDemo

NIST SP 800-108 counter-mode KDF is a universal primitive used wherever a master secret must produce multiple purpose-specific keys. This demo uses QKD as the input source, but the same KDF applies to:
KEM Shared Secrets ML-KEM encapsulation produces a 32-byte random secret. SP 800-108 derives encryption, MAC, and IV keys with domain separation (label + context).
Pre-Shared Keys (PSK) TLS 1.3 external PSK or IPsec IKEv2 PSK imported into an HSM, then expanded via KBKDF to produce per-session traffic keys.
Password-Based (PBKDF2) CKM_PKCS5_PBKD2 derives key material from passwords. Often chained with SP 800-108 for key hierarchy (master → KEK → DEK).
Input: A single fixed-length key handle (e.g., QKD master secret) already in HSM storage
Output: One or more purpose-specific sub-keys, each never leaving the HSM
Use when: Key hierarchy expansion (master → KEK → DEK) must stay within the HSM security boundary
Where: Software layer or HSM via CKM_HKDF_DERIVE (PKCS#11 v3.0)
Input: Variable-length IKM + optional salt (extract phase), then context info (expand phase)
Output: Arbitrary-length OKM; each caller context produces independent key material
Use when: TLS 1.3 key schedule, QUIC, or Signal — where IKM arrives from a DH/KEM exchange in software

chunks.title: Quantum Key Distribution — HSMKeyDerivationDemo
chunks.content:
Module: Quantum Key Distribution
Component: HSMKeyDerivationDemo

This demo uses KBKDF because the QKD secret is imported as a non-extractable HSM key. HKDF would require the raw key bytes to be visible in the software layer — acceptable for KEM-based TLS but undesirable for QKD where the secret must never leave the HSM.
QKD scenario below: This demo follows the ETSI GS QKD 014 key retrieval API → PKCS#11 v3.0 HSM import → NIST SP 800-108 counter-mode KDF pipeline. Both Alice and Bob run identical steps independently — the session key is never transmitted.
GET /api/v1/keys/{SAE_ID}/1 Authorization: Bearer {client_cert}
Both Alice and Bob independently call their local QKD key managers. They request the same key_ID — the secret bytes are identical on both sides because they were produced by the QKD hardware.
Once imported, CKA_EXTRACTABLE = FALSE ensures the raw QKD secret never leaves the HSM. Only derived keys can be exported.
Live HSM — C_CreateObject returned CKR_OK · handle stored in HSMKeyInspector
Illustrative mode — enable Live HSM above to run real C_CreateObject.
The shared secret from a KEM or QKD channel has zero domain separation — if used directly as a key, the same 32 bytes would be reused for encryption, MAC, and IV across every session, allowing cross-protocol correlation.

chunks.title: Quantum Key Distribution — HSMKeyDerivationDemo
chunks.content:
Module: Quantum Key Distribution
Component: HSMKeyDerivationDemo

Counter-Mode KDF (SP 800-108) addresses this by deriving additional keying material from an existing key: K(i) = PRF(KI, [i] ‖ Label ‖ 0x00 ‖ Context ‖ [L]). Different Label values ("session-key-v1", "mac-key-v1") produce cryptographically independent sub-keys from the same master secret. The Context field (session ID below) carries per-session data. SP 800-56C Rev 2 defines Context as "a bit string of context-specific data", a subcomponent of the FixedInfo.
Choosing L: L is the requested length of the derived keying material in bits: L = 256 for a 256-bit AES key, L = 384 for a 384-bit key for HMAC-SHA-384, L = 512 for 512-bit material for HMAC-SHA-512 (an HSM call that takes a byte count would be given 32, 48 or 64 bytes). The label & context bind purpose and session so all three can be derived from the same QKD secret without leaking information between them.
Both HSMs derive the identical key independently. The session key is never transmitted over any network. The shared secret was established exclusively via the quantum channel.
Suitable for MACsec link-layer or IPsec ESP payload encryption.
The derived session key becomes the HKDF input keying material. RFC 9258 wraps it with an ImportedIdentity context that binds it to a specific hash and TLS version, preventing cross-protocol reuse. Used in ClientHello PSK extension — see Part 4 → TLS 1.3 tab for the live handshake demo.

chunks.title: Quantum Key Distribution — HSMKeyDerivationDemo
chunks.content:
Module: Quantum Key Distribution
Component: HSMKeyDerivationDemo

QKD continuously generates fresh key material. The HSM can be programmed to rotate session keys on a schedule by fetching a new key_ID from the QKD key manager and repeating the SP 800-108 derivation with an incremented context counter. See NIST SP 800-108 §5.1 .
Standards used: ETSI GS QKD 014 · PKCS#11 v3.0 · NIST SP 800-108 Rev.1 · RFC 9258 (TLS 1.3 PSK Import)

chunks.title: Quantum Key Distribution — PostProcessingDemo
chunks.content:
Module: Quantum Key Distribution
Component: PostProcessingDemo

Run BB84 with 64 qubits (no eavesdropper) to produce a sifted key for post-processing.
In real QKD, Cascade or LDPC codes correct bit errors introduced by natural channel noise (simulated here at 5%). This demo shows parity-check blocks — each block of 4 bits is checked for odd parity, and errors are located via binary search.
Privacy amplification uses a universal hash function (such as Toeplitz matrix multiplication) to compress the corrected key, mathematically removing any partial information Eve may have gained. For this browser demo, we simulate this compression step using SHA-256.
Combine the QKD-derived key with a PQC KEM shared secret (simulated ML-KEM-768) via HKDF. The resulting hybrid key is secure even if one source is compromised.
This key combines information-theoretic security from QKD with computational security from ML-KEM — defense in depth against both present and future threats.

chunks.title: Quantum Key Distribution — ProtocolIntegrationDemo
chunks.content:
Module: Quantum Key Distribution
Component: ProtocolIntegrationDemo

RFC 9846 (TLS 1.3) derives session keys from a shared secret produced by the key exchange (e.g., ECDH or ML-KEM). RFC 9258 adds an external PSK importer: a QKD key delivered via the ETSI GS QKD 014 REST API can be bound to a specific KDF hash and imported as a pre-shared key, replacing or augmenting the key-exchange-derived secret (not sourced in the Library).
ImportedIdentity { external_identity: key_ID, hash: SHA-256 }
The QKD key is the PSK: it is the input of the Early Secret; an (EC)DHE shared secret, if used as well, is the input of the Handshake Secret, and binder_key is derived from the Early Secret (RFC 9846 §7.1)
Without a PSK: Early Secret = HKDF-Extract(0, 0); the (EC)DHE shared secret enters at the Handshake Secret
With the QKD key as PSK (RFC 9258): Early Secret = HKDF-Extract(PSK=QKD key, 0); with psk_ke no (EC)DHE secret is used, with psk_dhe_ke it still enters at the Handshake Secret
RFC 9258 is an interface for importing external PSKs into TLS 1.3: imported PSKs use the binder label "imp binder", so a client and server negotiate the PSK if and only if both endpoints import it or neither does
This 32-byte secret becomes the TLS 1.3 PSK. It is never transmitted — both endpoints independently retrieved the same key_ID from their local QKD key manager.

chunks.title: Quantum Key Distribution — ProtocolIntegrationDemo
chunks.content:
Module: Quantum Key Distribution
Component: ProtocolIntegrationDemo

IKEv2 uses nonces Ni (initiator) and Nr (responder) in the IKE_SA_INIT exchange to derive SKEYSEED: prf(Ni | Nr, g^ir). When QKD is deployed on the same fiber backbone as an IPsec link, the QKD-shared secret can replace or be mixed into g^ir, making SKEYSEED information-theoretically secure even against a quantum adversary.
Initiator sends Ni (random nonce, 32 bytes) alongside DH proposal
“Nonces used in IKEv2 MUST be randomly chosen, MUST be at least 128 bits in size, and MUST be at least half the key size of the negotiated PRF.” A QKD-sourced random value meets this requirement while providing information-theoretic quality.
MACsec (IEEE 802.1AE) encrypts Ethernet frames with AES-GCM using a Secure Association Key (SAK). Normally the SAK is negotiated via MACsec Key Agreement (MKA). ETSI GS QKD 002 says QKD "may also be used to provide keys for the IEEE 802.1 MACsec layer 2 protocol"; this workshop's design derives the SAK from key material delivered through ETSI GS QKD 014. The same document says the overall security level of a QKD link encryptor "is determined by both the QKD component, and the link encryptor component", so the link is not information-theoretically secure end to end.
SAK injected; GCM nonce = Packet Number (PN) || IV. Frames encrypted at wire speed.

chunks.title: Quantum Key Distribution — ProtocolIntegrationDemo
chunks.content:
Module: Quantum Key Distribution
Component: ProtocolIntegrationDemo

MACsec supports GCM-AES-128, GCM-AES-256, and XPN variants for high-speed links. The SAK is a 128- or 256-bit AES key — exactly the output size produced by HKDF from a 256-bit QKD secret. In this workshop's design, the QKD-derived key stands in for the MKA-negotiated SAK.
Both link endpoints independently derive the same SAK. It is never sent over the wire.
SSH (RFC 4253) generates a 16-byte random cookie in both the client and server's KEXINIT messages to ensure neither party fully controls the session keys. The session ID H is computed as hash(V_C || V_S || I_C || I_S || K_S || e || f || K) where K is the DH shared secret. A QKD-sourced entropy value can replace or be mixed into K, making the session ID and all derived keys information-theoretically secure.
Client cookie (16 bytes) + Server cookie (16 bytes) — both randomly generated per RFC 4253 §7.1
“The cookie MUST be a random value generated by the sender. Its purpose is to make it impossible for either side to fully determine the keys.” QKD-sourced randomness provides information-theoretic quality for this role, exceeding CSPRNG guarantees.
Protocols that accept nonces or pre-shared keys can integrate QKD without protocol changes. Select a protocol to see the exact injection point, the relevant RFC clause, and a live simulation using a randomly generated mock QKD secret.

chunks.title: Quantum Threats — QuantumThreatsExercises
chunks.content:
Module: Quantum Threats
Component: QuantumThreatsExercises

Work through these scenarios to understand how quantum computing threatens current cryptography and why PQC algorithms are resistant. Each exercise pre-configures the Workshop — click "Load & Run" to begin.
1. RSA-2048 Under Quantum Attack
Use the Security Level tool to see how RSA-2048's 112-bit classical security drops to 0-bit quantum security. Compare with RSA-4096 to see that larger keys don't help against Shor's algorithm.
Notice that RSA-2048, RSA-3072, and RSA-4096 all drop to 0-bit quantum security. Key size increases provide no defense against Shor's algorithm.
Compare how Grover's algorithm affects AES-128 (a ~64-bit theoretical bound) versus AES-256 (~128-bit) in the Security Level tool. The practical takeaway: prefer AES-256 for long-term confidentiality.
The tool shows AES-128 at a ~64-bit Grover bound and AES-256 at ~128-bit. In practice Grover's enormous circuit depth makes even AES-128 far stronger than 64 bits, so NIST still rates AES-128 at security category 1 — but AES-256 (category 5) is the safer choice for long-term data.
3. Vulnerability Matrix: Who Survives?
Open the full vulnerability matrix to see every algorithm's exposure to Shor's and Grover's attacks. Identify which algorithms are broken, weakened, or safe.
All asymmetric algorithms based on factoring or discrete logs are marked "broken." Symmetric algorithms are "weakened" but survivable with larger keys. PQC algorithms are fully safe.
4. HNDL Risk: Healthcare Records

7. ECC Blockchain Under Quantum Attack

chunks.title: Quantum Threats — QuantumThreatsExercises
chunks.content:
Module: Quantum Threats
Component: QuantumThreatsExercises

A Bitcoin transaction is broadcast to the mempool but not yet confirmed. Google Quantum AI (Mar 2026) estimated that breaking secp256k1 ECDLP would require\u22641,200 logical qubits — roughly half prior estimates. Use the Security Level tool to compare secp256k1 with RSA-2048 and see why fast-clock CRQCs pose an on-spend threat before PQC migration.
secp256k1 would require an estimated\u22641,200 logical qubits — fewer than RSA-2048 (~1,537 per Gidney 2025). A fast-clock CRQC (superconducting) reaching this threshold could derive the private key from an exposed public key within the mempool confirmation window (~10 min for Bitcoin). Migration to PQC signatures is critical for blockchain infrastructure.
6. PQC Algorithms: Built for Quantum
Compare ML-KEM-768 and ML-DSA-65 in the Key Size Analyzer. Verify that their classical and quantum security levels are identical — no degradation under quantum attack.
PQC algorithms maintain identical classical and quantum security bits. Their security is based on lattice problems, not factoring or discrete logs, so Shor's algorithm provides no advantage.

chunks.title: Quantum Threats — QuantumThreatsIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Quantum Threats
Component: QuantumThreatsIntroduction

Classical computers store information as bits — each is definitively 0 or 1. A quantum computer uses qubits , which exploit two quantum phenomena to process information fundamentally differently.
Always in a definite state. N bits represent exactly one of 2N values at a time.
Superposition: exists in a combination of 0 and 1 simultaneously. Entanglement: qubits can be correlated so measuring one instantly determines the other. Together, N qubits hold a superposition over all 2N basis states at once — though a measurement still returns only one of them.
Key insight: Quantum speedup doesn't come from "trying all answers at once." It comes from carefully constructing interference patterns that amplify correct answers and cancel wrong ones. Only specific algorithms (like Shor's and Grover's) can exploit this structure.
Peter Shor showed in 1994 (Polynomial-Time Algorithms for Prime Factorization and Discrete Logarithms on a Quantum Computer) that a quantum computer can solve two hard mathematical problems exponentially faster than any classical computer:
RSA relies on the difficulty of factoring large numbers (N = p × q).
RSA-2048 requires ~1,537 logical qubits (Gidney 2025, down from the 2016-era ~4,098 estimate). A CRQC could factor it in under a week, not billions of years.
ECC (ECDSA, ECDH, EdDSA) and Diffie-Hellman rely on the hardness of discrete logarithms.

chunks.title: Quantum Threats — QuantumThreatsIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Quantum Threats
Component: QuantumThreatsIntroduction

Google Quantum AI (30 March 2026) gives, for the 256-bit elliptic-curve discrete logarithm on secp256k1, at most 1,200 logical qubits with at most 90 million Toffoli gates, or at most 1,450 logical qubits with at most 70 million Toffoli gates; its paper gives no estimate for P-256. All ECC variants (P-256, P-384, X25519, Ed25519) are vulnerable to Shor's algorithm.
Impact: Every public-key algorithm based on integer factorization or discrete logarithms — RSA, DSA, ECDSA, ECDH, EdDSA, DH — provides zero security against a quantum adversary. Key size increases do not help because Shor's algorithm scales polynomially.
Lov Grover showed in 1996 (A fast quantum mechanical algorithm for database search) that a quantum computer can search an unstructured database quadratically faster. This affects symmetric encryption and hash functions:
Practical note: Grover's algorithm is less threatening than Shor's. It provides only a quadratic speedup (halving security bits), and the algorithm requires sequential oracle queries — it cannot be parallelized effectively. The fix is simple: double the key size (AES-128 → AES-256).
A Cryptographically Relevant Quantum Computer (CRQC) is one powerful enough to run Shor's algorithm against production-size keys. Experts disagree on when this will happen, but major agencies are planning for it now:

chunks.title: Quantum Threats — QuantumThreatsIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Quantum Threats
Component: QuantumThreatsIntroduction

Bottom line: Whether a CRQC arrives in 2030 or 2040, migration takes years. Organizations handling long-lived data (government, healthcare, finance) must begin now because of the Harvest Now, Decrypt Later threat.
The most urgent quantum threat is not future code-breaking — it's data being intercepted today for future decryption. This attack is called Harvest Now, Decrypt Later (HNDL), also known as "Store Now, Decrypt Later" or "retrospective decryption."
Adversaries intercept encrypted traffic today (VPN, TLS, email) and store it.
Data is archived — storage is cheap. Adversaries wait for quantum capability.
Once CRQC is available, Shor's breaks the key exchange. Symmetric keys are recovered, all data is decrypted.
HNDL targets confidentiality. HNFL targets authenticity and integrity. Adversaries collect signed artifacts today — firmware images, certificate chains, code-signing blobs — and store them. Once a CRQC arrives, Shor's algorithm recovers the signer's private key, enabling forged signatures on any document or binary.
Collect signed artifacts — firmware images, CA certificates, code-signing blobs. Public-key material is often publicly accessible.
Archive for years to decades. No active attack is needed — the adversary waits for quantum capability.
CRQC runs Shor's algorithm on the signer's public key, recovers the private key, and forges arbitrary signatures retroactively.
• Firmware signing (medical devices, industrial, automotive)

chunks.title: Quantum Threats — QuantumThreatsIntroduction
chunks.content:

Component: HNDLTimeline

Fast-clock CRQCs (superconducting, photonic) arriving first enable "on-spend" interception of unconfirmed transactions. Slow-clock CRQCs (trapped ion, neutral atom) enable "at-rest" attacks on archived ciphertext — the HNDL threat modeled here. Google Quantum AI, Mar 2026

chunks.title: Quantum Threats — HNFLTimeline
chunks.content:
Module: Quantum Threats
Component: HNFLTimeline

Calculate when signing credentials must migrate to PQC. Any credential still valid when a CRQC arrives can be retroactively forged — an adversary recovers the signing private key and issues fraudulent signatures on any document, firmware, or certificate.
Fast-clock CRQCs (superconducting, photonic) enable "on-setup" key compromise during handshakes. Once a CRQC can forge signatures, every credential signed by a compromised CA becomes retroactively forgeable — the HNFL threat modeled here. Google Quantum AI, Mar 2026
Key difference from HNDL: HNFL does not require the adversary to intercept any traffic. Signed artifacts — certificate chains, firmware images, code-signing blobs — are often publicly accessible. Any organization relying on RSA or ECDSA signatures must rotate to ML-DSA or SLH-DSA before a CRQC arrives, or every past and future signature becomes forgeable.

chunks.title: Quantum Threats — quantumConstants (data)
chunks.content:
Module: Quantum Threats
Data: quantumConstants

Shor's algorithm factors N in polynomial time. Current best published estimate: Gidney 2025 (Google Quantum AI, arXiv:2505.15917) — 1,409 logical qubits active at peak, 1,537 including idle patches (“fewer than 1600”), factoring RSA-2048 in under a week on fewer than 1M noisy physical qubits. Supersedes Chevignard–Fouque–Schrottenloher (ePrint 2024/222, published at CRYPTO 2025), which reached 1,730 logical qubits but at 2^36 Toffoli gates, and the older 2016-era estimate, where 2n+2 gives 4,098 (arXiv:1611.07995) — matches CRQC_QUBIT_THRESHOLDS.rsa2048.
Larger key does not help — Shor's scales polynomially with key size, and the revised circuits scale as n/2 + o(n). Gidney 2025 estimates 2,043 logical qubits for RSA-3072, as reported by Chevignard et al. (EUROCRYPT 2026) — down from the older 2016-era 2n+2 estimate, which gives 6,146 (arXiv:1611.07995). Note this is BELOW the 2,124 qubits the best space-optimised attack needs for a 256-bit elliptic curve at comparable classical security.
Even 4096-bit RSA provides zero post-quantum security. Gidney 2025 (Table 5) gives a revised estimate for this key size: 2,692 logical qubits and 4.0e+10 Toffoli gates, far below the older 2016-era 2n+2 figure of 8,194 (Häner–Roetteler–Svore 2016, arXiv:1611.07995).
Google Quantum AI (Mar 2026) gives \u22641,200 logical qubits (or \u22641,450) for the 256-bit ECDLP on secp256k1; its paper gives no estimate for P-256, and this module applies the secp256k1 figure to P-256 as its own approximation. Fewer qubits needed than RSA at equivalent security. Low-end estimate; other published work puts 256-bit ECC at ~2,330+ logical qubits (Roetteler et al. 2017, arXiv:1706.06752).
Shor’s algorithm applies to elliptic-curve cryptography at every curve size; a larger curve needs more logical qubits (Roetteler et al. 2017: 3,484 for a 384-bit curve).
Curve25519 ECDH falls to Shor's just like NIST curves. This module applies Google Quantum AI’s Mar 2026 secp256k1 estimate (\u22641,200 logical qubits) to Curve25519 as its own approximation; the paper gives no estimate for it. Low-end estimate; other published work puts 256-bit ECC at ~2,330+ logical qubits.
EdDSA signatures rely on discrete log — vulnerable to Shor's. This module applies Google Quantum AI’s Mar 2026 secp256k1 estimate (\u22641,200 logical qubits) to Ed25519 as its own approximation; the paper gives no estimate for it. Low-end estimate; other published work puts 256-bit ECC at ~2,330+ logical qubits.
Google Quantum AI & Ethereum Foundation (Mar 2026): \u22641,200 logical qubits + \u226490M Toffoli gates breaks secp256k1 ECDLP via Shor\u2019s algorithm. Used in Bitcoin, Ethereum, and most blockchain protocols. Low-end estimate; other published work puts 256-bit ECC at ~2,330+ logical qubits.
Grover's provides quadratic speedup: 128-bit → 64-bit. Below security threshold.
Grover's reduces to 96-bit — considered adequate for some legacy systems but below the 128-bit post-quantum threshold.
Grover's reduces to 128-b

chunks.title: SLH-DSA (Stateless Hash-Based Signatures) — SLHDSAExercises
chunks.content:
Module: SLH-DSA (Stateless Hash-Based Signatures)
Component: SLHDSAExercises

Hands-on scenarios to build intuition for FIPS 205 parameter tradeoffs, context strings, deterministic mode, and the Pure vs HashSLH-DSA distinction.
1. Small Signature vs Fast Signing
Generate keys with SHA2-128s (small/slow) then SHA2-128f (fast/large). Observe signature size and how the hypertree layer count (d) drives the tradeoff.
SHA2-128s produces 7,856 B signatures with d=7 layers. SHA2-128f produces 17,088 B signatures with d=22 layers. More layers = faster signing, bigger proof.
2. Context String Domain Separation
Sign a message with context string "protocol:codesign", then attempt verification with a different context "protocol:tls". Observe CKR_SIGNATURE_INVALID.
The same (SK, M) pair produces valid signatures under each context, but cross-context verification fails. This prevents replay attacks across protocol boundaries.
3. Randomized vs Deterministic Signing
Select deterministic signing and use “Sign twice and compare”. Repeat with hedged signing, keeping the key, message and context unchanged. Inspect both signatures and their verification results.
Both signatures should verify. Repeatability does not prove random-generator quality or resistance to attacks. Deterministic signing still requires randomness for key generation.
Sign with Pure SLH-DSA, then switch to HashSLH-DSA (SHA-256 pre-hash). Observe that the PKCS#11 mechanism changes from CKM_SLH_DSA to CKM_HASH_SLH_DSA_SHA256.

chunks.title: SLH-DSA (Stateless Hash-Based Signatures) — SLHDSAIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: SLH-DSA (Stateless Hash-Based Signatures)
Component: SLHDSAIntroduction

SLH-DSA (Stateless Hash-Based Digital Signature Algorithm) is the NIST-standardized post-quantum signature scheme published as FIPS 205 in August 2024. It is the standardized form of SPHINCS+, the hash-based signature scheme selected by NIST in Round 3 of the PQC competition.
FIPS 205 §1: its security “relies on the presumed difficulty of finding preimages for hash functions as well as several related properties of the same hash functions” — no new hardness assumptions beyond what we already rely on for HMAC and TLS.
Signing state (leaf index) must be persisted and never reused
Key exhaustion = catastrophic failure (no more valid signatures)
Cannot be used in stateless or distributed environments safely
Approved in NIST SP 800-208; specified in RFC 8554 (LMS) and RFC 8391 (XMSS), both Informational RFCs
No per-key leaf counter; this does not mean unlimited signatures
Safe for serverless, distributed, and HSM-pooled environments
Hedged (randomized) signing is the default, recommended where side-channel attacks are a concern (§9.2)

chunks.title: SLH-DSA (Stateless Hash-Based Signatures) — SLHDSAIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: SLH-DSA (Stateless Hash-Based Signatures)
Component: SLHDSAIntroduction

For the 12 parameter sets in FIPS 205 §11 , the security claims assume at most 2^64 messages signed with one key pair. This is a limit assumed by the security analysis, not a leaf counter that must be saved after every signature as in LMS or XMSS. It does not predict an immediate failure on the next signature beyond that limit. Keep planned use within this bound. For scale, even one billion signatures per second with the same key would take about 585 years to reach 2^64.
Technical enforcement is a separate challenge: a counter on one HSM does not account for signatures made by other copies of the same key. An exact cutoff would need coordinated accounting across devices and protection against resetting the count through backup restore or rollback. This lesson does not establish that an HSM counts these signatures or enforces a cutoff. A practical planning approach is to bound total signing volume across all key copies over the key lifetime and keep it far below the analysis limit. This is not a recommendation to add an LMS/XMSS-style per-signature counter to SLH-DSA.
Set a maximum signing-key lifetime and rotate keys on schedule.
Record where each key is deployed, including copies and backups.
Estimate total signing volume across all deployments over that lifetime, with a generous safety margin. Revisit the estimate when volume or deployments change.
Preserve the original key's retirement date when restoring a backup: restoring the same key does not start a new usage lifetime.

chunks.title: SLH-DSA (Stateless Hash-Based Signatures) — SLHDSAIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: SLH-DSA (Stateless Hash-Based Signatures)
Component: SLHDSAIntroduction

These controls support a documented estimate that expected use stays far below the analysis bound. They do not enforce an exact signature count. This is a practical planning example, not a claim that FIPS 205 prescribes this checklist or that it alone establishes certification compliance.
The tradeoff: SLH-DSA signatures are significantly larger (7,856 to 49,856 bytes, FIPS 205 Table 2, against about 0.8 to 9 KB for LMS across the SP 800-208 parameter sets, by the RFC 8554 byte layout) and signing is slower due to the hypertree traversal. Whether the stateless design is worth that cost depends on the deployment: a signing key that is used from several places, or restored from a backup, makes a leaf counter hard to keep safe. The three lists below are planning heuristics drawn from the sizes and speeds above, not requirements of FIPS 205 or of any policy.
National security systems: this list does not apply. NSA's CNSA 2.0 FAQ (version 2.2, October 2026) says SLH-DSA “is not part of CNSA and is not approved for any use in NSS”. See “What the lab tests” in the HashSLH-DSA Modes step.
SLH-DSA stacks three primitives. Understanding them explains why signatures are large, why some parameter sets are slow, and what's actually inside a 7,856-byte signature.

chunks.title: SLH-DSA (Stateless Hash-Based Signatures) — SLHDSAIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: SLH-DSA (Stateless Hash-Based Signatures)
Component: SLHDSAIntroduction

WOTS+ signs a single n-byte hash value by representing it as a sequence of base- w digits and computing a hash chain of length up to w for each digit. The signer walks down the chain (easy); the verifier walks up (also easy); forging requires inverting the hash (infeasible).
Sign digit d: output chain[d]. Verify: apply w−1−d more hashes and compare to pk_i.
Winternitz parameter w = 2^lg_w = 16. Each WOTS+ digit is 4 bits. Larger w → fewer chains needed → smaller sig, but each chain is longer → slower.
WOTS+ is one-time: each key may sign one message, and forgeries become feasible if a key is used twice (FIPS 205 §6, §8). In the hypertree each WOTS+ key signs one fixed value: a FORS public key at the lowest layer, or an XMSS public key of the layer below (§7).
FORS is a few-time signature scheme. It holds k binary trees each of height a, giving k × 2^a leaf secret values. To sign, the message digest selects one leaf per tree; the signature reveals those leaves plus authentication paths.
FORS provides few-time security: revealing up to q signatures is safe as long as k and a are chosen so that the probability of a collision in any tree position is negligible. FORS signs the message digest and produces a FORS public key, which is then signed by the hypertree.
The hypertree is a d-layer stack of XMSS trees, each of height h/d. Each layer authenticates the root of the layer below using a WOTS+ signature. The top root (PK.root), together with PK.seed, is the SLH-DSA public key.

chunks.title: SLH-DSA (Stateless Hash-Based Signatures) — SLHDSAIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: SLH-DSA (Stateless Hash-Based Signatures)
Component: SLHDSAIntroduction

Fewer layers (d small, e.g. 7) and taller per-layer trees (h/d large, e.g. 9). Each XMSS tree has more leaves and needs more hash rounds to traverse; fewer layers means fewer WOTS+ signatures, so the total signature is smaller (a hypertree signature is (h + d · len) · n bytes, §7.1).
More layers (d large, e.g. 22) and shorter per-layer trees (h/d small, e.g. 3). Each XMSS tree is shallow → fast traversal per layer, but the additional WOTS+ signatures for each extra layer add to signature size.
A SHA2-128s signature (7,856 B) contains: randomness R (16 B) + FORS signature (k × (a+1) × n B) + HT signature (d × WOTS+_sig + auth_path per layer). The dominant cost is the FORS trees + HT auth paths, all scaled by n (hash output size in bytes).
FIPS 205 defines 12 parameter sets (6 SHA-2 variants shown, each has a SHAKE counterpart with identical parameters). Every set uses lg_w = 4 (Winternitz parameter w = 16).
SHAKE variants (SHAKE-128s/f, SHAKE-192s/f, SHAKE-256s/f) use identical (n,h,d,a,k) values but replace SHA-2 with SHAKE-256 as the tree hash function.
Built from SHA-256, with SHA-512 added for security categories 3 and 5 (FIPS 205 section 11.2)
Every function is instantiated with SHAKE256 (FIPS 205 section 11.1)
Same security category as the matching SHA2 parameter set (FIPS 205 Table 2)
Pre-hash examples (§10.2.2): SHA-256, SHA-512, SHAKE128 and SHAKE256. SHA-256 and SHAKE128 are appropriate only for category 1 parameter sets.

chunks.title: SLH-DSA (Stateless Hash-Based Signatures) — SLHDSAIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: SLH-DSA (Stateless Hash-Based Signatures)
Component: SLHDSAIntroduction

Context strings (0–255 bytes) are supported, identically to pure SLH-DSA
Use when the protocol mandates pre-hashing (e.g. legacy interop)
HashSLH-DSA message construction (§10.2.2): M' = 0x01 ‖ len(ctx) ‖ ctx ‖ OID_DER ‖ H(M). The OID identifies the pre-hash algorithm; example DER encodings appear in Algorithm 23.
The live demo provides separate signing and verification contexts for pure and pre-hash modes. Leave both empty for zero bytes, or use the same label in both fields. Change only the verification context to test rejection. A space is not empty. An engine error does not demonstrate correct rejection; it means the test did not complete successfully.
A context string is an optional 0–255 byte value passed at sign and verify time. It binds the signature to a specific protocol or application context, preventing cross-context signature replay attacks.
Example: A CA signs both OCSP responses and firmware blobs with the same key. By using context "ca:ocsp" for one and "ca:firmware" for the other, a valid OCSP signature cannot be repurposed as a firmware signature — verification returns CKR_SIGNATURE_INVALID.
Supported in both pure SLH-DSA and HashSLH-DSA (Algorithm 23 takes ctx)
Context must be supplied identically at both sign and verify time
Empty context (0 bytes) is the default — most applications use this
PKCS#11 v3.2: passed via CK_SIGN_ADDITIONAL_CONTEXT.pContext
Deterministic: signing the same message with the same key, context and settings produces the same signature.

chunks.title: SLH-DSA (Stateless Hash-Based Signatures) — SLHDSAIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: SLH-DSA (Stateless Hash-Based Signatures)
Component: SLHDSAIntroduction

Hedged: signing adds fresh randomness, so repeating the operation normally produces a different signature. Both signatures should still verify.
Sign the same inputs twice and compare the results. Identical signatures are expected in deterministic mode; different signatures are normally expected in hedged mode.
This demonstrates the difference between signing modes. It does not prove that the random generator is good or that the implementation resists attacks.
Deterministic signing does not need fresh randomness for each signature, but generating the key still requires randomness.
Technical note: in deterministic SLH-DSA, opt_rand uses PK.seed, a public value belonging to the key, not zeros. See FIPS 205 §9.2 . In the existing demo, select a signing mode and use “Sign twice and compare” to inspect both signatures and their verification results with identical inputs.
PKCS#11 v3.2: set hedgeVariant = CKH_DETERMINISTIC_REQUIRED in the CK_SIGN_ADDITIONAL_CONTEXT parameter.
A validated SLH-DSA module is checked in three separate ways, and none of them replaces another: algorithm tests, the module's own self-tests, and the certificate path. A fourth question, whether the algorithm may be used at all, is answered by CNSA 2.0 for national security systems.
SLH-DSA has three ACVP modes: keyGen, sigGen and sigVer, all against FIPS 205. Each has one test type, AFT (Algorithm Functional Test).

chunks.title: SLH-DSA (Stateless Hash-Based Signatures) — SLHDSAIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: SLH-DSA (Stateless Hash-Based Signatures)
Component: SLHDSAIntroduction

keyGen: the implementation generates a key pair from the provided seed and key values (SK.seed, SK.prf and PK.seed). The server provides at least 10 tests for each combination of capabilities. sigGen: it generates a valid signature from the provided private key, message, context (external interface) and randomness (non-deterministic signing), with at least 13 tests for each combination.
sigVer: the server makes its tests by modifying a valid signature: a modified message, modified signature R, SIGFORS or SIGHT parts, a signature that is too long or too short, plus the valid case. The workshop's NIST sigVer panel replays a few published cases of this kind.
Not tested by ACVP, in the specification's words: “that fresh seed values are used for fresh invocations of key generation, that approved deterministic random bit generators (DRBGs) are used with the correct security strengths, that sensitive data is destroyed, that key validation is performed, and that floating point arithmetic is not used.”
parameterSets: any of the 12 names, from SLH-DSA-SHA2-128s to SLH-DSA-SHAKE-256f.
preHash: “pure”, “preHash” (described as “Whether SLH-DSA or HashSLH-DSA are supported”). hashAlgs is used if preHash.
deterministic (sigGen only): “A value of ‘true’ indicates that deterministic signature generation is supported and a value of ‘false’ indicates that non-deterministic signature generation is supported.” sigVer has signatureInterfaces and preHash but no deterministic field.

chunks.title: SLH-DSA (Stateless Hash-Based Signatures) — SLHDSAIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: SLH-DSA (Stateless Hash-Based Signatures)
Component: SLHDSAIntroduction

messageLength (8 to 65536 bits, step 8) and contextLength (0 to 2040, step 8) as ranges.
For each of signature generation, signature verification and key generation that the module implements, IG 10.3.A requires a cryptographic algorithm self-test (CAST), run before the algorithm's first use in the approved mode. The signature generation CAST is a known-answer test: fixed values go in and the output is compared with a pre-computed signature (SIG). The verification CAST checks that a known signature verifies (returns true). The key generation CAST uses fixed SK.seed, SK.prf and PK.seed and compares the private key; the public key need not be compared, “as the private key contains a copy of the public key”.
Pure and pre-hash (Notes 27 and 28): if both are implemented and “they both share the same underlying cryptographic implementations, a CAST on either one of them is sufficient to meet the CAST requirements for both”. This holds for signature generation and, separately, for verification.
Hash families (Note 29): a module that supports both SHA2 and SHAKE parameter sets in the approved mode must run the CASTs on at least two parameter sets, one SHA2 and one SHAKE. A module with only one family needs at least one. It is recommended, but not required, to test at least one “s” and one “f” set if both are implemented.
Tree height (Note 30): the CASTs need only exercise the smallest parameter set (lowest height trees) the module supports.

chunks.title: SLH-DSA (Stateless Hash-Based Signatures) — SLHDSAIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: SLH-DSA (Stateless Hash-Based Signatures)
Component: SLHDSAIntroduction

Pairwise consistency test: for FIPS 205 keys it “may be limited to confirming the same key identifier (I in the case of LMS, SEED in the case of XMSS and PK.SEED for SLH-DSA) is shared by the resulting public and private key following generation”.
NIST's CAVP page: “Cryptographic algorithm validation is a prerequisite of cryptographic module validation.” But “a product or implementation does not meet the FIPS 140 module validation requirements by simply implementing an Approved security function and acquiring validations for each of the implemented algorithms.”
ACVTS testing “is entirely black-box. The implementation is never provided to NIST or the CAVP in order to receive a validation certificate”, and CAVP “is not responsible for running those test vectors through the implementation”. The CASTs above are a FIPS 140-3 module requirement set by CMVP guidance (IG 10.3.A), separate from the ACVP tests.
CNSA 2.0 (NSA FAQ, version 2.2, October 2026): “While SLH-DSA is hash-based, it is not part of CNSA and is not approved for any use in NSS.” The CNSA 2.0 algorithm table lists ML-DSA-87 for digital signatures and LMS and XMSS (NIST SP 800-208) for signing firmware and software. See the stateful signatures module for how those are validated.

chunks.title: SLH-DSA (Stateless Hash-Based Signatures) — SLHDSAComparison
chunks.content:
Module: SLH-DSA (Stateless Hash-Based Signatures)
Component: SLHDSAComparison

All three schemes are hash-based: their security rests only on hash-function properties (BSI TR-02102-1 section 5.3.4), which are believed to withstand large-scale quantum computers (SP 800-208). The choice comes down to state management requirements, signature size constraints, and signing frequency.
How to choose: start with the policy that applies to you. Under CNSA 2.0, SLH-DSA is not approved for any use in national security systems, while single-tree LMS and XMSS are approved for firmware and software signing (ML-DSA-87 is also allowed). Outside that scope, the main difference is state: SLH-DSA has no leaf counter to protect, at the cost of the larger signatures above. SP 800-208 requires LMS and XMSS key and signature generation to run in a hardware cryptographic module that does not allow secret keying material to be exported, even in encrypted form.
Parameter set shown in the size rows

chunks.content:

Smallest signature (7,856 B) at NIST Level 1; slower signing due to d=7 layers.
Faster signing (d=22 layers) at the cost of a larger signature (17,088 B).

chunks.title: Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) — SbomIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Software Bill of Materials (SBOM)
Component: SbomIntroduction

A Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) is a machine-readable inventory of every software component a build depends on — packages, libraries, their versions, suppliers, and how they relate to each other. It answers what is in this build?
It does not answer what cryptography is inside it? — that is the CBOM module 's job, one layer up. An SBOM lists software; a CBOM extends that list with algorithm, key size, protocol, and quantum-vulnerability fields the SBOM has no place for. Keep the two separate: this module is the software inventory, not the crypto one.
SPDX (Linux Foundation; standardized as ISO/IEC 5962:2021) grew out of license-compliance tooling and has the deeper license/provenance model. CycloneDX (OWASP; standardized as ECMA-424) grew out of application-security tooling and is the more extensible object model — SaaSBOM, HBOM, ML-BOM and VDR/VEX are all sibling BOM types built on the same schema.
Neither format has a cryptography object model built in for general use. CycloneDX does have a crypto-specific extension (assetType: cryptographic-asset) — that extension, and the SPDX-vs-CycloneDX trade-off for a crypto inventory specifically, is covered in the CBOM module, not repeated here. Likewise, CycloneDX's own cross-tool algorithm/curve naming registry is covered in the CycloneDX Cryptography Registry module .

chunks.title: Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) — SbomIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Software Bill of Materials (SBOM)
Component: SbomIntroduction

NTIA's 2021 Minimum Elements for a Software Bill of Materials defines seven required fields per component: Supplier Name, Component Name, Version, Other Unique Identifiers, Dependency Relationship, Author of SBOM Data, and Timestamp. Two of the seven — author and timestamp — live at the document level, not per component.
CISA finalized a successor on 29 July 2026 — the 2026 Minimum Elements for a Software Bill of Materials, v2.1 — co-authored with NSA, FBI, and 15 international partner cyber agencies. It keeps all seven of the above and adds ten more; see the next section for what changed and why.
The seven elements above went unchanged for four years while SBOM tooling matured well past what they were designed for. The 2026 update adds ten new required elements: seven at the document level ( SBOM Author Signature, SBOM Data Format Name, SBOM Data Format Version, SBOM Tool Name, SBOM Tool Version, SBOM Version, and SBOM Generation Context) and three per component ( Component Hash Algorithm, Component Hash Value, and Component License). Existing elements are revised rather than carried over unchanged: Appendix B replaces Supplier Name with Component Producer , Other Unique Identifiers with Component Identifiers, Author of SBOM Data with SBOM Author, and Version of the Component with Component Version, and removes the Access Control element. Check anything built against the 2021 baseline against Appendix B.

chunks.title: Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) — SbomIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Software Bill of Materials (SBOM)
Component: SbomIntroduction

Real-world tooling hasn't caught up yet. We checked seven generators' actual current default output (not the format's theoretical capability) against these ten elements: none is fully 2026-compliant out of the box. npm's native npm sbom comes closest at 9 of 10 fields (missing only the signature); pip-audit trails furthest behind at 2 of 10, and still emits the older CycloneDX 1.4 schema. Two gaps are universal across every tool checked: none sign the SBOM automatically, and SBOM Generation Context has no clean mapping in any of them. Treat this as an August 2026 snapshot, not a fixed verdict — SBOM generators are actively adding fields as adoption of the 2026 baseline spreads, so expect these numbers to climb; re-check a tool's current release before relying on it for a real compliance claim.
An SBOM lists what is present; it says nothing about whether a listed component's known vulnerabilities are actually reachable in this product. VEX (Vulnerability Exploitability eXchange) — Profile 5 of OASIS CSAF 2.0 — closes that gap with a machine-readable affected / not affected / fixed / under investigation statement per CVE per product.
Without VEX, a CVE in a widely-used component (a compression library, a crypto library) fires an alert for every product that merely lists it in an SBOM, regardless of whether the vulnerable code path is ever called. VEX turns that into a triage decision instead of a fire drill.

chunks.title: Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) — SbomIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Software Bill of Materials (SBOM)
Component: SbomIntroduction

US Executive Order 14028 (May 2021) requires software vendors selling to the federal government to provide an SBOM (not sourced in the Library) — the requirement that produced NTIA's minimum-elements work above. The EU Cyber Resilience Act (Regulation EU 2024/2847) requires manufacturers of products with digital elements to maintain an SBOM covering top-level dependencies, with the main obligations applying from 11 December 2027.
Neither mandate is PQC-specific — they are general software supply-chain requirements. The reason a PQC migration program cares is downstream: an SBOM built to satisfy EO 14028 or the CRA is exactly the existing data source a crypto-discovery effort should integrate rather than duplicate.
An SBOM is Phase 1 discovery input, not a Phase 2 output: it is one of the existing data sources a crypto-discovery effort should cross-reference rather than rebuild from scratch. Skipping that cross-reference — building a CBOM without linking it back to SBOM dependency chains — is a named common failure in PQC migration programs.
Need to know what cryptographic algorithms, keys, and certificates a component uses? That's the CBOM module .
Need to resolve the same mechanism named differently across an HSM, a certificate, and a library string? That's the CycloneDX Cryptography Registry module .

chunks.title: Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) — SbomGenerationPicker
chunks.content:
Module: Software Bill of Materials (SBOM)
Component: SbomGenerationPicker

The right SBOM tool depends on what you're building, not on a single org-wide choice.
Two gaps are universal across every tool surveyed above: none of them sign the SBOM automatically — SBOM Author Signature needs a separate step (e.g. Cosign/Sigstore attestation) regardless of which generator you pick — and SBOM Generation Context has no clean 1:1 mapping in any of them; the closest analog (CycloneDX's lifecycles field) is inconsistently supported. Component hash and license fields are frequently present but not guaranteed — coverage depends on the package ecosystem and, for compiled languages, on whether a lock file was available to the generator.
Verified against each tool's own source, docs, and changelog as of August 2026 — SBOM tooling moves fast; re-check before treating this as a compliance decision.
Both scan image layers directly; pick the format your downstream tooling (CBOM pipeline, registry scanner) already consumes.
npm’s own `npm sbom` command ships CycloneDX output by default; use it before reaching for a third-party generator.
pip-audit doubles as the VEX-relevant step: it cross-references the generated SBOM against the OSV vulnerability feed in the same run.
Runs as a build-lifecycle plugin, so the SBOM is regenerated on every release rather than drifting from what actually shipped.

chunks.title: Secrets Management & PQC — SecretsManagementIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Secrets Management & PQC
Component: SecretsManagementIntroduction

Organizations manage two distinct categories of sensitive material: secrets (API keys, credentials, tokens, seed phrases) and cryptographic keys (KEKs, signing keys, DEKs). Understanding the distinction matters for PQC migration because they have different protection mechanisms and different risk profiles.
Secrets themselves are often not directly encrypted with asymmetric cryptography — they are stored in vaults that use envelope encryption. In envelope encryption, a Data Encryption Key (DEK) encrypts the secret, and a Key Encryption Key (KEK) wraps the DEK. The KEK is the quantum-vulnerable component when it uses RSA-OAEP or ECDH-ES. Migrating to ML-KEM for the KEK protects all secrets in the vault without touching the secrets themselves.
Key insight: The "Secret Zero" problem — how do you securely introduce an application to the vault without hardcoding a first credential? — is addressed by SPIFFE/SPIRE injecting verified workload identity. For the vault itself, migrating the master seal key to ML-KEM cascades PQC protection to all stored secrets.
Harvest Now, Decrypt Later (HNDL) applies differently to secrets than to general encrypted data. The risk depends on the secret's lifetime and the sensitivity of what it protects.

chunks.title: Secrets Management & PQC — SecretsManagementIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Secrets Management & PQC
Component: SecretsManagementIntroduction

A long-lived API key harvested from a TLS session today remains valid for months or years. When a Cryptographically Relevant Quantum Computer (CRQC) arrives, the attacker can decrypt the harvested TLS session, extract the API key, and use it to access your systems — or re-sell it. Short-lived OAuth tokens (1h TTL) have much lower HNDL risk since they expire before a CRQC is practically deployable.
Strategic insight: Switching static DB credentials to dynamic secrets (Vault DB engine, 8h TTL) eliminates their HNDL risk entirely — no algorithm migration needed. This "quick win" should be the first operational step before any cryptographic algorithm change.
Dynamic secrets are credentials generated on-demand with a Time-To-Live (TTL) and automatically revoked on expiry or lease revocation. HashiCorp Vault's database secrets engine is the canonical example: Vault creates a unique DB user for each requester, with configurable TTL (1h to 24h), then drops the user automatically.
The PQC consideration for dynamic secrets is not the secrets themselves (they expire too quickly to matter for HNDL) but the mechanisms that generate and deliver them. The TLS channel from Vault to the database backend must use hybrid ML-KEM, and the Vault token used by the application to request secrets must be issued via an ML-DSA-verified identity.
Vault Issues Scoped Token (TTL = 24h) — Auth via ML-DSA K8s JWT (planned)
Dynamic DB Credentials Generated (TTL = 8h, unique per lease)

Module: Secrets Management & PQC

Application Reads Credentials from tmpfs (never stored in env vars)
Vault Transit Engine performs crypto operations server-side. Migrating key types from rsa-4096 to ml-dsa-65 (an Enterprise-only transit key type in the Vault documentation) — with ml-kem-768 not among the documented transit key types — changes the internal transit key store without breaking the API surface. Applications simply update the key_type parameter during key creation, and Vault mechanically handles the larger PQC ciphertexts and nested encapsulation transparency.
Dynamic credential TTLs (e.g., 1-8 hour bounds) completely eliminate HNDL risk for the credential itself, as it expires long before a CRQC appears. Contrast this with PQC rotation bounds for static KEKs (30-90 days), which require complex re-wrapping operations. Short TTLs negate the need for PQC migration of the secret value itself.
Cloud secrets managers vary significantly in their PQC readiness. Understanding each provider's roadmap is essential for multi-cloud strategies and migration timeline planning.
All cloud providers use envelope encryption: DEK (AES-256-GCM) encrypts the secret, KEK wraps the DEK. The KEK is stored in the provider's KMS and is the quantum-vulnerable component. Switching the KEK to ML-KEM protects all secrets without re-encrypting secret content.
