BYOK lets you generate and manage the KEK in your own HSM or Vault instance. With BYOK + ML-KEM, you control the PQC upgrade timeline independently of the cloud provider's roadmap. AWS CloudHSM and Azure Managed HSM support BYOK with HSM-backed keys.
Kubernetes Secrets are base64-encoded, not encrypted — they are stored in etcd as plaintext unless encryption-at-rest is explicitly enabled. The CIS Kubernetes Benchmark v1.9 (section 1.2.33) mandates secrets encryption for production clusters. Without it, secret sprawl into etcd creates a massive HNDL attack surface.
Zero-trust secrets management eliminates static credentials entirely. Every workload authenticates via short-lived, dynamically issued credentials:

CI/CD pipeline crypto, container signing, and policy enforcement
Classify secrets by risk, simulate Vault transit PQC, design rotation policies, and compare cloud providers.

Use Azure Key Vault with "Key Vault references" in App Service/Container Apps to avoid storing secrets in app config. When PQC keys are available, only the Key Vault config changes.
Secret Manager has no PQC setting of its own. Data at rest is protected with AES-256 (optionally your own CMEK); the quantum-relevant exposure is the TLS connection to the API.
Configure --encryption-provider-config on kube-apiserver with a KMS provider. Use the KMS v2 plugin (Kubernetes 1.25+) pointing to a cloud KMS or Vault instance. With AWS KMS ML-KEM key spec as the KMS provider, all etcd secrets are ML-KEM protected. The External Secrets Operator (ESO) pattern keeps secrets in the vault and injects them at runtime, so they are not duplicated into etcd.
External Secrets Operator (ESO)
ESO syncs secrets from external stores (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault) to Kubernetes Secret objects at runtime. The Secret lives only in the external vault (PQC-protected) and in-memory in the pod. GitOps repos never contain secret values. PQC protection comes entirely from the external store's KEK algorithm.
SPIFFE/SPIRE Workload Identity
SPIFFE (Secure Production Identity Framework for Everyone) issues X.509-SVIDs (SPIFFE Verifiable Identity Documents) to workloads via short-lived certificates (TTL 5-60min). SPIRE (SPIFFE Runtime Environment) is the reference implementation. Migrating SVID signing from ECDSA to ML-DSA eliminates HNDL risk for workload identity entirely.

chunks.title: Secrets Management & PQC — secretsConstants (data)
chunks.content:
Module: Secrets Management & PQC
Data: secretsConstants

Long-lived tokens used to authenticate service-to-service calls, third-party API integrations, and platform access. Often embedded in configuration files or environment variables.
Tokens transmitted over TLS channels are at risk if the session is recorded and later decrypted by a CRQC. Long-lived tokens amplify this risk since they may still be valid years later.
API keys stored in vault are protected by envelope encryption. The KEK wrapping the DEK must be ML-KEM protected to prevent offline decryption of harvested vault backups.
Store all API keys in a PQC-protected vault (ML-KEM-768 envelope encryption). Implement short TTLs (90 days max). Use ML-DSA-signed webhook payloads to authenticate requests.
Username/password or connection string credentials for database access. Often static and long-lived in legacy systems, creating significant HNDL exposure for sensitive data stores.
Database connections over TLS 1.2 using RSA or ECDSA key exchange are vulnerable to harvest-now-decrypt-later attacks. A CRQC can decrypt the entire connection including credentials and query results.
Static DB credentials stored in vault represent a high-value target. Compromise of the vault master key (if RSA/ECDSA wrapped) exposes all credentials simultaneously.
Replace static credentials with dynamic secrets (Vault database engine: TTL 1h, max 24h). Upgrade DB connection TLS to hybrid ML-KEM. Rotate master keys with ML-KEM-1024 wrapping.
X.509 certificates and their corresponding private keys used for TLS/mTLS authentication. The private key material is the most sensitive component — compromise enables identity spoofing.
TLS private keys used in RSA/ECDSA handshakes are retroactively compromisable. Recorded TLS sessions can be decrypted once the server private key is recovered by a CRQC.
Private keys stored in vault or HSM must be protected with ML-KEM-based key wrapping. PKCS#12 bundles encrypted with legacy algorithms (3DES, RC4) are immediately vulnerable.
Issue hybrid ML-DSA-65 + ECDSA P-256 certificates for all TLS endpoints. Store private keys in FIPS 140-3 Level 3 HSMs with ML-KEM firmware. Automate rotation via ACME/cert-manager.
Private keys used to sign software packages, firmware images, container images, and legal documents. Compromise enables supply chain attacks via forged signatures on malicious artifacts.
Signing operations performed over unprotected channels expose the signature to HNDL. An attacker harvesting signed artifacts today can forge new signatures after recovering the private key.
Code signing keys stored in software keystores (JKS, PKCS#12) with RSA/ECDSA are directly at risk from CRQC offline attacks. HSM storage is mandatory for critical signing keys.
Migrate all signing operations to ML-DSA-87 (FIPS 204 Level 5) for long-term artifacts. Use Sigstore for keyless signing with short-lived certificates (ECDSA P-256 today; ML-DSA is a proposed future upgrade). Store root signing keys in HSMs.

chunks.content:
Module: Secrets Management & PQC
Data: secretsProviderData

Enumerate all secrets, their types, lifetimes, and protection mechanisms. Identify which vault instances use RSA/ECDSA for master key wrapping and key transport. Tools: HashiCorp Vault audit logs, AWS Config rules, truffleHog for secret sprawl detection.
Classify each secret category by HNDL exposure window. Longest-lived secrets (signing keys, encryption keys, seed phrases) with immediate HNDL exposure get Priority 1 treatment. Short-lived tokens (OAuth 1h TTL) are lowest priority.
Replace static database credentials with dynamic secrets (Vault DB engine, max TTL 24h). This eliminates the HNDL risk of long-lived DB credentials without requiring any algorithm migration. Immediate security improvement achievable in weeks.
HashiCorp Vault's transit documentation lists Enterprise-only ml-dsa, slh-dsa and hybrid sign/verify key types and no ML-KEM type; we found no PQC seal mechanism announced. Track the roadmap and plan to migrate seal key wrapping to a quantum-safe mechanism when available, since a harvested vault backup with classical seal wrapping is exposed to offline decryption.
Re-key DEKs Under ML-KEM Envelope Encryption
For each secret category using envelope encryption, generate new ML-KEM-768 or ML-KEM-1024 KEKs and re-wrap the DEKs. For DEKs whose old wrapped form was never exposed this is a key metadata operation, and the data does not need re-encryption (AES-256-GCM is already quantum-safe). For DEKs whose RSA- or ECDH-wrapped form was transmitted where an adversary could have saved it, NIST SP 800-57 says such keys may need to be considered compromised even after re-encryption for storage; treat those DEKs as exposed, generate new DEKs and re-encrypt the data they protect, knowing that this cannot protect copies of the data an adversary has already saved.
Replace all ECDSA/RSA signing keys in vault with ML-DSA-65 or ML-DSA-87. Update applications that verify signatures (JWT validators, package managers, CI systems). Re-sign historical artifacts if long-term validity is required.
Enable PQC Encryption for Kubernetes etcd
Configure Kubernetes KMS provider with ML-KEM-backed master key for etcd encryption-at-rest. Kubernetes Secrets stored in etcd are base64 only by default — enabling encryption is critical. CIS Kubernetes Benchmark v1.9 section 1.2.33.
Replace Service Account Keys with Workload Identity + ML-DSA
Eliminate all downloaded service account key files. Implement SPIFFE/SPIRE with ML-DSA X.509-SVID certificates for workload identity. Replace GitHub Actions service account keys with OIDC federation + ML-DSA JWT signing.

Measured Boot itself is quantum-safe (SHA-256 PCR extends). A TPM Quote signed with an RSA AIK is a forgery risk once a CRQC exists, not a harvest-now-decrypt-later one: the signature protects no secret, so urgency follows how long the TPM and its AIK certificate chain stay in service (the designer estimates about 10 years). Remote TLS attestation carries both risks: the TLS key exchange can be recorded now and decrypted later, while the embedded attestation signatures can only be forged later (estimated about 15 years in service).
6. Boot Verify Latency on an MCU
Open the Boot Verify Latency calculator at its defaults (2 MB/s SPI flash, 120 MHz Cortex-M4-class core). Compare the load and verify columns for ECDSA P-256, RSA-3072, ML-DSA-44 and LMS H10/W4, then drop the clock to 48 MHz and see which algorithm crosses the illustrative 100 ms budget.
Flash read is never the problem. Verify time dominates. ML-DSA-44 and LMS verify in the same league as ECDSA P-256. RSA-3072 in software is the one that blows the budget. These are model estimates; the 100 ms budget is illustrative, not a standard.

chunks.title: Secure Boot & Firmware PQC — SecureBootIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Secure Boot & Firmware PQC
Component: SecureBootIntroduction

UEFI Secure Boot establishes a cryptographic chain of trust from hardware power-on through the OS kernel. Each stage must be verified by a trusted key before it executes. The hierarchy is: Platform Key (PK) → Key Exchange Key (KEK) → Authorized Signature Database (db) → Bootloader/Kernel signatures.
In this module's reading, every RSA-2048 and ECDSA key in the UEFI Secure Boot hierarchy can be broken by a Cryptographically Relevant Quantum Computer (CRQC) via Shor's algorithm. This is a forgery risk (“trust now, forge later”), not a harvest-now-decrypt-later one: a signature protects no secret, so nothing recorded today is exposed later. Once a CRQC exists, anyone who holds a public key (the verifying keys are stored on every device) could derive its private key and sign firmware that existing devices accept — enabling undetectable firmware rootkits. How urgent that is depends on how long the device and its trust anchors stay in the field. NSA's CNSA 2.0 FAQ (v2.2, p.13) notes that in many firmware-signing cases the validation algorithm is not easily updated, so firmware-signing algorithms are “frequently locked in for the life of a system”. Harvest-now-decrypt-later applies to confidentiality, such as the TLS key exchange that carries remote attestation, not to signatures.

chunks.content:
Module: Secure Boot & Firmware PQC
Component: SecureBootIntroduction

ML-DSA-65 is this module's general-purpose target (NIST Security Level 3). For National Security Systems (NSS), the NSA's CNSA 2.0 FAQ (Ver. 2.2, p. 7–8) specifies ML-DSA-87 for all classification levels and allows LMS and XMSS (NIST SP 800-208) for signing firmware and software; HSS and XMSSMT are not allowed and SLH-DSA is not approved for NSS (p. 11). The CNSA 2.0 / NSS column shows the NSS choice.
The db size impact is a key operational concern: a minimal self-signed ML-DSA-65 X.509 certificate is about 5.5 KB (5,538 bytes) against about 0.8 KB (809 bytes) for RSA-2048, measured with OpenSSL 3.6.3. Certificates with more fields are larger. Secure Boot variable storage is platform-specific; firmware reports it through QueryVariableInfo() (UEFI 2.11 section 8.2.4). A full PQC db migration may require platform NVRAM reallocation — verify UEFI NVRAM capacity before planning.
ML-DSA-65 (FIPS 204, formerly CRYSTALS-Dilithium3) is the NIST-standardized post-quantum signature algorithm at NIST Security Level 3. It is a common choice for firmware signing because its signature size (3,309 bytes) balances security and UEFI storage overhead better than ML-DSA-87. For National Security Systems, CNSA 2.0 specifies ML-DSA-87 for all classification levels, so firmware for NSS customers uses ML-DSA-87 or LMS/XMSS.

chunks.title: Secure Boot & Firmware PQC — SecureBootIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Secure Boot & Firmware PQC
Component: SecureBootIntroduction

The last column uses two different measures. PQC rows show the NIST security category from FIPS 204 and FIPS 205. Classical rows show the comparable security strength in bits from NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 Rev. 5, Table 2 (RSA-2048: 112, P-256: 128, P-384: 192; RSA-4096 is not a listed size and falls between RSA-3072 at 128 and RSA-7680 at 192), which assumes no large quantum computer. SLH-DSA-SHA2-128s has the smallest public key (32 B) but the largest signature (7,856 B). For firmware signing where signature size is the bottleneck, ML-DSA-65 is a common choice. Outside National Security Systems, SLH-DSA may suit long-lived root keys where signing is rare; for NSS it is not an option, because the CNSA 2.0 FAQ (p. 11) says SLH-DSA is not part of CNSA and is not approved for any use in NSS. CNSA 2.0 prefers stateful hash-based signatures (LMS or XMSS, NIST SP 800-208) to start firmware/software signing now; validated ML-DSA-87 is also approved for firmware/software signing.
During the transition period, firmware images can carry both an RSA-2048 and ML-DSA-65 signature. Legacy systems that do not support ML-DSA fall back to RSA verification. New systems validate the ML-DSA signature. This dual-signature approach requires careful UEFI variable budget planning — the combined overhead is approximately 3,565 bytes (3,309 B ML-DSA-65 + 256 B RSA-2048 ≈ 3,565 B) per signed component; with an RSA-4096 second signature it is about 3,821 bytes (3,309 B + 512 B).

chunks.title: Secure Boot & Firmware PQC — SecureBootIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Secure Boot & Firmware PQC
Component: SecureBootIntroduction

Firmware signing has two sides, and they are tested differently. The verifier is the code on the device that checks a signature. The signer is the module that holds the private key and produces the signature. CAVP is NIST's algorithm validation program (its tests are specified in ACVP documents). CMVP is NIST's cryptographic module validation program. A CAST is a cryptographic algorithm self-test that a validated module runs on its own algorithms. In the quotations, IUT means implementation under test, OTS means one-time signature, and HBS means hash-based signature. Every quotation below is verbatim from the document named after it, with footnote and reference-number markers left out.
NIST's ACVP specification drafts include signature verification for ML-DSA (ML-DSA / sigVer / FIPS204) and for LMS (LMS / sigVer). Both use the test type AFT (algorithm functional test). For LMS:
The ACVP server generates a series of signatures to communicate to the IUT. The IUT is REQUIRED to determine the validity of the signature given the tree structure, key, and message.
For ML-DSA, the server starts from a valid signature and changes the message or one part of the signature (commitment, z or hint); each changed version is not a valid signature. The same specification says what ACVP does not test:
An ACVP server will not test the zeroization of intermediate values, security strength of the deterministic random bit generators (DRBGs), or incorrect length signatures or public keys.

chunks.title: Secure Boot & Firmware PQC — SecureBootIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Secure Boot & Firmware PQC
Component: SecureBootIntroduction

No ACVP specification is published for XMSS, XMSS^MT or HSS (NIST's ACVP specification list, October 2026). The FIPS 140-3 Implementation Guidance (IG) C.N, last modified September 2024, describes the same state:
CAVP tests are undergoing development with testing available for LMS but not yet for XMSS, HSS, or XMSSMT.
So CNSA 2.0 accepts XMSS as well as LMS for firmware (see part 2), but of the SP 800-208 schemes only LMS has an ACVP test.
NIST SP 800-208 sets this rule for key generation and signing with its stateful hash-based schemes (LMS and XMSS, and their multi-tree forms HSS and XMSS^MT):
Implementations of the key generation and signature algorithms in this document shall only be validated for use within hardware cryptographic modules. The cryptographic modules shall be validated to provide FIPS 140-2 or FIPS 140-3 Level 3 or higher physical security, and the operational environment shall be non-modifiable or limited.
That rule is for key generation and signing only. For a module that only verifies:
Modules that only support signature verification need to comply with requirements from section 8.2 of SP 800-208, but do not need to meet requirements from section 8.1.
ACVP cannot check two of the signer requirements, the ban on exporting a private key and the one-time use of each signing key:

chunks.title: Secure Boot & Firmware PQC — SecureBootIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Secure Boot & Firmware PQC
Component: SecureBootIntroduction

Many requirements outlined in this section are not testable by ACVP. ACVP does not test the inability of an implementation to export a private key. ACVP does not provide any guarantees on the inability to reuse private OTS pairs of an implementation.
The NSA CNSA 2.0 FAQ (version 2.2, October 2026, pp. 11-12) says which part needs which validation for National Security Systems (NSS). A product that only verifies:
Signature verification is expected to be performed by code that has been validated by NIST's Cryptographic Algorithm Validation Program (CAVP). … If your product is only verifying signatures, CAVP testing is all that is required.
Code sources and signature generation processes (signers) that are NSS are required to produce signatures according to NIST SP 800-208, which requires hardware validated by NIST's Cryptographic Module Validation Program (CMVP), or via other NSA guidance. Waivers for this will not be granted.
A signer that is not an NSS, such as a commercial vendor's development environment:

Module: Secure Boot & Firmware PQC

… the signature generation processes for that code (signers) are often not themselves NSS. For example, for many commercial vendors with commodity products used in an NSS, their development environments are not NSS. In this case, those signers are expected to use code in their signature generation processes that is at least at the same operational quality as the code being put on the device, but the only part NSA will validate is that the signature verification code on the device passes CAVP.
The same FAQ applies this to NIAP Protection Profile evaluations of products that only verify:
Where signing occurs outside the Target of Evaluation (TOE) boundary, such as for commercial products being certified where only firmware signature verification is performed within the TOE while the firmware signing is performed outside the TOE by an HSM or other external signing service, Protection Profile requirements only apply to signature verification. As signature generation is the component of LMS/XMSS that requires state management, if only signature verification is being performed only CAVP validation (not CMVP) will be expected to meet CNSA 2.0 for such products.
LMS and XMSS (the same table lists ML-DSA-87 for “signing firmware and software”, p. 7):
All parameters approved for all classification levels. LMS SHA-256/192 is recommended.
From NIST SP 800-208, NSA has only approved LMS and XMSS for use in NSS. The multi-tree algorithms HSS and XMSSMT are not allowed.

Module: Secure Boot & Firmware PQC
Component: SecureBootIntroduction

While SLH-DSA is hash-based, it is not part of CNSA and is not approved for any use in NSS.
A signer or verifier that is a FIPS 140-3 module also runs self-tests (CASTs). IG 10.3.A (last modified 19 August 2026) sets the timing and the content:
The requirements of this IG apply prior to the first operational use of the cryptographic algorithm.
If the module implements LMS signature generation then it shall also implement key generation and shall have CASTs for both LMS signature generation and key generation.
If the module implements signature verification for LMS, it shall have a CAST for it.
if the module implements digital signature verification, the module shall have an ML-DSA digital signature verification CAST.
For the hash-based schemes the size of the tree sets the testing effort:
it is sufficient that the CASTs exercise the smallest (or any other single) parameter set (e.g., a single table row with the lowest height trees) supported by the module to provide assurance that the algorithm is operating correctly.
Every generated key pair also gets a pairwise consistency test (PCT), which for SP 800-208 key pairs may be limited:
may be limited to confirming the same key identifier (I in the case of LMS, SEED in the case of XMSS and PK.SEED for SLH-DSA) is shared by the resulting public and private key following generation.
Subsequent generations of the key pair from the stored seed are considered a reconstitution of the key pair and a PCT is not required.

chunks.title: Secure Boot & Firmware PQC — SecureBootIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Secure Boot & Firmware PQC
Component: SecureBootIntroduction

Module type. SP 800-208 asks for a hardware module. IG C.N Resolution 9 reads:
Provided the hardware components of any FIPS 140-3 certified module satisfies the latter two requirements, it is not required that modules are module type: ‘hardware’ and may separately include modules of type ‘firmware’ and ‘hybrid firmware’. For any permitted module type, these shall support a certification claim to the Level 3 requirements from section 7.7, Physical security, of ISO/IEC 19790:2012. This resolution excludes software and hybrid software modules on the basis that these are not by definition in ISO/IEC 19790:2012 permitted to include a limited or non-modifiable operating environment (OE) as required by SP 800-208.
In this IG a hybrid firmware module is a module “whose cryptographic boundary delimits the composite of one or more firmware component(s) and a disjoint hardware component” (IG 1.B, p. 13). It has nothing to do with hybrid key exchange.
4. What a certificate for the signing module does and does not cover
It covers the module the lab tested. A module claiming SP 800-208 has to meet its Section 8 conformance requirements:
Modules claiming compliance with SP 800-208 and use of the approved security functions described therein shall meet, and make clear in the documentation, the conformance requirements noted in Section 8 of the standard including, but not limited to, the following that apply when a module implements key generation and signature generation:

chunks.title: Secure Boot & Firmware PQC — SecureBootIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Secure Boot & Firmware PQC
Component: SecureBootIntroduction

The cryptographic module shall not allow for the export of private keying material. The entropy source for any approved random bit generator used in the implementation shall be located inside the cryptographic module's physical boundary.
In addition to the prohibition of the export of private keys, this resolution extends this to include the prohibition of the import of private key material for use with an approved HBS service, including the prohibition of importing private keys as a restore operation from a backup.
The lab checks the one-time-key rule by testing, not by paperwork alone:
Documentation review in isolation is not sufficient to confirm compliance with these requirements.
the tester shall confirm they verified the module prevents the use of an OTS key to generate a digital signature more than one time.
The verification code on the device. The FAQ (part 2) says that for a signer that is not an NSS, “the only part NSA will validate” is that this on-device code passes CAVP.
Anything outside the module boundary. For a signature scheme split across components:
If the module is part of a distributed signature scheme per Section 7 of SP 800-208, the CASTs described above only apply to the functionality implemented within the module's boundary.
a product or implementation does not meet the FIPS 140 module validation requirements by simply implementing an Approved security function and acquiring validations for each of the implemented algorithms.

chunks.content:
Module: Secure Boot & Firmware PQC
Component: SecureBootIntroduction

The FAQ also advises on where to keep the signing state and on backups:
Note: To avoid weakening the security of these signatures, one should implement signing and state management in hardware, such as an HSM. Backup flows, which may involve transferring keys between modules, must prevent state re-use.
Related: how the ACVP tests are run in ACVP Lab Workflow , how the signing state is managed in Stateful Hash-Based Signatures , and how a module is validated in FIPS 140-3 Certification .
Two integrity checks beside the signature: SP 800-193 and the FIPS 140-3 integrity test
NIST SP 800-193, Platform Firmware Resiliency Guidelines (May 2018), is aimed at developers and engineers who implement firmware-level security.
It has three principles. Protection keeps platform firmware code and critical data in a state of integrity, for example by ensuring the authenticity and integrity of firmware updates. Detection finds when they have been corrupted or changed from an authorized state. Recovery restores them to a state of integrity.
The mechanisms are founded in Roots of Trust, defined by function: Update, Detection and Recovery. The guideline applies to any device in the platform that contains firmware. Its example list for x86 platforms includes the embedded controller, TPM, baseboard management controller, SPI flash and host boot firmware.

chunks.title: Secure Boot & Firmware PQC — SecureBootIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Secure Boot & Firmware PQC
Component: SecureBootIntroduction

In an authenticated update, the Root of Trust for Update holds the signature verification algorithm and the key store. Both change only through an authenticated update or a secure local update. Update images must be signed with a FIPS 186-4 algorithm at a security strength of at least 112 bits. For detection, the guideline lists integrity verification with a digital signature algorithm or a cryptographic hash before code outside the Root of Trust for Detection runs. The text names FIPS 186-4, which FIPS 186-5 has since superseded, and does not mention post-quantum schemes.
FIPS 140-3 takes its technical requirements and test methods from ISO/IEC 19790:2012 and ISO/IEC 24759:2017. The CMVP records changes in the SP 800-140 series and answers lab and vendor questions in the Implementation Guidance (IG).
The integrity test is a pre-operational self-test (ISO/IEC 19790:2012, 7.10.2.2). The module verifies all software and firmware inside its cryptographic boundary with “an approved integrity technique or EDC”; if verification fails, the test fails. Code in non-reconfigurable memory, as the IG defines it, is exempt. The IG notes that a bootloader will have a pre-operational test for firmware integrity/authenticity.

chunks.title: Secure Boot & Firmware PQC — SecureBootIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Secure Boot & Firmware PQC
Component: SecureBootIntroduction

For the software and firmware of a hybrid module, the IG names the technique by security level: level 1, “an approved integrity technique”; level 2, “an approved digital signature or keyed message authentication code”; levels 3 and 4, “an approved digital signature”. For a hardware module, an EDC is sufficient for its software and firmware. The algorithm behind the technique first has to pass its own algorithm self-test. The Security Policy states which techniques the module uses.
For PQC signatures, the CMVP list of security functions includes ML-DSA, SLH-DSA, LMS, HSS, XMSS and XMSSMT. The IG's worked example for the integrity technique's self-test uses RSA; it gives no PQC example.
SP 800-193 is a design guideline for platforms and names no validation program. The integrity test is a requirement on a cryptographic module, tested by an accredited laboratory and validated by the CMVP.

TPM 2.0 (ISO/IEC 11889:2015) is a cryptographic module that can establish a platform's device identity, securely store keys and credentials, and help measure and report system state. TCG standards are supported by technologies deployed in enterprise-class clients and servers and other platforms.
TPM 2.0 Library v185 Defines ML-DSA and ML-KEM; Installed TPMs Predate It

chunks.title: Secure Boot & Firmware PQC — SecureBootIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Secure Boot & Firmware PQC
Component: SecureBootIntroduction

The Trusted Computing Group (TCG) published the TPM 2.0 Library Specification v185 on 12 March 2026. Its change history (Part 0) states: “Introduced support for ML-DSA, HashML-DSA, and ML-KEM.” The PC Client Platform TPM Profile (PTP) 1.07 adds larger data transport and defines which ML-KEM Endorsement Key certificates are required. The ISO/IEC 11889:2015 edition dates from before ML-KEM and ML-DSA were standardized (FIPS 203 and FIPS 204).
A TPM offers these algorithms only if its vendor built it to v185 or later. A TPM2_GetCapability query for TPM_PT_REVISION (specification version) and TPM_PT_ML_PARAMETER_SETS (supported ML-KEM and ML-DSA parameter sets) shows what a given part supports. Chips and platform firmware follow the specification, so check a vendor’s own documentation for which version a shipping part implements.
PCR[7] records all Secure Boot key changes (PK/KEK/db enrollment). When you migrate UEFI keys to ML-DSA, PCR[7] will change. Any secrets sealed against PCR[7] (notably BitLocker TPM protectors on Windows) must be re-sealed after the key migration. Plan for BitLocker recovery key backup and re-sealing as part of your UEFI PQC migration procedure.
BIOS and firmware vendors are at different stages of PQC adoption. Understanding each vendor's timeline is critical for infrastructure refresh planning, especially for organizations with CNSA 2.0 or EU NIS2 compliance requirements.

chunks.title: Secure Boot & Firmware PQC — SecureBootIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Secure Boot & Firmware PQC
Component: SecureBootIntroduction

The UEFI Forum published a white paper, Post-Quantum Cryptography: UEFI Specification Updates (29 April 2026), that “consolidates proposed specification changes for additional feedback and to validate implementation feasibility.” It states: “These proposals are not yet approved and may change or be rejected.” Organizations should monitor UEFI Forum publications and engage their firmware vendors for preview access.
At scale, firmware integrity requires end-to-end supply chain controls. The threat model extends beyond network attackers to include insider threats at OEMs, compromised build systems, and hardware implants in manufacturing. PQC migration must secure the entire signing pipeline.
OS-level crypto providers, SSH host keys, and system TLS policy
Analyze UEFI key hierarchies, migrate firmware signatures, and explore TPM attestation flows.
TPM RSA AIK signs quote (hardware-backed proof)
The TPM's RSA-2048 AIK produces a quote over PCR values — this proves hardware integrity but is quantum-vulnerable for long-lived secrets.
Software ML-DSA-65 key co-signs the same nonce
An ML-DSA-65 key pair generated in software (outside the TPM) signs the same challenge nonce, providing quantum-safe attestation. The ML-DSA public key is bound to the TPM AIK certificate.
Verifier validates both signatures
The relying party checks: (1) TPM AIK certificate chain (hardware binding), (2) ML-DSA signature (quantum-safe proof). Both must pass.

chunks.title: Secure Boot & Firmware PQC — SecureBootIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Secure Boot & Firmware PQC
Component: SecureBootIntroduction

ML-DSA private keys used for firmware signing should be stored in FIPS 140-3 Level 3 HSMs (best practice). For LMS and XMSS, NIST SP 800-208 §8.1 says the key generation and signature algorithms "shall only be validated for use within hardware cryptographic modules". Key ceremony procedures must be updated for ML-DSA-65 key generation.
NIST SP 800-161r1 says the enterprise should ensure that code authentication mechanisms, such as digital signatures, are implemented to ensure the integrity of software, firmware, and information. Signing firmware manifests (SWID tags, SBOM attestations) with ML-DSA is one way to carry this out.
Automated firmware update systems (iDRAC, iLO, iSUM) must validate ML-DSA signatures before applying updates. Update catalogs and manifests must use ML-DSA-65 throughout.
Enterprise attestation services (Microsoft Azure Attestation, Google Confidential Space) must handle ML-DSA AIK certificates and PQC TPM quote signatures as hardware support becomes available.
Catalog all firmware signing keys, identify platforms, assess UEFI NVRAM capacity, engage OEM vendors for PQC timelines.
Deploy firmware with hybrid RSA + ML-DSA signatures. Begin PK/KEK/db migration on new platforms. EDK2 OVMF for lab validation.
Retire RSA-only firmware signing. Complete PK/KEK/db migration on all production platforms. Enable ML-DSA-only mode once legacy systems are retired.

A signature protects no secret, so this is a forgery risk, not harvest now, decrypt later. Once a CRQC exists, whoever holds the public key could derive the private key and produce attestation evidence the verifier accepts. The longer the device and its trust anchors stay in the field, the more likely a CRQC arrives while they still do, so migration urgency follows device lifetime.
The TLS key exchange in this flow is different: a recorded session can be decrypted later, so that leg is a true harvest-now-decrypt-later exposure.

chunks.title: Secure Boot & Firmware PQC — BootVerifyLatencySimulator
chunks.content:
Module: Secure Boot & Firmware PQC
Component: BootVerifyLatencySimulator

On a microcontroller root of trust, the boot ROM or first-stage loader reads the signature and public key from SPI flash into SRAM, then verifies the next stage in software before handing over. This calculator splits that delay into flash-read time and verify time for a Cortex-M4-class core, so you can see which part PQC actually changes.
What the numbers say: the PQC signature-plus-key payloads are 20-30× larger than ECDSA's 128 bytes, but at realistic SPI speeds that costs only a couple of milliseconds of flash reading (this module's planning assumption, not a measurement). In this module's model, verify time is what dominates — ML-DSA-44 (~1.4 M cycles) and LMS (~2.7 M) stay within a few times ECDSA P-256 (~1 M), while RSA-3072 verify in software is roughly 25 M cycles and is by far the slowest of the four.
For memory, power and network constraints on IoT devices, see IoT & Embedded Device PQC

chunks.title: Secure Boot & Firmware PQC — FirmwareSigningMigrator
chunks.content:
Module: Secure Boot & Firmware PQC
Component: FirmwareSigningMigrator

UEFI Secure Boot verifies every firmware image against signed db certificates at boot
TPM PCR measurements attest firmware integrity — signatures must survive quantum attacks
Supply chain compromise via forged signatures is a critical threat — PQC eliminates Shor's algorithm risk
Signing mode: Pure   [Standard per RFC 9882 §3.1 & RFC 9814 §1]
ML-DSA uses SHAKE-256 and SHAKE-128 internally ( FIPS 204 §3.7); SLH-DSA-SHA2-128S uses SHA-256 internally (the "SHA2" in the name; SHA-512 appears only in the 192- and 256-bit SHA2 sets, FIPS 205 §11.2.2). Both are called in pure mode: the signer is handed the message directly, with no separate pre-hash step. HashML-DSA (pre-hash) is not specified for CMS ( RFC 9882 §3.1) and must not be used in X.509 certificates (RFC 9881 §8.3). Your hash selection applies to: firmware digest display + classical signature mechanism (e.g. CKM_SHA256_RSA_PKCS).
“… in most situations, CMS signatures are computed over a set of signed attributes that contain a hash of the content, rather than being computed over the message content itself. Since signed attributes are typically small, use of pre-hash modes in the CMS wouldn't significantly reduce the size of the data to be signed, and hence offers no benefit.”

chunks.title: Secure Boot & Firmware PQC — FirmwareSigningMigrator
chunks.content:
Module: Secure Boot & Firmware PQC
Component: FirmwareSigningMigrator

What ML-DSA is given ( RFC 9882 §3.2 ): with signedAttrs, the complete DER encoding of the signed attributes, which must include a content-type attribute and a message-digest attribute (the hash of the content). Without signedAttrs, the content itself. Signed attributes are the preferred form, and an HSM then receives only that small attribute set ( §5).
This demo builds SignedData without signedAttrs and signs the short manifest text directly, so it shows the pure-mode signing call but not the signed-attributes step. With no signed attributes the SignerInfo digestAlgorithm carries no weight, and the PQC envelope names the value the RFCs prescribe: SHA-512 for ML-DSA ( RFC 9882 §3.3, MUST) and the tree hash, SHA-256, for SLH-DSA-SHA2-128S (RFC 9814 §4, SHOULD), whatever hash you picked for the classical signature.
X.509 is a separate rule. RFC 9881 §8.3 bars HashML-DSA from certificates mainly for interoperability: a verifier would have to be told whether to run ML-DSA.Verify or HashML-DSA.Verify.
ML-DSA-44 — NIST Level 2 · smallest ML-DSA keys/sigs · non-critical firmware where size matters
ML-DSA-65 — NIST Level 3 · balanced · recommended general-purpose firmware signing
ML-DSA-87 — NIST Level 5 · required by CNSA 2.0 for NSS; approved for firmware signing alongside the preferred LMS/XMSS (SP 800-208)

chunks.content:

Component: FirmwareSigningMigrator

SLH-DSA-SHA2-128S — NIST Level 1 · smallest pubkey (32 B) but very large signature (7,856 B) · This module's advice: use it only for root-of-trust and infrequent signing (e.g. UEFI PK/KEK), not per-image signing. Not part of CNSA and not approved for any use in NSS (NSA CNSA 2.0 FAQ v2.2, p. 11)

This demo uses a stub SignerInfo (issuer="demo", serial=1) with no certificate chain. In production the CMS certificates field carries an X.509 cert binding the PQC public key: RFC 9881 for ML-DSA ( id-ML-DSA AlgorithmIdentifier in SubjectPublicKeyInfo) or RFC 9909 for SLH-DSA. The UEFI db stores that cert as an EFI_CERT_X509 signature list entry.
NSA CNSA 2.0 prefers LMS/XMSS (SP 800-208, stateful hash-based signatures) to start software/firmware signing now, with CNSA 2.0 required exclusively by 2030. Explore TPM 2.0 key hierarchies and understand the path to post-quantum attestation. TPM 2.0 Library v185 adds ML-DSA and ML-KEM — see how each key type changes, and learn the hybrid approach for TPMs built to earlier versions.
TPM 2.0 Library v185 Defines ML-DSA and ML-KEM; Installed TPMs Predate It
The Trusted Computing Group (TCG) published TPM 2.0 Library v185 on 12 March 2026. Its change history states: “Introduced support for ML-DSA, HashML-DSA, and ML-KEM.”
The TPM's primary identity key, provisioned by the manufacturer. The EK's public key is enrolled in the TPM vendor's certificate authority. Used to establish trust in the TPM itself during attestation.
The primary key of the Storage Hierarchy. All user-created keys are ultimately protected by the SRK. Applications create keys under the SRK (or SRK-derived parent keys). The SRK is not exportable.
A restricted signing key used for TPM quotes. The AIK signs PCR values to prove system state to a remote verifier. The AIK certificate is issued by a Privacy CA or by TPM vendor direct attestation.
IEEE 802.1AR Initial Device Identity — a long-lived key provisioned at manufacture, used to prove device identity in network access (802.1X, TEAP). Embedded in TPM at factory.
The Platform Hierarchy is controlled by the platform owner (OEM). It manages TPM initialization and is typically locked during normal operation. Platform authorization is not a keypair but an auth value.

chunks.title: Skills & Team Structure — Introduction
chunks.content:
Module: Skills & Team Structure
Component: Introduction

PQC migration requires a combination of skills that rarely coexists in a single team: deep cryptographic knowledge (algorithms, protocols, PKI architecture), enterprise program management at scale (governance, stakeholder management, multi-year planning), and domain-specific technical expertise (network security, application security, OT engineering, cloud architecture). The market for professionals who combine even two of these is thin.
The realistic approach is not to hire a complete team of PQC specialists. It is to build the program around a small core of cryptographic expertise, supplement it with existing enterprise security and IT staff upskilled on PQC-relevant topics, and augment with external specialists for capabilities the organization cannot develop internally in the required timeframe.
A dedicated nucleus of cryptographic expertise: program management, architecture, and PMO that exists regardless of estate size.

Buy in scarce specialists (OT, strategic quantum CTI) you cannot develop in the required timeframe.

chunks.title: Software Supply Chain PQC — SoftwareSupplyChainIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Software Supply Chain PQC
Component: SoftwareSupplyChainIntroduction

Software reaches a device through a series of hand-offs, and at each hand-off some control is meant to tell the receiver that what arrived is what was sent. Many of those controls are signatures. This lesson reads the signature links from their own documents, one link at a time, and says for each what the document states about post-quantum signatures and where it is silent.
This table is the lesson’s own map, not a statement from any source. It shows which kind of control each link relies on and where the topic is taught in depth, so that this lesson can leave those parts to the modules that own them.
Two sourced statements anchor the map. The first is from NIST’s Secure Software Development Framework, the second from its guidance on integrating supply chain security into DevSecOps.
For each ecosystem below, the lesson reports what the held edition of one document says. A label next to a sentence says what kind of statement it is. The labels are about the document, never about a plan or a date.
A silent entry means the held text of one edition contains none of these terms: post-quantum, quantum, PQC, ML-DSA, SLH-DSA, Dilithium, SPHINCS, LMS, XMSS, hash-based signature, Kyber, ML-KEM. It does not say that anyone plans or declines a migration, and it does not describe other editions of the same document.
TUF and Uptane are two update frameworks that spread trust across several roles and keys. This section reads them from their specifications.

chunks.title: Software Supply Chain PQC — SoftwareSupplyChainIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Software Supply Chain PQC
Component: SoftwareSupplyChainIntroduction

A role that requires t signatures from n keys is trusted only when at least t of its keys signed. By simple counting, an attacker who holds fewer than t of the role’s keys cannot sign for it alone, and an attacker who holds t or more can. With t equal to 1, any single key is enough. The Roles and Thresholds step of the Workshop lets you set t, n and the keys an attacker holds.
Two further documents describe the signature elements of firmware updates. For SUIT and device constraints, see IoT .
Provenance records how an artifact was built. The SLSA v1.2 pages call it an attestation and ask for it to be signed from Build L2. This section reads the SLSA v1.2 Build pages and the in-toto Statement page for what each says about signatures.
Because none of these pages names a signature algorithm, the algorithm behind a provenance signature is not decided on these pages. In this lesson’s reading, the status of that signature is the status of its algorithm’s encodings in section 2: a hash-based or ML-DSA signature can be carried only where an encoding exists for it. The Provenance Chain Check step of the Workshop traces one artifact through build, provenance and verification and marks, at each signature, which section 2 entry applies.
The hard case is a verifier that is already deployed. This section reads what the documents say about verifiers that cannot be updated, about carrying two signatures during a change, and about combining algorithms.

chunks.title: Standards, Certification & Compliance Bodies — Introduction
chunks.content:
Module: Standards, Certification & Compliance Bodies
Component: Introduction

The PQC transition involves three fundamentally different types of organizations, each playing a distinct role. Confusing them is a common source of compliance mistakes.
Think of it like building construction: standardization bodies write the building codes (what materials are safe), certification bodies are the inspectors who verify that a specific building meets those codes, and compliance frameworks are the zoning laws that say "in this jurisdiction, meeting code is mandatory for these buildings." All three are necessary; none is redundant.
Create technical standards: algorithm specifications, security levels, protocol integration. Their output is a published document, not a certificate.
Certify that products/systems correctly implement standards. Their output is a certificate (or certificate number) tied to a specific product version.
• EUCC certification bodies → EU product certs ( ENISA publishes them)
Regulations and mandates that reference standards and require certifications. Their output is a legal/regulatory obligation, not a technical specification.
The three roles form a chain: a standards body publishes an algorithm specification → a certification body validates that a product correctly implements it → a compliance framework can require regulated entities to use certified products.
Key insight: You can comply with a framework, be certified against a standard, and the standard body writes the standard — three verbs, three different relationships.

chunks.title: Standards, Certification & Compliance Bodies — Introduction
chunks.content:
Module: Standards, Certification & Compliance Bodies
Component: Introduction

Whether an organization is governmental or non-governmental determines whether its outputs can be legally mandatory or only advisory. This distinction matters enormously for compliance.
Government agencies with regulatory authority. Their technical guidelines and mandates can be legally binding. Authority derives from government statute, not membership consensus.
Industry consortia and open membership bodies. Their standards gain authority through broad adoption, not government mandate. Anyone can contribute; consensus drives output.
Governments can mandate nationally-specific algorithms that differ from NIST standards. This creates interoperability challenges for multinational organizations.
China's Office of State Commercial Cryptography Administration (OSCCA) mandates SM2 (asymmetric), SM3 (hash), and SM4 (symmetric) algorithms for regulated sectors.

chunks.title: Standards, Certification & Compliance Bodies — Introduction
chunks.content:
Module: Standards, Certification & Compliance Bodies

Korea's KpqC competition (2022–2025), run by the research group that the National Security Research Institute (NSR) and the National Intelligence Service (NIS) set up in 2021, selected HAETAE and AIMer (signatures), SMAUG-T and NTRU+ (KEMs) as Korean national algorithms — distinct from NIST's selections. As of April 2026, Korean Standard proposals for the two KEMs have been submitted and the two signature algorithms are under review; no standardization date is published. The July 2023 national master plan (NIS and the Ministry of Science and ICT) targets 2035 for spreading PQC. Korean telecom operators may require support for KpqC algorithms alongside FIPS 203/204/205.
Crypto-agile architectures (abstraction layers, pluggable algorithm providers) are essential for organizations operating across jurisdictions with divergent algorithm mandates. Design your key management and protocol stacks to support algorithm negotiation, not hard-coded algorithm choices.
Global bodies gain authority through broad adoption and multi-country consensus, not government mandate. Their standards are recognized worldwide but not legally binding in themselves.
Practical guidance: For most products, start with NIST FIPS 203/204/205 (US procurement), add ETSI TS 103 744 (hybrid key establishment, if you need it), then layer national guidance (BSI TR-02102 for Germany, ANSSI hybrid for France). chunks.title: Standards, Certification & Compliance Bodies — workshopScenarios (data)
chunks.content:
Module: Standards, Certification & Compliance Bodies
Data: workshopScenarios

Your US federal agency is procuring a new HSM to store ML-KEM keys for classified communications. A vendor claims their product "supports FIPS 140-3". You need to verify this claim before signing the purchase order.
Which program certifies that an HSM correctly implements FIPS 140-3?
CMVP (Cryptographic Module Validation Program)
CMVP is the certification body. FIPS 140-3 is the standard being validated. NIST wrote FIPS 140-3 (standards body), but CMVP administers the validation program.
FIPS 140-3 is the NIST standard that defines security requirements for cryptographic modules — it specifies what a module must do. The CMVP (jointly run by NIST and Canada's CSE) is the certification body that validates whether a specific product actually meets those requirements through NVLAP-accredited testing labs. Always verify CMVP status on the official NIST CMVP database (csrc.nist.gov/projects/cmvp) using the exact certificate number, as vendors sometimes claim "FIPS compliance" without having an actual CMVP certificate. For US federal procurement under FISMA, you need a current CMVP certificate, not just a vendor claim.
Your multinational bank's French subsidiary must deploy PQC for customer authentication. A colleague says you need ANSSI approval for your cryptographic choices. You need to understand what ANSSI requires and what type of organization it is.
What type of body is ANSSI, and what is its primary position on PQC?
Standards Body (creates technical standards)
Government Agency (issues government mandates)
Hybrid PQC (classical + PQC combined; mandatory inside ANSSI's regulated perimeter)
ISO 27001 (information security management)
ANSSI is a governmental regulatory agency. Its key PQC position is hybrid cryptography: it strongly recommends using classical and PQC algorithms together (not PQC standalone), and makes that mandatory inside the French regulated perimeter.
ANSSI (Agence nationale de la sécurité des systèmes d'information) is France's national cybersecurity authority — a governmental regulatory agency. Unlike ISO or IETF, ANSSI has government authority, but its PQC publications are recommendations: ANSSI states that its PQC recommendations, including hybridisation, are not regulatory obligations today. Hybridisation is mandatory inside the regulated perimeter (defence-classified and Diffusion Restreinte information, vital information systems, and products certified or qualified through ANSSI security visas). ANSSI's distinctive PQC position (2022/2023 papers) is to combine a classical algorithm (e.g., ECDH) with a PQC algorithm (e.g., ML-KEM-768) in parallel, not replace classical cryptography outright. This is more conservative than NIST's approach. The rationale: if a PQC algorithm is broken, the classical component still provides protection. The exception is hash-based signatures (SLH-DSA, XMSS, LMS): ANSSI does not recommend systematic hybridisation for them, because it considers their underlying problem well studied, although the
...(truncated)

chunks.title: Stateful Signatures — SchemeForUseSection
chunks.content:
Module: Stateful Signatures
Component: SchemeForUseSection

Each row shows one example parameter set and the number of signatures it can ever make. Every signature uses up one one-time key, so that number is a hard limit; estimate what your use needs and pick a set that covers it. The record of which keys are used (the state) must stay inside the signing hardware module; a device that only verifies keeps none.

chunks.title: Stateful Signatures — StatefulSigsExercises
chunks.content:
Module: Stateful Signatures
Component: StatefulSigsExercises

Work through these scenarios to understand stateful hash-based signatures, parameter trade-offs, and the critical importance of state management. Each exercise pre-configures the Workshop — click "Load & Run" to begin.
Take the PQC quiz to test what you've learned about stateful signatures.
Start with H5/W8 (smallest signatures, fewest keys), then switch to H20/W4. Observe how tree height controls signing capacity while the Winternitz parameter controls the signature size vs signing speed trade-off.
Per RFC 8554, H5/W8 produces only 32 signatures at ~1.3 KB each. H20/W4 produces over 1 million signatures at ~2.8 KB each (RFC 8554 sizes). The public key stays the same size as you change H and W (56 bytes for these SHA-256 sets); it changes only with the hash output length.
Select XMSS-SHA2_10 and compare its signature size, key sizes, and security properties against LMS H10/W4. Understand why different regulatory bodies prefer different schemes.
At the same tree height (H=10), XMSS and LMS produce comparably-sized signatures (the exact order depends on the Winternitz parameter). In the current version of XMSS, the security analysis uses the random oracle only for randomized hashing and bitmasks, while LMS uses it to a greater degree.
3. Multi-Tree Scaling (HSS / XMSS^MT)
In the XMSS step, switch Structure to XMSS^MT and pick 60/6. See how chaining sub-trees enables effectively unlimited signing capacity while keeping individual trees manageable — and note the keygen time.

chunks.title: Stateful Signatures — StatefulSigsExercises
chunks.content:
Module: Stateful Signatures
Component: StatefulSigsExercises

XMSS^MT-SHA2_60/6 provides 2^60 signatures (over 10^18) by chaining 6 layers of 10-level trees. Increasing the number of layers reduces key generation time exponentially and signing time linearly, at the cost of a linear increase in signature size.
Use the State Management simulator with H5 (32 signatures). Sign messages until the key is exhausted. Observe the warning thresholds at 80% usage and the catastrophic exhaustion message.
At 80% capacity (26/32 signatures), a rotation warning appears. At 32/32, the key is permanently exhausted. In production, you must rotate BEFORE exhaustion. There is no way to "refill" a stateful key.
Sign several messages, then click "Simulate State Loss". The simulator asks the HSM to take the key back to an earlier signature, the way a restored backup or a cloned key would, and prints the PKCS#11 reply to each attempt. Then sign again and read the leaf numbers in the log.
The HSM engine refuses all three attempts (counter write, state read-out, key copy), so the counter does not move and the next signature uses the next leaf. This is how this emulator answers, not proof that any certified module does. A signer that keeps its state in an ordinary file would reuse the rolled-back leaves, and two signatures on different messages from one one-time key make forgery computationally feasible (SP 800-208 §1.2). That is why §8.1 requires that the cryptographic module not allow private keying material to be exported.

chunks.title: Stateful Signatures — StatefulSigsIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Stateful Signatures
Component: StatefulSigsIntroduction

Hash-based signatures derive their security solely from the properties of cryptographic hash functions, which have a longer standardization history than lattice-based or code-based constructions. Unlike those schemes, they require no new hardness assumptions. LMS requires its hash function to have second-preimage resistance (RFC 8554 §9); XMSS does not rely on the collision resistance of its hash functions but on weaker properties (RFC 8391).
“This recommendation specifies profiles of LMS, HSS, XMSS, and XMSS^MT that are appropriate for use by the U.S. Federal Government.”
— NIST SP 800-208: Recommendation for Stateful Hash-Based Signature Schemes (October 2020)
Security relies only on hash function properties — no lattices, no codes, no isogenies.
SP 800-208 standardized LMS/HSS and XMSS/XMSS^MT for federal use.
NSA CNSA 2.0 approves single-tree LMS and XMSS (not HSS or XMSS^MT) for firmware and software signing in national security systems, and prefers LMS with SHA-256/192; ML-DSA-87 is also allowed for this use. Phased timeline:
The core idea is a Merkle tree of one-time signature (OTS) key pairs. Each leaf contains the hash of a unique OTS public key. The tree root is the overall public key. To sign, you use the next unused OTS leaf and provide an authentication path from that leaf to the root.
Green = next available OTS key. Each leaf can only be used ONCE.

chunks.title: Stateful Signatures — StatefulSigsIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Stateful Signatures
Component: StatefulSigsIntroduction

Each OTS key pair (e.g., Winternitz OTS+) can sign exactly one message. Reusing an OTS key leaks the private key, enabling forgeries.
The signature includes the OTS signature plus the sibling hashes needed to recompute the path from the used leaf to the root. Verifiers check that the path produces the known root.
How Winternitz Hash Chains Work — and Why Reuse is Catastrophic
Each OTS secret key is a set of random values. To sign, each value is hashed a number of times based on the message digest — revealing an intermediate chain value. The public key is the fully hashed end of each chain.
sk → H¹(sk) → H²(sk) → … → H&sup7;(sk) = pk
Signing message A reveals H³(sk); signing message B (different digit) reveals H&sup5;(sk). An attacker who sees both can compute the full chain and forge arbitrary messages — this is why OTS reuse is a complete break, not a partial leak. The checksum field prevents attackers from simply “advancing” the chain to forge messages with higher digit values.
The Leighton-Micali Signature Scheme (LMS) is defined in RFC 8554. It uses a single Merkle tree with LM-OTS (Leighton-Micali OTS) at the leaves. The Hierarchical Signature System (HSS) extends LMS with multiple levels of trees, where each non-leaf tree signs the root of the tree below it.
• Small public key: 24 bytes plus the hash output length – 48 bytes for the SHA-256/192 sets, 56 bytes for the SHA-256 sets (RFC 8554, SP 800-208) (not sourced in the Library)

chunks.title: Stateful Signatures — StatefulSigsIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Stateful Signatures
Component: StatefulSigsIntroduction

• Signature size: 1.3 – 9.3 KB depending on H, W (RFC 8554) (not sourced in the Library)
Security note: W has zero impact on security level. It only controls the size / speed trade-off. Security is determined by the hash function and n (hash output length), not by W.
NIST SP 800-208 §8.1 requires key generation and signing within a FIPS 140-validated hardware cryptographic module with no private keying material export. The profile specifies Level 3 or higher physical security and a non-modifiable or limited operational environment. Consult applicable CMVP implementation guidance for validation details. The workshop explains how to review state protection and what its demonstration cannot prove.
The eXtended Merkle Signature Scheme (XMSS) is defined in RFC 8391. It shares the same Merkle tree approach as LMS but adds features like a bitmask-based tree hash construction (for multi-target attack resistance) and a different OTS scheme (WOTS+). XMSS^MT is the multi-tree variant, analogous to HSS.

chunks.title: Stateful Signatures — StatefulSigsIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Stateful Signatures
Component: StatefulSigsIntroduction

XMSS internals: Two key constructions distinguish XMSS from LMS. An L-tree compresses the WOTS+ public key (up to 67 hash values) into a single leaf via an unbalanced binary tree. RAND_HASH randomizes each internal node by XOR’ing inputs with PRF-derived bitmasks before hashing, providing domain separation and multi-target attack resistance. These add ~4× the hash computations of LMS but yield a security proof that does not rely on the collision resistance of the hash functions (RFC 8391).
Both LMS and XMSS are approved by NIST SP 800-208. NSA CNSA 2.0 allows only the single-tree LMS and XMSS (HSS and XMSS^MT are not allowed) and prefers LMS with SHA-256/192; BSI TR-02102-1 recommends all SP 800-208 parameter sets of both families (not sourced in the Library).
The critical operational challenge with stateful schemes is that the signer MUST track which OTS keys have been used. Each leaf index can be used exactly once. If state is lost, reset, or duplicated, the same OTS key may be used twice — completely breaking the signature scheme.
If a one-time signature key is reused (signing two different messages with the same leaf), an attacker can compute enough of the OTS private key to forge arbitrary signatures. This is not a theoretical weakness — it is a complete break of the scheme. There is no recovery; the entire key must be revoked.
FIPS 205 parameter sets meet their security categories when each key pair signs at most 2^64 messages; no leaf counter

chunks.title: Stateful Signatures — StatefulSigsIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Stateful Signatures
Component: StatefulSigsIntroduction

Approved for firmware/software signing (LMS SHA-256/192 recommended; ML-DSA-87 also allowed)
LMS/XMSS and SLH-DSA are complementary, not competing. Stateful schemes are typically more compact in signature and key sizes than stateless alternatives like SLH-DSA.
A FIPS 140-3 certificate for a module that signs with LMS or XMSS rests on four different kinds of check. The algorithm tests are only the first.
• ACVP has an LMS specification with three modes: keyGen, sigGen and sigVer. Each has one test type, AFT (Algorithm Functional Test).
• keyGen: the implementation must “generate a key pair based on an approved tree structure”. sigGen: it must “generate valid signatures based on the ACVP provided message”. sigVer: it must “determine the validity of the signature given the tree structure, key, and message”.
• A vendor registers LMS modes and LM-OTS modes by hash, tree height (for example LMS_SHA256_M24_H5 through LMS_SHA256_M32_H25) and Winternitz setting (W1, W2, W4, W8). The pair must follow SP 800-208 Section 4, “namely M = N, and the hash is the same”.
• On NIST's CAVP prerequisites page, LMS keyGen, sigGen and sigVer each list “All hash functions and XOFs used.”
• Not covered, in the specification's words: “ACVP does not test the inability of an implementation to export a private key. ACVP does not provide any guarantees on the inability to reuse private OTS pairs of an implementation.”

chunks.title: Stateful Signatures — StatefulSigsIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Stateful Signatures
Component: StatefulSigsIntroduction

• XMSS, XMSS^MT and HSS: no ACVP specification is published for them. The ACVP index at pages.nist.gov/ACVP lists LMS, ML-DSA, ML-KEM and SLH-DSA as its post-quantum entries (checked 23 October 2026). IG C.N, last modified 10 September 2024, says CAVP tests are “available for LMS but not yet for XMSS, HSS, or XMSSMT”. IG C.O, of the same date, records that “Support for the LMS scheme was added to the ACVTS production server in April 2023” and that “the other schemes (including HSS) remain untestable by the CAVP as of the last modified date of this IG”.
• The module runs cryptographic algorithm self-tests (CASTs). IG 10.3.A applies its requirements “prior to the first operational use of the cryptographic algorithm”.
• A module that implements LMS signature generation must also implement key generation and have CASTs for both. The same holds for HSS, XMSS and XMSS^MT. Signature verification needs its own CAST. HSS builds on LMS, so the HSS CASTs cover the LMS ones; XMSS^MT likewise covers XMSS.
• Hash functions: a CAST for SHA-256 is required; for SHA-256/192 if it is implemented without SHA-256; for SHAKE256/256; and for SHAKE256/192 if it is implemented without SHAKE256/256. These can be satisfied as part of the LMS, HSS, XMSS or XMSS^MT CASTs.

chunks.title: Stateful Signatures — StatefulSigsIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Stateful Signatures
Component: StatefulSigsIntroduction

• Testing cost depends on tree height, so the CASTs only need to exercise the smallest (or any single) supported parameter set. “It is also not necessary to test both LM-OTS + LMS modes”, but a CAST covering the different underlying SHA or SHAKE functions is still required.
• Every generated key pair also needs a pairwise consistency test. For SP 800-208 keys it “may be limited to confirming the same key identifier (I in the case of LMS, SEED in the case of XMSS and PK.SEED for SLH-DSA) is shared by the resulting public and private key following generation”.
• SP 800-208 §8.1: “Implementations of the key generation and signature algorithms in this document shall only be validated for use within hardware cryptographic modules.” The module must also provide Level 3 or higher physical security and a non-modifiable or limited operational environment, operate only in an approved mode with no bypass mode, not allow export of private keying material, and keep the entropy source of its random bit generator inside its physical boundary.
• Firmware modules (IG C.N, resolution 9): where the hardware components of a certified module meet the Level 3 physical security and the non-modifiable or limited operational environment, “it is not required that modules are module type: 'hardware' and may separately include modules of type 'firmware' and 'hybrid firmware'”. Software and hybrid software modules are excluded.

chunks.title: Stateful Signatures — StatefulSigsIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Stateful Signatures
Component: StatefulSigsIntroduction

• Signature verification only (IG C.N, resolution 1): the §8.1 requirements “exclusively apply to modules supporting HBS key generation and signature generation”. Modules that only support signature verification “need to comply with requirements from section 8.2 of SP 800-208, but do not need to meet requirements from section 8.1”.
• Where ACVP is silent, the lab checks. IG C.N prohibits importing private keys, including “importing private keys as a restore operation from a backup” (resolution 3), seeding key generation from an external entropy source outside the hardware perimeter (resolution 5), and creating “independent copies of keys internal to the cryptographic boundary” (resolution 7). The vendor “shall justify the implementation strategy taken to eliminate the possibility of OTS private key re-use”, and “Documentation review in isolation is not sufficient”: the tester confirms the module prevents the use of an OTS key to generate a digital signature more than one time, cannot create an independent copy of an HBS key, and, if it stores keys in non-volatile memory, updates the leaf index there before exporting a signature value or accepting a request to sign another message (resolution 12).
4. CNSA 2.0: verifier and signer are validated differently (NSA CNSA 2.0 FAQ, version 2.2, October 2026)

Section 10.2 says the digest needs at least 8n bits of classical security strength against both collision and second-preimage attacks (n = 16, 24 or 32, by parameter set). An SLH-DSA signature is a randomizer R, a FORS signature and a hypertree signature (d XMSS signatures, each a WOTS+ signature plus a Merkle authentication path) — see FIPS 205 §9.2, Figure 17 (FORS is §8, the hypertree §7).

chunks.title: Stateful Signatures — SLHDSALiveDemo
chunks.content:
Module: Stateful Signatures
Component: SLHDSALiveDemo

Enable Live WASM Mode above to generate real SLH-DSA keys, sign, and verify using the SoftHSM3 PKCS#11 v3.2 emulator.
Why is SLH-DSA stateless? SLH-DSA keeps no counter. A key pair is a very large set of few-time FORS keys; each signature hashes the message with a randomizer, uses part of the digest to select one of them, and authenticates it through the hypertree. A FORS key can be selected again, and its security degrades gradually; the parameter sets are designed for up to 2^64 signatures per key. Because SLH-DSA keeps no counter, a copy of the private key cannot cause the one-time key reuse that NIST SP 800-208 section 9.1 warns about for LMS and XMSS. Signatures made by all copies of a key still count towards the same limit of 2^64 signatures per key (FIPS 205 section 11). FIPS 205 gives no rules for backing up or replicating keys, so follow your module's key-management requirements.
A known-answer check compares the engine's output with a value fixed in advance by a standard or by NIST. A functional round trip signs and verifies with the same engine, so it shows the pieces work together and nothing more.

Select an SP 800-208 parameter set, then sign messages to watch the one-time key counter advance. See what happens at exhaustion, and how the HSM answers an attempt to roll the state back.
NSA CNSA 2.0 approves only single-tree LMS and XMSS for National Security Systems; the multi-tree HSS is not allowed (FAQ v2.2, p. 11). L2 and L3 are shown for education.
Each chain encodes W bits of the message hash and is 2^W − 1 hash steps long (RFC 8554 §4.1). The signer applies up to 2^W − 1 steps to produce the signature; the verifier completes the remaining steps. Larger W → fewer chains needed → smaller signature bytes → but each chain requires more hash steps → slower to sign and verify.
Simulate State Loss asks the HSM to take this key back to an earlier signature, as a backup restore or a cloned key would, and shows how it answers.
In stateful hash-based signatures, the private key state includes a monotonic counter tracking the next unused OTS leaf. If this counter is lost (via VM snapshot restore, backup restoration, or crash without flush), the signer may unknowingly reuse a one-time key.
The HSM engine in this simulator does not let you cause any of the scenarios below: Simulate State Loss shows it refusing to rewind the key. They describe a signer that keeps its state where it can be restored or copied.

chunks.title: Stateful Signatures — StateManagementVisualizer
chunks.content:
Module: Stateful Signatures
Component: StateManagementVisualizer

VM is snapshotted at counter=100. Signing continues to counter=150. VM is restored to snapshot. Counter resets to 100. Leaves 100–149 will be reused. An attacker with both signatures from any reused leaf can forge.
System signs at counter=50 but crashes before persisting counter=51 to disk. On restart, counter reads 50. Leaf 50 will be reused on next signature.
Private key (including counter) is copied to a second server for redundancy. Both servers sign independently, reusing all leaves. Every signature from the clone is potentially forgeable.
Mitigation: SP 800-208 §8.1 requires a durable leaf-index update before signature output or acceptance of another signing request. Section 9.1 discusses hardware monotonic counters as a possible aid; do not assume every validated HSM uses them. Inspect the actual implementation.

chunks.title: Stateful Signatures — StateReviewGuide
chunks.content:
Module: Stateful Signatures
Component: StateReviewGuide

A leaf represents a one-time signing key. After using leaf 42, the signer must remember not to use it again—even after a crash. Skipping a leaf wastes capacity; reusing it breaks the single-use rule.
NIST requirement: SP 800-208 §8.1 requires incrementing and durably storing the leaf index before exporting a signature or accepting another signing request. It prohibits generating more than one signature with the same one-time key. This is the NIST profile, not a universal CC/EUCC test procedure.
Practical assessment methods—not a prescribed NIST test checklist:
Design and code review: trace the counter update, persistent write and signature output. Check saving failures; a cached write may not survive power loss.
Crash and power-loss tests: interrupt around the state update, restart and sign again. Check that consumed leaves cannot be reused.
Concurrent requests: check that two requests cannot reserve the same leaf.
Recovery and rollback: examine whether restore, failover or cloning can make consumed leaves available again.
Reading results: associate signature leaf indices with the signing key and, for multi-tree schemes, the relevant tree. Two different messages signed with the same one-time key demonstrate failure even if both signatures verify. Repeated appearance of a stored parent-tree signature is not by itself evidence of generating it again.

chunks.title: Stateful Signatures — StateReviewGuide
chunks.content:
Module: Stateful Signatures
Component: StateReviewGuide

No reuse observed in finite tests does not prove reuse impossible. Combine results with design and implementation evidence. An algorithm-test pass alone does not establish crash-safe state management.
Hub limit: this exercise does not perform hardware power-loss testing or prove validated hardware, persistent-storage guarantees or rollback resistance—even when live signing succeeds.

XMSS applies bitmasks via pseudo-randomly generated tree hashes, removing the requirement for collision resistance. It uses standard CKM_XMSS keys.
No keys yet — generate a key pair in the XMSS / MT Explorer above first.
LMS (RFC 8554) and XMSS (RFC 8391) are stateful hash-based signature schemes; SP 800-208 "approves the use of some but not all of the parameter sets" defined for them. Both build Merkle trees over one-time signatures of the Winternitz type: LMS uses the Leighton-Micali one-time signature (LM-OTS), and XMSS uses WOTS+ ("Both XMSS and XMSS^MT use WOTS+ as a main building block").
Cryptographic Base: Relies on Collision Resistance of the underlying hash function (e.g., SHA-256).
Hashing Design: Standard, straightforward Merkle tree concatenations: H(Left || Right).

chunks.title: Stateful Signatures — StatefulSignaturesDemo
chunks.content:
Module: Stateful Signatures
Component: StatefulSignaturesDemo

Multi-Tree: Called HSS (Hierarchical Signature System). HSS is formally just a layered set of standard LMS trees.
Performance: Generally faster key generation times compared to XMSS because there are no complex bitmasking iterations during the tree build process.
Cryptographic Base: Does not rely on the collision resistance of the hash functions, but on weaker properties such as multi-target second-preimage resistance (RFC 8391).
Hashing Design: Applies pseudo-randomly generated Bitmasks via XOR before hashing nodes: H( (Left ⊕ Mask) || (Right ⊕ Mask) ).
Performance: Key generation is more computationally expensive because every hash call is randomised: each step of a WOTS+ chain runs PRF twice, for a key and for a bitmask, XORs the bitmask into the intermediate value and then applies F (RFC 8391 section 3.1.2), where an LM-OTS chain step makes one call to H (RFC 8554 section 4.3).
Multi-tree variants (HSS, XMSS^MT) raise the number of signatures per key without long key generation. NSA CNSA 2.0 approves only the single-tree LMS and XMSS for National Security Systems; HSS and XMSS^MT are not allowed (FAQ v2.2, p. 11).

chunks.title: Stateful Signatures — StatefulSignaturesDemo
chunks.content:
Module: Stateful Signatures
Component: StatefulSignaturesDemo

LMS and XMSS are stateful — each key can sign a bounded number of messages (2H). Once exhausted, the key is retired. SLH-DSA (FIPS 205 / SPHINCS+) is stateless — no persistent leaf counter, and FIPS 205 designs its parameter sets to meet their security categories when each key pair signs at most 2^64 messages — at the cost of significantly larger signatures. Use this tab's Workshop Step 4 to generate and compare real SLH-DSA keys.
Verify the WASM PKCS#11 engine against RFC reference test vectors. Select a scheme, then run the KAT. The PKCS#11 call trace appears below.
RFC 8554 Appendix F Test Case 1 · LMS_SHA256_M32_H5 · L=2 · imports RFC pubkey → C_VerifyInit + C_Verify with RFC signature
NIST SP 800-208 / RFC 8391 XMSS-SHA2_10_256 · h=10 · deterministic keygen via known seed → pubkey comparison → C_VerifyInit + C_Verify
Note: This test injects a known seed via the softhsmv3 _set_kat_seed hook, derives the public key deterministically, and compares it against a pre-computed golden value.

chunks.title: Stateful Signatures — ThresholdSigningDemo
chunks.content:
Module: Stateful Signatures
Component: ThresholdSigningDemo

Set the number of trustees n and the signing threshold t. Any t of n trustees can produce a valid signature. Only single-level LMS is supported — HSS hypertrees are impractical (see CRV table →).
This is an educational simulation. Shares and signatures are illustrative — no real LMS cryptography is performed. Real CRV sizes are shown in the side panel.
A trusted dealer generates an LMS key pair and splits the Winternitz OTS tables into shares using a PRF. Each trustee receives a secret share. The Common Reference Value (CRV) holds correction values for each Merkle tree node; it is published and accessible to an aggregator.
One device crash or bug → same OTS leaf reused → private key exposed. Catastrophic.
Common Reference Value grows explosively with tree levels — making HSS hypertrees impractical for thresholdisation.
HSS hypertrees require correction values for every node at every level. Each authorised signing subset needs its own set of correction values. For 2+ levels the CRV reaches GB–TB scale, making the Haystack construction explicitly impractical for HSS.
RFC 8554 and RFC 9858 define no threshold variant. This demo is restricted to single-level LMS only.
Kelsey, Lang & Lucks — threshold stateful hash-based signatures via trusted dealer + Common Reference Value. Practical only for small thresholds (n ≤ 5–6) on single-level trees.
For larger thresholds, lattice-based threshold schemes (e.g., threshold Dilithium / FROST variants) are currently more practical.
