chunks.title: TLS Basics — TLSDowngradeScenario
chunks.content:
Module: TLS Basics
Component: TLSDowngradeScenario

An active adversary blocks every TLS connection that offers a PQC key_share, pushing the client into its classical "maximum compatibility" fallback retry — so both endpoints end up on a classical-only session even though both support PQC. TLS 1.3 transcript integrity prevents in-flight tampering with the ClientHello, but it cannot stop the client from downgrading itself on retry. This is distinct from passive HNDL harvesting: the attack actively prevents PQC from being used.
Analysis by Bas Westerbaan (Cloudflare Research) · PQCrypto 2025 · Root Causes Podcast ep. 614
Both client and server negotiate X25519MLKEM768. The session is quantum-safe: an adversary recording the ciphertext cannot break it without both a classical compute break of X25519 AND a quantum break of ML-KEM-768.
Downgrade attack — induced fallback to a classical ClientHello
The attacker exploits maximum compatibility mode: when a handshake fails, the client retries with a more conservative ClientHello that omits the ML-KEM key_share. The attacker only has to make PQC attempts fail (drop, reset, timeout) — the client downgrades itself, and the resulting classical retry is self-consistent, so neither endpoint can detect it. The session is quantum-vulnerable.
PQ Lock + proposed PQC Continuity — attack blocked after a prior PQC visit

chunks.title: TLS Basics — TLSDowngradeScenario
chunks.content:
Module: TLS Basics
Component: TLSDowngradeScenario

PQ Lock (HTTP-layer, Chromium): browser caches that this server supports PQC; future classical-only negotiations are rejected. PQC Continuity ( draft-sheffer-tls-pqc-continuity, an individual Internet-Draft by Sheffer et al., not adopted by the TLS working group): a TLS extension that allows a TLS client to cache a server's declared commitment to present PQC or composite certificates for a specified duration, for TLS clients other than browsers too. Both need one earlier successful PQC connection; neither protects the first visit.
Client advertises key_share entries: X25519 + ML-KEM-768 (hybrid X25519MLKEM768). Both classical and PQC options offered.
Server selects X25519MLKEM768. Responds with its own key_share using both X25519 and ML-KEM-768 encapsulated key.
Both sides derive the same shared secret: KDF(ML-KEM_ss ∥ X25519_ss) — concatenated in that order per RFC 10024 §4.3. Session is quantum-safe — breaking X25519 alone is insufficient.
Handshake completes. Session uses AES-256-GCM-SHA384 with a hybrid-derived key. Protected against both classical and quantum adversaries.
Client sends a key_share with X25519MLKEM768. Client supports PQC and intends a hybrid connection.

chunks.title: TLS Basics — TLSDowngradeScenario
chunks.content:
Module: TLS Basics
Component: TLSDowngradeScenario

Attacker drops or resets every connection offering a PQC key_share. Note: silently rewriting the ClientHello in flight would NOT work — the server signs the transcript as it received it (CertificateVerify, RFC 9846 §4.5.2), so the client, hashing its original ClientHello, would detect the mismatch and abort. The attacker can only make the PQC attempt fail.
After the failure, the client retries in "maximum compatibility" mode: a fresh ClientHello with no ML-KEM key_share — classical X25519 only. This retry is the client's own genuine message, so the new handshake is fully self-consistent. TLS has nothing left to detect.
Server sees only X25519 offered and selects it. From the server's view this is a normal classical client — it cannot know a PQC attempt was sabotaged moments earlier.
Session key derived from X25519 only. No ML-KEM contribution. This session is vulnerable to Harvest-Now-Decrypt-Later: an adversary recording the handshake can decrypt it with a quantum computer.
Attacker records the ciphertext. Today it is unreadable — but once a CRQC (cryptographically-relevant quantum computer) exists, the X25519 key exchange can be broken and all session data decrypted.
Client has PQ Lock cached from a prior session: server previously signalled PQC support. ClientHello includes the X25519MLKEM768 key_share as before.
Attacker drops the PQC connection attempt to push the client into classical fallback. Same induced-failure attack as before.

chunks.title: TLS Basics — TLSDowngradeScenario
chunks.content:
Module: TLS Basics
Component: TLSDowngradeScenario

The client is about to retry without ML-KEM, but PQ Lock is cached for this server. The cached signal says: "this server supports PQC." Downgrading the retry to classical-only would be inconsistent with that promise.
Client refuses the classical retry and surfaces a connection error instead of a silently-downgraded session. The attacker can deny service but cannot force a quantum-vulnerable session. PQC Continuity (draft-sheffer-tls-pqc-continuity, an individual Internet-Draft, not adopted by the TLS working group) addresses a related certificate rollback: it defines a TLS extension by which a server declares, for a stated duration (for example one year), a commitment to present PQC or composite certificates, which the client caches and then uses to reject traditional-only certificates. Like PQ Lock, it needs one earlier successful PQC connection, so neither can protect the very first visit.

Run these scenarios in order to compare classical, PQC, and hybrid TLS configurations. Each exercise pre-configures the simulator — click "Load & Run" to apply the settings and switch to the Simulate tab. Use the Comparison Table to track overhead across runs.
▸ Algorithm trade-off reference (security level × size × speed)
Take the Protocol Integration quiz to test what you've learned.
Run a standard TLS 1.3 handshake with RSA-2048 certificates and X25519 key exchange — the baseline configuration used by most websites today.
Record the baseline handshake byte count (~4 KB) — you will compare it against every subsequent scenario. Note the RSA signature in the CertificateVerify message.
Switch to ML-DSA-87 post-quantum certificates while keeping classical X25519 key exchange. See how PQC signatures affect handshake overhead.
Compare handshake bytes vs Scenario 1. ML-DSA-87 signatures are significantly larger than RSA, increasing the Certificate and CertificateVerify messages.
Use X25519MLKEM768 hybrid key exchange with RSA certificates. This is the combination already deployed in Chrome and Firefox for quantum-safe key agreement.

Module: TLS Basics

Record the handshake bytes and check the "vs #1" column in the Comparison Table — this shows the percentage increase from the ML-KEM key share (1,184 B, FIPS 203). The Key Exchange badge will show the hybrid group name. Forward secrecy note: because ML-KEM keys are generated fresh per handshake, compromising the server's long-term ML-DSA signing key later cannot decrypt past sessions.
4. Full PQC (ML-DSA-87 + ML-KEM-1024)
Maximum post-quantum configuration: ML-DSA-87 certificates with ML-KEM-1024 key exchange. See the full cost of a quantum-safe TLS connection.
This will have the largest handshake overhead. Compare the total bytes with Scenario 1 to quantify the PQC migration cost.
Enable server-side client certificate verification. Both parties authenticate with certificates, commonly used in API security and zero-trust architectures.
Watch for the CertificateRequest message from the server, and the client Certificate + CertificateVerify responses. Both cert verification statuses should show "Verified".
6. PQC Mutual TLS (ML-DSA-87 + Hybrid)
The worst-case PQC overhead scenario: mutual authentication with ML-DSA-87 certificates on both sides, combined with X25519MLKEM768 hybrid key exchange.
Compare total bytes with Scenario 5 (RSA mTLS) — both sides now send large PQC certificates and signatures, roughly doubling the PQC certificate overhead. Record the handshake bytes for the Comparison Table.
7. HelloRetryRequest — Missing Key Share

chunks.title: TLS Basics — TLSExercises
chunks.content:
Module: TLS Basics
Component: TLSExercises

The client supports both X25519 and X25519MLKEM768 but lists X25519 first, so its ClientHello carries a key share only for X25519. The server supports only X25519MLKEM768. Because the client did list the hybrid group in supported_groups, the server replies with a HelloRetryRequest naming X25519MLKEM768, and the client resends its ClientHello with a hybrid key share.
Look for the "HRR" badge and the 2-RTT indicator in results. The Protocol Log shows two ClientHellos: a small first one (X25519 key share, about 200 B) and a retry of about 1.4 KB carrying the ML-KEM-768 + X25519 key share. The negotiated group is X25519MLKEM768. Compare with Scenario 3 (same group, 1-RTT): listing X25519MLKEM768 first on the client removes the retry.
8. No Common Group — Handshake Failure
The client offers only pure ML-KEM-1024; the server supports only the hybrid X25519MLKEM768. These are different group codepoints, so the two sides share no group at all. A HelloRetryRequest cannot fix this — the server can only ask for a group the client listed — so the server aborts with a handshake_failure alert.
The handshake fails with no HRR: the Protocol Log shows one ClientHello, then a fatal handshake_failure alert from the server ("no suitable key share"). A hybrid group does not match a pure ML-KEM or a pure X25519 offer. To fix it, add X25519MLKEM768 to the client groups: listed first it negotiates in 1-RTT; listed after ML-KEM-1024 it triggers an HRR, as in Scenario 7.

chunks.title: TLS Basics — TLSExercises

Module: TLS Basics

The client offers all five TLS 1.3 cipher suites; the server accepts only TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256. Observe which cipher is selected and why. Then swap the scenario to understand server-preference ordering.
The negotiated cipher in the result banner should be TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 — the only cipher the server accepts, regardless of client ordering. This shows that the server controls cipher selection in TLS 1.3. To test ordering: add a second cipher to the server (e.g. TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 first) and re-run to see which wins.

chunks.title: TLS Basics — TLSIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: TLS Basics
Component: TLSIntroduction

Prerequisites: Familiarity with public-key cryptography (asymmetric keys, digital signatures, certificates) and basic HTTPS concepts.
Explain the TLS 1.3 handshake and how it differs from TLS 1.2
Compare overhead of classical, hybrid, and PQC TLS configurations quantitatively
0-RTT early data (optional) — TLS provides no inherent replay protection for 0-RTT data (RFC 9846 §8)
The handshake establishes a secure connection in a single round trip. The client sends its supported parameters and a key share; the server responds with its choice and key share. After the ServerHello, all remaining handshake messages are encrypted using handshake traffic keys derived via HKDF.
TLS 1.3 cipher suites only specify the symmetric encryption algorithm and hash — key exchange and authentication are negotiated separately. This is why there are only 5 suites compared to hundreds in TLS 1.2.
TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 AES-256 in GCM mode (AEAD) + SHA-384 for HKDF
TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 AES-128 in GCM mode (AEAD) + SHA-256 for HKDF
TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256 ChaCha20-Poly1305 (AEAD) + SHA-256 — optimized for mobile/ARM
TLS_AES_128_CCM_SHA256 AES-128 in CCM mode + SHA-256 — designed for constrained environments (IoT)
TLS_AES_128_CCM_8_SHA256 AES-128 in CCM mode with 8-byte auth tag + SHA-256 — for highly constrained devices
TLS 1.3 uses ephemeral key exchange for every connection, ensuring forward secrecy. With post-quantum cryptography (PQC), three approaches are available:

chunks.title: TLS Basics — TLSIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: TLS Basics
Component: TLSIntroduction

X25519, P-256, P-384. Fast and small (~32 byte keys). Vulnerable to quantum computers.
ML-KEM-512/768/1024. Quantum-resistant. Larger keys (1,184 B for ML-KEM-768, FIPS 203) increase handshake size.
X25519MLKEM768 combines both. Already deployed in Chrome and Firefox. Secure even if one algorithm is broken.
TLS 1.3 derives all session keys through a structured key schedule using HKDF (HMAC-based Key Derivation Function). The shared secret from key exchange feeds into a chain of Extract and Expand operations:
1. Early Secret — derived from PSK (or zero for full handshake)
2. Handshake Secret — derived from ECDHE/KEM shared secret → produces CLIENT_HANDSHAKE_TRAFFIC_SECRET and SERVER_HANDSHAKE_TRAFFIC_SECRET
3. Master Secret — produces CLIENT_TRAFFIC_SECRET_0 and SERVER_TRAFFIC_SECRET_0 for application data
These exact secrets are visible in the Simulate tab after running a handshake.
After a successful handshake, the server issues a Pre-Shared Key (PSK) ticket. On reconnection, the client presents this PSK, which feeds into the Early Secret stage — enabling a faster resumed handshake and optionally 0-RTT early data. In a full handshake with no prior session, the PSK input is zero.

chunks.title: TLS Basics — TLSIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: TLS Basics
Component: TLSIntroduction

A client lists every group it supports in supported_groups but usually sends a key share for only one or two of them. If the server selects a group that both sides support but the ClientHello carried no key_share for it, the server responds with a HelloRetryRequest instead of a ServerHello, naming the group it wants. The client resends its ClientHello with a key share for that group, making a 2-RTT handshake instead of the standard 1-RTT (RFC 9846 §4.2.1, §4.2.4). If client and server have no supported group in common, no retry can help: the server aborts the handshake with a handshake_failure alert.
Client supports X25519 and X25519MLKEM768 but sends a key share only for X25519; the server selects X25519MLKEM768
Client supports ML-KEM-768 and ML-KEM-1024 with a key share only for ML-KEM-768; the server accepts only ML-KEM-1024
Not an HRR: no group in common (e.g. client X25519 only, server X25519MLKEM768 only) ends in handshake_failure
During PQC rollout, clients often send a classical key share first and an HRR upgrades them to the hybrid group the server prefers
X25519MLKEM768 is its own group codepoint (RFC 10024): a classical-only client matches only if the server also supports plain X25519 as a separate group
Offering X25519 as a fallback needs a policy that prevents silent downgrade to classical-only key exchange
HRR costs a round trip; a server with no group in common fails the handshake instead

chunks.title: TLS Basics — TLSIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: TLS Basics
Component: TLSIntroduction

In the simulator, set the client groups to X25519 then X25519MLKEM768 and the server to X25519MLKEM768 only to observe an HRR. Set the client to ML-KEM-1024 only and the server to X25519 only to observe a handshake failure with no common group.
Quantum computers threaten classical key exchange (ECDH) through Shor's algorithm. The "harvest now, decrypt later" attack means adversaries can record encrypted traffic today and decrypt it once quantum computers are available. PQC integration into TLS addresses this by using lattice-based KEMs (ML-KEM) and signatures (ML-DSA).
The trade-off: PQC algorithms have larger keys and ciphertexts, increasing handshake overhead. For example, ML-KEM-768 public keys are ~1,184 bytes vs 32 bytes for X25519. The hybrid approach (e.g., X25519MLKEM768) provides quantum resistance while maintaining classical security as a fallback.
SLH-DSA (formerly SPHINCS+) is a hash-based signature scheme standardized alongside ML-DSA. It relies on hash function security rather than lattice problems, providing cryptographic diversity— if lattices are broken, SLH-DSA remains secure. The trade-off is significantly larger signatures (~7.9 KB (7,856 B) for SLH-DSA-SHA2-128s vs 2,420 B, about 2.4 KB, for ML-DSA-44). The simulator's signature options offer ML-DSA only: no IETF working-group draft yet specifies SLH-DSA for TLS 1.3 (only an individual Internet-Draft, draft-reddy-tls-slhdsa, exists, and it has expired).

chunks.title: TLS Basics — TLSIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: TLS Basics
Component: TLSIntroduction

PQC signatures are significantly larger than classical ones — an ML-DSA certificate chain can add several kilobytes to every TLS handshake. For the web, where billions of connections happen daily, this overhead is a serious scalability concern. The ecosystem is deploying multiple mitigations.
TLS certificate compression is available, and certificates are compressed before transmission and decompressed by the peer. The IETF UTA working-group draft on PQC recommendations for TLS-based applications states that its impact on PQ and PQ/T hybrid certificates is limited, because the larger public keys and signatures are high-entropy fields that constrain compression effectiveness.
Certificate Transparency (CT) requires CAs to log all issued certificates in publicly auditable append-only logs. Browsers verify that certificates appear in CT logs, preventing misissued certificates from going undetected. Understanding CT is essential context for Merkle Tree Certificates, which leverage this same log infrastructure.
Google's MTC program (announced February 2026) goes further than compression — it replaces entire certificate chains with compact Merkle proofs.
Traditional TLS uses a chain of X.509 certificates, each containing a public key and a signature from the issuing CA. With PQC signatures (3,309 B, about 3.3 KB, for ML-DSA-65), a typical 2-certificate chain adds ~7 KB+ to the handshake — a substantial bandwidth increase.

chunks.title: TLS Basics — TLSIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: TLS Basics
Component: TLSIntroduction

MTCs replace the serialized signature chain with a compact Merkle inclusion proof. A single CA-signed "Tree Head" represents potentially millions of certificates. Browsers receive a lightweight proof-of-inclusion rather than full certificate chains.
Phase 1 (Now) Feasibility testing with Cloudflare on live traffic; all MTC connections backed by traditional X.509 certificates as fallback
Phase 2 (sample plan, Q1 2027) Inviting Certificate Transparency log operators to bootstrap public MTC infrastructure
Phase 3 (sample plan, Q3 2027) Establishing Chrome Quantum-resistant Root Store (CQRS) with new requirements for MTC Certificate Authorities
PQC protects the content of TLS connections from quantum attack, but the initial ClientHello — including the Server Name Indication (SNI) — is sent in plaintext, revealing which site a user is connecting to. Encrypted Client Hello (ECH) solves this by encrypting the ClientHello using a key published in DNS.
Major browsers are deploying ECH alongside hybrid PQC key exchange (X25519MLKEM768). Together, they protect both the metadata (who you connect to) and the content (what you exchange) against current and future adversaries.

You used hybrid key exchange, combining classical ECDH with post-quantum ML-KEM for security against both classical and quantum attacks.

chunks.title: Talking About PQC Accurately — Introduction
chunks.content:
Module: Talking About PQC Accurately
Component: Introduction

Most online security — the padlock in a browser, signed software updates, bank transfers — relies on mathematics that a large enough quantum computer could undo. No such computer exists yet. But data copied today could be read once one does, which is why people call the risk “harvest now, decrypt later”.
That is the whole story in three sentences: a real risk, a published fix, and years of work to apply it.
Every real date belongs to someone and applies to specific systems. Before you quote a date, say whose it is and what it covers.
A private company outside these scopes may have no legal deadline at all — but its customers may. Other countries set their own schedules; the Timeline lists them with their sources.
In this module's reading, “Certified” is the word most often stretched. In the US and Canada, the FIPS 140-3 programme has three stages that are easy to confuse:
Algorithm tested (CAVP certificate). One implementation of one algorithm passed its tests. It says nothing about the rest of the product.
In process. The module appears on NIST’s Modules In Process list: validation has started, not finished.
Validated (FIPS 140-3 certificate). The module passed. The certificate has a number anyone can look up, and it covers a specific version and configuration.

chunks.title: Talking About PQC Accurately — Introduction
chunks.content:
Module: Talking About PQC Accurately
Component: Introduction

Other schemes — Common Criteria and the EU’s EUCC, for example — work differently, but the same rule applies: read what a certificate covers before you read its level. Post-quantum algorithms added in a later version are not covered by an older certificate.
This site’s product catalogue shows these same three stages, taken from the public records, for every product it lists.
A useful answer has three parts, each with something the listener can check:
What is protected today — which parts of the product, with which algorithms, from which version.
What is planned, and when — a public roadmap is stronger than a promise in a meeting.
The evidence — certificate numbers, a roadmap page, or a cryptography bill of materials (a list of the cryptography a product uses).
If part of the answer is “we don’t know yet”, say so. Customers comparing suppliers notice a confident answer that cannot be checked.
This site lists every product on the same terms, whoever makes it, and links each claim to its source. It is evidence you can point to — not a ranking.

chunks.title: Trust Services & Long-Term Signatures — TrustServicesIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Trust Services & Long-Term Signatures
Component: TrustServicesIntroduction

Under eIDAS, an advanced electronic signature is uniquely linked to its signatory and detects later changes to the data. A qualified signature adds two things: it is created with a qualified signature creation device, and it rests on a certificate issued by a qualified trust service provider. Only the qualified form carries automatic legal equivalence to a handwritten signature across the Union.
That legal equivalence is why this module exists. Once a signature has legal weight, the question stops being “is this cryptographically valid today” and becomes “can a court establish that it was valid when it was made” — potentially decades later.
Scope note. Wallet activation, PID issuance and the eIDAS 2.0 wallet flows are covered in Digital ID ; CMS and S/MIME signing mechanics in Email & Document Signing ; certificate chain fundamentals in PKI . This module deliberately does not repeat them — it covers what happens to a signature over time, which none of them cover.
A signature does not fail all at once. It degrades in stages, and each stage has a different remedy that must be in place before the stage arrives.
Crypto agility is usually argued from principle. In this area it can be argued from documents: the same standard, by the same committee, before and after post-quantum algorithms existed.
ETSI TS 119 312 V2.1.1, Table 3.3 (algorithm-level hybrid combinations).

chunks.title: Trust Services & Long-Term Signatures — TrustServicesIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Trust Services & Long-Term Signatures
Component: TrustServicesIntroduction

A qualified trust service provider is not simply a CA with good intentions — it is an audited entity on a national trusted list, assessed against the ETSI EN 319 4xx series. That audit relationship is what makes a migration in this sector slow: changing signing algorithms means re-establishing conformity, not just deploying software.
The hardware that holds a provider's signing keys is certified too. The EU implementing rules for qualified certificates (Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/1943) and qualified time-stamps (Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/1929) list reference standards, and supervisory bodies should presume that a provider that follows them complies, although a provider may still rely on other practices. Those standards require the secure cryptographic device that holds the provider's certificate-signing (CA) key, or a time-stamping unit's key, to be certified to Common Criteria or the EU scheme EUCC at EAL 4 or higher — or, until 31 December 2030, to FIPS 140-3 level 3. In the text adopted on 29 September 2025, only the Common Criteria and EUCC routes remain after that date. This requirement covers the provider's own keys, not the signer's device.

chunks.title: Trust Services & Long-Term Signatures — TrustServicesIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Trust Services & Long-Term Signatures
Component: TrustServicesIntroduction

The practical sequence for a TSP is therefore: the suites document gains PQC modes (done — TS 119 312 V2.1.1), the timestamp and policy standards have to follow (EN 319 422 dates from 2016 and defers algorithm choice to the suites document, although for qualified time-stamps Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/1929 lists a version of EN 319 422 in which those clauses are replaced by clauses under which hash and time-stamp signature algorithms shall be compliant with the Agreed Cryptographic Mechanisms endorsed by the European Cybersecurity Certification Group), conformity assessment schemes absorb the change, and only then can a qualified service issue post-quantum signatures under audit. Each step gates the next. One caution on the first step: V2.1.1 (June 2026) says of itself that it is incomplete for the EU Digital Identity Wallet and for certain other trust services, including preservation and electronic registered delivery, with an update already in preparation, and it says that scheduling of the post-quantum migration is planned to be addressed in a separate document under development.

chunks.title: Trust Services & Long-Term Signatures — trustServicesData (data)
chunks.content:
Module: Trust Services & Long-Term Signatures
Data: trustServicesData

RSA, DSA, EC-DSA, EC-SDSA-opt — classical only
RSA, ECDSA + ML-DSA, SLH-DSA, LMS, XMSS, and hybrid modes
ETSI-TS-119-312-V2-1-1-Electronic-Signatures-and-Trust-Infra
Eighteen months apart, same standard, same committee. Anything built against V1.5.1 has no post-quantum path in it at all — not because the design was wrong, but because the suites document had not caught up yet. This is what standards evolution looks like from the inside.
Hash functions and asymmetric algorithms for secure e-signatures
TS 119 312 V2.1.1 marks its predecessor explicitly: "Withdrawn; superseded by ETSI TS 119 312." Citing the withdrawn document is a live risk in this area, because it was the reference for years and is still widely linked.
For hybrid signatures, implementations shall combine a classical signature and a post-quantum signature. Acceptance requires both signatures to be valid.
The same algorithms, two authorities, different defaults. ETSI specifies hybrid modes and the exact pairs to use; NSA will not require NSS developers to use hybrid certified products for security purposes, although product availability and interoperability requirements may lead to adopting hybrid solutions in specific cases. Neither is wrong — they are protecting different things over different lifetimes. Which one applies to you is a jurisdiction question, not a cryptography question.
RFC 3161 (August 2001, Standards Track), updated by RFC 5816 for ESSCertIDv2.
ETSI EN 319 422 V1.1.1 (March 2016) profiles RFC 3161 and RFC 5816 for European qualified timestamps. It names no algorithm itself — it defers to ETSI TS 119 312.
A timestamp is a proof of existence: a TSA signs a hash of your data plus a time. It is what lets a signature made with a certificate that has since been revoked — or with an algorithm since broken — still be evaluated against the moment it was made.
In this module's reading, because RFC 3161 carries the algorithm in the TSA certificate rather than in the protocol, a TSA can migrate to ML-DSA without a protocol change. The layer that has to move is the trust list and the validation policy, not the wire format.
Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/1929 (September 2025) applies V1.1.1 to qualified time-stamps, and TS 119 312 V2.1.1 (June 2026) still cites that 2016 edition. For qualified time-stamps the Regulation’s version of the profile replaces its algorithm clauses with clauses under which hash and time-stamp signature algorithms shall be compliant with the Agreed Cryptographic Mechanisms endorsed by the European Cybersecurity Certification Group, rather than the TS 119 312 clauses the profile points to.
None yet — the certificate is valid and the algorithm is current.

chunks.content:
Module: VPN & SSH PQC
Component: VPNSSHExercises

Work through these scenarios to compare VPN and SSH protocol behavior with classical, hybrid, and post-quantum key exchange. Each exercise pre-configures the Simulator — click "Load & Run" to begin.
Take the PQC quiz to test what you've learned about VPN and SSH protocols.
1. Classical IKEv2 Handshake (ECP-256)
Step through a standard IKEv2 handshake using elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman (ECP-256, DH Group 19). Observe the IKE_SA_INIT and IKE_AUTH phases, payload structure, and the compact message sizes with classical ECDH.
The total handshake is approximately 1,400 bytes across 2 round trips. The KE payload carries a 64-byte ECP-256 public value (RFC 5903). This baseline is quantum-vulnerable to Shor's algorithm.
2. Hybrid IKEv2 with ML-KEM + Additional KE
Run a hybrid IKEv2 handshake per draft-ietf-ipsecme-ikev2-mlkem Appendix A. Classical ECP-256 runs in IKE_SA_INIT; ML-KEM-768 follows as Additional Key Exchange 1 in the encrypted IKE_INTERMEDIATE exchange (RFC 9370).
The handshake grows to approximately 3,784 bytes and adds a third round trip for IKE_INTERMEDIATE. IKE_SA_INIT stays small; the ML-KEM encapsulation key (1,184 B) and ciphertext (1,088 B) travel in IKE_INTERMEDIATE, which RFC 7383 can fragment. Switch the ML-KEM size to 1024 and watch the same messages fragment instead of being dropped.
Observe the classical SSH key exchange using X25519. Step through SSH_MSG_KEXINIT negotiation, ECDH_INIT, and ECDH_REPLY messages. Note the compact 32-byte public keys.

Module: VPN & SSH PQC
Component: VPNSSHExercises

X25519 produces 32-byte public keys and a 32-byte shared secret. The total handshake is under 1 KB. This is the most widely deployed SSH KEX but is quantum-vulnerable.
4. SSH with ML-KEM-768 Hybrid (OpenSSH 9.9)
Switch to mlkem768x25519-sha256, the ML-KEM-768 + X25519 hybrid KEX added in OpenSSH 9.9 (and made the default in OpenSSH 10.0). Compare the message sizes with the classical X25519 exchange.
The public key grows from 32 bytes to 1,216 bytes (32 + 1,184 = 1,216: X25519 + ML-KEM concatenated). The total handshake is approximately 3,296 bytes — a 3.3x increase. The combined key material is 64 bytes (the 32-byte X25519 secret concatenated with the 32-byte ML-KEM secret) before being hashed into the final session key.
5. Cross-Protocol Size Comparison
View the comprehensive comparison table across IKEv2, SSH, WireGuard, and TLS 1.3. Filter by protocol and mode to understand the relative impact of PQC on each protocol.
WireGuard has the largest relative size increase (about 11x with Rosenpass: WireGuard's 240 B handshake plus Rosenpass's 2,464 B, in this workshop's model) due to its ultra-compact classical handshake. IKEv2 and SSH handle PQC sizes well through TCP or fragmentation support. TLS 1.3 maintains 1-RTT even with hybrid KEX.

chunks.title: VPN & SSH PQC — VPNSSHIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: VPN & SSH PQC
Component: VPNSSHIntroduction

IKEv2 (Internet Key Exchange version 2, RFC 7296) is the key negotiation protocol for IPsec VPNs. It establishes Security Associations (SAs) through a two-phase handshake: IKE_SA_INIT for key exchange and IKE_AUTH for identity verification.
The KE payload carries Diffie-Hellman public values. Both parties derive the same shared secret (SKEYSEED) from their DH exchange, nonces, and SPIs, then derive encryption and integrity keys for the IKE SA.
The IETF draft draft-ietf-ipsecme-ikev2-mlkem defines how to integrate ML-KEM (FIPS 203) into IKEv2 using the multiple key exchanges framework (RFC 9370). This enables hybrid key exchange while limiting the changes to the exchanged messages and the IKEv2 state machine (RFC 9370).
“The initiator generates an ML-KEM keypair (pk, sk) using KeyGen(), and sends the public key (pk) to the responder inside a KEi(1) payload. The responder will encapsulate a shared secret ss using Encaps(pk) and the resulting ciphertext (ct) is sent to initiator using the KEr(1).”
ECP-256 or MODP-2048 in KE payload during IKE_SA_INIT. Quantum-vulnerable.
ML-KEM-768 encapsulation key (1,184 B) in IKE_INTERMEDIATE. Adds one round trip.
SKEYSEED derived from both DH and KEM shared secrets via PRF. The keys stay secret as long as either exchange is unbroken, provided the PRF acts as a sound combiner.

chunks.title: VPN & SSH PQC — VPNSSHIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: VPN & SSH PQC
Component: VPNSSHIntroduction

A pure (quantum-resistant-only) IKEv2 handshake has no classical key exchange to fall back on, so ML-KEM must travel in the very first message, IKE_SA_INIT. That is where the draft's main restriction sits: IKEv2 fragmentation (RFC 7383) only works on encrypted messages, and IKE_SA_INIT is sent before any keys exist. In the draft's words, these messages “could not be IKEv2 fragmented”. A payload bigger than the path MTU falls back to IP fragmentation, which NATs and firewalls often drop and which is a known denial-of-service target.
CNSA 2.0 lists ML-KEM-1024 for key establishment. The draft says ML-KEM-512 MAY be used in IKE_SA_INIT as a quantum-resistant-only key exchange; implementations transporting IKE over UDP and not performing PMTU discovery SHOULD NOT use ML-KEM-768 or ML-KEM-1024 in IKE_SA_INIT on networks where the PMTU is unknown or restricted, and MAY use any ML-KEM parameter when reliable transport (for example RFC 9329) is used or a sufficient PMTU is guaranteed.
Appendix A runs a classical exchange in IKE_SA_INIT and carries ML-KEM-768/1024 in IKE_INTERMEDIATE (RFC 9242 / RFC 9370). Those messages are encrypted, so RFC 7383 fragmentation applies. The cost: the first exchange is no longer quantum-resistant on its own. That makes this a hybrid design, not pure PQC.

chunks.title: VPN & SSH PQC — VPNSSHIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: VPN & SSH PQC
Component: VPNSSHIntroduction

The draft also requires a fresh ML-KEM key pair and fresh encapsulation randomness for every exchange. The responder must check the initiator's encapsulation key (FIPS 203 §7.2) before encapsulating, and should reject a bad key with INVALID_SYNTAX to limit resource-exhaustion attacks. The draft further warns that an on-path attacker with a quantum computer could steer peers onto a classical-only group unless local policy forbids one. None of this makes the draft a dead end. It sits in the RFC Editor queue, and several firewall vendors already ship hybrid ML-KEM IKEv2. Only pure-PQC IKEv2 at the higher security levels over plain UDP remains an open engineering problem.
OpenSSH has been a pioneer in deploying post-quantum key exchange. Since version 8.5 (March 2021), it has shipped with sntrup761x25519-sha512 — a hybrid of Streamlined NTRU Prime and X25519. In OpenSSH 9.9 (September 2024), mlkem768x25519-sha256, OpenSSH’s hybrid of ML-KEM-768 (FIPS 203, standardised by NIST) and X25519, was added.
SSH hybrid KEX works by concatenating the classical and PQC public keys in SSH_MSG_KEX_ECDH_INIT, and concatenating the classical share and KEM ciphertext in SSH_MSG_KEX_ECDH_REPLY. The shared secret is derived from both components.
WireGuard uses the Noise IK protocol framework with a fixed cipher suite: X25519, ChaCha20-Poly1305, BLAKE2s. This minimal design makes WireGuard fast and auditable, but also means it has zero crypto agility — algorithms cannot be negotiated.

chunks.title: VPN & SSH PQC — VPNSSHIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: VPN & SSH PQC
Component: VPNSSHIntroduction

WireGuard's fixed X25519 is quantum-vulnerable. Adding PQC requires modifying the protocol or layering a separate negotiation on top.
Rosenpass runs a separate post-quantum key exchange (Classic McEliece for the static keys, the round-3 Kyber for the ephemeral keys — not FIPS 203 ML-KEM) and feeds the resulting PSK into WireGuard's pre-shared key slot.
The Rosenpass approach preserves WireGuard's simplicity while adding quantum resistance. The PSK is rotated periodically. WireGuard's classical security holds even if Rosenpass is compromised; the post-quantum protection does not.
Post-quantum key exchange significantly increases handshake sizes across all protocols. ML-KEM-768 adds approximately 1,184 bytes for the encapsulation key and 1,088 bytes for the ciphertext. For protocols like WireGuard that use UDP, this can cause IP fragmentation issues.

chunks.title: VPN & SSH PQC — VPNSSHIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: VPN & SSH PQC
Component: VPNSSHIntroduction

Sizes are this workshop's message model, not packet captures. WireGuard is not in the table: adding post-quantum protection with Rosenpass means four extra Rosenpass messages, InitHello 1,092 B, RespHello 1,132 B, InitConf 176 B and EmptyData 64 B, 2,464 B in total (Rosenpass white paper, Figure 2). The paper gives no comparison with WireGuard's own handshake, so none is stated here. Rosenpass's large McEliece public keys are exchanged out of band, not in the handshake. IKEv2 handles fragmentation explicitly (RFC 7383) over UDP, but only for encrypted messages, so it cannot help IKE_SA_INIT. SSH handles larger payloads natively because it relies on TCP transport.
While PQC Key Exchange (ML-KEM) secures connections against future decryption, Authentication using digital signatures secures against active attackers. Both IKEv2 and SSH uniquely require multiple layers of authentication that must be migrated.
In addition to the additional key exchanges, draft-ietf-ipsecme-ikev2-pqc-auth updates the IKE_AUTH phase to support ML-DSA (FIPS 204). The Auth payload verifies identities using post-quantum certificates.
SSH requires PQC host keys (server identity) and user keys (UserAuth). While OpenSSH 9.9 supports ML-KEM, standardizing ML-DSA keys for host and user authentication is still an active effort.

chunks.title: VPN & SSH PQC — VPNSSHIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: VPN & SSH PQC
Component: VPNSSHIntroduction

The migration to PQC only applies to the Control Plane (key exchange & auth). The actual Data Plane (the VPN tunnel) uses symmetric algorithms like AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305. The data plane’s symmetric algorithms are affected by Grover’s algorithm rather than Shor’s; per NIST (cited in RFC 9370), applications can continue using AES with a minimum key length of 128 bits, and a longer key size can be considered for data that must remain secure for many years.

Traditional IKEv2 using elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman (ECP-256, DH Group 19 — the aes256-sha256-ecp256 proposal this simulator runs). Vulnerable to HNDL (Harvest Now, Decrypt Later): traffic captured today can be decrypted retroactively by a future CRQC. Provides no quantum-safe forward secrecy.
Hybrid IKEv2 per draft-ietf-ipsecme-ikev2-mlkem Appendix A, using RFC 9370 multiple key exchanges over an RFC 9242 IKE_INTERMEDIATE round. Classical ECP-256 runs in IKE_SA_INIT; ML-KEM follows as Additional Key Exchange 1 in IKE_INTERMEDIATE. Because IKE_INTERMEDIATE is encrypted, the large ML-KEM payloads can use RFC 7383 fragmentation, which IKE_SA_INIT cannot. HNDL-safe: the chained SKEYSEED requires breaking both algorithms. Tradeoff: 1 extra round trip.

Your organization's quantum readiness is only as strong as your weakest vendor. Third-party software, hardware, and cloud services form the backbone of enterprise cryptographic infrastructure. If a critical vendor lacks PQC support, your entire migration timeline is at risk.
“Supply chain risks are among the most significant challenges for PQC migration. Organizations must evaluate vendors' cryptographic capabilities and ensure contractual commitments to post-quantum readiness.”
Vendors handling sensitive data in transit are immediate HNDL targets. Every unpatched vendor extends your exposure window. For the full HNDL risk quantification framework, see PQC Risk Management .
Regulatory deadlines (CNSA 2.0, FIPS 140-3) apply to your full supply chain, not just your own code.
A single vendor dependency on classical-only crypto can block your entire PQC migration program.

chunks.title: Decommissioning & Program Closure — VerificationClosureIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Decommissioning & Program Closure
Component: VerificationClosureIntroduction

The migration isn't done when PQC is added — it's done when the classical cryptography is gone. The defensible schedule is the deprecation timeline: NIST IR 8547 (final, October 2026) deprecates quantum-vulnerable public-key cryptography (RSA, ECC, finite-field DH) at 112-bit security and up after 2030 and disallows it under NIST standards after 2035; NCSC-UK sets phased targets — 2028 (discovery + plan), 2031 (highest-priority migration), 2035 (complete); NIST SP 800-131A carries the transition rules.
The discipline is four steps: deprecate → remove → verify removed → log. The step teams skip is the third — confirm by observation that the old key material is gone, not just that a new key exists.
A system is “migrated” when its behaviour shows it — the handshake negotiates ML-KEM/ML-DSA — not when a change ticket says so. Reuse the Active PQC Scanner (in the PQC Testing module) and passive handshake capture to collect the evidence. (Evidence-by-observed-behaviour is practitioner guidance.)
The control basis is independent: NIST CSWP 48 (draft) maps the NCCoE Migration-to-PQC capabilities to CSF 2.0 and SP 800-53.
You can't verify a large estate by hand, so decide which systems and what proof per tier: verify business-critical systems fully, sample the rest per migration wave, and let any sampled failure widen the check. (The specific sampling rule is practitioner guidance, not a named standard.)

chunks.title: Decommissioning & Program Closure — VerificationClosureIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Decommissioning & Program Closure

Web gateways — reverse proxies , load balancers, WAFs, and CDN edge nodes — are the primary TLS termination points in modern web infrastructure. They handle millions of TLS handshakes per day, making them the most impactful place to deploy PQC.
Unlike application-level PQC (covered in TLS Basics ), gateway-level deployment affects every client connection simultaneously. Upgrading a single reverse proxy to PQC hybrid can protect thousands of backend services without modifying application code.
CDN and load balancer operators manage certificates at enormous scale. Migrating these certificates from classical algorithms (RSA-2048, ECDSA P-256) to ML-DSA requires careful operational planning.
PQC algorithms produce larger keys and signatures, directly increasing TLS handshake size. At gateway scale (thousands of handshakes per second), this bandwidth cost is the primary operational concern — not CPU, which remains manageable with modern hardware.
Web Application Firewalls (WAFs) and Intrusion Detection Systems (IDS) rely on TLS interception to inspect traffic for threats, data loss, and compliance violations. PQC migration creates a critical decision point: if the gateway cannot terminate PQC TLS, it loses all visibility into traffic content.

chunks.title: Web Gateway & PQC — WebGatewayIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Web Gateway & PQC
Component: WebGatewayIntroduction

Content Delivery Networks deploy PQC at edge Points of Presence (PoPs) distributed globally. Cloudflare's edge network deploys X25519MLKEM768 hybrid key agreement in production across its global edge. AWS announced on 5 September 2025 that CloudFront supports hybrid post-quantum key establishment for client-to-edge connections across all existing TLS security policies, enabled by default with no customer configuration; it also launched a new TLS 1.3-only policy, TLS1.3_2025 (our proof-gated catalogue records the announcement). nginx supports X25519MLKEM768 through OpenSSL 3.5+. Browsers are further ahead than most gateways. Cloudflare's browser table lists post-quantum key agreement as the default for TLS in Chrome 131+, Edge 131+, Opera 116+, Firefox 132+ (desktop) and 145+ (Android), and Safari 26+; for QUIC/HTTP3 the same table gives Firefox 135+ (desktop). Cloudflare reports that the majority of human-initiated traffic to it uses post-quantum encryption (Cloudflare, 2025).

chunks.title: Web Gateway & PQC — WebGatewayIntroduction
chunks.content:
Module: Web Gateway & PQC

Gateway vendor PQC readiness varies significantly. F5 BIG-IP carries ML-KEM hybrid key exchange from the 17.5.1 PQC minor, generally available across the product in 21.1 (2026); Envoy supports hybrid PQC TLS in production. Broadcom Avi 31.2.1 introduced PQC support (pure ML-KEM, hybrid KEMs and ML-DSA); Imperva reports hybrid X25519 + ML-KEM-768 TLS for client-to-Imperva connections generally available from the start of 2026; ZIA inline inspection supports hybrid PQC key exchange (Zscaler, 17 February 2026). Understanding each vendor's status and upgrade path is critical for planning — and version numbers here move quickly, so confirm against the vendor's own release notes before committing to a date.

Category: Certification Schemes | Type: Compliance Guidance
Pillar: assurance | Maturity Level: 3 | Asset Class: software

chunks.title: FIPS 140-3 Implementation Guidance — September 2025 PQC update — Tier 3 lifecycle requirement
chunks.content:
Source: FIPS 140-3 Implementation Guidance — September 2025 PQC update
Category: Certification Schemes | Type: Compliance Guidance
Pillar: lifecycle | Maturity Level: 3 | Asset Class: software
Requirement: Re-validate algorithm implementations if the operational environment changes, such as moving from a 32-bit to a 64-bit platform.
Evidence: "If an implementation has been tested on an X-bit processor (e.g. 32-bit, 64-bit), a claim cannot be made that the implementation also runs on different bit size processors... In this case the operational environments are not the same; therefore, the algorithm implementations must be re-tested"
Evidence location: Section 2.3.A, Resolution, Item 2
Source URL: https://csrc.nist.gov/csrc/media/Projects/cryptographic-module-validation-program/documents/fips%20140-3/FIPS%20140-3%20IG.pdf
Confidence: high

chunks.content:
Source: Cryptographic Mechanisms: Recommendations for SSH
Category: Certification Schemes | Type: Compliance/Guidance
Pillar: governance | Maturity Level: 2 | Asset Class: all
Requirement: Establish documented policy mandating SSH-2 usage and prohibiting SSH-1 due to cryptographic vulnerabilities.
Evidence: "The use of SSH-2 is recommended. Using SSH-1 is not recommended, since this protocol version contains cryptographic vulnerabilities."
Evidence location: Section 3.2

chunks.title: Cryptographic Mechanisms: Recommendations for SSH — Tier 2 governance requirement
chunks.content:
Source: Cryptographic Mechanisms: Recommendations for SSH
Category: Certification Schemes | Type: Compliance/Guidance
Pillar: governance | Maturity Level: 2 | Asset Class: software
Requirement: Define policy to prioritize recommended strong algorithms over weak or obsolete algorithms specified in SSH standards.
Evidence: "The application should support the algorithms recommended in this document and the algorithms given in the specification, but be configured in such a way that the recommended (cryptographically strong) algorithms are used with high priority and the (possibly cryptographically weak or obsolete) algorithms from the SSH specification are used with low priority or, if possible, are not used."
Evidence location: Section 3.2.1
Source URL: https://www.bsi.bund.de/SharedDocs/Downloads/EN/BSI/Publications/TechGuidelines/TG02102/BSI-TR-02102-4.pdf
Confidence: high

chunks.title: Cryptographic Mechanisms: Recommendations for SSH — Tier 2 governance requirement
chunks.content:
Source: Cryptographic Mechanisms: Recommendations for SSH
Category: Certification Schemes | Type: Compliance/Guidance
Pillar: governance | Maturity Level: 2 | Asset Class: keys
Requirement: Mandate secure storage of private keys using certified hardware to prevent copying, misuse, and manipulation.
Evidence: "Private cryptographic keys, especially static keys and signature keys, must be stored and processed in a secure manner. This includes, among other things, the protection against copying, misuse and manipulation of the keys. Secure storage of the keys can be achieved, for example by using certified hardware (chip card, HSM)."
Evidence location: Section 4.1
Source URL: https://www.bsi.bund.de/SharedDocs/Downloads/EN/BSI/Publications/TechGuidelines/TG02102/BSI-TR-02102-4.pdf
Confidence: high

chunks.content:

Category: Certification Schemes | Type: Compliance/Guidance
Pillar: governance | Maturity Level: 2 | Asset Class: keys
Requirement: Enforce policy requiring irrevocable deletion of ephemeral keys after use and prohibit persistent storage.
Evidence: "It must be ensured that all ephemeral keys are deleted irrevocably after they have been used and that no copies of these keys were made. Ephemeral or session keys may only be used for one connection and generally not be stored persistently."
Evidence location: Section 4.2
Source URL: https://www.bsi.bund.de/SharedDocs/Downloads/EN/BSI/Publications/TechGuidelines/TG02102/BSI-TR-02102-4.pdf

chunks.title: CSWP.39 Step 1: Govern (Governance)
chunks.content:
NIST CSWP.39 (Dec 2025) — "Considerations for Achieving Crypto Agility"
Step 1 of 5: Govern
Section reference: §5.1–5.4
CPM pillar: Governance

Embed crypto policy into standards, mandates, supply chains, threats, business requirements, partner ecosystem, stakeholders, crypto policies, and crypto architecture.

Requirements:
- Documented organisation-wide crypto policy
- RACI (Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed) across crypto decisions
- Standards-watch subscription (IETF, NIST, CA/B Forum, ETSI, BSI, ANSSI)
- Stakeholder and partner-ecosystem register
- Exception-handling workflow with compensating-control record

chunks.title: CSWP.39 Step 2: Inventory (Inventory)
chunks.content:
NIST CSWP.39 (Dec 2025) — "Considerations for Achieving Crypto Agility"
Step 2 of 5: Inventory
Section reference: §5.2
CPM pillar: Inventory

Build an asset-centric Cryptographic Bill of Materials (CBOM) across all six CSWP.39 asset classes — not just certificates.

Requirements:
- CBOM covering Code, Libraries, Applications, Files, Protocols, and Systems
- Automated ingestion from SBOM / CMDB pipelines
- Annual refresh cadence at minimum (daily preferred)
- Asset criticality and data-sensitivity metadata per record
- Entropy Source Validation (SP 800-90B) status tracked alongside FIPS 140-3 cert number

chunks.title: CSWP.39 Step 3: Identify Gaps (Observability)
chunks.content:
NIST CSWP.39 (Dec 2025) — "Considerations for Achieving Crypto Agility"
Step 3 of 5: Identify Gaps
Section reference: §5.3
CPM pillar: Observability

Audit the Management Tools layer that sits between Assets and the Risk Management engine. Without this layer the Information Repository is populated manually and the Risk Analysis Engine has stale, incomplete data.

Requirements:
- Crypto scanners — algorithms, key lengths, cert details across code and traffic
- Vulnerability management — CVE feeds, library EoL tracking
- Asset management — CMDB / SBOM → CBOM pipelines
- Log management (SIEM) — crypto-drift events, cipher-suite anomalies
- Zero-Trust enforcement — policy engines that block disallowed cipher suites
- Data classification — sensitivity tags that drive prioritisation

chunks.title: CSWP.39 Step 4: Prioritise (Assurance)
chunks.content:
NIST CSWP.39 (Dec 2025) — "Considerations for Achieving Crypto Agility"
Step 4 of 5: Prioritise
Section reference: §5.4
CPM pillar: Assurance

Run a Risk Analysis Prioritisation Engine informed by crypto policy to produce a ranked asset list and KPIs the organisation can act on.

Requirements:
- Scoring model incorporating FIPS status, ESV status, PQC readiness, EoL, posture score
- Critical / High / Medium / Low queue with per-asset action guidance
- KPI set reviewed monthly (coverage, MTTR, drift events, validation freshness)
- Data-sensitivity multiplier applied to attack-surface score
- Feedback loop to Governance — KPI exceptions update policy-as-code

chunks.title: CSWP.39 Step 5: Implement — Mitigate or Migrate (Lifecycle)
chunks.content:
NIST CSWP.39 (Dec 2025) — "Considerations for Achieving Crypto Agility"
Step 5 of 5: Implement — Mitigate or Migrate
Section reference: §4.6 / §5.5
CPM pillar: Lifecycle

For each prioritised asset choose Migration (algorithm swap, preferred when agility allows) or Mitigation (crypto gateway / bump-in-the-wire, when direct modification is infeasible).

Requirements:
- Crypto-agility assessment per asset (source available? modular API? update cadence?)
- Migration path with algorithm target (ML-KEM-768, ML-DSA-65, SLH-DSA) and timeline
- Mitigation gateway spec when migration blocked — with mandatory sunset date
- §4.6 callout — "Mitigation is not a permanent solution"; decommission plan required
- Evidence artefacts per change type — CMVP cert number, ACVP run, CVE-scan clean

chunks.title: 3GPP TS 33.310: Network Domain Security – Authentication Framework (NDS/AF)
chunks.content:
Document: 3GPP_TS_33.310_NDS_AF_Certificate_Overview
Section: 3GPP TS 33.310: Network Domain Security – Authentication Framework (NDS/AF)

> **Official Documentation:** [3GPP TS 33.310 (Latest Version - V19.4.0)](https://www.3gpp.org/DynaReport/33310.htm)
>
> **ETSI Publication:** [ETSI TS 133 310](https://www.etsi.org/deliver/etsi_ts/133300_133399/133310/)
>
> **Technical Content:** [Tech-Invite TS 33.310](https://www.tech-invite.com/3m33/tinv-3gpp-33-310.html)

---

chunks.title: Overview
chunks.content:
Document: 3GPP_TS_33.310_NDS_AF_Certificate_Overview
Section: Overview

3GPP TS 33.310 specifies a **scalable entity authentication framework** for 3GPP network nodes using X.509 certificates. It defines certificate profiles, trust models, and protocols for securing inter-operator and intra-operator communications via IPsec (NDS/IP) and TLS.

---

chunks.title: Scope
chunks.content:
Document: 3GPP_TS_33.310_NDS_AF_Certificate_Overview
Section: Scope

| Domain                     | Description                                                                |
| -------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **NDS/IP**                 | IPsec-based security for Za (inter-SEG) and Zb (intra-domain) interfaces   |
| **TLS**                    | TLS-based authentication for inter-operator communications (IMS, GBA, SBA) |
| **Base Station Enrolment** | Certificate provisioning for eNodeB/gNodeB via CMPv2                       |
| **5GC SBA**                | Service Based Architecture certificates for NFs, SCP, SEPP                 |

---

chunks.title: Certificate Profiles Defined
chunks.content:
Document: 3GPP_TS_33.310_NDS_AF_Certificate_Overview
Section: Certificate Profiles Defined

### End Entity Certificates

| Profile                      | Use Case                                             |
| ---------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| **SEG Certificate**          | Security Gateway authentication (IPsec Za interface) |
| **NE Certificate**           | Network Element authentication (Zb interface)        |
| **TLS Client Certificate**   | TLS client authentication                            |
| **TLS Server Certificate**   | TLS server authentication                            |
| **Base Station Certificate** | eNodeB/gNodeB backhaul security                      |

### 5GC SBA Certificates (Release 15+)

| Profile               | Use Case                                          |
| --------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- |
| **NF Certificate**    | Network Function producer/consumer authentication |
| **SCP Certificate**   | Service Communication Proxy                       |
| **SEPP Intra-domain** | Security Edge Protection Proxy (within PLMN)      |

### Certificate Profile
