Q: What is the recommended approach for migrating SSH host keys to PQC on a large server fleet?
  A) Rotate all SSH host keys simultaneously during a single maintenance window
  B) Generate PQC SSH host keys alongside existing classical host keys and advertise both in sshd_config until client compatibility is confirmed
  C) Remove classical SSH host keys immediately to force PQC adoption
  D) Use a configuration management system to disable SSH and use certificate-based auth only
Answer: B
Explanation: Dual host key configuration allows SSH clients to negotiate the algorithm they support. New clients capable of ML-DSA-65 will use the PQC host key; legacy clients fall back to Ed25519. This parallel operation allows gradual fleet migration without breaking connectivity.

Q: True or False: Container image signing with Sigstore Cosign will produce the same signature size after migrating from ECDSA to ML-DSA-65.
Answer: FALSE
Explanation: False. Cosign signatures stored in OCI registries grow substantially with ML-DSA-65. An ML-DSA-65 signature is 3309 bytes.

chunks.title: Quiz: ops-quantum-impact
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: ops-quantum-impact

Q: A Prometheus alert fires when TLS handshake duration exceeds 8ms. After migrating to PQC what should the alert threshold be adjusted to?
  A) Keep it at 8ms — PQC migration should not increase handshake latency
  B) Increase to approximately 15ms to account for typical PQC handshake overhead
  C) Increase to 50ms because PQC is orders of magnitude slower than classical algorithms
  D) Remove the alert entirely as TLS latency monitoring is not useful post-migration
Answer: B
Explanation: Typical PQC TLS handshake latency increases from ~5ms to ~12ms due to larger certificate chains and PQC computation. Setting a threshold at approximately 15ms provides headroom for normal PQC-era variation while still alerting on genuine degradation.

Q: What is a crypto inventory and why is it the first step in PQC migration planning?
  A) A list of all software licenses for cryptographic products; required for compliance audits
  B) A complete mapping of all cryptographic algorithms in use across the infrastructure including where keys are stored and what data they protect; identifies migration scope and priority
  C) A hardware inventory of HSMs and TPMs; required for budget planning
  D) A vendor list of all cryptographic library suppliers; required for supply chain risk assessment
Answer: B
Explanation: A cryptographic inventory catalogs every algorithm in use, the systems where they appear, the key material involved, and the sensitivity of data they protect. Without this map, teams cannot prioritize migration or identify HNDL-exposed systems.

chunks.title: Quiz: ops-quantum-impact
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: ops-quantum-impact

Q: True or False: Rolling back a failed PQC migration is straightforward because classical algorithm certificates and keys are still valid while both are deployed in parallel.
Answer: TRUE
Explanation: True. A key advantage of deploying hybrid or dual-algorithm configurations during PQC migration is that rollback remains possible. If a PQC deployment causes compatibility issues, the classical algorithm configuration can be re-activated without service interruption.

Q: In a Kubernetes environment what resource most commonly needs updating to handle larger PQC TLS certificates?
  A) ConfigMap
  B) Service
  C) TLS Secret (kubernetes.io/tls type) and Ingress controller buffer configurations
  D) Namespace RBAC policy, because larger certificates require elevated permissions
Answer: C
Explanation: Kubernetes TLS secrets store certificate and key data that may exceed expectations sized for classical algorithms. More critically, ingress controllers (nginx, HAProxy, Envoy) have configurable proxy_buffer_size and proxy_buffers settings that may need increasing to handle PQC certificate chain sizes.

chunks.title: Quiz: ops-quantum-impact
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: ops-quantum-impact

Q: What does the multiple key exchanges extension in IKEv2 (RFC 9370) enable for PQC VPN migration?
  A) It allows two VPN endpoints to negotiate two separate SA tunnels simultaneously
  B) It adds a second key exchange round to IKEv2 allowing ML-KEM-768 to be combined with classical ECDH in a single IKE negotiation
  C) It replaces the Diffie-Hellman group entirely with ML-KEM, requiring both endpoints to be PQC-capable
  D) It adds post-quantum certificate validation to IKEv2 authentication
Answer: B
Explanation: RFC 9370 (Multiple Key Exchanges in IKEv2) adds a mechanism to perform additional key exchange rounds beyond the initial IKE_SA_INIT exchange. This enables hybrid key exchange: IKE establishes an initial ECDH key exchange, then an additional ML-KEM-768 exchange adds a second layer of key material.

chunks.title: Quiz: research-quantum-impact
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: research-quantum-impact

Q: Why does genomic research data require particular urgency in PQC migration compared to most enterprise data?
  A) Genomic databases use weaker encryption than financial systems
  B) Genomic data has an effectively permanent sensitivity horizon — an individual's DNA cannot be changed, making HNDL threats permanent and irreversible
  C) Genomic research data is publicly available and does not require encryption
  D) Genomic data files are too large for classical encryption algorithms
Answer: B
Explanation: Genomic data identifies individuals permanently. Unlike financial records where account numbers can be changed after a breach, DNA sequences are immutable identifiers tied to both the subject and their biological relatives, so participant-linked genomic data can stay sensitive for decades, for the subject's lifetime and beyond.

Q: True or False: Research publications signed with ECDSA today face a long-term quantum integrity threat because the publication record is permanent.
Answer: TRUE
Explanation: True. A digital signature on a research publication protects the integrity claim that the document has not been altered since signing. In this module's illustration, if a CRQC later allows signature forgery, adversaries could create fraudulent versions of foundational research papers with valid-looking classical signatures.

chunks.title: Quiz: research-quantum-impact
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: research-quantum-impact

Q: What security property is most at risk when research institutions share data in federated learning collaborations using classical TLS?
  A) Data accuracy and completeness of the training dataset
  B) Long-term confidentiality of research contributions transmitted between institutions — susceptible to HNDL if adversaries record the exchanges
  C) The intellectual property rights to the trained model
  D) Compliance with IRB approval requirements
Answer: B
Explanation: Federated learning transmits model gradients and potentially sensitive derivative data between institutions over TLS. If an adversary records these exchanges today they can potentially reconstruct sensitive training data from the gradients after CRQC arrival.

chunks.title: Quiz: research-quantum-impact
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: research-quantum-impact

Q: Under the EU Clinical Trials Regulation (EU) No 536/2014, Article 58, the clinical trial master file must be archived for at least 25 years after the end of the trial. What does this mean for the HNDL risk horizon?
  A) No additional action needed — 25-year retention periods predate quantum computing
  B) Classical encryption is sufficient because quantum computers will not exist within 25 years
  C) The retention period overlaps the period in which a CRQC may arrive (in the Global Risk Institute's 2025 expert survey, a clear majority judged a CRQC within 15 years at least as likely as not), so data encrypted today with RSA or ECDH may be decrypted before its retention period expires
  D) 25-year retention data should be deleted rather than encrypted
Answer: C
Explanation: EU Regulation 536/2014 Art. 58 requires the sponsor and investigator to archive the clinical trial master file for at least 25 years after the end of the trial. ICH E6(R3) (2.12.12) sets no fixed number of years: records are kept for the period required by applicable regulatory requirements or until the sponsor says they are no longer needed, whichever is longest. In the US, 21 CFR 312.62(c) requires investigators to keep records for 2 years after approval, or after the investigation is discontinued and FDA is notified. In the Global Risk Institute's Quantum Threat Timeline Report 2025, a clear majority of the 26 experts surveyed judged a CRQC within 15 years at least as likely as not, so data encrypted today may be decrypted before a 25-year retention period ends.

chunks.title: Quiz: research-quantum-impact
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: research-quantum-impact

Q: A research proposal's data management plan describes long-term protection of sensitive data. Which algorithms are NIST's standardised post-quantum choices for key establishment and digital signatures?
  A) RSA-4096 as the extended-lifetime standard
  B) AES-256 for all data protection with no PQC requirement
  C) ML-KEM (FIPS 203) for key establishment, and ML-DSA (FIPS 204) or SLH-DSA (FIPS 205) for signatures
  D) Elliptic-curve algorithms upgraded to P-521
Answer: C
Explanation: NIST published FIPS 203 (ML-KEM), FIPS 204 (ML-DSA) and FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA) in August 2024. This quiz does not claim that funders require them: check the funder's call text before stating a requirement. Describing PQC-ready data protection in a data management plan is good practice, not a general funder requirement.

Q: True or False: Code-based cryptography such as HQC derives its security from the hardness of decoding random linear codes — a problem believed hard for both classical and quantum computers.
Answer: TRUE
Explanation: True. Code-based cryptography relies on the syndrome decoding problem for random linear codes, studied since McEliece's 1978 proposal and not believed to be efficiently solvable by quantum computers.

chunks.title: Quiz: research-quantum-impact
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: research-quantum-impact

Q: What is a lattice-based cryptographic algorithm and what makes its security assumptions conservative?
  A) An algorithm using physical silicon lattice structures for key generation; conservative because hardware is hard to clone
  B) An algorithm whose security reduces to the hardness of lattice problems (LWE/SIS); conservative because these problems are well-studied and believed hard for quantum computers
  C) An algorithm built on graph theory; conservative because NP-hard problems are assumed quantum-safe
  D) An algorithm based on hash functions organized in a lattice structure; conservative because hash security is well understood
Answer: B
Explanation: Lattice-based algorithms (ML-KEM, ML-DSA) rely on the Learning With Errors (LWE) and Short Integer Solution (SIS) problems on high-dimensional lattices.

Q: Why are isogeny-based cryptographic schemes such as SIDH no longer considered viable PQC candidates?
  A) They are too slow for practical deployment
  B) A classical (non-quantum) attack published in 2022 completely broke the most efficient variants
  C) They were never formally submitted to the NIST PQC process
  D) They require quantum hardware to perform key generation
Answer: B
Explanation: In 2022, researchers Castryck and Decru published a classical polynomial-time attack that broke SIDH (Supersingular Isogeny Diffie-Hellman) and SIKE (a NIST candidate). The attack used auxiliary torsion point information to recover private keys classically. No quantum computer was needed.

chunks.title: Quiz: research-quantum-impact
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: research-quantum-impact

Q: True or False: The security of hash-based signature schemes like SLH-DSA rests on properties of the underlying hash function rather than on algebraic problems such as lattices or factoring.
Answer: TRUE
Explanation: True. SLH-DSA (FIPS 205) is built only from a hash function (SHA-2 or SHAKE), so its security reduces to properties of that hash function, such as preimage and second-preimage resistance, rather than to algebraic hardness assumptions. Quantum attacks are still accounted for: Grover-type search lowers the effective security of hash functions, which is why the parameter sets are sized for the NIST security categories. Implementation flaws such as side channels remain a separate risk.

Q: What is the primary challenge of 50-year data confidentiality requirements common in health and genetic research with respect to PQC migration?
  A) Modern computers cannot encrypt data with 50-year security guarantees
  B) Current PQC standards may themselves need to be replaced during a 50-year horizon, requiring cryptographic agility to be built into research data archives
  C) 50-year data must be stored offline and encryption cannot be applied
  D) HIPAA only requires 6-year data retention making 50-year encryption unnecessary
Answer: B
Explanation: 50-year confidentiality horizons extend well beyond the expected lifespan of any current cryptographic standard. Research data archives must implement crypto-agile storage: envelope encryption with version-tagged key identifiers that allow the outer encryption layer to be re-wrapped with updated algorithms as standards evolve.

chunks.title: Quiz: pqc-testing-validation
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: pqc-testing-validation

Q: Which tool operates in passive mode — inspecting TLS handshakes on a SPAN port without injecting any packets?
  A) pqcscan
  B) SSLyze
  C) CryptoNext COMPASS
  D) Keysight CyPerf
Answer: C
Explanation: CryptoNext COMPASS (and pqc-flow) operate in passive mode on a SPAN/TAP port — zero packets are injected, making them safe for production and OT environments. pqcscan, SSLyze, and CyPerf are active tools that initiate connections.

Q: What is the key limitation of passive discovery tools compared to active scanners?
  A) They require expensive hardware appliances
  B) They can only analyze OT protocols
  C) They cannot validate whether a remote endpoint actively supports PQC — only what is currently in use
  D) They inject packets that may disrupt production traffic
Answer: C
Explanation: Passive tools can only detect algorithms in currently observed flows. If no connection is being made using ML-KEM, a passive probe will not detect ML-KEM support on that endpoint. Active scanners probe endpoints directly to discover their full PQC capability.

Q: According to VIAVI TeraVM benchmark data, what is the approximate IKEv2 SA setup time for pure PQC on a WAN link (50ms RTT) compared to classical?
  A) 3× slower (720ms vs 240ms)
  B) 53× slower (12,626ms vs 240ms)
  C) 2× slower (480ms vs 240ms)
  D) 10× slower (2,400ms vs 240ms)
Answer: B
Explanation: IKEv2 SA establishment rises from 240ms (classical DH) to 12,626ms (pure PQC, WAN) — a 53× increase. This is why hybrid IKEv2 (380ms, 1.6×) is the recommended migration path rather than jumping directly to pure PQC for VPN gateways.

chunks.title: Quiz: pqc-testing-validation
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: pqc-testing-validation

Q: TCP fragmentation occurs when a TLS ClientHello exceeds approximately 1,400 bytes, adding one extra RTT to the handshake.
Answer: FALSE
Explanation: False. A post-quantum ClientHello can be larger than a typical TCP segment (about 1,460 bytes), so it is split over more than one TCP segment, but RFC 6928 proposes to raise the upper bound on TCP's initial window to 10 segments (maximum 14600 B). On a sender that uses an initial window of that size, a ClientHello of two segments goes out in the same first flight, so the split by itself does not add a round trip.

chunks.title: Quiz: pqc-testing-validation
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: pqc-testing-validation

Q: Why is a fixed-vs-random (non-specific) TVLA test alone not enough for ML-KEM and ML-DSA side-channel evaluation?
  A) Lattice algorithms run too fast for power measurement equipment
  B) It flags any input-dependent difference, public data included, so a failing result alone does not show that a secret leaks
  C) Welch's t-test requires more than 10,000 traces to be effective
  D) A fixed set is distinguishable by construction, so the test fails every implementation, masked or not
Answer: B
Explanation: The non-specific fixed-vs-random test compares traces recorded with a fixed input against traces recorded with random inputs. It needs no assumption about how the device leaks, so it can flag any input-dependent difference, including leakage of public data such as the ciphertext, and it "does not bring information about the hardness of mounting successful attacks" (Merino Del Pozo and Standaert). It does not fail every implementation: in the workshop, the masked ML-KEM target stays below the common |t| = 4.5 threshold (Goodwill et al., 2011) at every stage. TVLA therefore also uses specific tests on chosen intermediate values, so labs target the NTT/INTT, polynomial multiplication and modular reduction stages that handle secrets. A pass is still not proof of security (Standaert, CARDIS 2018).

chunks.title: Quiz: pqc-testing-validation
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: pqc-testing-validation

Q: What does CBOM stand for, and which tool generates it from source code repositories?
  A) Cryptographic Binary Object Model — generated by CBOMkit
  B) Cryptography Bill of Materials — generated by CBOMkit (IBM)
  C) Certificate Bundle of Materials — generated by pqcscan
  D) Crypto Baseline Operations Map — generated by PQC-LEO
Answer: B
Explanation: CBOM (Cryptography Bill of Materials) is standardized in CycloneDX 1.6. CBOMkit (open source, IBM-contributed) generates CBOM by scanning git repositories for cryptographic algorithm usage.

chunks.title: Quiz: pqc-testing-validation
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: pqc-testing-validation

Q: How does the TLS 1.3 hybrid key exchange construction (draft-ietf-tls-hybrid-design, published as RFC 9954) form the shared secret for a group such as X25519MLKEM768, and what should a hybrid interoperability test therefore check?
  A) Only the PQC component needs to complete — the classical component is optional for performance
  B) The two component shared secrets are concatenated, so both components must complete; a test should check that any fallback to a non-hybrid group is explicit, not silent
  C) Hybrid key exchange must always use X25519 as the classical component
  D) The shared secret is the PQC ciphertext XORed with the classical shared secret
Answer: B
Explanation: RFC 9954 section 3.3 forms the secret as "concatenated_shared_secret = MyECDH.shared_secret || MyPQKEM.shared_secret" and inserts it into the TLS 1.3 key schedule in place of the (EC)DHE secret, so a session only gets a hybrid secret if both components completed. Section 1.4 expects a non-hybrid result with a non-hybrid-aware peer only if the hybrid-aware endpoint is "willing to downgrade", which is why a test checks that a fallback is visible and intended. "Both components must complete, no silent downgrade" is this module's test practice built on that construction. RFC 9794 is an Informational terminology document ("This document defines terminology for such schemes") and sets no protocol rules. The construction is concatenation, not XOR, and other combinations such as SecP256r1MLKEM768 exist, so X25519 is not required.

chunks.title: Quiz: pqc-testing-validation
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: pqc-testing-validation

Q: Which TVLA threshold (|t| value) is the commonly used cutoff for declaring statistically significant side-channel leakage?
  A) 2.0
  B) 3.0
  C) 4.5
  D) 6.0
Answer: C
Explanation: The common TVLA threshold is |t| > 4.5. It comes from the methodology of Goodwill et al. (NIST Non-Invasive Attack Testing Workshop, 2011): "For n> 100, the pass fail criteria is C > 4.5 or C < -4.5." It is a widely used convention, not a NIST standard or a CMVP requirement: NIST SP 800-140F section 6.2 (approved non-invasive attack mitigation test metrics) reads "No additional requirements at this time". Crossing the threshold means leakage was detected, not that a key was recovered, and a lower threshold flags more points and makes false alarms more likely.

Q: Which of the following is an open-source passive PQC network discovery tool?
  A) VIAVI Observer
  B) Keysight Inspector
  C) pqc-flow (CipherIQ)
  D) VIAVI TeraVM
Answer: C
Explanation: pqc-flow (CipherIQ) is an open-source passive analyzer that detects PQC in encrypted network traffic — TLS, SSH, QUIC — without storing payload content. VIAVI Observer, VIAVI TeraVM, and Keysight Inspector are commercial tools.

chunks.title: Quiz: pqc-testing-validation
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: pqc-testing-validation

Q: When testing a pure PQC client (ML-KEM-768 only, no classical component) against Cloudflare, what result is expected?
  A) Full ML-KEM-768 negotiation — Cloudflare supports pure PQC clients
  B) Incompatible — Cloudflare lists only hybrid key agreements, so a client that offers only pure ML-KEM-768 has no group in common with it
  C) Partial — Cloudflare accepts pure PQC but disables QUIC
  D) Compatible — Cloudflare falls back to X25519+ML-KEM-768 automatically
Answer: B
Explanation: Cloudflare's post-quantum documentation lists two key agreements, both hybrid: X25519MLKEM768 (recommended) and X25519Kyber768Draft00 (obsolete). It does not list a pure ML-KEM group. In TLS 1.3 the server picks a group the client offered, and if there is no overlap between the client's supported_groups and the server's groups it must abort the handshake with a "handshake_failure" or "insufficient_security" alert (RFC 8446 section 4.1.1). A client that offers only pure ML-KEM-768 should therefore expect a failed handshake, not an automatic fallback to X25519MLKEM768. RFC 9794 is Informational terminology and does not require this; the outcome follows from the groups the server deploys, which can change, so confirm it against the live endpoint.

chunks.title: Quiz: pqc-testing-validation
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: pqc-testing-validation

Q: In a VIAVI white paper on PQC migration, what was VIAVI TeraVM Security Test used for?
  A) Passive network monitoring on SPAN ports
  B) Simulating millions of PQC-enabled TLS and IKEv2/IPsec connections to evaluate how components like HAProxy and Strongswan behave under enterprise-level load
  C) Source code scanning for cryptographic algorithm usage
  D) Side-channel power analysis of embedded devices
Answer: B
Explanation: In the VIAVI white paper, VIAVI TeraVM Security Test was used to simulate millions of PQC-enabled TLS and IKEv2/IPsec connections to evaluate how components like HAProxy and Strongswan behave under enterprise-level load.

Q: Which stage of ML-KEM's computation is most commonly identified as the primary leakage point in TVLA analysis?
  A) Randomness sampling (CBD sampling)
  B) Key serialization
  C) NTT (Number Theoretic Transform)
  D) Ciphertext compression
Answer: C
Explanation: The NTT (Number Theoretic Transform) is ML-KEM's core polynomial multiplication operation. It processes secret coefficients in a loop structure that creates key-dependent power patterns detectable with TVLA. Noise sampling (CBD) is not free of leakage either: in key generation it produces the secret vector s and the error vector e from a seed derived from the sensitive seed d (FIPS 203, Algorithm 13), so test plans cover it too.

Q: pqcscan is an open-source, Rust-based active TLS and SSH scanner that produces JSON and HTML report output.
Answer: TRUE
Explanation: pqcscan (Anvil Secure) is indeed written in Rust for high performance, supports TLS and SSH scan modes, and outputs results in both JSON and HTML formats. It is BSD-licensed and available for Linux, macOS, and Windows. It is classified as an active scanner — it initiates connections to probe endpoints.

chunks.title: Quiz: pqc-testing-validation
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: pqc-testing-validation

Q: In the recommended PQC test strategy for an OT/ICS environment, why must the inventory phase use passive-only tools?
  A) OT devices cannot handle TLS connections
  B) Active scanning tools are not licensed for OT environments
  C) Active probing can disrupt real-time safety systems and cause unplanned shutdowns
  D) OT networks use proprietary protocols that no active scanner supports
Answer: C
Explanation: OT/ICS environments run safety-critical systems with real-time constraints. Active scanning initiates unexpected connections that can trigger fault conditions, cause PLCs to enter safe-stop mode, or disrupt time-sensitive control loops. Passive-only discovery (CryptoNext COMPASS, pqc-flow in read-only mode) is mandatory for initial inventory of OT segments.

Q: What is the most significant performance overhead introduced by pure PQC certificates (ML-DSA + ML-KEM) compared to classical (ECDSA + ECDH)?
  A) Signing speed — ML-DSA signing is 100× slower than ECDSA
  B) Certificate size — pure PQC certificates (~17KB) force TCP fragmentation, adding an extra RTT
  C) Key generation time — ML-KEM key generation is 50× slower than ECDH
  D) Verification cost — ML-DSA verification requires more CPU than TLS record decryption
Answer: B
Explanation: Pure PQC certificates reach ~17KB vs 1.2KB for classical, causing TCP fragmentation in TLS handshakes (ClientHello + certificate chain exceeds MTU). This adds one extra RTT to every new connection — on WAN (50ms RTT) this is 50ms per connection, on satellite (600ms RTT) this is 600ms. The crypto computation overhead itself is under 1ms. This drives the recommendation to use hybrid schemes during the transition period.

chunks.title: Quiz: confidential-computing
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: confidential-computing

Q: What is a Trusted Execution Environment (TEE)?
  A) A virtual machine for testing software
  B) A hardware-isolated secure area within a processor that protects code and data during execution
  C) An encrypted network tunnel
  D) A secure operating system
Answer: B
Explanation: A TEE is a hardware-enforced isolated execution environment within a CPU that protects the confidentiality and integrity of code and data loaded inside it. Even privileged software (OS, hypervisor) cannot access TEE-protected memory. Examples include Intel SGX/TDX, AMD SEV-SNP, Arm CCA, and AWS Nitro Enclaves.

Q: What is remote attestation in the context of confidential computing?
  A) Logging into a remote server
  B) A cryptographic proof that code is running inside a genuine TEE with a specific software configuration
  C) Encrypting data before sending it to the cloud
  D) A backup verification process
Answer: B
Explanation: Remote attestation allows a relying party to verify that their workload is running inside an authentic TEE on genuine hardware, with the expected software loaded. The TEE generates a signed attestation report containing measurements (hashes) of the loaded code. The signature uses the TEE manufacturer's attestation key.

Q: True or False: Confidential computing protects data while it is being processed in memory, not just at rest or in transit.
Answer: TRUE
Explanation: True. Confidential computing addresses the third state of data protection: data in use. Traditional encryption protects data at rest (disk encryption) and in transit (TLS), but data must typically be decrypted for processing. TEEs keep data encrypted in memory and only decrypt it within the hardware-isolated enclave.

chunks.title: Quiz: confidential-computing
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: confidential-computing

Q: Which Intel technology provides VM-level confidential computing with hardware memory encryption?
  A) Intel SGX
  B) Intel TDX
  C) Intel AMT
  D) Intel vPro
Answer: B
Explanation: Intel Trust Domain Extensions (TDX) provides VM-level confidential computing, encrypting entire virtual machine memory and isolating VMs from the hypervisor. SGX provides application-level enclaves (smaller scope).

Q: What is AMD SEV-SNP?
  A) A network firewall technology
  B) AMD's confidential computing technology providing encrypted VM memory with integrity protection against hypervisor tampering
  C) A CPU overclocking feature
  D) A solid-state drive encryption standard
Answer: B
Explanation: AMD Secure Encrypted Virtualization - Secure Nested Paging (SEV-SNP) encrypts VM memory and adds integrity protection that prevents the hypervisor from modifying encrypted memory pages. SNP builds on earlier SEV and SEV-ES generations to provide the strongest protection against a compromised hypervisor.

Q: Why is confidential computing relevant to the PQC transition?
  A) TEEs replace the need for PQC algorithms
  B) TEE attestation keys and memory encryption use classical cryptography that is vulnerable to quantum attack
  C) Confidential computing is unrelated to quantum threats
  D) TEEs already use quantum-safe algorithms
Answer: B
Explanation: TEE attestation signatures typically use ECDSA or RSA, and memory encryption uses AES (quantum-safe for symmetric, but key agreement is classical). A CRQC could forge attestation reports by breaking the signing key, or compromise key provisioning. TEE vendors must migrate attestation to ML-DSA and key agreement to ML-KEM.

chunks.title: Quiz: confidential-computing
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: confidential-computing

Q: What is Arm Confidential Compute Architecture (CCA)?
  A) A cloud service from Arm
  B) Arm's hardware architecture for isolating workloads in Realms, providing confidential computing for Arm-based processors
  C) A certificate authority protocol
  D) An ARM assembly instruction set
Answer: B
Explanation: Arm CCA introduces Realms — hardware-isolated execution environments for Arm v9 processors. Unlike Intel TDX or AMD SEV-SNP (x86), CCA targets mobile, edge, and server workloads on Arm silicon. Realms are managed by a Realm Management Monitor (RMM) that runs at a new privilege level (EL2-Realm).

Q: What is the Confidential Computing Consortium (CCC)?
  A) A quantum computing research lab
  B) A Linux Foundation project promoting standards and open-source frameworks for hardware-based TEE technologies
  C) A government regulatory body
  D) A cloud provider alliance
Answer: B
Explanation: The Confidential Computing Consortium (CCC) is a Linux Foundation project with members including Intel, AMD, Arm, Google, Microsoft, Red Hat, and others. It promotes the adoption of confidential computing through open-source projects (Enarx, Gramine, Open Enclave SDK), standards, and best practices.

chunks.title: Quiz: confidential-computing
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: confidential-computing

Q: What is the primary quantum threat to TEE attestation?
  A) Quantum computers can break AES memory encryption
  B) A CRQC could forge attestation signatures by breaking the ECDSA/RSA attestation key, allowing fake TEE reports
  C) Quantum noise interferes with TEE hardware
  D) TEE memory becomes unstable near quantum computers
Answer: B
Explanation: TEE attestation relies on digital signatures rooted in manufacturer-provisioned keys. A CRQC running Shor's algorithm could derive these private keys, enabling an attacker to forge attestation reports that falsely claim code is running in a genuine TEE. This would undermine the entire trust model of confidential computing.

Q: How could a TEE-HSM integration improve PQC key management?
  A) TEEs replace HSMs entirely
  B) TEEs can provide a secure execution environment for PQC operations when HSM firmware lacks PQC support, using the HSM for key storage and the TEE for PQC computation
  C) TEEs and HSMs are incompatible
  D) HSMs provide better TEE attestation
Answer: B
Explanation: TEE-HSM integration allows organizations to bridge the gap during PQC transition: the HSM provides tamper-resistant key storage (FIPS 140-3 certified), while the TEE provides a secure environment for PQC computations that the HSM firmware does not yet support. Keys can be securely transferred between HSM and TEE for PQC operations.

chunks.title: Quiz: confidential-computing
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: confidential-computing

Q: True or False: AWS Nitro Enclaves use a dedicated Nitro Security Chip that is separate from the main CPU for attestation.
Answer: TRUE
Explanation: True. AWS Nitro Enclaves run on dedicated hardware managed by the Nitro Security Chip, which is separate from the main CPU. This chip handles attestation, provides a hardware root of trust, and ensures the hypervisor cannot access enclave memory. The Nitro attestation document includes PCR measurements signed by the Nitro Security Chip.

Q: What is memory encryption in the context of confidential computing?
  A) Encrypting files stored on disk
  B) Hardware-level encryption of DRAM contents in the memory controller so that physical memory access reveals no plaintext
  C) Using VPN for network traffic
  D) Compressing memory to save space
Answer: B
Explanation: Memory encryption in confidential computing uses hardware AES engines integrated into the memory controller. Encryption, integrity and replay protection are applied to data just before it leaves the chip, so physical access to memory reveals no plaintext. Defending against an attacker on the memory bus usually needs only a handful of keys, for example one pair of keys for encryption and integrity protection (Intel SGX) or a separate key per world (Arm CCA).

chunks.title: Quiz: confidential-computing
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: confidential-computing

Q: Which of the following are valid use cases for confidential computing in PQC transition? (Select all that apply)
  A) Running PQC algorithms in a TEE when the underlying OS or hypervisor is not yet PQC-ready
  B) Protecting PQC key generation inside an enclave, isolated from other software on the host
  C) Using TEE attestation as a replacement for PQC certificates
  D) Securely migrating classical keys to PQC keys within a hardware-isolated environment
Answer: A|B|D
Explanation: This module's own judgement, not a statement of the NIST IR 8320E initial public draft: a TEE can run PQC code where the operating system or hypervisor is not yet PQC-ready, can isolate PQC key generation from other software on the host, and can provide an isolated environment for key migration. The initial public draft of NIST IR 8320E covers remote attestation: it gives cryptographic evidence that a VM is running on hardware equipped with TEE capabilities and that the VM's memory and state are isolated and protected from other tenants and the hypervisor. Attestation verifies the execution environment, while certificates verify identity, so attestation does not replace PQC certificates; each has to migrate to PQC algorithms on its own.

Q: What does Google Confidential VMs use for memory encryption?
  A) Software-based encryption at the OS level
  B) AMD SEV or SEV-SNP hardware memory encryption
  C) Intel SGX enclaves exclusively
  D) Application-layer TLS
Answer: B
Explanation: Google Cloud Confidential VMs leverage AMD SEV (and SEV-SNP on newer hardware) to encrypt VM memory with hardware-managed keys. The hypervisor and other VMs cannot decrypt the protected VM's memory. This provides lift-and-shift confidential computing without requiring application modifications.

chunks.title: Quiz: confidential-computing
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: confidential-computing

Q: What is the key difference between Intel SGX and Intel TDX?
  A) SGX is newer than TDX
  B) SGX protects individual application enclaves while TDX protects entire virtual machines
  C) TDX is for consumer devices and SGX is for servers
  D) They are identical technologies with different names
Answer: B
Explanation: Intel SGX (Software Guard Extensions) creates small application-level enclaves with limited memory (originally ~128MB). Intel TDX (Trust Domain Extensions) provides VM-level isolation, encrypting the entire VM memory space. TDX is designed for cloud workloads requiring full VM confidentiality without application redesign.

chunks.title: Quiz: emv-payment-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: emv-payment-pqc

Q: What does EMV stand for in payment card technology?
  A) Electronic Mobile Verification
  B) Europay, Mastercard, and Visa
  C) Encrypted Message Validation
  D) Enhanced Multi-Vendor
Answer: B
Explanation: EMV stands for Europay, Mastercard, and Visa — the three companies that originally developed the chip card standard. EMV specifications define how chip cards, terminals, and payment networks interact to authenticate transactions. EMVCo now manages the standard with six member organizations.

Q: What cryptographic operations do payment cards perform during a chip transaction?
  A) Only symmetric encryption of the PIN
  B) Dynamic data authentication (DDA) using RSA signatures and symmetric session key derivation
  C) Quantum key distribution
  D) No cryptographic operations — the terminal handles everything
Answer: B
Explanation: EMV chip cards perform RSA-based dynamic data authentication (DDA/CDA) to prove card authenticity, and use symmetric key derivation for transaction-specific session keys. The card's RSA private key signs transaction data, and the terminal verifies it against the CA public key hierarchy. This RSA dependency is the primary PQC concern.

Q: True or False: Payment tokenization (replacing card numbers with tokens) is already quantum-safe because tokens are random values.
Answer: FALSE
Explanation: Partially true but misleading. While token values themselves are random, the tokenization infrastructure relies on classical cryptography for: token provisioning (TLS with RSA/ECDH), token vault protection, and the binding between tokens and original PANs. These surrounding cryptographic operations must migrate to PQC.

chunks.title: Quiz: emv-payment-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: emv-payment-pqc

Q: What is the primary PQC challenge for EMV chip cards?
  A) Cards lack internet connectivity
  B) PQC signatures and keys are too large for the constrained storage and bandwidth of chip card hardware
  C) Chip cards already use quantum-safe algorithms
  D) Payment networks do not use public-key cryptography
Answer: B
Explanation: EMV chip cards have severely constrained resources: limited NVM storage (typically 80-256KB), slow processors, and narrow communication bandwidth with terminals. ML-DSA-65 signatures (3,309 bytes) are ~13x larger than RSA-2048 signatures (256 bytes), creating significant challenges for card storage, transaction speed, and contactless communication bandwidth.

Q: Approximately how many EMV chip cards were in global circulation at the end of 2024?
  A) About 1.5 billion
  B) About 4-5 billion
  C) About 14.7 billion
  D) About 50 billion
Answer: C
Explanation: EMVCo reported over 14.7 billion EMV chip cards in global circulation at the end of 2024 (2025 EMV User Meeting), growing roughly 7% a year. This installed base is what makes PQC migration a logistics problem as much as a cryptographic one: cards turn over on a 3-5 year cycle, terminals must verify any new signature scheme, and the EMVCo CA hierarchy has to issue under it first.

chunks.title: Quiz: emv-payment-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: emv-payment-pqc

Q: What role does the EMV CA (Certificate Authority) hierarchy play in payment security?
  A) It encrypts all transaction data
  B) It provides the trust chain for card authentication — the payment network CA signs issuer certificates, which sign individual card certificates
  C) It stores cardholder PINs
  D) It manages network routing
Answer: B
Explanation: The EMV CA hierarchy is a multi-level PKI: Payment Network Root CA (Visa, Mastercard) → Issuer CA → Card Certificate. During DDA/CDA, the terminal walks this chain to verify the card's authenticity. Migrating this hierarchy to PQC requires coordinated upgrades across networks, issuers, and terminals worldwide.

Q: What is the HNDL risk for payment transactions?
  A) There is no HNDL risk because transactions are real-time
  B) Recorded transaction authentication data could be used to forge cards if the CA signing keys are later broken by a CRQC
  C) Harvest Now Decrypt Later only applies to email
  D) Payment PINs could be decrypted offline
Answer: B
Explanation: While individual transaction data has limited replayability, the HNDL threat to payments focuses on the CA key hierarchy. If an adversary captures RSA-signed card certificates and later breaks the CA root key with a CRQC, they could forge new card certificates, potentially enabling card cloning at scale. This makes CA key migration urgent.

chunks.title: Quiz: emv-payment-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: emv-payment-pqc

Q: Which card network has publicly described testing PQC algorithms on a cloud virtual network and checking whether existing hardware could support them through software updates?
  A) Mastercard
  B) Visa
  C) American Express
  D) Discover
Answer: A
Explanation: Mastercard described those prototypes in its official quantum-security account. This is evidence of prototype testing—not a production network pilot. Visa has separately published quantum-readiness guidance for stablecoins and digital payments, while American Express publicly describes an enterprise readiness program.

Q: What is the approximate size increase when replacing RSA-2048 DDA signatures with ML-DSA-65 on EMV cards?
  A) 2x larger (512 bytes)
  B) 5x larger (1280 bytes)
  C) 13x larger (3309 bytes)
  D) 100x larger
Answer: C
Explanation: ML-DSA-65 signatures are 3,309 bytes compared to RSA-2048 signatures at 256 bytes — approximately 13x larger. Combined with larger public keys (1,952 bytes vs 256 bytes for RSA-2048), this creates significant storage and bandwidth challenges for the constrained chip card environment, especially for contactless (NFC) transactions with limited communication windows (not sourced in the Library).

chunks.title: Quiz: emv-payment-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: emv-payment-pqc

Q: Which components of the payment ecosystem must be upgraded for PQC? (Select all that apply)
  A) Payment network root CA keys and certificates
  B) POS terminal firmware and certificate stores
  C) Card chip operating systems and key storage
  D) All of the above
Answer: A|B|C
Explanation: PQC migration for payments requires a coordinated upgrade across the entire ecosystem: network CAs must issue PQC certificates, terminals must verify PQC signatures and store larger certificates, and new card chips must support PQC key generation and signing. This makes payment PQC migration one of the most complex migration challenges due to the massive scale and hardware constraints.

Q: What is the impact of larger PQC signatures on contactless (NFC) payment transactions?
  A) No impact — NFC bandwidth is unlimited
  B) Larger signatures may exceed the contactless transaction time budget (typically 500ms), potentially causing timeouts
  C) NFC transactions do not use signatures
  D) PQC signatures are faster over NFC
Answer: B
Explanation: Contactless (tap) payments have strict time budgets (~500ms total) dictated by the ISO 14443 protocol. Transferring 3,309-byte ML-DSA signatures plus larger certificates over the relatively slow NFC interface (106-848 kbit/s) may exceed this budget, causing transaction failures. This is a key constraint driving research into smaller PQC signature schemes for payments.

chunks.title: Quiz: emv-payment-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: emv-payment-pqc

Q: What is 3D Secure and why does it need PQC migration?
  A) A 3D printing security protocol
  B) An e-commerce authentication protocol that uses RSA/ECDSA for server authentication and message signing between merchants, issuers, and card networks
  C) A physical card security feature
  D) A contactless payment standard
Answer: B
Explanation: 3D Secure (3DS) authenticates online card-not-present transactions through a challenge flow between the cardholder, merchant, and issuer. It uses TLS (RSA/ECDH) for channel security and digital signatures for inter-party message authentication. Both the TLS layer and the signing mechanisms must migrate to PQC algorithms.

Q: What approach might EMVCo take to address PQC signature size constraints on chip cards?
  A) Abandon chip card authentication entirely
  B) Explore hash-based signatures, algorithm compression techniques, or split authentication across online and offline paths
  C) Require all transactions to be online only
  D) Use quantum key distribution for each transaction
Answer: B
Explanation: EMVCo and payment networks are exploring multiple approaches: using smaller PQC signature schemes (if standardized), compressing certificate chains, moving more authentication online (where bandwidth is not as constrained), and potentially splitting authentication between offline (card-present) and online (network verification) paths to reduce on-card storage requirements.

chunks.title: Quiz: emv-payment-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: emv-payment-pqc

Q: True or False: The symmetric key derivation used in EMV for session keys (e.g., AES-based) is already quantum-safe and does not need migration.
Answer: TRUE
Explanation: True. Symmetric key derivation (AES, 3DES-based) used for EMV session keys and transaction authorization codes is resistant to quantum attack. Grover's algorithm only halves the effective key length (AES-256 → ~128-bit security), which remains secure. The quantum vulnerability is in the public-key operations (RSA-based DDA/CDA and key exchange).

Q: In this module's estimate, what is the timeline for full PQC migration across the global payment card ecosystem?
  A) 1-2 years
  B) 3-5 years
  C) 8-12+ years
  D) It will never be completed
Answer: C
Explanation: In this module's estimate, full PQC migration for payments takes 8-12+ years, driven by an assumed 3-5 year card replacement cycle across 14.7 billion EMV cards (EMVCo, end of 2024), terminal upgrade logistics, coordinated CA hierarchy migration across multiple payment networks, and the need for backward compatibility during the transition period. Early planning and hybrid approaches are essential.

chunks.title: Quiz: emv-payment-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: emv-payment-pqc

Q: In banking key management, what makes a "key block" more than just an encrypted key?
  A) It uses a longer key than standard encryption
  B) It binds the key to its permitted usage, so a key issued for one purpose cannot be repurposed
  C) It stores the key in a hardware security module
  D) It rotates the key automatically on a fixed schedule
Answer: B
Explanation: A key block wraps a key together with its usage attributes. The attribute binding is the security property, not the encryption alone: every cryptographic operation outside the declared usage fails. EPC 342-08 notes this only works if all parties use compatible control vectors with certified TRSMs enforcing the policy.

Q: Which standard is the current specification for payment key blocks?
  A) ANSI X9 TR-31
  B) ANSI X9.143
  C) ISO 8583
  D) PCI DSS v4.0.1
Answer: B
Explanation: ANSI X9.143 is the live specification; EPC 342-08 v16.0.1 cites it for key wrapping using AES and Triple DES, and X9.143 is formally the successor to TR-31. Material still teaching TR-31 as current is out of date — a common error because TR-31 is far more frequently cited.

chunks.title: Quiz: emv-payment-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: emv-payment-pqc

Q: Why can no single institution migrate a correspondent banking chain to PQC on its own?
  A) Regulators forbid unilateral cryptographic changes
  B) A payment traverses several institutions, each retaining its own records, so security is set by the weakest hop
  C) Correspondent banking uses only symmetric cryptography
  D) The messaging format cannot carry post-quantum signatures
Answer: B
Explanation: A cross-border payment crosses several institutions and each retains its own records independently, so harvest-now-decrypt-later exposure multiplies along the chain and the weakest hop sets the security of the whole path. This coordination problem is why the sector publishes jointly (BIS, G7 CEG, FS-ISAC) rather than per-bank.

Q: What drives harvest-now-decrypt-later exposure on interbank settlement rails?
  A) The number of transactions processed per second
  B) How long the data stays sensitive, rather than a predicted date for a quantum computer
  C) Whether the rail uses ISO 20022 or legacy FIN messages
  D) The physical distance between correspondent banks
Answer: B
Explanation: HNDL exposure is a function of data retention, not of a guessed CRQC year. Swift instruction metadata stays commercially sensitive for years and sanctions/AML records far longer, so traffic captured today remains worth decrypting later. The module’s Settlement Exposure Modeller is built on retention for exactly this reason.

chunks.title: Quiz: emv-payment-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: emv-payment-pqc

Q: Does the financial sector have a dated post-quantum algorithm mandate comparable to CNSA 2.0?
  A) Yes — PCI DSS v5.0 sets binding PQC deadlines
  B) Yes — DORA mandates ML-KEM by 2027
  C) No — sector pressure comes from operational-resilience regulation and HNDL exposure instead
  D) No — the sector is exempt from post-quantum requirements
Answer: C
Explanation: Unlike Government & Defense, no financial-sector body has issued a dated algorithm mandate of the CNSA 2.0 kind. DORA imposes operational-resilience obligations rather than naming algorithms, and PCI DSS v4.0.1 is current with no v5.0. The pressure is real but comes from resilience regulation and harvest-now-decrypt-later exposure.

Q: Why is e-commerce (card-not-present) TLS considered the fastest PQC migration path in the payments estate?
  A) Card-not-present transactions do not use cryptography
  B) Hybrid ML-KEM TLS 1.3 is already supported by major CDN providers and browsers, needing no hardware change
  C) E-commerce payments are exempt from PCI DSS
  D) Merchants can disable encryption for low-value transactions
Answer: B
Explanation: E-commerce protection is transport-layer, and hybrid ML-KEM key establishment is already deployable in TLS 1.3 across major CDN and browser stacks. Nothing physical has to be reissued — unlike cards, which turn over on a 3-5 year cycle, or terminals, which run 7-12 years.

chunks.title: Quiz: emv-payment-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: emv-payment-pqc

Q: What is the quantum exposure in 3-D Secure 2.x cardholder authentication?
  A) The per-transaction cryptogram, which uses AES
  B) ECDSA challenge signing and device binding, which a quantum computer could forge
  C) The merchant’s inventory database
  D) Nothing — 3-D Secure is already post-quantum
Answer: B
Explanation: 3-D Secure 2.x (Visa Secure, Mastercard Identity Check) uses ECDSA to sign the cardholder challenge and bind the device. Shor’s algorithm breaks ECDSA, so forged 3DS authentication would enable unauthorised card-not-present transactions. Migration needs an EMVCo 3DS specification update, so it lags the pure-TLS work.

Q: What does PSD2 Article 97 require for online account access and remote payment initiation?
  A) A single password is sufficient if it is long enough
  B) Strong customer authentication using at least two of three elements — knowledge, possession, inherence — with the code dynamically linked to the payment's exact amount and payee
  C) Biometric authentication only, with no other factor permitted
  D) Authentication is only required for payments above EUR 500
Answer: B
Explanation: Article 97 requires two-factor strong customer authentication (at least two of knowledge/possession/inherence) for online account access, remote payment initiation, and any action carrying fraud risk. For remote payments specifically, the authentication code must be dynamically linked to the exact transaction amount and payee — a static one-time code is not sufficient.

chunks.title: Quiz: emv-payment-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: emv-payment-pqc

Q: What legal instrument creates the EU's open banking APIs — the interfaces fintechs use to access a customer's bank account?
  A) A voluntary industry standard banks may choose to adopt
  B) PSD2's implementing RTS (Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2018/389), Article 30's "dedicated interface" obligation
  C) A private contract between each bank and each fintech
  D) An ISO standard with no legal force
Answer: B
Explanation: Article 30 of the RTS requires every EU bank offering online-accessible accounts to expose a dedicated interface that account information and payment initiation service providers can use to identify themselves, request data, and initiate payments. This is a binding legal obligation, not a voluntary program — it is the actual legal basis for EU open banking.

Q: What does the RTS on SCA (Art. 35) require for encrypting the dedicated-interface communication channel — and what does this mean for PQC migration?
  A) It mandates TLS 1.2 with AES-128, which must be formally amended before any upgrade
  B) It requires "strong and widely recognised encryption techniques" without naming an algorithm or TLS version — technology-neutral wording that needs no legislative change to move to hybrid ML-KEM
  C) It does not address channel encryption at all
  D) It mandates a proprietary EU-developed cipher suite
Answer: B
Explanation: Article 35 requires "strong and widely recognised encryption techniques" for data exchanged over the internet, and Article 34 separately requires eIDAS qualified certificates (QWAC or QSealC) for AISP/PISP identification — but neither article names a specific algorithm or TLS version. Because the wording is technology-neutral, migrating a dedicated interface to hybrid ML-KEM TLS is an implementation change, not a legislative one.

chunks.title: Quiz: mls-group-messaging
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: mls-group-messaging

Q: Which IETF RFC defines Messaging Layer Security (MLS)?
  A) RFC 8446
  B) RFC 9420
  C) RFC 9180
  D) RFC 8032
Answer: B
Explanation: MLS is defined in RFC 9420 (July 2023). RFC 8446 is TLS 1.3, RFC 9180 is HPKE (used inside MLS), and RFC 8032 is EdDSA.

Q: MLS arranges group members as leaves of a binary tree. What is the asymptotic cost of a key update in a group of N members?
  A) O(1)
  B) O(log N)
  C) O(N)
  D) O(N²)
Answer: B
Explanation: MLS uses TreeKEM: each leaf is a member, and only the nodes on the path from that leaf to the root need updating. That makes Add / Remove / Update operations O(log N). RFC 9420 contrasts this with distributing sender keys over 1:1 channels, which needs a number of key update messages that scales as the square of the group size to achieve post-compromise security.

Q: Which IETF draft defines the post-quantum ciphersuites for MLS?
  A) draft-ietf-jose-pqc-kem
  B) draft-ietf-mls-pq-ciphersuites
  C) draft-ietf-tls-hybrid-design
  D) draft-ietf-lamps-pq-composite-sigs
Answer: B
Explanation: draft-ietf-mls-pq-ciphersuites-06 registers MLS cipher suites using ML-KEM, either on its own or alongside traditional elliptic curve KEMs. The other drafts cover JOSE/JWS, TLS hybrid key exchange, and X.509 composite signatures respectively.

Q: Which production messaging services have publicly shipped MLS?
  A) Signal and Telegram
  B) WhatsApp and Cisco Webex
  C) Slack and Discord
  D) Microsoft Teams and Zoom
Answer: B
Explanation: WhatsApp, Cisco Webex, AWS Wickr, and Google Messages have publicly adopted MLS. Signal still uses its Double Ratchet (which is pairwise rather than group-native).

chunks.title: Quiz: mls-group-messaging
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: mls-group-messaging

Q: MLS uses Hybrid Public Key Encryption (HPKE) to encrypt path-update messages between members.
Answer: TRUE
Explanation: True. RFC 9420 specifies HPKE (RFC 9180) as the encryption primitive for path updates inside TreeKEM.

Q: Which property ensures that a member who leaves or rotates keys can no longer decrypt subsequent group messages?
  A) Forward secrecy
  B) Post-compromise security
  C) Deniable authentication
  D) Algorithm agility
Answer: B
Explanation: Post-compromise security (PCS) is achieved via TreeKEM ratcheting: once the leaving member's leaf is removed and the path is re-keyed, prior secret state cannot recover future messages. Forward secrecy protects past messages from a future compromise.

Q: How does the OpenMLS HSM provider keep MLS signature keys non-exportable from the HSM?
  A) CKA_SIGN=TRUE
  B) CKA_PRIVATE=TRUE
  C) CKA_SENSITIVE=TRUE and CKA_EXTRACTABLE=FALSE
  D) CKA_DECRYPT=TRUE
Answer: C
Explanation: Signature keys are generated as PKCS#11 token objects with CKA_SENSITIVE=TRUE and CKA_EXTRACTABLE=FALSE. What OpenMLS persists as the private key is an opaque HsmKeyHandle (PQTH magic + CKA_ID), never raw bytes.

Q: What problem does TreeKEM solve that pairwise ratcheting (e.g. Signal's Double Ratchet) does not handle well?
  A) End-to-end encryption
  B) Efficient key updates in large groups
  C) Forward secrecy
  D) Authentication of senders
Answer: B
Explanation: Pairwise ratcheting requires O(N) work per group key update because each member pair maintains an independent ratchet. TreeKEM reduces this to O(log N), making large encrypted groups practical.

chunks.title: Quiz: pqc-candidates
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: pqc-candidates

Q: When did NIST select HQC as an additional KEM standard alongside ML-KEM?
  A) August 2024
  B) March 2025
  C) October 2024
  D) January 2026
Answer: B
Explanation: NIST selected HQC as an additional KEM in March 2025 to provide a code-based alternative to lattice-based ML-KEM. ML-KEM/ML-DSA/SLH-DSA were finalised in August 2024 (FIPS 203/204/205).

Q: Which NIST Internal Report documents the first round of the PQC additional-signature (on-ramp) process?
  A) NIST IR 8413
  B) NIST IR 8528
  C) NIST IR 8547
  D) NIST IR 8545
Answer: B
Explanation: NIST IR 8528 (October 2024) is the Status Report on the First Round of the Additional Digital Signature Schemes, recording the candidates advancing to the second round. NIST IR 8413 is the third-round PQC status report (2022); IR 8547 is the deprecation timeline; IR 8545 is the HQC selection (2025).

Q: Which of these is a multivariate signature candidate in the PQC on-ramp?
  A) FAEST
  B) HAWK
  C) MAYO
  D) SQIsign
Answer: C
Explanation: MAYO is a multivariate signature scheme. FAEST is MPC-in-the-Head (AES-based), HAWK is lattice-based (integer Falcon variant; withdrawn from the NIST process in July 2026), and SQIsign is isogeny-based.

Q: Which PQC candidate scheme has the smallest combined public key + signature size?
  A) HAWK
  B) SQIsign
  C) MAYO
  D) FAEST
Answer: B
Explanation: SQIsign produces ~148-byte signatures at NIST Cat 1 — the smallest combined pk+sig of any PQC candidate. Trade-off: constant-time signing remains an open implementation challenge.

chunks.title: Quiz: pqc-candidates
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: pqc-candidates

Q: Which 2025 cryptanalytic result affected multiple UOV and MAYO parameter sets?
  A) Castryck–Decru attack
  B) Ran wedge attack
  C) Lattice basis reduction
  D) Shor's algorithm
Answer: B
Explanation: The 2025 Ran wedge attack pushed 3 of 4 UOV parameter sets below their security target and hit MAYO-2 by ~30 bits. Reparameterisation to odd-characteristic fields restores security. Castryck–Decru broke SIKE in 2022.

Q: Which Korean PQC standardization competition selected SMAUG-T and HAETAE among its winners?
  A) CRYPTREC
  B) CACR
  C) KpqC
  D) KISA-PQC
Answer: C
Explanation: KpqC is South Korea's national PQC competition. It selected SMAUG-T, NTRU+, PALOMA, REDOG, Layered ROLLO-I (KEMs) and HAETAE, AIMer, SOLMAE (signatures). CRYPTREC is Japan; CACR is China.

Q: HAWK is a lattice-based signature scheme designed as an integer-only alternative to FN-DSA (Falcon).
Answer: TRUE
Explanation: True. HAWK is lattice-based but uses integer arithmetic to eliminate the floating-point side-channel hazards that complicate Falcon implementations. Its team withdrew it from NIST's additional signatures process on 29 July 2026, after a new key-recovery attack.

Q: What is the main motivation behind NIST's signature on-ramp standardization process?
  A) Replace ML-DSA because it has known weaknesses
  B) Provide algorithmic diversity beyond lattice-based signatures
  C) Reduce signature sizes below 100 bytes
  D) Standardize a single multivariate signature
Answer: B
Explanation: The on-ramp exists so the PQC signature portfolio is not entirely lattice-based. If a future cryptanalytic advance broke lattices, jurisdictions would still have hash-based, code-based, multivariate, MPC-in-the-Head, or isogeny-based alternatives ready.

chunks.title: Quiz: SLH-DSA
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: SLH-DSA

Q: Which NIST FIPS standard defines SLH-DSA?
  A) FIPS 203
  B) FIPS 204
  C) FIPS 205
  D) FIPS 186-5
Answer: C
Explanation: SLH-DSA is defined in FIPS 205 (Stateless Hash-Based Digital Signature Standard, August 2024). FIPS 203 is ML-KEM, FIPS 204 is ML-DSA, FIPS 186-5 is the classical DSS family.

Q: What was SLH-DSA formerly known as during the NIST PQC competition?
  A) CRYSTALS-Dilithium
  B) SPHINCS+
  C) Falcon
  D) Kyber
Answer: B
Explanation: SLH-DSA was standardized from SPHINCS+, a stateless hash-based signature scheme. Dilithium became ML-DSA, Falcon became FN-DSA, and Kyber became ML-KEM.

Q: SLH-DSA is a stateless hash-based signature scheme — the signer does not have to track which one-time keys have been used.
Answer: TRUE
Explanation: True. Statelessness is SLH-DSA's defining property. FIPS 205 section 3: a key pair is a very large set of few-time FORS keys. A signature computes a randomized hash of the message, uses part of the digest to pseudorandomly select one FORS key, and authenticates it with a hypertree signature, so there is no leaf counter to track as in LMS/XMSS. The security of a FORS key degrades gradually as the number of signatures increases (section 8), and the parameter sets are designed for at most 2^64 signatures per key (section 11).

Q: Which two component signature schemes are layered inside SLH-DSA?
  A) FORS and XMSS
  B) Merkle and Lamport
  C) OTS and HORS
  D) LMS and XMSS
Answer: A
Explanation: SLH-DSA builds a hypertree of XMSS trees whose leaves are WOTS+ keys, with FORS acting as the few-time signature layer that signs the message digest.

chunks.title: Quiz: SLH-DSA
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: SLH-DSA

Q: In SLH-DSA parameter set names like SLH-DSA-SHA2-128s and SLH-DSA-SHA2-128f what do the -s and -f suffixes mean?
  A) secure vs fast
  B) small (signature) vs fast (signing)
  C) single vs full
  D) standard vs final
Answer: B
Explanation: -s variants use fewer hypertree layers so signatures are smaller but signing is slower; -f variants use more layers for faster signing at the cost of larger signatures. Both are equally secure at their stated NIST level.

Q: Why is SLH-DSA considered a conservative PQC signature scheme?
  A) It uses the largest key sizes
  B) Its security relies on the presumed difficulty of finding preimages for hash functions and several related properties of those functions
  C) It was the first PQC algorithm standardized
  D) It is the only PQC signature scheme that is deterministic by default
Answer: B
Explanation: SLH-DSA's security relies on the presumed difficulty of finding preimages for the underlying hash functions (SHA-2 or SHAKE) and several related properties of them (FIPS 205, section 1.1). FIPS 205 says that even if it is feasible to compute collisions on those functions there is believed to be no adverse effect on the security of SLH-DSA (section 10.2), although applications that need message-bound signatures may still be affected.

Q: Approximately what is the smallest SLH-DSA signature size at NIST Level 1?
  A) 1312 bytes
  B) 7856 bytes
  C) 17088 bytes
  D) 49856 bytes
Answer: B
Explanation: SLH-DSA-SHA2-128s produces ~7,856-byte signatures at NIST Level 1. The largest set (SLH-DSA-SHAKE-256f) reaches ~49,856 bytes. Compare to roughly 2.4-4.6 KB for ML-DSA (2,420 B for ML-DSA-44, 3,309 B for ML-DSA-65, 4,627 B for ML-DSA-87).

chunks.title: Quiz: SLH-DSA
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: SLH-DSA

Q: What does NSA CNSA 2.0 say about SLH-DSA versus LMS/XMSS for firmware and software signing?
  A) SLH-DSA is mandated and LMS/XMSS deprecated
  B) LMS and XMSS are approved for firmware and software signing; SLH-DSA is not approved for any use in national security systems
  C) All three are forbidden
  D) Only ML-DSA is approved for firmware signing
Answer: B
Explanation: NSA's CNSA 2.0 FAQ (version 2.2, October 2026) allows the NIST SP 800-208 stateful hash-based signatures LMS and XMSS for signing firmware and software ("any choice of XMSS or LMS satisfies CNSA 2.0 requirements"; LMS with SHA-256/192 is preferred), but not HSS or XMSS^MT. On SLH-DSA it says: "While SLH-DSA is hash-based, it is not part of CNSA and is not approved for any use in NSS." Validated ML-DSA (ML-DSA-87) is also approved for all signing use cases and may be the most appropriate choice where state tracking is impractical, for example distributed signing, so in national security systems the stateless option is ML-DSA, not SLH-DSA.

chunks.title: Quiz: crypto-mgmt-modernization
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: crypto-mgmt-modernization

Q: By what date does CA/B Forum Ballot SC-081v3 reduce TLS certificate maximum validity to 47 days?
  A) March 2027
  B) March 2028
  C) March 2029
  D) March 2030
Answer: C
Explanation: The CA/B Forum SC-081v3 ballot (April 2025) phases certificate maximum validity from 398d → 47d in March 2029.

Q: How does Crypto Management Modernization (CMM) differ from crypto-agility?
  A) CMM is technical; crypto-agility is a program
  B) CMM is a continuous management program; crypto-agility is the technical capability to swap algorithms
  C) They are synonyms
  D) CMM is short-term; crypto-agility is long-term
Answer: B
Explanation: CMM (or Cryptographic Posture Management) is the management discipline — inventory, governance, lifecycle, observability, assurance. Crypto-agility is the technical capability to actually swap an algorithm. Both are needed, but they answer different questions.

Q: What are the five pillars of Cryptographic Posture Management (CPM)?
  A) Plan, Do, Check, Act, Review
  B) Inventory, Governance, Lifecycle, Observability, Assurance
  C) Discover, Detect, Defend, Deter, Document
  D) Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover
Answer: B
Explanation: CPM's five pillars are Inventory (unified CBOM), Governance (policy + ownership), Lifecycle (CLM automation), Observability (posture metrics), and Assurance (FIPS / CMVP tracking). The PDCA loop wraps strategic execution; NIST CSF describes a different scope.

chunks.title: Quiz: crypto-mgmt-modernization
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: crypto-mgmt-modernization

Q: Which six operational stages make up the continuous CPM loop?
  A) Discover → Classify → Score → Remediate → Attest → Reassess
  B) Plan → Do → Check → Act → Review → Restart
  C) Inventory → Validate → Sign → Verify → Deploy → Monitor
  D) Detect → Analyze → Contain → Eradicate → Recover → Improve
Answer: A
Explanation: The operational continuous loop is Discover → Classify → Score → Remediate → Attest → Reassess. PDCA wraps it at the strategic annual layer. The other options describe NIST CSF or generic IR playbooks.

Q: In this module's cost model, roughly what average cost per certificate-outage event is assumed?
  A) ~1M USD
  B) ~5M USD
  C) ~11M USD
  D) ~50M USD
Answer: C
Explanation: This module's cost model assumes about 11M USD per certificate-outage event and an 86% annual incidence. Both are illustrative assumptions of this module, not figures from a held study. They drive the outage-avoidance stream of the CLM-automation ROI case.

Q: FIPS 140-3 CMVP certificates are bound to specific versions firmware and platforms — meaning a routine library update can invalidate the certificate.
Answer: TRUE
Explanation: True. Every CMVP certificate is version- and platform-specific. The FIPS 140-3 Implementation Guidance added self-test requirements for ML-KEM / ML-DSA / SLH-DSA in August 2024 and, in September 2025, let their key-generation tests check against the private key only. CMVP Modules-in-Process queue runs 18–24 months, so this is a monthly monitor, not an annual audit.

chunks.title: Quiz: crypto-mgmt-modernization
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: crypto-mgmt-modernization

Q: Which of these is NOT one of the four asset classes tracked by Cryptographic Posture Management?
  A) Certificates
  B) Cryptographic libraries
  C) Network firewalls
  D) Key material
Answer: C
Explanation: The four CPM asset classes are: certificates, cryptographic libraries (OpenSSL, BoringSSL, Bouncy Castle, liboqs, …), application software that uses crypto, and key material in HSMs / KMS. Network firewalls are an adjacent control but not a CPM asset class.

Q: What is the relationship between SBOM and CBOM?
  A) They are interchangeable
  B) CBOM is a crypto-focused view derived from or layered on top of SBOM
  C) SBOM replaces CBOM
  D) They cover entirely different domains
Answer: B
Explanation: CBOM (OWASP CycloneDX Cryptography BOM) is a crypto-specific extension to SBOM. The same dependency tree feeds both — SBOM lists components, CBOM enriches them with algorithm, key, certificate, and protocol facts so a posture-management program can score crypto risk.

chunks.title: Quiz: sbom
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: sbom

Q: What question does an SBOM answer?
  A) What cryptography is inside this build
  B) What is in this build
  C) Which CVEs are exploitable in production
  D) Which vendor supports this component
Answer: B
Explanation: An SBOM is a machine-readable inventory of every software component a build depends on. It answers "what is in this build?" — not "what cryptography is inside it?", which is the CBOM's job.

Q: An SBOM tells you what cryptographic algorithms and keys a component uses.
Answer: FALSE
Explanation: False. An SBOM answers "what is in this build" (packages, versions, suppliers, dependencies) — the cryptographic-asset question is answered by the CBOM, a separate, sibling discipline.

Q: Which standards body/process standardized SPDX, and as what?
  A) OWASP, as ECMA-424
  B) Linux Foundation, as ISO/IEC 5962:2021
  C) OASIS, as CSAF 2.0
  D) NIST, as SP 800-161
Answer: B
Explanation: SPDX grew out of the Linux Foundation's license-compliance tooling and was standardized as ISO/IEC 5962:2021. CycloneDX, by contrast, is OWASP's format, standardized as ECMA-424.

Q: Which of the two general-purpose BOM formats has the deeper license/provenance model, and why?
  A) CycloneDX, because it grew out of application-security tooling
  B) SPDX, because it grew out of license-compliance tooling
  C) Both are identical in their license model
  D) Neither format models license or provenance data
Answer: B
Explanation: SPDX grew out of license-compliance tooling and has the deeper license/provenance model. CycloneDX grew out of application-security tooling and has the more extensible object model, with sibling BOM types like SaaSBOM, HBOM, ML-BOM, and VDR/VEX.

chunks.title: Quiz: sbom
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: sbom

Q: Which of these are among NTIA's seven "Minimum Elements" required fields for an SBOM component? (select all that apply)
  A) Supplier Name
  B) Version
  C) Component Hash
  D) Timestamp
Answer: A|B|D
Explanation: NTIA's 2021 Minimum Elements defines seven required fields: Supplier Name, Component Name, Version, Other Unique Identifiers, Dependency Relationship, Author of SBOM Data, and Timestamp. Component Hash is one of four additions proposed in a 2025 CISA successor draft, which remained a pre-decisional public-comment draft — not part of the final baseline.

Q: CISA's 2026 Minimum Elements for a Software Bill of Materials, published on 29 July 2026, marks SBOM Generation Context, SBOM Tool Name, Component Hash Value, Component Hash Algorithm and Component License as new elements.
Answer: TRUE
Explanation: True. The 2026 Minimum Elements for a Software Bill of Materials (published 29 July 2026 by CISA with international partners) "updates and replaces" the NTIA Minimum Elements, and its element list marks SBOM Generation Context, SBOM Tool Name, Component Hash Value, Component Hash Algorithm and Component License as "(New)".

chunks.title: Quiz: sbom
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: sbom

Q: What does VEX stand for, and what problem does it solve?
  A) Vulnerability Exploitability eXchange — whether a listed component's known vulnerability is actually reachable in this product
  B) Vendor Exchange eXtension — mapping suppliers to component licenses
  C) Verified Encryption eXtension — confirming a component's crypto is FIPS-validated
  D) Version Exchange indeX — tracking component version history
Answer: A
Explanation: VEX (Vulnerability Exploitability eXchange) is Profile 5 of OASIS CSAF 2.0. An SBOM lists what is present; VEX closes the gap by stating, per CVE per product, whether that vulnerability is affected/not-affected/fixed/under-investigation.

Q: VEX is defined as which profile of which OASIS standard?
  A) Profile 2 of OASIS PKCS#11
  B) Profile 5 of OASIS CSAF 2.0
  C) Profile 1 of OASIS KMIP
  D) Profile 3 of OASIS SAML
Answer: B
Explanation: VEX is defined as Profile 5 of OASIS CSAF 2.0 (Common Security Advisory Framework).

Q: What does VEX turn a raw CVE-in-my-SBOM alert into?
  A) A compliance violation
  B) A triage decision
  C) A license dispute
  D) A cryptographic risk score
Answer: B
Explanation: VEX turns a raw CVE-in-my-SBOM alert into a triage decision instead of a fire drill, by stating per CVE per product whether the vulnerability is actually exploitable.

Q: Which US Executive Order requires software vendors selling to the federal government to provide an SBOM, and produced the NTIA minimum-elements work?
  A) Executive Order 14028 (May 2021)
  B) Executive Order 14144
  C) Executive Order 14306
  D) Executive Order 14412
Answer: A
Explanation: Executive Order 14028 (May 2021) requires software vendors selling to the US federal government to provide an SBOM, which is what produced NTIA's 2021 minimum-elements work.

chunks.title: Quiz: sbom
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: sbom

Q: When do the EU Cyber Resilience Act's main SBOM obligations (Regulation EU 2024/2847) begin to apply?
  A) 1 January 2026
  B) 11 December 2027
  C) 31 December 2030
  D) They already apply as of this module's review
Answer: B
Explanation: The EU Cyber Resilience Act (Regulation EU 2024/2847) requires manufacturers of products with digital elements to maintain an SBOM covering top-level dependencies, with the main obligations applying from 11 December 2027.

Q: Both Executive Order 14028 and the EU Cyber Resilience Act SBOM requirements are PQC-specific mandates.
Answer: FALSE
Explanation: False. Neither mandate is PQC-specific — both EO 14028 and the EU CRA require SBOM coverage for general software supply-chain transparency, independent of cryptographic migration.

Q: How should an SBOM be treated relative to a CBOM discovery effort?
  A) As a Phase 2 output that a CBOM produces
  B) As a competing, mutually exclusive inventory format
  C) As Phase 1 input — an existing data source to cross-reference, not rebuild from scratch
  D) As irrelevant to cryptographic discovery
Answer: C
Explanation: An SBOM is Phase 1 input, not a Phase 2 output: it is one of the existing data sources a discovery effort should integrate. Cross-referencing SBOM data against a certificate management system, a crypto scanner, and manual investigation is how a CBOM gets built.

Q: What is the named common failure in PQC migration programs regarding SBOMs?
  A) Using SPDX instead of CycloneDX
  B) Ignoring the SBOM-CBOM linkage
  C) Filing SBOMs with the wrong regulator
  D) Omitting the Timestamp field
Answer: B
Explanation: Skipping the cross-reference between SBOM data and cryptographic discovery is a named common failure: "ignoring the SBOM-CBOM linkage."

chunks.title: Quiz: sbom
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: sbom

Q: If your question is "what does this vendor call ML-KEM in their KMIP inventory versus their TLS stack," which module should you consult instead of the SBOM module?
  A) The CBOM module
  B) The CycloneDX Cryptography Registry module
  C) The VEX profile
  D) The NTIA minimum-elements guidance
Answer: B
Explanation: Cross-tool naming normalization for the same cryptographic mechanism (e.g. what an HSM, a cert, and a protocol each call ML-KEM) is the Cryptography Registry module's scope, not the SBOM module's.

Q: A federal vendor's SBOM (provided under EO 14028) lists a component with a CVE reported against it, but no VEX statement accompanies it. What evidence gap does this leave for a GRC reviewer?
  A) Whether the CVE is actually exploitable in this specific deployment
  B) Whether the component is open source
  C) The component's license terms
  D) Nothing — an SBOM alone is sufficient to close a CVE finding
Answer: A
Explanation: VEX turns a raw CVE-in-my-SBOM alert into an actual exploitability determination (sbom-009) — it exists precisely because an SBOM only lists presence, not exploitability. Without a VEX statement, the reviewer knows the vulnerable component is present but not whether the specific deployment is actually affected, which is the missing evidence a treatment decision needs.

Q: A vendor states: "Our SBOM proves we are quantum-ready." Is this a supported compliance claim?
Answer: FALSE
Explanation: False. Neither EO 14028 nor the EU CRA's SBOM mandates are PQC-specific (sbom-012) — an SBOM lists what components and dependencies are present, not whether their cryptography is quantum-safe. A GRC reviewer should treat this as an unsupported claim until it is backed by a CBOM or registry-mapped cryptographic inventory, not the SBOM alone.

chunks.title: Quiz: cbom
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: cbom

Q: What is a Cryptography Bill of Materials (CBOM)?
  A) A list of software licenses
  B) A machine-readable inventory of cryptographic assets — algorithms, keys, certificates, protocols, and configurations — and their relation to software components
  C) A vendor risk scorecard
  D) A record of quantum computing hardware inventory
Answer: B
Explanation: A CBOM is a machine-readable inventory of every cryptographic asset — algorithms, keys, certificates, protocols and their configurations — and how they relate to software components.

Q: Where does the CBOM sit in the PQC migration lifecycle?
  A) Phase 1: discovery itself
  B) Phase 2: fed by discovery, consumed by risk scoring
  C) Phase 3: risk scoring
  D) It is outside the migration lifecycle entirely
Answer: B
Explanation: The CBOM extends the SBOM and sits as Phase 2 of the migration lifecycle: discovery (Phase 1) feeds it, risk scoring (Phase 3) consumes it.

Q: Why is CycloneDX the practical CBOM format today rather than SPDX?
  A) SPDX has no dedicated cryptography object model yet
  B) CycloneDX is the only ISO-standardized BOM format
  C) SPDX was deprecated in 2025
  D) CycloneDX is mandated by NIST IR 8547
Answer: A
Explanation: CycloneDX (OWASP; ECMA-424, current spec v1.7) is the practical CBOM format today because SPDX (Linux Foundation; ISO/IEC 5962) has no dedicated cryptography object model yet.

Q: The PKI Consortium CBOM-Profiles Working Group is building a neutral methodology mapping profiles onto both CycloneDX and SPDX.
Answer: TRUE
Explanation: True. The PKI Consortium CBOM-Profiles Working Group is building a neutral methodology that maps CBOM profiles onto both CycloneDX and SPDX.

chunks.title: Quiz: cbom
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: cbom
