Q: What is "ghost crypto"?
  A) Cryptography that has been formally deprecated
  B) Every cryptographic usage that is not in any inventory — shadow-IT, forgotten certificates, hardcoded algorithms, embedded/OT crypto, default library crypto
  C) A quantum-safe algorithm with no known implementation
  D) Encrypted data with no recoverable key
Answer: B
Explanation: Ghost crypto is every cryptographic usage that is not in any inventory: shadow-IT services, forgotten-but-live certificates, hardcoded algorithms, embedded/OT crypto, and default library crypto.

Q: Why must discovery layers (source, binary, network, infrastructure, cloud) be combined rather than relying on just one?
  A) Because regulators require five separate reports
  B) Because you cannot migrate what you cannot find, and ghost crypto hides across all of these layers
  C) Because each layer uses a different programming language
  D) Because CycloneDX requires five discovery passes by specification
Answer: B
Explanation: "You cannot migrate what you cannot find" — ghost crypto can hide in any layer, so source, binary, network, infrastructure, and cloud discovery must be combined for real coverage.

Q: By what year does the EU PQC Roadmap (June 2025) recommend that all Member States have implemented the First Steps, which include supporting mature cryptographic asset management?
  A) 2026
  B) 2028
  C) 2030
  D) 2035
Answer: A
Explanation: The roadmap's Milestone 1 is 31.12.2026: by then at least the First Steps, including supporting mature cryptographic asset management, are to be implemented by all Member States. It is a recommended timeline for Member States, not a requirement on organisations.

chunks.title: Quiz: cbom
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: cbom

Q: Which of the following are content-derived key identifiers that correlate across systems (as opposed to locally-assigned identifiers that don't)? (select all that apply)
  A) X.509 SKI/SPKI hash
  B) PKCS#11 CKA_ID
  C) JWK Thumbprint (RFC 7638)
  D) KMIP Unique Identifier
Answer: A|C
Explanation: Content-derived identifiers (X.509 SKI/SPKI hash, KMIP Digest, JWK Thumbprint, KCV) correlate across systems because they are computed from the key material itself. Assigned identifiers (PKCS#11 CKA_ID, KMIP Unique Identifier, KMS key-id, JWK kid) are local and don't correlate.

Q: What is described as the "join key" across systems for correlating the same cryptographic key?
  A) The KMS key-id
  B) The SPKI fingerprint
  C) The PKCS#11 CKA_ID
  D) The JWK kid
Answer: B
Explanation: The SPKI (SubjectPublicKeyInfo) fingerprint is content-derived and is described as the join key across systems, unlike locally-assigned identifiers such as CKA_ID or kid.

Q: What does key provenance attestation prove?
  A) That a key is quantum-safe
  B) That a key was generated in hardware and is non-exportable
  C) That a certificate chain is complete
  D) That a key has never been rotated
Answer: B
Explanation: Provenance attestation (HSM/TPM attestation, Android Key Attestation, FIDO2/WebAuthn) proves a key was generated in hardware and is non-exportable — recording whether a key is software-, HSM-, or cloud-KMS-managed drives risk and migration feasibility.

chunks.title: Quiz: cbom
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: cbom

Q: Why does PQC multiply the naming-normalization problem for a CBOM?
  A) PQC algorithms use fewer OIDs than classical algorithms
  B) PQC multiplies parameters per mechanism and proliferates OIDs — e.g. ML-DSA uses one OID per parameter set with parameters absent (RFC 9881)
  C) PQC algorithms cannot be represented in CycloneDX at all
  D) PQC removes the need for OID-based identification
Answer: B
Explanation: PQC multiplies parameters per mechanism and proliferates OIDs (ML-DSA uses one OID per parameter set with parameters absent, per RFC 9881); hybrid and composite ciphers add combination × nomenclature on top.

Q: Machine-verifiable CBOM policy-as-code classifies each asset as quantum-safe, quantum-vulnerable, n/a, or unknown.
Answer: TRUE
Explanation: True. Policy-as-code (e.g. CBOMkit OPA/Rego) classifies each cryptographic asset quantum-safe / quantum-vulnerable / na / unknown over a REST API, making the inventory machine-verifiable.

Q: Why must a CBOM itself be secured?
  A) Because it is publicly required to be disclosed
  B) Because it is a map of an organization's weakest cryptography
  C) Because CycloneDX requires encryption of all BOM files
  D) Because unsecured CBOMs violate the EU CRA
Answer: B
Explanation: A CBOM is a map of an organization's weakest cryptography — if it leaks, an attacker gets a prioritized target list. Securing the CBOM itself is treated as a first-class concern.

chunks.title: Quiz: cbom
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: cbom

Q: Which algorithms are used as CBOM examples in this module (both classical and post-quantum)?
  A) ML-KEM-768, ML-DSA-65, ECDSA P-256, Ed25519, RSA-2048
  B) SLH-DSA only
  C) AES-256 and SHA-384 only
  D) FN-DSA and HQC only
Answer: A
Explanation: The module's worked examples cover ML-KEM-768, ML-DSA-65, ECDSA P-256, Ed25519, and RSA-2048 — a mix of post-quantum and classical algorithms, as a CBOM must inventory both.

Q: Onto what canonical model should inconsistent cryptographic mechanism names be normalized, without over-collapsing security-relevant parameters?
  A) The OASIS CSAF 2.0 VEX profile
  B) The CycloneDX Cryptography Registry
  C) The NTIA minimum-elements list
  D) The NIST CSWP 48 control catalog
Answer: B
Explanation: The same mechanism is named differently across OID, PKCS#11, KMIP, IETF/IANA, JOSE/COSE, and libraries. Normalize onto a canonical model — the CycloneDX Cryptography Registry — without over-collapsing security-relevant parameters.

chunks.title: Quiz: cbom
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: cbom

Q: An organization presents a CBOM covering only its source-code repositories as proof of a "full cryptographic inventory." What should a GRC reviewer flag as missing?
  A) Ghost crypto in the layers a source-only scan cannot see: network, cloud, infrastructure and binary-only components
  B) Nothing — source code is where all cryptography originates
  C) The CBOM's file format
  D) The names of the engineers who ran the scan
Answer: A
Explanation: Ghost crypto is every cryptographic usage not in any inventory — shadow-IT, forgotten certificates, hardcoded algorithms, embedded/OT crypto, default library crypto (cbom-005) — and discovery layers (source, binary, network, infrastructure, cloud) must be combined rather than treated as substitutes for each other (cbom-006). A source-only CBOM cannot support a "full inventory" claim; the reviewer should treat the other layers as unverified.

Q: An organization tells a GRC reviewer it has followed the EU PQC Roadmap's recommended cryptographic-inventory First Step. What should the reviewer ask to see before accepting this, rather than a verbal assurance?
  A) A dated CBOM whose coverage matches the scope the organisation states
  B) A press release announcing the achievement
  C) The vendor's marketing website
  D) Nothing further is needed once the claim is made
Answer: A
Explanation: The EU PQC Roadmap (June 2025) recommends that Member States support the creation and maintenance of cryptographic inventories, with First Steps by 31.12.2026 (cbom-007). A verbal assurance is not evidence; a reviewer needs the actual, dated CBOM to confirm the inventory exists and covers the scope claimed.

chunks.title: Quiz: crypto-registry
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: crypto-registry

Q: In which CycloneDX version was the Cryptography Registry introduced?
  A) v1.5
  B) v1.6
  C) v1.7
  D) v2.0
Answer: C
Explanation: The CycloneDX Cryptography Registry was introduced in CycloneDX v1.7.

Q: What does the Cryptography Registry catalog?
  A) 96 cryptographic algorithm families and 246 elliptic curves
  B) Only NIST-standardized algorithms
  C) A list of vulnerable ciphers to avoid
  D) Certificate authorities and their root programs
Answer: A
Explanation: The registry is a standalone, versioned catalog of 96 cryptographic algorithm families and 246 elliptic curves.

Q: What single problem does the registry exist to solve?
  A) Slow key generation for PQC algorithms
  B) The same mechanism having a different name in every tool that touches it
  C) Insufficient entropy in random number generators
  D) Lack of FIPS 140-3 validated modules
Answer: B
Explanation: The registry solves the "one mechanism, many names" problem: the same algorithm or curve is named differently by an HSM, a certificate, a protocol, a library, and a CBOM.

Q: Algorithm families in the registry are grouped by primitive. Which of these are named primitive groupings? (select all that apply)
  A) Signature
  B) KEM/PKE
  C) AEAD
  D) License compliance
Answer: A|B|C
Explanation: Algorithm families are grouped by primitive: signature, KEM/PKE, key-agreement, block/stream cipher, AEAD, MAC, hash, XOF, KDF, key-wrap, and DRBG. License compliance is not a cryptographic primitive — that is SPDX's domain, not the registry's.

chunks.title: Quiz: crypto-registry
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: crypto-registry

Q: Into how many standardization categories are elliptic curves grouped in the registry?
  A) 5
  B) 10
  C) 15
  D) 246
Answer: C
Explanation: Elliptic curves are grouped into 15 standardization categories (NIST, SECG, Brainpool, ANSSI, BLS, GOST, X9.62/X9.63, and more) — 246 is the total curve count, not the category count (not sourced in the Library).

Q: What information does each elliptic curve entry in the registry carry?
  A) Only its bit strength
  B) Its OID, form (Weierstrass/Edwards/Montgomery), and cross-referenced aliases
  C) Only the vendor that first implemented it
  D) A CVE history for known attacks against it
Answer: B
Explanation: Each curve entry carries its OID, form (Weierstrass/Edwards/Montgomery), and cross-referenced aliases — enabling resolution across different tools' naming conventions.

Q: ML-KEM, ML-DSA, SLH-DSA, XMSS, and LMS are registered as first-class families alongside classical algorithms, not a separate list.
Answer: TRUE
Explanation: True. PQC families are registered as first-class entries alongside their classical counterparts — the registry does not treat PQC as an afterthought bolted onto a legacy list.

Q: What does registering PQC families as first-class entries give a PQC-readiness review?
  A) A discount on FIPS 140-3 validation
  B) One place to check whether a discovered mechanism is quantum-safe
  C) Automatic remediation of quantum-vulnerable code
  D) A guarantee that all PQC algorithms are interoperable
Answer: B
Explanation: Because PQC families are first-class registry entries, a PQC-readiness review gets exactly what it needs: one place to check whether a discovered mechanism is quantum-safe.

chunks.title: Quiz: crypto-registry
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: crypto-registry

Q: How is the registry published relative to the CycloneDX specification?
  A) It is bundled inside the CycloneDX spec and released only with it
  B) As its own versioned JSON + JSON Schema, decoupled from the CycloneDX release cycle
  C) It is not versioned at all
  D) It is published only as a PDF appendix
Answer: B
Explanation: The registry ships as its own versioned JSON + JSON Schema, decoupled from the CycloneDX specification release cycle, and is explicitly usable by tooling that has nothing to do with CBOM or CycloneDX.

Q: Which of the following could adopt the registry's canonical names, per the module's framing of its independence? (select all that apply)
  A) An SPDX-based scanner
  B) A homegrown inventory format
  C) A compliance dashboard
  D) Only CycloneDX-native tooling
Answer: A|B|C
Explanation: The registry is explicitly designed for use outside CBOM/CycloneDX tooling entirely — an SPDX-based scanner, a homegrown inventory format, or a compliance dashboard can all adopt the same names.

Q: What does the Algorithm Name Normalizer workshop step in this module practice?
  A) Generating new certificates
  B) Resolving different tools' names for the same mechanism to one canonical registry entry
  C) Rotating HSM firmware
  D) Building an SBOM from source code
Answer: B
Explanation: The Algorithm Name Normalizer workshop step exercises the registry's core purpose: taking different tool-specific names (e.g. an HSM mechanism string, a JOSE alg value) and resolving them to one canonical registry entry.

chunks.title: Quiz: crypto-registry
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: crypto-registry

Q: What does the Curve Identifier Lookup workshop step let you resolve?
  A) License compatibility between curve implementations
  B) An elliptic curve's cross-tool aliases and identifiers (e.g. OID, name) to its canonical registry entry
  C) The manufacturing date of an HSM
  D) Whether a curve is patented
Answer: B
Explanation: The Curve Identifier Lookup workshop step resolves an elliptic curve's various cross-tool aliases and identifiers to its single canonical registry entry, carrying OID, form, and standardization category.

Q: The Cryptography Registry module covers the full CBOM document model and layered crypto-discovery methodology.
Answer: FALSE
Explanation: False. That is explicitly out of scope for this module — the full CBOM document model and layered discovery methodology are covered by the CBOM module, which the registry module cross-links.

Q: Give an example of how the same mechanism might be named differently across tools, per this module.
  A) An HSM names it by PKCS#11 mechanism, a certificate by OID, a protocol by code point, a library by config string, and a JOSE/JWT service by its `alg` value
  B) It is always named identically across all tools because of ASN.1 standardization
  C) Only the algorithm's marketing name varies; technical names are always identical
  D) Naming only varies between programming languages, never between tool categories
Answer: A
Explanation: The module gives exactly this example: an HSM (PKCS#11 mechanism), a certificate (OID), a protocol (code point), a library (config string), and a JOSE/JWT service (`alg` value) can all name the same mechanism differently.

chunks.title: Quiz: crypto-registry
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: crypto-registry

Q: Which module publishes this Cryptography Registry?
  A) ISO/IEC JTC 1
  B) OWASP, as part of CycloneDX
  C) NIST
  D) The Linux Foundation
Answer: B
Explanation: The CycloneDX Cryptography Registry is published by OWASP as part of the CycloneDX project (standardized as ECMA-424).

Q: A vendor's SBOM lists "secp256r1" in one system and "prime256v1" in another for what is claimed to be the same elliptic curve. Before accepting these as the same control, what should a GRC reviewer confirm?
  A) That both names resolve to the same canonical entry in the crypto registry
  B) That the vendor uses the newer name in future releases
  C) That the mechanism appears in a CVE database under either name
  D) Nothing — differently named mechanisms are always distinct controls
Answer: A
Explanation: Differently-named entries in different tools are exactly the naming-inconsistency problem the crypto registry exists to solve (see creg-003). A GRC reviewer cannot treat two differently-labeled entries as the same control on trust alone — the registry's canonical entry for the curve (P-256, with secp256r1 and prime256v1 listed as aliases) is what lets a reviewer confirm they refer to the identical mechanism before recording it as one piece of evidence rather than two open items.

chunks.title: Quiz: crypto-registry
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: crypto-registry

Q: An auditor asks whether a vendor's cryptography is quantum-safe, and the vendor points to internal documentation that uses its own non-standard names for the algorithms in use. What should the GRC reviewer request before accepting this as evidence?
  A) A mapping of the vendor's internal names to the crypto registry's canonical PQC family entries
  B) A notarized copy of the internal documentation
  C) Nothing further — internal documentation is sufficient on its own
  D) A live demonstration of the algorithm running
Answer: A
Explanation: The registry gives a PQC-readiness review one place to check whether a discovered mechanism is quantum-safe (creg-008) — but only once a name is mapped to a registry entry. Non-standard internal naming with no mapping to the canonical registry is not itself evidence of quantum-safety; it is an open item until the mapping is made.

  C) Hiring a CISO and writing a press release

Explanation: The end of a PQC migration is two distinct jobs that are routinely neglected: decommissioning the classical cryptography on a defensible schedule, and closing the program into business-as-usual.

Q: A system is considered "migrated" as soon as a change ticket says PQC was deployed.
Answer: FALSE
Explanation: False. A system is "migrated" when its behaviour shows it — the handshake actually negotiates ML-KEM/ML-DSA — not when a change ticket says so. This is the evidence-by-observed-behaviour standard.

  A) Deprecated after 2030; disallowed after 2035
  B) Deprecated after 2028; disallowed after 2030
  C) Deprecated after 2033; disallowed after 2040
  D) Deprecated after 2025; disallowed after 2030
Answer: A
Explanation: The final report deprecates it after 2030 and disallows it under NIST standards and guidelines after 2035.

Answer: B
Explanation: Where the SOC detects and responds, GRC measures, reports, and governs — producing the instruments the board uses to oversee the program, the CISO uses to manage it, and internal audit uses to verify it.

Q: What are the three levels of the KRI cascade, and their reporting cadence?
  A) Board (quarterly), CISO (monthly), Operational (weekly/real-time)
  B) Board (annual), CISO (quarterly), Operational (monthly)
  C) Executive (daily), Manager (weekly), Staff (monthly)
  D) All three levels report at the same monthly cadence
Answer: A
Explanation: Key Risk Indicators cascade across three levels at different cadences: Board (quarterly), CISO (monthly), and Operational (weekly/real-time) — each serving a different audience.

Q: At what Regulatory Compliance Buffer threshold does this module say a board intervention is triggered?
  A) Less than 24 months
  B) Less than 18 months
  C) Less than 6 months (red)
  D) Less than 1 month
Answer: C
Explanation: The Regulatory Compliance Buffer board KRI: less than 12 months triggers amber, and less than 6 months triggers red plus board intervention.

Q: What must a HNDL Residual Exposure board KRI do, per this module?
  A) Stay constant year over year
  B) Decrease each quarter
  C) Increase in proportion to data volume
  D) Reset to zero annually
Answer: B
Explanation: HNDL Residual Exposure is a board-level KRI that must decrease each quarter.

chunks.title: Quiz: pqc-grc

  B) A single numeric risk score updated daily
  C) Only a legal disclaimer reviewed by counsel
  D) A vendor-supplied risk template with no organizational input
Answer: A
Explanation: The Risk Appetite Statement operates at two levels: a strategic board-language sentence (e.g. complete migration of >10-year-secrecy data before earliest credible CRQC, with a 12-month regulatory buffer) plus measurable operational tolerances across HNDL, TNFL, regulatory compliance, and crypto-agility dimensions.

  A) Confirmed
  B) Proposed
  C) Signaled
  D) Closed
Answer: B
Explanation: The Regulatory Horizon Report classifies developments as Confirmed (enacted; immediate SteerCo assessment), Proposed (in process; impact assessment within 30 days), or Signaled (guidance/speeches; monitoring entry).

Q: Which third-party vendor tier requires a CycloneDX 1.6+ CBOM and a product-security review?
  A) Tier 3 (no dependency)
  B) Tier 2 (cryptographic dependency)
  C) Tier 1 (migration-constraining — HSMs, CAs, cloud, payment processors, MSSPs)
  D) All vendors regardless of tier

Explanation: Tier 1 migration-constraining vendors (HSMs, CAs, cloud, payment processors, MSSPs) require a CycloneDX 1.6+ CBOM and a product-security review; Tier 2 requires a standard assessment; Tier 3 requires none.

chunks.title: Quiz: pqc-grc

  D) Board meeting minutes only

Explanation: GRC produces four outputs the SOC consumes: the risk appetite statement (defines alert escalation thresholds), the compliance tracker (monitoring priority), vendor assessments (third-party connection treatment), and the exception/deferral register as a dynamic suppression list.

Explanation: True. The exception/deferral register acts as a dynamic suppression list — without it, drift-detection rules drown in alerts from legitimately deferred legacy systems.

  B) Timestamped inventory, quarterly CBOM snapshots, SteerCo minutes, the board-approved appetite statement, Horizon Reports, vendor records, and the exception register
  C) Only the vendor contracts
  D) No formal artifacts are required beyond emails
Answer: B
Explanation: The auditable artifact set includes: inventory with timestamps, quarterly CBOM snapshots, SteerCo minutes, board-approved appetite statement, Horizon Reports, vendor records, and exception register — audited at under 6 months, 18-24 months, then annually.

  C) Insurance is unaffected by cryptographic posture
  D) Only government entities can be insured against quantum risk

Explanation: No insurer has published a quantum-specific exclusion the module could find, so cover turns on general cyber wording and state-backed attack exclusions (e.g. Lloyd's Y5381). The module advises asking the broker and keeping the program's documentation presentable to underwriters.

Q: What is the recommended approach to staffing a PQC migration, per this module?
  A) Hire a complete team of PQC specialists
  B) Build a small core of cryptographic expertise, upskill existing staff, and augment with external specialists where needed
  C) Outsource the entire migration to a single vendor
  D) Assign it entirely to the existing help desk team
Answer: B
Explanation: The realistic approach is not to hire a complete team of PQC specialists but to build a small core of cryptographic expertise, supplement it with upskilled existing security and IT staff, and augment with external specialists for capabilities that cannot be developed internally in time.

Q: What is the team-sizing heuristic taught in this module?
  A) One dedicated FTE per 500 cryptographic instances in the CBOM (dropping to 1 per 1,000 during production rollout)
  B) One FTE per employee in the organization
  C) A fixed team of 3 regardless of estate size
  D) One FTE per certificate authority only
Answer: A
Explanation: The sizing heuristic: one dedicated FTE per 500 cryptographic instances in the CBOM for the first two years, dropping to one per 1,000 during production rollout as tooling matures.

Q: Which are among the seven core roles this module names? (select all that apply)
  A) Quantum-Readiness Program Manager
  B) Cryptographic Architect
  C) OT Security Specialist
  D) Chief Marketing Officer
Answer: A|B|C
Explanation: The seven core roles are: Quantum-Readiness Program Manager, Cryptographic Architect, Security Engineers (PQC), Application Security Lead, OT Security Specialist, Vendor/Procurement Lead, and PMO Analyst. A Chief Marketing Officer is not among them.

chunks.title: Quiz: skills-team-structure

Explanation: Training operates at four levels: (1) Executive education, (2) PQC foundations (3-5 days), (3) Deep technical (ongoing, lab-based), and (4) the Crypto Champion Program.

chunks.title: Quiz: soc-implementation-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: soc-implementation-pqc

Q: What is the SOC's dual mandate during and after a PQC migration, per this module?
  A) Only detect attacks; migration monitoring is GRC's job
  B) During migration, verify hybrid implementations are not silently downgraded and systems don't drift back to classical-only; permanently after, maintain cryptographic posture and respond to future algorithm transitions
  C) Write the migration roadmap
  D) Approve the migration budget
Answer: B
Explanation: The SOC has a dual mandate: during migration it verifies hybrid implementations are not silently downgraded and migrated systems do not drift back to classical-only cryptography; permanently after migration it maintains cryptographic posture, detects drift, and responds to future algorithm transitions.

Q: What single prerequisite does every SOC detection capability in this module depend on?
  A) A dedicated quantum computer for testing
  B) A queryable, continuously updated cryptographic posture registry mapping each system to its expected cryptographic configuration
  C) A signed vendor SLA
  D) A fully quantum-resistant firewall
Answer: B
Explanation: Every detection capability depends on a queryable, continuously updated cryptographic posture registry — derived from the Phase 1/2 inventory and CBOM — that must be machine-readable and SIEM-integrated.

Q: What does Hybrid Downgrade Detection (Use Case 1) flag?
  A) Any use of AES-256
  B) Connections negotiating classical-only key shares (NamedGroups) when the registry expects hybrid
  C) Slow DNS resolution times
  D) Expired TLS certificates only
Answer: B
Explanation: Hybrid downgrade detection flags connections negotiating classical-only key shares when hybrid is expected — e.g. a TLS 1.3 session between two ML-KEM-capable systems that completes using only ECDH.

chunks.title: Quiz: soc-implementation-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: soc-implementation-pqc

Q: What is the most common false positive source for hybrid downgrade detection, per this module?
  A) An actual attacker performing a downgrade attack
  B) The organization's own middleboxes: oversized hybrid ClientHello messages fragmented or stripped by legacy firewalls/SSL inspection proxies
  C) DNS cache poisoning
  D) Expired root CA certificates
Answer: B
Explanation: The most common false positive is the organization's own middleboxes: oversized hybrid ClientHello messages are fragmented or stripped by legacy firewalls and SSL inspection proxies, forcing a benign fallback that looks identical to an attack.

Q: What distinguishes TNFL (Trust Now, Forge Later) from HNDL?
  A) TNFL enables present-tense exploitation once signatures can be forged; HNDL compromises past data once decryption becomes possible
  B) They are the same threat with different names
  C) TNFL only applies to symmetric encryption
  D) HNDL requires a quantum computer today; TNFL does not
Answer: A
Explanation: TNFL (Trust Now, Forge Later) enables present-tense exploitation once an adversary can forge signatures (forged software updates, fabricated financial instructions, impersonation) — unlike HNDL, which compromises past data.

Q: What is the target MTD-Signing (mean time to detect unauthorized signing) metric in this module?
  A) Under 15 minutes for production code signing
  B) Under 24 hours
  C) Under 1 week
  D) There is no target; it is monitored qualitatively only
Answer: A
Explanation: MTD-Signing targets under 15 minutes for production code signing, measured via red-team exercises.

chunks.title: Quiz: soc-implementation-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: soc-implementation-pqc

Q: Which are among the three CTI (Cyber Threat Intelligence) horizons this module defines? (select all that apply)
  A) Tactical (hours-days)
  B) Operational (weeks-months)
  C) Strategic (months-years)
  D) Retroactive (post-incident only)
Answer: A|B|C
Explanation: The three CTI horizons are Tactical (hours-days: CVE/side-channel triage), Operational (weeks-months: adversary collection-shift watch), and Strategic (months-years: CRQC hardware and national-program tracking). "Retroactive" is not one of the three.

Q: What must the SOC be careful NOT to mistake for an attack, per Playbook 4?
  A) A phishing campaign
  B) An authorized emergency algorithm rotation (mass revocations, cipher-suite changes, KMS spikes)
  C) A routine software update
  D) A scheduled vulnerability scan
Answer: B
Explanation: Playbook 4 (Emergency Algorithm Rotation) warns that the SOC must not mistake an authorized rotation for an attack, keeping the rotation-drill false-positive rate under 10%.

Q: How many named tabletop exercises does this module define, and how often should they run?
  A) Three, run once at project kickoff only
  B) Five, run at least annually
  C) Ten, run monthly
  D) One combined exercise, run biannually
Answer: B
Explanation: Five named tabletop exercises (The Friday Afternoon CVE, The Ambiguous Cryptanalysis Paper, Silent Downgrade, The CRQC Announcement, Signing Key Compromise) should run at least annually with the migration program office, CISO, GRC, and application owners.

chunks.title: Quiz: soc-implementation-pqc
chunks.content:

Q: What is the "protocol-parsing gap" described in this module's Skills & Tooling Gaps section?
  A) Most SIEMs/network tools cannot yet parse PQC cipher-suite identifiers, hybrid key-exchange groups, or PQC TLS extensions, requiring custom engineering per platform
  B) A shortage of network cabling for new hardware
  C) The inability to parse XML configuration files
  D) A licensing gap for commercial SIEM products
Answer: A
Explanation: The protocol-parsing gap: most SIEMs and network tools cannot yet parse PQC cipher-suite identifiers, hybrid key-exchange groups, or PQC TLS extensions — plan 2-4 weeks of custom Suricata/Zeek/SIEM engineering per platform plus ongoing maintenance.

Q: As of this module's review, a quantum-capable adversary campaign has been publicly attributed against PQC supply chains.
Answer: FALSE
Explanation: False. Operational-horizon CTI takes a watch-and-wait posture on adversary collection shifts toward PQC supply-chain probing, since no campaign has been publicly attributed as of mid-2026.

Q: Which RFC governs where hybrid key shares are negotiated by NamedGroup codepoints rather than X.509 OIDs?
  A) RFC 9420
  B) RFC 7638
  C) RFC 8446 (TLS 1.3)
  D) RFC 5280
Answer: C
Explanation: RFC 8446 (TLS 1.3) is where hybrid key shares are negotiated by IANA NamedGroup codepoints, not X.509 OIDs — which is why those codepoints must be added to traffic-analysis rules for downgrade detection.

  A) 14
