Q: Which public DNS resolver announced default ML-DSA-44 DNSSEC validation on 2026-09-10?
  A) Google Public DNS (8.8.8.8)
  B) Quad9 (9.9.9.9)
  C) Cloudflare (1.1.1.1)
  D) OpenDNS
Answer: C
Explanation: Cloudflare announced that 1.1.1.1 validates ML-DSA-44 (DNSSEC algorithm 18) by default. The announcement does not establish worldwide chronological priority.

Q: Roughly how much larger is an ML-DSA-44 DNSSEC signature than a classical ECDSA P-256 signature, and what does that force?
  A) ~2x larger; no practical effect
  B) ~10x larger; slower validation only
  C) ~38x larger (2,420 B vs 64 B); forces a TCP fallback
  D) ~100x larger; requires a new transport protocol
Answer: C
Explanation: ML-DSA-44 signatures are 2,420 bytes versus ECDSA P-256's 64 bytes, about 38x larger. That exceeds DNS's practical ~1,232-byte UDP response ceiling, forcing a fallback to TCP.

Q: True or False: Cloudflare's 2026-09-10 milestone means production DNS zones are now signed with a post-quantum algorithm.
Answer: FALSE
Explanation: False. Cloudflare's milestone is resolver-side validation of ML-DSA-44 against a dedicated test zone (dnstest.dev).

chunks.title: Quiz: dnssec-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: dnssec-pqc

Q: Per Cloudflare's own roadmap, what two features has it committed to next for PQ DNSSEC?
  A) Faster resolvers and bigger UDP buffers
  B) Authoritative-side signing support and registrar DS-record support
  C) A new DNS root and a new TLD system
  D) Browser support and OS-level DNS-over-HTTPS
Answer: B
Explanation: Cloudflare's stated next steps are authoritative-side signing support (so zones can actually be signed with ML-DSA, not just validated) and registrar DS-record support (so parent-zone delegation can carry algorithm-18 DS records). Full end-to-end PQ DNSSEC also needs the root and other registries to adopt it.

Q: Why is DNSSEC's post-quantum motivation about signature forgery risk rather than 'harvest now, decrypt later'?
  A) DNSSEC is signature-only with no confidentiality dimension, so there is no ciphertext to harvest — only a signature a future quantum computer could forge
  B) DNS traffic is already encrypted end-to-end, so harvesting is impossible
  C) DNSSEC keys rotate too frequently for harvest-now attacks to work
  D) Quantum computers cannot break signature schemes, only encryption schemes
Answer: A
Explanation: DNSSEC signs DNS answers for authenticity and integrity; it never encrypts them. With no ciphertext to capture and decrypt later, the quantum risk is that a future cryptographically relevant quantum computer could forge RSA/ECDSA signatures outright, the day it exists.

chunks.title: Quiz: fips-140-3-certification
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: fips-140-3-certification

Q: An HSM’s ML-KEM implementation passed ACVP testing and has a CAVP algorithm certificate. What does that establish about the HSM’s FIPS 140-3 status?
  A) The HSM is FIPS 140-3 validated, at the level its design targets
  B) Only that the implementation gives correct results for the tested functions and parameters — necessary evidence for a module validation, not the module certificate
  C) The HSM is FIPS 140-3 validated provisionally, until the CMVP finishes its review
  D) Nothing — algorithm validation plays no part in a FIPS 140-3 module validation
Answer: B
Explanation: CAVP algorithm validation (tested through ACVP) shows that an identified implementation computes the tested algorithm functions correctly. It is one input to a module validation: an accredited lab must still test the whole module against FIPS 140-3, and only the CMVP reviews that report and issues the module’s validation record. Each approved function on a FIPS 140-3 certificate carries its CAVP reference for exactly this reason (not sourced in the Library). Source: NIST CMVP FIPS 140-3 Management Manual v2.7 (9 April 2026).

chunks.title: Quiz: fips-140-3-certification
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: fips-140-3-certification

Q: A vendor datasheet says “FIPS 140-3 validation pending at Level 3” and points to the CMVP Modules in Process (MIP) list. What can a buyer conclude?
  A) The module will be validated at Level 3 once the CMVP review ends
  B) The lab has confirmed Level 3 and only the paperwork is outstanding
  C) Only that a submission sits in the CMVP queue at a stated state and date — the MIP list shows no level and does not imply that validation will follow
  D) The module may be bought as validated for new federal systems while it is on the list
Answer: C
Explanation: The MIP list is a queue: it shows module name, vendor, standard, state (for example Review or Comment Resolution) and date, with no level field. The Management Manual says posting on the list “does not imply or guarantee FIPS 140 validation”, so a level written into a MIP claim is the vendor’s label, not a CMVP result. Source: NIST CMVP FIPS 140-3 Management Manual v2.7 (as of 24 September 2026).

chunks.title: Quiz: fips-140-3-certification
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: fips-140-3-certification

Q: A FIPS 140-3 validated HSM’s new firmware adds ML-KEM and ML-DSA as approved algorithms, with new services and self-tests. Under the CMVP Management Manual v2.7, which submission route is the candidate?
  A) UPDT if the change stays under 30 % in each of the five change categories, otherwise a Full Submission (FS)
  B) ALG, because the change only adds algorithms
  C) CVE, because it closes a quantum vulnerability
  D) TRNS, because customers have a PQC deadline
Answer: A
Explanation: New approved algorithms, services and self-tests are security-relevant changes. UPDT (Manual §7.1.10) covers security-relevant changes under 30 %, assessed separately for functions/algorithms, SSPs, services, self-tests and FSM states; the lab justifies it and the CMVP may decide it is a Full Submission. ALG allows no code or configuration change, CVE changes “shall not introduce new features or cryptography”, and TRNS needs a published CMVP algorithm transition — not a market deadline. Source: NIST CMVP FIPS 140-3 Management Manual v2.7, §7.1 (as of 24 September 2026).

chunks.title: Quiz: fips-140-3-certification
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: fips-140-3-certification

Q: Which statements about CMVP revalidation routes are correct under the Management Manual v2.7? (Select all that apply.)
  A) TRNS is only for changes made solely to meet a published CMVP algorithm transition that would move modules to the Historical list
  B) ALG permits no code or configuration changes: it adds CAVP evidence for an algorithm already available in the approved mode
  C) A CVE submission may add new cryptography when the fix addresses a quantum threat
  D) A customer’s PQC deadline makes an algorithm addition eligible for TRNS
Answer: A|B
Explanation: Route eligibility follows the Manual, not the calendar. TRNS (§7.1.12) is for changes made solely to meet a published CMVP algorithm transition that would move modules to Historical; ALG (§7.1.6) says “code or configuration changes are not permitted”; CVE (§7.1.11) changes “shall not introduce new features or cryptography”. A market or policy deadline creates urgency, not eligibility. Source: NIST CMVP FIPS 140-3 Management Manual v2.7, §7.1 (as of 24 September 2026).

chunks.title: Quiz: fips-140-3-certification
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: fips-140-3-certification

Q: As of 24 September 2026, what is the status of FIPS 140-2 module validations?
  A) They remain Active until 2030 alongside FIPS 140-3
  B) They moved to the CMVP Historical list on 21/22 September 2026: supported for existing systems; Federal Agencies should not include them in new systems
  C) They were revoked because the modules failed re-testing
  D) They were converted automatically into FIPS 140-3 certificates
Answer: B
Explanation: Every FIPS 140-2 validation moved to the Historical list on 21/22 September 2026 (NIST’s pages give both dates). The CMVP transition page says it still supports buying and using Historical FIPS 140-2 modules for existing systems, and the CMVP Validated Modules page says Federal Agencies should not include them in new systems. The certificates did not fail — the scheme moved on, which is what a scheme transition looks like. Source: NIST CMVP FIPS 140-3 Transition Effort page (as of 24 September 2026); the Federal Agencies statement is from the CMVP Validated Modules page (read 27 October 2026).

chunks.title: Quiz: fips-140-3-certification
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: fips-140-3-certification

Q: As of 24 September 2026, what has Executive Order 14412 §6(b) done to FIPS 140-3 validation?
  A) It replaced FIPS 140-3 Level 3 with a new PQC security level
  B) It lets vendors self-certify PQC modules until the CMVP backlog clears
  C) It directs NIST to revise CMVP processes to accelerate validations within 180 days of 22 June 2026 (about 19 December 2026); that revision has not been issued, and FIPS 140-3 itself is unchanged
  D) It already shortened CMVP review to 90 days
Answer: C
Explanation: EO 14412 (signed 22 June 2026) §6(b) says that within 180 days NIST “shall … revise the processes used by the Cryptographic Module Validation Program to accelerate validations of cryptographic modules” — a date around 19 December 2026. As of 24 September 2026 the revision is pending and its content is not public; the standard and its levels are unchanged. Source: Executive Order 14412, Securing the Nation Against Advanced Cryptographic Attacks.

chunks.title: Quiz: cc-eucc-certification
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: cc-eucc-certification

Q: An EU qualified trust service provider asks for proof that an HSM was certified against the EN 419221-5 Protection Profile. Which certificate can answer that?
  A) An eIDAS 2.0 certificate, because eIDAS 2.0 is the Protection Profile for trust-service HSMs
  B) A FIPS 140-3 Level 3 validation
  C) A PCI PTS HSM approval
  D) A Common Criteria-based certificate issued under the EUCC scheme, claiming conformance to EN 419221-5
Answer: D
Explanation: Protection Profile conformance is a Common Criteria concept, and in the EU CC-based certification now runs under EUCC (Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/482, applicable from 27 February 2025), whose Annex II lists EN 419221-5 for remote QSCDs. eIDAS 2.0 (Regulation (EU) 2024/1183) is the regulation that leads there — it is not a Protection Profile and issues no device certificate. FIPS 140-3 and PCI PTS HSM are separate evaluations that do not show PP conformance. Source: Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/482.

chunks.title: Quiz: cc-eucc-certification
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: cc-eucc-certification

Q: Two HSM listings both read “EAL4+”. What does the shared headline tell you about their assurance?
  A) Only that each EAL4 package was augmented — you must read each list of named components (for example whether AVA_VAN.5 is included) before comparing them
  B) That both have identical assurance
  C) That both were evaluated at a level above EAL4, such as EAL5
  D) That both are equivalent to FIPS 140-3 Level 4
Answer: A
Explanation: The “+” means the EAL4 package was augmented by named assurance components that add to or replace components in the package; the named components are the claim. Two “EAL4+” HSMs can differ in vulnerability analysis, development security and flaw remediation, an augmented EAL4 is not a higher EAL, and an EAL (how thoroughly claims were evaluated) does not convert into a FIPS level. Source: Common Criteria CC:2022 Part 5 (EAL packages and augmentation).

Q: A Security Target claims “EAL4 augmented with AVA_VAN.3”. What is wrong with that claim?
  A) Nothing — AVA_VAN.3 is the highest vulnerability-analysis component
  B) AVA_VAN.3 is already part of the EAL4 package, so it adds nothing; augmenting vulnerability analysis would mean substituting AVA_VAN.4 or AVA_VAN.5
  C) AVA_VAN components can only be claimed in EUCC certificates
  D) AVA_VAN.3 lowers EAL4 to EAL3
Answer: B
Explanation: EAL4 already contains AVA_VAN.3. An augmentation of vulnerability analysis replaces it with a higher component — AVA_VAN.4, or AVA_VAN.5 (the evaluator assumes a High attack potential). Reading which components were actually added is how you decode an “EAL4+” claim. Source: Common Criteria CC:2022 Part 5 (EAL4 package contents) and Part 3 (AVA_VAN components).

chunks.title: Quiz: cc-eucc-certification
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: cc-eucc-certification

Q: As of 24 September 2026, what does the applicable EUCC cryptography guidance (ECCG Agreed Cryptographic Mechanisms v2) say about ML-DSA?
  A) Nothing yet — PQC mechanisms arrive only with ACM v3
  B) ML-DSA is agreed, preferably ML-DSA-87 or ML-DSA-65, and lattice-based mechanisms should be combined with a classical mechanism rather than used standalone
  C) Any NIST-approved ML-DSA parameter set is accepted as-is, standalone
  D) ML-DSA-44 is recommended, standalone
Answer: B
Explanation: ACM v2 (the document is dated April 2025; ENISA lists it with the date 6 May 2025) already lists ML-KEM, FrodoKEM, ML-DSA, SLH-DSA, XMSS and LMS. For ML-DSA it recommends “either ML-DSA-87 or ML-DSA-65”, and it says (M)LWE-based mechanisms “shouldn’t be used in a standalone way” but should be combined with a classical mechanism — hash-based signatures may be standalone. ACM is the EU’s own list, so NIST approval does not import NIST’s parameter choices. Source: ECCG Agreed Cryptographic Mechanisms v2 (as of 24 September 2026).

chunks.title: Quiz: cc-eucc-certification
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: cc-eucc-certification

Q: As of 24 September 2026, what is the status of ECCG Agreed Cryptographic Mechanisms v3 under EUCC?
  A) It is a draft: ENISA posted it for public review (2 June 2026, review until the end of July 2026), and v2 remains the applicable version
  B) It is applicable and replaced v2 on 1 July 2026
  C) It is applicable only to products certified at EUCC level high
  D) It was withdrawn, so no PQC guidance applies under EUCC
Answer: A
Explanation: ACM v3 is a draft — ENISA posted the “draft for public review” on 2 June 2026, with review until the end of July 2026. ENISA’s EUCC Guidelines on Cryptography page lists v2 as applicable and v3 as the draft for public review, so treating v3 as applicable is a draft-cited-as-current error. Source: ENISA, EUCC Guidelines on Cryptography page (as of 24 September 2026).

chunks.title: Quiz: cc-eucc-certification
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: cc-eucc-certification

Q: A vendor adds an ML-DSA signature service to a EUCC-certified HSM. Under EUCC as amended by Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/2462, which statement is correct?
  A) The vendor declares the change minor, and the certification body issues a new certificate for the new version
  B) The certification body classifies the change from the holder’s impact analysis; a confirmed minor change gets a maintenance report and no new certificate — and a new cryptographic service changes the claimed SFRs, so expect it to be major (re-evaluation, then a new certificate)
  C) A market PQC deadline lets the certification body treat the change as minor
  D) Changes to a certified product never involve the certification body until the certificate expires
Answer: B
Explanation: Under the amended assurance-continuity rules the certification body — not the vendor — decides minor versus major. For a confirmed minor change “no new certificate shall be issued”: the holder gets a maintenance report. Adding a signature service changes the claimed security functional requirements, which CCRA assurance-continuity guidance (CCDB-014) lists as a typical major change, leading to re-evaluation and a new certificate. A deadline does not change the classification. Source: Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/2462.

chunks.title: Quiz: pci-certification
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: pci-certification

Q: A PCI PTS HSM listing carries the post-quantum (PQC) notation. What does that notation mean?
  A) PCI SSC has approved ML-KEM and ML-DSA for PIN and key-management use on that device
  B) The device’s PQC algorithms were each validated under ACVP
  C) The device meets a PCI deadline for PQC migration
  D) The lab evaluated whether the device supports PQC — the notation “is for the existence of PQC support”; the algorithms are named in the device Security Policy and readiness details come from the vendor
Answer: D
Explanation: The listing field definitions say that for v3-and-higher HSMs the device “has been evaluated to determine if it supports PQC” and that the notation “is for the existence of PQC support”, with implementation details in the Security Policy and readiness details from the vendor. PTS approval is device-security approval, not algorithm validation, and public PCI material names no approved PQC algorithm, parameter set or deadline. Source: PCI PTS approved-device listing field definitions (as read 24 September 2026).

chunks.title: Quiz: pci-certification
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: pci-certification

Q: A payment processor runs PIN processing on an HSM that has a FIPS 140-3 Level 3 certificate but no PCI PTS HSM approval. Which statement is correct?
  A) The FIPS certificate counts as PTS HSM approval, so the device is PCI-approved
  B) A FIPS 140-3 certificate is issued by PCI SSC, and PTS approvals are issued by NIST
  C) The FIPS certificate is not a PTS HSM approval: PTS approvals are assigned by PCI SSC and listed per device, while a FIPS 140-3 certificate is separate evidence from a different scheme
  D) A PTS approval is assigned to the processor that operates the HSM, not to the device
Answer: C
Explanation: A FIPS 140-3 certificate comes from the Cryptographic Module Validation Program (CMVP). A PTS HSM approval is a separate scheme: PCI SSC assigns the approval number to a device at the time of approval, and the number remains the same for the life of the device’s approval. A FIPS certificate is therefore not a PTS approval. Which HSM evidence a PCI standard accepts is set out in that standard, which this lesson does not read. Source: PCI SSC, Approved PTS Devices listing, field definitions.

chunks.title: Quiz: pci-certification
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: pci-certification

Q: What does the expiry table on the PCI SSC Approved PTS Devices listing give as the “Expiration of Device Models” for HSM v4.x?
  A) April 2033
  B) June 2027
  C) April 2036
  D) April 2028
Answer: A
Explanation: For HSM v4.x the table gives “Expiration of Requirements Approval” June 2027 and “Expiration of Device Models” April 2033. For v5.x the two dates are May 2030 and April 2036, and for v3.x they are December 2022 and April 2028. The page says device approvals expire six years past the effective date of a subsequent major update of the applicable Security Requirements. These are approval expiry dates; no PCI page this lesson reads ties them to post-quantum timing. Source: PCI SSC, Approved PTS Devices listing, field definitions.

chunks.title: Quiz: crypto-product-certification
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: crypto-product-certification

Q: A customer’s PQC deadline arrives before a vendor’s new ML-KEM firmware is certified. Which plan keeps the vendor’s certification claims correct?
  A) Request a lighter change route (CMVP TRNS, an EUCC minor change or a PCI delta), citing the deadline
  B) Describe the PQC firmware as covered by the existing certificate, because ML-KEM is a NIST standard
  C) Run two lanes: keep the certified build as the only certified claim, and move the PQC build through each scheme’s real route with no inherited certification claim
  D) Advertise the PQC firmware as validated once it appears on the CMVP MIP list
Answer: C
Explanation: A market deadline creates urgency, not a shortcut: it does not make a PQC addition eligible for CMVP TRNS (which needs a published CMVP algorithm transition that would move modules to Historical), an EUCC minor change or a PCI delta. The certified lane stays valid while the PQC candidate goes through the scheme’s route; an algorithm standard is not a validation, and a MIP entry is a queue position. Source: NIST CMVP FIPS 140-3 Management Manual v2.7, §7.1.12 (as of 24 September 2026).

chunks.title: Quiz: crypto-product-certification
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: crypto-product-certification

Q: An HSM appliance holds a FIPS 140-3 Level 3 validation. The vendor’s client SDK runs on customer hosts, outside the tamper-responsive enclosure. What does the Level 3 validation tell you about the SDK?
  A) The SDK is covered at Level 3, because it ships with the validated appliance
  B) Nothing: the SDK sits outside the validated module boundary, so the validation does not describe it
  C) The SDK is covered at Level 1, the software-only level
  D) The SDK is covered whenever its version matches the appliance firmware version
Answer: B
Explanation: A level describes a defined boundary at a version, in a configuration: read the object first, the grade second. A FIPS 140-3 module is bounded by what its Security Policy defines (here the enclosure: hardware, firmware, the crypto library compiled into it). Components that run on customer hosts normally stay outside, and the validation then says nothing about them.

Q: A buyer asks "is this HSM certified?". What should be checked first?
  A) The security level printed on the certificate
  B) The name of the testing laboratory
  C) The scope: which module, version and configuration the certificate actually covers
  D) Whether the vendor's datasheet mentions FIPS
Answer: C
Explanation: Scope before level. A certificate covers a defined module, target or device at a specific version and configuration; the level only means something inside that scope.

Q: A vendor adds ML-KEM to an already-certified product. The existing certificate automatically covers the new ML-KEM capability.
Answer: FALSE
Explanation: Adding ML-KEM or ML-DSA changes the certified product. Each scheme has its own route for handling that change, so the existing certificate does not extend to it automatically.

chunks.title: Quiz: crypto-product-certification
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: crypto-product-certification

Q: A product is fully crypto-agile in code: it can switch to ML-DSA with a configuration change. Why might it still be unable to ship a certified ML-DSA capability next month?
  A) Crypto agility and certification are the same thing, so it can ship
  B) Certification latency: the change must still go through the scheme's change route before the certificate covers it
  C) ML-DSA cannot be certified under any scheme
  D) Only hardware products can be certified
Answer: B
Explanation: Crypto agility versus certification latency: a product can be agile in code and still wait on a scheme's change route before a certified claim is correct.

chunks.title: Quiz: pqc-hw-acceleration
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: pqc-hw-acceleration

Q: On PQC Today's KV260 board, two FPGA ML-DSA-65 signers raised throughput from 404 to 522 signatures/s (+29%). What capped the gain?
  A) The FPGA fabric was too slow to compute a signature
  B) The ARM cores still did key decoding, matrix expansion, data copies and PKCS#11 work for every signature
  C) ML-DSA cannot be implemented in hardware
  D) The FPGA clock was limited to 100 MHz
Answer: B
Explanation: The two signers could reach about 1,316 signatures/s on their own, but the ARM side still did key decoding, ExpandA, copying data in and out, cache syncs and PKCS#11 for every signature. Speeding up only part of a job cannot beat the part left alone (Amdahl's law).

Q: Why does SLH-DSA-SHA2-128s sign faster than SLH-DSA-SHAKE-128s on Cortex-A53/A55 cores?
  A) SHA-2 needs fewer hash calls per signature
  B) The A53/A55 have SHA-256 instructions but no SHA-3 instructions, so SHAKE runs in software
  C) SHAKE signatures are larger
  D) SHA-2 variants use a smaller Merkle tree
Answer: B
Explanation: The two variants have the same structure; only the hash differs. Cortex-A53 and A55 implement the Armv8 SHA-256 instructions but not the SHA-3 (Keccak) ones, so on those cores the SHA-2 variant is about a third faster in PQC Today's measurements.

chunks.title: Quiz: pqc-hw-acceleration
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: pqc-hw-acceleration

Q: Which statement about x86 instruction support for PQC hashing is correct?
  A) x86 has had a SHA-3 instruction since AVX-512
  B) SHA-NI covers SHA-1 and SHA-256 only; there is no SHA-3/Keccak instruction on x86
  C) SHA-NI accelerates SHA-512 on all Intel CPUs since 2016
  D) AES-NI can be used to compute SHAKE
Answer: B
Explanation: Intel's SHA extensions support only SHA-1 and SHA-256. SHA-512 instructions arrived only with Arrow Lake-S / Lunar Lake, and no x86 SHA-3/Keccak instruction exists — x86 speeds up SHAKE with SIMD, running several Keccak states in parallel.

Q: Why is GPU acceleration efficient for large batches but not for one low-latency signature?
  A) GPUs cannot run integer arithmetic
  B) Each launch has a fixed start-up cost and thousands of lanes only pay off when many independent operations are in flight
  C) GPUs are slower per clock than any CPU
  D) GPU memory cannot hold a private key
Answer: B
Explanation: A GPU trades latency for throughput: launch overhead is paid per batch and memory delays are hidden only with many operations in flight. In PQC Today's Metal study, ML-DSA-65 key generation lost to the CPU at a batch of 256 and was 9.3x faster at 65,536.

Q: What does Montgomery reduction avoid when computing a·b mod N?
  A) Multiplication
  B) Addition
  C) Division by N
  D) Storing intermediate values
Answer: C
Explanation: Montgomery reduction adds a multiple of N so the low digits become zero and then shifts them away — a free operation in binary — so no trial division by N is needed. It is used in RSA/ECC and in ML-DSA coefficient arithmetic (FIPS 204 Appendix A).

chunks.title: Quiz: pqc-hw-acceleration
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: pqc-hw-acceleration

Q: True or False: An FPGA design always runs at the same clock frequency regardless of how many engines you place on it.
Answer: FALSE
Explanation: False. The clock is limited by the design's critical path, which grows as the design grows and routing gets crowded. PQC Today's 4-lane Keccak engine missed 250 MHz by 0.010 ns and ships at 240 MHz.

Q: Why is a typical NPU (AI accelerator) a poor fit for PQC acceleration?
  A) It lacks memory for keys
  B) It performs rounded 8-bit multiply-accumulate, while PQC needs exact modular arithmetic and Keccak is bitwise logic
  C) It is always slower than a CPU
  D) NPUs cannot be used on embedded boards
Answer: B
Explanation: NPUs are int8 multiply-accumulate arrays designed to tolerate rounding. ML-DSA needs exact arithmetic mod 8,380,417 and Keccak uses only XOR/AND/NOT/rotate. PQC Today evaluated the i.MX 95 NPU for PQC and ruled it out.

Q: Which parameter sets does the Adams Bridge PQC accelerator in Caliptra 2.0 support?
  A) All ML-DSA and ML-KEM parameter sets
  B) ML-DSA-87 and ML-KEM-1024 only
  C) ML-DSA-44 and ML-KEM-512 only
  D) SLH-DSA only
Answer: B
Explanation: Adams Bridge supports only ML-DSA-87 and ML-KEM-1024 (the highest security level), keeping the silicon small — an example of how an ASIC fixes its parameter sets at tape-out.

chunks.title: Quiz: government-defense-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: government-defense-pqc

Q: Which CNSA 1.0 primitive survives unchanged into CNSA 2.0?
  A) ECDH P-384
  B) RSA-3072
  C) ECDSA P-384
  D) AES-256
Answer: D
Explanation: CNSA 2.0 replaces every public-key line of CNSA 1.0 (with ML-KEM-1024, ML-DSA-87, and LMS/XMSS for firmware). AES-256 is unchanged, so "replace all cryptography" is the wrong budgeting model.

Q: ML-KEM-768 is FIPS 203-approved. Can it be used as the CNSA 2.0 key-establishment algorithm in a National Security System?
  A) No. CNSA 2.0 approves only the Level-5 parameter set, ML-KEM-1024
  B) Yes. Any FIPS 203 parameter set is CNSA 2.0-approved
  C) Yes, but only inside a hybrid construction
  D) Only until 2030
Answer: A
Explanation: CNSA 2.0 approves ML-KEM-1024 and ML-DSA-87 exclusively. The smaller parameter sets are FIPS-approved but not CNSA 2.0-approved; this is an NSS-specific narrowing of the NIST standards.

Q: Under CNSSP 15, as quoted in CNSA 2.0 FAQ version 2.2, from which date must all new National Security System acquisitions be CNSA 2.0-compliant unless otherwise noted?
  A) 31 December 2030
  B) 1 January 2027
  C) 31 December 2031
  D) 2035
Answer: B
Explanation: 1 January 2027 for new acquisitions. 31 December 2030 is the date to phase out equipment and services that cannot support CNSA 2.0 unless excepted, 31 December 2031 is when CNSA 2.0 algorithms are mandated unless otherwise noted, and 2035 is the separate NSM-10 quantum-risk objective.

Q: NSA prohibits hybrid (classical + post-quantum) products in National Security Systems.
Answer: FALSE
Explanation: NSA will not require hybrids for NSS, but it explicitly allows that product availability and interoperability may lead to adopting hybrid solutions. Calling this a ban is a common misreading.

chunks.title: Quiz: government-defense-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: government-defense-pqc

Q: A federal civilian agency system that is not a National Security System. Which statement is correct?
  A) It must meet the CNSSP 15 CNSA 2.0 dates
  B) It has no post-quantum obligations at all
  C) It falls under the QCCPA and OMB M-23-02 / M-26-15: inventory and reporting obligations, but no equivalent dated algorithm deadline
  D) It follows NIST SP 800-171 Rev. 3 only
Answer: C
Explanation: NSS and federal civilian systems are governed by different instruments. Civilian agencies have inventory and reporting duties without a CNSA-style algorithm deadline, which is why "which stack applies?" is the first question.

chunks.title: Quiz: pki-enrollment-protocols
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: pki-enrollment-protocols

Q: Why can't EST's standard proof-of-possession enroll an ML-KEM key?
  A) EST does not support TLS 1.3
  B) EST's proof-of-possession is the signed CSR itself, and an ML-KEM key cannot sign
  C) ML-KEM public keys are too large for HTTPS
  D) EST was withdrawn in 2025
Answer: B
Explanation: EST (RFC 7030) proves possession by the CSR signature. That works for ML-DSA but not for ML-KEM, a key-encapsulation key that cannot produce signatures.

Q: Which CMP proof-of-possession mode lets a requester prove it holds an ML-KEM private key?
  A) signature
  B) raVerified
  C) PBM-MAC
  D) encrCert: the CA encapsulates under the requester's new public key, and only the key holder can decapsulate
Answer: D
Explanation: RFC 9810 adds KEM-aware proof-of-possession via encrCert. raVerified relies on an RA vouching, and PBM-MAC protects the message rather than proving key possession.

Q: Which RFC (July 2025) obsoleted RFC 4210 and enabled CMP enrollment of KEM keys that cannot sign?
  A) RFC 7030
  B) RFC 4211
  C) RFC 9810
  D) RFC 9881
Answer: C
Explanation: RFC 9810 is the current Certificate Management Protocol specification. It obsoletes RFC 4210 and adds KEM-aware proof-of-possession.

Q: In 2026, how do production PKIs typically give one end-entity both a post-quantum and a classical certificate?
  A) Parallel chains: one ML-DSA certificate and one classical certificate for the same end-entity
  B) A single composite certificate, standardised in RFC 9810
  C) By re-signing the classical certificate with ML-DSA
  D) They don't; classical certificates were retired in 2025
Answer: A
Explanation: Composite signature and KEM OIDs are still IETF drafts (not yet shipped in OpenSSL 3.6), so deployments such as Cloudflare and AWS use parallel certificate chains.

chunks.title: Quiz: pki-enrollment-protocols
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: pki-enrollment-protocols

Q: A CA signs certificates with ML-DSA. Which RFC defines the algorithm identifiers it puts in the certificate's signatureAlgorithm field?
  A) RFC 9935
  B) RFC 9881
  C) RFC 9909
  D) RFC 9629
Answer: B
Explanation: RFC 9881 defines the ML-DSA identifiers in X.509. RFC 9935 does the same for ML-KEM public keys, RFC 9909 covers SLH-DSA, and RFC 9629 covers KEMs in CMS.

chunks.title: Quiz: acvp-lab-workflow
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: acvp-lab-workflow

Q: What does CAVP validate, and how does it relate to CMVP?
  A) Whole modules; it replaces CMVP for PQC
  B) Algorithm implementations; it is a prerequisite of CMVP module validation
  C) Operating systems; CMVP then validates the algorithms
  D) Nothing formal; it is a vendor self-test
Answer: B
Explanation: CAVP validates algorithm implementations (run black-box through NIST's ACVTS) and is a prerequisite of CMVP, which validates modules to FIPS 140-3 through accredited laboratories.

Q: Which ACVTS environment can produce CAVP certificates?
  A) Demo, for anyone with an account
  B) Either, as long as every test group passes
  C) Prod, used by accredited labs; Demo is a sandbox
  D) Neither; certificates come from the CMVP
Answer: C
Explanation: ACVTS Demo is a sandbox. Only Prod, used by accredited laboratories, creates CAVP certificates.

Q: Once issued, an ACVP vector set can be reused for another validation.
Answer: FALSE
Explanation: Vector sets are one-time use for a validation authority (ACVP spec §14). Separately, the Hub's own rule is that nothing issued to a real ACVTS session is committed to the repository.

Q: The Hub's two engines produce identical results for the same vector set. What does that agreement show?
  A) Independent validation of both implementations
  B) A CAVP certificate for both engines
  C) Nothing, because agreement is meaningless
  D) Differential evidence only: the engines share adapter code, so agreement is not independent validation
Answer: D
Explanation: Cross-implementation agreement is differential evidence. Because the two engines share adapter code, it cannot stand in for independent validation, and results bind to an operational environment.

chunks.title: Quiz: acvp-lab-workflow
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: acvp-lab-workflow

Q: Why can't a PKCS#11 v3.2 adapter answer an ML-KEM encapsulation AFT test group?
  A) The test supplies a server-chosen message m, and C_EncapsulateKey cannot accept one
  B) PKCS#11 has no ML-KEM support at all
  C) AFT tests only apply to hash functions
  D) The vectors are too large for PKCS#11 buffers
Answer: A
Explanation: ML-KEM encapsulation AFT fixes the randomness m server-side; C_EncapsulateKey generates its own, so the test group cannot be driven through PKCS#11. That is an adapter boundary, not a missing algorithm.

chunks.title: Quiz: talking-about-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: talking-about-pqc

Q: A security module appears on NIST's Modules In Process list. Which statement about it is accurate?
  A) It is FIPS 140-3 validated
  B) Its validation has started but is not finished
  C) NIST has approved the product
  D) Its algorithms have been retired
Answer: B
Explanation: The Modules In Process list follows a module's test report from its submission to the CMVP through validation, and the Validation Authorities issue a certificate number for inclusion in the database after confirming the information.

Q: Which phrase should you avoid when describing a product's post-quantum protection?
  A) Post-quantum
  B) Quantum-resistant
  C) Quantum-proof
  D) Uses ML-KEM (FIPS 203)
Answer: C
Explanation: No cryptography is proven unbreakable. Naming the standard and the version, such as ML-KEM (FIPS 203), gives the customer something they can check.

Q: True or False: NIST approves individual products as quantum-safe.
Answer: FALSE
Explanation: False. Validation programs test specific implementations, and each result covers a specific version.

Q: NIST IR 8547 sets dates for deprecating quantum-vulnerable public-key algorithms after 2030 and disallowing them after 2035. What is the status of those dates since 27 October 2026?
  A) Final NIST guidance: deprecated after 2030, disallowed after 2035
  B) Proposals in a draft report
  C) They were withdrawn
  D) They apply only in Europe
Answer: A
Explanation: NIST published the final NIST IR 8547 on 27 October 2026, so the dates are final NIST guidance for systems that follow NIST standards; they are not a law. The November 2024 initial public draft had proposed them, so say "final" when you quote them now.

chunks.title: Quiz: talking-about-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: talking-about-pqc

Q: What does 'hybrid' mean when a product describes its key exchange as hybrid?
  A) A halfway step that is less secure than full post-quantum
  B) A traditional and a post-quantum algorithm used together, protected as long as either holds
  C) A marketing term with no technical meaning
  D) Encryption that works only on quantum computers
Answer: B
Explanation: Hybrid combines a traditional and a post-quantum algorithm, so the connection stays protected as long as either one holds. It is a deliberate design for the transition, and a good word once you explain it.

Q: True or False: A FIPS 140-3 certificate for version 4 of a module also covers post-quantum algorithms added in version 5.
Answer: FALSE
Explanation: False. A certificate covers a specific version and configuration. Algorithms added in a later version are covered only once a validation that includes them is complete.

Q: A customer asks: 'Are you quantum-safe?' Which answer is strongest?
  A) Yes, fully.
  B) Quantum is not a real risk yet.
  C) Here is what is protected today, what is planned and when, and the evidence for each.
  D) We will be ready when quantum computers arrive.
Answer: C
Explanation: A strong answer separates what is done, what is planned and what is unknown, and links evidence for each part, such as certificate numbers or a public roadmap. A bare 'yes' cannot be checked.

chunks.title: Quiz: homomorphic-encryption
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: homomorphic-encryption

Q: How does fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) protect data in use differently from a Trusted Execution Environment (TEE)?
  A) FHE relies on the CPU vendor's attestation chain, while a TEE relies on lattice mathematics
  B) FHE decrypts the data inside a hardware enclave and re-encrypts the result before it leaves
  C) FHE lets the server compute directly on ciphertexts, so it trusts lattice mathematics instead of trusted hardware
  D) FHE runs at near-native speed, while a TEE is orders of magnitude slower than computing in the clear
Answer: C
Explanation: A TEE protects data in use by trusting hardware: its root of trust is the CPU vendor, its firmware and the attestation chain, and the data is plaintext inside the enclave. FHE trusts mathematics instead. The server computes directly on ciphertexts and returns an encrypted result, so the data on the server is always ciphertext and there is no enclave to attest. The price is speed: FHE is roughly 10^3 to 10^6 times slower than computing in the clear, while a TEE runs near native speed. FHE also does not prove that the result is correct, because ciphertexts are malleable.

chunks.title: Quiz: homomorphic-encryption
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: homomorphic-encryption

Q: In FHE, what is ciphertext noise and what does bootstrapping do about it?
  A) Noise is a small random error in every ciphertext that grows with each operation; bootstrapping refreshes it by running decryption homomorphically under an encrypted copy of the key
  B) Noise is a random mask the client adds so the server cannot read the data; bootstrapping lets the server remove the mask with the secret key
  C) Noise is leakage from the server's CPU through side channels; bootstrapping encrypts the server's memory to stop it
  D) Noise is jitter on the network link that delays ciphertexts; bootstrapping retransmits the lost packets
Answer: A
Explanation: Every FHE ciphertext carries a small random error. Additions grow it a little and multiplications grow it a lot, and once it is too large decryption fails, which is why multiplications limit how deep a computation can go. Bootstrapping refreshes the noise by running the decryption step homomorphically under an encrypted copy of the secret key, so the server never sees the key or the data. It is the expensive step: BGV and BFV usually run leveled instead, while TFHE bootstraps after every gate or nonlinear operation.

chunks.title: Quiz: homomorphic-encryption
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: homomorphic-encryption

Q: Which FHE scheme computes on approximate real or complex vectors, which makes it the usual choice for machine learning, statistics and signal processing?
  A) BGV
  B) CKKS
  C) BFV
  D) TFHE / CGGI
Answer: B
Explanation: CKKS works on approximate real and complex vectors and supports (approximate) bootstrapping, so it suits machine learning, statistics and signal processing. BGV and BFV compute exactly on integers modulo t packed into SIMD slots, which suits counts and matching. TFHE/CGGI (with FHEW) works on bits and small integers and handles arbitrary functions through lookup tables, comparisons and branching logic, with programmable bootstrapping.

Q: True or False: BGV, BFV, CKKS and TFHE are all defined in ISO/IEC 28033, which is still in draft and has no part published yet.
Answer: TRUE
Explanation: True. All four schemes are being standardized in ISO/IEC 28033, but no part is published yet: part 2 (BGV and BFV) is at Draft International Standard (DIS) stage, while parts 3 (CKKS) and 4 (TFHE/CGGI with FHEW) are at Final Draft International Standard (FDIS) stage. The FHE schemes are also not NIST-standardized, so a deployment that needs a stated post-quantum level has to pick its parameters deliberately from the HE Standard's quantum tables.

chunks.title: Quiz: homomorphic-encryption
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: homomorphic-encryption

Q: Which of these FHE keys are public keys that do not have to be kept secret? (Select all that apply)
  A) Public (encryption) key
  B) Secret key
  C) Relinearization key
  D) Rotation (Galois) keys
Answer: A|C|D
Explanation: The secret key is the only secret in an FHE key set: a small polynomial that can be regenerated from a 32-byte seed. The public encryption key, the relinearization key (which switches s squared back to s after every ciphertext multiplication) and the rotation keys (one per allowed slot rotation) are public but large, from megabytes up to gigabytes for a CKKS bootstrapping key set (order-of-magnitude estimates). Public does not mean unprotected: evaluation keys encrypt functions of the secret key, so they need integrity. There is also no standard encoding yet: no PKCS#11 or KMIP object type and no X.509 OID.

Q: In an FHE workflow, which step is run by the key holder because it needs the secret key?
  A) Decrypting and decoding the final result
  B) Encrypting the input data
  C) Multiplying two ciphertexts and relinearizing
  D) Bootstrapping to refresh the noise
Answer: A
Explanation: Encoding and encrypting is done by the client with the public key. Add, multiply plus relinearize, rescale, rotate and bootstrap are run by the server, which needs only public evaluation keys or no key at all. Decrypt and decode is the only evaluation-time operation that needs the secret key, so it belongs to the key holder, which is where an HSM fits. (Key generation needs the secret key too.)

chunks.title: Quiz: homomorphic-encryption
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: homomorphic-encryption

Q: A client already protects its data with AES-GCM. Why can an FHE server not simply add two of those ciphertexts, and what bridges the gap?
  A) The server must first decrypt the AES-GCM ciphertexts with the AES key and then re-encrypt them under FHE
  B) FHE works directly on AES-GCM ciphertexts, but only for addition and not for multiplication
  C) An AES-GCM ciphertext has no structure the server can compute on; transciphering runs the symmetric cipher's decryption inside FHE, so the server turns it into an FHE ciphertext without seeing the data
  D) No library implements a bridge, so the client has to upload the data as full-size FHE ciphertexts
Answer: C
Explanation: You can only compute on ciphertexts from a homomorphic scheme, and an AES-GCM ciphertext has no structure a server can exploit. Transciphering is the bridge: the client uploads data at plaintext size under a stream cipher, together with the stream key encrypted once under FHE, and the server runs the cipher's keystream inside FHE to obtain FHE ciphertexts of the data. TFHE-rs ships it for Kreyvium and AES-128-CTR; the workshop shows Kreyvium because it is cheaper. Prefer Kreyvium's 128-bit key over Trivium's 80-bit key, which is already below the 112-bit minimum before Grover's algorithm.

chunks.title: Quiz: homomorphic-encryption
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: homomorphic-encryption

Q: What does the core of an FHE scheme such as BGV, BFV, CKKS or TFHE rely on, and what is its quantum status?
  A) Integer factoring, which Shor's algorithm breaks
  B) Elliptic-curve discrete logarithms, which Shor's algorithm breaks
  C) Hash functions only, so it is quantum-safe for any parameter choice
  D) (Ring-)Learning With Errors lattices, the family behind ML-KEM, with no known quantum break
Answer: D
Explanation: The FHE schemes are lattice-based: they rest on the (Ring-)Learning With Errors family that also underlies ML-KEM (FIPS 203), and no quantum break is known. The FHE schemes themselves are not NIST-standardized, and common defaults target classical 128-bit security, so choose parameters from the HE Standard's quantum tables when you need a stated post-quantum level. That covers only the scheme: the parts of a deployment around it are a separate question.

chunks.title: Quiz: homomorphic-encryption
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: homomorphic-encryption

Q: Which parts of a typical FHE deployment are still classical and would be broken by a cryptographically relevant quantum computer? (Select all that apply)
  A) The lattice-based FHE scheme itself (BGV, BFV, CKKS or TFHE)
  B) The ECDHE key exchange in the TLS 1.3 channel that carries ciphertexts and evaluation keys
  C) ECDSA or RSA signatures protecting the integrity of evaluation keys and results
  D) RSA-OAEP or ECDH key wrapping used for secret-key backup
Answer: B|C|D
Explanation: The FHE scheme has no known quantum break; the components around it are usually classical. The channel needs a hybrid key exchange such as X25519MLKEM768, the signatures on evaluation keys and results need ML-DSA or SLH-DSA (FHE is malleable, so integrity matters), and the secret-key backup needs a post-quantum design: a non-extractable seed replicated only HSM to HSM, sealed with FIPS 203 ML-KEM-768 and signed with FIPS 204 ML-DSA-65. Two more weak spots from the module: additively homomorphic layers built on Paillier or exponential ElGamal, and Trivium's 80-bit key for transciphering.

chunks.title: Quiz: homomorphic-encryption
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: homomorphic-encryption

Q: In the HSM key-custodian pattern for FHE, how is the secret key created and protected?
  A) The client generates the secret key and wraps it with an AES key held in the HSM for storage
  B) A 32-byte seed is generated inside the HSM as a non-extractable key, the secret key is derived from it inside the HSM, and the seed is backed up only HSM to HSM
  C) The HSM exports the secret key under RSA-OAEP so any cloud key service can hold a backup
  D) The cloud server derives the secret key from a seed that the HSM shares with it over TLS
Answer: B
Explanation: The pattern generates a 32-byte seed inside the HSM as a non-extractable key (ordinary key wrapping refuses it), derives the secret key from it inside the HSM, streams the public and evaluation keys out, signs the parameter set and evaluation-key hashes with ML-DSA, decrypts under policy with an audit log, and backs up the seed (not gigabytes of keys) only HSM to HSM. Treat it as a deployment pattern: the module notes that no FHE library or paper defines an HSM role, and no standard PKCS#11 mechanism exists for any of this today.

chunks.title: Quiz: homomorphic-encryption
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: homomorphic-encryption

Q: Which statement correctly describes what an HSM can and cannot do for FHE?
  A) Seed and secret-key generation and decryption fit in an HSM; homomorphic evaluation and bootstrapping do not
  B) Homomorphic evaluation and bootstrapping should run in the HSM because they need the secret key
  C) An HSM can generate every FHE key of every scheme, including multi-gigabyte CKKS bootstrapping key sets
  D) An HSM can store the secret key but cannot run decryption
Answer: A
Explanation: Seed and secret-key generation and decryption take small inputs and milliseconds of compute, so they fit. Evaluation-key generation is size-limited: TFHE's server key of about 30 MB fits, but a CKKS bootstrapping key set (gigabytes, estimated) does not, and the planned engine in the workshop refuses it by design. Homomorphic evaluation and bootstrapping need gigabytes of keys in memory plus GPU or FPGA acceleration, and they need no secret, so running them in the HSM would add nothing but load.

chunks.title: Quiz: homomorphic-encryption
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: homomorphic-encryption

Q: Why must an HSM not act as a raw decryption oracle for FHE ciphertexts?
  A) Decryption is too slow inside an HSM, so it would become a performance bottleneck
  B) Each decryption consumes part of the seed, so the HSM runs out of key material after a fixed number of requests
  C) Published attacks can recover the secret key from decryptions of even honestly computed ciphertexts, so the HSM must release only approved result shapes, with rate limits
  D) Decrypting inside an HSM makes the non-extractable seed extractable
Answer: C
Explanation: If a party can get decryptions back, even of ciphertexts honestly computed from inputs it knows, published attacks recover the key: Li and Micciancio (2021) on CKKS, and decryption-failure attacks on BFV, BGV and TFHE (for example Cheon et al., CCS 2024 and Checri et al., CRYPTO 2024). This module's advice: for CKKS the HSM floods the decryption noise (OpenFHE NOISE_FLOODING_DECRYPT); for BFV, BGV and TFHE it uses parameters with negligible failure probability. In every case it releases only approved result shapes with rate limits, and a refusal still counts against the limit.

chunks.title: Quiz: homomorphic-encryption
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: homomorphic-encryption

Q: How do the OpenFHE and Lattigo threshold FHE scenarios in the workshop differ?
  A) OpenFHE uses t-of-N shares so any two of three parties can act, while Lattigo needs all N parties for every decryption
  B) Both need every party online for every decryption; the only difference is BFV versus BGV
  C) Neither library supports threshold FHE, so both require a single HSM to hold the whole key
  D) OpenFHE (BFV) is N-of-N, so every party must contribute a partial decryption; Lattigo (BGV) is t-of-N, so one of three parties can be offline
Answer: D
Explanation: Threshold FHE splits the key across several parties, each ideally holding its share in its own HSM, so no single decryptor exists. In the OpenFHE scenario (BFV, 3-of-3) the joint secret is the sum of three shares and every party must contribute a partial decryption, so one unavailable HSM blocks everything. Lattigo (BGV, 2-of-3) uses Shamir shares so any two of three can act, replaces bootstrapping keys with an interactive refresh among the key holders, and re-encrypts the result to the data owner's own public key. Its protocols assume honest-but-curious parties.

Q: True or False: TFHE-rs is published under a BSD-3-Clause-Clear licence, so its maintainer places no further conditions on commercial use.
Answer: FALSE
Explanation: False. Although the code is BSD-3-Clause-Clear, Zama states that commercial use requires a separate patent licence. This is one of the caveats in the module's table of open-source implementations of the ISO/IEC 28033 draft schemes, which lists Lattigo as Apache-2.0, OpenFHE as BSD-2-Clause and Microsoft SEAL as MIT without such a caveat.

chunks.title: Quiz: media-drm-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: media-drm-pqc

Q: Which statement about an edition of a content-protection specification is supported by reading its text?
  A) The organisation behind it has no plan to move to post-quantum cryptography
  B) The text of that edition does not mention quantum computing
  C) It was written before quantum computers were proposed
  D) It will be revised to add ML-KEM by 2030
Answer: B
Explanation: The editions read in the Media, Entertainment & DRM module (AACS Rev 0.953, CI Plus v1.3.2, MovieLabs ECP v1.4, C2PA 2.4) do not mention quantum computing in their text. That is a statement about a document; it says nothing about what any organisation plans, and nothing about other editions.

Q: In the AACS edition read in this module (Introduction and Common Cryptographic Elements Book, Revision 0.953), all digital signatures use ECDSA.
Answer: TRUE
Explanation: Section 2.3 of the book says all digital signatures in AACS utilize the ECDSA digital signature scheme defined in ANSI X9.62 and FIPS 186-2. The key tree itself is built from AES-128, so ECDSA and the Bus Key exchange are the public-key parts.

Q: How does AACS revoke a compromised set of Device Keys?
  A) It adds the device to a TLS certificate revocation list
  B) It releases an updated Media Key Block that stops devices with those Device Keys from calculating the correct Media Key
  C) It re-encrypts the content with a larger RSA key
  D) It changes the elliptic curve used for ECDSA
Answer: B
Explanation: AACS LA generates the Media Key Block. If a set of Device Keys is compromised, an updated block can be released that stops devices with those keys from calculating the correct Media Key (section 3.2 of the book).

chunks.title: Quiz: media-drm-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: media-drm-pqc

Q: In CI Plus Specification v1.3.2, which hash do the certificate signatures use?
  A) SHA-1 (RSASSA-PSS with MGF1 using SHA-1)
  B) SHA-256
  C) SHA-3
  D) MD5
Answer: A
Explanation: Table 9.1 sets the hash algorithm to SHA-1, the mask generation to MGF1 using SHA-1 and the salt to 20 bytes, and Annex I describes the scheme as RSA + SHA1. SHA-256 is used for derived values such as the UCK.

Q: In CI Plus v1.3.2, which scrambler option is mandatory for the CICAM and for both SD and HD hosts?
  A) AES-128 in CBC mode
  B) DES-56 in ECB mode
  C) AES-256 in GCM mode
  D) ChaCha20
Answer: B
Explanation: Table 5.5 makes DES-56-ECB mandatory for the CICAM and for both SD and HD hosts, and AES-128-CBC optional for the CICAM and mandatory for HD hosts only.

Q: Which of these are on the C2PA Technical Specification 2.4 allowed list for generating new claim signatures? Select all that apply.
  A) ES256
  B) PS384
  C) EdDSA (Ed25519 instance)
  D) ML-DSA-65
Answer: A|B|C
Explanation: The allowed list is ES256, ES384, ES512, PS256, PS384, PS512 and EdDSA (Ed25519 instance only); the deprecated list is empty. ML-DSA-65 is not on the list, although RFC 9964 specifies a COSE serialization for ML-DSA.

Q: RFC 10024 (IETF Standards Track, August 2026) defines which kind of mechanism for TLS 1.3?
  A) Pure ML-KEM key agreement
  B) Hybrid key agreement that combines ML-KEM with an ECDHE exchange
  C) Post-quantum X.509 certificates
  D) ML-DSA signatures for TLS handshakes
Answer: B
Explanation: RFC 10024 defines three hybrid key agreement mechanisms for TLS 1.3, X25519MLKEM768, SecP256r1MLKEM768 and SecP384r1MLKEM1024, each combining ML-KEM with an ECDHE exchange.

chunks.title: Quiz: media-drm-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: media-drm-pqc

Q: According to C2PA Technical Specification 2.4, how are time-stamps handled in a claim signature?
  A) Every signature must carry an RFC 3161 time-stamp
  B) A signature may carry an RFC 3161 time-stamp in the sigTst2 header; with no time-stamp, neither header is present
  C) Time-stamps replace the signer certificate
  D) Time-stamps are only allowed with ES256
Answer: B
Explanation: The specification stores a v2 time-stamp in a COSE unprotected header named sigTst2 (the v1 sigTst form is deprecated) and says that if no time-stamps are included, neither header is present.

Q: The dates in NIST IR 8547 (quantum-vulnerable public-key cryptography deprecated after 2030 and disallowed after 2035) are best described as:
  A) A deadline set by the media licensing bodies
  B) NIST’s schedule for NIST standards and guidelines
  C) A mandate that every studio must meet
  D) Dates stated in the AACS and CI Plus specifications
Answer: B
Explanation: IR 8547 says NIST will deprecate quantum-vulnerable public-key cryptography after 2030 and disallow its use under NIST standards and guidelines after 2035. The ECP, AACS, CI Plus and C2PA editions read in the module do not mention quantum computing and state no deadline.

Q: In the 2023 paper on Widevine, FairPlay and PlayReady, which key is described as protected by the license server’s public key in FairPlay?
  A) The content key
  B) The unique AES-128 session key that encrypts the license
  C) The device key
  D) The Media Key
Answer: B
Explanation: The paper says FairPlay requires the license to be encrypted with a unique AES-128 session key, generated by the FairPlay client and protected by the license server’s public key. It is the authors’ analysis of FairPlay, held in the Library as the arXiv preprint.

chunks.title: Quiz: software-supply-chain-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: software-supply-chain-pqc

Q: The Software Supply Chain module marks the CA/Browser Forum Code Signing Baseline Requirements v3.11 and the UEFI Specification Release 2.11 as 'Silent in this edition' for post-quantum signatures. What does that label say?
  A) The organisations behind them have decided not to adopt post-quantum signatures
  B) The text of each of those editions contains no post-quantum term
  C) Those editions forbid the use of post-quantum signatures
  D) Those editions will add post-quantum signatures in their next release
Answer: B
Explanation: A silent entry is a statement about one document: the text of the CA/Browser Forum Code Signing Baseline Requirements v3.11 and the text of the UEFI Specification Release 2.11 each contain no post-quantum term. It says nothing about what either body plans or has decided, and nothing about any other edition.

Q: How does the Sigstore algorithm registry list ML-DSA-44, ML-DSA-65 and ML-DSA-87?
  A) As sign/verify algorithms on the same footing as ECDSA and Ed25519, with no caveat
  B) As verify-only algorithms, the way it lists the 2048-bit RSA entries, with no warning
  C) As experimental ('Pure variant. Not yet fully functional.'), with a warning that they are currently not operational within Sigstore
  D) It lists no post-quantum algorithm; its algorithm table stops at classical schemes
Answer: C
Explanation: The Sigstore algorithm registry, a living page, lists ECDSA and Ed25519 as sign/verify, lists the 2048-bit RSA entries as verify only and not recommended, and lists ML-DSA-44, ML-DSA-65 and ML-DSA-87 as experimental ('Pure variant. Not yet fully functional.'), with the warning that they are currently not operational within Sigstore. This describes the page as read for the module.

chunks.title: Quiz: software-supply-chain-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: software-supply-chain-pqc

Q: Which statement about JOSE and COSE serializations for ML-DSA and for SLH-DSA matches the documents read in the module?
  A) Both are Standards Track RFCs published in May 2026
  B) Both are still Internet-Drafts, so neither is an RFC
  C) SLH-DSA has an RFC, while ML-DSA is still an Internet-Draft
  D) ML-DSA has an RFC (RFC 9964, Standards Track, May 2026), while SLH-DSA is in a working-group Internet-Draft that is not yet an RFC
Answer: D
Explanation: RFC 9964 (Standards Track, May 2026) specifies JOSE and COSE serializations for ML-DSA, a post-quantum digital signature scheme defined in FIPS 204. The serializations for SLH-DSA (FIPS 205) are in a working-group Internet-Draft, draft-ietf-cose-sphincs-plus-10 (28 July 2026); it is a draft and is not yet an RFC.

chunks.title: Quiz: software-supply-chain-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: software-supply-chain-pqc

Q: In TUF 1.0.37 every role requires a threshold of signatures from the role's keys. A role has five keys and a threshold of three, and an attacker has stolen two of the keys. Using only that rule, what follows?
  A) The attacker can already sign for that role alone, because one stolen key is enough
  B) The attacker cannot sign for that role alone yet; one more key would reach the threshold
  C) The attacker must hold all five keys before clients can be made to trust anything for that role
  D) The threshold applies only to the root role, so the two keys are enough for every other role
Answer: B
Explanation: TUF 1.0.37 says all roles can use one or more keys and require a threshold of signatures of the role's keys to trust a given metadata file. With a threshold of three, two stolen keys are one short, so the attacker cannot meet the role's threshold alone, and a third key would be enough. The counting is an application of the rule, not a figure from the specification. One of the specification's stated goals is that an attacker who compromises a single key, or fewer than a given threshold of keys, cannot compromise clients.

chunks.title: Quiz: software-supply-chain-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: software-supply-chain-pqc

Q: Which description of the TUF 1.0.37 root and timestamp keys matches the specification?
  A) The root role's private keys should be kept offline; the timestamp key must be kept online, and the risk to clients from its compromise is minimal
  B) Both the root role's private keys and the timestamp key must be kept offline, in the same secure storage
  C) The root role's private keys should be kept online so they can sign every update, while the timestamp key is kept offline
  D) Both must be kept online, because clients check the root and timestamp keys on every update
Answer: A
Explanation: TUF 1.0.37 says the root role's private keys must be kept very secure and so should be kept offline, and that the timestamp key must be kept online; even so, the risk posed to clients by the compromise of the timestamp key is minimal. The two roles are treated differently.

chunks.title: Quiz: software-supply-chain-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: software-supply-chain-pqc

Q: In Uptane 2.1.0, what does full verification of metadata compare, and which ECUs perform it?
  A) It compares the Root metadata held by the Primary ECU with the Root metadata held by each Secondary ECU; only Primary ECUs perform it
  B) It compares each image's hash with a list stored on the ECU at manufacture; Secondary ECUs shall and Primary ECUs should perform it
  C) It compares the Targets metadata about images from the Director repository with the Targets metadata about the same images from the Image repository; Primary ECUs shall and Secondary ECUs should perform it
  D) It compares the Director repository's clock with the Image repository's clock; every ECU shall perform it
Answer: C
Explanation: Uptane 2.1.0 (section 5.4.4.2): full verification of metadata means that the ECU checks that the Targets metadata about images from the Director repository matches the Targets metadata about the same images from the Image repository. The standard says this provides resilience to a key compromise in the system. Full verification shall be performed by Primary ECUs and should be performed by Secondary ECUs.

chunks.title: Quiz: software-supply-chain-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: software-supply-chain-pqc

Q: Select all that SLSA v1.2 says verification should include.
  A) Checking that the builder identity is one of the trusted builders
  B) Verifying the signature on the provenance envelope
  C) Checking buildType and externalParameters against expected values
  D) Confirming that the provenance is signed with a post-quantum algorithm
Answer: A|B|C
Explanation: The SLSA v1.2 page on verifying artifacts says verification should include checking that the builder identity is one of the trusted builders, verifying the signature on the provenance envelope, and checking buildType and externalParameters against expected values. It adds that a verifier's roots of trust are likely a map from the builder's public key identity and builder.id to a SLSA Build level. The text of that page names no signature algorithm and contains no post-quantum term, so it does not ask for one.

chunks.title: Quiz: software-supply-chain-pqc
chunks.content:
Quiz Category: software-supply-chain-pqc

Q: What does RFC 9019 (April 2021, Informational) say about unchangeable bootloader code in ROM?
  A) It must use RSA-2048 signatures so that every update server can verify them
  B) It may keep using ECC signatures indefinitely, because ROM code is never exposed to quantum computers
  C) It should be replaced over the air with post-quantum code whenever the manifest changes
  D) It is recommended to use post-quantum secure signature schemes such as hash-based signatures, because RSA and ECC signature schemes may become vulnerable to quantum-accelerated key extraction
Answer: D
Explanation: RFC 9019 says that, because signature schemes based on RSA and ECC may become vulnerable to quantum-accelerated key extraction in the future, unchangeable bootloader code in ROM is recommended to use post-quantum secure signature schemes such as hash-based signatures. It adds that a bootloader author must carefully consider the service lifetime of the product and the time horizon for quantum-accelerated key extraction. The wording is a recommendation in an Informational document.
