- Cited sources from the Library, Timeline, and Compliance pages

Deep-link share params (single-letter codes used to reconstruct a report from a URL): ?i=<industry>, ?cy=<country>, ?c=<currentCrypto>, ?d=<dataSensitivity>, ?f=<frameworks>, ?m=<migrationStatus>, ?u=<useCases>, ?r=<retention>, ?s=<systemCount>, ?t=<teamSize>, ?a=<agility>, ?n=<infrastructure>, ?v=<vendor>, ?p=<timelinePressure>.

If someone asks 'how do I get a PQC assessment report', 'view my report', 'show me my risk score', 'PQC executive report', or 'assessment results' — direct them to /report (after completing /assess).

chunks.title: PQC Today — Terms of Service
chunks.content:
PQC Today — Terms of Service

PQC Today has a dedicated Terms of Service page at /terms. The Terms cover:

1. Acceptance of Terms — using the platform constitutes agreement.
2. License — source code is licensed under GPL-3.0-only.
3. Educational Purpose & Cryptographic Disclaimer — all crypto operations are for educational and demonstration purposes only. Do not use generated keys for production systems.
4. Export Compliance & Sanctions — the platform embeds open-source cryptographic software classified under ECCN 5D002. Distribution is authorized under License Exception TSU (§740.13 EAR) and ENC (§740.17 EAR). Users in sanctioned countries (Cuba, Iran, North Korea, Syria, Crimea/Donetsk/Luhansk) are prohibited from accessing the platform.
5. Acceptable Use — no unlawful use, no misrepresentation, no interference.
6. No Warranty — provided 'as is' without warranties.
7. Limitation of Liability — maintainers not liable for damages.
8. Third-Party Content — references NIST, ETSI, IETF, BSI, ANSSI, ISO/IEC, Common Criteria. Not affiliated with or endorsed by these organizations.
9. Intellectual Property — source code GPL-3.0; original content copyright PQC Today maintainers.
10. Privacy and Analytics — no user accounts and no server of its own that processes your data; all cryptography runs in the browser. Google Analytics 4 runs on every visit and records page views and interaction events (typed search text is scrubbed of email addresses, web addresses, IP addresses and long key-like strings before it is sent); it sets cookies, and Google also receives the visitor's IP address. Analytics are off on localhost and can be blocked with a content blocker for google-analytics.com, by blocking cookies for the site, or with Google's opt-out browser add-on. Preferences and progress stay in the browser (localStorage). Chat messages go to Google only in the PQC Assistant's cloud (Gemini) mode, with the user's own API key; the Local LLM mode keeps everything in the browser.
11. Modifications — terms may be updated; continued use constitutes acceptance.
12. Governing Law — State of Texas, United States.
13. Contact — via GitHub Discussions.

For full details, visit the Terms of Service page: /terms

If someone asks about 'terms of use', 'terms of service', 'legal terms', 'privacy policy', 'data privacy', 'license', 'export controls', 'ECCN', 'sanctions', or 'acceptable use' — direct them to the Terms of Service page at /terms.

chunks.title: Global Migration Timeline — User Guide
chunks.content:
Global Migration Timeline

Compare post-quantum cryptography migration roadmaps across nations and track phases from discovery to full migration.

Region & Country Filters: Use the region dropdown to filter by Americas, EU, APAC, or Global. Select a specific country to see its migration phases highlighted on the Gantt chart. Filters sync with the URL so you can share filtered views.

Gantt Chart: Each row represents a country. Colored bars show migration phases (Research, Planning, Early Adoption, Transition, Full Migration). Hover over a bar to see phase dates and details. Click a row to expand milestones.

Export & Sharing: Use the Export button in the header to download the full timeline dataset as CSV. The Share button copies a deep link to your current filtered view.

Sources & Endorsements: Click Sources to see the authoritative government documents behind each data point. Use the Endorse/Flag buttons to provide community feedback on data accuracy.

Tips:
- Bookmark a filtered URL to quickly return to a specific region view.

chunks.title: PQC Algorithms — User Guide
chunks.content:
PQC Algorithms

Learn how post-quantum algorithms differ, explore candidate transition paths, inspect evidence, and run scoped implementation checks.

Transition Tab: Shows candidate migration paths from classical algorithms (RSA, ECDH, ECDSA) to post-quantum algorithms (ML-KEM, ML-DSA, SLH-DSA and others). Each row shows the classical algorithm on the left and a candidate migration path on the right, with region, publication status and transition timing. A row is educational context, not a drop-in replacement or a compliance determination.

Detailed Comparison Tab: Deep-dive into algorithms in a sortable table covering security levels, key/ciphertext/signature sizes, catalogue estimates, and reviewed use cases. Toggle Browse ↔ Compare mode. Baselines help explain size differences; they are not universal performance rankings. Filter by crypto family, function group, or security level.

Compare Panel: Select up to 3 algorithms to compare side-by-side. Click the compare icon on algorithm cards to add them to the comparison bar at the bottom of the page. The panel shows a detailed table comparing all properties.

URL Parameters: Deep link to specific views: ?tab=transition|detailed|support|landscape|validation, ?family=, ?fn=, ?level=, ?region=, ?status= and ?q= to filter, ?quickview=nist-picks|final-nist-standards|none (the older fips-validated value still opens Final NIST standards), ?mode=compare for the Detailed tab, ?section=attacks|kat|coverage for the Validation tab, ?protocol=<id> to open a Protocol Support row, ?industry= for the Landscape tab, ?highlight= to highlight algorithms, ?transition=<row> to open and highlight one Transition Guide row, ?compare= for pre-selected comparisons. On the Protocol Support tab: ?matrixView=detailed, ?matrixQ=, ?matrixStatus=, ?matrixAvailability=, ?matrixSort=key:direction. Use the Share button to copy a link to your current selection.

Tips:
- Use the Detailed tab filters to quickly narrow down algorithms by security level or standardization status.
- The compare panel is great for preparing algorithm selection reports.
- Toggle Browse ↔ Compare mode on the Detailed tab, or open the Validation tab for implementation attacks and live KAT tests.

chunks.title: PQC Library — User Guide
chunks.content:
PQC Library

Search and browse 1,200+ post-quantum cryptography standards, drafts, RFCs, and reference documents from NIST, IETF, ETSI, and other organizations.

Search & Filters: Type in the search bar to search across titles, descriptions, and tags. Use the category sidebar to filter across 13 categories (Digital Signature, KEM, PKI Certificate Management, Protocols, Government & Policy, NIST Standards, International Frameworks, Migration Guidance, Algorithm Specifications, Industry & Research, Compliance & Certification, Blockchain Standards, Implementations). Filter by organization or industry. Persona-aware category boosting surfaces the most relevant categories for your role.

View Toggle: Switch between Card view and Tree Table view using the toggle in the toolbar. Card view shows document summaries; Tree Table groups documents by category with sortable columns.

Document Details: Click any document card to see full details including abstract, status, dependencies, related standards, and a direct link to the source. Documents with local cached copies show a preview icon.

Activity Feed: The activity feed shows recently added or updated documents. New and Updated badges appear on documents that changed since the previous data version.

Tips:
- Use the URL parameter ?ref=REFERENCE_ID to deep-link directly to a specific document.
- Export the full library as CSV for offline analysis or reporting.
- URL params: ?ref= opens a document; ?cat=, ?org=, ?sector=, ?q=, ?sort=, ?view=cards|table are all combinable for shareable filtered views.

chunks.title: Interactive Playground — User Guide
chunks.content:
Interactive Playground

Generate real post-quantum cryptographic keys, encrypt data, and sign messages directly in your browser using WebAssembly. 34 workshop tools, an interactive crypto lab, and a full PKCS#11 HSM emulator — all running locally.

Workshop Grid: The main /playground view shows a searchable catalog of 34 workshop tools across 7 categories: HSM / PKCS#11, Entropy & Random, Certificates & Proofs, Protocol Simulations, Blockchain & Digital Assets, Digital Identity, and OpenSSL Studio (includes TLS 1.3 Simulator). Persona-aware filtering highlights recommended tools with difficulty badges (beginner/intermediate/advanced).

Interactive Crypto Lab: The /playground/interactive route provides 7 tabs: Key Store (keypair generation), Data (hex editor), KEM & Encrypt (ML-KEM + X25519 ECDH), Sym Encrypt (AES/ChaCha), Hash (SHA/SHAKE), Sign & Verify (PQC + classical), and Logs (operation history). Use ?tab= to deep-link to specific operations.

HSM Playground: The /playground/hsm route emulates a PKCS#11 v3.2 HSM via SoftHSMv3 WASM with 10 tabs: Keystore, Symmetric, Key Wrap, Hashing, Sign/Verify, Key Agreement, Key Derivation, Mechanisms, Validation (mixed-evidence workbench: selected NIST ACVP-Server reference samples, standard KATs, oracle and functional tests), and Logs. Supports C++, Rust, and Dual engine modes with parity cross-check.

Individual Tools: Each workshop tool has its own route at /playground/:toolId with lazy-loaded components, breadcrumb navigation, and community endorse/flag buttons.

Tips:
- All generated keys are for educational purposes only — not for production use.
- The Logs tab records every operation with timestamps for review.
- Use the SoftHSM tab to understand how real HSMs handle PQC operations via PKCS#11.

chunks.title: OpenSSL Studio — User Guide
chunks.content:
OpenSSL Studio

Interactive OpenSSL v3.6.3 environment running entirely in your browser via WebAssembly. Build and execute real OpenSSL commands with a visual workbench.

Command Categories: Select a command category from the top menu: genpkey (key generation), req (certificate requests), x509 (certificates), enc (encryption), dgst (digests), hash, rand (random), kem (key encapsulation), and more.

Workbench: The workbench provides a file manager and code editor. Upload or create input files, edit command parameters, and see the generated OpenSSL command. Click Run to execute against the in-browser OpenSSL instance.

Terminal Output: Command output appears in the terminal panel below the workbench. View generated keys, certificates, and operation results. Collapsible sections help navigate long outputs.

File Viewer: Generated files (keys, certificates, CSRs) appear in the file manager. Click to inspect file contents, copy to clipboard, or use them as inputs for subsequent commands.

Tips:
- Use the URL parameter ?cmd= to deep-link to a specific command category.
- Start with genpkey to generate a PQC key, then use req to create a certificate request.
- The Logs tab shows raw OpenSSL output for debugging.

chunks.title: Quantum Threats — User Guide
chunks.content:
Quantum Threats

Explore industry-specific threat analysis showing which cryptographic assets are at risk from quantum computers and the recommended PQC replacements.

Industry Filters: Filter threats by industry using the multi-select dropdown — select multiple industries simultaneously (e.g., Finance + Healthcare). Each industry shows its specific threat landscape and affected cryptographic protocols. A persona-aware summary card highlights the most impactful threats for your role.

Criticality & Search: Filter by criticality level (Critical, High, Medium-High, Medium, Low) to focus on the most urgent threats. Use the search bar to find threats by keyword across all fields.

Threat Details: Click any threat card to expand full details: affected algorithms, at-risk protocols, timeline to quantum risk, recommended PQC replacements, trust score badges, and references to compliance frameworks.

Sort Options: Sort threats by industry, threat ID, or criticality level. The default view groups threats by industry with the most critical items first. URL params: ?industry= (comma-separated), ?criticality=, ?q=, ?sort=, ?dir=, ?id=.

Tips:
- Use Endorse/Flag buttons to provide community feedback on threat assessments.
- Threats link to related compliance frameworks — click through to see requirements.

chunks.title: PQC Leaders — User Guide
chunks.content:
PQC Leaders

Discover the organizations and experts driving post-quantum cryptography adoption worldwide, organized by region, sector, and leadership category.

Region & Sector Filters: Filter by region (Americas, EU, Asia-Pacific) with country drill-down, or by sector (Public, Private, Academic). Use the category sidebar to browse by leadership type.

View Toggle: Switch between Card view (visual profile cards) and Table view (sortable columns). Both views support the same filtering and search capabilities.

Leader Details: Click a leader card to see their full profile: organization, contributions to PQC, key publications, and links to related library resources. 330+ leaders are currently profiled.

Search: Search by name, organization, or keyword to quickly find specific leaders or organizations. Results update in real-time as you type.

Tips:
- Leader profiles link to related documents in the Library via their Key Resource URLs.
- Use the consent/removal form to submit corrections or request profile removal.

chunks.title: Compliance Frameworks — User Guide
chunks.content:
Compliance Frameworks

Use this educational reference to learn which rules, standards and certification records may be relevant to a country and sector, why they were included, what their sources say about post-quantum cryptography, and the dates they state. It is not a GRC system, legal advice, an applicability decision or proof of compliance. The page has eight views: Rules & Standards, Sources & Practices, Progress, Products, Landscape, Product Records, For You and CSWP.39 Agility.

Eight Views: The tab bar has eight views: Rules & Standards, Sources & Practices, Progress, Products, Landscape, Product Records, For You and CSWP.39 Agility. Rules & Standards opens first for most roles, and operations roles open on Progress. A link that carries a certificate, a source passage, a product or a CSWP.39 reference opens the view it belongs to. On a narrow screen the tab bar scrolls sideways.

Rules & Standards, Sources & Practices and Progress: Rules & Standards lists instruments associated with the selected country and sector, why each one was included, and what its source says about post-quantum cryptography. Each item carries a tier (Binding, Relevant / recognized, Cross-border, Advisory, Related via IR 8477 or Informational) from the same educational applicability model as For You. Binding requires a reviewed binding status and a stated basis; an issuer match alone is not enough, and the site does not decide whether an instrument applies to a real organisation. Sources & Practices shows machine-extracted source passages, where they appear and which model extracted them. Verify the primary passage and obtain the appropriate legal or assurance review before treating it as an obligation. Progress compares dates stated by scoped sources; a date does not by itself prove implementation is overdue.

Products and Product Records: Products maps the inventory you keep on Migrate to reviewed evidence. It distinguishes NIST CAVP/ACVP algorithm validation, FIPS 140 module validation, and algorithms named in evaluated-product documentation; those evidence classes are not interchangeable. Product Records is a searchable snapshot of NIST CMVP module validations, NIST CAVP algorithm validations, NIST entropy source validations (the Entropy (ESV) tab), Common Criteria and EUCC certificates, and ANSSI CSPN certificates. Search by product, vendor or type, filter by source and status, and use the source and freshness fields before relying on a record. A link with ?cert= opens one specific record.

Landscape: Landscape lays the field out as a chain of three groups. Standardization Bodies define the algorithms and publish the standards. Certification Schemes (FIPS 140-3, ACVP, Common Criteria, EUCC) test that products implement them correctly. Compliance Frameworks (for example CNSA 2.0, NIS2 and DORA) set the requirements and deadlines. Switch between the three groups at the top, filter by organization, industry or search, and sort by name, deadline or finish date.

For You and CSWP.39 Agility: For You presents standards, threats, library documents and timeline milestones associated with the selected industry, country and region, tuned by the role selected in the top bar. The executive CSV is a learning worksheet, not an audit or management register. CSWP.39 Agility presents a PQC Today learning sequence based on NIST CSWP 39, with links to the source PDF and related Learn module; its steps are not NIST’s section structure.

Framework Details: Click any framework to open its details drawer: source and trust information, a Learn this link, the traceability chain, deadline phases, and related and overlapping frameworks.

Tips:
- Framework entries cross-reference both Library documents and Timeline milestones.
- Old links still work: ?tab=standards, ?tab=certification and ?tab=compliance open Landscape.
- URL params: ?tab=obligations|requirements|progress|products|foryou|records|cswp39 chooses a view; ?framework=<id> opens a framework, ?cert=<id> a certification record, ?reqfw=<id> a framework in Requirements, ?prod=<id> a product, ?evref= a CSWP.39 reference; ?org=, ?ind=, ?q= and ?mcat= filter.

chunks.title: Migration Workbench — User Guide
chunks.content:
Migration Workbench

Browse 880+ PQC-ready software products organized across 9 infrastructure layers with certification cross-references and migration planning tools.

Infrastructure Layer Stack: Products are organized across 9 layers: Cloud, Network, Application Servers, Libraries & SDKs, Security Software, Database, Security Stack, Operating Systems, and Hardware & Secure Elements. Click a layer to filter. The stack shows readiness counts per layer.

Product Search & Filters: Search by product name or vendor. Filter by infrastructure layer, category, sub-category, vendor, verification status, and migration step. Persona-based recommendations highlight relevant layers. URL params: ?product=<product id> opens one product, ?productIds= lists several, ?tab=replace|plan|roadmaps|vendorrisk picks a tab, and ?tab=roadmaps&vendor=<vendor id> opens a vendor roadmap.

Product Details: Click any product to see its full migration profile: current PQC support, migration timeline, certification status (FIPS 140-3/CAVP/CC cross-references), vendor links, and product briefs.

My Products & Comparison: Add products to your comparison list using the bookmark icon. The "My Products" panel lets you compare up to 3 products side-by-side via the sticky compare bar.

View Modes: Three view modes: Stack (grouped by infrastructure layer, default), Cards (flat grid), and Table (sortable columns). Hidden products can be managed via the settings icon.

Tips:
- Hidden products can be managed via the settings icon — useful for excluding irrelevant entries.
- Certification cross-references link directly to the Compliance page for each product.
- Community members can submit product update requests via the contribution cards.

chunks.title: Risk Assessment — User Guide
chunks.content:
Risk Assessment

Complete a guided assessment wizard to evaluate your organization's PQC readiness. Choose Quick (6 steps, ~3 min) or Comprehensive (13 steps, ~5 min) mode.

Assessment Modes: Quick mode covers 6 essential questions (Industry, Country, Crypto, Sensitivity, Compliance, Migration) for a rapid readiness check. Comprehensive mode adds 7 deeper steps: Use Cases, Data Retention, Credential Lifetime, Organization Scale, Crypto Agility, Infrastructure, and Timeline Pressure.

13 Comprehensive Steps: Industry → Country → Crypto Stack → Data Sensitivity → Compliance → Migration Status → Use Cases → Data Retention → Credential Lifetime → Organization Scale → Crypto Agility → Infrastructure → Timeline Pressure. Four risk categories scored: Strategic, Operational, Compliance, and Vendor.

Progress & Navigation: A progress bar shows your position in the wizard. You can navigate back to previous steps to change answers. Your progress is saved automatically — you can leave and resume later.

Results: After completing the assessment, you are directed to the Report page with personalized recommendations based on your answers. The assessment also pre-filters other pages (Compliance, Migrate) for your context.

Tips:
- Your assessment data persists in localStorage — it survives page refreshes.
- Persona-based mode recommendations appear on the mode selector to help you choose.

chunks.title: Readiness Report — User Guide
chunks.content:
Readiness Report

View your personalized PQC readiness report generated from your assessment responses, with actionable recommendations and links to relevant resources.

Report Overview: The report summarizes your PQC readiness across multiple dimensions: risk level, compliance gaps, migration priority, and recommended next steps. Includes Board Brief, KPI Trending, Migration Roadmap, ROI Calculator, and HNDL/HNFL risk window analysis.

Recommendations: Each section includes specific, actionable recommendations tailored to your industry, country, and cryptographic stack. Persona-aware CTAs adapt the report sections to your role. Recommendations link to relevant pages (Compliance, Migrate, Library) for deeper exploration.

URL Hydration & Sharing: Reports can be shared via URL parameters encoding your assessment context (?i=industry, ?cy=country, ?c=crypto, ?d=sensitivity, ?f=frameworks, etc.). Recipients see the same personalized view. Supports Print/PDF output.

Navigation & History: Action buttons link directly to pre-filtered views on the Compliance and Migrate pages. Assessment snapshots provide historical tracking of readiness changes over time.

Tips:
- Complete the Assessment wizard first for the most accurate report.
- Share the report URL with colleagues — it encodes your assessment context.

chunks.title: Command Center — User Guide
chunks.content:
Command Center

Your PQC readiness command center for managing risk artifacts, compliance documents, governance plans, vendor evaluations, and action items.

Getting Started: The welcome state shows CTA buttons to begin: Risk Assessment, Compliance Review, and Executive Learning Track. Complete the assessment first to populate your context banner with industry and country.

Artifact Sections: Five sections organize your work: Risk Management, Compliance & Regulatory, Governance, Vendor/Supply Chain, and Action Items. Each section contains artifact cards that you can create, edit, and manage.

Artifact Drawer: Click any artifact card or the "New" button to open the artifact drawer. Write and edit documents with rich text. Artifacts are saved to localStorage and persist across sessions.

Filter & Export: Filter artifacts by type using the dropdown. Export all artifacts as a ZIP file for offline use or to share with your team.

Tips:
- Complete the Assessment wizard to populate the context banner with your industry and country.
- The Learning Bar at the bottom links to relevant executive learning modules.

chunks.title: Learning Center — User Guide
chunks.content:
Learning Center

Structured PQC education with 73 interactive modules covering PKI fundamentals, quantum threats, hybrid cryptography, industry-specific topics, and hands-on workshops.

Module Tracks: Modules are organized into nine tracks: Foundations, Strategy, Protocols, Hardware Infrastructure, Software Infrastructure, Applications, Industries, Executive and Role Guides. Use the sidebar or dashboard to browse by track.

Module Tabs: Each module opens on Learn (the lessons). Depending on the module it also has Visual, Workshop (hands-on exercises), Exercises, References and Tools & Products tabs.

Progress Tracking: The sidebar shows completion status for each module with checkmarks. Your progress is saved automatically. The dashboard view shows overall track completion percentages.

Navigation: Use the Previous/Next buttons to navigate between lesson steps within a module. The "Next Module" CTA appears when you complete a module to guide you to the recommended next topic.

Achievements: Earn achievement badges as you complete modules, tracks, and milestones. Achievement toasts appear when you unlock new badges. View your full collection in the progress dashboard.

Tips:
- Start with the Foundations track if you are new to PQC.
- Workshop exercises use real WASM-based crypto — all operations run locally in your browser.
- The quiz module tests your knowledge across all tracks.

chunks.title: Frequently Asked Questions — User Guide
chunks.content:
Frequently Asked Questions

Browse common questions about post-quantum cryptography, the PQC Today platform, and how to get started with your migration planning.

Category Navigation: Questions are organized by category with quick-link navigation pills at the top. Click a category pill to jump directly to that section.

Search: Use the search bar to filter questions across all categories. Multi-term search is supported — results match any word in both questions and answers.

Deep Links: Each answer includes direct links to relevant app pages and features for further exploration.

Tips:
- Can't find your answer? Use the "Ask the PQC Assistant" button at the bottom to chat with the AI assistant.

chunks.title: PQC Today v4.193.0 — Release Notes (2026-11-01)
chunks.content:
Version 4.193.0 released 2026-11-01.

The Protocol Support Matrix catches up with the IETF's October decisions and gains a row for EDHOC, another round of lesson statements, quiz questions and data rows is corrected to follow its documents, and five certification lessons show the owner's review again.

### Added

Its pure post-quantum key exchange and ML-DSA signature cells are working-group drafts; the hybrid cells are marked as not yet defined.
- **Four new IETF drafts in the Library**: composite ML-DSA authentication for TLS 1.3, composite-signature authentication for IKEv2, post-quantum KEMs for COSE, and KEM-based authentication for EDHOC, with their details completed.

COSE lists the post-quantum KEM draft next to its HPKE registrations, and Kerberos notes the KITTEN working group's call for adoption of the PKINIT draft. The X.509 and CMS rows and the IKEv2 key-exchange row say that working-group drafts define FrodoKEM and that FrodoKEM is not a NIST-standardised algorithm.

chunks.title: PQC Today v4.192.0 — Release Notes (2026-11-01)
chunks.content:
Version 4.192.0 released 2026-11-01.

Hybrid cryptography gets a fuller lesson and a Migrate filter, the Executive Overview simulation is reworked, and the last line-by-line reading fixes land: 102 more lesson statements and 12 quiz questions now follow their sources or are marked as the lesson's own advice.

### Added

- **Hybrid Cryptography lesson: risks, who recommends hybrid, key combiners and crypto APIs**: new sections cover the risks of hybrid versus pure post-quantum, who recommends hybrid, how key combiners compare (including X-Wing), and how hybrid is handled in crypto APIs and HSMs. The workshop has a Hybrid KEM step with a combiner comparison, and the lesson has eight more quiz questions. The workshop steps were reordered, so a saved link that names a step number may now open a different step.
- **Migrate shows hybrid support in crypto libraries**: crypto libraries carry hybrid key-exchange and composite-signature support badges, with a filter, each backed by the vendor's own page (17 libraries: OpenSSL, BoringSSL, AWS-LC, Go, rustls, Bouncy Castle, SymCrypt, Windows 11, Windows Server 2025, .NET 10, Java 27, LibreSSL, oqs-provider, CIRCL and NSS). Fourteen products now have a category, and LibreSSL, oqs-provider, CIRCL and NSS show their current versions.
- **48 new Library documents for the hybrid lessons**: the documents the new hybrid sections cite, including the X-Wing and CFRG hybrid drafts, the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security guidance, and the NSS, rustls and Bouncy Castle release notes, with their details completed.
- **Executive Overview simulation reworked**: the standard and deep routes keep all ten chapters, including Foundations, sample labels are preserved, and playback resumes at chapter boundaries on desktop and phone. The sample bank journey puts discovery before programme estimates and keeps services, costing and proposed milestones consistent; its assumptions are kept apart from established costs, and the example private bank no longer inherits federal deadlines. Execu…

chunks.title: PQC Today v4.191.0 — Release Notes (2026-11-01)
chunks.content:
Version 4.191.0 released 2026-11-01.

The next part of the line-by-line reading: 34 more lesson sentences and 32 quiz questions follow their documents, including several that needed a person's decision.

### Changed

- **More Learn lesson sentences keep to what their documents say**: across 18 lessons, including Standards Bodies, Product Certification, Quantum Threats, Executive Quantum Impact, Secure Boot, Payment Card and Verification Closure, a further 34 sentences that no cited document supports were removed, rewritten to say what the source says, or marked as the lesson's own reading or advice. The Standards Bodies card for the PQUIP working group now describes what its charter says and names its published guidance document (RFC 9958); the NSA CNSA 2.0 lines say the 2030 dates are an anticipated timetable; the Quantum Threats note on IBM's Nighthawk chip follows IBM's announcement; the FIPS 140-3 Level 3 physical-security line names tamper detection and response and environmental failure protection; and the Secure Boot lesson now says the EDK2 ML-DSA pull request was closed without merging in favour of a newer one.
- **More quiz questions stay within their sources**: 32 quiz questions were corrected. The IBM Kookaburra question no longer states a qubit count that no document gives. The OpenPGP question now reflects RFC 9980, which defines ML-DSA for OpenPGP only combined with Ed25519 or Ed448. The code-signing question now asks which secret most urgently needs a post-quantum plan, because NIST says signatures are not vulnerable to harvest-now-decrypt-later attacks. The EUDI Wallet question names the private services that must accept wallets and labels its calendar dates as the lesson's own reading. The memory-encryption answer no longer says every VM gets its own key, the HSM question now cites the FIPS 204 publication date and a FIPS 140-3 Level 3 certificate that lists ML-DSA, the NIST SP 800-227 answer no longer says NIST recommends hybrid key exchange, and the Linux FIPS-mode answer now follows…

chunks.title: PQC Today v4.190.0 — Release Notes (2026-10-31)
chunks.content:
Version 4.190.0 released 2026-10-31.

The next part of the line-by-line reading that could be finished safely: 25 more lesson sentences, 47 quiz questions and 19 HSM comparison notes follow their documents.

### Changed

- **More Learn lesson sentences keep to what their documents say**: across 19 lessons, including the Secrets Management, Key Management, Standards Bodies, Secure Boot, Healthcare and Entropy lessons, a further 25 sentences that no cited document supports were removed, rewritten to say what the source says, or marked as the lesson's own reading or assumption.
- **More quiz questions stay within their sources**: 47 quiz questions were corrected. In 45 of them the explanation lost a claim that no document supports, says what the source says, or is marked as this lesson's own reading. The IBM Kookaburra question no longer states a qubit count that no document gives, and the intrusion-detection question's answer option names the ML-KEM-768 group code the source gives (0x0201) and no longer lists browser versions that no document supports.

- **HSM comparison notes keep to their sources**: 19 evidence notes in the HSM comparison table (Futurex, Utimaco, Entrust nShield, Thales Luna, Marvell LiquidSecurity 2, Crypto4A and Google Cloud HSM) now keep only what the vendor pages, release notes, NIST certificate pages and security policies say; statements no document supports were taken out and two dates were corrected.

### Fixed

chunks.title: PQC Today v4.174.0 — Release Notes (2026-10-23)
chunks.content:
Version 4.174.0 released 2026-10-23.

Rosenpass and WireGuard are now described correctly across the Learn modules, the Library, the product catalogue and the glossary, the VPN simulator says clearly when it is not ready, and the Migrate page gains a Vulnerabilities tab with refreshed data for cryptographic libraries.

### Added

- **A Vulnerabilities tab on the Migrate page**: after "Evidence gaps", it lists the known vulnerabilities (CVEs) for the products you selected, the top 20 per product at Medium severity and above, with a link to the full NVD list. Products whose data was refreshed after the snapshot show a "refreshed" date. With nothing selected it points back to the Replace tab. It is shown on desktop; the Business Center tool is unchanged.

### Fixed

- **Rosenpass uses Classic McEliece and Kyber-512, not ML-KEM**: the VPN and SSH module, its Q&A, the glossary, the protocol table, the Library entry and the product catalogue now say that Rosenpass pairs Classic McEliece 460896 with the pre-standard round-3 Kyber-512, not the standardized ML-KEM of FIPS 203. Its message sizes come from its white paper (four messages, 2,464 bytes in total) and WireGuard's normal handshake is 240 bytes (148 + 92) from WireGuard's own paper; the earlier 6,800-byte and "22x" figures had no source and are removed. WireGuard's catalogue entry now says the protocol has no post-quantum algorithm of its own and that Rosenpass supplies it.
- **OpenSSH and strongSwan hybrid key exchange details corrected**: OpenSSH made sntrup761x25519 its default from 9.0, added mlkem768x25519-sha256 in 9.9 and made it the default in 10.0; strongSwan's configuration uses the mlkem768 prefix. Planning timeframes in the Operations lesson are now marked as estimates, and the certificate size comparison is tied to its worked example. The Hybrid Cryptography summary now names RFC 10024 for hybrid TLS.
- **The 2030 RSA and ECC deprecation date names its document**: the Migration Program lesson attributes the date to the NIST IR 8547 initial p…

chunks.title: PQC Today v4.173.0 — Release Notes (2026-10-23)
chunks.content:
Version 4.173.0 released 2026-10-23.

A new lesson in Common Criteria, EUCC & eIDAS Certification explains what NIAP's protection profiles offer and require for post-quantum cryptography, and 15 NIAP documents join the Library.

### Added

- **A lesson on NIAP and post-quantum cryptography**: "NIAP and post-quantum cryptography: what its profiles require" leads with the Dedicated Security Component profile, explains that NIAP's Technical Decisions add the CNSA rule for the Product Compliant List so post-quantum is one allowed route rather than the only one, separates a NIAP certificate from a CMVP module certificate, and ends with questions to put to the lab. A table lists the 11 NIAP documents that carry post-quantum selections beside the classical ones, with the algorithms, the classical choices still allowed, the date NIAP shows for each and a quote from each. Passages that are the module's own reading are marked "Module analysis". The Common Criteria path goes from 70 to 76 minutes and the module from 60 to 66; the role learning-path totals follow.
- **15 NIAP documents in the Library**: the protection profiles and modules for dedicated security components (with their Supporting Document), network devices, general-purpose computing platforms, full-drive encryption, virtualization, VPN clients, hardcopy devices and file encryption; NIAP Technical Decisions 1010, 1011 and 1064; and NIAP's announcements notice on its Policy 33 decisions.

### Changed

- **Patents in the certification engineer's main page list**: certification engineers now see Patents in their main page list, next to Leaders, instead of only under More.
- **Recent Library entries show their key details**: NIAP's Protection Profile for Application Software v2.0 (published 16 June 2025) and the FS-ISAC paper on post-quantum risk in ATM and card-terminal PIN handling now carry a description, publisher, region, category and urgency taken from the documents themselves, instead of appearing as unverified entries. NIAP's Policy Letter 26 and …

chunks.title: PQC Today v4.172.0 — Release Notes (2026-10-23)
chunks.content:
Version 4.172.0 released 2026-10-23.

Three new lessons for certification engineers explain what a FIPS 140-3 certificate shows about side-channel and fault attacks, how a hybrid appears in a certificate's scope, and what carries over to a new platform. The change analyzer's Common Criteria and EUCC answers are corrected.

### Added

- **A lesson on side-channel and fault attacks in FIPS 140-3**: it explains that non-invasive security has no CMVP test metrics yet, what a lab does check under "Mitigation of other attacks", where attack testing does exist (Common Criteria vulnerability analysis) and what to ask a vendor. Passages that are the module's own reading of the sources are marked "Module analysis". Study time goes from 60 to 65 minutes.
- **Two lessons on hybrids and new platforms in Cryptographic Product Certification**: "Reading a hybrid in a certificate's scope" maps each part of a hybrid key exchange to where it shows on paper and what is tested; "A new platform, chip or accelerator: what carries over?" covers vendor affirmation, the operational environment, revalidation, processor acceleration and the Common Criteria view. Study time goes from 90 to 95 minutes, and the role learning-path totals follow.

### Fixed

- **The change analyzer answers Common Criteria and EUCC cases correctly**: adding ML-KEM is shown as a typical major change under Common Criteria and EUCC, beside the CMVP answer that now uses the Management Manual's own limits (under 30% overall and no category above 30%). Random number generator, tamper-sensor, new isolation and exploitable-vulnerability changes are shown as major, the FIPS enclosure route is limited to enclosure-only changes with no operational impact, the FPGA case names the bitstream and hardware-description rules, and an Intel-to-Arm move is rated as ENISA rates it.
- **The CCRA assurance-continuity document is named CCDB-015**: the lessons called it CCDB-014; its own front page gives 015. The document and its links are unchanged.

chunks.title: PQC Today v4.171.0 — Release Notes (2026-10-23)
chunks.content:
Version 4.171.0 released 2026-10-23.

The certification engineer journey now follows what the standards and vendors actually say: wrong statements in the Learn modules, quizzes and answers are corrected against their sources, the Product Records and validation workbench pages are easier to read, and HSM post-quantum statements are re-checked against each vendor's newest release notes.

### Added

- **"What the lab tests" panels and real NIST test cases in the certification modules**: Stateful Signatures, SLH-DSA, Secure Boot and HSM PQC show which checks a validation lab runs, and a hybrid panel explains what the validated-module guidance allows. The SLH-DSA, LMS, ML-KEM and ML-DSA known-answer panels replay published NIST cases through the in-browser engines, and the remaining round trips are labelled as round trips.
- **A new Library paper on card and PIN handling**: the post-quantum PCI use cases for ATMs and point-of-sale devices, with three matching maturity requirements for terminal keys, device certificates and boot code.

### Changed

- **Product Records open on the search and the table**: the page says plainly that the table is a snapshot, labels retrieval dates in UTC, shows a one-line PQC summary on phones, and no longer shows an internal identifier as a Common Criteria certificate number.
- **The validation workbench opens with one algorithm family ticked**: it explains what "test groups" and "test cases" mean, fits its results table to the panel, and lets you filter result rows by status and by evidence class.
- **The certification engineer path is shorter and its page matches it**: PQC Network Testing leaves the six essentials (it stays on the full path with a short certification route), Product Certification shows its measured 90-minute duration, the module header shows the duration of the path you are on, the Standards Bodies module is optional orientation at the start, and the "Testing & validation" line on the role page states the real order of the path.

chunks.title: PQC Today v4.170.0 — Release Notes (2026-10-23)
chunks.content:
Version 4.170.0 released 2026-10-23.

The certification engineer journey has been reviewed source by source and its five certification modules were reviewed end to end: its Learn modules, Library entries, Timeline milestones, maturity requirements and citations now match the current standards and documents. The browser HSM gains a PKCS#11 v3.3 working-draft track and more ACVP test coverage, certificate records are refreshed, and the Sources panel links each source to its trusted-source record.

### Added

- **A PKCS#11 v3.3 (working draft) lesson track in the browser HSM**: six lessons run real PKCS#11 calls for composite ML-DSA and ML-KEM, external µ, signatures remaining on stateful keys, and renamed identifiers. Each lesson has a quiz, glossary terms and plain-English log lines. The draft is unpublished, and the engine still reports Cryptoki 3.2.0.
- **A v3.3 test bench and a separate "v3.3 draft features" compliance group**: pick any of the 30 composite parameter sets and run IETF LAMPS known-answer checks in the browser. Draft results are kept apart from the v3.2 profile results, and the key inspector and PKCS#11 log decode composite keys, ciphertexts and signatures.
- **The ACVP lab runs the NIST test groups that need an optional test input**: deterministic ML-DSA and SLH-DSA signing with a given random value, internal verification, and ML-KEM encapsulation with a given seed now run through a clearly marked test-only extension. All 909 cases pass on both browser engines, and a new lesson section explains why a production module must never accept these inputs.
- **Ten new Library entries for certification work**: the SOG-IS notice on the end of national certificates under the agreement (27 February 2026), the ECCG Agreed Cryptographic Mechanisms v3 draft, composite ML-KEM draft -23, RFC 10042, RFC 9955, RFC 10033, the COSE HPKE post-quantum draft, Google's Chrome ML-KEM post and two PCI SSC posts.
- **A France milestone for buying products with PQC from 2030**: ANSSI's FAQ advises that from 2030 i…

chunks.title: PQC Today v4.168.0 — Release Notes (2026-10-18)
chunks.content:
Version 4.168.0 released 2026-10-18.

The repository entry point now reflects the current educational product, its evidence boundaries and its actual maintenance process. Generated facts and documentation checks prevent release, dataset and navigation claims from silently becoming stale again.

### Changed

- **The project guide now starts learners and contributors in the right place**: the README replaces its historical feature ledger with role-specific routes, clear browser and optional-service boundaries, reproducible setup instructions and the explicit statement that PQC Today is an education and demonstration platform rather than a production cryptographic, certification or GRC system.
- **Published evidence follows the official-source boundary**: repository guidance now explains that public records retain official publisher URLs and reviewed educational extractions without publishing downloaded third-party documents or private maintenance artifacts.

### Fixed

- **Repository facts can no longer drift silently**: release, module, catalogue, glossary and assistant-corpus figures are derived from the committed sources. Local and pull-request checks reject stale figures, broken repository links, product routes that would misdirect GitHub readers and superseded claims about GRC, scraping, archives or unfinished-tool badges.
- **Testing guidance matches the gates that actually run**: the contributor and testing guides now distinguish fast pre-push checks, full local suites, the final release gate and manual KMIP/CACP checks without promising repeated work that is not wired into the workflow.

chunks.title: PQC Today v4.167.0 — Release Notes (2026-10-18)
chunks.content:
Version 4.167.0 released 2026-10-18.

The browser Playground and Business Tools now tell learners what each result represents, what it can establish, and where an educational demonstration or planning artifact stops short of certification, compliance, approval or production evidence. Role journeys, phone layouts, standards references, exports and exercises follow the same evidence-first model.

### Changed

- **Every browser tool explains the strength of its evidence**: cards and tool pages identify real cryptographic execution, protocol models, calculators and simulations before learners interpret a result. Certification-shaped experiences state that a local pass is not an ACVP, CAVP, CMVP or product-certification verdict, and downloaded run records carry the same evidence class, assumptions, implementation identity, time and limitation.
- **Each role gets one coherent Playground journey**: desktop and phone now agree on the first tools, why they matter and which Learn module should follow. Executive and GRC learners receive a short demonstration before returning to role-appropriate education; certification engineers begin with entropy and test evidence.
- **Exercises ask learners to predict, run and explain**: correct answers are no longer always in the first position, and prompts distinguish an observed result from the broader conclusions it cannot support.
- **Business Tools identify the kind of artifact they produce**: all 37 tools now distinguish financial and threat scenarios, planning worksheets, draft templates, evidence organizers and technical design worksheets. Each tool says what its output can show and what it cannot prove, including explicit boundaries around forecasts, legal advice, audits, certification, compliance and security approval.
- **Every role gets an intentional Business Tools starting sequence**: architect, certification-engineer, operations and curious paths no longer fall back to a generic ROI-first journey, and the selected role's short sequence is now available on phones …

chunks.title: PQC Today v4.166.0 — Release Notes (2026-10-18)
chunks.content:
Version 4.166.0 released 2026-10-18.

Library, Threats, Migrate, Assess, Report, Timeline, Community and Navigate now teach learners how to interpret their evidence without turning source records, estimates or planning inputs into applicability, certification, readiness or ranking claims.

### Changed

- **Library records distinguish source facts from PQC Today teaching notes**: source scope, lifecycle, access, freshness and trust language have been reconciled across desktop and phone views. Reviewed records retain official publisher links and educational extractions without publishing locally held third-party documents, while inferred categories and purpose counts are identified as navigation aids rather than authoritative classifications.
- **Threat records now say what kind of evidence they are**: a short primer explains harvest-now-decrypt-later and harvest-now-forge-later, while every card, table row and detail view distinguishes threat scenarios, implementation vulnerabilities, migration constraints, policy signals, adoption milestones, quantum-capability evidence and educational guidance. A shareable record-type filter prevents unlike entries from being compared as though they were equivalent threats.
- **CRQC evidence is taught as uncertain source claims, not a smooth forecast**: the former continuous trajectory graphic is replaced by discrete demonstrations and roadmap markers with their scope and comparability limits. Source cards retain their individual estimates and lineage instead of being turned into a percentage-complete story.
- **Candidate responses are framed as questions to validate**: catalogue suggestions no longer read as prescribed mitigations. Detail views explain that each response is site-derived educational guidance and prompt the learner to verify maturity, applicability and evidence before using it.
- **Migrate presents evidence and planning inputs instead of product verdicts**: capability, certification, roadmap and replacement signals now state their evidence boundary; mis…

chunks.title: PQC Today v4.165.0 — Release Notes (2026-10-17)
chunks.content:
Version 4.165.0 released 2026-10-17.

Compliance source labels now explain who published an item, why it appears for the selected profile, and what its evidence can establish. Official publications open at their publisher; copied third-party documents are excluded from the public Library.

### Changed

- **Compliance source relationships are explained instead of guessed**: domestic, foreign, international and unclassified sources now come from reviewed organization records. Government guidance, regulators, standards bodies, certification schemes, professional bodies and industry groups keep distinct labels, while legal force remains a separate fact. The same “Why this is shown” evidence is available in compact assessment, report and export views.
- **Certification engineers have a tested evidence journey**: the role-specific path moves from local validation and known-answer tests through the product-certification workshop to jurisdiction-aware guidance and product records. Recorder instructions identify every click, wait and scroll for producing the matching explainer video.

### Fixed

- **U.S. organizations are no longer described as foreign in a U.S. profile**: NIST NCCoE, CISA, NIAP and AICPA now use their reviewed U.S. organization type and relationship. CCRA is identified as an international recognition arrangement, and unresolved metadata uses a neutral prompt to verify the primary source rather than inventing a foreign authority.
- **NIST CSWP 39 opens at its official source**: the broken local PDF route is removed. Public Library builds retain official publisher URLs and educational extractions, and a release gate prevents third-party source documents from being copied into the deployable Library.

chunks.title: PQC Today v4.164.0 — Release Notes (2026-10-17)
chunks.content:
Version 4.164.0 released 2026-10-17.

Algorithms now distinguish standards, validation, maturity and measured evidence; Compliance is framed as an educational reference with visible evidence limits; and the FHE module offers a general path plus optional advanced key custody. Current ANSSI and BSI material is included from official sources.

### Changed

- **Algorithm comparisons now separate facts, maturity, missing evidence, and measured hardware results**: standards are no longer called validations; published standards, pending selections, drafts, candidates, regional recommendations, non-selected schemes, non-standardized schemes, and unverified evidence are distinct filters. Migration rows are taught as candidate paths rather than drop-in replacements, and blanks say whether a field is not applicable, not specified, not measured, or not researched. Heterogeneous catalogue performance estimates are withheld from comparisons and exports; a scoped same-engine hardware case study shows measured signing throughput on M4 Pro, i.MX 95, and KV260—including which KV260 rows used FPGA acceleration. Phones can compare up to three algorithms, old filter links normalize to current terminology, and filtered exports include their source snapshot, scope, caveats, maturity, and provenance.
- **Compliance lessons say exactly what their evidence proves**: the page is explicitly an educational reference, not a GRC system or applicability decision. Binding classifications require a reviewed basis instead of a regulator-name match; ACVP, FIPS module validation and algorithms named in evaluated product documentation have distinct labels; certification and GRC views use guided evidence questions; source freshness and extraction-review gaps are visible; and phones include compact date, evidence and role-lens lessons. Extracted source material is called practices rather than legal requirements, and the CSWP 39 sequence is clearly labelled as a PQC Today synthesis.
- **FHE now starts with the general lesson and offers custody…

chunks.title: PQC Today v4.163.0 — Release Notes (2026-10-17)
chunks.content:
Version 4.163.0 released 2026-10-17.

The KMIP protocol workshop now runs its own local engine with a real audit trail, entropy and certification lessons separate test results from compliance claims, and workshop controls and results fit phone screens.

### Changed

- **Open gaps explain the lesson before the investigation history**: the coverage register now separates what a finding means, why it limits a claim, its scope and disposition, and the underlying technical record. General readers start with a guided overview; certification engineers start with structured evidence. Status explanations, search, filters and expandable history replace the previous walls of text, including on phones.
- **Entropy learning paths for both audiences**: general practitioners get a concepts-first route while certification engineers get the validation and evidence route. The random-generation workshop now makes a predictable generator visibly different, recovers its parameters as an exercise, and separates statistical observations from claims about entropy.
- **Validation workbenches fit the role and screen**: certification engineers open on technical evidence and traces; other roles get plain-language interpretation with raw details available. Phones get a compact ACVP runner, readable KAT results and an ordered KMIP policy-to-protocol-to-PKCS#11 timeline instead of compressed desktop panes.
- **The KMIP lesson now runs the local engine**: the protocol workshop executes browser-local KMIP requests and shows their real result and audit trail. Cloud-provider commands and cross-provider states are clearly marked as teaching examples, and the wrap and rotation exercises name where their runnable analogue differs from the exact KMIP operation.

### Fixed

- **The Entropy Evidence Lab opens and explains each dataset choice**: both learning paths can now open the six-screen SP 800-90B lab, including from a direct workshop link. The first screen makes clear that its choices are stored evidence datasets rather than live entropy…

chunks.title: PQC Today v4.162.0 — Release Notes (2026-10-16)
chunks.content:
Version 4.162.0 released 2026-10-16.

Each role now starts from its own questions and downloads (including a new operations pack for IT Ops), beginner pages keep their qualifiers, Library labels say what stage a document is at and how far to trust it, and 20 new certificates join the certification records. The Terms of Service now cover the website only.

### Added

- **Engineering migration plan download**: developer and IT ops reports can download one ZIP with the algorithm backlog, the products you bookmarked (each with its FIPS state, whether its post-quantum algorithms are inside the certificate, and an evidence link), your latest saved Crypto API Refactor Audit, and a release test checklist.
- **Language runtimes table**: a new tab shows, for Go, Python, .NET, Java, Windows, OpenSSL and Bouncy Castle, which of ML-KEM, ML-DSA and SLH-DSA each supports, from which version, with an official source and the date it was checked.
- **An architecture pack in the Command Center**: download your scope, saved architecture artifacts, decision records and test plan as one Markdown or PDF document. Sections you haven't produced yet are listed, and each cited Library source shows its current status.
- **A three-step quick run on the KMIP Migration tab**: create a signing key by name, change the policy, use the key again, and compare the old and new key. You can copy the result, which states its limits: an in-browser software token and a committee-draft protocol.
- **An operations pack for IT Ops**: the Command Center now builds one document for a change board or on-call team from what you have saved: scope, renewal and refresh windows, HSM and certificate capacity, configuration fragments, roadmap, deployment playbook, a VPN rehearsal, test plan, KPI thresholds and closure evidence, each with its review status. Missing sections link to the tool that produces them. Download it as Markdown, PDF, or a zip that adds every table as a CSV.
- **Save results to the operations pack**: the HSM and certificate capacity cal…

chunks.title: PQC Today v4.161.0 — Release Notes (2026-10-15)
chunks.content:
Version 4.161.0 released 2026-10-15.

The site now links the exact source code of the version you are viewing and lists the licence of every third-party package and engine it ships. The repository no longer redistributes full copies of third-party documents, and one Library title is corrected.

### Added

- **A "Source code" link on every page**: the footer links to the exact source of the version you are viewing, and the About page shows that link next to the version number.
- **Open-source licences at /licenses/**: the page gives the licence text of every npm package in the site's production bundle and a notices file for each WebAssembly engine. strongSwan is listed under GPL-2.0-or-later, with a link to its exact source.
- **Credit for adapted framework material**: Learn pages that adapt CC BY 4.0 framework material now credit it on the page.

### Changed

- **No more full copies of third-party documents in the repository**: the 11 reference PDFs and two copied texts are removed. A list now gives each one's publisher link and checksum, and our own extracted data stays. The KMIP test cases carry the OASIS notice.
- **How to contribute**: feedback is welcome through GitHub issues; code changes are made by the maintainer.

### Fixed

- **/report shows a sample report instead of an empty page**: visitors who have not run the assessment yet see the sample report, under a banner that marks it as a sample, with a button to start their own. Its link no longer changes between releases.
- **Two broken links fixed**: the SOC Implementation guide now links Quantum Threats, and the KMIP playground's "Docker sandbox" link opens the Docker sandbox.
- **A Library paper shows its correct title**: IACR ePrint 2010/560 is "On CCA-Secure Somewhat Homomorphic Encryption" (it read "Fully").

chunks.title: PQC Today v4.160.0 — Release Notes (2026-10-15)
chunks.content:
Version 4.160.0 released 2026-10-15.

Five certification modules now name the official document behind ten more of their statements. The Homomorphic Encryption module adds a two-round refresh that restores precision, runs the encrypted scoring service on an x86 machine and an MX95 Pro board, and generates the OpenFHE key set on both boards. The playground retires the Step-CA scenario, and the TPM emulator now comes from a tagged release.

### Added

- **Certification modules name their sources for ten more statements**: five modules now list the document that states each of these sentences:
  - PCI: the PCI SSC announcement of PIN Security Standard v3.1.
  - EUCC: ENISA's EUCC Guidelines on Cryptography page, the CMVP Management Manual, ENISA's 2024 State of Cybersecurity report and NIAP's CCEVS Policy 33.
  - FIPS 140-3: NIST's CMVP FIPS 140-3 standards page and a published CMVP certificate.
  - Product certification: NIST's CMVP FIPS 140-3 standards page and ETSI EN 319 411.
  - ACVP lab workflow: NIST's ACVP ML-DSA test specification.

  The module text is unchanged; only the reference lists grow.

- **OpenFHE's two-round refresh lifts precision from about 13 to about 32 bits with the HSM's own keys**: one refresh keeps 13.2 bits. Two rounds at OpenFHE's recommended setting give 21.1 bits, and the best setting gives 31.7–31.8 bits, close to a fresh ciphertext's 32.1. The cost is about twice the time and one level. This was measured on one Mac with one test input, not on a board.
- **The encrypted risk-scoring service runs on an x86 virtual machine and on an MX95 Pro board, with the token on a second board**: each batch scores 32,768 customers. A batch takes 277 ms on the virtual machine and 4.29 s on the MX95 Pro, about 21 times the Mac's 0.2 s. Peak memory is 1,311 MiB and 1,870 MiB. Both machines give identical scores (21.00 bits, AUC 0.717298). The runs use test certificates and a published test seed, so they show time, memory and correctness only.
- **The OpenFHE key set is also generated on both…

chunks.title: PQC Today v4.159.0 — Release Notes (2026-10-14)
chunks.content:
Version 4.159.0 released 2026-10-14.

The Homomorphic Encryption module adds the HSM key set running in OpenFHE and an encrypted risk-scoring service, its workshop now works on phones and its HSM scenario shows what the engine already does; the build now pins the compiled engine files the site ships and fails loudly when one differs.

### Added

- **The HSM's own key set now works in OpenFHE**: a third CKKS parameter set follows OpenFHE's own 128-bit settings, so the 79 keys the token streams out (6.56 GB in 17.8 s on a Mac) bootstrap in OpenFHE with no keys of its own, at the same precision (13.28 bits against 13.20 with OpenFHE's keys). Results go to the data owner only, and it has not run on the boards yet.
- **An encrypted risk-scoring service, measured end to end**: a reference service scores 32,768 customers' encrypted credit records per request in about 200 ms and ranks them exactly as the plaintext model does (AUC 0.717298 against 0.717299, the same decision for every customer). It accepts only token-signed keys, uses post-quantum TLS 1.3 with a client certificate, never holds a secret key, and only the data owner can read a score. Its limits are stated alongside: test certificates, one tenant, memory only, one Mac.

### Changed

- **The Homomorphic Encryption workshop now works on phones**: the Workshop tab opens on a phone instead of the "not built for mobile yet" note. All eight HSM flow scenarios step through to the end, the key-rotation and shared-decryption views respond to touch, and the six concept views open and work, with no horizontal scrolling.
- **"What can run in the HSM?" shows what the merged engine already does**: five steps that said "planned" now say "in engine today": key generation, streaming the evaluation-key set as bounded calls, the application's decrypt request, decryption under policy, and the release. The streaming step now states the second parameter set (4.41 GB in 1,201 calls, generated in 96.9 s on the MX95 Pro and 99.2 s on the MX95), the 31.5 MB rotation key tha…

chunks.title: PQC Today v4.158.0 — Release Notes (2026-10-11)
chunks.content:
Version 4.158.0 released 2026-10-11.

The Homomorphic Encryption module corrects its figures for releasing CKKS results to others and adds key rotation and shared decryption as interactive views. The certificate records behind Compliance and Migrate are refreshed, six classical-only FIPS 140-3 modules show their certificates again, and twelve NIST certification documents in the Library carry checked details.

### Added

- **Key rotation and shared decryption as interactive views**: a step-through of replacing an HSM key without decrypting stored data (who may start it, what the token refuses, 31.5 MB key, about 1.5 bits of precision lost, old key no longer decrypts), and a two-board shared-decryption view with switches for "approvals independent" and "noise on or off" that show the measured outcome. Both are in the workshop and in the HSM flow diagrams.
- **Releasing CKKS results to others: the corrected result at a thin margin**: with the published noise sizing, today's default parameters cannot release results to third parties, while a second parameter set (higher-precision bootstrapping, scale 2^90) keeps 11.1–11.4 bits against a bar of 10, on a Mac and with the token on both MX95 boards, for programs of 0, 1 and 3 multiplications after a refresh. The margin is about 1 bit; the section says so, and states the costs: refreshes take about twice as long, 3 multiplications fit between refreshes instead of 9, and the key set is about 12 % larger.
- **Cross-checks against OpenFHE, Microsoft SEAL and TFHE-rs**: OpenFHE's own CKKS keys at comparable 128-bit settings take 80 keys and 13.26 GB, and keys in Lattigo's layout ran in OpenFHE with equal precision; Lattigo decrypted all seven SEAL ciphertexts exactly as SEAL did; TFHE-rs 1.8.1 reproduced 28 of its 36 published test vectors byte for byte on the Mac and both boards (the other 8 differ in floating-point rounding but are identical across our platforms and decrypt correctly).

chunks.title: PQC Today v4.157.0 — Release Notes (2026-10-11)
chunks.content:
Version 4.157.0 released 2026-10-11.

Bouncy Castle's three Migrate rows move to the current releases, the Singapore handbook draft is backed by its own saved copy, and a broken Timeline source link is repaired.

### Fixed

- **A broken source link on the Timeline is repaired**: the Australian ASD milestone on quantum-vulnerable algorithms (Diffie-Hellman, ECDH, ECDSA and RSA not approved beyond 2030) linked to a web page that no longer exists. It now links to the June 2025 Guidelines for cryptography PDF it describes.

### Data

- **Migrate: Bouncy Castle at the current releases**: Java moves to 1.86 (announced 15 September 2026), Java LTS to 2.73.13 (22 September) and C# .NET to 2.7.0 (7 August), each with the vendor's own announcement as the proof page. The capability text now matches those announcements: C# .NET 2.7.0 adds hybrid ML-KEM key exchange and ML-DSA and SLH-DSA authentication for TLS 1.3, Java 1.86 names post-quantum and hybrid key encapsulation across CMS/S-MIME, HPKE and TLS, and the Java LTS row no longer says composite signatures are unconfirmed. The Migrate counts do not change.
- **Singapore Quantum-Safe Handbook: the draft is backed by the draft**: the Library entry for the October 2025 draft for public consultation shared a saved file with the final V1 handbook of 16 July 2026. It now has its own copy of the draft; the entry for the final handbook is unchanged.

chunks.title: PQC Today v4.156.0 — Release Notes (2026-10-10)
chunks.content:
Version 4.156.0 released 2026-10-10.

The Homomorphic Encryption module is reorganised into nine sections and gains measured key-streaming results, workshop views and sourced sections on operations, standards and market position; the Library gains thirteen primary papers behind it. The Executive's first Library suggestion shows the right document, two Migrate rows describe their certification and post-quantum status accurately, and a bundled sanitiser library is brought up to date.

### Added

- **New hands-on workshop step: FHE concepts**: four interactive views, namely noise budget and bootstrapping, encoding and rounding, a program turned into an FHE circuit, and key streaming with a chunk-size control backed by measured times.
- **CKKS evaluation keys scale when streamed, measured on Mac and MX95 boards**: an HSM token produced the full 3.94 GB bootstrappable key set as 1,001 bounded calls, never holding more than about 16 MB. On one MX95 core this took about 8 minutes; it was limited by the CPU, not the network. Chunk size trades memory for time, and every limb matched the reference exactly.
- **Decryption results are noisy: how to read them, and the decryption limits**: CKKS gives approximate fixed-point values that you read by rounding, while TFHE decrypts exactly. Explains why anyone allowed to ask for decryption can recover the key, what the HSM's decryption policy controls, and the value and limits of threshold decryption, all with sources.
- **Where FHE is used, what it costs, and how it is positioned**: use cases ranked by evidence (in production for private lookups; peer-reviewed or pilots for genomics, biometrics, AI inference and financial crime); compute overhead next to enclaves, MPC, differential privacy and federated learning; GPU, FPGA, chip and algorithm speedups; and FHE's market position among privacy technologies, with analyst estimates labelled.
- **Standards and compliance status of FHE**: no FHE scheme is FIPS-approved, in CNSA 2.0 or Common Criteria-certified, and ISO/IEC 280…

Certification engineers now start the Library on the documents their work depends on, the Glossary gains twelve terms for module validation, the Timeline records when FIPS 140-2 validations move to NIST's historical list, and the Migrate page no longer shows certificates that belong to other products.

chunks.title: PQC Today v4.154.0 — Release Notes (2026-10-09)
chunks.content:
Version 4.154.0 released 2026-10-09.

The OT & Industrial Control Systems module now shows the three ways attackers reach a plant, and its Zone & Conduit Planner separates firmware signing from command authentication and adds industrial IoT.

### Added

- **OT attack surface: three paths in**: a new Learn section shows how attackers reach industrial control systems. They move from the office network through the industrial DMZ into the plant, come in over remote access and internet-connected industrial IoT devices, or get on site, where most installed field equipment accepts commands from anyone. Each path gets its own fix, from separate OT accounts and a guarded DMZ to hybrid post-quantum key exchange on remote links and classical authentication at the field level. The December 2015 Ukraine grid attack is worked through as an example that used all three paths.

### Changed

- **Zone & Conduit Planner: industrial IoT and command authentication**: the planner adds an "IIoT & cloud connectors" zone on its own segment next to the industrial DMZ, and shows a cloud link that skips the DMZ as a connection that should not exist. Each zone now has separate settings for firmware and project signing and for command authentication; controllers and field devices start with unauthenticated commands, which the planner flags as a gap to fix today rather than a quantum risk. Every conduit is labelled with its attack path and can be filtered by it. The exercise on zone ranking is now "Where attacks start vs where they hurt".
- **IoT module: where industrial IoT sits in a plant**: a short note explains that industrial IoT gateways should connect through the plant's industrial DMZ, and links to the new OT section.

### Data

- **Four new OT security documents in the Library**: CISA's 2026 study "Barriers to Secure OT Communication: Why Johnny Can't Authenticate", the CISA, FBI, EPA and DOE fact sheet "Primary Mitigations to Reduce Cyber Threats to Operational Technology", CISA advisory AA21-131A on the 2021 pipeline ransom…

chunks.title: PQC Today v4.153.0 — Release Notes (2026-10-09)
chunks.content:
Version 4.153.0 released 2026-10-09.

The Report now says which compliance frameworks are binding and which are guidance, phone visitors see the page they asked for instead of a role question, and the Merkle Tree Certificates workshop proves the tree you built.

### Added

- **The Report separates laws from guidance**: for the frameworks from your own country's bodies, the Report no longer calls them all "Mandatory". Each one now sits under Binding (a law, regulation or enforceable rule that applies to organisations like yours), Guidance and drafts (recommendations, goals and drafts nobody is required to follow), or Not yet classified, and the same label appears beside each framework you selected. 171 of the 191 active frameworks are classified so far; the other 20 stay Not yet classified until their documents settle, and a blank is never treated as guidance.

### Fixed

- **On a phone, the page you asked for opens straight away**: a first-time visitor on a phone used to be asked "Who's asking?" on every page before seeing anything. The role picker now takes over the home page only. Every other page opens normally with a one-line "Pick your role" prompt above it, which you can dismiss for good. Visitors who have already chosen a role, and the computer layout, are unchanged.
- **Merkle Tree Certificates: the proof steps now use the tree you built**: in the Learn workshop, Step 2 (Inclusion Proof) and Step 3 (Verify Proof) used to start from eight sample certificates even after you built your own tree in Step 1. They now prove and verify the certificates you added, with a note that your tree is loaded. If you skip Step 1, they say so and use the sample set. Resetting the workshop clears the tree.

### Security

- **Dependency updates**: the HTML sanitising library (DOMPurify) moves from 3.4.13 to 3.4.16.

chunks.title: PQC Today v4.149.0 — Release Notes (2026-10-03)
chunks.content:
Version 4.149.0 released 2026-10-03.

FHE key custody now runs across two appliance boards with a backup and a failover, the data owner checks the custodian's attestation before trusting its keys, and the FHE compute service runs on a small Arm board over mutual TLS. Every "Validated" badge in the workshop now opens its results on the page, and the Threats and related pages now say plainly that some quantum estimates are still unresolved, with the BSI, NSA and ANSSI entries corrected to what those organisations actually state.

### Added

- **FHE key custody with a backup board**: the client key for the encrypted-computation demo is now held in a software token on one i.MX 95 appliance board, with a protected backup on a second board made over KMIP. On the same encrypted inputs both boards made identical decisions: six results released, all correct, and the 64-bit result its policy forbids refused. The KV260 compute board refused tampered and foreign keys before any computation. The same boards also passed a signed administration test over KMIP, accepting only properly signed requests and refusing every forged, replayed or wrong-role one. All of this is an educational test on software tokens, not certified hardware custody.
- **Destroy and restore of the key**: the key was wiped from the main board, after which it refused every result while the backup board still decided them all; it was then restored from the backup over KMIP and decided the same encrypted results again, all correct, and a fresh export from the restored board passed the attestation check. A copy to a destination without the FHE policy was refused.
- **Failover to the backup board**: when the backup board takes over and publishes its own signed keys, encrypted computation continues and both boards still make the same decisions.
- **The data owner checks the custodian's attestation**: before trusting a custodian's keys, the data owner now verifies its attestation, including the certificate chain, current revocation lists, a check tied to…

chunks.title: PQC Today v4.148.0 — Release Notes (2026-10-03)
chunks.content:
Version 4.148.0 released 2026-10-03.

The FHE + HSM workshop's key-custody flow now runs with the key held on the MX95 appliance board, the Lattigo threshold scenario gets its first board measurements, Library dates cite their NIST sources, and shared links are now checked every night.

### Added

- **FHE key custody on the MX95 board**: the single-HSM TFHE scenario ran end to end with the client key in a software token on the MX95 appliance board, the data owner on a Mac and the FHE server on a KV260. The board refused tampered and foreign server keys before loading them. The token released the six results its policy allows, all correct, and refused the 64-bit result its policy forbids. Every run now shows on each step, the MX95 run first; the earlier run with the token on a Mac is labelled as such.
- **Lattigo threshold timings on a small ARM board**: the Lattigo threshold scenario is now reference-validated on a KV260 (four Cortex-A53 cores), as 2-of-3 and 2-of-2. A threshold decryption took about 0.35 s and a multiplication about 0.19 s on the board, with every party in one process; a missing share stops decryption, as it should.
- **8- and 16-bit encrypted arithmetic timed on the KV260**: small integers are much cheaper than 64-bit ones on the board's Cortex-A53 cores. A 16-bit encrypted multiply takes about 15 s, against about 3.5 minutes for 64-bit, and 16-bit additions and comparisons take 1.6–3 s each. All 18 results decrypted correctly; the step badges and cost panel now show these runs.

chunks.title: PQC Today v4.147.0 — Release Notes (2026-10-03)
chunks.content:
Version 4.147.0 released 2026-10-03.

The FHE + HSM workshop now shows which steps have been validated, with measured runs on a Mac and on a KV260 board, including a first end-to-end run of TFHE key custody in a software token.

### Added

- **FHE + HSM Flows show what has actually been validated**: every step now has a "Validated" line and each scenario a validation-evidence summary, backed by signed, hash-pinned evidence records. The OpenFHE threshold scenario is the first one validated: a reference run of OpenFHE v1.6.0 (3 and 5 parties) reproduces the upstream example, and its result files are published for anyone to check. Other steps read "not yet" until lab runs land: the data owner on a Mac, the FHE server on a KV260 (untrusted compute) and the custodian as a software token on an MX95, backed up to an MX95 Pro. None of it is shown as hardware custody.

The earlier estimates were about four times too high.

- **First hardware numbers: the FHE server on a KV260**: the TFHE scenario's server steps are now validated on a KV260 board (four Cortex-A53 cores) running the untrusted compute side with software-held keys: all 27 encrypted operations decrypted correctly, a 64-bit add took about 13 s and a multiply about 3.5 minutes, and peak memory was 203 MB. The result files are published with the evidence.

chunks.title: PQC Today v4.145.0 — Release Notes (2026-10-02)
chunks.content:
Version 4.145.0 released 2026-10-02.

The FHE + HSM workshop now shows plainly when data is encrypted, computed on and decrypted, who may decrypt, and where every key sits; every HSM Learn lesson now runs on a fresh page, and the Library adds fhe.rs, the fourth open-source homomorphic-encryption library.

- **What an HSM decryption policy can and cannot do**: the decrypt steps explain the typed-ciphertext policy (authenticated requester, allowed result types checked before decrypting, a plaintext check before release, rate limits), that FHE ciphertexts carry no access-control metadata, and its limits: it caps how much one release reveals but cannot prove which computation produced a ciphertext.
