- **The migration timeline now covers ten national programs**: Australia (protect by 2030) and India (2033) join the countries with proof-backed migration deadlines, the EU's final compliance year is set to 2035, and an unsupported 2027 Czech deadline was removed — so the Timeline page and a non-US simulation run reflect a wider, more accurate set of national deadlines.
- **"Watch the full migration" is now paced by its narration**: the auto-run lets the spoken explanation drive each transition instead of a fixed timer, reads out the resources it touches at each step, shows it…

chunks.title: PQC Today v4.1.0 — Release Notes (2026-06-23)
chunks.content:
Version 4.1.0 released 2026-06-23.

Version 4.1 lets you watch a complete post-quantum migration run itself in the Migration Simulation, rebuilds that run around three plain goals tied to the new US Executive Order, and brings the redesigned Library, Migrate, Assess, Compliance, Learn, Algorithms, Patents, Report and Threats pages — each rebuilt around a single role selector — out of preview.

### Added

- **Watch your whole migration play out on its own**: a new "Watch the full migration" mode runs the simulation from start to finish for you — moving through every phase, filling each tool with sensible example answers, and narrating what's happening as it goes. You can speed it up, slow it down, or step in at any point, and it ends on a short celebration of the goals you set out to hit. It's the quickest way to see what a complete migration looks like before you run your own.

### Changed

- **The Simulation now tracks three clear goals instead of a countdown you couldn't win**: the old "you're N years past the danger line" gauge is replaced by a progress panel built around what a migration actually has to achieve — put governance in place, protect your most sensitive "harvest-now" data first, and finish migrating everything — each shown against its target year. Four bars below it track the real order of work (urgent data first, then signatures, then the rest), and a "harvest-now exposure" figure falls as you protect data, so you watch the risk closing instead of staring at a number you can never beat.
- **A US run now follows the new Executive Order's deadlines**: a United States migration is now paced to the June 2026 US post-quantum Executive Order — protect key exchange by 2030 and signatures by 2031 — and the goals, dates and standards shown in the run (FIPS 203 for key exchange, FIPS 204 for signatures) match it. Because the dates are read from each country's timeline data, other national timelines can drive their own version of the same three goals.
- **Backing up your progress to Google Drive…

chunks.title: PQC Today v4.0.0 — Release Notes (2026-06-20)
chunks.content:
Version 4.0.0 released 2026-06-20.

Version 4.0 makes the Migration Simulation the heart of the app — your learning modules, business tools, workshops, the product catalog, the timeline and the algorithm comparisons now run _inside_ the simulation instead of sending you elsewhere — and adds a real in-browser KMIP control plane + PKCS#11 HSM, a much-expanded and re-validated protocol-support matrix, and new SOC / GRC / Team learning modules. The PQC VPN simulator now also runs the post-quantum IKEv2 handshake for real — hybrid key exchange, message fragmentation, and tunnel (CHILD_SA) negotiation all execute in the browser instead of being narrated — and every byte is inspectable in a new live packet capture.

Behind it, five new IETF drafts were added to the searchable Library and the Cryptsoft KMIP/PKCS#11 SDK was added to the product catalog.

Three guided steps: pick a policy and watch the _same_ operation get allowed, blocked, or automatically upgraded to a post-quantum algorithm (and only when the engine truly upgrades it — the page won't claim an upgrade that didn't happen);…

chunks.title: PQC Today v3.19.5 — Release Notes (2026-06-09)
chunks.content:
Version 3.19.5 released 2026-06-09.

The Threats page is fresher and more accurate — corrected post-quantum standards status, more sources you can open, and consistent severity labels.

### Fixed

- **Corrected the status of NIST's fourth signature standard**: The cross-industry "NIST standards finalization" threat said FIPS 206 (FN-DSA/Falcon) was published in August 2024 alongside ML-KEM, ML-DSA and SLH-DSA. In fact only those first three were finalized then — FIPS 206 remains in development; NIST has not published an Initial Public Draft or final standard. The entry now says so, and the HQC backup-algorithm note (now tracked toward FIPS 207) was refreshed to a 2026 draft and 2027 final.
- **Consistent severity labels across every threat**: A few threats showed severity in mixed casing ("CRITICAL", "HIGH") or an off-scale "Medium-High" value that could sort or filter oddly. Every threat now uses the standard Critical / High / Medium scale.

### Changed

- **More threats link to a primary source you can actually open**: Re-verified the source documents behind the threat catalog and re-captured fresh copies. The share of active threats backed by an authoritative primary source rose from roughly a quarter to well over half, and every active threat now has an archived copy of its source on file.

### Data

- **Refreshed quantum-threats dataset (2026-06-09)**: New self-contained snapshot covering the 110 active industry threats, with refreshed source links, complete industry tags, and updated standards references.

chunks.title: PQC Today v3.19.4 — Release Notes (2026-06-08)
chunks.content:
Version 3.19.4 released 2026-06-08.

Compliance frameworks now say plainly whether PQC is required or just recommended, and sector names read in plain English.

### Fixed

- **Compliance frameworks no longer over-state legal force**: Several frameworks were flagged as hard mandates when they are actually recommendations or expectations. ANSSI is now shown as a recommendation (not a legal mandate), DORA as resilience obligations that imply but don't explicitly require PQC, and eIDAS 2.0 and FedRAMP as expected/indirect rather than in force today. In all, 42 frameworks were re-characterized so you can tell at a glance what is required versus advised.

### Changed

- **Readable industry names in the compliance views**: Frameworks that were tagged with raw industry codes (e.g. "54") now show the real sector name — "Government & Defense", "Finance", "Healthcare" — in the framework chips, the detail panel, and the focus view.

chunks.title: PQC Today v3.19.3 — Release Notes (2026-06-08)
chunks.content:
Version 3.19.3 released 2026-06-08.

A cleaner, more accurate Algorithms page — no duplicate entries, corrected standardization labels, and a live algorithm count.

### Fixed

- **Algorithms page now shows the real count and a working "Top picks" link**: The page advertised a fixed "42 algorithms" even though the catalog had grown well beyond that — it now shows the actual number loaded. The executive "View Top" shortcut was labeled "Top 5" but highlighted only four, and pointed at an algorithm name that no longer exists (so nothing highlighted); it now correctly shows the top four and links to the right entry (FN-DSA-512).

### Data

- **Duplicate algorithm rows removed and standardization labels corrected**: Four algorithms (HQC, Classic McEliece, LMS, XMSS) showed up both as a generic row and as their specific parameter sets (e.g. HQC-128/192/256), double-counting in filters and totals — the redundant generic rows are gone. Several standardization labels were also corrected: FrodoKEM is now shown as a NIST Round 3 alternate (it was never in Round 4), BIKE reflects Round 4 concluding in 2025 with HQC selected, and Classic McEliece 460896 is labeled BSI Level 3 (it was mislabeled Level 1).

chunks.title: PQC Today v3.19.2 — Release Notes (2026-06-07)
chunks.content:

chunks.title: PQC Today v3.19.0 — Release Notes (2026-06-07)
chunks.content:

chunks.title: PQC Today v3.18.0 — Release Notes (2026-06-04)
chunks.content:

Playground gets Learn-style views and filtering plus a live sandbox-availability check, with eight learn-module fact corrections and a multi-source data refresh.

They're now generated deterministically and re-signed, so signatures stay valid until the underlying data actually changes.

- **Playground sandbox terminal accepts input again**: The interactive terminal in embedded sandbox scenarios (VPN, TLS 1.3, SSH) showed a cursor but ignored keystrokes; the live connection behind it is fixed, and separate browser tabs no long…

chunks.title: PQC Today v3.17.5 — Release Notes (2026-06-02)
chunks.content:
Version 3.17.5 released 2026-06-02.

Fixed 10 reported issues across the Learn catalog and crypto workshops, plus several in-browser HSM engine corrections.

chunks.title: PQC Today v3.17.0 — Release Notes (2026-05-30)

Role-aware ("persona") personalization across all seven main pages, a NICE Framework workforce view, a TLS downgrade-attack workshop, and many new references.

Version 3.14.7 released 2026-05-11.

### Reverted — v3.14.6's Gemini-extracted xwalk edges (trust-engine violation)

**v3.14.6 promoted 9 IR 8477 xwalk edges sourced from a Gemini 3.1 Pro extraction run.** During that session it became evident that at least 3 of the 9 emitted `evidence` quotes closely echoed the example row in the orchestrator prompt rather than literal text from the source PDFs — i.e. the model was almost certainly hallucinating the evidence string while emitting plausible-looking `(from, to, relationship_type)` tuples. None of the 9 promoted rows had been verified against the actual source-doc text before merge.

The trust-engine architecture is "source-grounded by construction" (doc §16.1) — every claim must anchor to a cached source passage and pass the cross-check validators (N20/N21). Allowing un-verified evidence into production poisons the audit trail the entire platform depends on: downstream OSCAL + CBOM exports inherit the trust signal, SME signatures aggregate into reviewer attribution, and the corpus regeneration ingests the rows as authoritative.

The right answer when an SME-grade source like ASC X9 or NY DFS doesn't yet have edges in the production xwalk is **"this concept has no graph yet"** — not "fill it in with a less-trusted extraction path".

### What was reverted

- `src/data/concept_xwalks_05112026_r2.csv` — restored to v3.14.5 state (948 rows, was 957 after v3.14.6).
- `src/data/concept_xwalks_05112026_r1.csv` — restored to v3.14.5 state (1037 rows, was 1045 after v3.14.6).
- `src/data/concept_xwalk_candidates_05112026.csv` — public mirror restored to v3.14.5 state.

chunks.title: PQC Today v3.11.0 — Release Notes (2026-05-10)
chunks.content:
Version 3.11.0 released 2026-05-10.

### Highlights

- **Search now understands what you mean, not just what you type.** Typing "TLS hybrid" on Library, Migrate, Patents, Compliance, Threats, Timeline, Community, or Algorithms now also returns documents that talk about KEM hybrid in TLS 1.3 — even when none of those words appear literally. The classic keyword search is still the floor; semantic matches are added on top.
- **Free-text Compliance suggestions in the Assessment.** Step 5 has a new "Describe your context" textarea that recommends the top 5 frameworks for your situation and lets you add them with one click.
- **Five new behind-the-scenes data-quality watchers** that surface candidate fixes (missing references, possible duplicates, possible counter-claims, weak topic coverage) for SME review. They generate review queues; they don't auto-edit data.
- **Trust-tier baseline captured** at 47 Authoritative / 446 High / 786 Moderate / 2,035 Low so future shifts can be measured against this snapshot.

### Changed

Version 3.1.3 released 2026-04-11.

Bug fix for embedded widget brand theming, plus vendor certificate infrastructure cleanup.

### Fixed

  were incorrectly treated as URL fragment separators, causing the vendor token and signature to
  be silently dropped. The embed URL builder now percent-encodes color values before signing.

### Changed

- **Vendor certificate registry simplified**: All vendor certificates (including development ones)
  are now loaded from PEM files at build time. The separate dev-mode fixture merge step has been
  removed, making the embed boot path faster and more predictable.

- **Trust anchor certificates can be committed to version control**: Root CA and vendor
  certificate PEM files (public trust anchors only) are now tracked by git so they can be
  bundled by the build system.

### Security

- **No private key material is stored in the repository**: Root CA private keys, P12 bundles,
  and `.key` files are blocked by gitignore rules. Only public certificate PEM files (trust
  anchors) are ever committed.

  keep internal `pqcMode` in sync with the `initialPqcMode` prop when the same component

chunks.title: PQC Today v2.87.0 — Release Notes (2026-04-07)
chunks.content:
Version 2.87.0 released 2026-04-07.

### Added

- **5G SUCI — Profile B (P-256) dedicated step content**: Profile B now has its own `SUCI_STEPS_B`
  constant with step titles, descriptions, and code snippets tailored to P-256 (secp256r1) —
  previously it displayed Profile A (X25519) labels throughout.

- **5G SUCI — Profile B compressed key encoding**: The scheme output for Profile B now uses the
  33-byte COMPRESSED P-256 ephemeral public key (02/03 prefix + x-coordinate) per TS 33.501
  Annex C.4, down from 65 bytes. ECDH inside the HSM still uses the full uncompressed form.

- **5G SUCI — educational content: compressed vs uncompressed EC point encoding**: Steps 9, 10
  and terminal output for Profile B now show both encoding forms side by side, explaining when each
  is used and why. Includes the application-layer compression formula (no `C_CompressECPoint` in
  PKCS#11) and how the SIDF recovers y via the P-256 curve equation y²=x³−3x+b (mod p).

- **5G SUCI — PKCS#11 mechanism accuracy**: Code snippets for all X25519 operations now correctly
  cite `C_DeriveKey(CKM_EC_MONTGOMERY_KEY_DERIVE)` per PKCS#11 v3.2, distinguishing it from
  `CKM_ECDH1_DERIVE` which applies to Weierstrass curves (P-256/P-384). Affected: Profile A
  step 5, Profile A step 11, Profile C hybrid steps 5 and 11.

### Fixed

- **5G SUCI — profile transitions always reset to step 1**: Switching between Profile A → B → C
  (hybrid) → C (pure) now lands on step 1 each time. The `useStepWizard` hook gained a `reset()`
  method called at all transition sites (onClick handlers and `onComplete`).

- **5G SUCI — profile state set before every step executes**: `fiveGService.state.profile` is now
  assigned at the top of every `executeStep` call, preventing `computeMAC` and
  `visualizeStructure` from seeing a stale or undefined profile on early steps.

- **5G SUCI — B→C transition no longer double-cleans**: `changeProfile('C')` now internally sets
  `pqcMode` to `'hybrid'`, so `onComplete` can call it once without a redundant `changeP…

chunks.title: PQC Today v2.85.0 — Release Notes (2026-04-07)
chunks.content:
Version 2.85.0 released 2026-04-07.

### Added

- **5G SUCI — Profile C visualization corrected**: The SUCI structure panel now correctly shows
  the hybrid Profile C output format — the scheme output starts with the ML-KEM ciphertext, not
  an ephemeral key. The abbreviated SUCI string and description both reflect the actual
  `kemCiphertext ‖ msinCiphertext ‖ macTag` layout per 3GPP TS 23.003.

- **Library — 3 new records with proper titles and download links**:
  - _Study of Post Quantum Status of Widely Used Protocols_ (Cisco Research, arXiv 2603.28728, Mar 2026) — PQC migration survey across TLS, IPsec, BGP, DNSSEC, SSH, QUIC, OpenID Connect, OpenVPN, and Signal.
  - _Securing Elliptic Curve Cryptocurrencies against Quantum Vulnerabilities_ (Google Quantum AI + Ethereum Foundation, Mar 2026) — new resource estimates for breaking secp256k1 with a quantum computer; on-spend attack analysis.
  - _Protecting Subscriber Identifiers with SUCI_ (NIST CSWP 36A ipd, Aug 2024) — NIST guidance on enabling 5G subscriber identity concealment to prevent IMSI-catching.

- **5G SUCI — removed WIP badge**: The 5G SUCI Construction tool is now complete and no longer
  marked as Work in Progress in the Playground.

### Fixed

- **5G SUCI — HSM and OpenSSL cross-check now agree on key derivation**: The dual-engine
  comparison was previously using different ephemeral key bytes for the KDF — the HSM used its
  internal EC point while OpenSSL used an SPKI-wrapped version. The HSM key bytes are now synced
  into the shared state before derivation runs, so both engines produce matching output.

- **HSM — AES-GCM per-message encrypt/decrypt enabled on Rust engine**: The per-message AEAD
  functions (`C_MessageEncryptInit`, `C_EncryptMessage`, etc.) are now fully wired to the Rust
  WASM engine, which implements them in softhsmv3 v0.4.10. Previously they returned an error.

chunks.title: PQC Today v2.84.0 — Release Notes (2026-04-07)
chunks.content:
Version 2.84.0 released 2026-04-07.

### Added

- **VPN Simulation — SKEYSEED key derivation step**: After the ML-KEM shared secret is verified,
  a new panel shows exactly how IKEv2 derives the session master key (SKEYSEED) — using
  `prf(Ni ‖ Nr, shared_secret)` with the actual KEM secret bytes displayed. Pure-PQC and hybrid
  modes each show their respective PRF inputs. References RFC 9370 and the ML-DSA IKEv2 draft.

- **VPN Simulation — IKE exchange phase labels on logs**: Each line in the charon.log panel is now
  tagged with its IKE exchange phase (SETUP / IKE_SA_INIT / IKE_INTERMEDIATE / IKE_AUTH). This
  makes it easy to see where ML-KEM fits into the handshake — encapsulation happens during
  IKE_INTERMEDIATE in hybrid mode, IKE_SA_INIT in pure-PQC mode.

- **VPN Simulation — payload size note**: A callout explains that PQC key exchange payloads are
  10–16× larger than classical ECDH (ML-KEM-768 public key: 1,184 bytes vs P-256: 64 bytes),
  and why IKEv2 uses the IKE_INTERMEDIATE exchange to handle the extra fragmentation load.

- **VPN Simulation — QKD toggle clarified**: The QKD PSK option now shows
  "(informational — not simulated)" so it is clear this is a display label, not an active feature.

### Fixed

- **5G SUCI — dual-engine comparison uses real HSM output**: The encrypted MSIN and MAC tag
  shown in the comparison panel now come directly from the HSM rather than the parallel
  OpenSSL computation, giving an accurate side-by-side result. The MAC tag is correctly
  truncated to 8 bytes per 3GPP TS 33.501.

- **5G SUCI Profile C — KEM ciphertext carried forward correctly**: The HSM-produced ML-KEM
  ciphertext is now stored in the shared state after the key encapsulation step, so downstream
  SUCI assembly and visualization use the real ciphertext.

- **Stateful Signatures — default message aligned across panels**: Both the XMSS key generation
  demo and the Stateful Signatures workshop now default to `"Hello, world!"`, making cross-engine
  verification work without any manual inp…

chunks.title: PQC Today v2.83.0 — Release Notes (2026-04-07)
chunks.content:
Version 2.83.0 released 2026-04-07.

### Added

- **VPN Simulation — full IKEv2 + ML-KEM-768 handshake working end-to-end**: The VPN simulator
  now completes a real PKCS#11-based ML-KEM-768 key encapsulation through the HSM, including
  key generation, encapsulation, shared secret extraction, and SKEYSEED derivation. This is the
  first full IKEv2 post-quantum handshake running entirely inside the browser HSM.

### Fixed

- **VPN Simulation — engine stability**: Switched back to the C++ HSM engine for VPN simulation
  after finding that the Rust WASM engine has compatibility issues in the browser's secure context
  that prevent it from running correctly in this scenario.

- **HSM — encapsulation bug fixed in softhsmv3**: A bug in the C++ HSM engine caused key
  encapsulation to return an error when reading standard key attributes. The WASM binary has been
  updated with the fix.

- **HSM — 8 additional Rust engine functions now active**: Pre-bound signature verification
  (`C_VerifySignatureInit/Final/Update`) and PKCS#11 v3.2 session functions that were previously
  disabled are now fully wired to the Rust engine.

chunks.title: PQC Today v2.82.0 — Release Notes (2026-04-06)
chunks.content:
Version 2.82.0 released 2026-04-06.

### Added

- **5G SUCI — 3GPP TS 33.501 reference vectors modal**: A "Reference Vectors" button on the SUCI
  flow panel opens an expandable modal with the official 3GPP TS 33.501 Annex C.4 test vectors
  for Profile A (X25519) and Profile B (P-256) — including home network keys, ephemeral keys,
  scheme output breakdown (EphPub ‖ Ciphertext ‖ MAC), and copyable hex fields.
- **Profile C hybrid mode — full TR 33.841 §5.2.5.2 implementation**: Hybrid Profile C now
  generates two separate HN keypairs (ML-KEM-768 + X25519), derives Z_ecdh via ECDH and Z_kem
  via ML-KEM encapsulation, then combines them as `Z = SHA256(Z_ecdh ‖ Z_kem)` inside the HSM
  using `C_Digest`. Key derivation uses ANSI X9.63-KDF with SHA3-256 producing AES-256 + HMAC-SHA3-256 keys.
- **Stateful Signatures — cross-engine sign and verify**: The Stateful Signatures workshop can now
  sign on the Rust engine and verify on the C++ engine. Public key bytes are cached at generation
  time, imported into the C++ session via `C_CreateObject`, and verified with `C_VerifyInit` /
  `C_Verify`. Includes tamper-detection toggles (flip message / flip signature) and a live
  verification result indicator.
- **VPN Simulation — RSA-3072 certificate generation and inspection**: The VPN panel now generates
  a real RSA-3072 key pair via the HSM, constructs a TBS certificate using `@peculiar/asn1-x509`,
  signs it with `C_Sign` (SHA256withRSA), and shows a certificate inspector modal with full field
  breakdown. A warning badge notes that RSA-3072 is classical (not quantum-safe) per
  draft-ietf-ipsecme-ikev2-mldsa.

### Changed

- **5G SUCI — spec-correct ANSI X9.63-KDF replaces HKDF**: Key derivation now follows 3GPP TS
  33.501 §C.3.3 exactly — `block1 = SHA-256(Z ‖ 0x00000001 ‖ sharedInfo)`,
  `K_enc = block1[0:16]`, `K_mac = block1[16:] ‖ block2[0:16]`. HKDF was never in the 3GPP spec.
- **5G SUCI — AES-128-CTR with zero IV (was AES-GCM)**: MSIN encryption now uses AES-128-CTR per
  TS 33.501 §C.3.3 with a ze…

chunks.title: PQC Today v2.81.1 — Release Notes (2026-04-06)

chunks.title: PQC Today v2.81.0 — Release Notes (2026-04-06)
chunks.content:
Version 2.81.0 released 2026-04-06.

- **Envelope Encryption — accurate sizes and wrap overhead**: The PQC column always shows correct ML-KEM reference sizes regardless of which key-encryption algorithm is selected. AES-KWP wrap overhead corrected to 48 bytes (per RFC 5649 §4.2).
- **Bitcoin Playground — pure HSM path**: The Bitcoin key derivation flow no longer relies on OpenSSL — all operations now run entirely through the in-browser PKCS#11 HSM.

chunks.title: PQC Today v2.78.0 — Release Notes (2026-04-05)
chunks.content:
Version 2.78.0 released 2026-04-05.

### Added

- **VPN simulation — all crypto through the in-browser HSM**: ECDH key exchange and random number generation during the IKEv2 handshake now run entirely through the in-browser SoftHSMv3 PKCS#11 module. OpenSSL is no longer used for IKE crypto — every cryptographic operation is visible in the PKCS#11 log.

chunks.title: PQC Today v2.77.0 — Release Notes (2026-04-05)
chunks.content:
Version 2.77.0 released 2026-04-05.

### Added

- **VPN Simulation with ML-KEM-768**: A complete IKEv2 handshake now runs entirely in your browser — no server required. Two Web Worker instances of strongSwan 6.0.5 (initiator and responder) negotiate a post-quantum secure tunnel using ML-KEM-768 key exchange, completing IKE_SA_INIT and IKE_AUTH across 4 packets. Watch every PKCS#11 call, packet exchange, and key agreement step in real time.

- **Stateful Hash-Based Signatures Workshop**: LMS, HSS, and XMSS key generation and signing now run through the in-browser PKCS#11 HSM. Remaining signature capacity is tracked live — H5 trees are limited to 32 signatures, matching the real-world constraint on stateful schemes.

### Fixed

- **VPN simulation no longer crashes on start**: Fixed a threading incompatibility in the strongSwan WASM build that caused an "Unreachable" crash in single-threaded Emscripten mode.

### Data

- **strongSwan product entry updated**: ML-DSA experimental support added with 5 verified source URLs. Validation status: VALIDATED.
- **RAG corpus regenerated**.

chunks.title: PQC Today v2.75.0 — Release Notes (2026-04-02)
chunks.content:
Version 2.75.0 released 2026-04-02.

### Added

- **ACVP tests 23 & 24 — X25519/X448 ECDH round-trip**: The HSM ACVP compliance suite now covers Montgomery-curve Diffie-Hellman. Test 23 generates two X25519 keypairs, derives shared secrets from each side, and asserts they match. Test 24 does the same for X448. Both tests run on both the C++ and Rust engines in dual-mode (40 total assertions). A `extractMontgomeryPubKey` helper abstracts the engine difference: Rust stores raw bytes in `CKA_VALUE`; C++ stores a DER-wrapped point (`04 len raw`) in `CKA_EC_POINT`.
- **ACVP test 25 — X9.63 KDF with SHA3-256 / SHA3-512 (PKCS#11 v3.2 §5.2.12)**: Verifies `C_DeriveKey(CKM_ECDH1_DERIVE, CKD_SHA3_256_KDF)` and `C_DeriveKey(CKM_ECDH1_DERIVE, CKD_SHA3_512_KDF)` produce matching derived keys on both engines. Constants `CKD_SHA3_256_KDF = 0x0B` and `CKD_SHA3_512_KDF = 0x0D` are now exported from `softhsm/constants.ts`.
- **`hsm_pqcEncap` / `hsm_pqcDecap` wrappers (PKCS#11 v3.2 §6.3)**: String-variant API (`'ML-KEM-512' | 'ML-KEM-768' | 'ML-KEM-1024'`) over the existing `hsm_encapsulate` / `hsm_decapsulate` functions, for compatibility with the 5G SUCI Profile C UI layer.
- **`hsm_generateX25519KeyPair`**: PKCS#11 v3.2 compliant X25519 keypair generation via `CKM_EC_MONTGOMERY_KEY_PAIR_GEN` with `CKA_DERIVE=true` on the private key. Exported from `src/wasm/softhsm/classical.ts`.
- **`hsm_importECPrivateKey`**: Injects an EC private key scalar into the HSM via `C_CreateObject` for use in GSMA SUCI known-answer test injection. Supports P-256, P-384, P-521. Includes an inline warning documenting the `C_UnwrapKey` path that real hardware HSMs require.
- **`DerivedKeyProfile` interface + `buildDerivedKeyTemplate`**: Flexible PKCS#11 v3.2 attribute builder for `C_DeriveKey` templates. Replaces hardcoded `CKK_GENERIC_SECRET` templates in `hsm_ecdhDerive` and `hsm_ecdhCofactorDerive` — callers now pass a profile (`{ keyLen, derive, encrypt, decrypt, … }`) that maps 1-to-1 to `CKA_*` entries. Unspecified optional attributes a…

chunks.title: PQC Today v2.72.0 — Release Notes (2026-04-01)

Version 2.72.0 released 2026-04-01.

The browser URL also updates to include `?ref=` when the modal opens and clears when it closes, so the address bar is always shareable. Deep links open the modal automatically.

Clicking it copies `/timeline?country=<Country>` to your clipboard — send it to a colleague to open the timeline pre-filtered to that country's roadmap.

Because the Playground already syncs `?tab=` and `?algo=` to the URL on every selection, sharing copies a fully-resolved deep link — e.g. `/playground?tab=hashing&algo=SHA3-256` — that lands a recipient directly on the right panel and algorithm.

chunks.title: PQC Today v2.71.0 — Release Notes (2026-04-01)
chunks.content:
Version 2.71.0 released 2026-04-01.

### Added

- **SLH-DSA context string support (FIPS 205 §9.2)**: The SLH-DSA sign and verify operations in the HSM Playground now accept an optional context string — a short byte sequence that is cryptographically bound to the signature. A signature produced with context "A" will not verify with context "B", giving you a built-in domain-separation primitive for multi-protocol deployments.
- **SLH-DSA deterministic signing (FIPS 205 §10)**: A new "Deterministic" option in the SLH-DSA panel forces the HSM to derive its randomness from the key itself. Signing the same message twice with the same key produces identical signature bytes, making it easier to build reproducible test vectors and auditable log entries.
- **ACVP tests 21 & 22 — SLH-DSA context binding and deterministic mode**: The ACVP compliance test suite now covers the two new FIPS 205 capabilities. Test 21 verifies that context-bound signatures reject cross-context and no-context verification. Test 22 verifies that deterministic signing produces bit-identical signatures across two calls and that the result still verifies correctly. Both tests run on both the C++ and Rust engines in dual mode (44 total assertions).
- **Copy button on ACVP execution log**: A clipboard button in the ACVP log header lets you copy the full test output with one click — useful for attaching results to issue reports or compliance evidence packages.

### Fixed

- **SLH-DSA multi-message signing correctness**: The C++ HSM engine's message-API path (`C_MessageSignInit` / `C_SignMessage`) incorrectly lost session parameters (context string, deterministic flag) between the mandatory PKCS#11 size-query call and the actual signing call. Context binding and deterministic mode had no effect when using the message API. Parameters are now preserved across both steps.

chunks.title: Which 3GPP specification defines the core security architecture for 5G networks, including SUCI concealment and 5G-AKA?
chunks.content:
Q: Which 3GPP specification defines the core security architecture for 5G networks, including SUCI concealment and 5G-AKA?
A: The core security architecture for 5G networks is defined by 3GPP TS 33.501. This specification covers the three pillars of 5G security: subscriber privacy via SUCI concealment, mutual authentication through 5G-AKA, and SIM key provisioning.
Module: 5g-security
References: 3GPP TS 33.501 Rel-19

metadata.sourceCitations: RAG Summary: Key Concepts, Related Standards

chunks.title: What are the three specific SUCI concealment profiles mentioned in the module, and which one utilizes the ML-KEM algorithm?
chunks.content:
Q: What are the three specific SUCI concealment profiles mentioned in the module, and which one utilizes the ML-KEM algorithm?
A: The three SUCI concealment profiles are Profile A (X25519), Profile B (P-256), and Profile C. Profile C is the only one that utilizes the lattice-based ML-KEM (Kyber) algorithm to provide quantum-resistant key encapsulation.
Module: 5g-security
Algorithms: KEM;X25519

chunks.title: Which NIST standard defines the ML-KEM algorithm used in 3GPP Profile C for post-quantum security?
chunks.content:
Q: Which NIST standard defines the ML-KEM algorithm used in 3GPP Profile C for post-quantum security?
A: The ML-KEM algorithm is defined by FIPS 203. This standard establishes ML-KEM as the quantum-resistant key encapsulation mechanism, which is being studied for integration into 5G security under 3GPP TR 33.841.
Module: 5g-security
References: FIPS 203
Algorithms: KEM
Compliance: NIST

chunks.title: How does the SUCI mechanism specifically address the security vulnerability known as 'IMSI catching' found in previous mobile generations?
chunks.content:
Q: How does the SUCI mechanism specifically address the security vulnerability known as 'IMSI catching' found in previous mobile generations?
A: SUCI addresses IMSI catching by encrypting the subscriber's permanent identity (SUPI/IMSI) before it is transmitted over the air interface. This prevents adversaries from intercepting and identifying subscribers, a flaw that plagued 2G, 3G, and 4G networks where identities were sent in plaintext.
Module: 5g-security
References: NIST-CSWP-36A

metadata.sourceCitations: RAG Summary: Key Concepts, Curious Summary

chunks.title: Why is the MILENAGE algorithm used in 5G-AKA considered quantum-resistant despite the vulnerabilities of asymmetric cryptography?
chunks.content:
Q: Why is the MILENAGE algorithm used in 5G-AKA considered quantum-resistant despite the vulnerabilities of asymmetric cryptography?
A: MILENAGE relies on the symmetric AES-128 algorithm, which remains quantum-resistant because Grover's algorithm only reduces its effective key length to 64 bits rather than breaking it entirely. In contrast, the asymmetric ECDH used in SUCI concealment is vulnerable to Shor's algorithm.
Module: 5g-security
References: A-fast-quantum-mechanical-algorithm-for-database-search

chunks.title: What is the primary difference in cryptographic primitives between Profile A/B and Profile C regarding their vulnerability to quantum computers?
chunks.content:
Q: What is the primary difference in cryptographic primitives between Profile A/B and Profile C regarding their vulnerability to quantum computers?
A: Profiles A and B use elliptic curve cryptography (X25519 and P-256 respectively), which are vulnerable to Shor's algorithm on a quantum computer. Profile C uses the lattice-based ML-KEM algorithm, which is designed to be resistant to quantum attacks.
Module: 5g-security
Algorithms: KEM;X25519

chunks.title: In a scenario where an operator wants to migrate to post-quantum security for SUCI concealment, which specific algorithm and profile must they implement?
chunks.content:
Q: In a scenario where an operator wants to migrate to post-quantum security for SUCI concealment, which specific algorithm and profile must they implement?
A: The operator must implement Profile C, which utilizes the ML-KEM (Kyber) algorithm. This migration replaces the quantum-vulnerable ECIES-based profiles (A and B) with a lattice-based key encapsulation mechanism to secure subscriber identities against future quantum threats.
Module: 5g-security
Algorithms: KEM

chunks.title: If a network engineer needs to derive KAUSF during the 5G-AKA process, what inputs and algorithm are required according to the module?
chunks.content:
Q: If a network engineer needs to derive KAUSF during the 5G-AKA process, what inputs and algorithm are required according to the module?
A: To derive KAUSF, the engineer must use the CK and IK keys generated by MILENAGE as inputs. These are processed through an HMAC-SHA-256 function bound to the Serving Network Name.
Module: 5g-security

A: The 5G key hierarchy derives KgNB from KAMF, which is derived from KSEAF (the anchor key), which is derived from KAUSF, which in turn is derived from CK and IK generated by MILENAGE. chunks.title: Does harvest-now-decrypt-later (HNDL) apply to signed JWTs?
chunks.content:
Q: Does harvest-now-decrypt-later (HNDL) apply to signed JWTs?
A: Not in the usual sense. A signed JWT (JWS) is not encrypted, so anyone holding it can already read its claims and there is nothing to decrypt later. The quantum risk to a JWS is forgery: a cryptographically relevant quantum computer could recover a signing key from its public key and mint tokens that verifiers still trusting that key would accept. HNDL does apply to encrypted JWTs (JWE using ECDH-ES) and to the TLS connection carrying tokens, which can be recorded now and decrypted later.
Module: api-security-jwt
References: RFC 7515;RFC 7516

chunks.title: Why is HMAC-based HS256 less exposed to quantum attack than RS256 or ES256?
chunks.content:
Q: Why is HMAC-based HS256 less exposed to quantum attack than RS256 or ES256?
A: HS256 is a symmetric MAC: it uses a shared secret, not a public-key problem, so Shor's algorithm does not apply. Grover's algorithm only reduces its effective key strength, so a 256-bit key remains adequate. Its weakness is the shared secret itself, which every verifier must hold and protect.
Module: api-security-jwt
References: RFC 7519

chunks.title: How does ML-KEM replace ECDH-ES in JWE encryption?
chunks.content:
Q: How does ML-KEM replace ECDH-ES in JWE encryption?
A: ML-KEM replaces the Diffie-Hellman step with key encapsulation: ML-KEM.Encaps(recipient public key) returns a ciphertext and a shared secret. In the current design, HPKE with JWE (draft-ietf-jose-hpke-encrypt, using the ML-KEM suites of draft-ietf-jose-hpke-pq-pqt), the HPKE suite fixes the key derivation and AEAD: HPKE-12 (ML-KEM-768) and HPKE-9 (ML-KEM-768 + X25519) both use SHAKE256 and AES-256-GCM, and the 1,088- or 1,120-byte encapsulated secret travels as the JWE Encrypted Key. An earlier direct-KEM JOSE draft (revision -05, narrowed to COSE in -06) derived the content encryption key with KMAC256.
Module: api-security-jwt
References: FIPS 203;draft-ietf-jose-hpke-encrypt;draft-ietf-jose-hpke-pq-pqt-01
Algorithms: KEM

chunks.title: What changes, and what stays the same, when a JWT deployment migrates to ML-DSA?
chunks.content:
Q: What changes, and what stays the same, when a JWT deployment migrates to ML-DSA?
A: The token format stays the same: the compact serialization is unchanged and the header's "alg" value changes, for example from ES256 to ML-DSA-65. Around it much more changes: keys move to the AKP JWK type (RFC 9964) and every JWKS consumer must understand it; verifiers need explicit per-key algorithm allowlists (RFC 8725); tokens grow to several kilobytes, straining header and cookie limits; JOSE libraries must add support; and classical keys need a retirement plan so the transition cannot be used as a downgrade path.

Algorithms: ML-DSA-65

chunks.title: In a scenario where mobile bandwidth is constrained, how does the adoption of ML-DSA-65 impact API performance?
chunks.content:
Q: In a scenario where mobile bandwidth is constrained, how does the adoption of ML-DSA-65 impact API performance?
A: For one fixed payload, a ~300-byte ES256 JWT grows to about 4.7 KB with ML-DSA-65: roughly 16 times for the whole token, while the signature alone grows about 51 times (64 to 3,309 bytes). chunks.title: What are the two ways to combine a classical and a PQC signature in a JWT, and what does each require of verifiers?
chunks.content:
Q: What are the two ways to combine a classical and a PQC signature in a JWT, and what does each require of verifiers?
A: A composite signature (draft-ietf-jose-pq-composite-sigs-04) uses one alg such as ML-DSA-65-Ed25519, and both component signatures must verify, so every verifier must support the composite algorithm. A nested JWT puts a classical JWT inside a PQC-signed JWT (cty "JWT") and verifiers must validate both layers (RFC 8725 Section 3.3). Neither lets an unmodified classical verifier accept the token by itself: serving legacy verifiers needs a gateway or protocol that unwraps the inner token, and that path has no PQC protection. Each verifier's algorithm allowlist is what prevents a downgrade.
Module: api-security-jwt
References: draft-ietf-jose-pq-composite-sigs;RFC 8725

chunks.title: How does key derivation in an ML-KEM JWE differ from ECDH-ES?
chunks.content:
Q: How does key derivation in an ML-KEM JWE differ from ECDH-ES?
A: With ECDH-ES both sides compute the same Diffie-Hellman value and run the Concat KDF (RFC 7518). With a KEM the sender runs ML-KEM.Encaps to get a ciphertext and a shared secret, and the recipient recovers the same secret with ML-KEM.Decaps. What derives the key depends on the profile: in the current HPKE/JWE design the HPKE key schedule runs the suite's KDF (SHAKE256 for the ML-KEM suites of draft-ietf-jose-hpke-pq-pqt) and, in Integrated Encryption, encrypts the payload directly with no separate content encryption key; the earlier direct-KEM JOSE draft (revision -05) used KMAC256.
Module: api-security-jwt
References: FIPS 203;draft-ietf-jose-hpke-encrypt
Algorithms: KEM

chunks.title: Do long-lived refresh tokens need urgent PQC migration because of harvest-now-decrypt-later?
chunks.content:
Q: Do long-lived refresh tokens need urgent PQC migration because of harvest-now-decrypt-later?
A: Usually not for that reason. Refresh tokens are commonly opaque handles that the authorization server looks up, so a quantum computer cannot forge them unless they are themselves signed tokens. What does need planning is the signing keys behind JWTs that verifiers trust for a long time, and the confidentiality of the TLS channel that carries any bearer token, which is exposed to harvest-now-decrypt-later.

A: ML-DSA-87 produces a larger signature of 4,627 bytes compared to ML-DSA-65's 3,309 bytes. This represents a trade-off where higher security (NIST Level 5) is achieved at the cost of significantly increased token size and bandwidth consumption.

Q: How does the 'JWT Inspector' workshop tool assist in understanding the vulnerability of current production tokens?
A: The JWT Inspector decodes a token's header, payload and signature and classes the algorithm its header declares as classical or post-quantum. That class is a claim the token makes, not proof of protection: only verifying the signature against a key you trust, with the algorithm you expect, establishes that.

chunks.title: Does FIPS 204 approval of ML-DSA by itself make a JWT signing service CNSA 2.0 compliant?
chunks.content:
Q: Does FIPS 204 approval of ML-DSA by itself make a JWT signing service CNSA 2.0 compliant?
A: No. CNSA 2.0 is the NSA's algorithm suite for National Security Systems and specifies ML-DSA-87 for signatures, so ML-DSA-44 and ML-DSA-65 do not satisfy it. FIPS 204 standardizes all three parameter sets, but approval under FIPS 204 is not the same as CNSA 2.0 conformance, which also covers the other algorithms, parameter choices and transition dates the suite sets.

chunks.title: Why must a JWT verifier never choose the verification algorithm from the token's "alg" header?
chunks.content:
Q: Why must a JWT verifier never choose the verification algorithm from the token's "alg" header?
A: The header is written by whoever made the token. A verifier that follows it can be tricked into accepting alg "none", or into checking an HMAC computed with a public key as the secret. RFC 8725 Section 3.1 requires the library to let the application specify the allowed algorithms and to use only those; PQC adds new algorithms to that allowlist but does not remove the need for it.

chunks.title: Which claims must an API validate on a JWT access token besides the signature?
chunks.content:
Q: Which claims must an API validate on a JWT access token besides the signature?
A: Check the issuer (iss) and audience (aud) against the values you expect, enforce expiry (exp) and not-before (nbf) with a small clock skew, and use the token identifier (jti) where replay matters. RFC 9068 also requires explicit typing (typ "at+jwt") so an ID token cannot be replayed as an access token. A valid signature on a token for another audience is still the wrong token.

Q: How must a verifier validate a nested JWT such as an ES256 token wrapped in an ML-DSA-65 token?
A: It must validate both layers, each with the key and algorithm the application expects: the outer ML-DSA-65 signature, the cty "JWT" header that says the payload is itself a JWT, and then the inner ES256 signature. chunks.title: Why does a JWS that signs and verifies in the same library not prove interoperability, and what does?

Q: Why does a JWS that signs and verifies in the same library not prove interoperability, and what does?

Interoperability needs known-answer vectors from an independent source. Q: How is a composite ML-DSA-65-Ed25519 JWS signature built under draft-ietf-jose-pq-composite-sigs-04?

The signature is the 3,309-byte ML-DSA-65 signature followed directly by the 64-byte Ed25519 signature, with no length prefix, and both must verify. chunks.title: How does the TLS handshake latency for X25519MLKEM768 hybrid compare to classical P-256?
chunks.content:
Q: How does the TLS handshake latency for X25519MLKEM768 hybrid compare to classical P-256?
A: Real-world measurements show the overhead is much smaller than often assumed. A peer-reviewed benchmark of the TLS 1.3 handshake layer (ClientHello to Finished) found X25519MLKEM768 hybrid key exchange at approximately 6.5ms (P50) and 13.7ms (P99), versus classical X25519 at 5.5ms (P50) and 12.7ms (P99) — an increase of under 1ms at both percentiles. Google's own production telemetry reports a similarly modest ~4% median increase in handshake latency after switching to the hybrid scheme. The extra round-trip cost from larger PQC key-exchange messages is real, but it rarely threatens a sub-50ms SLA budget on its own — network and application-layer latency typically dominate.
Module: arch-quantum-impact
References: Layered-Performance-Analysis-of-TLS-1-3-Handshakes-Classical

chunks.title: How do the different hybrid certificate formats (Composite, Alt-Sig, Related Certificates) trade off against each other in terms of operational complexity and size?
chunks.content:
Q: How do the different hybrid certificate formats (Composite, Alt-Sig, Related Certificates) trade off against each other in terms of operational complexity and size?
A: Composite X.509 certificates (draft-ietf-lamps-pq-composite-sigs-19, in the RFC Editor queue) put both algorithms under one OID: one certificate, both signatures are required, but legacy validators cannot parse it. Alt-Sig certificates (ITU-T X.509 alternative-signature extensions) keep a classical certificate that legacy validators accept and carry the PQC key and signature in extensions, at the cost of a larger certificate. Related Certificates (RFC 9763) keep two separate certificates, linked one-way by a hash of the existing one, which is the simplest for legacy systems but doubles what must be issued, stored and sent. Chameleon certificates (draft-bonnell-lamps-chameleon-certs-07) expired as an individual draft and are a historical design, not a deployment option.
Module: arch-quantum-impact
References: draft-ietf-lamps-pq-composite-sigs-19;RFC-9763;draft-bonnell-lamps-chameleon-certs-07

This creates a conflict where an organization must maintain dual cryptographic stacks to satisfy both the US exclusive requirement and the European hybrid mandate simultaneously.

chunks.title: What is the specific impact of Grover's algorithm on current TEE memory encryption engines using AES-128-XTS?
chunks.content:
Q: What is the specific impact of Grover's algorithm on current TEE memory encryption engines using AES-128-XTS?
A: Grover's algorithm halves the effective security margin of symmetric encryption, downgrading AES-128-XTS to an effective 64-bit security level. This reduction makes current TEE memory encryption engines vulnerable to quantum attacks that could decrypt data-in-use. Consequently, hardware vendors must upgrade to AES-256 to maintain adequate security margins.

chunks.title: Which classical cryptographic algorithm is currently used for signing attestation quotes in Intel SGX/TDX, AMD SEV-SNP, and ARM CCA?
chunks.content:
Q: Which classical cryptographic algorithm is currently used for signing attestation quotes in Intel SGX/TDX, AMD SEV-SNP, and ARM CCA?
A: All major attestation quotes today, including those from Intel SGX/TDX, AMD SEV-SNP, and ARM CCA, are signed using classical ECDSA with curves P-256 or P-384. This reliance on ECDSA creates a critical vulnerability because Shor's algorithm can completely break these signatures. An adversary with a quantum computer could forge these signatures to impersonate an enclave.

chunks.title: What is the primary function of a Sealing Key in the context of TEE memory encryption?
chunks.content:
Q: What is the primary function of a Sealing Key in the context of TEE memory encryption?
A: A Sealing Key is used to derive keys that allow data to be encrypted and stored securely within the TEE's memory or persistent storage. It ensures that only the specific enclave instance with the matching hardware identity can decrypt and access the sealed data. This mechanism protects data even if it leaves the immediate execution context.

A: The transition to ML-DSA is critical because current attestation chains rely on ECDSA, which is vulnerable to Shor's algorithm. If an adversary can forge ECDSA signatures using a quantum computer, they can impersonate a trusted enclave and steal secrets provisioned from an HSM. ML-DSA provides the necessary quantum resistance to guarantee the integrity of the trust chain.

chunks.content:
Q: What is the relationship between the Quoting Enclave (QE) and the Attestation Key (AK) in Intel DCAP?
A: In the Intel DCAP flow, the Quoting Enclave verifies the REPORT structure locally using a REPORT key before signing it. It then uses the platform's Attestation Key (AK) to sign the report and produce a Quote. This process ensures that the quote is cryptographically bound to the specific hardware platform.

A: Intel DCAP uses an Intel PCK Certificate signed with ECDSA P-256 as its root of trust for remote attestation. In contrast, ARM CCA relies on an ARM CCA Platform Token signed with ECDSA P-384. Both roots are currently vulnerable to quantum attacks due to their reliance on classical elliptic curve cryptography.

chunks.title: What is the significance of the TCB (Trusted Computing Base) status check in the Intel DCAP verification process?
chunks.content:
Q: What is the significance of the TCB (Trusted Computing Base) status check in the Intel DCAP verification process?
A: The TCB status check ensures that the platform running the enclave is up-to-date and free from known vulnerabilities. The Relying Party validates the TCB level from the Quote against the latest TCB Info signed by the Intel Provisioning Certification Service (PCS). This step is crucial for maintaining the integrity of the trust chain before accepting the attestation.

chunks.content:
Q: Why is mutual attestation required for a secure TEE-HSM trusted channel?
A: Mutual attestation ensures that both the TEE enclave and the HSM verify each other's identity and integrity before establishing a connection. This prevents an attacker from impersonating either party to intercept or inject malicious data into the communication channel. It is a prerequisite for safely provisioning PQC keys between the two components.

TEEs extend this protection to the 'Data-in-Use' phase by keeping data encrypted within the processor's memory, even during processing. This closes the security gap where the host OS or hypervisor could otherwise access sensitive information.

chunks.content:
Q: How would you prioritize the migration of a TEE system that uses both AES-128 memory encryption and ECDSA attestation?
A: The highest priority is migrating the Remote Attestation protocol from ECDSA to a post-quantum signature such as ML-DSA, because attestation reports are signed by the TEE's attestation key, which relies on public-key signatures that a cryptographically relevant quantum computer running Shor's algorithm could break. The second priority is upgrading the memory encryption engine from AES-128 to AES-256, because Grover's algorithm roughly halves the effective strength of symmetric keys (a crude figure). Addressing the attestation chain first prevents impersonation of enclaves once such a computer exists.

chunks.content:
Q: How does the vulnerability of ECDSA in attestation chains impact the overall trust model of Confidential Computing across different vendors?
A: The reliance on ECDSA by Intel, AMD, and ARM creates a systemic vulnerability where the entire trust model collapses if an adversary can forge signatures. This means that regardless of the hardware isolation provided by SGX, SEV-SNP, or CCA, an attacker can impersonate any enclave to steal secrets. The trust model is only as strong as its weakest cryptographic link, which is currently the classical signature algorithm.
Module: confidential-computing

chunks.title: Compare the quantum threat vectors for memory encryption versus attestation signatures in TEEs.
chunks.content:
Q: Compare the quantum threat vectors for memory encryption versus attestation signatures in TEEs.
A: Memory encryption faces a threat from Grover's algorithm, which roughly halves the effective strength of symmetric keys (a crude figure), so a shift from AES-128 to AES-256 restores the margin. Attestation signatures face a different threat from Shor's algorithm: a cryptographically relevant quantum computer could break ECDSA, which would allow forged attestation and impersonation of enclaves. While the loss of symmetric margin is manageable with longer keys, signature forgery requires moving to a post-quantum signature algorithm.
Module: confidential-computing

chunks.title: Design a migration strategy that addresses both the immediate quantum threat to attestation and the long-term need for PQC in memory encryption.
chunks.content:
Q: Design a migration strategy that addresses both the immediate quantum threat to attestation and the long-term need for PQC in memory encryption.
A: The strategy should prioritize migrating Remote Attestation to ML-DSA (FIPS 204) immediately to prevent signature forgery, as this is the most critical vulnerability. Simultaneously, plan a phased upgrade of memory encryption engines from AES-128 to AES-256 to counter Grover's algorithm. This approach secures the trust chain first while gradually hardening the data-in-use protection layer.
Module: confidential-computing
References: FIPS 204

chunks.title: How do the timelines for PQC migration in Intel DCAP (2027) and ARM CCA (2028) influence enterprise adoption strategies?
chunks.content:
Q: How do the timelines for PQC migration in Intel DCAP (2027) and ARM CCA (2028) influence enterprise adoption strategies?
A: The staggered timelines suggest that enterprises cannot rely on a single vendor's roadmap to achieve full quantum safety immediately. Organizations must adopt a hybrid approach, potentially using software-based PQC wrappers or multi-vendor strategies until hardware support is universal. This necessitates early planning and testing of PQC algorithms like ML-DSA in non-production environments.

chunks.title: Evaluate the role of PKCS#11 v3.2 in enabling a quantum-safe TEE-HSM ecosystem.
chunks.content:
Q: Evaluate the role of PKCS#11 v3.2 in enabling a quantum-safe TEE-HSM ecosystem.
A: PKCS#11 v3.2 acts as the critical interface standard that allows HSMs to natively support PQC algorithms like ML-KEM and ML-DSA. Without this standard, integrating quantum-resistant keys into the TEE-HSM trusted channel would require custom, non-interoperable implementations. It enables the seamless provisioning of PQC keys between enclaves and hardware security modules.

Algorithms: KEM

chunks.title: What are the three dimensions of crypto agility defined in the module?
chunks.content:
Q: What are the three dimensions of crypto agility defined in the module?
A: The three dimensions of crypto agility are algorithm agility, which allows swapping algorithms via configuration; protocol agility, which supports multiple protocol versions simultaneously; and implementation agility, which enables switching between crypto providers without application changes. These dimensions ensure systems can adapt to new cryptographic standards like FIPS 203 without significant code rewrites.

chunks.content:
Q: What is the public key size for the hybrid X25519MLKEM768 algorithm?
A: The public key size for the hybrid X25519MLKEM768 algorithm is 1,216 bytes. This represents a significant increase from classical algorithms like RSA-2048 but provides quantum resistance through the combination of classical and post-quantum primitives.

chunks.title: How does the Service Mesh architecture pattern achieve crypto agility for data-in-transit?
chunks.content:
Q: How does the Service Mesh architecture pattern achieve crypto agility for data-in-transit?
A: The Service Mesh pattern achieves agility by offloading cryptographic operations, such as mTLS, to infrastructure proxies like Envoy or Istio. This allows applications to communicate in plaintext with the proxy, meaning zero code or configuration changes are needed at the application level when migrating protocols.

chunks.title: Why is the Provider Model considered less agile than External KMS for enterprise-wide upgrades?
chunks.content:
Q: Why is the Provider Model considered less agile than External KMS for enterprise-wide upgrades?
A: The Provider Model needs a configuration change in each application, whereas an External KMS centralizes crypto operations in a service such as AWS KMS or Azure Key Vault. Upgrading the central service changes the algorithm in one place, but each application still adopts the new key types, handles larger keys, signatures and ciphertexts, and is re-tested, so the change is not instant.

References: NIST CSWP 39

chunks.title: What is the primary risk of using hardcoded buffer sizes in cryptographic implementations?
chunks.content:
Q: What is the primary risk of using hardcoded buffer sizes in cryptographic implementations?
A: Hardcoded buffer sizes pose a critical risk because post-quantum algorithms often require significantly larger key and ciphertext sizes than classical ones. If an application allocates fixed memory or database columns based on classical sizes, it will fail to process data from quantum-safe algorithms like ML-KEM.
Module: crypto-agility
Algorithms: KEM

chunks.title: If an organization wants to move from RSA-2048 to ML-KEM-768 with the fewest application code changes, which architecture pattern should they prioritize?
chunks.content:
Q: If an organization wants to move from RSA-2048 to ML-KEM-768 with the fewest application code changes, which architecture pattern should they prioritize?
A: The Provider Model or External KMS patterns, because their abstraction layers keep the call sites the same and select the algorithm through configuration. Some changes remain: buffer and storage sizes, peer negotiation, and any code that encrypts directly with RSA, because a KEM cannot encrypt data directly and must be used through an encapsulate-then-wrap (envelope) pattern (NIST SP 800-227).

A: The Service Mesh pattern completely hides cryptographic operations from the application, offering maximum agility but reducing direct control over specific crypto parameters. chunks.title: How does the increase in key size from classical to hybrid PQC algorithms impact database schema design in a crypto-agile system?
chunks.content:
Q: How does the increase in key size from classical to hybrid PQC algorithms impact database schema design in a crypto-agile system?
A: The jump from 32-byte classical keys to over 1,000-byte hybrid keys (like X25519MLKEM768) requires database schemas to use variable-length fields rather than fixed-size columns. A crypto-agile design must anticipate these size changes to prevent data truncation or storage failures during migration.

chunks.title: Evaluate the role of FIPS 203 and CNSA 2.0 in driving the necessity for the 'Hybrid Migration' phase of the framework.

Q: Why is the Harvest Now, Decrypt Later (HNDL) threat considered an immediate risk even if a CRQC does not exist yet?
A: The HNDL threat is immediate because adversaries are actively collecting encrypted data today to decrypt it later once a Cryptographically Relevant Quantum Computer becomes available. Data that must remain confidential beyond the estimated CRQC arrival year is already at risk of being harvested now. Therefore, protection measures must be implemented before the quantum computer exists.
Module: data-asset-sensitivity
References: Cybersecurity-in-an-Era-with-Quantum-Computers-Will-We-Be-Re

A: Data retention period directly influences PQC migration urgency because any data that must remain confidential beyond the estimated CRQC arrival year is vulnerable to HNDL attacks. If a CRQC arrives in 2030, data retained past 2030 requires immediate protection. Shorter retention periods may allow for delayed migration if the data expires before quantum threats materialize.

A: Key material such as root Certificate Authorities (CAs) and Hardware Security Module (HSM) secrets must be classified as Critical because their compromise would undermine the security of all dependent systems. These assets are high-value targets for HNDL attacks due to their long-term validity and broad impact. Their classification ensures they receive the highest priority in PQC migration efforts.

A: Composite Risk Scoring combines multiple weighted dimensions, including sensitivity, retention, compliance obligations, and HNDL window, to produce a single urgency score. This approach allows organizations to prioritize assets that pose the highest combined risk rather than focusing on a single factor. It ensures a balanced migration strategy that addresses both technical vulnerabilities and regulatory deadlines.

Q: In a scenario where GDPR and HIPAA apply to the same dataset, how should sensitivity be classified?
A: When multiple regulations like GDPR and HIPAA apply, the organization must adopt the highest sensitivity tier required by any of the mandates. This 'highest common denominator' approach ensures compliance with all applicable laws. For example, if HIPAA requires a higher protection level for health data than GDPR does for personal data, the asset is classified at the HIPAA-mandated level.

A: To apply the FAIR model, one must calculate the Threat Event Frequency (TEF) and vulnerability to determine the Loss Event Frequency. This is then multiplied by the probable loss magnitude to derive the Annualized Loss Expectancy in USD. This quantifies the financial impact of a potential breach due to delayed PQC migration, aiding in budget justification.

So an organization can prioritize by compliance urgency or HNDL exposure, but can't directly trade those off against technical migration effort within the scoring engine itself.

chunks.title: How does the 'Hold Your Own Key' (HYOK) architecture differ from 'Bring Your Own Key' (BYOK) regarding key exposure in cloud environments?
chunks.content:
Q: How does the 'Hold Your Own Key' (HYOK) architecture differ from 'Bring Your Own Key' (BYOK) regarding key exposure in cloud environments?
A: In HYOK, the customer's key never leaves the on-premises infrastructure, and the cloud database receives only encrypted Data Encryption Keys (DEKs). In contrast, BYOK involves uploading a wrapped Customer Master Key (CMK) to the cloud KMS, where it is briefly held unwrapped in HSM memory, creating residual exposure.

ML-KEM-1024 wrapping is therefore a design target to check per cloud KMS service, not an AWS KMS feature.

Q: Analyze the interplay between AES-256 data encryption and ML-KEM-1024 key wrapping in the context of a 'harvest now, decrypt later' threat.
A: While AES-256 protects the data itself from quantum decryption, the 'harvest now, decrypt later' threat targets the RSA-wrapped keys. If an adversary captures the wrapped DEK today, they can wait for a quantum computer to break RSA and unwrap the key to decrypt the AES-256 data. Migrating the wrapping to ML-KEM-1024 neutralizes this specific vector.

chunks.content:
Q: How does the encryption workflow in PQC-enabled S/MIME differ from classical RSA key transport?
A: Classical S/MIME uses RSA key transport to directly encrypt the content-encryption key (CEK) with the recipient's public key, which is vulnerable to Shor's algorithm. Q: Which NIST FIPS standards define ML-KEM and ML-DSA, and where does each land in an OT network?
A: ML-KEM is defined in FIPS 203 and ML-DSA in FIPS 204. In OT, ML-KEM goes into the key exchange of TLS, VPN and SSH at the boundary, for example hybrid ML-KEM in front of jump hosts, or a hybrid ML-KEM group added to BACnet/SC, which already uses TLS 1.3. ML-DSA, alongside LMS/HSS, replaces RSA and ECDSA for firmware and project signing, where an ML-DSA-87 signature is 4,627 B. OPC UA's RSA and ECC SecurityPolicies have no published PQC policy yet.

chunks.title: How does IEC 62351-6 protect GOOSE and Sampled Values, and where is their quantum exposure?
chunks.content:
Q: How does IEC 62351-6 protect GOOSE and Sampled Values, and where is their quantum exposure?
A: IEC 62351-6 (2020) protects GOOSE and Sampled Values with profiles that include HMAC-SHA256 and AES-GMAC, symmetric MACs that a quantum computer does not break. Their group keys come from a key distribution centre over GDOI (IEC 62351-9, RFC 8052), not from RSA certificates. The quantum exposure is therefore in key management: the GDOI registration channel and the PKI behind it, which are open to both forgery and harvest-now-decrypt-later.

chunks.title: Which part of DNP3 Secure Authentication v5 is actually exposed to a quantum computer?
chunks.content:
Q: Which part of DNP3 Secure Authentication v5 is actually exposed to a quantum computer?
A: DNP3 SAv5 uses an HMAC challenge-response, wraps session keys with AES key wrap, and keeps update keys pre-shared by default; where they are changed remotely, the default method is symmetric (AES-256 key wrap plus HMAC-SHA-256), so all three are quantum-safe. Only the optional RSA/DSA update-key change methods are exposed. IEEE moved 1815-2012 to inactive status in 2023, the P1815 revision runs to 2027, and "SAv6" is unpublished. The Protocol Analyzer (protocol-security-analyzer) checks HMAC-SHA-256 against a NIST ACVP vector and AES-256 key wrap against RFC 3394 §4.6.
Module: ot-pqc
References: FIPS-198-1;RFC 3394

Q: A utility is planning PQC for a DLMS/COSEM smart-meter fleet. Which parts of its cryptography change, and how does the Fleet Key Manager (fleet-key-manager) model them?
A: Symmetric crypto stays: AES and SHA-2 are weakened only modestly by a quantum computer, and Suite 0's symmetric key wrap has no public-key exchange to break. What PQC replaces is the ECDH key agreement of Suite 1 (P-256) and Suite 2 (P-384). The Fleet Key Manager takes today's key establishment (DLMS Suite 0/1/2) and an ML-KEM parameter set as inputs, and its known-answer tests cover NIST ACVP ML-KEM-768 decapsulation, NIST CAVP AES-256-GCM decryption and an ECDH P-256 round-trip for the classical baseline.

Q: In the Fleet Key Manager's default scenario (2 million smart meters, 1,000 per collector, G3-PLC, ML-KEM-768, standard HSM), what limits a fleet-wide key rotation?
A: Each collector finishes its radio exchanges in about 16 minutes, sending 2,472 B per meter (7.5× today's 328 B), but the head-end HSM needs about 1.1 hours for 4 million operations, so the HSM is the bottleneck rather than the power-line link. chunks.title: How do IEC 62443 zones, conduits and security levels frame a PQC migration, and what does the standard say about quantum-safe cryptography?
chunks.content:
Q: How do IEC 62443 zones, conduits and security levels frame a PQC migration, and what does the standard say about quantum-safe cryptography?
A: IEC 62443 groups assets with the same security needs into zones and treats every communication path between zones as a conduit with its own controls. Each zone carries a target (SL-T), capability (SL-C) and achieved (SL-A) security level from SL 1 to SL 4. SR 4.3 (IEC 62443-3-3) and CR 4.3 (IEC 62443-4-2), both titled 'Use of cryptography' and applying from SL 1, ask for cryptography that follows commonly accepted (SR 4.3) or internationally recognized and proven (CR 4.3) security practice; neither names an algorithm or PQC, so PQC enters through risk assessment and procurement rather than through the standard's text.
Module: ot-pqc
References: IEC 62443;IEC-62443-4-2-2019-Security-for-industrial-automation-and-co

chunks.title: Why should PQC authentication not be inserted into the real-time path of IEC 61850 Sampled Values from a merging unit?
chunks.content:
Q: Why should PQC authentication not be inserted into the real-time path of IEC 61850 Sampled Values from a merging unit?
A: IEC 61869-9 defines Sampled Value rates including 4,000, 4,800 and 14,400 samples per second, a frame every 250, 208 and 69 µs. A 1,776-byte LMS or 4,627-byte ML-DSA-87 signature on every frame is neither needed nor practical, because the symmetric MAC already protecting the stream is quantum-safe. The PQC work goes into key distribution, firmware and the boundary; substation time sync is secured by IEEE 1588-2019 Annex P, not NTS.

Q: How do 20–50-year OT asset lifecycles affect PQC decisions made today?
A: A protection relay or PLC typically lasts 15–25 years, rail signalling 25–40 and substation primary plant 30–50, so a device installed today may still run in the 2040s. Forgery of the signatures these devices trust needs no harvesting and starts the day a cryptographically relevant quantum computer exists, so their signing roots have to be migrated first. Changing crypto in a safety-related device can mean re-testing a protection scheme, re-running a SIL assessment or re-opening a rail safety case, far more than a software update.

chunks.title: A utility wants PQC signatures for vendor firmware and for PLC project downloads. What does the Firmware & Project Signing Lab (firmware-project-signing-lab) show about LMS versus ML-DSA, and which NERC CIP requirements apply?
chunks.content:
Q: A utility wants PQC signatures for vendor firmware and for PLC project downloads. What does the Firmware & Project Signing Lab (firmware-project-signing-lab) show about LMS versus ML-DSA, and which NERC CIP requirements apply?
A: An LMS H10 tree holds 1,024 signatures, so used for project signing at 5,000 signatures a year it is exhausted after 0.2 years, and keeping a stateful counter consistent across engineering workstations is hard. ML-DSA-87 is stateless (no counter, no exhaustion) at the cost of a 4,627-byte signature, so the usual split is LMS or HSS in a vendor HSM for rare firmware releases and ML-DSA for high-volume project signing. NERC CIP-010-4 R1.6 requires verifying the software source and integrity before a baseline change on high and medium impact systems, and CIP-013-2 is the contractual lever for asking vendors for PQC firmware signing.

Q: A manufacturer is deciding how its devices will prove their identity over their whole service life. Which identity and onboarding mechanisms does the module describe, and why must the PQC decision be made before manufacture?
A: An IEEE 802.1AR initial device identifier (IDevID) is a certificate and key installed in the factory; NIST SP 1800-36B shows it anchoring trusted network-layer onboarding. FIDO Device Onboard 1.1 transfers ownership late with an ownership voucher, and EST-coaps (RFC 9148) enrols operational certificates over CoAP. Each of these is a long-lived signature key that PQC must replace, and an IDevID baked into silicon today cannot be swapped later.

chunks.title: What random inputs do ML-KEM and ML-DSA key generation draw, and does their 32-byte length set the required RBG strength?
chunks.content:
Q: What random inputs do ML-KEM and ML-DSA key generation draw, and does their 32-byte length set the required RBG strength?
A: ML-KEM.KeyGen draws two 32-byte values, d and z, and ML-DSA.KeyGen draws one 32-byte seed, ξ. The length does not set the RBG strength. FIPS 203 §3.3 requires an approved RBG with at least 128, 192 or 256 bits of security strength for ML-KEM-512, -768 or -1024. FIPS 204 §3.6.1 requires at least 192 bits for ML-DSA-65 and 256 bits for ML-DSA-87; for ML-DSA-44 the RBG shall have at least 128 bits and should have at least 192.

chunks.title: What is the primary difference between a TRNG and a QRNG in terms of their entropy source?
chunks.content:
Q: What is the primary difference between a TRNG and a QRNG in terms of their entropy source?
A: Both are noise sources. A TRNG uses a classical process such as thermal noise or timing jitter; a QRNG uses a quantum process such as photon detection or tunnelling. For FIPS 140-3 purposes both are judged by the same SP 800-90B requirements — a noise-source model, an entropy estimate from raw data, and health tests. CMVP has issued Entropy Validation Certificates for both kinds, for example E280 (a CPU-jitter source) and E145 (QuintessenceLabs qStream 100).
Module: entropy-randomness
References: NIST-SP-800-90B

chunks.title: Why should a design document not cite an "XOF_DRBG" as an approved DRBG for PQC?
chunks.content:
Q: Why should a design document not cite an "XOF_DRBG" as an approved DRBG for PQC?
A: Because no such mechanism is specified. NIST's SP 800-90A Rev. 2 page is a pre-draft call for comments (2025-09-04) that only announces a planned SHAKE-based DRBG; no draft exists. The approved DRBG mechanisms are those of SP 800-90A Rev. 1, and FIPS 203 and FIPS 204 place their requirement on the RBG's approval and security strength, not on whether the DRBG uses SHAKE.
Module: entropy-randomness
References: NIST-SP-800-90A-R1;FIPS 203;FIPS 204
Compliance: NIST

chunks.title: What does XOR-combining two entropy sources guarantee, and under what condition?
chunks.content:
Q: What does XOR-combining two entropy sources guarantee, and under what condition?
A: If the two inputs are independent, their XOR is at least as unpredictable as the stronger input, so one failed source does not erase the other's contribution. The guarantee is lost if the sources are correlated or an attacker can influence one input. Whether the resulting RBG is acceptable still depends on its SP 800-90C construction and on the validated entropy of the source that remains.
Module: entropy-randomness
References: NIST-SP-800-90C
Compliance: NIST

chunks.title: What is the relationship between NIST SP 800-90A, 800-90B, and 800-90C?
chunks.content:
Q: What is the relationship between NIST SP 800-90A, 800-90B, and 800-90C?
A: NIST SP 800-90A defines DRBG mechanisms, SP 800-90B covers entropy source validation, and SP 800-90C provides constructions for combining sources with DRBGs to create fully constructed Random Bit Generators. Together they form a complete framework from raw entropy to secure output.
Module: entropy-randomness
References: NIST-SP-800-90A-R1
Compliance: NIST

chunks.title: Why is "quantum-safe" the wrong test for a hardware TRNG?
chunks.content:
Q: Why is "quantum-safe" the wrong test for a hardware TRNG?
A: A hardware TRNG does not rest on a computational hardness assumption, so a quantum computer does not break it the way it breaks RSA. But that says nothing about whether it works. Its security depends on the noise source actually delivering its claimed min-entropy — SP 800-90B calls the noise source the root of security for the entropy source and the RBG — which is established by entropy assessment of raw data and by health tests that detect failures.
Module: entropy-randomness
References: NIST-SP-800-90B

chunks.title: You must generate ML-KEM-768 key pairs. What must the randomness source meet?
chunks.content:
Q: You must generate ML-KEM-768 key pairs. What must the randomness source meet?
A: KeyGen draws two fresh 32-byte values, d and z, from an approved RBG (SP 800-90A, 90B and 90C) with a security strength of at least 192 bits (FIPS 203 §3.3 and Table 2). If random bit generation fails, KeyGen returns an error instead of a key. The seed (d, z) can recompute the decapsulation key, so it must be protected like one.
Module: entropy-randomness
References: FIPS 203
Algorithms: KEM

chunks.title: If you are validating an entropy source for NIST ESV, which specific tests must be performed continuously?
chunks.content:
Q: If you are validating an entropy source for NIST ESV, which specific tests must be performed continuously?
A: SP 800-90B §4.3 requires both continuous and start-up health tests. The continuous tests shall include either the two approved tests of §4.4, the Repetition Count Test and the Adaptive Proportion Test, or developer-defined tests that meet the substitution requirements of §4.5. The start-up tests run the continuous tests over at least 1,024 consecutive samples, the source must support on-demand testing, and all of these run on the noise-source samples before any conditioning (§4.3 item 6).
Module: entropy-randomness
References: NIST-SP-800-90B
Compliance: NIST

chunks.title: How would you evaluate a design that combines a local TRNG with a remote QRNG service?
chunks.content:
Q: How would you evaluate a design that combines a local TRNG with a remote QRNG service?
A: State the assumptions first: whether the sources are independent; whether an attacker can observe, delay, replay or choose the remote data; what min-entropy each source is validated to provide; and which SP 800-90C construction the design follows. XOR and conditioning do not repair a correlated or attacker-controlled input. If those questions cannot be answered, the conclusion is "not enough evidence", not "secure".
Module: entropy-randomness
References: NIST-SP-800-90C

chunks.title: When estimating the min-entropy of a noise source under SP 800-90B, which estimator looks for long repeated substrings?
chunks.content:
Q: When estimating the min-entropy of a noise source under SP 800-90B, which estimator looks for long repeated substrings?
A: The Longest Repeated Substring (LRS) estimate, one of the SP 800-90B non-IID estimators (§6.3.6). It counts repeated substrings (tuples) in the dataset and complements the t-tuple estimate for tuple sizes that are too large for it. The estimators are run on a sequential dataset of at least 1,000,000 samples obtained directly from the noise source (§3.1.1); running them on DRBG or other generated output assesses the post-processing, not the source.
Module: entropy-randomness
References: NIST-SP-800-90B
Compliance: NIST

chunks.title: If your system uses the Web Crypto API, what is the underlying mechanism generating the randomness?
chunks.content:
Q: If your system uses the Web Crypto API, what is the underlying mechanism generating the randomness?
A: crypto.getRandomValues() returns output of a pseudorandom number generator in the browser, seeded with entropy from an external source such as the platform's random-number function or /dev/urandom (MDN). The Web Cryptography specification mandates no minimum degree of entropy, and the generator may vary across user agents. The output is not raw noise-source data, so its quality depends on the platform's entropy source and RNG.
Module: entropy-randomness
References: Crypto-getRandomValues-method-Web-APIs-MDN

chunks.title: How does an Entropy Validation Certificate differ from a FIPS 140-3 module certificate?
chunks.content:
Q: How does an Entropy Validation Certificate differ from a FIPS 140-3 module certificate?
A: An Entropy Validation Certificate covers an entropy source: an accredited lab submits its SP 800-90B conformance justification through the ESV Server, and a CMVP reviewer decides whether it is sufficient. A FIPS 140-3 certificate covers a whole cryptographic module, whose submission must document SP 800-90B conformance where applicable. SP 800-90C constructions receive a separate Random Bit Generator Validation Certificate (IG D.T). NIST publishes no review duration.
Module: entropy-randomness
References: NIST-SP-800-90B;FIPS-140-3-STANDARD
Compliance: NIST

chunks.title: In the QRNG comparison simulation, why do the simulated QRNG sample and the CSPRNG sample give the same kind of results?
chunks.content:
Q: In the QRNG comparison simulation, why do the simulated QRNG sample and the CSPRNG sample give the same kind of results?
A: Because the simulated "QRNG" sample is itself crypto.getRandomValues() output; no QRNG hardware is involved. The lesson is that tests on output cannot tell good generators apart. Any real difference between a QRNG and a CSPRNG lies in the noise source, which only an SP 800-90B assessment of raw noise-source data can address.
